The Archive of the Second Vatican Council, which exists as a special collection within the Vatican Apostolic Archive, is the primary source of documentation for the great assembly convened and presided over first by John XXIII and then by Paul VI in St Peter’s Basilica in Vatican City. In this archive are preserved the major share of the documents produced by the various commissions established following the initial announcement of the council which remained active for the duration of the event.[^c05-5]

[^c05-5]: Vincenzo Carbone, ‘L’Archivio del Concilio Vaticano II’, _Archiva Ecclesiae_ 34–35 (1991–92): 57–67; Sergio Pagano, ‘Riflessioni sulle fonti archivistiche del concilio Vaticano II: In margine ad una recente pubblicazione’, _Cristianesimo nella_ _storia_ 23, no. 3 (2002): 775–812; Piero Doria, ‘L’Archivio del Concilio Vaticano II: Storia e sviluppò’, _Anuario de historia de la_ _Iglesia_ 21 (2012): 135–55; Piero Doria, ‘L’Archivio del Concilio Vaticano II: Inventario e nuove proposte di ricerca’, _Cristianesimo nella storia_ 34, no. 1 (2013): 29–40; Doria, ‘L’Archivio del Concilio Vaticano II all’Archivio Vaticano: Istituzione, inventario e nuove prospettive di ricerca’, in _Religiosa Archivorum Custodia: IV Centenario della Fondazione dell’Archivio_ _Segreto Vaticano (1612–2012); Atti del Convegno di Studi Città del Vaticano 17–18 aprile 2012_ (Vatican City: Vatican City Archives, 2015), 497–53; ‘L’Archivio del Concilio Vaticano II’, in _Il Concilio ecumenico Vaticano II alla luce degli archivi dei_ _Padri Conciliari nel 50° anniversario dell’apertura del Concilio Vaticano II (1962–2012)_, ed. Philippe Chenaux (Vatican City: Vatican City Archives, 2015), 47–65.

**[p. 71]** However, since Vatican II is the first council celebrated in the age of advanced technology and mass media, its archive is also marked by that presence. Indeed, in addition to the printed materials (correspondence, votes, reports, etc.), the collection is in possession of a rich selection of recordings, now restored and accessible to scholars, including both the sessions of the Theological Commission and those of the general congregations, with recorded voices of the council fathers who took the floor of the council hall.

In addition to these important sound recordings, the holdings include a large collection of photographs which are spread throughout the archive, as well as a large, although incomplete, collection of press items from many newspapers around the world with the reactions of the principal observers to Vatican events during the years of the council. On the other hand, there are very few videotapes, with only a few brief recordings available.[^c05-6]

[^c05-6]: Federico Ruozzi, _Il Concilio in diretta: Il Vaticano II e la televisione tra informazione e partecipazione_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2012).

Finally, for the dissemination of news, it was immediately necessary to establish a council Press Office. Through the publication of almost daily bulletins, it provided accredited journalists with information in various languages on the work of the council sessions. A complete copy of these documents has been maintained from the four conciliar sessions in the archive of the council. And, as noted, the establishment of this Press Office was a first step towards the development of what is now known as the Vatican News Office.[^c05-7]

[^c05-7]: Giuseppe Alberigo and Joseph A. Komonchak, eds., _History of Vatican II_, 5 vols. (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1995–2006); Alberto Melloni, _L’altra Roma: Politica e S. Sede durante il Concilio Vaticano II (1959–1965)_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2000); Giuseppe Alberigo, _A Brief History of Vatican II_, trans. Matthew Sherry (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2006); John O’Malley, _What Happened at_ _Vatican II_ (Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press, 2008); Roberto De Mattei, _Il Concilio Vaticano II: Una storia mai scritta_ (Turin: Loreto, 2010); Riccardo Burigana, _Storia del Concilio Vaticano II_ (Turin: Lindau, 2012); Philippe Chenaux, _Il Concilio Vaticano_ _II_ (Rome: Carocci, 2012); Philippe Chenaux, _Le Temps de Vatican II: Une introduction à l’histoire du Concile_ (Paris: Desclée de Brouwer, 2012); Alberto Melloni, _Atlante storico del Concilio Vaticano II_ (Bologna: Jaca Book, 2015); Piero Doria, _Storia del_ _Concilio ecumenico Vaticano II: Da Giovanni XXIII a Paolo VI (1959–1965)_ (Todi: Tau Editrice, 2016); Alberto Melloni, _Il Concilio_ _e la grazia: Saggi di storia sul Vaticano II_ (Milan: Jaca Book, 2016).

### 2. Collecting the Archive of the Second Vatican Council

The initial plan for the future work development of the Vatican II Archive began on 20 November 1965. It was made official on 7 December, the day before the conclusion of the council, when it was still fully active, voting to approve the promulgation of the decrees on the Apostolate of the Laity, _Apostolicam Actuositatem_; **[p. 72]** on the Mission Activity of the Church, _Ad Gentes_; on the Ministry and Life of Priests, _Presbyterorum Ordinis_; and on the Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World, _Gaudium et Spes_. Among the initiatives to be undertaken on that day was the official establishment of the archive, an action recorded in a ‘note on the constitution of post-conciliar commissions for the application of Decrees approved by the [^c05-8] Second Vatican Ecumenical Council’: ‘Finally, it should be noted that it will be necessary to create an organism to provide for the archival arrangement and the printing of the numerous conciliar acts, as it was [^c05-9] already done for the pre-preparatory phase and in part for the preparatory phase of the Council.’

[^c05-8]: AAV, _Conc. Vat. II_, b. 343, fasc. 3.

[^c05-9]: Ibid.

In a second letter from the hand of Pericle Felici, former secretary general of the council, dated 13 December 1965 and presented to Pope Paul VI during the audience on 17 December, it is written:

In accordance with the Holy Father’s instructions, currently the General Secretariat of the Council is providing … for the establishment of the Vatican II Archives, arranging for the gathering of the vast array of materials from the Preparatory and Conciliar Commissions. When all the materials have been collected and organized, they will be handed over to the Vatican Secret Archive for conservation.[^c05-10]

[^c05-10]: AAV, _Conc. Vat. II_, b. 344, fasc. 1.

Subsequently, on 14 and 29 December 1965, following the official conclusion of the council proceedings, Felici sent a letter to the presidents of the conciliar commissions and secretariats informing them of the forthcoming constitution of the Central Archive of the Second Vatican Council and requesting that they collect and hand over to the General Secretariat all the documentation produced by their individual commissions and secretariats by January 1966.

However, despite the goodwill of the various institutional bodies, the procedures for the transfer of the documents were more complicated than expected and needed more time, as was appropriately underlined by Vincenzo Carbone, head of the Vatican II Archive and the person responsible for other delicate tasks linked to its development. He wrote:

For various reasons, the delivery [of the documentation] extended throughout 1966, with some addenda in 1967. The committees, in fact, needed more time to sort the documents and complete the lists. Moreover, the commissions, which were engaged in the post-conciliar phase, still needed their archives to prepare the norms for the implementation of the conciliar decrees. The provision given, even if it could not be carried out within the fixed term, served to establish clearly that all the documentation must flow into the central archives of the Council. The dispersal that might have occurred at the end of the Council was therefore avoided, with the dissolution of the **[p. 73]** commissions and secretariats. The clarification was all the more appropriate as some entities wanted to keep their documentation for the activity to be carried out after the Council. This was the thinking of several dicasteries of the Roman Curia and post-conciliar authorities who hoped to edit the papers. Paul VI, however, confirmed the requirement for the deposition of all documents, adding that the organs of the Holy See would have the ability to consult the archive of the Council as needed for the completion of their work.[^c05-11]

[^c05-11]: Carbone, ‘L’Archivio del Concilio Vaticano II’, 59.

Once the work of gathering all (or almost all) the conciliar documentation was complete, an office was established and equipped with qualifled personnel to proceed with the classification of the papers and the publication of the most important documents. Indeed, on 2 September 1967, Cardinal Felici wrote to Giovanni Benelli, titular archbishop of Tusuro and substitute (deputy) for general affairs of the Secretariat of State, recalling the _Promemoria_ that had already been sent to Cardinal Giovanni Amleto Cicognani, Secretary of State, on 1 July 1967 and requesting pontifical approval for the establishment of the Vatican II Archive.[^c05-12]

[^c05-12]: AAV, _Conc. Vat. II_, b. 701, fasc. 1 and fasc. 2.

Below is the part of the _Promemoria_ that is of interest:

The Motu Proprio _Finis Concilio_ entrusts to the Secretary of the Central Commission the task of printing and of archiving the Acts of the Council. At present, the printing of pre-conciliar acts is almost finished and all the material of the Acta SS. Concilii Vaticani II is ready for printing. Furthermore, although the Archive has been gathered and arranged at the premises of Via Pfeiffer 12, it needs more complete scientific organization.

To accomplish all this work, which is of the utmost importance for the History of Vatican II, it is necessary (as there no longer exists a real General Secretariat of the post-conciliar Central Commission) to form a separate office, which could temporarily be called the Archive of the Council, under the direct responsibility of a Prelate. We believe it will also be necessary to maintain relations with the Commission for the Revisions of the Code of Canon Law, who will need to consult the material of the Council Archive. The appointed Prelate might come under the President of the Commission for the Code.

Cardinal Felici, as General Secretary of the Central Post-Conciliar Commission, is bound to report the names of the officers being assigned new tasks to a Higher Authority.

The proposed Head of the Council is Monsignor Vincenzo Carbone who has laudably worked with dedication for the preparation and the celebration of the Council. Other possible staff of the Archives include Monsignors Emilio Governatori, Nazareno Cinti, Marcello Venturi and Mr Gianni Malpassi.[^c05-13]

[^c05-13]: Ibid., fasc. 1.

On 27 September, Giovanni Benelli replied to Cardinal Felici, communicating the decision of Paul VI, who **[p. 74]** approved the institution of ‘a separate office for the printing of the Acts of the Council, and for the arrangement of scientific documentation of all the archive material’. The office, called Archive of the Second Vatican Council and placed under the responsibility of Cardinal Felici, was assigned the following personnel: Vincenzo Carbone, director of the Archive office; Emilio Governatori; Nazareno Cinti; Gianni Malpassi; and [^c05-14] Nello Venturini. In all, it took about two years (December 1965 to September 1967) and Felici’s firm resolve that all the documentation kept at the General Secretariat and the various commissions and secretariats should be collected, rearranged, and assembled at the Via Pfeiffer headquarters.

[^c05-14]: Ibid., fasc. 2.

The office at Via Pfeiffer was but the first location for the collection of the Archive of Vatican Council II. According to the _Annuario Pontificio_, Felici became a cardinal on 26 June 1967. At that time, the staff of the archive included the director, Vincenzo Carbone; assistants Mariano De Nicolò and Emilio Governatori; writer-archivist Nazareno Cinti; and writer Gianni Malpassi. In July 1975, the Archive of Vatican Council II was transferred to the Palace of the Congregations in Piazza Pio XII no. 10, in the rooms formerly housing the Congregation for Divine Worship, where they remained until 9 March 2000. By that time, they were staffed by a sole officer, Vincenzo Carbone, who had recently retired.

In the years following its establishment until 1998, the Archive of the Second Vatican Council was enriched by other important archives or by items not yet deposited by the secretariats of the commissions and [^c05-15] secretariats. In 1985, for example, Carbone wrote:

[^c05-15]: Doria, _L’Archivio del Concilio Vaticano II all’Archivio Vaticano_, 507–11.

The increase came from the Sacred Congregation for the Catholic Education. In addition to the abundant material delivered at the time, it transferred to the Archives of the Council many other collections that were promptly ordered and placed. In this way, it was possible to completely reconstruct the section of the Preparatory and Conciliar Commission for Seminaries and University of Studies.[^c05-16]

[^c05-16]: _Att. S. Sede_ (1985), 1415.

In conclusion, the Archive of the Second Vatican Council—which, since its establishment within the Vatican Secret Archives, had as its ultimate purpose the preservation of documents relating to the council—was also tasked, according to the intentions of Paul VI, with providing scholars access to it and, gradually, for obvious reasons, with publishing at least part of the massive documentation. The latter work was completed in 1999 with the publication of the final volume of the _Acta Synodalia_, edited with particular care and competence by Vincenzo Carbone.

### 3. The Transfer of the Archive of Vatican II to the Vatican Secret

### Archives

**[p. 75]** On 3 March 2000, Carbone addressed the following letter to Giovanni Battista Re, titular archbishop of Vescovio and substitute of the Secretariat of State: ‘Excellency _Reverendissima_, to execute the instructions given by Your Most Reverend Excellency for the transfer of the Vatican Council II Archives to the Vatican Secret Archives, I beg Your Excellency to kindly inform me of the day and the name of the person to whom I must hand over the massive documentation.’[^c05-17]

[^c05-17]: AAV, _Conc. Vat. II_, b. 724, fasc. 71.

On 6 March, Archbishop Re, noting Carbone’s availability to proceed with the delivery of the documentation of the archive, indicated the person to whom this delivery was to be made: Jorge Maria Mejía, titular archbishop of Apollonia and archivist and librarian of the Holy Roman Church. Re indicated that ‘he will make contact with you on Thursday, March 9th. Starting from that day, the documentation can be [^c05-18] transferred.’ On 7 March, Jorge Maria Mejía addressed the following note to Vincenzo Carbone:

[^c05-18]: Ibid., fasc. 73.

Most Reverend Monsignor: I am pleased to inform you that, according to the letter from his Excellency, Monsignor Substitute (Prot. N. 471.408 dated 6 March 2000), and subject to your availability, next Thursday, March 9, at 10.00 a.m. I will present myself to the Vatican II Archives to receive the documentation stored there for the purpose of beginning its transfer to the Vatican Secret Archive. With sincere wishes. 7 March 2000. Jorge Mejía, Archivist and Librarian of Holy Roman Church.[^c05-19]

[^c05-19]: Ibid., fasc. 74.

At the appointed time, Mejía and Sergio Pagano, prefect of the Vatican Secret Archives, met Carbone in the offices at no. 10, Piazza Pio XII, officially taking possession of the archive. The deposition of the documentation took place in the following days, from 11 to 13 March, under Pagano’s guidance, with the collaboration of Piero Doria and other employees of the office. Once the documents had been transferred— and given the importance of the papers—the prefect offered Carbone the opportunity of having his own office within the Vatican Secret Archives so he might complete his work there and gradually introduce Doria to the archives. The proposal, although much appreciated, was politely declined by Carbone. Once the documentation of the Second Vatican Council arrived in the archive and was placed on the first floor of the new premises, Doria was able to begin an initial survey of the archive. At the end of May, with permission from the Secretariat of State, the prefect made the archive available to scholars for consultation, in accordance with the will of Paul VI.

**[p. 76]** In this regard, as early as 1990, Carbone wrote: ‘The Archives have not yet been fully opened to scholars because the work of organization continues. To facilitate their research, however, the consultation of [^c05-20] individual documents was permitted on request.’

[^c05-20]: _Att. S. Sede_ (1990), 1350.

At the same time, the work plan was decided by the prefect. The documentation would faithfully maintain the arrangement established by Carbone and his collaborators, both in the external ordering of the boxes and in the internal arrangement of the individual files. Given their importance, in addition to the writings of John XXIII, who convened the council, numerous other papers are preserved from the four subsequent pontiffs—Giovanni Battista Montini, Albino Luciani, Karol Wojtyła, and Joseph Ratzinger—as well as numerous cardinals, bishops, and experts. These have been catalogued in an analytical inventory. In 1983, Carbone suitably observed (although not exactly with appropriate terminology):

The first work of collecting, sorting, and organizing the documents in the various sections is very advanced. As soon as it is completed, it will proceed to the cataloguing of the thousands of binders and the filing of all the documents. Given the huge quantity of the material, only through an accurate filing system will it be possible to find, with ease and promptness, the desired documents.[^c05-21]

[^c05-21]: _Att. S. Sede_ (1983), 1293.

At the time of their deposition in the Vatican Secret Archives, the documentation of the Vatican II Archive included 2,001 boxes, divided as follows:

Segreteria Generale (General Secretariat):

_Congregazioni Generali_ bb. 1–87

_Animadversiones Patrum_ bb. 88–147

_Modi_ bb. 148–256

_Segreteria Generale—Varia_ bb. 257–727

Commissioni e Segretariati (Commissions and Segretariats):

_Commissio theologica_ bb. 728–807

_Commissio de Ecclesiis Orientalibus_ bb. 808–960

_Commissio decretis Concilii Vaticani II interpretandis_ bb. 961–72

_Varia_ bb. 973–76

_Commissio de Episcopis et de Dioecesium regimine_ bb. 977–1051

_Secretariatus de Scriptis prelo edendis et de Spectaculis moderandis_ bb. 1052–53

_Commissio de Sacramentis_ bb. 1054–67

_Commissio de Missionibus_ bb. 1068–1106

_Commissio de Seminariis, de Studiis et de Educatione Catholica_ bb. 1107–68

_Commissio de Apostolatu Laicorum_ bb. 1169–1214 _Commissio de Religiosis_ bb. 1215–1301

_Indici_ bb. 1302–10

**[p. 77]** _Commissio de Disciplina Cleri et Populi Christiani_ bb. 1311–49

_Commissio de Sacra Liturgia_ bb. 1350–1400

_Commissio de Studiis, de Seminariis et de Educatione Catholica (doppioni)_ bb. 1401–21

_Secretariatus ad Christianorum unitatem fovendam_ bb. 1422–1494

Varia (Various):

_Ufficio Stampa_ bb. 1495–1514

_Permessi per l’Aula Conciliare_ bb. 1515–44

_Schemi_ bb. 1545–94

_Registrazioni—Bobine_ bb. 1595–1800

_Traslationes—Cliché – Registrationes—Varia_ bb. 1801–43

_Stampa sul Concilio_ bb. 1844–2001

To this substantial documentation was added an ‘Appendix’, according to the prefect’s disposition, the conciliar fathers’ section, now present in the Vatican Secret Archives, for a total of 152 boxes.

Therefore, part of the Vatican II Archive includes:

• one file—twenty (20) dark brown boxes—handwritten and typewritten cards

• eighteen (18) bound volumes of proceedings of the conciliar documents (_textus et acta praeparatoria_)

• thirty-five (35) dark brown bound volumes with a list of the conciliar fathers who took part in the 168 general congregations and the 10 public sessions

• fourteen (14) light brown bound volumes entitled _Sedes in Aula Conciliari_

• fifteen (15) light grey bound volumes of lists or alphabetical indexes of the conciliar fathers

• eight (8) dark grey volumes _Index Suffiragationum_

• sixteen (16) dark blue bound volumes concerning _animadversiones_ to the plans of dogmatic constitutions

• one hundred and eight (108) volumes bound in two copies of the 544 _Suffiragationes_

• sixty-eight (68) bound volumes of the Press Office

• numerous other copies of volumes printed _durante concilio_

[^c05-22] In the Archive are found numerous printed texts, such as the complete collection of _Acta et Documenta_ (_AD_) [^c05-23] and _Acta Synodalia_ (_AS_), now available to scholars in the Leone XIII Room of the Vatican Apostolic Archive; [^c05-24][^c05-25] **[p. 78]** the _Storia del Concilio Vaticano_by Eugenio Cecconi; the _Geschichte des Vatikanischen Konzils_; and the [^c05-26] _Histoire du Concile du Vatican_ by Theodor Granderath, SJ. These last three works have been transferred to the Sisto V Halls of the Vatican Apostolic Archive. Besides these, other works are kept in the archive next to the documentation for consultation by scholars. Finally, the archive includes five printing plates of the [^c05-27] council chamber used for printing the volume _Aula Sancti Concilii_ and the recordings of the general congregations and of the Theological Commission, restored and edited in 1994–95 by Vatican Radio.

[^c05-22]: _Acta et Documenta Concilio Oecumenico Vaticano II apparando_, Series I Antepraeparatoria, vol. 4, no. 16 (Vatican City: Typis Polyglottis Vaticanis, 1960–61); _Acta et Documenta Concilio Oecumenico Vaticano II apparando_, Series II Praeparatoria, vol. 4, no. 11 (Vatican City: Libreria Editrice Vaticana, 1964–88).

[^c05-23]: _Acta Synodalia Sacrosancti Concilii Oecumenici Vaticani_, Series II Praeparatoria, vol. 4, no. 35 (Vatican City: Typis Polyglottis Vaticanis, 1970–99).

[^c05-24]: C. Cecconi, _Storia del Concilio Vaticano_, 4 vols. (Rome: 1872–79).

[^c05-25]: See note 5 above.

[^c05-26]: Théodore Granderath, SJ, _Histoire du Concile du Vatican depuis sa première annonce jusqu’à sa prorogation d’après les_ _documents authentiques_, ed. Conrad Kirch, SJ, 4 vols. (Brussels: Librairie Albert Dewit, 1907–19).

[^c05-27]: Pericle Felici and Francesco Vacchini, _Aula Sancti Concilii_ (Vatican City: Concilio Ecumenico Vaticano, 1967).

Of course, given the extent of the conciliar collection, the typology of the documents in the archive are varied and numerous. There is a considerable body of correspondence from exchanges between Vatican offices. In fact, letters were widely used by the various conciliar bodies to communicate with bishops, general superiors of religious orders, apostolic prefects, nuncios and apostolic delegates, auditors, observers, and others. They were also used to communicate with the pope, the General Secretariat, and the various secretariats of individual commissions. Besides the incoming correspondence, which is almost always the original document, we find, for outgoing correspondence, letters in draft, copy, or photocopy. Through correspondence, observations and studies were requested and presented, appointments communicated, personal papers and oaths transmitted, members and consultors convened to take part in the various meetings, schemas sent out, and so on.

Next to the correspondence, as mentioned, another type of documentation that is abundantly present is the _animadversiones_ or observations and studies prepared and presented by bishops, individually or with the signatures of other conciliar fathers, or from entire episcopal conferences, experts, and even parish priests, laypeople, women, nuns, religious, and simple priests who, while not having a direct role to play in the assembly, wished to make a contribution to the council.

The press was very active at the council. This is apparent in the materials amassed in special boxes which consist of publications of various kinds—books, pastoral letters, offprints of articles, conference texts, and so on. The collection also includes photographs of John XXIII, Paul VI, the council chamber, the cardinal moderators, papal audiences, press conferences, individual members, and experts or commissions gathered in the presence of the pope, and the machinery used for tabulating the votes according to the criteria: _placet_, _non placet_, _placet iuxta modum_, etc. Finally, the collection includes the extensive documentation of the _Modi_ that occupy more than 100 boxes (bb. 148–256).

**[p. 79]** In addition to the documentary material already mentioned, the individual commissions and secretariats have a very special role. Of particular significance are the protocol register, even if not always present or not always correctly drafted, and the minutes of the plenary meetings or of the individual subcommissions. The latter sometimes remain in the form of handwritten notes or first drafts and are difficult to read. Also of interest are the various drafts of corrected schemata, copies of printed, corrected, and revised schemata, etc.

To this consistent documentation, schematically inventoried, one must add the presence of four particular collections belonging to conciliar cardinals, now available through special arrangement by the prefect (_Fondo cardinale Pietro Parente_, bb. 684–85; _Fondo cardinale Clemente Micara_, b. 686; Cardinal Arcadio Larraona, CMF Fund, bb. 687–89; and the _Fondo cardinale Dino Staffia_, b. 690). Also worthy of mention are the manuscript diaries of Sebastian Tromp, SJ (bb. 789–91), the bull _Humanae Salutis_ (25 December 1961), and the closing brief of the council, _In Spiritu Sancto_ (8 December 1965), by John XXIII and Paul VI respectively, and five boxes (bb. 589–92/A) containing the volumes of the constitutions, decrees, and declarations signed by the pope and endorsed by all the bishops. Finally, the archive has recently benefited from the addition of an important documentary testimony, the conciliar diaries of the general secretary, Pericle Felici.[^c05-28]

[^c05-28]: Piero Doria, _Le agende conciliari di Pericle Felici (1959–1967): Analisi di una fonte_ (forthcoming).

On 18 November 2015, the day on which this volume, _The Conciliar Diaries of Monsignor Pericle Felici_, was presented in the Pietro da Cortona Hall of the Capitoline Museums at the Campidoglio in Rome, transcribed [^c05-29] by Vincenzo Carbone and edited by Agostino Marchetto for the Vatican Library Press, Raffaele Di Nardo, a parish priest of San Pietro di Acerra (Naples), delivered a box containing diaries, notebooks, and some of Cardinal Felici’s handwritten papers to the Secretariat of State on behalf of Carbone’s heirs. Subsequently, on 7 June 2016, Angelo Becciu, titular archbishop of Roselle and substitute of the Secretariat of State, addressed the following letter to Sergio Pagano recording the deposition of the documents received in the special collection of the Archive of Vatican Council II:[^c05-30]

[^c05-29]: Vincenzo Carbone and Agostino Marchetto, _Il ‘Diario’ conciliare di Monsignor Pericle Felici Segretario Generale del Concilio_ _Ecumenico Vaticano II_ (Vatican City: Libreria Editrice Vaticana, 2015). See also Agostino Marchetto, _Il ‘Diario’ Conciliare di_ _Monsignor Pericle Felici: Addendum_ (Vatican City: Libreria Editrice Vaticana, 2016).

[^c05-30]: AAV, Arch. Prefettura, _Versamenti_, fasc. 222, f. n. n.

From the Vatican, 7 June 2016

No. 301734

Reverend Excellency,

18 November 2015, the Reverend Don Raffaele Di Nardo, pastor of San Pietro di Acerra (NA), in the name of the heirs of Monsignor Vincenzo Carbone, formerly in charge of the **[p. 80]** Archive of the Second Vatican Ecumenical Council, has returned to the Secretariat of State a box containing the following manuscript documents belonging to Cardinal Pericle Felici, Secretary General of the Council from 1962 to 1965:

- N. 8 agendas

- N. 4 notebooks

- N. 2 envelopes of manuscript sheets in a blue folder.

I have taken care to ensure that these documents are entrusted to the archival records of [^c05-31] the Second Vatican Council.

[^c05-31]: Ibid.

And the prefect’s reply:

Vatican, 14 June 2016

Prot. N. 59.101

Most Reverend Excellency,

I write in reply to your important missive, n. 301.734, dated 7 June, which accompanied the delivery of archival materials containing manuscripts of Cardinal Pericle Felici, which until now were in possession of the heirs of Monsignor Vincenzo Carbone. In this regard, I am pleased to confirm to your Excellency the reception on 13 June, of these archival materials and the perfect correspondence of the content with your records. I have already made provision for the inclusion of the aforementioned documentation in the collection [^c05-32] of the Second Vatican Council.

[^c05-32]: Ibid.

On 14 June, the day following the deposition of the documents of Cardinal Felici in the archive, Doria was summoned by the prefect, who informed him of these developments and arranged for the aforementioned agendas to be placed in the collection. After making a full inventory, he placed the documentary material in two specially designated boxes (b. 727A and b. 727B) in the archive of the General Secretariat, adding to the extensive documentation there.

### 4. The Inventory

As already underlined, once the deposition of the Vatican II Archive in the Vatican Secret Archives was completed in accordance with the directives given by the branch office, Doria began to consult the documentation to establish the criteria and typology to be used in the preparation of the inventory. It was **[p. 81]** immediately obvious that one could not proceed to a sample survey using the methods that are customary in these cases to get a precise idea of the various papers present in the archive. Although it was a recent archive, its complex nature soon became apparent. Faithfully following the organizational system established by the branch office, each box was carefully numbered before its removal.

The complexity of the collection was confirmed in the correspondence of the archivist Emilio Governatori, [^c05-33] who sought to avoid jumping to ‘easy conclusions and judgments’ concerning the pre-preparatory and preparatory phases:

[^c05-33]: AAV, _Conc. Vat. II_, b. 702, fasc. 60.

for two years all the documents concerning the replies of the bishops, which constituted the nucleus first and largest part of the Archive, were used for the preparation of the volumes of the _Acta et documenta_ … The same originals were used for this, as there was no efficient photocopying machine. Often the order of the collection was tampered with and re-established many times, since the persons in charge of proofreading borrowed the necessary documents without informing the archivist.[^c05-34]

[^c05-34]: Ibid.

And again:

There has never been a single person whose sole task it was to be in charge of the Archive and the Protocol. Many, including some of the most important documents, were kept in a special archive by the Secretary himself. Only in 1962, just before the opening of the Council, was the Secretary able to organize his collection of the many documents that passed into the general archive. Many were never recorded or were only recorded very late … Therefore, it may be that many documents are not in chronological order, either in their organization or in relation to the protocol.[^c05-35]

[^c05-35]: Ibid.

With regard to the reorganization of the archive, Governatori drafted this note, following the establishment of the office:

Returned to the headquarters of the Secretariat of the Post-conciliar Commission and of the Vatican II Archives in Via Pfeiffer 10. Monsignor Governatori looked after the arrangement of all documentary material relating to the pre-preparatory phase and of almost the entire preparatory period (Central Commission, Preparatory Commissions). This work, left dormant since 1962, from the beginning of the conciliar event, was taken up again from November 1967, the date of his return to Via Pfeiffer, to December 1968, when he was transferred to the Pontifical Commission for Social Communications.[^c05-36]

[^c05-36]: Ibid.

These testimonies, combined with a number of unfortunate findings (such as the excessive presence of **[p. 82]** photocopies, the use of original texts for publication, the poor organization of materials, and accompanying letters that were sometimes unsigned, undated, or lacking protocol numbers), led the prefect of the Vatican Secret Archives to decide in favour of preparing an extensive analytical inventory, recording all the materials in the Vatican II Archive document by document. While he recognized that this project would take considerable time, the result would be a useful research tool for scholars, providing a complete record of the holdings.

The work of inventorying and surveying the Vatican II Archive is now complete. The results can be found in the Indices Hall of the Vatican Apostolic Archive, readily accessible to scholars. The Index for the Archive of Vatican II is found in twenty-one volumes, which inventory 1,198 of a total of 2,001 inventoried boxes. They total approximately 8,000 pages. The following is a complete list of volumes in the archive:

1.  _Congregazioni Generali_, bb. 1–87, 2005, pp. 188.

2.  _Animadversiones Scriptae_, bb. 88–147, 2005, pp. 206.

3.  _Modi_, bb. 148–182, 2005, pp. 471.

4.  _Modi_, bb. 183–217, 2005, pp. 460.

5.  _Modi_, bb. 218–256, 2005, pp. 459.

6.  _Segreteria Generale_, bb. 257–337, 2005, pp. 405.

7.  _Segreteria Generale_, bb. 338–402, 2005, pp. 423.

8.  _Segreteria Generale_, bb. 403–510, 2005, pp. 443.

9.  _Segreteria Generale_, bb. 511–621, 2006, pp. 429.

10.  _Segreteria Generale_, bb. 622–727, 2006, pp. 414.

11.  _Commissio Theologica et Commissio De doctrina fidei et morum_, bb. 728–807, 2007, pp. 360.

12.  _Commissio De Ecclesiis Orientalibus—Varia_, bb. 808–976, 2007, pp. 366.

13.  _Commissio de Episcopis et de dioecesium regimine—Secretariatus de scriptis prelo edendis et de spectaculis moderandis_, bb. 977–1053, 2008, pp. 361.

14.  _Commissio de Sacramentis—Commissio de Missionibus_, bb. 1054-1106, 2009, pp. 240.

15.  _Commissio de Seminariis, de Studiis et de Educatione Catholica_, bb. 1107–68, 2009, pp. 403.

16.  _Commissio de Apostolatu Laicorum—Commissio de Religiosis_, bb. 1169–1301, 2010, pp. 602.

17.  _Indici; Commissio De disciplina cleri et populi christiani; Commissio De sacra liturgia; Commissio De studiis, de seminariis et de educatione catholica (Doppioni)_, bb. 1302–1421, 2011, pp. 600.

18.  _Secretariatus ad christianorum unitatem fovendam_, bb. 1422–94, 2012, pp. 483.

19.  _Ufficio Stampa—Permessi per l’Aula_, bb. 1495–1544, 2013, pp. 584.

20.  _Schemi—Registrazioni—Varia (Traslationes. Cliché, Registrazioni, Suffiragationes, Centro Meccanografico, Carte Antonelli, Segretariato per l’Unione dei Cristiani)_, bb. 1545–1843, 2014, pp. 538.

21.  _Stampa sul Concilio_, bb. 1844–2001, 2014, pp. 167.

**[p. 83]** A decision was taken by the prefect of the Vatican Secret Archives to publish this inventory, and confirmed by Jean-Louis Bruguès, OP, former archivist and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on 7 May 2013, on the occasion of the presentation of the fifth edition of _Archivi Secreti Vaticani Humanae Salutis_. Besides the inventory, Pagano also approved the restoration of a series of audio recordings of the seven sessions of the Central Preparatory Commission. These had escaped the attention of the staff of Vatican Radio in the 1990s, when other tapes were restored.

Vatican Radio has also restored a series of other recordings, including the celebration of the Byzantine- Slavic Liturgy in the Papal Chapel of the Vatican Basilica on 13 November 1960; the papal audience on 14 November; and seven sessions of the Central Preparatory Commission: the first, 12–20 June 1961; the second, 7–17 November 1961; the third, 15–23 January 1962; the fourth, 19–27 February 1962; the fifth, 26 March to 3 April 1962; the sixth, part I, 3–12 May 1962; the sixth, part II, 3–12 May 1962; the seventh, part I, 12–20 June 1962; and the seventh, part II, 12–20 June 1962. The Information Service of the Vatican Secret Archives has secured a special storage area for the long-term preservation of cassettes and compact discs of the audio recordings of the general congregations and the Theological Commission that were restored by Vatican Radio in 1994–96.

Consideration is being given to the possible digitization of important documentary material relating to the work of the Vatican Press Office to allow for easier consultation by scholars. Moreover, the archive has digitized a significant share of the photographic material present in the collection. Finally, the photographic laboratory of the Vatican Apostolic Archive has already begun to digitize the diary of Sebastian Tromp, SJ, secretary of the Theological Commission and of the Commission _De doctrina fidei et morum_. Plans are under way to digitize the photo cards of the council fathers who participated in the assembly, which are kept in the section of the _Padri Conciliari_.

The work accomplished by Carbone and his colleagues is worthy of praise. Nonetheless, one cannot escape the impression that instead of focusing on the organization and cataloguing of materials, much more effort in this initial period went into publishing the volumes of _Acta Synodalia_. This task absorbed most or almost all of the energies of the employees of the office, especially after Governatori’s departure in December 1968. He had served as archivist of the General Secretariat since November 1967. With his transfer to the Pontifical Commission for Social Communications, the reorganization was interrupted or, at the very least, it does not seem to have been continued with the same enthusiasm by his successors.

This may explain the sometimes haphazard ordering of the documentation, especially that pertaining to the General Secretariat. Boxes were sometimes arranged in a confusing manner, rather than in chronological or thematic order. In some cases, boxes were not numbered and were then misplaced after consultation. Today, these anomalies can no longer be corrected, since the misordering of materials predates its deposition in the Vatican Apostolic Archive. The organization of materials pertaining to the conciliar commissions appears to be more accurate, probably due to the reorganization carried out before their delivery to the General Secretariat.

**[p. 84]** It must be borne in mind that those who played the role of archivist in these many commissions did not all have the necessary skills. Only a few were trained in the fleld. For the most part, all were guided by the criteria of the protocol register for drafting documents and reports. On the other hand, these same criteria have at times been overly personalized, with at times contradictory results. This is the case for the protocol registers prepared by the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity, some of which are useless, or almost so. We must add that very often, the same few employees carried out this heavy work with great difficulty, given the tight timelines and burden of other responsibilities.

A further challenge worth mentioning is the dispersal of documentation which occurred during the conciliar period but which does not necessarily imply the loss of papers. Unfortunately, especially in the case of the secretaries of the commissions, it happened that office papers were taken home. In some cases, documents have been lost. In others, they have fortunately been recovered. Two examples come to mind. The first concerns the protocol register of the Theological Commission and the Commission _De doctrina fidei et morum_. At least for now, we must speak of the loss of this precious research tool. In 2006, in fact, Doria reported this lacuna to the prefect, who wrote to the undersecretary of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith. Regrettably, the congregation’s answer was negative, as was the survey carried out by the Jesuit fathers of the Pontifical Gregorian University, where Sebastian Tromp, SJ, had lived and where his papers are preserved. The second example, a more positive one, concerns the archive of the Preparatory Commission _De sacra liturgia_ which, as Felici wrote to Ferdinando Antonelli, OFM, on 4 March 1967, was discovered in the possession of Annibale Bugnini.

Unfortunately, as Doria was able to verify from the records kept in the archives of the Prefecture of the Vatican Apostolic Archive, there does not seem to have been any request for collaboration or guidance in the tasks relating to the organization of the archive of the General Secretariat and other offices. Some, like the newly established Secretariat for Christian Unity, could not rely upon established structures like those of the congregations of the Roman Curia that had supported other conciliar commissions. Their staff had little or no instruction in the appropriate methods for organizing and preserving archival materials. Regrettably, this was also the case from 1967 onwards, when it would have been appropriate to enlist the skills of a true archivist to carry out the dual task of ordering and inventorying the huge amount of documentation. In all likelihood, if we had immediately resorted to the skills of Martino Giusti and his close collaborators, many of the inconsistencies that we have been obliged to report might have been avoided, and we might have offered to the Church and to scholars an archive of the Second Vatican Council more befitting the great event. In short, the overall impression remains that in the preparation of the Second Vatican Council, those who ought to have done so neglected their responsibility to organize the office in a manner that would ensure the preservation of the memory of the assembly. Still, as Carbone has written, there was no lack of awareness among the protagonists at the highest levels:

At the beginning of the preparation of Vatican II, Cardinal Domenico Tardini, President of the **[p. 85]** pontifical Pre-Preparatory Commission, considered it appropriate to consult the documentation of Vatican I, held in the Vatican Secret Archives, in search of suggestions and operational directions.

Obtaining permission from Pope John XXIII and accompanied by the Prefect, Monsignor Martino Giusti, I was able to study the documentation stored there.

I did not find much for our purpose. The investigation, however, served to underline the need to take, from the outset, great care in preserving the documents during the course of the council proceedings, and to gather them all, as soon as the council concludes, to avoid dispersion.

To this end, certain directives for the conservation of each page, for the care of the protocols, for the drafting of the minutes of the meetings, etc. were promptly established.

This commitment of the General Secretariat and the other conciliar bodies (commissions, secretariats, and offices) ensured the preservation of the abundant documentation now amassed in [^c05-37] the Vatican II Archives.

[^c05-37]: Carbone, ‘L’Archivio del Concilio Vaticano II’, 58.

Subsequent events, including the visionary decision of Paul VI and the silent, discreet service of many good priests, made the constitution of the Vatican II Archive possible. However imperfect, they remain an inexhaustible mine of information for scholars.

A number of recent publications on the Second Vatican Council and related topics allow us to introduce briefly the theme of new prospects for research. In fact, one must ask whether the documents published in _Acta et Documenta_ and _Acta Synodalia_ are sufficient to reconstruct the conciliar dynamics. As some recent studies show, their consultation alone does not necessarily constitute in-depth archival research. It must be noted that the Vatican II Archive contains a series of still unexplored papers and documents, especially in the archives of the commissions and secretariats. These are most useful for reconstructing the elaboration of the various schemata. They are of great value for understanding both the spirit of the council and the correct hermeneutic of documents approved by the assembly of bishops gathered in the Vatican Basilica and by Paul VI.[^c05-38]

[^c05-38]: Massimo Faggioli, _Il vescovo e il concilio: Modello episcopale e aggiornamento al Vaticano II_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2005); Gilles Routhier, _Vatican II: Herméneutique et réception_ (Montreal: Fides, 2006); Christoph Theobald, _La Réception du Concile_ _Vatican II_ (Paris: Cerf, 2009); Massimo Faggioli, _Vatican II: The Battle for Meaning_ (Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 2012); Philippe Chenaux and Nicolas Bouquet, _Rileggere il Concilio: Storici e teologi a confronto_ (Vatican City: Lateran University Press, 2012); Gilles Routhier, _Un concilio per il XXI secolo: Il Vaticano II cinquant’anni dopo_ (Milan: Vita e Pensiero, 2012); Massimo Faggioli, _True Reform: Liturgy and Ecclesiology in Sacrosanctum Concilium_ (Collegeville, MN: Paulist, 2012). Alberto Melloni, _Galileo al Concilio_ (Bologna: Edizioni Dehoniane Bologna, 2013). Massimo Faggioli, _Nello spirito del concilio: Movimenti_ _ecclesiali e recezione del Vaticano II_ (Milan: San Paolo Edizioni, 2013). Christoph Theobald, _Le Concile Vatican II: Quel_ _avenir?_ (Paris: Cerf, 2015).

### 5. Other Archives Related to Vatican II

**[p. 86]** Besides the Archive of Vatican II, which contains the most complete documentary collection relating to the conciliar event itself, there are several thousand other small or medium-sized archives throughout the world belonging to the many protagonists who came to Rome from the four corners of the earth: council fathers (3,058 of whom took part in at least one session), general superiors of religious orders (129), experts (479), male lay (29) and female auditors (23), and observers and guests (154); to this must be added consultors, journalists, diplomats, government representatives, and, in several cases, representatives of political parties.[^c05-39]

[^c05-39]: Massimo Faggioli and Giovanni Turbanti, eds., _Il Concilio inedito: Fonti del Vaticano II_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2001); Philippe Chenaux, _Il Concilio Vaticano II alla luce degli archivi dei padri conciliari_ (Vatican City: Lateran University Press, 2015); Philippe Chenaux and Kiril Plamen Kartaloff, _Il Concilio Vaticano II e i suoi protagonisti alla luce degli Archivi_ (Vatican City: Libreria Editrice Vaticana, 2017).

The vast array of papers, photos, and images made the council one of the most closely followed events in the [^c05-40] history of contemporary Christianity. We cannot omit to mention the important contribution made by those who lived through these events and whose participation is witnessed in the writings they left us in books, articles, newspapers, and television interviews broadcast on networks around the world that enhance the often unpublished details and stories. These materials frequently reflect the new debates that arose in the immediate aftermath of the council that sought to address the consequences of its teachings— not merely from an emotional perspective, but also and perhaps above all from a scientific one. They sought to understand the implications for the life of the Church in the short term and for the long term. An important venue of this debate was the international magazine _Concilium_, founded in 1965 by some of the great theologians of the council, including Yves Congar, Hans Küng, Karl Rahner, Edward Schillebeeckx, Joseph Ratzinger, and Jorge Maria Mejía.

[^c05-40]: See the bibliographical surveys of Massimo Faggioli in _Cristianesimo nella storia_: 24, no. 2 (2003): 335–60; 26, no. 3 (2005): 743–67; 29, no. 2 (2008): 567–610; 32, no. 2 (2011): 755–91; 34, no. 3 (2013): 927–55; and 37, no. 3 (2016): 675–715. See also Philippe Roy-Lysencourt, _Bibliographie du Concile Vatican II_ (Vatican City: Libreria Editrice Vaticana, 2012).

In this same period, the Fondazione per le Scienze Religiose Giovanni XXIII, located in Bologna, Italy, was a major player. Born in 1953 from an intuition by Giuseppe Dossetti (1913–96), it was directed by Giuseppe Alberigo (1926–2007) for almost fifty years. Today, under the direction of Alberto Melloni, it has become the first major protagonist of a post-conciliar historiographical debate nourished by the collection and study of documentary materials, research, conferences, publications, and, since 1980, through the publication of _Cristianesimo nella storia,_ a multidisciplinary journal that has become the host to significant studies on the council. One of the foundation’s largest achievements is the publication of the five-volume **[p. 87]** _History of Vatican II_, a work produced through the collaboration and contributions of distinguished scholars from around the world. This work has been subject to some criticism. At times less than complete, it was drawn up when the Archive of the Second Vatican Council was only partially open to consultation and remains a fundamental and indispensable reference work for every student and scholar. The foundation’s library is unique in the world for its collection of texts on the council and for its archive, which includes the remarkable collections of papers belonging to Cardinal Giacomo Lercaro, archbishop of Bologna, and Giuseppe Dossetti.

Still in Italy, we find at least three other important centres of interest: the Istituto Paolo VI of Brescia (1979) and the Fondazione Papa Giovanni XXIII of Bergamo (1993), where the archives preserve numerous papers of the two conciliar popes; and the Centro per l’ecumenismo per l’Italia, based in Venice (2008), directed by Riccardo Burigana. More recently, in 1998, the Centro Studi e Ricerche sul Concilio Vaticano II was established in connection with the Pontifical Lateran University by Cardinal Angelo Scola, then rector of the university. Under the direction of Philippe Chenaux, the centre is in possession of important archives (Cardinal Georges Cottier, Michele Maccarrone, Cardinal Pietro Pavan, etc.) and produces a series and a magazine (now online) entirely dedicated to the Second Vatican Council.

Beyond the borders of Italy, we wish to mention three other important institutions. First, in Belgium, the Centre for the Study of the Second Vatican Council was founded in 1970 by two professors from the University of Louvain, Maurits Sabbe (1924–2004) and Jan Grootaers (1921–2016). Located in the Faculty of Theology and Religious Studies of Louvain and currently under the direction of Mathijs Lamberigts, the centre holds numerous archives belonging primarily to Belgian protagonists of the council (Gérard Philips, Edward Schillebeeckx, Emiel-Jozef De Smedt, Jozef-Maria Heuschen, etc.) and promotes an intensive programme of scientific research. The second, in the Netherlands, is the Cardinal Willebrands Research Centre. Linked to the University of Tilburg, the centre is directed by Karim Schelkens. Its collection is entirely focused on the figure of Cardinal Johannes Willebrands, who was the protagonist, together with Cardinal Augustin Bea, on matters of ecumenical and interreligious dialogue from the first days of the council. (Since 2013, at the Pontifical Gregorian University in Rome, the Centro Cardinal Bea per gli studi giudaici has been directed by Étienne E. Vetö, SJ.) The centre has produced important research and publications of unquestionable scientific value. Finally, a third research centre worthy of mention is the Vatican II et le Québec des années 1960 centre, located in the Faculty of Theology and Religious Studies of Université Laval in Quebec, under the direction of Gilles Routhier. The centre promotes the study of the history of the council and its reception.

### 6. Conclusion

As we have noted, the Second Vatican Council is the most widely known and most studied event of **[p. 88]** contemporary church history. Yet significant gaps remain and await new study and reflection. We know a great deal concerning the principal protagonists and themes of the council. Yet there is more to learn about how topics were proposed and selected and how the schemata were prepared and debated in the various phases, from the work of the commissions and subcommissions to the council hall. Each of the sixteen documents approved by the council fathers and promulgated by Pope Paul VI has been studied and examined in detail in scientific works too numerous to count.

The conciliar season brought great changes without abandoning tradition. These changes helped the People of God better understand the Gospel, as John XXIII intended, sweeping away the dust that had accumulated through the centuries. That season, however, has not yet exhausted its driving force and its effects. Indeed, with the pontificate of Francis, we have embarked on its path of reform in the awareness that it is no longer possible to turn back.

## 6. Other Sources for the Study of Vatican II: Journalism,

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 89]** Recent conciliar historiography has highlighted how the celebration of a council is preserved in a varied corpus of sources: not only through approved texts, minutes, or theological treatises, but also, for example, through private papers, letters, diaries, images, and recordings. The same conciliar iconography (from painted icons to frescoes, engravings, and prints) represents a type of documentation in which certain traces are discernible, and, if duly examined, can prove useful for a deeper understanding of the events in [^c06-1] question, as pointed out by Hermann Josef Sieben, André Grabar, and Christopher Walter. The photographs of Vatican I and the audiovisual images of Vatican II represent the natural evolution of that iconography preserved in museums and churches around the world. At Vatican II, more than two thousand council fathers arrived in Rome from five continents and in such numbers as to give ‘universal’ a new meaning. They arrived with _periti_ (experts), observers, and listeners, but that was not all: the media (newspapers, [^c06-2] magazines, radio, television) were present, and, through them, the whole of society ‘participated’ as well.

[^c06-1]: André Grabar, _Christian Iconography: A Study of Its Origins_ (Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press, 1968); Christopher Walter, _L’Iconographie des conciles dans la tradition byzantine_ (Paris: Institut français d’études byzantines, 1970); Hermann Josef Sieben, _Konzilsdarstellungen—Konzilsvorstellungen: 1000 Jahre Konzilsikonographie aus Handschriffen und_ _Druckwerken_ (Würzburg: Echter, 1990).

[^c06-2]: Federico Ruozzi, _Il concilio in diretta: Il Vaticano II e la televisione tra informazione e partecipazione_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2012).

### 2. Vatican II: Between Traditional Sources and Twentieth-Century

### Sources

**[p. 90]** One of the peculiarities of Vatican II is the sheer wealth of documentation that the event generated. In fact, no council has ever produced so many decisions. Those of Vatican II represent more than a quarter of the [^c06-3] total number deliberated at the other twenty councils, from Nicaea I to Vatican I. The final documents form an important body of work for understanding what went on and for understanding the leap forward that the Catholic Church made in the last council of the second millennium, beyond the easy enthusiasm, criticism, or foreseeable resistance to its reception. However, the final documents are not the only ones. Other types of sources appear to be equally fundamental for arriving at a deeper knowledge, as the historiography of recent [^c06-4] years on Vatican II has shown. The final documents have come with the publication of the conciliar sources proper, collected in the volumes of the _Acta Synodalia Sacrosanti Concilii Oecumenici Vaticani II_. In addition to these, there are the acts of the pre-preparatory period (_Acta et Documenta Concilio Oecumenico Vaticano II apparando, Series I, Antepraeparatoria_) and those of the preparatory period (_Acta et Documenta Concilio Oecumenico Vaticano II apparando, Series II, Praeparatoria_); these are preserved in the Archive of the Second Vatican Council, which is currently at the Vatican Apostolic Archive. All of these documents were collected and published under the direction of Vincenzo Carbone as early as 1960; in addition, ninety-seven issues of the _Notiziario_ were published by the Pontifical Central Preparatory Commission, the General Secretariat of [^c06-5] the council, and the Press Office for the period June 1960 to June 1962.

[^c06-3]: Giuseppe Alberigo, ‘Transition to a New Age?’, in _History of Vatican II_, ed. Giuseppe Alberigo and Joseph Komonchak (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis; Leuven: Peeters, 2006), 5:573–74; also in Giuseppe Alberigo, _Transizione epocale: Studi sul concilio_ _Vaticano II_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2009).

[^c06-4]: Alberto Melloni, ‘Tipologia delle fonti per la storia del Vaticano II’, _Cristianesimo nella storia_ 13 (1992): 493–514.

[^c06-5]: Vincenzo Carbone, ‘Genesi e criteri della pubblicazione degli atti del concilio Vaticano II’, _Lateranum_ 44 (1978), 579–94; Gerard Lefeuvre, ‘Les Actes du Concile du Vatican’, _Revue théologique de Louvain_ 11 (1980): 186–200, 325–51; Umberto Betti, ‘A proposito degli _Acta Synodalia Sacrosancti Concilii Oecumenici Vaticani II_’, _Antonianum_ 56 (1981): 3–42.

Contrary to what had happened for previous councils, in the case of Vatican II the problem of reordering the documents was immediately raised to facilitate the study of the event based on documentation that was as complete and accessible as possible. On 20 November 1965, two weeks before the closing ceremony, the secretary general, Msgr. Pericle Felici, sent the pope a ‘Note about the establishment of post-conciliar commissions for the application of the decrees approved by the Second Vatican Ecumenical Council’. He also wrote about the opportunity to establish a body that would provide ‘the archival arrangement and **[p. 91]** publication of the numerous conciliar acts’, as had happened for the pre-preparatory and part of the [^c06-6] preparatory periods, marking ‘a new period in the life of the Church and its relations with the world’. This opened a new phase in the study of councils. The concern for care with the documentation was also felt by Paul VI himself: at the end of the council, he made provision for the establishment of the Vatican II Archive, arranging the publication of the synodal acts and, above all, access to the documentation by scholars. This approach was in contrast to the traditional restrictive rules that regulate the other funds of the Vatican [^c06-7] Secret Archive (called the Vatican Apostolic Archive since 2019). Historians could thus begin to study Vatican II through the numerous sources made immediately available, which continued to be published and released over the years.

[^c06-6]: Vincenzo Carbone, ‘L’archivio del concilio Vaticano II’, _Archiva Ecclesiae_, 34–35 (1991–92): 58.

[^c06-7]: Vincenzo Carbone, ‘Il cardinal Domenico Tardini e la preparazione del concilio Vaticano II’, _Rivista di storia della Chiesa in_ _Italia_ 45 (1991): 42–88; ‘L’Archivio Vaticano II (1965–1999): Trentacinque anni di inventari e pubblicazioni; Intervista a mons. Carbone’, _Centro Vaticano II–Ricerche e documenti_, 1, no. 0 (2000): 42–46; Sergio Pagano, ‘Riflessioni sulle fonti archivistiche del concilio Vaticano II’, _Cristianesimo nella storia_ 23 (2002): 775–812; Piero Doria, ‘L’Archivio del Concilio Vaticano II: Storia e sviluppo’, _Anuario de historia de la Iglesia_ 21 (2012): 135–55.

[^c06-8] Similarly, resuming the system proposed for the publication of the documents of the Council of Trent, the sources cited earlier constitute the ‘acts’ and are specifically kept in the central archive. However, the approach used for the Tridentine council also considers other types of conciliar sources, such as diaries, letters, and treatises—the most interesting part of the conciliar documents. For these types of documents, scholars of Vatican II made use of other archives, mainly diocesan, local, or private, with all the [^c06-9] complications that arise from problematic archiving processes and complex cataloguing. These sources are difficult to quantify and, precisely for that reason, pose unprecedented and equally stimulating problems to scholars: if read between the lines, they reveal aspects of the conciliar event that escape the _Acta_. At the intersection of all these sources, ‘it is possible to gain a more nuanced and realistic picture of the course of [^c06-10] Vatican II than the necessarily more impersonal official sources could produce’. Indeed, as early as December 1965, Giuseppe Dossetti—_peritus_ (expert) of Cardinal Giacomo Lercaro, archbishop of Bologna (Italy), and the leader of the group Church of the Poor—during a lesson at the Documentation centre/Institute for Religious Sciences in Bologna directed by the historian Giuseppe Alberigo, reiterated that
