[^c06-9]: Massimo Faggioli and Giovanni Turbanti, eds., _Il concilio inedito_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2001); Jan Grootaers and Claude Soetens, eds., _Sources locales de Vatican II_ (Leuven: Bibliotheek van de Faculteit Godgeleerdheid van de K.U. Leuven, 1990); Philippe Chenaux and Karil Plamen Kartaloff, eds., _Il Concilio Vaticano II e i suoi protagonisti alla luce degli archivi_ (Vatican City: Libreria Editrice Vaticana, 2017).

[^c06-10]: Giuseppe Alberigo, ‘The Sources for the Second Vatican Council’, in Alberigo and Komonchak, _History of Vatican II_, 5:648– 49.

the conclusion of the council undoubtedly means, in the end, the conclusion of a whole series of **[p. 92]** stimuli which are not only revealed by the individual documents, but which have also manifested themselves in the history of the council, in its overall atmosphere, even in the orientations that have not been documented, but which have come true, and which can be captured through other data, other instruments that are not single acts and which together make the global [^c06-11] history and the global grace of the council.

[^c06-11]: Dossetti, ‘Per una “Chiesa eucaristica” ’, (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2002): 22. For a biographical overview on Giuseppe Dossetti (partisan, professor of Canon Law, politician, theologian, funder of the Bologna Documentation centre, priest and monk) see Alberto Melloni, ed., _Giuseppe Dossetti. Studies on an Italian Catholic Reformer_ (Berlin: Lit, 2008).

However, the publication of the sources is also closely related to another non-marginal issue that has mostly characterized the history of the councils as they took place: the confidentiality of the discussions. This tradition ended with Vatican II. Since its preparatory period, despite the meagre information that was leaked, chronicles, memoirs, and correspondence began to emerge—through channels outside the Vatican —which would later turn into the first essential sources for the history of Vatican II. As we will see, these broke the seal of privacy that weighed on the works at the beginning. During Vatican I, some attempts were [^c06-12] made to inform the faithful and public opinion about the conciliar discussions. Yet, the papers remained under archival secrecy for almost half a century, as had also happened with the acts of the Tridentine Council: those documents were shelved for three centuries, thus hindering a full understanding of them. Much of the documentation relating to the preparatory period of Pius IX’s council was, for that matter, also dispersed or stashed away, without any criteria, in the Vatican Secret Archives.

[^c06-12]: Cosimo Ceccuti, _Il Concilio Vaticano I nella stampa italiana (1868–1870)_ (Rome: Edizioni Cinque Lune, 1970).

Vatican II differs from most of the past councils for several reasons. Among those that need to be remembered is, on the one hand, as mentioned earlier, the care aimed at avoiding any dispersion and sketchy collection of documents—not only internal Vatican ones—so as to have a heterogeneous corpus of sources. On the other hand there was the awareness of the Church itself, which had set the goal of improving [^c06-13] ‘the cognitive state of the gospel message in the modern world’. Thus, the problems relating to the modern means of the popularization of thought, such as the press, radio, television, and the cinema, were brought to the council (_Superno Dei nutu_, 5 June 1960). Moreover, for the first time, and at a time when the clergy was still forbidden to read newspapers that were not Catholic, the Holy See decided to inform public opinion by using not only ecclesiastical channels, but also secular ones. This meant a careful consideration of the reception of the event by society and, therefore, an organization of the information that would serve that goal. World public opinion thus formed a conciliar consciousness to a degree and level unthinkable, for example, only for the Vatican I, celebrated just a century before **[p. 93]** Vatican II - in addition to making use of a well-established press, the key role of Vatican typography, and international journalism that was certainly more prepared and perceptive than in the past - was at the same time able to use a series of tools that the technological revolutions of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries made available. Not only were the typewriter, the mimeograph, the photocopier, or the telephone—ordinary but essential work instruments for the facilitations they introduced—in use, but so were microphones, tape [^c06-14] recorders, satellites, telecommunication bridges, films, cameras, and movie and television cameras. In the [^c06-15] 1960s, the media circuit was gaining ground, and television was showing its ‘splendour’ to the world. The audio and radio recordings and the television and cinematographic images that were the result of these [^c06-16] technologies would eventually become in all respects conciliar sources. Historiographic research has demonstrated that they cannot be ignored when studying the history of the Church and the papacy in the twentieth century. Once underestimated by historians and relegated to the confines of media studies or to cultural or social history, the audiovisual document, as a tool for the historian and after critical scrutiny, is now considered a source of the conciliar event itself. It also becomes, for its nature and specificity, an actor of the event, as we will see.

[^c06-13]: Giancarlo Zizola, ‘La comunicazione del Concilio Vaticano II: Storia inedita di qualche problema’, _Desk_ 4 (2002): 28.

[^c06-14]: Klaus Wittstadt, ‘On the Eve of the Second Vatican Council’, in Alberigo and Komonchak, _History of Vatican II_, 1:405–500. See also Leo Declerck and André Haquin, eds., _Mgr Albert Prignon, Recteur du Pontificio Collegio Belga: Journal conciliaire_ _de la 4° Session_ (Leuven: Peeters, 2003).

[^c06-15]: Alberto Abruzzese, _Lo splendore della TV: Origini e destino del linguaggio audiovisivo_ (Genoa: Costa & Nolan, 1995).

[^c06-16]: Ruozzi, _Il concilio in diretta_; Ruozzi, ‘La voce del concilio: Il fuorionda del 13 ottobre 1962; Le fonti audio del Vaticano II’, _Cristianesimo nella storia_ 34 (2013): 161–99.

The study of Vatican II, as the various historiographical traditions have shown, can therefore rely on its protagonists’ private diaries and letters, the correspondence and journalistic reports, and also on thousands of miles of magnetic tape (the Belgian company Philips installed a modern recording system in the conciliar chamber, under the direction of Vatican Radio), and film. These recordings were mainly kept in the Vatican Apostolic Archives and in the audiovisual archives of the various television networks, including, in particular, the Italian ones (Teche RAI and Luce Institute), which played an international important role and had connections and exclusive rights with the Holy See.

### 3. Media, Public Opinion, and Vatican II

Vatican II was thus the first council in the history of the Church to take place in front of the cameras as well [^c06-17] **[p. 94]** as radio microphones, in the century that was defined as the Media Age. For the first time, the whole world was able to follow live the work of the conciliar assembly and be informed of it at the very moment at which the event was taking place. As well as a great ecclesial, political, and socio-cultural event in history, [^c06-18] Vatican II was also a great twentieth-century media event.

[^c06-17]: Mario Morcellini, ed., _Il mediaevo: TV e industria culturale nell’Italia del XX secolo_ (Rome: Carocci, 2000); Peter C. Rollins, Gary R. Edgerton, eds., _Television Histories: Shaping Collective Memory in the Media Age_ (Lexington: The University Press of Kentucky, 2001)

[^c06-18]: Daniel Dayan, Elihu Katz, _Media Events. The Live Broadcasting of History_ (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1994).

The world’s public opinion was therefore able to form a conciliar consciousness at a level that would have been unthinkable, for example, for Vatican I. The debates that a more detailed knowledge of the conciliar issues generated outside the Vatican walls, starting during the years of preparation for Vatican II, deeply affected the dynamics and strength of the assembly. It is no coincidence, therefore, that ‘spectators’ became ‘influential’ thanks to the different role played by magazines, newspapers, and audiovisual media in [^c06-19] general. The hopes and expectations that the conciliar debate brought to the fore and that emerged autonomously within the composite ecclesial body, therefore, from the activities of the curial offices, were precisely what helped to overturn consolidated practices during the council. They lifted the veil on a Roman minority that was ultimately surprised to see itself as such, allowing John XXIII’s council to take its first important steps forward and without restraints.

[^c06-19]: Alberto Melloni, ‘Lo spettatore influente: Riviste e informazione religiosa nella preparazione del Vaticano II (1959–1962)’, in _Il Vaticano II fra attese e celebrazione_, ed. Giuseppe Alberigo (Bologna: Il Mulino, 1995), 119–92.

The media, as mouthpiece and major protagonist, were certainly not alone, but they played a role—to different degrees—that cannot be overlooked. Books, public lectures, magazines, and periodicals fuelled a historical-theological debate among scholars and produced a degree of awareness among Christians which later provided the basis for the perspectives of the conciliar years: ‘theologians, Christians, [and] institutionally marginalized, in that four-year period, took an active part in the preparation itself with all [^c06-20] the weight of their expectations, at various levels’. Newspapers and radio and television networks, while remaining in the background at least in the preparatory phase and keeping an apparently mainstream approach, offered a more indefinite conciliar image compared to specialist magazines. They acted as conveyors of information that would inform public opinion while also interpreting the mood. Moreover, at certain moments they became the lens providing a focal point on the debates, currents, and decisions.

[^c06-20]: Ibid., 121.

This is not a novelty of Vatican II. Public opinion, even before being theorized as such, had always played a [^c06-21] non-secondary role and one of ‘mutual fertilization’ with the synodal moments of the Church, despite the [^c06-22] **[p. 95]** marginality of the direct participation of the Christian people in such events. The epigraphs and epistles reveal this internal–external exchange process. The advent of the press, on the one hand, gave to the diffusion of the conciliar texts and minutes such an impulse that the great historiographic season on the councils was opened (this culminated in _Saepenumero Considerantes_ of 1881, with which Leo XIII opened the doors of the Vatican Archives). On the other hand, it made it more possible to influence and become part of the council itself. As the Italian journalist and Vaticanist Ettore Masina recalled in his introduction to the conciliar newspaper of a French colleague, Henri Fesquet:

[^c06-21]: Marie-Dominique Chenu, ‘Vox populi vox Dei’, _Idoc-Documenti nuovi_ 7 (1968): 209–26.

[^c06-22]: Giuseppe Alberigo, ‘Concili’, in _Dizionario del sapere storico-religioso del Novecento_, ed. Alberto Melloni (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2010), 540.

It is with Vatican I … that a new protagonist—journalism—enters the history of the great assemblies of the Catholic hierarchy. No longer just the Holy Spirit, the pope, the bishops and their _periti_ [experts], often battling furiously with each other; or the pious or unscrupulous chroniclers writing down, for a select few, events and doctrines; or the secular powers directing their emissaries and pawns in purple or violet for highly mundane purposes; or Rome’s sneering mob; or the parish priests from all over the world interpreting the decrees on the basis of their faith or their own interests. If the Council of Trent ended with the first timid attempts to create a newspaper, Vatican I opened at a time when the press was already a major power player; and with the press, public opinion entered the conciliar room.[^c06-23]

[^c06-23]: Ettore Masina, ‘Nota del curatore’, in Henri Fesquet, _Diario del Concilio: Tutto il Concilio giorno per giorno_, ed. Ettore Massina (Milan: Mursia, 1967), xv–xvii, at xv.

The media of the twentieth century opened an additional new season in the history of conciliar reception and, therefore, in the history of the councils.

### 4. The Media at Vatican II: The Creation of the Press Office

When on 5 October 1962, at noon, the new headquarters of the council’s Press Office was inaugurated, in via Serristori 12 in Rome, it was evident to all that the Holy See had realized that it was no longer practicable in [^c06-24] the 1960s to manage information based on the consolidated practices of the past. In the century of the media, it was impossible, in fact, to think of sharing news on the council in dribs and drabs, or to limit it exclusively to publication in _L’Osservatore Romano_ or the news on Vatican Radio. It was not as if the press or, more generally, the secular media did not exist; indeed, Pope John XXIII and the media had established a [^c06-25] **[p. 96]** special relationship since the first days of his pontificate. The council of Pius IX had contributed to establishing the extent and limits of censorship and ecclesiastical secrecy, with unexpected results. In the mid-nineteenth century, despite the fact that the press had an international circulation, the lack of a centre for the management and dissemination of information by the Holy See led journalists interested in the council to go in search of news, ‘drawing too often on sources poisoned by partisan interests’, as journalist [^c06-26] Ettore Masina pointed out. The controversies or exposés published in their articles could not be thwarted by Fr D’Alzon, the founder of the Augustinians of the Assumption, who sent 400 letters, conceived as dispatches and newsletters on the council, to various countries. By doing so, he revealed even more the limits of this initiative. Louis Veuillot, a well-known exponent of the Ultramontanist movement and correspondent of _L’Univers_, commented harshly enough in his diary of Vatican I on the attitude of ‘those foreigners who are hunting here’, concluding, ‘I am referring to all those who know nothing or talk [^c06-27] nonsense’. This secrecy mentality can be discerned in the discussion on papal infallibility in the pages of the diary of Fr Dehon, founder of the religious congregation Priests of the Sacred Heart of Jesus (Dehonians), which specialized in media and publications: ‘the Holy Father prohibited the publication in Rome of articles on controversies relating to the council. Thank heavens! Otherwise we would have had [^c06-28] another council in the newspapers, along with the one in St Peter’s.’

[^c06-24]: Giancarlo Zizola, ‘La nascita dell’Ufficio stampa della S. Sede: Appunti e testimonianze per una storia; 1953–2003’, _Cristianesimo nella storia_ 25 (2004): 997–1013.

[^c06-25]: Federico Ruozzi, ‘L’icona Giovanni XXIII’, in _L’ora che il mondo sta attraversando: Giovanni XXIII di fronte alla storia_, ed. Giovanni Grado Merlo and Francesco Mores (Rome: Storia e Letteratura, 2009), 47–103.

[^c06-26]: Masina, ‘Nota del curatore’, xiv.

[^c06-27]: Louis-François Veuillot, _Œuvres complètes_, vol. 12, _Rome pendant le concile_ (Paris: Lethielleux, 1927).

[^c06-28]: Léon Dehon, _Diario del Concilio Vaticano I_ (Vatican City: Tipografia Poliglotta Vaticana, 1962), 80.

This is not to say, however, that there were no attempts to politicize the news at Vatican II or to go for sensationalism. However, to avoid simply leaving the council in the hands of the media, which were interested in the event due to its newsworthiness, it seemed natural to satisfy that need for information and think about how to allow and help the press to follow first the preparatory phases of the council and then its development. This led to the establishment of a press office that was able to manage—and control—the flow of news and the relationship with the media. Secretary of State Cardinal Domenico Tardini announced it during what is remembered as the first press conference in the history of the Holy See, on 30 October 1959. Welcomed with hope, after a few public announcements, it began operating on 18 April 1961 as the Press Office of the Central Preparatory Commission, when Msgr. Felici, secretary of the Preparatory Commission, announced to journalists the opening of the office in via Serristori. In October 1962 it became the Council Press Office, led by the Italian Msgr. Fausto Vallainc, who was supported by the coordinators of the seven language sections: German, North American, French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, and Polish. Today it is known as the Holy See Press Office.

### 5. The World of Journalism, the News, and Communications

**[p. 97]** Vatican II thus opened in the presence of more than 1,200 journalists accredited to the Holy See from all five continents. The radio and television services of the Italian public broadcasting company RAI were used; these were broadcast by sixty-six international organizations. The flow of news and coverage of the event that public opinion expected—according to the most classical logic of media events as researched by Daniel Dayan and Elihu Katz—was therefore remarkable. The Dutch Catholic radio network, KRO (Katholieke Radio Omroepverenéging), arrived at the council with an impressive organization. It was coordinated by the Roman correspondent, Jan Dykgraaf, who, thanks to the work of numerous technicians, a radio link, and a direct air service, managed to get constant audio and video updates on the conciliar events. The Canadian French radio network (Radio-Canada) featured a daily broadcast dedicated to the council. The commitment to information of these two countries guaranteed, as of September 1963, a representative for each of them [^c06-29] on the council’s press committee. The press and radio and television companies then collaborated directly and frequently with the Council Documentation Centre in Rome (IDOC).

[^c06-29]: Jan Grootaers, ‘Ebb and Flow between Two Seasons’, in Alberigo and Komonchak, _History of Vatican II_, 2:546–47.

The denominational and specialized periodicals were not the only ones that began to offer significant coverage of the event, thus providing a lively theological reflection that contributed to the maturity of the topics on the council’s agenda while increasing their own circulation. Also worth mentioning, in addition to _La Croix_, which could boast at the start of the council approximately 67,000 subscribers, with an increase of more than 60 per cent, are _Irenikon_, _Informations catholiques internationales_, _The Ecumenist_, _The Ecumenical Catholic Quarterly_, and _Oecumene_. New periodicals that were launched, created specifically for this purpose, included the Catalan _Concil Aviu_ and the Dutch _Vaticanum Secundum_. Moreover, the most notable international newspapers decided to send their correspondents. Those who made this choice included Germany’s _Frankfurter Allgemeine_ and _Die Zeit_; the British _The Times_; the Dutch _Nieue Rotterdamse Courant_; Italy’s _Corriere della Sera_ and _L’Espresso_; the US _Newsweek_, _The New Yorker_, with writer Xavier Rynne (a pseudonym of the American Redemptorist priest Francis X. Murphy), and _Time_, with articles signed by Robert G. Kaiser; and from France, _Le Figaro_, with articles by René Laurentin, and _Le Monde_, featuring those by Henri Fesquet. In particular, articles written by Fesquet, according to the Spanish chronicler José Luis Martín Descalzo, ‘were undoubtedly the most sought after in Roman newspaper stands; they went from [^c06-30] **[p. 98]** hand to hand not only in the press room, but in the council hall’. The major expenses that the regular presence of a correspondent entailed were considered necessary to have direct coverage of the event.

[^c06-30]: Hilari Raguer, ‘An Initial Profile of the Assembly’, in Alberigo and Komonchak, _History of Vatican II_, 2:230.

In addition to Robert Kaiser, René Laurentin, and Xavier Rynne (Francis X. Murphy), the following correspondents should also be remembered: Antoine Wenger, José Luis Martín Descalzo, Raniero La Valle, Manfred Plate, Robert Rouquette, Michael Novak, David Andreas Seeber, Mario von Galli, and Jan Grootaers, along with Giovanni Caprile’s precise and detailed reports for _La Civiltà Cattolica_. These articles are even more important because of the ‘informal’ imprimatur of the Secretariat of State; their articles were immediately collected in volumes, with the dual purpose of informing and mobilizing public opinion starting in 1963. The articles were also able to convey the dynamism that characterized that particular conciliar climate.[^c06-31]

[^c06-31]: ‘The kind and generous reception of our two articles on the Council in _The New Yorker_ has prompted us to complete the story in depth. … The book is an attempt to give the reader a meaningful account of the proceedings during the eight weeks of the first session of Vatican Council II, with enough background material to enable him to understand what the debates and discussion were all about.’ X. Rynne, _Letters from Vatican City: Vatican Council II—First Session: Background_ _and Debates_ (London: Faber and Faber, 1963), xi, xiii; Melloni, ‘Lo spettatore influente: Riviste e informazione religiosa nella preparazione del Vaticano II (1959–1962)’; Jean Vavasseur-Desperriers, ‘L’Image de Vatican II à travers la chronique de l’abbé Laurentin’, in _Le Deuxième Concile du Vatican (1959–1965)_, edited by Philippe Levillain (Rome: École française de Rome, 1989), 379–403.

The non-religious press was therefore in the front row and at times more prepared and motivated than the religious one, which was much more submissive and respectful, at least at the beginning, of the need for confidentiality. The Church was making the news. Lercaro, in his preface to the edition of Raniero La Valle’s conciliar chronicles (La Valle was editor-in-chief of _Avvenire d’Italia_, the newspaper that was distributed to all the bishops during the conciliar years), wrote that the Church owed something to the press ‘for opening channels of communication and contact between the reality of the council and that of Christians and ordinary people … For some time now no Italian newspaper, not even a Catholic one, has provided any [^c06-32] significant coverage of a strictly religious topic.’ It was also a type of chronicle that would eventually become history, offering a precious source of information. Even in the analysis of the French chronicles by Yves Poncelet, it becomes clear how the historicization of the council was also based on these chronicles:

[^c06-32]: Giacomo Lercaro, ‘Introduzione’, in Raniero La Valle, _Il Concilio nelle nostre mani_ (Brescia: Morcelliana, 1996), ix–xi, at x.

It made use of their rich factual contribution and looked for elements of an initial analysis of the process for developing documents and of the phenomenology of the work of the council fathers. It has sometimes included their writings as archival material of a reflection on religious information and on the expression of opinions and impressions.[^c06-33]

[^c06-33]: Yves Poncelet, ‘Les Grands Chroniqueurs français du Concile’, in _La France et le Concile Vatican II_, ed. Bernard Barbiche et Christian Sorrel (Brussels: Peter Lang, 2013), 77. Translations from this source are my own.

**[p. 99]** The reporter Descalzo tried to jot down his first impressions on the attitude of the world press in the first conciliar period (1962), identifying some specific traits of national journalism. In his opinion, indiscretion characterized, for example, the French press; sensationalism was to be found in weekly publications; politicization in the Italian press (where the “Vaticanist” played a major role); mediocrity in the Spanish press; and so on. Such categorizations risk, as always, distorting experiences, publications, writers, and reflections that cannot be compared. It is therefore appropriate to refer to specific studies that have come [^c06-34] out over the years. Here, however, it is important to highlight ‘the opening up to religious information [^c06-35] that Vatican II represented for the Church’ and how, within this context, we need to distinguish not only between the contributions of the different media, but also between periods and specific moments.

[^c06-34]: For analyses of the Belgian, Chilean, German, British and Irish, Italian, Polish, Spanish, Swiss, Soviet, and American press, see _Paolo VI e I problemi ecclesiologici al concilio_ (Brescia: Istituto Paolo VI-Studium, 1989).

[^c06-35]: René Laurentin, ‘L’Information au Concile’, in Levillain, _Le Deuxième Concile du Vatican (1959–1965)_, 359–78, at 360.

After the initial enthusiasm and a great deployment of forces wanted by the Pope, it was clear from the early weeks of October 1962 that proclamations or good intentions were not enough to undermine the mechanisms of the Roman Curia’ secular mentality of distrust and aversion to the media. Despite the Press Office, the reports that were disseminated through the official bulletins at first were inadequate abridgements. The news reports on the morning discussions in the general congregations, or on the afternoon work of the commissions, which allowed journalists to understand and therefore to inform their readers, were few and vague. Although the attitude of secrecy and hegemony of the Holy Office had been finally abandoned only a few years earlier, at least in intention, the scarce information on what the council machine was up to was a limit felt, to different degrees, by all the media. In the aftermath of the council, the key word on information remained ‘confidentiality’.

Behind this impenetrable but strategic reserve were far more relevant ecclesiological motives, as Yves Congar noted: ‘but secrecy is also a means of isolating people and neutralizing all opposition. It reduces us, in effect, to the status of men who have direct contact only with Rome, but not with one another; it [^c06-36] amounts, in practice, to destroying horizontal Catholicity for the sole benefit of the vertical one.’ This situation prompted several representatives of the documentation centres, religious informants, journalists, and experts (such as Raniero La Valle and Fr Roberto Tucci) to be promoters of various initiatives, not always coordinated, to ask for more insight. For example, they would ask for more information on the texts in progress, the interventions in the general congregations, discussions and other conciliar activities, and the profiles of the bishops who intervened.

[^c06-36]: Yves Congar, _My Journal of the Council_, trans. Mary John Ronayne, OP and Mary Cecily Boulding, OP (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2012), 16.

### 6. 1963 and the Revival of Information

**[p. 100]** Once the first conciliar session ended, the intersession of 1963 appeared to be a real ‘second preparation’ amid uncertainties and confusion: a laboratory of sorts where bishops and the _periti_ attempted to reclaim the threads of autonomy and freedom gained in the last months of 1962, which translated into a desire to revise the schemas of the preparatory period.

Information—within the context of the ebbs and flows described by Grootaers—was also the topic of discussion. It was understood by many that the success of the council also depended on a correct and complete ability on the part of the media to follow and understand what was happening: ‘if our contemporaries have not been suitably informed about the Council, it will not be possible for them to live [^c06-37] the Council later on’, wrote Francis Mayor. The Bologna group that gravitated around Cardinal Lercaro, his _peritus_ Giuseppe Dossetti, and the ‘Documentation Centre’, which would play an important role in the historicization of the council, knew this well. Hence, they were able to convince Italian public television to air a series of television programmes on the history of the councils for a mainstream audience in the early [^c06-38] evening hours beginning in September 1962.

[^c06-37]: Grootaers, ‘Ebb and Flow between Two Seasons’, 550.

[^c06-38]: Federico Ruozzi, ‘La chiesa a concilio: Uomini e problemi; L’officina bolognese e la Rai-Tv (novembre–dicembre 1962)’, _Cristianesimo nella storia_ 34 (2013): 611–670.

In those first few months, the media euphoria had more to do with particular enthusiasms, like the one shown by the Catholic newspaper _La Croix_. At the end of October 1962, _La Croix_ began to mention the names of the bishops who intervened in the general congregations; having received no special prohibitions or [^c06-39] sanctions, ‘the editor felt justifled in continuing the practice’, a correspondent observed. Starting with the first intersession, an attempt was made to reorganize and coordinate the various initiatives to avoid unnecessary competition and useless overlaps and, above all, to try to force the Vatican’s hand to increase the flow of information conveyed by the Press Office.

[^c06-39]: Concerning _La Croix_, Descalzo commented: ‘If I had to give a personal judgment on the facts and the fruits, I would fully absolve “La Croix” from this “sin”, immensely useful for the bishops and informers in the months spent in Rome, and of decisive utility for all those who today write the history of the first conciliar period.’ Francis X. Murphy, ‘Secrecy at the Council’, _America_ (27 July 1963).

At a meeting held on 2–3 February 1963 in Geneva, chaired by Fr Tucci, director of _La Civiltà Cattolica_ and with the participation of representatives of 46 different religious information organisations (press, radio, television), and then in March and May in Rome, relations with the press were on the agenda, to devise better cooperation for future work. One of the most visible outcomes of these consultations was the establishment of the Centrum Coordinationis Communicationum de Concilio, designed to coordinate and strengthen the existing centres, a real innovation of Vatican II. Among the identifled tasks that the Centrum **[p. 101]** was expected to have were those of ensuring rapid translation services of press bulletins, reports and documents, of helping all Centres, especially the less well-equipped ones, to organize conferences and meetings in a common central hall, of providing all the information services to Africa and Asia, which did not have such facilities. In conciliar Rome, there were eight autonomous national media centres, supported by their respective episcopates, which liaised with the Press Office and journalists: the American, Canadian, Brazilian, Italian, German, Spanish, French, and Dutch centres. Together with the press, the television networks, and secular radio, the flow of information created by these centres had as a first clear result the breaking of the Vatican’s hold on information. Until then, that hold had been rather rigid and controlled, with any news coming from outside the designated traditional channels being dismissed as false. It was a monopoly that, in the mid-twentieth century, was impossible to sustain. Those years saw the coexistence of new demands, which were also the result of the openings triggered by John XXIII’s pontificate and legacies of the past leading to tensions and revealing contradictions. These contradictions included the coexistence of article 26 of the _Ordo Concilii_, which imposed the obligation of secrecy on the council fathers (‘The Fathers are bound to keep secrecy concerning the discussions which take place at the Council and the declarations of each Father’), and the decision to open a press office. Journalists lived those obvious contradictions first hand, with repercussions on their work and therefore on their effectiveness in describing what was happening.

As mentioned earlier, the dizzying enthusiasm of the first months made it possible to avoid various difficulties, yet they persisted and needed to be addressed: ‘the reorganization of the general policy regarding news during the second period of the Council supposed one other step. The official press office had to be freed from its feudal connection with the Secretary General of the Council, and news about the [^c06-40] Council had to be placed under the authority of representatives of the assembly itself.’ For this reason, Grootaers has talked about a boomerang effect, because ‘the rule of secrecy and silence contributed to an [^c06-41] explosion of unrestricted news’. As described in a subtitle of an article published in 1963 in _America_, the magazine of the US Jesuits, and signed by correspondent Fr Francis X. Murphy, ‘The Council’s dilemma: [^c06-42] when everything is a secret, nothing is kept a secret.’ In the past, the secret, Murphy explained, ‘has frequently been used to intimidate individuals and destroy careers and reputations in both civil and ecclesiastical societies. This kind of thing is no longer tolerable. The reportage of Vatican Council II thus far [^c06-43] proves that such secrecy is both useless and unnecessary’.

[^c06-40]: Grootaers, ‘Ebb and Flow between Two Seasons’, 553.

[^c06-41]: Ibid., 552.

[^c06-42]: Murphy, ‘Secrecy at the Council’, 98.

[^c06-43]: Ibid., 97.

If, at the beginning, the majority was the one that benefited from a freer and more open relationship with **[p. 102]** the media, the minority, traditionally more devoted to secrecy in relation to public opinion, experimented at its own expense with what a press blackout could mean in the century of the media. As for the second session, it began to use, even deceptively, the unprecedented relationship established with the world of journalism, especially through pamphlets handed out among the assembly. Thus, in the years of the council, a very close relationship was established between the conciliar assembly and the media and, through it, public opinion. That same public opinion, however, assumed an unprecedented importance and influence on the council itself, taking on old roles that were part of a long tradition. As Cardinal König wrote: ‘instead of kings and princes, today we have public opinion; the role of messengers and ambassadors is now played by journalists. The news that spreads around the world in a few seconds replaces the old secret [^c06-44] messages.’

[^c06-44]: Franz König, ‘Stampa: libertà e responsabilità’, in _Laici sulle vie del Concilio_ (Assisi: Cittadella, 1967), 255.

The degree of freedom of the discussions that was perceived outside Vatican walls was possible thanks to the media, which helped to uncover what was happening at the event. There was a real freedom of opinion within the Church, which had always been seen as monolithic. Open and free information showed the public the real level of confrontation, which at times was harsh, among the council fathers. More importantly, it showed the existence of different positions as well as the vitality of discussions that distinguished the ecclesial body, which the religious or Vatican press tended mostly to anaesthetize. George Lindbeck of the Lutheran World Federation wrote from the pages of _Istina_: ‘Catholic Christians, whether Roman or not, had to acknowledge, thanks to these criticisms made public for the first time, that there was a wider dynamism [^c06-45] and greater reforming zeal within the Church of Rome than they had thought.’ Among the factors that contributed to this dynamism were no doubt the press conferences—one of the novelties that most distinguished the formal or informal afternoon conciliar activities.

[^c06-45]: George Lindbeck, ‘Helsinki, Rome et Montréal: Impressions sur l’Église en concile’, _Istina_ 9 (1963), 487.

### 7. Press Conferences and Interviews: A Church that Speaks

During the years of preparation and the first session, public interest was high. The various international circuits, as mentioned earlier, lacked first-hand information and had to make do with the meagre official press releases published later in _L’Osservatore Romano_. However, these international groups managed to **[p. 103]** find channels to obtain information, in more or less informal ways, which became more official as of the second session. On the other hand, Fesquet himself, in an issue of _Témoignage chrétien_, commented, not without irony: ‘With time, perseverance, a little luck and physical stamina, anyone could have found out what transpired behind the Vatican walls.’ Voting results were sought after to understand the general orientation of the assembly on certain topics on the agenda, along with reports of the work by the council fathers or the most talkative _periti_. But, above all, the afternoon press conferences were well attended. For the first time, the press agencies specialized in religious matters and began to spread what would be considered the real novelty of Vatican II, a tangible sign of a Church that was opening up, speaking without the mediation of spokespersons, and discussing without fear: the press conferences and, as a corollary, the interviews. They were held mostly in the afternoons with the council fathers or _periti_ most directly involved in the work and discussions, after the General Congregations in the morning.

Press conferences and interviews thus became an important tool for journalists, offering direct testimonials on which to draw heavily. In fact, many of the bishops who arrived in Rome were not shy of being filmed or interviewed. They appeared in front of television cameras which, for the first time, took notice of the heterogeneity of the ecclesial body on which they decided to focus the spotlight, giving them space and, above all, a voice. In some cases, the bishops spoke even more freely than what was put in writing in journals and newspapers. This created the media rebound effect: newspapers kept an eye on what journals reported, which in turn cited from spontaneously generated debates, which in turn were based on press conferences of some prelates who had attended or whose audio or video recording had been recovered. Some of these press conferences were not only recorded in audio and video formats, but also incorporated in the conciliar documents. As the _Avvenire d’Italia_ itself remarked during the first session, ‘one of the characteristics of the first session of the conciliar works, and only apparently unrelated to them, was precisely that of the press conferences’. The interventions of the fathers during the general congregations in the first session remained completely confidential. The press releases were ‘parsimonious’ when expressing real opinions: ‘however, there were some who offered more than just a glimpse on the actual substance of the “things with which the council is concerned”; and these were just a few, better yet, numerous council fathers’ and ‘the means they used were the press conferences’.[^c06-46]

[^c06-46]: ‘Le conferenze stampa’, _Avvenire d’Italia_ (17 November 1962).

The news agencies were coordinated to facilitate the collection and dissemination of information. For example, in via Silvieri 30, the RICI (Romanae Informationes Catholicae Internationalis), formed by Kathpress (Austria), KNA (Germany), and KIPA (Switzerland), was later joined by KNP (Holland) and CIP (Belgium). The documentation and information centres of the episcopates or religious congregations **[p. 104]** organized themselves to follow the conciliar works: the Documentation Centre of the Catholic Church of the Netherlands; the Information Center of the Canadian bishops; the Brazilian centre; the Spanish centre; the French centre; the American bishops’ centre; the German centre; the Italian centre; the Pan-African centre; the Information Centre of the Oblates of Mary Immaculate; the centre of the White Fathers; or that of the Society of the Divine Word. At the end of the second period, the results obtained by the Centrum Coordinationis Communicationum de Concilio were substantially positive: active translation service, 770 different documents distributed, plus the Press Office’s daily bulletin, contacts with RAI-TV for radio and television recordings, as well as own broadcasts, generally for Africa and Latin America, more than 40 conferences organised by 8 affiliated centres, over 60 newspapers in 5 languages available to the people attending the C.C.C.

The afternoon activities of the council fathers who were speaking, especially the theologians, became so intense that on 15 September 1964, a list was distributed with some rules the _periti_ had to follow, which Paul VI himself had communicated to the Coordinating Commission at the end of December 1963. The rules recommended ‘objectivity’ and above all ‘prudence’ in speaking of the council, as well as abstaining from criticism of the debate; they also went on to prohibit the formation of currents of opinion, the public defence of personal ideas, and giving interviews. It all sounded like a formal rebuke to the intense _extra aulam_ activity of the group of _periti_; failure to respect the rules could lead to the loss of one’s title. The directives evidently sought to sanction a practice which was frequent but still poorly tolerated in certain circles.

The vanguard of theological, biblical, liturgical, and ecumenical reflection, the representatives of the episcopates, and the voices of observers, through interviews or press conferences, found unprecedented openings and an audience eager to listen. Radio and television networks and the press gave a voice and a face to names which, as the weeks passed, became increasingly recognizable, above all to the lethargic Italian Catholics, who were used to identifying the Church with the image of the pope only. For example, various figures made their appearance on television screens: transalpine theologians who had been condemned a few years earlier under Pius XII; the bishops of local churches (from Africa to Asia); and non- Catholic observers and representatives of other churches. Some became real media stars. Cardinal Augustin Bea, in the preparatory period, was relentlessly sought after by international radio and television to get the latest on his secretariat. The same can be said of cardinals like Leo Jozef Suenens and Julius Döpfner; theologians like Yves Congar and Hans Küng; and observers and guests like Oscar Cullmann and Roger Schutz.

In particular, Italian television, for the exclusive relationship with the Holy See, became a real instrument of the conciliar majority. This intense activity can be observed from the private diaries and memoirs of council fathers and _periti_, who would keep track every week of their numerous appointments with the staff of radio stations, newspapers, and international television networks.

### 8. Diaries, Written Records, Televised Broadcasts, and Other

### Communications

**[p. 105]** Memoirs and diaries enrich historical research on the councils of the modern age. They provide scholars with the opportunity to look at the event and its dynamics from within, creating a perspective on the events [^c06-47] that is different from sources such as conciliar acts. This was not new to Vatican II, as previously mentioned; see, for example, the diaries of Cardinal Guillaume Fillâtre for the Council of Constance, or of Andrea Gatari for the Council of Basel; the _diaria privata_ used by the publisher of the _Concilium Florentinum_ or the prolegomena of Sebastian Merkle, who consecrated the importance of the genre (even if in an apologetic perspective against the enemies of the Roman Curia). Disregarded both by the editions of the documents of Vatican I and the _Acta_ of Vatican II, they were rediscovered, edited, and studied a few decades later the end of the Vatican II itself. They became essential sources for the historicization of the council, starting in the 1990s. Aside from the ‘flourishes’ they provide on the conciliar events or the curiosities they [^c06-48] bring to light, they help to make ‘the real history of Vatican II’. Moreover, they unveil its complexity, helping people to understand the formation of an _opinio communis_, going beyond the well-known and established paths and revealing what is not always in plain sight: ‘scholars may now understand the [^c06-49] complexity of the factors playing in the Council’s decision-making process’. In 1996, Alberto Melloni noted that the diaries for the study of Vatican II were still ‘a little-known source’. The reason for this, he pointed out, was the type of research conducted up to then, which was more focused on doctrinal analysis and on the ‘objective’ principle adopted by the _Acta_. For decades, these were considered the most complete and reliable sources for the publication both of a large number of memoirs and of the journalistic correspondence that had appeared during the conciliar period. This had the effect of exhausting the more **[p. 106]** general interest in the genre and, above all, overwhelming further documentary findings. From the mid- 1990s, thanks to the international work set in motion by the _History of Vatican II_, edited by Giuseppe Alberigo, a further series of diaristic sources and memoirs emerged ‘without which full commentaries could [^c06-50] be written, but not the real history of Vatican II’. This opened a new phase in the history of the editions of the conciliar sources and their interpretation.

[^c06-47]: Joseph Famerée, ‘Uso comparativo dei diari: Una settimana di lavori conciliari (5–15 novembre 1963)’, in _L’evento e le_ _decisioni: Studi sulle dinamiche del concilio Vaticano II_, eds. Maria Teresa Fattori and Alberto Melloni (Bologna: Il Mulino, 1997), 321–54.

[^c06-48]: Melloni, ‘Introduction’, in Marie-Dominique Chenu, _Vatican II Notebook,_ ed. A. Melloni, trans. Paul Philibert (Adelaide: ATF, 2015), 1–56, at 7; Joseph Famerée, ‘Instruments et perspectives pour une histoire du Concile Vatican II: La “Carte” des sources privée (mise à jour)’, in _À la veille du concile Vatican II_, ed. Mathijs Lamberigts and Claude Soetens (Leuven: Bibliotheek van de Facuteit der Godgeleerdheid, 1992), 258–68; Nicolas Egenter, ‘Note sur les cinquante ans de Vatican II, pt. I’, _Irénikon_ 83 (2010), 41–91; M. Lamberigts, ‘The Importance of Diaries for the Study of Vatican II’, in _The Council Notes of_ _Edward Schillebeeckx 1962–1963_, ed. Karim Schelkens (Leuven: Peeters, 2011), ix–xiii.

[^c06-49]: Leo Kenis, ‘Private Sources for Study of the Second Vatican Council’, in _The Belgian Contribution to the Second Vatican_ _Council_, ed. D. Donnelly et al. (Leuven: Peeters, 2008), 31.

[^c06-50]: Melloni, ‘Introduction’, 7.

Even within the same literary genre, the types of diaries vary considerably. They represent a litmus test of the polyphony of voices that played a role at Vatican II. The same can be said of the writing styles, the goals [^c06-51] they pursued, or the underlying intentions. Memoirs of journalists should also be included, as mentioned earlier, as well as those of non-Catholic observers and those of the diplomats (above all, the one by the Italian ambassador to the Holy See, Bartolomeo Migone), personal diaries, starting with Pope John XXIII’s _Journal of the Soul_ and his other ‘agendas’, and those of bishops and cardinals, and diaries by those who began to have a role in the preparatory phase as well as those commenting on the conciliar event, each with their own purposes and level of maturity. There are also diaries _pro memoria sua_, of a more personal nature, [^c06-52] and diaries of the conciliar leaders. Finally, we have the diaries of theologians (from the fundamental _My Journal_ of Yves Congar to those of Henri de Lubac and Marie-Dominique Chenu, for instance) and the laity, including those of auditors, freelance journalists, and other individuals who were directly or indirectly involved.

[^c06-51]: Kenis, ‘Private Sources for Study of the Second Vatican Council’.

[^c06-52]: Melloni, ‘Introduction’, 14.

At Vatican II, however, in addition to individual written diaries, a new kind of record was inaugurated thanks to television, which made it immediately available to the general public: the collective diary. From 1962 to 1965, Italian television, through a series of programmes it produced, offered its viewers a wealth of interviews and analyses that cannot be underestimated. The council fathers, theologians, experts, observers, auditors, scholars, and journalists took turns in front of the cameras. This body of television programming can be compared to diary and memoir sources, such as the personal diaries the council fathers kept during their stay in Rome.

The televised source, like the diaries and memoirs of the conciliar events, provided readers and observers with an interpretative key to understand what was happening. Above all, it conveyed the idea of a Church that was asking questions about the problems of the modern world without formulas or ready-made answers. To scholars today, this same source offers a story that colours those moments and gives them a particular shape while softening their rigidity. And like the private diaries of Vatican II, it provided something more than just a simple assertive role, as had been the case for the Council of Trent. Like all other sources with their partial, subjective, partisan, narrow, or wide-ranging vision, and at the mercy of the narrating ‘I’—here plural rather than singular—it contributes to the history of the council. But it is **[p. 107]** characterized by a significant difference from other sources: if private papers give us the point of view of the individual—priest, expert, observer, layperson—the television diary is instead a public and choral diary of the council or an unredacted and useful memoir of the entire assembly, broadly understood as a commentary in progress. However, it is also a _pro memoria sua_ diary, a diary of the council leaders, of theologians, of laypeople, of journalists and observers. The polyphony of the voices interviewed allows the researcher to grasp the overall dimensions of the council as well as the atmosphere of that experience of communion and to receive an assessment of the formation of an _opinio communis_. Moreover, in this collective diary we find silences, mediations, and contradictions, in addition to the intrinsic logics of television (the time factor, the compression, the simplification, the synthesis, the programming) and those of the same audiovisual image with its signs and procedures (framing, editing, intervals, direction). All this, however, cannot and must not lead us to underestimate the wealth of knowledge that this source offers.

### 9. Ad Intra and Ad Extra: Television’s Role and Effects

Television interviews with the protagonists of the council allows to introduce the role played by television more generally. If television played a role of primary importance, Italian TV had a particular one: the historical, privileged relationship between RAI-TV (the Italian public radio and television broadcasting system, owned by the Italian State) and the Holy See. RAI, the only network to hold rights to the pope’s image since its establishment in January 1954, received the exclusive right to broadcast from the Vatican, having already tested its ability to transmit great events with the 1960 Rome Olympics. The network was headed by Ettore Bernabei, a long-time Catholic who was very close to the prime minister, the Christian Democrat Amintore Fanfani. At that early stage, Italian public television was led by people who were ideologically and culturally close to Giuseppe Dossetti and the cardinal of Bologna, Giacomo Lercaro. The Italian ambassador to the Holy See (1969–77), Gianfranco Pompei, referred to Bernabei in his personal diary as ‘the cardinal’ for his strong ties with Italian political and ecclesial circles. Bernabei had in fact decided to support the Centre Left’s political project and John XXIII’s _aggiornamento_ for the Catholic Church. In addition to the live coverage of the ceremonies broadcast on Eurovision, RAI produced a wealth of television and radio shows: documentaries and programmes for children about the council; interviews and weekly segments (_Il diario del concilio_, hosted by Luca Di Schiena on the Programma Nazionale from 8.05 to 8.20 p.m.); programmes of historical-religious in-depth analysis (with the series _Chi è il vescovo?_); programmes on the history of the councils (with the series _1962 anno del concilio_ and _La chiesa a concilio_: **[p. 108]** _Uomini e problemi_ on the second channel). It was a group of young Bolognese professors (Giuseppe Alberigo, Paolo Prodi, and Boris Ulianich), who in those years were studying the history of the councils under the guidance of Dossetti, who agreed to take care of a series of television programmes trying to explain the importance that these synodal moments had for the life of the Church, providing viewers with some coordinates by which to navigate the not always simple discussions in Latin of the conciliar fathers.

#### Television: A Window on the Event

From 1962 to 1965, the Italian television was a ‘window’ on that great council meeting, to use a typical promise of news programmes, as underlined by the historians of television.

Live broadcasts of the Vatican II ceremonies were shown on the Eurovision network to many public television in other countries. In addition to a simple chronicle of the event, television showed the universality of the Catholic Church for the society of the 1960s, in particular in Italy, which tended to identify the Church with the pope, who had a monopoly on TV screens. Direct from their living rooms, on black-and-white TV, viewers were able to follow the long opening ceremony of 11 October, with the procession of African, Latin American, and Chinese and other Asian bishops, with their different skullcaps and vestments. Those watching were able to see the diversity of the traditions within Catholicism and listen live to John XXIII’s impromptu speech, the famous ‘Moonlight Speech’ on the first evening of the council. But there was more. Television also helped to reveal catholicity to the rest of the Catholic world. Local churches and the various episcopates became truly aware of their participation in the event, including through the unprecedented attention given to them by the media, especially radio and television. Prime time TV interviews with the great theologians gave faces to names that until then had only been read on paper. Thanks to those interviews, voices of Christianity were also made known that were usually ignored by the isolated and lethargic world of Italian Catholicism. In his letters, Cardinal Lercaro repeatedly referred, for example, to the compelling interviews broadcast by TV with the brothers of the Taizé community, and with Roger Schutz and Max Thurian themselves. They were recognized by other religious figures thanks to their television appearance.

Through comparison with the interviews of Vatican Radio, a more profound and useful aspect emerges that helps us to grasp the different strategies that animated the two media. The Radio of the Holy See decided to summon bishops, not experts, to appear in front of its microphones (respecting the decree of 1964). On the public television network RAI, however, various Christian figures took turns week after week in front of the camera: from council fathers to theologians, including African or African American bishops or cardinals, from laypeople to Protestant observers, from journalists to members of the Orthodox world. This was a significant moment for the television of the 1960s, where, except for sporting events, showing and giving to different cultures and ethnicities the floor was still new.

#### Television as an Agent of History

**[p. 109]** However, television did not simply act as a window on the conciliar events: it played a significant role as a true _agent of history_, a real protagonist of the conciliar history, and on different levels.[^c06-53]

[^c06-53]: As for the terminology used, see Giovanni De Luna, _La passione e la ragione. Fonti e metodi dello storico contemporaneo_ (Firenze: La Nuova Italia, 2001); Peppino Ortoleva, _Mediastoria. Mezzi di comunicazione e cambiamento sociale nel mondo_ _contemporaneo_ (Milano: Net, 2002); Peppino Ortoleva, _Il secolo dei media_ (Milano: Il Saggiatore, 2009).

First, the live broadcast of the opening and closing ceremonies of the four sessions allowed the council fathers, non-Catholic experts, and observers who could not be present to ‘participate’ in those liturgies, which in effect influenced the council’s reception. This can be seen from some pages of the diaries of the council fathers and theologians as well. For example, Charles Moeller, one of the Louvain theologians, watched the ceremony on television. And in the pages of his diary, the young bishop of the small Melkite Church, Néophytos Edelby, adviser and secretary to Patriarch Maximos IV Saigh, described how the [^c06-54] patriarch, who was unable to participate in that ‘solemn and moving’ ceremony, managed to watch it on television. Congar himself wrote in his journal: ‘Father de la Brosse, who saw it all on TV (until 12.30 pm), told me that it was splendid, very well photographed, transmitted and explained. And to think that with Telstar [the satellite], the whole world could see it all, at the very moment at which things were happening [^c06-55] …!’

[^c06-54]: Néophytos Edelby, _Il Vaticano II nel diario di un vescovo arabo_, ed. R. Cannelli (Cinisello Balsamo: San Paolo, 1996), 45.

[^c06-55]: Congar, _My Journal of the Council_, 87 (11 October 1962).

The live broadcasts of the council did not end with the opening ceremony of 11 October 1962. RAI’s first channel—the more institutional one—broadcast all the opening and closing ceremonies of the sessions, which were simultaneously broadcast on Eurovision. RAI also aired some special events, general congregations, and public sessions for the proclamation of the texts. Congar wrote on 28 October 1965 that ‘we had, after all, on TV in a nearby room, the Holy Father’s speech (nothing very remarkable: the Church IS [^c06-56] ALIVE!) and the result of the votes’. He was referring specifically to the television broadcast of the congregation during which two declarations and three decrees were proclaimed; he was unable to participate, as he was in a parallel meeting of the drafting subcommittee on _De Presbyteris_. On 8 December 1965, he resorted to the live broadcast on RAI Television to watch the closing ceremony in St Peter’s Square, which, again, he was unable to attend: ‘I watched the whole thing on Italian TV. Pretty good reporting, with [^c06-57] a well-prepared text, varied and technically excellent pictures.’ That liveliness of information also served to bring bishops and theologians closer to the media, which they usually ignored. The live broadcasts **[p. 110]** positively affected the council fathers, which helped them to understand television as a means of service. A very attentive observer like Congar, as we have seen, understood the new possibilities that television was opening up at that time. On Sunday, 25 November 1962, on the occasion of a live conversation on French television from Paris, he wrote enthusiastically in his journal: ‘We were in direct contact with the people in Paris, who asked us questions to which we replied there and then, the viewers seeing all this in front of them at the very same time. All the same it is quite sensational! Our great nephews and nieces see things even [^c06-58] more sensational!’

[^c06-56]: Ibid., 827 (28 October 1965).

[^c06-57]: Ibid., 874 (8 December 1965).

[^c06-58]: Ibid., 204 (25 November 1962).

Second, television was configured as an agent of the conciliar story in different ways, influencing the debate and the work of the assembly. The weekly programmes and summaries that RAI broadcast were used, for example, by the council fathers themselves, together with newspapers and magazines, as a compass to understand the progress of the debate on certain schemas. Understanding these was not always easy, complicated as it was by a Latin that was pronounced in the most disparate accents. The Jesuit Roberto Tucci, editor of _La Civiltà Cattolica_, for example, enthusiastically wrote in his diary about the way Archbishop Gabriel-Marie Garrone of Toulouse explained the functions and roles of the episcopal conferences to an Italian public and clergy who were not aware of how these were organized.

Moreover, the extent to which the council itself was receptive to the media’s mouthpiece role, in particular through the live broadcasts, can be seen on the occasion of specific events. RAI covered Paul VI’s visit to New York and his speech to the United Nations on 4 October 1965 on Eurovision. The council fathers and experts also followed the event from Rome via worldwide broadcasts. As the Brazilian Hélder Câmara, archbishop of Olinda and Recife, pointed out: ‘Telstar has allowed us to be there at the UN, watching and [^c06-59] certainly more comfortably than the participants at the ceremony.’ Congar also reported in his diary that ‘At 2.15 pm, the arrival of the pope in New York was shown live on TV (2.27 pm). Thus we witnessed it at the [^c06-60] very moment it was happening. It’s fantastic.’ The pope’s words, heard live, carried a certain weight on the progress of discussion in the general congregations of the council. In those days, the bishops were dealing with the chapter on war and peace in Schema XIII; they could not but be influenced by his words and implement his requests, hearing him live in Rome. Thus, they adapted to the papal requests and toned down the most radical proposals oriented towards an unmitigated condemnation of war.

[^c06-59]: Hélder Camara, _Circulares conciliares_, ed. Luíz Carlos Luz Marques and Roberto De Araujo Faria (Recife: Cepe, 2009), 1/3:84.

[^c06-60]: Congar, _My Journal of the Council_, 798 (4 October 1965).

At a third level, however, radio and television were used to direct the perception on some documents under discussion outside the conciliar hall as a counterpoint to the active propaganda fuelled in some countries. If the information conveyed by the small screen had an impact inside the council, this was even more true for those outside. There are many instances of this. For example, the influence of television or radio **[p. 111]** information on the conciliar debate, the perception of this, and its impact on public opinion were particularly evident in the discussion that the _De religionibus non christianis_ group was having in February 1965. Congar noted in his diary that ‘Msgr. Willebrands explained clearly that the Arabs of the Near East (whose very lively reactions we had to hand) had been very much disturbed by the propaganda put out in Arabic by Israeli radio: they listen to their broadcast a lot. But this radio chanted the refrain: the council has [^c06-61] declared that the Jews are innocent.’ The usefulness of a proper dissemination of news by the media was perceived precisely in those cases that touched on delicate issues associated with maintaining peaceful relations with other monotheistic faiths. On 15 September, Congar was finally able to note: ‘The pope also wanted the Muslim world to be better informed not only about this issue but about the work of the council in general. An attempt is being made to provide reliable information and explain things on the radio, to bring together various competent and influential people to create a favourable climate of opinion.[^c06-62]

[^c06-61]: Ibid., 735 (26 February 1965).

[^c06-62]: Ibid., 777 (15 September 1965).

If the mainstream media was able to involve public opinion, raising hopes and expectations, and though specialized journals and periodicals helped the bishops, offering reflections that eventually had an impact on the same debates, in reality the extent and level of influence of the media was more varied and fluid. We can conclude by saying that they all acted together and had an impact inside and outside St Peter’s, thus giving the conciliar assembly an unprecedented structure in terms of information and participation.

### 10. The Post-Conciliar Period on Television

Almost seven years after John XXIII announced his decision to celebrate an ecumenical council and hundreds of hours of filming on the part of television networks from all over the world, the post-conciliar period began. Right from the start, the issue of the reception of Vatican II became crucial. This is not the place to discuss the complex scenario of the reconstruction of the council’s reception or to offer an analysis of the post-conciliar period, which to a certain extent is a historiographic reflection that still needs to be written, despite the extensive and varied bibliography. However, we cannot overlook the role that the media, and in particular television, had in the reception of Vatican II.

The examples presented here are exclusively Italian, but the impact they had on Vatican II is such that they are worth mentioning. Leaving aside single programmes and the more-or-less successful commentaries or **[p. 112]** analyses of the post-conciliar Church, the programme that immediately brought the attention of all Italian society to one of the most visible changes brought about by the liturgical reform was the broadcasting of Sunday Mass. The live broadcast of the Sunday Eucharist in Italy, from the most famous basilicas and sanctuaries to the smallest parish churches, is among the longest-standing and successful broadcast programmes, so to speak, since the days of radio. From Vatican II onwards, television contributed to bringing the liturgical reform to every home. Television thus became the first real and essential vehicle for the diffusion of the implementation of conciliar decisions, reaching every Italian household: the first liturgies according to the new formulas; the first concelebrated rites; the first meetings dedicated to reading and discussing the sacred texts. The first images of the post-conciliar period were broadcast on television while the council was still in session. During the January–August 1963 intersession, an episode of the RAI TV program _Diario del concilio_, which was dedicated to the Liturgical Commission, showed a Mass with commentary, celebrated by Cardinal Lercaro in a parish on the outskirts of Bologna. It adhered fully to the new liturgical reform and aimed to facilitate greater participation of the faithful in the liturgical celebrations. The live Eurovision broadcast of the opening ceremony of the third session, on 14 September 1964, showed viewers the implementation of an ancient rite, also reintroduced by the liturgical reform: a concelebrated Mass.

In addition, the 18 September episode of _Diario del concilio_ showed video footage that RAI filmed on 17 May 1964 in the metropolitan Cathedral of San Pietro in Bologna: the Mass was concelebrated by Lercaro with four other bishops (not surprisingly, the bishop of Bologna was one of the most active in applying the conciliar reforms). There were interviews with young countryside priests and foreign cardinals on the changes they would implement in their dioceses on the basis of the new reform. For example, Bishop Thomas McGucken of the diocese of San Francisco in the US detailed the construction plan of his new cathedral, which would be carried out with the new schema in mind, according to the approved liturgical modifications. What RAI offers, therefore, is not a valuable commentary on the events and achievements of the Council after the fact, but one that is still in progress.

Italian television thus entered its new phase in its own way, with its own genres and formats, which is why we can rightly speak of a ‘post-conciliar period on television’. Indeed, and without exaggeration, it is possible to predate the official beginning of the conciliar reception to a specific date: that of 11 October 1962. That day of the opening ceremony of Vatican II, thanks to Eurovision, the live afternoon broadcast from Italy to the US for the first time and evening show with John XXIII’s ‘Moonlight Speech’ were the first form of participation and worldwide simultaneous reception of the event itself. Even before the discussions on the schemas and the promulgation of the first documents, the images that RAI broadcast and disseminated on a planetary level created the first awareness of the council, anticipating and confirming the directions and developments it would later take: openness to the world, pastorality, unity, and dialogue. The translation of what was happening in Rome into the language of television, therefore, revealed a new and unprecedented way of making discernible to world public opinion that ‘leap forward’ of the Church that Pope John XXIII wished for.

**[p. 113]** Through live reporting, programme series, interviews with priests and experts, and weekly reflections, television helped to make public the dimension of communion, discussion, and _aggiornamento_ that was taking place at the council, setting in motion a process and facilitating a degree of awareness on those issues that had never been reached before. Paul VI’s televised travels, his embrace with the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, Athenagoras I which the TV cameras helped to spread round the globe and transform into a great ecumenical gesture, the hopes placed in the council and expressed in front of the cameras by the African or Latin American bishops provide a foretaste of the tangible and visible signs of the fruits of the council: a preview of the messages and channels of dialogue that Vatican II would open.

## 7. The Unique Character of Vatican II’s Teaching

Peter Hünermann

### 1. Problems Connected with This Theme and a Possible Solution

**[p. 114]** Is the title of this essay—‘The Unique Character of Vatican II’s Teaching’—a rhetorical exaggeration, or does something fundamentally new happen with this council, compared with the long series of the great councils, from Nicaea down to Vatican I? There are, of course, differences among the individual councils. Like all historical events, each council has its own historical character; they differ in their specific historical and ecclesial situations and bear the imprint of varying cultural and societal contexts. The topics they deal with cover a large spectrum of questions concerning faith and church order, prompted by various circumstances and reasons. The legal forms have their own characteristics in the different epochs. Besides this, the specific flavour of the councils depends on their members and actors, and on their character and educational level. The outcomes and consequences for each council differ. In short, councils are as unique and ‘individual’ as historical events and arrangements necessarily always are.

If the title of this essay were understood in this way, it would be an expression of banality. The title might suggest a simple presentation of the teaching of the Second Vatican Council in its historical specificity and character, while making it impossible to emphasize the uniqueness of the council. Yet this title envisages a qualitative uniqueness that sets this council fundamentally apart from the series of preceding councils. Accordingly, we shall look for a quality that is not immediately obvious. When the title is understood emphatically, it suggests a quality characteristic of the teachings of the Second Vatican Council. This council **[p. 115]** was held in accordance with the customary conciliar forms of development, discernment, and impact, but we find a quality here that distinguishes it from the traditional historical type of councils.

If we are to demonstrate a uniqueness defined in this way, we must take as our starting point that which is common to all councils and which happens in all of them and ask: How did things look at Vatican II? What happened there that differs from other councils? Can we identify a unique quality or character? What kind of quality is this? Is there perhaps a particular series of events in the course of the council, with a gradual intensification in the expressions of this quality? How is this special quality manifested in the history of the council; that is to say, in its reception? It is a question of a quality that permeates transversally (so to speak) all the elements of the council, both its events and its teachings. But does anything like this exist? Our aim is to identify something that cannot be found elsewhere in the history of the councils; otherwise, it would be less than unique! To help us to identify this element, we must turn to academic disciplines outside theology. The most obvious candidate is philosophy, which serves as an institutionalized inquiry into wisdom, given that philosophy has a traditional place in theology.

A look at the philosophy or the history of thought in the modern period can help us to find a path here. Immanuel Kant drew a sharp dividing line in the development of his own thought, distinguishing between his early ‘uncritical’ and the later ‘critical’ philosophy. With these adjectives, he demarcates his discovery of transcendental logic and of the transcendental form of reflection that is linked to it. He stipulates that ‘All our knowledge has its origin from the senses, passes from thence to the understanding, and ends at the reason. There is nothing higher in the reason that can be found in us, to work on the matter that has been [^c07-1] seen and to bring it under the highest unity of thought.’ If one follows this pointer and consults the _Historisches Wörterbuch der Philosophie_, one finds a description of this path, from transcendentals to transcendental thinking and transcendental logic with numerous details, under the heading [^c07-2] ‘Transzendentalien, Transzendentalphilosophie’.

[^c07-1]: Immanuel Kant, _Kritik der reinen Vernunff, Transzendentale Dialektik_ (Hamburg: Felix Meiner, 1993), II A, 298 (B, 355); series _Philosophische Bibliothek_, t. 37a, 338.

[^c07-2]: See ‘Transzendentalien, Transzendentalphilosophie’, in _Historisches Wörterbuch der Philosophie_, ed. Joachim Ritter, Karlfried Gründer, and Gottfried Gabriel (Darmstadt: Wissenschaffliche Buchgesellschaff, 1998), 10:1358–1438.

An intellectual step has occurred in philosophy, finding expression continuously in the various great figures of modern philosophy. It emerges in Kant and passes from German Idealism to phenomenology and Wittgenstein’s analytical philosophy of language (to mention only the most outstanding elaborations). This new way of philosophizing is fundamentally different both from the roots in antiquity and the Middle Ages **[p. 116]** and from the definitions of the transcendentals in the modern period. Until Kant, the transcendentals were ‘defined _ontologically (that is to say, presupposing the possibility of the immediate knowledge of objects)_, [^c07-3] [as] the most general definitions of the existent’. From Kant onwards, this defines the _most general conditions that make experience possible at all_.

[^c07-3]: Ibid., 10:1359.

There is a corresponding tradition specific to Catholic theology, beginning with the early Tübingen theologians in the nineteenth century and continuing down to theologians like Karl Rahner or Edward Schillebeeckx, who played a decisive role at the council; the list continues to the present day. It was radically interrupted in the Catholic Church in the nineteenth century by the return to the ‘philosophy of antiquity’ [^c07-4] and the ‘theology of antiquity’ by Joseph Kleutgen, SJ and by the harsh attacks on modern philosophy and [^c07-5] science by writers such as Tilmann Pesch, SJ.

[^c07-4]: See Joseph Kleutgen, _Die Theologie der Vorzeit verteidigt_, 1st ed., 4 vols. (Münster: 1853–70); 2nd ed., 5 vols. (Münster: 1867–74); Joseph Kleutgen, _Die Philosophie der Vorzeit verteidigt_, 2 vols. (Münster: 1860–63).

[^c07-5]: The works of Pesch, president of the Görres Society, include eight volumes of the _Philosophia Lacensis_ and the following writings against Kant and the consequences of his thought: _Die modern Wissenschaff betrachtet in ihrer Grundfeste_, _Haltlosigkeit der modernen Wissenschaff_, _Das Welphänomen_, suppl. vols. 1/3 and 16 of the series _Stimmen von Maria Laach_. See Joseph Koch, ‘Pesch, Tilmann’, in _Lexikon für Theologie und Kirche_, ed. Michael Buchberger, 10 vols. (Freiburg im Breisgau: Herder, 1930–38), 8:107 f.

This pre-modern type of theology and philosophy prevailed in the Catholic Church from the second half of the nineteenth century onwards under the influence of the Roman Curia. Yet the general pre-modern guidelines laid down for philosophy and theology encountered problems in the twentieth century, due to the [^c07-6] in-depth theological and historical studies undertaken in the same period. If we trace the path of transcendental thinking in philosophy—and the approaches taken in theology—it is possible to discern in the conciliar texts and in the pronouncements of the magisterium a new holistic understanding of faith and thus a qualitative uniqueness of this council.

[^c07-6]: Bernhard Welte explored these tensions encountered by the Catholic theological faculty at the time of the convocation of the council: ‘Die Theologie zwischen Erbe und Neubeginn’, in _Festschrift der Universität Freiburg zur Eröffnung des Zweiten_ _Kollegiengebäudes_, ed. Johannes Vincke (Freiburg im Breisgau: Verlag Eberhard Albert Universitätsbuchhandlung, 1961), 9–30.

If it is indeed the case that the Second Vatican Council involves a new holistic understanding of faith, the problems linked with this issue must manifest themselves from the outset in the discussions, demands, and confiicts of the council. In particular, the disputed questions must each involve the whole in this sense, or the integration of individual details into the totality. Basically, what is at stake is this new position of individual doctrines within the context of the whole. Debates may indeed begin at individual points of doctrine, but this new approach itself must always be involved.

### 2. Can We Discern in the History of the Council, Beginning from Its

### Convocation, a Qualitative Uniqueness of This Council?

#### The Convocation of the Council and the Pope’s Opening Speech

**[p. 117]** Conflict, demands, misunderstanding, and debate broke out as soon as John XXIII issued the convocation of the council: the Second Vatican Council was to be a ‘pastoral council’ that proclaimed the traditional faith in a ‘new language’; that is to say, bringing it ‘up to date’ (_aggiornamento_) and thus launching a spiritual [^c07-7] awakening in the Church, ‘a new Pentecost’. This accent in the texts of the convocation is elaborated with [^c07-8] greater emphasis in the opening speech of John XXIII, _Gaudet Mater Ecclesia_.

[^c07-7]: See Joseph A. Komonchak, ‘The Struggle for the Council during the Preparation of Vatican II (1960–1962)’, in _History of_ _Vatican II_, ed. G. Alberigo (Leuven: Peeters, 1995), 1:167–356.

[^c07-8]: See Alberto Melloni, ‘L’allocuzione Gaudet Mater Ecclesia (11 ottobre 1962), Sinossi critica dell’allocuzione’, in _Fede,_ _tradizione, profezia: Studi su Giovanni XXIII e sul Vaticano II_, ed.
