Giuseppe Alberigo (Brescia: Paideia, 1984), 223–83. For an English translation, see ‘Pope John’s Opening Speech to the Council’, in _The Documents of Vatican II_, ed. Walter M. Abbott (Piscataway, NJ: New Century, 1966), 710–19.

The four characteristics of the council that I have just mentioned are certainly peculiar. None of them refers to a given doctrine or to any particular complex of doctrines. According to John XXIII, the Second Vatican Council was not to be a council of the Church that would fill the gaps left by Vatican I (which was interrupted [^c07-9] prematurely), or anything of the sort. It was to be a ‘pastoral council’. ‘Pastoral’ designates the activity of a shepherd that Jesus Christ himself carried out: his self-giving, his work, his testimony, his death on the Cross, and his Resurrection—in short, his entire mission, which the Lord of the community of believers has entrusted to the Church as a whole and given as a commission to the disciples and apostles. The council fathers must now implement this mission for the people of the modern era.

[^c07-9]: On the use of the term ‘pastoral’ by John XXIII, see Giuseppe Ruggieri, ‘Appunti per una teologia in Papa Roncalli’, in _Papa_ _Giovanni_, ed. Giuseppe Alberigo (Rome: Laterza, 1987), 245–71; Giuseppe Ruggieri, _Chiesa sinodale_ (Bari: Editori Laterza, 2017), 6–19. On the use of the terms ‘pastoral’ and ‘pastoral theology’ in the Middle Ages and in the post-Tridentine period, see E. Stolzi, ‘Pastoraltheologie’, in Buchberger, _Lexikon für Theologie und Kirche_, 7:1023–25. On the conception of a ‘practical theology’, see H. Schuster, ‘Praktische Theologie’, in Buchberger, _Lexikon für Theologie und Kirche_, 8:682–85.

The faith to which the council must testify in this way is to be proclaimed in a ‘new language’. It is not a matter of a new doctrine or of a special question of ethics, but of the faith itself, which, in its entirety, is to **[p. 118]** be proclaimed by the council in a new and different language. The characterization of this task by the keyword _aggiornamento_ indicates that the faith is to be thought through and expressed in the contemporary context, in the historical present: that means in the language of this age.

The term ‘a new Pentecost’ refers to the hoped-for effect of the council. The pope does not hope for the resolution of a conflict (as in the period of the Council of Trent), or for fresh light and decisions on questions of faith and morals. He hopes that the Spirit of God himself will make the Church’s faith ‘come alive’. This will come about when the council fathers, as successors of the apostles, carry out their mission as shepherds who care for people in the modern age; and the process will take fiight thanks to the new language and the positioning of this testimony in the historical present.

An analysis of the _vota_, the hopes and requests for the conciliar agenda sent in by the bishops, reveals that the great majority took up questions that would help them to carry out the duties of their office in a less complicated manner. They also raised ecclesiological questions in continuity with the First Vatican Council and a number of spiritual questions. A few individual bishops presented fundamental questions concerning a theological-ecclesial renewal in faith. Only a few _vota_ were drawn up or sent in by groups of bishops or episcopal conferences. We should also mention that some publications spoke of the need for a comprehensive renewal.

These _vota_ were studied and processed by the preparatory commissions on the basis of the neo-scholastic schemata and following the pattern of the 1917 Code of Canon Law, which made it impossible for tentative new approaches to come to light. The picture is sobering, if we prescind from the fact that about 25 per cent of the _vota_ refer to the liturgy. The message of John XXIII in the convocation of the council aims at something comprehensively new, but this lay beyond the horizon of most of the bishops and beyond the condition and understanding of the Church at that time.

#### The Council’s Message to the World

[^c07-10] On the basis of a preliminary text submitted by Marie-Dominique Chenu, a group of council fathers proposed that the council should address a public message to all people and all nations in order to explain what the council was about: the great concern of the council was to proclaim the importance for humanity of the Gospel, the ‘message of salvation’. Many of the phrases in this text sound like a prelude to _Gaudium et Spes_, and it was approved with applause after a short discussion. From the very outset, therefore, the Second Vatican Council speaks in the modern public arena. The council fathers define as follows what the council intends to do: ‘to inquire how we ought to renew ourselves, so that we may be found increasingly faithful to [^c07-11] **[p. 119]** the Gospel of Christ’. They are moved to speak by their pastoral concern, thus opening a dialogue with contemporary peoples and the nations concerning the Gospel that is God’s message of salvation for the world. They do not address selected groups of people, nor do they speak to Catholics or to Christians alone; they address all peoples and all nations. At the centre of their dialogue with the human public arena is God’s word to human beings, the message of salvation. The conciliar event, its importance, and its content could scarcely be expressed in more universal terms.

[^c07-10]: See André Duval, ‘Chenu’, in _Lexikon für Theologie und Kirche_, ed. Walter Kasper, 3rd ed. (Freiburg: Herder, 1994), 2:1034.

[^c07-11]: Abbott, ‘Message to Humanity’, in Abbott, _The Documents of Vatican II_, 3–7, at 3–4.

In accordance with this message, after the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy (the first conciliar document to be promulgated), all the constitutions (_Lumen Gentium_, _Dei Verbum_, _Gaudium et Spes_) explicitly address believers and the ‘whole world’ (literally, ‘all men’) in their introductions. The entire _linguistic style_ is determined by this definition of the addressees, as is the language of the documents that makes the constitutions concrete and amplifles them. Three documents (_Inter Mirifica_, _Nostra Aetate_, _Dignitatis Humanae_) speak of the relationship of the church to societal developments, other religions, and human rights, including religious freedom. Here, therefore, the ‘new language’, the new ‘pastoral style of speaking’, emerges clearly.

#### The Rejection of the Proposed Conciliar Schemata and the Elaboration of New Ones

We follow the progression of the council. Both the intention of John XXIII—seen in his announcement of the council and above all in his opening discourse, _Gaudet Mater Ecclesia_—and the first spontaneous grasping of this conciliar intention by the council fathers in the ‘Message to Humanity’ find their continuation and development on a deeper level in the way in which the council fathers deal in the first session with the conciliar schemata that had been prepared. These had been substantially drafted and written by the Roman Curia, its officials, and their colleagues in the theological institutions in Rome on the basis of the _vota_ that the bishops submitted. The first session of the council is particularly important, because it was here that fundamental decisions with regard to the subsequent work of the council were taken.

The First Session of the Council (1962)

What were the crucial themes of the first session? The opening speech of the pope was the central point in the first general congregation; in the second, the council fathers themselves elected the members of the commissions that would be responsible for elaborating the documents on the proposed topics. In the third congregation, the council fathers’ _Message to the World_ was presented and approved. The presentation of the prepared schema on the liturgy began with the fourth general congregation on 22 October and lasted until the nineteenth general congregation on 14 November. This debate concluded with the acceptance in principle of the schema, recognizing the need for further work.

**[p. 120]** The important dogmatic schema _De Fontibus Revelationis_ was presented on the same day. The heated discussion, taking up fundamental issues, ended on 20 November with a vote on the preparatory schema, which failed to receive the necessary percentage of the vote required. The outcome of this vote led to a vigorous debate and an intervention by the pope. Already on 23 November, in the twenty-fifth general congregation, the preparatory schema on the Church and on Mary, and the schema on the means of social communication, were presented. The first vote, with a positive outcome, on the schema _Inter Mirifica_ (Decree on the Mass Media), took place on 27 November during the twenty-eighth general congregation. A more thorough discussion of the schema did not take place; it was intended from the outset to leave such questions to the elaboration of post-conciliar pastoral regulations.

Cardinal Ottaviani presented the preparatory schema on the Church on 1 December, in the thirty-first general congregation. It encountered sharp criticism from the start, and arrangements were made for a thoroughly revised version. The last three days of the first council session were devoted to discussing and making improvements to the first chapter of the schema on the liturgy, _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ (_SC_), and approving it. Thus, in the first session, the council debated three of the four authoritative constitutions that the fathers would ultimately approve. These are the central documents of the council.

The conciliar debates on the preparatory schemata begin with a consideration of the schema on the liturgy, which has a special place in the context of the prepared schemata and is itself a model of the uniqueness that was lacking precisely in the schemata that were discussed in subsequent weeks. The high number of _vota_ by [^c07-12] the council fathers—roughly a quarter of all those submitted —is an indication not only of the universally shared consciousness of the importance of the liturgy, but also of the great pastoral importance that the bishops attributed to it. This reflects an extremely significant element of a radical new ecclesial orientation after the Napoleonic upheavals and the ensuing secularization in Western and Central Europe. The revival of monasticism, and especially of the Benedictine order, from the first half of the nineteenth century onwards, and the development of critical studies in the history of the liturgy opened the door to a rediscovery of the liturgy. This can be seen in the early attempts to involve the laity in the liturgy, in the great liturgical congresses. Its effects are evident in the pastoral reforms of Pius X with regard to the frequent reception of communion and in the reform of the liturgies of Holy Week and Easter by Pius XII. A fundamental distinction was reintroduced between the liturgy and the numerous devotions that had their origin in earlier centuries, such as processions and the practice of receiving communion outside Mass once a year. At the same time, this new way of looking at the liturgy gave form to a new understanding of the Church, especially due to the rediscovery of the essence of the Church as _mysterium_ (mystery or sacrament). **[p. 121]** Attention was directed to the individual’s personal path of faith, to the Church’s path of faith, and to [^c07-13] their integration into this _mysterium_. Unlike the other schemata, this schema had been drawn up by leading theologians of the liturgical renewal. It was the only preparatory schema that was evaluated positively by Edward Schillebeeckx, who published a widely read theological critique of all the preparatory [^c07-14] schemata. The fundamental first chapter, which was originally envisaged in the schema as a ‘Dogmatic Prologue: _De mysterio sacrae liturgiae eiusque relatione ad vitam ecclesiae_’ (On the Sacred Mystery of the Liturgy and Its Relation to the Life of the Church), offered an outstanding ‘synthesis of the doctrinal and the [^c07-15] pastoral’.

[^c07-12]: See Rainer Kaczynski, ‘Theologischer Kommentar zur Konstitution über die heilige Liturgie _Sacrosanctum Concilium_’, in _Herders Theologischer Kommentar zum zweiten Vatikanischen Konzil,_ ed. Peter Hünermann and Bernd Jochen Hilberath (Freiburg: Herder, 2004–5), 2:43.

[^c07-13]: See Massimo Faggioli, _True Reform: Liturgy and Ecclesiology in Sacramentum Concilium_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2012), 59–93.

[^c07-14]: See Gerald P. Fogarty, ‘The Council Gets Underway’, in Alberigo, _History of Vatican II_, 2:73.

[^c07-15]: Joseph A. Komonchak, ‘The Struggle for the Council during the Preparation of Vatican II (1960–1962)’, in Alberigo, _History_ _of Vatican II_, 2:211.

The schema of the Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation was discussed immediately after the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy. This was because, when the first schemata were sent to the council fathers in July 1962, it was the first to arrive. It was followed, next, by the schema of a dogmatic constitution on the preservation of the purity of the faith; third, the schema of a dogmatic constitution on the Christian moral order; fourth, the schema of the dogmatic constitution on chastity, marriage, the family, and virginity; fifth, the schema of the constitution on the liturgy; sixth, the schema of the constitution on the means of communication; and seventh, the decree about the unity of the Church (including the Eastern churches). The first four schemata of the ‘Dogmatic Constitutions’ were drawn up by the Preparatory Theological Commission, under the presidency of Cardinal Ottaviani. Its secretary was Fr Tromp, SJ. Taken as a whole, they were strongly marked by the neo-scholastic Roman theology.

In the aforementioned schema, revelation was understood as an objectively existing divine structure present partly in Scripture and partly in the oral tradition. It maintained that the evaluation of the two ‘sources of revelation’ belongs exclusively to the Church’s magisterium.[^c07-16]

[^c07-16]: The second schema deals with questions that the Holy Office at that period regarded as its special remit, namely ‘to preserve in its purity the deposit of faith’. It treats, in a corresponding structure, the tasks involved in guaranteeing this deposit of faith. See Klaus Wittstadt, ‘On the Eve of the Second Vatican Council (July 1–October 10, 1962)’, in Alberigo, _History of Vatican II_, 1:412. The third schema dealt with the foundations of the ethical order in accordance with the distinction between _ius naturale_ (natural law) and _ius Evangelii_ (the law of the Gospel); conscience, ethical subjectivism, and relativism; sin and the natural and supernatural dignity of the human person. The fourth schema treats questions of sexual morality and the regulation of marriage and the family.

The drafts of the four Dogmatic Constitutions clearly display everywhere the ‘logic of the application’ of the [^c07-17] order of creation and revelation, posited by God, to human praxis. Immediately after the prepared **[p. 122]** schemata were sent out, they were sharply criticized, especially the first dogmatic schema, because this fundamental document risked orienting all subsequent work of the council.

[^c07-17]: Max Seckler is correct in speaking of an ‘instruction-theoretical model of revelation’. Max Seckler, ‘Der Begriff der Offenbarung’, in _Handbuch der Fundamentaltheologie_, ed. Walter Kern, Hermann-Josef Pottmeyer, and Max Seckler, 2nd ed. (Tübingen: UTB GmbH, 2000), 2:45–47.

Gustave Martelet, SJ and Charles Moeller wrote a critical report for the French bishops; Karl Rahner wrote a report for the German-speaking bishops, and Edward Schillebeeckx for the Dutch and Belgian bishops. Around 160 bishops sent _vota_ to the council secretariat. On the eve of the conciliar discussion, on 13 November, new drafts by Karl Rahner, together with Joseph Ratzinger, Edward Schillebeeckx, and Gérard Philips, circulated among the bishops. On that very evening, representatives of the various international episcopal conferences met in the Domus Mariae to discuss the schema that had been presented.

When the nineteenth general congregation opened on 15 November, Cardinal Alfredo Ottaviani and then Bishop Salvatore Garofalo did not make a detailed presentation of the commission’s schema. Both began in medias res with a defence of this schema against the alternative schemata that were being circulated. This led to a heated debate. The eighty-five contributions to the discussion did not take up particular disputed questions, such as the relationship between Scripture and Tradition, the definition of the Gospel, revelation as the sole source of Scripture and Tradition, the inerrancy of Scripture, and new exegetical insights about the historical character of the Bible. The central issue in this debate was the whole approach of the schema towards revelation and the orientation of the council as a whole. It is noteworthy that, of the eighty-five contributions to the discussion, sixty-one referred in one form or another to the opening speech of John XXIII, _Gaudet Mater Ecclesia_. Cardinal Bea got to the heart of the debate: ‘_a_) The Pope has given the council a pastoral purpose; _b_) the council has already made this purpose its own in its opening “Message”; and _c_) the [^c07-18] need now is consciously to ratify this purpose by rejecting a schema that runs counter to it’. He emphasized strongly that one must not prescind from human beings, because after all, it is to them that the truth of the faith is to be proclaimed. He insisted on the essential need to pay heed to the _modus tradendi_ of the Gospel: the Gospel must be proclaimed in a new way in modern times. It was a question of the ‘pastoral’ and ‘ecumenical’ orientation of the schema.

[^c07-18]: Giuseppe Ruggieri, ‘The First Doctrinal Clash’, in Alberigo, _History of Vatican II_, 2:253.

The outcome of these highly controversial discussions was the decision by the Council of Presidents, after the general congregation of 19 November, to hold a vote and interrupt the discussion. The announcement of this decision on the following day led to questions and puzzlement, because many bishops did not understand the point of the interruption. This led to a clarification by Archbishop Pericle Felici, the general secretary of the council, and Cardinal Ernesto Ruffini: a vote in favour of _interrumpatur_ meant that the schema should be revised and rewritten, while _non interrumpatur_ would signify support for a continuation of work on the existing schema. Eleven minutes later, Felici gave a further clarification; one may presume that most of the bishops had voted in the meantime. The result: 822 council fathers voted for the continuation, **[p. 123]** and 1,368 for the interruption. This was 105 votes short of a two-thirds majority required for the interruption. Since such a case was not envisaged in the procedural rules of the council, John XXIII declared on the next day that a ‘mixed commission’, with members from the Theological Commission and the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity, would be formed to improve this schema, shortening it and giving it a more appropriate form. This mixed commission would have two presidents, Cardinals Ottaviani and Bea, as well as two secretaries, Sebastian Tromp, SJ and Mgr Johannes Willebrands. It was comprised of members of the commission ‘De doctrina fidei et morum’ and the members of the Secretariat for Unity in addition to other cardinals, nominated by the pope: Liénart, Frings, Ruffini, Meyer, Lefebvre, and Quiroga y Palacios—here, too, there was a mixture of positions.

This new commission, with its richly contrasting membership, produced in the course of the next conciliar sessions a completely revised document characterized by new questions and themes that had not yet been treated in this form. This is apparent above all in the first chapter on revelation itself, which introduces a new way of looking at the ‘transmission of revelation’ through Scripture and oral teaching, and presents new insights into the inspiration of Scripture, the character of the Old and New Testaments, and their place in the Church’s life.

In the immediate aftermath of the debate on revelation, the discussion in the general congregations concentrated on questions of ecclesiology. The preparatory schema _De Ecclesia_ and _De Beata Maria Virgine_ [^c07-19][^c07-20] was distributed on 23 November 1962. The schema _De Ecclesiae Unitate_, on the Eastern churches, was presented on 26 November and was accepted for further treatment on 1 December, with the instruction that it be combined with the submissions of the Secretariat for Unity under Cardinal Bea and material from the draft of _De Ecclesia_ to form a single document.

[^c07-19]: See Peter Hünermann, ‘Theologischer Kommentar zur dogmatischen Konstitution über die Kirche: _Lumen Gentium_’, in Hünermann and Hilberath, _Herders Theologischer Kommentar zum zweiten Vatikanischen Konzil_, 2:291–319.

[^c07-20]: Bernd Jochen Hilberath, ‘Theologischer Kommentar zum Dekret über die katholischen Ostkirchen “_Orientalium_ _Ecclesiarum_” ’, in Hünermann and Hilberath, _Herders Theologischer Kommentar zum Zweiten Vatikanischen Konzil_, 3:5–18.

[^c07-21] At the same time, work on the schema on the Church began in the same general congregation. Eighty [^c07-22] speeches were made, and fifty-seven objections were submitted in writing. The debate was marked from the start by the conviction that this schema needed a thorough transformation. The controversial points were closely related to the objections and the critique evoked by the schema on revelation. When he presented the schema, Cardinal Ottaviani complained that it had been ‘condemned in advance’. He lamented the circulation of new drafts and the expected criticism that the schema was not pastoral, that it **[p. 124]** was too scholastic, not ecumenical, too negative, and so on. At the close of the debate on the last working day of the first session, no vote was taken on the schema on the Church under discussion. Felici, the general secretary, announced that written proposals for revision should be submitted by 28 February 1963.

[^c07-21]: See Hünermann, ‘Theologischer Kommentar zur dogmatischen Konstitution über die Kirche’, 2:320–24.

[^c07-22]: See Ruggieri, ‘Beyond an Ecclesiology of Polemics: The Debate on the Church’, in Alberigo, _History of Vatican II_, 2:281–358.

What Was the Decisive Turning Point in the Events of the First Session?

Alberigo entitled the second volume of his history _The Formation of the Council’s Identity_. The third is entitled _The Mature Council_. This reflects the fact that the events of the first session and the elaboration of the drafts in the period between sessions up to August 1963 marked a decisive turning point. What is the nature of this turning point, and how is it manifested? What is the decisively new element that we see in _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ and the constitutions on revelation and on the Church? If we compare the introductory chapters of these three constitutions, we clearly see a new structure of speaking and a new mode of approach in the argumentation.

We read in _Sacrosanctum Concilium_:

For it is the liturgy through which, especially in the divine sacrifice of the Eucharist, ‘the work of our redemption is accomplished’, and it is through the liturgy, especially, that the faithful are enabled to express in their lives and manifest to others the mystery of Christ and the real nature of the true Church. The Church is essentially both human and divine, visible but endowed with invisible realities, zealous in action and dedicated to contemplation, present in the world, but as a pilgrim, so constituted that in her the human is directed toward and subordinated to the divine, the visible to the invisible, action to contemplation, and this present world to that city yet to come, the object of our quest. (_SC_ 2)

This understanding of the liturgy is fundamentally different from the pre-modern understanding of the liturgy—for example, that of the Eucharist—as an essentially earthly action that, as such, has the character of a direct symbolic, analogical referent. By virtue of his divine authority, Christ has added to this earthly action a supernatural reference function, pointing beyond it and thereby making it an effective sacramental sign.

In the conciliar text, on the other hand, the liturgy is presented as the very mystery of redemption in Jesus Christ—a divine–human _mysterium_ of the believers and of the believing community, the Church—that is enacted whenever the earthly action is performed in faith. In this very celebration, the Church is fortifled and built up. Individual believers and the community of believers are strengthened on their pilgrim path towards the full realization of redemption.

The language here is immediately pastoral, stating what is at issue without recourse to the pre-modern clarification and laborious explanations of the meaning of the liturgy. It is in the human action itself that the divine–human action of Jesus Christ, and the reconciliation carried out and bestowed by the Father in the Son, are manifested.

The first chapter of _Dei Verbum_ (_DV_), the Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation, speaks of ‘revelation itself’. How does revelation take place?

**[p. 125]** It pleased God, in his goodness and wisdom, to reveal himself and to make known the mystery of his will (cf. Eph 1:9). His will was that men should have access to the Father, through Christ, the Word made flesh, in the Holy Spirit, and thus become sharers in the divine nature (cf. Eph 2:18; 2 Pet 1:4). By this revelation, then, the invisible God (cf. Col 1:15; 1 Tim 1:17), from the fullness of his love, addresses men and women as his friends (cf. Ex 33:11; Jn 15:14-15), and moves among them (cf. Bar 3:38), in order to invite and receive them into his own company. This economy of Revelation is realized by deeds and words, which are intrinsically bound up with each other. As a result, the works performed by God in the history of salvation show forth and bear out the doctrine and realities signifled by the words; the words, for their part, proclaim the works, and bring to light the mystery they proclaim. (_DV_ 2)

God’s eternal plan of salvation, which exists from before all time, ‘shines forth in Christ, who is himself both the mediator and the sum total of Revelation’ (_DV_ 2). Jesus Christ is God’s self-revelation, which he communicates to human beings. How does he do so? In his living together with human beings, ‘the invisible God, from the fullness of his love, addresses men and women as his friends’ (_DV_ 2). This self-revelation of God was made known by God ‘to our first parents from the very beginning’. God then ‘buoyed them up with the hope of salvation’ through Abraham, Moses, and the prophets. Finally, ‘in these last days he has spoken to us in the Son’ (_DV_ 4).

Here, as in _Sacrosanctum Concilium_, the starting point is God’s own action, the _mysterium_ of God, his plan of salvation. God discloses himself in history from the very beginning, to our first parents. This self-disclosure of God is then communicated further through Abraham and the patriarchs and the prophets; it reaches its fulfilment in Jesus Christ, who is the Word of God. The second chapter of _Dei Verbum_, on the transmission of the divine revelation, speaks of how this event of communication is handed on further.

We read nothing here about a ‘supernatural revelation’ that ‘has come down to us in written books and unwritten traditions that were received by the apostles from the mouth of Christ himself or were [^c07-23] transmitted from hand to hand (so to speak) by the apostles themselves at the dictation of the Holy Spirit’. God himself acts. God reveals himself to human beings, and this revelation reaches us in such a way that we believe on the basis of the authority of the God who discloses his very self to us. This disclosure takes place through Jesus Christ. It is handed on through the testimony of the Church’s faith, through the witness of the faith of believers.

[^c07-23]: See First Vatican Council, Dogmatic Constitution _Dei Filius_’, translated from Heinrich Denzinger and Peter Hünermann, eds., _Enchiridion symbolorum definitionum et declarationum de rebus fidei et morum_, 43rd ed. (Freiburg im Breisgau: Herder, 2010), no. 3006.

The Word of God, proceeding from the Father and becoming flesh, is proclaimed here in ‘pastoral language’, in a new language that is spoken in the manifold testimonies of the faith. The Word of God is not simply words and sentences that the historical Jesus spoke or that he directed the apostles through the Holy Spirit **[p. 126]** to hand on by word of mouth. God’s Word himself encounters the human being in, through, and under the words of Jesus and of the disciples. But how is this envisaged?

Let us conclude by turning to the first chapter of _Lumen Gentium_ (_LG_), which speaks of the mystery of the Church. ‘Christ is the light of humanity; and it is, accordingly, the heart-felt desire of this sacred Council, being gathered together in the Holy Spirit, that, by proclaiming his Gospel to every creature (cf. Mk 16:15), it may bring to all humanity that light of Christ which shines out visibly from the Church.’ The Church is then described as being like a ‘sacrament—a sign and instrument, that is, of communion with God and of unity among all men’ (_LG_ 1). How does this occur?

The eternal Father, in accordance with the utterly gracious and mysterious design of his wisdom and goodness, created the whole universe, and chose to raise up men and women to share in his own divine life; and when they had fallen in Adam, he did not abandon them, but at all times held out to them the means of salvation, bestowed in consideration of Christ, the Redeemer, ‘who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature’ (Col 1:15). All the elect the Father foreknew and predestined before time began ‘to become conformed to the image of his Son, that he should be the firstborn among many brethren’ (Rom 8:29). He determined to call together in a holy Church those who should believe in Christ. Already present in figure [_praefigurata_] at the beginning of the world, this Church was prepared in marvelous fashion in the history of the people of Israel … and made manifest in the outpouring of the Spirit, it will be brought to glorious completion at the end of time. (_LG_ 2)

‘All the just, “from Abel, the just one, to the last of the elect” ’ belong to this Church (_LG_ 2). In this way, the Church belongs to the _mysterium_ of Christ as ‘the seed and the beginning of the kingdom’ on earth and is sent like Christ ‘to serve and to give its life as a ransom for many’ (_LG_ 5). On its path through history, however, this Church is ‘at once holy and always in need of purification’ and ‘follows constantly the path of penance and renewal’ (_LG_ 8), because it contains sinners in its bosom and is itself on the path of conversion.

If we compare the way _Lumen Gentium_ speaks of the Church—of its presence in the Father’s plan of salvation, in the revelation of Jesus Christ, and of the life of the Church in history, with the way in which the other constitutions speak of these matters—we must conclude that here, in exactly the same way as in _Dei Verbum_ and _Sacrosanctum Concilium_, we are obliged to speak of a highly complex divine–human event of communication.

### 3. A Conceptual Clarification

How are we to understand the change in language and total outlook that we meet in these initial descriptions of liturgy, revelation, and the Church? The epistemological presuppositions of Vatican II are no **[p. 127]** longer those that characterized the definitions of Vatican I. The First Vatican Council gave a very precise definition of its epistemological presuppositions in the Constitution _Dei Filius_:

The abiding understanding of the Catholic church also held and holds firmly that there is a twofold order of knowledge, which is distinct not only in the principle, but also in the object, because in the one (order) we know with the natural reason, and in the other with the divine faith; but also in the object, because in addition to that which the natural reason can attain, mysteries hidden in God are presented to us to be believed in. If these had not been revealed by God, they could not have been known.[^c07-24]

[^c07-24]: Ibid., no. 3015.

This twofold order of knowledge thus means that there are different principles of knowing and different objects of knowing. This makes it necessary to demonstrate to reason the credibility of the faith. The First Vatican Council does so primarily by pointing to external reasons such as miracles and the fulfilment of prophecies, but also adds explicitly that the Spirit of God is decisive for believing the faith. At the same time, it emphasizes that there can never be a contradiction between the faith and natural knowledge and its objects.

This created the fatal situation where the exercise of the magisterium in the aftermath of Vatican I would claim that only the Church is authorized to make judgements concerning the ‘supernatural objects’ of faith, such that rational scholarly investigation could not make valid claims concerning (by way of example) the authorship of Deuteronomy or other statements of the Old and New Testaments, with the intention of correcting the tradition.

It is precisely with regard to these epistemological presuppositions that a fundamental redefinition takes place in the Second Vatican Council. How are we to describe this redefinition? In conceptual terms, it means that God’s plan of salvation—that is to say, God’s self-disclosure—is (from a human perspective) the transcendental and also transcendent ground of all human capacity: of our freedom, our reason, our will, our loving, believing, and hoping—our selfhood. God’s plan of salvation, that is to say, God’s self-disclosure, is incomprehensibly anterior to all that is creaturely. In other words, it is transcendent. At the same time, it concerns the deepest aspiration of the human being: it is transcendental, emerging as the absolute precondition of all being.

This means that the epistemological position of Vatican I, the language of two principles—of the parallelism between revelation/faith and creation/reason, and the categorical separation between two types of objects, the natural and the supernatural—is taken up into a perichoretic unity that has an essentially historical character. This is because what is involved here is the God who discloses himself to the human being who, in their self-realization in freedom in history, de facto continually fails to meet God’s self-disclosure. It is God who holds fast to this self-disclosure to the human being in his sinfulness. This is manifested in the Cross of Jesus Christ and in his Resurrection.

**[p. 128]** Schleiermacher, with his discovery of the solidly established freedom and selfhood of the human being, paved the way to a transcendental theology which presupposes God’s incomprehensible self-disclosure in [^c07-25] freedom, a self-disclosure that is never at the disposal of human beings. Schleiermacher’s approach was received critically in Catholic theology by Johann Sebastian von Drey and his pupils and colleagues, [^c07-26] Hirscher, Staudenmeier, and Johann Evangelist von Kuhn. I touched on this fact briefly in the introduction. In the Anglo-Saxon world, we should mention Newman, who, in his _Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine_, presented a similar historical sketch in contrast to the epistemological basis of the First [^c07-27] Vatican Council. This new theological approach was vehemently contested by the neo-scholastic theology that was to dominate Catholic school philosophy from Kleutgen in his _Philosophie der Vorzeit_ and _Theologie_ [^c07-28] _der Vorzeit_ down to the theses prescribed by the _Congregatio studiorum_. We can only mention these developments briefly.

[^c07-25]: See C. Cesa, ‘Transzendental; transzendentale Philosophie, Schleiermacher’, in _Historisches Wörterbuch der Philosophie_, eds. Joachim Ritter, Karlfried Gründer, Gottfried Gabriel (Basel: Schwabe, 1998), vol. 10, 13, 95: ‘But the ego is only one of the original elements; and thinking, its internal activity, is inspired by a claim to totality that can be fulfilled only in union “with something else that is original, namely, the consciousness of the highest being [_Wesen_]”, which is also called the Absolute or the deity. This is the transcendental basis to which everything must be ascribed; understood in this form as being [_Sein_], it represents the boundary of discursive or reflexive thinking.’

[^c07-26]: See A. Kustermann, ‘Drey, Sebastian von’, in Buchberger, _Lexikon für Theologie und Kirche_, 3:373–4.

[^c07-27]: See Peter Walter, ‘Neuscholastik, Neuthomismus’, in Buchberger, _Lexikon für Theologie und Kirche_, 7:779–82.

[^c07-28]: See Denzinger, _Enchiridion symbolorum definitionum et declarationum de rebus fidei et morum_, nos. 3601–24.

The elaboration of this theological approach proceeded step by step, as a counterpart to the development and continuation of transcendental philosophy. Important steps were taken by French-speaking thinkers such as Maréchal, Blondel, Rousselot, de Lubac, Chenu, and Congar; among German-speaking theologians, von Balthasar, Lotz, Rahner, and Welte; in the Dutch–Flemish world by Schillebeeckx; and among English-speakers by Lonergan. There are considerable differences in the concrete ways in which this transcendental approach in theology was put into practice in the post-conciliar period. One need only consider Rahner’s post-conciliar works, with his _Grundkurs_ (_Foundations of Christian Faith_); Welte with his phenomenological analysis of faith in its dual aspect as constitutive of existence and as a historical-Christian faith in freedom; Lonergan’s _Method in Theology_; or Christoph Theobald’s _Selon l’Esprit de Sainteté: Genèse d’une théologie systématique._ The mutual criticism is sharp. But this approach makes possible in principle the integration of culturally and historically diverse approaches to the _mysterium_ of revelation in Christ and to the _mysterium_ of the Church. It also makes possible a variety of methodologies, including the modern linguistic-philosophical and social analyses, such as we find in Wittgenstein, Strawson, or Ricoeur, and the use of new methods in exegesis, church history, systematic theology, and practical theology.

**[p. 129]** This shows the uniqueness of the council, which is linked to the approach of transcendental theology. But it also shows the serious tasks that still await theological reflection. Numerous traditional doctrinal propositions and forms of Church life and of ecclesiastical order stand in need of critical study and redefinition. Conciliar documents such as _Dignitatis Humanae_ (Declaration on Religious Freedom) and _Nostra Aetate_ (Declaration on the Relation of the Church to Non-Christian Religions) are but a prelude to this task.

### Suggested Reading

Alberigo, G., ed. _History of Vatican II_, 5 vols. English edition edited by Joseph A. Komonchak. Maryknoll, NY: Orbis; Leuven: Peeters, 1995–2005.

Berger, Peter L., and Thomas Luckmann. _The Social Construction of Reality: A Treatise in the Sociology of Knowledge_. New York: Anchor, 1996.

Denzinger, Heinrich, and Peter Hünermann, eds. _Enchiridion symbolorum definitionum et declarationum de rebus fidei et morum_, 43rd ed. Freiburg im Breisgau: Herder, 2010.

Hünermann, Peter, and Bernd Jochen Hilberath, eds. _Herders Theologischer Kommentar zum Zweiten Vatikanischen Konzil_, 5 **[p. 130]** vols. Freiburg: Herder, 2004–5.

## 8. Expunged and Forgotten Texts and Messages of Vatican II

### 1. The Myth Concerning the Corpus of Vatican II’s Texts

**[p. 133]** After the end of Vatican II, the work of publishing the documents of the council proved to be fraught with critical and philological issues of no less importance than those that have marked all the other great [^c08-1] councils of the past. Moreover, this time there was no longer a _camera papae_ (papal official) in charge of a final editing of the texts and manipulating the will of an assembly convened _ad solemnitatem tantum_ (for the [^c08-2] sole purpose of solemnizing the papal agenda). Nor was there (at least there was not believed to be) a resistant minority that refused and disavowed the conciliar pronouncements.

[^c08-1]: See Silvia Scatena, ‘Filologia delle decisioni conciliari: Dal voto in congregazione generale alla Editio Typica’, in _Volti di fine_ _concilio: Saggi di teologia e storia sulla fine del Vaticano II_, ed. Joseph Doré and Alberto Melloni (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2000), 53–97; for the most recent councils of the Catholic Church, see Klaus Ganzer, ‘La conclusione dell’edizione degli atti del concilio di Trento’ and Alberto Melloni, ‘Vaticano I, Vaticano II: L’edizione dei concili in età contemporanea’, in _Annali_ _dell’Istituto storico italo-germanico in Trento/Jahrbuch des italienisch-deutschen Instituts in Trient_ 29 (2003): 389–403 and 495–510 respectively.

[^c08-2]: See Hermann Joseph Sieben, _Die Konzilsidee des lateinischen Mittelalters (847–1378)_ (Paderborn: Schöningh, 1984); Wilhelm Imkamp, ‘Sermo ultimus, quem fecit Dominus Innocentius papa tercius in Lateranensi concilio generali’, _Römische Quartalschriff für christliche Altertumskunde und Kirchengeschichte_ 69 (1974): 149–79.

Yet, tensions that accumulated during the conciliar celebration—especially those of the first intercession [^c08-3] **[p. 134]** (January–August 1963) and of the third period (autumn 1964) —had repercussions that would be [^c08-4] reflected in the creation of the conciliar corpus, in those editions (with or without commentary) which communicated the texts of the council to the People of God who had participated in it _modo proprio_.

[^c08-3]: See Giuseppe Alberigo, ed., _Storia del concilio Vaticano II_, 5 vols, 2nd ed. (Bologna, 2012–15), and my ‘Post-scriptum’, 5:ix– xix. I cite the English translation: Alberigo, ed., _History of Vatican II_, ed. Joseph A. Komonchak (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1995– 2005); for bibliographical updates, see Alberto Melloni, ed., _Vatican II: The Complete History_ (Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 2015).

[^c08-4]: See Christoph Theobald, ‘Vatican II: Un corpus, un style, des conditions de réception’, _Laval théologique et philosophique_ 67, no. 4 (2011): 421–41. On the hermeneutics of theological statements, see Walter Kasper, _Teologia e Chiesa_ (Brescia: Queriniana, 1989), 302–12; and Christoph Theobald, ‘ “L’Herméneutique de réforme” implique-t-elle une réforme de l’herméneutique?’, _Recherches de science religieuse_ 100, no. 1 (2012): 65–84.

The task was by no means impartial and cannot be reduced to the fate of the many voices raised at the end of [^c08-5] Vatican II. The point was not, as one of the young theologians who would go on to attain the highest position in the Church, the future Benedict XVI, would later claim, a matter of _two_ hermeneutics [^c08-6] ‘quarrelling’ with each other. The post-conciliar phase of each council—and Vatican II was no exception— has been the terrain where dozens of interpretative readings clashed. Leaving aside the historical aspects, these different interpretations tried to reconstruct a posteriori alliances, canons, systematics capable of capturing the synodal language in a neo-scholastic syntax. In other words, they did exactly what Pope John XXIII sought to avoid because of the ‘new Pentecost’ that he had imagined and convoked with a primatial [^c08-7] act.

[^c08-5]: See Joseph Doré and Alberto Melloni, eds., _Volti di fine concilio: Saggi di teologia e storia sulla fine del Vaticano II_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2000).

[^c08-6]: See Massimo Faggioli, _Vatican II: The Battle for Meaning_ (Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 2012); on the interpretation of Benedict XVI’s address to the Roman Curia of 22 December 2005, see Joseph A. Komonchak, ‘Benedict XVI and the Interpretation of Vatican II’, _Cristianesimo nella storia_ 28 (2007): 323–37; Alberto Melloni, ‘Breve guida ai giudizi sul Vaticano II’, in _Chi ha_ _paura del Vaticano II?_, ed. Alberto Melloni and Giuseppe Ruggieri (Rome: Carocci, 2009), 107–45.

[^c08-7]: See Alberto Melloni, _Papa Giovanni: Un cristiano e il suo concilio_ (Turin: Einaudi, 2009), 195–225; John W. O’Malley, _What_ _Happened at Vatican II?_ (Cambridge, MA: The Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 2008), 15–18.

Towards the end of the conciliar proceedings on 8 December 1965 and at the outset of the reception process, the problem could not be reduced to a dialectic between the ‘letter’ and the ‘spirit’ of the council. Even this simplistic dichotomy, in fact, fails to capture adequately the historical reality of that period for at least two reasons.

On the one hand, the polarization between the letter and spirit of the council was used (in the opposite sense [^c08-8] to the New Testament model from which it originated) by both traditionalist and anti-conciliar factions to give equal value to those lines in which they remained, along with certain incipient formulas, mature doctrinal developments, and concessions in the opposite direction. The aim was to gain sufficient consent to [^c08-9] **[p. 135]** pass from the canonical majority to the quasi-unanimity desired by Paul VI. Indeed, Paul VI himself used [^c08-10] that polarization in an opposite sense, and not occasionally, when he defined how the spirit of the council was that capacity for synthesis experienced in the assembly to temper the implementation of some [^c08-11] decisions, especially those related to the liturgy.

[^c08-8]: Daniele Menozzi, ‘L’anticoncilio’, in _Il Vaticano II e la Chiesa_, ed. Giuseppe Alberigo and Jean-Pierre Jossua (Brescia: Paideia, 1985), 433–64; Philippe Roy, _Les Membres du Coetus Internationalis Patrum au concile Vatican II_ (Leuven: Peeters, 2014).

[^c08-9]: Norman Tanner, ‘How Novel Was Vatican II?’, _Ecclesiastical Law Journal_ 15, no. 2 (2013): 175–82.

[^c08-10]: On Paul VI’s use of that polarization, see Alberto Melloni, _Il concilio e la grazia: Saggi di storia sul concilio Vaticano II_ (Milan: Jaca Book, 2015), 612–14.

[^c08-11]: See the first-hand testimony of Annibale Bugnini, _The Reform of the Liturgy (1948–1975)_ (Collegeville MN: Liturgical Press, 1990); for an analysis, see Francis M. Mannion, ‘The Catholicity of the Liturgy: Shaping a New Agenda’, in _Beyond the_ _Prosaic: Renewing the Liturgical Movement_, ed. Strafford Caldecott (Edinburgh: T&T Clark, 1998), 11–48; Massimo Faggioli, _True Reform: Liturgy and Ecclesiology in Sacrosanctum Concilium_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2012); _Vatican Council_ _II: Reforming Liturgy_, ed. Carmel Pilcher, David Orr, and Elizabeth Harrington (Adelaide: ATF, 2013); Kevin Irwin, _What We_ _Have Done, What We Have Failed to Do: Assessing the Liturgical Reforms of Vatican II_ (New York: Paulist, 2014).

On the other hand, to provide an ‘order’ to the corpus—whether editorial or to ‘teach’ Vatican II to seminarians, priests, and laypeople—meant expressing a way of reading what took place between December 1965 and 1968, which is still considered something of a hot potato today.

One of the most interesting and revealing hypotheses is that formulated by Herbert Vorgrimler and Karl Rahner in the commentary which supplements the _Lexikon für Theologie und Kirche_. Beyond the positions expressed in the essays commenting on documents, it suggests an articulation based on the literary genre to which each segment of Vatican II belonged: dogmatic and pastoral constitutions, decrees, and [^c08-12] declarations. This proposal, at the upper level, left open the question of the primacy of _Dei Verbum_ or _Lumen Gentium_, but was not afraid of relegating to a lower position those texts, such as _Nostra Aetate_ or _Dignitatis Humanae_, which would prove to be among the most fruitful for a holistic reception of the [^c08-13] council.

[^c08-12]: For the history of the commentaries, see Peter Hünermann, ‘Einleitung’, in _Die Dokumente des Zweiten Vatikanischen_ _Konzils: Theologische Zusammenschau und Perspektiven_, in _Herders Theologischer Kommentar zum Zweiten Vatikanischen_ _Konzil_, ed. Bernd-Jochen Hilberath and Peter Hünermann (Freiburg i.B.: Herder, 2006), 5:1–101; the theological question is examined in Christoph Theobald, ‘Mise en perspective: Transmettre l’histoire del Vatican II ou/et commenter ses textes? Un débat nouveau sur la réception du Concile’, in _Vatican II sous le regard des historiens: Colloque du 23 septembre 2005,_ _Centre Sèvres–Facultés jésuites de Paris_, ed. Christoph Theobald (Paris: Médiasèvres, 2006), 3–23.

[^c08-13]: On Dossetti’s expression, see Giuseppe Ruggieri, ‘Cos’è stato il Vaticano II?’, in _A quarant’anni dal Concilio della speranza:_ _L’attualità del Vaticano II_, ed. Duilio Bonifazi and Edoardo Bressan (Macerata: Edizioni Università Macerata, 2008), 59–79.

Other readings, editions, collections, and commentaries (think of the great commentaries of L.A. Barauna, which have been translated into many languages) instead gave top priority to the Dogmatic Constitution on the Church (_Lumen Gentium_) along with, or as an alternative to, the Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World (_Gaudium et Spes_). The thinking here was, not without reason, that the conciliar agreement on ecclesiology had been the basis of the conclave of 1963, and that Paul VI, elected by that conclave, had brought the council to its completion in 1965.

### 2. The Expunged Documents

**[p. 136]** A common but revealing point of these two perspectives was the deletion from the list of conciliar documents of the messages delivered during the first session on 20 October 1962 and at the close of the council in December 1965 (messages to heads of state, to scientists, to women, to the poor, to the sick and suffering, to workers, and to youth). This genre, which ranks alongside the constitutions, decrees, and declarations with equal dignity, was instead downgraded in the _editio typica_ (the official Latin version) of the documents of Vatican II prepared in Rome as an example of how the historical understanding of the council as an event is marked by a before and an after, even in its own philology.

It is worth noting that the messages expunged by a systematic and anti-historical reading of the conciliar corpus are concentrated in two precise moments of time during the council. The first forgotten text is _Message to the World_ (_Ad omnes homines ac nationes nuntium_), approved by the council fathers on 20 October 1962 by an indicative vote as they stood up or remained seated in their places. This text was expunged from the _editio typica_ of the texts of Vatican II produced in Rome by the former General Secretariat of the council.

That short text approved just a week after the opening of the council would constitute an incomprehensible anomaly to the council fathers and to post-conciliar theologians. It was voted on by standing up, a very [^c08-14] traditional method of conciliar deliberation. But the various editions of the conciliar texts do not include it, referring instead (and inexplicably) to an imaginary classification of ‘sixteen’ documents.

[^c08-14]: Also, the Bolognese edition: Josephus Alberigo et al. (eds.), Huberto Jedin (consultant), _Conciliorum Oecumenicorum_ _Decreta_ (Bononiae: Istituto per le scienze religiose, 1973).

Why this _damnatio_? Perhaps because it did not undergo a proper hearing procedure and did not pass with the usual approvals? Was it due to a papist hypercorrectness that did not recognize the authority of the council, one that spoke with its own voice (a synodal voice that includes Peter’s successor) and did not require an official act of modern papal promulgation (i.e., a papal signature: _Ego PP_ …)? Or perhaps there was an instinctive antipathy in some Roman circles to a text that originated from two French Dominican theologians, Yves Congar and Marie-Dominique Chenu, who had been the bêtes noires of the Holy Office?[^c08-15]

[^c08-15]: See Étienne Fouilloux, ‘L’Affaire Chenu 1937–1943’, _Revue des sciences philosophiques et théologiques_ 98, no. 2 (2014): 261– 352; Yves Congar, ‘Mon témoignage’, in his _Journal d’un théologien, 1946–1956_, ed. Étienne Fouilloux (Paris: Cerf, 2000), 57– 62; Dominique Dubarle, ‘Le Temps des enthousiasmes’, in _L’Hommage différé au père Chenu_ (Paris: Cerf, 1990), 194–206. See André Duval, ‘Le Message au monde’, in _Vatican II commence … Approches francophones_, ed. Étienne Fouilloux (Leuven: Peeters, 1993), 105–18; Marie-Dominique Chenu, _Notes quotidiennes au Concile_, ed. Alberto Melloni (Paris: Cerf, 1995); Yves Congar, _Mon journal du Concile_, ed. Éric Mahieu (Paris: Cerf, 2002).

[^c08-16] **[p. 137]** The question of the origin of the message should perhaps not be dismissed entirely. However, the two Dominicans (the only ones in the twentieth century who could boast the double title of historian and theologian) who were the authors of the _Message to the World_, had conceived those few lines on the basis of an erroneous conviction. Congar and Chenu were convinced, during the preparatory phase and in light of the documents produced in that first phase, that Vatican II would be a disaster if the council fathers came away from the first session without having spoken. Roman scholastic theology—fractured by the clash between various close-minded schools, cut oft from international networks, and rooted in a repression that in the 1950s had taken on the features of a theological totalitarianism—had poured into the preparatory schemas its visions, idiosyncrasies, and subservience to a curial structure dominated by clerics and guided by the logic of condemnation. It was not pessimistic to assume that an episcopate formed in that environment, and often with those same Roman professors, would have approved everything prepared between 1960 and 1962, and that John XXIII’s sincere desire for a ‘new Pentecost’ might have resulted in a funeral procession for all those involved in movements of renewal, except for the liturgical reform. Only the latter’s ability to make use of the great ancient tradition to question the practices of an anti-modern obsession, which, after all, was rather recent, helped the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy to pass without a hitch.

[^c08-16]: Etienne Fouillous, _Le message au monde,_ in _Vatican II commence… Approches francophones_ (Leuven: Bibliotheek van de Faculteit der Godgeleerdheid, 1993), 105–18.

Moreover, even in John XXIII’s radio message of 11 September 1962—which, according to Cardinal Leo Jozef Suenens who had drafted it, should have been the opening speech of the council—there were no signs suggesting that the pope was willing to set aside a preparation led by the Curia, to which he had guaranteed an unexpected autonomy of action. The Curia, in turn, was preparing to seal its victory by simply transforming the preparatory commissions into conciliar commissions. Their victory was considered so certain by those who had led the preparations that they did not consider dangerous the idea that Chenu helped to spread in the days before the start of the council: the idea of a brief message ‘to the world’, which [^c08-17] would allow those like him to have a word or two imbued with the authority of the council. ‘A few pages’ is how the cardinal of Genoa, Giuseppe Siri—a leading figure in Italian conservative circles and beyond, and a [^c08-18] potential candidate for all conclaves of the second half of the twentieth century—described them. What harm could there ever be in ‘a few pages’, even if they came from the French Dominicans who were considered to be the bêtes noires and subjected to the ‘wrath’ of being expunged by the Holy Office?

[^c08-17]: Chenu, _Notes quotidiennes au Concile_.

[^c08-18]: See Nicla Buonasorte, _Siri—Tradizione e Novecento_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2006).

Thus, those few pages did not go through the preparatory commissions, which indeed had changed, in comparison to those of the preparatory phase, when the assembly imposed its first decisive will during the [^c08-19] **[p. 138]** first general congregation. The text of the future _Message to the World_ instead went through what would be the qualifying instances of Vatican II: the Belgian team, the colleges, the informal groups. The author of the message, Chenu, had the impression that his brainchild was ‘drowned in holy water’. But if he wanted a ‘citable’ text within the dull theory of curial and Roman schemas destined for approval, he achieved what he was looking for. All that it was believed Vatican II might never achieve—the Church of the poor, collegiality, unity, the primacy of the Word, the push for liturgical and ecumenical renewal—found a home in those few lines.

[^c08-19]: See Alberigo, _History of Vatican II_, 2:50–54; O’Malley, _What Happened at Vatican II?_, 99; Melloni, _Vatican II: The Complete_ _History_, 120–21.

However, it is a fact that the message, due to an extremely serious conciliar error, remains marginalized. Even in the present volume it is treated as ‘supplementary’ material, to use an expression that diminishes its importance and continues to foster a manualistic, rather than a historical-critical, conception of Vatican II.

The second example of a forgotten text is the _Nuntia_ at the closing of the council on 8 December 1965. In chiasmatic relationship with the _Message to the World_, announced nine days after the solemn opening of Vatican II, we find the seven messages read in St Peter’s Square on 8 December 1965 and delivered to a series of recipients chosen according to a very clear symbolic protocol. It addressed, in succession, world leaders; the world of culture and science; artists; women; workers; the poor, the sick, and the suffering; and [^c08-20] young people. These messages—_This Is a Unique Moment_; _A Very Special Message_; _To All of You Now_; _And Now_; and _During This Council_—undoubtedly were in all respects part of the conciliar corpus. They were created as messages from the conciliar fathers, including Peter’s successor. They were read before the council in liturgical and solemn session and were approved by acclamation in a traditional way of the Church. Yet they, too, were expunged from the conciliar corpus and forgotten, even at the earliest stages of the post-conciliar period.

[^c08-20]: See Alberigo, _History of Vatican II_, 5:549–552; Alberto Melloni, ed., _Conciliorum oecumenicorum generaliumque decreta:_ _Editio critica_, 3 vols (Turnhout: Brepols, 2006–13), 3: 628–36; O’Malley, _What Happened at Vatican II?_, 288–89; Melloni, _Vatican II: The Complete History_, 236–23.

The reasons, in this case, are more complex. Once again, those texts did not go through the channels of the assembly even though these were by now working efficiently and were capable—as seen in the fourth and last period—of working on several issues with a technical-procedural consistency unthinkable in 1962. But these messages were not moved by the same sense of urgency as the one conceived by the two theologians who were still not freed from inquisitorial suspicions (Chenu never would be; Congar would be only after his elevation to cardinal in November 1994, a few months before his death), but by the _mens_ of the first conciliar father, the pope himself. In the messages of 8 December 1965, in fact, we can see the attempt to incorporate in the conciliar provision the principle of ‘dialogue’, theorized in Paul VI’s 1964 encyclical, _Ecclesiam Suam_. If the Chenu–Congar foray into the opening _Nuntium_ is qualitatively high, despite the oblivion in which it is still immersed, that of the closing ceremonies, imbued with Montini’s ethos, is less vibrant.

**[p. 139]** Those messages might have been delivered within a conclusive magniloquent choreography like the one Hélder Câmara, archbishop of Recife, envisioned as a sort of final liturgy. Câmara had imagined a ceremony where the pope would leave the basilica and ask the bishops for forgiveness for the abuses of power committed by the Chair of Peter. Then, after receiving forgiveness, the pope and the bishops would ask forgiveness of the faithful, women, Jews, members of other religious traditions, and of the contemporary [^c08-21] world, culminating in a penitential tone and triumphant staging. Montini instead opted for a mutual dialogue with the ‘categories’ of those that the pastoralist jargon of the time defined as ‘the distant ones’.

[^c08-21]: See Hélder Câmara, _Vaticano II: Correspondência conciliar; Circulares á família do São Joaquim_, ed. Luiz Carlos Marques, in _Obras completas_, 1 (Recife: Editora Universitária da Universidade Federal de Pernambuco Recife, 2004–12).

Written, for this reason, in French and without a Latin version, these final messages were not composed in the forms of constitutions, decrees, and declarations, but, like those, they could still claim an intrinsic [^c08-22] value. Moreover, they were preceded by another ‘message’—usually also considered part of the acts and not the decisions of the council—that is, the lifting of the excommunications between Rome and Constantinople, proclaimed on 7 December 1965.

[^c08-22]: See the discussion concerning the authority of the various conciliar documents in Melloni, _Vatican II: The Complete History_, 6–13; Melloni, _Conciliorum oecumenicorum generaliumque decreta: Editio critica_, 3:639–40; _AS_ III/ 8, 10–13.

With two solemn acts, read in French in St Peter’s conciliar hall (not at the Lateran, seat of the pope, but in the presence of Vatican II) and, at the same time, in Greek in St George’s Cathedral, seat of the Ecumenical Patriarchate in Constantinople (Istanbul), the throne of St Andrew and the See of St Peter removed the mutual excommunications of 1054. It was a watershed moment, stemming from a sudden acceleration along the ecumenical path which, prior to John XXIII, was characterized by a recalcitrant Roman Catholic Church; after the embrace in Jerusalem between the pope and the Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras in January 1964, this had become a priority agenda. Thus, the ‘Catholic ecumenism’ that Congar had defended [^c08-23] even at the cost of being condemned by what he called the Roman ‘Gestapo’ emerged as a permanent dimension of the life of the Church of Rome and of its pastor at the council and with the council.

[^c08-23]: The expression is used by Congar in _Journal d’un théologien_.

Supported by the presence and participation of the observers of the other churches in the conciliar works, Vatican II thus presents a new type of ecumenicity. It is not the classical one of the seven councils convened by the Christian emperor to gather all the bishops of the political _oikumene_, or the Bellarminian type; namely, a council where the pope’s actions—to convene, regulate, preside, and promulgate—conferred universal value to the Church of Rome, thus making it, in his opinion, ‘ecumenical’. Rather, the ecumenical nature of Vatican II must be understood in the entirely modern sense of an experience of encounter and liturgical communion (in its essence, the council is a liturgical act) on the path towards visible unity.

**[p. 140]** For this reason, the ceremony of lifting the excommunications between Rome and Constantinople was held while the council was still officially in session (_concilio sedente_) and is part of the council’s history, even though it would only became part of the conciliar corpus with the critical edition of the _Conciliorum_ [^c08-24] _Oecumenicorum Generaliumque Decreta_ of 2008. This did not happen on an erudite whim, but rather to suggest that the council must be interpreted through its history. The inclusion of these documents is necessary to organize its internal and external doctrinal production. Without them, the council might remain imprisoned in a _glossa ordinaria_ which could lead the reader to ignore its most powerful and profound characteristics, including its principal aim of fostering unity.

[^c08-24]: See Melloni, _Conciliorum oecumencorum genraliumque decreta: Editio critica_, 3: 550–52; _AS_ IV/ 7, 652–54.

The text elaborated by the delegation of the Phanar and the Secretariat for Christian Unity, led by Cardinal Augustin Bea, presents itself as an act of obedience in which the churches respond to the call of that divine grace, bringing two churches to ‘overcome their differences’ to realize the unity that Jesus asked for in his prayer to the Father, as in the Gospel of John 17:21. Among the principal obstacles were the mutual excommunications of 1054. The churches ‘cannot pretend that these events were not what they were’, but, in the light of history, they can affirm that the intention was not a perpetual break of communion. And it is for this historical reason (‘c’est pourquoi’) that the pope and the patriarch assume the attitude commanded by the Lord: before presenting their gifts at the altar, they are reconciled with a text that declares the will to ‘regret’ and ‘deplore’ the offences, gestures, sentences, and suspicions that have marked the centuries that now end with this act, which opens instead a path of purification.

Signed by Paul VI, the text was read at the council and accompanied by a kiss of peace between the secretary of the Secretariat for Christian Unity, Archbishop Johannes Willebrands, and Metropolitan Meliton, the Phanar delegate. The symbolic gesture was met with applause from the council, marking its significance, which had an undeniable historical and theological value, albeit a neglected one.

### 3. Forgotten Interpretative Keys

The expunging of the conciliar messages obeys a dehistoricization of Vatican II, which marked the great season of the conciliar commentaries, as if the meaning and implication of the event could be found in what was voted and not what happened. As evidence of this trend and its consequences, in terms of the global understanding of the event and what defines it, it is worth considering the fate of a few other papal texts/documents. They are inscribed in the council and, while not in any way part of the decisions of Vatican II, they serve nonetheless as interpretative keys. Other casualties of this tendency to forget essential texts in **[p. 141]** conciliar history are John XXIII’s two fundamental addresses announcing the council in 1959 and his opening address in 1962, which gave Vatican II its particular imprint; Paul VI’s address at the beginning of the second period of the council in September 1963; and the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy promulgated by Paul VI in December 1963. The neglect of these texts shows how the relevance of those interpretative keys was even then difficult to grasp in all its significance.

#### The Feast of the Conversion of St Paul, 25 January 1959

That unity which at the end of the council came to dictate the agenda of the post-conciliar Church was already present at the beginning of Vatican II, in the act with which John XXIII convoked it. The council he envisioned was intended not as an opportunity to close Vatican I, which Pius IX suspended indefinitely after the Franco-Prussian War, but as a ‘banquet of grace’ open to the mystical commensality of the churches.

Announcing on 25 January 1959 the primatial decision to convene a new council (a ‘Second’ Vatican Council; for that reason, the previous Vatican council would come to be known as the ‘First’ Vatican Council following these events), Pope John XXIII placed his choice in a wider context. It was the same decision he had communicated to the Secretary of State a few days earlier and to which the newly elevated cardinal [^c08-25] Domenico Tardini adhered, perhaps underestimating the timeline that the ageing Roncalli had in mind. Thus, on that same day, Roncalli announced the reform of the Code of Canon Law, a Roman diocesan synod, [^c08-26] and, almost as if it were something of the same import, a ‘general council’. As he was an expert in conciliar history, stemming from a scholarly inclination that marked his formation and career, Roncalli’s use of the word ‘general’ was not casual as he read from the text of his announcement in the sacristy of the Basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls. Gathered in consistory, the pope read it in the presence of a mere seventeen cardinals, a small number compared to the seventy who at that time held that title. We know from Monsignor Josep Höfer, who was behind the pope as assistant cleric and who reported the news to the chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany, Konrad Adenauer, that it was from those ‘seven handwritten [^c08-27] pages’ that the pope read the address which would lead to Vatican II. The council was defined as a ‘general’ rather than an ‘ecumenical’ one. This choice did not deprive the assembly of significance but was rather proof of the knowledge of the sensitivity of the other churches, above all of those of the Christian East. It also served to make more acceptable the complex sentence, typical of Roncalli’s style, stating the desire that ‘other churches’ ‘participate with us’ in ‘this banquet of grace’, by which he meant the council. In Roncalli’s **[p. 142]** intention, therefore, there is a conscious redefinition of the ‘ecumenicity’ of the future council, marked by the participation of Christians of the other churches and desired from the very moment of his decision to [^c08-28] convoke it. But in the way the announcement was made by the Vatican press, nothing remained of those subtle nuances: what the pope called ‘churches’ became ‘communities’; the ‘general’ council became ‘ecumenical’, like the previous one; instead of equal participation, the other churches were said to merely [^c08-29] ‘follow’. However, Pope John’s intention of unity is still apparent; it makes this unknown text of the address in which he announced his intention to convoke the council a sort of watermark discernible through the long spring of 1959, when everyone thought that the unity of the separated churches was an imminent [^c08-30] possibility.

[^c08-25]: Melloni, _Papa Giovanni e il suo concilio_, 210–14.

[^c08-26]: Pope John, in his manuscript, defines it as a ‘general’ council. On the importance of this, see Alberto Melloni, ‘Concili, ecumenicità e storia: Note di discussion’, _Cristianesimo nella storia_ 28 (2007): 509–42; also Melloni, _Il concilio e la grazia_, 633–64.

[^c08-27]: Melloni, _Papa Giovanni e il suo concilio_, 216.

[^c08-28]: Giuseppe Alberigo, _Transizione epocale: Studi sul Concilio Vaticano II_ (Bologna, 2009), 325–50; for another perspective, see Mauro Velati, _Separati ma fratelli: Gli osservatori non cattolici al Vaticano II (1962–1965)_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2014).

[^c08-29]: Melloni, _Papa Giovanni e il suo concilio_, 224.

[^c08-30]: Mauro Velati, _Una difficile transizione: Il Cattolicesimo tra unionismo ed ecumenismo (1952–1964)_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 1996).

#### Gaudet Mater Ecclesia, 11 October 1962

The unity of the Church would not be the main theme of the preparatory period. The handing over of the entire preparatory machine to the autonomy of the Roman Curia was a choice John XXIII would not revoke —nor was it revocable. A source of bewilderment for many, that mountain of schemas destined to crumble at the opening of the council would also be the reason for those sentiments mentioned earlier that convinced theologians like Chenu and Congar to write that first _Message to the World_ as a possible guarantee clause for a council that many feared might fail.

But precisely the freedom guaranteed to the Roman Curia engendered the freedom that the pope kept for himself when they tried to force his hand with an encyclical on the use of Latin, intended to undermine the ongoing liturgical reform—a freedom that the pope intended to guarantee to the council. He would eventually defend it again against the regulatory language when the will of the assembly appeared vulnerable to the filibustering of the conservative minority.[^c08-31]

[^c08-31]: On the downfall of the _De fontibus_, see Alberigo, _History of Vatican II_, 2:233–66; O’Malley, _What Happened at Vatican II?_, 141–52; Melloni, _Vatican II: The Complete History_, 138–39.

The link between these two freedoms—of pope and council—was clear, especially in the opening address, _Gaudet Mater Ecclesia_. In the long season of conciliar commentaries and conciliar nominalism, little weight was given to it. The former, in fact, considered the celebration of the council as a sort of threshing machine in which exciting and dramatic things had certainly happened but which ultimately delivered a corpus to an uneven intellectual theological reflection. This approach considered it appropriate to use parts of the corpus **[p. 143]** of decisions or acts, or equivalent theological literature, or the papal magisterium, whenever it became [^c08-32] necessary. Punctuated by the question of the corpus, this approach would give to the _Nota explicativa praevia_ to chapter 3 of _Lumen Gentium_ (a commission act that never claimed to become a conciliar act, and to which Paul VI never gave particular coverage apart from ordering to have it read to the assembly) the status of an ecclesiological principle and source of very distant events in time. One of the consequences of this attitude was the project of a _Lex ecclesiae fundamentalis_, which, if passed, would have changed forever the [^c08-33][^c08-34] Church’s self-understanding, or the creation of a doctrinal policy on the definitive magisterium, as an [^c08-35] alternative to the infallible one, which was so well delimited by Vatican I to have become in fact unusable.

[^c08-32]: For example, the commentary of the future John Paul II. See Robert Skrzypczak, _Karol Wojtyla na Soborze Watykanskim II:_ _Zbiór Wystapien_ (Warsaw: Centrum Myśli Jana Pawła II, 2011).

[^c08-33]: The battle against _Lex Ecclesiae Fundamentalis_ is marked by a work promoted by Alberigo and now included in _Legge e_ _Vangelo: Discussione su una legge fondamentale per la Chiesa_ (Brescia: Paideia, 1971); Daniel Cenalmor, ‘Ley fundamental de la Iglesia’, in _Diccionario General de Derecho Canonico_, ed. Javier Otaduy, Antonio Viana, and Joaquín Sedano (Pamplona: EUNSA, 2013), 5:80–87; Luigi Rosa, ‘La “Lex Ecclesiae Fundamentalis”: Il lungo e faticoso “iter” di un progetto’, _Aggiornamenti sociali_ (1977): 319–26.

[^c08-34]: On the note _Ad tuendam fidem_ issued by the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith in 1998, see ‘Disciplinare la verità?’, special issue _Cristianesimo nella storia_ 21 (2000).

[^c08-35]: See Christoph Theobald, ‘La Constitution dogmatique Dei Filius du concile de Vatican I’, in _La Parole du salut_ (Paris: Desclée, 1996), 259–313.

Conciliar nominalism, on the other hand, needed only a _legenda_ of Vatican II, of which Jean Guitton, in a television interview, ultimately provided the most elaborate literal synthesis: the council is like ‘a Caravelle’ (a French jet airliner): John XXIII took it to high and dangerous altitudes, and Paul VI brought it back, intact, [^c08-36] to earth. End of story: a story in which everything was reduced to details, learned minutiae, and historical curiosities in the most derivative sense of the term.

[^c08-36]: See Federico Ruozzi, _Il concilio in diretta: Il Vaticano II e la televisione tra partecipazione e informazione_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2012).

It is only when the work of historicizing Roncalli’s papacy and Vatican II begins, in the 1980s, that new [^c08-37] questions begin to shed new light on the sources and reveal new ones. In the wake of the lesson of Hubert Jedin, the leading historian of the Council of Trent and one of the great historians of the twentieth century, Giuseppe Alberigo proposed interrogating the sources not so much to know how the conciliar decisions were reached as to understand the conciliar event in its historical objectivity: without compromising its interpretation, without being dominated by its ‘documents’, or by the external sequencing of the phases of an assembly that was punctuated by intercessions. Instead, the aim was to grasp, in the event as such, an object worthy of historical investigation. In this perspective, what becomes essential is understanding the way in which the conception of the council by John XXIII allowed a vision opposed to the curial perspective **[p. 144]** to be freely expressed and how this, in turn, guaranteed that same freedom to the assembly and to the pope himself. The text of the opening address of the council is, in this respect, a fundamental starting point.

[^c08-37]: See Enrico Galavotti, ‘ “È un cristiano sul serio”: Alberigo e l’interpretazione di Giovanni XXIII’, in ‘Giuseppe Alberigo (1926– 2007): La figura e l’opera storiografica’, special issue _Cristianesimo nella storia_ 29, no. 3 (2008): 761–874.

In the address delivered at the opening session of the council on 11 October 1962, _Gaudet Mater Ecclesia_, the freedom that the curial machine and the Roman schools had used—with the sole exception of the commission on the liturgy—in a short-sighted logic, becomes the moment for the pope to freely lay out his vision for Vatican II.

John XXIII’s inspiration was a vision, not a programme. And a programme was shared by the leaders of what was to become the conciliar majority, and what the conclave of 1963 would hope for. For while everyone, starting from Montini, was preparing to demand a structuring of the agenda that would make the council look a little more like a handbook, Roncalli instead enunciated his own idea of the council: a necessary act intended to avoid repeating what had been and to make instead that ‘leap forward’ in understanding the [^c08-38] Gospel in an era where Messianic signs were discernible, an act that authoritatively distinguished the substance of the Gospel from its doctrinal form, whose transformation was not intended as an adaptation to modernity but as an act of fidelity to the Gospel itself.

[^c08-38]: For an overview, see the sources cited by Gilles Routhier, ‘ “Les Signes du temps”: Fortune et infortune d’une expression du Concile Vatican II’, _Transversalités_ 2, no. 118 (2011): 77–102. For a historical theological analysis, see Giuseppe Ruggieri, ‘Zeichen der Zeit: Herkunff und Bedeutung einer christlich-hermeneutischen Chiffre der Geschichte’, and Christoph Theobald, ‘Zur Theologie der Zeichen der Zeit. Bedeutung und Kriterien heute’, in _Das Zweite Vatikanische Konsil und die_ _Zeichen der Zeit heute_, ed. Peter Hünermann (Freiburg i.B.: Herder, 2006), 61–70, 71–84.

Finally, in that opening address, Roncalli articulated his own conception of the ‘pastoral’ dimension of the magisterium. It is a conception so complex and refined as to be incomprehensible to the ‘baroque’ culture that considered pastorality as a set of compromises and tricks or of indulgences and simplifications providing the people with what they were able to understand, leaving untouched, immovable, and distant a doctrine understood as a fixed reality. For Roncalli, the question was exactly the inverse: the pastoral is the evangelical duty to proclaim the Gospel, which must continually _aggiornare_ (update) the doctrinal language [^c08-39] to prevent it from becoming an obstacle to the understanding of the Gospel itself.
