This idea made inroads in the assembly and slowly shaped the conscience of Vatican II which, thanks to the orientation provided by [^c08-40] John XXIII, would develop its own identity in the subsequent weeks of November 1962.

[^c08-39]: On the issue of pastorality, see Christoph Theobald, ‘Le Style pastoral de Vatican II et sa réception postconciliaire: Élaboration d’une critériologie et quelques exemples significatifs’, in _Vatican II comme style: L’Herméneutique théologique_ _du Concile_, ed. Joseph Famerée (Paris: Cerf, 2012), 267–288.

[^c08-40]: See Alberigo, _History of Vatican II_, 2:566–84; Melloni, _Vatican II: The Complete History_, 106–40; Enrico Galavotti, ‘Il concilio continua: Giovanni XXIII e la lettera “Mirabilis Ille” of 6 January 1963: Introduzione e sinossi critica’, in _Tutto è grazia: In_ _omaggio a Giuseppe Ruggieri_, ed. Alberto Melloni (Milan: Jaca Book, 2010), 115–69.

#### Salvete, Fratres, 29 September 1963

**[p. 145]** The address with which Paul VI opened the second conciliar session in September 1963 and which he, expressing the view of the conciliar majority, presented to the assembly, does not have the same importance and weight as _Gaudet Mater Ecclesia_. As he did throughout the council, Montini felt the need to reassure the (conservative) minority, which would remain hostile towards him for the rest of his life and even after his death. For Paul VI, the council was an epiphany of the Church’s ‘hierarchical orders’, and he placed the [^c08-41] theme of the Church at the centre of his address. The chances that Paul VI’s remarks concerning the Church would be accepted by the minority, who would make him its target in the following twelve months, were minimal. Despite citing Pius XII, Montini anticipated the document that would become _Lumen Gentium_: a collegiality that places the relationship between Peter and the apostles in symmetrical relation to that between pope and bishops.

[^c08-41]: He began his speech by saying, ‘Salvete, Fratres in Christo dilectissimi, quos undecumque gentium vocavimus, quo sancta et catholica Ecclesia suae protulit _Hierarchiae_ ordines’.

While distancing himself from the language of _aggiornamento_ and reform, Paul VI nevertheless explicitly and expressly recalled Pope John’s conciliar vision: he paid homage to his predecessor; to the convocation of the council; to _Gaudet_ (while omitting the reprimand against the prophets of doom and emphasizing the other, so-called pastoral, task). However, he also set four goals for the conciliar works: ‘conscientia Ecclesiae, eius renovatio, unitatis redintegratio inter christianos universos, et Ecclesiae collocutio cum nostrae aetatis hominibus’ (the conscience of the Church, its reform, the restoration of unity among all Christians, and the dialogue of the Church with contemporary humanity).

After excluding the need for ecclesiological dogmas, Paul VI reveals the parameters of the dialogue that the Church sought to initiate, which, apart from the theme of Christian unity, concern precisely the ‘worlds’ of political powers, cultures, and work. These concerns were to return in the final message of the council to the world, where, in addition, women would also make an appearance.

#### Una cum patribus

Another reason for not including John XXIII’s announcement of the council of January 1959 in the editions of the conciliar documents had to do with the fact that for a few decades, what was alive and hidden beneath the ashes of the protocol imposed on the pope’s manuscript was ignored. On the other hand, a formula of approval of the conciliar documents, which has a lot to do with unity, made the cut. The formula was worded by the Italian canon and constitutional lawyer Fr Giuseppe Dossetti, German church historian Fr Hubert **[p. 146]** Jedin, and Italian church historian Giuseppe Alberigo. As Alberigo himself pointed out in a scrupulous [^c08-42] essay, Paul VI did not adopt the formula of Vatican I, recovered in the regulation of Vatican II and elaborated by the General Secretariat of Archbishop Pericle Felici, but, with unchanged rules, made the solemn proclamation his own:

[^c08-42]: Giuseppe Alberigo, ‘ “Una cum patribus”: La formula conclusiva delle decisioni del Vaticano II’, in _Ecclesia a Spiritu Sanctu_ _edocta: Mélanges théologiques; Hommage à Mgr Gérard Philips_ (Gembloux: Duculot, 1970), 291–319.

In nomine Sanctissimae et Individuae Trinitatis Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti. Decreta, quae in hac sacrosancta et universali synodo Vaticana secunda legitime congregata modo lecta est, sunt placuerunt Patribus. Et Nos, Apostolica a Christo nobis tradita potestate, illam, una cum Venerabilibus Patribus, in Spiritu Sancta approbamus, decernimus ac statuimus, et quae ita synodaliter statuta sunt ad Dei gloriam promulgari iubemus.

(In the name of the Holy and Undivided Trinity of Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The decrees, which have been read in this holy and universal Second Vatican Council, legitimately assembled, were approved by the Fathers. And we, by virtue of the apostolic power which We have from Christ, in union with the venerable Fathers, We approve them, resolve and decree in the Holy Spirit, and We order that what has thus been established in Council be promulgated for the glory of God.)

That phrase ‘una cum Venerabilibus Patribus’ had a doctrinal value of great significance and expressed a theology of primacy in which there is a shift from the lexical prominence of the papal _ego_, which dominated the syntax of the promulgation of Vatican I, to Vatican II’s large-scale adoption of the conciliar tradition of the East and West.

It is therefore surprising, but understandable, that this formula, which did not reveal the pope as _solus_ agent but included the signature of the bishop of Rome together with that of the other bishops, was amended and [^c08-43] altered in the _Acta Apostolicae Sedis_. The ecumenical need and the demand for collegiality had taken a prominent place in the very conscience of the papacy and the whole Church, which only two years earlier appeared to Chenu so incapable of reform or _aggiornamento_. It was a turning point that provoked reactions of censorship and revisions comparable to those mentioned above.

[^c08-43]: Ibid., n. 11 notes the changes in the _AAS_ 56 (1964), 134.

Thus, the formula was not repeated in the closing apostolic letter of the council, _In Spiritu Sancto Congregatum_, of 8 December, which ratifled the canonical validity of the conciliar decisions, but which gave a quadripartition (_Constitutiones, Decreta, Declarationes et Vota_, ‘Constitutions, Decrees, Declarations and Votes’) broader than the one that has had a considerable weight in discussions on the council and its reception.[^c08-44]

[^c08-44]: In the closing brief, apart from the remarkable beginning where the council is said to be ‘assembled in the Holy Spirit’, the wording of the canonical ratification of the decisions returns. However, following the Tridentine model, it constitutes a universal approval of the _corpus ‘ad omnes iuris effectus’_.

### 4. Conclusion

**[p. 147]** At this point in our path, it should be clear that the question of the conciliar corpus, after Alberigo’s historicization of the council and the redefinition of the normative question of the style of Vatican II faced by Christoph Theobald, does not permit—or, better, should no longer allow—a graduation of the texts based on an ideological orientation. The pastoral and dogmatic qualification cannot be used to cut up, as in Zeno’s paradox, the scope of Vatican II’s decisions. Nor can the council endure a literary type of classification that differentiates the weight of the constitutions from the other documents in a descending order with supplementary and insignificant materials at the bottom of the pile. The torn limbs of Vatican II have their own unity that is not created by the homogeneity of the generating process or despite the inhomogeneity of the process that each followed, but by the global meaning of an event. The corpus of the conciliar documents is a lens that magnifles the eye that scrutinizes it.

Paris: Médiasèvres, 2006.

## 9. The Constitution on Sacred Liturgy

John F. Baldovin, SJ

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 148]** Mother Church earnestly desires that all the faithful should be led to that full, conscious, and active participation in liturgical celebrations which is demanded by the very nature of the liturgy, and to which the Christian people ‘a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a redeemed people’ (1 Pet. 2:9, 4-5), have a right and obligation by reason of their baptism … for it [the liturgy] is the primary and indispensable source from which the faithful are to derive the true Christian spirit. (_SC_ 14)

_Sacrosanctum Concilium_ (_SC_), the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy, was approved on 4 December 1963. It was the first of the council’s documents and has been widely regarded as having far-reaching effect, perhaps more than any other conciliar document as far as ordinary Catholics are concerned. The aim of this chapter is threefold: to discuss the significance of the document itself and its context in the liturgical movement of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, to situate it within the council documents, and to reflect on its implementation and reception.

### 2. The Liturgy Constitution in the Light of the Liturgical Movement

_Sacrosanctum Concilium_ was the fruit of several centuries of scholarship and pastoral experience. Although the liturgy of the Roman Rite remained relatively stable in the centuries following the Council of Trent, a [^c09-1] **[p. 149]** massive amount of historical and textual scholarship revealed that Trent’s desire to return to the norm [^c09-2] of the Early Fathers was greatly impeded by a lack of historical sources. These studies, as well as the philosophical concerns of the Enlightenment, led to decrees of the Synod of Pistoia (Tuscany) in 1786 under Bishop Scipione de’ Ricci. In liturgical terms, the synod decreed a major streamlining and modernization of the liturgy, for example, by decreeing that there be only one altar in a church, as well as limiting statues and processions. Although its decrees were swiftly suppressed by Pope Pius VI (1794), much of Pistoia’s agenda survived in _Sacrosanctum Concilium_.

[^c09-1]: Some of the better known early liturgical scholars are Jean Mabillon (d. 1707), Edmund Martène (d. 1739), Giuseppe Tommasi (d. 1713), Ludovico Muratori (d. 1750), and Giovanni Mercati (d. 1865).

[^c09-2]: To restore ‘the Missal itself to the original form and rite of the holy Fathers’, in Pope Pius V, ‘_Quo Primum:_ Promulgating the Tridentine Liturgy [1570]’, Papal Encyclicals Online, 22 February 2018, http://www.papalencyclicals.net/pius05/p5quopri.htm.

The twentieth-century liturgical movement which produced _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ had diverse starting points. One major step in the previous century was the establishment of the Benedictine monastery of Solesmes in France by Prosper Guéranger in 1833. Guéranger was determined to restore Gregorian chant as well as to remove neo-Gallican elements particular to French dioceses especially after the Reformation, from the Roman Rite. At the same time there was a revival of interest in the Early Church (the Tractarians or Oxford Movement) and medieval liturgy (the Cambridge Camden Society) in England. Shortly after his election to the papacy, Pope Pius X issued a motu proprio entitled _Tra le Sollecitudini_ (_Among the Concerns_) (1903), calling for the restoration of Gregorian chant. It was this document that provided inspiration for the memorable phrase about active participation in liturgy as the indispensable font of the Christian life in our quotation above.

The true twentieth-century liturgical movement, however, is widely considered to have begun with a Belgian Benedictine, Lambert Beauduin, who founded the abbeys of Mont-César and Chèvetogne in Belgium and encouraged more popular liturgical knowledge and participation by means of educating the laity on the nature and meaning of worship. A number of other pioneers followed, including Romano Guardini, Pius Parsch, Odo Casel, and (in the United States) Virgil Michel. On an official level, following the Second World War, Pope Pius XII issued an encyclical on the liturgy entitled _Mediator Dei_ (1947), which gave a blessing (albeit a rather conservative one) to the liturgical movement and prompted the establishment (in 1948) of a papal commission for the reform of the liturgy.

Although many of the liturgical reforms inspired by Vatican II seem bold, it should not be forgotten that the 1950s saw some significant reforms, including the reform of the Holy Saturday Vigil (1953) and the rest of the Holy Week liturgies (1956) as well as the shortening of the fast required before receiving Holy Communion: from midnight to three hours and, eventually, one hour. These reforms were a foretaste of the reforms later undertaken by the council.

### 3. The Constitution

#### Preparation: Early Schemas

**[p. 150]** As with other areas that the council would deal with, a preparatory Liturgical Commission prepared the [^c09-3] early drafts or schemata of _Sacrosanctum Concilium_. The commission divided into subcommittees to deal with a number of issues, including participation of the faithful, the Eucharist, the other sacraments, the Liturgy of the Hours, the liturgical year, music, art, and particular subjects like concelebration and the [^c09-4] vernacular. Many of these subjects were sharply contested in the course of conciliar debates.

[^c09-3]: See Giuseppe Alberigo and Jospeh Komonchak, eds., _History of Vatican II_, 5 vols (Leuven: Peeters, 1995–2005), 1:206 {. Reiner Kaczynski, ‘Theologischer Kommentar zur Konstitution über die Heilige Liturgie _Sacrosanctum Concilium_’, in _Herders theologische Kommentar zum zweiten vatikanischen Konzil_, ed. Peter Hünermann and Bernd Jochen Hilberath, 5 vols (Freiburg: Verlag Herder, 2004–6), 2:44 {.; J. A. Jungmann, ‘Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy’, in _Commentary on the_ _Documents of Vatican II_, ed. Herbert Vorgrimler, 5 vols (New York: Herder & Herder, 1967–1969), 1:4 {. The secretary of the commission was Fr. Annibale Bugnini, later to steer the implementation of the Constitution.

[^c09-4]: Alberigo and Komonchak, _History of Vatican II_, 2:112–33.

#### Conciliar Debates

While the principles and proposals that were made in the schema presented to the council were met with general approval during the debates and discussions of the first session (October–November 1962), a number of influential figures, like Alfredo Ottaviani (Curia), Enrico Dante (Curia), and Ernesto Ruffini (Palermo), and even the prefect of the Congregation of Rites, Arcadio Larraona, mounted a vigorous opposition to several proposals.

Towards the end of the first session, a preliminary vote was taken on the liturgy schema. The vast majority [^c09-5] of the bishops voted in favour of the document. The eventual approval and promulgation of _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ took place towards the end of the second session, on 4 December 1963, but not without a great deal of further debate on issues like the use and extent of vernacular languages, the anointing of the sick, concelebration of the Eucharist, the Divine Office (Liturgy of the Hours), and communion under both kinds. With regard to the vernacular, for example, a number of bishops wished to retain Latin for the ‘form’ (i.e., verbal formula) of each sacrament.

[^c09-5]: Ibid., 2:159.

#### Basic Principles of Sacrosanctum Concilium

**[p. 151]** As far as the Church’s official teaching was concerned, _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ marked a profound development in theology and had far-ranging implications for liturgical reform and renewal. A conciliar document, however, cannot elaborate all the details of a subsequent reform. These needed to be worked out by post-conciliar commissions, just as the revision of the Roman Missal (1570) in the sixteenth century was undertaken only after the Council of Trent had ended (1563). The bishops of Vatican II did, however, lay out the general principles and mandates of the reform, which I will divide into theological principles and pastoral directives/principles of revision. Admittedly, this distinction is somewhat artificial since what I am labelling ‘pastoral’ has profound theological implications as well.

Theological Principles

1. The introductory paragraphs of _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ are programmatic, since the aims of the Constitution were the aims of the council in general: enhancing the life of the Church, adaptation to contemporary culture, ecumenical advance, and evangelization (_SC_ 1). Next comes a potentially revolutionary affirmation: the liturgy is the primary manifestation of the Church. This relativizes the institutional, hierarchical, and structural elements of the Church in favour of the Church’s manifestation in coming together to worship (_SC_ 2). The importance of this priority plays out in a pastoral way when the communal nature of all liturgy is emphasized (_SC_ 26–32).

2. The second fundamental theological principle in the document is even more important: the liturgy is first of all the action of Christ in the midst of his people. _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ quotes a classic liturgical text to the effect that every time the Eucharist is celebrated, ‘the work of our redemption is [^c09-6] accomplished’ (_SC_ 2). This activity of Christ relies on the unity of the human and divine in Christ: ‘humanity united with the Word of God’ (_SC_ 5); i.e., the Incarnation. Without this unity, there would be no foundation for sacramental theology as the Catholic Church understands it. The Constitution then links Incarnation with the Paschal Mystery (the passion, death, resurrection, and ascension) as the apex of Christ’s activity. The use of ‘Paschal Mystery’ is significant, because much of Catholic sacramental theology in the second millennium focused only on the passion and death of Christ as salvific. Emphasizing the Paschal Mystery makes it clear that it is the Risen Lord who is active in the liturgy. It is through the making present of the Paschal Mystery that Christ’s priestly office is exercised (_SC_ 7). It should be noted here that there is little evidence of the role of the Holy Spirit in **[p. 152]** _Sacrosanctum Concilium_. This lacuna is remedied in subsequent conciliar documents, like the Constitution on the Church. In addition, the Constitution introduces (I believe for the first time in official Catholic teaching) the notion that Christ is present in four different ways in liturgical celebrations: in the person of the ordained minister, (especially) in the Eucharistic elements, in the proclamation of the word, and when ‘the Church prays and sings’. This fourfold participation would be reiterated in Pope Paul VI’s encyclical on the Eucharist (_Mysterium Fidei_), issued while the council was in session. There the pope asserted that this fourfold presence of Christ is real; i.e., that his presence in the assembly, the word, and the minister is no less real than in the consecrated Eucharistic elements. The same affirmation is made in the General Instruction of the Roman Missal (2002) 27.

[^c09-6]: From the prayer over the gifts for Holy Thursday and for the Second Sunday in Ordinary Time. _How_ this happens must of course be left to the reflection of theologians, as conciliar documents do not offer a detailed theology.

3. At this point the document defines the twofold purpose of the liturgy as glorification of God and the sanctification of the people. Hence the liturgy is ‘the summit [glorification] toward which the activity of the Church is directed; it is also the fount [sanctification] from which all her power flows’ (_SC_ 10).

4. A most important corollary to the idea of liturgy as ‘summit and source’ is _Sacrosanctum Concilium_’s insistence that the ‘full, conscious, and active participation’ of the faithful is the primary aim to be [^c09-7] considered in the reform of the liturgy (_SC_ 14). Citing 1 Peter 2:9 on the common baptismal priesthood, the document’s rationale for this kind of participation is based on the baptismal status of Christians, not a delegation, as it were, from above; i.e., from the Church’s hierarchy. This affirmation is clearly one of the most important theological statements of the constitution and has had enormous pastoral consequences as well. Perhaps because of _Sacrosanctum Concilium_’s insistence on the centrality of the assembly’s full, conscious, and active participation in the liturgy, the document’s framers also found it necessary to insist on a balance between the role of the priest ‘who, in the person of Christ, presides over the assembly’ (_SC_ 33) and the vital importance of communal celebration of the liturgy. Thus the liturgy is communal and hierarchical at the same time. By the same token, _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ notes the importance of a variety of ministerial roles in the liturgy, above and beyond that of the priest (_SC_ 26–31). Precisely _how_ priest and people are related in liturgical celebration is an ongoing theological issue.

[^c09-7]: The meaning of active (Latin _actuosa_) participation continues to be hotly contested by those who insist that the word refers to interior understanding rather than to outward participation, e.g. by singing or joining in prayers; see Martin Stuflesser, ‘The Many Meanings of “Active Participation”: A Contemporary Perspective’, in _Mediating Mysteries,_ _Understanding Liturgies: On Bridging the Gap between Liturgy and Systematic Theology_, ed. Joris Geldhof (Leuven: Peeters, 2015), 143–64.

5. Another major theological feature of the Constitution is the insistence on the importance of faith, conversion, and preaching (_SC_ 9, 24, 35). Although Catholic worship never abandoned the use of **[p. 153]** Scripture in the liturgy, the council found it important to emphasize the scriptural foundation of the liturgy. It can be fairly said that in light of Reformation polemics, this was an important ecumenical advance.

Pastoral Directives/Principles of Revision

1. The most obvious and perhaps significant practical liturgical reform to come out of the council was the decision to allow the use of the vernacular in the liturgy. Official permission had already been granted to translate certain parts of the sacramental rites, such as baptism, into the people’s language, but this was a more extensive endeavour. However, the council fathers did not have a complete translation of the liturgy in mind. After stating that Latin is to remain the language of the Roman Rite, the constitution notes: _‘_But since the use of the vernacular, whether in the Mass, the administration of the sacraments, or in other parts of the liturgy, may frequently be of great advantage to the people, a wider use may be made of it, especially in readings and directives, and in some prayers and chants’ (SC 36.2). Supervision of translations is to be given over to national or regional episcopal conferences (_SC_ 22.2), along with the decision on the extent of the translations (_SC_ 36.3–4). The subsequent fortunes of this issue will be dealt with below, in Section 4. With regard to the Eucharist, the Constitution further specifles what parts of the Mass might be translated into the vernacular: A suitable place may be allotted to the vernacular in Masses which are celebrated with the people, especially in the readings and ‘the common prayer’, and, as local conditions may warrant, to those parts which pertain to the people, according to the rules laid down in article 36 of this Constitution. Nevertheless, care must be taken to ensure that the faithful may also be able to say or to sing together in Latin those parts of the Ordinary of the Mass which pertain to them. Wherever a more extended use of the vernacular in the Mass seems desirable, the regulation laid down in article 40 of this constitution is to be observed (_SC_ [^c09-8] 54). Many critics regarded the post-conciliar implementation of the constitution, especially on matters like the vernacular, as a betrayal. Despite what they contend, the last sentence demonstrates that latitude regarding the extent of translation can be found in the document itself. This is not to say, [^c09-9] however, that the issue of the vernacular was not hotly debated on the council floor.

[^c09-8]: _SC_ 40 provides for more radical adaptation of the liturgy. It will be discussed below. _SC_ 63 applies the principle of vernacular usage to the sacraments and sacramentals. _SC_ 101 gives a somewhat grudging extension of the use of the vernacular in the Divine Office to clerics.

[^c09-9]: See Joseph Komonchak, ‘The Constitution on the Liturgy: The Debate at the First Session’, _In Verbo Veritatis: Thoughts and_ _Writings of Fr. Joseph Komonchak_, https://jakomonchak.files.wordpress.com/2012/10/liturgy-debate.pdf.

2. Another important principle for reform that was to have enormous pastoral consequences was the **[p. 154]** desire to enrich the liturgy’s use of Scripture, expressed in a general mandate to broaden the use of the Bible (_SC_ 24). Further, to show the connection between actions and words in the liturgy, _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ 35.1 states: ‘In sacred celebrations a more ample, more varied, and more suitable reading from Sacred Scripture should be restored’. With regard to the Eucharist, the constitution is even clearer: ‘The treasures of the Bible are to be opened up more lavishly, so that richer fare may be provided for the faithful at the table of God’s word. In this way a more representative portion of the holy scriptures will be read to the people in the course of a prescribed number of years’ (_SC_ 51). Eventually, this mandate led to a three-year Sunday cycle of readings (that included the Old Testament for the first time during most of the liturgical cycle) as well as a two-year cycle of weekday readings. A similar recommendation to increase the amount of Scripture is made with regard to the Liturgy of the Hours (_SC_ 92).

3. The exact nature of the reform to be undertaken provides for a fourth pastoral principle. Here the Constitution requires distinguishing between unchangeable elements of the liturgy divinely instituted and a judgement regarding liturgical developments that are out of harmony with the nature of liturgy itself so that the rites might themselves be able to communicate more clearly ‘the holy things, which they signify’ (_SC_ 21). Moreover, the document stresses that the revision of these elements is to proceed with caution on the basis of historical, theological, and pastoral study. The most delicate formulation comes at the end of _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ 23: ‘Finally, there must be no innovations unless the good of the Church genuinely and certainly requires them; and care must be taken that any new forms adopted should in some way grow organically from forms already existing.’ Precisely what constitutes ‘organic’ development was to become a bone of contention in the post-conciliar reform.

4. Another principle that was contended after the council had to do with the presentation of the rites:

‘The rites should be distinguished by a noble simplicity. They should be short, clear, and free from useless repetitions. They should be within the people’s powers of comprehension, and normally should not require much explanation’ (_SC_ 34). Critics labelled this approach to liturgical reform ‘modernist’ and criticized it for being based on a naïve and outdated anthropology that did not take [^c09-10] into account the complex nature of ritual.

[^c09-10]: See my reflections on the sociological and anthropological critiques of the reform in John Baldovin, _Reforming the Liturgy:_ _A Response to the Critics_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2008), 90–104.

5. The pastoral implications of _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ (37–40) are evident in the treatment of the [^c09-11] cultural adaptation of the liturgy (later to be called ‘inculturation’) —perhaps the most adventurous **[p. 155]** section in the document. In light of the Church’s sharp rejection of liturgical adaptation in China and India in the seventeenth century, this section of the constitution is indeed revolutionary. A ‘rigid uniformity’ (37) of the rites is to be avoided and ‘legitimate variations’ (38) permitted; ‘[i]n some places and circumstances, however, an even more radical adaptation is needed’ (40). Those more radical adaptations needed to be approved by the episcopal conferences in consultation with the Vatican.

[^c09-11]: See Anscar Chupungco, ‘Liturgy and Inculturation’, in _Handbook for Liturgical Studies_, vol. 2, _Fundamental Liturgy_, ed. Anscar Chupungco (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 1998), 337–75.

6. It is hard to imagine that the celebration of the Eucharist in the rites of the various churches in union with Rome (e.g., Melkite, Ethiopic, Syrian, Byzantine) at the beginning of many daily sessions did not open the eyes of the council fathers to the historical reality of ‘legitimate variations’ in the worship of the Church.

7. Finally, in what is more of a pastoral strategy than a principle, attention is given to liturgical education and formation. In the first place, centres for training liturgical professors are to be established (_SC_ 15). In addition, the study of liturgy in its various aspects (historical, pastoral, theological, juridical) is to be made a compulsory subject in seminaries, and seminarians are to be formed spiritually in the liturgy as well (_SC_ 16–17). Those already ordained are to be educated in the liturgy so they can serve and form their people (_SC_ 18–19). Moreover, national and diocesan liturgical commissions are to be established to implement the liturgical reform set in motion by the council (_SC_ 44).

#### The Eucharist

The second chapter of the Constitution turns to the Eucharist in particular. This chapter reaffirms a number of the theological and pastoral principles set out in the first chapter, among them the richer use of Scripture (_SC_ 51), a more readily understood connection between word and sacrament (_SC_ 50), and the simplifying of parts of the rite that had become overgrown with added ceremonies over time (_SC_ 50)—all to foster more active participation. We can focus here on several specific issues, which move significantly beyond the pre- Vatican II Mass.

First, the homily is made mandatory (except when not possible) on Sundays and feast days of obligation (_SC_ [^c09-12] 52). This emphasis on preaching couples nicely with the renewed emphasis on Scripture and the richer lectionary that would result from the council’s principles.

[^c09-12]: This had previously been mandated in the sixteenth century in the Council of Trent, _Doctrine on the Holy Sacrifice of the_ _Mass_ [1545], Session XXII, Ch. VIII. See _The Council of Trent_, ed. J. Waterworth (London: Dolman, 1848), 157–58.

Second, the common prayer (or general intercessions or prayer of the faithful) were restored, with the expectation that the people would take part in them (_SC_ 53). Except for the Solemn Prayers on Good Friday, they had disappeared from the Roman Rite Mass after the late fifth century. The General Instruction of the Roman Missal 69 would later call these intercessions an exercise of the baptismal priesthood.

**[p. 156]** In another major move, the council fathers introduced Eucharistic concelebration. This was somewhat of an [^c09-13] innovation, in that sacramental concelebration had hitherto been limited to priestly ordination. The reason given is to manifest ‘the unity of the priesthood’ (_SC_ 56). From the council debates it is clear that part of the motivation for introducing concelebration was the desire to discourage the so-called private or solitary Mass. Permission was given for several occasions, such as Holy Thursday (both the Mass of the Lord’s Supper and the Chrism Mass) and the blessing of an abbot and bishops’ meeting. The diocesan bishop was allowed to grant permission for conventual Masses (the daily Mass of a religious community).

[^c09-13]: Rose C. McGowan, _Concelebration: Sign of Unity of the Church_ (New York: Herder and Herder, 1964).

In addition, _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ ‘warmly recommends’ that the people receive holy communion from ‘the same sacrifice’ that has been offered to ensure ‘a more perfect participation’ in the Eucharist (_SC_ 55). Given the frequent pre-conciliar practice of distributing communion independently of the priest’s communion and indeed the communion rite itself, this change encouraged lay participants in the Eucharist [^c09-14] to appreciate that this was indeed their offering as well as that of the priest. Here the council fathers settled on a somewhat ambiguous formulation with regard to the very important issue of how the offering [^c09-15] of the priest and people are related (_SC_ 48). The Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, _Lumen Gentium_, refers to the role of the faithful in offering the Eucharistic sacrifice in virtue of their common baptismal priesthood (_LG_ 10).

[^c09-14]: On the preconciliar practice, see Bernard Botte, _From Silence to Participation: An Insider’s View of Liturgical Renewal_ (Washington, DC: Pastoral Press, 1988), 2–3. Unfortunately, the persistence of the practice of regularly distributing communion from the tabernacle frustrates this aim of the council.

[^c09-15]: The participation of the people in the Eucharistic sacrifice is also alluded to in Pope Pius XII’s encyclical _Mediator Dei_ 28 [1947]. See also _Mediator Dei_ 80–98, where the pope makes a number of distinctions with regard to the difference between the priest’s offering and that of the people.

Finally, the constitution marks a striking advance over the Council of Trent on the issues of communion from the cup. While maintaining Trent’s insistence on concomitance (namely, that the whole Christ, body and blood, is present in the consecrated bread by reason of the consecration), _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ allows that under certain circumstances, with the approval of the Apostolic See, communion under both kinds might be given to the people (_SC_ 55). When taken together, all these elements paved the way for an Order of Mass in the wake of the council that was remarkably different from the pre-conciliar liturgy.

Somewhat oddly, given that the council was still in session, Pope Paul VI issued an encyclical letter, _Mysterium Fidei_, in September 1965. There he praised the liturgical reform undertaken by the council but at the same time expressed concerns about the dilution of Eucharistic faith, especially with regard to transubstantiation and the sacrifice of the Mass. Such caution was to be characteristic of Pope Paul in the post-conciliar period.

#### Sacraments and Sacramentals: Rites of Initiation, Penance, Anointing of the

#### Sick, Holy Orders, and Matrimony

**[p. 157]** The third chapter of the constitution is devoted to reforms pertaining to the other sacraments and to sacramentals (those rituals which do not have a sacramental character, like blessings, but are still part of the Church’s liturgy). The reforms proposed in this chapter correspond to the general principles enunciated in chapter 1. Since sacraments are ‘sacraments of faith’, they need to be more intelligible to help the faithful respond better to God’s grace offered in them (_SC_ 59). In this vein, celebration of the sacraments in the vernacular languages is encouraged (under the direction of the bishops, of course) (_SC_ 63).

The other two sacraments of initiation, baptism and confirmation (in addition to the Eucharist), are dealt with first not simply because of chronological priority but also because of the great importance the council attached to baptism. Baptism, it should be recalled, is the basis for the people’s right to participation in the liturgy (_SC_ 14). The baptismal priesthood is fundamental not only to _Sacrosanctum Concilium_, but also to the council’s ecclesiology in general.[^c09-16]

[^c09-16]: See Jean-Pierre Jossua, ‘La Constitution _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ dans l’ensemble de l’œuvre conciliare’, in _La Liturgie_ _après Vatican II: Bilans, études, prospective_, ed. J. Jossua and Y. Congar (Paris: Cerf, 1967), 131–35.

Three issues with regard to baptism were primary in the considerations of the council fathers. First, _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ calls for the restoration of the adult catechumenate (_SC_ 63). Though the primary concern was ‘mission lands’, the subsequent Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults (1972) caught on elsewhere very well, especially in North America. The rites associated with adult initiation were to become most capable of the adaptation foreseen in _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ 37 to 40.

The second issue was infant baptism. Since the Middle Ages, baptism was administered in a manner that was not adapted to infants but rather as an abbreviated form of adult initiation that might be given, for example, to those in danger of death (_SC_ 67). For this reason, the role of parents and godparents was reconsidered, with the result being that in the revised rite, the parents professed their own baptismal faith. Previously, the godparents had proclaimed the faith as if they were infants.

Finally, the rite of confirmation was to be revised such that its connection with baptism as a rite of initiation was made clearer. For this reason, the Constitution recommends that the renewal of baptismal promises be included in the revised rite. The rite could now be celebrated in the context of the Eucharist (_SC_ 71). That indeed became the preferred practice.

The constitution deals very briefly with the sacrament of penance, directing only that the rite and formulae more clearly express ‘the nature and effect of the sacrament’ (_SC_ 72). Only in the subsequent reform was it [^c09-17] **[p. 158]** made clear that penance is an act of reconciliation with the Church as well as with God. There is also no mention in the Constitution of what later became three forms of celebration of the sacrament: individual penance, communal sacramental penance with individual confession, and communal sacramental penance [^c09-18] with general absolution (in extraordinary circumstances).

[^c09-17]: ‘Rite of Penance: Introduction #5’, in _The Liturgy Documents_, vol. 2, _Essential Documents for Parish Sacramental Rites and_ _Other Liturgies_, 2nd ed. (Chicago: Liturgy Training Publications, 2012), 169. See Karl Rahner, ‘Penance as an Additional Act of Reconciliation with the Church’, in _Theological Investigations_, vol. 10, _Writings of 1965–1967_ (New York: Seabury, 1973), 125–49.

[^c09-18]: See ‘Rite of Penance: Introduction #15–35’, in _The Liturgy Documents_, 2:174–79.

The Constitution takes a major step in rearticulating the sacrament of the anointing of the sick, a title it finds more suitable than ‘Extreme Unction’ (_SC_ 73). Now the sacrament was to be celebrated not so much at the point of death, but rather as soon as one is in danger of death and in old age. Viaticum, or communion for the dying, is clearly recognized as the ‘last’ sacrament. The document also makes a point about the adaptability of the prayers for the anointing to the varying circumstances of the sick (_SC_ 75). This is a point worth underlining, since the council is rejecting a one-size-fits-all approach to sacramental/liturgical celebration.

The directions for the revision of the ordination rites are rather brief. They did, however, open the way for a [^c09-19] very significant change in the ordination liturgies. For example, the entire ceremony for the ordination of a presbyter (priest) now takes place not before the Gospel but after it. In the pre–Vatican II rite, the bishop imposed hands on the candidates twice: before the Gospel to confer the power to celebrate the Mass and after communion to confer the power to absolve sins.

[^c09-19]: See Antonio Santantoni, ‘Ordination and Ministries in the West’, in _Handbook for Liturgical Studies_, vol. 4, _Sacraments and_ _Sacramentals_, ed. Anscar Chupungco (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2000), 240–51. James Puglisi, _The Process of_ _Admission to Ordained Ministry_, vol. 3, _Contemporary Rites and General Conclusions_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 1996), 21–42.

With regard to the marriage liturgy, _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ expresses a clear preference that the celebration of matrimony take place during the Eucharistic liturgy—after the homily and before the prayer of the faithful (_SC_ 78). This is a change from the pre–Vatican II rite, in which the marriage ceremony took place before Mass began. A great deal of adaptation in accordance with local customs is to be permitted for this celebration (_SC_ 77).

Finally, and perhaps most important in this section, the funeral rites were to be revised so that they might ‘express more clearly the Paschal character of Christian death’ (_SC_ 81). This directive was to inspire a significant move away from a more penitential approach to Catholic funerals, perhaps best symbolized by the use of the medieval sequence _Dies Irae_, which was excised from the Catholic funeral rite in the post-conciliar reform. The emphasis on the Paschal Mystery rather than purgatory, as the earlier rite had done, also led to a more positive focus on the resurrection of the body.

#### Liturgical Time: The Liturgical Year and Calendar

**[p. 159]** In addition to the rite of the Mass itself, the Christian articulation of time throughout the calendar year has a very strong influence on the practice of Catholic faith. The liturgical calendar had been pruned after the Council of Trent, but the framers of the constitution judged that a number of changes were necessary to accommodate to contemporary culture, especially since historical research had revealed how much of the calendar had been determined by its root in the urban liturgy of Rome, such as in the retention of the indication of those churches in the city at which the pope celebrated on different days.

One of the more important emphases in the calendar reform is the renewed focus on the observance of Sunday as the primary day for the celebration of the Paschal Mystery. Thus the council fathers wished to return to the very origins of the liturgical cycle (_SC_ 102, 106). Only then did they mention the major feasts of the Christ cycle (Easter, Christmas, Lent, and Advent) and those dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary and to the saints and martyrs. They eliminated many of the observances that had been added over time (such as the Holy Wounds) but also provided for the development of individual (national, diocesan, religious order) calendars (_SC_ 107, 111). The observance of Lent was to be reformed so that two foci were prominent: penance and the preparation of candidates for initiation at Easter (_SC_ 109).

The principles enunciated in this chapter paved the way for a radical transformation of the liturgical calendar, which included eliminating the three pre-Lenten Sundays (known as Septuagesima), which were originally a local Roman observance, and the octave which followed Pentecost Sunday (in favour of the integrity of the great fifty days of Pentecost). Other changes included a renewal of Advent as both a time of eschatological (end-time) expectation and a preparation for the feasts of the Incarnation, and a major pruning of the number of saints’ days celebrated in the general Roman calendar. An appendix to the constitution promoted (ecumenical) discussion regarding agreement on a fixed date for Easter.

#### The Liturgy of the Hours (Divine Office)

Reforming the Church’s daily prayer occasioned a good deal of debate on the council floor because of its implications for the life of priests. Two major principles govern this chapter: that in the Liturgy of the Hours, Christ is praying to the Father through the Church (_SC_ 83–85), and that the divine office is meant to ‘sanctify the day’ (_SC_ 88). The fathers were clearly concerned that the office be reformed in accord with the needs of modern culture, especially of those priests whose main occupation was pastoral ministry. Though the entirety of the daily office was still mandatory, the document prioritizes the importance of the various hours. Morning Prayer and Evening Prayer (Vespers) have priority of place and were to be considered the ‘chief hours’. They are to be prayed at the times of day appropriate to them. (It had long been the practice of **[p. 160]** priests to pray the whole office, including compline, at one sitting without regard to the appropriate time of day.) Matins, later named the Office of Readings, had traditionally taken place at night or at the break of day, but now it was to be adapted so it could be prayed at any hour of the day. A morning office called ‘Prime’, a relatively late monastic addition to the daily order of prayer, was suppressed. Finally, only one of the three shorter offices that occupied the time between Morning and Evening Prayer (terce = midmorning, sext = midday, and none = mid-afternoon) need be recited. The entirety of the psalter had previously been recited over one week. Now it was to be spread out over a longer period (eventually, four weeks) (_SC_ 91). _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ encouraged public and communal celebration of the Liturgy of the Hours as belonging to the entire people of God, especially the celebration of Sunday Vespers (_SC_ 100). Finally, provision was made for the possibility of praying the Divine Office in the vernacular (_SC_ 101).

Of all the particular aspects dealt with in _Sacrosanctum Concilium_, the principles for the reform of the Divine Office are perhaps the least satisfactory. The council had the opportunity to inspire a new (but very traditional) approach to the Liturgy of the Hours as the prayer of the whole Church but settled for concentrating on priests and religious. The post-conciliar reform attempted to promote the Liturgy of the Hours as the prayer of God’s people but ended up with a reformed prayer book for priests.

#### Music, Sacred Art, and Sacred Furnishings

The final two chapters of _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ are anything but an afterthought, since in practice music and architecture are among the most influential factors in Christian worship. The chapter on music begins [^c09-20] by insisting on the importance of what it calls ‘sacred music’ as well as on the retention of the ‘treasury of sacred music’ handed on from the past (_SC_ 112–44). Accordingly, it gives pride of place to Gregorian chant and, to some extent, to polyphonic music. On the other hand, other kinds of sacred music are not excluded (_SC_ 115). This possibility was to be exploited in the post-conciliar instruction _Musicam Sacram_, which gave great latitude in the choice of music that could replace the traditional chants of the Mass (introit, gradual, [^c09-21] offertory, communion). This chapter’s retention of tradition along with an opening to freedom is typical of the desire to balance the old and the new.

[^c09-20]: Many today would want to differentiate between ‘sacred’ music and ‘liturgical’ music; see Jan Michael Joncas, _From_ _Sacred Song to Ritual Music: Twentieth Century Understandings of Roman Catholic Worship Music_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 1997).

[^c09-21]: Sacred Congregation of Rites, ‘Instruction on Music in the Liturgy (_Musicam Sacram_)’, _Acta Apostolicae Sedis_ 59 (1967), 32.

A similar openness to freedom is repeated in the final chapter. In line with the principle of simplicity and clarity urged in _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ 21 and 34, moderation in the placement and number of sacred images in churches is recommended, even though their retention for the devotion of the faithful is praised **[p. 161]** (_SC_ 124). A somewhat laconic statement in paragraph 128 mandates that in line with the Constitution, liturgical law be amended with regard to ‘the worthy and well-planned construction of sacred buildings, the shape and construction of altars, the nobility, placing, and security of the eucharistic tabernacle, the suitability and dignity of the baptistery, the proper ordering of sacred images, and the scheme of decoration and embellishment’.

Note that _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ made no mention here of a change in the arrangement of liturgical space which was to become one of the hallmarks of the post-Vatican II liturgical reform, namely that the principal altar in each church must be separated from the wall so that the priest might be able to face over the altar towards the congregation. This issue had been debated in the pre-conciliar commission, but a free-standing altar was mandated only by the instruction _Inter Oecumenici_ of 1964.

### 4. Echoes in Other Conciliar Documents

Connections and influences between the conciliar documents have become an important focus of the study of Vatican II over the past few decades. Just as the Bible needs to be studied and understood intertextually, so do the various constitutions and decrees of a council. Moreover, the relation between _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ and the other conciliar documents depends on the hermeneutics of the council itself. Here we can simply note that there are several contenders for the hermeneutical key to the council: _Sacrosanctum_ [^c09-22] _Concilium_ and the Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation, _Dei Verbum_. Massimo Faggioli, for example, argues for the priority of the former, not only because it was the first document to be approved but also because of its overall theological import for the council. Ormond Rush and Christoph Theobald, on the other hand, argue for _Die Verbum_ because of the overall significance of Scripture.

[^c09-22]: See Massimo Faggioli, _True Reform: Liturgy and Ecclesiology in Sacrosanctum Concilium_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2012), 71, 50; Ormond Rush, _Still Interpreting Vatican II: Some Hermeneutical Principles_ (Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 2004), 42–43; Christoph Theobald, _La Réception de Vatican II: Accéder à la source_ (Paris: Cerf, 2009), 769.

A survey of the citations of the rest of the Vatican documents reveals a surprising paucity of references to _Sacrosanctum Concilium_. Perhaps most surprising of all is that there are none in either _Lumen Gentium_ or _Die Verbum_, although _Lumen Gentium_ 10 does refer to the people’s participation in the offering of the Eucharist, as does paragraph 4 of the Decree on the Ministry and Life of Priests, _Presbyterorum Ordinis_. This suggests that there were a good number of lost opportunities in adopting the vision of _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ in the rest of the documents. For example, _Sacrosanctum Concilium_’s insistence on full, conscious, and active participation in the liturgy could have inspired bolder thinking around the relation between priest and **[p. 162]** people in liturgical celebration, especially that of the Eucharist. A number of citations from _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ appear in the Decree on the Ministry and Life of Presbyters, but they do not reflect the liturgy Constitution’s implicit ecclesiology, which might have inspired a more profound reflection on the sacramental role of the priest vis-à-vis the rest of the people of God.

On the other hand, despite the lack of citations and some failed opportunities, one can discern some influence of _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ on the rest of the documents. Jean-Pierre Jossua has related _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ to the other documents under six main headings: a homogeneous ecclesiology, baptismal priesthood, catholicity (which includes adaptation and diversity), the word of God, the [^c09-23] ministerial priesthood, and dialogue with the world. Aimé-Georges Martimort has found that the sources employed in _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ give a good example of moving away from scholastic terminology in [^c09-24] favour of the wider Church tradition (_ressourcement_). Massimo Faggioli has argued for a Eucharistic reading of the council’s ecclesiology based on _Sacrosanctum Concilium_, since a Eucharistic reform implies an [^c09-25] ecclesial reform according to the principle that the Eucharist makes the Church. In addition, _Sacrosanctum Concilium_’s mandate that national episcopal conferences have responsibility for translating the liturgy, as well as other issues of adaptation (see _SC_ 22, 36, 39, 40, 44, 63, 77, 120, 128), had major ecclesiological implications with regard to collegiality, itself a hotly contested issue in the debate over the Dogmatic Constitution on the Church.

[^c09-23]: See Jossua, ‘La Constitution _Sacrosanctum Concilium_’, 127–56.

[^c09-24]: Aimé Georges Martimort, ‘La Constitution liturgique et sa place dans l’œuvre de Vatican II’, in _Le Deuxième Concile du_ _Vatican (1959–1965)_, Publications de l’École française de Rome 113 (Rome: École française de Rome, 1989), 504.

[^c09-25]: Faggioli, _True Reform_, 123–24.

### 5. Implementation and Reception of Sacrosanctum Concilium

As Ormond Rush and others have pointed out, no interpretation of Vatican II can be complete without [^c09-26] reflection on its reception. Needless to say, that remains a story in progress—a story so complex that we can make only a few observations here.

[^c09-26]: On reception in general, see Ormond Rush, _Still Interpreting Vatican II: Some Hermeneutical Principles_ (New York: Paulist, 2004), 52–68; _The Vision of Vatican II: Its Fundamental Principles_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2019); Christoph Theobald, _La Réception du concile Vatican II_ (Paris: Cerf, 2009); Gilles Routhier, _Réceptions de Vatican II: Le Concile au risqué_ _de l’histoire et des espaces humains_ (Leuven: Peeters, 2004); Massimo Faggioli, _Vatican II: The Battle for Meaning_ (New York: Paulist, 2012); Matthew Lamb and Matthew Levering, eds., _Vatican II: Renewal within Tradition_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2008). On the reception of the liturgical reform in particular, see Faggioli, _True Reform,_ and Baldovin, _Reforming the_ _Liturgy_.

But first, a brief chronology of the implementation of _Sacrosanctum Concilium_. No conciliar documents could **[p. 163]** provide detailed directions for the implementation of its principles. And so, a month after the [^c09-27] promulgation of _Sacrosanctum Concilium_, Pope Paul VI established a commission for its implementation and within a few weeks issued a motu proprio (_Sacram Liturgiam_), which initiated the implementation of the [^c09-28] reform. The document has been called ‘disappointing’, since it legislated very few of the individual reforms mandated by _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ and especially since it changed the principles established in paragraph 36.4, which had granted full authority for vernacular translations to episcopal conferences. Now they had to be confirmed by Rome. The issue was only resolved by a motu proprio of Pope Francis, _Magnum Principium_ of 3 September 2017, which favoured the authority of the various national episcopal conferences with regard to translation but retained the Vatican’s right of final approval.

[^c09-27]: _Consilium ad Exsequendam Constitutionem de Sacra Liturgia._ One can find the narrative in Annibale Bugnini, _The Reform_ _of the Liturgy 1948–1975_, trans. M. J. O’Connell (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 1990), and Piero Marini, _A Challenging_ _Reform: Realizing the Vision of Liturgical Renewal_, ed. M. Francis, J. Page, and K. Pecklers (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2007). The relevant documentation is collected in _Documents on the Liturgy 1963–1979_, ed. The International Commission on English in the Liturgy (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 1982).

[^c09-28]: Reiner Kaczynski, ‘Volume II: Theologischer Kommentar zur Konstitution über die Heilige Liturgie’, 248–56.

The first of five major instructions implementing the liturgical reform was _Inter Oecumenici_ (_IO_), issued on 26 September 1964. It notably recommended the construction of free-standing altars (_IO_ 91), as mentioned above. It also reiterated the prescriptions of _Sacram Liturgiam_ with regard to final approval of translations by the Vatican (_IO_ 29–31). A second instruction was issued in 1967. Among other changes, the instruction mandated the recitation of the Eucharistic Prayer (Canon) aloud (10) and permitted its translation into the vernacular (28). The third instruction (_Liturgicae Instaurationes_) was issued in September 1970 in the wake of the publication of the new Roman Missal by Pope Paul VI. This document adopted a rather defensive tone, lamenting the unlawful innovations that had been undertaken in many places immediately after the council as well as rejecting the claim that the new liturgy was ‘secularizing’. In addition to the Roman Missal (1970), the reform of other liturgical books proceeded apace: Ordination (1968), Infant Baptism (1969), Marriage (1969), Christian Funerals (1969), Rite of Confirmation (1971), Liturgy of the Hours (1971), Anointing of the Sick (1972), Christian Initiation of Adults (1972), and Penance (1973). Thus, nearly all of the liturgical books were revised prior to 1975, when a concerted effort prompted the removal of Archbishop Annibale Bugnini, the major architect of the liturgical reform, from his position as secretary of the Congregation of Rites.

Subsequent decades, especially after the election of Pope John Paul II (1978), were to witness a conservative move that moderated many of the impulses of _Sacrosanctum Concilium_.

A fourth instruction, _Varietates Legitimae_, On the Inculturation of the Liturgy, appeared in 1994. It manifested a rather cautious approach to applying the principles on adaptation found in _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ 37–40. The most recent (fifth) instruction, _Liturgiam Authenticam_ (2001), was perhaps the most **[p. 164]** significant salvo against what had been a progressive understanding of the principles of translating liturgical texts. This document completely rejected the previous translation strategy of dynamic equivalence that characterized _Comme le prévoit_ (1969). The 2001 instruction determined the 2010 translation of the [^c09-29] third edition of the Roman Missal (2003) into English.

[^c09-29]: For a trenchant critique of _Liturgiam Authenticam_, see Peter Jeffery, _Translating Tradition: A Chant Historian Reads_ _Liturgiam Authenticam_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2005). On the current English translation, see Gerald O’Collins and John Wilkins, _Lost in Translation: The English Language and the Catholic Mass_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2017).

What of the major issues of the liturgical reform and thus the fate (up to now) of _Sacrosanctum Concilium_? I will limit myself to three areas: forms of resistance to the post-conciliar reform, inculturation, and the realization of the Constitution’s vision of full, conscious, and active participation.

Resistance to the liturgical reform began as soon as _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ was approved. Much of the resistance had to do with changes that were made by the _Consilium_ even before the council ended, especially with regard to the permission for the priest to face the assembly across the altar. Opposition mounted as further reforms were implemented. They reached a kind of crescendo with the publication of the Roman Missal of 1969 and its implementation in 1970. Officials of the reform were accused of (among many other things) downplaying the theology of the Mass as sacrifice in favour of a convivial banquet and in general with breaking with the organic continuity that was mandated by _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ 23.

All in all, however, it is possible to discern three different types of opposition. The first group consists of the Traditionalists, like the Society of St Pius X associated with Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre of the Priestly Fraternity of Saint Peter, which reject the council as a whole (Pius X) or simply the liturgical reform in particular (Fraternity). These groups achieved a certain vindication with the publication of the motu proprio _Summorum Pontificum_ of Pope Benedict XVI in 2007, a document that gave widespread permission for the celebration of the pre-Vatican II liturgy, now referred to as the Extraordinary Form of the Roman Rite. _Summorum Pontificum_ gave encouragement for the celebration of the older rite especially to young priests and seminarians of a traditional bent. It could be argued that this development has been a serious setback to the project of liturgical reform launched by _Sacrosanctum Concilium_. Pope Francis, after consulting the bishops, reversed the provisions of _Summorum Pontificum_ for the celebration of the Tridentine Rite in his 2021 Apostolic Letter _Traditionis Custodes_, in an effort to restore greater unity. He rightly observes in the attachment of certain groups to the Missal of Pius V an open resistance to the Revised Roman Rite and a harmful rejection of the Second Vatican Council itself, insisting that the liturgy as revised after Vatican II is the sole _lex orandi_ (or operative rule of prayer) for the whole Church.

The second form of resistance to _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ is characterized by a movement which has been called the Reform of the Reform. This group has accepted _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ but found its official implementation by the _Consilium_ seriously deficient. Mass facing the people, the translation of the entire **[p. 165]** liturgy into the vernacular, and the introduction of multiple Eucharistic prayers (among other innovations) had not been specifically mandated by the Constitution. Here, opponents (Joseph Ratzinger/Benedict XVI foremost among them) argued that there was a serious rupture in the reform’s implementation with the organic development that the council had called for. This group achieved its ‘triumph’ with the publication of the Fifth Instruction, _Liturgiam Authenticam_, mentioned above. More recently, however, Pope Francis gave national episcopal conferences themselves the right to make more of the important decisions with regard to translation. Finally, another group of the liturgical reform’s critics have objected not so much to _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ or to its official implementation as to how it has been put into practice in the pastoral realm.

The last two issues have more to do with the limited success of realizing _Sacrosanctum Concilium_’s vision. As we have seen, paragraphs 37 to 40 were a call for the cultural adaptation of the liturgy, especially in ‘mission lands’. In the wake of the council, there were indeed serious attempts to follow up on what came to be called the project of inculturation. Culturally innovative rites were produced in Congo (Zaire), India, and the Philippines. In the United States, there were several official designated experimental liturgical centres, such as St John’s Abbey (Collegeville, Minnesota), the Woodstock Centre for Liturgy (New York), and the Centre for Pastoral Liturgy at the University of Notre Dame. Interest in these rites and projects began to wane after the mid-1970s, when strong resistance to the excesses of putting the liturgical reforms into practice began to increase, especially in the Vatican. Suspicion of liturgical innovation and inculturation increased even more during the pontificate of Pope John Paul II, even though many of the liturgies he presided over in his international travels did include significant elements of inculturation, due in large part to his papal master of ceremonies, Msgr (later Archbishop) Piero Marini.

Finally, _Sacrosanctum Concilium_’s primary aim of promoting ‘full, conscious, and active participation’ has had, in the opinion of this observer, mixed success—at least in post-industrialized societies—because of strong cultural forces like individualism and consumerism. Helping the liturgy to become a truly corporate activity in practice as it is in theory/theology is an ongoing project.

### 6. Conclusion

[^c09-30] It is a commonplace to say that it takes a long time for the work of an ecumenical council to be received. Some fifty years later, this is clearly the case with _Sacrosanctum Concilium_. There can be little doubt that in practical terms, it has been the most influential of all the council documents. The liturgy is celebrated in the **[p. 166]** common tongue, the sacraments have been revised in a way that makes them (at least potentially) truly pastoral experiences, and the repertoire and performance of liturgical music have been transformed, as have liturgical spaces. The Liturgy of the Hours and the liturgical calendar have been radically transformed. For the most part, all of these reforms have been received and implemented rather well, but, as noted, there has been considerable resistance in the past decades. And so, it remains to be seen to what extent the vision and principles of _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ will stand the test of time. But that is for future scholars to discern.

[^c09-30]: See Bernard Sesboué, ‘La Réception de Vatican II est-elle achevée?’, in _La Réception de Vatican II: En cinquante ans, quels_ _effets pour les Églises?_, ed. Jean-Noël Pérès (Paris: Desclée, 2015), 121–52.
