Faggioli, Massimo. _True Reform: Liturgy and Ecclesiology in Sacrosanctum Concilium_. Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2012.

Ferrone, Rita. _Liturgy: Sacrosanctum Concilium_. Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 2007.

Grillo, Andrea. _Beyond Pius V: Conflicting Interpretations of the Liturgical Reform_. Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2013.

Klockener, Martin, and Benedikt Kranemann, eds. _Liturgiereformen: historische Studien zu einem bleibenden Grundzug des christlichen Gottesdienstes_. Münster: Aschendorff, 2002.

Marini, Piero. _A Challenging Reform: Realizing the Vision of Liturgical Renewal_. Edited by M. Francis, J. Page, and K. Pecklers. Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2007.

Martimort, Aimé Georges. ‘La Constitution liturgique et sa place dans l’œuvre de Vatican II’. In _Le Deuxième Concile du Vatican (1959–1965)_, 497–509. Publications de l’École française de Rome 113. Rome: École française de Rome, 1989.

## 10. The Ecclesiology of Vatican II

Richard Gaillardetz

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 167]** Like most ecumenical councils, Vatican II marked the culmination of a wide range of cultural, spiritual, and theological developments already at work in the Church. At the same time, it was the impetus for the post-conciliar Church’s engagement with a new set of ecclesial issues and concerns.

The freshness of Vatican II’s deliberations and principal teachings can mask the way in which it drew on a variety of pre-conciliar sources: the contributions of the nineteenth-century Tübingen School and the writing of John Henry Newman, the fruit of the liturgical and biblical renewal movements, a growing (if too tentative) Catholic participation in the budding ecumenical movement, new developments in papal teaching (particularly Pius XII’s encyclicals, _Divino Aflante Spiritu_, _Mystici Corporis_, and _Mediator Dei_), Catholic Action’s empowerment of the laity, and the scholarly contributions of the _nouvelle théologie_.

The council has also set a new course for the Church over the past decades. Every post-conciliar papacy must be interpreted in the light of the teaching of the council. It has been an indispensable starting point for theology and pastoral life, inspiring developments that could be identifled only inchoately in the council’s teaching, whether it be the burgeoning liberation theologies of the global South or the flourishing of lay ecclesial ministries in North America.

Although the Second Vatican Council was undeniably preoccupied with ecclesiological concerns, one cannot find in the documents a single systematic and comprehensive treatise on the Church. Nevertheless, when considered diachronically, as the council texts were developed over the course of the council, and synchronically, as we consider their many intertextual connections, it is possible to draw from the council’s **[p. 168]** work a deeply coherent theological vision of the Church. This essay will explore key features of that ecclesiological vision under five headings: (1) The Church’s Liturgico-Sacramental Foundations; (2) The Church’s Trinitarian Origins and Eschatological Destiny; (3) The Church’s Missionary Nature; (4) The Church’s Ecumenical Commitment; and (5) The Church’s Collegial Exercise of Authority.

### 2. The Church’s Liturgico-Sacramental Foundations

Amidst a wide range of fresh theological currents surfacing in the first half of the twentieth century, the fact remains, as Antonio Acerbi observed, that Catholic ecclesiology during this period was marked by the dominance of the manual tradition of neo-scholastic theology, particularly in Catholic seminaries and key [^c10-1] magisterial documents. The preparatory schema, _De Ecclesia_, one of seven draft documents submitted to the bishops for their consideration during the first session of the council, largely reflected this theological framework. While not entirely lacking fresh theological insight, in the main the draft reflected much of the ecclesiological temper of the manual tradition. It was dominated by questions of church membership, Church–State relations, the authority of the bishops, and matters of ecclesiastical jurisdiction. In spite of a more promising chapter on the laity, overall one is inclined to agree with the assessment offered on the council floor by Bishop Emiel De Smedt of Bruges, who effectively summarized the draft’s three decisive shortcomings: (1) the tone of the document was _triumphalist_; (2) it presupposed a _clericalist_ view of the Church; and (3) its account of the Church was excessively _juridicist_. Much of the council’s work over the remaining sessions represented an effort to overcome these failings. We see this in particular in the council’s appropriation of a profoundly sacramental view of the Church.

[^c10-1]: Antonio Acerbi, _Due ecclesiologie: Ecclesiologia giuridica e ecclesiologia di comunione nella ‘Lumen Gentium’_ (Bologna: Edizioni Dehoniane, 1975).

The council was able to take advantage of significant theological contributions of such figures as Karl [^c10-2] Rahner, Otto Semmelroth, and Edward Schillebeeckx. In the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy, _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ (_SC_), the council taught that it was ‘from the side of Christ … that there came forth the wondrous sacrament of the whole church’ (_SC_ 5). Later, the Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, _Lumen Gentium_ (_LG_) would refer to the Church as a kind of sacrament, ‘a sign and instrument, that is, of communion with God and the unity of the entire human race’ (_LG_ 1), and, still later, in the chapter on the **[p. 169]** pilgrim Church, it would refer to the Church as ‘a universal sacrament of salvation’ (_LG_ 48). This analogous application of sacramentality to the Church itself provided a more adequate response to the struggle, since the Reformation, to find a more adequate articulation of the relationship between the visible and the invisible dimensions of the Church. The Church’s visibility, evident in its many institutional forms, exists not for its own sake but to sacramentally realize the saving work of Christ in human history.

[^c10-2]: Karl Rahner, _The Church and the Sacraments_ (New York: Herder, 1963); originally published in German (Freiburg: Herder, 1961); Edward Schillebeeckx, _Christ the Sacrament of the Encounter with God_ (London: Sheed & Ward, 1963); originally published in Dutch (Antwerp: ’T Groeit, 1957); Otto Semmelroth, _Church and Sacrament_ (Notre Dame, IN: Fides, 1965); originally published in German (Frankfurt a. M.: Knecht, 1960).

This more sacramentally grounded ecclesiology enabled a fresh consideration of the role of Christian baptism, one developed in the documents along two distinct trajectories. The first trajectory is evident in _Sacrosanctum Concilium_. In that document it is baptism that draws believers into the paschal mystery (_SC_ 1– 5) and participation in the triune life of God. The liturgy constitution’s rich sacramental ecclesiology began consideration of the liturgy from the perspective of the whole worshipping assembly, thereby stressing that the Christian’s primary identity was not as lay or cleric but as a baptized believer called to participate in the life and worship of the Church. It was the liturgical celebration that represented the ‘summit’ and ‘source’ of the Church’s activity (_SC_ 10). As Massimo Faggioli has noted, this ecclesiological trajectory, beginning [^c10-3] with baptism and culminating in the Eucharist, made a distinctive ecclesiological contribution. The liturgy Constitution’s presentation of the Eucharist as the privileged sacramental enactment of the Church introduced a theology of the local Church as something more than a mere jurisdictional subset of the universal Church; rather, the eucharistic _synaxis_, marked by ‘the full, active participation of all God’s holy people’, particularly when presided over by the bishop (_SC_ 41), constitutes ‘the principal manifestation’ of the Church. This Eucharistic context also suggested a new framework for considering ordained ministry. The essential features of the ministry of the ordained were disclosed not in the conferral of distinctive sacramental powers, but in the nexus of ecclesial relationships exhibited in the liturgy.

[^c10-3]: Massimo Faggioli, _True Reform: Liturgy and Ecclesiology in Sacrosanctum Concilium_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2012); translated into Italian (Bologna: EDB, 2013); translated into German (Freiburg i.B.: Herder, 2015).

The transposition from a clericalist, triumphalist, and juridicist ecclesiology to a more sacramentally grounded one is explored along a second, complementary trajectory in _Lumen Gentium_, the Dogmatic Constitution on the Church. Although its development is less successful, we see here as well a renewed focus on the theological integrity and significance of the local Church (_LG_ 26). The council taught that it is ‘in and from these [particular churches] that the one and unique catholic church exists’ (_LG_ 23).

The manualist tradition had generally apprehended the Church from the perspective of Holy Orders, and therefore conceived it as essentially constituted by two ranks: the laity and the clergy. In contradistinction, _Lumen Gentium_ begins with the priority of baptism and the _Christifideles_, the Christian faithful. The first decisive shift in this direction came after a second draft of the _De Ecclesia_ was sent to the Central **[p. 170]** Commission in the summer of 1963. At that point, Cardinal Suenens made the famous suggestion that the third chapter, then on the ‘People of God and Especially the Laity’, be separated into two chapters, with the chapter on the people of God being placed in front of the chapter on the hierarchy.

This suggested a new sacramental starting point, one in which the Church is defined not by whether one is ordained but by the ecclesial belonging effected through faith and baptism. In that second chapter, the council interwove the pre-conciliar ‘mystical body’ theology into a series of ecclesial reflections that drew on a much wider range of biblical and patristic images (such as a sheepfold, a piece of land to be cultivated, an olive tree, a building, the household of God, the temple of the Holy Spirit, the bride of Christ, a Messianic people).

This emphasis on the _Christifideles_ informs much of the council’s teaching. It brought to the foreground of theological reflection the fundamental equality of all Christians in the Church: ‘Although by Christ’s will some are appointed teachers, dispensers of the mysteries and pastors for the others, yet all the faithful enjoy a true equality with regard to the dignity and the activity which they share in the building up of the body of Christ’ (_LG_ 32).

Among the many biblical images appropriated by the council, ‘people of God’ was given a privileged place, largely because of its emphases on baptism and divine election. We belong to God’s people not through our own merit or distinguishing rank but by God’s free action on our behalf.

For those who believe in Christ, who are reborn, not from a corruptible but from an incorruptible seed, through the word of the living God, not from flesh but from water and the holy Spirit, are finally established as a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his possession … who in times past were not a people, but now are the people of God. (_LG_ 9)

Prior to the council, John Henry Newman had, somewhat inconsistently, applied to the Church the three [^c10-4] offices of Christ as priest, prophet, and king, with mixed results. The _tria munera_ schema would be developed with unprecedented systematic rigour, however, by Yves Congar, who, in his major pre-conciliar work on the laity, applied the threefold office of Christ not just to the ministry of the clergy but to all the [^c10-5] baptized. This schema would largely be adopted by the council, particularly in _Lumen Gentium_. This ecclesiological framework, beginning with baptism, bore considerable fruit. The council began with a consideration of the one priesthood of Christ and then affirmed two overlapping participations in that one priesthood: the ministerial priesthood and ‘the common priesthood of the faithful’. These two priesthoods differed ‘essentially and not only in degree’ (_LG_ 10). This development marked a rehabilitation of the biblical **[p. 171]** theme of the baptismal priesthood that had been largely neglected in Catholic thought since the Reformation.

[^c10-4]: John Henry Newman, _An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine_, 6th ed. (1878; Notre Dame, IN: University of Notre Dame Press, 1989), 76–77.

[^c10-5]: Yves Congar, _Lay People in the Church_, rev. ed. (Westminster, MD: Christian Classics, 1985); originally published in French (Paris: Cerf, 1953).

The council then considered the participation of the baptized in the prophetic office of Christ. As Ormond Rush has recognized, the council’s treatment of the prophetic office opened the door for a broader consideration of the ways in which not only the bishops but also theologians and all the baptized share a [^c10-6] responsibility for church teaching. In particular, the council acknowledged that the baptized possess a supernatural instinct for the faith (_sensus fidei_) that allows them to receive the faith of the Church, discovering its meaning more profoundly and applying it more fully in their daily lives (_LG_ 12). The Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation, _Dei Verbum_ (_DV_), would, in similar fashion, affirm the ways in which the whole Christian faithful contribute to the development of tradition (_DV_ 8). Finally, although the council was less successful in this regard, it considered the participation of the baptized faithful in the kingly office of Christ as a participation in the work of the Church in establishing the kingdom of God in human history (_LG_ 13). This final aspect receives a fuller development in the Decree on the Apostolate of the Laity, _Apostolicam Actuositatem_ (_AA_).

[^c10-6]: Ormond Rush, _The Eyes of Faith: The Sense of the Faithful & the Church’s Reception of Revelation_ (Washington, DC: The Catholic University of America Press, 2009).

It is within this commitment to a baptismal ecclesiology that we can better comprehend the council’s efforts to articulate a more positive theology of the laity. The significant contributions of Catholic Action and its advocacy of a form of Christian engagement in the world, marked by the three-step process ‘see—judge— act’, forced many theologians and church leaders to acknowledge the need for a more positive theology of the laity. This commitment was evident in the preparatory schema on the Church, which affirmed not only the obligations but also the rights of the laity and exhorted the laity to an active participation in the work of the Church.

If the council bishops widely shared a commitment to produce a more positive theology of the laity, they were somewhat less successful in their execution of that commitment. Giovanni Magnani has identifled two [^c10-7] different theological approaches to the laity in the council documents. The first he terms a _contrastive_ theology, one which defines the active role of the laity in the Church and world by way of contrast to the clergy. Typical of this approach would be _Lumen Gentium_ 31, which speaks of secularity as ‘the special characteristic of the laity’. This view appears as well in _Apostolicam Actuositatem_, particularly in articles 4 and 29.

[^c10-7]: Giovanni Magnani, ‘Does the So-Called Theology of the Laity Possess a Theological Status?’, in _Vatican II: Assessment and_ _Perspectives_, ed. René Latourelle (New York: Paulist, 1988), 1:568–633.

According to Magnani, one can identify a second, more _intensive_ view of the laity, one which presents the layperson not as radically distinct from the clergy or professed religious but rather as living out a more intensive realization of the situation of all the Christian faithful. This view is evident in the council’s assertion in chapter 5 of _Lumen Gentium_ that all Christians, ‘each in their own state of life’, are called to **[p. 172]** holiness and ‘the perfection of charity’ (_LG_ 39). The bishops acknowledged that ‘not everyone walks along the same path, yet all are called to holiness and have obtained an equal privilege of faith through the justice of God’ (_LG_ 32).

### 3. The Church’s Trinitarian Origins and Eschatological Destiny

Interwoven into the council’s richly sacramental account of the Church is a more developed consideration of the Church’s participation in the Trinitarian missions of Word and Spirit. In _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ we are told that ‘by baptism men and women are implanted in the paschal mystery of Christ; they die with him, are buried with him, and rise with him. They receive the spirit of adoption as sons and daughters “in which we cry, Abba, Father” and thus become true adorers such as the Father seeks’ (_SC_ 6).

_Dei Verbum_ presents divine revelation as drawing all people ‘near to the Father, through Christ, the Word made flesh, in the holy Spirit’ (_DV_ 1). It is God who addresses men and women ‘as friends’. Christ is ‘both the mediator and the sum total’ of this revelation (_DV_ 2). This revelation is received through the help of the Holy Spirit, ‘who moves the heart and converts it to God, opens the eyes of the mind, and “makes it easy for all to accept and believe the truth” ’ (_DV_ 5).

_Lumen Gentium_ also calls attention to the Trinitarian origins of the Church manifested at Pentecost, when believers were ‘given access to the Father through Christ in the one Spirit’ (_LG_ 4). The council, quoting St Cyprian, affirms that the Church is ‘a people made one by the unity of the Father, the Son and the holy Spirit’ (_LG_ 4).

The council’s thoroughly Trinitarian account of the Church becomes more significant when one considers the common Orthodox accusation that Latin ecclesiology was guilty of a persistent Christomonism. Congar had challenged this critique, which he believed was overstated, yet even he admitted the failure of preconciliar Catholic ecclesiology to offer a sufficiently integrated account of the missions of Word and Spirit in the life of the Church.[^c10-8]

[^c10-8]: Yves Congar, _Spirit of God: Short Writings on the Holy Spirit_, ed. Susan Mader Brown, Mark E. Ginter, and Joseph G. Mueller, SJ (Washington, DC: The Catholic University of America Press, 2018), 162–96; originally published in French: (Paris: Cerf, 1981–85).

The council presents Christ as the ‘light of the nations’ (_LG_ 1) and the one Mediator (_LG_ 8; _DV_ 2). The essential sacramentality of the Church is grounded in Christ (_SC_ 5), who is encountered in the liturgico-sacramental life of the Church in multiple modalities (_SC_ 7). At the same time, the council avoided the excesses of the late nineteenth-century Roman School, which described the Church as the ‘continuation of the incarnation’. Moreover, the Church is only occasionally referred to as the ‘mystical Body’ (_LG_ 7; _Ad_ **[p. 173]** _Gentes_ (_AG_) 7, 9, 19) and, according to the council, only by way of analogy can one look to Christ for a consideration of the complex union of the divine and human aspects of the Church (_LG_ 8). According to _Presbyterorum Ordinis_ (_PO_), the Decree on the Ministry and Life of Priests, priests exercise their ministry ‘in persona Christi capitis’ (in the person of Christ the head) (_PO_ 2). This Christological understanding of the ordained priesthood stressed a more dynamic and relational understanding of the priest’s sacramental configuration to Christ. It is noteworthy that the council carefully avoided employing the more static view of the priest as _alter Christus_, ‘another Christ’, that had been prominent in post-Tridentine theologies of the priesthood.

As Congar observed, the council’s ecclesial Christocentrism escapes a more reductive Christomonism by integrating the missions of Christ with that of the Spirit. Together, Christ and the Spirit ‘co-institute’ the [^c10-9] Church. Indeed, according to Congar, there are 258 references to the Spirit in the council documents. One particularly rich text captures much of the council’s renewed pneumatology:

[^c10-9]: Yves Congar, _I Believe in the Holy Spirit_, 3 vols (New York: Crossroad, 1997), 2:5–14.

The Spirit dwells in the church and in the hearts of the faithful, as in a temple, prays and bears witness in them that they are his adopted children. He guides the church in the way of all truth and, uniting it in fellowship and ministry, bestows upon it different hierarchic and charismatic gifts, and in this way directs and adorns it with his fruits. By the power of the Gospel he rejuvenates the church, constantly renewing it and leading it to perfect union with its spouse. (_LG_ 4)

It is the Spirit that effects in the Church that spiritual communion that moves the Church beyond a static institutional reality, drawing believers into a deeper, twofold communion with God in Christ and one another. The Spirit is the divine principle of the Church’s rejuvenation and renewal. The Spirit is also the interior principle of tradition’s own growth and development (_DV_ 8).

This emphasis on the Spirit helps overcome the tendency towards a reductive, competitive account of the respective roles of the clergy and the laity in the Church. In the above text, the council recognizes that it is the one Spirit who is the source of both the work of the hierarchy and those charisms given to all the baptized. Here we see the fruit of the council’s recovery of the biblical notion of charism, so central to the thought of St Paul. Affirming the charisms of the faithful strengthened the council’s commitment to the active participation of all the faithful in the life of the Church. This pneumatological commitment resisted the tendency to place charism and church office in competition. The council bishops insisted that, when considering those charisms given to the ‘faithful of every rank’, the clergy are not to ‘extinguish the Spirit’ but rather ‘should judge the genuineness and orderly use of these gifts’ (_LG_ 12; see also _AA_ 3 and _PO_ 9). In the post-conciliar period, this renewed appreciation of the role of baptismal charisms would provide a crucial theological opening for the development of lay ecclesial ministries in the life of the Church. As we **[p. 174]** saw above, this pneumatological ecclesiology of the council further underscored the active participation of all the faithful through the exercise of their supernatural instinct for the faith (_sensus fidei_).

The council’s rediscovery of the role of the Spirit is evident as well in its affirmation of the eschatological conditioning of the Church. The council presented the Church not just as a community comprised of individual pilgrims, but as itself a pilgrim people living fully in history. The Spirit draws this pilgrim Church towards a perfection that will be in its possession ‘only in the glory of heaven, when the time for the renewal of all things will have come’ (_LG_ 48). It is precisely by situating the Church in human history that the council could consider more fully the possibility and necessity of ecclesial reform and renewal. Living fully in human history, the council taught, ‘the church, however, clasping sinners to its bosom, at once holy and always in need of purification, follows constantly the path of penance and renewal’ (_LG_ 8). This commitment to ongoing reform and renewal flows from a confidence in the Spirit of Christ to rejuvenate and renew the Church: ‘Every renewal of the church essentially consists in an increase of fidelity to her own calling. Undoubtedly this explains the dynamism of the movement towards unity. Christ summons the church, as she goes her pilgrim way, to that continual reformation of which she always has need, insofar as she is a human institution’ (_Unitatis Redintegratio_ (_UR_) 6). In this recovery of the Church’s eschatological orientation, the council left behind a pre-conciliar conception of a static and immutable Church residing safely on some ethereal plane.

### 4. The Church’s Missionary Nature

The Church’s eschatological destiny follows from its complete immersion in human history; it is in history that the Church realizes its essential mission. In the council’s Decree on the Church’s Missionary Activity, _Ad Gentes_, the bishops firmly asserted that the Church is ‘by its very nature missionary’ (_AG_ 2). This conviction proceeds not from a pragmatic determination to increase the Church’s membership rolls, but from a heightened appreciation for the Trinitarian foundations of the Church considered above. The Church is missionary because ‘it has its origins in the mission of the Son and the Holy Spirit’ (_AG_ 2). The Trinitarian missions reveal God’s fundamental orientation towards the world. God’s stance towards the world is marked both by a respect for the world’s proper autonomy and an invitation to communion: ‘the invisible God, from the fullness of his love, addresses men and women as his friends, and lives among them, in order to invite and receive them into his own company’ (_DV_ 2).

The Church is at the service of the triune God’s mission to the world as a ‘universal sacrament of salvation’ (_AG_ 1; _LG_ 48). Just as God’s triune being is fundamentally oriented towards the world, so the Church is an effective sign of God’s irrevocable commitment to the world. It is the task of the Church ‘to render God the Father and his incarnate Son present and as it were visible, while ceaselessly renewing and purifying itself **[p. 175]** under the guidance of the holy Spirit’ (Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World, _Gaudium et Spes_ (_GS_) 21). The council, to be sure, acknowledged the reality of sin and the woundedness of the world (_GS_ 13, 37). And yet, the overall tone of the council is affirming of the world’s goodness and the real possibility of human achievement (_GS_ 34).

This missionary commitment to the world undergirds the Pastoral Constitution’s poetic affirmation of the Church’s solidarity with all humankind: ‘The joys and hopes, the grief and anguish of the people of our time, especially of those who are poor or affiicted, are the joys and hopes, the grief and anguish of the followers of Christ as well. Nothing that is genuinely human fails to find an echo in their hearts’ (_GS_ 1). The Church, the council stressed, ‘travels the same journey as all of humanity’. Consequently, the Church fulfils its mission by acting in the world as a ‘leaven’ (_GS_ 40). The laity, in particular, are to realize their baptismal vocation by bringing their faith to bear on their daily engagements in the workplace, in the home, and in their various civic and political commitments (_GS_ 43).

Christian solidarity with all humankind can only be sustained by a commitment to respectful dialogue. Christians must not hesitate to preach the Good News of Jesus Christ to all peoples, but such a proclamation must be offered in a dialogical key, one which also affirms that the Church ‘has profited from the history and development of humankind’ (_GS_ 44). This dialogical commitment was doubtless affirmed by Pope Paul VI’s first encyclical, _Ecclesiam Suam_ (1964), which illuminated the Church’s various dialogical commitments. In this spirit of dialogical mission, the council affirmed all that is ‘true and holy’ in the great world religions; it warranted the council’s encouragement for Christians to witness to their own faith even as they ‘acknowledge, preserve and encourage the spiritual and moral truths found among non-Christians’ (_Nostra Aetate_ (_NA_) 2). It led the council to insist that even modern atheism does not merit an unqualifled condemnation but rather a sympathetic hearing, and for several reasons. First, because the criticisms modern atheism levels against theistic belief are not always without merit. Believers have at times perpetuated deeply problematic understandings of God and God’s activity in the world. Second, because atheism often proceeds from a deeply human capacity for self-reflection which can raise difficult questions regarding the meaning and purpose of human existence. Third, many people’s atheistic commitments are motivated by ‘a violent protest against the evil in the world’ (_GS_ 19).

The Trinitarian shape of the Church’s mission, with its emphasis on the co-instituting role of Word and Spirit, opened the council up to a far richer and more expansive account of the Church’s catholicity. The first stirrings of this renewed catholicity may have been instigated by the presence of over 150 bishops from the Eastern Catholic churches. These churches, often of ancient origin, had long been reduced, in the eyes of the West, to exotic ecclesial ornamentation. Yet, the Eastern bishops exerted a tremendous influence on the consciousness of the council as they gave stirring testimony to the distinctive theological, spiritual, liturgical, and canonical traditions that their churches had preserved, all while maintaining fidelity to the Church of Rome (Decree on the Catholic Churches of the Eastern Rite, _Orientalium Ecclesiarium_ (_OE_) 3). The **[p. 176]** extended interaction between the Eastern Catholic bishops and those belonging to the Latin Church _sui iuris_ helped tremendously to deepen the Western bishops’ appreciation for a more differentiated ecclesial unity, a unity-in-diversity.

_Ad Gentes_ offered a beautiful reflection on the significance of Pentecost for appreciating the Church’s deep catholicity (_AG_ 4). The Holy Spirit is, of course, the divine principle enabling the Church’s unity; it is at the same time the animating principle underlying its catholicity, for it is the Spirit that enables the Church to embrace, ‘in so far as they are good, people’s abilities, resources and customs’. It is in the ‘unity of the Spirit’ that the Church ‘strives to recapitulate the whole of humanity and all its riches under Christ the Head’. Through the Spirit of Pentecost and ‘in virtue of this catholicity, each part contributes its own gifts to other parts and to the entire church, so that the whole and each of the parts are strengthened by the common sharing of all things and by the common effort to achieve fullness in unity’ (_LG_ 13).

At the same time, the Incarnation provides an analogue for what would, in the decades after the council, be termed the process of inculturation:

The seed which is the word of God grows out of good soil watered by the divine dew, it absorbs moisture, transforms it, and makes it part of itself, so that eventually it bears much fruit. So too indeed, just as happened in the economy of the incarnation, the young churches, which are rooted in Christ and built on the foundations of the apostles, take over all the riches of the nations which have been given to Christ as an inheritance. (_AG_ 22)

What the missionary decree affirmed regarding the ‘young’ churches is theologically applicable to the life of every local Church. Every local Church is called to be genuinely ‘autochthonous’, offering its own distinctive gifts and customs to the Church universal (_AG_ 6). In this regard, the missionary decree represents a genuine maturation of the theology of the local Church which first appeared in _Sacrosanctum Concilium_.

### 5. The Church’s Ecumenical Commitment

The ever-deepening experience of the Church’s catholicity extended beyond the boundaries of the Roman Catholic Church to the Catholic Church’s relationship to other Christian bodies. It must be recalled that for most of the second millennium, Roman Catholicism had understood itself to be in complete historical continuity with the Church of the New Testament. As divisions emerged within the Christian tradition, the Roman Catholic perspective was generally to interpret these splits within the framework of either heresy or schism. Indeed, for much of the first half of the twentieth century, Catholic leadership remained quite suspicious of the burgeoning ecumenical movement. In 1928, Pope Pius XI, in his encyclical _Mortalium_ **[p. 177]** _Animos_, condemned ‘indifferentism’, which for him meant ‘indifference’ to the unique claim of the Roman Catholic Church to be the one true Church of Jesus Christ here on earth. In his encyclical _Mystici Corporis_ (_MC_) (1943), Pius XII admitted that non-Catholic Christians are in ‘a certain relationship with the Mystical Body of the Redeemer’ by an ‘unconscious desire and longing’, but he insisted that they still could not be considered true members of Christ’s Church (_MC_ 103).

In spite of these decades of caution and a persistent Catholic triumphalism, John XXIII insisted that the council make more constructive overtures towards separated Christian communities. Thus, the gentle flame of Catholic ecumenism was nurtured during the council by the inspiration of Pope John and the work of the Secretariat (and, after Vatican II, Pontifical Council) for Promoting Christian Unity conducted under the courageous leadership of Cardinal Augustine Bea.

A significant number of bishops were committed to establishing a new basis for engaging other Christian communities, one that wished to establish the substantial bonds that connected all Christians before engaging the obstacles to full communion among the churches. In its Decree on Ecumenism, _Unitatis Redintegratio_, the council affirmed the many ‘ecclesial elements’ that could be found in other Christian churches: ‘the written Word of God; the life of grace; faith, hope and charity, with the other interior gifts of the holy Spirit, as well as visible elements’ (_UR_ 3). In light of these many elements, separated Christians were in ‘some, though imperfect, communion with the Catholic Church’. The council admitted that although these separated communities ‘suffer from … defects’, nevertheless the Spirit was still able to work through them ‘as means of salvation’ (_UR_ 3).

This growing consciousness of the real, if imperfect, communion that existed between the separated Christians and the Catholic Church stood uneasily alongside Pius XII’s absolute identification of the Roman Catholic Church with the Church of Christ. That assertion had appeared, almost word for word, in an early _De Ecclesia_ draft. This led to perhaps the most controversial single word change in the history of the sixteen council documents. Where _Mystici Corporis_ had asserted that the Church of Jesus Christ _is_ the Roman Catholic Church, the council instead affirmed that

this church, constituted and organised as a society in the present world, _subsists in_ the Catholic Church, which is governed by the successor of Peter and by the bishops in communion with him. Nevertheless, many elements of sanctification and of truth are found outside its visible confines. Since these are gifts belonging to the church of Christ, they are forces impelling towards catholic unity. (_LG_ 8)

The post-conciliar period has been marked by protracted debates regarding the import of this text, but the soundest interpretation would be to see here an acknowledgement that although the Church of Christ has always existed in history, and continues to do so in the Catholic Church, the Church of Christ can be [^c10-10] encountered beyond the boundaries of Catholicism. Indeed, it is this recognition of the elements of the **[p. 178]** Church present outside the boundaries of Catholicism that led the council to speak of non-Catholic Christian communities as ‘churches and ecclesial communities’ (_LG_ 15; _UR_ 3).

[^c10-10]: Francis A. Sullivan, ‘The Significance of the Vatican II Declaration that the Church of Christ “Subsists in” the Roman Catholic Church’, in Latourelle, _Vatican II: Assessment and Perspectives_, 2:272–87.

The intent of the council’s teaching on the presence of ecclesial ‘elements’ outside the Catholic Church here was not so much to diminish the ecclesiality of other Christian churches as to insist on the institutional integrity of the one Church of Christ that has continued to exist across the centuries in the Roman Catholic Church. But the limits of this assertion must not be overlooked, as Sullivan notes:

Of course it must be kept in mind that this is a question of _institutional integrity_: of fullness of the _means_ of salvation. There is no question of denying that a non-Catholic community, perhaps lacking much in the order of means, can achieve a higher degree of communion in the life of Christ in faith, hope and love than many a Catholic community.[^c10-11]

[^c10-11]: Francis A. Sullivan, _The Church We Believe In_ (New York: Paulist, 1988), 22.

[^c10-12] Here we can distinguish between _institutional integrity_ and _ecclesial vitality_. The council insisted on the distinctive institutional integrity that has been maintained in the Catholic Church across the centuries, as it alone has maintained ‘the fullness of the means of sanctification’. But this assertion should be distinguished from any claims regarding the concrete experience of ecclesial vitality that can be encountered in a given Christian community. Put simply, there is nothing in the council’s teaching that precludes one from holding that the Catholic Church, alone in possessing an institutional integrity rooted in its possession of the fullness of the means of sanctification, may nevertheless lack much in comparison to other Christian churches at the level of concrete ecclesial vitality.

[^c10-12]: Richard R. Gaillardetz, _Ecclesiology for a Global Church: A People Called and Sent_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2008), 114.

In the light of the council’s heightened appreciation for the imperfect union that existed between the Catholic Church and other Christians, the council grappled with the vexing question of church membership in the second chapter of _Lumen Gentium_. The binary approach to church membership that had been assumed in papal documents of the first half of the twentieth century no longer seemed adequate. An early draft document on the Church had insisted that only Roman Catholics who acknowledge the whole structure of the visible Roman Catholic Church (profession of faith, sacraments, and church governance) were incorporated in the fellowship of the Church ‘in the true and absolute sense of the term’. This passage was emended to read that those who accept the Roman Catholic Church and its entire structure and all the means of salvation are ‘fully incorporated’ (_plene incorporantur_) into the Church. This alternative wording suggested that there were degrees of ‘incorporation’ into the body of Christ such that even if one were not a member of the Roman Catholic Church one could, in some sense, belong to the body of Christ. According to the council, the Church is ‘joined to [_coniunctum esse_] the baptised who are honoured by the name of **[p. 179]** Christian’ (_LG_ 15). No longer would the Catholic Church hold, as it seemed to in the teaching of Pius XII, that other Christians could be saved only in spite of their non-Catholic Christian identity.

According to the council, Catholics were not just permitted to participate in ecumenical activities; they must positively commit themselves to the work of Christian unity. This commitment requires that they ‘avoid expressions, judgments and actions which are not truthful and fair in representing’ other Christian traditions. This commitment also imposes on Catholics the primary duty ‘to make a careful and honest appraisal of whatever needs to be renewed and done in the Catholic household itself’ (_UR_ 4).

### 6. The Church’s Collegial Exercise of Authority

When the bishops gathered in Rome for the first session of the council, they were well aware that they would need to address several as yet unresolved questions regarding the structures and exercise of authority in the Church. As is well known, the First Vatican Council had been suspended in 1870 after issuing two constitutions: one on the Catholic faith, focusing in particular on the relationship between faith and reason (_Dei Filius_), and the second on the papacy (_Pastor Aeternus_). A draft text on the Church itself had been sent back to committee and could not be considered prior to the council’s suspension. The principal consequence of the promulgation of a text on the papacy, absent a more comprehensive treatment of the Church, was the perpetuation of an excessively papocentric and Ultramontane theology of Church authority.

At the heart of Vatican II’s reconsideration of the structures and exercise of church authority was its extended treatment of the episcopate in both the third chapter of _Lumen Gentium_ and the Decree on the Pastoral Office of Bishops in the Church, _Christus Dominus_ (_CD_). For much of the second millennium, the Church’s theology of ordained ministry had focused on the ministry of the priest. Thomas Aquinas, and many who followed him, considered the bishop primarily as a priest with greater jurisdictional authority. Yet by the time of the Council of Trent in the sixteenth century, important questions had emerged regarding the role of the bishop. It was not clear in Catholic doctrine, for example, whether the episcopal office itself was of divine institution. Although it was commonly acknowledged that a bishop’s power of orders was conferred at ordination, it was less clear whether the bishop received the power of jurisdiction at ordination as well. Some felt the latter was conferred only later by the pope. These issues re-emerged at Vatican I but, again, the suspension of the council prevented their resolution. The council’s one-sided stress on papal authority gave some the impression that bishops were little more than vicars of the pope. This view would later be refuted by the German bishops in an 1875 statement, the substance of which was confirmed by Pius IX and later by Leo XIII. Nevertheless, the sense of a diminished episcopal authority endured up to the time **[p. 180]** of Vatican II. This diminishment was doubtless exacerbated by the practice of the papal appointment of bishops, made universal only in the nineteenth century due to the cataclysmic changes in the relations between Church and State after the French Revolution and the end of the Papal States.

The council’s rediscovery of a more ancient theology of the local Church provided an opening for a reconsideration of the ministry of the bishop. As we saw above, the liturgy Constitution had situated the ministry of the bishop within a more developed Eucharistic ecclesiology (_SC_ 41), and in _Lumen Gentium_ the council repudiated any sense that bishops were simply papal representatives. Rather, the council insisted that the bishops received a pastoral charge that was proper to them as pastors of their churches. They were not ‘to be regarded as vicars of the Roman Pontiff; for they exercise a power which they possess in their own right’ (_LG_ 27). In a preliminary draft of the Decree on the Pastoral Office of Bishops in the Church, an appendix had been added that listed the faculties to be granted to bishops, suggesting that the essential features of episcopal ministry were only conceded to the bishops by the pope. In the final text, however, it was assumed that these faculties were proper to the ministry of the bishop, and reference was made only to certain matters that were ‘reserved’ to the pope (_CD_ 8). _Lumen Gentium_ settled the hitherto open questions regarding whether episcopal consecration was in fact a distinct participation in the sacrament of Orders and whether the power of jurisdiction was conferred on the bishop at consecration:

The holy synod teaches, moreover, that the fullness of the sacrament of Orders is conferred by episcopal consecration, and both in the liturgical tradition of the church and in the language of the Fathers of the church it is called the high priesthood, the summit of the sacred ministry. Episcopal consecration confers, together with the office of sanctifying, the offices also of teaching and ruling, which, however, of their very nature can be exercised only in hierarchical communion with the head and members of the college. (_LG_ 21)

The council re-emphasized the teaching and preaching ministry of the bishops and in general affirmed that the bishops should not be seen as mere administrators; they were, first and foremost, pastors of their flock (_CD_ 15). The council also acknowledged the legitimate function and authority of the Roman Curia while emphasizing that the Curia was to act ‘for the good of the churches and in the service of the sacred pastors’ (_CD_ 8). The council did call for a curial reform necessary to render it ‘more appropriate to the needs of our time and of different regions and rites’ (_CD_ 9).

Proceeding from this dramatic reappraisal of the office and ministry of the bishop was a consideration of the role of the bishops regarding leadership of the universal Church. Since the nineteenth-century rise of Ultramontanism and the papocentrism that emerged from Vatican I, Catholicism had embraced a substantially monarchical conception of papal authority, one influenced, as Herman Pottmeyer [^c10-13] **[p. 181]** demonstrated, by political theories of sovereignty. If, in fact, bishops were true pastors of their local churches and not mere papal proxies, and if local churches were not simply subdivisions of the universal Church but the concrete locus for the realization of the universal Church, then it followed that the bishops should have some share in the leadership of the universal Church. From these insights emerged one of the council’s most controversial teachings: the doctrine of episcopal collegiality.

[^c10-13]: Hermann Josef Pottmeyer, _Unfehlbarkeit und Souveränität: Die päpstliche Unfehlbarkeit im System der ultramontanen_ _Ekklesiologie des 19_. _Jahrhunderts_ (Mainz: Matthias-Grünewald-Verlag, 1973).

Grounded in the bishops’ role as successors to the authority of the apostles, the council asserted, ‘the collegiate character and structure of the episcopal order’ was rooted in ‘the very ancient discipline whereby the bishops installed throughout the whole world lived in communion with one another and with the Roman Pontiff in a bond of unity, charity and peace’ (_LG_ 22). The council insisted that the college of bishops held no authority except when in communion with its head, the pope. Nevertheless, the college ‘is the subject of supreme and full authority over the universal church; but this power cannot be exercised without the consent of the Roman Pontiff’ (_LG_ 22). The emphasis in article 22 was on the authority of the college when in union with the pope. This reflected a view of the college, however, that functioned as a quasi-governing board over the universal Church. This emphasis stood in a certain tension with the orientation of the following article, which was more successful in grounding the authority of the college in the bishops’ relationship to their local churches: ‘Individual bishops are the visible source and foundation of unity in their own particular churches … and for that reason each bishop represents his own church, whereas all of them together with the pope represent the whole church in a bond of peace, love and unity’ (_LG_ 23).

No other ecclesiological teaching at the council would be so hotly contested. In spite of a widespread openness to the doctrine, a persistent and vocal minority of bishops feared that any acknowledgement that the bishops shared authority over the universal Church would undermine Vatican I’s teaching on papal primacy. In consequence, the council’s treatment of episcopal collegiality, for all its advances, was hobbled by a preoccupation with preserving the teaching of Vatican I. The force of the council’s teaching was further weakened by the controversial _Nota Explicativa Praevia_ that was attached to chapter 3 ‘by higher authority’ and was not subject to conciliar vote. The _Nota_ appeared to return to a more juridical account of the relationship between the pope and the college of bishops.

Perhaps because of the controversial nature of the teaching, the council was reluctant to prescribe formal structures that would give expression to its teaching on collegiality. There were a number of interventions calling for the creation of a permanent synod of bishops modelled on those in force in the Eastern churches. These requests would go largely unheeded as Pope Paul VI, on his own authority, would create on 15 September 1965 a much-weakened Synod of Bishops that would meet only intermittently and would exercise only consultative authority.

The council openly encouraged the development of regional episcopal conferences. _Christus Dominus_, the Decree on the Pastoral Office of Bishops in the Church, rooted episcopal conferences in the ancient practice of convening regional synods and provincial councils (_CD_ 36). These conferences were given considerable authority in the liturgy constitution (_SC_ 22, 36), but there was little formal consideration of the nature and **[p. 182]** scope of their authority. This lack of development may explain why, in the decades since the council, the implementation of its teaching on episcopal collegiality has been fraught, particularly regarding the teaching authority of episcopal conferences.

### 7. Conclusion

It is a commonplace in church history to note that it generally requires many decades before the teaching of a council can be fully received in the life of the Church. If this is true of councils in general, it must be especially true of the Second Vatican Council. Its corpus is unprecedented in its length. Vatican II’s sixteen documents represent almost one-third of all the texts of all twenty-one ecumenical councils combined. Moreover, unlike many prior councils, Vatican II did not limit itself to a few focused issues but rather set into motion a vigorous and comprehensive programme for pastoral reform and renewal of the Church in all its aspects. Not surprisingly, this programme has yet to be fully realized. As the Church continues on its ‘pilgrim way’, it must have the courage to discern the gentle impulse of the Spirit and respond to the pressing questions and concerns of each new era. In doing so, John Paul II reminded us in _Novo Millennio Ineunte_ (2001), the Church must always keep before it the teaching of the council, for ‘there we find a sure compass by which to take our bearings in the century now beginning’ (57).
