## 11. Gaudium et Spes: From the Binary ‘Church–World’ to the

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 183]** For a very long time, the Catholic Church distinguished itself from the world and saw itself as a sort of perfect supernatural society (_societas perfecta supernaturalis_) which was visibly differentiated from the surrounding natural states. Originating in the early seventeenth century, the theological understanding of the Church as a _societas perfecta_ reached its peak after the First Vatican Council. According to this idea, to protect its holiness, the Church ought not to get involved with this troubled world. The world’s relativity must not intrude on its internal life, which is ruled by morality and faith. Yet, the Church was a vulnerable human society exposed to worldly powers. It expected states, especially those governed by Catholic kings and emperors, to protect it and accord it a privileged place within the wider society.

Unchallenged ecclesial supremacy never succeeded in achieving sufficient authority to be obeyed by world powers or even by all members of the Church. There was for centuries, and still is today, an inevitable struggle between the Church and the world in all varieties of political, cultural, and religious matters. There are ups and downs, give and take. This binary relationship was never a fixed and stable reality. Vatican II would overcome the way of conceiving this relationship as a Church–world binary by daring to embrace a more complex understanding of itself, of the world, and of their dynamic interrelationship. This development was achieved by taking greater account of the pastoral activities of faith rooted in history, the great teacher of life. Thus, the Church–world binary was left behind, and a triad emerged based on the **[p. 184]** pillars of Church, world, and peoples living in the here and now. At Vatican II, this triad converges in the Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World, _Gaudium et Spes_.

### 2. A Magisterium That Is Pastoral in Nature: Redefining Ecclesial Identity

Pope Pius XII wanted to teach using an approach that would speak to the whole world in any way possible. He sought to do so primarily through moral teaching, but his efforts did not stop there. He expanded the idea of exercising indirect power (_potestas indirecta_), seeking to influence various domains from politics to culture, medicine, and even science. Thus, he taught in his encyclical _Humani Generis_ (_HG_) in 1950 that the biblical truth claims concerning Adam and Eve could not be reconciled with scientific anthropology (_HG_ 37).

Here, doctrinal claims reveal a truth of faith even in cases where the works of science may prove the falsity of their literal claims, as in the case of monogenism. Pope Pius XII’s teaching placed the Catholic Church in a marginal position in comparison with Protestantism and its ability to influence the progress of the world. The doctrine of historical monogenism was not the only case where official teaching was effectively defending nonsense. Such teachings suggested that the papacy was out of touch with the world. Its inaction in the face of the Holocaust was not an exception, but rather reflected the tragic normality of an institution trying to distance itself from history. For that reason, the papacy was no longer respected as a major international player. While it exercised considerable power within the Church, it had no credible authority outside it. Rather than being viewed as an asset, the papacy had become a burden for the Church.

Pope John XXIII wanted to change that. He was well aware that the world had lost patience with a Church that always seemed to arrive on the scene too late. He knew this from his long years of service as papal nuncio in Eastern Europe and Turkey, and later in the secularized West (France). Understanding that a radical step was needed for the Church to break out of its bubble, Pope John decided to call a council. Still, the preparation of the council from 1960 to 1962 followed the regime of the old neo-scholastic magisterium standing over and against history. It defended the idea that the ecclesial magisterium stands above all other truth claims because it cannot be relativized by history or secular forms of knowledge and belief. The ante-preparatory and preparatory phases produced texts which seemed to suggest that the upcoming council would not need to take account of those who might receive it. The council’s rule would be tradition and loyalty to those ruling in the name of this tradition. None of the preparatory texts dealt constructively with the issue of the Church and the contemporary world. Many of the texts concerned the moral shortcomings of the world and the errors of secular culture.

**[p. 185]** On 11 October 1962, Pope John XXIII’s opening address, _Gaudet Mater Ecclesia_, presented a completely different point of view. It turned the ahistorical magisterium on its head. Rather than attack secular errors or the world’s shortcomings, Pope John drew attention to the shortcomings of the Church. He warned the council fathers against following the ‘prophets of doom’ and emphasized that it would not suffice for the council to simply recapitulate the established tradition. He called the council fathers to listen to history, the great teacher of life. Further, he pointed to the need for another type of magisterium—one that would be defined by its pastoral character. The deposit of faith, he observed, must be presented in ways that make it understandable and invite assent: ‘This way of speaking will require a great deal of work, and it may be, much patience. Types of presentation must be introduced which are more in accord with a teaching authority which is primarily pastoral in character’ (par. 15).

This opening address was a blow to all the work done before in preparation for the council, which lacked a pastoral approach in its formulation of doctrine. As a result, most of the documents tabled in the first session were sent back to be revised. Up to this period, modern theological developments were suspected of falling into the modernist heresy and so had little more than a hidden influence on the council. The Holy Office, whose men dominated in the Preparatory Theological Commission, had little tolerance for theologians looking to make a difference, often meeting in the absence of non-Roman experts. Thus, the pope’s opening address had no immediate impact on the agenda of the Holy Office for the council. They sought to push through their prepared drafts no matter the cost. For that reason, the first session of the council was characterized by a difficult struggle between more progressive bishops and conservative hardliners who deeply mistrusted each other. This was no surprise. It might be seen as a reflection of the tensions present in the world of that time.[^c11-1]

[^c11-1]: See Peter Neuner, _Turbulenter Aufbruch: Die 60er Jahre zwischen Konzil und konservativer Wende_ (Freiburg: Herder, 2019).

During the first session, theologians and bishops who were dismayed by the approach of the prepared texts formed networks to form a common plan of action. They came together to do the unthinkable: to prepare new, alternate drafts. Thus the first act of the council evolved into a heated debate concerning the mode of presenting the doctrine of the Church.[^c11-2]

[^c11-2]: See _Herders Theologischer Kommentar zum Zweiten Vatikanischen Konzil_, ed. Peter Hünermann and Bernd Jochen Hilberath (Freiburg: Herder 2005), 4:581–886; Dries Bosschaert, _The Anthropological Turn, Christian Humanism, and Vatican_ _II: Louvain Theologians Preparing the Path for ‘Gaudium et Spes’ (1942–1965)_ (Leuven: Peeters, 2019); _Vatican 21: Die_ _bleibenden Aufgaben des Zweiten Vatikanischen Konzils im 21. Jahrhundert_, ed. Christoph Böttigheimer and René Dausner (Freiburg: Herder, 2016), 29–58; Franz-Xavier Kaufmann, Karl Lehmann, and Franz-Josef Overbeck, _Freude und Hoffnung:_ _Die Kirche in der Welt von heute und die Aktualität des Konzils_ (Ostfildern: Grünewald, 2017); Massimo Faggioli, _Catholicism_ _and Citizenship: Political Cultures of the Church in the Twenty-first Century_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2017). For a counter-narrative, see Stephen Bullivant, _Mass Exodus: Catholic Disaffiliation in Britain and America Since Vatican II_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2019); for world–Church relations, see Antonio López, ed., _Enlightening the Mystery of Man:_ _Gaudium et Spes Fifty Years Later_ (Washington, DC: Humanum Academic Press, 2018).

**[p. 186]** The principal object of concern for a pastoral magisterium was not to be the error of others, an approach to be avoided. It would focus, rather, on the world, on all human persons, especially on their struggles and suffering. The first impulse of this magisterium is not to recall that which is to be believed or to be done. It begins by seeking common ground and working with others to find solutions. There is an important empirical dimension in this magisterium or way of exercising the pastoral teaching office: it attends to the world as it is here and now. One cannot begin from the perspective of doctrine or faith if one wishes to reach this world. One begins rather with the world and the people living in it. Only then can one discern whether one’s own truth claims might bring healing—or how they may be contributing to the problem.

In line with this shift away from an approach of ‘us’ (Church) and ‘them’ (world), Cardinal Suenens introduced a plan to organize the council’s agenda at the end of the first session in December 1962. He proposed that the council place the Church at the centre of its reflection. He envisioned that the council might address the problem of the Church’s self-understanding by asking, first, what the council might say concerning the Church itself; and second, what it might say in relation to what the Church is not, that is, the world. The Church–world binary was set aside and replaced by a triad: _ecclesia ad intra_, _ecclesia ad extra_, and the pastoral position of the Church in the world of today. This meant that the Church is present to the world as it is today: her true place is in the world. In this approach, the sense of ecclesial identity has evolved from a perspective that considered it as distant and aloof from the world to one that considers her place in and with the world of our time. Such a shift would entail a precarious confrontation, for it revealed all the shortcomings of the Church in relation to the world and not the other way around.

Long before the council fathers began to grasp it fully, Pope John had sensed that such an engagement with the world would help the Catholic Church throughout the world become more deeply aware of itself as a global Church of catholic faith. This is suggested in his call to elaborate a completely new kind of magisterial document. He promoted not only a development of doctrine but also a new form of teaching. In this formative orientation, he sought to have the council address its doctrinal teaching to every member of the Christian Church, not only to Catholics. In his view, doctrine was not to be used to divide people but ought to impel them towards a commitment while respecting the others. This was a decisive action to counter the danger of both intra-ecclesial resentment and the self-righteousness of a resentful minority over and against ‘the world’.

This major magisterial turnaround was accomplished in Pope John’s encyclical _Pacem in Terris_ (11 April 1963). For the first time in history, a papal document was addressed ‘to all people of good will’. Here the Church was presented as being in the world, and the people of the world were clearly at the centre of concern for the Church’s magisterium. The letter resonated with the longing for world peace—a peace endangered by the Cuban Missile Crisis between the major nuclear powers in October 1962. Its doctrine did not begin with Catholic truth claims but with the fact that all life on earth is in danger if peace fails and war **[p. 187]** erupts. In another significant move, the pope called upon the Church to commit itself to reading the signs of the times, including the overwhelming human desire for world peace in this context.

### 3. From Pacem in Terris to Schema XVII/Schema XIII

Pope John XXIII’s encyclical impelled the council fathers to consider the precarious condition of the Church and to address this challenge. Initially, the council was called to bring the Catholic Church into contact with the longings and problems of the human community in an effort to do what the pope called _aggiornamento_, updating. No one had ever seen a papal agenda quite like this. Soon, people around the world began to see that the council’s elementary goal was related to the aspiration of improving of their lives. By undertaking this renewal, the council shifted from being an internal affair of the Catholic Church to a widely accepted human undertaking of coming to terms with the new movement of globalization in the world. The Church made a U-turn from a road that led away from the world to the pilgrim path of solidarity with all human efforts to create a more just and peaceful world for all peoples.

This was a surprising, even miraculous turn. Ecclesial habits of exploring the supernatural were abandoned in favour of the search for the true locus of God’s supernatural presence in concrete history. This entailed a deeper appreciation of how God was present and active more widely than among the Church’s rank and file. The world responded almost immediately and showed great interest in the Church’s internal debate concerning its position in the world. This general and worldwide public interest was considered by the overall majority of the council fathers as a confirmation of the calling to become a different sort of Church than they had known in the past.

The council took up its responsibility and tried to fulfil this vocation. The council fathers realized that it would no longer be possible to consider the Church simply in reference to itself: it must always be viewed in relation to others, including its own problematic response to the world’s expectation. The council opted to accept the pastoral grammar of _ecclesia ad intra_ and _ecclesia ad extra_ proposed by Suenens. Exercising his leadership as a cardinal of the Coordinating Commission, he proposed the elaboration of two conciliar documents concerning the Church. This resulted in two separate, but internally related, constitutions: the Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, _Lumen Gentium_ (_LG_), and the Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World, _Gaudium et Spes_ (_GS_). The centrepiece of this unprecedented ecclesial grammar is a rethinking of the Church–world relationship. The Church is a sign and instrument of God’s relationship with all of humanity, and thus is like a sacrament (‘veluti sacramentum’, _LG_ 1). This Church is located in the world and not apart from it (_Gaudium et Spes_). The Church–world relationship requires the recognition of a **[p. 188]** world–Church dynamic. The Church cannot meaningfully present the Gospel message without some concrete relationship to developments in the world where humans struggle to realize their full dignity— that is to say, without taking into account the _signs of the times_.

Here we have an unusual solution to a highly complex challenge. It was not easy to leave behind a binary like the Church versus the world and to find a position for the Church as distinct from the world yet not standing apart from it. There were many ups and downs as the text evolved. Even after Cardinal Suenens had convinced the council’s Coordinating Committee of the need for two separate constitutions treating the Church, many continued to think along the lines of the Pian era (the century running from the papacy of Pius IX to that of Pius XII).

At first, a Joint Commission was created in February 1963. Here, the minority attempted to push all material dealing with the moral insufficiency of the world into this second text concerning the Church, now known as Schema XVII. Suenens put an end to these efforts within the Coordinating Commission, arguing that such an approach was not sufficiently pastoral. Instead, he called for something like a social catechism. In June 1963, Cardinal Urbani of Venice brought this proposal to the Joint Commission, where Suenens did not have a seat. This idea was in line with the tacit agreement between minority and majority bishops in the days when John XXIII was on his deathbed, shortly after the publication of _Pacem in Terris_. (Pope John died on 3 June.)

Both sides had to accept something from the other. It was obvious that the idea of placing the Church over and above the world had no future. But the majority had no real alternative at the time, apart from this idea of a social catechism. _Pacem in Terris_, published only two months earlier (11 April 1963) would serve as a model for the doctrinal approach in the first part of the document. This would have the support of the council. In a second part, materials treating more specific worldly affairs would offer guiding principles and advice rather than doctrinal definitions. The latter part would not be accorded the same doctrinal character. With this understanding, Cardinal Suenens organized meetings at his residence in Mechelen, Belgium, shortly before the opening of the second session, bringing together leading theologians from France, Belgium, and Germany to work on the first doctrinal part of the text. The overall approach adopted was one of evangelizing the world by a Church that no longer claimed to dominate on moral grounds. In November 1963, the draft from Mechelen was essentially rejected by Cardinal Ottaviani in the Joint Commission. He argued that its approach was not sufficiently doctrinal. The two sides were deadlocked, objecting that the drafts were either ‘not sufficiently pastoral’ or ‘not sufficiently doctrinal’.

In this context, the Joint Commission created a new subcommission for the redaction of the text. The subcommission made a surprising move: it added to the complexity of the document’s method by introducing the notion of the ‘signs of the times’ from _Pacem in Terris_. From now on, a dual system of ‘Church versus world’ would no longer hold. In the zone of contact with these signs, the Church itself is implicated in the world and placed in relationship with the times; the world came to be considered as an integral part of the Church. This was a major breakthrough in the grammar of the document. The doctrinal reflections in part one would call for reading the signs of the times, while part two would address the **[p. 189]** significant events of the present context. This shift took place over the summer of 1964, when the Joint Commission agreed on two separate drafts: a doctrinal one, sent to the council fathers for further debate, and a so-called _adnexa_ or appendices which were sent to the bishops with the remark that they would not be subject to further debate. The two documents were printed under separate covers, each booklet having a different colour. Obviously, the grammar linking Church and world by means of the signs of the times still lacked a coherent methodology. A method that might honour the promise of this new grammar had not yet been invented. Initially, it looked as if the council would accept this state of affairs, as no one intervened during the intersession.

But by the beginning of the third session in the fall of 1964, a major struggle developed between one of the presidents of the Joint Commission, Cardinal Cento, and the secretary of the council, Pericle Felici. Motivated by a concern he shared with Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre to leave traditional doctrinal positions unchallenged, Felici denounced the status of the appendices as ‘_documentum mere privatum_’ (merely a private document). This was unacceptable to Cento, who had signed the _adnexa_ together with the doctrinal part of the text; the appendices could not be considered simply as matters of private concern. They had official status, though it was not clear at what level. In a flerce struggle behind the scenes involving not only Felici and Cento, but also Cardinal Ottaviani, president of the Doctrinal Commission, and the four council moderators (Agagianian, Lercaro, Döpfner, Suenens), an important decision was made: the entire Schema XIII—as Schema XVII was now known—was to be rewritten; the appendices would become an integral part of the council’s doctrine. The traditional separation between doctrinal positions standing over and above worldly matters and the strict division between dogmatic decisions and pastoral concerns no longer held. A completely new form of teaching agenda had emerged. Daily living in the here and now, including its deep-rooted problems, would have a direct impact on the Church’s doctrine. At last, the council was embracing John XXIII’s call for magisterium with a pastoral character.

In the final phase of drafting, two further steps were taken that reflect the pastoral character of the magisterium. The first was the development of the inductive ‘see–judge–act’ method borrowed from the Young Christian Workers (Jeunesse ouvrière chrétienne, or JOC) movement; it was applied to every article of Schema XVII (later Schema XIII), the draft of the future _Gaudium et Spes_. This method would later nourish the spirit of liberation theology and contextual theologies that are prevalent today. Finally, it was necessary to clarify the doctrinal authority of the Constitution through a series of four separate votes by the council fathers. The schema became an entirely new form of constitution: a pastoral constitution. The significance of this decision and of its doctrinal character was established by the addition of an extraordinary footnote. This footnote is an important part of the constitution’s text and was approved by a deliberative vote. It confirms the title ‘Pastoral Constitution’, indicating that the doctrinal principles of part I cannot be dissociated from ‘the relation of the church to the world and to the people of today’. Similarly, it explains that the pastoral actions of the Church presented in part II are not simply the result of higher doctrinal **[p. 190]** positions. Rather, they are realized in the mutual relationship between the pastoral and doctrinal dimensions of the Church, which ‘constitutes an organic unity’ (_GS_, footnote n. 1 to par. 1).

This has an important consequence: the doctrinal and the pastoral position of the Church in its relationship to the world has shifted from the binary of _Church–world_ to the more complex triad _Church–contemporary world–pastoral mutuality_. This triad has not yet been fully implemented in the Church as it presently stands. In this respect, one might consider that in the development of _Gaudium et Spes_ we witness a rare and exceptional moment in church history where the conciliar magisterium adopts a forward-looking theological approach. It did so to address a long-standing deficit, a fact to which the Catholic faith community can pay tribute today.

### 4. The Structure of the Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World

The Pastoral Constitution was intended as a complement to the council’s Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, _Lumen Gentium_, which considers the inner life of the Church, the vocations of the baptized, the universal call to holiness, and the structures and ministries that exist to aid them on their pilgrim way. _Gaudium et Spes_ reflects on the ways that the Church is to live out its calling in the context of the world of our time, with attention to a number of urgent questions that call for a renewed witness.

As we saw in the preceding discussion, the text of _Gaudium et Spes_ was elaborated in two parts. These interdependent parts remain in the structuring of the final document approved by the council fathers. Part I contains a densely formulated Christian anthropology, laying out the Church’s conviction concerning the dignity of every human person created in the image and likeness of God, whose vocation is most perfectly realized in the person of Jesus Christ. Remarkably, it affirms that God’s saving plan in Christ concerns ‘all people of good will’ and that the Holy Spirit offers to all the ‘possibility of being made partners, in a way known to God, in the paschal mystery’ (_GS_ 22). No longer standing over and against the world and contemporary human societies from a distance, the Church is located firmly in the world and acknowledges the proper autonomy of the secular order of society (_GS_ 76). Its members share the most basic conditions and aspirations of every human person and join with them in solidarity, sharing in their joys, hopes, griefs, and anxieties: ‘Nothing that is genuinely human fails to find an echo in their hearts’ (_GS_ 1).

The doctrine concerning the dignity and equality of human persons impels the council to embrace the basic principles of social justice and universal human rights. The council rejects all forms of discrimination on the basis of ‘sex, race, colour, social conditions, language or religion’ (_GS_ 29). Transcending individualistic **[p. 191]** models of morality, it points to the shared obligation of all persons to contribute to the ‘common good according to one’s means and the needs of others’ (_GS_ 30). The council does not hesitate to acknowledge that human persons and communities are deeply marked by the reality of sin, pride, and the disorder of self-love (_GS_ 37). Still, it affirms the redemptive presence of God’s Spirit who works in and through history and whose love is made manifest ‘above all in the ordinary circumstances of daily life’ (GS 38).

Part II turns to a series of particular issues that press in on the life and witness of the Church in the contemporary context, requiring new reflection and inviting the application of gospel principles. These include the dignity of marriage and the family, the proper development of culture, economic and social life, the political community, and the role of the Christian community in fostering peace among the community of nations. In each case, the document calls upon the heritage of Catholic social teaching and indicates the principles that ought to guide the Church’s witness.

Remedying an overemphasis in Catholic moral theology on the procreative end of marriage, _Gaudium et Spes_ gives renewed attention to the unitive dimension of the mutual love between the spouses (_GS_ 48–50). The vexing question of the use of artificial means of birth control was withdrawn from the conciliar agenda to be treated by a special papal commission, and so was not dealt with directly here.

In its discussion of human culture, the constitution gives expression to a new consciousness, the product of an industrialized and increasingly technological age, that men and women have become ‘the architects and moulders of the community’s culture’, implying at one and the same time a new sense of ‘autonomy and responsibility’ and signalling the ‘birth of a new humanism’ (_GS_ 55). In sum, human persons have become more deeply aware of their interdependence and thus of their co-responsibility for one another. These reflections, and those that follow on the principles of social justice and peace, are deeply influenced by Pope John XXIII’s encyclical _Pacem in Terris._ The principles of social justice are extended to _Gaudium et Spes_’s consideration of economic and social life, where the council observes that increasingly efficient yet destructive modes of production can wreak havoc on nature and contribute to social inequalities. It calls for economic systems that serve the human community and avoid the concentration of power in the hands of a few. Resisting absolute theories of the right to property, it considers that the goods of the earth are given for the good use of all (_GS_ 69–71). The Catholic conviction that government and the political community exist to serve the common good, ‘the sum total of all those conditions which enables individuals, families and organizations to achieve complete and effective fulfillment’ (_GS_ 74), is related to the obligation of all to participate in public life and to contribute to building of a just society (_GS_ 75). Respecting the autonomy of the political order, the Church ‘is not identifled with any political community nor is it tied to any political system’ (_GS_ 76).

The Pastoral Constitution’s treatment of peace and war was elaborated at the height of the Cold War and in the shadow of the threat of nuclear conflict signalled by the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962. It rightly observes that peace cannot be reduced to ‘the absence of war’ nor to ‘a balance of power between opposing forces’—alluding to the theories of nuclear deterrence that prevailed in the nuclear arms race of the 1960s **[p. 192]** (_GS_78, 81). Humanity now found itself confronted with the prospect of ‘total war’ and mutual annihilation, essentially changing the meaning of war and challenging the classical principles of just war theory. While war may be justifled as a measure of self-defence, the indiscriminate destruction of civilian populations cannot (_GS_ 80). The council deplored the sums of money being poured into the arms race while the needs of the poor go unanswered. In the context of these new and critical threats and injustice, the Church encourages the development of new international community organizations for international cooperation on matters of economic development and peace.

### 5. Church and State as Societas Perfecta

From the time of the sixteenth-century Reformation, the Catholic Church had clung to an understanding of the Church–world binary in terms of a unidirectional dynamic moving from the Church to the world, yet never in the reverse direction. Thus, it excluded any creative influence of the world in its consideration of the nature of the Church. Instead, it conceived of the two realms of the supernatural and the natural, and thus of the Church and the secular realm, as being in constant tension, if not opposition. As a result, it maintained two basic dispositions: exceptional access to exercise its dominant influence in the world on moral questions while defending itself from the intrusion of a morally corrupt world into the purity of its inner life.

In the wake of the Reformation, the Catholic Church developed a state-like identity as a way of contending with the reality represented by the newly established nation states. Following the dissolution of the medieval order, early modern states were governed by absolute monarchs who ruled by divine right, claiming God himself as the source of their authority. They no longer had use for a Vicar of Christ to confirm the divine origin of their worldly power. They now acted as autonomous subjects. So, too, church leaders, in particular the popes, sought to establish their autonomy from other temporal powers. Out of necessity they sought to establish the independence of the Church from outside influence. Some form of autonomous subjectivity became a modern necessity.

While flercely defending itself against modernity, the Catholic Church nonetheless took on a modern grammar in her own self-definition. Without this independent self-identity, the Church would not have the capacity or ability to self-govern or maintain sovereignty in the face of conflicting powers. This new form of sovereign ecclesial identity had three characteristics. First, the Catholic Church was considered a natural entity in and of itself, a perfect society (_societas perfecta_) equipped with all the structures needed to govern its own affairs. Second, the Church was understood as a supernatural state thanks to the grace given by its founder. This grace was visible at every level of the perfect society. Third, these two perfect social realities— **[p. 193]** the natural and the supernatural—were understood as interdependent and organically linked. This ecclesiology was developed principally by the Jesuit Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621). In answer to the question of the worldly or temporal power of the pope and the authority of the Church in relation to the nation-state, now restricted considerably, Bellarmine proposed the strategy of indirect power (_potestas_ [^c11-3] _indirecta_). This meant that in certain important matters of human life, the papacy could no longer lay claim to supreme power. The Church ceded to the secular states’ claim of autonomy and sovereign authority in temporal affairs.

[^c11-3]: See Enrica Fabbri, _Roberto Bellarmino e Thomas Hobbes: Teologie politiche a confronto_ (Rome: Aracne, 2009), 129–86.

In opposition to Hobbes and other theorists of his day, Bellarmine argued that the Church must visibly [^c11-4] demonstrate her nature as a state and become an ‘empire of souls’. He feared that in the absence of this imperial claim, the Catholic Church would inevitably share the fate of the established ‘state churches’ of Protestantism. The papacy was the primary symbol of this utopia. While it argued for limiting the power of the state in ecclesiastical affairs, given the Church’s supremacy in matters of salvation, it neglected to recognize the relativity of its own authority in matters of state. The early modern notion of _potestas indirecta_ [^c11-5] is typical of the temporal–spiritual binary. Temporal matters pertain to the state, and spiritual affairs concern the Church. Only a supernatural society, that is, the Church, could properly order spiritual matters such as the forgiveness of sin, the conferral of sacraments, or excommunication in cases of grave and obstinate sin. Still, in matters of marriage and sexual ethics, the Church sought the collaboration of the secular state, at times using its privileged place in a given society to impose its mores through the coercive power of the state. Many ‘Catholic’ states were sympathetic to this indirect exercise of the Church’s power in the world, especially when it fostered the loyalty of the citizenry.

[^c11-4]: Stefania Tutino, _Empire of Souls: Robert Bellarmine and the Christian Commonwealth_. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2010), 9–48.

[^c11-5]: See Godehard Brüntrup, _Philosophie des Geistes: Eine Einführung in das Leib-Seele-Problem_ (Stuttgart: Kohlhammer, 2018).

### 6. Continuing Tensions with the Values of Modernity

Following the collapse of the _ancien régime_ at the hands of the French Revolution, other modern states gave themselves authority over spiritual matters in the name of freedom, peace, and liberal citizenship. For revolutionary states like France, founded on the principle of _laïcité_, or the United States, which adopted a strict separation of Church and State, religious freedom was—and had to be—guaranteed as an essential human right. Authoritarian states like Germany, united by Bismarck’s Prussia, or Italy, united by the liberal **[p. 194]** ideology of the Risorgimento, wanted to garner the undivided loyalty of their citizens. They perceived the intrusions of any foreign power, even of the pope’s spiritual leadership, as a threat.

In 1864, Pope Pius IX reacted to the challenges of religious freedom and authoritarian domination with the [^c11-6] _Syllabus of Errors_, a long list of heresies that appeared to deny the Church’s autonomy. Two articles formulated against the dangers of modernity were directly relevant to the world–Church relationship. Article 55 condemned the separation of Church and State, and article 77 denied the claims of secular religious pluralism: ‘In the present day it is no longer expedient that the Catholic religion should be held as the only religion of the State, to the exclusion of all other forms of worship.’ The _Syllabus_ was not the last ecclesial intervention against secular modernity. The same grammar would dominate in the Church’s response to the modernist crisis of the early twentieth century, including its anti-modernist oath, social teachings on heavily contested economic questions, and strict anti-communism. The _Syllabus_ defended the superiority of a Church which could not be guaranteed by its own efforts but relied upon the protection of a secular state. There is a contradiction in play: the Church needed a modern state to grant it the autonomy needed to defend true religion against modernity.

[^c11-6]: See Hubert Wolf, ‘Der Syllabus errorum (1864); Oder: Sind katholische Kirche und Moderne unvereinbar?’, in _Kirche im 19._ _Jahrhundert_, ed. Manfred Weitlauff (Regensburg: Pustet, 1998), 115–39.

A Catholic counterculture emerged which functioned as an integral alternative to liberal society until the 1960s. The secular world was seen as a hostile environment. To shield the laity from its influence, a long series of intra-ecclesial organizations were founded to channel their creativity. Catholics could live their whole social lives within the framework of this culture, ‘from the cradle to the grave’. Within this milieu, Catholics believed in the dominance and moral supremacy of the Catholic Church in contrast to the secular state. This was the predominant attitude within the Catholic Church until the eve of Vatican II. The Church saw itself largely as a self-sufficient perfect society, with little need for input from external sources. The Church also regarded itself as superior to the _societas perfecta naturalis_, the secular state, and considered that the Church ought never to be subject to the law of the state (see Leo XIII, encyclical _Immortale Dei_, 1885).

This claim to be a state power was at once the backbone and the weakness of the modern Church. Considering itself in principle undisturbed by the affairs of the secular state, the Church remained aloof and appeared disinterested in brutal biopolitical matters such as the unofficial practice of serfdom in Italian agricultural business, total war in the First and Second World Wars, and finally the Holocaust. The popes and most Catholic leaders preferred the path of silence over active resistance to defend their own independence.

This notion of a Church detached from the world stands in marked contrast to the separation of Church and State practised in democratic societies. The normal separation of Church and world is protected by the secular state to ensure religious freedom for all religious communities, requiring that each grant this same right to others. This separation aims to prevent the domination of any single religion—even those that **[p. 195]** claim to be the ‘true’ religion—over others. Until the Second Vatican Council, the position of the Catholic Church was that due to the error of their ways, other religions had no rights and therefore should not be protected by the State. Nonetheless, the Church sought state toleration and privilege for itself, the one true religion (_religio vera_), where it was the dominant religious community. In addition, in those countries where [^c11-7] Catholic communities were a minority, the Church sought the toleration and protection of the State. This position was set aside in Vatican II’s Declaration on Religious Liberty, _Dignitatis Humanae_ (_DH_). A residue of pre-conciliar attitudes towards the secular state can be seen in the recent efforts of Catholic bishops to deal with the crime of sexual abuse by the clergy through internal systems of canonical justice and avoid accountability to existing secular courts. This failed strategy has led to a loss of credibility for the witness of the Church in the world. It was a mimicry of the modern world, but it failed to reach the level of human relations immediately within the institution.

[^c11-7]: See John Courtney Murray, _Religious Liberty: Catholic Struggles with Pluralism_, ed. J. Leon Hooper (Louisville, KY: Westminster/John Knox Press, 1993); Felix Hafner, _Kirchen im Kontext der Grund- und Menschenrechte_ (Freiburg i.Ue.: Universitätsverlag, 1992).

In contrast, the principle of religious liberty adopted in _Dignitatis Humanae_ is rooted in an understanding of faith as something to be embraced freely and of the dignity of the conscience of each person. _Gaudium et Spes_ describes conscience as ‘people’s most secret core and their sanctuary’, the privileged space where God speaks to the human heart. All people are urged to pursue the truth and to develop an informed conscience. The Church, following the example of its master, does not impose its teachings but summons all to ‘love and to do what is good and to avoid evil’ (_GS_ 16; _DH_ 2–3).

### 7. The Heterotopic Location of a Real Church in a Real World

For 1,500 years, binaries dominated in the manner of conceiving the Church–world relationship. All of them placed the Church in an initiating and superior position: divine versus malign civilization (Augustine); a higher moral order for a world longing for goodness (Jesuit neo-Thomism); a supernatural versus a secular state (from the baroque era to Pius XII); and a pure Church of Christ versus a disenchanted and impure [^c11-8] modernity. These concepts derive from differing thought systems, but the binary of Church versus world is **[p. 196]** ever present. The notion of ecclesial superiority never left the realm of ideas, though it was far from the lived reality. For 1,500 years, the Church failed to overcome its disdain for the world.

[^c11-8]: See Benedict XVI, ‘Freiburger Rede 2011’, in _Entweltlichung der Kirche? Die Freiburger Rede des Papstes_, ed. Jürgen Erbacher (Freiburg: Herder, 2012), 11–17; translated as ‘Address of His Holiness to Catholics Engaged in Church and Society, Freiburg im Brisgau, 25 September 2011’, http://w2.vatican.va/content/benedict- xvi/en/speeches/2011/september/documents/hf_ben-xvi_spe_20110925_catholics-freiburg.html.

Those outside the Church—that is, not having a special interest in Christianity, not having accepted the Church as morally superior, following non-Christian faith systems, or sceptical of Christian truth claims— have always constituted the overwhelming majority of humankind. Catholics and other Christians have always been in a minority position in human history and expect to remain so into the predictable future. Even prior to Vatican II, Karl Rahner called this diaspora situation ‘ein heilsgeschichtliches Muß’—an [^c11-9] inevitable necessity of salvation history. One might ask whether a failure to accept this condition by opposing the world was perhaps less an indication of a strong and sovereign belief system than it was a sign of a minority’s deep-rooted resentment. The latter was expressed in the claim of a universal mandate for salvation by the chosen few who proved themselves incapable of generating broader interest in their project for over 2,000 years.

[^c11-9]: Karl Rahner, _Theologische Deutung der Position des Christen in der modernen Welt_, in _Sämtliche Werkem_, vol. 10, ed. Josef Heislbetz (Solothurn: Benziger, 2003), 266.

This problem has deepened since the extent of the sexual abuse of minors by Catholic priests has come to light. In spite of all the attempted cover-up, the Church is clearly not above, not better than, the world. Its culture is deeply enmeshed in the darker habits of the world. On the other hand, many continue to try to make the world a better place through the separation of powers. Others dissent in favour of human rights, criticize the self-righteousness of the powerful, promote the ecological agenda, seek peace through dialogue between enemies, and fight against the sexual abuse of the vulnerable. The human community has only one planet on which to live, and it is high time to fight for improved living conditions. Otherwise, the apocalypse of Christian expectation might arrive much sooner than expected. A Church that places itself apart from the world will never be in a position to prevent this. A faith that disregards the world will only contribute to the acceleration of calamity, as one can observe in certain charismatic denominations.

The hypothesis of the Church as a ‘chosen’ few was completely abandoned by Vatican II, as was neo- Thomism’s formula of a supernatural ecclesial order over and above the natural conditions of life, reflected in the Pian era’s contention for the moral superiority of the Church. Following the council, and on the basis [^c11-10] of a revanchist reformulation of Catholic faith, these two intra-ecclesial strategies would battle again for [^c11-11] intra-ecclesial power. A first attack on the new world–Church doctrine was led by a neo-Augustinian battling modernity. The seeds of this debate can be traced to the conciliar discussion of _Gaudium et Spes_; they reached a first crescendo in the publication of the encyclical _Humanae Vitae_ by Pope Paul VI, which **[p. 197]** resented sexuality as an identity marker for modern men and women. The ensuing effort to defend the council’s teaching triggered a new more transcendental Thomist revival, one more open to the social sciences, modern philosophies, and political revolution. These movements gave birth to liberation theology.

[^c11-10]: See Gilles Kepel, _The Revenge of God: The Resurgence of Islam, Christianity and Judaism in the Modern World_ (University Park, PA: Pennsylvania State University Press, 1994; originally published as _La Revanche de Dieu_ (Paris: Éditions du Seuil, 1991).

[^c11-11]: See Massimo Faggioli, _Vatican II: The Battle for Meaning_ (Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 2012).

The struggle between these two grammars of faith is still prevalent in Catholic theology and in the Church today. It is expressed in a debate concerning correct ways to envision the Church–world relationship:

The Augustinian school is wanting to set the Church and world in a situation of rivals; it sees the world in a negative light; evil and sin so abound in the world that the church should be always suspicious and distrustful. Any openness to the world would be ‘naïve optimism.’ … The ‘Thomist’ school is is wanting to set church and world in a situation of dialogue; it sees the world in a positive light; despite evil and sin, grace abounds and will eventually overcome evil; attention to the ‘signs of the times’ reveals new perspectives on God’s salvific presence in the world here and now; the present redeeming activity in the world of the same God witnessed to in scripture provides the surest hermeneutical lens for interpreting faithfully those scriptures.[^c11-12]

[^c11-12]: Ormond Rush, _Still Interpreting Vatican II: Some Hermeneutical Principles_ (Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 2004), 15–16.

Vatican II generally accepted that the People of God who make up the Church constitute a significant minority and are called to work together with all people of good will for the transformation of the world to make it a better place for all. Karl Rahner’s category of the ‘must of salvation history’, which structurally and permanently locates Christian belief in the diaspora, was transformed by the council’s _ressourcement_ as it reconsidered the Church’s very reason for existing. The world wants to know why there is need for a Church; what does it contribute to human life? If it cannot provide a convincing answer, the Church will fail not only the world, but also its own supernatural calling. The council had to face the hard truth that had been confronting Catholics the world over for some time.

[^c11-13] Ecclesial existence cannot rely on self-constructed utopias. Two different sorts of herotopias form the basis for ecclesial existence: one is the Gospel, and the other is the world as it really is today. Both come together in the zones of encounter with the world, including human histories big and small, with all their dangers and possibilities for progress, in all their relativity and universality. These are ‘other spaces’: they are really and already there and cannot be avoided by a Church seeking genuine encounter. ‘The joys and the hopes, the grief and the anguish of the people of our time, especially those who are poor or in any way affiicted’ (_GS_ 1): this is no utopia. This is the world that awaits the Church in the future if it is willing to discipline itself enough to become a place of encounter. There are heterotopias present here and now, accessible to a Church willing to enter into solidarity with the people who experience them.

[^c11-13]: See Michel Foucault, ‘Des espaces autres’, in _Dits et écrits 1954-1988_, vol. 4, _1980–1988_ (Paris: Gallimard, 1994), 752–62.

**[p. 198]** In contrast to utopias, which are little more than self-indulgent future realities, other spaces (heterotopias) are actually there. They are not self-indulgent. They are forced upon people in such a way that they cannot avoid taking them into account. They are open to contact with anyone seeking to enter into relationship. Entering into that other space inevitably changes the normal order of things, the ways we seek to maintain sovereignty, as Michel Foucault has observed.

There are also, probably in every culture, in every civilization, real places—places that do exist and that are formed in the very founding of society—which are something like counter-sites, a kind of effectively enacted utopia in which the real sites, all the other real sites that can be found within the culture, are simultaneously represented, contested, and inverted. Places of this kind are outside of all places, even though it may be possible to indicate their location in reality. Because these places are absolutely different from all the sites that they reflect and speak about, I shall call them, by way of contrast to utopias, heterotopias.[^c11-14]

[^c11-14]: Ibid., 48.

The world today offers its heterotopic nature to all those wanting to enter into relationship. In this heterotopology, the world as it is now becomes a _locus theologicus_ (a starting point for theological reflection); yet for those in the Church who are only interested in the assurance that all is right with their own house, the world remains a _locus theologicus alienus_ (a space that is alien to and unworthy of theological reflection), and any encounter is a risky experience. The world of today does not alienate the Church from its mission. Rather, it reveals its shortcomings and possibilities for mission. This is a precarious enterprise —a true adventure, with God long preceding the Church. The way of coming to terms with a _locus theologicus alienus_ is by respecting its proper authority in the formulation and proclamation of faith and belief.

The first of these precarious heterotopias invites the transformation of the Church into an urban religious matrix in the world, since urbanization is one of the major signs of the times. From the beginning, there has been an urban reason why a Church is necessary in the world. _Ecclesia_, the gathered assembly, was Paul’s conceptual choice for theorizing the faith community in Christ. It was not ‘synod’, which means a purely religious gathering. _Ecclesia_ was not a religious gathering, but a worldly assembly to improve the world, uniting the people that live in a given place. This was a specific action in Hellenistic cities in the lifetime of Paul. It was a sort of urban parliament of all full citizens in a Hellenistic polis. The _ecclesia_ had to resolve the problems of daily life in urban areas.

What, then, is it that the Christian _ecclesia_ has to bring forward as its contribution to the City? It is faith in the Gospel, in Christ, in the Holy Spirit, in God, in Mary, in grace and justification, and so on. Nothing less than this is expected from the Church. But nothing more, either. The faith that the Church offers to human **[p. 199]** beings is proposed in the context of urban activity and in relation to the life of the people in a city. The ecclesial nature of faith does not contradict the world but serves those activities in the world that enhance living conditions. The faith-based nature of the Church contributes to making this world a better place. The basic formula for this worldly enterprise can be found in _Gaudium et Spes_ 92:

For our part, our eagerness for such dialogue, conducted with appropriate discretion and leading to truth by way of love alone, excludes nobody; we would like to include those who respect outstanding human values without realizing who the author of those values is, as well as those who oppose the church and persecute it in various ways. Since God the Father is the beginning and end of all things, we are all called to be brothers and sisters; we ought to work together without violence and without deceit to build up the world in a spirit of genuine peace.

The Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World does not hesitate to say that in and through this dynamic of mutual dialogue, the Church can—and indeed has done for many centuries—receive and learn from the knowledge and insights of the natural sciences, philosophies, and the patterns of human cultures. _Gaudium et Spes_ affirms, ‘the church is not unaware how much it has profited from the history and development of humankind’ (_GS_ 44). It has often borrowed from the language and thought systems of human cultures to express the Gospel message and to deepen its understanding of God’s supernatural revelation:

It profits from the experience of past ages, from the progress of sciences, and from the riches of various cultures, through which greater light is thrown on human nature and new avenues to truth are opened up. The church learned early in its history to express the Christian message in the concepts and languages of different peoples and tried to clarify it in light of the wisdom of their philosophers: it was an attempt to adapt the Gospel to the understanding of all [ … ] Indeed, this kind of adaptation must ever be the law of all evangelization. (_GS_ 44)

The Church itself is ‘enriched through this mutual exchange’, a dialogue that belongs ‘in the very constitution which Christ gave to the church (_GS_ 44). The dominant stance of the church in _Gaudium et Spes_ is one of empathy and solidarity with all of humanity, as a community that ‘travels the same journey of all humanity and shares the same earthly lot with the world’ (_GS_ 40). Without departing from her mission to witness to Christ and proclaim the Gospel, the council’s teaching locates the Church decisively _in_ the world, acknowledging that ‘the earthy and the heavenly city penetrate one another’ (_GS_ 40).

By transforming the binary of Church and world into the triad of the contemporary world, pastoral concern for all human persons, and a Church acknowledging her duty to engage with others, the Second Vatican Council ensured that the Church cannot be reduced to a purely worldly community. Its spiritual task does not exclude anything or anyone. Its strength is in its offer of dialogue with others. It is a ‘Contemplation in a [^c11-15] **[p. 200]** World of Action’, plain and simple, constantly reminding the world of its higher calling for the sake of all of its inhabitants. This pastoral activity opens the space for the Church to discover its true self—locating its Gospel faith in the midst of this world.

[^c11-15]: See Thomas Merton, _Contemplation in a World of Action_ (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, 1971).

Faggioli, Massimo. _Catholicism and Citizenship: Political Cultures of the Church in the Twenty-first Century_. Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2017.

Lopez, Antoni, ed. _Enlightening the Mystery of Man: Gaudium et Spes Fifty Years Later_. Washington, DC: Humanum Academic Press, 2018.

Rahner, Karl. _Theologische Deutung der Position des Christen in der modernen Welt_. In S_ämtliche Werke_, edited by Josef Heislbetz , 10:251–73. Solothurn: Benziger, 2003.

Rush, Ormond. _Still Interpreting Vatican II: Some Hermeneutical Principles_. Mahwah, NJ: Paulist.

Sander, Hans-Joachim. ‘Theologischer Kommentar zur Pastoralkonstitution über die Kirche in der Welt von heute’. In _Herders Theologischer Kommentar zum Zweiten Vatikanischen Konzil_, edited by Peter Hünermann and Bernd Jochen Hilberath, 4:581– 886. Freiburg: Herder, 2005.

## 12. Vatican II’s Theology of Revelation

Gerald O’Collins, SJ

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 201]** Unquestionably, the central conciliar document on the divine self-revelation in Jesus Christ is the Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation, _Dei Verbum_ (The Word of God), a text which emerged from debates that began in November 1962, during the first session of Vatican II, and was finally promulgated on 18 November [^c12-1] 1965. But, equally unquestionably, we should attend to other conciliar texts for a complete account of Vatican II’s integral teaching on revelation (Tradition and the Scriptures). We begin with _Dei Verbum_ (_DV_).

[^c12-1]: Francisco Gil Hellín, _Concilii Vaticani II Synopsis in ordinem redigens schemata cum relationibus necnon patrum orationes_ _atque animadversiones_: _constitutio dogmatica de divina revelatione, Dei Verbum_ (Vatican City: Libreria Editrice Vaticana, 1993); Jared Wicks, ‘The Fullness of Revelation in Christ in _Dei Verbum_’, _Josephinum Journal of Theology_ 23 (2016): 176– 204.

### 2. The Divine Self-Communication

In its opening chapter, _Dei Verbum_ presents revelation as _primarily_ being the tripersonal God’s personal self-manifestation: ‘in his goodness and wisdom it pleased God to reveal himself’ (_DV_ 2). Produced by the First Vatican Council (1869–70), the Dogmatic Constitution on the Catholic faith, _Dei Filius_ (the Son of God), **[p. 202]** spoke only once of revelation as the divine self-revelation: ‘it pleased his [God’s] wisdom and goodness [^c12-2] to reveal himself and his eternal decrees’. Unlike Vatican I, _Dei Verbum_ repeatedly uses the language of self-revelation: for instance, in the Old Testament, ‘by words and deeds [God] revealed himself as the one, true, living God’ (_DV_ 14). Then Christ ‘established on earth the kingdom of God, revealed his Father and himself by deeds and words’ (_DV_ 17). In the primary sense, revelation brings an intimate communion with the tripersonal God.

[^c12-2]: Heinrich Denzinger and Peter Hünermann, eds., _Enchiridion Symbolorum_, 42nd ed. (Freiburg im Breisgau: Herder, 2009), no. 3004; Josef Neuner and Jacques Dupuis, eds., _The Christian Faith in the Doctrinal Documents of the Catholic Faith_, 7th ed. (Bangalore: Theological Publications in India, 2001), 113.

_Secondarily_, the divine revelation discloses hitherto unknown truths about God and the destiny of human beings—propositional revelation. The loving dialogue that God’s self-disclosure initiates (_DV_ 2) communicates something. Hence chapter 2 (on tradition) of _Dei Verbum_ opens with these words: ‘God graciously arranged that what he had once revealed for the salvation of all peoples should last forever in its entirety and be transmitted to all generations’ (_DV_ 7). Since it deals with the transmission of revelation in tradition, that chapter speaks of ‘all revealed truths’ (_DV_ 9) and uses a classical term for the content of the revelation communicated through Christ and his apostles: ‘all that it [the magisterium] proposes for belief as being divinely revealed [_divinitus revelata_] it draws from this sole _deposit of faith_’ (_DV_ 10; emphasis added). At the end, _Dei Verbum_ speaks of ‘_the treasure of revelation_ entrusted to the Church’ (_DV_ 26; emphasis added), which is to be faithfully preserved and proclaimed. Nevertheless, the full revelation of this ‘treasure’ of divine ‘truths’ (lower case and in the plural) derives from the primary and personal revelation of Christ, ‘the Truth’ (upper case and in the singular; John 14:6). The model of information-revelation has been subordinated to the model of encounter-revelation.

In chapter 1 of _Dei Verbum_, two verbs glossed ‘revelation’: ‘by divine revelation God wished to _manifest_ and _communicate_ both himself and the eternal decrees of his will concerning the salvation of humankind’ (_DV_ 6). Here the language of divine ‘communication’ and ‘self-communication’ entered official Catholic teaching. It could be found as far back as the work of St Thomas Aquinas, who drew on Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite to say, ‘goodness implies self-communication; it is appropriate for the highest good to communicate itself to the creature in the highest possible way’ (_Summa Theologiae_ IIIa.1.1 resp.). After Vatican II, the ‘self-communication’ of God was used by Pope John Paul II in a 1980 encyclical, _Dives in Misericordia_ (Rich in Mercy, 7) and then repeatedly in a 1986 encyclical on the Holy Spirit, _Dominum et Vivificantem_ (Lord and Giver of Life, 13 [twice], 14, 23, 50 [four times], 51 [twice], and 58 [twice]). As a term, ‘self-communication’ holds together God’s self-_revelation_ and self-_giving_ through saving grace. The divine communication is not merely cognitive but constitutes a real self-communication of God, which not only makes salvation known but also brings it in person.

### 3. Salvific and Sacramental

**[p. 203]** Right from its prologue, _Dei Verbum_ indicates how God’s self-revelation and the offer of salvation coincide. The council aimed to ‘set forth the genuine doctrine on divine revelation’, because it wanted ‘the whole world to hear the summons to salvation’ (_DV_ 1). The ‘economy’ or plan of revelation is equivalent to ‘the history of salvation’ (_DV_ 2). Repeatedly and without hesitation, the document passes from the language of revelation to that of salvation and then back to revelation (_DV_ 3, 6, 7, 14, 15, 17, 21). This recognition of these two inseparable, if distinguishable, realities reaches a high point at the heart of chapter 1: Christ ‘completes and perfects revelation’ and does this by ‘his presence and his manifestation of himself … [by] words and works, signs and miracles, but above all by his death and glorious resurrection from the dead, and finally by his sending the Spirit of truth’. This revelation has the deeply salvific scope of showing that ‘God is with us, to deliver us from the darkness of sin and death, and to raise us up to eternal life’ (_DV_ 4). God’s revealing words and works embody the offer of the eternal life of salvation. In Johannine terms, since Jesus is the revealed Truth in person, he is also eternal Life in person.

Linking ‘the economy of revelation’ with the concomitant ‘history of salvation’ matches the _sacramental_ language of ‘words’ (revelation) and ‘works’ (salvation) that features prominently in _Dei Verbum_ (e.g., _DV_ 2, 4, 14). Just as in the administration of the sacraments the words and actions of a person (the minister, or the ministers in the case of the sacrament of matrimony) join to convey God’s revelation and salvation, so the words and deeds of a person, Jesus himself, mediated the saving self-manifestation of God (_DV_ 6, 17). In short, revelation displays a sacramental face.[^c12-3]

[^c12-3]: Gerald O’Collins, _Revelation_: _Towards a Christian Interpretation of God’s Self-Revelation in Jesus Christ_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2016), 39–55.

This ‘sacramental’ way (words and works) of representing God’s revealing and saving self-communication does not appear to have enjoyed a contemporary ecumenical origin. It was not that the drafters of _Dei Verbum_ combined (1) the language of ‘word of God’ theologians like Karl Barth and Rudolf Bultmann with (2) that favoured by Oscar Cullmann and George Ernest Wright about God’s saving acts in history. Such sacramental language of ‘word and deed’ had turned up much earlier: for instance, in the _Katholische Dogmatik_ of Hermann Schell that appeared in 1900. He wrote: ‘the supernatural revelation of God means the free self-communication of God through word and deed [_durch Wort und Tat_] to a personal and real community of life with the created spirit’ (trans. mine). A few years earlier, a posthumous book by Johann Baptist Franzelin (d. 1886), _Tractatus de Divina Traditione et Scriptura_, used similar language when explaining revelation to be ‘a divine locution, made up of _words_ stating a truth and of _facts_ proving that these words are a divine locution’ (trans. mine; emphasis added).

**[p. 204]** A year before _Dei Verbum_ was promulgated in late 1965, Vatican II’s Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, _Lumen Gentium_ (_LG_) (The Light of the Nations), recalled Jesus’s proclamation of God’s kingdom: ‘this kingdom shines out before humanity in the word, the works, and the presence of Christ’ (_LG_ 5). But two years before that, in November 1962, the language of ‘word(s)’ and ‘works’ had already entered the making [^c12-4] of _Dei Verbum_ through a draft prepared by Jean Daniélou. Several months earlier, Pieter Smulders, SJ, in a text sent to the papal nuncio to the Hague, Archbishop Giuseppe Beltrami, maintained that revelation embraces not only the ‘locutio Dei’ (the word of God) but also the ‘magnalia Dei’ (the great deeds of God). A world expert on St Hilary of Poitiers, Smulders, when drafting what was to become chapter 4 of _Dei Verbum_, picked up the language of Hilary. In the opening article of _Tractatus Mysteriorum_, Hilary wrote of the biblical ‘words’ (_dicta_) and ‘facts’ (_facta_) that ‘announce’ (_nuntiare_) and ‘make known’ (_exprimere_) the coming of Christ. Of course, one can note how _Dei Verbum_ joins together themes developed by different schools of Protestant theologians. Nevertheless, through Smulders the scheme of ‘words and deeds’ as the vehicle of [^c12-5] divine revelation comes rather from Hilary.

[^c12-4]: Wicks, ‘The Fullness of Revelation in Christ in _Dei Verbum_’, 190–93.

[^c12-5]: Gerald O’Collins, _Retrieving Fundamental Theology_ (Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 1993); Jared Wicks, _Investigating Vatican II_ (Washington, DC: The Catholic University of America Press, 2018).

### 4. Revelation Past, Present, and Future

_Dei Verbum_ speaks of the divine self-disclosure in a triple time-key: as past, present, and future. Let us examine what _Dei Verbum_ says about this time-key.

#### Past

As regards revelation in the past, we observed above how the constitution says that ‘God revealed [past] himself in words and deeds’ (_DV_ 14); likewise, Christ ‘revealed [past] his Father and himself’ (_DV_ 17). The document had already quoted 1 John 1:2: ‘we proclaim to you the eternal life which was with the Father and was made manifest [past] to us’ (_DV_ 1). Echoing John 1:14, 17, it characterizes Christ as ‘the fullness’ of all revelation (_DV_ 2). He ‘completes and perfects’ (historical present) revelation with ‘the divine witness’. With all that, he brought ‘a new and definitive’ covenant (_DV_ 4).

Neither here nor elsewhere did Vatican II ever allege that the historic, divine self-disclosure in Christ was ‘definitive’ or ‘final’. It called the new covenant ‘definitive’ but not the revelation in and through Christ. To be full, complete, and perfect is one thing, but to be ‘definitive’ goes further. It would mean that this **[p. 205]** revelation has proved unconditionally full, totally complete, and utterly conclusive, so that all of God’s self-manifestation is simply over and done with. There is no further revelation to wait for. Such a position is [^c12-6] incompatible with the New Testament’s teaching on the final revelation to come and with _Dei Verbum_, which appealed to Titus 2:13 and 1 Timothy 6:14 and spoke of expecting the future ‘glorious manifestation of [^c12-7] our Lord Jesus Christ’ (_DV_ 4).

[^c12-6]: O’Collins, _Revelation_: _Towards a Christian Interpretation_, 106–7.

[^c12-7]: Ibid., 108–10.

#### Present

_Dei Verbum_ also portrays revelation as a _present_ event that invites human faith: ‘ “The obedience of faith” (Rom. 16:26; see Rom. 1:5; 2 Cor.10:5–6) must be our response to God who reveals’ (_DV_ 5). In the next chapter, the Constitution associates revelation as it happened in the past with revelation as it happens now (in the Church): ‘God, who spoke in the past, continues to converse with the spouse of his beloved Son.’ At once the document varies its language to concentrate on revelation here and now: ‘the Holy Spirit, through whom the living voice of the Gospel rings out in the Church—and through it in the world—leads believers to the full truth and makes the word of Christ dwell in them in all its richness’ (_DV_ 8).

Other documents of Vatican II also recognize the divine revelation to be a _present_ reality. Apropos of the various liturgical presences of the risen Christ, the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy, _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ (_SC_), teaches that ‘it is he himself who speaks when the holy Scriptures are read in the church’ (_SC_ 7). Later, the same Constitution declares: ‘in the liturgy God speaks to his people, Christ is still proclaiming the Gospel’ (_SC_ 33). The Decree on the Mission Activity of the Church, _Ad Gentes_ (_AG_) (To the Nations), highlights the present event of revelation: ‘in manifesting Christ, the Church reveals to men and women their true situation and calling’ (_AG_ 8). In the mystery of Christ ‘the charity of God is revealed’ (_AG_ 12). Holding together revelation and salvation, the Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World, _Gaudium et Spes_ (_GS_), describes the Church as ‘the universal sacrament of salvation’ (see _LG_ 48), ‘manifesting and actualizing the mystery of God’s love for humanity’ (_GS_ 45). The same document admits that, through their failures, Christians may here and now ‘conceal’ rather than ‘reveal the true nature of God and religion’ (_GS_ 19).

The same awareness that revelation is not only a past but also a present event turns up in John Paul II’s 1979 Apostolic Exhortation on Catechesis in Our Time, _Catechesi Tradendae_ (_CT_ 35, 36), and even more in his 1980 encyclical _Dives in Misericordia (DM)._ Over eighty times he uses the verb ‘reveal’ or the noun ‘revelation’— not to mention other revelational terms like ‘manifest’, ‘sign’, and ‘proclaim’. As well as portraying revelation as something completed in the past, the encyclical repeatedly portrays divine self-revelation as a present event (e.g., _DM_ 6, 7, 9, 15).

**[p. 206]** Some allege that ‘present’ revelation is not revelation in the proper sense but only a growth in understanding the revelation completed and closed once and for all with Christ and his apostles. Undoubtedly, such a developing appreciation takes place: ‘the tradition that comes from the apostles makes progress in the Church, with the help of the Holy Spirit. There is growth in insight into realities and words that are being passed on’ (_DV_ 8). _Gaudium et Spes_ puts this growing understanding as a duty: ‘with the help of the Holy Spirit, it is the task of the whole people of God, particularly of its pastors and theologians, to listen and to distinguish the many voices of our time and to interpret them in the light of God’s word, in order that _the revealed Truth may be more deeply penetrated_, _better understood_, and more suitably presented’ (_GS_ 44; emphasis added).

Nevertheless, we belittle the ‘living tradition’ (_viva traditio_) (_DV_ 12) if we credit it only with developing our understanding of past revelation. _Dei Verbum_ offers no such low version of tradition:

through the tradition … the holy Scriptures themselves are more thoroughly understood _and constantly actualized_ in the church. Thus God, who spoke in times past, continues to converse with the spouse of his beloved Son. And the Holy Spirit, through whom the living voice of [the] Gospel rings out in the Church—and through her in the world—leads believers to the full truth. (_DV_ 8; emphasis added)

Here the council teaches that, through tradition guided by the Holy Spirit, the divine self-revelation recorded by the Scriptures is not only more deeply understood but also ‘constantly actualized’ as a living revelation of God to the Church and the world.

To deny present revelation is to doubt the active power here and now of the Holy Spirit as enlivening the tradition and communicating the presence of the risen Christ. This also means reducing faith to the acceptance of some revealed truths inherited from the past rather than taking faith in its integral sense as a full submission prompted by the Holy Spirit and given to God revealed here and now (_DV_ 5). Denying the present revelation of God sells short the human response to this revelation, faith.

Of course, if one persists in thinking that revelation _primarily_ and even exclusively involves the communication of revealed truths, it is easier to relegate revelation to the past. As soon as the whole set of revealed doctrines is complete, revelation ends or is ‘closed’. For this way of thinking, later believers cannot directly experience the divine self-revelation. All they can do is remember, understand, interpret, and apply truths revealed long ago to the apostolic Church. But, as we have seen, this is not the thinking of the Second Vatican Council and John Paul II: revelation is primarily God’s personal self-disclosure and is both a past and a present event.

We can sum up the teaching of Vatican II on revelation: present revelation actualizes the living event of the divine self-manifestation but _does not add_ to the ‘content’ of what was fully revealed through Christ’s life, death, resurrection, and sending of the Holy Spirit. In worship and life, revelation continues as an actual **[p. 207]** encounter with God. But this living dialogue adds nothing to the core of the divinely revealed truths, which essentially amount to Jesus Christ crucifled and raised from the dead, along with the coming of the Spirit.

#### Future

_Dei Verbum_ does not dedicate much attention to the _future_ and _final_ revelation of God, apart from referring to 1 Timothy 6:14 and Titus 2:13 and recalling ‘the glorious manifestation of our Lord Jesus Christ’ that is to come at the end of human history (_DV_ 4). In a chapter on ‘the pilgrim Church’, _Lumen Gentium_, promulgated a year earlier, had already appealed to a broad range of New Testament texts to picture the final, glorious self-disclosure of Christ that will bring heavenly happiness (_LG_ 48–51). This constitution understood the mission of the Church to ‘reveal faithfully in the world’ the mystery of her Lord, ‘until, in the end, it [the mystery of Christ] shall be manifested in full light’ (_LG_ 8). _Gaudium et Spes_, promulgated less than a month after _Dei Verbum_, would add its teaching on ‘the new heaven and the new earth’ that will appear in a transformed universe (_GS_ 38–39).

To sum up: a triple time-key of past, present, and future revelation underpins the teaching of _Dei Verbum._ The past reception of revelation in the apostolic teaching is transmitted in the Church’s ‘doctrine, life, and worship’. Believers ‘experience’ now an ‘intimate sense of spiritual realities’ (present revelation), and ‘the Church is always advancing towards the plenitude of divine truth, until … the words of God are fulfilled’ in her (future revelation) (_DV_ 8).

### 5. A Biblical Orientation

In presenting revelation (and the associated themes of tradition and the inspired Scriptures), _Dei Verbum_ includes eighty-eight references to or citations of the Scriptures. It shows itself much more biblical in its language and mentality than Vatican I’s Constitution on Faith, _Dei Filius._

Chapter 1 of _Dei Verbum_ sets the tone for the rest of the document by picking out three classical biblical texts on revelation. The prologue quotes 1 John 1:2–3, verses which indicate the personal character of the divine self-revelation, its Christocentrism, its salvific aim, and its apostolic, ecclesial mediation (_DV_ 1). _Dei Verbum_ then refers to Ephesians 1:9, another classic passage on God revealing ‘the mystery’ of the divine will— namely, the saving plan for all humanity now disclosed in Christ (_DV_ 2). The same chapter presses on to cite in part the opening verses of the Letter to the Hebrews (_DV_ 4): ‘After God had spoken many times and in various ways through the prophets, “in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son” (Heb 1:1–2).’ _Dei Verbum_ has already made it clear that not only words but also deeds are integral to revelation (_DV_ 2). By **[p. 208]** having already named the patriarchs and Moses (_DV_ 3), the document implies that ‘the prophets’ of Hebrews 1:1 should be understood more broadly as all those Old Testament figures through whom God spoke and acted and not merely as those who gave their names to the prophetic books.

Chapter 2 endorses a _reductio in mysterium_, which highlights _the_ mystery of the tri-personal God revealed through Christ in the history of salvation and inviting human beings to share in the new communion of love. This language is based on the Pauline letters: Romans 16:25–26; Ephesians 1:9; 3:4, 9; 6:19; and Colossians 1:27; 4:3. Talk of this ‘mystery’ forms a leitmotif in _Dei Verbum_; five times the constitution speaks of ‘mystery’ in the singular (_DV_ 2, 15, 17, 24, 26) and, unlike Vatican I’s _Dei Filius_, never of ‘mysteries’ in the plural. The same tendency pervades all the texts of Vatican II: the sixteen documents use ‘mystery’ in the singular 114 times and ‘mysteries’ in the plural only fourteen times. Right from his first encyclical, _Redemptor Hominis_ (The Redeemer of the Human Person) of 1979, John Paul II followed suit. He wrote fifty-nine times of ‘the mystery of redemption’, ‘the paschal mystery’, ‘the mystery of Christ’, ‘the mystery of the divine economy’, and so forth, without ever using the term ‘mystery’ in the plural. His 1980 encyclical _Dives in Misericordia_ uses ‘mystery’ thirty-nine times, but ‘mysteries’ only twice.

The examples just given should establish the profoundly biblical orientation of _Dei Verbum._ It comes as no surprise to find the document inviting theologians to make the study of the Scriptures ‘the soul’ of their work (_DV_ 24), an invitation already found in a text published three weeks earlier, the Decree on the Training of Priests, _Optatam Totius_ (The Desired [Renewal] of the Whole [Church]), 16. The Second Vatican Council nowhere says that the Scriptures should be the very soul of the teaching office of bishops. Nevertheless, the nature of magisterial teaching exemplifled by the conciliar documents, along with the clear affirmation that the magisterium of the bishops is ‘not superior to the word of God, but is rather its servant’ (_DV_ 10), clearly implies that the official teaching of the Church should also find its ‘soul’ in the inspired Scriptures.

### 6. Christ and the Holy Spirit

[^c12-8] The fullness of the divine revelation in Christ dominates _Dei Verbum_. At the General Congregations of Vatican II, all held in St Peter’s Basilica, the Book of the Gospels was solemnly enthroned each day right through the four sessions (including the sessions dedicated to the elaboration of _Dei Verbum_) and symbolized the presiding presence of the risen Christ.

[^c12-8]: Wicks, _Investigating Vatican II._

Even though _Dei Verbum_ refers twenty-three times to the Holy Spirit, it remains very Christocentric and displays a Western tendency to subordinate the work of the Holy Spirit to that of the Son. The chapter on the **[p. 209]** Old Testament (_DV_ 14–16), for example, is oriented towards Christ and says nothing about the Holy Spirit active in the history of God’s chosen people.
