On 5 October 1964, during a debate on the revised text of _De Divina Revelatione_, which was to become _Dei Verbum_, an Eastern archbishop, Néophytos Edelby, indicated in a remarkable speech the need to recognize more fully the role of the Holy Spirit in revelation and its [^c12-9] transmission through tradition and the inspired Scriptures. Unfortunately, Edelby’s speech came too late and hardly affected the final version of _Dei Verbum._

[^c12-9]: O’Collins, _Retrieving Fundamental Theology_, 174–77.

If the Second Vatican Council had met in the 1990s or later, the Holy Spirit would have bulked larger in _Dei Verbum._ Since Vatican II, the members of the Catholic Church and their leaders, especially those in the Western Church, who make up the overwhelming majority of the Church’s members, have become much more sensitive to the role of the Holy Spirit. The charismatic renewal and increased contacts with Eastern Christians, both Orthodox and Catholic, have helped to bring about this change. John Paul’s 1986 encyclical _Dominum et Vivificantem_, the first papal encyclical on the Holy Spirit since 1897, was emblematic of this development. His 1990 encyclical on the Church’s missionary mandate, _Redemptoris Missio_ (_RM_) also embodied much on the Spirit (see _RM_ 21–30).

### 7. The Other Documents on Revelation

To grasp Vatican II’s teaching on revelation, _Dei Verbum_ is beyond question _the document_. Nevertheless, it is at our peril that we neglect other texts of the council. As we have already seen, at times they repeat and amplify the teaching of _Dei Verbum_: for instance, on (1) the present revelation that takes place in the liturgy, an essential part of Christian life which is barely mentioned in _Dei Verbum_ (_DV_ 25), and (2) the full and final manifestation of Christ at his Second Coming. At times, these other documents add new and important points about the divine self-revelation and its reception. Let us consider three examples: the prophetic mediators of revelation are not restricted to bishops; there are various means of revelation (sanctity, missionary activity, and the signs of the times) other than the Scriptures and the liturgy; and the human condition is open to the divine self-disclosure.

First, as well as being ‘the fullness of revelation’, Jesus Christ is ‘the Mediator’ of revelation (_DV_ 2). _Dei Verbum_ also speaks about some of those who, as subordinate mediators (lower case), share in the communication of the divine self-disclosure. Successors to the apostles, the bishops are called to transmit the word of God integrally, being ‘enlightened by the Spirit of truth [so that] they may faithfully preserve, expound, and disseminate [the word of God] by their preaching’ (_DV_ 9). As servants of this word, the **[p. 210]** magisterium ‘listens to this [Word] devotedly, guards it reverently, and expounds it faithfully’ (_DV_10). In its lyrical closing chapter, _Dei Verbum_ recognizes how priests, deacons, and catechists also share in this ‘ministry of the Word’ (_DV_ 25).

A year earlier, _Lumen Gentium_ insisted that the bishops’ prophetic ministry of ‘preaching the Gospel’ and communicating the divine self-revelation takes precedence over their priestly duty to administer the sacraments and their pastoral, ‘kingly’ leadership (_LG_ 26–27). ‘Among the more important duties of bishops, preaching the Gospel has pride of place. For the bishops are heralds of the faith … Under the light of the Holy Spirit they cause that faith to radiate, drawing from the storehouse of revelation new things and old (see Matt. 13:52)’ (_LG_ 25). Since _Lumen Gentium_ centres here on the _transmission_ of revelation through the bishops’ ministry of the word, the _content_ of the divine self-revelation comes naturally to the fore: ‘the Gospel’, ‘the faith’ (= the _fides quae_ or ‘faith which’ we confess), and ‘the treasure of revelation’. Like public heralds, the bishops announce God’s revelation in Christ which the light of the Holy Spirit illuminates and makes credible. The ‘external’ word of the bishops and the ‘internal’ word of the Spirit conspire in witnessing to the divine revelation and evoking faith.

_Lumen Gentium_, while highlighting the bishops’ prophetic role as mediators of revelation, in no way proposes an episcopal monopoly. Priests, deacons, and _all the baptized_ share, albeit somewhat differently, in the triple office of Christ as priest, _prophet_, and king/shepherd. Yves Congar and Gérard Philips had written [^c12-10] on this triple office and helped to make it a major theme at the council: in particular, all the members of ‘the holy people of God share also in Christ’s _prophetic_ office’; their ‘living witness … aroused and sustained by the Holy Spirit’, communicates to others Christ’s revelation of God (_LG_ 12).

[^c12-10]: Gerald O’Collins, _The Second Vatican Council_: _Meaning and Message_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2014), 19–20, 40– 43.

Chapter 4 of _Lumen Gentium_ elaborates the threefold ‘office’ of the laity as priests, prophets, and kings. First of all, Christ Jesus, ‘the supreme and eternal Priest’, ‘intimately joins’ all the baptized to his ‘life and mission’ and gives them ‘a share in his priestly office’ so that they may offer spiritual worship in the Holy Spirit ‘for the glory of the Father and the salvation’ of the world (_LG_ 34). Second, ‘Christ … the great prophet who proclaimed the kingdom of the Father’ now ‘fulfils this prophetic office not only by the hierarchy who teach in his name … but also through the laity’. He ‘establishes them as witnesses’ and ‘powerful heralds of the faith’ (_LG_ 35). Third, ‘the Lord also desires that his kingdom be spread by the lay faithful’ through the exercise of their kingly office (_LG_ 36).

Apropos of the prophetic function, the council speaks of laypeople engaged in ‘evangelisation’, which it describes as ‘the proclamation of Christ by word and the testimony of life’. Married people must be ‘witnesses of the faith and love of Christ to one another and to their children’. As for the Christian family and its contribution to the mediation of revelation, such a family ‘proclaims aloud both the virtues of the kingdom of God here and now and the hope of the blessed life’. Hence, ‘by their testimony’, they ‘enlighten **[p. 211]** those who seek the truth’ (_LG_ 35). The passage is heavy with language for revelation and its present mediation (‘evangelisation’, ‘proclamation’, ‘testimony’, ‘witnesses’, ‘proclaims’, ‘light’, and ‘truth’).

Second, referring to Christians of heroic sanctity, no matter what their specific place is in the Church, _Lumen Gentium_ remarks: ‘In the lives of those companions of ours in the human condition who are more perfectly transformed into the image of Christ God shows [_manifestat_], vividly, to humanity his presence and his face’ (_LG_ 50). Unlike bishops, priests, deacons, catechists, and other official mediators of and witnesses to God’s revelation in Christ, saints cannot produce a document to prove that they have received such a commission. They show themselves to be such mediators and witnesses through their impact on others. They do so in ordinary ‘life’, communicating vividly the ‘presence’ and ‘face’ of God. Here the present tense of ‘shows’ highlights the divine self-disclosure here and now. The Constitution continues to press the present force of revelation by adding that in the saints God ‘speaks to us’ and ‘offers us’ both ‘a sign of his Kingdom’ and a witness to ‘the truth of the Gospel’ (_LG_ 50).

[^c12-11] A footnote (_LG_ 50 n. 12) directs readers to the First Vatican Council. The link with _Dei Filius_ also indicates a difference between the two councils. For Vatican I, eminent holiness works as one of the signs or ‘notes’ that establish the credibility of the Catholic Church and show how she was instituted by Christ. But _Lumen Gentium_ interprets outstanding sanctity as primarily a sign revealing God, Christ, the divine Kingdom, and ‘the truth of the Gospel’.

[^c12-11]: Denzinger and Hünermann, eds., _Enchiridion Symbolorum_, no. 3013; Neuner and Dupis, eds., _The Christian Faith_, 123.

The sign of sanctity within the Church figures prominently among the _means_ that in the present time disclose the divine self-revelation in Christ. The missionary activity of the Church towards those ‘who are outside’ does the same. Above we quoted two passages from _Ad Gentes_ which embody similar teaching on the present event of revelation (from _AG_ 8, 9). Let me add a third such passage, which deftly associates revelation with salvation: ‘missionary activity’ is ‘the manifestation of God’s purpose, its epiphany, and realisation in the world and its history—that by which God, through mission, manifestly brings the history of salvation to its conclusion’ (_AG_ 9).

A _further means_ of divine revelation goes by the biblical name of ‘the signs of the times’ (Matt. 16:3). _Gaudium et Spes_ pays particular attention to interpreting these signs ‘in the light of the Gospel’ (_GS_ 4). In ‘the events, needs, and longings’ of our time, there can be ‘genuine signs of the presence or purpose of God’ (_GS_ 11). In other words, the signs of our times may show us _where_ God is present in a special way and _what_ God wants to bring about in our world. A later article draws together what we read in _GS_ 4 and 11 by spelling out the duty to attend to ‘the voices of our times’: ‘with the help of the Holy Spirit, it is the task of the whole people of God, particularly of its pastors and theologians, to listen and to distinguish the many voices of our time and to interpret them in the light of God’s word, in order that the revealed Truth may be more deeply **[p. 212]** penetrated, better understood, and more suitably presented’ (_GS_ 44). An openness to God’s revelatory presence and redemptive purposes calls for such attention to the signs of the times and the voices of our age.

_Dei Verbum_, above all in its final chapter (_DV_ 21–26), stresses the ways in which the inspired Scriptures, which it called ‘the utterance of God [_locutio Dei_]’ (_DV_ 9), convey the divine self-manifestation. It also mentions the liturgy, ‘full of the divine words’ (_DV_ 25), as a channel of God’s self-revelation. A canonical reading of the documents of Vatican II adds further means that convey divine revelation: eminent sanctity, missionary activity, and the signs of the times.

Third, those other conciliar texts also add to the brief account that _Dei Verbum_ provides of the human faith that responds to God’s self-revelation (_DV_ 5). The Declaration on Religious Freedom, _Dignitatis Humanae_ (_DH_), naturally underscores the freedom with which human beings are called to receive the divine revelation (_DH_ 9–11). Like _Dei Verbum_ (e.g., _DV_ 2–5), _Gaudium et Spes_ acknowledges the priority of the divine self-witness over any human search for God (e.g., _GS_ 36, 58). As Augustine put it in his _Expositions of the Psalms_, ‘he [God] has searched for you before you search for him; and he has found you so that you will find him’ (138.14; trans. mine). But, going further than _Dei Verbum_, both _Gaudium et Spes_ and _Nostra Aetate_ correlate divine revelation with a vision of the human condition.

In October 1965, _Nostra Aetate_ (_NA_), the Declaration on the Relation of the Church to Non-Christian Religions, summarized the basic questions about the meaning of life, suffering, happiness, existence after death, and other primordial issues that open human beings up to religious responses (_NA_ 1). Less than two months later, _Gaudium et Spes_ developed at greater length a similar list, which served to correlate the human questions with the divine answers offered by God’s saving self-revelation. Aligning itself with a tradition that goes back to St Paul (Rom. 7:13–25), the Constitution presented the human being as a radically questioning reality (_homo interrogans_): ‘For people will always be keen to know, if only in a general way, what is the meaning of their life, their activity, and death’ (_GS_ 41; see _GS_ 10, 21). The divine revelation stands in correlation with these questions: ‘in God alone, who created women and men in his own image and redeemed them from sin; and this answer is given in the revelation in Christ his Son who became man’ (_GS_ 41). Revelation meets the need of human beings as essentially questioners. _Gaudium et Spes_ also correlated the divine revelation with deep human experiences (_GS_ 13, 33).

The human condition is characterized by radical experiences and deep questions. Matching these experiences and questions, the divine self-disclosure of God brings the revelation of humanity: ‘Christ the new Adam, in the very revelation of the mystery of the Father and of his love, fully reveals humanity to itself and brings to light its very high calling’ (_GS_ 22). In her revelatory role, ‘the Church is entrusted with the task of manifesting to them the mystery of God, who is their final destiny; in doing so, it discloses to them the meaning of their own existence, the innermost truth about themselves’ (_GS_ 41). One might argue that _Dei Verbum_ implies, along with the revelation of God, the revelation of the true situation of human beings. Yet one must turn to _Gaudium et Spes_ to find this clearly stated and explained.

### 8. Saving Revelation Reaching the ‘Others’

**[p. 213]** Finally, what of the saving revelation of God reaching those who follow other faiths or none at all? In four [^c12-12] documents, but not in _Dei Verbum_, Vatican II addresses their religious situation. Here the council characteristically uses a double-sided terminology: true/good, true/holy, truth/grace, and light/life. These dyads express the two distinguishable but inseparable dimensions of the divine self-communication: revelation and salvation.

[^c12-12]: Gerald O’Collins, _The Second Vatican Council on Other Religions_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2013), 73–142.

In his first encyclical, _Ecclesiam Suam_ (His Church) of 1964, Pope Paul VI wrote of what is ‘true and good’ in the Muslim worship of God (_Acta Apostolicae Sedis_ (_AAS_), 56:654–5). Within a few months, similar language surfaced in what _Lumen Gentium_ found among ‘those who, without any fault of theirs, have not yet arrived at an explicit knowledge of God, and who, not without grace, strive to lead a good life. Whatever _good or truth_ is found amongst them is … a preparation for the Gospel and given by him who _enlightens_ all men and women, so that they may at length have _life_’ (_LG_ 16; emphasis added). The Johannine language for revelation and salvation—‘enlightens’ and ‘life’—(John 1:4, 9) alternates with the recognition of elements of salvation and revelation (‘whatever is good and true’) to be found among upright non-believers.

In three documents—_Nostra Aetate_, _Ad Gentes_, and _Gaudium et Spes—_from its last session (October– December 1965), Vatican II employed similar double terminology. Implying that other religions, even often, can exhibit elements of truth and holiness, _Nostra Aetate_ declared: ‘the Catholic Church rejects nothing of what is _true and holy_ in these religions. She has a high regard for the manner of life and conduct, the precepts and doctrines which, although differing in many ways from her own teaching, nevertheless, often reflect a _ray of that Truth_ [upper case in the original Latin] _who enlightens all human beings_’ (_NA_ 2). Once again echoing John’s Gospel, the council followed here the usual order of revelation and salvation (‘true and holy’). Six weeks later it followed the same order, while being more critical in its thinking about other religions: missionary activity delivers from evil influences every ‘element of _truth and grace_ found among peoples, and which are, as it were, a secret presence of God; and it restores them [these elements] to Christ their source’ (_AG_ 9; emphasis added).

This double-sided terminology reminds us that we may not raise the question of salvation without raising that of revelation, and vice versa. When interpreting anyone’s situation before God, we need to recall the two inseparable dimensions of the divine self-communication. The conciliar language witnesses to the way **[p. 214]** Christ’s mediation involves his being universal Revealer as well as universal Saviour. He cannot be accepted as Saviour of all without being accepted as Revealer for all, ‘the true light that enlightens everyone coming into the world’ (John 1:9).

What Vatican II teaches about those who come to embrace Christian faith opens a window on how it views the followers of other faiths. Those who accept the Gospel undergo a revelatory and salvific process of being ‘enlightened and healed’ (_AG_ 3). For their part, Christ’s followers, while respecting ‘the riches which a generous God has distributed among the nations’, should ‘endeavour to illuminate these riches with the _light_ of the Gospel, set them free, and bring them once more under the dominion of God _the Saviour’_ (_AG_ 11; emphasis added). Despite the cultural and religious ‘riches’ they already enjoy through the divine initiative, non-Christians need to be further ‘enlightened’ by revelation and ‘healed’ by the liberation of salvation.

_Lumen Gentium_ interprets in three ways the change for those who accept the revelation of Christ. They move from an implicit to an ‘explicit knowledge’, from ‘shadows’ to light, and from a state of ‘preparation for the Gospel’ to the ‘fullness’ of maturity (_LG_ 16; see _AG_ 3). There is no question of starting from zero. Implicit knowledge, while not yet a ‘full and conscious acceptance’ (_AG_ 7), is still some kind of knowledge. ‘Shadows’ differ from mere formless darkness. A ‘preparation’ has already set people in movement towards the full goal.

Three verbs imply Vatican II’s vision of those who do not yet accept the Gospel. Their situation leaves them somehow wounded, at a lower level, and imperfect. Through accepting the good news, ‘whatever good is found sown in the heart and mind of human beings and in the particular [religious] rites and cultures of peoples’, so far from being lost, is ‘_purifled_, _raised up_, and _perfected_ for the glory of God’ (_LG_ 17; emphasis added). Yves Congar saw to it that the key verbs (_sanare_, _elevare_, and _consummare_) were repeated a year later [^c12-13] in _Ad Gentes_. Through missionary activity, ‘whatever goodness is found in the minds and hearts of human beings, or in the particular customs and cultures of peoples, so far from being lost, is _purifled_, _raised to a higher level_, and _reaches its perfection_ for the glory of God’ (_AG_ 9; emphasis added).

[^c12-13]: Ibid., 109–10, 213.

While expressing the impact of conversion to Christianity, both passages imply that some measure of revelation is already known in the human _mind_ prior to accepting the Gospel. The process of healing, elevating, and perfecting obviously bespeaks some continuity between the pre-Christian and the Christian state.

Apropos of the revealing and saving activity of Christ before and beyond Christianity, _Ad Gentes_ quotes St Irenaeus on ‘the Word’ through whom ‘all things were made and who was always present to the human race’. The decree adds a further passage from Irenaeus: ‘from the beginning, the Son, being present in his creation, reveals [_revelat_] the Father to all whom the Father desires, at the time and in the manner desired by the Father’ (_AG_ 3 n. 2). Since the second century, this real but hidden presence of the Word has been named as ‘the seeds of the Word’ (_AG_ 11). It is only in _Ad Gentes_ 3 n. 2, that Vatican II uses ‘reveal’ of the **[p. 215]** human knowledge of God mediated through the created world and its history. In contemporary terms, Irenaeus was talking about the general or universal history of revelation (and salvation) impinging on the existence of human beings.

Even more than _Ad Gentes_, the constitution _Gaudium et Spes_ offers much teaching about the situation of those who follow other religious faiths or none at all. The voice of God is heard in the human conscience, and the (natural) law is written by God on human hearts (_GS_ 10). This implies some kind of divine self-revelation to all human beings. The Holy Spirit gives all human beings ‘the _light_ and strength’ needed to respond to their supreme calling (_GS_ 10; emphasis added). Through the same Spirit, all human beings can be united with the crucifled and risen Christ (_GS_ 22), and the risen Christ is at work in the hearts of human beings everywhere (_GS_ 38). We should recall that faith forms the human response to revelation, when the council significantly remarks that all human beings can receive the gift of faith (_GS_ 15). This implies that in some real, albeit mysterious, way, all human beings, whether or not they are addressed by the Christian [^c12-14] good news, are open to receiving the divine self-revelation by responding to it through God-given faith. Here Vatican II presents God’s revelation and salvation within a universal horizon.

[^c12-14]: Gerald O’Collins, _A Christology of Religions_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2017), 100–122.

### 9. Fundamental Theology

We can describe fundamental theology as the discipline which studies fundamental issues: the divine revelation in the history of Israel and Jesus Christ; the conditions that open up human beings to this self-communication of God; the signs that make faith in and through Jesus Christ a reasonable option; the transmission through tradition and the inspired Scriptures of the experience of revelation; and theological [^c12-15] method. Since revelation (and the response of human faith), tradition, and the Scriptures (including their role as the ‘soul’ of theology (_DV_ 24)) are the chief topics treated in _Dei Verbum_, the Constitution has become the official _magna carta_ for much Catholic fundamental theology. A canonical reading of other documents of Vatican II, as we have just seen, will fill out what we glean from _Dei Verbum._

[^c12-15]: Gerald O’Collins, _Rethinking Fundamental Theology_: _Toward a New Fundamental Theology_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2011).

[^c12-16] This makes it strange that the council never mentioned fundamental theology by name. In _Optatam Totius_ (_OT_), it listed various branches of theology: sacred Scripture, dogmatic theology, the Church Fathers, moral theology, sacred liturgy, canon law, church history, Christian ecumenism, and the study of other faiths. But **[p. 216]** fundamental theology was not included, even though the document mandated the close study of the principal ‘themes of divine revelation’ (_OT_ 16). Eventually, the conciliar omission was remedied when the 1979 Apostolic Constitution on Ecclesiastical Universities and Faculties, _Sapientia Christiana_ (Christian Wisdom), listed fundamental theology among the obligatory disciplines (art. 51).

[^c12-16]: René Latourelle, ‘Absence and Presence of Fundamental Theology at Vatican II’, in _Vatican II_: _Assessment and Perspectives_, ed. René Latourelle, 3 vols (Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 1989), 3:378–415.

### Suggested Reading

O’Collins, Gerald. _Revelation_: _Towards a Christian Interpretation of God’s Self-Revelation in Jesus Christ_. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2016.

O’Collins, Gerald. _The Second Vatican Council_: _Meaning and Message_. Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2014.

Rush, Ormond. _The Eyes of Faith_: _The Sense of the Faithful and the Church’s Reception of Revelation_. Washington, DC: Catholic University of America Press, 2009.

Wicks, Jared. ‘The Fullness of Revelation in Christ in _Dei Verbum_’. _Josephinum Journal of Theology_ 23 (2016 [published 2017]): 176–204.

Wicks, Jared. _Investigating Vatican II_. Washington, DC: The Catholic University of America Press, 2018.

## 13. Church Governance and Forms of Christian Vocation

Joachim Schmiedl, Isch

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 217]** In the fourth session (1965), the council passed three decrees dealing with the Church’s leadership: bishops, priests, and religious. Among them was a Decree on the Apostolate of the Laity, an issue that had never before been dealt with by a council. A strategic decision influenced the course of the council. The chairman of the Theological Commission, Cardinal Alfredo Ottaviani, insisted that doctrinal, strictly dogmatic-theological issues should be dealt with by his commission alone. All other commissions were to content themselves with pastoral applications. Upon this premise, issues had already been determined in a preparatory phase of the council. As a result, chapters in the Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, _Lumen Gentium_, contain sections on the People of God, to which belong the so-called laypeople, as well as the bishops, priests, and religious. The application to the practice of the Church is found in the decrees, which clarifled the profile of the respective groups of persons and their missions as well as the juxtaposition of different charisms and functions within the Church.

### 2. The Situation before the Council

The reform decrees of the Council of Trent (1545–63) had determined the function and role of bishops, priests, and religious for more than three centuries. It was not until the nineteenth century that the reversal of a long held feudal culture among the bishops was begun. Priests lived in the tension between the roles of **[p. 218]** ‘Reverend Father’, pastor, and civil servant. By their consecration they were sanctifled and were expected to demonstrate this sanctity through their lives. The religious were able to maintain a degree of independence in the plurality of their orders and congregations. Laypeople had no rights in the Church, only duties. Lay movements emerged in countries like Italy and Germany in the nineteenth century. Self-determined organizations in the form of unions and associations were possible, but the apostolate remained strictly the task of the ecclesiastical hierarchy, and laypeople were permitted to participate in this role only in the sense of Catholic Action.

The need for reform had already become clear during the period of consulting the future council fathers. The First Vatican Council was only able to deal with the pope’s singular position, the definition of his infallibility, and the primacy of his jurisdiction. Now the bishops demanded a theologically based re-evaluation of their positions. In addition to the Council of 1869–70, the following topics were to be addressed: the collegiality of bishops; their powers that are not derived from the pope or the Curia; the leadership of their dioceses; their relationships to their dioceses and their priests; their share in the ordinary magisterium of the Church. For priests, the bishops called for a commitment to holiness through frequent confession and a zealous life of prayer, priestly attire, and celibacy. With regard to religious, the main concern of the bishops was an appropriate regulation of the orders’ relationship with the diocese, in the sense of the orders being incorporated into the pastoral structures controlled by the bishops. The extent of their exemption from episcopal oversight was criticized. This concern was raised in vehement terms by bishops who had only a small number of diocesan clergy. As persons responsible for diocesan congregations of sisters—they were generally favoured by the bishops over those under papal jurisdiction—the bishops were concerned with reform in outward appearance. For this reason, they submitted a plethora of suggestions to simplify religious habits, reduce privileges in the area of popular liturgy, implement regulations about enclosure, and provide restrictive rules for the confession of religious sisters.

The demand, however, that the issue of the laity be dealt with in a comprehensive way was new. This reflected the great congresses which had taken place in Rome on the initiative of Pope Pius XII in the 1950s and which were accompanied, theologically, by the contributions of theologians like Yves Congar, Gérard Philips, Hans Urs von Balthasar, Alfons Auer, Karl Rahner, and Edward Schillebeeckx. It was necessary that the council occupy itself with the lay apostolate and lay associations and, in particular, clarify the relationship between Catholic Action and existing organizations.

### 3. The Historical Development of the Decrees

The four decrees dealt with here each have their own complicated history of development. They began as **[p. 219]** drafts from the time of the preparation for the council, were revised several times, discussed in the general congregations, and finally adopted in the fourth session.

#### Christus Dominus

The Decree on the Pastoral Office of Bishops in the Church, _Christus Dominus_ (_CD_), emerged from the discussion of two drafts: ‘On the Bishops and the Leadership of Dioceses’ and ‘On Pastoral Care’. Both schemas were redrafted several times from scratch. From 5 to 15 November 1963, the schema on the bishops was discussed in the council hall for the first time. Criticism of the schema was primarily based on the lack of emphasis on collegiality as a guiding principle. The bishops’ participation in the leadership of the universal Church was to be clarifled in the form of a representative body of the College of Bishops to assist the pope. The Roman Curia ought to be internationalized and, through the involvement of laypeople, become more open. A highlight of the discussion was the open criticism by Cardinal Joseph Frings, archbishop of Cologne, of the highest ecclesiastical office, the Supreme Congregation of the Holy Office in the Roman Curia.

When the draft text _De cura animarum_ was set aside, a number of other aspects were added to the schema on the bishops so that it now concerned the tasks of the bishops at various levels of ecclesial life. The working title was accordingly _De Pastorali Episcoporum Munere in Ecclesia_, the Pastoral Office of the Bishops in the Church. The role of the bishops was treated in three chapters: their relationship to the universal Church; their relationship to the particular churches, their dioceses; and their cooperation with one another. After further discussion in three general congregations and the incorporation of the _modi_, the decree was widely accepted and, in the final votes, was solemnly accepted on 28 October 1965 with only two votes against.

As mentioned above, the decree is divided into three chapters. The bishops are seen in their relationship with the universal Church (_CD_ 4–10), including their role in advising the administration of the Curia. As diocesan bishops they are in charge of a particular Church, which they are ‘to teach, to sanctify and to govern’ (_CD_ 11). The dioceses should be viable entities. The bishops are to be assisted by co-workers assigned to them, such as auxiliary bishops, a diocesan curia, a pastoral council, the diocesan clergy, and the religious working in the diocese. The bishops are called upon to ‘promote the common good and the good of the individual churches’ (_CD_ 36). The council mentions synods, councils and bishops’ conferences, ecclesiastical provinces, and bishops with extra-diocesan tasks.

#### Presbyterorum Ordinis

Several smaller schemes were presented by the Preparatory Commission on the discipline of the clergy and **[p. 220]** the Christian people. But since a commission on the apostolate of the laity existed at the council, this commission focused its attention on clerics and priests. A first draft, _De Clericis_ (1963), was renamed, after its revision, _De Sacerdotibus_, On Priests (1964). After endeavours to synthesize them, twelve guiding principles, together with a message to the priests, were, after a short discussion in October 1964, integrated into a Decree on the Ministry and the Life of Priests, which was adopted as _Presbyterorum Ordinis_ in October 1965.

The first chapter presents the priesthood as part of the Church’s mission. The second chapter is devoted to the priestly ministry. The tasks of proclamation, sanctification, and pastoral guidance are entrusted to priests. Priests are to be united with their bishops and with the presbytery, and they have a special ecumenical responsibility towards their congregations. Care should be taken to ensure a proper distribution of priests across the diocese. The priests are called to a life of perfection. Helpful to this are the evangelical councils of obedience, celibacy, and poverty. Priests are to cultivate unity with Christ through prayer and the Holy Eucharist, and they should regularly improve their knowledge. They should receive a fair wage.

#### Perfectae Caritatis

Questions about the life of religious orders were among the most pressing issues in the preparation of the council. In an effort to ensure that the issue would not be overlooked, the Commission for Religious devised a schema of 132 pages. At the council, however, the commission was marginalized. The streamlining of texts demanded by Cardinal Julius Döpfner was of particular concern to the Commission for Religious. After several sessions, the extensive text was revised and boiled down to a series of ‘propositions’, which were discussed in the General Congregations from 10 to 12 November 1964. From the interventions and _modi_, submitted in writing by the bishops, and a consultation of female superiors of religious orders, a text emerged which was finally approved on 28 October 1965.

The twenty-five paragraphs of the Decree on the Adaptation and Renewal of Religious Life, _Perfectae Caritatis_ (_PC_), required that religious orders undertake a process of renewal and adaptation. The decree establishes norms for an accommodation to conditions of time and place (_PC_ 25). To all forms of consecrated life—contemplative, active, monastic, lay, secular—belong the vows of chastity, poverty, and obedience, as well as life in community. Adaptations were to be made with respect to the enclosure of nuns, religious habit, education, and the promotion of mergers.

#### Apostolicam Actuositatem

One of the preparatory commissions set up by John XXIII was required to attend to the apostolate of the laity. It focused on three themes: lay apostolate, Catholic Action, and communities and associations. A first **[p. 221]** text was submitted to the council fathers at the end of the first session. From 1963, laypeople were involved in the development of the text. Only in the third session and after several new versions could the draft be discussed in the council hall, where portions were strongly criticized. After incorporating references to the two Constitutions on the Church, the decree was the subject of voting in the fourth session and was solemnly approved on 18 November with 2,340 votes in favour and only two negative votes.

The introduction to the Decree on the Apostolate of Lay People, _Apostolicam Actuositatem_ (_AA_), points to the necessity for the lay apostolate and the rationale for this; namely, ‘continuing population increases, progress in science and technology, and growing interdependence of people worldwide’ (_AA_ 1). The vocation of the laity to the apostolate is the subject of the first chapter. Any activity directed towards the expansion of the kingdom of Christ is considered as belonging to the apostolate. Lay people exercise it ‘when they work to evangelize people and make them holy, [and] when they endeavour to have the Gospel spirit permeate and improve’ (_AA_ 2). Baptism and confirmation lead, by their very nature, to this participation in the apostolate. The fruitfulness of the mission of the lay apostolate depends upon ‘their living union with Christ’ (_AA_ 4) and the cultivation of a deep spiritual life.

The objectives of the lay apostolate (chapter 2) concern both the spiritual and secular order: ‘The lay person, at one and the same time a believer and a citizen of the world, has only a single conscience, a Christian conscience, by which to be guided in both domains’ (_AA_ 5). This is to be done through the witness of life and the proclamation of the word. It is the task of the laity to shape the temporal order according to Christian principles. The exercise of love as a private and public attitude is essential. Various areas of the apostolate are mentioned and described in the third chapter: ‘church communities, the family, the young, the social enviironment, national and international spheres’ (_AA_ 9).

The forms of the lay apostolate (chapter 4) may differ. Lay persons may practise it as individuals or in associations. Here, the role of laypeople in situations of persecution or ‘where Catholics are few or scattered’ receives special recognition (_AA_ 17). Communal and organized apostolates are to be promoted in any event:

While preserving intact the necessary link with ecclesiastical authority, the laity have the right to establish direct associations, and to join existing ones. Dissipation of forces must, however, be avoided; this would happen if new associations and works were created without sufficient reason, if old ones now grown useless were retained, if out-of-date methods continued to be employed. It will not always be a wise procedure, either, to transfer indiscriminately into some particular country forms that have originated in another. (_AA_ 19)

To be recognized as a Catholic organization, groups or associations of laypersons must embrace as their immediate purpose contributing to the Church’s apostolic aim; ‘that is, the evangelisation and sanctification of men and women and the Christian formation of their consciences, so as to enable them to imbue with the Gospel spirit the various social groups and enviironments’ (_AA_ 20). There must be **[p. 222]** collaboration with the church hierarchy in the manner of a corporation and under the guidance of the hierarchy. Lay apostolates are ‘regarded as Catholic Action, even if they have forms and names that vary according to the requirements of localities and peoples’ (_AA_ 20).

According to the fifth chapter, the lay apostolate must be integrated into the apostolate of the universal Church. The hierarchy should promote the lay apostolate and has the right to judge the catholicity of works and institutions (_AA_ 24). Consultative bodies are to be established in dioceses and parishes, but also at regional, national, and international levels to ‘assist the Church’s apostolic work, whether in the fleld of evangelisation and sanctification or in the fields of charity, social relations and the rest, the clergy and religious working with the laity’ (_AA_ 26). ‘For the service and promotion of the lay apostolate’ (_AA_ 26), a special secretariat was to be established at the Holy See. This happened with the founding of the Pontifical Council for the Laity, created by Paul VI on 6 January 1967 by the motu proprio _Catholicam Christi Ecclesiam_. In 2018, this office was integrated into a new Dicastery for the Laity, the Family and Life.

Finally, the document refers to the formation for the apostolate (chapter 6). The lay apostolate receives its special character from the ‘secularity proper to the lay state and from its particular type of spirituality’ (_AA_ 29). Formation for the apostolate is styled as a lifelong task which is to be carried out in accordance with one’s area of responsibility. ‘Many aids are now at the disposal of the laity who devote themselves to the apostolate: namely, seminars, congresses, recollections, retreats, frequent meetings, conferences, books, and periodicals’ (_AA_ 32), which ‘take into account the various types of the apostolate exercised in this or that particular area’ (_AA_ 32).

### 4. Central Themes

#### The Bishop

Following the secularization of the nineteenth century, the role of the bishops in the Church changed dramatically. The separation of Church and state and the secularization of Western society in the Western world had also made it possible for priests of lowly origin to rise to high ecclesiastical office. Since the First Vatican Council, however, the pope had risen in dominance. The Second Vatican Council needed to clarify how the relationship between bishops and the pope was to be shaped and to define their respective tasks. The Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, _Lumen Gentium_ 21 establishes that, by episcopal consecration, the fullness of the sacrament of Orders is conferred and that bishops are thus brought into communion with others: into a collegium whose head is the pope, the bishop of Rome, who shares in the episcopal office and has not received any additional sacramental consecration. The unfolding of this dogmatic doctrine was left to the Decree on the Pastoral Office of Bishops in the Church, _Christus Dominus_ (_CD_). In this decree, **[p. 223]** statements are made concerning the responsibilities of the individual bishop, but the formulations are in the plural. It was always the council’s intention to be mindful that an individual bishop is part of the episcopal college, part of a larger whole.

In describing the role of the bishop, the council refers to the teaching concerning the ‘threefold office’ of Christ as priest, prophet, and king. The pastoral duty of the bishop is one of ‘teaching, sanctifying and governing’ (_CD_ 11). The bishops should not only present the teaching of the Church in an unabridged manner, but also help to interpret in faith so ‘that worldly things and human institutions are ordered, according to the plan of God the Creator, towards the salvation of humanity’ (_CD_ 12). They should seek and promote dialogue with all people. The bishops are the first catechists of their dioceses. They are also the first liturgists, presiding over the prayer of the community, and should lead others to perfection (_CD_ 15). Among the groups of people to whom the bishops should pay particular attention, the council names first priests and the faithful, but also non-Catholic Christians and the non-baptized. The bishops are invited to go to the peripheries of their local Church (a theme reactualized by Pope Francis). The council addresses present-day problems when it draws the special attention of the bishops to ‘migrants, exiles and refugees, sailors and airmen, itinerants and others of this kind’ (_CD_ 18).

A special role is assigned to the bishops with respect to his priests. _Christus Dominus_ 16 states that they should be ‘true fathers’ to all. Paragraph 28 says that diocesan clergy ‘form one priestly body and one family of which the bishop is the father’. The council assigns to the bishops a responsibility that goes beyond an employer–employee relationship. The bishop is urged to care for his priests with affection, and to meet with them regularly to discuss current issues. This relationship of mutual esteem belongs to the spirituality of the bishop and especially to the diocesan priests. It may at times be in tension with the role of the bishop as employer and as the person ultimately responsible for the—sometimes erroneous, indeed unlawful— behaviour of the priests and other employees of the diocese. Closely related are the deliberations on a meaningful territorial and personal determination of the dioceses (_CD_ 22–24).

The council’s discussion of the role of auxiliary bishops who are nominally assigned to a no longer existing diocese as their ‘titular see’ was somewhat controversial. The council, however, assigns them to the bishop in whose diocese they work, where they exercise their office in all matters such that they ‘act in in single minded accord with him’ (_CD_ 25) with him. In contrast to pre-conciliar practices of appointing auxiliary bishops as coadjutors with the right of succession to an elderly bishop, the council does not provide for this as a rule. However, auxiliary bishops are normally to be appointed as vicars general, or, at least, areas are to be entrusted to them in which they can exercise their own responsibility as episcopal vicars. The auxiliary bishops represented at the council followed the discussions of their role with great interest. One consequence was that in Germany, from the time of the council, the auxiliary bishops have participated in the twice-yearly plenary of the episcopal conference and thus, at least, have a say in the election of the president. Important decisions, however, are still made by the diocesan bishops or by a permanent council.

#### Participation and Co-responsibility

**[p. 224]** On 30 October 1963, after securing more than three-quarters of the votes cast, the council fathers decided to affirm that episcopal ordination confers the fullness of sacramental ordination; that every legitimately ordained bishop is a member of the episcopal college; that this college has the full and supreme power in the universal Church; and that this power, in union with the pope, is of divine law. This marked a decisive change in relation to the First Vatican Council. The doctrine of collegiality requires a new relationship between pope and bishops. In the discussion of the Decree on the Pastoral Office of Bishops, therefore, the concept of a continuously existing council of bishops co-governing with the pope played an important role. Even before _Christus Dominus_ was passed, Paul VI issued the motu proprio _Apostolica Sollicitudo_ (15 September 1965) and instituted a Synod of Bishops, which according to its nature would meet periodically, for a limited period. This institution is anchored in _Christus Dominus_ as a body ‘representative of the entire Catholic episcopate’ that reflects their ‘communion in the care of the universal Church’ (_CD_ 5).

Since 1967, the popes have convened a Synod of Bishops every two to four years on issues determined by them. Participants are bishops delegated by the various bishops’ conferences and persons invited by the pope, with or without voting rights. After fifty years, it has treated an impressive panorama of topics. The international synods of bishops have dealt with evangelization and catechesis; bishops, priests, and religious; the Eucharist and the word of God. Extraordinary synods were held for the Netherlands, Africa, Asia, Europe, Lebanon, the Middle East, Oceania, and the Amazon region. Three synods (1980, 2014, and 2015) were devoted to marriage and the family. Their post-conciliar writings do not provide many answers to concrete questions, but serve to motivate and strengthen the Church’s faith consciousness. They are part of the self-reassurance of a global religious community and are an important part of the Church’s ordinary teaching office, derived from a vital engagement with both tradition and the present.

The bishops seek to discern responses and deliberate on the pressing questions of the day when they gather in synods or as episcopal conferences. These are ways of practising collegiality and synodality. In Germany, the bishops have been meeting in formal gatherings since 1848. The German bishops’ conference was officially constituted at the end of the Second Vatican Council. During the council, the assemblies of the bishops of one or several countries met in groups where the directions for debate and joint submissions were voted upon and the speakers appointed for the plenary sessions. Today, worldwide, there are more than a hundred conferences of bishops of various countries, regions, or continents. As much as they determine the practical life of a particular church, their efficacy remains limited to the organization and encouragement of joint action. Any doctrinal teaching by a bishops’ conference still requires unanimity or quasi-unanimity to be regarded as binding.

**[p. 225]** The way the documents of national or regional bishops’ assemblies have been received by the universal Church has differed according to the pontificates of the various bishops of Rome. While Pope John Paul II, in his many writings, referred repeatedly to the documents of continental episcopal conferences, in the writings of Benedict XVI there is no indication of any reference to the work of the conferences. This changed fundamentally under Pope Francis. Twenty-two references to publications of episcopal conferences can be found in each of the pope’s first two documents: _Evangelii Gaudium_ (2013) and _Laudato Si’_ (2015). The final document of the Assembly of the Latin American Episcopate in Aparecida (2007) is conspicuous in this regard. It was written under Cardinal Bergoglio’s leadership. Also, reference is made to various documents from the Congo, India, Paraguay, New Zealand, Mexico, Portugal, and Bolivia. More than his predecessors, Francis draws from the magisterial statements of regional churches. The next step in the development of synodality and collegiality will have been attained when those magisterial statements are not only tolerated but also come to be regarded as complementing those that derive from the exercise of the papal teaching office.

For Francis, this ‘spirit of collegiality and synodality’ (6 October 2015) is indispensable. To understand the tension, however, in which this spirit is to be conceived, two statements by the pope should be considered. At the celebration of the fiftieth anniversary of the institution of the Synod of Bishops by Paul VI on 17 October 2015, Francis said:

The world in which we live, and which we are called to love and serve, even with its contradictions, demands that the Church strengthen cooperation in all areas of her mission. It is precisely the path of _synodality_ which God expects of the Church of the third millennium. …

… The _sensus fidei_ [the supernatural sense of faith] prevents a rigid separation between an _Eccelsia docens_ [the teaching Church] and an _Ecclesia discens_ [a learning Church], since the flock likewise has an instinctive ability to discern the new ways that the Lord is revealing to the Church.

Synodality is manifested on three levels of ecclesial life: in the advisory councils of the individual diocese, at the level of episcopal conferences, and finally the universal Church.

On the same occasion, Francis pointed to the limitation of synodality through the office of the pope:

The Synod process culminates in listening to the Bishop of Rome, who is called to speak as ‘pastor and teacher of all Christians’, not on the basis of his personal convictions but as the supreme witness to the _fides totius Ecclesiae_ [the faith of the entire Church], ‘the guarantor of the obedience and the conformity of the Church to the will of God, to the Gospel of Christ, and to the Tradition of the Church’.

The fact that the Synod always acts _cum Petro et sub Petro_—indeed, not only _cum Petro_, but also _sub Petro_—is not a limitation of freedom, but a guarantee of unity. For the Pope is, by will of the Lord, **[p. 226]** ‘the perpetual visible source and foundation of the unity both of the bishops and of the whole company of the faithful’. Closely related to this concept of ‘_hierarchica communio_’ as employed by the Second Vatican Council: the Bishops are linked to the Bishop of Rome by the bond of episcopal communion _(cum Petro)_ while, at the same time, hierarchically subject to him as head of the college _(sub Petro)_.

This marks the opportunities in, but also the limits of, synodality in the Catholic Church: synods are advisory bodies. The structure of participants varies. Since the Second Vatican Council, synods, especially at diocesan and national levels, have been a reflection of a particular church: priests and laity, professionals and volunteers, various professional groups, and members of religious orders, congregations, and spiritual communities. They remain, however, assemblies in which central issues of the respective Church are discussed, but the final decision on their implementation remains with the bishop or, in the case of synods of bishops, with the pope. The fact that Francis quoted the First Vatican Council in this context shows this tension between consultation on the one hand and co-determination and decision-making on the other.

This tension continues at the level of dioceses. The bishops are committed to collegial advisory structures. Vatican II prescribes structures of consultation, whose forms may vary. These include cathedral chapters, a college of consultors, a presbyteral council, as well as diocesan and parish pastoral councils, which also include laypeople. The involvement of the bishop in committees comprised of specialists is becoming increasingly important. Thus, the associations of laypeople and their organization are autonomous bodies. Due to a variety of cases of economic mismanagement, a sound reliance on competent persons by the bishop becomes more and more urgent, especially with respect to financial matters. In its 2018 document _Synodality in the Life and Mission of the Church_ (69), the International Theological Commission correctly points to the difference between decision-making and decision-taking (the pastoral implementation of the decisions). The document recognizes in synodality a new style which will have an effect on ecclesiastical processes.

#### The Roman Curia

The Decree on the Pastoral Office of Bishops defined the departments of the Roman Curia as institutions acting in the name, and with the authority, of the pope to assist him ‘in exercising supreme, full, and immediate power in the universal Church’ (_CD_ 9). The council called for a reform of those institutions ‘as regards their number, name, competence and peculiar method of procedure’ (_CD_ 9). In addition, an internationalization of the Curia was required through the appointment of diocesan bishops and laypeople.

Paul VI responded to these calls by undertaking a reform of the Curia. With the motu proprio _Pro Comperto Sane_ (6 August 1967), he broadened the membership of the curial congregations with the addition of a few **[p. 227]** diocesan bishops who attend the plenary assemblies. The Apostolic Constitution _Regimini Ecclesiae_ (15 August 1967) changed the names and responsibilities of congregations and added secretariats for the unity of Christians, non-Christians, non-believers, and the Pontifical Council for the Laity. Twenty years later, John Paul II transformed the secretariats, according them the status of pontifical councils and adding councils for the family, for justice and peace, for the pastoral care of migrants, for the pastoral care of those working with the sick, for the interpretation of legislative texts, for culture, and for the social means of communication. As much as this diversity in the variety of pastoral activities corresponds to the work of the Church, it is, at the same time, a reflection of an inflated administrative apparatus of the central Roman authorities.

The reform of the Curia under Pope Francis first concentrated on economic affairs, which had got out of control. The media activities of the Vatican were reorganized. He sought to establish greater equality between the various councils and congregations of the Curia and merged several responsibilities under one roof: for example, in a new Dicastery for Laity, Family, and Life, and the Dicastery for Integral Human Development. In individual cases, laypersons already occupy the offices of several councils and commissions. Women sometimes act as undersecretaries in dicasteries. But the de-clericalization of the Curia is not yet complete. Pope Francis issued a new set of statutes for the Roman Curia in his Apostolic Constitution, _Praedicate Evanglium_ (19 March 2022), placing all dicasteries on the same level, and opened the possibility for lay men and women to preside over them.

#### Religious Life: Principles of Reform

_Perfectae Caritatis_ (_PC_), the Decree on Renewal of Religious Life, assimilated into its very title the hopes of John XXIII for an _aggiornamento_ for the Church through a ‘new Pentecost’ of the council. How does such reform occur? _Perfectae Caritatis,_ chapter 2 provides answers with regard to religious which are also applicable to other groups and communities. It considers five criteria to guide the return to the sources and the adaptation to the conditions of our time.

The first criterion for successful reform is orientation to the Gospel. The biblical emphasis of the council is demonstrated in the contention that the example of Jesus Christ receives a new radiance in meeting the present time. Since the council, ecclesiastical documents have therefore been more based on Scripture and seek a responsible biblical foundation. The second criterion concerns tradition and history. This requires religious orders to follow the _spirit_ of their founders and sound traditions of the past, thus ensuring continuity but also granting opportunity for numerous reforms. The third criterion requires that creative reforms be informed by ‘their own characteristics’ and by the charisms granted to a group or community (parish, diocese). For the council, ‘renewal’ is not a uniform process but must reflect ‘catholic’ diversity.

From the core spirit of the council emerges the fourth criterion for reform, which can be summed up in the **[p. 228]** concept of reading and understanding the ‘signs of the time’. The fifth criterion for reform is that renewal must be a spiritual exercise that takes place in a spiritual process. Ecclesiastical reforms are more than mere administrative acts.

For orders and religious communities, these conciliar mandates for reform meant that, in the meetings of general chapters, they were to acquire a new awareness of their spiritual roots, translating them into new statutes and constitutions. Following the introduction of a revised Code of Canon Law, which came into force in 1983, they undertook yet another process of renewal. However, clear specifications with respect to reform have not precluded the effect of internal and external influences. In Europe and the Americas, religious orders have suffered dramatic reductions in numbers since the council. The focus has shifted mainly to Africa and Asia, where religious orders are experiencing new growth. Nevertheless, for religious orders, as for the Church as a whole, the council’s prerequisites with respect to reform have remained constant.

#### Priests

The bishops desired that the council reinforce disciplinary provisions with respect to priests. The latter were to be conscious of their duties as priests, including, in particular, commitment to a life of holiness, to regular confession, and to ardent prayer. Obedience and poverty are required from priests, as is appropriate dress. The obligation of celibacy was to be enforced and attendance at film and theatre performances restricted. The Synod for the Diocese of Rome, called by John XXIII and celebrated in January 1960 (the first synod of the diocese of Rome in modern times), set the tone for these restrictive requirements. It took four sessions for the council to pass a coherent document on the ministry and life of priests.

Different models of priesthood can be found in the council’s teaching. There is thus a cultic image of a priest which understands his role in terms of his liturgical functions and emphasizes personal holiness. Alongside that image is the functional image of the priest defined by the three ministries of proclamation, administration of sacraments, and governance: this includes a greater openness towards the world. Another image sees the priest in terms of his relationship to others. Priests are so united with the other baptized that they are ‘brothers among brothers’ (_PO_ 9). The bishops should consider their priests as ‘their brothers and friends’ (_PO_ 7). Belonging to a presbyteral college calls for mutual support and hospitality. However, the recommended spirituality for priests is largely guided by the practices that have been tried and tested in religious communities.

During the council’s deliberations on priestly ministry and life, a great crisis with respect to the form of priestly life emerged. Some had hoped or expected that the council might relax or even abolish the obligation of celibacy for diocesan priests. Paul VI, however, disappointed those expectations when he withdrew the discussion on priestly celibacy from the council’s competence. The first synods of bishops, in 1967, dealt with this question but maintained the obligation for priestly celibacy, just as the pope himself had done in his encyclical letter _Sacerdotalis Caelibatus_ of 24 June 1967. Petitions for dispensation from the **[p. 229]** obligation to celibacy have increased worldwide and influenced the resignation of 63,972 priests between 1965 and 2000. Although, over the same period, the overall number of diocesan and religious priests increased slightly (1970: 425.553; 2001: 438.920), a substantial increase in the Catholic population in this same period has reduced the ratio of priests able to administer pastoral care. The popes have tried to address this issue by concentrating on improving the education of priests. Since the end of the council, alternative models had been developed in addition to the traditional model of seminaries instituted after the Council of Trent. The biblical image of a priest portrayed from John Paul II to Pope Francis is that of the Good Shepherd, as previously espoused by the Council of Trent.

In addition to the crisis concerning the requirement of celibacy and internal ecclesiastical clashes, which have emerged from the newly created pastoral ministries for laypeople, allegations of sexual abuse have undermined the credibility of the priestly way of life. These allegations concern priests and bishops, religious, and above all church institutions involved in youth work. Since the 1990s, allegations of abuse have made their way through canonical trials, leading to some priests’ removal from office as well as convictions issued by both ecclesiastical and secular courts. Guidelines for safeguarding young people have been strengthened, as have the sanctions for abuse. Especially since the tenures of Benedict XVI and Francis, the Catholic Church has intensifled its measures against sexual abuse in its ranks. The abuse scandals have resulted in an as-yet-unquantiflable loss of credibility of the Church and, for example, contributed to the collapse of the structures of the Catholic Church in a Catholic country like Ireland within a few short years. The global impact has not yet been quantifled.

#### The Charisms of Laypeople

_Apostolicam Actuositatem_ concedes that while laypersons have gained autonomy in ‘numerous sectors of human life’, this is ‘sometimes accompanied by a certain loss of moral and religious values’, making their witness more urgent (_AA_ 1). The Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World, _Gaudium et_ Spes, acknowledging these fears, recognizes in the autonomy of ‘earthly affairs … [which implies] the gradual discovery, utilisation and ordering of the laws and values of matter and society’ (_GS_ 36). This legitimate autonomy ‘is at once the claim of humankind today and the desire of the Creator’ (_GS_ 36). It is, above all, the Pastoral Constitution that elaborates the role of the laity as mission bearers of the Church in the secular realm. The laity ensure the presence of the Church in marriage and family, in the world of politics, and in the struggle for a peaceful world order. The Dogmatic Constitution on the Church states: ‘The secular is the special characteristic of the laity’ (_LG_ 31).

However, the emphasis of the decree on the laity concerns the importance of the laity for the apostolate of the Church and the participation of the laity in the immediate ministry and mission of the Church. Although this endeavour is primarily a matter for priests, the laity, too, share ‘in the mission of the whole people of **[p. 230]** God in the Church and in the world’ (_AA_ 2). The council acted as a catalyst for movements that were already in progress: laypeople began to study theology and made their way into the pastoral careers, in most countries on a voluntary basis, and full time in the economically stable countries of Central Europe and North America. Lay pastoral ministers, assistants, and consultants, working with the same qualifications as priests, had to seek and fight for their place between liturgy and catechesis in the area of parish work and in pastoral tasks. This provided a further opportunity for women to occupy certain leadership roles within the Church. In the countries of the global South, voluntary professions for laypeople as catechists and leaders of grass-roots communities have also emerged. In many countries of Latin America, Africa, and Asia, the leadership of the laity, which is still often rejected in Europe, has become a matter of fact.

The decree on priests envisions laypeople as important collaborators with priests. The description of how the mutual relationship should take shape includes a rejection of any form of open or hidden clericalism. Priests

should have an unfailing respect for the just liberty which belongs to everybody in civil society. They should be willing to listen to laypeople, give brotherly consideration to their wishes, and recognize their experience and competence in the different fields of human activity. In this way they will be able to recognize along with them the signs of the times. While testing the spirits to discover if they be of God, they must discover with faith, recognize with joy, and foster diligently the many and varied charismatic gifts of the laity, whether it be of a humble or more exalted kind. Among the other gifts of God, which are found in abundance among the faithful, special attention ought to be devoted to those graces by which a considerable number of people are attracted to greater heights of the spiritual life. Priests should confidently entrust to the laity duties in the service of the Church, giving them freedom and opportunity for activity and inviting them, when opportunity offers, to undertake projects of their own initiative. (_PO_ 9)

Priests are thus given the important task of paying attention to, discovering, and promoting the charisms of the laity. Laypeople are the lead players in evangelization, which, according to Paul VI’s 1975 Apostolic Exhortation, _Evangelii Nuntiandi_ (_EN_), consists of ‘bringing the Good News into every level of humanity, and through its influence transforming humanity from within’ (_EN_ 18).

The role of the laity in both the secular realm and in the ecclesiastical apostolate requires a new spirituality that ‘should take its particular character from the circumstances of one’s state of life—married and family life, celibacy, widowhood—from one’s state of health and from one’s professional activity’ (_AA_ 4). The council thus assimilates some elements which were developed in the writings of St Francis of Sales at the beginning of the seventeenth century. The general vocation to holiness, as developed in _Lumen Gentium_, is outlined only briefly in _Apostolicam Actuositatem_. The 2018 Apostolic Exhortation _Gaudete et Exsultate_ (_GeE_) **[p. 231]** of Pope Francis mentions concrete elements of this lay spirituality: perseverance, patience and meekness, joy and sense of humour, boldness and passion, community, and constant prayer (_GeE_ 112–57).

In several places, _Apostolicam Actuositatem_ points out the communal nature of the apostolate. The apostolate takes place within ecclesiastical communities of parish, diocese, and universal Church (_AA_ 19); in and through the family (_AA_ 11); in the social environment, among the youth (_AA_ 12; 13); and on national and international levels (_AA_ 14). The council prefers the ‘collective and organised form’ of apostolate (_AA_18) and praises, alongside the movement of Catholic Action promoted since the time of Pius XI (_AA_ 20), the diversity of Catholic associations, with a caveat against ‘a dissipation of forces’ (_AA_ 19).

The communal apostolate has experienced tremendous diversification since the council. In addition to religious movements founded before the council (such as the Schoenstatt Apostolic Movement, Legion of Mary, Focolare), a variety of movements (such as the Catholic Charismatic Renewal, Neo-Catechumenal Way, Community of Sant’Egidio) and charismatic initiatives, especially in Latin-speaking countries, have had a significant impact on society and Church. Their origins are often based upon the experiences of individual founding personalities or circles of friends. Some have developed into pluriform movements whose members are priests and laypeople, families, and celibates. While Catholic lay associations, which originated in the late nineteenth century, could easily be integrated into the structures of the Catholic Action in the first half of the twentieth century, a parallel structure of Church has come into being with these movements, which are largely independent on the traditional structures of parish and diocese. Their integration into the territorially constituted Church must be aligned with the proviso that these initiatives are still in the process of development and remain in search of adequate forms of organization.

### 5. Outlook

In its documents, the Second Vatican Council issued general guidelines which were to lead a centuries-old government and administration into a new era. The leadership of the Catholic Church is also subject to the requirement to exercise good governance. To this day it is imperative to supplement a monarchical form of governance (the papacy) and monocratic structures and hierarchies (cardinals, bishops) with democratic elements such as synods and structures that represent the lay apostolate. Since the council, the popes, in different ways, have linked and sought to implement the three aspects of good governance: transparency, participation, and decision-making. This demonstrates that the Catholic Church, after the Second Vatican Council, is a Church ‘on the way’ and a Church ‘on the move into the future’.
