## 14. Faith Formation in Light of Vatican II

Jane E. Regan

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 233]** The process by which Christians—adults, youth, and children—grow in faith is a complex and multifaceted reality. It is most effectively accomplished when it is made up of a rich mix of life in the Christian community, liturgy and prayer, opportunities for service, and both systematic and occasional instruction. Taking place in both contextual experience and intentional activities, the process endeavours to foster a relationship with Jesus Christ, strengthen one’s commitment to the Christian community, and enhance [^c14-1] involvement in the Church’s mission of service and transformation of the world. It is primarily the intentional activities designed to enhance the lived faith of adults, youth, and children that are the focus of this chapter.

[^c14-1]: Jane Regan, _Where Two or Three Are Gathered: Transforming the Parish through Communities of Practice_ (New York: Paulist, 2016), 8–18.

A word about terms: from the time of Vatican II (1962–65), a variety of words have been used to indicate the broad category of these intentional activities. They have included ‘religious instruction’, ‘religious education’, ‘Christian education’, ‘catechesis’, ‘faith formation’, and others. In some ways, the shifting in these terms has both pointed to and expedited the shift in focus and breadth of this intentional activity. ‘Religious instruction’ was seen as too limited, looking only at the cognitive elements of the experience; thus the move to ‘religious education’. As an awareness of the diversity of religious expressions grew, ‘Christian education’ provided an important specificity.

In the years following the council, numerous ecclesial documents, both international and the product of national conferences of bishops, have examined dimensions of intentional activities in service to lived **[p. 234]** Christian faith. In those documents, the dominant term that is used is ‘catechesis’. An ancient term in the Christian tradition, its etymology points to the action of echoing or re-echoing the heart of the Christian message. This early understanding has been developed into a more robust meaning that refers to ‘the whole of the efforts within the Church to make disciples, to help people to believe that Jesus is the Son of God, so that believing they might have life in His name, and to educate and instruct them in this life and thus build up the Body of Christ’ (John Paul II, Apostolic Exhortation _Catechesi Tradendae_ (1979), 1). While a common term in ecclesial documents and academic writings, its continued usage within the United States context is primarily in the designation ‘catechist’ for those engaged in this endeavour.

Finally, a term that is common when speaking of adult catechesis is ‘formation’ or ‘faith formation’. Eschewing vocabulary related to education because of its perceived connection with schooling and children, those engaged in the intentional activities designed to enhance the lived faith of adults speak of ongoing formation in the faith. The term ‘formation’ is used along with ‘catechesis’ throughout _Adult Catechesis in the Christian Community_, a 1990 document published by the International Council for Catechesis, a consultative body to the Vatican office of the Congregation for the Clergy. _Our Hearts Were Burning Within Us,_ a 1996 document from the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, acknowledges the multiplicity of terms and decides on ‘faith formation’. While the term is not without its critics, who argue that language of formation can connote an uncritical socialization into the status quo, for this chapter, catechesis and faith formation are used interchangeably.

Focusing on the contemporary understanding of faith formation of adults, youth, and children as it has evolved in the decades following Vatican II, primarily as it is expressed within the United States, which is the author’s context, this chapter begins with a consideration of _Gravissimum Educationis_. Looking at two key themes present in the documents of the council—theological anthropology and evangelization—the chapter traces aspects of their development from the council documents and examines the implications for the focus and practice of faith formation. Closing comments set out some issues for further consideration.

### 2. Gravissimum Educationis

During the closing days of Vatican II, several documents were reviewed, discussed, and given final approval by the assembled bishops. Among these was the Declaration on Christian Education, _Gravissimum Educationis_ (_GE_), promulgated by Pope Paul VI on 28 October 1965. One of the council’s briefer documents, counting some 4,500 words in twelve articles, this declaration sets out the bishops’ views concerning the significance of education as a right that is shared by all peoples and is essential for the common good; the centrality of moral education and governments’ responsibilities to provide for it; and the necessity that **[p. 235]** Christians receive education in the Christian faith. The document then points to the particular importance of Catholic formation of children and youth and, in that context, of the role of Catholic schools and Catholic higher education. It is worth noting that in the evolution of this document, the title and focus shifted from a lengthy preparatory draft entitled ‘On Catholic Schools’ to this final document that situates the role of Catholic schools within the broader enterprise of education, and Christian education in particular.

The document begins by attending to the nature and agents of education and then of Christian education. First, the writers of the document set the discussion of education in terms of human rights. The opening paragraph states that all persons, ‘of whatever race, condition or age, in virtue of their dignity as human persons, have an inalienable right to an education’ (_GE_ 1). Education is not the privilege of the few but the right of everyone. The document emphasizes particularly the rights of children and young people to an education that develops ‘their physical, moral and intellectual qualities’; that provides appropriate sexual education; and that prepares the children and young people to be engaged in society and community organizations. In addition, ‘They should be open to dialogue with others and should be willing to devote themselves to the promotion of the common good’ (_GE_ 1). Education is seen as an essential human right in service to human fulfilment and the common good.

Second, Christian education is set within the context of the right of all to education. While education in general strives to support the maturing of the human person, Christian education addresses the needs of those who have been baptized to live out fully their baptismal call, to align their lives to the commands of Christ, to witness willingly to their faith, and to work for the transformation of the world and the good of society (_GE_ 2).

Finally, prominence is given in several places to the primary responsibilities of parents to educate their children in service both to society and to Christian faith. Families are the ‘principal school of the social virtues which are necessary to every society’ and the context for children and youth to experience an environment marked by love of God and neighbour (_GE_ 3). Beyond the importance of family life, parents are encouraged to be sure that the education their children receive is sound and effective. This is most advantageously done in the setting of Catholic schools.

The last half of the document looks specifically at Catholic schools at the elementary and secondary level as well as higher education (_GE_ 8–12). It points to the right of the Church to establish Catholic schools, the relationship between Catholic schools and the social order, and the essential role of teachers and others involved in Catholic schools to enhance the human and spiritual formation of all participants.

It must be noted that _Gravissimum Educationis_ is not without its deficits. It is a fairly weak document and, in [^c14-2] many ways, does not build on the insights achieved by developments during the council. In particular, the [^c14-3] **[p. 236]** theological anthropology that runs through other council documents is not fully reflected in this one. In _Gaudium et Spes_ (_GS_), for example, the understanding of human beings and their relationship with one another and with God is richly developed. Human persons experience the challenges of life (‘the grief and anxieties’) as limited creatures. At the same time they experience themselves being called to the ‘more’ of life from which flow true human ‘joys and hopes’ (_GS_ 1). The human person, though confiicted and sinful, is nonetheless marked by dignity by being made in the image of God, the God who is inviting each one into the divine relationship. In many ways, it seems that _Gravissimum Educationis_ embodies an earlier anthropology with its understanding of the aim of education as ‘a formation which is directed toward their final end and the good of that society to which they belong’ (_GE_ 1). Throughout the document, their ‘final end’ is the primary aim, with the common good being present but secondary. In this area of Christian anthropology, which is developed later in this chapter, one can see some development when comparing it to Pius XI’s 1929 encyclical on Catholic education, _Divini Illius Magistri_. However, in many ways _Gravissimum Educationis_ builds on the principles concerning education set out in the earlier document.[^c14-4]

[^c14-2]: Gerald Grace, ‘Vatican II and New Thinking about Catholic Education: _Aggiornamento_ Thinking and Principles into Practice’, in _Vatican II and New Thinking about Catholic Education_, ed. Sean Whittle (New York: Routledge, 2017), 13.

[^c14-3]: Dermot A. Lane, _Catholic Education in the Light of Vatican II and Laudato Si’_ (Dublin: Veritas, 2015), 23.

[^c14-4]: Lieven Boeve, ‘Belgium: New Thinking on Catholic Education Fifty Years after Vatican II’, in Whittle, _Vatican II and New_ _Thinking about Catholic Education_, 55.

In the context of this chapter, one of the more significant aspects of _Gravissimum Educationis_ is the already mentioned name change that took place during the final session of the council. The shift from ‘The Catholic School’, which was the title for the first six drafts of the document, to ‘Declaration on Christian Education’ is a move towards a more inclusive understanding of Christian education from schools alone. Universities and theological faculties are included under that rubric, and, one could argue, so are the other ways in which children, youth, and adults are intentionally formed in the Christian faith.

### 3. Christian Education: Beyond Catholic Schools

To see Christian education as inclusive of but not coextensive with Catholic schools invites one to look beyond _Gravissimum Educationis_ for tracings of the influence of Vatican II on Christian education or catechesis more broadly. For the rest of this chapter, attention turns to two core themes that have influenced the shape and direction of the process by which persons and communities grow in faith. These two themes—theological anthropology and evangelization—are examined both for their understanding in light of the council and for their implication for the process of intentional activities designed to enhance the lived faith of adults, youth, and children.

#### Theological Anthropology: Nature of Faith Formation

**[p. 237]** One of the significant themes that was present throughout the discussions held by the participants of Vatican II and that can be found both explicitly and implicitly in the council documents is theological anthropology: What does it mean to be human? How do humans relate to one another, to creation, and ultimately to God? Our presumptions about the human being have a significant impact on how we understand the nature of faith formation, its approaches and aims. To consider the dynamics of faith formation from Vatican II to the present, this section begins with a brief survey of some of the core characteristics of a theological anthropology that can be traced from Vatican II and continues with a discussion of the implications for faith formation.

#### From Gaudium et Spes to Gaudete et Exsultate: The Human as Graced, Relational, and in Solidarity

While tracings of an operative anthropology can be found across the writings of Vatican II, one of the documents where this is most clearly set out is _Gaudium et Spes._ One of four constitutions proceeding from the council, it was accepted by the bishops in the final session and promulgated by Pope Paul VI on 7 December 1965, the day the council ended. Alternatively described as the document on the Church’s relationship to the world, on social justice, on the foundation of pastoral work of the Church in society, and others, it can be argued that this document also expresses the outline of a distinctive anthropology that echoes across subsequent church documents, theological developments, and faith formation up to the present. In this chapter, attention is given to three themes that have particular implications for and expression in the intentional process of enhancing the lived faith of adults, youth, and children: the human being as graced by God, as formed in relationships, and as in solidarity with other humans and the rest of creation.

Humans as Graced

To say that humans are graced is to reaffirm a core theological conviction that in the work of creation God proclaimed it all ‘good’ (Gen. 1:1–29). All of creation—including human beings—is graced by God. Before any action or decisions on our part, the spark of divine life is already present; we are, so to speak, ‘wired’ for God. While a consistent part of Catholic theology and spirituality across time, the theological expression of this as set out in the council documents can be summed up in the Jesuit theologian Karl Rahner’s notion of [^c14-5] supernatural existential. The Rahnerian notion of God’s always present offer of grace serves as the **[p. 238]** foundation of the fundamental connection between human nature and divine life. The very offer of grace given to all in the moment of creation, before any thought or experience on the part of the human, makes it part of how the human is constituted in the world.

[^c14-5]: Karl Rahner, ‘Concerning the Relationship between Nature and Grace’, in _Theological Investigations_, vol. 1, _God, Christ,_ _Mary and Grace_ (Baltimore: Helicon, 1961), 297–317.

More recent theologians raise the question of the inherent anthropocentrism that permeates _Gaudium et Spes_. Considering humans as the ‘crown’ of the material world (_GS_ 12) is viewed today as an inadequate theological framework. Particularly in light of the publication of the Apostolic Exhortation _Laudato Si’_ (_LS_) by Pope Francis in 2015, it is essential that attention be given to the graced nature of all of creation and the concomitant multifaceted call for what he describes as ‘ecological conversion’ (_LS_, part III). This points to the breadth and depth of the second aspect of a theological anthropology rooted in Vatican II: relationality.

Human Beings in Relationship

As graced beings, all humans are called to relationship with God and with one another; this fundamental relationality of being human is central to the theological anthropology expressed and implied at the council. We become most fully Christian and human through our relationships with others. From some of the earliest documents of Vatican II (see, for example, _LG_ 7) to the last (see _GS_ 16), the theme of the necessity of human relationships is developed. The images of Church as ‘body of Christ’ and ‘people of God’ point to the central role not only of human beings’ relationship with God but also of their relationship with one another. The human person cannot experience human flourishing or the full Christian life without the fellowship of believers.

The importance of relationality is brought into the present with Pope Francis’s 2018 Apostolic Exhortation on holiness, _Gaudete et Exsultate_ (_GeE_). Here he points to the essential place of relationship in human and Christian life as the context of our salvation and of God’s self-communication. ‘We are never completely ourselves unless we belong to a people. That is why no one is saved alone, as an isolated individual. Rather, God draws us to himself, taking into account the complex fabric of interpersonal relationships present in a human community’ (_GeE_ 6).

Human Beings in Solidarity

The graced nature of humanity and indeed all of creation, as well as the relational character of human beings, points to solidarity as an essential Christian response to the world around us. Among the most often quoted lines from the Vatican II documents are those that open _Gaudium et Spes_: ‘The joys and the hopes, the grief and anguish of the people of our time, especially those who are poor or affiicted, are the joys and hopes, the grief and anguish of the followers of Christ as well. Nothing genuinely human fails to find an echo in their hearts’ (_GS_ 1). These words point to the essence of Christian solidarity with all of human existence, those experiences that point us to the ‘more’ of human being as well as those that remind us of the limits of human life and our mortality. These are experiences common to all human existence in which the followers of Christ participate.

**[p. 239]** This discussion of solidarity returns us to the document with which the chapter began: _Gravissimum Educationis._ The writers of the document point to the importance of all education and particularly Christian education—not only because it prepares the learner for their final end, but also because it forms them to contribute to the common good (_GE_ 1). Christian education develops in learners the skills and commitment to engage in the work of the community and to engage in discourse in service to human solidarity.

As mentioned earlier in this chapter, the nature of solidarity has been broadened since the time of the council to include solidarity with all creatures and with the full created order. Pope Francis writes: ‘In the present condition of global society, where injustices abound and growing numbers of people are deprived of basic human rights and considered expendable, the principle of the common good immediately becomes, logically and inevitably, a summons to solidarity and a preferential option for the poorest of our brothers and sisters’ (_LS_ 158). Francis recognizes that the interconnection of all life is essential for human thriving and for sustaining the world, and he requires this solidarity with particular attention to those who are oppressed.

#### Implications for Faith Formation

This understanding of the human person—as graced, as shaped and sustained in relationships, and as giving expression to that relational nature in solidarity with all of the created order, particularly that which is most vulnerable or oppressed—has implications for faith formation. Embedded in this anthropology is an understanding of revelation pointing to faith formation that builds on human experience, is rooted in the work of traditioning, and aims at fostering lived faith.

Builds on Human Experience

For the human being marked by the gratuitous gift of divine grace, God’s self-revelation takes place in and through human experience. The process of the intentional activities that foster the lived faith of adults, youth, and children has as its point of reference the awareness of God’s presence in the experience of being human. This serves as the beginning spot of the theological reflection that shapes faith formation in its most effective expressions.

Rooted in the Work of Traditioning

While recognizing that the fullness of divine revelation took place in Jesus, its ongoing manifestation is in the lived experience of believers and of communities of faith. The tradition of Jesus’s life, death, and resurrection becomes a tradition in action as it is continued in each generation. This handing down, or traditioning, keeps alive the dynamic tradition of the Christian story and at the same time shapes the community of faith in which each believer comes to know his or her faith in the retelling.

**[p. 240]** Aims at Fostering Lived Faith

The Christian story is never told for the sake of information alone. It is a story that touches the heart of the hearer and invites a response of lived faith: faith that puts into action the call to accompaniment as an expression of solidarity. Ultimately, this lived faith is one that responds to the invitation to be and become ever more effective agents of evangelization. This is the second theme to which we now turn.

### 4. Evangelization: Aim and Context of Faith Formation

Influencing the direction of faith formation in the years following the council is the increasing clarity with which the call to evangelization has developed. With the promulgation of the Decree on the Mission Activity of the Church, _Ad Gentes_ (_AG_), the Church reaffirmed its commitment to its core mission of proclaiming the saving work of Jesus Christ to all peoples. In subsequent documents, the understanding of evangelization has been sharpened and a vision of its implementation and implications has expanded in response to situations in Church and society.

From the earliest post-conciliar document on evangelization, the link between catechesis and evangelization is made clear. Pope Paul VI’s 1975 Apostolic Exhortation _Evangelii Nuntiandi_ (_EN_), sees the proclamation of the Gospel—preaching and catechesis—as second only to Christian witness in the work of evangelization. From that point on, the call to evangelization appears in a variety of ecclesial documents that together set out a rich sense of evangelization and with it a renewed understanding of catechesis. In this section, attention turns to a brief survey of these documents with a consideration of international documents only. Many documents from various bishops’ conferences have also contributed to enriching the understanding of evangelization as it comes to expression in the local context. This is followed by a consideration of the core implications for evangelization and therefore for catechesis and faith formation.

#### From Ad Gentes to Evangelii Gaudium: Insight into the Nature of Evangelization

The Decree on the Mission Activity of the Church, _Ad Gentes_, sets the framework for the discussion of the nature and expression of evangelization. Promulgated on 7 December 1965, it reiterates the mission given by the risen Christ to ‘Go, therefore, and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you’ **[p. 241]** (Matt. 28:19–20). While expressed in different ways in response to diverse settings, this mission is the responsibility of the bishops with the ‘prayers and help of the whole Church’ (_AG_ 6). It is this role of the whole Church that is expanded over subsequent documents.

_Evangelii Nuntiandi_ affirms the centrality of this mission to the life of the Church: ‘Evangelising is the special grace and vocation of the Church. It is her central function’ (_EN_ 14). In this context, evangelization is described as the ‘carrying forth of the good news to every sector of the human race so that by its strength it may enter into the hearts of [all] and renew the human race’ (_EN_ 18).

A few years later, on 16 October 1979, Pope John Paul II presented the Apostolic Exhortation on catechesis, _Catechesi Tradendae_ (_CT_), the papal response to the fourth Synod of Bishops held in Rome in 1977 on catechesis, with particular reference to the catechesis of children and young people. Building on _Evangelii Nuntiandi_, _Catechesi Tradendae_ describes catechesis as a stage of evangelization that gains its meaning and purpose from its relationship to this essential pastoral activity. Catechesis builds on the initial witness and proclamation of the Gospel ‘with a view to initiating the hearers into the fullness of Christian life’ (_CT_ 18). The document recognizes that at times, participants in catechesis have not been effectively evangelized and that the work of catechesis can include the initial teaching.

About ten years after _Catechesi Tradendae_, two other Apostolic Exhortations examined the nature of evangelization and included focus on the concept of ‘re-evangelization’, later to be called ‘new evangelization’. The first of these, _Christifideles Laici_ (_CL_), issued on 30 December 1988, is the statement from John Paul II following the synod on the role of the laity. Reflecting on the reality of de-christianized contexts and the rise of secularism, John Paul II calls for a re-evangelization, which begins with addressing the Christian community. We must ‘first remake the Christian fabric of the ecclesial community itself’ so it can reflect what it means to live in Christ (_CL_ 34).

Two years later, on 7 December 1990, the twenty-fifth anniversary of _Ad Gentes_, the encyclical from John Paul II on the missionary activity of the Church, _Redemptoris Missio_ (_RM_), was promulgated. With its emphasis on a new evangelization, the document stresses the necessity of being aware of the dynamics shaping the situation within which evangelization and, by extension, catechesis takes place. In paragraph 33, the document highlights three distinct settings. First is evangelization addressed to ‘peoples, groups, and socio-cultural contexts in which Christ and his Gospel are not known, or which lack Christian communities sufficiently mature to be able to incarnate the faith in their own environment and proclaim it to other groups’. This is the classic evangelization _ad gentes_. The second group are those living in stable, effective ecclesial communities: ‘They are fervent in their faith and in Christian living. They bear witness to the Gospel in their surroundings and have a sense of commitment to the universal mission. In these communities the Church carries out her activity and pastoral care.’ The third group, reflective of the impact of secular culture, refers to those who have heard the Gospel and been baptized but ‘have lost a living sense of the faith, or even no longer consider themselves members of the Church, and live a life far removed from Christ and his Gospel. In this case, what is needed is a “new evangelisation” or a “re-evangelisation”.’ **[p. 242]** These three contexts, within which the pastoral life of the Church is expressed, are particularly important in the discussion of a _new evangelization_, which rose to prominence under John Paul II, Benedict XVI, and Francis.

The next document that warrants attention in this discussion is the _General Directory for Catechesis_ (_GDC_), which was approved by John Paul II on 15 August 1997. As a directory, it is designed to provide guidance in the work of catechesis throughout the Church, setting out in fairly broad terms the aims and tasks of catechesis and how they are to be accomplished, leaving the details to be developed by the conference of bishops in each specific location. Two themes that have emerged from the earlier documents apply here as well. First, the directory reiterates that catechesis, the process by which we intentionally form adults, youth, and children in lived faith, must be understood in relationship to evangelization. The _General Directory for Catechesis_ describes evangelization as consisting of different but essential moments and then, quoting _Catechesi Tradendae_, states that catechesis is one of those ‘moments—a very remarkable one—in the whole process of evangelisation’ (_GDC_ 63). It is by looking at the overarching category of evangelization that catechesis or faith formation is effectively understood. Second, the directory, like the other documents mentioned, is attentive to the situation within which evangelization takes place. It takes the three categories set out in _Redemptoris Missio_ and develops them somewhat in light of the years between the documents (_GDC_ 58–59).

One further point from the _General Directory for Catechesis_: although the full cycle of evangelization is perhaps presumed in earlier documents, the directory explicitly names it. Evangelization does not come to completion with catechesis; the point of an evangelizing catechesis is to form vibrant faith communities and believers who are themselves called forth and strengthened with further formation to be evangelizers (_GDC_ 58b). This idea is central to the final document we consider here: _Evangelii Gaudium_ (_EG_).

In November 2013, Pope Francis issued the Apostolic Exhortation _Evangelii Gaudium._ Written following the 2012 Synod of Bishops on the new evangelization, the document begins with the challenge to all believers to participate in the work of evangelization, a work that begins with the invitation to enter into a ‘renewed personal encounter with Jesus Christ’ (_EG_ 3). This is seen as the source and inspiration for all forms of evangelization. At the same time, from the first pages of the text, it is clear that at the heart of the call to engage in evangelization is the need to renew the life of the Church. ‘To make this missionary impulse ever more focused, generous and fruitful, I encourage each particular Church to undertake a resolute process of discernment, purification, and reform’ (_EG_ 30). Participating in and building up the Christian community is an essential component of evangelization. But the building-up of the Christian community is always in service to the missionary task of the Church. The themes that Francis chose to develop in some detail in this exhortation give an indication of the breadth of his understanding of how this ‘new chapter in evangelisation’ comes to expression: ‘the reform of the Church in her missionary outreach; the temptations faced by pastoral workers; the Church, understood as the entire People of God which evangelises; the homily and its preparation; the inclusion of the poor in society; peace and dialogue within society; the spiritual **[p. 243]** motivations for mission’ (_EG_ 17). This evangelizing faith, rooted in relationship with Jesus and nurtured within the Christian community, is ultimately in service to the world.

In light of these documents, what are the core essentials of evangelization and what are the implications of this for catechesis? That is the question that shapes the next section of this chapter.

### 5. Catechesis as a Moment of Evangelization

A review of these documents indicates several key themes that shape our understanding of evangelization and thus of catechesis. While there are certainly other important themes, these four are particularly pertinent to our discussion of catechesis. Evangelization and catechesis are Christocentric, multidimensional, the responsibility of the Church and all its members, and attentive to the situation of the participants. Summarizing each point in light of evangelization, the chapter continues with a discussion of its expression and implication for catechesis.

#### Christocentric

The Great Commission in Matthew 28 highlights the focus of the task of the eleven disciples and of Christians today: the person and teachings of Jesus. ‘Go, therefore, and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, until the end of the age’ (Matt. 28:19– 20). It is this _kerygma_, the central message of the apostolic teaching, that is at the heart of evangelization today.

And at the core of catechesis, its fundamental aim, is relationship with Jesus Christ. All faith formation, regardless of the setting in school, parish, or faith community, and regardless of the audience—adults, youth, or children—is oriented to establishing and enhancing each person’s relationship with Jesus Christ. In evangelizing catechesis, both catechists and participants are invited to deepen their relationship with Jesus Christ by reflecting on their experience as believers, engaging with the Christian message, and recognizing the implications of the message for lived Christian faith.

Enhancing one’s relationship with Jesus Christ and being shaped by his message always take place within the context of the Christian community. It is within the Christian community, beginning with the family as domestic Church, that one hears the message of Christ and sees it expressed in the quotidian rhythm of life. Relationships with family and friends as well as with members of the community of faith serve as the settings where one sees articulated the reality of lived faith. So to say that evangelizing catechesis is **[p. 244]** Christocentric is also to affirm its fundamentally communal nature. Enhancing one’s relationship with Jesus Christ goes hand in hand with strengthening one’s commitment to the Christian community.

But the Christian message is never simply for our personal enrichment or even just for the enhancement of the community of believers. Just as the first disciples were gathered on the mountain in Galilee for the purpose of being sent to spread the message of Jesus, so too is every Christian community gathered to be sent to speak the Gospel in word and action to a world that is also in need of the saving action of God in Jesus Christ. The aim of evangelizing catechesis, then, includes strengthening participation in the Church’s work of evangelization.

#### Multifaceted

One of the most significant developments across the documents dealing with evangelization over the years since Vatican II has been the growing awareness of the complexity of evangelization and the multiple ways in which it comes to expression. In the _General Directory for Catechesis_, this point was clearly articulated: evangelization is ‘a dynamic reality which contains within it interdependent activities which are to be kept in creative tension: witness and proclamation, word and sacrament, interior change and social transformation’ (_GDC_ 46).

It cannot be reduced to a set of tasks or be assigned to a particular group within the Church. It has to do less with _what_ the school or parish or faith community does and more with _how_ the work is accomplished. We can speak of an evangelizing catechesis or an evangelizing liturgy, an evangelizing youth group or an evangelizing finance committee, and ultimately of an evangelizing school or parish. In each case, those responsible for these aspects of Church life engage in their endeavours with an eye to how their actions, attitudes, and decisions contribute to bringing the message of the reign of God into the world around us.

Catechesis or faith formation, as an element of the broader work of evangelization, is itself a dynamic and multifaceted reality. While at times it has been equated with instruction and often with a schooling model, the charge and expression of catechesis builds on instruction and goes beyond it.

In the 1976 book _Will Our Children Have Faith?_ religious educator John Westerhoff critically examines the ‘schooling model’ of religious education/catechesis and refers to that paradigm as a ‘broken ecology’. While the _General Directory for Catechesis_ has been revised twice over the intervening years, the core thesis remains: we form and transform people in faith not only through instruction but also through the multiple ways in which the community of faith gathers to give expression to its life and commitments. To rely exclusively on instruction is to ignore the wider ecology through which the faith is expressed and embodied in past, present, and future generations. In this sense, catechesis consists of peer groups and multigenerational gatherings, entails both systematic and occasional teaching, and is designed to be in service to the building-up of the believing community for the sake of the transformation of the world.

**[p. 245]** One can argue that rooting catechesis in evangelization and seeing it as broader than instruction moves the enterprise in the direction of ‘situated learning’; that is, learning that takes place in the doing of Christian life. The _General Directory for Catechesis_ speaks of catechesis as apprenticeship: ‘Catechesis initiates [believers] in knowledge of faith and apprenticeship in the Christian life, thereby promoting a spiritual journey which brings about a progressive change in outlook and morals’ (_GDC_ 56c). Catechesis as apprenticeship points to the formative role of intentional engagements with the various expression of the Christian life—liturgy and prayer, preaching and teaching, community and service. Providing opportunities for all members of the faith community to engage in these activities and reflect on their experience is the heart of catechesis from this perspective.

#### Essential to the Church and the Responsibility of All

An oft-quoted statement from _Evangelii Nuntiandi_, the first post-Vatican II document to examine evangelization in detail, makes clear this important fact: ‘Evangelising is the special grace and vocation of the Church. It is her central function’ (_EN_ 14). Established by the evangelizing work of Jesus and the first disciples, the Church is fully itself when, through the witness and words of its members, it proclaims to each generation the good news of God’s love conveyed in Jesus. ‘Thus it is the whole Church that receives the mission to evangelise, and the work of each individual member is important for the whole’ (_EN_ 15). One of the key implications of this is the centrality of the catechesis of adults to the life and mission of the Church.

One of the documents written in response to Vatican II is the _General Catechetical Directory_, published in 1971 following the directive in _Christus Dominus_ (_CD_), the Decree on the Pastoral Office of Bishops in the Church (_CD_ 44). In a statement that is cited in many subsequent ecclesial documents on catechesis, the directory points to the importance of adult catechesis: ‘catechesis of adults, since it has to do with persons who are capable of fully responsible commitment, must be accepted as the principal kind of catechesis’ (_CD_ 20). While the catechesis of children and youth is not to be slighted, adults have both the capacity and the responsibility to live lives of faithful discipleship. This includes the injunction to be and to become ever more effective evangelizers. Catechesis must prepare them for this work.

The tasks of adult faith formation are the same as all catechesis—to deepen relationship with Jesus Christ, enhance commitment to the Christian community, and strengthen participation in the Church’s mission of evangelization. But for adults, this takes on added focus, since it has the immediate outcome of preparing adults to be evangelizers within their context in the world.

What does this mean for catechesis? First, it involves inspiring and empowering adults in their roles as agents of evangelization. It is not uncommon to hear catechists remind parents that they are the first teachers of their child in the faith, a point made clear at the time of the child’s baptism. But the connection is seldom made with the wider calling to be evangelizers not only to their children but also to the wider **[p. 246]** society and culture. Second, it requires that catechesis gives adults the opportunity to be in conversation with other adults about things that matter to them; that is, about the issues related to how they live their faith in their homes and in the world. It is when one has the chance to talk about faith and hear others talking about it that adults become comfortable and ready ‘to give an explanation to anyone who asks for a reason for [their] hope’ (1 Pet. 3:15); they become more effective evangelizers.

Finally, in setting catechesis in the context of forming evangelizers, the centrality of catechesis to the life and mission of the Church is clear. The 1990 document from the International Council for Catechesis, _Adult Catechesis in the Christian Community_ affirms the importance of evangelization to the life of the Church and the place of all adults in this work. The writers of the document come to this conclusion: ‘Hence, it is not only legitimate, but necessary, to acknowledge that a fully Christian community can exist only when a systematic catechesis of all its members takes place and when an effective and well-developed catechesis of adults is regarded as the _central task_ in the catechetical enterprise’ (25).

#### Attentive to the Situation of the Participants

Evangelization always takes place in a particular time and place. While at one point the work of evangelization emphasized the mission _ad gentes_, the development of the understanding in later documents has a broader scope. As highlighted in _Redemptoris Missio_, evangelization is also directed to active members of the Christian community, who are always in need of renewing their relationship with Christ, with the Christian community, and with the mission of the Church. In addition, the evangelizing task includes attention to baptized persons who are in need of a new evangelization that beckons them into life in Christ. Each of these situations of the participants of evangelization requires a distinctive approach; always Christocentric, evangelization takes a different shape and emphasis depending on the audience.

Similarly, in catechesis, attention is given to the setting of the participants, their age, and their relationship with the Christian community. From the start, this means that religious educators need to attend to the insights of the social sciences and education. Developmental theories provide guidance in understanding the perspective out of which persons might be hearing the Christian message and how that might be presented in a suitable and effective way. Educational theories give the religious educator a framework for sequencing elements of the Christian tradition and integrating a variety of approaches, activities, and experiences into the intentional formative process.

In addition, it is important for the catechist to recognize the situation of the participants relative to the movement from initiatory to ongoing catechesis through liturgical catechesis and theological study towards being an evangelizer (see _GDC_ 51). Initiatory catechesis, with its focus on the clear articulation of the heart **[p. 247]** of the Christian message, is particularly appropriate for children and youth. When working with adults, it is essential to build on this initiatory catechesis and connect the Christian message with the lived faith of the adult community.

As a moment of evangelization, catechesis shares in the work of the Spirit in inviting, forming, and sending forth believers as proclaimers of the Gospel in word and action.

### 6. Conclusion and Future Questions

_Gravissimum Educationis_ serves as the point of entry to this discussion of faith formation in light of Vatican II. Within this document, Catholic schools are set in the broader context of Christian education and education in general; this is the foundation for our examining the more inclusive perspective of intentional activities designed to enhance the lived faith of adults, youth, and children. It is within that perspective that Catholic schools, parish programmes, youth ministry, and adult formation are all able to find a common foundation.

It is also in light of the contribution of Vatican II that two core themes are brought forward: theological anthropology and evangelization. Rooted in the milieu of the Second Vatican Council and expressed in various documents, these two categories serve as lenses for seeing core elements of the present expression of catechesis/faith formation as it has evolved over the fifty-plus years since the council.

In this concluding section, I propose a series of questions that emerge from the prior discussion and that might serve as the beginnings of imagining the future expression of faith formation. At the heart of these questions is this overarching question: if we accept as given the elements of a theological anthropology and the understanding of evangelization set out here, what might faith formation look like in a future that continues to be shaped by such dynamics as postmodernity, increasing religious diversity, the considerable movement of migrants and refugees, rising ecological damage, the cumulative effect of ongoing secularism, and so forth?

#### Centrality of Adult Formation

For fifty years, ecclesial documents have repeatedly emphasized the centrality of the faith formation of adults to the work of catechesis and to the vitality and effectiveness of the Church. Within the same fifty years, with increasing clarity, has come the call that the whole Church be about the work of evangelization. What are the intentional activities that foster mature adult faith—that is, evangelizing faith? This question often leads to discussion of adult programmes and these subsequent questions: What do adults need to know? or What do we need to teach them? But instead of first thinking about gathering adults for **[p. 248]** instruction, we might ask instead: How do we draw upon the formative aspect that is the potential of each gathering of adults within the community of faith? We can think of each gathering of adults—from small faith-sharing groups or Bible study, to staff or faculty of a Catholic school, to parish council or finance committee—as a potential community of Christian practice. From that perspective, they become a setting in which one enters into an apprenticeship that is the Christian life. When this is done intentionally, by integrating prayer and theological reflection into these gatherings, they can become truly faith formative communities of practice.

#### Challenge of Human Relationality in an Increasingly Individualistic Context

Whether we are looking at discussions within the Church or debates within the political context, the dearth of opportunities for people to build relationships through conversation is evident. Taking the time for conversation even among people who generally agree is a challenge. As we think about engaging in intentional activities that form an evangelizing people, how does the local faith community serve as a gathering place and as a context where sustained, engaged, critical conversation can take place? One of the primary contributions of faith formation is providing adults with the opportunity to talk about things that matter in their lives—how to make a living, how to raise their children, how to care for the earth, how to express their faith.

Educate for Solidarity

Continuing the topic of sustained critical conversation, engagement across differences adds another complexity. To truly be in solidarity with someone who is different from us requires learning the challenging skills of honest speaking and active listening. It also means being able to affirm the truth that the other speaks without forgoing one’s own faith commitments and beliefs. How does the local faith community provide opportunities for these kinds of conversations across differences? How does the wider Church model an openness to this type of conversation?

Evangelization as Accompaniment

In the work of evangelization, all parties are graced by God’s presence. The evangelizer and the one being evangelized are both recipients of God’s gratuitous gift of love. God’s always-and-everywhere offer of grace shapes each person. In light of that, the work of evangelization is not proselytizing but invitation, not cajoling but accompaniment. In writing about preparing evangelizers, Francis wrote in _Evangelii Gaudium_, ‘The Church will have to initiate everyone—priests, religious and laity—into this “art of accompaniment” which teaches us to remove our sandals before the sacred ground of the other’ (_EG_ 169). What changes will have to happen in the Church and among the people to make that possible? Catechesis/faith formation must prepare believers for this task.
