## 15. Vatican II’s Missiology: Foundation for a Missionary

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 250]** We live in a world that is vastly different from the world of 1965, when the Second Vatican Council ended. Globalization, increasing poverty, mass migrations, tensions between cultures and religions, unimagined scientific progress in medicine, communications, and transportation, the end of the Cold War, the rise of global terrorism, the urgent need for reconciliation among peoples, and a loss of credibility of the Church and its leadership all make today’s world one of increasing complexity and unforeseen dangers.

In this vastly different world, however, ‘the joys and hopes, the grief and anguish of the people of our time, especially of those who are poor or affiicted’, are still ‘the joys and hopes, the grief and anguish of the followers of Christ’ (_Gaudium et Spes_ (_GS_) 1). These famous first lines of Vatican II’s Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World point to a basic concern of Christians and, indeed, love for the world that can only be called ‘missiological’. As the text goes on to say, the community of believers in Christ are united in him and guided by the Holy Spirit to be ‘bearers of a message for all of humanity’ (_GS_ 1). This is the reason Christians are in such deep solidarity with humanity and its history, and why ‘nothing that is genuinely human fails to find an echo in their hearts’ (_GS_ 1). There is no better summary of the Church’s evangelizing mission.

This chapter on the missiological perspective of Vatican II proposes that, while key to an interpretation of the council, mission can also be key in interpreting the council and its documents for today, a time that calls for a truly missionary Church.

### 2. Missiology at the Council

#### A Missionary Council

**[p. 251]** [^c15-1] Although it has not always been recognized as such, Vatican II may well be called a ‘missionary council’. Italian theologian Serena Noceti speaks of the theme of mission as a defining factor in the reception and [^c15-2] interpretation of the council’s documents for the post-conciliar period. A vision of mission, however, was there from the beginning. As John XXIII’s goals of the council matured, it became clear that he ‘wanted a council that would mark a transition between two eras, that is, that would bring the Church out of the post- [^c15-3] Tridentine period and … into a new phase of witness and proclamation’. All four of the council’s constitutions—primary documents for interpreting all sixteen (_Final Report_ of the 1985 Bishops’ Synod)— [^c15-4] emphasize the importance of the Church’s mission in their opening paragraphs. Indeed, every council document mentions the importance of mission, and the documents refer to mission in one way or another over one hundred times. In addition, the documents on religious freedom and non-Christian religions deal with issues at the heart of the missionary commitment of the Church in the world. In addition, after some [^c15-5] significant hesitation and struggle, the council produced a document that focused specifically on mission, stating at the beginning that mission was constitutive of the Church itself, since the Church participated in the very mission of God, who sent the Son and Spirit into the world and its history (see _Ad Gentes_ (_AG_) 2).

[^c15-1]: Johannes Schütte, ‘Ce que la mission attendait du Concile’, in _Vatican II: L’Activité missionaire de l’église_, ed. Johannes Schütte (Paris: Cerf, 1967), 120.

[^c15-2]: Serena Noceti, ‘Pensare il post-concilio: Tra recezione ed ermeneutica’, _Ad Gentes: Teologia e antropologia della missione_ 16 (2012): 20.

[^c15-3]: Giuseppe Alberigo, ‘The Announcement of the Council: From the Security of the Fortress to the Lure of the Quest’, in _History of Vatican II_, ed. Giuseppe Alberigo and Joseph A. Komonchak (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1995), 1:1–54, at 42.

[^c15-4]: Stephen B. Bevans, ‘Revisiting Mission at Vatican II: Theology and Practice for Today’s Missionary Church’, _Theological_ _Studies_ 74, no. 2 (2013): 263–66.

[^c15-5]: Stephen B. Bevans, ‘Decree on the Church’s Missionary Activity’, in _Evangelization and Human Freedom: Ad Gentes,_ _Dignitatis Humanae_, ed. Stephen B. Bevans, SVD and Jeffrey Gros, FSC (Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 2009), 3–29.

#### A Broader Notion of Mission

One must admit, however, that mission at the council was understood somewhat ambiguously. The documents can read in places as quite church-centred, territorial, and focused on an otherworldly salvation (e.g., _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ (_SC_) 1; _Lumen Gentium_ (_LG_) 5, 15; _AG_ 6), fitting a certain stereotype in the minds of many. Nevertheless, there is evidence of efforts to understand mission in a wider and more comprehensive way. The opening paragraphs of the document on the Church rooted the Church’s mission **[p. 252]** first and foremost in the mission of the Triune God (_LG_ 1–4). This perspective is made even plainer in _Ad Gentes_ 2, with a footnote reference to _Lumen Gentium_ 1 and language that alludes to the theology of the [^c15-6] _missio Dei_ developed in Protestant theology in the years preceding the council. Such rootedness in God’s mission makes mission not one thing among others that the Church does, but an activity essential to its being, the work of God that calls it forth. The Church is, indeed, ‘by its very nature missionary’ (_AG_ 2).

[^c15-6]: Ibid., 32–34.

Even though in _Ad Gentes_ and in other documents a more traditional, territorial understanding of mission is expressed (see, e.g., _AG_ 6, 19; _SC_ 38), the council ‘moves the centre of gravity … from the geographical and [^c15-7] territorial sphere to an almost exclusively human and sociological conception’. Mission is focused on people, not places. It is ‘one and the same everywhere and in all situations’ (_AG_ 6), although it takes different forms according to the concrete circumstances of a particular situation. The Church exercises its mission in a particular way among peoples who have not yet heard of Christ. This way differs from the way it cares for the pastoral needs of those already baptized and from the way it works to restore unity among Christians. Each of these ways, however, ‘are very closely connected’ (_AG_ 6) with each other. They are simply different ways of engaging in the same mission.

[^c15-7]: Suso Brechter, ‘Decree on the Church’s Missionary Activity’, in _Commentary on the Documents of Vatican II_, ed. Herbert Vorgrimler, 5 vols. (Freiburg im Breisgau: Herder and Herder, 1969), 4:120.

A number of passages also give the impression that mission is about the expansion of the Church (see, e.g., _SC_ 1; _LG_ 15; _Dignitatis Humanae_ (_DH_) 1). Nevertheless, the council does hint at an understanding of mission beyond numbers. Mission is about ‘proclaiming and establishing the kingdom of Christ and God’ (_LG_ 5). Thus, the kingdom is understood as something larger than the Church, although the Church is its ‘seed and the beginning’ (_LG_ 5). The perspective of _Gaudium et Spes_ is that the Church is at the service of the world, not simply seeking to enlarge its own membership. Here, the Church proclaims ‘humanity’s noble destiny’, ‘that there exists in it a noble seed’ (_GS_ 3). The Church wants to enter into dialogue with the world and offers it ‘sincere cooperation … in fostering a sense of sisterhood and brotherhood to correspond to their destiny’ (_GS_ 3). The Church offers itself to serve individuals and society, to cooperate in the world’s work, and acknowledges that it receives much from the world itself (_GS_ 41–44). Chapters 3, 4, and 5 of the second part of the Pastoral Constitution reflect on the role of the Church in regard to the world’s economic life, its political life, and its commitment to justice and peace. The Church’s mission, it becomes clear, is bound up with the flourishing of the human race. The salvation to which the Gospel witnesses and proclaims is a holistic one of healing, compassion, justice, and human emancipation and development.

#### Mission, Culture, and Dialogue

_Gaudium et Spes_ also deals extensively with the promotion of human culture in general and local cultures in **[p. 253]** particular. As the council says powerfully, sensitivity to culture ‘must ever be the law of all evangelisation’ (_GS_ 44). In order that the faithful may be able to better understand and participate in the liturgy, the liturgy may need to be changed (_SC_ 21), something recognized by the council’s allowance of local languages in the liturgy and its call for the adaptation of the liturgy ‘to the temperament and traditions of peoples’ (_SC_ 36–37). _Lumen Gentium_ 16 acknowledges that whatever goodness and truth is found among the world’s cultures is to be considered a preparation for the Gospel. This is also articulated eloquently in _Ad Gentes_ 11. Here Christians in various cultures are urged to enter into a ‘sincere and patient dialogue’ so they ‘might learn of the riches a generous God has distributed among the nations’. _Ad Gentes_ also calls for the development of local theologies in dialogue with the ‘customs, attitude to life and social structures’ of local peoples (_AG_ 22).

The declarations on religious freedom and non-Christian religions build on _Lumen Gentium_’s recognition that non-Christians and even non-believers who follow the ‘dictates of their conscience’ (_LG_ 16) can indeed find their way to salvation. All peoples have the right to religious freedom (_DH_ 2), and those religions other than Christianity possess ‘a ray of that truth which enlightens all men and women’ (_Nostra Aetate_ (_NA_) 2). Christians are not thereby absolved from proclaiming the Gospel (_NA_ 2), but such recognition does shape the way the Gospel is proclaimed. As Paul VI urged in his 1964 encyclical _Ecclesiam Suam_ (_ES_) (published the summer before _LG_ was promulgated), the Church should relate to the world ‘in the nature of a dialogue’ (_ES_ 78). The word should ‘confidently and perseveringly’ be proclaimed, but only ‘whenever God opens a door for the word’ (_AG_ 13). In no uncertain terms, _Ad Gentes_ forbids any kind of forcing or manipulation of people to accept the faith (_AG_ 13).

The spirit of mission pervades the council. The Church is to be missionary—reaching out to the world around it—in every circumstance in which it finds itself. The council’s missiology is comprehensive. It is concerned not for itself but for the kingdom. It embraces the world in its commitment to human development and justice and peace. It witnesses and proclaims and celebrates in a critical appropriation of local cultures. Like the Triune God in whom its mission is rooted, it engages in mission in dialogue with other Christians, with people of other religions, and with people who have no faith. All of these features of the council’s missiology would be developed further in the years after the council and into our own day.

### 3. Post-Conciliar Reception of Vatican II’s Missiology

#### Mission in Crisis

In a seminal article describing the changes in Catholic mission thinking from the nineteenth until the late **[p. 254]** twentieth century, Robert J. Schreiter characterizes the years before Vatican II as a ‘period of certainty’. In these years, no one questioned the validity and necessity of missionary work in its traditional sense, [^c15-8] although mission was done ‘with virtually no attention’ to its theological foundations. Vatican II’s missiology was formulated just at the end of this era. One can see these traditional attitudes present in the documents, but, as noted above, Vatican II offered a renewed sense of mission that saw the whole Church as missionary.

[^c15-8]: Robert Schreiter, ‘Changes in Roman Catholic Attitudes toward Proselytism and Mission’, in _New Directions in Mission and_ _Evangelization_, vol. 2, _Theological Foundations_, ed. James A. Scherer and Stephen B. Bevans (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1994), 113–25, esp. 115.

Schreiter describes Vatican II as taking place in a ‘period of ferment’ that was the result of epochal change both in the world at large and in the world of traditional mission. The end of the ‘period of certainty’ was marked by the end of the Western colonialism, the resulting rise of nationalism, and a renaissance of the world’s major religions—thought by many at the beginning of the twentieth century to be on the brink of being overtaken by Christianity. The council responded with its renewed theology and missiology, but the effect of its more open theology on missionary understanding and practice in ‘mission lands’ was initially quite negative. Foreign mission was plunged into a ‘period of crisis’. Many in the Church, under the influence of the council’s openness to salvation outside the Church, and its positive attitude towards non- Western cultures and other religions, began to wonder about the validity of mission itself. There were calls [^c15-9] for withdrawal from foreign mission work altogether. Schreiter reports that just after the council, the number of missionaries in the world continued to increase, but after 1968 the numbers went into steep decline. Some of this decline was due to the exodus of priests and religious after the council. ‘But the growing insecurity about what was the exact nature of mission in a post-Vatican II church surely fuelled [^c15-10] this development as well’. This crisis contributed to the fact that the robust missiology—especially the essential missionary nature of the Church—developed by the council was eclipsed by the other great move in ecclesiology of the council: the move from institution to community, from hierarchy to People of God or communion. Rather than focusing on its mission in the world, the Church focused on itself.

[^c15-9]: Bevans, ‘Decree on the Church’s Missionary Activity’, 59–60.

[^c15-10]: Schreiter, ‘Changes in Roman Catholic Attitudes toward Proselytism and Mission’, 120.

#### Mission Reborn

Schreiter traces a ‘rebirth’ of mission theology to the publication of Paul VI’s 1975 Apostolic Exhortation _Evangelii Nuntiandi_ (_EN_). One might say, however, that the earliest glimmers of rebirth came as early as 1968, with the meeting of the Latin American bishops in Medellín, Colombia. The bishops met with the goal of implementing the insights and decisions of Vatican II in their Latin American context; what began to **[p. 255]** emerge was that, in such a context, issues of justice and liberation needed to be foremost in their [^c15-11] concerns. The Medellín conference surely influenced the bishops’ discussions at the 1971 Synod of Bishops and its final document on justice in the world. It was in this document that working for justice was identifled [^c15-12] as a constitutive part of the Church’s evangelizing mission. In 1974, the recently formed Federation of Asian Bishops’ Conferences (FABC) met in preparation for the upcoming Synod of Bishops, to be held later that year. The result was a document that articulated for the first time the ‘triple dialogue’ that was to distinguish the FABC through the years: the dialogue with Asian poverty, Asian cultures, and Asian [^c15-13] religions.

[^c15-11]: Conference of Latin American Bishops, _The Church in the Present-Day Transformation of Latin America in the Light of the_ _Council: Second General Conference of Latin American Bishops, Bogotá 24 August, Medellín 26 August–6 September, 1968_ (Bogotá: General Secretariat of CELAM, 1970–73); Margaret Eletta Guider, OSF, Félix Palazzi, and O. Ernesto Valiente, eds., _The Grace of Medellín: History, Theology and Legacy_ (Miami: Convivium, 2018).

[^c15-12]: Synod of Bishops, ‘Justice in the World [1971]’, in _Catholic Social Thought: The Documentary Heritage_, ed. David J. O’Brien and Thomas A. Shannon (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1992), 287–300.

[^c15-13]: Federation of Asian Bishops’ Conferences, ‘Evangelization in Modern Day Asia’, in _For All the Peoples of Asia: Federation of_ _Asian Bishops’ Conferences_, vol. 1, _Documents from 1970 to 1991_, ed. Gaudencio Rosales and Catalino G. Arévalo (Quezon City: Claretian, 1992), 14–16.

_Evangelii Nuntiandi_ was written as a papal response to the 1974 synod that had focused on evangelization in response to the period of missionary crisis. At the synod, strong voices from the global South were heard— from Asia and Africa about the need for more attention to local cultures, and from Latin America for more attention to justice and liberation. Paul’s remarkable document stressed again the council’s emphasis on the essential missionary nature of the Church, insisting that ‘evangelising is in fact the grace and vocation proper to the Church’, its ‘deepest identity’. The Church ‘exists in order to evangelise’ (_EN_ 14).

Initially, Paul’s definition of evangelization focused on witnessing to and preaching the Gospel message, but he goes on to expand this understanding, cautioning against reducing mission to one or the other aspect (_EN_ 17). For Paul, evangelization includes the evangelization of cultures (_EN_ 20). In paragraph 20 he uses the word ‘liberation’, no doubt influenced by the emergence of the theology of liberation in many parts of the world. This is the first time that ‘liberation’—connected to human development and the Church’s commitment to justice—appears in a document of the Roman magisterium. Later in the document, Paul reaffirms Vatican II’s respect for non-Christian religions, but he also insists that non-Christians have a right ‘to know the riches of the mystery of Christ’ (_EN_ 53).

Paul VI does not anchor his treatment of evangelization in the mystery of the Trinity or the mission of God. His starting point is rather Jesus’s preaching the kingdom of God. The reason for this is not clear, but it could very well be that in the years after the council—particularly in more liberal Protestant theology—the idea of the _missio Dei_ had become controversial, to the extent that the necessity of the Church for mission [^c15-14] was called into question. The advantage, however, of Paul’s starting point is that he is able to develop **[p. 256]** much more clearly the relationship between Church and kingdom, and so makes mission less ecclesiocentric. As Paul writes, ‘As an evangeliser, Christ first of all proclaims a kingdom, the kingdom of God; and this is so important that everything else becomes “the rest” which is “given in addition” [cf. Matt 6:33]. Only the kingdom therefore is absolute, and it makes everything else relative’ (_EN_ 8). As the reception of Vatican II’s missiology continues, the relationship between the Church and kingdom will be clarifled even more exactly.

[^c15-14]: David J. Bosch, _Transforming Mission: Paradigm Shifts in Theology of Mission_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1990), 389–93.

#### Mission as a Single, Complex Reality

A major step in the reception of Vatican II’s missiology was taken in 1981 with a seminar in Rome at SEDOS, the centre of ‘Service of Documentation and Study’ on global mission that had been founded in Rome by several missionary congregations in 1969. In the document summarizing the seminar, four ‘principal [^c15-15] activities’ of mission were singled out: proclamation, dialogue, inculturation, and liberation of the poor. Three years later, a similar list of activities was offered by the Vatican’s Secretariat for Non-Christians (created by Paul VI in 1964). Mission in this document, _Dialogue and Mission_ (_DM_), was called a ‘single but complex and articulated reality’; it was comprised of (1) presence and witness, (2) commitment to social development and human liberation, (3) liturgical life, prayer, and contemplation, (4) interreligious dialogue, and (5) proclamation and catechesis.

[^c15-15]: ‘Agenda for Future Planning, Study, and Research in Mission’, in _Trends in Mission: Towards the Third Millennium_, ed. William Jenkinson and Helene O’Sullivan (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1991), 399–414.

What had begun to develop in this ‘period of rebirth’ of mission in the wake of Vatican II was an expansion of mission to include several constitutive elements. This development continued in Pope John Paul II’s 1990 encyclical _Redemptoris Missio_ (_RM_). In words alluding to the 1984 document of the Secretariat for Non- Christians, John Paul II noted that ‘mission is a single but complex reality’ (_RM_ 41). He goes on to outline missionary activity as involving mission and proclamation, engaging in inculturation, interreligious dialogue, and the promotion of development and liberation (see _RM_ 42–60).

Another noteworthy aspect of _Redemptoris Missio_ is John Paul II’s treatment of the kingdom of God. While insisting on not separating the kingdom from the Church or from Christ, he does go a step further than _Lumen Gentium_ 5’s cautious distinction between Church and kingdom and continues Paul VI’s development in _Evangelii Nuntiandi_. He writes: ‘one must not separate the kingdom from the Church. It is true that the Church is not an end unto herself, since she is ordered towards the kingdom of God, of which she is the seed, sign and instrument. Yet, while remaining distinct from Christ and the kingdom, the Church is indissolubly united to both’ (_RM_ 8). The relationship of the kingdom to the Church is further articulated in a 1991 **[p. 257]** document entitled _Dialogue and Proclamation_ (_DP_), issued by two Vatican dicasteries shortly after the publication of _Redemptoris Missio_. The continuity between Church and kingdom is again stressed (_DP_ 34–35, 58–59), although the relationship is ‘mysterious and complex’ (_DP_ 34). Nevertheless, the document goes on to say, quite significantly, that

The Church’s mission is to foster ‘the kingdom of our Lord and his Christ’ (Rev 11:15), at whose service she is placed. Part of her role consists in recognising that the inchoate reality of this kingdom can be found also beyond the confines of the Church, for example in the hearts of the followers of other religious traditions, insofar as they live evangelical values and are open to the action of the Spirit. (_DP_ 35)

In this way, official church teaching seems to have validated ideas about the relationship between Church and kingdom proposed quite soon after the conclusion of Vatican II by theologians such as Hans Küng, John Füllenbach, and Richard P. McBrien.[^c15-16]

[^c15-16]: Hans Küng, _The Church_ (New York: Sheed and Ward, 1967); John Füllenbach, _The Kingdom of God: The Message of Jesus_ _for Today_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1995); Richard P. McBrien, _Do We Need the Church?_ (New York: Harper & Row, 1969).

Since the 1990s, a number of missiologists have offered their own list of what might be called constitutive dimensions of mission, among whom are the Protestant David J. Bosch, Evangelical Samuel Escobar, [^c15-17] Anglican J. Andrew Kirk, and Catholics Anthony Gittins and Donal Dorr. The work of Robert J. Schreiter has added a new element to the ones proposed by the magisterium and these theologians: reconciliation, [^c15-18] suggesting that it might even be the best way to speak of mission in today’s divided and violent world. Stephen Bevans and Eleanor Doidge proposed a synthesis of all these elements, naming six essential components: (1) witness and proclamation; (2) liturgy, prayer, and contemplation; (3) commitment to justice, peace, and the integrity of creation; (4) the practice of interreligious dialogue; (5) efforts of [^c15-19] inculturation; and (6) the ministry of reconciliation. In 2004, Bevans and Roger P. Schroeder developed these six elements more fully in their book on the history and theology of mission, _Constants in Context._ Bevans and Schroeder proposed in this book and in subsequent reflections that the theology, spirituality, and practice of ‘prophetic dialogue’ was perhaps the best way to characterize missionary understanding and practice today. Fundamental to all mission is a basic openness, respect, and willingness to find the Spirit operative in every ministerial and missionary context. Ultimately, mission is about the communication of a **[p. 258]** Gospel message that brings women and men into an authentic encounter with Jesus Christ, gives a word of hope in difficult and seemingly impossible situations, and offers a clear confrontation with injustice at [^c15-20] every turn.

[^c15-17]: David J. Bosch, _Transforming Mission: Paradigm Shifts in Theology of Mission_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1990); Samuel Escobar, _Changing Tides: Latin America and World Mission Today_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2000); Andrew J. Kirk, _What Is Mission?_ _Theological Explorations_ (Minneapolis, MN: Fortress Press, 2000); Anthony J. Gittins, _Reading the Clouds: Mission_ _Spirituality for New Times_ (Ligouri, MO: St Pauls, 1999); Donal Dorr, _Mission in Today’s World_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2000).

[^c15-18]: Robert Schreiter, ‘Reconciliation as a Model of Mission’, _Neue Zeitschriff für Missionswissenschaff_ 52 (1996): 243–50; Robert Schreiter, ‘Globalization and Reconciliation’, in _Mission in the Third Millennium_, ed. Robert J. Schreiter (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2001), 121–43.

[^c15-19]: Stephen Bevans and Eleanor Doidge, ‘Theological Reflection’, in _What MISSION Confronts Religious Life Today?_, ed. Barbara Kraemer (Chicago: Center for the Study of Religious Life, 2000), 37–48.

[^c15-20]: Stephen B. Bevans and Roger P. Schroeder, _Prophetic Dialogue: Reflections on Christian Mission Today_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2011); Stephen B. Bevans and Roger P. Schroeder, _Constants in Context: A Theology of Mission for Today_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2004); Roger P. Schroeder, _What Is the Mission of the Church? A Guide for Catholics_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2018).

#### An Ecumenical Convergence

Contemporary Catholic missiology is highly ecumenical and takes into account missiological thought of all of the world’s major churches—Protestant, Evangelical, Pentecostal, and Orthodox. This is another way in which it has engaged in the reception of Vatican II. There is a real convergence—although not, of course, total agreement—about the nature of mission across church lines. This was evident in the 2010 _Common Call_ from the conference held in Edinburgh, Scotland, to commemorate the 100th anniversary of the 1910 Edinburgh World Mission Conference (which is often considered the birthplace of the modern ecumenical movement). This short document presents an understanding of mission that is thoroughly holistic, [^c15-21] committed to justice, respectful of cultures, and respectful of other religions. The same can be said of the document from the celebration of the Edinburgh centenary by the Evangelical churches, _The Cape Town Commitment_, the landmark document issued in 2013 by the World Council of Churches’ Commission on World Mission and Evangelism (CWME), _Together towards Life_, and _The Arusha Call_, a short document from the World Mission Conference sponsored by the CWME in Arusha, Tanzania, in 2018. The Holy and Great [^c15-22] Council of the Orthodox Churches of 2016 also offers a perspective on mission that is holistic and inclusive.

[^c15-21]: Kenneth R. Ross et al., eds., _Ecumenical Missiology: Changing Landscapes and New Conceptions of Mission_ (Oxford: Regnum Books International, 2016).

[^c15-22]: _The Cape Town Commitment: A Confession of Faith and Call to Action_ (Peabody, MA: Hendrickson, 2011); Commission on World Mission and Evangelism, _Together Towards Life: Mission and Evangelism in Changing Landscapes_ (Geneva: World Council of Churches, 2013); ‘Arusha Call to Discipleship Arusha (2018)’, World Council of Churches, 13 March 2018, https://www.oikoumene.org/en/resources/documents/commissions/mission-and-evangelism/the-arusha-call-to- discipleship; ‘The Mission of the Orthodox Church in Today’s World’, Russian Orthodox Church, 28 January 2016, https://mospat.ru/en/2016/01/28/news127353.

#### Towards a Missionary Church

As Catholic understandings of mission have developed after the council, there has been a growing sense among missiologists and some theologians that mission should not be confined to ‘overseas mission’ or the primary evangelization of non-Christian peoples. These missiologists and theologians point to Vatican II’s **[p. 259]** teaching on the essential missionary nature of the Church, affirmed in both _Evangelii Nuntiandi_ and _Redemptoris Missio_, to press for the Church to be—in the words of the Latin American and Caribbean bishops [^c15-23] at the Aparecida Conference in 2007—‘permanently in a state of mission’. Mission, they argued, needed to [^c15-24] be at the centre of theology and ecclesial thinking.

[^c15-23]: Conference of Bishops of Latin America and the Caribbean, _Aparecida: Documento Conclusivo_ (Bogotá: CELAM, 2007), no. 51.

[^c15-24]: Kirk, _What Is Mission?_; Stephen B. Bevans, ‘Theological Education as Missionary Formation’, in _Reflecting on and Equipping_ _for Christian Mission_, ed. Stephen Bevans et al. (Oxford: Regnum Books International, 2015), 93–105.

John Paul II’s call for a ‘new evangelization’ during his pontificate was an acknowledgement that mission needed to be understood more widely to include the witness of the Church in contexts which had been previously Christianized but had become indifferent to the faith. Benedict XVI also emphasized this aspect of mission and in 2010 created the Pontifical Council for Promoting the New Evangelization, calling for the 2012 Synod of Bishops to take up the new evangelization as its theme. The result of the synod, however, was in some ways quite different from what Benedict had foreseen. Several of the most striking interventions called not for more boldness of purpose in mission, but for openness, vulnerability, and listening. Rather than the Church pretending to have all the answers, the Church would be more credible if it were silent and more able to listen and learn from people who struggle with their faith today. Rather than the narrow focus in the West and the need for its re-evangelization, many of the bishops called for a more missionary Church [^c15-25] wherever it finds itself. Just as _Ad Gentes_ 6 spoke of mission as ‘one and the same everywhere and in all situations’, and yet because of circumstances ‘not always to be exercised in the same way’, so the members of the synod called for a multifaceted missionary Church.

[^c15-25]: Stephen Bevans, ‘Beyond the New Evangelization: Toward a Missionary Ecclesiology for the Twenty-First Century Church’, in _A Church with Open Doors: Catholic Ecclesiology for the Third Millennium_, ed. Richard R. Gaillardetz and Edward P. Hahnenberg (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2015), 3–22, esp. 8–10.

Pope Francis’s 2013 post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation _Evangelii Gaudium_ (_EG_) followed along these lines. In this lengthy document of some 288 paragraphs, he makes reference to the ‘new evangelisation’ only twelve times. Yet his focus is overwhelmingly missionary. He calls the Church, in a reference to the 2007 Aparecida document, ‘a community of missionary disciples’ (_EG_ 24) and alludes to _Ad Gentes_ 2’s programmatic statement about the missionary nature of the Church (_EG_ 179). In a powerful passage near the beginning of the document, Francis writes that he dreams ‘of a “missionary option”, that is a missionary impulse capable of transforming everything, so that the Church’s customs, ways of doing things, times and schedules, language and structures can be suitably channelled for the evangelisation of today’s world rather than for her self-preservation’ (_EG_ 27). Francis writes powerfully of issues of justice (_EG_ 53–58), care for and inclusion of the poor (_EG_ 186–216), the importance of inculturation (_EG_ 68–70, 117–18), the centrality of witness (_EG_ 99–100, 150), and the art of proclaiming the Gospel message (_EG_ 127–29). He emphasizes the **[p. 260]** need for the Church to be open, listening, and inviting—to be ‘a mother with an open heart’, the house of the father of the prodigal son, with its doors always open (_EG_ 46). In the 2015 encyclical _Laudato Si’_ (_LS_), Francis makes a case for placing the care of creation at the centre of the Church’s mission today. In _Amoris Laetitia_ (_AL_), the 2016 Apostolic Exhortation after the two-part Synod on the Family in 2014–15, Francis wrote compassionately of married couples who live in ‘irregular situations’ of civil marriage, or as divorced and remarried persons, insisting that they be allowed to participate as fully as possible in the life of the Church (_AL_ 291–312). Francis’s ecclesiology and missiology might be called an ‘ecclesiology’ or ‘missiology [^c15-26] of attraction’.

[^c15-26]: Stephen Bevans, ‘Pope Francis’s Missiology of Attraction’, _International Bulletin of Mission Research_ 43, no. 1 (2019): 20–28.

As the missiology of Vatican II has been developed through the process of reception of the council, the seeds sown at the council and in its documents have reached a genuine maturity. It is a holistic missiology that recognizes the ‘single complex reality’ (_RM_ 41) that mission is, one that includes a clear witness to and proclamation of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, and yet is constituted by its commitment to justice, to inculturation, to interreligious, secular, and ecumenical dialogue, and commitment to working for reconciliation in its individual and social dimensions. It is a missiology that, while recognizing the importance of the Church, is focused not on the Church itself but on the kingdom to which it gives witness and that it proclaims. It is a missiology that calls the Church to be thoroughly missionary, a ‘community of missionary disciples’ (_EG_ 24), a Church ‘by its very nature missionary’ (_AG_ 2). It is a missiology that can truly help the Church minister in this world that is so different from the world of the council’s immediate aftermath.

### 4. The Shape of a Missionary Church

What might the Church look like if it would take seriously the missiology of Vatican II and its development over a half-century of reception? How might a ‘missiological hermeneutic’ shape a ‘missiological imagination’ for mission and ministry in today’s world?

#### A Missionary God

Perhaps the first step in answering these questions would be for the Church to be firmly rooted in faith in a dynamic, missionary God. Ecclesiology can never be separated from the doctrine of God. In a stunning way, a missionary God is imaged in ways that resonate with understandings of God proposed by theologians in **[p. 261]** dialogue with contemporary astrophysics and evolutionary theory. The Triune God is ‘the “Verb” in which [^c15-27][^c15-28] all beings participate, live and move and have their being’. God’s Being is ‘sheer livingness’, coursing [^c15-29] through all things. It is ‘an act of communion’, revealed in the world as all-pervading creator Spirit, made flesh in Jesus of Nazareth, who reveals God as loving, merciful, tender Holy Mystery. The ‘Verb’ that is God is a God of mission. God’s ‘ “fountain-like love” … freely creates us and moreover calls us to share in his life and glory’ (_AG_ 2; see _LG_ 1–4), anointing the community at Pentecost in the same way as Jesus was anointed [^c15-30] at his baptism.

[^c15-27]: Elizabeth A. Johnson, _She Who Is: The Mystery of God in Feminist Theological Discourse_ (New York: Crossroad, 1992), 239; Elizabeth A. Johnson, _Ask the Beasts: Darwin and the God of Love_ (New York: Bloomsbury, 2014), 144.

[^c15-28]: Johnson, _She Who Is_, 236.

[^c15-29]: Ibid., 238.

[^c15-30]: Bevans and Schroeder, _Prophetic Dialogue_, 9–18.

#### Church as Communion-in-Mission

The narrative of a Triune, missionary God who shares the divine mission with the followers of Jesus points to a development in the usual interpretation of the Church as communion. This interpretation was proposed [^c15-31] as ‘the central and fundamental idea in the council’s documents’, but the ‘missiological hermeneutic’ developed in this chapter reveals another strand of interpretation just as crucial for an adequate understanding of the council’s intentions. Taking into account the council’s missiological vision, refined and developed over fifty years since its conclusion, the Church is best described not simply as a ‘communion’, but also as a ‘communion-in-mission’, expressed also by Pope Francis as a ‘community of missionary disciples’ (_EG_ 24).

[^c15-31]: ‘The Final Report of the 1985 Extraordinary Synod’, in _A Message to the People of God and the Final Report_ (Washington, DC: National Conference of Catholic Bishops, 1986).

A more dynamic interpretation opens up a missiological interpretation of the council’s description of the Church as ‘sacrament’ (see _LG_ 1, 48; _AG_ 1; _GS_ 42, 45), as sign and _instrument_ of salvation. The gradual development of the distinction between Church and kingdom (_LG_ 5; _RM_ 18; _DP_ 35) is also illuminated by understanding the Church as communion-in-mission. It is because the Church already participates in the communion of the kingdom that it is able to bear witness to it in the world.

Describing the Church as a communion-in-mission also enhances the council’s emphasis on baptism. Baptism is the sacrament of communion of Christians with the Triune God and with one another. But the life of the Trinity into which one is baptized is the life of a _missionary_ God, and so baptism is the sacrament of mission. As Pope Francis expresses it, ‘All members of the People of God have become missionary disciples (cf. Mt 28:19). All the baptised … are agents of evangelisation’ (_EG_ 120). There are no passive Christians, because they have been baptized into a missionary Church, a communion-in-mission.

**[p. 262]** The missionary Church of today, however, should heed the voices of those bishops who spoke at the 2012 [^c15-32] Synod on the New Evangelization and the 2018 Synod on Youth and Vocation. The Church should first be silent and respectful in the face of the complexities of our contemporary world, then listen carefully to the voices of women, youth, the poor, and even those who have left the Church. Pope Francis’s ‘missiology of attraction’ should be the way that the Church engages in mission today. Only by listening, being hospitable, and being inclusive can the Church hope to regain its credibility in the wake of the sexual abuse and financial scandals of the past years. As Paul VI said famously in _Evangelii Nuntiandi_, echoed by Pope Francis in _Evangelii Gaudium_, people today are more interested in witness than in words (_EN_ 41, see also 21; _EG_ 150).

[^c15-32]: ‘Documento finale e Votazioni del Documento finale del Sinodo dei Vescovi al Santo Padre Francesco (27 ottobre 2018)’, Holy See Press Office, 27 October 2018, http://press.vatican.va/content/salastampa/it/bollettino/pubblico/2018/10/27/0789/01722.html.

#### Structure that Serves Mission

A Church that takes seriously Vatican II’s missiology and its reception will be a Church organized for mission. Structure, in other words, serves mission, and not vice versa. A missionary Church will be rooted in the fact that its fundamental structure is actually no structure—it is one of the basic equality of missionary discipleship conferred on every Christian at baptism. It would be, in the resonant phrase of Richard [^c15-33] Gaillardetz, a ‘non-competitive church’. Such an understanding is rooted in the theology of the sacrament of Holy Orders at Vatican II. The title of the document on priesthood favours ministry over state and is rooted in an acknowledgement of the priesthood of all believers, which a person is ordained to serve (see _Presbyterorum Ordinis_ (_PO_) 2). As Pope Francis wrote in _Evangelii Gaudium_, ‘the ministerial priesthood [and one might add episcopacy as well] is one means employed by Jesus for the service of his people, yet our great dignity derives from baptism, which is accessible to all’. Francis goes on to say that ordination, although it conforms the ordained to Christ the head of the Church, ‘does not imply exaltation which would set him above others. In the Church, functions “do not favour the superiority of some vis-à-vis the others” ’ (_EG_ 104).

[^c15-33]: Richard R. Gaillardetz, _An Unfinished Council: Vatican II, Pope Francis, and the Renewal of Catholicism_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2015), 91–114.

Authority in the Church, inspired by its mission, would not be a strictly hierarchical, top-down authority but one that takes seriously the reality that the entire People of God is endowed with the infallibility of belief ‘through a supernatural sense of the faith of all the people walking together’. This is a point that Pope Francis makes strongly. ‘Thinking with the church’, he says, is about thinking theologically and pastorally **[p. 263]** as part of this People. ‘When the dialogue among the people and the bishops and the pope goes down this [^c15-34] road,’ Francis says in a remarkable sentence, ‘then it is assisted by the Holy Spirit.’

[^c15-34]: Antonio Spadaro, _A Big Heart Open to God: A Conversation with Pope Francis_ (New York: Harper One, 2013), 25–26; originally published as ‘Intervista a Papa Francesco’, _La civiltà cattolica_, 3918, year 164 (19 September 2013), 449–77.

In _Evangelii Gaudium_, Francis describes episcopal ministry (one could also say _presbyteral_ ministry) as fostering ‘missionary communion’. The bishop, he says, sometimes walks before the people, showing the way. At other times, he will simply be present within the community, no doubt with openness and a listening heart. At still other times, the bishop must walk after the people, ‘helping those who lag behind’, but ‘above all’, he walks behind them to allow them ‘to strike out on new paths’. The main purpose, he says finally, of developing participatory processes in the Church, ‘should not be ecclesiastical organisation but rather the missionary aspiration of reaching everyone’ (_EG_ 31). Such a missionary aspiration is surely why Francis speaks so much of ‘synodality’, even in a way that recasts the notion of episcopal collegiality. The final document of the 2018 synod calls for changes that would go more in the direction of synodality—more participation by women in the Church as a ‘duty of justice’, and more participation by laity and youth as well. A synodal Church, the document states, would be ‘more participative and co-responsible … welcoming [^c15-35] with gratitude the contribution of lay faithful’. If mission is taken seriously, these aspirations could well be fully implemented.

[^c15-35]: Joshua J. McElwee, ‘Synod Ends, Calling Women’s Inclusion in Catholic leadership a “Duty of Justice” ’, _National Catholic_ _Reporter Online_, 27 October 2018, https://www.ncronline.org/news/vatican/synod-ends-calling-womens-inclusion- catholic-leadership-duty-justice.

#### A Church of Inculturation, Dialogue, and Justice

A Church that takes mission seriously would be a Church committed to communicating the Gospel in ways that people in their local contexts can understand. It would be a Church committed to prophecy—the clear and challenging articulation of the Gospel message to women and men, a result of profound respect and listening to people’s cultures, concerns, and aspirations, their struggles for dignity and justice. A missionary Church would recognize that all preaching, all teaching, all liturgical celebrations, all Church organization needs to be profoundly contextual. Today’s Catholicism is a _world_ Catholicism, in which the centre of gravity of the Church has shifted from the global North to the global South. No longer can there be conceived one way of expressing things or doing things. Each local Church—in the North or in the South— needs to articulate its own theology, its own way of worship, its own way of organizing itself. A robust practice of catholicity—defined as constant change and communication among the world’s churches—will ensure a rich unity.[^c15-36]

[^c15-36]: Robert J. Schreiter, _The New Catholicity: Theology between the Global and the Local_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1997).

**[p. 264]** Such a commitment to contextual theologizing and inculturation would demand some courage and risk. It would be much easier simply to repeat orthodox formulae (or traditional ways of doing things), but, as Pope Francis points out, it would not be safer. The ‘greatest danger’, he writes, is holding ‘fast to a formulation while failing to convey its substance’ (_EG_ 41). ‘A missionary heart’, he adds, ‘never closes itself oft, never retreats into its own security, never opts for rigidity and defensiveness’ (_EG_ 45). Being a Church committed to inculturation would follow one of the clearest trajectories laid out by the missiology of Vatican II and its post-conciliar reception.

Another clear trajectory from the council and post-conciliar thought is that of dialogue in all its forms— ecumenical, interreligious, and secular. Ecumenical activity was closely tied to mission at Vatican II (see _AG_ 6; _UR_ 1), and has remained central in the World Council of Churches’ Commission on World Mission and [^c15-37] Evangelism, in which the Catholic Church has full membership. Pope Francis affirmed that link in his 2018 [^c15-38] visit to the World Council of Churches headquarters in Geneva. A Church committed to the missionary legacy of Vatican II will also be fearless in its commitment to interreligious dialogue. In a world in which religion is often seen as the cause of violence and terrorism, women and men working to live together in peace and understanding can be an articulation of the Gospel that is truly prophetic. A deep, even passionate recognition of the ‘rays of truth’ (see _NA_ 2) found in the world’s religions can be a small but powerful way that Christians can work for peace in today’s fractured world (see _EG_ 250). Francis has called the Church to be a ‘listening Church’ (_LS_); one way a missionary Church can do this is to listen to those who do not believe, or who no longer believe, or who even oppose belief. In a genuine development of _Gaudium et Spes_’s sympathetic treatment of atheism (see _GS_ 19–21), Francis writes that Christians feel close to those who do not identify with religious traditions but ‘seek the truth, goodness and beauty which we believe have their highest expression and source in God’, regarding them as ‘precious allies’. Referring to a recommendation of the 2012 synod, Francis calls for spaces where ‘believers and non-believers are able to engage in dialogue about fundamental issues of ethics, art and science, and about the search for transcendence’ (_EG_ 257).

[^c15-37]: Commission on World Mission and Evangelism, _Together Towards Life_, 59–66.

[^c15-38]: Elise Harris, ‘Mission Is a Prerequisite to Unity, Pope says in Geneva’, _Catholic News Agency_ (21 June 2018), https://www.catholicnewsagency.com/news/mission-is-a-prerequisite-to-unity-pope-says-in-geneva-62886.

A month before the council opened, John XXIII spoke of the need for the Church, especially in [^c15-39] ‘underdeveloped countries’, to become ‘a Church for all, particularly a Church of the poor’. This theme of solidarity with the world’s poor was taken up by the council, especially in _Gaudium et Spes_ (e.g., _GS_ 1, 63–72), and was championed by a group of bishops, mostly from Latin America, who met regularly at the Belgian College in Rome during the council. This was the group, led by the legendary Dom Hélder Câmara of Brazil, **[p. 265]** who signed the ‘Pact of the Catacombs’ in the final days of the council and committed themselves to [^c15-40] simple living, identification with the poor, and social justice. The Latin American bishops called for a poor Church committed to justice in their deliberations at Medellín, Colombia, in 1968, surely influencing the 1971 Synod of Bishops declaration on the constitutive nature of working for justice in the missionary work of the Church. Such a commitment to the poor and to justice has been a hallmark of papal and episcopal teaching ever since, and Pope Francis has made ‘a Church which is poor and for the poor’ (_EG_ 198) a central motif of his papacy. A Church shaped by mission can only be a Church ‘where the poor feel at home’, such a witness being ‘the most effective presentation of the good news of the kingdom’ (_EG_ 199). The centrality of a commitment to the poor and working for their empowerment in justice is undoubtedly one of the clearest legacies of the council’s missiology—even though the Church in actuality struggles to make it a reality. A ‘missiological hermeneutic’ of the council, however, will never let the Church oft the hook.

[^c15-39]: John XXIII, ‘Nuntius radiophonicus universis catholici orbis christifidelibus, mensae ante quam Oecumenicum Concilium simeret initium’, in _Enchiridion Vaticanum: Documenti del Concilio Vaticano II_ (Bologna: EDB, 1968), 2:28.

[^c15-40]: Xabier Pikaza and José Antunes da Silva, eds, _The Pact of the Catacombs: The Mission of the Poor in the Church_ (Estella, Spain: Editorial Verbo Divino, 2015).

### 5. Conclusion

The missiology of Vatican II, and its development in the council’s wake, can be a framework within which the Church can adequately respond to the challenges of our present day. A missionary Church is a Church that is not concerned with itself but is wholly committed to working with God for the completion of creation and so the full, integral salvation of the world. Such a Church is a true sign and instrument of the God who manifested Godself fully by self-emptying and service in incarnation within cosmic and human history and in full solidarity with the world’s poor. A missionary Church may well be one of the most significant results [^c15-41] of the dream of St Pope John XXIII for the council: to bring about ‘a new Pentecost’. Like the Triune God, from whom it draws its life, a missionary Church embraces ‘the joys and hopes, the grief and anguish of the people of our time, especially of those who are poor or affiicted’ (_GS_ 1).

[^c15-41]: John XXIII, ‘Constitutio Apostolica qua Ss. Oecumenicum Concilium Vaticanum II indicitur’, in _Enchiridion Vaticanum_, 2:12–13.
