## 16. Religious Liberty at Vatican II

Silvia Scatena

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 267]** Intended as a personal and collective right to immunity from coercion and restriction in the practice and diffusion of one’s beliefs, the right to religious freedom was the last topic to be considered with regard to the Catholic doctrine on human rights. Before John XXIII’s 1963 encyclical _Pacem in Terris_, for over a century, the interventions of the magisterium were repeatedly aligned with a disdainful rejection of the challenges of political modernity, understood, essentially, as an unstoppable process of secularization. This refusal—as is well known—derived from the conflict that began with European continental secularism and the response of the Catholic Church to the traumas of the French Revolution.

On the eve of the council, this was no longer relegated to a distant past. At the end of the 1950s, Pius XII’s pontificate ended remarkably with the preparation of some definitive condemnation procedures against authors who, from the second half of the 1940s, had variously engaged in an overall rethinking of the question of the confessionalism and secularism of the State, and of the notion of tolerance and religious liberty. At the beginning of 1958, the Dominican priest Rosario Gagnebet, former secretary of the Commission for Studies of the Order of Preachers (OP) and since 1954 an official of the Holy Office, prepared a list of forty-two propositions summarizing the positions of some Catholic authors who had been engaged for years in an attempt to overcome the classic thesis–hypothesis dualism and to rethink the problem of [^c16-1] **[p. 268]** religious liberty. Reduced to twenty-one by a special commission and translated into Latin, they constituted the second part of a document printed in June 1958. Only Pius XII’s death in October of that year [^c16-2] seemed to have prevented their definitive publication.

[^c16-1]: They were printed in French in March 1958: _Concezioni di diversi autori sulle relazioni tra Chiesa e Stato; Troisième partie:_ _Liste des propositions résumant les positions soutenues ci-dessus_. A copy of the document is found in the Gagnebet Fund (FGn), III, 1, 64, in the Archives at the John XXIII Foundation for Religious Studies, Bologna. Of these twenty-one propositions, there is a second, revised version dated 30 April 1958, _Conceptions de divers auteurs sur les devoirs de l’État_ _catholique_, FGn III, 1, 74.

[^c16-2]: Suprema Congregatio Sancti Offici, Mense Iunio 1958, Prot. N. 551/53/1, _Ecclesia et Status: De officiis Status catholici erga_ _religionem_, FGn III, 1, 18.

This document of the Holy Office opened with a synthesis of the ‘immutable’ Catholic doctrine, founded on the ‘immutable rights of God’: the distinction between Church and civil society; the subordination of temporal ends to spiritual ends; the Church’s duty to intervene in the temporal order when supernatural goals were at stake; the duty of civil powers to support religion without remaining indifferent to it; the duty, therefore, to fulfil religious obligations by the civil authority itself; the exclusion from its legislation and public acts of anything that the Church considered contrary to its purpose and, therefore, the effort to create the moral, intellectual, and social conditions that facilitated man’s ability to discover divine truth; the evaluation of the conditions in which the good of religion and society require the Catholic State to grant a ‘certain just tolerance’; and, finally, the establishing that this doctrine could be applied only in a Catholic State. Five years after the well-known speech given at the Lateran University in Rome by Cardinal Alfredo Ottaviani, pro-secretary of the Holy Office, _Duties of the Catholic State in Regard to Religion_—a vigorous defence of the Catholic confessional State, which expressly legitimized the use of the criterion of ‘two [^c16-3] weights and two measures’, one for truth, the other for error —the perennial validity of the principles of ecclesiastical public law, still hinging on the theory of _potestas indirecta in temporalibus_ (the indirect power of the Church in temporal affairs), was thus reaffirmed. At the same time, the positions of some ‘proponents of new doctrines’—convinced that the traditional doctrine of the Church could be reduced to a set of principles to be applied in a way that differed necessarily from the approach of the past—were therefore condemned. According to the redactor of the document, a new theory—indeed, a ‘new _thesis_’—was being formulated, one that was clearly distant from the magisterium of the popes of past centuries and a source of some confusion among Catholics. For this reason, an explicit suppression of these new propositions, which ‘cannot be taught by Catholics’, was necessary.

[^c16-3]: Alfredo Ottaviani, _Doveri dello Stato cattolico verso la religione_ (Rome: Libreria del Pontificio Ateneo Lateranense, 1953).

Until the end of Pius XII’s long pontificate, the attempt to revise the traditional doctrine on relations between Church and State and on religious tolerance was therefore forbidden. It was only with the new perspectives opened by John XXIII’s choice to entrust his programme for the _aggiornamento_ of the Church to the conciliar process that a significant advance could be made by the Catholic magisterium on the subject of human rights.

### 2. The Ecumenical Genesis of the Conciliar Schema

**[p. 269]** Directly urged by the representatives of the separated communities, in November 1960 the new and controversial theme of religious freedom was immediately included in the agenda of the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity, a body originally created earlier that year by John XXIII to help non-Catholic Christians follow the progress of the ecumenical assembly. However, it soon became an alternative body alongside the other preparatory commissions of Vatican II. Religious freedom would specifically be one of the four schemas prepared by the new Secretariat. The schema was examined by the Central Preparatory Commission of the council in June 1962, the year when the ‘conciliar’ history on religious freedom formally began. And a difficult story it would be, mainly because of the heated confrontation that would take place until the final day of debate and voting in St Peter’s between differing, if not opposing, interpretations of the political, social, and cultural developments that had changed the world and with which the Church was now called to dialogue. From the beginning to the end of the council, the categories in which the problem of tolerance and relations between Church and State had traditionally been set—the same categories found in the manuals of ecclesiastical public law that had been absorbed by generations of seminarians and students of pontifical universities—would still have a profound influence as they provided deep resistance to the various efforts under way for an overall reset of the whole problem of freedom in religious matters. Thus the issue, and the schema, of religious freedom would soon become a coalescing element of different dissatisfactions and obstructions: bishops from curial circles who would repeatedly try to circumscribe the authority of the Secretariat presided over by Cardinal Bea; those belonging to an increasingly organized minority; and those from significant sectors of the episcopate, in particular the Italian- and Spanish-speaking countries, which were strongly marked by the experience of Francoism and, soon after, of Fascism, and held the deep-rooted idea that the State ought to ensure a condition of legal privilege to the Catholic Church.

Placed on the agenda essentially to respond to requests from within the World Council of Churches, during the preparatory period the question of religious freedom immediately acted as a magnet for a series of issues which, although familiar to those who had navigated in ecumenical circles, were nevertheless substantially new for many bishops. With regard to the more traditional arguments bearing on the rights and duties of conscience, several themes quickly emerged: in particular, the problem of collaboration among Christians, especially in mission countries, and the problem of the link between ecumenism and mission. The latter was a fundamental topic from the beginning of ecumenical reflection. It took centre stage at the annual meeting of the Catholic Conference for Ecumenical Questions in 1959 and the following year at the meeting of the Faith and Order commission of the World Council of Churches in Geneva. There **[p. 270]** was also the question of Church–State relations, the starting point for discussions on religious freedom within the ecumenical movement beginning after the Second World War. Finally, there was a need to rethink certain categories of Thomistic social ontology, which revolve around the controversial and much-debated notion of the common good.

On the eve of the council, this plurality of issues and levels of reflection evidently found an echo in internal discussions at the Secretariat and in the first drafts of the schema prepared by a small group of redactors. The personalist approach of the presenter of the schema, the bishop of Bruges, Emiel De Smedt, and of the moral theologian of Leuven, Louis Janssens—author of a first text presented in Freiburg in December 1960, entirely centred on the concept of the immutable dignity of the human person—was immediately confronted with two other perspectives destined to meet with greater favour in the gathered assembly of bishops. On the one hand, the American theologian Gustave Weigel, a colleague of the Jesuit John Courtney Murray who had been ‘silenced’ by the Holy Office in 1955 and was destined to become the kingpin of the _Dignitatis Humanae_ drafting committee at the council, became in particular a spokesman for the demands raised by the pre-preparatory _vota_ of the US bishops and, more generally, of the expectations of American Catholicism for a clear official pronouncement by the Catholic Church in favour of religious freedom. Weigel insisted above all on two central and qualifying points of Murray’s reflection: the subjective character of rights and the need to take into account the variation, in time and place, of the organizational structure of States. Alongside this perspective, which primarily emphasized the need for an in-depth study of all the problems inherent in Church–State relations, there emerged other combining approaches, themes, and ideas that at times were very different from one another. Some were destined to make no lasting impression. Among these were the main issue of freedom within the Church, raised by the English Jesuit Maurice Bévenot and the Swiss Johannes Feiner, and the question, raised by the Dutch Franz Thijssen, of the eschatological dimension of the problem of religious freedom. In his view, only a careful consideration of the pilgrim nature of the Church would make it possible to set aside the fundamentally negative approach with which the question of tolerance of error had traditionally been framed and give the whole question a solid theological foundation. In an eschatological perspective, the Church was called to put up with error and to renounce the will to extirpate sin from the world, not for an opportunistic adaptation to the present situation and circumstances, but rather out of conformity to its very nature, to its condition of expectation, its being in a pilgrim state (_statu peregrinationis_). Similar reflections did not give rise to a sustained debate within the Secretariat. However, combined with other ideas (such as those of Fr. Pierre Michalon from the Lyons school of the pioneer of spiritual ecumenism, Paul Couturier, or those of the German bishop of Mainz, Hermann Volk), they contributed to keeping alive a certain tension and desire for a deeper reflection on the biblical-scriptural aspects of the question of religious freedom and for considering the neglected ‘mystery’ of God’s plan. A more solid biblical anchoring of the schema would be a crucial concern with regard to relations with Protestant Christians.

### 3. An Impossible Compromise: The Language of Abstractions and That of Situations

**[p. 271]** After this intense phase of reflection in the ‘laboratory’ of the preparatory work by the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity, the true ‘conciliar’ history of religious freedom would begin, as stated earlier, with the presentation of the text prepared by Cardinal Bea’s office for the examination of the Central Preparatory Commission of Vatican II in June 1962. This debut was marked by a significant clash between two different and conflicting schemas on religious freedom and tolerance, developed separately by the Secretariat for Unity and the Theological Commission presided over by Cardinal Ottaviani. The latter’s text —chapter 9 of the preparatory ecclesiological schema on relations between Church and State—represented the theological perspective that had dominated for over fifty years, assuming an essentially defensive stance. It proposed in particular the perennial validity of the principles of ecclesiastical public law, including the duty of civil powers to support religion without remaining indifferent to it; the exclusion from its legislation and from public acts of everything the Church considered contrary to its purpose; and, last but not least, the evaluation of the conditions in which the good of religion and society required the Catholic State to grant ‘just tolerance’ to other confessions to avoid greater evil.

The schema of the Secretariat was characterized instead by a decidedly pastoral structure. Its distinguishing elements were the disappearance of the concept of tolerance in favour of the proclamation of freedom of conscience and ensuing responsibilities for all people; greater differentiation between the concepts of State and civil society; an awareness of the spiritual and universal character of the mission of the Church and of its clear separation from temporal power; and the explicit recognition of the equal dignity of all religious expression. From this perspective, the person erring in matters of faith was considered equally worthy of esteem, while the right to religious freedom was affirmed on the basis of the free nature of the act of faith, without which the redeemed person cannot adhere to revelation. Called by God’s free gift of grace, he or she must respond in a free and rational way. The schema of the Secretariat affirmed that this right was not only to be asserted but also concretely exercised as the right to proclaim and to observe, publicly and privately, individually and in groups, one’s duties regarding God and human beings, according to the dictates of one’s consciousness.

This first confrontation that took place within the Central Preparatory Commission represents in many ways a kaleidoscope through which we can discern some of the essential lines of the assembly’s subsequent dialectic, as well as some of the reefs on which the confrontation would founder.

After a prolonged absence from the conciliar debate due to the objective difficulty of finding a compromise **[p. 272]** between two radically different approaches, the schema of the Secretariat was presented for the first time to the assembly only at the end of the second session of Vatican II, in November 1963, as the fifth chapter of the schema on ecumenism. This ecumenical guise was given to it by the new Commission for the Coordination of the Council’s Works to ensure that the schema remained under the responsibility of Bea’s office, in this way eluding the Theological Commission. Distributed to the assembly when the debate on the first three chapters of the schema on ecumenism had already begun, the text on religious freedom, as well as that on the Jews, was not, however, put to a preliminary vote of acceptance and was not the object of a specific assembly meeting, even though there were references to its content in several of the interventions dedicated to an overall evaluation of the schema on ecumenism. Hailed by many, especially by the North American bishops, as an essential prerequisite for any serious discourse on ecumenism, it was criticized by other groups of bishops above all for the confusing overlap they saw in it between the consideration of religious freedom as an ecumenical issue on the one hand and as a political issue on the other.

Expectation outside St Peter’s was such, however, that the debate that did not take place at the council immediately shifted outside the conciliar hall, where, in the meantime, the impatience of large sectors of world public opinion, both Catholic and non-Catholic, had grown. Many people followed closely the council’s dealing with religious freedom; the reason for this was simultaneously psychological, ecumenical, and doctrinal. Regarding the last, after Pius XII’s interventions and John XXIII’s encyclicals, the need was felt in particular for a tangible confirmation of the sincerity of the Catholic conversion to the cause of human rights.

The debate that sparked the second intersession was often an abstract confrontation of principles. The problem still had to do with establishing the very language of the debate: What exactly was meant by religious freedom? The variety of approaches to the problem was indeed remarkable and was immediately demonstrated by the large dossier of the written observations sent to the Secretariat and, even more so, by the first real assembly debate of September 1964. Opening the debate with a firm attempt to repropose the traditional arguments for the ‘rights of truth’ by the cardinal of Palermo, Ernesto Ruffini, and ending with Cameroonian Jean Zoa’s heartfelt words on the need to recognize without hesitation, and in a doctrinally rigorous manner, the right to religious freedom, this late assembly debate revealed a clash between two different discourses: one focused on principles and abstractions, and the other more attentive to the different situations affecting the life and concrete needs of Christians in the various contexts in which they found themselves.

Given the profound diversity of the bishops’ backgrounds and their conflicting and culturally diverse intellectual perspectives, and to avoid the pitfall of traditional controversies over the rights of truth and conscience in erroneous good faith, the schema underwent a sort of progressive ‘filtering’. This eventually helped to shift the discussion from the ecumenical terrain, from which the schema originated, to the more defined one of Church–State relations, civil liberties, and intersubjective rights. In the face of resistance by those whom Congar in his diary calls the ‘tenors’ of the opposition, and due to the difficulties that **[p. 273]** supporters of the right in question faced in connecting the different meanings of ‘religious freedom’ (freedom of faith; evangelical freedom; freedom from coercion, from restriction, from the all-pervasive State), in the autumn of 1964 the redactors sought a solution by shifting the question of religious freedom to the constitutional terrain. They also retained a ‘negative’ approach, so to speak, by affirming a right to freedom that is understood essentially as immunity from coercion by public authorities in religious matters. Therefore, they decided to favour the historical-legal perspective, which was apparently less complex and challenging than other approaches.

### 4. The ‘American Schema’, Vatican II’s ‘Black Week’, and the Debate of the Third Intersession

The drafting of the schema prepared in October 1964 received a decisive contribution from John Courtney Murray. Already a _peritus_ (expert) of the archbishop of New York, Cardinal Francis Spellma, Murray officially joined the team of _periti_ of the Secretariat in the autumn of 1964, but his direct involvement in the drafting of _De libertate_ was delayed after he was sidelined at the beginning of that year by a serious heart attack. The great novelty of the schema was the recognition of the historically determined nature of a right of an essentially juridical-political nature, which was closely related to the structure of modern constitutional governments and to the twofold and parallel distinction between civil society and State, the common good and public order. At the same time, the reference to the dignity of the human person was becoming more clearly articulated as the fundamental motive of the schema, together with the decidedly new importance acquired by the contemporary historical consciousness of religious freedom as an indispensable right of the person and the reality of the role of modern constitutional governments. The first consequence of the new approach to the problem was the division of the arguments into those from reason (_ex ratione_) and those based in revelation (_ex revelatio_)—that is, the separation between the natural and the supernatural orders. In line with this new approach, any allusion to erroneous conscience was definitively eliminated from the text. A reference to freedom of conscience was retained, but it was condensed and combined with four other themes: the integrity of the person, from a strictly anthropological perspective; the duty of seeking the truth, which would acquire a growing importance in the continuation of the redaction history of the declaration; the very nature of the act of faith; and, finally, the incompetence of the public powers in religious matters, which would now acquire new significance, as it essentially grounded the very special dignity of the human person in the transcendence of the relationship with God, which goes beyond the limits of earthly societies.

It was precisely at the end of this delicate redaction phase, in the hectic week of 14–21 November 1964—the **[p. 274]** so-called ‘black week’ of the council—that the schema of the Secretariat came close to being excluded from the conciliar agenda. Cardinal Dean Eugène Tisserant announced that the vote on the text as a whole and on individual chapters would be postponed. He then announced the postponement of the preliminary vote to decide whether to retain the text as a basis for further consideration, following a first petition of the opponents of _De libertate_ to the Council of Presidents and the administrative court of the council, to allow ‘adequate time’ for study before proceeding to vote. It was a text, as was pointed out, that touched on a matter of great delicacy from both a doctrinal and a pastoral perspective. It also differed considerably from the schema discussed in September. In this case, the new-found ability of the organized minority to appeal to the council regulations played a crucial role. The reservations of some members of the curia in important positions of authority played a role as well. The section that raised the greatest difficulty was that which laid out the rational arguments in support of the right to religious freedom. In particular, the passage treating the duty or right to seek the truth and to express one’s beliefs in religious matters was deemed incoherent and was therefore rejected.

The presentation of the cardinal dean made a profound impression on the assembly. A contributing factor was Paul VI’s choice not to intervene in the procedure, thus ensuring respect for the vote by the majority of the fathers. The reason behind the request for a postponement of the vote, as Fr Congar wrote, was no doubt the hope of ‘some, who do not want to have anything to do with the declaration on freedom, and who think that suspending this vote means postponing it to next summer, therefore, dedicating the months ahead to other matters’.[^c16-4]

[^c16-4]: Yves-Marie Congar, _Mon journal du Concile_, 2 vols. (Paris: Cerf, 2002), 2:281.

For the second consecutive year, the debate thus shifted to the pages of a large dossier of observations, criticisms, and proposals. Theologians and _periti_ continued to guide and accompany the reflection of the episcopate. The debate of September 1964 helped to familiarize the bishops with a problem that had the attention of both the World Council of Churches and the United Nations. In principle, they were able to define and examine in depth the options, the _vota_, and the dissatisfactions which had emerged in the previous year and in the months of the third session and were crucial in the redaction history of _Dignitatis Humanae_.

Leaving aside the feelings and intentions of the organized minority as well as those of certain episcopal and curial sectors, which would continue to have reservations about the text of the Secretariat right to the end, the debate was particularly animated in North American and francophone circles, usually referred to as the ‘American’ and ‘French’ schools.

The Americans essentially identifled with the approach of the Jesuit theologian from Woodstock College, John Courtney Murray. The main lines of his approach—which would be the one adopted, in essence, by the final version of the conciliar declaration—found a particularly effective and concise presentation in _America_, the magazine of the American Jesuits. At the end of the second session, on 30 November 1963, a **[p. 275]** short, dense article titled ‘On Religious Liberty’ represented his first explicit public ‘return’ after being [^c16-5] censored in 1955. In this contribution, soon translated into four other languages, the American theologian presented the essential points of his long reflection on religious freedom developed from the late 1940s. Distinguishing between the tradition of European liberalism and the Anglo-Saxon political tradition which was immune from the ‘monism’ that had informed the genesis of the modern European secular States, Murray stressed that the cornerstone of American constitutionalism represented in some ways a modern reframing of the principle of the incompetence of secular political authority in religious matters, a principle deeply inscribed in the authentic political tradition of the Christian West. From the second half of the 1950s especially, the salient features of the American model—the non-immediacy of the relationship between religion and politics whereby the State is strictly neutral or non-denominational, even if religion, not defined in a confessional way, is recognized as one of the very sources of democratic life—were being configured in Murray’s work as a sort of modern constitutional reversal of one of the fundamental principles of the Western Christian tradition: the institutional separation of powers, the _sacerdotium_ and the _imperium_, which had remained in the dark for centuries, largely as a consequence of the affirmation of royal absolutism and the union of the throne and the altar. Moreover, this evoked the concealment, in the unfolding of history, of a principle long considered constitutive of the life of the Church and now reframed in the apparently problematic aspects of Murray’s other main line of inquiry that had been the cause of censorship. He pointed to the need to adopt a method based on the analysis of historical development, attentive to the distinction between that which is historically conditioned and that which belongs to the fundamental principles of church life. The question concerning the ‘development of doctrine’ was present in Murray’s thought from the very first formulations of his reflections on religious freedom. It basically underlined the problem of defining the concept of tradition and the other crucial issue of the Church’s relationship with history.

[^c16-5]: For the list of locations where Murray’s article was published in French, German, Italian, and Spanish translation during 1964, see the chronology of the production of the American Jesuit in appendix to John Courtney Murray, _Religious Liberty:_ _Catholic Struggles with Pluralism_, ed. J. Leon Hooper (Louisville, KY: Westminster/John Knox Press, 1993), 256.

As for the so-called ‘French school’, whose dissatisfaction with the ‘American’ structure of the scheme that relegated the doctrina ‘sub luce revelationis’ to an ‘appendix’ has been widely emphasized, in reality, it comprised a wide range of positions. There was no lack of voices, such as that of Dominican Marie-Joseph Le Guillou, who found the starting point of the ‘American schema’ excellent regarding the willingness of the Church to listen first of all to the world and its questions. Or that of Jacques Maritain and, above all, of the Jesuit Jean Daniélou, who on several occasions wanted to distance themselves from those who asked to begin from the data of revelation, because this would enable the council to treat the problem of true religion and the duties it entailed, with all the risks that involved. For Daniélou, the true foundation of religious **[p. 276]** freedom, unquestionable and valid for all, was the natural right of the human person to be religious. Moving from radically different perspectives, the Dominican Henri-Marie Féret, consulted by the bishops of eastern France for the preparation of a ‘French schema’ on religious freedom, made clear that he was against the inversion of the order of the different sections of the amended schema: if the rational methodology adopted in the text drafted in the autumn of 1964 was preserved, the scriptural part, in his opinion, ought to be eliminated. In his view, either the council opted for a document that started from faith and revelation—in which case the whole schema would have to be deeply rewritten—or for a ‘mosaic’ of confusing texts that did not draw from the pages of biblical theology. Rather than recalling a series of scriptural passages completely out of context, it would make more sense for a solemn declaration by the conciliar magisterium that might be seen ‘as an act that, at a certain moment in the history of the Church, [^c16-6] intervenes in the unfolding of the providential economy and the progressive explicitation of revelation’.

[^c16-6]: Henri-Marie Féret, _Le Schéma sur la liberté religieuse_, 28 January 1965, 17 typed pages, Murray Archives, Woodstock College Archives, Georgetown University, Washington DC, 18, 1000.

Nonetheless, many more diverse French-speaking voices spoke in favour of a schema that would begin with the data of revelation and emphasize the need for evangelical self-criticism. Among these voices were Pierre Haubtmann, René Laurentin, and Philippe Delhaye. The last underlined the need for Vatican II to say something doctrinally rigorous on the fundamental matter of the rights of a conscience that is erroneous yet acting in good faith. The Benedictine exegete Jacques Dupont gave voice to the different groups who were unhappy with an approach to the right to religious freedom limited to the context of the relations between citizens and the State, and favouring the addition of new passages that would draw up the data of revelation. The free character of the act of faith was obviously not coextensive with religious freedom, as it was commonly understood by contemporaries. Nevertheless, in Dupont’s opinion, it clearly expressed its primary essence. He deemed it essential to begin with revelation to avoid the impression of a schema [^c16-7] dictated by reason of a ‘diplomatic opportunism’. This impression would be difficult to avoid if the declaration were only to acknowledge the universal aspiration to religious freedom, without highlighting at the same time its profound correspondence with the principles of revelation. In this sense, Dupont also gave voice to the widespread unease present in various Protestant circles with the redactors’ choice to establish the right in question from the outset on the basis of arguments drawn from natural law, no doubt valid in themselves, but not adequate to highlight the roots of religious freedom at the very heart of the Gospel message. Among Protestants, one of the most significant voices was that of Pastor Hébert Roux, president of the commission of the French Reformed Church for relations with Catholics. During the final session of the council, Dupont, who was commissioned by the supervisor of the schema, De Smedt, to prepare a draft on the scriptural part of _De libertate_ for the French episcopate, consulted him several times.

[^c16-7]: See Jacques Dupont, _Réflexions sur le schéma De Libertate Religiosa_, 11 February 1965, 2 typed pages, Fonds J. Dupont, UCLouvain, Louvain-la-Neuve, 1521.

### 5. The Activism of the Minority and the Role of Paul VI

**[p. 277]** In the months of the third and final conciliar intersession, the various minority voices did not relent, starting with those of the _Coetus internationalis patrum_. After the postponement of the vote announced in November 1964, the team of redactors was increasingly forced to consider the ‘redaction measures’ in anticipation of the objections that might yet be raised within the assembly and to prepare modifications in advance of the debate.

In these final phases of the editorial work—during which the text would increasingly narrow its focus on the juridical-political sphere of religious freedom—Paul VI’s intention to exercise the role of ‘supervisor’ for the schema when it was still being drafted had a significant effect. Although he always had a favourable attitude towards _De libertate_, which was considered a necessary document for dialogue with contemporary society, the pope repeatedly proved to be sensitive both to the grievances of the hardcore minority and to the more concealed perplexities of an indefinite, but significant, group of fathers for whom the affirmation of a right to religious freedom represented a strong element of concern.

A biblically based introduction drafted by Congar bore the brunt of the pontiff’s concern and of the ‘realism’ of the redactors after the events of the autumn of 1964. In an attempt to situate juridical and civil liberty, which by now had become the main point of the schema, Congar’s prooemium was intended, in essence, to integrate the two different perspectives and methodological options which had divided the redactors of the schema. Aware of the difficulties of an immediate biblical _ressourcement_, Congar had not sought to provide a ‘proof’ to the right to religious freedom. However, starting from the passage from the Old to the New Testament and from the new awareness of contemporary men and women, he tried to highlight how freedom was at the heart of the path of salvation itself. Although brief and succinct, the presentation of the cause of freedom in the history of salvation immediately raised doubts and reservations about its possible post-conciliar use, generating questions and concerns in the same protagonists of the _aggiornamento_. Congar’s draft was thus shelved while the thorny issue, implicit in his proposed text, of the foundation of freedom in the history and life of the Church was left for further consideration in the post-conciliar period.

Another issue dealt with in the schema of the autumn of 1964, though it was dropped in later versions, was that of the relationship between _De libertate_ and the intransigent magisterium of the nineteenth century. The dangerous doctrinal discontinuity of the conciliar text with the documents of the nineteenth-century magisterium became the increasingly recurrent argument of the opponents of the text of the Secretariat in the months of both the third intersession and fourth sessions of Vatican II. Although the group of those who shared the positions of the organized minority of the council was rather small, the insistence with which it **[p. 278]** raised the problem of a certain neglect of the authority of the ecclesiastical magisterium led to some concern within the Secretariat. Opponents of the schema remained active until the end, with an orchestrated series of interventions on the floor, petitions to the pope, and increasingly systematic pressure on wavering bishops with letters, leaflets, and files of proposed amendments.

Until the very last minute, and even after the final approval in the general congregation of 19 November 1965, the text on religious freedom thus continued to face resistance and difficulties, despite the ‘revisions’ inserted in the last hectic weeks of the council at the pope’s express request. In particular, a statement affirming that the right to religious freedom left intact the Catholic doctrine on the one true religion and the one true Church of Christ was placed at the beginning of the schema. The responsibilities and duties of persons in the exercise of freedom, especially with regard to religious truth, were also underlined. Finally, there was a greater insistence on the relationship between moral and legal orders. The ‘traditional’ doctrine, as stated in a note added at the last moment, therefore remained ‘intact’. As it was stressed in even more detail in a passage prepared by Italian theologian Fr Carlo Colombo—a passage that Paul VI wanted in the text of the last accompanying report on the schema—in the teaching of the most recent popes there was doctrinal ‘progress’ that tended to coincide with what was stated in the conciliar text. Even this intervention in the drafting of the presentation of the schema was evidently explained by the pope’s desire to maximize the level of consensus as much as possible, in terms of the vote, and to reassure the minority. Despite the concessions he made to the latter, the voting projections did not appear particularly encouraging.

### 6. Reaching the Final Declaration and the Complex Paths of Its Reception

Although the majority in favour of the declaration remained firm, the voting results of 19 November 1965 confirmed the previous day’s projections: in the overall vote on the whole schema, 249 fathers voted against (_non placet_). Beyond the results of the individual votes, however, a fact became clear that was confirmed in the last public session of 7 December, during which 70 negative votes were recorded, an unusually high number for this type of vote. By the fact that on 7 December, in the last public session, the discontented minority did not hesitate to depart from the standard conciliar practice—whereby in the final vote and in the presence of the pope the opposition goes along with the majority vote—it became clear that in the matter of religious freedom, with evident caution, Vatican II had made a decisive paradigm shift. If the idea of the dignity of the human person, conceived in the image of the Creator and called to become an adopted child of God, belonged to the earliest heritage of Christian doctrine, the social and political interpretation of this dignity evidently had arrived at a decisive turning point. Identifying and ratifying some of the lines of development that were outlined in John XXIII’s encyclical _Pacem in Terris_, the conciliar declaration _Dignitatis_ **[p. 279]** _Humanae_established the inevitability of the link between this same dignity and the rights and freedoms in which the former cannot but become manifest. In other words, there could be no authentic recognition of the dignity of the person if that person was not able to actually exercise the inalienable rights and freedoms that are proper to him or her.

With the affirmation of this link, the traditional view of the ‘rights of truth’ was abandoned. On the other hand, this view was implicit in the magisterium of Pius XII, which, faced with the totalitarianism and upheavals of the Second World War, put a certain emphasis on human rights, on the basis of a new relationship between civil and ecclesiastical rights. Instead, what Vatican II asserted was the personal character of the right to civil liberty in religious matters, while acknowledging the role of the State as guarantor, albeit in negative terms, of the conditions that allow a peaceful coexistence among human beings. Recognizing the individual subject as the holder of the right to religious freedom in the concreteness of his or her being—prior to the efforts made to seek the truth—Vatican II reversed the previous subordination of the recognition of this right to the permanence, or not, of ethical and religious truths. Moreover, it made clear, in very different terms from those of the nineteenth-century magisterium, the distinction, in content and purpose, between the order of law and the order of moral duty while also attaining a profound shift from the heteronomy of conscience to the truth of the dignity of the person. For this reason, despite being aware of the ambiguity of certain passages and the heterogeneity of certain statements in the declaration, the acceptance by the Church of the principle that all religions have the same right to public expression in a democracy was seen as an epochal turning point for the Catholic Church.

The significant differences in backgrounds—cultural, theological, and socio-political—of the council fathers, and therefore the multiplicity of approaches to the new and controversial theme of religious freedom, would be reflected in the subsequent phases of the post-conciliar period. Moreover, the different perspectives from which the different episcopates (from Central Europe to North America, and from the African-Asian Christian minority to the Iberian one) followed the complex events of _De libertate_ at Vatican II inevitably had an impact on the many paths of its reception. In this sense, it is not necessary to underline how Karol Wojtyła’s ascent to the chair of St Peter, and then his long pontificate, gave an entirely distinctive orientation and a ‘universal’ importance to the perspective with which the archbishop of Krakow first followed the conciliar debate on _De libertate_, later renamed _Dignitatis Humanae_.

As a member of the episcopate who was interested, for obvious reasons, in a conciliar declaration on religious freedom and who intervened on several occasions in support of the schema of the Secretariat, Wojtyła showed his support of _De libertate_ through several comments and frequent petitions during the council. First, he called for a greater emphasis on the fact that only truth makes women and men free and that only responsibility, understood as awareness of duty by a properly formed conscience, effectively qualifles freedom. He also emphasized the necessary correlation between the moral and legal orders. This last point—raised together with the identification of the limitative criterion of religious freedom in a ‘public order’ whose protection was entrusted to civil authorities—was the object of a difficult and tight debate **[p. 280]** until the final days of the council even within the majority in favour of the declaration. The stakes were high: it was a matter of assuming as universally valid for the Church notions and formulations—and basically the same idea of the State as guarantor of religious freedom and ‘arbitrator’ of any form of intolerance—which for the most part took into account primarily the culture and political-constitutional experience of the West. On the final day of the conciliar debate on religious freedom, speaking on behalf of over seventy Polish council fathers, the archbishop of Krakow thus underlined in particular how the right to religious freedom—as a natural right, founded, that is, _in lege naturae ergo divina_—finds its regulating norm [^c16-8] only in moral law.

[^c16-8]: _AS_, IV/2, 11–13.

These petitions and proposals for amendments were accepted to some extent in the definitive version of the schema, albeit while retaining the basic structure of the declaration. In addition, the new concept of ‘public order’ and the significant rejection of the traditional notion of the common good gave the schema one of its most characteristic elements. On the other hand, these points of emphasis would later acquire new relevance and resonance during John Paul II’s long pontificate. This can be seen, for example, in his frequent references to the unavoidable link between freedom and truth; in the objective dimension of the latter, as well as in the certainty of its ‘attainability’; moreover, in his insistent emphasis that ‘conscience [^c16-9] has rights because it has duties’ and that, therefore, in the human conscience there is always deeply inscribed ‘a principle of obedience vis-à-vis the objective norm’ which transcends, justifles, and supports conscience itself (_Dominum et vivificantem_ 43 and _Veritatis Splendor_ 60). There will be those who will read here a reasonable inversion of a conciliar magisterium that had underestimated the risks of an alliance between democracy and ethical relativism. For some, this may even be the only reason for a full reinstatement of _Dignitatis Humanae_ to the authentic magisterial tradition. However, there will also be those who see instead a disavowal of the instances of freedom that emerged from Vatican II. John Paul II’s repeated proposition of the universal exemplarity of an experience based on a supreme ethical-religious _ratio_ to protect the freedom and dignity of the human person, combined with the tendency to resolve a certain number of problems in an authoritarian manner, also generated a certain diffidence towards his commitment to the defence of human rights—in particular, the right to religious freedom. A constant commitment, no doubt, starting with the well-known message of 1980 to the heads of State who were signatories of the Final Act of Helsinki, which represented an undeniable basis of credibility for the positions taken by the Holy See within the international community.

[^c16-9]: See esp. _Veritatis Splendor_ 34. The statement is borrowed from John Henry Newman’s well-known letter to the Duke of Norfolk: _A Letter Addressed to His Grace the Duke of Norfolk: Certain Difficulties Felt by Anglicans in Catholic Teaching_ (London: Longman, Green and Co., 1868–81), 2:250.

Was this an unquestionable reversal of the _metanoia_ of the Church inaugurated by Vatican II, or ‘presumption’ to avoid the risks of a democracy without values, thus guaranteeing an ethical foundation for the civil, national, and international communities through the recovery of the inseparable link between **[p. 281]** freedom and truth? As many have stressed, Wojtyła’s magisterium in this regard appears ambivalent. The same might be said of the line between a dialogically offered contribution to a reflection on the ethical coordinates of civil coexistence and the contrasting claim of imposing concrete legal solutions in the name of a supreme ethical-religious _ratio_. It is the same ambivalence that we find in the most comprehensive Vatican-approved document on religious liberty since Vatican II, the document of the International Theological Commission of 26 April 2019: ‘Religious Freedom for the Good of All: Theological Approach to Contemporary Challenges’. The document is built on the fundamental theological impulses of _Dignitatis Humanae_: the need to update the previous posture of papal teaching (especially that of Pius IX) against religious liberty for all; and the teaching and life of Jesus as the primary theological source for the magisterium of the Church on religious liberty. The document walked in the footsteps of Vatican II in ‘the refusal of the attempt to make of political power an instrument for proselytism’ (8), offering a critique of the claim of neutrality by liberal modernity but at the same time warning against the regression towards confessionalism or theocracy.
