## 17. Ecumenism: A Principal Concern of the Second Vatican

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 282]** ‘The restoration of unity among all Christians is one of the principal concerns of the Second Vatican Council’. So begins the council’s Decree on Ecumenism, _Unitatis Redintegratio_ (_UR_ 1). This chapter explores the ways that this overarching concern for Christian unity shaped the event of the council and the orientations of its teaching. The twentieth-century ecumenical movement, which had emerged independently of the Catholic Church’s participation, provoked a deeper self-reflection on the Catholic share of responsibility for the continuing separation of the churches and invited a clarification of the doctrinal basis for Catholic ecumenical engagement. We will consider the ecumenical intention of the council, developments in Catholic ecclesiology that undergird Catholic ecumenical commitment, the practice of dialogue in the search for unity, consequences of shared faith for the pastoral practice of common prayer and sacramental life, and a number of post-conciliar developments. This presentation is by no means exhaustive. It aims to introduce the reader to the salient features of Catholic ecumenism and their roots in the event and teachings of Vatican II.

### 2. The Ecumenical Intention of the Second Vatican Council

Pope John XXIII chose to announce the coming council during a celebration of the Week of Prayer for **[p. 283]** Christian Unity in the papal Basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls on 25 January 1959 to underline the ecumenical intention of Vatican II. An ‘ecumenical’ council is one of concern to the whole of Christianity. Representatives of the Eastern Orthodox churches had been invited to previous councils even after the Great Schism of 1054, though participation hinged on the acceptance of papal authority and the form it had taken in an age of division—a precondition to which they could not, in conscience, agree. Similarly, Protestant representatives had been invited to the sessions of the Council of Trent, but years of violence and tension had undermined any confidence that they might receive a fair hearing or be granted safe passage to the meeting.

John XXIII, building on the acknowledgement of his predecessor, Pius XII, that the ecumenical movement that had formed through the first half of the twentieth century was truly inspired by the Holy Spirit, saw this fresh desire for Christian unity as a ‘sign of the times’ that required fresh thinking and a generous response on the part of the Catholic Church. Pope John XXIII called for an _aggiornamento_, an updating, that would require not only that Catholicism contend in a more constructive way with modernity but also that it seriously consider the concerns of other Christians, especially their aspiration for ecclesial unity. The renewal and reform of the Catholic Church could not be dissociated from the quest to restore full, visible ecclesial communion.

#### The Context of the Ecumenical Movement

The opening paragraphs of the Decree on Ecumenism acknowledge the Second Vatican Council’s debt to the wider ecumenical movement, a fruit of divine grace at work in the corporate life of many non-Catholic communities:

In recent times, God has begun to bestow more generously upon divided Christians remorse over their divisions and longing for unity. Everywhere, large numbers have felt the impulse of this grace, and among the members of the separated Christian communities also there increases from day to day a movement, fostered by the grace of the Holy Spirit, for the restoration of unity among all Christians. (_UR_ 1)

The modern ecumenical movement is commonly dated from the first World Missionary Conference in Edinburgh, which in 1910 brought together representatives from Protestant and Anglican missionary societies to reflect on the need for greater collaboration in the work of spreading the Gospel to the ends of the earth. A number of leading figures at this meeting were acutely aware that the rivalry of the churches for new converts to the Christian faith and the deep divisions among the churches gave a counter-witness to the world, contradicting Christ’s message of reconciling love. While no Catholic took part in the conference, a sympathetic letter was sent by Archbishop Geremia Bonomelli of Cremona, Italy, to an American **[p. 284]** Episcopalian, Silas McBee. Bonomelli hailed the many common elements shared by the various Christian [^c17-1] denominations and their aspiration to unity in faith and practice.

[^c17-1]: Joan Delaney, ‘From Cremona to Edinburgh: Bishop Bonomelli and the World Missionary Conference of 1910’, _Ecumenical_ _Review_ 52 (2000): 418–31.

Any triumphalism that may have tainted the missionary project of Edinburgh was soon chastened by the outbreak of World War I. How was it possible, many wondered, for the Christian peoples of Europe to engage in such wanton destruction? The impulse of Edinburgh gave rise to new efforts of ecumenical collaboration in response to the needs of refugees and the poor in the wake of the war through the establishment of Life and Work in 1925. And in 1927, the Anglican bishop Charles Brent convened a first international meeting on Faith and Order to address the doctrinal causes of ecclesial division. These two movements came together to form a new World Council of Churches (WCC) in 1948, headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. In 1961 the International Missionary Council, founded at Edinburgh in 1910, was formally incorporated into the structure of the WCC. Those churches belonging to this movement sought unity in faith, church order, and witness to better serve the mission of Christ in the world.

#### Early Catholic Responses to the Ecumenical Movement

Catholics looked upon these developments with a mix of suspicion and sympathy. In response to an invitation to send a Catholic delegation to the 1927 meeting of Faith and Order, Pope Pius XI wrote the letter _Mortalium Animos._ While affirming the importance of ecclesial unity, his judgement of this effort was unequivocal: ‘the union of Christians can only be promoted by promoting the return to the one true Church of Christ of those who are separated from it, for in the past they have unhappily left it’. Deeply influenced by the teaching of Cyprian of Carthage, Pius XI’s encyclical narrowly identifled the Church of Rome with the one Church of Christ and took no account of ecclesial realities beyond the bounds of the Roman Catholic Church. While the search for Christian unity was laudable, he considered this new ecumenical movement as tragically mistaken in its approach.

A programme of ‘return’ to Rome was advanced by the Octave of Prayer for Unity proposed by Paul Wattson, founder of the Franciscan Friars of the Atonement of Graymoor, New York. Originally a ‘High Church’ Anglican, Wattson himself adopted this path to unity when he and his Franciscan community of Episcopalian Friars and sisters entered into communion with Rome en masse in 1908. During the annual observance of the Octave, Catholics were to pray for the ‘conversion’ of other Christians to Rome. In the first quarter of the twentieth century, a number of religious orders, including the Jesuits and the Assumptionists, adopted the ‘unionist’ project of urging other Christians along the path of return.

**[p. 285]** A number of Catholics had misgivings about this approach, given their positive interactions with other Christian communities. In 1935, Paul Couturier, a French priest in Lyons, France, recast the unity Octave as a ‘universal’ Week of Prayer, where Christians of every confession might intercede for the unity that Christ desires and according to the means that Christ wills. In so doing, he fostered a shift from a Roman-centred model of unity to one that is Christ-centred. Couturier favoured a spirituality characterized by ecclesial humility and repentance, cognizant that Christians on all sides bore responsibility for the sin of division. In the place of conversion or return to Rome, he envisioned the way to reconciliation—much like the Early Church Fathers—as one of conversion and return to Christ. Vatican II would opt for Couturier’s approach in the Decree on Ecumenism, which states, ‘There can be no ecumenism worthy of the name without interior conversion.’ It envisions this ‘spiritual ecumenism’ as ‘the soul of the whole ecumenical movement’ (_UR_ 7– 8).

In the same period that Couturier was looking to foster a humble spiritual practice to support Catholic ecumenical commitment, a young French Dominican, Yves Congar, turned to the theological tradition for resources to reframe the Catholic appraisal of other Christian communions. His reflections were developed in his first major work, _Chrétiens désunis_ (_Divided Christendom_), published in 1937. In contrast to Pope Pius XI, Congar recalled, previous popes and councils had rather consistently considered the Eastern Orthodox communities as churches in the full theological sense of the word after the Great Schism of 1054. Further, he contended, it was inappropriate to apply the term ‘heretics’ to members of the communities rooted in the sixteenth-century Protestant Reformation; those born 400 years after the fracturing of communion could not be said to bear a direct moral responsibility for the division of the Western Church. What is more, he argued, given that they share many common elements of ecclesial life with the Catholic Church and manifest a growing desire for ecclesial unity, the corporate life of these groups must be recognized as effective vehicles of God’s grace. Where Calvin had spoken of ‘vestiges’ and Luther recognized ‘embers’ of Christ’s Church remaining in the Church of Rome, Congar sought a more affirmative language to describe Protestant communities. He considered the elements of their corporate life derived from a shared patrimony as positive gifts and endowments from the Holy Spirit.

By the time the WCC was founded in 1948, sustained contacts had been established between Catholics and Protestants on the European continent—at times prodded by the need for collaboration throughout the period of World War II. By 1950, the Holy Office authorized the participation of Catholics in official ecumenical meetings. Congar’s effort to find a more positive appraisal of the separated churches found a sympathetic hearing in the wider ecumenical movement. When the central committee of the WCC set out a ‘Basis’ or criteria for membership, it stipulated that member churches must recognize at a minimum ‘vestiges’ or ‘elements’ of Christ’s Church in other Christian communities (Toronto Statement, 1950).

In the Netherlands, a young professor of philosophy, Johannes Willebrands, established the Catholic Conference on Ecumenical Questions in 1952 to foster deeper reflection among Catholic theologians on **[p. 286]** matters of ecumenical concern. The notion of ‘vestiges’ or ‘elements’ of the Church was explored extensively in this context as Catholic theologians wrestled with Pius XI’s, and later Pius XII’s, narrow identification of the Church of Christ with the Roman Church (_Mystici Corporis_, 1943) against the horizon of a broader tradition that acknowledged a wider and more diverse ecclesial reality. Among the participants in this series of nine gatherings from 1952 to 1963 were many who would serve as expert advisers to the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity during the Second Vatican Council, including Franz Thijssen, Gustav Thils, Johannes Feiner, Christophe Dumont, Emmanuel Lanne, Charles Boyer, Eduard Stakemeier, and Jerome Hamer.

### 3. The Ecumenical Agenda and Conciliar Debate

#### The Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity

To attend to the ecumenical dimension of the council’s work, John XXIII established a new office within the Roman Curia in 1960: a Secretariat for the Promotion of Christian Unity. Its president, Cardinal Augustin Bea, was a widely respected biblical scholar and former rector of the Pontifical Biblical Institute. When Bea needed a secretary and trusted adviser to carry out the many diplomatic tasks of this new office, he turned naturally to Willebrands, who by now was familiar with the network of Catholic ecumenical scholars and in regular contact with Protestant and Orthodox ecumenical leaders.

One of the major tasks of the new secretariat would be to facilitate the participation of official ecumenical observers from other Christian communions in the council proceedings. In addition, it was to advise the conciliar commissions concerning matters of ecumenical concern. While the observers did not have an official voice or vote in the conciliar debate, they regularly attended the general congregations and met weekly with bishops and theologians to discuss and share their reactions to the draft documents under consideration. Among the more notable ecumenical observers and guests were the Swiss Reformed and Orthodox theologians Lukas Vischer and Nikos Nissiotis, representing the WCC; André Scrima, representing the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople; Vitaly Borovoy for the Russian Orthodox Church; John R. Moorman for the Anglican Communion; Oscar Cullmann and George Lindbeck for the Lutheran World Federation; Hébert Roux of the World Alliance of Reformed Churches; Albert Outler for the World Methodist Council; David Du Plessis of the World Pentecostal Conference; Alexander Schmemann of St Vladimir’s Orthodox Seminary, New York; and Brothers Roger Schutz and Max Thurian of the Taizé Community. By the fourth and final session of the council in 1965, ninety observers and sixteen ecumenical guests were in attendance.

**[p. 287]** Members of the secretariat met for six plenary sessions during the preparatory phase of the council. During this period, fifteen subcommissions worked on a host of topics including membership in the Church, the nature of the Church and the hierarchy, the priesthood of the baptized faithful, religious freedom, the word of God (including the relationship of Scripture and tradition), liturgical questions, ‘mixed’ marriage, prayer for Christian unity, theological conceptions of ecumenism, and relations with the Jewish people. In October 1962, Pope John expanded the mandate of the Secretariat, granting it the authority to act as a conciliar commission and to participate directly in the drafting of council documents. By the time the council concluded, it had contributed directly to the elaboration of four key conciliar texts: the Decree on Ecumenism (_Unitatis Redintegratio_), the Declaration on Religious Liberty (_Dignitatis Humanae_), the Declaration on Non-Christian Religions (_Nostra Aetate_), and the Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation (_Dei Verbum_). The Secretariat for the Promotion of Christian Unity became a permanent office within the Roman Curia to oversee the implementation of the council’s principles of ecumenism and to maintain relations with churches and ecclesial communities not in full communion with the Catholic Church. It was reduced to the status of a pontifical council while continuing to carry out the same tasks when Pope John Paul II introduced a revised set of statutes for the curial offices in 1988, in the Apostolic Constitution _Pastor Bonus._ With Pope Francis’s curial reform in 2022, it has come to be known simply as the Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity.

#### The Elaboration of the Decree on Ecumenism

During the preparatory period, the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity prepared four separate schemas for the council fathers to consider: _De libertate religiosa_ (On Religious Liberty), _Necessitas orationis pro unitate christianorum maxime temporibus nostris_ (On the Great Need of Prayer for Christian Unity in Our Time), _De oecumenismo catholico_ (On Catholic Ecumenism), and _De Verbo Dei_ (On the Word of God). To these was attached an appendix on the Jewish question, elaborated in response to a task entrusted to Cardinal Bea [^c17-2] by John XXIII: _De Judaeis_ (On the Jews). Because the status of the new secretariat was disputed by Cardinal Ottaviani, secretary for the Congregation of the Holy Office and president of the Preparatory Theological Commission, and by Cardinal Amleto Cicognani, the Secretary of State, who simultaneously served as president of the Commission for the Oriental Churches and the council’s Secretariat for Extraordinary Affairs—none of these documents reached the bishops or was put on the council agenda prior to the first session. In all, three schemas treating the question of relations with other Christian communities had been prepared in advance of the first session: _De ecclesiae unitate_, a schema produced by the Commission for the **[p. 288]** Oriental Churches; chapter 11 of the schema _De ecclesia_, submitted by the Preparatory Theological Commission; and _De oecumenismo catholica,_ drafted by the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity.

[^c17-2]: _AD_ III/2, 431–58.

The first of these was debated during the first session of the council, from 26 to 30 December 1962. It dealt with the diverse Eastern Catholic churches and relations with the Eastern Orthodox, yet took no account of the Reformation communities. Many bishops were disappointed by its approach to interchurch relations, one that reflected more of a ‘unionist’ agenda than the growing theological consensus concerning the providential character of the emerging ecumenical movement. Sending this document, together with the schema _De ecclesia_ that was debated from 1 to 7 December, back to the drawing board, Pope John issued a directive (_Mirabilis Ille_, 1963) requiring that a new mixed commission be established to combine the materials in these three drafts into a single new schema on ecumenism. The Dutch Jesuit Jan Witte, principal drafter of chapter 11 of _De ecclesia_ for the Doctrinal Commission, worked with the experts of the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity, led by the Belgian Gustav Thils, to propose a new schema that was debated during the second session between 18 November and 2 December 1963. All efforts at collaboration with the Commission for the Oriental Churches were consistently obstructed.

The schema tabled during the second session of the council by the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity included three chapters on ecumenism. In a move not unlike a sort of ‘omnibus’ bill, the draft that was tabled included two additional chapters on the questions of religious liberty and on the Jews. The latter chapters would form the basis for the council’s Declaration on Religious Liberty (_Dignitatis Humanae_)—a question of no little importance for ecumenical or interchurch relations—and the Declaration on the Relation of the Church to Non-Christian Religions (_Nostra Aetate_). When the original schema on revelation was rejected by a large majority of council fathers during a vote on 20 November 1962, Pope John established a joint commission with experts from both the Doctrinal Commission and the Secretariat to draft a new text that would take sufficient account of ecumenical discussion concerning Scripture and tradition. This new joint commission, co-chaired by Cardinals Bea and Ottaviani, produced the Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation (_Dei Verbum_).

The ultimate draft of the Decree on Ecumenism was debated and voted upon _in aula_ in the third session, on 5–8 October, 10–11 and 14 November, and was finally approved on 21 November 1964 together with the Dogmatic Constitution on the Church (_Lumen Gentium_) and the Decree on the Catholic Eastern Churches (_Orientalium Ecclesiarum_ (_OE_)). The final days of the decree’s passage were overshadowed by the unprecedented intervention of Pope Paul VI when, after the council fathers had finished voting chapter by chapter to approve the final text, he submitted a proposal for some forty amendments aimed at placating the conciliar minority. Willebrands hastily gathered three consultors (Gustav Thils, Emmanuel Lanne, and Pierre Duprey) for an urgent meeting to consider the pope’s proposed amendments one by one. On 19 November, the secretariat presented a final version of the decree with nineteen minor revisions which did not alter the substantial meaning of the previously approved text. In the eyes of the ecumenical observers **[p. 289]** and many council fathers, these events reflected a heavy-handed and arbitrary exercise of papal authority. Many commentators refer to this episode and the related events as the ‘black week’ of the council. The document was finally approved by a decisive vote of 2,054 in favour and 64 against on 21 November 1964.

### 4. From an Ecclesiology of Return to Ecclesial Recognition

#### ‘Truly Christian Endowments from Our Common Heritage’

All three of the draft texts relating to Catholic ecumenical commitment from the preparatory period included language aimed at affirming a measure of shared faith with other Christian communities. When referring to the Eastern and Oriental Orthodox churches not in communion with the Church of Rome, the document of the Preparatory Commission for the Eastern Churches, _De Unitate_, spoke of the ‘dissident Christians’ belonging to the ‘venerable Eastern Churches’ as being united to the one flock of Christ by the ‘spiritual bonds’ of a ‘common patrimony’. Still, it maintained that while they were not ‘strangers to the church’, they were nonetheless ‘deprived of many means of salvation’ due to their separation. The council fathers were highly critical of this schema, in particular of its insistence that these churches, whose origins were quite independent of Rome, must ‘return’ to the communion of the Latin Church.[^c17-3]

[^c17-3]: _AS_ I/3, 528–45; see esp. the speeches of the Melchite bishops: _AS_ I/3, 616–20 (Metropolitan Maximos IV Saigh); _AS_ I/3, 638– 40 (Edelby); _AS_ I/3, 640–43 (Zoghby).

Chapter 11 of the schema _De Ecclesia_, presented by the Preparatory Theological Commission, _De Oecumenismo_, acknowledged ‘with joy’ that all Christians are joined together through the sacrament of baptism, the grace of which ‘impels’ them to unity and communion with the Roman pontiff. It recognized the presence of ‘elements of the church’ and ‘authentic spiritual goods’ in other Christian communities, including Holy Scripture and the sacraments, that served as ‘means and efficacious signs’ of union with Christ and contribute to the catholicity of the Church. While acknowledging ‘a kind of communion’— however ‘illicit and imperfect’—with the separated Eastern churches, it insisted that these spiritual goods existed ‘in a twisted form’. The halting recognition of this chapter contradicted affirmations contained in chapter 2 of the same schema, which repeated the ill-fated claim of Pope Pius XII’s encyclical _Mystici Corporis_ (_MC_) that the ‘true church of Jesus Christ’ is ‘the One, Holy, Catholic, Apostolic and _Roman_ Church’ (_MC_ 13, 91). Within the Doctrinal Commission, a conservative minority sought to defend an exclusivist identification of the Church of Rome and the Church of Christ, maintaining that the separated Christian communities could not be considered anything more than sociological gatherings and their corporate life of prayer of no consequence for the life of grace and salvation. The theological consensus of the majority, **[p. 290]** however, drawing from the facts of history and a wider theological tradition, sought to return to an ecclesiology of diverse churches in communion reflected in the Scriptures and the tradition of the first millennium.

Already in the early days of October 1962, Cardinal Suenens, seeing the inadequacies of the schema _De Ecclesia_, called upon Gérard Philips—_peritus_, later named the secretary of the Theological Commission—to begin drafting an alternate schema with the collaboration of other _periti_ from the Doctrinal Commission. In February 1963, this schema was chosen from among several others as the basis for a new draft of what would become the Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, _Lumen Gentium._ In a fateful move, Philips juxtaposed material from the contradictory affirmations of chapters 2 and 11 of the original schema, _De Ecclesia_. In the version presented to the council fathers during the second session in the autumn of 1963, the schema read that the one, holy, catholic, and apostolic church of the creed ‘is [_est_] the catholic church … although outside its full structure many elements of sanctification can be found, which, as elements proper to the church of Christ, impel toward unity’.[^c17-4]

[^c17-4]: _AS_ II/1, 219–20. For a detailed historiography of these few lines and the context of their contested interpretation, see Karim Schelkens, ‘_Lumen Gentium_’s “_subsistit in_” Revisited: The Catholic Church and Christian Unity after Vatican II’, _Theological Studies_ 69 (2008): 875–93.

Many bishops complained that this formula failed to express sufficiently the bond of communion established by baptism and nourished by many other means of salvation which are acknowledged as present and effective beyond the institutional structure of the Catholic Church. Taking these requests into account, the Doctrinal Commission revised the text to affirm that while the Church of Christ subsists in (_subsistit in_) —continues to exist or is found in—the Catholic Church, it is also present and active in other Christian ‘churches and ecclesial communities’ (_LG_ 8). Indeed, the council opted for an ecclesiology of communion, recognizing that both individuals and whole communities participate in the reality of Christ’s Church according to differing degrees—a reality established by their sharing in the life of grace, the fruit of God’s reconciling love. _Lumen Gentium_ affirms that ‘those who, possessing the Spirit of Christ, accept the entire structure and all the means to salvation established within it and who in its visible structure are united with Christ’ are ‘fully incorporated’ into the Church (_LG_ 14). Still, it is ‘joined to the baptized who are honoured by the name of Christian’ and who belong to ‘churches and ecclesial communities’ having their own sacramental life, episcopate, life of prayer and witness, and devotion to Mary (_LG_ 15). Finally, it considers that even non-Christians, including Jews, Muslims, and members of other religious traditions, are ‘related to the people of God in various ways’ (_LG_ 16).

The Decree on Ecumenism, _Unitatis Redintegratio_, develops in greater detail this theology of differentiated ecclesial recognition and draws from it a number of pastoral consequences, distinguishing especially between the separated churches of the East and the separated churches and ecclesial communities of the **[p. 291]** West. To underline the unbroken bond that joins the other Christian communions to Christ and his Church despite the wounds of schism and division, this decree speaks of other Christians as estranged brothers and sisters—a fact that is most often lost in translation. The Latin text opted to use _fratres sejuncti_ rather than _fratres separati_ (separated brethren—the common English rendering). The sacrament of baptism, celebrations of word and sacrament, devotion to the Mother of God, witness, and martyrdom pertain not only to individuals or aggregates of believers, but also to entire Christian communions.

#### The Special Position of the Eastern Churches

The council applies the term ‘church’ to Eastern Orthodox communities in accordance with a long-established tradition and in deference to their episcopal structuring. Expressing esteem for the diverse traditions of the Orthodox, the Decree on Ecumenism ‘gladly’ recalls that ‘in the east there flourish many particular churches’ among whom ‘the patriarchal churches hold first place’ and affirms the ‘communion of faith and charity’ that binds them to the Catholic Church ‘as between sisters’ (_UR_ 14). It acknowledges the many expressions of common faith reflected in the Trinitarian confession of faith and the dogmas of the early ecumenical councils, and in the rich and diverse liturgical, spiritual, and monastic traditions, and canonical disciplines of the Eastern churches, whose legitimate diversity is to be encouraged and preserved (_UR_ 15–16). Moreover, the decree acknowledges that the Catholic Church might be enriched by the methods and insights of their diverse theological traditions, observing: ‘sometimes one tradition has come nearer to a full appreciation of some aspects of a mystery of revelation than the other, or has expressed them better’. Eschewing an approach that would confuse unity with uniformity, even in the use of theological language, it contends, ‘In such cases, these various theological formulations are often to be considered complementary rather than conflicting’ (_UR_ 17). The model of communion among the diverse particular churches that obtained in the first millennium is commended as a model for the restoration of unity (_UR_ 14).

#### The Separated Churches and Communities of the West

The separated Christian communities of the West originate from a variety of historical contexts, including the sixteenth-century Protestant Reformation, which gave birth to the Lutheran and Reformed churches, and the conflict between Henry VIII and the papacy, which resulted in the separation of the Church of England from Rome; the seventeenth-century revivals that fostered the Religious Society of Friends and Baptist communities; the Pietism of the eighteenth century that spawned Methodism and Evangelical communities; the rejection of the First Vatican Council in the nineteenth century, which led to the Old Catholic schism; and the twentieth-century charismatic renewal that set in motion a worldwide Pentecostal movement. The drafters of the Decree on Ecumenism faced the impossible task of establishing a set of **[p. 292]** constructive principles for engagement in dialogue and common witness with the multifaceted and much-fractured reality of Western Christianity.

To acknowledge this complexity, the Decree on Ecumenism speaks of ‘churches and ecclesial communities separated from the Apostolic See of Rome during the grave crisis that began in the West at the end of the middle ages or in later times’ (_UR_ 19). The ‘churches’ in question here include the Old Catholic Church, which broke communion with the Catholic Church while retaining valid sacraments and orders of the Catholic tradition when it failed to receive the teachings of the First Vatican Council. The decree also takes pains to recognize the ‘special place’ of the Anglican Communion ‘in which catholic traditions and institutions in part continue to exist [_subsistere_]’ (_UR_ 13).

To affirm the corporate ecclesial reality of those Christian communities born from the fragmentation of the Western Church from the sixteenth-century Reformation onwards, the council coined the term ‘ecclesial communities’ (_LG_ 8, 15; _UR_ 19, 22). It is meant to be broad and inclusive, taking into account the fact that some of these communities (such as the Society of Friends and the Salvation Army) do not consider themselves to be churches. This language does not claim to be an exhaustive or all-encompassing description of Western Christian communities. It aims, rather, to affirm their churchly character and the real if imperfect communion that exists between them and the Catholic Church as a result of their participation in the one Church of Christ. The explication accompanying the revised draft of the decree in September 1964 highlights the connection between their corporate ecclesial life and the constitutive elements of the one Church:

It must not be overlooked that the communities that have their origin in the separation that took place in the West are not merely a sum or collection of individual Christians, but they are constituted by social ecclesiastical elements which they have preserved from our common patrimony, and which confer on them a truly ecclesial character. In these communities the one sole Church of Christ is present, albeit imperfectly, in a way that is somewhat like its presence in particular churches, and by means of their ecclesiastical elements the Church of Christ is in some way operative in them.[^c17-5]

[^c17-5]: _AS_ III/2, 335. This same page contains the examples of the Old Catholic Church and those communities who themselves reject being called churches.

The decree points to the constitutive nature of these elements when it affirms: ‘some, even very many, of the most significant elements and endowments which go together to build up and give life to the church itself, can exist outside the visible boundaries of the Catholic Church’. The centre of unity here is not the Catholic Church, but Christ himself; since these elements ‘come from Christ and lead back to Christ, [they] belong by right to the one Church of Christ’ (_UR_ 3).

Thirty years after the close of Vatican II, Pope John Paul II would echo this fundamental insight of the **[p. 293]** council’s teaching in his 1995 encyclical letter On Catholic Commitment to Ecumenism, _Ut Unum Sint_ (_UUS_)—which moves from the recognition of the effective mediation of faith, word, sacrament, and witness in and through the corporate life of other Christian communities to the recognition of their ecclesiality:

Indeed, the elements of sanctification and truth present in the other Christian Communities, in a degree which varies from one to the other, constitute the objective basis of the communion, albeit imperfect, which exists between them and the Catholic Church. To the extent that these elements are found in other Christian Communities, the one Church of Christ is effectively present in them. (_UUS_ 11)

When bishops of the conservative minority objected to the use of the expression ‘churches and ecclesial communities’ in the decree—language already accepted by the vote of the council fathers on _Lumen Gentium_ —the drafters replied in early November 1964 that the custom of the Catholic tradition is to refer to the separated communities of the East as churches and, further, that ‘it is not the business of the council to [^c17-6] decide which of the other communities ought to be called churches in the theological sense’. This last comment would seem to suggest that, in the absence of a consensus (many bishops argued for the application of the term ‘church’ to Protestant communities), it seemed best to leave the question open, or that it might be answered more appropriately in dialogue with the various communities in question.

[^c17-6]: _AS_ III/7, 35.

#### Foundations for Dialogue and the Practice of Ecumenism

The purpose of the council’s teaching on ecumenism was to provide a doctrinal and pastoral foundation for the engagement of all Catholics, ‘the whole church, faithful and clergy alike’ (_UR_ 5), in the work of reconciliation with other Christians. By acknowledging both the communion of faith that already exists and areas of continuing disagreement, it aimed to create the conditions for genuine dialogue. The decree noted the necessity for dialogue on ‘the Lord’s supper, the other sacraments, worship, and ministry in the church’ (_UR_ 22). Pope Paul VI, elected in June 1963 following the death of John XXIII, eloquently called the Church to adopt a culture of dialogical engagement in the first encyclical letter of his pontificate, _Ecclesiam Suam_, issued in August 1964, between the second and third sessions of the council.

Religious Freedom, Conscience, and the Avoidance of Proselytism

Pope Paul VI’s teaching on the importance of dialogue surely influenced the drafting of the Declaration on Religious Liberty, _Dignitatis Humanae_, a text prepared by consultors of the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity. Indeed, on the eve of the council, the general secretary of the WCC, W. Visser ’t Hooft, had conveyed his hope to Willebrands that the council might clarify the Catholic position on this question, since **[p. 294]** many Protestant Christians in so-called Catholic countries, in particular in Spain and Latin America, were deprived of the requisite freedom to exercise their faith in accordance with their convictions. In the absence of an embrace of the right to religious freedom, many Christians might justiflably suspect that the Catholic approach to ecumenism remained little more than a strategic ploy to advance a proselytizing agenda, an exercise of subtle coercion aimed at a ‘return’ to Rome. _Dignitatis Humanae_ (_DH_) provides an important clue to understanding the dialogue’s purpose. It presents dialogue as the search for a shared understanding of the truth instead of an effort to convert the other to one’s point of view. In this process, ‘people share with each other the truth they have discovered, or think they have discovered, in such a way as they help one another in the search for truth’ (_DH_ 3). A fundamental respect for the freedom of conscience and the religious adherence of other Christians grounds every effort of ecumenical dialogue.

A Careful and Honest Appraisal of the Catholic Household

The Decree on Ecumenism lays out the attitudes that guide Catholic experts called upon to engage in dialogue concerning doctrinal and pastoral differences. First among these is a commitment to understand the other as they understand themselves, which entails ‘every effort to avoid expressions, judgments and actions which are not true and fair’ in their representation or characterization of others’ beliefs and practices (_UR_ 4). Official dialogues, which often entail detailed studies of the Scriptures or of historical conflict, are carried on ‘in a religious spirit’ and accompanied by moments of common prayer and fellowship. While seeking a fuller appreciation of the view of ecumenical partners, Catholics aim to present their own tradition in all honesty and humility. In this process, they ‘are led to examine their own faithfulness to Christ’s will for the church, and wherever necessary, undertake with vigour the task of renewal and reform’ (_UR_ 4). These reforms extend even to the language of Catholic teaching which may stand in need of clarification or completion, especially if it has been elaborated in a context of polarizing debate: ‘Consequently, if, in various times and circumstances, there have been deficiencies … even in the way that church teaching has been formulated—to be carefully distinguished from the deposit of faith itself —these should be set right in the opportune moment and in the proper way’ (_UR_ 6). The ‘manner and order’ in which Catholic doctrine is expressed must be clear, the decree insists, and ‘should in no way become an obstacle to dialogue’ (_UR_ 11).

The Hierarchy of Truths

Those engaged in theological dialogue are to keep in mind what _Unitatis Redintegratio_ calls the ‘hierarchy of truths’, that is to say, an ordering in the truths of faith which ‘vary in their relation to the foundation of the Christian faith’ (_UR_ 11). Stated simply, this hermeneutical principle recognizes that while all Christian doctrines are related, they are not all of equal weight or importance. In a historic intervention during the debate of the second session, Archbishop Pangrazio of Gorizia urged the bishops to bear in mind that the faith all Christians share in Christ and in his saving cross and resurrection is of far greater importance than **[p. 295]** the doctrinal questions that divide. He distinguished carefully between those truths that relate more directly to the final goal of salvation (Trinity, Incarnation, redemption, God’s merciful love) from those that pertain to the means of obtaining it (sacraments, ministries, apostolic succession). Pleading for an approach to doctrinal division marked by a fitting sense of proportion, he argued, ‘doctrinal differences among Christians have less to do with these primary truths on the level of our goal, and deal mostly on the [^c17-7] level of means, which are absolutely subordinate to those primary truths’. Catholics engaged in ecumenical dialogue must apply this principle in the presentation of the Catholic faith and in evaluating the nature of doctrinal differences.

[^c17-7]: For an English translation of Pangrazio’s speech, see ‘The Mystery of the History of the Church’, in _Council Speeches of_ _Vatican II_, ed. Hans Küng, Yves Congar, and Daniel O’Hanlon (Glen Rock, NJ: Paulist, 1964), 188–92, at 191. Cf. _AS_ II/6, 32– 35.

The council’s teaching on the practice of dialogue reflects the fundamental connection between the two principal aims of the council set out by John XXIII: Catholic renewal and Christian unity. The renewal of the Catholic Church by returning to the Gospel and the sources of tradition brings it closer to other Christian communities that, through the ecumenical movement, have also embarked upon a process of renewal and reform, of becoming church more fully. The path of renewal and reform entails humility and repentance and requires that Catholics acknowledge and repent of their share of responsibility for ecclesial division. The decree does not hesitate to ask ‘pardon of God and of our separated brothers and sisters’, citing 1 John 1:10: ‘If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us’ (_UR_ 7).

Common Prayer and Sacramental Life

As we have seen, Vatican II’s Decree on Ecumenism considers Paul Couturier’s spiritual ecumenism, which entails ‘change of heart and holiness of life’, ‘the soul of the whole ecumenical movement’ (_UR_ 8). This personal and corporate spirituality and prayer for unity is linked to the dynamism of ‘continual reformation’ of which the pilgrim Church will always have need (_UR_ 6). It also calls for the practice of public prayer in common with other Christians where we recall all that unites us and repent of all that continues to keep us apart.

The practice of ecumenism is rooted in the sacramental bond of baptism and a shared confession of faith in Christ and the tri-personal God, a bond that orients us and carves out in us a hunger for full ecclesial communion that will one day be sealed and signifled through our sharing in one Eucharist. While Christians agree that sharing in the body and blood of Christ is a sign of ecclesial unity, some see it as a means, a nourishment along the path to full communion; others consider Eucharistic sharing the crowning sign of full ecclesial unity. The Decree on Ecumenism is carefully nuanced, laying out two principles that guide the practice of sacramental sharing: first, ‘the unity of the church which ought to be expressed … generally forbids it’; and second, ‘sharing in the means of grace sometimes commends it’ (_UR_ 8). In the first case, because sharing in the Eucharist is a sacramental sign of full ecclesial unity, Christians not in full **[p. 296]** communion with the Catholic Church are not generally invited to receive the sacraments of the Catholic Church. Nonetheless, it can and does happen that other Christians belonging to churches and ecclesial communities of the West whose faith in the sacrament is consonant with that of the Catholic Church who find themselves in situations of serious spiritual need appropriately ask for and receive the sacraments of reconciliation, anointing of the sick, or Eucharist from a minister of the Catholic Church.

The council adopts a more generous attitude towards the Eastern Orthodox churches, given the high degree of communion in faith and the recognition that many Orthodox Christians may find themselves as members of small diaspora communities, far from the clergy of their own church. Members of the Eastern churches in communion with Rome are especially urged to foster closer unity with Eastern Orthodox Christians (_OE_ 24). This includes the offering of ‘a common sharing in the sacraments’ (_OE_ 26), with due respect for the canons and tradition of the other churches. Catholics who find themselves in similar circumstances are in the same way authorized to receive the sacraments ‘from non-Catholic ministers in whose church there are valid sacraments’ (_OE_ 27). Because they have remained in the apostolic succession, the Catholic Church recognizes the validity of the sacraments of the Orthodox churches (_UR_ 15).

Catholics, however, are not authorized to receive the sacraments from ministers of those Western communities who are not recognized as validly ordained. The question of the recognition of ministry is at the core of sacramental and ecclesial recognition, particularly in churches that have not retained an episcopal structure, as the bishop’s ministry of oversight is understood as the faithful handing on of the apostles’ teaching. Where this visible sign of succession in the ministry and teaching of the apostles is not evident, the council considers that ‘the sacrament of orders is lacking’ (_UR_ 22). Regrettably, some translations refer to the ‘absence of the sacrament of order’. The Latin term refers to a deficiency or weakness (_defectum_) in the sacrament of orders, which should be understood not so much in the order of grace, as at the level of the visible sacramental sign. This is the root of the reservation of the Catholic Church when it says that these communities ‘have not preserved the proper reality of the eucharist in its fullness’ (_UR_ 22). This judgement must be read together with the decree’s previous affirmation that the ‘liturgical actions’ of these same communities are efficacious means of salvation (_UR_ 3). These vexing questions have been the object of considerable debate and growth in mutual understanding in the decades following the council.

Norms to guide the pastoral application of these principles are found in the revised Code of Canon Law (CIC/1983 c. 844) for the Latin Catholic Church, in the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (CCOE c. 671), and are spelled out in the Directory for the Application of the Principles and Norms of Ecumenism (1993). The ecumenical directory also provides helpful guidelines for the pastoral care of marriages between Catholics and other Christians and for the sharing of other spiritual and material resources, including schools, church buildings, and cemeteries. Episcopal conferences and diocesan bishops are encouraged to provide further directives to assist members of their local churches and to take into account the particularities of the local context. Every case of sacramental sharing or sharing of other resources requires **[p. 297]** an exercise of pastoral discernment and respect for the convictions and the ecclesiastical discipline of other Christians.

### 5. Ecumenical Progress Since the Second Vatican Council

Other doctrinal developments during the Second Vatican Council had a profound ecumenical significance and opened the path to continuing dialogue with other Christian communions. Among them one might mention _Lumen Gentium_’s embrace of the collegial character of church governance—an important corrective to an unbalanced emphasis on papal primacy (_LG_, ch. 3); the decision to place reflections on Mary within the context of its teaching on the Church and the communion of saints (_LG_, chs. 7–8); _Dei Verbum_’s framing of Scripture and tradition as ‘flowing from the same divine well-spring’ of God’s self-revelation in Christ (_DV_ 9); and its affirmation that the magisterium ‘is not superior to the Word of God, but is rather its servant’ (_DV_ 10). These teachings each relate to the exercise of teaching authority and the interpretation of the word in the life of the Church, areas of persistent disagreement and continuing friction with churches and communities not in full communion with the Catholic Church. Finally, Vatican II’s communion ecclesiology would prove to be a fertile ground for a growing ecumenical consensus on the nature and mission of the Church.

In the dramatic closing act of the council, Pope Paul VI and Athenagoras I, Ecumenical Patriarch of the Orthodox Churches, jointly declared the lifting of the mutual excommunication of 1054, preparing the way for the establishment of official dialogue aimed at addressing doctrinal disagreements that underlie the separation of the churches. During the third and fourth sessions of the council, exploratory conversations began between ecumenical observers and the Secretariat for Christian Unity, laying the groundwork for a future of sustained dialogue and collaboration. In 1963, five Catholic theologians attended the Montreal meeting of the WCC’s Commission on Faith and Order for the first time as official delegates. In the spring of 1964, the first meeting of a new Joint Working Group between the World Council of Churches and the Roman Catholic Church was held. These structures continue to serve as important vehicles of collaboration today. Mandates were soon agreed to for official theological dialogues with the Lutheran World Federation, the Methodist World Council, the Anglican Communion, and the Orthodox Church.

In the decades since Vatican II, the Catholic Church has pursued an ambitious and sustained series of theological dialogues in the pursuit of full ecclesial communion and greater mutual understanding with at least fourteen different Christian communions: Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches, Assyrian Church of the East, Old Catholic Church, Anglican Communion, Lutheran World Federation, Methodist World **[p. 298]** Council, World Communion of Reformed Churches, Baptist World Alliance, Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), Pentecostals, Evangelicals, Mennonites, and the Salvation Army. These international commissions are often complemented by dialogues at national, regional, and local level where Catholics and members of the various communities live together.

Careful study and dialogue have helped to dispel many misunderstandings and have led to mutual agreement on issues that were once considered church-dividing. Significant growth in agreement has been achieved in many bilateral dialogues and in the multilateral forum of the WCC’s Commission on Faith and Order, where Catholics have been full members since 1968, on doctrinal questions relating to the sacraments and ecclesiology. This emerging consensus is reflected in the groundbreaking Faith and Order documents on _Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry_ (1983) and _The Church: Towards a Common Vision_ (2013). Dialogue with a number of Oriental Orthodox churches has helped to overcome disagreements relating to the Christology of the early ecumenical councils. In the West, a historic agreement was signed in 1999 between the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church on the central dispute of the sixteenth century, the doctrine that we are justifled by faith alone through the free gift of God’s grace. Subsequently, Methodist, Reformed, and Anglican communions formally expressed their adherence to this agreement, signifying a new context in ecumenical relations—one that calls for new concrete measures to signify growing ecclesial recognition.

British Catholic theologian Paul Murray has suggested that this new stage of growing communion requires [^c17-8] the churches to enter more intentionally into a process of ‘receptive ecumenism’. Building on Vatican II’s theology of ecclesial recognition, Murray calls on the churches to take greater ownership of their shortcomings and ask what they might learn from and receive from other churches as they seek to renew their ecclesial life and practice. Pope Francis captures well the spirit of receptive ecumenism in the context of his reflections on the need for a pastoral and missionary conversion of the Catholic Church in his 2013 Apostolic Exhortation, The Joy of the Gospel (_Evangelii Gaudium_ (_EG_)): ‘How many important things unite us! If we really believe in the abundantly free working of the Holy Spirit, we can learn so much from one another! It is not just about being better informed about others, but rather about reaping what the Spirit has sown in them, which is also meant to be a gift for us’ (_EG_ 246). This mutual exchange of gifts is integral to the ongoing renewal of the Catholic Church and the growth of unity with other Christian communions.

[^c17-8]: Paul D. Murray, ‘Receptive Ecumenism and Catholic Learning—Establishing the Agenda’, in _Receptive Ecumenism and the_ _Call to Catholic Learning: Exploring a Way for Contemporary Ecumenism_, ed. Paul D. Murray (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2008), 5–25.

The Second Vatican Council marked a new and growing awareness of the fundamental nature of the Church as a communion, ‘a sign and instrument, that is, of communion with God and of the unity of the entire human race’ (_LG_ 1). The restoration of full ecclesial unity is even more urgently needed today if the Church is to accomplish its reconciling mission in the service of a deeply divided human community.

Congar, Yves M.-J. _Chrétiens désunis: Principes d’un œcuménisme catholique_. Unam Sanctam 1. Paris: Cerf, 1937. Translated as _Divided Christendom: A Catholic Study of the Problem of Reunion_. London: G. Bles, 1939.

Murray, Paul D., ed., _Receptive Ecumenism and the Call to Catholic Ecumenical Learning: Exploring a Way for Contemporary Ecumenism_. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2008.

Kasper, Walter. _Handbook of Spiritual Ecumenism_. New York: New City Press, 2006.

Ryan, Thomas. _Christian Unity: How You Can Make a Difference_. New York: Paulist, 2015.

Thils, Gustav. _Le Décret sur l’œcuménisme: Commentaire doctrinal_. Paris: Desclée de Brouwer, 1996.
