## 18. Interreligious Dialogue at Vatican II

John Borelli

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 300]** Without the original ecumenical intention of John XXIII, interreligious dialogue might not have ascended as a major theme of Vatican II. Relations with Jews emerged as a topic when the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity suggested both ecumenical dialogue and fraternal conversations with Jews and others in the first draft of ‘On Ecumenism’ in November 1963. This chapter explores the issue of interreligious dialogue, focusing primarily on relations with Jews, as an example that suggests that what applies to ecumenical relations is true, with modifications, for conversing and collaborating with non-Christians as well.

Council fathers from Africa and Asia wanted specific references to the religious traditions of the peoples among whom they lived; others, especially Middle Eastern and North African bishops, wanted relations with Muslims discussed. The secretariat gradually expanded that chapter into the Declaration on the Relation of the Church to Non-Christian Religions (_Nostra Aetate_ (_NA_)), which exhorts Christians to recognize, preserve, and foster the spiritual, moral, and socio-cultural values found among other religions through dialogue and collaboration.

Two other factors were important for the inclusion of interreligious dialogue in _Nostra Aetate_: the slowness of the Commission on Missions in finding agreement on foundational propositions for a decree on missions and Pope Paul VI’s promotion of a Church in dialogue with the world. His recommendations for the council’s agenda included recognizing what is true, good, and human in other religions. He established a Secretariat for Non-Christians, once the idea of interreligious relations was discussed in the council, to implement what it might decree; his encyclical _Ecclesiam Suam_ offered strong support. The council overwhelmingly approved the expanded version of _Nostra Aetate_ in November 1964 for preparation for a **[p. 301]** final vote and promulgation in 1965. Three additional documents, issued after _Nostra Aetate_, referred to interreligious dialogue. The doctrine on interreligious dialogue in _Nostra Aetate_, minimal as it was, was the result of the conciliar process, yet it left considerable room for significant development.

### 2. Placing Interreligious Dialogue on the Council’s Agenda

While both of the original aims for the council that Pope John XXIII proposed to the cardinals who had joined him on 25 January 1959 when he announced this undertaking were ‘tantalizingly vague’ and ‘unqualifledly positive’, they were ecumenical in scope: ‘the enlightenment, edification, and joy of the entire Christian people’ and ‘a renewed cordial invitation to the faithful of the separated communities to [^c18-1] participate with us in this quest for unity and grace’. To maintain a truly ecumenical character for the council, such that it would involve other Christians and relations with them, John XXIII agreed to establish the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity, which he identifled in his announcement of the preparatory commissions on Pentecost Sunday (5 June) 1960. He appointed the esteemed biblical scholar Augustin Bea, SJ, whom he had created a cardinal in December 1959, as the secretariat’s president.

[^c18-1]: John W. O’Malley, _When Bishops Meet_ (Cambridge, MA: The Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 2019), 24; John W. O’Malley, _What Happened at Vatican II_ (Cambridge, MA: The Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 2008); _AAS_ 51 (1959), 69.

Eight days later, on 13 June 1960, the pope received Jules Isaac in a private audience. Isaac was a venerable scholar, a Holocaust survivor, and a recognized advocate for Jewish–Christian reconciliation. Isaac brought a portfolio with him which included the results of meetings from the immediate post-war period, as well as conclusions from his own research, and asked the pope to form a commission to address church teaching on the Jews. According to Isaac’s account, Pope John told him that he thought of the idea as soon as he saw [^c18-2] Isaac. With the secretariat in place for just eight days, Pope John could refer both Jules Isaac and his suggestion that the Church explore relations with Jews in the preparations for the council to Cardinal Bea. In a memorandum dated 22 March 1966, just over three months after the council, Msgr Loris Capovilla, the pope’s private secretary, wrote that John was extremely impressed by that meeting, talked about it for a long time, had not considered that the council would address relations with Jews until that day, but [^c18-3] afterwards was completely taken with the suggestion. When the pope and cardinal met next, on 18 September 1960, Bea offered to facilitate relations with Jews along with the ecumenical preparations for the council. At that early date, no one could accurately predict an outcome. The pope had not yet authorized the **[p. 302]** secretariat to prepare conciliar documents, no one had a clear sense if a draft on relations with Jews would succeed, and not very many involved with preparations for the council were pondering interreligious relations.

[^c18-2]: Norman C. Tobias, _Jewish Conscience of the Church: Jules Isaac and the Second Vatican Council_ (Cham, Switzerland: Palgrave Macmillan, 2017), 186–189.

[^c18-3]: _AAV_, Vatican II, 1452.

The ecumenical context out of which the topic of interreligious dialogue emerged is significant. From the beginning of the twentieth century, the Catholic Church had instructed the faithful not to host or participate in discussions of faith and morals with dissenters from the Catholic religion. Pope Leo XXIII advised Catholic bishops to stay away from such gatherings in 1895, after Cardinal Gibbons, a few bishops and other [^c18-4] Catholic leaders participated in the World’s Parliament of Religions in 1893 in Chicago. This ban applied to formal and public discussions about religious topics with other Christians as well as with Jews and the followers of other religions.

[^c18-4]: _Acta Leonis XIII Pontificis Maximi_, 23 vols. (Rome: Typographia Vaticana, 1881–1905), 14:323–24.

As the twentieth century unfolded, Christians from various churches increased their ecumenical efforts to address the scandals and deficiencies of their disunity and to converse on the principles for Christian unity. The ecumenical movement began to take shape amidst these efforts, reaching important milestones with the Faith and Order conference in 1927 and the establishment of the World Council of Churches in 1948. A few Catholic individuals sought to participate in that movement, and in 1952 ecumenically minded Catholic theologians and other scholars began meeting as a transnational organization, the Catholic Conference for Ecumenical Questions, directed by two Dutch priests, Johannes Willebrands and Frans Thijssen. Several participants would become members and consultors of the secretariat, and Cardinal Bea would invite Willebrands to be its secretary.

Out of these ecumenical efforts, Christians in the United States, and later in England and elsewhere, began joining primarily with Jews in interfaith associations, an effort that gained momentum with purpose during World War II. After the war, some Protestant and Eastern Christian leaders began raising questions about Jewish relations in ecumenical settings, notably the Second Assembly of the World Council of Churches, which took place in Evanston, Illinois, in 1954. The significant point is that interfaith relations in Europe and North America emerged out of the developing ecumenical movement; similarly, a secretariat primarily dedicated to ecumenical relations at Vatican II assumed the task of facilitating Jewish relations and then developed a rationale for promoting interreligious dialogue.

Both terms, ‘interreligious’ and ‘dialogue’, were new to conciliar language with Vatican II. Putting the two words together indicated an activity that Catholic officials had discouraged the faithful from doing before the council. In fact, the use of the term ‘religion’ in appreciation of the beliefs and practices of anyone other than Christians was new in the history of the councils. At Vatican I, any tradition other than ‘the Christian religion’ was deemed ‘false religion’ (_Dei Filius_, ch. 4). According to Thomas F. Stransky, CSP, who helped staff the development of _Nostra Aetate_ for the secretariat, ‘The method of the Declaration is to recognize, **[p. 303]** evaluate and respect _faith-communities_, whose collective life has taken and is developing options of [^c18-5] thought and responsible action before the mystery of human existence.’ This represented quite a change in attitude for Catholics. Forty years later, Stransky commented on the benefits of that change: ‘the all-embracing positive character of the entire _Nostra Aetate_ makes it of commanding import in Catholic history’, and it ‘helped open the church to living dialogue with each community of faith—respecting its own [^c18-6] identity, ritual and conduct’.

[^c18-5]: Thomas F. Stransky, ‘The Declaration on Non-Christian Religions’, in _Vatican II: An Interfaith Appraisal_, ed. John H. Miller (Notre Dame, IN: University of Notre Dame Press, 1966), 335–48, at 340.

[^c18-6]: Thomas F. Stransky, ‘The Genesis of _Nostra Aetate_: An Insider’s Story’, in _Nostra Aetate: Origins, Promulgation, Impact on_ _Jewish–Catholic Relations_, ed. Neville Lamdan and Alberto Melloni (Berlin: Lit Verlag, 2007), 29–53, at 53.

While no bishops called for an examination of the Church’s relationship with Jews in their responses to the pre-conciliar survey, two pontifical faculties did: the Biblicum in Rome (_ADA_ IV/1, 131–2) and Fribourg in Switzerland (_ADA_ IV/2, 784–6). Two other pontifical faculties had suggestions for what amounted to interreligious appreciation. In their response, the faculty of the Urbaniana in Rome designed a section entitled ‘Adaptation of Ascetical Doctrine in Mission Lands’ and offered several pages of reflections on the teachings and practices of Asian traditions and, specifically, ‘Confucian spirituality’, ‘Taoist spirituality’, and Buddhist spirituality’ (_ADA_ IV/1, 1, 488–92). The pontifical faculty in Pune, India, suggested that the council ‘determine the relation between the only revealed religion and the moral and religious values of other religions’ (_ADA_ IV/2, 727). No proposals as specific as these were raised in the working sessions during the contentious first period of the council.

Without the shift to ecclesiology as the focus of the council’s work that took place as that first session was drawing to a close in late 1962, interreligious dialogue may not have arisen as a major theme. On 5 December, Cardinal Giovanni Battista Montini (Milan) spoke in support of proposals made the previous day by Cardinal Léon-Joseph Suenens (Malines-Brussels) for the council to focus on the Church’s inner life (_ad intra_) and the relations of the Church with the world (_ad extra_). Six months later, on 21 June 1963, Cardinal Montini was elected as Paul VI after the death of Pope John earlier that month. Before and during the conclave that elected Paul VI, missionaries and bishops from Africa and Asia suggested that the council needed ‘another secretariat’ like the one connecting with Christians but for relations with the followers of other religions. The newly elected pope received the proposal in a letter from Cardinal Thomas Tien Ken-sin, archbishop of Peking. Then, at summer’s end, in his apostolic letter _Quod Apostolici_, dated 12 September 1963, laying out the changes he was making for the council, Paul VI indicated that ‘in due time’ there would be another secretariat (_AS_ II/1, 12). Paul VI eventually created a Secretariat for Non-Christians on 19 May 1964, after making a formal announcement—significantly on Pentecost Sunday—two days earlier (_AAS_ 56 (1964), 560).

As pope, Paul VI more easily managed to have the council shift the focus to the study of the Church’s inner **[p. 304]** life and the resulting possibilities for renewal, to promotion of the restoration of unity among Christians, and to engagement with the world. He accomplished this by articulating in some detail these three aspects for the council’s agenda in a lengthy opening address for the second session on 29 September 1963. In the final section, entitled ‘The Situation of the Church with Humanity in Our Times’ (_Nostra Aetatis_), he prepared the ground for interreligious dialogue to emerge as a topic for deliberation and for the work of the secretariat that he would eventually create to carry on such dialogue after the council.

In those concluding paragraphs, Pope Paul recalled how the message from the opening address of his predecessor, John XXIII, the year before, had inspired council fathers to want to open the doors of the assembly and to shout to all humanity greetings, fraternity, and hope. He observed that they had already decided to dialogue (_colloqui_)—not just among themselves but with the whole human family. Then, in the concluding paragraphs, he invited the council fathers to look beyond their own sphere and observe other religions and, with qualifications, he declared that ‘the Catholic religion holds in just regard all that which in them is true, good, and human’ (_AAS_ 55 (1963), 854-8). The one use by Pope Paul of the term ‘dialogue’ in that opening address in 1963 was in the final section promoting an agenda of openness to the world. He thereby connected in the minds of the council fathers any inclination they had developed to reach out to those beyond the Christian family with his own appreciation of the values of other religions.

### 3. The Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity Takes the Lead

Before Pope Paul VI could offer considerably more suggestions on the topic of dialogue, especially with the followers of other religions, in his first encyclical, _Ecclesiam Suam_, the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity distributed a draft for discussion at the council that would suggest ‘dialogue’ with Christians and with those who were not Christian. In November 1963, towards the end of the third session, the secretariat explicitly introduced the topic of interreligious dialogue into the council in the fourth chapter of its draft ‘On Ecumenism’. Cardinal Bea believed that inserting into a single draft a chapter entitled ‘On the Relation of Catholics to Non-Christians, above all, to Jews’ to follow three chapters on ecumenical relations provided the best opportunity for placing the topic of relations with Jews on the council’s agenda. The strategy included a fifth chapter on another controversial topic: religious liberty. The analogous connection with ecumenical relations, specifically with dialogue, and a general reference to relations with all who were not Christian served to moderate the controversial changes that the secretariat was proposing for relations of the Church with Jews, including the suggestion of theological dialogue.

The secretariat had prepared a previous draft, entitled ‘On the Jews’, which had been removed from the **[p. 305]** council’s agenda in June 1962, ostensibly for political reasons. Cardinal Amleto Cicognani, Secretary of State and presiding over the Central Preparatory Commission, also voiced theological concerns and the lack of a specific reference to Muslims (_ADP_ II/4, 22–3; III/2, 458). Cardinal Bea successfully gained the approval of Pope John XXIII in December 1962, after the close of the first session, to put a purely religiously oriented draft, without any political concerns or implications, back on the council’s agenda. The secretariat revised and expanded its previous draft into one entitled ‘On the Relation of Catholics to Non-Christians, above all, to the Jews’. Material added to the old draft made two references to dialogue, which the old draft had not proposed. This new draft opened with this sentence:

After we have treated the principles of Catholic Ecumenism, we do not wish to pass over in silence the fact that, taking account of diverse conditions, these same principles ought to be applied to the way of conversing [_de modo colloquendi_] and collaborating with those who are not Christians, who nevertheless worship God, or at least spirited with good will, strive to follow their conscience in carrying out the moral law inserted in human nature. (_AS_ II/5 431–2)[^c18-7]

[^c18-7]: All English translations of the drafts leading up to the final text of _Nostrae Aetate_ were provided by Thomas F. Stransky working in collaboration with the author to examine the genesis and development of the declaration.

Aside from the fact that the Secretariat later changed the opening expression to ‘Catholic principles for ecumenism’ for all subsequent drafts of the _Decree on Ecumenism_, it had also referred to ‘dialogue’ in the preceding chapters as among those principles for the best way to discern with separated Christians the state of their communion and to address the obstacles that separated them as fellow Christians. Presumably, the ‘diverse conditions’ that would make interreligious dialogue distinct from ecumenical dialogue would include the eventual goals of ecumenists for restoring unity among Christians and tending to their shared ecclesial life in the one Church. Actually, the draft gave no reasons in this opening sentence for interreligious dialogue between Catholics and those who ‘worship God’ or are ‘spirited with good will’. By adding that alternative to worshipping God, conversing and collaborating would also apply to relations with non-believers who followed their conscience and lived moral lives. The introduction did not provide a definition for interreligious dialogue but presented the idea almost as tentatively as Paul VI had done several weeks previously in his opening address.

The 1963 draft offers more insight into interreligious dialogue in its concluding paragraphs, added to the discarded first draft. It lays out profoundly theological reasons for Christians’ appreciation of their Jewish heritage and explains how it is an injustice to accuse Jews of being accursed and deicidal. Then, urging care in preaching and catechesis to prevent contempt of Jews, the text continues with strong language to affirm the fruits of dialogue with Jews: ‘Since the common heritage of the Church with the synagogue is so great, this Holy Synod intends in every way to foster and commend mutual understanding and esteem, which is **[p. 306]** the fruit of theological studies and fraternal conversations.’ Thus, mutual understanding and esteem are declared goals for interreligious dialogue, and one could suggest that theological insight might be suggested as a goal as well if the conversations touched on theological topics and even involved joint theological studies. In the next sentence, the Holy Synod declares that it rejects injustices and decries and condemns hatreds and persecutions against the Jews (_AS_ II/5, 431–2). Reconciliation and healing of past wrongs and injustices by implication are goals for fraternal conversation, especially between Jews and Christians.

### 4. Paul VI Promotes Interreligious Dialogue

Six months later, on 17 May 1964—appropriately, Pentecost Sunday—the Church feast when Pope John in 1960 had announced the founding of the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity and the other preparatory commissions, Pope Paul VI revealed that he was establishing a Secretariat for Non-Christians. Neither his homily that Sunday nor the official document by which he established the secretariat two days later mention the term ‘dialogue’. Nevertheless, the pope spoke eloquently of one of the most significant consequences for this new agency: ‘No pilgrim, no matter how distant he may be religiously or geographically, no matter his country of origin, will any longer be a complete stranger in this Rome, ever faithful to the historic program the Catholic faith has reserved to it as a common homeland [_patria communis_]’ (_AAS_ 56 (1964), 433). Thus, from that time forward, for visitors to the Holy See from religions other than Christianity, an office existed specifically to receive them for conversation and dialogue.

Speaking again in Italian to the College of Cardinals one month later, on 23 June 1964, Pope Paul specifled that he had established the Secretariat for Non-Christians to become ‘a means for sincere and respectful dialogue [_dialogo_] with those who still believe in God and worship him’ (_AAS_ 56 (1964), 584). Then, on 6 August 1964, six weeks before the start of the third session, Pope Paul issued his encyclical _Ecclesiam Suam_ (_ES_). The pope himself suggested a freely translated title for his first encyclical, ‘The Ways of the Church’, for it laid out the same tripartite agenda for his pontificate as he had offered for the council in his opening address eleven months earlier: guiding the Church towards deeper spiritual insight into its inner nature, renewal of the Church for moral strength, and dialogue with the world. The council and the world focused on the third part, taking one of its subheadings, ‘Church in Dialogue’, as its primary message. Paul VI employed the concept of dialogue throughout the text, using the term over seventy times; among those instances, the expression ‘the dialogue of salvation’ appears seven times.

After reflecting on the desire of the Church to speak with the whole of humanity, including non-believers, Pope Paul identifled a circle of believers that included the Jewish people, Muslims, and the followers of the great Afro-Asiatic religions in a concentric relationship around the Catholic Church. He expressed the **[p. 307]** conviction that ‘the Catholic religion is the only true religion’ and the hope that ‘all who look for God and worship Him will acknowledge it as such’. He then extended an offer for dialogue, not turning ‘a blind eye to the spiritual and moral values of the various non-Christian religions’ and declaring his willingness ‘to join with them in promoting and defending common ideals’ (_ES_ 107). He suggested that ‘dialogue is possible in all these great projects’ and disclosed his willingness to join such discussions when his offer was ‘received in genuine, mutual respect’ (_ES_ 108).

So new, and more imagined than practised, was this suggestion for interreligious dialogue that from the perspective of decades afterwards, these come across as conflicting hopes that those who worship God in ways other than Christianity will accept an offer for dialogue with genuine, mutual respect and that they will likewise come to acknowledge the ultimate truth of the Christian religion (_ES_ 107–8). In his opening address to the council, there is a similar ambiguity in Pope Paul prejudging that the Catholic Church perceives in these other religions ‘gaps, insufficiencies, and errors’, while at the same time wanting them to know that the Church esteems what they hold that is true, good, and human. By describing interreligious dialogue within the apostolic mission of the Church in _Ecclesiam Suam_, while holding that interreligious dialogue can be a form of spiritual interaction, Pope Paul VI left unanswered several questions about the relationship between dialogue and mission and how dialogue can take place in an environment of trust, respect, and openness to learning. The German theologian Otto Hermann Pesch has suggested that the council—and we can add Pope Paul VI—did not indicate concrete ways for the recommended dialogue because there were few experts: ‘Until the time of the Council, advocates for “interreligious dialogue” were solitary voices in the wilderness.’[^c18-8]

[^c18-8]: Otto Hermann Pesch, _The Second Vatican Council: Prehistory—Event—Results—Posthistory_, trans. Deirdre Dempsey (Milwaukee, WI: Marquette University Press, 2014), 280.

Despite generalities and ambiguities, the encyclical provided a strong endorsement for ‘dialogue’, and the concept of ‘interreligious dialogue’ may not have emerged as a major theme of the council without the effect of how the encyclical broadened the term ‘dialogue’. In _Ecclesiam Suam_, Paul VI applied ‘dialogue’ to any number of relationships, not just those bridging religious traditions. The single word ‘dialogue’ spoke volumes on what the council was all about. Some have suggested that the pope appropriated the term and its interpersonal meaning from Martin Buber, author of _I and Thou_ and a number of other writings on dialogue. There is no evidence that Paul VI ever read Buber. Bishop Pietro Rossano, who served in the early years of the Secretariat for Non-Christians, proposed that ‘dialogical thought’, emblematic of the work of Buber and others that influenced a whole generation of philosophers, theologians, and teachers in the first half of the twentieth century, accounted for the pope’s profuse use of the term ‘dialogue’, rather than any particular [^c18-9] individual, including Buber, or even the philosophical movement known as ‘personalism’. Other students **[p. 308]** of the council and of Paul VI concur that there is no evidence of the singular influence on the encyclical by any person or movement and that the encyclical was thought out and composed by the pope himself.

[^c18-9]: Istituto Paolo VI, _‘Ecclesiam Suam’: Première lettre encyclique de Paul VI_, Colloque International, Rome, 25–26 octobre 1980, Publicazioni dell’Istituto Paolo VI, 2 (Brescia: Istituto Paolo VI, 1982), 175–76.

Throughout the promulgated Latin text of the encyclical, cognates for _colloquium_, ‘dialogue’ or ‘conversation’, and for _colloqui_, ‘to dialogue’ or ‘to converse’, were used and usually translated into English as ‘dialogue’. The one instance of ‘to dialogue’ in the Latin text of Pope Paul’s opening address to the council is _colloqui_. In the three instances in the 1963 draft of ‘On Ecumenism’, the Latin word _dialogus_ and its cognates appear. This preference would continue with several more instances added to the final, promulgated _Decree on Ecumenism_. In the two instances in the fourth chapter of the 1963 draft for interreligious ‘conversations’, _colloquia_ and _colloquiis_ are used. This would continue to the promulgated text of _Nostra Aetate_. Some have judged that something more is intended by the consistent use of distinct terms by the secretariat for ecumenical dialogue and for interreligious dialogue. One might ask if the intense formal discussions on matters of doctrine and practice in ecumenical dialogue, where participants are seeking to overcome the obstacles towards ecclesial unity, differ in depth and significance from friendly, interreligious conversations drawing the participants into trusting and respectful relationships of cooperation and spiritual sharing.

_Ecclesiam Suam_ makes no such distinction. Translations of the encyclical and conciliar documents have overwhelmingly rendered both terms as ‘dialogue’. When asked to explain why different terms appear in the same draft in 1963 and were used by the secretariat, Thomas F. Stransky, CSP, who served on the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity from its beginning in 1960, explained that two different Latinists were responsible for the difference. Long before the encyclical was prepared for promulgation in Latin, the group of the secretariat writing the first three chapters on ecumenical relations for the 1963 draft worked in French; their Latinist, Erich Salzmann, preferred ‘dialogus’. The working group for the fourth chapter on relations particularly with Jews communicated more comfortably in English, and the Latinist who prepared the draft in Latin, Emilio Springhetti, SJ, preferred ‘colloquium’.[^c18-10]

[^c18-10]: John Borelli, ‘Correcting the _Nostra Aetate_ Legend: The Contested, Minimal and Almost Failed Effort to Embrace a Tragedy and Amend Christian Attitudes to Jews, Muslims and the Followers of Other Religions’, in _Nostra Aetate, Non-Christian_ _Religions, and Interfaith Relations_, ed. Kail C. Ellis, OSA (Cham: Palgrave Macmillan, 2020).

### 5. A Separate Declaration

On 24 September 1964, Cardinal Bea pointed out in his report on revision of the 1963 chapter, now distributed for discussion as the separate ‘Other Declaration’ (_Declaratio altera_) and entitled ‘Declaration on Jews and Non-Christians’, that this occasion was the first time in the history of the Church that a council **[p. 309]** was addressing the subject of relations with non-Christians. He reviewed how there was now a new Secretariat for Non-Christians, providing a special office for relations with members of other religions, and that among the tasks before the Church that Paul VI had outlined in his encyclical was ‘dialogue with them’ (_dialogo cum eis_) (_AS_ III/2, 562–3).

Bea’s strategy had proved successful. A review of relations with Jews, with suggestions requiring major shifts in Catholic attitudes and understanding, was on the agenda as a draft declaration. The same was true for religious liberty, which was now the ‘First Declaration’ (_Declaratio prior_). Despite his emphasis on the historical moment for the Church’s relations with non-Christian religions for conciliar deliberation, this draft declaration had only one more reference to interreligious dialogue than the previous one. It still commended mutual understanding and esteem, the fruit of theological studies and fraternal conversations between Jews and Catholics. Something new was added, suggesting another reason for interreligious conversations having a theological character. The secretariat added an unmistakable reference to John 1:9, without providing a note, to state that, motivated by love, ‘we ought to pay great attention to the opinions and teachings which although they differ from our own in many ways, contain nevertheless many rays of that Truth which enlightens everyone in this world’. This is followed by the first explicit reference to Muslims in a draft: Muslims are said to ‘stand close to us in a religious sense’, but it does not develop the idea beyond that (_AS_ III/2, 329).

The draft resulted from a series of required and imposed edits and emendations of a simpler text that the secretariat had submitted the previous March with the consequence that the passages do not always fit well together. Even with the draft’s weaknesses and shortcomings, Cardinal Bea received thunderous applause before and after delivering his report, which sought to explain some aspects of the draft’s turbulent journey. The majority who spoke favourably in the debate that followed for the next two days offered numerous suggestions for improvement, including considerably more expansion and more precise reasons for dialogue.

Two months later, on 18 November 1964, the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity distributed a greatly expanded draft for a first round of voting. Bearing the initial words ‘in our time’ (_nostra aetate_) for the first time, it opened with a broad and positive statement of purpose: ‘Day by day humankind is being drawn close together, and the bonds of friendship between different peoples are being strengthened, the Church examines with greater care her relations to non-Christian religions’(AS III/8, 637).

Two days later, when Cardinal Bea gave his report, he drew attention to the importance of the declaration with regard to non-Christian religions: ‘No Council in the history of the Church, unless I am mistaken, has ever set out so solemnly the principles concerning them.’ He spoke then of ‘the grave duty of initiating dialogue’ with the billion-plus members of humanity who had never heard of Christ and his redemptive work, even though they could be saved if they obeyed the dictates of conscience (_AS_ III/8, 650–51). The Dogmatic Constitution on the Church (_Lumen Gentium_ (_LG_)) was ready for promulgation the next day. The council fathers had agreed to particular language in the constitution which declared that the followers of other religions stand in a relationship with the Church and that by seeking God, living a sincere life, and **[p. 310]** moved by grace to try to do what is right ‘may attain eternal salvation’ (_LG_ 16). If adopted, this language would represent a development in the teachings of the Catholic Church with regard to other religions.

This broad and positive statement of purpose in the opening sentence of the 1964 draft of _Nostra Aetate_ indicated that this development in Church teaching concerning the followers of other religions would receive further discussion. It was followed immediately by an engaging discourse on how various religions sought to answer the basic enigmas facing the whole human family. The text identifled the responses of two specific religions, Hinduism and Buddhism, and then referred to ‘other religions found everywhere’. After the exhortation to dialogue and collaboration, Muslims and Jews were addressed, and greater detail was given as to why these traditions are close to Christians.

In the proposed text, in a passage that would remain unchanged in the final version, the council pleads with all, Christians and Muslims especially, to make ‘a sincere effort … to achieve mutual understanding’ and so to work together to ‘preserve and promote peace, liberty, social justice, and moral values’ for all humankind’ (_NA_ 3). The draft adds ‘biblical’ as an area for joint studies for Jews and Christians in promoting mutual knowledge and esteem, ‘the fruit, above all, of biblical and theological studies and fraternal conversations’ (_NA_ 4; AS III/8, 638–40). Though expanded, the document remains brief, leaving much to be imagined and undertaken by those willing to embrace its message. The final, promulgated document was, in fact, the shortest of the council’s sixteen documents.

The voting was overwhelmingly positive for the expanded draft. A year later, the final draft of _Nostra Aetate_, distributed in October 1965 for final voting, was not fundamentally changed but improved by various suggestions. To the initial statement of purpose for the document, a second was added affirming the value of serious conversation even in daily life: ‘Ever aware of its duty to foster unity and charity among individuals, and even among nations, it [the Church] reflects at the outset on what people have in common and what tends to bring them together’ (_NA_ 1). The declaration confirms that ‘a profound religious sense’ draws humanity together. Thus, interreligious dialogue, the mutual discernment of truth and the sharing of values and insights, guided by the light that enlightens all, is a spiritual exercise of a natural religious sense that all participants in dialogue share. To ‘preserve and promote’, the final draft adds ‘recognize’ those spiritual and moral goods and other values among the followers of other religions.

The secretariat, the council fathers, and the pope were probably less certain about what the future held for interreligious relations than they were about ecumenical dialogue, although they probably sensed that they stood on the threshold of unimaginable possibilities for interreligious relations. _Nostra Aetate_’s proposal for interreligious dialogue was truly the beginning. Although precautions were put into the final text, reminding Catholics that differences matter, especially in that they believe that in Christ is ‘the fullness of religious life’ and through him ‘God has reconciled all things to himself’ (_NA_ 2; cf. 2 Cor. 5:18–19), the encouragements to form relationships of cooperation and dialogue were palpable. _Nostra Aetate_ laid out extraordinary possibilities in only a few sentences, compared with the other conciliar documents, but it **[p. 311]** grew in pastoral importance and theological significance over the next five decades, when interreligious dialogue and collaboration became more and more necessary for addressing adequately so many issues facing humanity.

### 6. The Impact of Nostra Aetate on Other Conciliar Documents

Those drafting the eventual Decree on the Mission Activity of the Church (_Ad Gentes_) started to incorporate the topic of interreligious dialogue into their text after the council fathers approved the expanded draft of _Nostra Aetate_ in November 1964 for a final vote and promulgation in October 1965. The Commission on [^c18-11] Missions was slow in drafting a decree. A debate unfolded over four days in early November 1964 on an outline and propositions for a draft; the council fathers voted in favour of significant revision. Just as the expanded draft of _Nostra Aetate_ was being readied for distribution and a vote prior to adjournment of the third period, the Commission for Missions decided to begin practically afresh. Fortunately, _Nostra Aetate_ provided a position on interreligious dialogue that the drafters of that new draft could incorporate. The final text of _Ad Gentes_, promulgated at the end of the council on 7 December 1965, recommended dialogue as an instrument of mission so that Christ’s disciples might discern with the followers of other religions ‘the riches which a generous God has distributed among the nations’ and ‘illuminate’ them ‘with the light of the Gospel’ (_AG_ 11). _Ad Gentes_ recognized, with _Nostra Aetate_, that God reaches out to humanity through their religions: ‘This universal plan of God for the salvation of humanity is not carried out secretly, as it were in people’s souls, nor by the efforts, including religious efforts, by which they seek God in many ways “and perhaps grope for him and find him—though indeed He be not far from each one of us (cf. Acts 17:27)” ’ (_AG_ 3). Furthermore, _Ad Gentes_, drawing from the New Testament witness, affirms that through various ways, God causes divine faith to arise among the followers of other religions: ‘in ways known to himself God can lead those who, through no fault of their own, are ignorant of the Gospel to that faith without which it is impossible to please him (Heb. 11:6)’ (_AG_ 7).

[^c18-11]: Eddy Louchez, ‘La Commission De Missionibus’, in _Les Commissions conciliaires à Vatican II_, ed. Mathijs Lamberigts, Claude Soetens and Jan Grootaers (Leuven: Bibliotheek van de Faculteit Godgeleerdheid, 1996), 251–78.

For humanity’s quest for peace, _Ad Gentes_ recommended ‘fraternal dialogue’ (_fraterno dialogo_) so that those who were not Christian might find ‘the peace and light of the Gospel’ (_AG_ 12). _Ad Gentes_ explicitly called for preparation for fraternal dialogue to be incorporated into the training of priests (_AG_ 16), the formation of missionaries (_AG_ 34), and the work of the laity in their academic study of religions and cultures (_AG_ 41).

**[p. 312]** _Nostra Aetate_’s sister text, the Declaration on Religious Liberty (_Dignitatis Humanae_ (_DH_)), which the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity had also sheltered in its first draft of ‘On Ecumenism’, makes an important reference to dialogue that serves to expand its application to public life. The text identifles dialogue as an important instrument in the public quest for truth, enhancing ‘the free exercise of religion in society’. Since the practice of religion ‘sets the course of one’s life directly toward God’, dialogue provides opportunities for persons ‘to explain to one another the truth they have discovered, or think they have discovered, in such a way that they help one another in the search for truth’. This allows mutual spiritual enrichment, which animates ongoing interreligious conversation and collaboration that contribute to a healthy public life for a given society (_DH_ 3). The secretariat chose to place in the section on relations with Muslims in _Nostra Aetate_ its plea for everyone to make sincere efforts ‘to achieve mutual understanding, for the benefit of all’ and so to work together to preserve and promote ‘peace, liberty, social justice and moral values’ for all humankind (_NA_ 3). _Dignitatis Humanae_ argues that religious freedom empowers citizens ‘to act with greater responsibility in fulfilling their obligations in society’ (_DH_ 8).

The Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World (_Gaudium et Spes_ (_GS_)), the final text promulgated by the council, insisted that ‘the right order in this world’ cannot be realized ‘without a dialogue that is sincere and prudent’ (_GS_ 21). The Constitution emphasizes throughout the social nature of the human person and observes that such dialogue, whether interreligious or simply public without specific reference to religion, reaches its perfection ‘on the deeper level in a community of persons which calls for mutual respect for each one’s full dignity’ (_GS_ 23). _Gaudium et Spes_ urges all the faithful to do their part ‘to enter into dialogue with the world’ (_GS_ 43) and offers numerous examples. In its only reference to ‘religions’, the constitution acknowledges the significance of ‘a steadily growing respect for men and women of other opinions or other religions’, which advances the life of political communities and safeguards minority populations within them (_GS_ 73). Along with _Dignitatis Humanae_, _Gaudium et Spes_ encourages Catholics to imagine public spaces for interreligious dialogue for the sharing of insights and good will in the service of justice.

### 7. The Many Forms and Purposes of Interreligious Dialogue

In 1984, to mark the twentieth anniversary of its foundation and the same anniversary of _Ecclesiam Suam_, the Secretariat for Non-Christians held a plenary assembly of its members and consultors and evaluated their experiences of dialogue, reflected on the Church’s attitudes towards other believers, and considered the relationship between dialogue and mission. The secretariat then published a document that is both a **[p. 313]** status report on what the participants had learned about interreligious dialogue since Vatican II and a vision statement for the Secretariat’s future work. The report is entitled _The Attitude of the Church toward Followers of Other Religions: Reflections and Orientations on Dialogue and Mission_ (_DM_).

The document described dialogue, before all else, as ‘a manner of acting, an attitude; a spirit which guides one’s conduct’ (_DM_ 29). The secretariat suggested that mission is a complex but unifled reality consisting of several elements. One of these elements is dialogue, through which ‘Christians meet the followers of other religious traditions in order to walk together toward truth and to work together in projects of common concern’ (_DM_ 13). The document urged that all Christians are called to dialogue, and thus the simplest form of interreligious dialogue is the dialogue of daily life (_DM_ 29–30). The document also identifled the dialogue of works and collaboration and applied the council’s plea in _Nostra Aetate_ 3 for persons of differing religious traditions to join together in projects for social justice, moral welfare, and peace and freedom (_DM_ 31–32). To these two forms of interreligious dialogue, the text added dialogue that involves experts: those who undertake theological and biblical studies and the academic study of religions. As _Nostra Aetate_ 4 recommends, participants in this form of intense scholarly exchange grow in mutual understanding and appreciation of one other’s spiritual and cultural resources and thereby promote communion and fellowship (_DM_ 33–34). Finally, the document identifled a fourth form of interreligious dialogue, that of religious experience, in which participants share their experiences of prayer, contemplation, faith, and duty as well as their expressions and ways of searching for the Absolute. Experience had taught those who prepared the document that profound differences between their religious traditions did not prevent this dialogue from growing and nurturing all who draw from it (_DM_ 35–36).

As the third millennium was opening, Pope John Paul II identifled interreligious dialogue as one of the most significant ways for the human family to face the uncertainties of the future in his apostolic letter released at the beginning of the new millennium, _Novo Millennio Ineunte_ (_NMI_) He reviewed how, in the formal preparations he had instituted for the Great Jubilee Year of 2000, he had held ‘a series of highly symbolic meetings’ in his efforts to build ‘a relationship of openness and dialogue with the followers of other religions’. He then declared that, ‘in the climate of increased cultural and religious pluralism which is expected to mark the society of the new millennium, it is obvious that this dialogue will be especially important in establishing a sure basis for peace and warding oft the dread spectre of those wars of religion which have so often bloodied human history’ (_NMI_ 55).
