## 19. Women and the Council: Catholic Women’s

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 315]** When on 11 October 1962 some 2,500 conciliar fathers filed into St Peter’s Basilica to inaugurate the Second Vatican Council, women were mere onlookers. More than three years later, by the fourth conciliar session, the situation had changed substantially. At the close of the council, on 8 December 1965, Pope Paul VI delivered, among others, an address to ‘women of all nations—girls, wives, mothers and widows, consecrated virgins and women living alone’. According to the pope, the Church felt proud of having ‘glorifled and liberated woman’ and having ‘brought into relief her basic equality with man’. The pope added that ‘the hour is coming, in fact has come, … in which woman acquires in the world an influence, an effect and a power never before achieved’. At the end of his message, the pope asked women to ‘bring the [^c19-1] spirit of this council into institutions, schools, homes and daily life’. During the four sessions of the council, women had come more and more into the Church’s focus. Women contributed to the discussions of the assembly by writing petitions and letters. They attended the third and fourth sessions as so-called lay auditors, including both female lay catholics and religious sisters. They contributed to the formulation of texts by working in different subcommissions. They had shaped places of communication as hosts. Women **[p. 316]** travelled to Rome to meet bishops, theologians, and Christian women from all over the world had brought the spirit of the council to women’s organizations, religious orders, and parishes. Those who had been involved in the council’s work in some way were determined to continue their commitment as multipliers after its conclusion.

[^c19-1]: Paul VI, ‘Address of Pope Paul VI to Women’ (8 December 1965), https://www.vatican.va/content/paul- vi/en/speeches/1965/documents/hf_p-vi_spe_19651208_epilogo-concilio-donne.html.

### 2. Conciliar Vota

Already in the run-up to the council, women raised their voices. When in June 1959 Pope John XXIII asked bishops, religious superiors, Catholic universities, and ecclesiastical faculties to express their hopes and concerns for the forthcoming council, laypeople were not addressed. Nevertheless, as early as June 1960, the World Union of Catholic Women’s Organisations (WUCWO)—representing 36 million Catholic women from every continent—presented a number of requests and suggestions to the council’s Central Preparatory Commission. Their primary concern was for a Christian formation that would enlarge the possibilities of women to work for the good of the Church ‘in accordance with the reality of the present time’. WUCWO asked that the council acknowledge ‘the personal and not only sexual value of woman’ and that it recognize the position of women in the family, in the workplace, in society, and in the apostolic commitment of the Church. Furthermore, the organization encouraged the council to take a stand against the Marxist tendency of ‘woman’s masculinization’ in order to achieve a ‘distinct development for women’ on the one hand, and against the ‘pseudo-catholic’ tendency to idealize women on the other.[^c19-2]

[^c19-2]: Suggerimenti e voti dell’Unione delle organizzazioni femminili cattoliche (UMOFC), in AAV, _Conc. Vat. II_, b. 606. The organization is also known as Union Mondiale des Organisations Féminines Catholiques (UMOFC = WUCWO).

These requests of a more general nature were accompanied by suggestions concerning the formation and pastoral work of priests. Above all, WUCWO pleaded for an end to all expressions of misogyny! It appealed for better psychological, pedagogical, and theological training of priests to improve women’s experience of spiritual direction and to inspire greater confidence in the self-organized pastoral activities of women on the part of the clergy. In a nutshell, Catholic women dealt with the issue of priestly formation because they did not feel comfortable with the pastoral approach of priests towards women. To conclude, the authors announced a second memorandum on birth control.

WUCWO’s memorandum on birth control was sent in the autumn of 1960. Whereas the first letter had been quite outspoken, this theme demanded a more cautious description of the situation and respective suggestions. The women acknowledged that birth control was sometimes motivated by rather selfish motives, yet at the same time could be a question of reason. According to the memorandum, Catholic women the world over suffered from anxieties and confiicts of conscience. The authors therefore suggested **[p. 317]** that the Church ought to enlighten the faithful and underline the fact that its teaching was not a ‘pro-birth doctrine’ but rather a ‘family doctrine’, one that concerned both the procreation _and_ education of [^c19-3] children.

[^c19-3]: ‘Note de l’Union Mondiale des Organisations Féminines Catholiques sur “La famille et la fécondité” ’ (autumn/winter 1960), in _Katholikinnen und das Zweite Vatikanische Konzil_, ed. Regina Heyder and Gisela Muschiol (Münster: Aschendorff, 2018), 62–70, at 66–68.

These two letters from WUCWO were representative of the many initiatives of women’s organizations both before and during the council. The role and dignity of women in Church and society, the status of laypeople in general, pastoral attitudes towards women, priestly formation, liturgy, ecumenism, Jewish–Christian relations, the understanding of marriage, and birth control (and the respective experiences of women in the confessional) were among the most important themes for women. More often than Catholic men, they chose not to act as individuals, but addressed the council under the cover of Catholic women’s organizations. Some petitioners also asked that women be allowed to participate in the council as experts.

These suggestions received due attention in the preparatory commissions of the council, where extracts and translations at least of some texts originating from the major women’s organizations were made. The memorandum on birth control, for example, was brought to the attention of the Preparatory Theological Commission and Central Preparatory Commission as well as the Preparatory Commission for the Lay Apostolate. However, the women had expressed themselves so cautiously that Jesuit Sebastian Tromp SJ, a member of the Preparatory Theological Commission, added a handwritten comment to the page: ‘What do women themselves think about this issue?’[^c19-4]

[^c19-4]: Ibid., 68.

Among the other international organizations sending suggestions to the preparatory commissions was the St Joan’s International Alliance, a group originally founded in Great Britain in 1911 as the Catholic Women’s Suffrage Society. Their members were mostly intellectuals, and the Alliance itself was proud of its good relations with popes Pius XII, John XXIII, and Paul VI. The activists intensifled their work after the announcement of the council. A first ‘suggestion’, brought forward in May 1961, claimed that ‘if in future diaconal duties are to be entrusted to laymen as an independent ministry, this ministry should be open to [^c19-5] both men and women’. Later, the Alliance pleaded for the participation of women in the council, a revision of canon law, and a reform of the rite of marriage.

[^c19-5]: ‘Votum der St. Joan’s Alliance’ (27/28 May 1961), in Heyder and Muschiol, _Katholikinnen_, 74–75.

Catholic women, among them religious sisters, continued to submit written requests throughout the whole of the council. What all texts had in common was their concern to address the negative experiences of women in the Church. Few referred to theological matters, given that up until this period women had rarely been afforded the opportunity to study theology. As in the case of the expectations of the council fathers, a certain diversity, regionality, and a-synchronicity is to be noted in women’s perspectives. African women, for example, hoped the council would speak against polygamy and forced marriages. While German women **[p. 318]** generally longed for a liturgy in the vernacular, letters to the editor of _The Tablet_ of London revealed that [^c19-6] a significant number of English Catholic women preferred to retain Latin as a liturgical language. The same range of opinions is to be noted regarding birth control, with English Catholic women again being more in accordance with the traditional Church teaching. However, attention to and tolerance for this diversity of views was perhaps never greater than during the years of the council.

[^c19-6]: Alana Harris, ‘A Fresh Stripping of the Altars: Vatican II, Liturgical Language and the Legacy of the Reformation in England, 1964–1984’, in _Catholics in the Vatican II Era: Local Histories of a Global Event_, ed. Kathleen Cummings, Timothy Matovina, and Robert Orsi (Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press, 2018), 245–74.

One of the most important figures of the Second Vatican Council, Cardinal Josef Frings of Cologne, a member of the Central Preparatory Commission, wrote a letter in Latin in 1961 to accompany the petitions of two German women’s associations, urging that ‘the voice of the laity not be despised, even if I do not [^c19-7] totally agree with them’. One suggestion in particular had provoked Frings’s scepticism—namely, the women’s plea that the Church make a pioneering statement concerning the ‘needs’ of married couples. With regard to birth control, Frings himself faced a dilemma between pastoral necessity and theological impossibility. In the long run, the women’s appeals had a twofold effect: first, Catholic women became more deeply aware of the need for a more profound understanding of theology; and second, following the close of the council, they felt proud to have contributed through their petitions to its discussions and decisions. This ‘success’ motivated them to bring the council’s spirit to the different places, as Pope Paul VI had asked.

[^c19-7]: Kardinal Josef Frings, ‘Begleitschreiben zu den Eingaben der Frauenverbände’ (4 July 1961), in Heyder and Muschiol, _Katholikinnen_, 114.

### 3. Women Priests? The Requests of Women Theologians

In November 1965, the official newspaper of the Holy See, _L’Osservatore Romano_, published a three-part series on ‘women and the priesthood’. Its author, Franciscan Gino Concetti, referred to a publication of essays in 1964 edited by the Swiss lawyer Gertrud Heinzelmann, entitled, ‘_Wir schweigen nicht länger!_ We [^c19-8] Won’t Keep Silence Any Longer!’. The German- and English-speaking authors—including Heinzelmann; German theologians Iris Müller, Ida Raming, and Josefa Theresia Münch; and the Americans Mary Daly and Rosemary Lauer—argued that the Catholic Church should allow women’s ordination to the diaconate and **[p. 319]** priesthood. Concetti was furthermore alarmed by a booklet, ‘Concerning the Ordination of Women’, produced by the World Council of Churches. He stated that ‘some theologians, even qualifled ones’ had supported the women’s initiatives for priesthood, which however had not found an echo in the texts of the council. Concetti’s testimony noted that the women theologians spoke of a number of supportive conciliar fathers. Indeed, the American-German Benedictine Placidus Jordan OSB, for example, was intrigued by Heinzelmann’s petition and sought contact with its author even before the council began. However, after his arrival in Rome, he advised Heinzelmann to change her strategy and to focus primarily on a less misogynistic theology, not on women’s ordination. As a journalist for the American National Catholic Welfare Conference (NCWC) News Service—maintained by the US bishops and today known as Catholic News Service—and as a _peritus_ of the fourth session, Jordan was able to cover the issue of women in the Church in several articles and to work for the dissemination of the women activists’ texts. Above all, Jordan was an expert in networking and persuasion: twenty-five years later, the council father and auxiliary bishop Augustinus Frotz recalled how Jordan had urged him to address the topics of the laity and women in his conciliar speeches. Furthermore, Frotz acknowledged that his thoughts had been shaped by conversations [^c19-9] with the German lay activist Gertrud Ehrle, who became an auditor in 1965.

[^c19-8]: Gertrud Heinzelmann, _Wir schweigen nicht länger! We Won’t Keep Silence Any Longer! Frauen äußern sich zum 2._ _Vatikanischen Konzil. Women Speak Out to Vatican Council II_ (Zurich: Interfeminas, 1964).

[^c19-9]: ‘Weihbischof Augustinus Frotz an Sr. Carmel McEnroy RSM’ (July 1989), in Heyder and Muschiol, _Katholikinnen_, 539–42.

Another activist for women’s ordination was the young German theologian Josefa Theresia Münch, who in 1964 included in her ten-page collection of reform suggestions (_vota_) for the revisions of canon law—most of them concerning women and women religious—the suggestion that CIC/1917 canon 968, §1, ‘only a baptized _man_ can validly receive sacred ordination’, be changed to ‘only a baptized _person_ can validly receive sacred ordination’. She argued that the medieval sources of canon law had dealt with the question of the validity of orders in a very different context, where the primary concern was to avoid cases where unbaptized persons might inadvertently be ordained. When Josefa Theresia Münch sent her suggestions to Cardinal Augustin Bea, he thanked her warmly and encouraged her to continue with her work: ‘I have taken note of everything and will make use of your proposals when the Commission for the Revision of the Code of [^c19-10] Canon Law meets. If you have any further suggestions, I am at your disposal.’ Cardinal Bea saw no need to convince Münch of the impossibility of this specific suggestion concerning CIC/1917 canon 968, §1. Münch, who had been making this point since the days of Pope Pius XII, intensifled her work at the beginning of the council and regularly sent her petitions to all the German bishops.

[^c19-10]: See the complete dossier: Josefa Theresia Münch, ‘Vorschläge zur Reform des Kirchlichen Gesetzes in Bezug auf Frauenrechte’ (15 October 1964), in Heyder and Muschiol, _Katholikinnen_, 275–88; ‘Kardinal Augustin Bea an Josefa Münch’ (20 March 1965), in Heyder and Muschiol, _Katholikinnen_, 293.

The council brought together Gertrud Heinzelmann and the German theologians Josefa Theresia Münch, Ida Raming, and Iris Müller—the last a former Protestant theologian, trained as a vicar, a convert to **[p. 320]** Catholicism, and a refugee from the German Democratic Republic (East Germany). Each woman had different motives for her commitment to women’s ordination. While Heinzelmann lamented discrimination against women in the tradition of St Thomas Aquinas and demanded equal rights for men and women in the Church, Münch, Müller, and Raming felt a personal vocation to priesthood. Münch stressed the pastoral needs resulting from a shortage of priests, especially in developing countries, suggesting this might be easily resolved by the ordination of women. Prior to the publication of _Ordinatio Sacerdotalis_ by Pope John Paul II in 1994, appeals for women’s ordination had greater plausibility. Neo-scholastic handbooks on dogmatic theology had left a small space open for this idea. Today, the women’s appeals can be found in the conciliar records of many bishops. To their credit, the activists succeeded in drawing the attention of the council to the topic of women in the Church.

### 4. Women’s Participation in the Council: Initiatives, Lay Auditors, and Guests

Lay Catholics had long requested that women be allowed to participate in the council. In October 1962, this was still an exotic idea. When, during a press conference, Josefa Theresia Münch asked if women would be present in the assembly, her question was met with laughter. One journalist among those present supposed she was a Protestant, since a Catholic woman would know, of course, that such an idea was absurd.

The following year, on 22 October 1963, the Belgian Cardinal Suenens, archbishop of Mechelen-Brussels, observed in a speech which was soon to become famous, that women make up half of humankind and [^c19-11] should therefore also be invited as auditors. In 1963, thirteen male lay auditors had already taken their seats in the conciliar _aula_. Suenens’s speech raised the hopes of women religious superiors and lay Catholics —and fears among many churchmen. Just a few days later, a rather unpleasant incident occurred. On 30 October 1963, the American journalist Eva Fleischner, a member of the Grail community, took part in the council Mass together with about twenty male colleagues. She had intended to receive communion with her colleagues but was prevented from doing so at the communion rail. The presumably spontaneous action of a functionary in St Peter’s Basilica set a precedent for what would become a principle: in the course of the second session, the council secretariat explicitly excluded women from invitations to council Masses. The reason given was a fear that many women religious superiors would, inspired by Suenens’s speech, ‘rush’ to the council. Only at the closing of the second session were women again permitted to attend the conciliar liturgies.

[^c19-11]: _AS_ II/3, 175–78, at 177.

### 5. Women Auditors

**[p. 321]** The hour of women arrived in the year 1964. On 14 September, at the inauguration of the third conciliar session, Pope Paul VI welcomed the women auditors, ‘our beloved daughters, … who for the first time have [^c19-12] gained the possibility to attend certain conciliar assemblies’. The decision to include women among the lay auditors had been announced only one week earlier. In a homily to religious sisters on 8 September 1964, Pope Paul VI surprised them with the announcement:

[^c19-12]: _AS_ III/1, 140–51, at 149.

We have given instructions that some qualifled and dedicated women should assist, as auditors, at several solemn functions and General Congregations of the forthcoming Third Session of the Second Vatican Council: at those Congregations which will be discussing matters of special interest for the life of women. … The women present will, naturally, be few in number; but it will be a significant and, as it were, a ‘symbolical’ representation.[^c19-13]

[^c19-13]: Rosemary Goldie, _From a Roman Window: Five Decades—The World, the Church and the Laity_ (Melbourne: Harper Collins, 1998), 70.

Australian lay auditor Rosemary Goldie and the American Sr Mary Luke Tobin, SL were convinced that _all_ aspects of the Church’s life were of importance to women. Tobin therefore expressed her intention to attend all general congregations. In their various texts on the council, all women lay auditors resisted the initial idea of a merely ‘symbolic’ or passive representation and stressed the contributions of women.

Despite the inaugural speech of the pope, no female auditor was present in the conciliar _aula_ on 14 September 1964. Only a week later, on 21–22 September 1964, did the secretary general of the council, Pericle Felici, send the first letters of invitation to fifteen women auditors, among them eight religious sisters (mostly superiors or leaders of national associations of women religious), one woman member of a secular institute, two war widows, and four leaders of international Catholic women’s organizations (see Appendix). In October 1964, two more women were added, with the group expanding to twenty-three by 1965. As was the case with their male colleagues, the women auditors represented international Catholic organizations, various fields of activities, different regions of origin, and different rites. The appointment of two war widows was intended to honour ‘those women who, in their mourning and pain, are an eloquent condemnation of war and at the same time a symbol of humanity’s deepest hopes for a just and Christian [^c19-14] peace’. As religious sisters, leaders of lay organizations, or widows—unlike their male colleagues—most of the women auditors were celibate or single. The lay activists had turned their commitment into a ‘profession’ and could therefore dispose of their time more freely than the male auditors, some of whom **[p. 322]** had to ask employers for leave. This imbalance can be seen in photographs of the auditors’ tribune in the conciliar _aula_: the sisters in their different religious habits and the laywomen wearing a mantilla attract more attention than the relatively small number of the male auditors present. It was only in the final year of the council, in 1965, that Luz María Alvarez Icaza was invited to the council as a married woman, with her husband, José. Together they were the founders of the Mexican Movimiento Familiar Cristiano (Christian Family Movement). Originally, only José received an invitation. He agreed on the condition that Luz could also participate. Before arriving in Rome, the couple conducted a survey of the hopes of families for the council. More than 40,000 people in some thirty-five countries answered their questionnaire. The results were presented in a press conference and disseminated in different languages. Again, the responses revealed a broad variety of opinion, including encouraging the lay apostolate, the study of the Bible, various and contradicting suggestions concerning birth control, ecumenism, and a desire for better marriage [^c19-15] preparation.

[^c19-14]: _La civiltà cattolica_ 115, no. 4 (1964): 173 f.

[^c19-15]: José and Luz María Alvarez Icaza, ‘Was erwartet die Familie vom Konzil?’, in Heyder and Muschiol, _Katholikinnen_, 302–6.

On 24 September 1964, Marie-Louise Monnet and Rosemary Goldie were the first women auditors to join the weekly assembly of what had been until then a male-only group of lay auditors. The next day, Monnet was the first woman participant to arrive in the conciliar _aula_. Both Monnet and Goldie had been present in Rome from the opening of the council to follow its proceedings: Australian-born Rosemary Goldie, as executive secretary of COPECIAL, the Permanent Committee for International Congresses of the Lay Apostolate, and Monnet as a leader of MIAMSI, the Mouvement International d’Apostolat des Milieux Sociaux Indépendants. Goldie had also been part of an informal study group which formulated thirteen papers concerning current problems requiring the council’s attention, ranging from international activities of Catholics to the role of women in Church and society. The examples of Goldie and Monnet reveal that women were involved in conciliar politics even before they received the official invitation to serve as lay auditors.

As the lay auditors had no right to speak or to vote in the council’s general congregations, their main activities might be described generally as networking. The laywomen attended the regular meetings of the lay auditors, where on only three occasions a religious sister was present. The women formed a Groupe de travail des auditrices (Working Group of Women Auditors) to intensify the collaboration between religious sisters and laywomen and to study together the council’s texts concerning women especially. From these activities there emerged comments on the drafts of _Apostolicam Actuositatem_, _Gravissimum Educationis_, and _Gaudium et Spes_ (Schema XIII). Rosemary Goldie, Sr Mary Luke Tobin, Hedwig von Skoda, Sr Suzanne Guillemin, María Pilar Bellosillo, and Luz María Alvarez Icaza were members of different subcommissions for Schema XIII. Even before being invited to the council, from the summer of 1963, Rosemary Goldie wrote **[p. 323]** more than ten sets of ‘observations’ on the schemas _De apostolatu laicorum_ and _Ecclesia in mundo huius_ [^c19-16] _temporis_. Luz María Alvarez Icaza is said to have influenced and mitigated the perspective on birth control of the council fathers and that of Pope Paul VI. Other auditors, such as the Germans Sr Juliana Thomas and Gertrud Ehrle, tried to dispel prejudices against religious women in various conversations with council fathers and to put the subject of women on the council’s agenda. However, in the conciliar _aula_, the task of the women auditors was to listen, not to speak. While six male auditors were granted the right to speak, the lay auditors’ request that María Pilar Bellosillo be permitted to publicly express gratitude for the opportunity accorded to the women was denied.

[^c19-16]: Piero Doria, ‘Le Uditrici del Vaticano II nell’Archivio e negli Acta’, in _Tantum aurora est: Donne e Concilio Vaticano II_, ed. Marinella Perroni, Alberto Melloni, and Serena Noceti (Vienna: LIT Verlag, 2012), 33–65, esp. 58–60.

The religious sisters among the auditors were especially interested in the formulation of the decree on religious life, _Perfectae Caritatis_ (_PC_). In January 1965, Fr Joseph Rousseau, secretary of the Commission for Religious, asked them to send their remarks and suggestions for the schema on the adaptation and renewal of the religious life. Most sisters responded to this request and were engaged in an ongoing process of conversation with council fathers on this topic. One idea raised by the sisters concerned the establishment of an international forum of women religious. This led to the foundation of the International Union of Superiors General (UISG), which had its first general assembly in March 1967.

#### Hosts of Informal Conciliar Gatherings

Throughout the four conciliar sessions and the intersessions, the guest houses of women’s congregations in Rome proved not only to be popular accommodations for the council fathers but also became meeting places for different working groups and assemblies. The histories of their various congregations and their regions of origin shaped the mixture of their guests. Similarly, the sisters became more deeply interested in the process of the council, often benefiting from reports and intense exchanges with their guests, and in the final years, from the opportunity to attend conciliar liturgies and events. Contacts between bishops, theologians, and sisters have perhaps never been as close as in these years of the council. In October 1965, for example, the Council for the Implementation of the Constitution on Sacred Liturgy met at the house of the Istituto Santissima Maria Bambina for the celebration of masses _ad experimentum_ in various languages. The sisters were a liturgically trained congregation, willing to provide the necessary vestments and vessels for masses _versus populum_ (facing the people) and concelebrations.[^c19-17]

[^c19-17]: Maria Clara Bianchi, _Il postconcilio e la suora: Documentazione relativa all’attività di madre Costantina Baldinucci come_ _‘uditrice’ al Concilio Ecumenico Vaticano II nella III e IV sessione_ (Viboldone: Tipografia S. Benedetto. 1967), 38.

#### The Women’s Ecumenical Meeting of October 1965

**[p. 324]** The ecumenical meeting of women, held in Vicarello and Rome on 22–29 October 1965, was the first official women’s ecumenical meeting of a comparable breadth. For those attending, it certainly was part of the conciliar ‘event’ (Giuseppe Alberigo). The initiator of this conference was Bishop Johannes Willebrands of the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity. Its planning—entrusted to Madeleine Barot from the World Council of Churches (WCC), and to Rosemary Goldie, one of the outstanding lay auditors—was itself ecumenical. The Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity invited twelve Catholic participants, among them four members of the international Grail Movement, to which Goldie belonged, and three lay auditors (María del Pilar Bellosillo, Sr Mary Luke Tobin, and Mrs Catherine McCarthy). The WCC also designated twelve Protestant and Orthodox participants, including Madeleine Barot, from the department on Cooperation of Men and Women in Church, Family and Society (WCC); Cynthia C. Wedel, who would become president of the National Council of Churches, USA, from 1969 to 1972 and a president of the WCC from 1975 to 1983; and Swiss theologian and ecumenical activist Marga Bührig, also a future president of the WCC (1983–91). Three of the Protestant women were deaconesses; one was an Anglican nun. Most of the participants came from Europe or North America. During the conference, Fr Bernhard Häring and Fr Paul Verghese served as ecumenical ‘observers’.

The conference began in Vicarello (near Lake Bracciano, north of Rome) with days of exchange and talks given by the women themselves. Each day, a ‘Mass in English following the latest liturgical use’ was held, as Anglican Sr Brigitta observed. Cynthia Wedel reported that the women discovered their common

concern for missions, for social action in our communities, for young people and better family life. All are seeking for more vital forms of prayer and devotional life. All want better education and training for the laity. All have an increasing number of women studying theology. … All feel restive under the restrictions placed upon women by the Church at a time when the secular world is rapidly removing such restrictions.[^c19-18]

[^c19-18]: Cynthia Wedel, ‘Church Women and Christian Unity’, _Catholic World_ 202 (1966): 278–82, at 280.

The days that followed in Rome, from 25 to 29 October 1965, were filled with conferences and receptions. The women heard from Fr Thomas Stransky (Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity) and Lukas Vischer (Official Observer for the WCC), who briefed them on the work of the council. They met Bishop Willebrands and Cardinal Bea. They visited the Foyer Unitas run by the Ladies of Bethany at Piazza Navona, where the non-Catholic Christian observers held regular meetings. They attended a supper at the home of the brothers of Taizé, who during the council sought to promote ecumenism through their ministry of hospitality. A **[p. 325]** highlight was the promulgation of five conciliar decrees on 28 October 1965, which the women attended in the conciliar _aula_. The next day they adopted a resolution stressing that ‘women in the Churches are longing for unity … and they believe that together they have a contribution to make towards achieving [^c19-19] unity’. One specific suggestion soon proved successful: the participants asked that Catholic women be allowed to participate in the ecumenical Women’s World Day of Prayer.

[^c19-19]: ‘Resolution der Ökumenischen Frauen in Vicarello und Rom’ (22–29 October 1965), in Heyder and Muschiol, _Katholikinninen_, 551–52.

### 6. Council Texts on Women

When speaking of the laity, the Latin conciliar documents oscillate between gender-inclusive language and generic male language. For example, the passage on ‘the people of God’ in the Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, _Lumen Gentium_ (9–17), uses terms like _credentes_ (believers), _fideles_ (the faithful), _homines_ (men, humankind), _baptizati_ (the baptized), _universi discipuli Christi_ (all the disciples of Christ), _filii Dei_ (sons of God), and _Ecclesiae filii_ (sons of the church, children of the church). Only on rare occasions do the conciliar texts, however, draw attention to specific developments and problems of particular concern to women. This was entirely in line with the wishes of two women auditors. In a strategizing conversation, Rosemary Goldie and María del Pilar Bellosillo had agreed that the council should abstain from defining women’s role in society and Church in a rigid or even poetic way.[^c19-20]

[^c19-20]: Rosemary Goldie, ‘La Participation des laïcs aux travaux du concile Vatican II’, _Revue de sciences religieuses_ 62, no. 1 (1988): 54–73, at 72.

The first text to be analysed here is, however, a conciliar text _avant la lettre_: Pope John XXIII’s final encyclical, issued on 11 April 1963, ‘on establishing universal peace in truth, justice, charity, and liberty’. This encyclical would become highly influential for the council as a whole, especially for the Declaration on Religious Freedom, _Dignitatis Humanae_, and for the Pastoral Constitution on the Church, _Gaudium et Spes_. The pope identifled several ‘characteristics of the present day’ or ‘signs of the times’, among them ‘the part that women are now playing in political life’: ‘Women are gaining an increasing awareness of their natural dignity. Far from being content with a purely passive role or allowing themselves to be regarded as a kind of instrument, they are demanding both in domestic and in public life the rights and duties which belong to them as human persons’ (_Pacem in Terris_ (_PT_), 41). This means nothing less than that the encyclical considered the women’s movement relevant and exemplary for the Church.

It is _Pacem in Terris_’s conviction that men and women possess an equal dignity as human persons and therefore have the right ‘to choose for themselves the kind of life which appeals to them: whether it is to found a family—in the founding of which both the man and the woman enjoy equal rights and duties—or to **[p. 326]** embrace the priesthood or the religious life’ (_PT_ 15). The idea of men and women enjoying equal rights and duties in marriage was revolutionary with regard to the Church’s teaching. Up until this time, the ‘ready subjection of the wife and her willing obedience’, as the encyclical _Casti Connubii_ (1930) put it, was a long-standing theological tradition, going back to St Paul. Theologians around Pope John XXIII had tried in vain to soften this passage of _Pacem in Terris_ by reiterating the subordination of wives to their husbands or by speaking of the ‘similar’ (not equal) rights and duties of women in matrimony. Yet, _Pacem in Terris_’s teaching won the day. When the Pastoral Constitution _Gaudium et Spes_ (_GS_) dealt with ‘promoting the dignity of marriage and the family’ (_GS_ 47–52), it reflected on the duties of parents without any consideration of a difference between sexes or the different roles of wives and husbands in family life. Other conciliar texts, however, strengthen the concept of an essential difference between sexes. The Declaration on Christian Education, _Gravissimum Educationis_ (_GE_), claims that teachers ‘should, together with the parents, make full allowance for the difference of sex and for the particular role which providence has appointed to each sex in the family and in society’ (_GE_ 8). This ‘difference of sex’ is not specifled. And when _Gaudium et Spes_ declares that ‘We must do everything possible to make everyone aware of their right to culture and their duty to develop themselves culturally’ (_GS_ 60), the constitution is aware of the various difficulties in realizing this concept. It explicitly mentions rural people, manual labourers, and women. Again, it refers to the signs of the times: ‘At present women are involved in nearly all spheres of life: they ought to be permitted to play their part fully in ways suited to their nature.’ Everyone, therefore, should ‘see to it that women’s specific and necessary participation in cultural life be acknowledged and developed’ (_GS_ 60). _Gaudium et Spes_ on this occasion draws on a difference between the sexes (‘suited to their nature’, ‘women’s specific and necessary participation’) to claim women’s participation in cultural life. Indeed, in the process of women’s emancipation, it was a well-known strategy to stress the differences between the sexes and therefore the necessary complement of men’s contribution to society or politics by women. This passage in _Gaudium et Spes_ may be, at least partially, a result of the influence of German lay auditor Gertrud Ehrle, who in her conciliar calendar on 16 September 1965 reports a colloquium with auxiliary bishop Augustinus Frotz and its intention: ‘Concerning Scheme XIII—insert a passage on “women” in several places.’[^c19-21]

[^c19-21]: ‘Gertrud Ehrle, Konzilskalender’, in Heyder and Muschiol, _Katholikinnen_, 523–29, at 525.

Equal rights flow from the essential equality in the orders of creation and redemption. In the words of _Gaudium et Spes_:

All women and men are endowed with a rational soul and are created in God’s image; they have the same nature and origin and, being redeemed by Christ, they enjoy the same divine calling and destiny; there is here a basic equality between all and it must be given ever greater recognition. … But any kind of social or cultural discrimination in basic personal rights on the grounds of sex, race, colour, social conditions, language or religion, must be curbed and eradicated as **[p. 327]** incompatible with God’s design. It is regrettable that these basic personal rights are not yet being respected everywhere, as is the case with women who are denied the chance freely to choose a husband, or a state of life, or to have access to the same educational and cultural benefits as are available to men. (_GS_ 29)

Discrimination against women, who in many regions still do not enjoy equal rights, remains an important fleld of activity for Christian social action.

_Pacem in Terris_ and the conciliar texts sought to promote women’s emancipation in society more than in the Church. It is only in the Decree on the Apostolate of the Laity, _Apostolicam Actuositatem_ (_AA_), that women’s contribution in the Church is mentioned: ‘The lay apostolate, in all its many aspects, is exercised both in the Church and in the world. … Since in our days women are taking an increasingly active share in the whole life of society, it is very important that their participation in the various sectors of the Church’s apostolate should likewise develop’ (_AA_ 9). Ferdinand Klostermann, a member of the conciliar Commission on the Lay Apostolate, observed in his commentary that this sentence was formulated as a proposed amendment by [^c19-22] two bishops at the insistence of the women auditors. Since the council, women’s active participation in societal life has increased substantially; it is an ongoing task to elucidate the relevance of this process for the life of the Church.

[^c19-22]: Ferdinand Klostermann, ‘Decree on the Apostolate of the Laity’, in _Commentary on the Documents of Vatican II_, ed. Herbert Vorgrimler, vol. 3 (New York: Herder and Herder, 1969), 335.

The last texts to be mentioned here are the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy, _Sacrosanctum Concilium_, and the Decree on Renewal of Religious Life, _Perfectae Caritatis_, both of which would have an impact on celibate women. According to the Constitution on the Liturgy, ‘the rite of the Consecration of Virgins contained in the Roman Pontifical is to be revised’. The council fathers originally intended to reform the consecration of virgins in connection with the monastic profession of nuns, but in the end the respective commission in 1970 developed a rite based on the ancient sources and destined for the consecration of women living in the ‘world’. Today, more than 5,000 women live as consecrated virgins.

The updating of the life of women religious had been a constant concern of Pope Pius XII. During the council, especially the religious sisters among the auditors contributed to this ongoing process of renewal. In the end, the decree _Perfectae Caritatis_ included only a few remarks on women religious and above all on contemplative nuns. Religious foundations of women were encouraged to establish only one class of sisters (formerly, there had been two convents in the same monastery: one consisting of nuns with solemn vows, and one of lay sisters under simple vows). The strict papal cloister of contemplative nuns was to be maintained, but adapted to the conditions of time and place (_PC_ 15).

For Catholic women as individuals and as members of women’s organizations, the council proved to be a catalyst. Bishops, theologians, and the conciliar (preparatory) commissions were soon invited to address **[p. 328]** various suggestions and petitions of women. Their texts covered issues such as the status of women— and of laypeople in general—in the Church, priestly formation, the attitude of priests towards women, liturgy, birth control, and ecumenism. Some women, especially theologians, asked that women be ordained to the diaconate and priesthood. The reasons given ranged from gender equality to pastoral needs and the conviction of a personal vocation.

Soon after the council was announced, Catholic women expressed their desire to participate in the assembly. In the third and fourth sessions of the council in 1964 and 1965, twenty-three female auditors attended the general congregations, contributed to the formulation of various texts, and shaped the work of the council through networking. In addition to the auditors, women were involved in the council’s work as experts, journalists, unofficial collaborators or advisers, and hosts. Following the council, a great number of Catholic women understood themselves as multipliers of this event. A general and perhaps overly optimistic impression was that the council had essentially contributed to women’s equality with men, at least in regard to the status of lay Catholics.
