## 20. Vatican II and the Theology of Reception

Gilles Routhier

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 333]** Any attempt to find an erudite presentation of the notion of reception in the documents of Vatican II would [^c20-1] be futile. While a search will find uses of the verb _recipere_ and the noun _receptio_, taken together they do not allow us to constitute a theory of reception. Any inquiry based on the term ‘reception’ in the documents of Vatican II would therefore yield disappointing results. Reception is certainly mentioned in _Lumen Gentium_ (_LG_) 22 and _Christus Dominus_ (_CD_) 4, in the context of the act of the Roman pontiff as he receives and [^c20-2] confirms the acts of an ecumenical council or of the College of Bishops scattered throughout the world. It has been suggested that a teaching on reception can be found in _Lumen Gentium_ 12, which deals with the _sensus fidei fidelium_, or at no. 25 of that same constitution, which deals with the requirement that the faithful adhere to the magisterial teachings of the pope or bishops. Olivier Clément states that ‘in light of the Vatican II texts, the issue of reception nevertheless finds expression in terms of obedience rather than synergy (cf. _LG_ 25). The supernatural sense of the faith of all the people can be made manifest only through [^c20-3] the consent expressed in the Dogmatic Constitution (_LG_ 12).’ The resulting impression, suggesting that reception is a unilateral process whereby the faithful adhere to the teachings of the magisterium, is **[p. 334]** somewhat amended elsewhere in the Constitution. _Lumen Gentium_ 45 says that pastors receive the rules presented by men and women (‘regulas praeclaris viris et mulieribus propositas recipit’). More importantly, and this seems to be a unique case, the decree _Inter Mirifica_ 24 discusses the reception of the teaching of the council by all the faithful.

[^c20-1]: The verb _accipere_ (ninety occurrences) is used more than _recipere_ (thirty-five occurrences) to provide the idea of receiving or of welcoming.

[^c20-2]: ‘Concilium Oecumenicum numquam datur, quod a Successore Petri non sit ut tale confirmatum vel saltem receptum’ (_LG_ 22) and ‘vel saltem episcoporum dispersorum unitam actionem approbet vel libere recipiat’ (_CD_ 4).

[^c20-3]: Olivier Clément, ‘Après Vatican II: Vers un dialogue théologique entre catholiques et orthodoxes’, _La Pensée orthodoxe_ 13 (1968): 46. Hermann Josef Pottmeyer comments on no. 25 in his study of its reception: ‘Rezeption und Gehorsam— Aktuelle Aspekte der wiederentdeckten Realität “Rezeption” ’, in _Glaube als Zustimmung: Zur Interpretation kirchlicher_ _Rezeptionsvorgänge_, ed. Wolfgang Beinert et al. (Freiburg i.Br.: Herder, 1991), 81–84.

On closer examination, other references to reception can be found. _Lumen Gentium_ 51 states that a council receives the teaching of previous councils: ‘magna cum pietate haec Sacrosancta Synodus recipit et decreta Sacrorum Conciliorum Nicaeni II, Florentini et Tridentini rursus proponit’. Similarly, _Gaudium et Spes_ (_GS_) 91 notes that the teaching of the Pastoral Constitution is ‘already accepted in the Church [_doctrina miam in Ecclesia receptam_]’.

Another aspect of reception is found in _Gaudium et Spes_ 44. In this case, it is the assistance the Church receives (_accipit_) from the modern world (‘De adiutorio quod Ecclesia a mundo hodierno accipit’), while further acknowledging all that it received from the history and development of humanity (‘Ecclesia non ignorat, quantum ex humani generis historia et evolutione acceperit’). It continues to receive wide-ranging assistance from people of all classes and conditions (‘varium adiutorium ab hominibus cuiusvis gradus vel condicionis accipere’). This idea can be found in many passages of the council’s documents, such as _Lumen Gentium_ 13, _Gaudium et Spes_ 62, as well as _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ (_SC_) (in the numerous passages dealing with adaptations for different peoples) and _Ad Gentes_ (_AG_) (in particular 22).

That being said, in the council’s document—and this is crucial—that which is received in the Church is the word of God (_LG_ 12, 37; _SC_ 6; _Presbyterorum Ordinis_ (_PO_) 13), the Gospel (_LG_ 16, 19; _GS_ 57; _AG_ 27; _Nostra Aetate_ (_NA_) 4), the books of the Old Testament (_Dei Verbum_ (_DV_) 15), Revelation (_LG_ 25; _NA_ 4), doctrine (_Dignitatis Humanae_ (_DH_) 12), truth (_DH_ 14), and the heritage of the apostles (_Unitatis Redintegratio_ (_UR_) 14). We are dealing here with the fundamental pairing of tradition and reception, understood from a wide and fundamental viewpoint, beyond the welcoming of a council’s decisions. This relates to the process by which the Church is built up: through the welcoming and free reception of God’s gifts. Thus, the Church and the faithful continue to receive God’s very self (_GS_ 32), the Spirit (_SC_ 6, 11), sanctification (_LG_ 40), grace (_LG_ 12, 13; _SC_ 11, 33, 59; _PO_ 12; _Apostolicam Actuositatem_ (_AA_) 3), and different gifts and charisms (_LG_ 43; _DV_ 8; _PO_ 6, 10; _AA_ 4). Among these gifts, faith stands out (_LG_ 11; _AG_ 14, 41; _DH_ 14). Finally, the Church and the faithful also receive their mission (_LG_ 5, 17, 24; _GS_ 34; _PO_ 1; _AA_ 11, 25), their vocation (_PO_ 12), and the impulse of the Spirit (_GS_ 92).

The Church is therefore a community of reception of the gift of God. This originating process of gift and reception is fundamental to developing a theology of reception. It is from this first and originating fact that **[p. 335]** the reception of magisterial teachings is derived. All other experiences of reception flow from this paradigmatic experience and are similar to it. Before speaking about the reception of a council, one must think of the Church as a place where God’s gifts are welcomed and received, and one must draw attention to the fact that this people is constituted by an act of tradition and reception. It is in welcoming God’s gifts and God’s word, and responding in faith to this word, that the Church is born and continues to be built up. Only this depth of understanding will allow a full comprehension of reception within Christianity.

There are, therefore, in the Vatican II documents a number of elements that could form the initial outline of a theology of reception. However, searching for words used by a council to establish a foundation on which to then build a theory of reception is not an adequate way forward. Such a method, which involves [^c20-4] discerning a reality based on the only words that refer to it, is limited, as Congar has noted. In any case, a council represents an experience of reception: reception of Scripture, reception of the creed, reception of the teachings of previous councils, reception of magisterial teachings, reception of the customs and traditions [^c20-5] that make up the heritage of the different churches within their cultural context, and so on. Rather than tracking down words, one must pursue realities. If a word cannot always be found, a reality remains apparent.

[^c20-4]: Concerning the potential and the limits of an investigation derived from the words used in the councils, see Yves Congar, ‘L’Église en cartes: À propos du traitement informatique des textes de Vatican I’, in _Le Concile de Vatican II: Son Église_ _peuple de Dieu et Corps du Christ_, Théologie historique 71 (Paris: Beauchesne, 1984), 73–78.

[^c20-5]: See Gilles Routhier, ‘Orientamenti per lo studio del Vaticano II come fatto di ricezione’, in _L’Evento e le decisioni: Studi sulle_ _dinamiche del concilio Vaticano II_, Testi e ricerche di scienze religiose nuova serie 20, ed. Maria Teresa Fattori and Alberto Melloni (Bologna: Il Mulino, 1997), 465–99.

Undoubtedly of greater importance is the fact that the teachings of Vatican II themselves provide the [^c20-6] necessary theological context for developing a theology of reception. As Congar pointed out, this presupposes a theology of tradition, a theology of the local Church, the restoration of communion between churches, and an unwavering espousal of a pneumatological perspective. Furthermore, any theology of reception presupposes that the Church is situated in history and enshrined in various cultures. That is the theological context within which a theology of reception can unfold. Even if its developments remain at times unfinished, Vatican II represents clear progress in these different areas by reintegrating these diverse elements into the discussion.

[^c20-6]: See Yves Congar, ‘La Réception comme réalité ecclésiologique’, _Revue des sciences philosophiques et théologiques_ 56 (1972): 392.

Vatican II therefore highlights and promotes ecclesial realities that will foster a practice of reception and the development of a theology of reception that started in the 1970s. The following paragraphs provide a brief overview of the fundamental elements proposed by Vatican II which, in time, will comprise the ecclesial and theological context that will foster the reception of Vatican II.

### 2. A Theology of Tradition

**[p. 336]** The issue of _tradition_ was the subject of bitter debates at Vatican II and, contrary to what one might think, these were not limited to discussions of _Dei Verbum_. In fact, the real debate on tradition is found elsewhere. The issue arose in the first few lines of the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy: ‘The Sacred Council has set out … to adapt more closely to the needs of our age those institutions which are subject to change’ (_SC_ 1). Already, a stumbling block is placed in the way of those who are mistakenly called traditionalists. In their view, nothing is subject to change; past ecclesial institutions and ways of Christian life are timeless and [^c20-7][^c20-8] sacred. For them, there is no ‘today’, a term that the council so often took up; there are no cultures or [^c20-9] customs; there are no traditions belonging to the different peoples in which the Church has taken root ) and who are to receive the spiritual heritage of the Church.

[^c20-7]: Thus, the adverb _hodie_ (today) occurs forty-six times in the documents of Vatican II and the term _hodiernus_ (of our time) appears eighty-nine times. The word _tempus_ (time) is used 243 times, and _ӕtas_ (epoch, age), eighty-five times. These terms often accompany the substantive _condicio_ (condition), which occurs 195 times, or are preceded by the possessive adjective: our times, our age. Vatican II calls us ‘to adapt more closely to the needs of our age’ (_SC_ 1), acknowledges that ‘some changes are necessary to adapt [the rites] to present day needs’ since ‘there have crept into the rites … certain features which have rendered their nature and purpose far from clear to the people of today’ (_SC_ 62). It invites us to attend to ‘the circumstances of our times’ (_SC_ 79), preserving and restoring them ‘to suit the conditions of modern times’ (_SC_ 107), etc.

[^c20-8]: Vatican II is the first council to treat the question of culture _ex professo_, consecrating an entire chapter to it in part II of the Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World, _Gaudium et Spes_. The term _cultura_ occurs ninety-one times in the conciliar corpus, while the adjective _culturalis_ appears thirty-four times. Vatican II affirms the importance of adapting the proclamation of the Gospel to the languages of diverse peoples, highlighting the wisdom of the philosophers and their contribution to the understanding of its message by all, noting that this is ‘the law of all evangelisation’ (_GS_ 44).

[^c20-9]: _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ speaks of the mentality and the traditions of the peoples (forty), the traditions found in various regions (eighty-one), and the musical traditions of the people (119). The Constitution speaks abundantly of the customs proper to each region or territory. In the Constitution on Sacred Liturgy alone, we find ten references to territories (_SC_ 22, 36, 39, 40, 44, 63, 77, 119, 120, 128), eleven to regions (_SC_ 23, 25, 36, 38, 63, 77, 110, 119, 119, 123, 127) and five to different peoples (_SC_ 37, 38, 77, 119, 123).

The most significant debate at Vatican II was about tradition. For some, nothing can be added to that which has already been said or done. All that matters is the past; one can only repeat or reproduce it. Local churches are not subjects that act and take initiative, but receivers, and receivers play no creative role. The local churches only implement, since they are not called to adapt, and to receive never means to assimilate that which is transmitted, make it one’s own, update it to fit new circumstances, and express it anew. Those who hold such a view see tradition simply as a repetition, whereas _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ proposes a revision of the rites ‘in the light of sound tradition, and that they be given new vigour to meet present-day circumstances and needs’ (_SC_ 4). While the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy wished to move forward **[p. 337]** while respecting the tradition, ‘[i]n order that sound tradition be retained, and yet the way remain open to legitimate progress’ (_SC_ 23), others wanted to stop time and the organic development of approaches. This debate about tradition permeates the whole of the council.

In his opening address to the council, John XXIII raised the issue of tradition when he stated what was at play: the proclamation of the Gospel over time and within the cultures of the world. The beginning of a new era requires that what has come from the apostles be received (reappropriated) and expressed anew. As he presented to the fathers the primary task of the council in his opening speech, _Gaudet Mater Ecclesia_, John XXIII broached the issue of tradition or, to be more precise, the issue of ‘transmission’, which is the action of passing on to others a heritage that will be updated and adapted for a new context and will be revitalized in a new situation. His wish was that the council’s work be rooted in tradition:

Its [the twenty-first Ecumenical Council] intention is to give to the world the whole of that doctrine … to transmit it in all its purity, undiluted, undistorted … And our duty is not just to guard this treasure, as though it were some museum-piece and we were the curators, but earnestly and fearlessly to dedicate ourselves to the work that needs to be done in this modern age of ours, pursuing the path which the Church has followed for almost twenty centuries. Nor are we here primarily to discuss certain fundamentals of Catholic doctrine, or to restate in greater detail the traditional teaching of the Fathers and of early and more recent theologians … There would be no need to call a council merely to hold discussions of that nature. What is needed at the present time is … the unreserved acceptance by all of the entire Christian faith … What is needed is that this certain and immutable doctrine, to which the faithful owe obedience, be studied afresh and reformulated in the contemporary terms. For this deposit of the faith, or truths which are contained in our time-honoured teaching, is one thing; the manner in which these truths are set forth (with their meaning preserved intact) is something else. This, then, is what will require our careful, and perhaps too our patient, consideration. We must work out ways and means of expounding these truths in a manner more consistent with a predominantly pastoral view of the Church’s teaching office. (https://www.vatican.va/content/john-xxiii/la/speeches/1962/documents/hf_j-xxiii_spe_19621011_opening-council.html)

The council is thus perceived as an act of tradition and reception, and, in the final analysis, as an act of re-expression of doctrine. In this respect, John XXIII is not really innovating. Rather, he found himself in continuity with the other councils, many of which were focused on formulating creeds to witness to the faith of the Church in new contexts and to express this faith to new people. Councils thus represent the highest form of witness to the Gospel, in that they carry out an act of tradition that allows for both the reception of the Gospel and the shedding of light on it in a manner suitable to the most diverse historical and cultural contexts.

In his address, John XXIII had in mind this living and innovating nature of tradition. The council is called upon to receive, to transmit, and to re-express. Its primary purpose is not to add new chapters to this **[p. 338]** doctrine so as to broaden it (additive tradition), nor is it ‘to repeat at length what the Fathers and ancient and more recent theologians have handed on’ (repetitive tradition). The council is called upon, on the one hand, to receive things from the past and, on the other, ‘to eagerly and without fear … devote ourselves to the task our age demands’. Tradition is therefore innovative and creative, since to transmit (or engage) the tradition is to make available to people of today or of our era the doctrinal and spiritual ‘heritage’ that we receive.

From the opening of Vatican II, the issue of tradition was raised in terms of the revitalization or re-expression of the spiritual heritage of Christianity. It is understood as an act of transmission of that which has been received, which led the council to find itself between two poles: on the one hand, the religious heritage received and inherited from the past, and, on the other, the present-day recipients to whom this heritage must be addressed and whose new context must be considered. As is the case in the baptismal catechumenate, tradition (_traditio_) combines with reception (_receptio_) and re-expression (_redditio_).

On this basis, it is not surprising that among the conciliar documents, it is in _Ad Gentes_, the Decree on the Missionary Activity of the Church, that are found some of the most important statements for an [^c20-10] understanding of the notion of tradition, particularly at nos. 18 and 22:

[^c20-10]: We find ninety-one occurrences of the term _traditio_ in the documents of Vatican II, of which fourteen appear in _Ad Gentes_ and twelve in _Dei Verbum._ Indeed, a full reading of the texts allows us to measure the importance of its different uses. Often, it refers to the traditions (to customs, and thus to culture) of diverse peoples (as in the case of _Sacrosanctum_ _Concilium_: seventeen times) and sometimes in _Ad Gentes_ as well. As for the verb _tradere_, it is used seventy-eight times, fiffeen of which are found in _Dei Verbum_ and four in _Ad Gentes._ We find it seven times in _Christus Dominus_ and _Presbyterorum Ordinis,_ when speaking of preaching and catechesis, and five times in _Optatam Totius_, when speaking of the priestly formation.

Religious institutes, which are working for the implanting of the Church and which are deeply imbued with those mystical graces which are part of the Church’s religious tradition [_traditio religiosa Ecclesiae_], should strive to give them expression and to hand them on [_exprimere et tradere_] in a manner in keeping with the character and outlook of each nation. (_AG_ 18)

This paragraph suggests that when it comes to the encounter with a new culture, there is still work to be done to rearticulate the Church’s heritage, taking into consideration the new context in which it finds itself at that particular time in its pilgrimage. This is taken up again at no. 22:

So too indeed, just as happened in the economy of the incarnation, the young churches … take [to themselves all] the riches of nations which have been given to Christ as an inheritance (see Ps 2:8). They borrow from the customs, traditions, wisdom, teaching, arts and sciences of their people everything which could be used to praise the glory of the Creator, manifest the grace of the saviour, **[p. 339]** or contribute to the right ordering of Christian life (_LG_ 13). To achieve this, it is necessary that in each of the great socio-cultural regions, as they are called, theological investigation should be encouraged and the facts and words revealed by God, contained in the sacred scripture, and explained by the fathers and magisterium of the church, submitted to a new examination in light of the tradition of the universal church. In this way it will be more clearly understood by what means the faith can be explained in terms of the philosophy and wisdom of the people, and how their customs, attitude to life and social structures can be reconciled with the standard proposed by divine revelation. Thus a way will be opened for a more profound adaptation in the whole sphere of Christian life. [In this way] the Christian life will be adapted to the mentality and character of each culture; and local traditions together with the special qualities of each national family, illumined by the light of the gospel, will be taken up into a Catholic unity. So new particular churches, each with its own traditions, have their place in the community of the church, the primacy of Peter which presides over this universal assembly of charity () all the while remaining intact.

In this interplay of tradition–reception–re-expression, one subject emerges: young churches, as active subjects, called to receive the Gospel in its fullness and to take for themselves the riches of the nations.

Only after reading these passages can we return to reading a paragraph of the Constitution _Dei Verbum_:

The tradition that comes from the apostles makes progress [_proficit_] in the church, with the help of the Holy Spirit. There is a growth [_crescit_] in insight into the realities and words that are being passed on. This comes about through the contemplation and study of believers who ponder these things in their hearts (see Lk 2:19 and 51). It comes from the intimate sense of spiritual realities which they experience. And it comes from the preaching of those who, on succeeding to the office of bishop, have received the sure chrism of truth. Thus, as the centuries go by, the church is always advancing towards the plenitude of divine truth, until eventually the words of God are fulfilled in it. (_DV_ 8)

Thus, the understanding of that which has been received from the apostles increases in the encounter with new situations, which leads to a rereading of the spiritual heritage of Christianity and to developing a new comprehension of things and new insights. It is therefore clear that a theology of reception presupposes a sound theology of tradition that presents the history of God’s gifts in particular human settings and the reception of these gifts by active subjects who internalize them to the point of making them their own.

The issue of tradition finds itself at the intersection of many other issues—that of the local Church, of the communion of churches—and assumes a theology of cultures. Vatican II represents a clear step forward in these many fields, even though its consideration of these areas often remains incomplete. Its theology of [^c20-11][^c20-12] **[p. 340]** the local Church remains underdeveloped, with a pneumatology that some see as deficient, and its theology of communion between churches has not yet assumed its rightful place. However, Vatican II laid the foundations for future development that would come.

[^c20-11]: See Gilles Routhier, ‘ “Église locale” ou “Église particulière”: Querelle sémantique ou option théologique?’, _Studia_ _Canonica_ 25 (1991): 277–334.

[^c20-12]: See Yves Congar, ‘La Pneumatologie du concile Vatican II’, _Je crois en l’Esprit Saint_ (Paris: Cerf, 1995), 227–35.

### 3. A Theology of the Local Church

The development of a _theology of the local Church_ clearly represents one of the most decisive contributions of [^c20-13] the post-conciliar era. This renewed appreciation of local churches as subjects having rights and being able to take action is crucial, since reception cannot be considered if local churches are not able, in an active and creative way, to welcome, internalize, integrate, and claim ownership of what is being offered to them. The local churches are not simply passive recipients of conciliar teaching. They are called upon not to pass judgement on the truth of such teaching, but to assess its advisability given their particular ecclesial, social, and cultural situation. They are not simply subordinate to a higher authority that would dictate their actions. Within the communion of churches, they have an active role to play so they can make their own whatever is offered to them, according to the particular character of the nation in which they have taken root.

[^c20-13]: See esp. the important work on this subject by Jean-Marie R. Tillard, _L’Église locale: Ecclésiologie de communion et_ _catholicité_, Cogitatio fidei 191 (Paris: Cerf, 1995).

The development of a _theology of the local Church_ not only allows the Church to be seen as a subject having rights, capable of action, and able to take initiative; it also allows a vision of a Church of subjects, all enabled to participate actively in different ways in the life of the Church. One can therefore speak of the reception of a council by a Church-subject and a Church of subjects. It is important to emphasize that these subjects are connected to a body and, all together, form a living body of which they are the members. Otherwise, reception is reduced to the individual judgement of each member of the faithful on the teaching of pastors. In such a situation, churches would no longer exist, and all that would remain is the relationship between individuals: pastors and believers disconnected from the body. As is too often the case today, reception is used to discuss what is seen as the possibility offered to the faithful to go along (or not) with the teaching of pastors, where they choose only what they like. Such an understanding of reception proposes that each of the faithful has the ability to express their consent or dissent. An appeal to the _sensus fidelium_ that is free of any organic link to the Church body or to the _sentire cum Ecclesia_ is not without its problems. Reception, considered as an ‘ecclesial reality’, therefore requires the renewal of the local churches. Reception is difficult to envisage unless the whole Church is considered in terms of local churches living in communion **[p. 341]** with each other, a communion that is nourished, fostered, protected, and preserved by bonds established between them and with the Church of Rome.

Vatican II certainly took a few steps in that direction, which allows for the development of a theology of reception even though its legacy remains ambiguous in this area. A study of Vatican II with respect to reception requires a review of the conciliar documents where the issue of the relationship between churches is broached (notably, _LG_ 13 and 23). Special attention needs to be paid to the passages dealing with the relationship between local churches and the whole Church (_tota Ecclesia_) as well as those that recognize the existence of churches enjoying their own traditions, their particular discipline, specific liturgical practices, or a distinctive spiritual and theological heritage (notably _LG_ 13; _Orientalium Ecclesiarium_ (_OE_) 3, 5–6; _UR_ 14–16), along with those where attempts were made to develop the joints and ligaments that enable a dialogue between churches and the development of this communion of churches (notably _LG_ 13 and _AG_ 22). Of particular significance is the passage dealing with ‘family ties between Churches’ in _Unitatis Redintegratio_ 14. While the term ‘reception’ is not used, the text points out that the Latin Church received many elements of liturgy, spiritual tradition, and law from the treasures of the Eastern churches. There is therefore a process of sharing and receiving of each Church’s gifts.

A theology of the local Church cannot be based solely on the passages that acknowledge it and on developments that promote a dialogue, in communion, between churches. An effective restoration of local [^c20-14] churches leads to a real concern for the _pleroma_ of the Church, to use a beautiful Orthodox expression. Thus, when relationships between churches are considered only through the lens of episcopal collegiality, they do not lead us down the path of a healthy theology of reception. In line with tradition, episcopal collegiality must be expressed within the framework of the communion of churches, which in turn involves [^c20-15][^c20-16] the synodal life of the local churches. Cyprian offers the model testimony on this matter.

[^c20-14]: See Alexandros Papaderos, ‘Quelques réflexions sur la réception sans laisser de côté la vie et le plérôme de l’Église’, _Proche-Orient Chrétien_ 33 (1983): 186–89.

[^c20-15]: See Nikos Nissiotis, ‘Die Ekklesiologie des zweiten vatikanischen Konzils in orthodoxer Sicht und ihre ökumenische Bedeutung’, _Kerygma und Dogma_ 10 (1964): 157–58.

[^c20-16]: Cyprian, _Letters_, 19.2.2 and 34.4.1. He articulates perfectly the internal synodality of his church, the communion of the churches, and the collegiality of the bishops.

### 4. A Consistent Pneumatology

Church-subjects are also churches of subjects: this involves a theology of the Holy Spirit, who pours out its charisms upon all members of the people of God. This is where _pneumatology_ comes into play. A rereading of Vatican II with respect to reception requires a reconsideration of its teaching on the various gifts bestowed **[p. 342]** on all the members of the Church and of the active participation of all the faithful in the life of the local [^c20-17] Church . This will lead to a careful examination of everything Vatican II affirms regarding the synodality of the local Church. It finds expression not only in the creation of a diocesan pastoral council (_CD_ 27) and of a presbyteral council (_PO_ 7), but also by all that the council affirms about listening, discussion, and dialogue [^c20-18] within the Church. These concrete processes are the foundation on which reception is built.

[^c20-17]: See Gilles Routhier, « La pneumatologie de Vatican II », _Perspectiva Teológica_ 52, n. 2 (2020): 375–392.

[^c20-18]: Gilles Routhier, ‘La Synodalité de l’Église locale’, _Studia Canonica_ 26 (1992): 111–61.

In describing the Church as the People of God, Vatican II first considers the _pleroma_ of the Church, thus avoiding the danger of reducing the Church to the hierarchy. From this perspective, the Church is seen as a whole. This leads to highlighting the value of the common priesthood of all the faithful and of the participation of all in the three functions of Christ—priest, prophet, and king—which the council established on the basis of a sacramental right bestowed through baptism and, more broadly, by the sacraments of Christian initiation. This also makes it possible to highlight the value of the gifts of the Spirit shared among all the faithful. Indeed, it has been noted that there are more references to the gifts of the Spirit in chapter 2 than in the rest of _Dei Verbum_.

The faithful’s participation in the prophetic function of the Church rests therefore on the acknowledgement of the fact that they have been anointed with the Holy Spirit. Such an acknowledgement is the basis upon which they have been given an active role in reception.

### 5. A Theology of Cultures

This is not, however, the final word on this theology of the local Church. Of note also is the new interest in cultures that is found in the conciliar documents. At Vatican II we witness a real discovery of culture from which the council will present an initial outline of a _theology of cultures_. The notion of culture emerges strongly in the conciliar documents, even though the issue of inculturation remains absent and even though there has been, since then, some resistance to integrating the given notion of culture in the development of [^c20-19] a theology of the local Church. Hervé Legrand, Joseph A. Komonchak, and Jean-Marie Tillard are perhaps the Catholic theologians of our time who have best taken into account the convergence of theological and socio-historical factors in what constitutes the Church. Legrand states that ‘from a theological perspective, [^c20-20] **[p. 343]** a Church’s particularity is foremost its relationship with the world’. Komonchak connects ‘generative principles’ (theological) and ‘individuating principles’ (socio-historical), seeing them as two essential [^c20-21] elements for the emergence of a local Church.

[^c20-19]: Certain theologians maintain that the essence of the local/individual church rests on the following theological criteria: the episcopacy, the Holy Spirit, the Gospel, and the Eucharist. This approach neglects the first element: the portion of the people of God, formed by its culture, its own traditions, and its customs. See Routhier, ‘ “Église locale” ou “Église particulière” ’, 15–16, 51–56. Here he develops the link between the Church, its human location, and its culture.

[^c20-20]: Hervé Legrand, ‘Enjeux théologiques de la revalorisation des Églises locales’, _Concilium_ 71 (1972): 55.

[^c20-21]: See Joseph A. Komonchak, ‘The Local Church and the Catholic Church: The Contemporary Theological Problematic’, _The_ _Jurist_ 52 (1992): 416–47.

Vatican II is the first council to address the issue of culture, and it is given great importance. In the conciliar documents, the relationship between the Gospel, the Church, and cultures was understood through the lens of ‘adaptation’. The term is used widely in both the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy and the Decree on the Missionary Activity of the Church. The issue is also addressed in the document on mass media (IM) and especially in _Gaudium et Spes_, where an entire chapter in part II is dedicated to a systematic presentation on culture.

Three basic statements of Vatican II regarding culture are particularly relevant to this discussion. The first is the acknowledgement of the diversity of cultures, which can also be found in _Lumen Gentium_ (13), in _Gaudium et Spes_ (53), and in the Decree on the Missionary Activity of the Church. The fact is that there are _numerous_ cultures, which implies that the Gospel and the Church must be well rooted in the human ground they encounter. In speaking of local churches, they are described as a ‘community of the faithful, endowed with the cultural riches of its own nation, [that] must be deeply rooted in the people’ (_AG_ 15). Vatican II then reflects on the issue of the emergence of new cultures. The constitution _Gaudium et Spes_ asserts that the ‘circumstances of life today have undergone such profound changes on the social and cultural level that one is entitled to speak of a new age of human history’ (_GS_ 54). A number of socio-historical factors contribute today to ‘create new mass-cultures which give birth to new patterns of thinking, of acting, and of use of leisure’. It is thus that ‘a more universal form of culture is gradually taking shape’. Lastly, Vatican II acknowledges that the proclamation of the Gospel is closely tied to culture and that it should be conveyed in the ideas and languages of various peoples. It recognizes that ‘this kind of adaptation and preaching of the revealed word must ever be the law of all evangelization’ (_GS_ 44). These three statements are the foundation that will lead to the assertion of the need to adapt the Church to different cultures.

These three facts—the acknowledgement of the plurality of cultures, the realization of the emergence of new cultures, and the affirmation of a connection between culture and the articulation of Christ’s message —led the council fathers to consider new opportunities for the Church: entering into dialogue with new cultures, communicating Christ’s teaching in a culturally relevant manner, and renewing its own ecclesial image. In thinking about culture, the council followed the opening made by John XXIII in his inaugural address when he noted that culture colours the way in which the faith is expressed, and that this meant that attention must be given to different cultures if the Gospel is to be expressed in a ‘adapted’ manner. Nos. 44 **[p. 344]** and 58 of _Gaudium et Spes_ are without a doubt the most critical passages in this area. The teaching of Vatican II leads to an understanding that the emergence of new questions, far from representing a threat to the proclamation of the Gospel or causing harm to the life of the faith (_GS_ 62), can ‘rather stimulate a more precise and deeper understanding of that faith’. This new understanding of the faith, which will ‘demand new scrutiny by theologians’, is an invitation to ‘develop more efficient ways of communicating doctrine to the people of today’ (_GS_ 62). It is therefore necessary that in each of the great socio-cultural regions … theological investigation should be encouraged and the facts and words revealed by God, contained in the sacred scripture, and explained by the fathers and magisterium of the church, submitted to a new examination in light of the tradition of the universal church. In this way it will be more clearly understood by what means the faith can be explained in terms of the philosophy and wisdom of the people, and how their customs, attitude to life and social structures can be reconciled with the standard proposed by divine revelation. Thus a way will be opened for a more profound adaptation in the whole sphere of Christian life. (_AG_ 22)

To attain that goal, Vatican II suggests highlighting once again the value of episcopal conferences, which, within each large socio-cultural territory, will be able to undertake the necessary ‘adaptation’ (_SC_ 63) so that ‘local traditions together with the special qualities of each national family, illumined by the light of the Gospel, will be taken up into a catholic unity’ (_AG_ 22). It also suggests an increase in dialogue between the Church and different cultures. To achieve this, the Church must first rely on the contribution of laypeople who are integrated into the culture. _Gaudium et Spes_ 44 emphasizes that the ‘church needs to step up this exchange by calling upon the help of people who are living in the world today, who are expert in its organizations and its forms of training, and who understand its mentality, in the case of believers and non-believers alike’. According to Vatican II (_AG_ 22), the laity are the most valuable point of contact between the Gospel and culture, even though this knowledge of cultures is also required for missionaries (_AG_ 16), pastors, and theologians, who are to ‘listen to and distinguish the many voices of our times and to interpret them in light of God’s word, in order that the revealed truth may be more deeply penetrated, better understood, and more suitably presented’ (_GS_ 44). Furthermore, a number of these writings describe a living process of exchange between Church and cultures.

These documents have certainly not fully adopted a perspective of inculturation. However, they represent a step that turned the Church in that direction. Above all, they emphasize the fact that a speaker must know the various audiences and adapt to them. Such a position reflects the level of understanding of communication theory in the 1960s. This focus on the addressee is on the threshold of a consideration of reception, since it involves more than just paying attention to the addressee. It begins with the act of [^c20-22] reading and interpretation by the addressee, with the action of the speaker becoming secondary. It **[p. 345]** depends on the action of the receiver, establishing them, as mentioned above, as an active subject. As a person who is culturally conditioned, who lives in history, the receiver is led to rework that which has been given them. It is within a determined human environment that the receiver receives, assimilates, and makes their own that which has been offered.

[^c20-22]: See Wolfgang Iser, ‘The Reading Process: A Phenomenological Approach’, _New Literary History_ 3 (1971): 279–305; _Der_ _implizite Leser: Kommunikationsformen des Romans von Bunyan bis Beckett_ (Munich: Wilhelm Fink, 1972); _The Act of_ _Reading: A Theory of Aesthetic Response_ (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1978). See also Hans R. Jauß, _Pour_ _une esthétique de la réception_ (Paris: Gallimard, 1978).

### 6. Conclusion

It is clear that the teaching of Vatican II introduced many elements that will allow the Church to navigate the process of reception. Looking back decades later, we are inclined to think that the theology of tradition, which was a bone of contention at the time of the council, remains the key element in this matter. Such a theology of tradition is impossible if one does not consider the subjective role of the local churches enshrined in diverse world cultures and living in communion with other churches, and especially with the Church of Rome. These local churches, which take over the riches of the nations that God has given them in inheritance, are not only subjects that have rights and can take action, but are also churches of subjects. ‘With the help of the Holy Spirit’, there is indeed growth in insight into the realities and words that have been handed down, due to the spiritual activity of all the faithful, either by study or contemplation, either by their experience of spiritual realities or by preaching (_DV_ 8).
