## 21. The History of Conciliar Reception

Salvador Pié-Ninot

### 1. First Period of Reception (1965–1985): From Conciliar Euphoria to the Extraordinary Assembly of the Synod of Bishops, 1985

**[p. 346]** The first few years after the council were lived in a sort of ‘conciliar euphoria’. The ideological spectrum of Catholic theologians regarding Vatican II seemed unanimous in their enthusiastic acceptance of the final documents and in their view of the novelty of the council. That kind of theological unanimity—arising from the ‘moral unanimity’ that Paul VI sought for the approval of the final documents—would not last. The ranks of theologians in the so-called majority accepted the council as a major turning point. The most international scholarly commentary that represented that interpretation is the German _Lexikon für Theologie_ [^c21-1] _und Kirche_, with authors such as Karl Rahner and Joseph Ratzinger, alongside commentaries on specific documents: Henri de Lubac, Umberto Betti, and Luis Alonso Schökel on _Dei Verbum_; Gerard Philips and Guilherme Baraúna on _Lumen Gentium_; and Yves Congar on _Gaudium et Spes._

[^c21-1]: Joseph Höfer und Karl Rahner, eds., _Lexikon für Theologie und Kirche_, 2nd ed. (Freiburg im Breisgau: Herder, 1957–68), translated as _Commentary on the Documents of Vatican II_, 5 vols., ed. Herbert Vorgrimler (New York: Herder and Herder, 1967–69).

In contrast, the ‘conservative’ minority at the council proved to be coherent in its fight against Vatican II. The small group created by Archbishop Lefebvre in 1970—the Society of St Pius X (SSPX)—represented quite effectively the awkward features of a contemporary Catholicism that deliberately rejected Vatican II. **[p. 347]** The _suspensio a divinis_ (disciplinary prohibition of the exercise of faculties for ministry) of Archbishop Lefebvre in 1976 did not alter the trajectory of the debate on Vatican II in the SSPX. (He would be [^c21-2] excommunicated in 1988.)

[^c21-2]: D. Menozzi, ‘Opposition to the Council’, in _The Reception of Vatican II_, ed. Giuseppe Alberigo et al. (Washington, DC: The Catholic University of America Press, 1987), 325–48.

[^c21-3] John Paul II’s election as pope in 1978 unleashed a new impulse for the reception of Vatican II. Twenty years after the end of the council, John Paul II announced an Extraordinary Synod of Bishops for 1985. The Catholic press was unanimous in declaring that the synod was a surprise, but immediately diverged in its [^c21-4] interpretation. On the one hand, the synod revealed the complexity of the interpretation of Vatican II, but on the other hand, the Final Report favoured harmonizing interpretations and presents some principles for a proper exegesis of the council documents that may be paraphrased as follows: (1) each passage and document must be interpreted in the context of all the others, so that the integral meaning of the council may be rightly grasped; (2) the four constitutions of the council are the hermeneutical key to the decrees and declarations; (3) the pastoral import of the documents ought not to be separated from or set in opposition to their doctrinal content; (4) no opposition may be made between the spirit and the letter of [^c21-5] Vatican II; (5) Vatican II must be accepted as illuminating the problems of our day.

[^c21-3]: Massimo Faggioli, _Vatican II: The Battle for Meaning_ (Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 2012), 9–11.

[^c21-4]: Salvador Pié-Ninot, ed., _La imposible restauración: El Vaticano II a la hora del balance del Sínodo de 1985_ (Madrid: PPC, 1986).

[^c21-5]: See ‘The Final Report of the 1985 Extraordinary Synod’, _A Message to the People of God and the Final Report_ (Washington, DC: National Conference of Catholic Bishops, 1986), 11.

The synod did not support a position for or against any theological or historiographical school but reaffirmed the complex relationship between tradition and transition in Catholic theology, saying that ‘the Council must be understood in continuity with the great tradition from the Council’s own doctrine for [^c21-6] today’s Church and the men of our time. The Church is one and the same throughout all the councils.’ Two major works witness to this stage. The first, prepared by the professors of the Pontifical Gregorian [^c21-7] University (Rome), focused on the contents of the council. The second is the work promoted by the so- [^c21-8] called Bologna school, which was oriented towards conciliar reception.

[^c21-6]: ‘The Final Report of Extraordinary Synod of 1985’, 5; see Avery Dulles, ‘The Extraordinary Synod of 1985’, in Alberigo et al., _The Reception of Vatican II_, 349–63; Francesco Saverio Venuto, _La recezione del Concilio Vaticano II nel dibattito_ _storiografico dal 1965 al 1985_ (Turin: Effatà, 2011).

[^c21-7]: René Latourelle, ed., _Vatican II: Assessment and Perspectives: Twenty-five Years after 1962–1987_, 3 vols (New York: Paulist, 1988–89).

[^c21-8]: Alberigo et al., _The Reception of Vatican II_.

From this period in the history of research on Vatican II, two studies have become classics: the historical analysis by Hermann Josef Pottmeyer which presents the global reception of the council during its first twenty-five years, and a study by Eugenio Corecco which offers a serious and measured criticism on the new **[p. 348]** Code of Canon Law of 1983, indicating that it does not entirely receive the ecclesiology of communion of Vatican II.

### 2. Second Period of Reception (1986–2012): Between Continuity and Discontinuity

During this phase of the council’s reception, two particularly relevant works were published which deal with the ‘battle for meaning’ between continuity and discontinuity of Vatican II. The first was the five-volume _History of Vatican II_, published in seven languages, that represented a major international historiographical [^c21-9] exploration of the debate on the council. It does not consist of a new series of commentaries on the documents; rather, it is a scholarly reconstruction of the council as a ‘historical event’. This edition was coordinated by Giuseppe Alberigo and the John XXIII Foundation for Religious Studies in Bologna, which led a major research effort to examine many yet undiscovered and unused archives: primary sources held in the Vatican II Archive of the Holy See (unpublished sources such as the acts of the preparatory phase, acts of commissions and committees of the council, reports and letters exchanged between the council’s various bodies) as well as sources from local archives. The international and multidisciplinary character of the team brought many new questions, issues, and perspectives to bear upon the debated interpretation of Vatican II. It produced new results and opened new paths for research. The main hermeneutical principles that guided Alberigo in the enterprise were the idea of the council as an ‘event’, John XXIII’s intention in announcing the council, the pastoral nature of the council, an understanding of _aggiornamento_ as the main goal of the [^c21-10] council, and the importance of compromise in understanding the council’s final documents. Its most important result was the expansion of international discussions on Vatican II in Latin America, Europe, North America, and throughout the world.

[^c21-9]: Giuseppe Alberigo and Joseph A. Komonchak, eds., _History of Vatican II_, 5 vols. (Leuven: Peeters, 1995–2006).

[^c21-10]: Faggioli, _Vatican II: The Battle for Meaning_, 15–16.

[^c21-11] The second work worthy of mention is _Herders Theologischer Kommentar zum zweiten vatikanischen Konzil_, a major set of commentaries on all the documents of Vatican II produced in the German-speaking world, but intended to provide the international theological community with a significant contribution on the council forty years after it ended. Hünermann qualifles the literary genre of conciliar documents as a **[p. 349]** ‘constitutive text of faith’, using a formula that would replace the textual genre ‘dogma’, considering the [^c21-12] council teachings as ‘constitutive texts’.

[^c21-11]: Peter Hünermann and Bernd Jochen Hilberath, eds., _Herders Theologischer Kommentar zum zweiten vatikanischen Konzil_, 5 vols. (Freiburg im Breisgau: Herder, 2004–6).

[^c21-12]: Peter Hünermann, ‘Der Text: Werden—Gestalt—Bedeutung: Eine hermeneutische Reflexion’, in Hünermann and Hilberath, _Herders Theologischer Kommentar zum zweiten vatikanischen Konzil_, 5:5–101, esp. 11–17, 85–87.

A third work emerges also as relevant, especially because of its impact in the English-speaking world: John O’Malley’s _What Happened at Vatican II_ (2008), where Vatican II is qualifled as a ‘language-event’ that needs to be read in its intertextual character to consider the so-called spirit of the council. Vatican II progressively offers a ‘linguistic game’ in a rhetorical key that culminates in _Gaudium et Spes_, which employs a persuasive [^c21-13] and exhortatory form to persuade the reader of the worth of its content (_epideictic genre_). It must be said, finally, that these three works, while not denying the deep continuity of the council’s teaching with tradition, emphasize the novelty of the council. Because of that, they have been qualifled as supporters of ‘discontinuity’, but these qualifications are too simplistic.

[^c21-13]: John O’Malley, _What Happened at Vatican II_ (Cambridge, MA: The Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 2008), 310.

#### The ‘Hermeneutic of Reform’ Proposed by Benedict XVI

In this context, the long speech of Pope Benedict on the fortieth anniversary of Vatican II, delivered in his annual Address offering Christmas greetings to the Roman Curia on 22 December 2005, is of decisive importance, generating a broad debate about the proposal of a ‘hermeneutic of reform’:

The question arises: Why has the implementation of the council, in large parts of the Church, thus far been so difficult? Well, it all depends on the correct interpretation of the council or—as we would say today—on its proper hermeneutic, the correct key to its interrelation and application. The problems in its implementation arose from the fact that two contrary hermeneutics came face-to-face and quarrelled with each other. One caused confusion, the other, silently but more and more visibly, bore and is bearing fruit. … On the one hand, there is an interpretation that I would call a ‘hermeneutic of discontinuity and rupture’; it has frequently availed itself of the sympathies of the mass media, and also one trend of modern theology. On the other, there is the ‘hermeneutic of reform’, of renewal of continuity of the one subject-Church that the Lord has given to us. She is a subject that increases in time and develops, yet always remaining the same, the one subject of the journeying People of God.

According to Benedict XVI, the ‘hermeneutic of discontinuity’ risks dividing the pre-conciliar and the post-conciliar Church and asserts that the texts of the council as such do not express its true spirit. It claims that they are the result of compromises in which, to reach unanimity, it was found necessary to keep and **[p. 350]** reconfirm many old things that are now pointless. In the ‘hermeneutic of discontinuity’, the true spirit of the council is not to be found in these compromises but instead in the impulses towards the new that are contained in the texts. In a word, it would be necessary not to follow the texts of the council but its spirit. In this way, according to Benedict XVI, a vast margin was kept open for the question of how this spirit should subsequently be defined, and room was consequently made for every whim.

In Benedict XVI’s speech of December 2005, the ‘hermeneutic of discontinuity’ is countered by the ‘hermeneutic of reform’ as it was first presented by John XXIII in his speech inaugurating the council on 11 October 1962 and later by Paul VI in his discourse for the council’s conclusion on 7 December 1965: ‘Here I shall cite only John XXIII’s well-known words, which unequivocally express this hermeneutic when he says that the council wishes “to transmit the doctrine, pure and integral, without any attenuation or distortion.” ’ Benedict continues,

Our duty is not only to guard this precious treasure, as if we were concerned only with antiquity, but to dedicate ourselves with an earnest will and without fear to that work which our era demands of us It is necessary that this certain and unchanging teaching, which is to be faithfully respected, be deeply studied and presented in a way that corresponds to the needs of our time. The substance of that ancient doctrine of the deposit of faith is one thing and the way in which it is presented is another, retaining nonetheless the same meaning and message.

Benedict XVI presented an argument in favour of a complex mix of continuity and change, especially in the cases of the teaching on faith and science, the relationship between Church and State, and religious tolerance:

It is clear that in all these sectors, which all together form a single problem, some kind of discontinuity might emerge. Indeed, a discontinuity had been revealed but in which, after the various distinctions between concrete historical situations and their requirements had been made, the continuity of principles proved not to have been abandoned. It is easy to miss this fact at a first glance.

He admitted a particular form of acceptable change in Church teaching:

It is precisely in this combination of continuity and discontinuity at different levels that the very nature of true reform consists—for example, certain practical forms of liberalism or a free interpretation of the Bible—should necessarily be contingent themselves, precisely because they refer to a specific reality that is changeable in itself.

The main argument of Benedict XVI’s speech was not about material continuity of teaching but the continuity of the one subject-Church:

The Second Vatican Council with its new definition of the relationship between the faith of the Church and certain essential elements of modern thought has reviewed or even corrected certain **[p. 351]** historical decisions, but in this apparent discontinuity it has preserved and deepened her inmost nature and true identity. The Church, both before and after the council, was and is the same Church, one, holy, catholic and apostolic, journeying on through time; she continues ‘her pilgrimage amid the persecutions of the world and the consolations of God’, proclaiming the death of the Lord until he comes (cf. Luke 8).

Benedict XVI concluded his argument by citing the spiritual exercises that the future John Paul II preached to Paul VI and the Roman Curia in 1976: ‘In our time too, the Church remains a “sign that will be opposed” (Luke 2:34).’ In this way, Benedict XVI connected the need for continuity to a view of the relationship between Church and the modern world: ‘The council could not have intended to abolish the Gospel’s opposition to human dangers and errors.’

Benedict’s speech was clearly not an argument delegitimizing Vatican II:

The dialogue between reason and faith, particularly important today, found its bearing on the basis of the Second Vatican Council. This dialogue must now be developed with great open-mindedness but also with that clear discernment that the world rightly expects of us in this very moment. Thus, today we can look with gratitude at the Second Vatican Council: if we interpret and implement it guided by a right hermeneutic, it can be and can become increasingly powerful for the ever-necessary renewal of the Church.

#### Conciliar Background in Vatican II Concerning Church Reform

The reference to ‘reform/renewal’ as a key for understanding Vatican II is present in two key citations of the [^c21-14] council texts where the famous formula _Ecclesia semper reformanda_, inspired in Luther but formulated by the Dutch Calvinist Voetius (1589–1676), resonates. The first text is _Lumen Gentium_ (_LG_). Describing the Church as at once a visible and spiritual reality, it states that ‘the Church, embracing in its bosom sinners, at the same time holy and always in need of being purifled, always follows the way of penance and renewal’ (_LG_ 8). In the following paragraph, the Spirit appears as the main character of this renewal, because ‘the Church … ceaselessly [renews] itself through the action of the Holy Spirit’ (_LG_ 9).

[^c21-14]: _D. Martin Luthers Werke_, Weimarer Ausgabe, 56 vols (Weimar: H. Böhlaus, 1883–1929), 1:627, 26–27; 6:404, 2; 6:458, 38–9.

The second text comes from the Decree on Ecumenism, _Unitatis Redintegratio_ (_UR_), which speaks explicitly of ‘continual reformation’:

Every renewal of the Church essentially consists in an increase of fidelity to her own calling. **[p. 352]** Undoubtedly this explains the dynamism of the movement toward unity. Christ summons the Church, as she goes her pilgrim way, to that continual reformation of which she always has need, insofar as she is a human institution here on earth. Consequently, if, in various times and circumstances, there have been deficiencies in moral conduct or in church discipline, or even in the way that church teaching has been formulated—to be carefully distinguished from the deposit of faith itself—these can and should be set right at the opportune moment. (_UR_ 6)

It is worth noting that the beginning of this text in _Unitatis Redintegratio_ 6 contains a reference to the Fifth Council of the Lateran (1517), which had stated the need for a general renovation of the Church, the last great appeal to church reform before the divisions of the Protestant Reformation. In this way, with this citation, Vatican II wants to underline that the appeal to the ‘reformation’ was present in the Church before Luther; this is the perspective from which Vatican II starts. We can understand here a comprehension of the movement of the so-called Catholic Reform, irreducible to a simple ‘Counter-Reformation’, with two elements: the awareness of the Catholic ideal of living, present in the Church during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries through an internal renewal or ‘Catholic Reform’; and the self-affirmation of the Church against the Protestant Reformation that would be known properly as the ‘Counter-Reformation’.[^c21-15] For example, the link to the liturgical reform of the Church is rooted in the fact that the liturgy of Vatican II embodies the spirit of true reform within the Church. It is true that the Eucharist makes the Church; a liturgical reform that reshapes the form of celebrating the Eucharist represents and anticipates a major reform of the Church. With reason, Massimo Faggioli has spoken of Vatican II’s Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy, _Sacrosanctum Concilium_, as representing a movement of ‘true reform’.[^c21-16]

[^c21-15]: See Salvador Pié-Ninot, ‘Reformar, ayuda fundamental a la Iglesia’, _Manresa_ 84 (2012): 260.

[^c21-16]: See Massimo Faggioli, _True Reform: Liturgy and Ecclesiology in Sacrosanctum Concilium_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2012).

#### Benedict XVI’s ‘Hermeneutic of Reform’ and the Social Teaching of the Church

Pope Benedict XVI applied his understanding of continuity and discontinuity in a significant and paradigmatic manner when, in the encyclical _Caritas in Veritate_ (_CV_) (2009), he made the following observation:

The link between _Populorum Progressio_ and the Second Vatican Council does not mean that Paul VI’s social magisterium marked a break with that of previous Popes, because the Council constitutes a deeper exploration of this magisterium within the continuity of the Church’s life. In this sense, clarity is not served by certain abstract subdivisions of the Church’s social doctrine, **[p. 353]** which apply categories to Papal social teaching that are extraneous to it. It is not a case of two typologies of social doctrine, one pre-conciliar and one post-conciliar, differing from one another: on the contrary, there is _a single teaching, consistent and at the same time ever new._ … It is one thing to draw attention to the particular characteristics of one Encyclical or another, of the teaching of one Pope or another, but quite another to lose sight of the coherence of the overall doctrinal _corpus_. Coherence does not mean a closed system: on the contrary, it means dynamic faithfulness to a light received. The Church’s social doctrine illuminates with an unchanging light the new problems that are constantly emerging.

This safeguards the permanent and historical character of the doctrinal ‘patrimony’ which, with its specific characteristics, is part and parcel of the Church’s ever-living Tradition. … Social doctrine is built on the foundation handed on by the Apostles to the Fathers of the Church, and then received and further explored by the great Christian doctors. This doctrine points definitively to the New Man, to the ‘last Adam [who] became a life-giving spirit’ (1 Cor 15:45), the principle of the charity that ‘never ends’ (1 Cor 13:8). It is attested by the saints and by those who gave their lives for Christ our Saviour in the fleld of justice and peace. It is an expression of the prophetic task of the Supreme Pontiffs to give apostolic guidance to the Church of Christ and to discern the new demands of evangelisation. For these reasons, _Populorum Progressio_, situated within the great current of Tradition, can still speak to us today. (_CV_ 12)

Thus, the starting point for an understanding of the ‘hermeneutic of reform’ proposed by Benedict XVI may reflect the formula applied by St Bonaventure (on this point in total agreement with Thomas Aquinas) to the relationship between faith and history: ‘explanation has access to faith but does not change the essence of [^c21-17] faith, so that the variation of time determines but does not vary the faith’. In short, then, such a hermeneutic emerges from an ontological understanding of truth that, on the one hand, reserves discontinuity for what is historic as contingent and accidental and, on the other hand, affirms continuity in the essential and enduring truth of faith. So, discontinuity is always related to continuity as a point for discernment. In this sense the dynamic comprehension of tradition adopted by Vatican II is applied and [^c21-18] related to a dynamics of the eternal within the realm of contingent realities.

[^c21-17]: Bonaventure, _III Sent_. d.24 a.1 q.3c.

[^c21-18]: Lieven Boeve, ‘La Vrai Réception du Vatican II n’a pas encore commencé: J. Ratzinger, révélation, et autorité de Vatican II‘, in _L’Autorité et les autorités: L’Herméneutique théologique du Vatican II_, ed. Gilles Routhier and Guy Jobin (Paris: Cerf, 2010), 13–50.

#### Magisterial Value of the Council as ‘Catholic Doctrine’

As a key for the ‘hermeneutic of reform’, Benedict not only refers to John XXIII’s discourse at the opening of the council, but also cites Paul VI in the final discourse on 7 December 1965. In this final speech, Paul VI addresses the matter of the authority of the council’s teaching in these words:

**[p. 354]** the teaching authority of the Church, even though not wishing to issue extraordinary dogmatic definitions, has made thoroughly known its authoritative teaching on a number of questions which today weigh upon man’s conscience and activity, descending, so to speak, into a dialogue with him, but ever preserving its own authority and force; it has spoken with the accommodating friendly voice of pastoral charity; its desire has been to be heard and understood by everyone; … sought to express itself in simple, up-to-date, conversational style, derived from actual experience and a cordial approach which make it more vital, attractive and persuasive; it has spoken to modern man as he is.

In these lines Paul VI considers the theological and magisterial value of Vatican II as ‘Catholic doctrine’; that is, as a teaching that, even though it is not proposed expressly and categorically as the word of God, teaches authentically the faith of the Catholic Church. Even though it does not take the form of a solemn definition, it is recognized as true and revealed and deserving of a ‘religious adhesion of the spirit [_religiosum animi obsequium_]’ (_LG_ 25). This comprehension of Catholic doctrine or Catholic truths by Paul VI reflects the orientations present in the theological teachings of the moment.[^c21-19]

[^c21-19]: See Sixtus Cartechini, _De Valore Notarum Theologicarum_ (Rome: PUG, 1951), 68–69. Yves Congar, _La Foi et la théologie_ (Tournai: Desclée, 1962), 43.

The clarifications of the conciliar Doctrinal Commission concerning the weight of the Dogmatic Constitutions _Lumen Gentium_ and _Dei Verbum_ must be taken into account: they must be understood ‘following the norms of the theological interpretation that are deduced, from the subject matter [_ex subiecta materia_], or from the manner of expression [_ex dicendi ratione_]’. On the other hand, an initial note in _Gaudium et Spes_ (_GS_) underlines that it is called a ‘Pastoral Constitution’ because, ‘while resting on doctrinal principles, it seeks to express the relation of the Church to the world and modern mankind’. Because of this, the first, more doctrinal part of the Pastoral Constitution (_GS_ 1–45) does not lack pastoral intention, and the second, more practical or pastoral part (_GS_ 47–93) does not lack doctrinal intention. ‘Consequently, the constitution must be interpreted according to the general norms of theological interpretation. Interpreters must bear in mind—especially in part two—the changeable circumstances which the subject matter, by its very nature, involves’ (_GS_ 1 n. 1).[^c21-20]

[^c21-20]: See Francis A. Sullivan, _Creative Fidelity: Weighing and Interpreting Documents of the Magisterium_ (Dublin: Gill & Macmillan 1996), 162–74; Salvador Pié-Ninot, _Eclesiología_ (Salamanca: Sígueme, 2015), 75–98.

#### The Anti-Conciliar Lefebvrist Perspective and the Catholic ‘Traditionalist’ Perspective

At the beginning of 2009, Benedict XVI’s lifting of the excommunications of the four bishops consecrated by Marcel Lefebvre in 1988 cast significant light on a very active rift within European and North American **[p. 355]** Catholicism concerning the role of Vatican II. The anti-conciliar followers of Archbishop Lefebvre in the SSPX published a harsh attack against Pope Benedict’s ‘hermeneutic of reform’ titled ‘Un nouveau magistère en rupture’. The SSPX concluded that Vatican II represents a ‘radical rupture’ with Catholic tradition: ‘Actually the “hermeneutic of continuity” suggested by Benedict XVI is a laudable effort, but ineffective, because it is not able to overcome a rift present in the very documents of the Second Vatican Council.’ They concluded, ‘it is essential to demythologize this Council which has been named as pastoral because of the instinctive fear of dogma and to make it easier to introduce liberal ideas in an official Church [^c21-21] text’.

[^c21-21]: See Jean Michel Gleize, _Vaticano II: Un dibattito aperto; Questioni disputate sul XXI Concilio Ecumenico_ (Albano Laziale: Ichthys, 2013), 222; Fraternité Saint Pie X, _Magistère de soufre: Études théologiques sur le Concile de Vatican II_ (Paris: Fraternité Saint Pie X, 2009), 7:218–21; Giovanni Miccoli, _La Chiesa dell’anticoncilio: I tradizionalisti alla riconquista di Roma_ (Rome: Laterza, 2011).

A more moderate tone, but equally combative, can be found in the writings of those who adopt an approach that might be classifled as ‘traditionalist’, including the former Lateran professor Bruno Gherardini, Roberto de Mattei, and Romano Amerio. In light of these debates, it might be said that ‘the definition of Vatican II as the ultimate and final moment of early twentieth-century Modernism has almost become, at the beginning of the twenty-first century, common language in the neo-traditionalist movement within contemporary Catholicism’.[^c21-22]

[^c21-22]: See Faggioli, _Vatican II: The Battle for Meaning_, 24–37, at 29.

#### Reception of Benedict XVI’s ‘Hermeneutic of Reform’

Benedict XVI’s ‘hermeneutic of reform’ has sparked interest especially in the English-speaking world. Representative of this approach is the collection of essays _Vatican II: Renewal within Tradition_, which examined the conciliar documents with contributions from Cardinals Avery Dulles and Francis George; Bishop Charles Morerod, OP; Richard John Neuhaus; and Geoffrey Wainwright. Its editor, Matthew Lamb, was careful to insist that ‘the chapters in this book have presented the documents of Vatican II within the fundamental continuity of Catholic tradition. Renewal and reform within this tradition are demanding projects for each generation of Catholics.’[^c21-23]

[^c21-23]: Matthew L. Lamb, ‘The Challenges of Reform and Renewal within Catholic Tradition‘, in _Vatican II: Renewal within_ _Tradition_, ed. Matthew L. Lamb and Matthew Levering (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2008), 440.

On the other hand, Catherine Clifford and Richard Gaillardetz produced an insightful study, _Keys to the Council: Unlocking the Teaching of Vatican II_, favouring the ‘reform in continuity’ view. They offer twenty conciliar keys from a reform perspective that assume continuity within Catholic faith. Its conclusion is clear: these keys ‘will unlock a vision of the Church that remains both challenging and liberating, a vision capable of guiding our Church in the decades to come’.[^c21-24]

[^c21-24]: Catherine Clifford and Richard Gaillardetz, _Keys to the Council: Unlocking the Teaching of Vatican II_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2012), 192.

**[p. 356]** In a dialogic mode, we find Thomas G. Guarino, _The Disputed Teaching of Vatican II: Continuity and Reversal in Catholic Doctrine_:

Through their artful combination of development, reform, and reversal, the conciliar theologians and bishops deftly advanced the doctrinal teaching of the Catholic Church _in eodem sensu eademque sententia_. Fundamentally, Catholics would recognise Vatican II —following Vicent of Lérins—not only as an extraordinary council but also as a _profectus_—‘legitimate advance’—_et non permutatio fidei_—‘not an alteration of faith’.[^c21-25]

[^c21-25]: Thomas G. Guarino, _The Disputed Teaching of Vatican II: Continuity and Reversal in Catholic Doctrine_ (Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 2018), 203 f.

As a conclusion of this second phase of reception, the Jesuit Christoph Theobald proposed a synthetic and suggestive study, _Le Concile Vatican II: Quel avenir?_ (2015). It attempts to coordinate four significant approaches to the hermeneutic of the council represented by Giuseppe Alberigo, Peter Hünermann, John O’Malley, and the discourse of Benedict XVI. Drawing insights from each of these, Theobald concludes with a synthetic proposal:

the idea of a ‘hermeneutic of reform’ could serve as a ‘Formula of Concord’ between Bologna (Alberigo), Tübingen (Hünermann), Washington (Georgetown: O’Malley) and Rome (Benedict XVI), but with one _condition_: the renunciation of a polemical approach to the opponent’s position and the understanding of tradition according to the conciliar statement found in _Ad Gentes_ 22: ‘a new examination’ of the words and deeds which God has revealed.[^c21-26]

[^c21-26]: Christoph Theobald, _Le Concile Vatican II: Quel avenir?_ (Paris: Cerf, 2015), 127.

### 3. Third Period of Reception: The ‘Francis Effect’

The pontificate of Francis signals the beginning of a new phase of reception of the council. However, it stands now as an element of periodization in the history of the reception of Vatican II and in a different way from that in which his predecessors received Vatican II. Francis’s papacy may mean the beginning of a new phase of both the reception of the council and of the research on the council given the difference in his approach when compared to those of John Paul II and Benedict XVI.

In a certain sense, one must beware of the risk of falling into a ‘conciliar nominalism’ that would uncritically associate ‘Vatican II’ with all that is new in the Church. Francis quotes Vatican II cautiously and sparingly; he has never addressed Vatican II directly and formally, in a speech or a written document, as a **[p. 357]** key moment in the life and renewal of the Church. At least not until his 2021 intervention to reduce the divisive influence of those who cling to the Tridentine liturgy as an expression of resistance or an outright rejection of the conciliar reform (_Traditionis Custodes_, 2021). Yet, the keywords of his pontificate—‘mercy’ and ‘the poor’—are unmistakably linked to John XXIII and Vatican II. The foundational document of his pontificate, _Evangelii Gaudium_ (2013), is an original interpretation of Vatican II. In March 2015, Francis claimed as his motive for the decision to call an Extraordinary Jubilee of Mercy a direct appeal to John XXIII’s opening speech at the council, _Gaudet Mater Ecclesia_ (_Misericordiae Vultus_ 4).

In this context, Francis, in his path-breaking September 2013 interview with the editor of _Civiltà Cattolica_, Antonio Spadaro, SJ, was forceful about the contemporary impact of the Second Vatican Council:

Vatican II was a re-reading of the Gospel in light of contemporary culture … Vatican II produces a renewal movement that simply comes from the same Gospel. Its fruits are enormous. Just recall the liturgy. The work of liturgical reform has been a service to the people as a re-reading of the Gospel from a concrete historical situation. Yes, there are hermeneutics of continuity and discontinuity, but one thing is clear: the dynamic of reading the Gospel, actualising its message for today—which was typical of Vatican II—is absolutely irreversible.[^c21-27]

[^c21-27]: ‘Pope Francis: The Interview’, ed. Antonio Spadaro, _America_ (19 September 2013), 30.

A profound act of this interpretation of Vatican II was the synodal process on family and marriage in two Synods of Bishops. The subsequent Apostolic Exhortation, _Amoris Laetitia_ (2016), constitutes a profound act of interpretation of Vatican II with many consequences, both ecclesiological (because of the implications for episcopal collegiality and synodality vis-à-vis the Petrine ministry) and theological (due to the _modus procedendi_ of the Synod, looking at the ‘signs of the times’). The time for polemics concerning the ‘two hermeneutics’ may soon have passed in the Church; it is certainly over for Pope Francis, who has never framed his interpretation of Vatican II in those terms.

In this context, the global approach of Francis to Vatican II, which is different from the Apostolic Exhortation _Verbum Domini_ of Benedict XVI and the encyclical _Lumen Fidei_ (written, for the most part, by Benedict XVI, but signed by Francis), represents an effort to develop the teaching of _Dei Verbum_. On the other hand, in Francis’s teaching there is an evident effort to overcome a certain latent scepticism concerning _Gaudium et Spes,_ which is abundantly cited in _Amoris Laetitia_.[^c21-28]

[^c21-28]: Salvador Pié-Ninot, _Guía de lectura e interpretación de ‘Amoris laetitia’_ (Madrid: PPC, 2017); ‘La eclesiología del Papa Francisco’, _Atualidade Teologica_ 22, no. 59 (2018): 255–86.

Francis’s approach to Vatican II is not only marked by a lack of interest in an abstract hermeneutical debate, but also visibly shaped by a pastoral concern that is markedly different from a nostalgic appeal to Vatican II —as opposed to the nostalgic memorialization of the pre-Vatican II Church. Francis’s approach to Vatican II **[p. 358]** is an update of its message in a deeply changed context of both Church and world. In this context, Francis speaks of the ‘Church of Yes’: ‘There was a “No” Church that said, “you cannot; no, no, you must not”, and a “Yes” Church that said, “but … let’s think about it, let’s be open to this, the Spirit is opening the door to [^c21-29] us”.’

[^c21-29]: From Francis’s homily at the Mass celebrated in Santa Marta on 2 May 2013. Cited in Paul Crowley, ed., _From Vatican II to_ _Pope Francis_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2014), xv–xvi.

Lakeland reflects with insight on Pope Francis’s priorities:

What we should expect to find consistent will be his focus on the poor, on making their concerns and their world the centre of the Church’s priorities, together with his critique of self-referentiality, both ecclesiastical narcissism in general, and clericalism in particular. It seems like both the bishop’s palace and the stock market will be displaced by the stable at Bethlehem, and this can only be a good thing.[^c21-30] Following Francis’s recognition of the need for a ‘pastoral conversion of the papacy’ in _Evangelii Gaudium_ 32, he notably speaks for the first time of a _diaconal primacy_ to give impulse to the relationship between collegiality and Petrine ministry envisioned by Vatican II. He cites John Paul II’s encyclical _Ut Unum Sint_, which refers to the ecclesial tradition of _diakonia_, and to the papal title _servus servorum Dei_ (Servant of the Servants of God), first introduced by Pope Gregory the Great (540–604).[^c21-31]

[^c21-30]: Paul Lakeland, _A Council that Will Never End_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2013), 155.

[^c21-31]: See Salvador Pié-Ninot, ‘Il “Primato diaconale”: nuovo titolo del papa Francesco’: _L’Osservatore Romano: 25.3.2018_.

[^c21-32] In conclusion, it is clear that recent publications on Vatican II have been under a particular ‘Francis effect’. The reform of the Church promoted by Francis, following the compass of Vatican II, is not his alone: he invites all, insisting that all must do their share, as we read in his very significant discourse about “The synodal Church” in 2015, who is followed with a global synodal proposal way with a diocesan level (2021– 2022), a continental level (2022–2023) and a universal level (Synod of Bishops: October 2023–October 2024).

[^c21-32]: Massimo Faggioli, ‘Council Vatican II: Bibliographical Overview’, _Cristianesimo nella Storia_ 37 (2016): 714–15. See also Mario de França Miranda, _A reforma de Francisco_ (Sao Paolo: Paulinas, 2017), 199; Santiago Madrigal, _El giro eclesiológico_ _en la recepción del Vaticano II_ (Santander: Sal Terrae, 2017), 515–23.

In fact, the synodality is a renewal fruit of Vatican II, speciality from the title of the Church as a People of God, the most beloved for the Pope Francis. In this sense, this ‘Francis effect’ is moving the Church towards a ‘lived experience’ of the Second Vatican Council, beyond ‘the way of the synodality’.[^c21-33]

[^c21-33]: International Theological Commission, _The synodality in the life and mission of the Church_ (Rom: Vatican, 2018); Dario Vitali, _Un popolo in cammino verso Dio: la sinodalità in Evangelii gaudium_ (Milano: San Paolo, 2018); Salvador Pié-Ninot, _La_ _Sinodalidad como el “caminar juntos” en la Iglesia_ (Barcelona: CPL, 2021); A. Borras, G. Routhier, R. Gaillardetz, C. Schickendanz, H.-M. Legrand…, ‘Synodality’, _Concilium_ 390 (2021): 7–143.

Faggioli, Massimo. ‘Council Vatican II: Bibliographical Overview 2013–2016’. _Cristianesimo nella storia_ 37 (2016): 675–715.

Faggioli, Massimo. _Vatican II: The Battle for Meaning_. Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 2012.

## 22. The Reception of the Second Vatican Council by

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 360]** There is a lack of research on the reception of the Second Vatican Council by traditionalist Catholics: work in this area is in its infancy and therefore does not offer any exhaustive understanding or provide a total, global perspective on the issue. Rather, the work done so far represents an invitation to further serious and in-depth research that will bear fruit only after years of study. This chapter will therefore not offer a true synthesis, but simply aims to give an initial overview of the question, which admittedly will be narrow in scope. It will therefore be far from exhaustive, especially given that the world of traditionalist Catholics is complex and that the individuals, movements, and networks that make up that world are far too numerous to be covered in these few pages. It will thus be limited to a presentation of the initial results of a historical inquiry that requires much further in-depth investigation.

We will not deal with the historical details of the development of post-conciliar traditionalism. Rather, we will focus on the issue of the reception of Vatican II and its evolution, while pointing out essential events that shed light on the issue without delving into either the circumstances or the people or groups formed along the way. Francophone and Italian spaces will seem to dominate. This is not due to any deliberate choice or to any limitations on the issue. Rather, it stems from the fact that we are dealing with a history of ideas; in this case, the theoretical reflections on the subject are found in these geographical areas. A history of Catholic traditionalism would have required a different geographical vista than a history of the reception of Vatican II by these same people.

**[p. 361]** Excluding the reception that took place during the council itself and taking as a starting point the close of the council, research suggests that the reception of Vatican II by traditionalists occurred in three phases, each of which will be addressed in separate sections of this chapter. First, there is the period of initial reception from 8 December 1965 to 30 November 1969, which takes us from the closing of the council to the implementation of the prescriptions of the Apostolic Constitution _Missale Romanum_ (3 April 1969). From that moment, the reception of Vatican II by those who opposed the council enters a second phase that extends to the year 2000, marked specifically by a pilgrimage to Rome by the Society of St Pius X (SSPX) during the Jubilee. It resulted in doctrinal discussions between its members and the Holy See, which inaugurated the third phase of the reception of Vatican II by traditionalists.

### 2. Phase One (1965–1969): A Reception in Light of Tradition

A study of the reception of the Second Vatican Council by traditionalists involves looking at the history and confrontations of the Cœtus Internationalis Patrum (CIP), the main opposition during this council. This ‘committee’, led by Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre (former archbishop of Dakar and, at the time of the council, superior general of the Congregation of the Holy Spirit), opposed the general orientation of the council because CIP members and sympathizers thought it went against the traditional doctrine of the Church. The antagonism of these conservatives began from the first session of the council, within a ‘piccolo comitato’, and continued throughout the event. The post-conciliar positions and battles of traditionalist Catholics can, for the most part, be traced back to the CIP’s struggles and the doctrinal inflexibility of its main members. It is therefore necessary to examine the first reception of the council by the former members of this group, which will be done in the next subsection, before moving on to study the reception of the event by other people and groups.

#### The Former Members of the Cœtus Internationalis Patrum

An examination of the reception of the Second Vatican Council by former CIP members reveals that initially none of them openly criticized the documents promulgated by the council. Quite the opposite: they defended the documents, calling for them to be interpreted according to the traditional doctrine of the Church. There are numerous examples. In 1966, Archbishop Geraldo de Proença Sigaud (Diamantina, Brazil) published an article in _La Pensée catholique_ in which he suggested a course of action for the ‘traditional priest’ against the ‘forces that dreamed of the Revolution-Council’ and who, ‘disappointed with the **[p. 362]** conciliar documents’, would attempt to ‘maintain confusion’ and ‘to convince traditional priests and [^c22-1] Catholics of the bad nature of the decrees of the documents of the Council’. In his view, ‘the traditional priest’ was not to disregard or oppose Vatican II, but rather ‘collaborate with the hierarchy, headed by the pope, for the wise, generous and supernatural implementation of the council, in faithfulness to the legitimate tradition of the Church’. Furthermore, according to Proença Sigaud, ‘to oppose the council would be for the traditional priest a betrayal of his past and a kind of suicide’. It would also be ‘to play into the hands of the enemies of the Church’ as well as ‘to resist the voice of the Holy Spirit, the breath of its action, [^c22-2] to be an obstacle to God’s activity in his Church’.

[^c22-1]: Mgr Geraldo de Proença Sigaud, ‘Le Concile et le prêtre traditionnel’, _La Pensée catholique_ 100 (1966): 17.

[^c22-2]: Ibid., 19–20.

That same year, another leading figure of the CIP published an article, also in _La Pensée catholique_. In searching through the conciliar documents, Bishop Luigi Maria Carli (Segni, Italy) was looking for ‘the [^c22-3] Church’s solemn response to the doubts and concerns raised by priestly obedience’. In the same issue could be found a homily by Archbishop Lefebvre delivered on 7 May 1966, in which he called for an interior [^c22-4] renewal by his listeners in the name of the council.

[^c22-3]: Luigi Maria Carli, ‘L’Obéissance du prêtre à la lumière de Vatican II’, _La Pensée catholique_ 102 (1966): 9.

[^c22-4]: Marcel Lefebvre, ‘Le Concile Vatican II, appel à la sainteté’, _La Pensée catholique_ 102 (1966): 38.

On 24 July 1966, Cardinal Alfredo Ottaviani, prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, sent a letter to the presidents of episcopal conferences and superiors of religious congregations. Eight months after the closing of the council, he drew attention to the ‘unfortunate news [that] has been reported from various areas about abuses regarding the interpretation of the conciliar doctrine’ and lamented that ‘some brazen opinions [were] circulating … causing great disturbance among the faithful’. The cardinal specifled that, these were ‘affirmations which easily go beyond the limits of hypothesis or simple opinion, seeming to undermine in some way the dogma itself and the foundations of the faith’. He gave ten examples of these opinions and errors and asked that the bishops strive to eradicate or prevent them, as well as tackling the issue and reporting back to the Holy See before Christmas.[^c22-5]

[^c22-5]: Alfredo Ottaviani, ‘_Epistula ad venerabiles praesules conferentiarum episcopalium_’, Rome (24 July 1966), in _AAS_ 58 (1966): 659–61. French translation in _La Pensée catholique_ 103 (1966): 14–16.

On 20 December 1966, Archbishop Lefebvre, in his capacity as superior general of the spiritans, answered [^c22-6] the cardinal. His response is invaluable for the light it sheds on his views of the council a year after its closing. He wrote to the cardinal that ‘when the Council introduced innovations, it unsettled the certainty of **[p. 363]** truths taught by the authentic Magisterium of the Church as unquestionably belonging to the treasure of Tradition’. In his view, ‘the Council has encouraged, in an inconceivable manner, the spreading of liberal errors’ so that ‘[f]aith, morals and ecclesiastical discipline are shaken to their foundations, fulfilling the [^c22-7] predictions of all the Popes’. A few months later, on 19 March 1967, he wrote to Fr Victor-Alain Berto, who had been his theological adviser at Vatican II, that ‘false theologians’ had distorted and corrupted the council, and that those who had prepared the schemas wanted to introduce doctrines contrary to the [^c22-8] ecclesiastical magisterium. In a second letter to the same correspondent in October 1968, just over a year and a half later, he wrote that ‘as long as the Church continues to remain trapped by the conciliar documents, it undermines itself’. In this same letter, he states that the Church resulting from the council is [^c22-9] a ‘new religion’. Even so, he did not yet reject Vatican II, as can be seen in an article he published in the journal _Itinéraires_ in November 1968: ‘The council documents … have been signed by the pope and the bishops and therefore there can be no doubt as to their content.’ This did, however, raise some questions: ‘Even so, how, for example, is one to interpret the text of religious freedom in which there is a certain [^c22-10] internal contradiction? … In the end, what is one to do?’ Questions were also asked by his Brazilian colleagues and friends, bishops Geraldo de Proença Sigaud and Antonio de Castro Mayer (Campos, Brazil), as evidenced by a letter de Castro Mayer addressed to Archbishop Lefebvre in June 1968.[^c22-11]

[^c22-6]: ‘Lettre de Mgr Marcel Lefebvre au cardinal Alfredo Ottaviani’, Rome (20 December 1966), Archives du Séminaire d’Écône (ASE), E02–19, 001; reproduced in Marcel Lefebvre, _J’accuse le Concile!_ (Martigny: Éditions Saint-Gabriel, 1976), 107–11; translated as _I Accuse the Council_ (St Marys, KS: Angelus Press, 1982).

[^c22-7]: Lefebvre, _J’accuse le Concile!_, 109–10.

[^c22-8]: ‘Lettre de Mgr Marcel Lefebvre à l’abbé Victor-Alain Berto’ (19 March 1967), Archives des Dominicaines du Saint-Esprit (ADSE), Fonds Victor-Alain Berto, folder ‘Le Deuxième Concile du Vatican’.

[^c22-9]: Letter, Rome (29 October 1968), ADSE, Fonds Victor-Alain Berto, folder ‘Le Deuxième Concile du Vatican’.

[^c22-10]: Mgr Marcel Lefebvre, ‘Lueurs d’espérance’, _Itinéraires: Chroniques et documents_ 127 (November 1968): 105.

[^c22-11]: ‘Lettre de Mgr Antonio de Castro Mayer à Mgr Marcel Lefebvre’, Campos (29 June 1968), ADSE, E05–01.

The conciliar documents and the evolution of the conciliar Church caused great psychological distress for the former members of CIP, at least the most ardent ones. Some of the Dominican nuns of the community [^c22-12] founded by Fr Berto are convinced that he died as a result of the council. Not an implausible explanation, [^c22-13] when one reads his letters. However, he clearly stated that he unreservedly accepted Vatican II in its [^c22-14] entirety. The Benedictine monks of Solesmes and even the alumni of the Pontifical French Seminary who worked with the CIP also accepted all the Vatican II documents. Their writings on the subject, notably those [^c22-15] of Dom Jean Prou (abbot-president of the Solesmes congregation), witness to this acceptance, as does the later evolution of the Solesmes community. Likewise, Bishop Carli, who remained conservative and **[p. 364]** traditionalist, accepted the conciliar documents and would later be appointed archbishop of Gaeta (Italy). [^c22-16] Cardinals Ottaviani, Siri, and Ruffini also took the position of acceptance.

[^c22-12]: Comments to the author by a religious sister of the community.

[^c22-13]: See his conciliar and post-conciliar correspondence in the ADSE.

[^c22-14]: ‘Projet de lettre (non envoyée) de l’abbé Victor-Alain Berto à l’abbé Harang’ (3 July 1968), ADSE, Collection Victor-Alain Berto, Folder ‘Le Deuxième Concile du Vatican’. See Berto’s complete post-conciliar correspondence in the ADSE.

[^c22-15]: Archives de l’abbaye Saint-Pierre de Solesmes (AASPS), Folder ‘Dom Jean Prou—Sur le Concile: Le Regard de la foi sur le Concile Vatican II’. See also AASPS, Collection ‘Dom Georges Frénaud’.

[^c22-16]: ‘Lettre de Mgr Antonino Romeo à Mgr Georges Cabana’ (29 March 1967), Service des Archives de l’Archidiocèse de Sherbrooke (SAAS), P43/7.1 1937–69 60.

#### The Reception of Vatican II by Other People and Groups

The reception of the Second Vatican Council by traditionalists who were not former members of CIP was not fundamentally different from those who were, but one can detect more radical views. Among priests, Fr Georges from Nantes was probably the first to resist Vatican II publicly. Among his famous _Lettres à mes amis_ is a letter dated 16 July 1966 addressed to Cardinal Ottaviani. It contained a passage that claimed that a ‘council assembled to reconcile the Church with the modern world seemed a contradiction in terms’ and that the council fathers had betrayed their mission and fallen into modernism.[^c22-17]

[^c22-17]: ‘Lettre de l’abbé de Nantes au cardinal Ottaviani’, La Contre-Réforme catholique au XXIe siècle, https://crc- resurrection.org/notre-pere-fondateur/la-situation-canonique-de-labbe-de-nantes/lettre-de-labbe-de-nantes-au- cardinal-ottaviani.html.

[^c22-18] Roger-Thomas Calmel, a Dominican, is another figure who cannot be overlooked. He maintained that Vatican II could be ignored outright: ‘Regarding the authority of the council … it defined nothing; therefore [^c22-19] we are not obligated—by virtue of the faith—to take seriously anything they have to say.’ Until his death in 1975, he continued to write articles about theology and spirituality for the journal _Itinéraires_. It was founded in 1956 by Jean Madiran as a traditionalist journal whose position on Vatican II was expressed in its first issue of 1966. An editorial entitled ‘Receiving the Decisions of the Council’ stated: ‘[W]e receive all the conciliar decisions and …, as far as it is up to us, we invite our readers to receive them’. The position was nuanced by the statement that such reception was done ‘in conformity with decisions of previous councils’, and therefore if any text could be subject to various interpretations, ‘the correct interpretation is precisely set by and in conformity with the previous councils and with the whole of the teaching of the [^c22-20] magisterium’.

[^c22-18]: Père Jean-Dominique Fabre, _Le Père Roger-Thomas Calmel 1914–1975: Un fils de saint Dominique au XXe siècle_ (Suresnes: Clovis, 2012).

[^c22-19]: ‘Lettre de Roger-Thomas Calmel’ (10 February 1966), ibid., 318.

[^c22-20]: Editorial II, ‘Recevoir les décisions du Concile’, _Itinéraires_ 99 (January 1966), 21–26.

During this phase, the struggles of Fr Louis Coache are of note. In February 1968, he founded _Le Combat de la Foi_, a monthly publication in support of his fight against the ‘modernist heresy’. During that first year, he published his famous _Vade Mecum du catholique fidèle_, signed by 170 priests—mostly from France, but from other countries as well. They were not taking a stand against the council, but they took issue with the ‘post-conciliar spirit, decried by Paul VI, that was inclined to abolish all external signs of adoration’. In terms of **[p. 365]** liturgy, they reminded priests that ‘the rules in effect before the Second Vatican Council remained in effect, apart from any explicit exemption stemming from laws enacted at a later date’. As a sign of faithfulness to the council, he insisted on the use of Latin in the liturgy, pointing out that ‘priests who [^c22-21] continued to use Latin while celebrating Mass were … not against the Council’.

[^c22-21]: _Vade Mecum du catholique fidèle: Face à la destruction concertée de l’Église 170 prêtres rappellent les principes essentiels_ _de la vie chrétienne_ (Paris: Ferrey, 1968), 5–7.

This publication foreshadows what was to become the main preoccupation of traditionalist Catholics at the end of the 1960s, a concern that would be a decisive element in the reception of the council: liturgical reform and its implementation. This reform marks the beginning of the second phase of the traditionalists’ reception of Vatican II.

### 3. Phase Two (1969–2000): Towards a Rejection of the Council

[^c22-22] The Apostolic Constitution _Missale Romanum_ was promulgated on 3 April 1969 and came into effect on 30 November, marking the beginning of a new phase in the reception of Vatican II by traditionalists. It is not that doctrinal issues were ignored—far from it—but the new Mass and liturgical abuses became one of the main bones of contention of those who opposed the council. After an examination of this issue, the focus will shift to Archbishop Lefebvre and the SSPX in order to examine the evolution of their views on the Second Vatican Council; we will end with an examination of the Ecclesia Dei communities that were formed after the episcopal consecrations by Lefebvre in 1988.

[^c22-22]: Paul VI, ‘Constitutio apostolica Missale Romanum’, _AAS_ 61 (1969): 217–22.

#### The Liturgical Issue

Before 1969, traditionalist Catholics had been critical of the conciliar liturgical reform. Many had already publicly expressed reservations about the reform and the way it was being implemented in dioceses and parishes. From 1964 on, many Catholics answered the call of Borghild Krane, a Norwegian psychologist, to form national associations for the defence of the traditional liturgy. An initial meeting in Rome in 1965 of delegates from six of these associations was followed on 8 January 1967 by the creation of Foederatio [^c22-23] Internationalis Una Voce in Zurich. It was in the offices of this organization, supported by Archbishop Lefebvre, that the famous _Bref examen critique du Nouvel Ordo Missæ_, dated 5 June 1969 and co-signed by Cardinals Alfredo Ottaviani and Antonio Bacci, was written. The cover letter for the document addressed to **[p. 366]** Paul VI (3 September 1969) contains the following statement: ‘the Novus Ordo represents, both as a whole and in its details, a striking departure from the Catholic theology of the Mass as it was formulated in Session XX of the Council of Trent’. The letter ends with a plea to the pope ‘not to want the possibility of [^c22-24] having recurse to the honest and fruitful Roman Missal of St Pius V taken away’.

[^c22-23]: Foederatio Internationalis Una Voce, ‘A Brief History, International Una Voce Federation’, http://www.fiuv.org/p/who-we- are.html.

[^c22-24]: Cardinaux Ottaviani et Bacci, ‘Bref examen critique de la nouvelle messe’, _Itinéraires_ 141 (1970): 216, 218.

The traditionalist attacks on the new Mass came from many quarters. Bishop Antonio de Castro Mayer of Campos, Brazil, a former member of the CIP steering committee, wrote to Paul VI to share the concerns that grieved his heart as a priest and bishop because of the reform of the Mass; he beseeched the pope to [^c22-25] ‘authorize the continued use of the _Ordo missae_ of Pius V’. Fr Raymond Dulac penned an article that [^c22-26] became authoritative in traditionalist circles in which he severely criticized the new _ordo_ and clearly stated [^c22-27] that he did not intend to use it. Fr Georges from Nantes used his journal _Contre-réforme catholique_ to denounce ‘the fraudulent replacement of the Holy Sacrifice of the Catholic Mass with a Lutheran Last [^c22-28] Supper and progressive celebration’. Jean Madiran thought it ‘absolutely impossible, in all conscience, that the new mass be accepted … except as a prudent, cautious, and regretful acceptance with [^c22-29] reservations’. Fr Calmel believed that it was his ‘duty as a priest to refuse to celebrate Mass using such a [^c22-30] questionable rite’; similarly, Fr Guérard des Lauriers, a future sedevacantist bishop (i.e., one who fails to acknowledge the pope as legitimate, and thus considers the chair of Peter vacant), stated that he ‘cannot use [^c22-31] the new _Ordo missae_’. Fr Coache urged ‘all the faithful, anxious about the true faith and union with God, to [^c22-32] not attend this new Mass’, and Paul Scrotesco declared that it ‘was the Mass of the Revolution’ and was [^c22-33] ‘no longer a sacrifice, but a sacrilege’. Finally, in 1971, Jean Vaquié wrote _La Révolution liturgique_, in which [^c22-34] he condemned the new Mass as part of a conspiracy and as the Protestantization of Catholic worship.
