#### Archbishop Lefebvre and the Society of St Pius X on Vatican II

During the 1970s and 1980s, Archbishop Lefebvre travelled the world, exhorting the faithful and establishing the SSPX that he has founded in 1970. His criticism of the council grew, and he compared its main doctrines to the ideals of the French Revolution: freedom of religion corresponded to _liberty_, [^c22-42] collegiality to _equality_, and ecumenism to _fraternity_. In 1974, a manifesto he wrote made the headlines and rallied people to his cause, but also had ramifications with respect to his relations with the Holy See. Dated 21 November, it contains the following sensational declaration: ‘We refuse, on the other hand, and have always refused to follow the Rome of neo-Modernist and neo-Protestant tendencies which were clearly [^c22-43] evident in the Second Vatican Council and, after the Council, in all the reforms which issued from it.’ Following this declaration, he was summoned to Rome and asked to explain himself, which he did on 13 [^c22-44][^c22-45] **[p. 368]** February and 3 March 1975. On 22 July 1976, he was struck by a suspension _a divinis_,to which he responded: ‘I have been asked to obey the “conciliar Church”, as it is called by Archbishop Benelli. But this conciliar Church is a schismatic Church, since it has broken with the Catholic Church that has always [^c22-46] been.’

[^c22-42]: e.g. Marcel Lefebvre, _Un évêque parle, Mgr Lefebvre: Écrits et allocutions 1963–1974_ (Jarzé: Éditions Dominique Martin Morin, 1974), 196–97; translated as _A Bishop Speaks: Writings and Addresses, 1963–1975_ (Kansas City: Angelus Press, 2007).

[^c22-43]: ‘Déclaration de Mgr Marcel Lefebvre’, _Itinéraires_ 189 (January 1975), 5–8.

[^c22-44]: Tissier de Mallerais, _Marcel Lefebvre_, 507.

[^c22-45]: Ibid., 514.

[^c22-46]: Mgr Marcel Lefebvre, ‘Quelques réflexions à propos de la “suspense _a divinis_” ’ (29 July 1976), in Tissier de Mallerais, _Marcel_ _Lefebvre_, 514.

On 29 August 1976, at the request of the ‘Traditional Associations’, Archbishop Lefebvre celebrated a Mass [^c22-47] at the Lille trade fair that was attended by about 7,000 people. On that occasion, he declared:

[^c22-47]: Tissier de Mallerais, _Marcel Lefebvre_, 516.

what the Revolution did is nothing compared to what the Council has done, nothing! It would have been better that the 30, 40, even 50 thousand priests who turned in their cassocks, who turned their back on the oath they made to God had been martyred, had been marched to the scaffold, as that would have at least preserved their soul. Now, they may lose it.[^c22-48]

[^c22-48]: Mgr Marcel Lefebvre, ‘Lille—29 août 1976’, in _Homélies ‘Été chaud 1976’_, Textes officiels—Fraternité Saint-Pie X (Martigny: Éditions Saint-Gabriel, n.d.), 28.

That same year, he published a book entitled _J’accuse le Concile_ (later published in English as _I Accuse the Council_); to justify such a title, he wrote that ‘the spirit that prevailed at the Council and inspired so many ambiguous and questionable and downright erroneous texts, is not the Holy Spirit, but the spirit of the modern world, a spirit that is liberal, Teilhardian, modernist, and contrary to the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ’.[^c22-49] Sedevacantism

[^c22-49]: Mgr Lefebvre, _J’accuse le Concile_, 9 {.

Alongside the criticism levelled by Archbishop Lefebvre, the SSPX, and associated communities, there grew a movement, _sedevacantism_, that would draw much more radical conclusions. In 1971, a Mexican Jesuit named Joaquín Sáenz y Arriaga published a book in which he claimed that Paul VI had founded a new [^c22-50] religion and could therefore not be the pope of the Catholic Church. Two years later, he published another [^c22-51] book in which he concluded that the See of Peter was vacant because of the heresies of Paul VI. These two books would play a part in the development of _sedevacantism_, which started in Mexico, spread to the United States and Spain, and reached France. One of its advocates there would be Michel-Louis Guérard des Lauriers, a Dominican who had had an important role in the writing of the aforementioned _Bref examen critique du nouvel Ordo Missae_. In 1979, he published a study entitled _Le Siège apostolique est-il vacant?_ in which his thesis is that Paul VI is pope _materialiter_ but not _formaliter_, because he no longer ‘habitually, really and effectively speaks’ so as to ‘promote the good purpose entrusted to the Church’. Guérard des Lauriers **[p. 369]** writes that, as a result, ‘there is no longer communication coming from Christ, nor true Authority being [^c22-52] exercised’. Since then, sedevacantist movements have developed, and many separate groups have appeared (sedeprivatists, _Semper Idem_ Catholics, conclavists). They all rally to a common cause: the rejection of the Second Vatican Council and all the reforms to which it gave rise, also holding to the idea that the See of Peter has been vacant since the death of Pius XII because of the heresies of the popes that followed him. There is a profound point of divergence with the SSPX and the communities that are close to it.

[^c22-50]: Joaquín Sáenz y Arriaga, _La nueva iglesia montiniana_ (Palmdale, CA: The Christian Book Club of America, 1971).

[^c22-51]: Joaquín Sáenz y Arriaga, _Sede Vacante: ‘Paulo VI no es legitimo papa’_ (Mexico City: Editores Asociados, 1973).

[^c22-52]: Père Guérard des Lauriers, ‘Le Siège apostolique est-il vacant?’, _Cahiers de Cassiciacum_ 1 (May 1979): 57.

#### From Rejection of the Council to Excommunication

In 1983, given the ‘self-destruction of the Church’, Archbishop Lefebvre and Bishop de Castro Mayer wrote an open letter to the pope to which they attached a ‘Brief summary of the main errors of conciliar ecclesiology’ in which they denounced the main errors that were at the origin of the situation in which the [^c22-53] Church found itself. Later, in August 1985, before the Extraordinary Synod of Bishops to be held on the twentieth anniversary of the closing of the council, both prelates wrote again to John Paul II to express their concerns and wishes. They denounced in particular the religious freedom and its consequences, stating that ‘if the coming Synod does not return to the traditional Magisterium of the Church, in the question of religious liberty, but instead confirms this serious error from which heresies flow, [they will be forced] to [^c22-54] think that the members of the Synod no longer profess the Catholic faith’.

[^c22-53]: ‘Lettre ouverte de Mgr Marcel Lefebvre et de Mgr Antonio de Castro Mayer à Jean-Paul II’, Rio de Janeiro (21 November 1983), ADSE, Fonds Marcel Lefebvre, E 03–17.

[^c22-54]: ‘Solennelle mise en garde de Mgr Lefebvre et de Mgr de Castro Mayer au Pape Jean-Paul II’, _Fideliter_ 49 (January–February 1986): 4–6.

On 25 January 1986, John Paul II announced that ‘there would be a special meeting in Assisi to pray for peace’, with representatives not only of various churches and Christian communions but also of other world [^c22-55] religions. As Archbishop Lefebvre saw it, this was ‘an insult to our Lord Jesus Christ’. Therefore, on 27 August 1986, he wrote to eight cardinals, asking them to protest against this ‘planned procession of [^c22-56] religions in the city of St Francis’. After the gathering, Archbishop Lefebvre and Bishop de Castro Mayer [^c22-57] protested publicly and very vigorously against this meeting.

[^c22-55]: COSPEC 117 B, 28 (January 1986).

[^c22-56]: In Tissier de Mallerais, _Marcel Lefebvre_, 565.

[^c22-57]: _Fideliter_ 55 (January–February 1987).

In 1987, Archbishop Lefebvre received the Holy See’s response to the _dubia_ about religious freedom that he [^c22-58] had submitted in October 1985 to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith. He was greatly **[p. 370]** disappointed with the response, which he considered even more serious than the interreligious gathering at Assisi: ‘It is one thing to commit a grave and scandalous act, and another to declare false and erroneous [^c22-59] principles, which consequently have disastrous conclusions in practice’. That same year he published a [^c22-60] book in which he decries what he called the ‘robber Council of Vatican II’, in reference to the ‘robber Council of Ephesus’. He also lays out an argument that traditionalists would call upon with increased regularity to reject, or at least no longer follow, the council. The argument centres on the pastoral nature of the event: ‘By declaring the council as “_pastoral_” and not dogmatic, by emphasizing _aggiornamento_ and _ecumenism_, these popes immediately deprived the Council and themselves of the intervention of the [^c22-61] charism of infallibility that would have safeguarded them against all error.’

[^c22-58]: Published under the title _Mes doutes sur la liberté religieuse_ (Étampes: Clovis, 2000); translated as Marcel Lefebvre, _Religious Liberty Questioned_ (Kansas City: Angelus Press, 2002). First edition in 1987 under the title ‘Dubia sur la déclaration conciliaire sur la liberté religieuse présentés à la S.C.R. pour la Doctrine de la Foi par S. Exc. Mgr Marcel Lefebvre, archevêque-évêque émérite de Tulle, fondateur de la Fraternité Sacerdotale Saint-Pie X’.

[^c22-59]: ‘Mgr Lefebvre: Rome est dans les ténèbres’, _Fideliter_ 58 (July–August 1987): 2.

[^c22-60]: See Marcel Lefebvre, _Ils l’ont découronné: Du libéralisme à l’apostasie; La Tragédie conciliaire_ (Escurolles: Fideliter, 1987); translated as _They Have Uncrowned Him: From Liberalism to Apostasy—The Conciliar Tragedy_ (Dickinson, TX: Angelus Press, 1988).

[^c22-61]: Lefebvre, _Ils l’ont découronné_, 163.

In light of Assisi, of the response to his _dubia_ on religious freedom, and of the failure to come to an agreement with Rome, Archbishop Lefebvre decided to consecrate bishops, which he did with Bishop de [^c22-62] Castro Mayer on 30 June 1988, incurring a _latae sententiae_ excommunication. The consecrations caused a deep division within the traditionalist world and affected their reception of the council. Those who chose to remain within the SSPX sphere of influence rejected the council more firmly and categorically, and ties with Rome became weaker, while a different future awaited those who refused to follow Archbishop Lefebvre.

[^c22-62]: On this subject, see _Fideliter_ 64 (July–August 1988).

#### The Ecclesia Dei Communities

On 2 July 1988, immediately following the consecrations, John Paul II issued the motu proprio _Ecclesia Dei_, which established a commission of the same name

whose task it will be to collaborate with the bishops, with the Departments of the Roman Curia and with the circles concerned, for the purpose of facilitating full ecclesial communion of priests, seminarians, religious communities or individuals until now linked in various ways to the Fraternity founded by Mons. Lefebvre, who may wish to remain united to the Successor Peter in the Catholic Church, while preserving their spiritual and liturgical traditions.

**[p. 371]** By the day of the ordinations, around fifteen priests and fifteen seminarians had left the SSPX. On 2 July, the day of the creation of the Ecclesia Dei Commission, they signed in Paris a declaration of intent in which they expressed

their hope that the ecclesiastical authorities would establish them canonically as a society, so that they might work for the realization of their own particular vocation: to dedicate themselves to the People of God and above all to the formation of future priests in an authentic Catholic spirit, and … to celebrate Divine Worship according to the guidelines of immemorial tradition’.[^c22-63]

[^c22-63]: Declaration published in Thierry Bouclier, _L’ Abbé Denis Coiffet: Zélé serviteur de l’Église_ (France: Terra Mare, 2016), 110–11; https://www.fssp.org/en/declaration-of-intention-by-the-founders.

A few days later, some of them were welcomed in Rome and encouraged to found a society of apostolic life [^c22-64] that would be named the Priestly Fraternity of St Peter. It was officially instituted on 18 July 1988 at [^c22-65] Hauterive Abbey (Switzerland) and canonically erected on 18 October 1988. It operated under the authority of the Ecclesia Dei Commission until 17 January 2019, when the commission was suppressed by Pope Francis in the motu proprio _Da oltre trent’anni_ on 19 January 2019.

[^c22-64]: Bouclier, _L’ Abbé Denis Coiffet_, 115.

[^c22-65]: Ibid., 121.

Many other members of the traditionalist movement renewed ties with the Holy See through this commission. As an example, Dom Gérard, the founder and first abbot of Sainte-Madeleine du Barroux Abbey (France), distanced himself from Archbishop Lefebvre as of the ordinations and signed an agreement with [^c22-66] Rome on 29 July 1988. This formalization entails a more positive reception of the council as well as a [^c22-67] recognition of the validity of the Mass and sacraments as set out by the post-conciliar popes. Archbishop Lefebvre was none too kind to those who sided with Rome: ‘It is clear that in siding with and trusting the current conciliar authorities, they implicitly accept the council and the reforms that followed, even though [^c22-68] they have been given only exceptional and provisional privileges.’

[^c22-66]: Yves Chiron, _Dom Gérard: Tourné vers le Seigneur_ (Le Barroux: Éditions Sainte-Madeleine, 2018), 399–400.

[^c22-67]: ‘Lettre du cardinal Mayer à dom Gérard’ (10 September 1988), in Chiron, _Dom Gérard_, 498–99.

[^c22-68]: ‘Lettre de Mgr Lefebvre à l’abbé Daniel Couture’ (18 March 1989), cited in Tissier de Mallerais, _Marcel Lefebvre_, 600.

The Ecclesia Dei communities followed instead the path of compromise. Given the current state of research, it is difficult to provide an accurate analysis of their reception of the Second Vatican Council. Such an analysis is further complicated by the fact that they are extremely guarded on the subject, as they are not in the same position as the SSPX—which, it could be said, has nothing to lose. In general, it could be said that these communities either give a minimal assent to Vatican II or turn a blind eye to it, or, since a 2005 address by Benedict XVI (‘Address of His Holiness Benedict XVI to the Roman Curia Offering them his Christmas Greetings’), adhere to ‘a hermeneutic of reform in the continuity of the one subject-Church’.

**[p. 372]** After the 1988 ordinations, an important fracture therefore appeared in the traditionalist world, leading to a different reception of Vatican II. From that moment, one needs to differentiate the reception of the council by the Ecclesia Dei communities—with their unenthusiastic ‘reception’ of the council or their silence on the subject—and the reception of the event by the followers of Archbishop Lefebvre who continued to reject the council.

### 4. Phase Three (2000– ): Further Theological Inquiry and Critical Reflection

Following the 1988 ordinations, discussions between the SSPX and Rome were practically non-existent, except for some informal and infrequent contacts. Things would change with the Great Jubilee of the Year 2000, as the SSPX organized a pilgrimage to Rome that brought together over 6,000 people. Cardinal Castrillón Hoyos, head of the Ecclesia Dei Commission, learned of it through the media and took it upon himself to meet with the bishops of the SSPX. The meeting led to the start of official doctrinal discussions, aimed at a reconciliation, and to which the SSPX requested two preconditions in order to continue: (1) that the Holy See allow all Catholic priests to celebrate the Mass according to the so-called Pius V rite, and (2) [^c22-69] that the excommunications against the four SSPX bishops be lifted. The Holy See agreed to meet these demands—on 7 July 2007 for the first (with Benedict XVI’s motu proprio _Summorum Pontificum_), and on 21 January 2009 for the second (by the Decree of the Congregation of Bishops lifting the excommunication of the bishops of the SSPX)—but discussions became bogged down for doctrinal reasons. There was one exception: the Union sacerdotale Saint-Jean-Marie-Vianney, founded by Bishop de Castro Mayer in 1982, which had been involved in the discussions, was established as a Personal Apostolic Administration on 18 January 2002 by decree of the Congregation for Bishops. The need for doctrinal discussions, with Vatican II at the centre of things, brought about a new phase in the reception of the council by the SSPX traditionalists that would require in-depth studies of the perceived difficulties raised by the council.

[^c22-69]: ‘Lettre du cardinal Darío Castrillón Hoyos à Mgr Bernard Fellay’ (5 April 2002), Fraternité Sacerdotale Saint Pie-X: La Porte Latine, http://laportelatine.org/vatican/sanctions_indults_discussions/2000_2005/05_04_2002_hoyos_fellay.php.

#### Discussions between the SSPX and Rome and More In-depth Reflection

The initial outcome of the doctrinal discussions between Rome and the SSPX was a number of conferences **[p. 373]** and publications by the latter in preparation for future discussions and the consolidation of a doctrinal foundation from which to discuss any issues. The SSPX organized four theological symposia on the council, [^c22-70] held annually in Paris from 2002 to 2005. SSPX priests, academics, and representatives of associated communities, such as the Dominicans from Avrillé and members of the Fraternity of the Transfiguration, attended the symposia. The aim, according to the inaugural address by Bishop Richard Williamson (one of the four bishops consecrated by Lefebvre in 1988), was to draw out ‘teachings in view of a dialogue with the [^c22-71][^c22-72] Roman authorities’. Others suggested that at stake was a ‘theological struggle’, a preparation for [^c22-73] ‘upcoming confrontations’. The idea was to build up ‘a small arsenal that will assist … in exposing the [^c22-74] undeniable responsibility that Vatican II bears in the crisis of the Church’.

[^c22-70]: _La Religion de Vatican II: Premier symposium de Paris, 4–5–6 octobre 2002_ (Paris: Les Cercles de tradition de Paris, 2003); _La_ _Conscience dans la religion de Vatican II: Deuxième symposium de Paris_ (Paris: Les Cercles de tradition de Paris, 2004); _Le_ _Sel de la terre_ 50 (2004); _L’Unité spirituelle du genre humain dans la religion de Vatican II: Troisième symposium de Paris_ (Avrillé: Le Sel de la terre, 2005); L’Institut universitaire Saint-Pie-X, _Vu de haut_ 12 (2005); _Autorité et réception du concile_ _Vatican II: Quatrième Symposium de Paris, 6–7–8 octobre 2005_ (Avrillé: Le Sel de la terre, 2006); L’Institut universitaire Saint- Pie-X, _Vu de haut_ 13 (2006).

[^c22-71]: Richard Williamson, ‘Allocution d’ouverture’, in _La Religion de Vatican II_, 5.

[^c22-72]: Arnaud Sélégny, ‘Préface’, in _La Conscience dans la religion de Vatican II_, 4.

[^c22-73]: Régis de Cacqueray, ‘Allocution d’ouverture’, in _Autorité et réception de Vatican II_, 10.

[^c22-74]: Ibid., 8.

Around sixty speakers produced a ‘final declaration’ at the end of the first symposium: it was presented as a synthesis of rejection of the council by the SSPX after forty years of resistance. It was also intended to be an [^c22-75] ‘effort of clarification and unity’ for themselves as well as with respect to the ‘official Church’. The document appears to be a summary of the views on Vatican II of the SSPX and its associates. It consists of eight points, including a statement that the council ‘develops a new Christianity’ which is a ‘different religion’ that ‘serves humanity’. The conciliar Church, according to the authors, only wishes ‘to be a “sign” of the invisible presence of God among men’; it renounces ‘being the only society of salvation’, and its pastoral approach ‘does without original sin and without human nature’s fall from grace’. The document also laments that the idea of Christendom seems obsolete and that the Church officially supports ‘the liberal vision of the secularism of the state, as the only one capable of fostering the unity of the human race’. The authors decry the post-conciliar liturgy as ‘a celebration that is a memorial not of the cross but of the Last Supper in which the assembly makes an offering of itself’. A statement in its conclusion declares that Vatican II seems to have made ‘a complete break with the Catholic Tradition … completely centred on God, his praise and service’, while ‘the Council has laid the foundation for a new religion whose primary aims are to exalt the human person and unite the human race’. Therefore, the participants at the symposium reaffirmed ‘their unwavering commitment to the Catholic religion as it has been lived out by the faithful and taught by all the popes until the eve of Vatican II’.[^c22-76]

[^c22-75]: Bernard Tissier de Mallerais, ‘Préface’, in _La Religion de Vatican II_, 1.

[^c22-76]: ‘Déclaration finale’, in _La Religion de Vatican II_, 357–59.

#### Benedict XVI’s Hermeneutic of Vatican II and Its Repercussions in the

#### Traditionalist World

**[p. 374]** Beyond the SSPX, an event would provoke a flurry of research in the wider traditionalist world. The occasion was a speech by Benedict XVI on 22 December 2005 in which he addressed the Roman Curia, sharing his Christmas greetings and marking the fortieth anniversary of the close of Vatican II. Speaking of the reception and hermeneutic of the council, he said that the difficulties in the reception of Vatican II were due to

the fact that two contrary hermeneutics came face to face and quarrelled with each other. One caused confusion, the other, silently but more and more visibly, bore and is bearing fruit. On the one hand, there is an interpretation that I would call ‘a hermeneutic of discontinuity and rupture’; it has frequently availed itself of the sympathies of the mass media, and also one trend of modern theology. On the other, there is the ‘hermeneutic of reform’, of renewal in the continuity of the one subject-Church which the Lord has given to us. She is a subject which increases in time and develops, yet always remaining the same, the one subject of the journeying People of God.

In 2009, in reaction to the debate sparked by this speech, Monsignor Brunero Gherardini, a professor of [^c22-77] ecclesiology and ecumenism at the Lateran University from 1968 to 1995, published a book in which he laments that so little has been done to show how Vatican II is rooted in the previous magisterium, with one [^c22-78] notable exception: the essays of Archbishop Agostino Marchetto. Gherardini railed against the _History of Vatican II_, edited by Giuseppe Alberigo, which in his view ‘only aim[s] at presenting a single idea: the _council_ [^c22-79] _as event_ as the means to get beyond the conflict between the pre-conciliar Church and modernity’. He suggests that ‘the need for a historical and critical analysis of the conciliar texts is required: a study that will [^c22-80] search for links (if there are any) between these texts and the whole of the unbroken Catholic Tradition’. He laments that ‘the magisterium, theologians and pastoral leaders have made of Vatican II an absolute’. In [^c22-81] doing so, he suggests, they have committed a ‘fundamental error … that now needs to be corrected’. He [^c22-82] therefore called for work to be done by a team of experts to ‘revise and re-evaluate’ the conciliar texts.

[^c22-77]: Brunero Gherardini, _Le Concile œcuménique Vatican II: Un débat à ouvrir_ (Frigento: Casa Mariana Editrice, 2009); translated as _The Ecumenical Vatican Council II: A Much Needed Discussion_ (Frigento, Italy: Casa Mariana Editrice, 2009).

[^c22-78]: See Agostino Marchetto, _Il Concilio ecumenico Vaticano II: Contrappunto per la sua storia_ (Vatican City: Libreria Editrice Vaticana, 2005); translated as _The Second Vatican Council: A Counter-point for the History of the Council_, trans. Kenneth D. Whitehead (Scranton, PA: University of Scranton Press, 2010). Marchetto followed up with the publication of _Il Concilio_ _ecumenico Vaticano II: Per una sua corretta ermeneutica_ (Vatican City: Libreria Editrice Vaticana, 2012).

[^c22-79]: Gherardini, _Le Concile œcuménique Vatican II_, 17.

[^c22-80]: Ibid., 19.

[^c22-81]: Ibid., 26.

[^c22-82]: Ibid., 27.

[^c22-83] **[p. 375]** As the years passed, Gherardini, whose sympathy for the views of the SSPX increased, became more and [^c22-84] more explicitly critical of the council. In 2011, he published a follow-up to his 2009 work. It was followed a year later by another book in which he responded to his critics and boiled down the problem of Vatican II to [^c22-85] its anthropocentrism. It is interesting to note that the French translation of his book _Concilio Vaticano II: Il discorso mancato_ was published by the _Courrier de Rome_, an association that organized a number of symposia [^c22-86] on Vatican II beginning from 2004.

[^c22-83]: Brunero Gherardini, _Quod et tradidi vobis: La tradizione, vita e giovinezza della Chiesa_ (Frigento: Casa Mariana Editrice, 2010).

[^c22-84]: Brunero Gherardini, _Concilio Vaticano II: Il discorso macato_ (Turin: Lindau, 2011); French translation: _Concile Vatican II: Un_ _débat qui n’a pas eu lieu_ (Versailles: Courrier de Rome, 2011).

[^c22-85]: Brunero Gherardini, _Il Vaticano II: Alle radici d’un equivoco_ (Turin: Lindau, 2012), 367.

[^c22-86]: _Penser Vatican II quarante ans après_ (Versailles: Publications du Courrier de Rome, 2004); _Vatican II, Un débat à ouvrir_ (Versailles: Publications du Courrier de Rome, 2011); _Vatican II, 50 ans après, quel bilan pour l’Église_ (Versailles: Publications du Courrier de Rome, 2013); _1914–2014: La Réforme de l’Église selon saint Pie X et selon Vatican II_, Actes du congrès théologique du Courrier de Rome, 2015 (Versailles: Publications du Courrier de Rome, 2016).

In the wake of Gherardini’s 2009 book, the Franciscan Friars of the Immaculate held a colloquium (16–18 [^c22-87] December 2010) aimed at a historical, philosophical, and theological analysis of the council. In general, their views align with those of Gherardini, that the problem stems essentially from the interpretation of the council and the dogmatization of the pastoral aspect of the event. In 2012, Fr Serafino Lanzetta of the Franciscan Friars of the Immaculate published a book in which he argued that Vatican II should be seen as a ‘moment’ within the Tradition and not as containing the whole of Tradition, while contending that Vatican II in its pastoral affirmations was not always sufficiently clear.[^c22-88]

[^c22-87]: Serafino Lanzetta, _Concilio Ecumenico Vaticano II, un Concilio Pastorale: Analisi storico-filosofico-teologica_ (Frigento: Casa Mariana Editrice, 2011).

[^c22-88]: Serafino Lanzetta, _Iuxta Modum: Il Vaticano II riletto alla luce della Tradizione della Chiesa_ (Siena: Cantagalli, 2012). About this joining of forces between different kinds of traditionalism during the pontificate of Benedict XVI, see Giovanni Miccoli, _La Chiesa dell’anticoncilio: I tradizionalisti alla riconquista di Roma_ (Rome: Laterza, 2011).

### 5. Conclusion

This chapter has shown that the reception of the Second Vatican Council by traditionalist Catholics is an extremely complex phenomenon that includes evolving interpretations and reactions that vary according to time and circumstance. We examined the reception by dividing the post-conciliar era into three periods which could be refined and debated but which allow for a useful overview of the issue.

Initially, most of the traditionalists and particularly the former members of the CIP seem to receive the documents interpreted in light of the Tradition but reject the spirit of the council, which they see as contrary **[p. 376]** to this same Tradition. For example, against those who interpreted Vatican II according to its ‘logic’ or [^c22-89] its ‘spirit’, Fr Luc J. Lefèvre insisted that only the documents should be retained. Such an approach was not tenable, since this famous ‘spirit of the council’ pervades all the documents of Vatican II. During this first phase, three reactions in the traditionalist world are gradually developing: (1) some accepted the conciliar documents in their entirety and progressively adhered to the ‘spirit’ of the council; (2) others, like Archbishop Lefebvre, wondered about the value of the teaching of Vatican II and how much they should accept it in the face of a growing crisis; and (3) still others—people who were not former members of the CIP—radically opposed the event. Two other points are worthy of note during this phase. First, on the whole, the reaction does not seem (further studies would be required to be more definite) to be grounded in any kind of in-depth intellectual and theological reflection, but rather on concrete observations regarding the post-conciliar crisis and its effects. Second, traditionalists belong to an intellectual and spiritual line of ‘Romans’ who were overly respectful towards the papacy and the magisterium before the council. The conciliar documents completely dismayed and devastated them, as they judged these as being in complete opposition to the traditional doctrine of the Church.

[^c22-89]: Luc J. Lefèvre, ‘Y a-t-il un concile Vatican II? oui ou non…’, _La Pensée catholique_ 121 (1969): 7.

In 1969, the promulgation and implementation of the Apostolic Constitution _Missale Romanum_ marked the beginning of a second phase, in which the issue of the reception of Vatican II would be greatly shaped by the issue of the reception of the new missal, around which those who were resisting the council rallied. During this second phase, three major trends in post-conciliar traditionalism can be detected over time. The first is that Archbishop Lefebvre, of the SSPX and its associated communities, gradually moved towards a complete rejection of the council as a whole, as well as a large part of the post-conciliar magisterium (viewed as contrary to the previous magisterium and the Tradition), culminating in the ordinations of 1988.

The second trend is that the so-called Ecclesia Dei communities, made up mostly of former members of the SSPX who disavowed the four consecrations by Lefebvre and the break with the conciliar Church, rallied around their refusal of the new Mass while, for the most part, remaining silent about their reception of the council.

The third trend is that of those most radical in their reaction, the sedevacantists: they defend the notion that the Apostolic See is to be considered vacant since the death of Pius XII because of the heresies of the popes since the Second Vatican Council, whose teaching they completely reject. Aside from the Ecclesia Dei communities, reception is characterized by a formal refusal of the council and by strong negative reactions. For these movements, the council is like a foreign body in the life of the Church, like a cancer to be fought.

Starting in the year 2000, the reception of the council by traditionalists entered a third phase, with the beginning of discussions between the Holy See and the movement founded by Archbishop Lefebvre. To properly assert its position to Rome, the SSPX needed to arm itself and to secure better and more in-depth **[p. 377]** theological reflections on the council. This was accomplished through conferences and publications, among which those on the subject of the magisterial value of Vatican II are notable. One of the consequences of these discussions was an end to the internal consensus that had prevailed in the SSPX, since they generated a ‘resistance’ movement that refused any and all relations with Rome until the authorities ‘converted’. In some cases, it is not only the principle of coming to agreement that is called into question, but also the principle of entering into discussions in the first place. Any future discussions would now take place under the authority of the Congregation of the Doctrine of the Faith, given the suppression of the Ecclesia Dei Commission in January 2019. Another key event of this period was the speech given by Benedict XVI on 22 January 2005. It is significant because in its wake, and for the first time, insiders, some with affinities to an older Roman school of theology, would officially express reservations about the council in ways that align more closely not only with the ideas of the SSPX, but also with the SSPX itself.

The reception of the Second Vatican Council by traditionalist Catholics is therefore a combination of evolution and disruption, division and convergence, surrender and radicalization. As a result, establishing clear and distinct periods within the post-conciliar era with regards to this reception is extremely complex and therefore somewhat artificial. As is the case in history in general, periodization is a construct of historians; a new period often entails more elements of continuity than of rupture. If the year 1969 can certainly be considered a point of rupture and therefore allows for the establishment of the beginning of a new period in the reception of the council, the year 1988—with its consecrations—could also have justifled the start of a new period, with the traditionalist world fracturing and the creation of the Ecclesia Dei Commission.

However, although there is undeniably a historical rupture within the traditionalist world, it does not appear as a true rupture when viewed uniquely from the perspective of the reception of the council. Indeed, the consecrations do not lead to any fundamental change in the stance taken by the SSPX and its associated communities and do not seem to have brought about—at least not immediately—any change in the thinking of the members of the fledgling Ecclesia Dei communities. For communities that had sided with Rome, their silence with respect to Vatican II seems more like a tactic to safeguard their privileges than a true adherence to the council. That is a question that warrants serious study, as do many of the other aspects of the issue of the reception of the Second Vatican Council by traditionalist Catholics.

## 23. The Papacy and Vatican II

Andrea Riccardi

### 1. The Papacy of John XXIII at the Origin of the Council

**[p. 379]** In the history of the councils, often the pressures to convene the event came from authorities and personalities other than the pope. In the case of Vatican II, the initiative was entirely John XXIII’s, as has [^c23-1] been abundantly demonstrated, overcoming the perplexities of the College of Cardinals. The idea of a council had been circulated at the beginning of the twentieth century. In the Catholic Church, it was definitively set aside by Pius XII. But even in the Eastern Orthodox churches the idea of holding a council circulated for a long time without coming to fruition. In the case of Vatican II, the decision was taken by John XXIII: in short, the papacy was at the origin of the council. Angelo Roncalli himself identifled the council’s mission with respect to its predecessors, not so much through the vast work of consulting the future council fathers and of preparation, in which the Curia played a notable role, but through the message that he himself delivered to the council fathers in the opening address of the council on 11 October 1962: _Gaudet Mater Ecclesia_.

[^c23-1]: On the preparation, convocation, and development of the Second Vatican Council, see Giuseppe Alberigo, ed., _History of_ _Vatican II_, 5 vols. (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1996–2006). See also Alberto Melloni, ‘ “Questa festiva ricorrenza”: Prodromi e preparazione del discorso di annuncio del Vaticano II’, _Rivista di storia e letteratura religiosa_ 28 (1992): 607–43.

The conciliar assembly, in fact, found itself faced with ‘impressive preparatory material produced under the direction of the Roman Curia, which was very dense in character, and which required more support and [^c23-2] assent than debate and research’, as Giuseppe Alberigo wrote. This corpus could have given the council its **[p. 380]** fundamental orientation. But instead, as we see in the personal interventions of the pope, he considered [^c23-3] as belonging to his ‘extraordinary form of governance’ reserved for himself and his initiative.

[^c23-2]: Giuseppe Alberigo and Alberto Melloni, ‘L’allocuzione _Gaudet Mater Ecclesia_ di Giovanni XXIII (11 ottobre 1962)’, in _Fede_ _tradizione profezia: Studi su Giovanni XXIII e sul Vaticano II_, ed. Giuseppe Alberigo, Giuseppe Battelli, and Alberto Melloni (Paideia: Brescia, 1984), 189.

[^c23-3]: See Andrea Riccardi, _Il potere del papa da Pio XII a Giovanni Paolo II_ (Rome: Bari, 1993), 176–84. See also Giuseppe Alberigo, ed., _Papa Giovanni_ (Rome: Bari, 1987).

The culmination of these personal interventions (including the radio message of 11 September 1962, in which John XXIII spoke of ‘the Church of all, and particularly the Church of the poor’) was the opening address of the council.

Roncalli himself wrote the speech addressed to the council fathers, defined by some as ‘the most personal [^c23-4] solemn act of the pontificate’. It is now well established that this intervention triggered a dynamic of greater attention and sense of responsibility among the bishops who had arrived in Rome. It helped to determine their attitude concerning the election of members to the various conciliar commissions and the vote on the schema of the two sources of revelation. Yet it is not a question of going into the dynamics of the relationship between the papacy and the council as far as the pontificates of John XXIII and Paul VI are concerned, but of noting how the approach of Vatican II was designed effectively (and personally) by Roncalli and communicated by him.

[^c23-4]: Alberigo and Melloni, ‘L’allocuzione _Gaudet Mater Ecclesia_’, 193.

‘Illuminated by the light of this Council,’ said John XXIII in his opening speech, _Gaudet Mater Ecclesia_,

the Church—we confidently trust—will become greater in spiritual riches and, gaining the strength of new energies therefrom, she will look to the future without fear. In fact, by bringing herself up to date where required, and by the wise organization of mutual cooperation, the Church will make men, families, and peoples really turn their minds to heavenly things.

Here, the pope outlined his intentions for the council, what distinguished it from the councils that preceded it, their methods of analysis and their condemnations. Through four long years of debates and the production of specific texts, it can be said that a common thread links this opening speech of John XXIII to the closing speech of Paul VI. Paul VI stated in that speech at the end of the council on 7 December 1965: ‘And what happened? Was there a clash, a battle, a condemnation? There could have been, but there was none. The old story of the Samaritan has been the model of the spirituality of the council. A feeling of boundless sympathy has permeated the whole of it.’ One must keep in mind the different contributions of the two popes to the council (the first was its initiator, the second the architect who brought it to a conclusion); nor must one forget the different characters of Roncalli and Montini. And yet, already in _Gaudet Mater Ecclesia_, there was the idea of a ‘new’ pastoral council. In fact, John XXIII distanced himself from the **[p. 381]** catastrophic reading held by those he called ‘prophets of doom’. ‘In the daily exercise of our pastoral office, we sometimes have to listen, much to our regret, to voices of persons who, though burning with zeal, are not endowed with too much sense of discretion or measure. In modern times they can see nothing but prevarication and ruin.’

He sets out the earlier attitude, and the contrasting approach that he proposes to adopt:

The Church has always opposed these errors. Frequently she has condemned them with the greatest severity. Nowadays, however, the Spouse of Christ prefers to make use of the medicine of mercy rather than that of severity. She considers that we meet the needs of the present day by demonstrating the validity of her teaching rather than by condemnations.

John XXIII concentrated his efforts, with the strength of the authority of the papacy and the charismatic and pastoral character of his person, on a process much greater than other reforms: the beginning of Vatican II and the responsible participation of bishops from all over the world. He was convinced of the need for change, but he felt that a single man, even if he was pope and charismatic, would not succeed; in short, the papacy needed to appeal to the bishops of the world and to the conciliar process.

### 2. The Conclave of Vatican II

From this perspective, following the death of John XXIII on 3 June 1963 after the conclusion of the first session of the council, the question of papal succession not only concerned the papacy and the government of the Church but also directly affected the continuation of Vatican II. For this reason, in the conclave of June 1963, the council itself was in some way at stake. Whether and how it might continue would depend on the future pope. It must be said that, within the ranks of the cardinal-electors of the new pope, those who were perplexed about Vatican II and the orientation of John were more numerous than among the bishops in general. The bishops, in the first session, had acclimatized to the council atmosphere created by John XXIII. The conclave could have put the council back on the path of the Curial preparations or limited its scope through the election of the pope.

In this sense, the conclave of 1963 was a delicate one; the council was open, although it was during the intersession when the bishops were not gathered in Rome. The decisive character of the June 1963 conclave was noted by the first observers, such as the Vatican scholar Giancarlo Zizola, who observed the harsh clash [^c23-5] in the Sistine Chapel between the ‘conciliar’ and conservative cardinals. The candidate with most press **[p. 382]** coverage, the archbishop of Milan, Cardinal Giovanni Battista Montini, was among the progressive leaders at the council and was considered a frightening figure by the ‘Roman party’, the group of prelates and cardinals of the Roman Curia who in 1954 had determined his departure from a position close to Pius XII [^c23-6] in the Secretariat of State, sending him to the Ambrosian archdiocese. The ‘Roman party’ had managed to prevent Montini from reaching the 1958 conclave after the death of Pius XII; without the cardinal’s red hat, he could not be a candidate.

[^c23-5]: See Giancarlo Zizola, _Il Conclave: Storia e segreti_ (Rome: Newton Compton, 1993). See also Giancarlo Zizola, _L’utopia di_ _Papa Giovanni_ (Assisi: Cittadella, 1973).

[^c23-6]: See Andrea Riccardi, _Il ‘partito romano’: Politica italiana, Chiesa cattolica e Curia romana da Pio XII a Paolo VI_ (Morcelliana: Brescia, 2007).

Another candidate in 1963 was the archbishop of Bologna, Cardinal Lercaro. He was clearly aligned with the progressive council majority, elected as the head of the conciliar Commission for Liturgical Reform, with an articulate and reforming vision. The German Cardinal Josef Frings (Cologne), together with the leaders of [^c23-7] the conciliar majority, sought to avoid opposition between the two conciliar cardinals in the conclave. Montini appeared to be an ideal candidate, sharing the views of the majority of council fathers, but with a more centralist position to the council. He was an expert in the Roman Curia as well and was linked to John XXIII, who, as soon as he was elected, had appointed him as cardinal. Although Montini was the object of strong hostility from the ‘Roman party’, he appeared perhaps more acceptable than Lercaro to the moderates.

[^c23-7]: See Alberto Melloni, _Il conclave_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2001), 126.

On the other hand, the conciliar minority, represented by a good number of cardinals in the conclave and capable of blocking the election of the new pope, promoted the nomination of Cardinal Ildebrando Antoniutti, a member of the Roman Curia, perhaps in the hope of reaching a compromise on a candidate [^c23-8] who was less committed to Vatican II. Cardinal Gustavo Testa, a friend of Pope John, reported that there [^c23-9] were moments of tension. Then, some of the conservatives moved to support the name of Montini, who [^c23-10] resisted the opposition and was eventually elected, taking the name Paul VI. It is easy to see how the conclave, while representing an assembly of a different nature and more restricted than the council, fully reflected the logic and dynamics that had already inhabited Vatican II.

[^c23-8]: See Riccardi, _Il potere del papa_, 223 {.

[^c23-9]: See Zizola, _Il Conclave_, 243–47.

[^c23-10]: Testimony of Cardinal Loris F. Capovilla to the author.

From the beginning, the papacy of Paul VI presented itself as a conciliar pontificate which fully embraced the objective of bringing to a successful conclusion the work begun to implement an incisive renewal of the Church. However, as a majority and a minority were becoming more sharply defined, Paul VI tended to take an inclusive position. He wanted to be the pope of all not only during the conciliar proceedings, but also during the period of the reception of Vatican II.

### 3. Between the Council and Its Reception

**[p. 383]** Paul VI was, in many ways, the architect of Vatican II through three intense sessions that led to its conclusion, on 8 December 1965, and to the promulgation of the council documents. We will not focus on [^c23-11] the role of the pope in the dynamics of the council’s proceedings, as this has already been done by others. It should simply be remembered that Montini emerged as a man of government with his ability to receive various requests, to mediate, to draw a line of progress in the works. Cardinal Franz König called him the ‘martyr of the Council’ for his attentive patience with different requests. In his testimony for the process of beatification, Romeo Panciroli portrayed Montini as an

[^c23-11]: See Alberigo, _History of Vatican II_, vols. 3–5.

attentive observer of the facts, willing to listen, respectful of the freedom of the fathers and of the conciliar bodies, firm when he reached personal conviction, firm when it came to Catholic doctrine. Beyond partisan interest, he sought to understand problems thoroughly and clearly: he invited study by the competent bodies and, after examining their results, he took decisions with his own authority.[^c23-12]

[^c23-12]: Congregatio de Causis Sanctorum, _Beatificationis et Canonizationis Servi Dei Pauli VI: Positio super vita, virtutibus et fama_ _sanctitatis_, 2 vols. (Rome: Nova Res, 2012), 1:189. See Giselda Adornato, _Giovanni Battista Montini—Paolo VI: Biografia_ _storica e spirituale_ (Cinisello Balsamo: San Paolo, 2018), 439–40.

The development of the council’s works led to the creation of new bodies in the life of Rome, a subject to which Montini was very attentive. Already in 1960, in the context of the conciliar commissions, the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity was born, led by the Jesuit Cardinal Augustin Bea. In 1964, Paul VI set up a special body to apply the council’s guidelines on liturgical matters, the Consilium ad exequendam constitutionem de sacra liturgia (Commission for Implementing the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy); it [^c23-13] was headed by Cardinal Lercaro, who had long been involved in the liturgical movement. The dynamics and the achievements of the council raised new questions for the structures of the Roman papacy, to which Montini was very sensitive.

[^c23-13]: See Alberigo, _History of Vatican II_, 3:241–47. See also Annibale Bugnini, _The Reform of the Liturgy_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 1990; originally published as _La riforma liturgica_ (1983).

Paul VI, himself a member of the Roman Curia for many years, was aware of the resistance to the council and its prospects that existed in these circles. Here the ‘Roman party’ had its strongest base. The great French theologian Yves Congar, present at the council’s proceedings as an expert, offers a description of the climate of the Curia towards the council’s work and the orientation given to it by the pope himself:

On all sides he [the Brazilian _peritus_ Antonio Guglielmi] hears bitter complaints about ‘this cursed **[p. 384]** council’ which is ‘ruining the Church’; not a financial ruin, but an ecclesiological one, I venture to say. What Church? What ecclesiology? They say: if only it was over, and these bishops went back home!!! But is ‘back home’ not the Church? The Romans have a strange conception of things. For them, there are bishops and dioceses; there are _materia circa quam_ [the matter about which], and there is ‘the Church’; that is, themselves, their authority, their administration, their legalism.[^c23-14]

[^c23-14]: Yves Congar, _My Journal of the Council_ trans. Mary John Ronayne and Mary Cecily Boulding, ed. Dennis Minns (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2012), 606 (2 October 1964).

Paul VI, who had been opposed by the ‘Roman party’ in the years spent in the Secretariat of State and in the conclave of 1963, was aware of the difficulties the Curia could create during the course and implementation of the council. That is why, from the outset, he posed the problem of the relationship between the new pope and his Curia. He quickly wanted to establish a direct dialogue with its members, whom he summoned to an audience. He received them on 21 September 1963, shortly after his election and before the second session of Vatican II, and delivered a very demanding speech. He explained that the Church was really living a ‘historic moment’ represented by the council, due to the inspired work of John XXIII, which he intended to continue.

Paul VI concluded, as if to build excitement among the members of the Curia: ‘the hour is great and sacred’. What role should the Curia play in this particular hour? His answer: ‘It seemed appropriate to us that the Roman Curia should become aware with us of this great event’. The historic moment demanded above all a profound unity of intent between the pope and his Curia, avoiding those episodes of disconnection or the contrasts that had marked the papacy of John XXIII: ‘If ever such conformity of mind to what the pope commands or desires must be strictly univocal on the part of the Roman Curia … this is the moment to give your firm and open profession.’[^c23-15]

[^c23-15]: Paul VI, ‘Discorso alla Curia romana, 21 settembre 1963’, Libreria Editrice Vaticana, http://w2.vatican.va/content/paul- vi/it/speeches/1963/documents/hf_p-vi_spe_19630921_roman-curia.html.

From the start of this speech, it is clear that the pope reserved a decisive role for Rome, not only in the leadership of the council but in its reception: ‘It is from Rome that the invitation to update starts’, he says. In this context, how can the Roman Curia, the first instrument of government of the papacy, be cold and hostile to the message of the council that the pope himself desires and makes his own? How can the Curia not go along with this? In 1963, Paul VI was convinced that the papacy must profoundly reform the instruments of government—hence the Curia—to help the reception of the council. A great Curia expert like Montini had accumulated over the years many observations, suggestions, and criticisms that led him to set to work as soon as possible on the reform of the Curia. This reform would play an integral part of the relationship between the papacy, the council, and its reception in the years to come.

### 4. The Papacy in a Renewed Rome

**[p. 385]** Rome and the Curia had to renew themselves to provide decisive help to a pope who intended to lead the reception of the council in direct contact with the episcopal conferences. First they would need to regard the local churches and the world with a different attitude. The closing speech, made by Paul VI during the last council session, set the tone:

The Church of the Council, yes, has been very concerned not only with herself and with the relationship that unites her to God, but also with man [_sic_] who is actually present today: the living man, the man who is completely occupied with himself, the man who not only becomes the centre of every interest, but dares to say he is the beginning.[^c23-16]

[^c23-16]: Paul VI, ‘Allocuzione: Discorso di chiusura della Quarta Sessione del Concilio Vaticano II’, 1084; also in _AS_ IV/7, 874–83.

In this framework, the papacy was called to dialogue not only with the Catholic churches of the world and the bishops, but also with humanity as it presented itself, the different Christian churches, non-Christian believers, Jews, non-believers, different cultures. The encyclical _Ecclesiam Suam_, published by Paul VI in August of 1964, presented itself as the ‘manifesto’ of his pontificate. In fidelity to tradition and doctrine, the Church of Paul VI emphasized sympathy in dialogue. The papacy would have to change, and this meant that more people than the pope alone would need to adopt a different attitude. An important decision came at the end of 1965, when the Congregation of the Holy Office—led by Cardinal Alfredo Ottaviani, who had represented the first Vatican department and the ‘bulwark’ against innovators—was reformed with less rigid rules, recognizing greater rights for those accused of error or whose works were examined by the congregation. The cardinals in charge of the congregation were no longer ‘general inquisitors’, and the department changed its name to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, according to the vote of various council fathers.[^c23-17]

[^c23-17]: See François-Charles Uginet, ‘La Constitution _Regimini ecclesiae universae_’, in École française de Rome, _Paul VI et la_ _modernité de l’Église_ (Rome: École française de Rome, 1984), 606–7.

The great work of reforming the papacy along the lines of the council, involved the introduction of organic changes to the Roman Curia, both in the institutions and their methods of government. This reform took up the expressed desire of the bishops at Vatican II by establishing a new relationship between the bishops and the Curia and enabling their participation as members of the Vatican congregations. In September 1965, an office for the Synod of Bishops was created—the first ordinary synod was held in 1967—with the participation of bishops delegated by the national episcopal conferences and others called by the pope. It is not a synod conceived in the manner of the Orthodox and Eastern churches, as some Eastern Catholic bishops at Vatican II had hoped, but an institution with consultative power that has an important role in connecting the papacy and the world’s episcopates to discuss matters of great importance for the whole Church.

**[p. 386]** Another important aspect that marked the post-conciliar period, extending well beyond the pontificate of Paul VI and indeed up to that of Pope Francis, was the internationalization of personnel in the Roman Curia. Until the time of the council, the Curia had been criticized for the fact that most members were of Italian origin and for its Rome-centered attitude, which seemed almost to consider the local and national churches as suburbs of Rome. Paul VI appointed Cardinal Jean-Marie Villot of France, whom he had already called to the Curia, as his Secretary of State. He opened up the top management and the ranks of the Roman administration to people from all over the world, although there remained a good share of Italians. This process made the papacy an institution more similar to international agencies, with personnel from a variety of national origins. Moreover, it is not unlikely that the pope had this model in mind in reforming the Vatican, seeking less a pontifical court and more a home at the service of world Catholicism and dialogue.

In this context, the reform of the Curia carried out by the constitution _Regimini Ecclesiae Universae_— promulgated in 1967, two years after the end of the council, by a commission of experts in close contact with the Secretary of State—played a decisive role. The Secretariat of State acquired a central place—a novelty— as the secretariat of the pope, while some institutions were progressively abolished, such as the Chancery and the Apostolic Chamber. A prefecture for economic affairs was created. Above all, there was room for institutions at the service of the new function that the papacy of the council was taking on in the world: the Pontifical Council for the Laity, the Commission ‘Iustitia et Pax’, the Secretariat for Non-Christians, the Secretariat for Christian Unity, and the Secretariat for Non-believers.

Leading the departments was no longer a life-long appointment, but would expire every five years and was subject to the pope, who could confirm someone in the position or make another appointment. This marked the end of the perpetuity of the cardinals who had been at the head of the Curia congregations for several pontificates. In the new Curia, much of the personnel came from the dioceses of the world, while various bishops were called to Rome to serve in administrative roles. The path for the traditional curial career was discussed again. In this way the papacy established new structures and brought in new faces to represent the Church of the council.

### 5. The Papacy and the Reception of the Council between Paul VI and John Paul II

The period of the initial reception of Vatican II, lasting from the conclusion of the council in 1965 until Paul VI’s death in 1978, was in many respects a time of difficulty and crisis. The pope was openly challenged by **[p. 387]** Catholic movements and groups that accused him of having buried the council’s impetus. The spirit and methods of the turbulent year 1968 also entered the Church, while, as Congar noted, the movements of that year also represented a filter in the reception of the council in some Catholic sectors. On the other hand, in a much more reserved way but no less effectively, Montini was criticized by the conservative sectors that had always opposed him and accused him of having ‘sold oft’ the Church to the world with the conciliar reforms.

It is not possible here to reconstruct the history of the reception of the council in the almost fifteen years of Paul VI’s pontificate, but it is sufficient to note that, amidst contrasting pressures and with strong concerns [^c23-18] for the stability of the Church, he was keen to reaffirm the centrality of the papacy in this ecclesial climate. In Italy, he supported the new national bishops’ conference as the motor to carry out the implementation of the council organically in the various dioceses, while he was against individual local churches following an itinerary that he considered too particular in the reception of the council. The reactions of various national episcopates to the encyclical _Humanae Vitae_, published in July 1968—characterized by proposals for attenuation with respect to the papal positions—show that the various conferences of bishops were not always willing to follow every Roman directive. This attitude can be seen well in the history of the Church in [^c23-19] the Netherlands, its Catechism, and its synods.

[^c23-18]: See Andrea Riccardi, _Paolo VI: Sfide della storia e governo della Chiesa_ (Milan: Jaca Book, 2018).

[^c23-19]: See Riccardi, _Il potere del papa_, 323–25.

The pope curbed the overly autonomous development of the episcopates. The years between 1968 and 1972 were characterized by his desire not to lose the leadership of conciliar reform, which he wanted to apply gradually, without fracture, by including as many bishops and Catholics as possible. In 1968, he proposed the ‘Creed of the People of God’, with which he intended to reaffirm the doctrine of the faith. The pope wanted to moderate the centrifugal thrusts, both traditional and progressive. This can be seen in the application of liturgical reform with the celebration of rites in the vernacular languages of various nations, a policy of which he was firmly convinced. He wanted the Mass to be celebrated everywhere in the revised rite; he responded negatively to Archbishop Lefebvre’s request to allow, in the name of ‘pluralism’ (an incredible motivation for a traditionalist!), the celebration of the Mass in the pre-conciliar rite.

The post-Vatican II Church appeared insufficiently organic to Paul VI. He was concerned that it risked becoming overly variegated, animated by many turbulent movements, marked by problems and confiicts, while crises of vocations among the clergy and men and women religious were emerging. Yet the conciliar papacy opened up new ways of contact with the complex and multifaceted reality that characterized the Catholicism of the 1960s and 1970s. It suffices to consider the ‘invention’ of international papal journeys by Paul VI, which would be taken up again in a systematic manner during the long pontificate of John Paul II, who almost came to define a ‘travelling papacy’. These were pastoral journeys, such as the longest ones to **[p. 388]** Asia, Oceania, and Australia (1970); they were ecumenical journeys, like those to the Holy Land to meet Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras (1964) or to Istanbul (1967) and Geneva to the World Council of Churches (1969); they were journeys to speak to the world, like that to the United Nations in October 1965. The pope, definitively, leaves the physical space of Rome: not only does his word reach everyone through the media [^c23-20] but also, in some way, he is reachable by all, travelling to various countries.

[^c23-20]: See Rodolfo Rossi, ed., _I viaggi apostolici di Paolo VI: Colloquio internazionale di studio_ (Rome: Brescia, 2004).

The papacy of Paul VI, despite various difficulties, opened up a perspective that was destined to be linked to that of John Paul II. Paul VI decided, despite criticism, to hold a Jubilee in 1975, albeit in a renewed form, but full of content. He wanted to go beyond the polarization of Catholic dissent and called for reconciliation. He himself, in Rome, could see so much attention on the figure of the pope. According to Alphonse Dupront, a [^c23-21] French scholar who observed the Jubilee closely, this showed the popular vitality of Catholicism. That season saw the publication of the last important document of the magisterium of Paul VI, after several other texts of value: the Apostolic Exhortation, at the conclusion of the 1974 Synod of Bishops, _Evangelii Nuntiandi_ (On Evangelization in the Modern World).

[^c23-21]: See Alphonse Dupront, _Puissances et latences de la religion catholique_ (Paris: Gallimard, 1993); Alphonse Dupront, _Du_ _Sacré: Croisades et pèlerinages, images et langages_ (Paris: Gallimard, 1987).

A reconciled Church, after the fractures of the post-council era, could not be introverted, but must be projected ad extra. Ten years after the end of Vatican II, the pope declared that the ‘objectives [of the council] are summed up, in the final analysis, in just one: to make the Church of the twentieth century ever more suitable for proclaiming the Gospel to the humanity of the twentieth century’. It is the perspective of evangelization that extends from the pontificate of Paul VI, passes through that of John Paul II, and continues in that of Pope Francis. Although the Church of Paul VI was aware of the many contributions it could make to the world, it particularly emphasized that of evangelization. Indeed, the papacy placed itself at the service of evangelization and as its engine, both in the world of the so-called missions and in the lands of ancient Christianization that are largely secularized. Paul VI stressed, several times, the symbolic fact of his having taken the name of Paul, the evangelizer and the apostle of the nations.

There are profound differences in the history and character of the pontificates of Paul VI and John Paul II. The election of a non-Italian pope in October 1978 reflected the process of internationalization of the papacy desired by Paul VI. The conclave in which Wojtyła was chosen also took place under the banner of debate on the council and its reception. In fact, two prominent candidates were Cardinal Giuseppe Siri (Genoa, Italy), ‘successor’ of Pius XII, critic of Montini’s openness, and Cardinal Giovanni Benelli, former substitute (deputy) of the Secretariat of State under Paul VI. The majority of non-Italians, finding the two candidatures unsatisfactory, turned to a figure from Eastern Europe who had experienced the persecution of religious freedom but who was well known for his identification with Vatican II.[^c23-22]

[^c23-22]: See Andrea Riccardi, _Giovanni Paolo II: La biografia_ (Cinisello Balsamo: San Paolo, 2011).

**[p. 389]** Karol Wojtyła had been a very active council father. Following his return to Poland, he was creatively engaged in the reception of Vatican II through a synod celebrated in a broad and inclusive way for the faithful. He also had a very close, if little publicized, relationship with Paul VI, who considered him one of the most significant personalities of the Church of the time. It can be said that John Paul II had a particular devotion to his predecessor, considering the decisions he made with great respect, and often referred to his behaviour and orientations. However, Wojtyła had a very strong and particular charisma which left a profound impression on his pontificate, in comparison to that of Paul VI.

Conservative or progressive? This was the question that surrounded him in the early days of his pontificate. His position towards communism was very clear, given the difficult experiences of the East. His personality was immersed in the religion of the Polish people which he cultivated rather than rejecting, as was often the case in the West with popular religiosity. But Karol Wojtyła was one of the original bishops of the council and saw himself as a disciple of Paul VI.

Yet the new pope was aware of the crisis the Church was going through and felt personally responsible—in his ministry—to point the way out of the crisis. Benedict XVI, who had been a member of the two conclaves of 1978 that led to the elections of John Paul I and John Paul II, recalled that at the time of the election of the latter, ‘the real problem to face was getting out of the crisis of the Church of those years. It was necessary to practise maximum fidelity to the Second Vatican Council. The reception of the council was also to be purifled. Above all, structural reform was not necessary, but a profound spiritual reform.’[^c23-23]

[^c23-23]: Conversation between the author and Benedict XVI, ibid., 168. Cardinal Albino Luciani was elected by a conclave in August 1978 and took the name John Paul I. He died after 33 days in office on September 28, 1978. His was the shortest pontificate in papal history.

### 6. The Council and the Papacy of John Paul II

Karol Wojtyła brought to the _cathedra_ of Peter his sense of profound identification with Vatican II: ‘A bishop who participated in Vatican II feels indebted to it.’ And, he concluded, ‘to pay back to the council is to implement it’. For him, the council was not the origin of the problems of the Church nor was it to be considered the close of a period of history to be overcome: certainly it is an ‘experience already closed historically but spiritually always in progress’, that of a Church that lives its mission in the world.[^c23-24]

[^c23-24]: Karol Wojtyła, _Alle fonti del rinnovamento_ (Soveria Mannelli: Rubbettino, 2007), 3, 5.

**[p. 390]** We read in the final words of the testament of John Paul II, added in 2000:

Standing on the threshold of the third millennium ‘in medio Ecclesiae’, I wish once again to express my gratitude to the Holy Spirit for the great gift of the Second Vatican Council, to which together with the whole Church—and especially with the whole episcopate—I feel indebted. I am convinced that for a long time to come the new generations will be given to draw on the riches that this Council of the twentieth century has bestowed upon us.

According to Wojtyła, Vatican II still has an important role in the Church of the twenty-first century, while its function and message are far from exhausted. He writes: ‘As a bishop who participated in the event from the first to the last day, I wish to entrust this great patrimony to all those who are and will be called in the future to realize it. For my part I thank the eternal Pastor who has allowed me to serve this great cause throughout all the years of my pontificate.’[^c23-25]

[^c23-25]: John Paul II, _Testamento_ (Rome: Vatican City, 2005), 13; ‘Testamento del Santo Padre Giovanni Paolo II’, Libreria Editrice Vaticana, http://www.vatican.va/gpII/documents/testamento-jp-ii_20050407_it.html.

It is clear that the council was the ‘great cause’ of the papacy of John Paul II. He served it with his approach, which was very different from that of the organic government of Paul VI, a gradualist marked by the tradition of institutional service in the Roman Curia as well as by a clear desire for reform. John Paul II was a council father, but he also felt like a son of Vatican II, which was for him a ‘pastoral-conciliar initiation’. The pontificate of Wojtyła was marked by a pastoral orientation which had matured during his long years of diocesan service in Krakow when he was in contact with the people; but it was also characterized by his multifaceted personality and his ability to establish contact with people and crowds. For this reason, elsewhere, I have defined the leadership of John Paul II as ‘charismatic government’.[^c23-26]

[^c23-26]: Andrea Riccardi, _Governo carismatico_ (Milan: Mondadori, 2003).

His lengthy pontificate passed through a range of historical situations and the most diverse scenarios. Pastorality always remained central to it and was expressed in his numerous trips to many parts of the world and through his contact with people. The pope is first of all a pastoral bishop, as Vatican II teaches, and that was how he presented himself. From this perspective, even if it seemed an arduous objective, John Paul II wanted to meet and be met by the greatest number of people possible. He practised a kind of ‘asceticism’ of encounter, not avoiding the most varied occasions.

For John Paul II, the papacy according to Vatican II meant that the pope was first and foremost the bishop of Rome. Certainly, he did not neglect his universal ministry: meetings, journeys, government, messages. However, the backbone of his episcopal ministry was in the diocese of which he was bishop. He affirmed this forcefully when, far from Rome, he presented himself as ‘bishop of Rome’. This was not an ecclesiastical **[p. 391]** formality, because the pope knew the problems of the diocese of Rome and dealt with them through his successive vicars, visited the diocesan institutions, and especially, every Sunday when able, visited the parishes of Rome (after having received at lunch the clergy who worked there). In John Paul II, the pope took on the mind and the commitment of the diocesan bishop.

Undoubtedly, in the long years of his pontificate, as Cardinal Carlo Maria Martini has noted, John Paul II’s presence on the Church stage was a strong one. His commitment, starting from the ‘Do not be afraid!’ of his initial speech, was intended to give new courage and a new sense of mission to the members of the Church.

He moved along Paul VI’s line of evangelization, which he shared deeply; he represented himself in some situations as the evangelizer, perhaps an extraordinary evangelizer, endowed with a particular charism.

Pope John Paul II took special care of the relationship with the world of young people. He was not eager to discipline or catechize them, but to build with them a relationship of sympathy and trust. This was the setting for World Youth Days, which were John Paul II’s own invention. Young people, for the pope, embodied the ‘Messianic people’ of the future: he was convinced of the need to witness to them, with sympathy, a great Gospel message without giving them lessons in morals or doctrine. Here we find the personal charismatic character of his papacy: it is not only words that are important, but also gestures and [^c23-27] looks, all aimed at meeting people, as Polish director Krzysztof Zanussi has noted. The papacy and charisma were deeply linked during the twenty-eight years of his pontificate. That was something new in comparison to the time of Paul VI.

[^c23-27]: See Krzysztof Zanussi, _Tempo di morire: Ricordi riflessioni aneddoti_ (Milan: Spirali, 2009), 3 {.

The gunman’s attack on the pope in 1981, where he was seriously wounded, changed public opinion towards him. The many meetings, trips, and talks solidifled a dense network of relations between the pope and the people, and not only through the media. A significant change occurred in the history of the papacy with respect to public opinion. The pope, who was often seen on television, was a person whom many people had met directly or who had visited their country. In short, the charism of the pope was witnessed in his encounter with millions of people.[^c23-28]

[^c23-28]: See Riccardi, _Giovanni Paolo II la biografia_, 468 {.

### 7. Vatican II and Benedict XVI

The election of Joseph Ratzinger, who was not endowed with John Paul II’s charism and pastoralism, marked a strong sea change. Benedict XVI was the last of the popes directly involved in the council: he was [^c23-29] an expert theological advisor at the council, following assiduously the work during all four sessions. The year of Ratzinger’s election, 2005, marked the fortieth anniversary of the closing of Vatican II. The papal **[p. 392]** theologian could not but be aware of this anniversary, and intended to remember it. As he said in the ‘Address of His Holiness Benedict XVI to the Roman Curia Offering them his Christmas Greetings’, on 5 December, ‘No one can deny that, in vast parts of the Church, the reception of the Council took place in a rather difficult way.’ What were the reasons for the problems and confiicts that had arisen? Here Benedict XVI presented his analysis as a scholar and witness of the years of the reception of the council, in which he noted the particular role of 1968. Where did the problems come from? For him, the ‘hermeneutical question’ of Vatican II was central, one on which he placed his attention during his pontificate:

[^c23-29]: See Benedict XVI, _Last Testament: In His Own Words_, interviewed by Peter Seewald, trans. Jacob Phillips (London: Bloomsbury, 2016), 119–42.

everything depends on the right interpretation of the Council or—as we would say today—on its right hermeneutics, on the right key of reading and application. The problems of reception arose from the fact that two opposing hermeneutics confronted and quarrelled with each other. One caused confusion, the other, silently but increasingly visibly, has borne fruit. On the one hand there is an interpretation that I would like to call ‘hermeneutics of discontinuity and rupture’; it has often been able to avail itself of the sympathy of the mass media, and also of a part of modern theology.

On the other hand, according to Ratzinger, there was the ‘hermeneutics of reform’, the authentic one attested to by the council texts:

[The Church] is a subject which increases in time and develops, yet always remaining the same, the one subject of the journeying People of God.

The hermeneutic of discontinuity risks ending in a split between the pre-conciliar Church and the post-conciliar Church. It asserts that the texts of the Council as such do not yet express the true spirit of the Council … it would be necessary not to follow the texts of the Council but its spirit. In this way, obviously, a vast margin was left open for the question of how this spirit should subsequently be defined and room was consequently made for every whim.

Benedict XVI’s pontificate undertook to bring the reception of the council back into the wake of what he considered the hermeneutics of the reform. Significantly, his last speech, before his resignation, was addressed to the clergy of the diocese of Rome and touched precisely on the topic of the council, recalling the enthusiasm with which he himself had gone to Vatican II, but also the disappointments that have come about. But then he observed that, next to the council of council fathers, there was that of the media, through which it reached the people of God (a fact that occurred only at Vatican II in the history of the councils). He went so far as to speak of a ‘Council of the media’, which created crises: ‘closed seminaries, closed convents, banalized liturgy’, while the true council struggled to establish itself. However, Benedict XVI affirmed, by now that ‘virtual’ council has become lost, while ‘the true Council appears with all its spiritual strength’.[^c23-30]

[^c23-30]: Benedict XVI, ‘Discorso del Santo Padre Benedetto XVI: All’incontro con i parroci e il clero di Roma, 14 febbraio 2013’, Libreria Editrice Vaticana, http://w2.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/it/speeches/2013/february/documents/hf_ben- xvi_spe_20130214_clero-roma.html.

### 8. The First Pope Who Is a Son of the Council: Francis

**[p. 393]** Pope Francis’s approach to Vatican II has been very different, even though he received and signed the encyclical _Lumen Fidei_, prepared by his predecessor before his resignation. There are various differences in the relationship between Pope Francis and the council compared to Benedict’s: this goes beyond the fact that Ratzinger had a reading of the council as a systematic theologian, unlike his successor, who cultivates an eminently pastoral perspective. The main difference between the two is existential and historical. Despite the fact that Ratzinger was not a bishop at Vatican II, but a theologian and council expert, he was involved in the events and the work of the council and followed it in the making, discussing its decisions. John XXIII and Paul VI were council fathers; John Paul I and John Paul II participated as council fathers. Jorge Bergoglio is a son of the council: he was ordained priest in 1969, four years after the closing of Vatican II, receiving it in the completeness of its texts and through the formation he received in the Argentine province of the Society [^c23-31] of Jesus, an environment that appreciated the novelty of the council. Bergoglio is a priest who, unlike his predecessors, has always celebrated the liturgy with the rite reformed by Paul VI.

[^c23-31]: See Austen Ivereigh, _The Great Reformer: Francis and the Making of a Radical Pope_ (New York: Holt, 2014). See also Andrea Riccardi, _La sorpresa di papa Francesco_ (Milan: Mondadori, 2013).

The conclave following the resignation of Benedict XVI in 2013 was played out around issues other than the council and its implementation, as the conclaves of 1963 and 1978 had done. In fact, the Church and the papacy, for Bergoglio, were incomprehensible without Vatican II, from the beginning of his priesthood and throughout his episcopate. This connaturality of Vatican II to the Church also explains why, as some have observed, he does not constantly mention the council in his texts and speeches, as is sometimes the case in ecclesiastical rhetoric. The editor of _La Civiltà Cattolica_, Antonio Spadaro, SJ, who had conversations with the new pope from the beginning and is familiar with his texts, wrote: ‘I have the impression that the pope simply considers the council as such an indisputable fact that it is not worth talking about it for too long, as if to have to reaffirm its importance’.[^c23-32]
