[^c23-32]: Antonio Spadaro, ‘Intervista a papa Francesco’, _La Civiltà Cattolica_ 3918 (19 September 2013): 467; translated as ‘A Big Heart Open to God’, _America_ 209, no. 8 (30 September 2013): 14–18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30, 32, 34.

Moreover, from the very first moments of Pope Francis’s pontificate, one can see his conciliar inspiration. [^c23-33] Soon after being elected, he declared: ‘How I would like a Church which is poor and for the poor!’ The **[p. 394]** programmatic text of his pontificate, the Apostolic Exhortation on the Joy of the Gospel, _Evangelii Gaudium_ (_EG_), published in November 2013, does not present a reinterpretation of Vatican II but is largely based on the council as an event and teachings lived and assimilated by the pope and by the Church itself. _Evangelii Gaudium_ is a full and mature assimilation of the council, a text inhabited by a strong concern for the reform of the Church in the pastoral sense—an expression of a new season of reception of Vatican II, no longer linked to its protagonists or to the controversies around the texts or interpretation.

[^c23-33]: Pope Francis, ‘Audience to Representatives of the Communications Media 16 March 2013’, Libreria Editrice Vaticana, http://w2.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/speeches/2013/march/documents/papa-francesco_20130316_rappresentanti- media.html. See also Antonio Spadaro, ‘Svegliate il mondo!: Colloquio di papa Francesco con i Superiori Generali’, _La_ _Civiltà Cattolica_ 3925 (4 January 2014): 3–17.

Significantly, in this text, Bergoglio quotes at length the speech of John XXIII at the opening of Vatican II against ‘the prophets of doom’: ‘we are far from naïve optimism’, but ‘greater realism must not mean less trust in the Spirit or less generosity’ (_EG_ 84). Francis reserves some explicit attention—that is, in the quotations—for Vatican II when he talks about the ‘People of God’ (‘He chose to summon them as a people and not as isolated beings’, _EG_ 83; cf. _LG_ 9). But substantially, the Council, assimilated and lived, is the plot of the reflection of the _Evangelii Gaudium_ and most of the body of Francis’s interventions and teachings.

In the conversation with Antonio Spadaro which took place at the beginning of the pontificate, Francis answered a question about what the council was. His response offered a key to understanding his relationship with the council, which has been confirmed in subsequent years:

Vatican II was a reinterpretation of the Gospel in the light of contemporary culture. It has produced a movement of renewal that simply comes from the Gospel itself. The fruits are huge. Just remember the liturgy. The work of the liturgical reform has been a service to the people as a reinterpretation of the Gospel starting from a concrete historical situation. Yes, there are hermeneutic lines of continuity and discontinuity, but one thing is clear: the dynamic of reading the Gospel as it is actualized in today’s Council is absolutely irreversible.[^c23-34]

[^c23-34]: Spadaro, ‘A Big Heart Open to God’, 30.

It is not a question here of insisting on the innovative elements of Francis’s pontificate. It must be said, however, that the Jesuit pope ‘naturally’ assumes the legacy not only of Vatican II but also of the conciliar pontificates—he canonized John XXIII, Paul VI, and John Paul II—while introducing to the practice of his predecessors changes that are typical of his character and his pastoral vision. Bergoglio governs the Church with instruments he intends to reform, but above all he receives from the council popes the pastoral vision of the ministry of the bishop of Rome, which is expressed in meetings, journeys, teaching, and the primacy of evangelization and the poor. In this context, perhaps the papacy of greatest reference for Francis is that of Paul VI. Francis looks with particular attention and for inspiration to _Evangelii Nuntiandi_, which is linked to the tenth anniversary of Vatican II and projects the Church towards the future in evangelization.

### Suggested Reading

**[p. 395]** Benedict XVI. _Last Testament: In His Own Words._ Interviewed by Peter Seewald. Translated by Jacob Phillips. London: Bloomsbury, 2016.

École française de Rome. _Paul VI et la modernité dans l’Église: Actes du colloque organisé par l’École francaise de Rome (2–4 juin 1982)_. Rome: École française de Rome, 1984.

Riccardi, Andrea. _Giovanni Paolo II: La biografia_. Cinisello Balsamo: San Paolo, 2011.

Riccardi, Andrea. _Il ‘partito romano’: Politica italiana, Chiesa cattolica e Curia romana da Pio XII_ a Paolo VI. Brescia: Morcelliana, 2007.

Riccardi, Andrea. _Il potere del papa da Pio XII a Giovanni Paolo II_. Rome: Laterza, 1993.

Zizola, Giancarlo. _Il Conclave:_ Storia e segreti. Rome: Newton Compton, 1993.

## 24. The Reception of Vatican II in Systematic Theology

Paul D. Murray

**[p. 396]** Councils do not have an effect or impact on church life independently of the interpretative and applicative work of receivers who make the potentiality of the council a reality. _Effiect_ and _reception_ go hand in hand; the history of a council’s effect is at the same time a history of its reception.[^c24-1]

[^c24-1]: Ormond Rush, _Still Interpreting Vatican II: Some Hermeneutical Principles_ (Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 2004), ix. I am grateful to Kristin Colberg, Karen Kilby, Paul Lakeland, Ormond Rush, and Gregory Ryan for comments on an earlier version of this chapter.

### 1. Introduction

The title for this chapter presents us with a number of problems. First, looked at in one way, it surely has things the wrong way round, with the conciliar cart placed before the theological horse. As Chapter 3 in this book relates, decades of systematic theological labour flowed into Vatican II as a key part of its context, [^c24-2] which altered the horizon of possibilities rather than simply following from it as constructive consequence. It was the event of the council which itself marked the reception of such work into formal Catholic teaching before there was any question about the reverberative reception of conciliar teaching into subsequent theology.

[^c24-2]: See Gabriel Flynn and Paul D. Murray, eds., _Ressourcement: A Movement for Renewal in Twentieth Century Catholicism_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2012).

Second, how important anyway is this question about the theological reception of Vatican II? As pointedly posed afresh in the Francis papacy, is it not the council’s reception into the life, habits, structures, and processes of Catholicism which really matters? To what extent has more than fifty years of post-conciliar **[p. 397]** systematic theology really served to effect, or even support, such ecclesial reception? That is a sobering question for Catholic theologians to consider. Perhaps with Pope Francis some of that endeavour—or at [^c24-3] least what of it he has himself absorbed and internalized—is now being taken oft the shelf and put to work.

[^c24-3]: See Massimo Faggioli, _Pope Francis: Tradition in Transition_ (Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 2015); Alana Harris and Duncan Dormor, eds., _Pope Francis, Evangelii Gaudium, and the Renewal of the Church_ (Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 2018), particularly Paul Murray, ‘_Ecclesia et Pontifice_: Delivering on the Ecclesiological Implications of _Evangelii Gaudium_’ 85–111.

Third, as that last question suggests, there is the sheer vastness of the fleld, wide enough to fill an entire [^c24-4] Handbook. Inasmuch as the council’s intention was the ‘renewal of the whole tradition … the whole of what [^c24-5] is Catholic’, all Catholic theology since the early 1960s has in a sense been an exercise in the varying [^c24-6] reception of Vatican II, an exercise in pursuing Catholic theology ‘after Vatican II’. Without reducing the task to a listing of names and positions, comprehensive treatment is impossible within a short essay, and selectivity inevitable. Attention here is largely confined to ecclesiological matters.

[^c24-4]: The most useful remains Francis Schüssler Fiorenza and John P. Galvin, eds., _Systematic Theology: Roman Catholic_ _Perspectives_, 2nd ed. (Minneapolis, MN: Fortress, 2011).

[^c24-5]: Walter Kasper, ‘The Continuing Challenge of the Second Vatican Council: The Hermeneutics of the Conciliar Statements’, in _Theology and Church_, trans. Margaret Kohl (London: SCM, 1989), 172.

[^c24-6]: See Paul D. Murray, ‘Catholic Theology After Vatican II’, in Ford’s _The Modern Theologians: An Introduction to Christian_ _Theology Since 1918_, eds. Rachel Muers, Ashley Cocksworth, and David F. Ford, 4th ed. (Oxford and Malden, MA: Wiley Blackwell, 2024), _forthcoming_. The wider-angle synthetic presentation here complements the more restricted ecclesiological focus of the current essay.

Fourth, just as the conciliar debates were sites of contestation and unresolved differences of substance and [^c24-7] approach, so also there has been no unifled reception of its teaching into subsequent Catholic theology; no common synthesis around which a new integrated and integrating Catholic consensus has been able to coalesce.

[^c24-7]: Giuseppe Alberigo and Joseph A. Komonchak, eds., _History of Vatican II_, 5 vols. (Leuven: Peeters, 1995–2006). More briefly, Giuseppe Alberigo, _A Brief History of Vatican II_, trans. Matthew Sherry (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2006).

With these four difficulties in view, this short chapter does three things. First, it provides a more extended treatment of this matter of the divergent theological receptions of Vatican II in order to offer clearer perspective on the specific challenges this presents for contemporary Catholic theology and life. Second, focusing on a subset of exemplary issues, it indicates something of the range of ways in which Catholic theologians have sought to resolve some of the ecclesiological matters opened up by the council’s documents. Third, in the process of so doing, it offers judgement on how these same issues might now best be taken forward in Catholic systematic theology and Catholic life in a manner capable of serving whole- [^c24-8] **[p. 398]** church Catholic flourishing. The aim is both to provide summary narrative and commentary on what has been and to indicate what might be, thereby seeking to contribute to the continuing story of Catholicism’s [^c24-9] reception of Vatican II and the role of systematic theology in that process.

[^c24-8]: On what is required theologically for ‘whole-church Catholic flourishing’, see Paul D. Murray, ‘Living Catholicity Differently: On Growing into the Plenitudinous Plurality of Catholic Communion in God’, in _Envisioning Futures for the Catholic Church_, ed. Staf Hellemans and Peter Jonkers (Washington, DC: Council for Research in Values and Philosophy, 2018), 109–58; and Paul D. Murray, ‘Ecclesiology as Political Theology: On Delivering on a Transformative Strategic Orientation in Ecclesiology’, _Theological Studies_, 80 no. 4 (December 2019): 822–44.

[^c24-9]: Thus, the aims of this chapter resonate with those of Paul Lakeland’s very helpful study, _A Council that Will Never End:_ Lumen Gentium _and the Church Today_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2013).

### 2. Differential Theological Receptions of Vatican II: The Ecclesial and Systematic Theological Significance of the Hermeneutics Industry

#### In-built Complexity

Despite the at-times significantly differing positions represented among the assembled bishops at Vatican II, Pope Paul VI was concerned that the council documents should nevertheless be capable of achieving as large a majority in their favour as possible. As such, it is perhaps inevitable that we are dealing here with compromise documents. In the rounds of drafting and seeking to accommodate the various proposed modifications, it was not uncommon for apparently contrary conceptual registers simply to be placed alongside each other, in a way allowing their respective advocates each to hear their concerns as having [^c24-10][^c24-11] been incorporated. Hermann Pottmeyer refers in this regard to the ‘two faces of the Council’. This, combined with the sheer volume of matters touched upon in the documents, gives them an open, under-defined quality, requiring, as Paul VI himself recognized when addressing the last General Meeting of the council on 7 December 1965, ‘further investigation’ and ‘application’. For his part, the pope sought to present this need for further work as a positive expression of the council’s ‘vitality’. Whichever is the case, it ensured that the need for an active interpretation of the council documents was written into their DNA.

[^c24-10]: See Hans Küng, ‘The Council: End or Beginning?’, _Commonweal_ 81 (1965): 631–37.

[^c24-11]: Hermann J. Pottmeyer, ‘A New Phase in the Reception of Vatican II: Twenty Years of Interpretation of the Council’, in _The_ _Reception of Vatican II_, ed. Giuseppe Alberigo, Jean Pierre Jossua, and Joseph Komonchak (Washington DC: The Catholic University of America Press, 1987), 34.

#### Subsequent Tensions

Of course, the very openness, under-definition, and even somewhat self-contradictory nature which enabled the documents to achieve large majority votes at the council proved incapable of forging any real **[p. 399]** consensus in the years afterwards. Leaving aside the small minority who remained implacably opposed to council teaching (whether ecclesially separatist in persuasion or not), among the approving majority, the years following the council witnessed the separating out of a number of distinct agendas and contrary instincts and concerns, which have remained largely separated out from one another ever since. Key differences pertain to such things as

(1) What it means to receive the council: Does it mean just repeating, disseminating, and applying the letter of the documents? Or does it also mean continuing in the line of questioning and updating [^c24-12] (_aggiornamento_) which the council had opened?

[^c24-12]: See Karl Rahner, ‘The Abiding Significance of the Second Vatican Council’, in _Theological Investigations_, vol. 20, _Concern for_ _the Church_, trans. Edward Quinn (London: DLT, 1981), 90–102.

(2) What it means to interpret the council’s relationship to previous Catholic tradition: Is there any real [^c24-13] change and, if so, in what does the continuity of the tradition consist?

[^c24-13]: See John W. O’Malley, _What Happened at Vatican II_ (Cambridge, MA: Harvard, 2010); David G. Schultenover, ed., _Vatican II:_ _Did Anything Happen?_ (London: Continuum, 2007).

(3) How the council’s relationship to the world is to be properly understood and followed: as [^c24-14] fundamentally world-affirming or as a calling to conversion in Christ?

[^c24-14]: For a helpful discussion, see Catherine E. Clifford, _Decoding Vatican II: Interpretation and Ongoing Reception_ (Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 2014), 77–92; see also Massimo Faggioli, _Vatican II: The Battle for Meaning_ (Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 2012), 66–90.

Differing inclinations in relation to this constellation of issues have frequently been associated with the movements around the two journals _Concilium_ and _Communio_. Although this is something of a caricature, much of the ecclesial-political ecology of Catholic theology since the council has been dominated by the tensions and differences between these two sets of instincts, particularly within global North Catholicism.[^c24-15]

[^c24-15]: See Tracey Rowland, _Catholic Theology_ (London: Bloomsbury, 2017), 3–5, 91–138, 139–66; see also Philip Trower, _Turmoil_ _and Truth: The Historical Roots of the Modern Crisis in the Catholic Church_ (San Francisco: Ignatius, 2003).

_Concilium_ was founded in Rome on 28 November 1963, during the council’s second session, by a group originally including Karl Rahner, Edward Schillebeeckx, Yves Congar, Hans Küng, Joseph Ratzinger, and Henri de Lubac. From the outset, the intention was to provide a vehicle for the continuation of the _aggiornamento_ aspect of the council’s work. With Rahner, Schillebeeckx, and Congar, it was also characterized by a Thomist-leaning concern ‘to set church and world in a situation of dialogue’, with the world viewed ‘in a positive light’ and the Church attending to the ‘signs of the times’, regarded as revealing [^c24-16] ‘new perspectives on God’s salvific presence in the world here and now’. For those of a more cautious persuasion, however, _Concilium_ came to be regarded as a byword for the over-hasty adaptation of Catholic **[p. 400]** tradition and the insufficiently critical affirmation of secular culture and understanding. Without intending the merest hint of praise, in 1982 Joseph Ratzinger would write, ‘The spirit of the Council was to [^c24-17] find in this publication a permanent organ for the perpetuation of its influence.’

[^c24-16]: Rush, _Still Interpreting Vatican II_, 15–16; see also Joseph Komonchak, ‘Thomism and the Second Vatican Council’, in _Continuity and Plurality in Catholic Theology: Essays in Honor of Gerald A. McCool_, ed. Anthony J. Cernera (Fairfield, CT: Sacred Heart University, 1998), 53–73. With this characteristic orientation to dialogue and engagement, there has also been strong resonance and overlap between _Concilium_ circles and liberationist and feminist theologians.

[^c24-17]: Joseph Ratzinger, _Principles of Catholic Theology: Building Stones for a Fundamental Theology_, ed. Mary Frances McCarthy (San Francisco: Ignatius, 1987), 383, see also 382; Joseph Ratzinger with Vittorio Messori, _The Ratzinger Report: An_ _Exclusive Interview on the State of the Church_, trans. Salvator Attanasio with Graham Harrison (San Francisco: Ignatius, 1985), 29–31; and for Ratzinger’s related view of the council as sharing in the ‘naïve optimism’ of the 1960s, see his _Principles of Catholic Theology_, 372, 378.

Indeed, Henri de Lubac had already been expressing such concerns about an insufficiently critical engagement with the world during the time of the council itself, thereby aligning himself with a more Augustinian sense of suspicion and distrust of the world as disfigured throughout by sin and evil, which can [^c24-18] only be judged aright in the redeeming light of Christ. Mix this both with the disillusioning shock effect which the cultural unrest of 1968 occasioned for Joseph Ratzinger and with Hans Urs von Balthasar’s Barthian-influenced, distinctively Christocentric mode of engaging with culture and we have the key theological ingredients which lay behind the rival founding of _Communio_ by Balthasar, de Lubac, and Ratzinger in 1972. Preaching at Balthasar’s funeral, Ratzinger pointedly described _Communio_ as ‘a powerful [^c24-19] source for correct renewal as opposed to its counterfeit forms’.

[^c24-18]: Drawing on de Lubac’s council diaries, Aaron Riches tells us that while de Lubac agreed to join the _Concilium_ editorial board at the 1963 founding meeting, he withdrew before the 1965 publication of the first issue. See Riches, ‘Henri de Lubac and the Second Vatican Council’, in _T&T Clark Companion to Henri de Lubac_, ed. Jordan Hillebert (London: Bloomsbury, 2017), 132, referring to de Lubac, _Carnets du Concile_ (Paris: Cerf, 2007), 2:49, 220–21, 247, 455.

[^c24-19]: Joseph Ratzinger, ‘Homily at the Funeral Liturgy of Hans Urs von Balthasar’, in _Hans Urs von Balthasar: His Life and Work_, ed. David L. Schindler (San Francisco: Ignatius, 1991), 294.

While it does violence to the subtlety and range of any of the aforementioned great names to press them into crude polarities, it is nevertheless the case that the broader circles respectively associated with _Concilium_ and _Communio_ did come to be characterized by their differing founding impulses. Where the former has tended to be more obviously _aggiornamento_-oriented, the latter has tended to be more obviously _ressourcement_-oriented. Where the former has tended to be more ecclesially critical and reforming in intent, the latter has tended to be more ecclesially celebratory. And where the former has tended to be more dialogically open and world-affirming, the latter has tended to be more focused on the need for the distinctive light, beauty, and judgement of the Gospel for right understanding and living.

The problem is that if it is artificial to pigeonhole any truly great theologian within either of these caricatured sets of instincts (even while allowing for differing personal emphases), this is so much more the case for the overall endeavour of Catholic theology in the round. As Johann Adam Möhler (1796–1838) recognized so clearly—albeit in somewhat idealized terms—the defining nature of Catholic unity, of Catholic truth, and hence of the role of Catholic theology is to be a living communion of valid corrective **[p. 401]** contrasts and distinctions (_Gegensätze/antitheses_) which, although inevitably standing in some dialectical tension with each other, require to be held together rather than separating out into opposed contradictions [^c24-20] (_Widersprüche_). By contrast, one of the pathologies of post-conciliar Catholicism—perhaps reflecting the [^c24-21] wider dynamics of secular culture during this period and exacerbated by the digital age —has precisely been its general bifurcation into opposed camps, a situation significantly further complicated and compounded by one of these camps enjoying the status of ‘court theology’ under the papacies of John Paul II and Benedict XVI. As a result, much Catholic theological conversation effectively became a process of respectively talking _to_ those who are already like-minded and of talking _past_—with occasional shouting at —the others.

[^c24-20]: See Johann Adam Möhler, _Unity in the Church or the Principle of Catholicism: Presented in the Spirit of the Church Fathers of_ _the First Three Centuries_, trans. Peter C. Erb (1825; Washington, DC: The Catholic University of America Press, 1996), no. 46, pp. 194–98; also no. 40, pp. 178–79; no. 44, p. 193. For further, see Murray, ‘Living Catholicity Differently’, 129–51.

[^c24-21]: See Massimo Faggioli, _Catholicism and Citizenship: Political Cultures of the Church in the Twenty-First Century_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2017), 125–26.

#### Discerning Dynamic Integrity

One of the nodal points of difference in this bifurcated context has related to whether and to what extent [^c24-22] Vatican II represents a genuinely fresh ‘event’ in Catholic tradition, introducing real novelty, or whether that represents a ‘progressivist’ misinterpretation and co-optation of a body of teaching which is to be [^c24-23] properly understood as standing in line with previous Catholic tradition. ‘Continuity’ and ‘discontinuity’, ‘constancy’ and ‘change’ have been the watchwords here, frequently played upon as straightforward binary opposites.

[^c24-22]: See Joseph Komonchak, ‘Vatican II as an “Event” ’, _Theology Digest_ 46 (1999): 337–52; also John W. O’Malley, ‘Vatican II: The Event’, in _Tradition and Transition: Historical Perspectives on Vatican II_ (Lima, OH: Academic Renewal Press, 2002), 11– 18; and Rahner, ‘The Abiding Significance of the Second Vatican Council’.

[^c24-23]: See Matthew L. Lamb and Matthew Levering, eds., _Vatican II: Renewal within Tradition_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2008); also ‘The Council must be understood in continuity with the great tradition of the Church … The Church is one and the same throughout all the Councils’, in the Second Extraordinary General Assembly of the Synod of Bishops on the Twentieth Anniversary of the Conclusion of the Second Vatican Council (24 November–8 December 1985), Final Report, no. I.5, https://www.ewtn.com/catholicism/library/final-report-of-the-1985-extraordinary-synod-2561. For de Lubac viewing the ‘progressivist’ interpretation of the council as opening a state of ‘permanent revolution’ within Catholicism, see Henri de Lubac, ‘L’Église dans la crise actuelle’, _Nouvelle revue théologique_ 91 (1969): 580–96.

In this regard, Joseph Ratzinger had long been identifled in his personal theological writings with the [^c24-24] continuity camp. Consequently, when, in January 2005 as Benedict XVI, he cautioned the Roman Curia against a hermeneutic of discontinuity as the appropriate organizing category for correctly interpreting the [^c24-25] **[p. 402]** Vatican II documents and emphasized instead their deep continuity with prior Catholic tradition, he was widely and perhaps inevitably interpreted as directing his fire primarily against the ‘progressivists’ and [^c24-26] as wanting thereby to use the papal office to qualify the degree of freshness introduced by Vatican II. Subsequently, however, Gilles Routhier and Joseph Komonchak each presented an interestingly different perspective on things. Speaking to the Curia at that point in his papacy, they argue, the driving concern was not to press home old scores against _Concilium_ rivals but to lay down a clear marker against the Lefebvrist [^c24-27] claim that Vatican II teaching is radically discontinuous with Catholic tradition. According to this analysis, far from rejecting the true freshness of Vatican II, the pope’s concern at this point was to defend it. Cogent and interesting though this is, perhaps it claims too much? For Ratzinger/Benedict XVI surely has a subtle enough mind to be making a related, if differently ordered, point on two fronts at once.

[^c24-24]: ‘There are no leaps in this history, there are no fractures, and there is no break in continuity. In no wise did the Council intend to introduce a temporal dichotomy in the Church’: Ratzinger with Messori, _The Ratzinger Report_, 35.

[^c24-25]: See Pope Benedict XVI, ‘A Proper Hermeneutic for the Second Vatican Council’, in Lamb and Levering, _Vatican II: Renewal_ _within Tradition_, ix–xv; in particular, ‘renewal in the continuity of the one subject-Church’, at x.

[^c24-26]: See Nicholas Lash, ‘In the Spirit of Vatican II’, in _Theology for Pilgrims_ (London: DLT, 2008), 253–84.

[^c24-27]: See Gilles Routhier, ‘The Hermeneutic of Reform as a Task for Theology’, _Irish Theological Quarterly_ 77, no. 3 (2012): 219– 43; Joseph Komonchak, ‘Novelty in Continuity’, _The Tablet_ (31 January 2009): 5–6; Komonchak, ‘Benedict and the Interpretation of Vatican II’, _Cristianesimo nella storia_ 28 (2007): 323–37; and Clifford, _Decoding Vatican II_, 16–19.

Equally, Routhier and Komonchak highlight the significance of the fact that at no point in this address does Pope Benedict ever speak simply of a straightforward continuity between Vatican II and broader Catholic tradition—which by itself could indeed be used to flatten out any supposed freshness in Vatican II teaching [^c24-28] —but, rather, precisely in terms of a _reform within the continuity of the tradition_. The implication is that here, when speaking as pontiff, as bridge-builder and structural and sacramental focus of Catholic communion rather than as personal theologian, Benedict XVI properly seeks to hold together both the fact [^c24-29] of change and something of the ‘dynamic integrity’ of Catholic identity.

[^c24-28]: e.g., most significantly, ‘It is precisely in this combination of continuity and discontinuity at different levels that the very nature of true reform consists’ and ‘In this process of innovation in continuity’, in Pope Benedict XVI, ‘A Proper Hermeneutic for the Second Vatican Council’, xiii.

[^c24-29]: I refer in the subtitle to this section to the ‘hermeneutics industry’. There is level upon level of this. Here we are dealing with the hermeneutics of the hermeneutics. For further on the concept of ‘dynamic integrity’, see Murray, ‘Living Catholicity Differently’, 110–11, esp. no. 7.

Even so, helpful though it may be, the trope of ‘reform in continuity’ itself has its limits, for it tends to suggest that the direct continuity of each reforming teaching can be traced in equal, specific detail, in such fashion as would limit the dynamics of doctrinal development to a matter of organic unfolding and cumulative growth. This still represents a significantly constrained understanding of doctrinal discernment when compared with the more episodic, genuinely historically rooted, ‘decision’-based account which, as early as 1966, the great Lutheran observer George Lindbeck noted as being suggested and required by [^c24-30] **[p. 403]** aspects of Vatican II teaching. The point is that some aspects of Vatican II—perhaps most notably its transformed Catholic teaching on religious liberty—evince clearer, more significant change and development than others. It is for good reason, then, that following O’Malley’s rule about needing to balance appreciation for fundamental continuity with the recognition of specific discontinuities, Ormond [^c24-31] Rush distinguishes between ‘macro-ruptures’ and ‘micro-ruptures’. As he writes: ‘In no way can the spirit of the Council be conceived as a desire for a macro-rupture with the tradition. However, a case can be made for the claims by various interpreters that Vatican II explicitly intended what I am calling certain [^c24-32] micro-ruptures.’

[^c24-30]: See George A. Lindbeck, ‘The Constitution on the Church: A Protestant Point of View’, in _Vatican II: An Interfaith Proposal_, ed. J. H. Miller (Notre Dame, IN: University of Notre Dame, 1966), 219–36; also George Lindbeck, _The Future of Roman_ _Catholic Theology_ (London: SPCK, 1970), esp. 101: ‘This might be called the “decision theory” of doctrinal development. … it denies that the church’s understanding of the faith grows continuously and progressively through the addition of new dogmas, and rather affirms that it needs to be constantly reformulated and corrected in the light of changing circumstances and renewed attention to the sources of the faith’. See also George Lindbeck, ‘The Problem of Doctrinal Development and Contemporary Protestant Theology’, _Concilium: Man as Man and Believer_ 21 (1967): 133–49. The most sustained and impressive post-conciliar Catholic account of doctrinal development which resonates with this is John E. Thiel, _Senses of Tradition: Continuity and Development in Catholic Faith_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2000); see also Paul D. Murray, ‘Discerning the Dynamics of Doctrinal Development in Post-foundationalist Perspective’, in _Faithful_ _Reading: New Essays in Theology and Philosophy in Honour of Fergus Kerr, O.P._, ed. Simon Oliver, Karen Kilby, and Tom O’Loughlin (London: Continuum, 2012), 193–220.

[^c24-31]: See Rush, _Still Interpreting Vatican II_, 7, referencing O’Malley, ‘Reform, Historical Consciousness, and Vatican II’s Aggiornamento’, in _Tradition and Transition_, 44–81.

[^c24-32]: Rush, _Still Interpreting Vatican II_, 25, also 58–59.

#### Towards an Integrated and Integrating Reception of Vatican II

To get beyond readings of the Vatican II documents as either a sophisticated form of straightforward continuity or as an unresolved ambiguity which can be all things to all people, Rush develops a three-fold hermeneutic: (1) the _authors_ (i.e., the historical processes leading to the drafting and settling of the documents and what can be discerned of the various authorial intentions which were at work there); (2) the _texts_ (i.e., both the intra-textual logic of each text as it now stands relative to the varying degrees of emphasis accorded to specific points and the inter-textual logic of how what is found in one text needs to be read in relation to what can be found in the other texts); and (3) the _reception_ of Vatican II teaching into subsequent theology, ecclesial teaching, and Catholic practice.

In developing this toolkit, the aspiration is to support a reading of the Vatican II documents which not only does justice to the real change in real continuity they represent but can also do justice to the different theological concerns and voices which they hold within them. In turn, the aim is thereby to provide the basis for an integrated and integrating synthesis of conciliar teaching and its genuine reception into the theology [^c24-33] **[p. 404]** and practice of contemporary Catholicism. This is an aim which chimes well with the agenda of the papacy of Francis, who has repeatedly called for the internal polarities in the Church to be overcome. One of the implications of this, however, which the Francis papacy has also served to highlight—but not resolve— is that whenever a creative move is made on the basis of the more innovative aspects of conciliar teaching, then, wherever possible, it is vital that reasons also be adduced which can speak to the more cautious by seeking to discern and address whatever constructive points really lie at the heart of their concerns.

[^c24-33]: See ibid., 63–64.

Rush is by no means the first to call for an integrating synthesis of council teaching. In 1979, Karl Rahner identifled the integrating core of the council as consisting in the self-conscious move to being a genuinely [^c24-34] world Church. In 1985, Hermann Pottmeyer articulated the need for the incorporation of ‘what is still [^c24-35] binding in pre-conciliar theology into the newly acquired foundation’ and, with this, the need to seek to reconcile ‘minority’ and ‘majority’ council teachings while paying heed to the council’s own emphasis and [^c24-36] priorities, according to whether they enjoyed majority or minority support. Similarly, in 1987, Walter Kasper called for a hermeneutics of conciliar statements subtle enough to treat continuity, change, and [^c24-37] disagreement.

[^c24-34]: See Rahner, ‘Towards a Fundamental Theological Interpretation of Vatican II’, trans. Leo J. O’Donovan, _Theological Studies_ 40, no. 4 (1979): 716–27.

[^c24-35]: See Pottmeyer, ‘A New Phase in the Reception of Vatican II’, 34; also ‘The limitation of the Council was that it did not succeed, and probably could not have succeeded, in going beyond juxtaposition to a new synthesis. … The needed synthesis is a task the Council sets for the Church and for theologians; it is a task of reception, which is far from being a merely passive process.’ And again: ‘Fidelity to the Council requires that both juxtaposed theses be taken seriously and that an attempt be made through more penetrating theological reflection and a renewed ecclesial praxis to reconcile them in a synthesis that will allow further advances.’ Ibid., 38–39.

[^c24-36]: Ibid., 39.

[^c24-37]: See Kasper, ‘The Continuing Challenge of the Second Vatican Council’, 171.

In his own constructive synthesis of Vatican II teaching for the Francis era, Richard Gaillardetz—drawing on Pottmeyer’s evocative image of Vatican II as ‘an unfinished building site’—identifles seven key pillars: (1) a kerygmatic and Trinitarian theology of revelation; (2) a practice of dialogical engagement; (3) the priority of baptism; (4) a renewed theology of the Holy Spirit; (5) an emphasis on episcopal collegiality; (6) a sustained emphasis on the Church as missionary; and (7) the image of the Church as the pilgrim people of [^c24-38] God. After decades of the perceived frustration of these pillars, Gaillardetz writes with a refreshing celebratory enthusiasm. A key question is whether this will be enough to achieve the required new Catholic consensus for the reforming openings of Vatican II to be secured long term.

[^c24-38]: See Richard R. Gaillardetz, _An Unfinished Council: Vatican II, Pope Francis, and the Renewal of Catholicism_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2015), 49–71; compare Hermann Pottmeyer, _Towards a Papacy in Communion: Perspectives from Vatican_ _Councils I & II_, trans. Matthew J. O’Connell (New York: Crossroad, 1998), 110.

Written in a somewhat different register is Rush’s 2019 work, _The Vision of Vatican II: Its Fundamental Principles_, representing a monumental and painstaking 600-page systematic delivery on the threefold **[p. 405]** hermeneutic he developed in _Still Interpreting Vatican II_. The analysis is built around a series of patient, chapter-length examinations of twenty-four paired ‘principles’, each of which explores and proposes a [^c24-39] ‘proper balance between two aspects of doctrine or church life which the council wanted to realign’. Six of these proposed paired principles are hermeneutical in orientation (e.g., Pastoral/Doctrinal, _Ressourcement_/_Aggiornamento_, and Continuity/Reform); five are broadly theological in orientation (e.g., Christological/Pneumatological and Soteriological/Ecclesiological), and thirteen are specifically ecclesiological in orientation (e.g., Unity/Diversity, People of God/Hierarchy, College of Bishops/Bishop of Rome, and Catholic/Ecumenical).

[^c24-39]: See Ormond Rush, _The Vision of Vatican II: Its Fundamental Principles_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2019), xv.

The next section of this chapter turns now to treat briefly a number of sites of required fresh and/or deepened reception of Vatican II into Catholic life. The chosen sites cut across and meld some of Rush’s pairings; by comparison, I merely trace some lines of proposed exploration and possible argument. But in each case the concern is to ask what constructive role systematic theology might play. A threefold pattern recurs: (1) identifying how the range of issues in view were introduced but left open by the council; (2) identifying something of the relevant post-conciliar debates and proposals; and (3) proposing a way forward which might repay closer scrutiny.

### 3. A Vision to Pursue: Some Possible Contributions of Systematic Theology to the Continued Reception of Vatican II into a Renewed Catholic Consensus and Life

#### Holiness, Sin, and Continual Reform in the Church

It is a consistent feature of Catholic tradition, maintained by Vatican II, that the unity, holiness, catholicity, and apostolicity of Christ’s Church pertain to the Catholic Church. More novel is that Vatican II maintains these claims while both expanding and qualifying previous default instincts.

The traditional claim for the Church’s indefectible holiness is clearly voiced (see _Lumen Gentium (LG)_ 39; also 5, 10, 12, 26): it is indefectible because it is properly Christ’s, not ours, and only ours in and through the Spirit of Christ (_LG_ 40). But helpfully expanding beyond what had become typical, the council emphasizes **[p. 406]** that each and every church member, regardless of rank or state of life, is called to this same ‘fullness of Christian life and … perfection of love’ (_LG_ 40; also 41). Moreover, such holiness is also expansively reconstrued as having an essential this-worldly dimension. These moves were decisive in shaping much [^c24-40] subsequent Catholic theology and practice of vocation, mission, spirituality, and sacramental theology. Particularly notable is the way the emergence of Latin American liberation theology represents the effective reception of these and other aspects of conciliar teaching.

[^c24-40]: This is too pervasive to allow for adequate documentation here. Emblematic is Johannes Baptist Metz, _Theology of the_ _World_, trans. William Glen-Doepel (New York: Scribner, 1968).

Alongside this teaching about the Church’s holiness is the council’s recognition of the church as being ‘at once holy and always in need of purification’, always following the ‘path of penance and renewal’ (_LG_ 8), and in need of ‘continual reformation’ as ‘she goes her pilgrim way … on earth’ (_Unitatis Redintegratio_ (_UR_) 6). This is a very different register than Vatican I’s _Dei Filius_ (ch. 3), where we hear of the Church’s ‘eminent holiness, and inexhaustible fruitfulness in everything that is good’. In the light of the clerical sexual abuse scandal, this difference of register is now absolutely crucial. Thus far, however, its full reception has been stunted.

The standard Catholic line is that while the Church _in via_ inevitably contains sinners, as a corporate, institutional reality it nevertheless remains sinless. Dissatisfled with this, Rahner drew upon the sacramental distinction between sign (_sacramentum_) and the graced reality signifled (_res_) to maintain a both/and approach. For Rahner, while sin really does diminish the quality of the Church’s collective sign value and effective corporate witness (_sacramentum_) to the life of grace in this order (_res_), it does not [^c24-41] compromise the Church’s fundamental graced reality as already lived fully in the communion of saints. Despite such sin, the Church in this order both acts as a basic pointer to that graced reality and can, on occasion, be an effective anticipation and living sign of it.

[^c24-41]: See Karl Rahner, ‘The Church of Sinners (1947)’ and ‘The Sinful Church in the Decrees of Vatican II’ (1965), in _Theological_ _Investigations_, vol. 6, _Concerning Vatican Council II_, trans. Karl-Heinz and Boniface Kruger (London: DLT, 1969), 253–69 and 270–94 respectively.

This both/and is helpful but now needs to be pressed further in light of what we are learning about the [^c24-42] seemingly systemic nature of Catholic clerical sexual abuse and its mishandling and cover-up. First, it needs to be pressed further by applying the category of ‘structural sin’ to the Church’s collective habits, [^c24-43] processes, and structures (i.e., routine modes of operating). Second, it is not enough simply to say that the Church’s graced _res_ can still be lived despite the sin-diminished quality of its sign value. We need to move to **[p. 407]** recognizing that the effective reality of graced holiness, the action of the Spirit, can be disclosed precisely in the form of the Church’s sinful human reality being seen as being in process of conversion and being [^c24-44] made holy in faith. That would in turn require a deepening of the fresh pneumatological emphases which feature at various points in the council documents. This opens a way to understanding the Church’s holiness and sharing in the Spirit not as a possession we can proudly claim; not as something delegated, fixed, and given, once and for all, but as something which, as with each of us individually, we must receive and re-receive, moment by moment, in poverty and continual absolute dependence on the sure gifting and initiating-transforming action of the Spirit. But that must remain a story for another occasion.[^c24-45]

[^c24-42]: See Marie Keenan, _Child Sexual Abuse and the Catholic Church: Gender, Power, and Organizational Culture_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2011).

[^c24-43]: See José Ignacio González Faus, ‘Sin’, in _Systematic Theology: Perspectives from Liberation Theology_, ed. Jon Sobrino and Ignacio Ellacuría (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1996), 197–200; see also Pope John Paul II, _Solicitudo Rei Socialis:_ Encyclical Letter on the 20th Anniversary of _Populorum Progressio_ (30 December 1987), 36–40 (Vatican City: Libreria Editrice Vaticana, 1987), http://w2.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/encyclicals/documents/hf_jp-ii_enc_30121987_sollicitudo-rei- socialis.html. For an insightful discussion and constructive proposal, see Bradford E. Hinze, ‘Ecclesial Repentance and the Demands of Dialogue’, _Theological Studies_ 61 (2000): 220–35.

[^c24-44]: See Paul D. Murray, ‘Receptive Ecumenism and the Quincentennial Anniversary of the Lutheran Reformation’, _Centro Pro_ _Unione: Semi-Annual Bulletin_ 92 (Fall 2017): 8–17.

[^c24-45]: Of significance here is Yves Congar, ‘Christological and Pneumatological Implications of Vatican II’s Ecclesiology (1981)’, in _Spirit of God: Short Writings on the Holy Spirit_, ed. Susan Brown et al. (Washington, DC: The Catholic University of America Press, 2018), 225–42.

#### Identity, Unity, and Ecumenism

The attentive reader will have noticed that the wording at the start of the previous subsection—that Catholic tradition has consistently maintained ‘that the unity, holiness, catholicity, and apostolicity of Christ’s Church pertain to the Catholic Church’—represents something of a sleight of hand. As recently as Pope Pius XII’s 1950 encyclical _Humani Generis_, and consistently prior to that point, pre-Vatican II Catholic teaching had spoken not merely of the creedal identiflers of Christ’s Church as _pertaining_ to the Catholic [^c24-46] Church but also of a straightforward identity between the Church of Christ and the Catholic Church. By contrast, Vatican II’s Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, _Lumen Gentium_, notoriously appears to soften this claimed strict identity.

[^c24-46]: See ‘the Mystical Body of Christ and the Roman Catholic Church are one and the same thing’, in Pope Pius XII, _Humani_ _Generis: Concerning Some False Opinions Threatening to Undermine the Foundations of Catholic Doctrine_, § 27 (Vatican City: Libreria Editrice Vaticana, 1950), http://w2.vatican.va/content/pius-xii/en/encyclicals/documents/hf_p- xii_enc_12081950_humani-generis.html. Also ‘If we would define and describe this true Church of Jesus Christ—which is the One, Holy, Catholic, Apostolic and Roman Church’, Pius XII, _Mystici Corporis Christi: On the Mystical Body of Christ_, § 13 (Vatican City: Libreria Editrice Vaticana, 1943), http://www.vatican.va/holy_father/pius_xii/encyclicals/documents/hf_p- xii_enc_29061943_mystici-corporis-christi_en.html.

The first seven sections of _Lumen Gentium_ present a theologically rich salvation-historical account of the Church of Christ without at any point specifically referring to the Catholic Church, as in no. 8: ‘This is the sole Church of Christ which in the Creed we profess to be one, holy, catholic and apostolic’. Only then, in the very next sentence, are we told, ‘This Church, constituted and organized as a society in the present world, subsists in [_subsistit in_] the Catholic Church.’ Following much protracted wrangling and prior consideration [^c24-47] **[p. 408]** of other possible terms, the ambiguous _subsistit in_ phrase had been introduced as another suggested replacement for the earlier, more straightforward, _est_ (is), but with significantly divergent readings of this both at the time and since. More ink has likely been spent on this one phrase in the intervening years than [^c24-48] on any other sentence within the conciliar documents.

[^c24-47]: Notably ‘_adest in_’ / ‘is present in’; see Avery Dulles, ‘Nature, Mission, and Structure of the Church’, in Lamb and Levering, _Vatican II: Renewal within Tradition_, 28.

[^c24-48]: For a sampling, see Francis Sullivan, ‘The Meaning of _Subsistit In_ as Explained by the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith’, _Theological Studies_ 69, no. 1 (2008): 116–24; also Francis Sullivan, ‘A Response to Karl Becker, S.J., on the Meaning of _Subsistit In_’, _Theological Studies_ 67, no. 2 (2006): 395–409; and for a helpful overview, see Richard R. Gaillardetz, _The_ _Church in the Making: Lumen Gentium, Christus Dominus, Orientalium Ecclesiarum_ (Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 2006), 116–18.

At one extreme, appealing to the council’s supposed ‘spirit’, or projected line of travel, some interpret _subsistit in_ as ‘exists in’ or ‘is present in’ and contrast this with the strict equivalence of ‘_est_/is’. On this basis, they appeal to _Lumen Gentium_ 8 as grounding an ecclesiological pluralism wherein the Church of Christ can be regarded as subsisting equivalently in many different traditions, one of which is the Catholic [^c24-49] Church. At the other extreme are those who argue that _subsistit_ is here functioning as a mere synonym for ‘is’, claiming that the rejected _adest_ was available if the looser ‘is present in’ had indeed been intended. Here, no amount of scholarship into the competing intentions of the drafters can resolve in a singular intended meaning. What we can say is that a careful intra-textual reading of _Lumen Gentium_ combined with an intertextual reading of the documents as a whole discloses a logic which does not support either of these [^c24-50] polar extremes.

[^c24-49]: e.g., Leonardo Boff, _Church: Charism and Power: Liberation Theology and the Institutional Church_, trans. John W. Diercksmeier (New York: Crossroad, 1985), 75.

[^c24-50]: See Paul D. Murray, ‘Ecumenism, Evangelization, and the Conflicting Narratives of Vatican II: Reading _Unitatis_ _Redintegratio_ with His Holiness Benedict XVI Roman Pontiff Emeritus’, in _The New Evangelization: Faith, People, Context_ _and Practice_, ed. Kirstin Kim (London: Bloomsbury, 2015), 99–120.

Running contrary to the claim that _subsistit in_ maintains a strict and exclusive identity between the Church of Christ and the Catholic Church is the clear acknowledgement in _Lumen Gentium_ 8 that ‘many elements of sanctification and of truth are found outside its [the Catholic Church’s] visible confines’. In turn, having [^c24-51] very clearly reinforced this in _Unitatis Redintegratio_ 3, the next paragraph proceeds to say that these gifts, ‘wrought by the grace of the Holy Spirit … can contribute to our own edification’ and can even ‘bring a more perfect realization of the very mystery of Christ and the Church’ (_UR_ 4). Pope John Paul II would later draw the implication from this that ‘certain features of the Christian mystery have at times been more effectively emphasized’ in other Christian communities in ways from which the Catholic Church itself has things to learn (_Ut Unum Sint_ (_UUS_) 14; also 48). Perhaps most remarkably of all, _Unitatis Redintegratio_ 4 identifles the **[p. 409]** ‘primary’ ecumenical ‘duty’ for Catholics as the need ‘to make a careful and honest appraisal of whatever needs to be renewed and done in the Catholic household itself’.

[^c24-51]: See ‘some, even very many, of the most significant elements and endowments which together go to build up and give life to the Church itself, can exist outside the visible boundaries of the Catholic Church’ (_UR_ 3). Reflecting both on this and on _LG_ 8, Pope John Paul II drew this striking conclusion: ‘To the extent that these elements are found in other Christian communities, the one Church of Christ is effectively present in them’ (_Ut Unum Sint_ (_UUS_), 11). This observation echoes, almost verbatim, the _relatio_ concerning the meaning of _Lumen Gentium_ during the third session of the council (_AS_ III/1, 178).

We are in a very different thought-world here compared to the attitude of unilateral return to Rome which had marked pre-Vatican II Catholic thinking about the other Christian traditions. Here it is not just the [^c24-52] Protestant and Orthodox traditions which have a journey to travel, but Catholicism also. This is the conciliar basis for all subsequent positive Catholic engagement in the ecumenical movement. More specifically, it represents the formal magisterial roots for what developed into the approach of Receptive Ecumenism, which places priority not on what we can _teach_ our ecumenical others but on what we can _learn_ from them. This is an approach clearly reflected in Pope Francis’s ecumenical teaching.[^c24-53]

[^c24-52]: For concise expression of this, see ARCIC III, _Walking Together on the Way: Learning to Be the Church—Local, Regional, and_ _Universal_, no. 124 (London: SPCK, 2018), 70–71. Some of these points were anticipated by Yves Congar in his first book, _Divided Christendom: A Study of the Problem of Reunion_, trans. M. A. Bousfield (1937; London: Geoffrey Bles, 1939), esp. 255–60.

[^c24-53]: See Paul D. Murray, ‘Introducing Receptive Ecumenism’, _The Ecumenist: A Journal of Theology, Culture, and Society_ 51 (2014): 1–8.

Equally, however, if the internal logic of the documents does not sanction a reading of _subsistit in_ as maintaining a direct equivalence between the Catholic Church and the Church of Christ, nor does it sanction the polar opposite claim for a simple equivalence between the Catholic Church and the other Christian traditions. For all the more positive valuing of the other traditions in _Lumen Gentium_ and _Unitatis Redintegratio_, something essential pertaining to the unity of the Church is still regarded as missing from these traditions that is uniquely to be found within the Catholic Church. As _Unitatis Redintegratio_ 3 puts it: ‘our separated brethren, whether considered as individuals or as communities and Churches, are not blessed with that unity which Jesus Christ wished to bestow on all those to whom he has given new birth into one body’. Whereas ‘This unity, we believe, subsists in the Catholic Church as something she can never lose’ (_UR_ 4, with ecclesial unity understood here as necessarily structured through communion with the bishop of Rome).

At one level, the sting can be drawn from this continuing claim for Catholic uniqueness by recognizing that here the Catholic Church is identifying one of its own core identifying characteristics and maintaining that it is an essential gift for all the churches. In some ways, this is comparable to a Pentecostalist maintaining that life in the Spirit is essential to true ecclesial existence or an Orthodox maintaining that fidelity to the tradition is essential to the being of the Church. This drawing of the sting from the continuing claim for Catholic uniqueness is further helped by the clear recognition that the functioning of the papal office and the lived character of ecclesial communion with the bishop of Rome each need to be reformed (see _UUS_ 95– 96).

More difficult to navigate, however, is the further claim—still formally pressed by the Catholic Church in relation to the other Western Christian traditions—concerning their apostolicity and, hence, their full **[p. 410]** ecclesial status being compromised. In my judgement, if this is to be resolved, it will require a shift in Catholic understanding comparable to that which occurred in the Porvoo agreement between the Anglican Communion and the Nordic Lutheran churches. It would involve a shift from thinking of apostolicity purely in terms of linear episcopal succession to it first being grounded in continuity of life, faith, and witness, with personal episcopacy as its appropriate sacramental expression and structural form. That could represent a further significant ecumenical and theological breakthrough for Catholicism.

#### The Common Dignity and Mission of the Baptized and the Specific Dignity and Ministry of the Ordained

The fresh emphasis which the council gave to the common dignity and calling of all the baptized to one and the same holiness, regardless of differences of state of life and rank, has already been noted. This is one of the council’s leitmotifs, encapsulated in the decision during the second session to place a chapter treating ‘The People of God’ as a whole ahead of the chapter treating the Church as hierarchical in _Lumen Gentium_, [^c24-54] thus opening the way to the ‘total ecclesiology’ for which Congar had called. Particularly notable is the emphasis placed on the whole People of God and not just the ordained as sharing in the prophetic, priestly, and kingly offices of Christ (_LG_ 31). This aspect of conciliar teaching was decisive in encouraging an [^c24-55] explosion of interest in the theology of the laity in the post-conciliar period.

[^c24-54]: See Yves Congar, _Lay People in the Church: A Study for a Theology of the Laity_ (1953), rev. ed., trans. Donald Attwater (London: Chapman, 1965), xvi.

[^c24-55]: Perhaps most evocatively captured by the title of Leonard Doohan, _The Lay-Centered Church: Theology and Spirituality_ (Minneapolis, MN: Winston, 1984). Of particular significance is Paul Lakeland, _The Liberation of the Laity: In Search of an_ _Accountable Church_ (London: Continuum, 2003).

For all this freshness of approach and emphasis, it was left unresolved as to how the hierarchical dimension of the Church relates to this common aspect and, most specifically, how the dignity and calling of lay and ordained are to be properly configured. Gaillardetz speaks in this regard of Vatican II as presenting us with a [^c24-56] ‘non-competitive’ theology of the Church. For sure the council opened ways towards such a resolution, but it is a task which has thus far eluded settled achievement. In fact, much post-conciliar theology has precisely been locked into a competitive binary dynamic of emphasizing either lay or ordained, to the [^c24-57] perceived cost of the other. The key conciliar sentence is found in _Lumen Gentium_ 10: ‘Though they differ essentially and not only in degree, the common priesthood of the faithful and the ministerial or hierarchical **[p. 411]** priesthood are none the less ordered one to another; each in its own proper way shares in the one priesthood of Christ.’ A great deal is placed together here, but the unresolved question is how the common priesthood and the ministerial priesthood can be necessarily ‘ordered one to another’, each participating ‘in the one priesthood of Christ’ while also differing ‘essentially’.

[^c24-56]: See Gaillardetz, _An Unfinished Council_, 91–114.

[^c24-57]: For an earlier attempt to indicate the most fruitful way to resolve this matter in a genuinely non-competitive manner, see Paul D. Murray, ‘The Need for an Integrated Theology of Ministry within Contemporary Catholicism: A Global North Perspective’, _Ministries in the Church: Concilium_ (2010/1): 43–54.

One move has been to forgo all language of ontological distinction between lay and ordained and to think of the latter as only functionally different, such as in terms of the degree of leadership and responsibility [^c24-58] exercised. Apart from the fact that such approaches fail to cohere with _Lumen Gentium_ 10’s point about differing ‘essentially and not only in degree’, they struggle to do justice to the traditional sacramental understanding of ordained ministry as something which the ordained _are_ and not simply something they _do_. Locked into a zero-sum binary, the official reaction throughout the pontificates of John Paul II and Benedict XVI was to give renewed emphasis to a sacerdotal understanding of ordained priesthood and to maintain a strict distinction between lay and ordained, to the point of discouraging even the use of the language of ministry in relation to laypeople (see John Paul II, _Christifideles Laici_ (1988), and Congregation for the Clergy, ‘Instruction on Certain Questions Regarding the Collaboration of the Non-ordained Faithful in the Sacred Ministry of Priests’ (27 November 1997)).

[^c24-58]: Although he later moved away from this bald position, Küng at one point espoused it; see Hans Küng, _Why Priests? A_ _Proposal for a New Church Ministry_, trans. John Cummings (London: Collins, 1972). Schillebeeckx’s critics also found this in his _Ministry: A Case for Change_, trans. John Bowden (London: SCM, 1981).

One of the most promising constructive proposals for moving beyond this binary has been made by Susan [^c24-59] Wood, Edward Hahnenberg, and others. Recognizing the need to retain a clear sense of ontological density around ordained ministry in Catholic understanding, they advocate a shift from _substance_ ontology (i.e., different kinds of things) to _relational_ ontology, which focuses on the way our formal relationships effect who we are. On this understanding, ordination initiates the ordained into a formal relationship of pastoral leadership vis-à-vis the ecclesial community in a way that gives specific orientation to their baptismal calling and shapes who they are.

[^c24-59]: See Susan K. Wood, ed., _Ordering the Baptismal Priesthood: Theologies of Lay and Ordained Ministry_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2003) and Edward P. Hahnenberg, _Ministries: A Relational Approach_ (New York: Crossroad, 2003).

The basic instincts at work here—to view ordination as giving specific orientation to the common baptismal calling and to recognize the ontological implications of our formal relations—are surely to be valued. The limitation, however, is in the central focus on active pastoral leadership as the distinguishing relationship, for what does that imply about the ordained distinctiveness of those who, for whatever reason, are effectively not able to serve in pastoral leadership? As such, a potentially fruitful further development would be to view ordained distinctiveness as primarily consisting in the ordained as being marked out—whatever the circumstances of their lives—as the official, authenticated, sacramental representatives of and witnesses to the prophetic, priestly, and kingly calling and dignity of the community as a whole. This would **[p. 412]** be to view ordained ministry (diaconal, priestly, and episcopal) as consisting in an essentially different _mode of performance_ of the one and the same fundamental baptismal calling in a way which appropriately [^c24-60] distinguishes but does not separate. Far from elevating the ordained over the community, this would provide sure grounds for their real accountability to the body of the Church, of which they are called to be its representatives and authenticated witnesses.

[^c24-60]: For an extended reflection on ordination and lay vocation as different ways of living the one baptismal calling, see Lakeland, _A Council that Will Never End_, 74–87, 70–73.

#### Discerning Catholicism: The Sensus Fidelium and Authoritative Catholic Teaching

The recognition that all the baptized share equally, if variously, in the prophetic office of Christ means that the common pre-conciliar distinction between the _ecclesia discens_ and the _ecclesia docens_, the ‘listening church’ and the ‘teaching church’, is significantly relativized. (See Pope Francis, ‘Address Commemorating the 50th Anniversary of the Institution of the Synod of Bishops’ (17 October 2015).) The implication is that the Church as a whole should be a listening church and the Church as a whole is a teaching church (see _LG_ 35). As _Lumen Gentium_ 12 puts it most dramatically, the infallibility of the Church ‘in matters of belief’ fundamentally pertains to the ‘whole body of the faithful’ on the basis of their ‘supernatural appreciation of the faith’.

In a literal sense, this teaching about the _sensus fidelium_ has radical potential for the at-root reorientation of the entirety of Catholic ecclesiology and ecclesial practice. By contrast, until its recent frequent referencing by Pope Francis and the 2014 document on the subject by the International Theological Commission (see ‘_Sensus Fidei_ in the Life of the Church’ (2014) 4), it received little attention in formal Catholic teaching beyond the basic acknowledgement in _Lumen Gentium_ 37 of laity having a right to be heard. With this, there was practically nothing by way of practical implementation, nor any real, deliberative involvement of laypeople in Catholic decision-making. What formal attention it did receive generally majored on rejecting any false understanding of the _sensus fidelium_ as equating with straightforward majority opinion in the Church (see, e.g., Benedict XVI, ‘Address to the International Theological Commission on the Occasion of Its Annual Plenary Assembly’ (7 December 2012)). This line of argument might well point to the recent ills of democratic populism for some corroboration.

Predictably, the _sensus fidelium_ has received greater attention in academic theology, exploring its potential [^c24-61] as a core structuring principle for a renewed Catholic ecclesiology and ecclesial practice. By far the most **[p. 413]** impressive such attempt is Ormond Rush’s _The Eyes of Faith: The Sense of the Faithful and the Church’s_ [^c24-62] _Reception of Revelation_. In line with his focus on reception hermeneutics and underpinned by a developed understanding of the Spirit as the agent of such reception, Rush presents a systematic account of the Church as a community of reception, continually re-receiving the living tradition afresh in the lived faith of the Church. In his published works thus far, however, he stops short of offering any specific proposals in relation to the various practical matters that would necessarily be attendant upon any attempt to structure Catholic decision-making around attending to the _sensus fidelium_ at any given level of Catholic life in a [^c24-63] manner beyond consultation.

[^c24-61]: Helpful literature reviews are provided by Daniel J. Finucane, _Sensus Fidelium: The Use of a Concept in the Post-Vatican II_ _Era_ (San Francisco: International Scholars, 1996) and John Burkhard, ‘_Sensus Fidei_: Theological Reflection Since Vatican II; Part I: 1965–1984’, _Heythrop Journal_ 34 (1993): 41–59; also Burkhard, ‘_Sensus Fidei_: Theological Reflection Since Vatican II; Part II: 1985–1989’, _Heythrop Journal_ 34 (1993): 123–36; Burkhard, ‘_Sensus Fidei_: Recent Theological Reflection (1990– 2001); Part I’, _Heythrop Journal_ 46 (2005): 450–75; and Burkhard, ‘_Sensus Fidei_: Recent Theological Reflection (1990–2001); Part II’, _Heythrop Journal_ 47 (2006): 38–54.

[^c24-62]: See Ormond Rush, _The Eyes of Faith: The Sense of the Faithful and the Church’s Reception of Revelation_ (Washington, DC: Catholic University of America, 2009).

[^c24-63]: For two significant works in this regard, see Bradford Hinze, _Practices of Dialogue in the Roman Catholic Church: Aims and_ _Obstacles, Lessons and Laments_ (London: Continuum, 2006); and Hinze, _Prophetic Obedience: Ecclesiology for a Dialogical_ _Church_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2016). Rush’s core involvement in helping to shape the multi-year process of the Fifth Plenary Council of Australia should also be noted.

For sure, this all requires far more than a matter of structural, organisational, and bureaucratic innovation alone in relation to the various levels of Catholic life—parochial, diocesan, national/regional, and international—itself a massive task. At its heart, the process of continually re-receiving the living tradition afresh in the lived faith of the Church is a spiritual-theological reality, and the changes it requires in Catholic life are pre-eminently spiritual and cultural—from a default hierarchical style to a fully conciliar and synodal style—before they are structural. Nevertheless, if the journey towards becoming the ‘full [^c24-64] synodal church’ that Pope Francis envisions is to have real force, considered attention must be given, as one key strand of work at least, to developing appropriate processes and structures of representational governance. This will need to include developing appropriate processes both for attending to the varied ordinary voices of the Church and for selecting representatives in such a way that can ensure the involvement of all relevant expertise, age groups, experience, and perspectives, including those not given to contributing to formal meeting processes, those on the margins of Catholic life, and those who are critical of current norms. It will also require developing processes for the genuinely deliberative rather than merely consultative involvement of Catholic laity in decision-making but in ways which cohere with the appropriate executive function of hierarchical leadership at each level of Catholic life.

[^c24-64]: See Pope Francis, ‘Address Commemorating the 50th Anniversary of the Institution of the Synod of Bishops’. Congar’s work is significant here, ‘The Council as an Assembly and the Church as Essentially Conciliar’, in _One, Holy, Catholic, and_ _Apostolic: Studies in the Nature and Role of the Church in the Modern World_, ed. Herbert Vorgrimler (London: Sheed and Ward, 1968), 44–88.

There are undoubtedly challenges here. But it is not beyond Catholic wit and wisdom to develop processes **[p. 414]** which allow _both_ for the combination of genuine lay initiative in decision-making with appropriate executive sanction and accountability _and_ for a genuine, if asymmetric, accountability of hierarchical executive initiative to whole-church discernment and deliberation. There is real potential here for much fruitful receptive Catholic learning from the other Christian traditions and their differing ecclesial polities [^c24-65] in such regards. Similarly, there is much significant experience and practice already intrinsic to Catholic tradition within the various religious orders and their various ways of pursuing whole-body discernment as [^c24-66] well as within the base community experience of the Latin American Church.

[^c24-65]: See ARCIC III, _Walking Together on the Way_, nos. 99–101, 120–22, 148; also Ormond Rush, ‘Revelation, _Sensus Fidelium_, and Receptive Ecumenism’, in _Receptive Ecumenism as Transformative Ecclesial Learning: Walking the Way to a Church Re-_ _formed_, eds. Paul D. Murray, Gregory A. Ryan, and Paul Lakeland (Oxford and New York: Oxford University Press, 2022), 349–360.

[^c24-66]: See James Sweeney, ‘The Experience of Religious Orders’, in _Authority in the Roman Catholic Church: Theory and Practice_, ed. Bernard Hoose (Aldershot: Ashgate, 2002), 71–80; and Leonardo Boff, _Ecclesiogenesis: The Base Communities Reinvent_ _the Church_, trans. Robert R. Barr (1977; Maryknoll, NY: Orbis 1986).

Moreover, far from a prospective substantive reception of conciliar teaching on the _sensus fidelium_ serving to compromise the traditional Catholic claim to be the authoritative witness to God’s truth in Christ and the Spirit, it can be held to take such truth and the complexity of its discerning radically seriously, recognizing that the whole-church nature of Catholic truth takes time to come into view and, even then, only ever partially.[^c24-67]

[^c24-67]: See Paul D. Murray, ‘On Valuing Truth in Practice: Rome’s Postmodern Challenge’, _The International Journal of Systematic_ _Theology_ 8 (2006): 163–83.

#### The Structures of Catholicity, Local and Universal: Collegiality and Papacy

As noted earlier, for Rahner the most significant thing about Vatican II was the shift it occasioned in Catholic self-understanding to being a genuinely world Church, with the assembled bishops representing the diverse local churches of the world, held in communion with each other in and through their respective [^c24-68] structural and sacramental communion with the bishop of Rome. This opened a way to understanding true [^c24-69] catholicity as consisting not in uniform repetition and the exporting of an ‘hegemonic universality’ from Rome to the world, as had characterized the ‘Pianische’ period from Pope Pius IX to Pope Pius XII, but as living between a centripetal gathering in communion and a centrifugal dispersal throughout the diverse localities of the world.

[^c24-68]: For Rahner’s understanding of papacy as the principle of unity and episcopacy as the principle of diversity in the whole Catholic Church, see Karl Rahner and Joseph Ratzinger, _The Episcopate and the Primacy_, trans. Kenneth Barker et al., Quaestiones Disputatae 4 (London: Burns and Oates, 1962).

[^c24-69]: See Johanna Rahner, ‘A Less Eurocentric Theology: Advantages, Tasks, and Challenges’, in Hellemans and Jonkers, _Envisioning Futures for the Catholic Church_, 160.

**[p. 415]** The most significant expression of this in the years since the council has undoubtedly been the various ways in which Catholic life, language, and liturgy have been adapted to local cultural norms. This was encouraged by _Ad Gentes_ (_AG_), the council’s Decree on the Mission Activity of the Church (_AG_ 22), and has been emphasized by Pope Francis, the first pope from the global South (_Evangelii Gaudium_ 117, 127). The theological principle at work here—noted under ‘Discerning Catholicism: The _Sensus Fidelium_ and Authoritative Catholic Teaching’—is the authentic need for the Church to receive ever afresh the living tradition in the varied specific circumstances in which the Church is situated.

This should naturally also express in the articulation of Catholic teaching in a manner fitted to the specificities of context. There have been many notable examples in this regard, particularly so from the Latin American Episcopal Council (CELAM), the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, and the Federation of Asian Bishops’ Conferences. The frequency with which Pope Francis cites such documents in his own magisterial teaching is significant. More generally, however, in the post-conciliar period, such initiatives have been constrained by unresolved matters pertaining to the teaching authority of bishops’ conferences, which in turn relate to unresolved matters in _Lumen Gentium_ about the appropriate relationship between the office of the papacy and the College of Bishops.

To placate the traditionalist minority who were opposed to the developing teaching on episcopal collegiality as a balance to monarchical papal power, Pope Paul VI personally authorized a _Nota Explicativa Praevia_ in relation to chapter 3 of _Lumen Gentium_. This _Nota_ clarifled both that the College of Bishops can only act with and under the pope as head of the college and that effective episcopal exercise of the ‘sacred functions’ of teaching, sanctifying, and governing is dependent on juridical empowerment through hierarchical communion with the pope. In effect, this both denies any intrinsic authority to gatherings of bishops and removes the possibility of the college acting either independently or in resistance to the pope.

Where some find here the key to the Catholic system, which gives it a strong centre and serves to hold it in unity, others find here the root of a structural dysfunction which serves to paralyse any real initiative and vitality in the local churches of Catholicism and which thereby serves to frustrate and diminish the quality and appeal of their mission and witness. Accordingly, Ladislas Orsy calls for Catholic law to ‘acknowledge the fundamental right and duty of bishops, flowing from their ordination, to assemble for pastoral [^c24-70] purposes’, not as ‘a concession from the Holy See’ but as something which exists ‘by divine institution’. Drawing on Jérôme Hamer, his vision is for there being different ‘modalities’ of effective episcopal [^c24-71] collegiality between the levels of diocese and the full College of Bishops.

[^c24-70]: Ladislas Orsy, _Receiving the Council: Theological and Canonical Insights and Debates_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2009), 29.

[^c24-71]: Ibid., 24–5 n. 10.

**[p. 416]** Such concern to give appropriate ecclesial density to the regional manifestation of _episcope_ is essential vis- [^c24-72] à-vis any prospect of further ecumenical progress in relation to the other Christian traditions and could be [^c24-73] significantly furthered by relevant Catholic receptive learning. As a complement to the routine existence and proper authority of such regional and international episcopal conferences and synods, it would also be [^c24-74] necessary to give renewed attention to the limits of the papacy and the development of appropriate, if asymmetric, mechanisms for real mutual accountability between the papacy and the episcopate. For example, it might be that any proposed significant papal initiative would require agreement by the College of Bishops (or its appropriate representatives) prior to implementation and that, correlatively, the college could routinely bring proposals to the pope for potential ratification. Moreover, in the latter regard, it could be that while a pope could rule against a repeated majority request of the college for the duration of his [^c24-75] papacy, he would not be able to rule it out in principle beyond that point.

[^c24-72]: Writing in 1976, Joseph Ratzinger recognized that ‘Rome must not require more from the East with respect to the doctrine of the primacy than had been formulated and was lived in the first millennium’, see ‘The Ecumenical Situation— Orthodoxy, Catholicism and Protestantism (1976)’, in _Principles of Catholic Theology_, 199.

[^c24-73]: See ARCIC III, _Walking Together on the Way_, no. 120–2, 145–8.

[^c24-74]: See Patrick Granfield, _The Limits of the Papacy: Authority and Autonomy in the Church_ (London: DLT, 1987).

[^c24-75]: See Paul D. Murray, ‘Redeeming Catholicity for a Globalising Age: The Sacramentality of the Church’, in _Believing in_ _Community: Ecumenical Reflections on the Church_, ed. Peter De Mey, Pieter DeWitte, and Gerard Mannion (Leuven: Peeters, 2013), 229–40.

### 4. Conclusion

Were the five interrelated points, here identifled, of fresh and continuing reception of Vatican II to be pursued, they would give us a Catholicism reformed because transfigured: not by return to a supposed earlier purity but through growth towards all that Catholicism is called to be. It presents us with a vision of whole-church Catholic flourishing which might equate to a process of comprehensive reception of Vatican II, but one which might in turn require a Third Vatican Council (howsoever feasible that might be) for its own ratification and formal reception. As Joseph Ratzinger accurately noted in 1975, ‘the real reception of [^c24-76] the Council has not yet even begun’. In the meantime, the servant task of Catholic systematic theology is (1) to diagnose the ills, difficulties, and open questions in Catholic life, structure, and understanding; (2) to identify and consider potentially constructive ways forward; and (3) to test such proposals rigorously for **[p. 417]** their degrees of dynamic integrity (on grounds of internal, external, and pragmatic coherence) and their [^c24-77] capacity to achieve theological and ecclesial consensus in service of whole-church Catholic flourishing.

[^c24-76]: Ratzinger, ‘Church and World: An Inquiry into the Reception of Vatican II (1975)’, in _Principles of Catholic Theology_, 390.

[^c24-77]: See Paul D. Murray, ‘Searching the Living Truth of the Church in Practice: On the Transformative Task of Systematic Ecclesiology’, _Modern Theology_ 30 (2014): 251–81.
