## 25. Moral Theology and the Paradigm Shift of Vatican II

James T. Bretzke, SJ

### 1. Looking Back

**[p. 418]** While John XXIII (1958–63) certainly surprised much of the world with his announcement on the Feast of the Conversion of St Paul on 25 January 1959 to convene an ecumenical council, John’s predecessor, Pius XII (1939–58) had already spoken in 1948 to the then head of the Supreme Sacred Congregation of the Holy Office, Cardinal Alfredo Ottaviani (1890–1979), about the preparation of a council to complete the [^c25-1] interrupted Vatican I. Ottaviani’s coat of arms proudly bore the motto _Semper Idem_ (Always the Same), and no doubt he and many other curial officials preparing for the council thought the work would be relatively minor and quickly concluded. Ottaviani was the president of the _De Doctrina Fidei et Morum_ (Faith and Morals) Commission, and he believed the council would quickly confirm the preparatory schema guided by the basic trajectory of his episcopal motto. However, as Vatican II unfolded, Ottaviani and a number of his ecclesial allies increasingly found themselves on the losing side of many of the pitched battles that took place in the four sessions of the council (1962–65), which are detailed elsewhere in this volume.

[^c25-1]: See François-Charles Uginet, ‘Les Projets de Concile général sous Pie XI et Pie XII’, in _Le Deuxième Concile du Vatican (1959–_ _1965)_ (Rome: École française de Rome, 1989), 65–78.

The formal discipline of moral theology did not emerge as such as a major theme of the council, at least not in comparison with the themes of liturgy and sacraments, divine revelation, ecclesiology, and the episcopacy. Explicit reference to moral theology as a discipline is found only in _Optatam Totius_ (_OT_), the Decree on the Training of Priests. This decree mandated that Scripture be the ‘soul’ of all theology, and that **[p. 419]** in particular moral theology’s ‘scientific exposition, nourished more on the teaching of the Bible, should shed light on the loftiness of the calling of the faithful in Christ and the obligation that is theirs of bearing fruit in charity for the life of the world’ (_OT_ 16). The moral manuals leading up to the dawn of the council were not all that different from the tomes in the preceding two to three centuries. These relied heavily on abstract understandings of the natural law, ethical norms, conscience, moral acts, and the virtues, all articulated in a heavily physicalist, classicist, and deductive manner. In terms of methodology, the pre- Vatican II moral manuals traditionally named three sources or ‘fonts’ for moral theology: Scripture, Tradition, and the magisterium. However, these sources were not used in equal measure. Scripture was employed largely for proof texts to confirm, or perhaps to give a pious exhortation to, a moral already established on other grounds. The usual approach began with the position of the magisterium on a particular topic and then worked backwards to show how this particular teaching was found in Scripture and then subsequently developed in the Tradition, especially in the patristic and medieval authors. Thus, Cardinal Ottaviani’s _Semper Idem_ mirrored well this discipline’s own self-understanding, also illustrated by the popular and encyclopaedic _Dictionary of Moral Theology_, edited by Cardinal Francesco Roberti (Italian edition, 1955, 1957; English translation, 1962), which produced definitive pronouncements on nearly everything that was understood as falling within the domain of ethics from the Roman Catholic perspective.

Nevertheless, in the decade before the council opened, there were the beginnings of some significant shifts in the genre of some of the moral manuals, such as Bernard Häring, CSsR. (1912–98)’s 1954 three-volume _Das Gesetz Christi_ (1963 translation: _The Law of Christ_) and Gérard Gilleman, SJ’s _Le Primat de la charité en théologie morale_ (1959 translation: _The Primacy of Charity in Moral Theology_). While not fully incorporating what _Optatam Totius_ seemed to be calling for in the renovation of moral theology, these works did employ a biblically grounded organizing metaphor for the exposition of Christian ethics. Häring in particular would go on to play a very important role as a _peritus_ at the council in the drafting of _Gaudium et Spes_ (_GS_), the Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World, as well as _Optatam Totius_ itself. Since the close of the council, the response of Roman Catholic moralists to this biblical mandate has been mixed at best.

There likely were several reasons for the sluggishness of many moral theologians to embrace this mandate which illustrated some of the difficulties encountered with significant paradigm shifts. First, a more biblically grounded approach to the discipline represented a considerable paradigm shift in itself. Few moralists of that era were adequately trained in scriptural studies to integrate the Bible into moral theology. Instead, it was the discipline of canon law that was wedded to moral theology. Second, the use of the Bible in theology, especially Christian ethics, seemed to many to be drawing too close to a domain long dominated by the _sola scriptura_ methodology of Protestant theologians. The nascent ecumenical movement in ethics and the 1964 conciliar decree _Unitatis Redintegratio_ (_UR_) were not yet sufficiently developed to encourage or support this sort of methodological shift. The decree did give a clear enough mandate for cooperation, suggesting that ‘ecumenical dialogue could start with the moral application of the Gospel’ (_UR_ 23), but at **[p. 420]** that time there was insufficient buy-in from either Protestant or Catholic theologians for a concentrated cooperation in addressing the moral problems the council did articulate in that decree, in _Gaudium et Spes,_ and elsewhere. Third, Roman Catholic moral theology had long given pride of place to a scholastic natural law approach, and greater utilization of biblical material would seem to call that methodology into considerable question.

Related to this last point was a debate that emerged in the years following the council between two major schools of thought among moral theologians over just what constituted the distinctiveness, or _proprium_, of Christian ethics. The ‘Moral Autonomy’ school, identifled with thinkers such as Josef Fuchs, SJ (1912– 2005), Alfons Auer (1915–2005), and Bruno Schüller, SJ (1925–2007), held that most of the normative content of ethics was discerned and then applied by individual conscience, and thus would essentially be the same for Christians and non-Christians alike. The Bible could be helpful in ‘confirming’ the truth of ethics and providing motivation and intentionality for right conduct. The content, though, could (and, in the view of some, such as Schüller, should) be found without recourse to the sacred claim of Scripture, since the natural law was seen as discoverable by all through Thomas’s understanding of _recta ratio_, or ‘right reason’.

The other side, often termed the _Glaubensethik_ or ‘Faith Ethics’ school, did not deny Thomistic natural law theory but did hold that Scripture was crucially important for fully and properly understanding and implementing what was in accordance with God’s eternal law. Inasmuch as Scripture was truly divine Revelation entrusted to the Church in the _depositum fidei_ (deposit of faith), then the magisterium would also exercise its proper roles not only in ‘safeguarding’ that deposit of faith, but also in interpreting it authoritatively along with the requirements of the natural law. This understanding of the magisterium’s role found expression in _Dei Verbum_ (_DV_) as it related to the charism of office that enjoyed the ‘special assistance of the Holy Spirit’, which certainly ‘is not above the word of God, but serves it, teaching only what has been handed on, listening to it devoutly, guarding it scrupulously and explaining it faithfully in accord with a divine commission and with the help of the Holy Spirit’ (_DV_ 10). In the _Glaubensethik_ school, the role of the magisterium was seen as both critical and indispensable in discerning the proper relationship between Scripture and ethics; Joseph Ratzinger (b. 1927), later Benedict XVI, was one of this school’s main proponents. Given other tensions in the post-Vatican II era, this emphasis on extrinsic authority by the whole _Glaubensethik_ raised a number of red flags for the Moral Autonomy school.

While this debate on fundamental moral theology was key for the moral theologians themselves in the years after the council, undoubtedly it was the moral issues connected with family planning that dominated the larger scene. Here again, Cardinal Ottaviani would play a key role, at least symbolically. In the same year that John XXIII called for Vatican II, he also created a special commission to re-examine the Church’s teaching on the regulation of births in light of new scientific, social, and economic developments as well as possible new moral understandings of various aspects of the relationship between procreation and marriage. Pope John made Ottaviani the president of this Pontifical Commission on Population, Family and Birth (aka the Birth Control Commission), which originally had just six other members—all European male **[p. 421]** theologians. When Paul VI (1963–78) became pope after John’s death, he expanded the commission to seventy-two members, including a number of laypeople, representing five continents. Most importantly, both symbolically and practically he supported simultaneous translation so that all of the participants could speak freely and would not be as constrained by the Latin philosophical and theological vocabulary.

Meanwhile, back at the council _aula_ in St Peter’s, when discussion eventually turned to the subject of marriage, Paul VI indicated that he did not want the council fathers to take up consideration of birth control.

The reason given for the pope’s decision to reserve this topic to himself was the ongoing work of this special commission, which had not yet arrived at the point of formulating its final report. The council therefore naturally obeyed the pope, but in a relatively brief section on marriage in _Gaudium et Spes_ (49–52), they adopted what would become a major paradigm shift of their own by employing personalist language and removing the exalted status of the _bonum prolix_ (good of procreation) as the ‘primary’ or highest end of the marital covenant. The married couple was charged with fulfilling their duties to each other and to the whole family, exercising what came to be called the principle of ‘responsible parenthood’. However, since the papal commission’s work was not yet complete, all that the council fathers said about methods of birth control was that the couple ‘may not undertake methods of birth control which are found blameworthy by the teaching authority of the Church in its unfolding of the divine law’ (_GS_ 51).

A year after the council closed, the Birth Control Commission drafted its final report, which was positively [^c25-2] endorsed by sixty-four of the sixty-nine voting members present. On the critical question on whether the Church could give a nuanced ‘yes’ to the possibility of a couple using artificial contraception for good reasons, the Final Report replied in the affirmative. However, the structure of the presentation and modes of argumentation employed showed how the abstract, deductive, classicist, act-centred, physicalist paradigm was being replaced by analysis that was much more inductive and personalist. The real questions shifted from ‘Is it _contra naturam_ to obstruct the biological procreative faculty?’ to a much broader consideration of all of the morally relevant features a married couple should take into consideration in planning their family size. This decision, as well as the concrete means employed, should be left up to the married couple themselves to decide in light of their own informed consciences. It should be noted here that of even greater importance was the implied paradigm shift in moral methodology, from a deductive analysis and application of a key principle (e.g., what is _contra naturam_) to a more inductive investigation into as many as possible of the morally relevant features which could be considered before arriving at a conclusion.

[^c25-2]: For a fascinating journalistic account of the work of the Pontifical Birth Control Commission, as well as the text of the Final Report, see Robert Blair Kaiser’s _The Encyclical that Never Was: The Story of the Pontifical Commission on Population,_ _Family and Birth, 1964–1966_ (London: Sheed & Ward, 1987).

The individual moral choice and resulting act of contraception still remained important, but its significance was not determined by taking it largely out of its concrete, personal context. Instead, the principle of totality was employed to weigh the couple’s own decision about contraception in light of the ensemble of the marital relationship. Moral norms remain very important, but it is difficult in the concrete to absolutize **[p. 422]** these completely: ‘since moral obligations can never be detailed in all their concrete particularities, the personal responsibility of each individual must always be called into play. This is even clear today because of the complexities of modern life: the concrete moral norms to be followed must not be pushed to an [^c25-3] extreme.’

[^c25-3]: Ibid., 4. See also the entries for ‘Pontifical Birth Commission and _Humanae Vitae_’, in James T. Bretzke, SJ, _Handbook of_ _Roman Catholic Moral Terms_ (Washington, DC: Georgetown University Press, 2013).

While this approach was ultimately rejected by the eventual papal encyclical (see especially _Humanae Vitae_ (_HV_) 3, 6, 14, 17), the moral reasoning was hardly obliterated from theological discourse. The grounds for the rejection of the Final Report counterproposed by the four commission dissenting theologians and Ottaviani can be deduced from the so-called Minority Report that was prepared largely by John Ford, SJ (1902–89), aided by a married lay philosopher, Germain Grisez (1929–2018); like the Final Report (aka the Majority Report), it was leaked to the press the same year. Many of the moral principles outlined in the Minority Report were ultimately adopted in _Humanae Vitae_, though there is considerable difference in tone and style. However, in terms of the foundational moral principles and judgements brought forward, the Minority Report foreshadowed a good deal of the tension that remains up to the present in how to ‘receive’ the thrust of the council as it relates to both the exposition and application of moral theology.

One of the commission members who had been most strident in his opposition was the famous Spanish moralist Marcelino Zalba, SJ (1908–2009), who located his principal difficulties not so much with the moral principles themselves adopted in the Majority Report as with the underlying assumptions about the nature of the Roman Catholic Church that any significant change or development of moral doctrine might involve. Zalba raised three primary objections in the course of the commission’s deliberations. First, any such change—which in effect would adopt the position articulated in 1930 by the Anglican Lambeth Conference —might suggest that the Holy Spirit was more present on this issue in the Anglican Communion than in the Catholic response to that decision promulgated in the same year in Pius XI’s encyclical _Casti Connubii_. This Catholic position, then, had been relatively recently reaffirmed in Pius XII’s 1951 Address to the Italian Midwives, which repeated the prohibition against artificial contraception (though explicitly allowing for the practice of natural family planning). Second, how could the Church now reconcile acceptance of a practice that earlier had been repeatedly denounced as condemning to eternal damnation Catholics who had knowingly violated this teaching of the magisterium? Third, any such significant change in such a position would undermine its credibility in the eyes of the faithful. This last point proved to be particularly persuasive for Paul VI, who was trying very hard to keep together the liberal and conservative factions among the council fathers. Change in this long-standing critical area of Catholic sexual morality must have seemed to be a ‘bridge too far’ for the Church’s papal magisterium at that time. While Paul VI undoubtedly saw that many of the paradigms of the pre-Vatican II Church were changing, he was likely afraid of being at the head of an institution that would be changing too much in too short a time.

**[p. 423]** In this context, three questions that occasioned the most debate at the time of _Humanae Vitae_’s release were the following: first, did the constancy of ‘the Church has always taught’-tradition allow for the possibility of genuine development of doctrine that went beyond linguistic expression of moral principles; second, who would have the responsibility of making the final moral decision about the legitimacy of means chosen to regulate birth; and third, what was the status of a deliberate act to employ artificial means to achieve contraception? Fifty years later, the one thing that is clear is that these three questions remain unresolved and thus continue to play a great role in how the Church continues to struggle with the challenges of implementing the authentic, Spirit-led dynamism of Vatican II.

For his part, Paul VI, who would be canonized in 2018, likely believed in 1968 that the exercise of a high level of papal magisterium such as an encyclical would be bolstered by the time-tested dictum of _Roma locuta, causa finita_ (‘Rome has spoken, the case is closed’, or ‘the cause is lost’) and together would ultimately function as a calming oil on the troubled waters this issue had caused. He belatedly discovered that this was no longer the case, and although he was to reign for another decade, he never again promulgated another encyclical. Again, while paradigms had begun to shift significantly, this change was neither quick nor easy. The year 1978, though, proved to be a remarkable year for both change and constancy.

Paul VI died on the Feast of the Transfiguration (6 August); he was succeeded, as a centuries-long tradition seemed to dictate, by another Italian, Albino Luciani, who sought to bridge some of the divide in the Church by combining the names of his two immediate predecessors. John Paul I’s thirty-three-day reign was one of the shortest in history, but the name itself stuck. In October 1978, the two leading Italian candidates were the arch-conservative Giuseppe Siri of Genoa and the more progressive Giovanni Benelli of Florence (substitute of the Secretary of State, 1967–77). While Benelli came very close in the early rounds of voting, his supporters could not quite close the deal. Another Italian put forward as a potential compromise candidate, Giovanni Colombo of Milan, indicated he would not accept if elected. To break the impasse, another candidate was proposed who would signal another paradigm shift—and he was elected. For the first time in 455 years, a non-Italian would take the helm of the Barque of Peter. Initially, Karol Wojtyła of Poland had considered taking the name of Stanislaus I, but settled quickly on the recent tradition established by Luciani and took John Paul II. At the age of 58, he was the youngest pope since Pius IX, who had been elected at the age of 54 in 1846 (and would reign for nearly thirty-two years). Wojtyła’s own reign would last just a few months shy of twenty-seven years and would exhibit strong forces of both change and retrenchment in many areas of the Church, including the reception of Vatican II in general and moral theology in particular.

### 2. Looking Around

In 1965, the year the council closed, Peter Knauer, a young German Jesuit studying in Paris, published an **[p. 424]** intriguing paper proposing a significant paradigm shift in the understanding and application of the [^c25-4] classic principle of the double effect. For the better part of the next twenty-five years, the intramural debates among moral theologians centred on the emerging moral theory which came to be called ‘proportionalism’ and which can be substantially traced back to Knauer’s seminal article, as well as many others writing on similar aspects involved in ‘doing evil to achieve good’. Some of these include Louis Janssens, Josef Fuchs, SJ, Richard McCormick, SJ, and Bernard Hoose, who supported the central claim that what distinguished moral evil from non-moral evil (often termed ‘physical’, ‘pre-moral’, or ‘ontic’ evil) was the presence or absence of proportionate reason for causing or allowing the evil effect so that the [^c25-5] desired and morally intended good effect would follow.

[^c25-4]: Peter Knauer, SJ, ‘La Détermination du bien et du mal par le principe du double effet’, _Nouvelle revue théologique_ 87 (1965): 356–76; translated as ‘The Hermeneutic Function of the Principle of the Double Effect’, in _Readings in Moral_ _Theology, No. 1: Moral Norms and Catholic Tradition_, ed. Charles E. Curran and Richard A. McCormick, SJ (New York: Paulist, 1979), 1–39.

[^c25-5]: For an excellent history of this movement, see Bernard Hoose’s revised Gregorian doctoral dissertation, completed under Josef Fuchs, SJ, _Proportionalism: The American Debate and Its European Roots_ (Washington, DC: Georgetown University Press, 1987).

This theory went far beyond the more limited application of the principle of the double effect and called into question a significant rethinking of moral absolutes and norms in general. Two pre-eminent American moral theologians, Charles Curran and Richard McCormick, SJ, launched a multi-volume topical series (twenty volumes by 2022) entitled _Readings in Moral Theology_, its first volume being _Moral Norms and the Catholic Tradition_ (1979). In these debates, the traditional concept of ‘intrinsic evil’ in particular did not converge well with this theory (discussed below). Space here does not permit even a concise summary of any more of this complex debate, but the theory had a large number of theologians and philosophers who were adamantly opposed to this paradigm shift, which they considered to be no less than a total capitulation to moral relativism and situation ethics. During the reign of Paul VI, both he and the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (CDF) largely stayed out of this particular battle. However, the ascent of John Paul II and his long-serving prefect of the CDF, Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger (1981–2005), later Benedict XVI (2005– 13), marked a significant change in the Vatican response to this debate. Those who strayed too far from the traditional theory were labelled dissenters who posed a dangerous threat to both the Church and the understanding of morality.

_L’Osservatore Romano_ announced in the autumn of 1990 that John Paul II’s long-awaited encyclical on fundamental moral theology would be released on the first Sunday of Advent that same year. Advance copies of the draft had been circulated to a small group of moral theologians so they could prepare the usual expected laudatory commentaries at the time of the encyclical’s release. However, Christmas came and went, but the promised encyclical did not make its appearance. Instead, it was more quietly acknowledged that the document had been withdrawn _sine die_ (without a given publication date). Tabling a document in this way usually meant it would never see the light of day, though the radiance of its understanding of the truth finally burst forth with the promulgation of _Veritatis Splendor_ (_VS_), signed on the Feast of the **[p. 425]** Transfiguration in 1993 (6 August) but not released until 5 October. Just how much the original text had been transfigured in the intervening three years must await an eventual archival historical investigation, but most likely the key sticking point was the level of extrinsic authority that would have been invoked in the original draft. So the final document did not fulfil the criteria for infallibility in the extraordinary papal magisterium as outlined in Vatican I’s 1870 _Pastor Aeternus_, and thus while we had a _Roma locuta_, it clearly was not yet in the minds of most experts a _causa finita_.

A ‘keywords’ listing of _Veritatis Splendor_ would certainly feature the following: natural law, human acts (_actus humanus_), moral object, intrinsic evil, moral relativism, consequentialism, proportionalism, fundamental option, and teleology. Other contrasting terms which have appeared since Vatican II, such as ‘personalism’ or ‘inductive reasoning’, are not to be found at all, while understandings of the principle of totality and freedom of conscience are either very narrowly described or appear in conjunction with contemporary trends that _Veritatis Splendor_ condemns. ‘Physicalism’ as such is not adopted, though _Veritatis Splendor_ asserts that many contemporary moral theories deny the existence of universal moral norms in claiming that only a false and superficial understanding of physicalism is employed to justify somehow a setting aside of such moral absolutes that would condemn a number of practices connected with sexual ethics (see _VS_ 47 |.).

This chapter cannot treat these items in detail, but it is clear that _Veritatis Splendor_ seems to be arguing strongly for a return to the status quo ante of the pre-Vatican II understanding of moral theology, rather than mapping a route to move with the challenges of the new millennium. In this sense, the encyclical confirms the dynamics of the great difficulties and resistance involved in paradigm shifts. Nevertheless, it is both necessary and important to consider carefully many of the objections _Veritatis Splendor_ has raised to different understandings of moral theology that have emerged since Vatican II. Chief among these is ‘intrinsic evil’, which is the bulwark that _Veritatis Splendor_ strongly reaffirms against the other ‘evils’ condemned in the encyclical.

However, _Veritatis Splendor_ clearly indicates that its purpose is not to innovate in moral analysis but rather to recover and emphasize the classic moral tradition. This means that a correct understanding of the papal text must be understood from within that tradition. In the pre-Vatican II moral manuals, the full expression for ‘intrinsic evil’ was _intrinsice malum in se_, literally ‘intrinsic evil in itself’. This ‘in itself’ (_in se_) is critical to a correct understanding of the term, since it expressly brings into consideration the ‘object’ of the moral action undertaken in light of both the circumstances in which the agent finds him/herself and the agent’s moral intention in performing the action, or what in classic moral theology is termed the _finis operantis_.

_Veritatis Splendor_ does correctly stress that no further additional motives or other mitigating circumstances would ever turn a morally evil object into a morally good one (see _VS_ 80–81). Thus murder, defined as the unjustifled taking of innocent life, is intrinsically evil and always wrong. But not every killing is murder. This last point is crucial to avoid the too common misunderstanding that somehow intrinsically evil acts constitute a different moral species that allows for no consideration whatsoever of intention and **[p. 426]** circumstances. This false view would then conclude that the simple commission of an act labelled in the abstract as ‘intrinsically evil’ is always and everywhere a serious moral evil. Regrettably, the language used in certain parts of _Veritatis Splendor_ adds to that confusion, such as the statement that ‘any kind of homicide’ constitutes an intrinsic evil (_VS_ 80). Many people would misinterpret ‘any kind of homicide’ to mean ‘every kind of killing’, and thus even the classic double-effect principle of legitimate deadly force in self-defence would also be disallowed.

However, an actual act without any consideration of either circumstances or intention could not qualify as a genuine moral act (_actus humanus_), since it would lack the necessary components of a moral intention, formulated in freedom, and in light of the concrete circumstances in which the agent’s intention aims at the action’s object (the _finis operis_). Though very few commentators note this, _Veritatis Splendor_ does allude to this key point by adding that intrinsically evil acts ‘are such always and per se, in other words, on account of their very object, and quite apart from the _ulterior_ intentions of the one acting and the circumstances [_aliorum adiunctorum ratione habita_]’ (_VS_ 80). ‘Ulterior’, then, is the crucial modifler that keeps _Veritatis Splendor_ within the moral tradition and negates the misunderstanding that there is a distinct species of moral actions that somehow automatically constitute serious moral evil without reference to circumstances and/or intention. Rhetorically, it seems that what _Veritatis Splendor_ wishes to underscore is that one can never transform a morally evil object (_finis operis_) somehow into a morally good act. In murder, for example, both the intention (_finis operantis_) and the action in itself (_finis operis_) are evil. Even if the individual killed were a serial paedophile, his or her murder would still be intrinsically evil.

### 3. Conscience

The notion of conscience may be the moral concept that has undergone the most discussion and development since Vatican II. _Veritatis Splendor_ references ‘conscience’ well over a hundred times, yet its overriding treatment primarily utilizes the manualist understanding of conscience simply as the faculty of right reason (_recta ratio_) which makes judgements about moral principles and their proper applications. Errors in moral judgement would be possible, though the subjective culpability would be judged on whether it could reasonably have been corrected or not; that is, whether the moral ignorance involved was ‘vincible’ or ‘invincible’. This understanding of conscience as a faculty of reason is somewhat analogous to exercising reason in solving an arithmetic problem. No one would knowingly conclude that seven times five equals seventy-five, but a young child or someone who is uneducated might conceivably make this error.

Taking this analogy further, the students would be encouraged to follow the guidance of their teachers as they progress in their mastery of mathematics. Similarly, the magisterium of the Church would exercise this function for the faithful in giving them moral guidance on a range of issues, from general principles to particular decisions like contraception. For their part, the faithful, by giving what _Lumen Gentium_ (_LG_) 25 **[p. 427]** termed the proper _obsequium religiosum_ (whether translated as ‘submission of the intellect and will’ or ‘religious respect’), acknowledge in a concrete, lived manner their desire both to live uprightly and to use the Church’s moral teachings as a way to discern what morality requires (see _VS_ 64).

There is, however, considerable tension on other possible understandings of conscience which first arose during the debates at Vatican II on the possibility of reformulating the Church’s understandings of religious liberty, as ultimately occurred in its Declaration on Religious Freedom, _Dignitatis Humanae_ (_DH_, especially 3, 4, 11). The _locus classicus_ for the council’s expanded understanding on conscience is found in _Gaudium et Spes_ 16, which speaks of the ‘sanctuary’ of conscience as being both a sacred place in which the individual meets God in a privileged manner and a safe place in which no other force or authority may legitimately intrude (including the official magisterium). The 1992 _Catechism of the Catholic Church_ echoes this last point in its section on erroneous conscience, which states that ‘A human being must always obey the certain judgment of his conscience. If he were deliberately to act against it, he would condemn himself’ (no. 1790).

If conscience is the inviolable sanctuary where the individual ‘is alone with God, Whose voice echoes in his depths’, then this relationship should transcend merely finding the right answer to moral dilemmas. This represents an important shift which views conscience not just as a faculty of right reason but as a core relational modality of the human person. In other words, ‘right conscience’ is no longer simply realized just in getting, or following, what are the external answers to moral questions but in an ongoing process of forming, informing, following, re-evaluating, and reforming again and again one’s very personhood in ‘obeying’ the call of conscience. In other words, the individual grows into a truly human person by continually seeking God as the transcendental Absolute, either explicitly or implicitly, and then following what is discerned to be in accordance with that Absolute. The seeds planted in Vatican II’s documents that involve conscience—_Gaudium et Spes_, _Lumen Gentium_, and _Dignitatis Humanae_—would continue to germinate and grow, but the struggles over the fruits of their cultivation further illustrate the thesis about the difficulties and tensions involved in deep-seated paradigm shifts.

The paradigm shifts in conscience also found a resonance in _Lumen Gentium_’s chapter 5 on the ‘Universal Call to Holiness’ and a renaissance in reconnecting moral theology with spirituality and renewed attention to virtue ethics, which focused much more on the development of moral character than on introspective review of the rightness or wrongness of discrete moral acts. One area in which these developments were played out is in the theology and practice of the sacrament of reconciliation. The whole discipline of moral theology as taught in the seminaries from Trent to Vatican II focused on forming priest confessors who could adequately function in the confessional, which in turn was seen primarily as a tribunal of God’s judgement of individuals on this side of the great divide. Prior to Vatican II, long lines in most parishes on Saturday afternoon gave ample evidence of the widespread reception of the theology of the sacrament of penance in place at the time.

Not very long after the close of the council, these lines of penitents shrunk considerably and in some places **[p. 428]** disappeared almost entirely. The reasons for these changes in pastoral practice are many and complex, including broad societal changes, as chronicled in well-known psychiatrist Karl Menninger’s (1893–1990) _Whatever Became of Sin?_ (1973). But theologically, certainly some key reasons involve a shifting and deepening understanding of conscience as the sanctuary in which the person is alone with God (see _GS_ 16), in which the priest’s role as external absolver of sin may seem less crucial. Other reasons involve the shift in the neo-scholastic moral manuals themselves from Heribert Jone’s famous _Moral Theology_ (translated into numerous languages)—a pocket-sized _vademecum_ that could easily be slipped into a cassock pocket, containing a short summary of confessional casuistry and canon law arranged according to the likely sins to be heard. This was reprinted in many editions up to 1957 and even figures in Graham Greene’s novel _Monsignor Quixote_, who takes it as a protective reference tome on his road trip with a communist mayor of a small Spanish town. Vatican II saw a major revision of the celebration of the sacrament now renamed ‘reconciliation’, which was also supported by more personalist elaborations of sin, grace, mercy, forgiveness, and reconciliation, such as those as developed in the moral theology of Bernard Häring and others.

### 4. Looking Forward: Halfway There

_Morto un papa, se ne fa un altro_ (‘when a pope dies, they just make another one’) is a common Italian adage combining the sentiments of ‘it’s not the end of the world’ with the French _plus ça change, plus c’est la même chose_ and the Latin _semper idem_. However, proving that all these generalizations indeed are false, on 11 February 2013, in a Latin discourse to those cardinals present in Rome, Benedict XVI shocked those whose Latin acumen allowed them to understand the pope’s discourse, as well as the rest of the world when the translation followed: for the first time since Pope Celestine V in 1294, a pontiff was resigning on his own initiative. This was a considerable paradigm shift on several levels. Benedict’s predecessor, John Paul II, despite advanced age, poor health, and the increasingly debilitating effects of advanced Parkinson’s disease, refused to consider stepping down as pope, stating that when God wanted the Wojtyła reign to end, God himself would call the pontiff home.

A month later, on the evening of 13 March 2013, the church bells in Rome, and around most of the world, began to ring in anticipatory confirmation of the election of a new pope, Cardinal Jose Maria Bergoglio of Buenos Aires, Argentina. This new pope ushered in a number of papal firsts, including being the first non- European and first Jesuit to ascend the throne of Peter. He chose as his papal moniker neither John Paul III nor Pius XIII, but rather became the first ‘Francis’. Pope Francis appeared on the loggia of St Peter’s clad in the traditional white cassock but without the ermine-lined scarlet mozzetta, gold pectoral cross, and red Prada shoes favoured by his immediate predecessor, Benedict XVI. Francis’s first words were a folksy ‘Fratelli e sorelle, Buona sera!’ (‘Brothers and sisters, good evening!’), and his next words and actions gave **[p. 429]** further indications of the continued paradigm shifts that have been seen throughout his pontificate. Before dispensing his inaugural _Urbi et orbi_ pontifical blessing, Francis bowed his own head and asked for the prayers of the gathered throng in St Peter’s Square. For some on the loggia, this was all clearly too much, as they were heard to mutter in horror, ‘Questa è la fine del mondo!’ (‘This is the end of the world!’).

Perhaps the end of a certain world, but not the eschaton yet. According to church historian John O’Malley, SJ, the documents of Vatican II for the most part are characterized by an epideictic genre in that ‘[t]hey hold up ideals, then draw conclusions from them and often spell out practical consequences. This is a soft style compared with the hard-hitting style of canons and dialectical discourse. It is rightly described as [^c25-6] “pastoral” because it was meant to make Christian ideals appealing.’ Pope Francis has echoed this epideictic rhetorical genre in a good deal of the exercise of both his teaching and governing, which recalls the ‘medicine of mercy, rather than that of severity’ enunciated by John XXIII in the latter’s opening [^c25-7] address to Vatican II, _Gaudet Mater Ecclesia_.

[^c25-6]: John O’Malley, SJ, _What Happened at Vatican II_ (Cambridge, MA: The Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 2008), 47.

[^c25-7]: ‘Mother Church Rejoices’ (_Gaudet Mater Ecclesia_), 11 October 1962, in which Pope John XXIII critiqued those ‘prophets of doom are who always forecasting disaster’ while at the same time encouraging the assembled council fathers ‘to use the medicine of mercy rather than the weapons of severity’ in their pastoral approach in responding to the primary purpose for the council itself. For the official Latin text, see ‘Ioannis XXIII allocutio in sollemni Sacrosancti Concilii inauguratione’, Libreria Editrice Vaticana, 11 October 1962, http://w2.vatican.va/content/john-xxiii/la/speeches/1962/documents/hf_j- xxiii_spe_19621011_opening-council.html. For an English translation, see _The Documents of Vatican II_, ed. Walter M. Abbott (New York: America Press, 1966), 710–19.

In contrast, the pontificates of both John Paul II and Benedict XVI focused primarily on presenting the Church itself as a necessary bulwark of ‘truth’ in an age profoundly disturbed, in their eyes, by secularism that was exacerbated by infections of relativism, nihilism, gender ideologies, and so forth. Magisterial documents such as _Fides et Ratio_, _Veritatis Splendor_, _Evangelium Vitae_, and _Dominus Iesus_ were offered as antidotes to these serious diseases. While not denouncing these initiatives, Pope Francis clearly is trying to refocus the attention of the Church on the Gospel itself. Moreover, his writings—such as his Encyclical _Laudato Si’_ and his post-synodal Apostolic Exhortations _Evangelii Gaudium_ and _Amoris Laetitia—_have all used a more inductive analysis to look carefully at the concrete challenges and problems facing the world in this twenty-first century. Francis’s oft-used metaphor of the Church as a ‘fleld hospital’ sees the Church’s mission more in relation to the Gospel than as an institution that fulfils the mission through the exercise of the ecclesial _munera_ of teaching, governing, and sanctifying.

With Francis, therefore, we find both an ecclesiology and pastoral ministry focused less on abstract doctrines and instead turning its attention to the many deeply wounded souls who need Gospel-grounded healing. Pastoral ministers, then, should be like fleld health-care workers who are not afraid to leave a citadel Church to go out to these suffering souls. Shepherding in this way will likely result in ‘smelling like **[p. 430]** the sheep’, to use Pope Francis’s oft-repeated term, and will characterize bishops, priests, religious, and all Christians, who minister to the flock in a mode of accompaniment. At the same time, this accompaniment must fundamentally respect the dignity and freedom of the individuals’ consciences while seeking to help in the ongoing discernment process of deeper integration. This theme surfaced strongly in the 2016 post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation _Amoris Laetitia_, which followed the two Synods on the Family in October 2014 and 2015.

In his opening address of the 2014 Extraordinary Synod on the Family, Pope Francis called for a radical [^c25-8] openness or παρρησία (Greek, _parrhesia,_ meaning to speak candidly or boldly, and without fear). This was an ecclesial cultural change of some significance, allowing the sort of frank discussions necessary for shifting to a Church that was more ‘synodal’ in the sense of ‘walking together on the way’, as the Greek word συν+οδος (_synodos_) literally suggests. In the past, the ‘walking together’ was perhaps seen as a long, straight, single-file line, with everyone in the Church _Cum Petro et sub Petro_—being ‘with Peter’ only by gathering together ‘under Peter’ (as explicitly referenced in _VS_ 116). Historically, any public disagreement was relabelled as ‘dissent’, and dissent could never be seen as legitimate. Dissent was treated fairly harshly during the years (1981–2005) that Cardinal Ratzinger headed the CDF during the pontificate of John Paul II, but relaxed slightly when Ratzinger himself became pope.

[^c25-8]: For an English translation of the Pope’s Italian address, see Pope Francis, ‘Greeting of Pope Francis’, Libreria Editrice Vaticana, 6 October 2014, http://w2.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/speeches/2014/october/documents/papa- francesco_20141006_padri-sinodali.html.

Nevertheless, strict adherence to the traditional moral teachings against contraception articulated in _Humanae Vitae_ and condemnation of same-sex activity, coupled with unwavering support of the papal ordinary magisterium, were widely viewed as a critical litmus test for episcopal promotion. The role of conscience vis-à-vis the _obsequium religiosum_ articulated in _Lumen Gentium_ 25 was given very little latitude for public theological discussion, much less disagreement, and theologians were instructed in the CDF’s 1990 Instruction _Donum Veritatis_ to suffer in prayerful silence if they believed even the ordinary magisterium to be incomplete or in error in some concrete teaching (see _Donum Veritatis_ 31).

### 5. Conclusion

This chapter was being written as the 2018 Synod on Youth was drawing to a close. Compared to the sharp debates in the previous synods, which ultimately resulted in _Amoris Laetitia_ with its major shifts in pastoral tone and articulation of the proper role of moral norms, the 2018 synod was relatively peaceful. Nevertheless, the Final Report probably gave little solace to those who longed for a return to the era of John Paul II. _Humanae Vitae_, _Veritatis Splendor_, and John Paul II’s 1981 _Familiaris Consortio_ were entirely absent in **[p. 431]** both letter and spirit. The ‘Theology of the Body’ got a quick mention at paragraph 39 in a long list of documents including the _Catechism of the Catholic Church_, Benedict XVI’s _Deus Caritas Est_, and Francis’s _Amoris Laetitia_, but nowhere else is this particular approach to sexuality elaborated upon. The deeper message of _Amoris Laetitia_ came through clearly in the triad of ‘accompaniment, conscience & discernment’ instead. This synod showed Francis not way ahead in the ecclesial vanguard of the Left, nor fighting a rearguard action with the Right, but rather leading resolutely from the centre. This in itself is another paradigm shift, though, as it moves moral theology after the council to the centre of the Gospel, which Pope Francis clearly believes must centre on God’s mercy, forgiveness, compassion, healing, and reconciliation.

As Isaac Newton has taught us in another discipline, for every action there is an equal opposite reaction, and so not even a pope is exempt from this law of (human) nature. As with every other section of this chapter, at least a book could be written outlining the growing resistance and rejection of the Francis effect in some conservative corners of the church community. In a meeting with a large group of Latin American Jesuits on 6 January 2018 in Santiago de Chile, Pope Francis repeated a point he has made several times in different venues: he referenced the common view of church historians that it takes a century before a council can really put down its roots, then added: ‘We are halfway there.’[^c25-9]

[^c25-9]: ‘Gli storici dicono che ci vuole un secolo prima che un Concilio metta radici. Siamo a metà strada’. The conversation took place in Spanish but was transcribed and published in Italian by Antonio Spadoro as ‘ “Dov’è che il nostro popolo è stato creativo?”: Conversazioni di papa Francesco con i gesuiti del Cile e del Perù’, _La civiltá cattolica_ 4024 (2018): 313–30. Available at http://www.laciviltacattolica.it/articolo/dove-che-il-nostro-popolo-e-stato-creativo.

Curran, Charles E. _The Development of Moral Theology: Five Strands_. Washington, DC: Georgetown University Press, 2013.

Häring, Bernard, CSsR. _Free and Faithful in Christ: Moral Theology for Priests and Laity_, 3 vols. Slough: St Paul Publications, 1978– 81.
