## 26. New Wine, Old Wineskins: The Reception of Vatican II in

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 432]** On 25 January 1959, Pope John XXIII announced that he was convoking an ecumenical council, summoned a synod for the diocese of Rome, and ordering the revision of the Code of Canon Law. In 1963, while the council was barely under way, a commission to oversee the revision of the 1917 Code was established. However, since it had already become apparent that this revision process was to give juridical form to the vision and principles enunciated by the council, the commission did not begin its work in earnest until the council had concluded. By the time the commission formally took up its task in November 1965, canon law had already begun to change, especially through the efforts of Paul VI to implement provisionally some of the council’s ecclesiological vision.

### 2. The Council and Canon Law

#### The Council and the Task of Revising the Code

From an early stage of its deliberations, the council opted to refrain from enacting new legislation and to content itself with sketching a grand vision of the Church and principles for the revision of canon law, while leaving to canonists the task of translating that vision and those principles into legal norms. To be sure, the council did on a few occasions simply change the existing law (e.g., _Christus Dominus_ (_CD_) 8b on the dispensing authority of the diocesan bishop), but more frequently it expressly directed that the future **[p. 433]** revision of canon law should be carried out in conformity with its teaching. Thus, the council documents had very little to say explicitly about canon law and the function it should play in the life and mission of the Church. Indeed, the absence of a theology of canon law is one of the great lacunae in the legacy of the [^c26-1] council. Not only did the council fail to provide those charged with revising canon law with an overarching vision of the role of law in the Church, but in several ways the council also complicated the task of revising canon law in its wake.

[^c26-1]: Louis Bouyer, _L’Église de Dieu: Corps du Christ et temple de l’Esprit_ (Paris: Cerf, 1970), 208–9.

First, the documents of Vatican II belong to a different genre than the output of previous councils. Earlier councils had usually framed their teaching in the form of ‘canons’, terse legislative texts enjoining external conformity in doctrinal and disciplinary matters with a threat of punishment for non-compliance. However, the style of the documents of Vatican II is ‘epideictic’; that is, less concerned with clarifying and defining [^c26-2] than enhancing appreciation, persuading, fostering reconciliation, and articulating an ideal to be emulated. By contrast, canon law, with its penchant for clarity and precision and its focus on external conformity to norms, goes against the grain of this epideictic approach. When this conciliar rhetoric is translated into canonical language, the latter almost inevitably seems cramped and restrictive by comparison to the former.

[^c26-2]: John W. O’Malley, _What Happened at Vatican II?_ (Cambridge, MA: The Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 2008), 46–48.

Second, although it was clear from its outset that the aim of the revision of canon law was to translate the ecclesiological teaching of the council into juridical norms, the council itself did not bequeath to the revisers of canon law a unitary vision of the Church. It has long been noted that at least two ecclesiologies seem to underlie the documents of Vatican II, especially its Dogmatic Constitution _Lumen Gentium_: a _communio_ [^c26-3] ecclesiology and a juridical ecclesiology. The latter so focuses on the external and visible dimensions of the Church, especially its hierarchical authority (exercised from the top down), that the internal and spiritual dimensions can disappear from view. The _communio_ ecclesiology, on the other hand, tries to hold the external and internal, visible and invisible aspects of the Church in dynamic balance in which the external, visible dimensions are the sacramental expression of the internal, spiritual dimensions and, in turn, reinforce and deepen them. This complex _communio_ or sacramental ecclesiology is perhaps most evident in _Lumen Gentium_ 8:

[^c26-3]: Antonio Acerbi, _Due ecclesiologie: Ecclesiologie giuridica ed ecclesiologie di communio nella ‘Lumen Gentium’_ (Bologna: EDB, 1975).

The one mediator, Christ, established and ever sustains here on earth his holy Church, the community of faith, hope and charity, as a visible organization through which he communicates truth and grace to all men. But, the society structured with hierarchical organs and the mystical body of Christ, the visible society and the spiritual community, the earthly Church and the Church endowed with heavenly riches, are not to be thought of as two realities. On the contrary, they form one complex reality which comes together from a human and a divine element. For this reason the Church is compared, in a powerful analogy, to the mystery of the incarnate Word. As the **[p. 434]** assumed nature, inseparably united to him, serves the Divine Word as a living organ of salvation, so, in a somewhat similar way, does the social structure of the Church serve the Spirit of Christ who vivifles it, in the building up of the body.

Throughout the post-conciliar era, it has been tempting for commentators, both theologians and canonists, simply to juxtapose these two ecclesiologies, as if they were incompatible. On the one hand, some have attributed the evidence of different ecclesiologies in the conciliar documents to the inevitable compromises between the conservative minority and the reformist majority in the conciliar _aula_. Overlooking the fact that the _communio_ ecclesiology also insists on the Church’s visible dimensions, these commentators have viewed the strands of conciliar ecclesiology emphasizing the Church as a visible society as concessions to the minority at the council and remnants of the now discredited _societas perfecta_ ecclesiology that had dominated the pre-conciliar era; meanwhile, they have seen the strands emphasizing the Church as an invisible, spiritual communion as the authentic ecclesiological teaching of the council. From this perspective, a canon law faithful to the legacy of Vatican II would downplay, if it did not totally ignore, the societal dimension of the Church and its consequences. On the other hand, some commentators concentrate on conciliar texts that stress the visible aspects of the Church and treat its invisible and spiritual aspects as non-juridical or merely ‘pastoral’ and so peripheral to the concerns of the law. This approach is especially tempting to canonists who, in the absence of a clearly articulated theology of canon law, are prone to resort to the default position that law in the Church flows from the demands of its societal nature and not from its theological identity.

If a too exclusive focus on the invisible and spiritual dimension of the Church can foster a sort of ecclesiological Monophysitism, too exclusive a concentration on its societal dimension can tend to a sort of ecclesiological Nestorianism. However, in _Lumen Gentium_, the council audaciously analogized the admingling of the visible society and the spiritual communion in the one Church of Christ to the unity of the divine and human natures in the one person of Christ. Just as orthodox Christology must maintain the delicate Chalcedonian balance of the human and divine natures in Christ, so canon law that is faithful to the teaching of Vatican II must keep the visible societal dimensions and the invisible spiritual dimensions of the one Church in balance. Although the drafters of the revised Code strove to find this delicate balance, it is hard to avoid the conclusion that, on the whole, they were more successful at drafting a law for a visible society than providing legislation for a _communio_.

#### The Problematic Option for a Revised Code

With little discussion, the Code Revision Commission opted to continue to organize the Church’s law in the form of a code in the style of the great secular codifications of the nineteenth century and the 1917 Code of Canon Law. This option had the inevitable consequence of exacerbating the tilt towards the visible **[p. 435]** dimensions of the Church inherent in the long-standing reliance of canon lawyers on the principle that the Church is a society as the rationale for ecclesial law. Codifled law as it emerged in continental Europe in the nineteenth century, and later in the Church with the 1917 Code of Canon Law, was an instrument for centralizing authority by identifying law with the enactments of the supreme legislator and recognizing only unencumbered individuals as subjects of law and the objects of official ministrations. Although the drafters of the revised Code jettisoned much of the ideology of ‘codification’, the code format inevitably fosters a positivism that grounds law in the will of the legislator instead of in the theological nature of the Church as community of faith and an individualism that sees the faithful as atomized subjects of hierarchical authority and not as individuals always enmeshed in communities. Thus, the underlying dynamics of the technique of codification has led the revised Code to accentuate the juridic dimension of the Church at the expense of its _communio_ dimension.

#### Disdain for Law in the Post-Conciliar Era

The late 1960s and 1970s were an inauspicious time in which to engage in legislative renewal. In the secular world, especially in North America and Western Europe, these were years of social and political upheaval. This period was marked by strident demands for freedom from oppressive social and political structures and even from the constraints of traditional morality. In this context, law often seemed an agent of oppression that needed to be overthrown. The Church was not immune to this tide of antinomianism. Already in the conciliar _aula_, Bishop Émile De Smedt (Bruges, Belgium) had denounced the clericalism, legalism, and triumphalism he believed permeated the initial drafts of conciliar documents. Under the banner of _aggiornamento_, the post-conciliar period was characterized by considerable experimentation in liturgy and in church governance at all levels. Efforts to set limits to this experimentation or even to bring it to an end were often scored as resurgent legalism. In this cultural context, efforts to translate the teaching of the conciliar documents into legislative texts were criticized by some as fixations on the ‘letter’ of the council rather than openness to its ‘spirit’. For others, the antidote to the anti-juridicism that had infected the Church was the prompt promulgation of a revised Code to provide clear and rigorously juridical norms for pastoral governance.

### 3. Reception of the Council in the Revised Code of Canon Law

Despite the inherent limitations and biases of the technique of codification and the turbulent times in which **[p. 436]** the work of code revision was carried out, the revised Code of Canon Law for the Latin Church was promulgated by ‘primatial act’ of John Paul II on 25 January 1983. This Code (CIC/1983) is not, of course, the entire corpus of the canon law of the Catholic Church. Canon law also includes the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches promulgated in 1990; the norms enacted governing the celebration of the sacraments and sacramentals contained in the several liturgical books; various special laws governing particular institutes like the Roman Curia; penalties; special procedures; the proper laws of religious institutes and societies of apostolic life; as well as the laws enacted by episcopal conferences, diocesan bishops, and, more rarely, particular councils. Moreover, the Code itself has been modifled several times since it was first promulgated in 1983. Nonetheless, the Code is, as John Paul II noted, ‘the Church’s principal legislative document’ and ‘an indispensable instrument to insure order both in individual and social life, and also in the Church’s own activity’. Indeed, the Code was lauded by John Paul II ‘as a great effort to translate the same conciliar [^c26-4] doctrine and ecclesiology into _canonical_ language’, and on several occasions, John Paul II described it as [^c26-5] ‘the last document of the Council’. Thus, it is fair to use the Latin Code as the standard for judging post-conciliar canon law’s fidelity to the teaching of the council itself.

[^c26-4]: John Paul II, ‘Apostolic Constitution _Sacrae disciplinae leges_’, 25 January 1983, in Canon Law Society of America, _Code of_ _Canon Law: Latin–English Edition; New English Translation_ (Washington, DC: Canon Law Society of America, 2020); emphasis in the original.

[^c26-5]: John Paul II, ‘Allocution to the Auditors and Officials of the Roman Rota’, _AAS_ 76 (1984): 644.

#### Organization of the Revised Code

Instead of reprising the classical triad of persons, things, and actions borrowed from the classical Roman jurist Gaius as its organizing principle, the revised Code divides its material into seven major sections or books. After an introductory book on General Norms, it devotes books to the People of God, the Church’s Teaching Office, the Church’s Sanctifying Office, Temporal Goods, Sanctions, and Processes. This overall organization of the revised Code is a distinct improvement on that of the 1917 Code. Instead of focusing on unencumbered individuals or ‘persons’, this organizational plan gives prominence to the Church as the People of God. Faithful to the schema of _Lumen Gentium_, this largest single book of the revised Code begins with the Christian faithful themselves and only then takes up, in turn, laity, clergy, associations, the hierarchical structures of the Church, institutes of consecrated life, and societies of apostolic life. The remaining five books exhibit a serious effort on the part of the Code Revision Commission to arrange material according to the schema of the three _munera_ of Christ and the Church that the council had adopted: teaching, sanctifying, and three key aspects of governing (temporal goods, sanctions, and processes). Despite its reprising of conciliar themes, this organizational structure is not entirely successful in providing an adequate framework for articulating the conciliar vision of the Church because it separates the discussion of the faithful—laity and clergy—and their respective obligations and rights from the matrix of the word **[p. 437]** and sacraments in which they are rooted; it also treats word and sacraments more as objects of the Church’s ministrations than as the sources from which the Church emerges and lives.

Book I: General Norms

The decision to begin the revised Code as the 1917 Code had begun, with a book on general norms, was unfortunate. While much of the material contained in this book would probably have had to be incorporated somewhere in the revised law, locating this highly juridical material at the very beginning of the Code leaves it deracinated from the kerygmatic and sacramental core of ecclesial reality and makes the Church appear as simply a society indistinguishable from all others. That there is no compelling reason of legal theory for beginning the revised Code with general norms is evident from the fact that the Eastern Code has not done so. Instead, it distributes the material on general norms at various places throughout the Code. Particularly unfortunate is the Latin Code’s treatment of physical persons in CIC/1983 canons 96 to 112, where, despite recognition that it is ‘by baptism that one is incorporated in to the Church of Christ and constituted a person in it’, the whole focus is narrowly juridical and devoid of theological content. This description of the ecclesiologically unencumbered individual physical person with obligations and rights contrasts sharply with the designation of the Christian faithful ‘incorporated into Christ through baptism’, ‘constituted as the People of God’, and ‘made sharers in their own way in Christ’s priestly, prophetic, and royal function’, introduced in canon 204, §1, the opening canon of Book II on the People of God. In fact, the juxtaposition of the definitions of the physical person in canon 96 and of the Christian faithful in canon 204 suggests an inability on the part of the Code’s drafters ‘to work out a coherent notion either of the Church or of the Code’.[^c26-6]

[^c26-6]: Joseph A. Komonchak, ‘Vatican II and the New Code’, _Archives des sciences sociales des religions_ 62 (1986): 111.

The decision to include a treatment of power of governance or jurisdiction among the general norms is also problematic. These norms are disconnected from the Code’s treatment of the sacramental source of empowerment in the Church and even from the Church’s hierarchical structure. As such, they seem to be indistinguishable from comparable norms in a secular legal text. In _Lumen Gentium_ 27 and elsewhere, the council tried to transcend the traditional bifurcation of power in the Church into power of orders and power of jurisdiction or governance—a bifurcation Rudolph Sohm had scored as the hallmark of the juridicization of the Church—by consistently avoiding the traditional terminology and speaking instead of ‘sacred power’, a phrase that has been understood by many canonists at least to embrace what have traditionally been called the powers of orders and jurisdiction. This language helped to identify sacramental ordination and not papal delegation as the source of the bishop’s share in the teaching and governing _munera_. However, reducing power in the Church to ‘one sacred power’ so links the Church’s teaching and governing functions to sacramental ordination that it is difficult to see how and even whether the non-ordained can participate **[p. 438]** in any meaningful way in these _munera_. The issue of lay participation in Church governance was hotly debated throughout the Code revision process and has not been resolved fully at the doctrinal level. Although it is a bit unfair to expect the Code to resolve this still debated theological issue, the absence of a resolution leaves considerable doubt about how the non-ordained can participate in the royal function of Christ and the Church and opens the way for a reclericalization of the Church.

Book II: The People of God

As introductions to major sections of Book II on the People of God, the revised Code faithfully incorporates citations from conciliar documents, especially _Lumen Gentium_, in rather juridicized forms. The juridicization of the conciliar texts sometimes entails conflations of several sources, truncations of the original texts, and other modifications, all of which tend to weaken the thrust of conciliar teaching. For example, CIC/1983 canons 208 to 222 reproduce all but one of the obligations and rights of the faithful mentioned in conciliar documents, but they have so qualifled these rights with caveats and conditions that they seem like begrudging concessions. The one right omitted from the listing in the revised Code is ‘the right and duty to exercise charisms’ (_Apostolicam Actuositatem_ (_AA_) 3), which the Code Revision Commission judged to be insufficiently juridical for inclusion. In a similar way, canon 205 faithfully echoes _Lumen Gentium_ 14 in enunciating ‘the bonds of the profession of faith, the sacraments, and ecclesiastical governance’ as criteria for full communion with the Catholic Church, but quietly omits ‘possessing the Holy Spirit’, which the conciliar text had included among these criteria. Here as elsewhere, the drafters of the revised Code ignored elements of conciliar teaching most expressive of the Church’s _communio_ dimension.

The large central section of Book II, on the Hierarchical Constitution of the Church, is divided into two sections: one devoted to the Supreme Authority of the Church and the other to Particular Churches and their groupings. The former is faithful to the council in recognizing that the College of Bishops shares in the supreme authority in the Church with the Roman Pontiff. However, its treatment of the College of Bishops is rather perfunctory, devoted mostly to its activity at ecumenical councils and the pontiff’s prerogative to convoke, direct, and approve the decisions of such councils. Unlike the council, which called for the establishment of a Synod of Bishops to ‘demonstrate that all the bishops in hierarchical communion share in the responsibility for the universal Church’ with the Supreme Pontiff (_CD_ 5), and the preamble to Paul VI’s motu proprio _Apostolica Sollicitudo_ of 1965, which established this Synod of Bishops, the revised Code treats the Synod only as a body which, like the College of Cardinals and the Roman Curia, assists the Roman Pontiff with their counsel. Suggestions that the Synod of Bishops might be an expression of collegiality have disappeared.

The rich post-conciliar discussion about the mutual inherence of the universal Church and the particular or local churches has had no impact on the Code’s presentation of the Church. One of the most important ecclesiological statements of the council affirmed that particular churches ‘are fashioned after the model of **[p. 439]** the universal Church’ and ‘[i]n and from such individual churches there comes into being the one and only Catholic Church’ (_LG_ 23). The revised Code acknowledges this ecclesiological datum but only in a subordinate clause (CIC/1983 c. 368), and it plays no further function in the articulation of the Code’s ecclesiology. Instead, the Code’s treatment of the hierarchical constitution of the Church takes the form of a descending ecclesiology. Throughout the revised Code, the Roman Pontiff is always mentioned before bishops, whether collectively or individually. Even the canon enjoining obedience on clerics mentions first their obligation to show reverence and obedience to the Supreme Pontiff and only then obedience owed to their own bishop or superior (CIC/1983 c. 273). Although the revised Code has not repeated the 1917 Code’s division of the hierarchy into ‘the supreme pontificate and the subordinate episcopate’ (CIC/1917 c. 108, §3), the mentality that spawned that phrase has not entirely disappeared.

The revised Code does make an advance by treating provincial and plenary councils and episcopal conferences as groupings of particular churches and as expressions of the collegial authority of the participating bishops rather than as manifestations of the authority of the Roman Pontiff, as was the case in the 1917 Code (CIC/1983 cc. 281–92). Representation by presbyters and other members of the Christian faithful at plenary and provincial councils is permitted as long as their number does not exceed half the number of bishops, diocesan officials, seminary and university rectors, and members of religious institutes and societies of apostolic life who must be convoked. However, their presence at these councils is not required, and, when they are present, they have only a consultative vote (CIC/1983 c. 443, §4). An ample number of presbyters and some lay members of the faithful must be called to diocesan synods, but they again have only a consultative vote (CIC/1983 c. 463, §1). Nevertheless, the revised Code exhibits considerable suspicion of the collaborative or joint exercises of episcopal authority at particular councils and in episcopal conferences. It is particularly parsimonious in allotting governance authority to episcopal conferences and, since 1983, the scope of even the teaching authority of these conferences has been [^c26-7] subjected to additional restrictions. Although preserving the integrity of the office of diocesan bishop from encroachments of conference bureaucracy was often the stated rationale for these restrictions, they have had the effect of inhibiting the development of collegial cooperation among bishops.

[^c26-7]: See John Paul II, ‘Apostolic letter _Apostolos suos_’, _AAS_ 90 (1998): 641–58, esp. no. 22,1.

Drawing on _Christus Dominus_ 11, CIC/1983 canon 369 asserts that

a diocese is a portion of the people of God which is entrusted to a bishop for him to shepherd with the cooperation of the _presbyterium_, so that adhering to its pastor and gathered by him in the Holy Spirit through the gospel and the Eucharist, it constitutes a particular church in which the one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church of Christ is truly present and operative.

Making a community of the faithful—indeed, a eucharistic community—and the presbyterate constitutive **[p. 440]** elements of a diocese is a definite improvement over the 1917 Code’s treatment of it as a merely administrative subdivision of the Church. The parish is also recognized as a stably constituted ‘community of the Christian faithful’ (CIC/1983 c. 515, §1). However, the idea of the parish as a eucharistic community prominent in the conciliar documents cited as sources for this canon has disappeared. In fact, the faithful fade from view in the revised Code’s treatment of the structures of the particular Church after their mention in the definitions of dioceses and parishes. After defining dioceses and parishes as communities of the faithful, the revised Code reverts quickly to treating them as juridical persons, artificial entities that are distinct from the persons or things that serve as their substratum and created by competent authority. It is of course true that dioceses and parishes only exist as such in virtue of the intervention of, respectively, the Roman Pontiff and the diocesan bishop. Nevertheless, by designating parishes and dioceses as juridical persons and consistently treating them as such, the revised Code allows them to be dealt with in abstraction from their underlying communities simply as things to be administered.

The revised Code, faithful to the council, requires that each diocese have a presbyteral council whose members ‘represent the _presbyterium_ … and who assist the bishop in the governance of the diocese’ (CIC/1983 c. 495, §1; see _CD_ 27–28). However, the revised Code stipulates only a handful of issues about which the diocesan bishop must consult the presbyteral council. Most of these issues mark important moments in the life of the local church but occur only relatively rarely (e.g., erecting, modifying, or suppressing parishes). Only the requirement of consultation with the presbyteral council prior to the levying of a diocesan tax touches on the ordinary affairs of diocesan governance. This reluctance of the revised Code to sketch a more substantial role for the presbyteral council in the day-to-day governance of the local Church and the reluctance of diocesan bishops to involve the presbyterate in such governance reflect a failure to appreciate and incorporate the conciliar view of presbyters not just as cooperators but also as ‘necessary cooperators’ (_Presbyterorum Ordinis_ (_PO_) 7) with the bishop, who is united with them in one _presbyterium_ (_LG_ 28). Consequently, the revised Code can only treat the admonition that bishops ‘attend to presbyters and listen to them as assistants and counselors’ (CIC/1983 c. 384) as a moral and legal obligation instead of one grounded in the very structure of _communio_ and the demands of synodal governance.

Presbyters can, of course, participate in diocesan governance by appointment to various offices in the diocesan curia. The non-ordained are eligible to be appointed to many of these curial offices as well, and they can be appointed to diocesan finance councils (CIC/1983 c. 492, §1) and, where they exist, to diocesan pastoral councils (CIC/1983 c. 512, §1). Although the council had presented diocesan pastoral councils as ‘highly desirable’ (_CD_ 27), the revised Code exhibits much less of a sense of urgency about their establishment. It is content to reproduce with slight modifications the skeletal norms on diocesan pastoral councils issued in 1966 by Paul VI in the motu proprio _Ecclesiae Sanctae_. The scope of the responsibility of the diocesan pastoral council is potentially vast: it ‘investigates, considers, and proposes practical conclusions about those things which pertain to pastoral work in the diocese’ (CIC/1983 c. 511). Since it is **[p. 441]** left to the diocesan bishop to establish a pastoral council, convoke it, and set its agenda, it is a rather fragile vehicle for structuring the right of the faithful ‘to manifest to the sacred pastors their opinion on matters which pertain to the good of the Church’ (_LG_ 37; CIC/1983 c. 212, §3).

Although the parish is now defined as ‘a certain community of the Christian faithful’, the forty-seven canons devoted to the parish deal with the non-ordained faithful primarily as the recipients of the ministrations of the pastor and his ordained vicars. The revised Code does admonish pastors to ‘recognize and promote the proper part which the lay members of the Christian faithful have in the mission of the Church’ but considerably weakens this exhortation by limiting the focus of the pastor’s solicitude to ‘fostering their association for the purpose of religion’ (CIC/1983 c. 529, §2). Books III and IV of the revised Code do offer opportunities for the lay faithful to participate in the Church’s teaching and sanctifying missions, especially at parish level. However, opportunities to participate in the Church’s governing mission in the parish are rather limited. The Code does foresee that, in cases of extreme shortage of clergy, a layperson may be entrusted with the pastoral care of a parish, as long as a priest is designated to direct this pastoral care (CIC/1983 c. 517, §2). The only other roles foreseen for laypeople in parish governance are as members of parish finance councils (CIC/1983 c. 537) and, where they exist, pastoral councils (CIC/1983 c. 538). The Code emphasizes that lay faithful enjoy ‘a consultative vote only’ on these councils. This restriction has been underscored by the 1997 instruction _Ecclesiae de mysterio_ on the participation of the non-ordained in the ministry of the ordained, which stipulated that these councils ‘cannot in any way become deliberative structures’. Pope John Paul II approved this provision of the instruction _in forma specifica_, thus making it part of canon law. The result of this repeated insistence on the merely consultative role of the lay faithful and the reluctance to identify issues about which they must even be consulted is that the revised Code continues the marginalization of the lay faithful in ecclesial governance and falls short of giving juridical form to the conciliar understanding of the Church as a _communio_ and of the complementarity between the ministerial priesthood and the common priesthood (e.g., _LG_ 10).

Although the drafters of the revised Code attempted to give form to the conciliar vision of collegial or synodal governance at all levels of the Church (e.g., _CD_ 5, 27–28, 36–38), the structures for articulating this vision were originally crafted in haste in the immediate aftermath of the council. Despite their already evident weaknesses, the provisional structures have been largely replicated with only a few modifications and juridical precisions in the revised Code. As a result, they have proved too feeble to resist the steady encroachment of bureaucracy, the Church’s ‘permanent government’. At the level of the universal Church, the Synod of Bishops, which the council hoped would ‘bear testimony to the participation of all the bishops in hierarchical communion in the care of the universal Church’ (_CD_ 5), has been largely co-opted by the Roman Curia. It has, at least until recently, been little more than an opportunity for bishops to pontificate rather than deliberate as a prelude to a papal apostolic exhortation that barely shows the imprint of the synod discussions. The same bureaucratic encroachment has occurred at the level of the particular Church. In the wake of Vatican II, diocesan curias expanded exponentially, with staffs of experts in various areas of pastoral activity to advise bishops, coordinate programmes, and direct activities. Dwarfed by the **[p. 442]** influence of the diocesan curia and its many offices, the role of collegial structures like presbyteral and pastoral councils, without staff and meeting only periodically, has withered.

Book III: The Church’s Teaching Office

Book III, on the Church’s Teaching Office, treats divine revelation more as a deposit of faith to be carefully protected and faithfully proclaimed by the Church than as ‘the plenitude of divine truth’ into which ‘the Church is always advancing … until eventually the words of God are fulfilled in her’ (_Dei Verbum_ (_DV_) 9). This emphasis is particularly marked in the introductory canons of Book III, which treat the deposit of faith, the prerogative of the Roman Pontiff and the College of Bishops to proclaim and protect it, and the obligation of the faithful to submit to their authoritative teaching. The revised Code follows the council rather faithfully in its regulation of the various means by which the Church carries out its teaching mission (_LG_ 23–26; _CD_ 4; _Gaudium et Spes_ (_GS_) 4–10; _Ad Gentes_ (_AG_) 2, 35). It gives pride of place to preaching the word of God, especially the liturgical homily. The norms governing preaching are less concerned with who has the faculty to preach than they are with the obligation of ordained ministers and even, at times, laypeople (CIC/1983 c. 766), to preach the Gospel. Catechesis is seen as a solicitude of the whole Church, and the role of bishops and pastors in catechesis is seen as organizing, supporting, and overseeing the efforts of others. Noteworthy is the recognition of the need for catechesis for the reception of the several sacraments and even for catechetical efforts to continue beyond childhood. Unlike the 1917 Code, which reserved responsibility for missionary activity to the Apostolic See, the revised Code holds evangelization to be ‘a fundamental duty of the People of God’ in which all the faithful have their part (CIC/1983 c. 781). The revised Code’s norms on Catholic education are drawn from the conciliar decree _Gravissimum Educationis_.

Book IV: The Church’s Sanctifying Office

The bulk of the revision of the law governing the Church’s sanctifying office occurred during the preparation of the several liturgical books the council had directed to be revised in light of its teaching (_Sacrosanctum Concilium_ (_SC_) 47). The revised Code has gathered many of these norms governing liturgy, sacraments, sacramentals, and sacred times into Book IV, on the Church’s sanctifying office. This organization of material is a considerable improvement over the arrangement in the 917 Code, where the sacraments and sacramentals are treated as ‘things’, and liturgy is barely mentioned.

The revised Code begins its treatment of the Church’s sanctifying function with a long and somewhat juridicized quotation from _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ 7 on the nature of liturgy and its centrality to the life of the Church (CIC/1983 c. 834, §1). This canon sets the tone for the canons which follow. A similar canon, drawn mostly from _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ 57, introduces the section dealing with the sacraments. Although more doctrinal than disciplinary, this canon emphasizes the role of faith in the celebration of the sacraments, underscores the role of the whole community of faithful in these celebrations, and recognizes **[p. 443]** the sacraments as constitutive of the Church. These conciliar themes were notably absent from the 1917 Code. Although the ecclesiological dimension of the sacraments was largely ignored by the 1917 Code, it is emphasized in the revised Code in the canons that serve as theological preambles for the treatment of six of the seven sacraments. The one exception is in the section on the sacrament of matrimony, where the council’s reference to the family as a ‘domestic church’ (_LG_ 11) is not even mentioned.

The revised Code does, however, incorporate other aspects of conciliar teaching on marriage. Its description of marriage itself (CIC/1983 c. 1055, §1) and of the matrimonial consent which brings it about (CIC/1983 c. 1057, §2) are drawn directly from the conciliar teaching on marriage in _Gaudium et Spes_ 48. In these opening canons, the revised Code also adopts the council’s preference for speaking of marriage as ‘a covenant’ rather than ‘a contract’. However, covenantal language disappears after the introductory canons and contractual language reappears; even in the introductory canons, it is not clear that this covenantal language is more than a rhetorical flourish.

Unlike the previous Code, the revised Code follows the council (_GS_ 50) in refusing to designate the procreation and education of offspring as the primary end of marriage and all others as merely secondary. It states simply that marriage is ‘ordered by its nature to the good of the spouses and the procreation and education of offspring’ (CIC/1983 c. 1055, §1). The revised Code’s description of marriage as ‘a partnership of the whole of life’, its recognition of the ‘good of the spouses’ as an end of marriage on a par with the procreation, and its description of matrimonial consent as an act by which the spouses give and accept ‘each other’ instead of, as the 1917 Code had phrased it, giving and accepting the perpetual and exclusive right to acts that are per se apt for the procreation of offspring have allowed for the interpersonal dimension of marriage to be accorded juridical weight. These conciliar contributions have opened the way for church tribunals to consider psychological factors that impeded or impaired a person’s capacity for forming and sustaining interpersonal relationships when judging the validity of marriage. Along with the simplification of procedural law, this opening is, for better or for worse, a major contributor to the proliferation of declarations of nullity by church tribunals since the council.

Books V, VI, and VII: Elements of the Church’s Governing Office

Books V, VI, and VII of the revised Code deal respectively with the temporal goods of the Church, sanctions, and processes. These books have been only lightly influenced by the teaching of the council.

Temporal Goods of the Church

Book V, on the Church’s temporal goods, begins with an unqualifled reaffirmation of the Church’s right to acquire, retain, administer, and alienate temporal goods ‘independently from civil power’ (CIC/1983 c. 1256, §1). This bald assertion ignores the careful effort of the council to redefine the Church’s relationship with civil authorities and to recognize the right of the latter to regulate the exercise of religious liberty, even the liberty of the Church, ‘in the interest of public order’ (_Dignitatis Humanae_ (_DH_) 7, 13). The revised Code also **[p. 444]** insists on the innate right of the Church (clearly, the hierarchical authority of the Church is intended here) to exact (_exigere_) from the faithful what is needed for carrying out the Church’s mission (CIC/1983 c. 1260). Although conciliar documents stress over and over the role of _communio_ in the acquisition, retention, and administration of temporal goods (e.g., _CD_ 6), little of this emphasis finds its way into Book V of the revised Code. Instead, the overriding emphasis of the norms on temporal goods is on preserving the Church’s possessions and preventing their dissipation. While good stewardship of the Church’s resources is important, a greater emphasis on stewardship and on placing the Church’s goods at the service of its mission, especially solicitude for the poor, would have been more in keeping with the spirit of the council. A small step in that direction is the revised Code’s acknowledgement that ‘it is right [_fas est_] for administrators of church goods to make donations for purposes of piety or Christian charity’ (CIC/1983 c. 1285). The previous Code had stipulated rather ungenerously that administrators of church goods ‘shall not presume to make donations out of the mobile goods of their churches beyond small and moderate ones’ (CIC/1917 c. 1535).

Faithful to the council, the revised Code incorporates provisions for diocesan and possibly supra-diocesan funds foreseen by the council to ensure adequate support for clerics and others who serve the Church (CIC/1983 c. 1274; see _PO_ 20–21). Perhaps in deference to the principle of subsidiarity, the revised Code does recognize the competence of episcopal conferences to enact norms for their territories governing fundraising campaigns (CIC/1983 c. 1262). It designates transactions as acts of extraordinary administration for diocesan bishops in their administration of the goods of their dioceses (CIC/1983 c. 1277), setting limits on the value of property a bishop or superior can alienate without first receiving the consent of his or her councils and of the Holy See (CIC/1983 c. 1292, §1) and regulating leasing of Church property (CIC/1983 c. 1297).

Sanctions in the Church

Perhaps no area of canon law was in greater need of a renewed theological rationale than penal sanctions. Grounded in the understanding of the Church as a _societas perfecta_ like the State, the 1917 Code treated the infiiction of penalties as the means by which superiors disciplined their inferiors. An approach to crime and punishment consistent with, or at least sensitive to, the Church as _communio_ would view offences as particularly egregious violations of communal order requiring intervention by representatives of the community to restore order and repair breaches in _communio_. Book VI of the revised Code, on sanctions in the Church, does make some progress in this direction. It makes clear that penalties are to be imposed only as a last resort for dealing with delinquents (CIC/1983 c. 1341). The number of offences subject to penalties, and especially the number prompting _latae sententiae_ or ‘automatic’ penalties, has been greatly reduced and simplifled. The penalty of suspension ‘from informed conscience’, which allowed a cleric to be suspended without any process, has been abrogated so that sanctions can now be imposed only pursuant to at least an administrative procedure in which the basic demands of ‘due process’ are met. Nevertheless, the revised law on penalties seems to have been shaped more by a desire to square canonical penal law with general legal theory than by an effort to incorporate conciliar ecclesiology into it.

**[p. 445]** Although there had been a plan to promulgate the section on penal law with an introductory motu proprio that sketched the theological underpinnings for penalties in the Church, this plan was scrapped. Instead, the opening canon of Book VI asserts baldly: ‘The Church has the innate and proper right to coerce offending members of the Christian faithful with penal sanction’ (CIC/1983 c. 1311), a norm which echoes both the letter and the spirit of the parallel canon of the previous Code (CIC/1917 c. 2214, §1). Most of the specific punishable offences or delicts listed in Book VI appeared in almost identical form in the previous Code. Although most of them could be presented as serious violations of _communio_, there is little evidence in the revised Code of any effort to do so. The delicts specifically mentioned in the Code, including those designated in post-Codal law as ‘more grave’, are primarily those for which the ‘ordinary’ faithful (laity, religious, and especially ‘lower’ clergy) are likely to be disciplined by ecclesiastical superiors. Even though arbitrary actions and negligent inactions by authorities may be more destructive of ecclesial communion than the failures of others, these offences are barely adverted to in the revised Code.

The Code revision process was a privileged opportunity to elaborate a compelling, theologically sound rationale for sanctions in the Church. The failure to exploit this opportunity in the revised Code helps to explain the reluctance, at least until recently, of Church authorities to use penal law to address reports of sexual abuse of minors by priests and other church ministers. Although the canonical penal process is complex and difficult, these difficulties could have been navigated by church leaders if they had had the will to do so. The lack of heart or stomach for the penal process was due, at least in part, to the failure of the revised Code to integrate penal law into a _communio_ vision of the Church. As a result, penal law could be dismissed by many bishops and others as ‘the dark side of the good news’.

In 2021, Pope Francis issued the apostolic constitution _Pascite gregem Domini_ to replace completely the penal law of Book VI promulgated in 1983. This constitution introducing the new norms does attempt to provide a theological grounding for penal law in the Church, but, even here, the _communio_ ecclesiology of Vatican II is not immediately evident. The new norms do incorporate most of the post-1983 innovations in penal law aimed at addressing the sexual abuse of minors and vulnerable persons, add new delicts for financial malfeasance, and make greater provision for delicts rooted in negligence.

Processes

Book VII of the revised Code, on processes, is considerably shorter than the comparable Book IV of the 1917 Code, but most of the abridgement results from the removal of the norms governing canonization and their relegation to special law outside the Code. Following the model of its predecessor, the current Code begins its presentation of procedural law with two long sections on trials in general, and the contentious trial in particular, before turning to consider certain special processes, the penal process, and some administrative procedures. While this systematic organization makes sense from the point of view of juridical science, it fits oddly in a law for the Church in which almost all the judicial processes are either marriage nullity cases **[p. 446]** (one of the Code’s ‘special processes’) or penal cases. This arrangement of material leaves the impression that these latter judicial processes are simply incidental business for church tribunals rather than critical determinations of the status of the faithful in the Church and of their consequent rights and obligations.

The law governing marriage nullity procedure has been modifled several times since the council, including twice since the promulgation of the revised Code. The effect of these revisions has been to streamline and shorten the process and to make it more accessible to ordinary faithful. Consistent with the council’s stress on the dignity of the human person, ongoing changes in the law have eroded the suspicion evident in the previous Code that those who sought the assistance of the tribunal could not be trusted to be truthful; the revised Code established the principle that the declaration of a party and the testimony of a single witness can provide full proof (CIC/1983 c. 1678, §1). Although the format of a contentious trial, with all of the procedural protections it affords for the defendant, may be an appropriate vehicle for addressing penal cases, it is not clear that it is the appropriate vehicle for probing the dynamics of ‘the intimate partnership of married life and love’ (_GS_ 48).

Excised from the revised Code during the last edit by Pope John Paul II were norms structuring the administrative tribunals. Such tribunals had been called for by the Principles to Govern the Revision of the Code, approved by the 1967 Synod of Bishops, ‘so that any suspicion whatsoever of arbitrariness in church [^c26-8] administration may completely disappear’. The revised Code does sketch the rudiments of a procedure for hierarchical recourse for the faithful who believe they have been dealt with unfairly by administrative authorities in the Church (CIC/1983 cc. 1732–39). Although new to codifled law, these norms largely reproduce the long-standing _praxis Curiae Romanae_ for dealing with such recourses against the decrees of hierarchical authorities, procedures which had been judged ‘lacking considerably in church practice and the administration of justice’ by the same principles. Perhaps creating a completely new system of administrative tribunals might not have been the optimal way to resolve confiicts between members of the faithful and church authorities. However, the revised Code’s failure to provide any other method than the long-discredited method of hierarchical recourse leaves the lingering suspicion that breaches of _communio_ caused by real and supposed administrative arbitrariness are not considered sufficiently important to warrant attention.

[^c26-8]: Pontifical Commission for the Revision of the Code of Canon Law, ‘Principia quae recognitionem Codicis Iuris Canonici dirigant [1967]’, _Communicationes_ 2 (1969): 77–85.

### 4. Conclusion

The revised Code of Canon Law appeared almost eighteen years after the close of the Second Vatican **[p. 447]** Council. Although it would probably have benefited from at least one more round of consultation and revision prior to promulgation, the revised Code can still be judged to be moderately successful in translating ‘conciliar doctrine and ecclesiology into _canonical_ language’. The reports of the deliberations of the Pontifical Commission for the Revision of the Code of Canon Law make clear that the disagreements and tensions that had accompanied the debates in the conciliar _aula_ continued throughout the Code revision process. Although the revised Code is more successful in its translation of the juridical aspects of conciliar teaching than of its _communio_ aspects, the areas where its fidelity to the council are most tenuous and [^c26-9] questionable are precisely those where the council itself left ‘lacunae and ambiguities’ and where debates about the proper interpretation of the council have been most heated. The relationship between the Roman Pontiff and the College of Bishops, the inherence of the universal and the local Church, the appropriate level of decentralization of decision-making, the nature of _sacra potestas_, and the role of the non-ordained in the Church’s governing mission in particular and in the ministry of the ordained in general—these are all areas where ambiguities about the teaching of the council and its implication remain even fifty years after its conclusion.

[^c26-9]: Knut Walf, ‘Lacune et ambiguité dans l’écclesiologie de Vatican II’, in _Les Églises après Vatican II: Dynamisme et_ _prospective; Actes du Colloque internationale de Bologne, 1980_, ed. Giuseppe Alberigo (Paris: Beauchesne, 1981), 207.

Canon law is a servant of the Church’s own self-understanding. It is, therefore, a bit unfair to criticize canon law for its failure to deal adequately with issues that are still in flux in the Church’s own theology. Less excusable is the failure of drafters of the revised Code to learn from experience and make revisions of the law in the light of disappointed expectations. By the time the revised Code was promulgated, it was already clear, for example, that the structures called for by the council and hastily enacted in law at various levels had proved ineffective as expressions of communion and the synodality desired by the council. From the Synod of Bishops to local pastoral councils, consultative structures were established with great expectations during the post-conciliar decades, but their results have been disappointing. Nevertheless, the drafters of the revised Code were content to replicate the post-conciliar legislation with only minor adjustments. Their willingness to treat these recent additions to canon law as if they constituted a hallowed part of canonical tradition marked a great failure of imagination.

When he met with the membership of the Council for the Revision of the Code of Canon Law for the first time in November 1965, Paul VI insisted that the revision of canon law had to be accommodated to the new [^c26-10] way of thinking (_novo mentis habitui_) proper to the Second Vatican Council. This ‘new way of thinking’ has not always been evident in the text of the revised Code, and it has also been lacking in its implementation. One painful example of the disconnect between the ‘new way of thinking’ inspired by the council and the old **[p. 448]** way of thinking that continues to be operative has been laid bare by the continuing crisis surrounding the sexual abuse of minors and other vulnerable persons by clerics. The council had proclaimed the fundamental equality of all the baptized in the Church (_LG_ 32), and that teaching was duly incorporated into the revised Code (CIC/1983 c. 208). Nevertheless, time and again church authorities at all levels chose to turn a blind eye to reports of such abuse, protected offending clerics, and tried to preserve their priestly vocations rather than protect the most vulnerable members of their flocks. Clearly, some Christian faithful were deemed ‘more equal than others’. As a result of such ecclesial practice that did not fully receive the council’s teaching, the Church, ‘at once holy and always in need of purification, follows constantly the path of penance and renewal’ (_LG_ 8).

[^c26-10]: Paul VI, ‘Allocutio ad eminentissimos Patres Cardinales et ad Conultores Pontificii Concillii Codici Iuris Canonici recognoscendo’, _AAS_ 57 (1965): 985–89.

## 27. Theologians, Theologies, Church: Feminist Theologies in

### 1. In the Context of the Ecclesial Reception of Vatican II: Women’s New Subjectivity

**[p. 449]** Far from being a mere application of conciliar texts, reception is an overall transformative ecclesial process which develops from the documents and the conciliar event over the course of decades and affects all [^c27-1] subjects, dynamics, and ecclesial contexts. This is particularly true if we take into account the female condition and the subjectivity of women in the Catholic Church in the past fifty years. The corpus of Vatican II documents includes only a few passages explicitly dedicated to women. These are largely contained in the last of the conciliar documents to be promulgated: _Gaudium et Spes_ (_GS_ 8–9, 29, 31, 49, 59, 60), _Apostolicam Actuositatem_ (_AA_ 9, 32), and _Ad Gentes_ (_AG_ 17, 21). The passages in question contain an initial recognition of the changes that for almost a century have marked the female condition: socially, culturally, and economically (changes described by John XXIII in _Pacem in Terris_ (1963) as a sign of the times). There is also **[p. 450]** an indirect attestation to the contributions that religious life and female Catholic associations made to the apostolate and ecclesial mission without, however, dealing with the question of women with the [^c27-2] necessary depth and breadth. It is in relation to the ecclesial transformation brought about by Vatican II, which affects all local churches, that the contribution of these ‘unacknowledged subjects’—that is, women —comes to light in terms of practice, intra-ecclesial relations, and reflection on faith. Women welcome the conciliar teaching in an active and responsible way, finding in its baptismal ecclesiological vision the basis of their identity and role after centuries of misunderstanding and underestimation. Since the first post-conciliar season, their condition as full human subjects has emerged as reshaped and is acknowledged as being in close relationship with the social and civil conquests for women’s rights under way along with the acquisition of unprecedented roles in professional, political, cultural, and family life. Women have become a primary subject in ongoing transformative dynamics, whether it be in religious life, or as protagonists in catechesis or mission, liturgy or pastoral activities. In affirming their identity as ecclesial subjects, in recalling the evangelical logic of inclusion, in denouncing the widespread patriarchal culture, and in revealing the mechanisms that generate gender injustice, women make real the vision of the Church as ‘People of God’, as revealed in chapter 2 of the Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, _Lumen Gentium_ (_LG_). Thus, they have contributed to the progressive deconstruction of the Gregorian-Tridentine model of Church. Moreover, by interacting with different currents of feminist thought or in participating in women’s emancipation movements, women significantly establish the Church _in_ the world as envisioned in _Gaudium et Spes_.

#### Trajectories of Development of the Presence/Action of Women in the Post- Conciliar Church

[^c27-3] In the initial reception of the council in terms of practice, which quickly led to the increased involvement of women in liturgical assemblies, pastoral services, and theological research (in close connection with the recovery of lay subjectivity and the renewal of religious life), there has been a development of extremely diversifled thought dynamics. This makes it difficult to outline a comprehensive and adequate periodization of women’s reception of Vatican II. However, we can point to some trajectories in all fields that mark the progressive maturation of conscience, the determination of proper and autonomous roles for women, and **[p. 451]** the consequent deconstructing/restructuring of the usual ecclesial procedures. But there are substantial differences in terms of timing and modalities of acquisition of speech, cultural elaboration, and mainstreaming. In a Church that was becoming a world Church as prefigured by Karl Rahner, the times and forms of women’s ‘irruption’ were different, as were the socio-cultural and religious factors that influenced it. Among the many factors that influence this process are both intra-ecclesial motives (biblical, historical, and theological-systematic studies; liturgical and catechetical reform; etc.) and solicitations emerging from [^c27-4] ecumenical dialogue (in particular, with the Protestant churches and with the World Council of Churches). Other more relevant factors are exogenous and are experienced at different times in different countries: achievements on a professional and legislative level; access to university education; contributions from philosophical, scientific, historical, and sociological reflections. These help to develop self-awareness and offer the categorical interpretative framework necessary to think about the ecclesial subjectivity of women within the context of the ecclesiological teachings of Vatican II.

[^c27-3]: For discussion of Franz Wieacker’s studies on the reception of Roman law in Germanic law, see Gilles Routhier, ‘La recezione dell’ecclesiologia conciliare’, in _La chiesa e il Vaticano II: Problemi di ermeneutica e di recezione conciliare_, ed. Marco Vergottini (Milan: Glossa, 2005), 3–45, at 32–38.

[^c27-4]: Natalie Maxson, _Journey for Justice: The Story of Women in the WCC_ (Geneva: WCC, 2015).

Moreover, in all cases, a similar set of trajectories structure the transition from an ‘initial reception’ towards a full reception. We cannot say that a full reception has been reached in any context, since there remain gender gaps and exclusion of women from decision-making contexts, forms of ordinary sexism and sexist stereotypes—expressions of a widespread patriarchal culture, resistance to discussing the question of women in ministry, and lack of acceptance of the contributions of feminist theologies. A first phase is always characterized by women’s ‘revelation of presence’, along with ‘finding their voice’ and the search for tools and opportunities for empowerment, albeit within the conceptual canon and established ecclesial structures in which women are found. In this first phase, women learn to express themselves with a dual linguistic register: acquiring that of the liturgy, theology, and catechesis, formulated in an androcentric perspective, but without denying or underestimating the ‘maternal’ language of the female experience. The second phase combines the consolidation of positions (roles and contribution of service to the community), the expansion of spaces and opportunities for apostolate and ecclesial service, and the confirmation of a specific form of action and thought which questions received categories. Women now ask for the recognition of their right to participate and to assume their share of responsibilities. In the third phase, [^c27-5] women, strengthened by an already acquired ‘active citizenship’, call for the institutional restructuring of communities, seek a codification of new developments, and the diffusion of women’s thought in the educational and training contexts, in the hope of instilling an awareness that men and women, together, are ‘doing gender-Church’.

[^c27-5]: Silvia Gherardi, _Gender, Symbolism and Organizational Cultures_ (London: Sage, 1995).

#### A Public, Authoritative, Competent Word that ‘Does Church’

**[p. 452]** Women find a space of identity in the council texts, incorporate the overall ecclesiological vision, actualize it in their ecclesial service, and contribute to defining the implications for the ecclesial journey. While the council documents and Paul VI’s _Final Message to Women_ of 8 December 1965 are elaborated in a patriarchal perspective, with an androcentric and universalizing language—an expression (after centuries of subordinationist readings) of an anthropology of equality, open to theorizing the complementarity of the sexes (a vision that not infrequently betrays the stereotype of a maternal female, of the care of life, of self-denial in service, of the sacrificial _animus_)— women reading of the conciliar texts _as a whole_ would unfold ‘other’ interpretative perspectives. By naming sexual and gender differences, a ‘decoding of the implicit’ takes place and the vision of a neutral and undifferentiated human identity and _Christifideles_ (Christian faithful) is overcome. Thus, it becomes possible to imagine and experiment with new forms of women’s subjectivity, which were only implicitly contained in the council’s teaching on laypeople and religious.

In the post-conciliar season, women—until then silent subjects considered irrelevant to ‘voice’ the Christian faith—acquire a _public, competent, authoritative, prophetic voice_ in the churches. Women have opportunities and the spaces to speak for and of themselves, after centuries in which they have been ‘spoken of by others’ (male clerics). They have become elaborators of a theological word that ‘does’ Church, with a reflective awareness and a recognized public authority: a _novum_ in the history of post-Tridentine Catholicism. The assessment of women’s theologies, in particular feminist theologies, offers therefore a key perspective to understanding one of the most fruitful (and unexpected) contributions to the reception of the council. For the epistemological system adopted and for the thematic articulations addressed, feminist theologies are the implementation and re-proposition of the conceptual _framework_ of the council. They also represent the realization and reinterpretation of the main categories of Vatican II’s ecclesiology and anthropology. As such, they constitute an essential contribution to the ongoing conciliar reception. A Church undergoing reform can find illuminating and essential perspectives in the political-transformative example of feminist theologies.

### 2. A Progressive Development: Women Theologians and Theologies

With regard to the theological proposals elaborated by women in the post-conciliar period, it is difficult to offer a systematic map. Different theological sensitivities, multiple philosophical conceptualizations, a non-synchronic development in the different countries and continents, and different access to academic studies allow us to identify only developmental factors and criteria common to many thinkers. The **[p. 453]** plurality of positions can be read as a sign of the richness of the currents of thought, which range from a theology elaborated by those women who shy away from the recognition of a gender-specificity for their works, to theological positions explicitly ascribed to militant feminism or queer thinking, and from those who recognize themselves in women’s studies to those who opt for a gender perspective. In all cases, Vatican II represents a _terminus a quo_: the presence of women as learners, and later as teachers in pontifical and Catholic universities, and the opportunity to pursue scientific studies in exegesis and systematic theology, represent some of the most significant and innovative signs and factors of the conciliar reception. Prior to 1965 only a small number of women were academically qualifled in theology, in particular in [^c27-6] Germany and in the United States. It is only with the guidelines provided by the council that new spaces and contexts for a conceptual elaboration and a new competent and public voice opened up for the laity, and for women (_AA_ 32)—until then reserved only for the thought and voices of clerics and men.

[^c27-6]: Nicoletta Capozza, ‘Voci inattese in lingua tedesca: Le prime teologhe (1954–1964)’, in Perroni, Melloni, and Noceti, _Tantum_ _aurora est_, 165–96.

The period from the 1960s to the 1980s saw an initial presence of women in the academic fleld: first in northern Europe and North America, and, later and with greater difficulty, also in southern European [^c27-7] countries. Those who achieved theological qualifications were professionally recruited in the life of the churches as pastoral ministers or pastoral assistants. Participation in feminist movements became widespread, and dialogue with ongoing cultural movements was frequent. Interdisciplinary dialogue with the human sciences and with other forms of knowledge grew. There was also a wide range of contributions [^c27-8] elaborated in relation to various assumed philosophical orientations. By the end of the 1980s, thousands of women in the world could say with Valerie Saiving in 1960, ‘I am a woman and I study theology.’ Women found their voice to speak of themselves, God, and the Christian faith, to speak of the Church and religious experience. The main features of feminist theology (or rather, in the plural, of feminist theologies) began to [^c27-9] take form. Since the 1990s, there has been a movement of internationalization and increasing [^c27-10] contextualization focused on liberationist perspectives, interreligious dialogue, and attention to cultures. **[p. 454]** In the 1980s the involvement in grass-roots movements in Latin America, which centred on reading the scriptures, led some women to complete their course of study in European and North American universities. In the following decade a unique form of Latin American feminist thought took shape within the framework [^c27-11] of liberation theologies: Mujerista theology, ecofeminism, and _teología india_. A similar liberationist approach marks theological developments in Asia (in particular in the Philippines, South Korea, and India), characterized by dialogue with other religious traditions and local cultures: inculturated Christologies, Dalit [^c27-12][^c27-13] theology. More recently, there has been the development of a Catholic theology of women in Africa.

New subjects who read the Gospel anew beginning from their experience shaped by gender and who re-elaborate the understanding of faith with categories borrowed from emancipatory practice and feminist thought contribute to reimagining the ecclesial tradition, with their perception and with their study of spiritual matters and of Scripture (_Dei Verbum_ (_DV_) 8). New figures—women biblical scholars and theologians—contribute their particular charisms to shaping the _sensus fidei ecclesiae_ (_LG_ 12). They attest, in the process of ecclesial reception, to the gender non-neutrality of the _Christifideles_, as all, men and women, are participants in the prophetic office of Christ. An important contribution has been made by women religious, who, following the council’s call to recover their founding charisms and seek forms of consecrated life better adapted to contemporary needs (_Perfectae Caritatis_), widened the spaces of women’s presence, created opportunities for autonomous action, and acquired high levels of education. Many of the women theologians of the first phase of reception of the council on the different continents were members of religious orders.[^c27-14]

[^c27-14]: Sandra Schneiders, _Finding the Treasure: Locating Catholic Religious Life in a New Ecclesial and Cultural Context_ (New York: Paulist, 2000); Mary John Mananzan, _Woman, Religion & Spirituality in Asia_ (Manila: Anvil and Institute of Women’s Studies, 2004); Virginia Fabella, _Der Weg der Frauen: Theologinnen der Dritten Welt melden sich zu Wort_ (Freiburg: Herder 1996).

As is typical of feminist thinking, alongside university classrooms and research centres, it is in the multifaceted world of practices and of struggles for the recognition of rights, in pastoral life, and in groups of feminist self-awareness that women’s thought has developed. Theology and political action, biblical exegesis, and narration of lived experiences develop in a virtuous reference to theory and practice. As early **[p. 455]** as the 1980s, several associations of theologians and scholars of religion were founded, most of them [^c27-15] clearly feminist in orientation. Chairs of feminist/gender theology were established as well (e.g.: Nijmegen [^c27-16] and Münster). What emerged were places for gathering, critical dialogue, and synthesis in journals, in [^c27-17][^c27-18] dictionaries of feminist thought, and in the publication of collective works.

### 3. Reception of the Council: Feminist Theological Perspective

Studies published on the occasion of the fortieth and fiftieth anniversaries of the council examined the contribution of the female auditors and of the council fathers who intervened on women’s issues, commenting on the few passages dedicated to women. There are only a handful of studies expressly [^c27-19] dedicated to the reception of the council by women. To reconstruct its main lines involves first understanding how the main tenets of the intention of the council, from the point of view of the method and of generating themes, have been welcomed and developed in a unique way precisely by feminist theologies. It is mainly on the epistemological level that we can see how feminist theologies fully embrace the conciliar lessons of the Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation, _Dei Verbum_, the Decree on the Training of Priests, _Optatam Totius_, and the Decree on the Church’s Missionary Activity, _Ad Gentes_, and the extent to which their contribution qualifles and orients, creatively and not by slavish repetition, the maturation efforts of the Church in the interpretative horizon traced by the Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World, _Gaudium et Spes_. With regard to structure, method, and categories, feminist theologies constitute a significant, though often overlooked, chapter of conciliar reception.

[^c27-19]: Marinella Perroni and Hervè Legrand, eds., _Avendo qualcosa da dire: Teologhe e teologi rileggono il Vaticano II_ (Cinisello Balsamo: Paoline, 2014); Cettina Militello, _Il Vaticano II e la sua recezione al femminile_ (Bologna: EDB, 2007); Margit Eckholt, _Ohne die Frauen ist keine Kirche zu machen: Der Aufbruch des Konzils und die Zeichen der Zeit_ (Ostfildern: Matthias Grünewald, 2012).

#### Theological Structure: From Scripture

**[p. 456]** At the outset, humanity, God, and faith are conceived _from_ the Judaeo-Christian Scriptures, which constitute an essential point of reference, an immediate source and ‘soul’ of theological reflection (_DV_ 24; _OT_ 16). The approach is diversifled: it ranges from synchronic, canonical-spiritual readings to sociolinguistics, from contributions to historical-social investigation to the more classical historical method, to suggestions that come from depth psychology. However, what remains common in feminist biblical studies is the denunciation of the patriarchal character of Scripture and the androcentric socio- [^c27-20] symbolic order reflected in it. Biblical research was the first fleld of research that opened up for women (Woman’s Bible, 1895–98) and is the discipline that has amply recognized women’s input in terms of dissemination and scientific contribution. The contribution of feminist methodologies to the study of the bible is also recognized by the magisterium (Pontifical Biblical Commission, ‘The Interpretation of the Bible in the Church’, 57). Women exegetes no longer limit themselves—as they did in the early stages of research —to the recovery of women figures, buried by an androcentric _Wirkungsgeschichte_, and the feminine language for naming or speaking about God. Instead, they approach Scripture and its normativity, bringing the questions and categories of contemporary women, deconstructing the implicit androcentric and patriarchal inheritances in the drafting of texts, translations, transmission, and exegesis, distinguishing between the theological meaning of a text and its mode of enunciation, always historically determined. It is a matter of _depatriarchalizing the biblical interpretation_ and offering _a non-sexist interpretation of the Bible_. The work of exegesis is never detached from the socio-political demands of struggle for emancipation and [^c27-21] equality of rights. The interest in the current ecclesial situation is evident in research on Christology and [^c27-22] Christian origins. The revelation of God occurs in history and as history (_DV_ 1–2): the Her/story provides a unique perspective for understanding the self-communication of God to humanity and overcoming interpretative categories used for centuries (divine omnipotence, sovereignty of the One). Three further traits—not expressly mentioned in the documents but related to what theologians and bishops experienced during the conciliar assembly—characterize the feminist theological approach: interdisciplinarity, **[p. 457]** ecumenical openness, and collective research. Theologizing lives on a continuous and dialectical ‘confrontation’ with sociology, history, philosophies, and the sciences; it is ‘conversation’ of women and among women, with the thought developed over the centuries in Christian churches; it is a ‘contribution’, as women theologians, to the development of the living Tradition of the Church (_DV_ 8); it is ‘sharing’ in [^c27-23] research and practice.

#### Method

Despite the wide variety of feminist discourse, several common methodological choices can be discerned dating from the works of the 1970s and then reiterated over the following decades. They all share the perspective of liberation and criticise the assumptions of traditional theological discourses, denounced as oppressive, partial, alienating, and an expression of a patriarchal order that justifles the exclusion and [^c27-24] subordination of women. Feminist methodologies aim to accomplish three specific tasks: to critically analyse and expose the occult dynamics of oppression, and deconstruct the systems and structures of thought on which male domination is based; to search for traces of an alternative, ignored, and oppressed feminine wisdom; and to elaborate new holistic theological interpretations, with new language and images, in the light of theoretical presuppositions of feminist philosophies (in particular, the politics of difference and gender studies) in order to rebuild ecclesial relations. Elizabeth Johnson defines these three passages as ‘demolition, discernment, reinterpretation’. Anne M. Clifford instead talks about the need to examine and bring the texts of the Christian tradition into dialogue with the female experience and develop [^c27-25][^c27-26] transformative strategies. Regina Coll speaks of ‘revising, claiming, rethinking (re/conceiving)’. The understanding of the relationship between the kingdom of God and human progress, in reconciliation, justice, the common good (_GS_ 39), and the call of all to salvation in communion in difference (_GS_ 24, 32) are developed in a gender perspective, in the search for gender equality, with recognition of sexual differences, in the perspective of an inclusiveness that is not the elimination of diversity but the enhancement of the plural faces of the human.
