#### Cultures and Contextual Theologies

_Gaudium et Spes_ 44 reminds us that it is necessary to know the languages of our time not only to guarantee effective and meaningful preaching, but also to be able to understand the Gospel in an appropriate way for the present. Women’s studies, philosophies of difference, gender studies, and the expressive languages with which women present their feelings and convey their peculiar experience have made possible a new understanding of the Gospel message, of its charge of liberation and humanization. Interrupting the monosexual male interpretation of the sources of the Christian tradition and communicating with ‘two voices’, according to gender difference, is a form of theological thinking that represents a fruitful turn not yet explored.

Second, the council insists on the necessary processes of inculturation of faith, of the Church, and of theology (_AG_ 22). In the context of a Church that is becoming a ‘world Church’ (as Karl Rahner has said) or ‘polycentric’ (in the words of Johann Baptist Metz), women promote ‘contextual theologies’ in dialogue with the challenges emerging from the place in which they live and the cultures in which they participate. Position and social location, which define us in an unequivocal way, become possibilities for intervention and spaces for the construction of meanings. The same feminist theologies produced in the North American and European context by white, privileged, middle–upper-class women are subjected to criticism: the mere ‘translation’ or the unproblematic ‘cultural hybridization’ must be overcome, to open up—with new myths, rituals, and symbols—a _transcoding_ of the Christian faith.

[^c27-33] **[p. 459]** Post-colonial feminist theologies criticize the alleged universal truth of Christianity and urge the disavowal of the Hellenistic-Latin colonialist, Eurocentric, and male chauvinist schemes with which theology was developed. This is achieved by unmasking the ‘_politics of othering_’ both on a cultural and gender level, which has been supported on a religious basis, in the awareness that there is an inextricable connection between colonialism, religion, and the subordination of women. The hegemonic system of thought and organization, spread with the colonies, is rooted in a fixed, essentialist binary structure. It must be overcome (‘post’ in the sense of ‘beyondness’) by promoting a vision of the identity of the intersectional person, which is built ‘in-between’: in/between border spaces, crossroads, intersections of race, gender, sexual orientation, social class, citizenship, culture, in the attestation of one’s irreducible partiality. If we take the case of Asia, feminist theology is necessarily multireligious and plurilingual. It renounces the development of Aristotelian thought and evokes the value of linguistic-conceptual structures of very ancient traditions to think about the relationship between female and male. Finally, it criticizes every universalizing claim typical of Western thought.

[^c27-33]: Kwok Pui-Lan, _Postcolonial Imagination & Feminist Theology_ (London: SCM, 2005).

A second example comes from _teología latina_, which was developed in the late 1980s by Latin American [^c27-34] theologians living in the United States. These critically analyse the peculiar form of ‘patriarchy’ among Latinos, who in a framework of exaggerated familism, and on the basis of a false and distorted Mariology, idealize a passive, silent, obedient woman figure. In denouncing the sexism and violence of which women are victims, _Latina_ theologians recognize themselves as close to the theological elaboration of Afro- [^c27-35] American _womanists_, who intertwine gender and race issues.

[^c27-34]: María Pilar Aquino, _Our Cry for Life: Feminist Theology from Latin America_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1993); Isasi-Díaz, _En la_ _Lucha—In the Struggle_.

[^c27-35]: Stephanie Y. Mitchem, _Introducing Womanist Theology_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2002).

### 4. Contribution of Feminist and Gender Theologies to the Life of the Post-Conciliar Church

The process of women’s reception of Vatican II in the Catholic Church develops at the intersection of an anthropological question and one concerning operative models of church. The research on categories for thinking about and defining women’s identity is associated with the reflection on roles, dynamics of recognition of ecclesial subjectivity and participation, and sustainable figures of a ‘church of men and women’. In the first post-conciliar phase discussion focused on the practices of inclusion and recognition, favouring ecclesial reform processes—made possible thanks to women and necessary for a real **[p. 460]** participation of those who for centuries have been unrecognized and unheard subjects. Since the mid- 1980s both theology and the magisterium have insisted on the anthropological question as a way to [^c27-36] determine a ‘female specificity’. This line of research has been privileged in the fields of biblical and systematic theology, as it is considered capable of contributing to ecclesial dynamics in a positive way. In more recent times, the acceptance of gender studies in ecclesiology, the revival of debate on ordained ministry, the development of post-colonial theologies, and the denunciation of persistent glass ceilings and crystal palaces have given rise to a focus on the interaction between anthropological and ecclesiological [^c27-37] perspectives.

[^c27-36]: Susan Ross, ‘Christian Anthropology and Gender Essentialism’, _Concilium_ 42, no. 1 (2006): 43–50.

[^c27-37]: Guntern Prüller-Jagenteufel, Sharon Bong, and Rita Perintfalvi, eds., _Toward Just Gender Relations: Rethinking the Role of_ _Women in Church and Society_ (Göttingen: Vienna University Press, 2019).

#### A Question of Identity

The first chapter of _Gaudium et Spes_ provides the main elements of council’s the anthropology, starting from the perspective of the human being created in the image and likeness of God. Explicit reference is made to ‘men and women’ (_GS_ 12). Sexism is condemned, as are those who discriminate, and the equal dignity of man and woman is recognized (_GS_ 29). These are a few indications that point to a movement away from the [^c27-38] readings of Augustine and scholastic thinkers on the subordination and inferiority of women which have marked the anthropological interpretation for centuries, with repercussions in terms of ecclesiological vision, spiritual theology, and liturgy. Studies in biblical exegesis, patristics, and the history of theology published by women in these fifty years have highlighted its fallacy and shown how much theological anthropology is still substantially unfinished. In _Gaudium et Spes_ itself, reference is made to an apparently neutral _anthropos_, which is actually a projection of a masculine identity, universalized and then declared neutral; once established, it is used to define an alleged feminine specificity.

[^c27-38]: Børresen, _Subordination et Equivalence_; Kari Børresen, ed., _The Image of God: Gender Models in Judaeo-Christian Tradition_ (Minneapolis: Fortress, 1995).

Starting from a different consideration of sexual corporeity, difference, and relationship, and in close correlation with the second and third waves of feminist philosophical thought, on the one hand feminist theologies have tried to define what is specific to the identity of women—overcoming any biological essentialism that might reduce the ‘feminine’ to the ‘maternal’. On the other hand, they have tried to account for the genesis and interpretation (linguistic, symbolic, cultural) of sexual difference, thanks to the contributions of women’s studies (primarily in the anglophone context) and reflections on gender difference (in France: Luce Irigaray, Hélène Cixous, Julia Kristeva; in Italy: Diotima group, Adriana [^c27-39] Cavarero). Use of the critical-analytical category of gender has brought to the foreground the processes of **[p. 461]** sexual differentiation, the construction of differences in social roles, and the need to think about the [^c27-40] masculine, which remains neglected even in the theological fleld. Intersectional approaches led to the correlation of sex/gender with other identity and discrimination markers (race, ethnicity, religion, class). [^c27-41] More recently, queer theology, which incorporates the orientations of Teresa de Lauretis and Judith Butler, invites us to set aside references to normative heterosexuality to overcome the binary, polar oppositions with which male and female are constructed, to enter into a reading of ‘identity without essence’, socially constructed, and performatively enacted. Along these lines, and based on post-structuralist and deconstructionist assumptions, Marcella Althaus-Reid has elaborated a counter-narrative concerning God and salvation which goes beyond the boundary of ‘decency’, subverting what is given and [^c27-42] understood as the ‘norm’.

[^c27-39]: Robert W. Connell, _Questioni di genere_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2006); Raewyn W. Connell and Rebecca Pearse, _Gender: In_ _World Perspective_ (Cambridge, UK: Polity, 2014); Dominique Fougeyrollas-Schwebel, Christine Planté, Michele Riot-Sarcey, et Claude Zaidman, eds. _Le Genre comme catégorie d’analyse: Sociologie, histoire, littérature_ (Paris: L’Harmattan, 2003).

[^c27-40]: Ursula King and Tina Beattie, _Gender, Religion, and Diversity: Cross-cultural Perspectives_ (London: Bloomsbury, 2005); Serene Jones, _Feminist Theory and Christian Theology: Cartographies of Grace—Guides to Theological Inquiry_ (Minneapolis: Augsburg Fortress, 2000).

[^c27-41]: Susannah Cornwall, _Controversies in Queer Theology_ (London: SCM, 2011).

[^c27-42]: Marcella Althaus-Reid, _Indecent Theology: Theological Perversions in Sex, Gender, and Politics_ (London: Routledge, 2000).

Faced with this process of women’s self-definition, the papal magisterium has repeatedly reiterated the ‘specificity of the feminine’. In 1988, with his Apostolic Letter on the Dignity and Vocation of Women, _Mulieris Dignitatem_, John Paul II delivered the first magisterial document on women: the identity of ‘woman’ (in the singular) is described on the basis of the Marian archetype of bride and mother. The relationship between men and women is brought back to a scheme of complementarity of predefined male and female characteristics (even though the text uses the word ‘reciprocity’), from which social roles and specific functions are deduced. Similar approaches are found in the letter of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith to bishops _On the Collaboration of Men and Women_ (2004). The resistance to the use of the term and the concept of ‘gender’, starting from the critical position taken by the Vatican delegation on the United Nations’ Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action (1995), and repeated criticisms of ‘gender ideology’ (referring to Butler’s thought and to queer theory), reinforce this interpretative scheme of the magisterium without accepting or debating the proposed rethinking of Christian anthropology (of difference or in a gender perspective) developed by Catholic women theologians. Pope Francis’s position in the 2016 post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation on Love in the Family, _Amoris Laetitia_ (_AL_), is more nuanced when he asks, for example, to distinguish sex and gender without separating them (_AL_ 56) and to recognize the historicity of the interpretations of sexual difference (_AL_ 256). However, on the whole, his thought concerning women appears unresolved: on the one hand, he calls the Church to empower them, while on the other he remains indebted to the Balthasarian interpretation of Marian and Petrine principles. Further, he does not recognize the steps taken thus far, the theological contributions already made, the persistence of a [^c27-43] **[p. 462]** Catholic patriarchal culture. In general, considering women as more ‘natural’ than men from a spiritual point of view has meant a lack of recognition of women’s important contributions and their exclusion from decision-making roles. Such an approach reflects an essentialist reading which interprets sexual difference by associating it with an ahistorical and unchanging nature.

[^c27-43]: Serena Noceti, ‘Unterwegs zu einer inklusiven Kirche (EG 103-104). Prinzipien für eine ekklesiologische Re/Vision’, in Kurt Appel and Jakob Helmut Deibl, eds., _Barmherzigkeit und zärtliche Liebe: Das theologische Programm von Papst Franziskus_ (Freiburg im Breisgau: Herder, 2016), 336–48.

#### A Church Model and an Ecclesiological Model

[^c27-44] The Church, like any other human institution, is gender-structured. Therefore, the ‘kyriarchic’ logic which shapes ecclesial practices and leads to the persistence of patriarchal structures that exclude women [^c27-45] must be denounced. The discipleship of equals of Jesus’s own movement, the practice of the early Church, [^c27-46] and the reformative contribution of some women whose memory remains in the history of the churches have inspired the building of spaces of inclusion, of participation for women, and the pursuit of a reinterpretation of the ‘ecclesial We’ in a gender perspective. The denunciation of the gender gap in pastoral practice, the request for gender equality and gender justice, and the recognition of the many forms of basic female leadership are not an expression of women’s claims. Nor are they a function of the inclusion of a hitherto disadvantaged group; they are steps necessary to generate a model of ecclesial life in line with the theology of the People of God and with the ecclesiology of communion embraced by the council. In the communicative and participatory decision-making dynamics that generate and regenerate the ecclesial body, the interlocutors are defined by sex/gender. The imbalance between the active participation of women and their limited presence in places of power, along with the a widespread exercise of ministeriality by women in the face of a lack of entitlement in the exercise of authority, weakens the _forma ecclesiae_ and [^c27-47] impoverishes the desired synodality. For a full reception of the demands of Vatican II, as women theologians point out, the dynamics of the style of the exercise of power and forms of co-optation in the roles of authority must be rethought, correlating in a new form the baptismal _exousia_ of laymen and **[p. 463]** laywomen and the clergy’s _potestas ordinis_and _iurisdictionis_ (power of orders and of jurisdiction). Feminist [^c27-48] ecclesiology has reread the conciliar texts favouring ‘circular’ church models which pursue participation, equality, and the structuring of right relationships between all components, expressed with images (e.g., the round table: an idea of Protestant scholar Letty Russell welcomed by Catholics) and categories (see the exodus community; the communion of friends; the communion of saints; friends of God and prophets; [^c27-49] communities of resistance and solidarity). However, Anne Carr rightly denounces the coexistence in the Catholic Church of patriarchal-hierarchical models and egalitarian-inclusive ones, both justifled by using the letter of _Lumen Gentium_. The former favours the ‘Christ–Church’ relationship; the latter favours the pneumatological and Trinitarian dimensions of Church teaching.

[^c27-44]: Schüssler Fiorenza, _In Memory of Her_.

[^c27-45]: Carolyn Osiek and Margaret McDonald, _A Woman’s Place: House Churches in Earliest Christianity_ (Minneapolis: Fortress, 2005); Marinella Perroni and Cristina Simonelli, _Maria di Magdala: Una genealogia apostolica_ (Roma: Aracne, 2016); Kevin Madigan and Carolyn Osiek, _Ordained Women in the Early Church_ (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 2005).

[^c27-46]: Adriana Valerio, _Donne e Chiesa: Una storia di genere_ (Rome: Carocci, 2016); Lucetta Scaraffia and Gabriella Zarri, eds., _Donne e fede_ (Rome: Laterza, 1994).

[^c27-47]: Phyllis Zagano, _Women and Catholicism: Gender, Communion and Authority_ (New York: Macmillan, 2011).

[^c27-48]: Natalie K. Watson, _Introducing Feminist Ecclesiology_ (Sheffield: Sheffield Academic Press, 2002); Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza, ‘The Forgotten Partner: The Professional Ministry of Women in the Church’, in _Discipleship of Equals: A Critical_ _Feminist Ecclesiology/Ekklesia-logy of Liberation_ (London: Crossroad, 1993), 13–22; Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza, _Empowering Memory and Movement: Thinking and Working across Borders_ (Minneapolis: Fortress, 2014).

[^c27-49]: Elizabeth Johnson, _Friends of God and Prophets: A Feminist Theological Reading of the Communion of Saints_ (New York: Continuum, 1998); Sharon D. Welch, _Gemeinschaffen des Widerstands und der Solidarität. Eine feministische Theologie der_ _Befreiung_ (Freiburg: Exodus-Verlag, 1988).

A sign of the still unfinished reception of the council is the liturgy. Undoubtedly, the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy, _Sacrosanctum Concilium_, required and oriented the subsequent liturgical reform, which changed profoundly the form of the liturgical celebration and had an impact on the self-awareness of the post-conciliar Church. However, reflection on liturgy and sacramental theology in a gender perspective remains weak. Ritual action is the expression of an experience and a self-understanding of faith of [^c27-50] believers, men and women, embodied in gestures and rites involving sexual bodies. In all the sacraments and liturgies there is a communicative dynamic that draws on tradition; at the same time, it involves a living inculturation in a socio-religious system that carries within itself a precise determination, interpretation, and organization of sexual differences. All this has emerged only to a limited extent. There have been celebratory proposals that trace exclusively female experiences and ‘existential rituals’, along with initial reflections on the verbal language used in the liturgies (Germany, United States, Australia, Canada). These, however, have not considered gender as perspective for an overall understanding of the sacraments, of the ritual form, of men and women’s agency of word and action, which is marked by an evident symbolic and performative outcome.

[^c27-50]: Teresa Berger, ed., _Liturgie und Frauenfrage: Ein Beitrag zur Frauenfrage aus liturgiewissenschafflicher Sicht_ (St Ottilien: EOS, 1990); Teresa Berger, _Gender Differences and the Making of Liturgical History_ (New York: Ashgate, 2011); Susan K. Roll et al., eds., _Women, Ritual and Liturgy_ (Leuven: Peeters, 2001).

The change in the life of women religious, in all its various forms, has contributed to the reconfiguration of the ecclesial model. The post-conciliar period has seen the acquisition of spaces of autonomy and expertise, along with substantial changes in lifestyles and professional activities. The Decree on the Renewal of **[p. 464]** Religious Life, _Perfectae Caritatis_, made specific references to women only in relation to cloistered life and religious habits. The reception of the ecclesiology of Vatican II, the revision of their constitutions in light of their founder’s charisms as required by the council, and the development of new forms of consecrated life [^c27-51] have meant the overcoming of borders—including symbolic ones—that defined female religious life. The tense confrontation between the Vatican Congregation for Institutes of Consecrated Life and the Leadership Conference of Women Religious between 2009 and 2014 centred on these issues: the meaning of the changes have disrupted centuries-long practice, as well as the critical stance against traditional gender expectations which women religious today deliberately forego.

[^c27-51]: Sandra Schneiders, _New Wineskins: Re-imagining Religious Life Today_ (New York: Paulist, 1986); Schneiders, _Finding the_ _Treasure_.

#### The Ordained Ministry: An Open and Essential Question

[^c27-52] The delicate issue of ministerial ordination remains open. Near the end of Vatican II, an international conference organized by St Joan’s International Alliance (born in the early twentieth century as a suffragist movement in London) issued a request for the priestly and diaconal ordination of women. Formulated by women jurists and theologians, it was distributed to all the conciliar fathers in a pamphlet with the [^c27-53] significant title _We Are No Longer Willing to Keep Silent!_ Immediately after Vatican II, research on this topic [^c27-54] developed in biblical, patristic, historical, systematic, and ecumenical fields. Two dates stand as watershed moments. Both are linked to magisterial documents: in 1976, the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith issued the Declaration on the Question of the Admission of Women to the Ministerial Priesthood, _Inter Insigniores_; and in 1994, John Paul II published the Apostolic Letter On Reserving Priestly Ordination to Men Alone, _Ordinatio Sacerdotalis_, in which he authoritatively affirmed the doctrinal position of the Catholic Church that restricts the sacrament of ordination to the priesthood and the episcopate to men (no. 4), insisting that this doctrine is to be “definitively held”. The theological research of women first deconstructed the reasons given in the 1976 document (the absence of women at the moment of the Last Supper; the symbolic representation of Christ by the male priest; the choice of only men in the group of **[p. 465]** Twelve). After 1994, the form of the document and its magisterial value were critically debated, as was the argument concerning ‘the will of Jesus and the _Traditio perpetuo serbata_ [preserved by the constant and universal Tradition]’, which is at the root of the veto. In 1975, the first Women’s Ordination Conference was celebrated in Detroit. In 2002, the Roman Catholic Women Priests movement was created with the priestly ordination of seven women (who were later excommunicated).

[^c27-52]: Walter Gross, ed., _Frauenordination: Stand der Diskussion in der katholischen Kirche_ (Munich: Wewel, 1996); Kelley A. Raab, _When Women Become Priests: The Catholic Women’s Ordination Debate_ (New York: Columbia University Press, 2000).

[^c27-53]: Gertrud Heinzelmann, ‘Frau und Konzil. Hoffnung und Erwartung’, in _Wir schweigen nicht länger! Frauen äussern sich zum_ _II. Vatikanischen Konzil_ (Zurich: Interfeminas, 1964), 20–44.

[^c27-54]: See Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza and Hermann Haring, eds., _Non-ordination of Women and the Politics of Power_, special issue _Concilium_ 35, no. 3 (1999); Serena Noceti, ‘Donne e ministero: Una questione scomoda; Orientamenti e prospettive interpretative nella riflessione teologica delle donne’, in Anna Calapaj Burlini, ed., _Liturgia e ministeri ecclesiali_ (Rome: Edizioni Liturgiche, 2008), 67–99.

Studies dedicated to the diaconal ordination of women are numerous and well founded, demonstrating its [^c27-55] possibilities and opportunities. The topic recently re-emerged when Pope Francis created in 2016 a study commission on a women’s diaconate and with the requests made during the Synod for the Amazon. The shift that occurred in the 1990s in the interpretation of the council documents weighs on the debate. In thinking about ordained ministry, perspectives shifted from the ecclesiological-functional foundation of the third chapter of _Lumen Gentium_ and of the Decrees on the Pastoral Office of Bishops, _Christus Dominus_, and on the Ministry and Life of Priests, _Presbyterorum Ordinis_, to embrace a more traditional Christological-ontological and priestly-cultic vision of the ministry (acting _in persona Christi capitis_, representation of Christ as the bridegroom of the Church). The oversight of the apostolicity of the faith and the service to the unity of the ‘ecclesial We’ are today carried out in the Catholic Church with exclusively male language and authority. While some women theologians believe it necessary simply to deconstruct the system of the priesthood and the traditional ministry, many men and women, from all continents, are asking for a resumption of the debate on the ordination of women, the central issue for the configuration of the Church.

[^c27-55]: Gary Macy, William T. Ditewig, and Phyllis Zagano, _Women Deacons: Past, Present, Future_ (New York: Paulist, 2011); Serena Noceti, ed., _Diacone: Quale ministero per quale chiesa?_ (Brescia: Queriniana, 2017); Ute E. Eisen, _Amtsträgerinnen im frühen_ _Christentum: Epigraphische und literarische Studien_ (Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1996); translated as _Women_ _Officeholders in Early Christianity: Epigraphical and Literary Studies_ (Collegeville, MN: Michael Glazier, 20000; Moira Scimmi, _Le antiche diaconesse nella storiografia del XX secolo_ (Milan: Glossa, 2004).

They consider it an authentic and possible development along the lines of the conciliar theology of ministry and ministries. As Rosemary Radford Ruether wrote in the 1990s, ‘Today the critical issue for Christianity has become that of the full inclusion of women in the ministry of Christian churches.’[^c27-56]

[^c27-56]: Rosemary Radford Ruether, ‘Women’s Difference and Equal Rights in the Church’, _Concilium_ 27, no. 6 (1991): 11–18.

### 5. On the Road to Reform: A Church of Women and Men

The convocation of Vatican II was linked from the outset to a desire for ecclesial reform, as was made clear in John XXIII’s reference to _aggiornamento_ in _Gaudet Mater Ecclesia._ Paul VI’s speech at the beginning of the **[p. 466]** second session included ecclesial renewal among the four aims of the council. This reform affected the consideration of ecclesial subjects and dynamics, the model of the Church and its practice, from the liturgy to missionary work. Several well-known conciliar passages recall the principles for an authentic reform of an institutional subject understood under the figure of provisionality, of the historicity of forms (_LG_ 48), and of the permanent principle of the Gospel of Jesus (_Unitatis Redintegratio_ 4, 6). The trends of theological reflection developed by Catholic women over the past fifty years, specifically in the fields of ecclesiology, liturgy, and theology of ministries, invite us to reflect further on the principles that must guide the desired reform of the Church.

#### Incremental Change and Structural Reform

First, the examination of what has happened—in particular regarding those developments and dynamics which have proven to be more effective and long-lasting implemented by women,—and the identification of resistance and oppositions that have emerged, show that every reform of a heterogeneous institutional [^c27-57] subject, as is the Catholic Church throughout the world, follows a threefold plan: the change of ecclesial self-awareness; the renewal of the form of ecclesial relations (participatory, communicative, communal, with a view to full participation and recognition of the subjects actively involved); and the transformation of the structures (training, decision-making, communication, exercise of authority and powers).

[^c27-57]: Nils Brunsson, _Reform and Routine: Organizational Change and Stability in the Modern World_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2009); Douglass C. North, _Istituzioni, cambiamento istituzionale, evoluzione dell’economia_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2005); Gervase R. Bushe and Robert J. Marshak, eds., _Dialogic Organization Development_ (Oakland, CA: Barrett-Köhler, 2015). See also Serena Noceti, ‘What Structures Are Needed for a Reform of the Church?’, _Concilium_ 54, no. 4 (2018): 85–99.

These three levels are interrelated: the assumption of consciousness and the role, or empowerment, of some subjects changes the form of ecclesial relations and calls for a reorganization of the supporting structures for common living and acting. At the same time, a change of ecclesial form, such as in the celebratory experience or widespread ministeriality, requires substantial changes in its formative structures and in its understanding of power—better yet, of powers—without which it is impossible to guarantee the continuity of innovative experiences, even those perceived as significant. The change that has led to the development and recognition (at least theoretically) of women’s condition as full human subjects in the Catholic Church, at different levels and in many cultural contexts, during the long post-conciliar season is indisputable. However, it entails not only a modification of the female subjects involved, but also the rethinking of the overall _forma ecclesiae_, of the many structures of the ecclesial organization, of the ‘ecclesiological theory’ and vision, including its symbols, categories, and language. What is more, structural changes, especially those that represent vital points or crucial intersections for articulating these issues, were not adequately **[p. 467]** thought out in the post-conciliar period for the implementation the ecclesiological vision of the People of God contained in the second chapter of _Lumen Gentium_.

The issue of the structural reform of the Church today remains largely unanswered: the condition of women —still subordinate and ‘secondary’—constitutes a ‘litmus test’ and a ‘missed opportunity’; that is, for an adequate reform of structures. Feminist ecclesiology and the requests for the ministerial ordination of women challenge the Church and theology on this necessary perspective and show the weakness of a ‘neutral’ reflection on the subjects that ‘make the Church’ and reveal the contradiction between the theoretical recognition of women’s subjectivity and a partial, or sometimes non-existent, entitlement. The supporting structures of the Roman Catholic Church, where the overall strategies are decided and the ‘ecclesial We’ is symbolized, are (almost) exclusively characterized by a male perspective, a rigid hierarchization, and a prerogative of the clerical class. The affirmation of a formal equality is not enough without a rethinking of the structured processes that underlie ecclesial development and a pluralization of powers, fields of practice, and forms of authority.

Second, the evolving role of women—a question not considered at the time of the council—shows that no reform is the result of a linear development, or based on a single transformative factor or guideline. The acquisition of an interpretative theory of reality is not enough, nor is the maturation of a theological vision, however widespread, for reform to take place. Cultural, social, and economic factors come into play and have a decisive influence. Feminist theology and the acquisition of an active and self-conscious subjectivity of women in the Church owes much to the various feminisms, to the paths of social transformation, to women’s philosophical, historical, and cultural anthropological thought, and to interreligious dialogue. The constant interplay between theory and practice and the cooperation between academic institutions and social movements, which are the essential principles and established methods of feminist thought, suggest a way to connect the related levels of reform and conscious recognition of the different factors that drive change.

Third, historical and sociological studies open up a further perspective: reforms (especially those _in_ the Church, rather than _of_ the Church) are prompted by the encounter with otherness, by perceived differences, and by those who, from the margins, develop an understanding of the whole according to criteria and sensitivities hitherto not considered (it is no coincidence that the more detailed passages of the council’s [^c27-58] teaching on reform are found in the Decree on Ecumenism, _Unitatis Redintegratio_). The possible and necessary reforms of the Church cannot ignore the proposals, the critical judgement, and the deconstruction of centuries-long positions, the interruption of what is obvious and consolidated, the requests made by women, the ‘other’ par excellence, in the eyes of the clergy, who for many centuries were considered the only intentional subjects of reform. Likewise, it will be essential to stress the contribution **[p. 468]** that comes from non-Western women, from post-colonial theologies, and from the liberationist practice at work in Asia, Africa, and Latin America.

[^c27-58]: bell hooks, _Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center_ (Cambridge, MA: South End, 2000).

#### Strategies and Paths of Reform

One of the recurring questions in feminist thought is whether women should continue to fight against the barriers of exclusion in order to knock them down or use their energies to shape something new. To put it differently, is it more effective to gradually become part of existing structures, dominated by men today, to change them from within, or create ‘habitable spaces’ as alternatives to existing ones? Can existing structures be reinvented? Moreover, should we privilege spaces for discussion, narration of experiences, maturation, and self-awareness for women only, to articulate our singular identities and ensure a female genealogy, or should women make alliances and cooperate with those men and theologians who are more [^c27-59] open to change? During the post-conciliar period, many feelings emerged with regard to these issues, and many were the strategies implemented. First, we should mention Women-Church (_ekklesia_ of women), which originated in the 1980s from the desire to create—while remaining in the Catholic Church, without becoming a movement or an alternative religious institution—a communal living space founded on discipleship of equals, with democratic forms of ministeriality and functioning to meet the needs of the community, where women might experiment with participatory forms of liturgical, beginning with feminine experiences and language. The idea and the movement matured in the context of the World Council of Churches programme for the Community of Women and Men in the Church (1974); the first international conference of Women-Church was held in 1983. The proposal developed in close connection with the North American movements for the ordination of women. Within the long-lasting dialectic in the Church between institution and charismatic community—the former male-dominated, the latter with a strong presence of female prophecy—‘the _Women-Church_ movement represents the first time when women collectively claimed to be church and they appropriated the exodus community as a community of liberation [^c27-60] from patriarchy’, as a community anticipating the desired future for the whole Church. While there are differences between Schüssler Fiorenza and Radford Ruether’s proposals, for both it would not be a matter of implementing a ‘theological separatism’ theorized by Mary Daly. The Women-Church is a necessary medium for the Church to develop the ‘co-humanity of men and women freed from patriarchy’, an intermediate phase for the formation of a critical conscience and a non-patriarchal culture. In this regard, the juridical aspect should not be underestimated, in terms of _de iure condendo_ vs. a matter _de iure condito_. A **[p. 469]** first essential task is to recognize new forms of _potestas iurisdictionis_ (the power of jurisdiction) on the basis of baptism. It is also necessary to rethink the exercise of ministry, with innovative pastoral practices that see women protagonists and show the obsolescence of the current codification. However, there are only a few women canon-law experts working in this direction, which nonetheless is essential for the development of new ecclesial structures.

[^c27-59]: Mary E. Hunt and Diann L. Neu, eds., _New Feminist Christianity: Many Voices, Many Views_ (Woodstock, VT: Skylight Paths, 2010).

[^c27-60]: Ruether, _Women-Church_, 56.

Feminist theologies are political theologies, characterized by a critical, militant, subversive intentionality, constitutively oriented towards social transformation. It is not a question of guaranteeing the inclusion of a ‘disadvantaged group’ (women) but of reconfiguring the relations of a participatory synodal Church as a whole, taking on a gender perspective (which is not only an analytical but also a political-transformative category), starting from the necessary rethinking of masculinity and the relationship between masculinity, power, and the sacred.[^c27-61]

[^c27-61]: Monika Egger, Livia Meier, and Katja Wißmiller, eds., _WoMan in Church: Kirche und Amt im Kontext der Geschlechterfrage_ (Münster: LIT, 2006; Susan Abraham, Geraldo De Mori, and Stefanie Knauss, eds., _Masculinities: Theological and Religious_ _Challenges_, special issue _Concilium_ 38 no. 2 (2020).

#### Reception of the Council: Process of Reform

At the beginning of the twenty-first century, the question of church reform emerges in a changed scenario: a new sensitivity to rapid changes, typical of the [post]modern condition, shapes the general mentality; the Church is seen against a polycentric and multicultural horizon and the reception of the council, more than fifty years after its conclusion, is in many respects still ongoing, due to a magisterial hermeneutics that for three decades has worked for a consolidation of Catholicism in a more traditional doctrinal and liturgical [^c27-62] form and excluded, from the lexicon and the practice, the perspective of reform. On the other hand, the desire to imagine the Catholic Church and the aspiration to work for a structural transformation of the Church found an unexpected voice in Francis’s pontificate, at least in terms of conversion and the renewal [^c27-63] of mentalities. The challenge to the patriarchal, male-dominated Church—in its unrecognized assumptions, in the patristic scriptural interpretation, and in the Scholasticism that supported it—is still open. Such a challenge is guided by the awareness of how deeply it still affects the life and religious experience of many women and how it still impacts society and the understanding of family life, especially in some parts of the world.

[^c27-62]: Massimo Faggioli, _Vatican II: The Battle for Meaning_ (New York: Paulist, 2012).

[^c27-63]: Gerard Mannion, ed., _Pope Francis and the Future of Catholicism_ (Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press, 2017); Kurt Appel and Jakob Helmut Deible, eds., _Barmherzigkeit und zärtliche Liebe: Das theologische Programm von Papst Franziskus_ (Freiburg: Herder, 2016).

Like any other institution, the Church is built and rebuilt by its members (men and women) through symbolically mediated and communicated interactions: institutions deal with intersubjective processes of [^c27-64] **[p. 470]** the re-elaboration of meanings and structuring of relationships. Formation of consciousness, conversion of mentality, and the overcoming of stereotypes must be related to a modification of structures, which always combine an objective-operational function and a symbolic-communicative dimension. In approaching the conciliar ecclesiology, women theologians have put the dynamic principle of the Gospel in [^c27-65] the foreground, which opens spaces of liberation for all, men and women. Moreover, they have privileged participatory logics and the procedural dynamics of ecclesial co-edification, reaffirming the prophetic role that the Church must play while denouncing the gender-related injustice that marks the ecclesial body. The necessary intervention of the ‘women’s question’, limited but still relevant in the public democratic context or in ecumenical and interreligious dialogue, cannot be ruled out. The entire ecclesiastical body is at stake. Women theologians present themselves today as subjects of reform ‘of’ the Church—and not only ‘in’ the Church or only for women—to participate in the elaboration of overall projects and help define global intervention strategies, thanks to their experience and competent and authoritative theological voices, even if today there is no real decision-making power connected to this speaking as full subjects. The unexpected [^c27-66] irruption of this ‘forgotten partner’ has changed the scenario of the post-conciliar Church by not asking for ‘concessions’ or spaces for itself, but through the overall rethinking of the ecclesial body, both in line with the implementation of the guiding principles of the ecclesiology of the People of God defined by Vatican II and the reception of new requests, critical contributions, and elaborative categories, matured within women’s movements of emancipation and women’s thought.

[^c27-64]: Peter L. Berger and Thomas Luckmann, _The Social Construction of Reality: A Treatise in the Sociology of Knowledge_ (New York: Anchor, 1966); Jürgen Habermas, _The Theory of Communicative Action_, 2 vols. (Boston: Beacon, 2005); originally published as _Theorie des kommunikativen Handelns_ (Frankfurt am Main: Suhrkamp, 1981).

[^c27-65]: Phyllis Zagano, _Women and Catholicism: Gender, Communion and Authority_ (New York: Macmillan, 2011).

[^c27-66]: See Schüssler Fiorenza, ‘The Forgotten Partner’.
