## 28. Non-Catholic Observers at Vatican II

Peter De Mey

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 475]** There are several ways to discuss the role of the observers at Vatican II. This chapter will follow a chronological approach that focuses on the immediate reactions and contributions of the observers during the sessions and intersessions. By way of introduction, I will describe the most important primary and secondary sources that help the scholar of Vatican II with this task.

An invaluable source of information are the reports of the weekly meetings which the Secretariat for Christian Unity organized to introduce and reflect together on the documents that were almost [^c28-1] simultaneously discussed by the council fathers in St Peter’s Basilica. At regular intervals, the observers also transmitted confidential reports to their sending bodies. These give an honest and sometimes critical [^c28-2] account of the conciliar events but also show how the event of the council had truly changed the observers. The American Methodist Albert Outler described this experience as a change ‘from an ecumenical tourist at a great ecclesiastical pageant into a participant observer in an epoch-making event, and then, into a partner [^c28-3] in the ongoing ecumenical enterprise which has been generated by that event’. Some of these observers— apart from Outler, the Reformed observers Douglas Horton and Robert McAfee Brown need to be mentioned [^c28-4] **[p. 476]** especially—decided to share their reports with a broader audience.Recently, two new collections of primary sources have been added to this documentation, pertaining to the Anglican observer Bernard [^c28-5] Pawley and the Old Catholic observer Werner Küppers. During each period of commemoration of the council, a number of essays were published that highlight the significance of particular groups of observers [^c28-6] or of individual observers. The Italian scholar Mauro Velati is the author of an indispensable reference work [^c28-7] for the study of the role of the observers during the Second Vatican Council. The German Lutheran Edmund [^c28-8] Schlink has recently been honoured with a monographic study.

[^c28-1]: These sources are preserved in the archives of the Second Vatican Council in the Vatican Apostolic Archive, b. 1468–1471.

[^c28-2]: Many of these reports can be consulted in the archives of the World Council of Churches, 4201.3.

[^c28-3]: Albert C. Outler, _Methodist Observer at Vatican II_ (Westminster: Newton, 1967), 16.

[^c28-4]: Douglas Horton, _Vatican Diary 1962: A Protestant Observes the First Session of Vatican Council II_ (Philadelphia: United Church Press, 1964), and subsequent volumes; Robert McAfee Brown, _Observer in Rome: A Protestant Report on the Vatican_ _Council_ (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, 1964).

[^c28-5]: Bernard Pawley, _Observing Vatican II: The Confidential Reports of the Archbishop of Canterbury’s Representative, Bernard_ _Pawley, 1961–1964_, ed. Andrew Chandler and Charlotte Hansen (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2013); Anne Hensmann-Eβer, ed., _Abenteuer im Rom: Texte aus dem Nachlass Werner Küppers im Alt-Katholischen Seminar der_ _Universität Bonn_ (Bonn: Alt-Katholischer Bistumsverlag, 2017).

[^c28-6]: Michael Quisinsky, ‘The Ecumenical Dynamic of Vatican II: Lukas Vischer between Geneva and Rome’, _Cristianesimo nella_ _storia_ 34 (2013): 273–314; Radu Bordeianu, ‘Orthodox Observers at the Second Vatican Council and Intra-Orthodox Dynamics’, _Theological Studies_ 79 (2018): 86–106; Peter De Mey, ‘The Role of the Observers during the Second Vatican Council’, _St Vladimir’s Theological Quarterly_ 60 (2016): 33–51.

[^c28-7]: Mauro Velati, _Separati ma fratelli: Gli osservatori non cattolici al Vaticano II 1962–1965_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2014).

[^c28-8]: Margarethe Hopf, _Ein Osservatore Romano für die Evangelische Kirche in Deutschland: Der Konzilsbeobachter Edmund_ _Schlink im Spannungsfeld der Interessen_ (Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 2019).

It is not easy to exactly determine the influence of the observers on the final version of the conciliar texts. When a commission appointed a _relator_ to introduce changes in a conciliar document, these could only refer to oral or written interventions by council fathers. This chapter will mention a few cases where staff members of the secretariat were able to convince one of the council fathers to read or submit an intervention that contained ideas suggested by a particular observer.

### 2. Inviting the Observers

The ‘invitation to the faithful of the separated Churches to participate with us in this feast of grace and [^c28-9] brotherhood’, which formed part of the announcement of the council by Pope John XXIII, could only materialize after the Secretariat for Christian Unity had been established on 5 June 1960. It was agreed that the secretariat should focus on contacts with the Protestant world, whereas the Commission for the Eastern Churches remained responsible for relations with the Eastern churches. A first proposal by Johannes **[p. 477]** Willebrands was discussed internally in December 1960, but it would be a whole year before the pope took [^c28-10] a final decision on the procedure. Observers would be welcome as auditors at public sessions and general congregations but could not participate in commission meetings. Only after the Catholic Church could finally agree to send official observers to the third general assembly of the World Council of Churches (WCC) was there hope that other churches would be able to accept its invitation. The secretary general of the WCC, Wilhelm Visser ʾt Hooft, was involved in the decision of the secretariat to contact confessional federations to attract a worldwide and representative group of observers.

[^c28-9]: Giuseppe Alberigo, ‘The Announcement of the Council from the Security of the Fortress to the Lure of the Quest’, in _History_ _of Vatican II_, ed. Giuseppe Alberigo and Joseph Komonchak (Leuven: Peeters, 1995), 1:1–54, at 15.

[^c28-10]: Joseph A. Komonchak, ‘The Struggle for the Council during the Preparation of Vatican II (1960–1962)’, in Alberigo and Komonchak, _History of Vatican II_, 1:167–356, at 319–22; Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 62–96.

The archbishop of Canterbury, who had appointed Bernard Pawley as his personal representative in Rome in April 1961, immediately agreed to send three observers. Positive reactions were also received from the Lutheran World Federation, the World Alliance of Reformed Churches, the International Congregationalist Council, the World Methodist Council, the World Convention of the Disciples of Christ, the Friends World Committee Consultation, and the International Association of Liberal Christianity and Religious Freedom, representing the Unitarian tendency within Protestantism. The Methodist José Miguez Bonino was the sole observer from Latin America. During the first session, the Old Catholic Church sent a professor from its seminary in Amersfoort, Peter J. Maan. Edmund Schlink, who had been a permanent delegate of the Evangelische Kirche Deutschlands in Rome since January 1962, continued to represent this federation during the first session of the council.

Because the Secretariat for Christian Unity had expected the Commission for the Eastern Churches to take the lead in inviting the heads of those churches, it began to send delegates on official visits to those churches beginning in June 1961. Because the first Pan-Orthodox Conference, which had been organized in Rhodes in the autumn of 1961, had pleaded to act as one Church in ecumenical matters, the Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras saw himself obliged to decline the invitation, even if privately he had shown great interest in the council. It was painful for the patriarch to learn that the Russian Orthodox Church, after a [^c28-11] secret visit by Willebrands one week before the start of the council, had agreed to send two observers. Even the WCC had originally intended to delegate one observer for the Protestant world and one for the Orthodox world but could only nominate the Reformed theologian Lukas Vischer. Apart from the forty-six official observers attending the first session, the secretariat also decided to invite eight guests. In the case of the two brothers of Taizé, this initially caused tensions with the Fédération protestante de France, but the decision to also invite private guests was the right move to secure the presence of Orthodox theologians such as Alexander Schmemann as of the first session.

[^c28-11]: Komonchak, ‘Struggle’, 324–26.

### 3. The First Experiences of the Observers

**[p. 478]** The observers left for Rome with modest expectations. Having read the first drafts in September 1962, Outler realized that if the opinion of the council on the relationship between Scripture and tradition did not change, this would be ‘wholly disastrous for the Catholic–Protestant dialogue almost before it is well [^c28-12] begun’. On the evening of the opening ceremony, the observers tried to define their policy. Schlink’s proposal to act with one voice was countered by the Anglicans, who did not want to give the impression to [^c28-13] the Catholics that the observers had formed ‘a bloc’.

[^c28-12]: Outler, _Methodist Observer_, 24.

[^c28-13]: Pawley, _Observing Vatican II_, 143 (Report no. 50, 29.10.62).

The observers were impressed by the ‘unrestricted brotherly love’ with which they were received, especially by the members of the secretariat, and soon they were able to characterize the atmosphere of the council as [^c28-14][^c28-15] ‘a hidden Reformation’. Sometimes they complained that ‘we rarely meet the conservatives’, but they [^c28-16] soon realized that their major contribution was to offer ‘indirect support for the progressives’. In their diaries and reports, the observers commented not only on the speeches but also on the liturgies they were confronted with. After hearing the heavenly sound of a boy treble soloist, Horton wrote: ‘The music here would make almost everyone want to turn Roman Catholic; it is only the little matter of theology and [^c28-17] government that stands in the way of conversion by canticle.’

[^c28-14]: Vilmos Vajta, ‘An Interpretation of the Vatican Council’, _Lutheran World_ 13 (1965): 412–30, at 413, 430.

[^c28-15]: McAfee Brown, _Observer in Rome,_ 115.

[^c28-16]: George Lindbeck, ‘Summary Report of the Lutheran Observers of the First Session of Vatican Council II’, 18 (WCC Archives, 4201.3.2).

[^c28-17]: Horton, _Vatican Diary 1962_, 43. Cf. Peter De Mey, ‘The Daily Eucharist at the Council as Stimulus and Test Case for Liturgical Reform’, _Questions liturgiques/Studies in Liturgy_ 95 (2014): 28–51.

The schema on the liturgy was considered by the observers the most mature and renovating document among all the preparatory texts. The council fathers had a true interest in hearing the opinion of the observers. The Reformed observer Hébert Roux could address a group of French bishops, and the notes of [^c28-18] brother Max Thurian of Taizé were conveyed to the appropriate commission. Because of the length of discussion on the liturgy, the observers worried that the council would be an endless event: ‘it will adjourn [^c28-19] in 1980, when some of us will be looking down at it from the high walls of (I hope) heaven’.

[^c28-18]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 142, and Silvia Scatena, _Taizé: Una parabola di unità; Storia della comunità dalle origini al_ _concilio dei giovani_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2018), 509–10.

[^c28-19]: Horton, _Vatican Diary 1962_, 44.

The observers had much greater difficulties with the draft on the sources of Revelation. Since they noticed **[p. 479]** that in some interventions, references were made to their presence, they even considered leaving the [^c28-20] _aula_ to avoid influencing the debate. The observers’ reactions on the quality of the prepared documents on the media and on unity were as negative as those pronounced by the council fathers _in aula_. With regard to the discussion on the means of communication, George Lindbeck reacts: ‘This was the point in the [^c28-21] proceedings when I felt most acutely the need for expert lay participation.’ Vischer knew that ‘the question [^c28-22] of unity and the question of ecumenism were only provisionally discussed during the first session’. His reaction on the final text under discussion during this session, the draft for a Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, also reflects the _communis opinio_ among both the observers and the majority of the council fathers: ‘It was too clerical; it spoke only of the hierarchy and did not sufficiently bring out the fact that the Body of [^c28-23] Christ includes all Christian believers—both clergy and laity. It was too triumphal.’ In their letters and reports at the end of the first session, the observers really felt they had encountered a Church on the move. [^c28-24] Frère Roger of Taizé wrote to his community that the council was ‘the sign of a new Pentecost’. The final judgement on the session by WCC representative Vischer was equally positive: ‘Doors which were thought to be permanently closed have been forced open; questions which were thought to be settled are being re- [^c28-25] examined.’

[^c28-20]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 152.

[^c28-21]: Lindbeck, ‘Summary Report’, 3.

[^c28-22]: Lukas Vischer, ‘Report on Second Vatican Council’, _The Ecumenical Review_ 16 (1963): 43–59, at 50.

[^c28-23]: Ibid., 47.

[^c28-24]: Scatena, _Taizé_, 513.

[^c28-25]: Vischer, ‘Report on the Second Vatican Council’. Velati refers to the difficult minority situation of the Protestant Church in Italy to explain the rather negative reaction by the Waldensian Vittoria Subilia, who considered the result of the first session ‘mediocre’. _Separati ma fratelli_, 184–86.

[^c28-26] The observers were also aware that ‘the Council-in-recess continues as the Council-in-process’. With the help of Edmund Schlink and Kristen Skydsgaard, in the first weeks of January 1963, Vischer prepared a memorandum to help improve the conciliar reflection on the Church and ecumenism. The observers were not informed about the new documents that were being produced by the secretariat. The Taizé brothers, however, were asked by the Louvain theologian and member of the secretariat, Gustave Thils, to send a contribution on ecumenism. An important point made by Max Thurian was that the Orthodox Christians would feel offended if they were not addressed as churches and only as communities. Understandably, he [^c28-27] also pleaded to extend this term to the communities that had emerged from the Reformation. When hearing that a schema was being prepared on the relationship between Church and world, Vischer sought information about this with the Jesuit priest Tucci, the Italian bishop Guano, and others and received an invitation to prepare a document that could help the drafting committee to elaborate their draft. Apparently, [^c28-28] his letter was decisive for this committee putting central emphasis on Christ’s Lordship. During the same **[p. 480]** intersession, the first conversations between Rome and Geneva took place concerning the creation of a Joint Working Group, and in August 1963 the Lutheran World Federation decided to create a centre for [^c28-29] ecumenical studies in Strasbourg.

[^c28-26]: Outler, _Methodist Observer_, 60.

[^c28-27]: Scatena, _Taizé_, 525–26.

[^c28-28]: Lukas Vischer, ‘The Council as an Event in the Ecumenical Movement’, in Alberigo and Komonchak, _History of Vatican II_, 5:485–539, at 498.

[^c28-29]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 200–13.

The secretariat chose not to send invitations for the coronation of Paul VI because the presence of the observers could be interpreted as an act of obedience to the pope. Some observers, however, chose to attend. In an exchange of letters, the different approach between the Anglican and Protestant observers became obvious. Schlink refused to participate for theological reasons, since the coronation ceremony for him represented ‘an inappropriate mixture of spiritual and material claims’. Whereas Pawley understood his role also as being a representative of the Anglican Church, Schlink saw it as his task to analyse the documents of the council from a Protestant perspective and to explain this perspective to his hosts.[^c28-30]

[^c28-30]: Hopf, _Ein Osservatore Romano_, 109–10.

### 4. Attempts to Improve Key Documents during the Second Session

At the start of the second session, the Ecumenical Patriarchate still was not able to send official observers, but the Romanian Orthodox monk André Scrima could attend the council as the personal representative of the Ecumenical Patriarch and guest of the secretariat; the Greek Orthodox lay theologian Nikos Nissiotis became one of the two observers of the WCC. Observers were also sent by the Church of South India, the Malabar Church, and the Malankara Orthodox Church.

During this session, the observers were very much interested in the debate on the revised schema on the Church. During a private meeting of observers, Vischer and Schlink proposed preparing a collective point of view, but this proposal was not accepted for lack of a common view on ecclesiology among the observers. Still, during the four weekly meetings with the secretariat dedicated to this theme, a ‘parallel debate’ took place in which twenty-five observers intervened.[^c28-31]

[^c28-31]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 272.

The Orthodox observers showed themselves to be quite critical; they especially deplored the lack of attention for the role of the Holy Spirit and for the local Eucharistic assembly. The revised schema was still [^c28-32] characterized by a Western approach to ecclesiology and could be read as an apology for papal primacy. With regard to the first chapter, many Protestant observers believed the schema was not ‘sufficiently clear [^c28-33] **[p. 481]** in its acknowledgment of the reality of sin within the life of the church’. The same critique also returned with regard to the chapter on holiness. For Lutheran observer Kristen Skydsgaard, ‘there is more a [^c28-34] lifted forefinger in it than of the freedom of the children of God, there is more morality than faith’. The same observer remained puzzled about the discussion on the hierarchy: ‘Some are dissatisfled because the schema speaks positively about the collegiality of the bishops _iure divino_, and others are disappointed because it speaks very unilaterally of the primate of the Pope. How the two viewpoints can be harmonized, I [^c28-35] do not see.’ For the same reasons, Methodist observer Outler hoped this would not be the final word in [^c28-36] Roman Catholic ecclesiology. Skydsgaard noticed that something had changed in the relationship between the secretariat and the observers. The previous year, they had been partners in criticizing the reports prepared by others; now the members of the secretariat felt ‘personally involved’ since they agreed with [^c28-37] several new schemes or had written them themselves. With regard to the discussion on the Church, the observers also followed the vote on whether to treat the Mother of God within the Dogmatic Constitution on the Church with great attention. McAfee Brown wrote in his diary: ‘Close as the vote was and difficult to interpret as it is, the Council fathers have nevertheless taken a step which has the possibility of being [^c28-38] ecumenically creative rather than ecumenically divisive.’

[^c28-32]: Ibid., 273. See also Nikos Nissiotis, ‘Ecclesiology and Ecumenism of the Second Session of the Vatican Council II’, _Greek_ _Orthodox Theological Review_ 10 (1964): 15–36.

[^c28-33]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 37.

[^c28-34]: Kirsten Skydsgaard, ‘Some Remarks on the 4th chapter of the Schema De Ecclesia at the Meeting of the Observers, 5.11.1963’, 1 (WCC Archives 4201.3.5).

[^c28-35]: Skydsgaard, ‘Report I, 2nd Session, Second Vatican Council; Oct. 28, 1963’, 9 (WCC Archives 4201.3.5).

[^c28-36]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 281.

[^c28-37]: Skydsgaard, ‘Report II, 2nd Session, 22.11.1963’, 3 (WCC Archives 4201.3.5).

[^c28-38]: McAfee Brown, _Observer in Rome_, 125.

During the two meetings which the secretariat had dedicated to discussion on the theme of ecumenism, twenty delegates intervened. Willebrands had invited the observers to react not only to the three chapters on ecumenism but also to the appendices on religious liberty and on the relationship with the Jews. A substantial document was prepared by Lukas Vischer and signed by Nissiotis, Schlink, Skydsgaard, Küppers, [^c28-39] Lindbeck, and Miguez Bonino. The observers also received useful background on the redaction history of the document:

[^c28-39]: The original German version was entitled ‘Bemerkungen zum schema _De Oecumenismo_’. The observers also did a translation in English, ‘Remarks on the Schema _De Oecumenismo_’. Both documents can be consulted in AAV, Conc. Vat. II, b. 1469. Cf. Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 304.

In discussion about this with responsible members of the Secretariat, we get the impression that the text of the Schema as it stands is the result of a long struggle with conservative elements on the Theological Commission, etc. and represents an optimum of what we can expect. We should therefore prepare ourselves and our public not to be disappointed if certain positions at present occupied are heavily attacked and even lost. Some of the texts (e.g. that on permission for corporate prayer) are deliberately vague, in the hope that they will be able to be given a favourable context later.[^c28-40]

[^c28-40]: Pawley, _Observing Vatican II_, 258 (Report no. 101, 14.11.63).

**[p. 482]** For the first time, Old Catholic theologian Werner Küppers intervened, wondering why his community, [^c28-41] which like the Orthodox was structured around its bishop, had not explicitly been defined as Church. Oscar Cullmann, however, understood why the Catholic Church could not recognize them as ‘churches’ without [^c28-42] betraying its ecclesiology. In Vischer’s remarks and in interventions by Lindbeck, the manner of ranking all Christian communities on a scale depending on the elements they had in common with the Catholic [^c28-43] Church was not judged favourably. Interestingly, Lindbeck’s final report on this session contains a _retractatio_ compared to the previous one. At the start of the debate on ecumenism, he had called the schema an ‘ecumenical catastrophe’ because of its quantitative ecclesiology of elements. Later he realized that [^c28-44] calling Protestant communities ‘churches’ ‘is probably too advanced for the majority’. Apart from the opening chapter, the third chapter was met with a lot of criticism as well, because neither the churches of the East nor those of the West are understood ‘as they understand themselves’. Vischer therefore proposed [^c28-45] dropping this chapter completely.

[^c28-41]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 306.

[^c28-42]: Ibid., 308.

[^c28-43]: Ibid., 311.

[^c28-44]: Compare Report IV from 18 November with Report V from 5 December (WCC Archives 4201.3.5).

[^c28-45]: ‘Remarks on the Schema _De Oecumenismo_’, 4; Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 312.

Some ideas by observers found their way into the speeches of council fathers. Cullmann was twice successful. On 22 November, the French bishop Huyghe presented his proposal that Catholic and Protestant parishes should not restrict the concern for the poor to their own parishes; three days later, the Italian archbishop Pangrazio read a speech prepared by a staff member of the secretariat, Johannes Feiner, who had [^c28-46] integrated ideas on the hierarchy of truths which Cullmann had shared with him. At the end of the session, Schutz and Thurian had the occasion to be received by the pope and proposed that he make ‘gestures of reconciliation’, including meeting the Ecumenical Patriarch during his upcoming pilgrimage to the Holy Land.[^c28-47]

[^c28-46]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 316. The speeches are found in AAV II/5, 753–56 and II/6, 32–34.

[^c28-47]: Scatena, _Taizé_, 558.

McAfee Brown read the abbreviated document on ‘Instruments of social communication’ (Decree on the Mass media, _Inter Mirifica_) in detail and was convinced that ‘its adoption by the Council would be a tragic mistake’ and that a _non-placet_ would give the message ‘We prefer not to speak at all unless we can speak [^c28-48] well.’ By the end of this session, McAfee Brown had revised his own ethos as observer. He had set out thinking he had only to observe, not to participate, and that it was ‘their’ council. Now he felt bound to [^c28-49] contribute so that the council ‘does the most creative job it can’.

[^c28-48]: McAfee Brown, _Observer in Rome_, 168–69.

[^c28-49]: Ibid., 172.

The second intersession proved to be one of intensive ecumenical contacts. After the encounter with the pope in Jerusalem, Patriarch Athenagoras was resolved to send delegates to Rome during the third session. At first, Athenagoras wished the Third Pan-Orthodox Conference to take this decision, but since it would **[p. 483]** not meet until November 1964, the local churches were allowed to decide about this issue. In early September, the Patriarchal Synod gave the green light so that the Ecumenical Patriarchate could finally send official observers to the third session. A Roman Catholic delegation attended a WCC colloquium on ministry in January 1964 and shared the new draft of Schema XIII with Vischer, who proposed introducing the idea of the Lordship of Christ in a paragraph of the schema dealing with the evaluation of culture and other religions. Together with Nikos Nissiotis, he also prepared written comments that Häring brought to the [^c28-50] attention of the drafting committee. In April 1964, the first official meeting between the WCC and the Secretariat for Christian Unity took place to discuss the new relationship and the issue of membership, and in July 1964 the WCC convened a meeting of all the churches that had sent observers to Rome to discuss the [^c28-51] implications of the council for the future of ecumenical dialogue.

[^c28-50]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 358–59.

[^c28-51]: Ibid., 335–36. One of the fruits of this conference was a famous article by Nikos Nissiotis, ‘The Main Ecclesiological Problem of the Second Vatican Council and the Position of the Non-Roman Churches Facing It’, _Journal of Ecumenical_ _Studies_ 2 (1965): 31–65.

### 5. Encountering the Slowness of the Catholic Church’s Renewal and Reform in Year Three

During the third session, the number of observers had grown to seventy-five. Not only the Ecumenical Patriarchate but also the Assyrian Church of the East sent a delegation for the first time, as did the Pentecostals, the Quakers, and even the Missouri Synod. Rome would also witness a conflict about the delegation of the Reformed churches. Vischer had proposed substituting Subilia for Roux, because the latter was seen as too friendly to Catholics, but the Fédération protestante de France decided to send Roux as their observer.[^c28-52]

[^c28-52]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 378.

At the start of the session, the observers could share their opinions on the concluding chapter of _Lumen Gentium_ with the members of the secretariat. Schlink considered the chapter ‘modest though not minimalist’ and believed that even an analogical use of the term _mediatrix_ for Mary would be a ‘big tragedy’, especially since ordinary believers do not usually make such theological distinctions. But even the Orthodox observers shared their mild criticism. According to Scrima, churches should be prudent in making theological claims about the Mother of God since what believers know about Mary is mostly mediated liturgically, and Nissiotis added that one would never be able to develop a good Christology by starting from Mariology.[^c28-53]

[^c28-53]: This information is based on the twelve-page report which the Louvain theologian Charles Moeller made of the meeting of 22 September. Cf. AAV, _Concilium Vaticanum Secundum_, b. 1470.

**[p. 484]** The observers were very interested in the debates on Jews and on religious freedom. For the Protestant [^c28-54] world, ‘it was a test for the credibility of the conciliar _aggiornamento_’. They also followed the discussion on the Decree on the Apostolate of the Laity with great attention. William B. Blakemore, one of the observers from the Disciples of Christ, considered this ‘one of the superb weeks of the Council’ and found it so exciting [^c28-55] that in the Catholic Church ‘an amazing renewal among its lay people’ could be observed. The number in the decree that rehearses the teaching of the Decree on Ecumenism that it is ‘desirable, and often imperative, that Catholics cooperate with other Christians, either in activities or in societies … and at national or international level’ (_Apostolicam Actuositatem_ (_AA_) 27) was drafted by Johannes Feiner, who made use of notes by Lukas Vischer.[^c28-56]

[^c28-54]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 399.

[^c28-55]: William B. Blakemore, ‘The Second Vatican Council: Third Session’, 15 (Report preserved in the personal archive of Fr. Stransky, Catholic University of America).

[^c28-56]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 429–30.

The Decree on Ecumenism was no longer exposed to public discussion, but it was still possible for the council fathers to submit _modi_. Edmund Schlink provided material that went into a _modus_ submitted by Bishop Kampe of Limburg that was supported by another forty-two council fathers. In its final version, the Decree on Ecumenism no longer states that ‘large communities have separated themselves [_se seiunxerunt_] from full communion with the Catholic Church’ but that they ‘became separated [_seiunctae sunt_]’ (_Unitatis_ [^c28-57] _Redintegratio_ (_UR_) 3). The council deliberately sought to leave the question of guilt abstract. The work on the Decree on the Catholic Churches of the Eastern Rite was, however, followed with great suspicion. In a document signed by seven Orthodox observers, André Scrima asked for this document to be rejected, since it reflected a different ecclesiology than the one found in the Decree on Ecumenism. The addition of a few words to recommend consultation of ‘the ordinaries of the separated churches’ (_UR_ 29) before taking [^c28-58] measures to promote Eucharistic sharing was partially the result of their efforts. At the end of the session, Lukas Vischer did not hide his criticism of this decree: ‘Now as the text is promulgated, the tension between the two possible views will remain and it is to be seen how things will develop in future. I hope that the text [^c28-59] on the Oriental churches will not determine the ecumenical style of the Roman Catholic Church.’

[^c28-57]: Ibid., 440.

[^c28-58]: Ibid., 446.

[^c28-59]: Lukas Vischer, ‘Concerning the Third Session of the Second Vatican Council. No. 7’, 14 (WCC Archives 4201.3.9).

A returning complaint during the debate on Schema XIII was that it had not sufficiently paid attention to the reality of evil or to the eschatological dimension. Instead of praising the progress of science, the schema should not forget the ‘dramatic view of man in this world’, as this became clear, as one example, in ‘the [^c28-60] horror of the concentration camps’. Horton’s diary reports a similar criticism by the Orthodox **[p. 485]** representative of the WCC, Nikos Nissiotis: ‘The Church as shown in the schema is an island of grace in the midst of a natural world, and he [Nissiotis] felt that the Latin distinction between nature and grace made [^c28-61] it impossible to relate the two.’ A positive assessment was submitted by representatives of the International Association of Liberal Christianity and Religious Freedom and of the Quakers: ‘The humility of the Church as it seeks dialogue with the modern world is exemplary for all bodies of Christian assembly and [^c28-62] convention which take upon themselves the responsibility of instructing the world.’

[^c28-60]: ‘Report No 7’, 2, 5 (WCC Archives 4201.3.8).

[^c28-61]: Horton, _Vatican Diary 1964_, 116.

[^c28-62]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 462.

Towards the end of the session, the observers were impressed that the council had dared to reject the Decree on Mission, despite Pope Paul VI’s explicit support during the only time he had attended a meeting of the council during this session. In the meeting with the secretariat on 10 November, the Anglican observer Pawley had criticized the proselytizing practices by Catholic missionaries in countries with a majority of [^c28-63] Catholics. The observers were also very interested in the discussion of a short schema on marriage prepared by a commission that Paul VI put in place under the presidency of the Louvain canonist Willy Onclin. The document was the last one to be discussed during the third session, on 19 and 20 November. The Leiden professor Van Holk, a representative of the Free Churches, was disappointed that the council failed to pay proper attention to this important theme:

[^c28-63]: Horton, _Vatican Diary 1964_, 150.

Rather late during the session a small schema on Marriage was proposed to the Council, and came up for discussion the last two days, when everybody’s interests was elsewhere and the voting-process cut painfully across the discussions. As it was generally acknowledged that this problem is urgent, both inside the Roman Catholic world, and in relation to the non-Catholic world (as a test for the sincerity of the ecumenical attitude), so short a discussion completely failed to do justice to the subject.[^c28-64]

[^c28-64]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 452.

Vischer, for his part, appreciated that the Catholic Church differentiated between marriages in which one of the partners was a baptized non-Catholic and marriages in which one of the partners was an unbaptized Christian; he agreed that this was a matter not to be decided by the council but by a motu proprio promulgated by the pope.[^c28-65] Many observers reacted to the events of the so-called _settimana nera_, which started with the publication of the _Nota Explicativa Praevia_. Vischer understood very well that ‘this additional text was written in order to [^c28-66] meet the opposition against the notion of collegiality’. For Schlink it is clear that the pope had been ‘an instrument of curial forces’. In unusually emotional terms, he considered the _Nota_ as an ‘attack on the **[p. 486]** foundations of the council’. Together with the last-minute changes in the Decree on Ecumenism, it now [^c28-67] had become clear to him that a pope ‘can deal with a text approved by the Council as he wishes’. The Anglican observers reacted with British humour but no less critically. From the stalls of St Longinus, they sent a _modus_ (a motion to amend) composed in perfect Latin, giving four reasons why the _Nota explicativa_ did not please the Anglicans and the other observers. The _modus_ contains the wise advice that the relationship between pope and bishops is not a matter of juridical definition but a ‘_modus vivendi_’; it is determined ‘along the way’. According to the Anglicans, the document also constituted ‘a severe obstacle [^c28-68] for the spirit of ecumenism and for the possibility of a future dialogue with other Christians’.

[^c28-65]: Vischer, ‘Concerning the Third Session of the Second Vatican Council. No. 7’, 10 (WCC Archives 4201.3.9).

[^c28-66]: Ibid., 15–16.

[^c28-67]: Hopf, _Ein Osservatore Romano_, 162–64.

[^c28-68]: We consulted the _Modus de modis a patribus conciliaribus preparatis et ab observatoribus anglicanis examinatis_ in the Vatican II archive of the Benedictine monk of Emmanuel Lanne, Chevetogne.

Many observers also objected to the papal _modi_ on the Decree on Ecumenism, introduced at the eleventh hour after the council fathers had voted to approve the final draft in an effort to placate the conciliar [^c28-69] minority. For Horton, the changes in the text cannot be easily explained away. ‘Many of them are alterations that take the text, often by only a hair’s breadth, back towards the days before Pope John when [^c28-70] the Roman Church saw in itself all good, and outside of itself, no good.’ The observers remained convinced, though, of the honest attempt made by their friends in the Secretariat for Christian Unity to solve this request by the pope in the best possible way, as appears from the following moving account of an intervention by Willebrands during the meeting with the observers:

[^c28-69]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 482–88.

[^c28-70]: Horton, _Vatican Diary 1964_, 179.

Bishop Willebrands’ reply left us with wet eyes. He too was sorry that the change had been made. … In the midst of the present strained circumstances, in which misunderstandings could so easily develop, he hoped that we would look past the temporary setbacks to the great gains that had already been established in the fleld of ecumenicity and which were registered in many paragraphs of the schema; and then, still speaking in French in response to Dr. Cullman, he said the equivalent for ‘Don’t give up on us!’ This became suddenly a moment of rededication. We observers saw, as by a flash of light, where the knife cut deepest—in the red flesh of the Secretariat. These men, dedicated to church unity, had unexpectedly had their plans scotched by brethren of their own household.[^c28-71]

[^c28-71]: Ibid., 187.

In hindsight, however, the observers looked with great satisfaction to the decree: ‘We now have an unprecedentedly open and generous statement … I know nothing to match it, certainly not in the literature of our denomination, nor in the literature of the World Council of Churches.’[^c28-72]

[^c28-72]: Outler, _Methodist Observer_, 99.

**[p. 487]** The negative effect of the nineteen amendments was amplifled by the decision to postpone the vote on the Decree on Religious Freedom until the final session. William Blakemore, who paid special attention to ‘Council procedures’ in his report on this session, knew that ‘the Roman Catholic Church seeks government not in terms of a majority—but in terms of a virtual unanimity’. They prefer to postpone finishing a [^c28-73] document until ‘nearly all members of the church can agree’. One last critical moment would follow: the proclamation of Mary as ‘Mother of the Church’ by Pope Paul VI during the concluding Eucharist. Schlink could not understand why Catholic ‘ecumenists’ could minimize the impact of this papal speech by insisting [^c28-74] that it was not clothed in the form of dogma. Horton doubted whether the proclamation of this new title would make much difference: ‘Protestants find the whole range of Mariology so foreign to their thinking that the addition of a new title for the blessed Virgin Mary can hardly tip the scales much further.’ He remained positive at the end of the session: ‘The obstacles to church unity loom, I think, larger than ever— [^c28-75] but not larger than our hope.’

[^c28-73]: Blakemore, ‘The Second Vatican Council: Third Session’, 15.

[^c28-74]: Hopf, _Ein Osservatore Romano_, 170.

[^c28-75]: Horton, _Vatican Diary 1964_, 109.

### 6. ‘Never Once in the Four Years Have We Felt Any Resentment at Your Presence’: How the Observers Lived the Final Year of the Council

During the last intersession, not only the general secretary of the council and the Secretary of State but even the pope himself started raising doubts about the continued presence of the observers during the fourth session. Willebrands strongly argued that ‘the observers were invited to the Council and not to one or more [^c28-76] sessions’. The number of observers and guests would reach its peak during the fourth session with 105— including, for the first time, representatives of the Bulgarian and Serbian Orthodox churches. Even before the session started, the observers had good reason to reflect on the tension between pope and council. The Hungarian Lutheran Vilmos Vajta noticed important differences between the encyclical on the Eucharist (_Mysterium Fidei_), which the pope had promulgated on the eve of this session, and the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy, and he clearly sensed that the papal institution of the Synod of Bishops was perhaps not [^c28-77] what the bishops had hoped for.

[^c28-76]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 522.

[^c28-77]: Vilmos Vajta, ‘Report no. 4 (22.10.1965)’, 2 (WCC Archives 4201.3.12).

**[p. 488]** The same Lutheran observer was also highly interested in the first document discussed during this session: the one dealing with religious freedom. In his initial reflections on the new schema, he expressed the hope that the Catholic Church would grant the same rights to others which she assumed for herself in minority situations. Moreover, in his opinion, ‘the Council should more clearly face the fact that the Church has [^c28-78] become a minority in today’s world. The defence of a _corpus Christianum_ is only based on an illusion.’ Still, he would consider the approval of the document ‘a great ecumenical achievement’, since it would mean that [^c28-79] the Catholic Church ‘would renounce the methods of the past’.

[^c28-78]: Vilmo Vajta, ‘Report no. 2 (22.09.1965)’, 1.

[^c28-79]: Vajta, ‘Report no. 4’, 5.

During the two meetings with the secretariat on Schema XIII, it became clear that the presence of Orthodox observers had become stronger this session. For Paul Evdokimov, the constitution should not only reflect on [^c28-80] ‘The Church in the World’ but also be interested in the reverse question. After the council, Nissiotis considered _Gaudium et Spes_ ‘a good example to other Churches, and especially to the Eastern Orthodox one, [^c28-81] of a sincere care on the part of the Church to serve and help the modern man in his human condition’. Vajta appreciated the addition of a ‘Christological dynamic’ but felt it still lacked attention to ‘the mystery [^c28-82] of the cross’. The observers were also interested in the practical part of the constitution. The Orthodox, defending the theme of married priesthood, believed that the Catholics cherished celibacy higher than marriage. The most pacifist theologians among the observers were the Quaker Douglas Steere and the Lutheran theologian Skydsgaard. They offered reflections on nuclear deterrence and conscientious objection. The observers were impressed by the fact that so many council fathers were willing to criticize the [^c28-83] excesses of capitalism.

[^c28-80]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 550–51.

[^c28-81]: Nissiotis, ‘Report on the Second Vatican Council’, _Ecumenical Review_ 18 (1966): 190–206.

[^c28-82]: Vajta, ‘Report no. 4’, 7.

[^c28-83]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 552–60.

Even before the start of the final session, the Secretariat for Christian Unity had agreed to set up an informal meeting with the WCC division on Mission and Evangelism on the newly prepared draft of the Decree on Mission, in the presence of many observers in April 1965. An important lacuna of the document was that it said nothing about ecumenical cooperation in a missionary context. The three references to _Unitatis Redintegratio_ in the final text would be motivated by the _relator_ Johannes Schütte—not only with a reference to the interventions by bishops but, exceptionally, also to documents submitted by Vischer, Bonino, and the Anglicans.[^c28-84]

[^c28-84]: Ibid., 577. Cf. AS IV/6, 248.

The tensions _in aula_ that accompanied the final work on _Nostra Aetate_ also affected the observers to some extent. Willebrands even had to organize a special meeting with the small group of observers from Arabic **[p. 489]** countries. The Quakers, who believed the Catholic Church could take more concrete steps to promote dialogue with Muslims, took the lead in organizing a meeting with the newly created Secretariat for Non- [^c28-85] Christians.

[^c28-85]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 581–84.

The observers appreciated the changes in the Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation. Vischer knew it [^c28-86] was ‘without doubt the most significant of the texts promulgated in the course of the fourth session’. Nissiotis believed that ‘great progress’ had been made in comparison to previous versions, especially with [^c28-87] regard to the council’s view on ‘the unity between Bible and Tradition’. They also followed the discussion on _Christus Dominus_ with great interest to find out how ‘the so-called collegiality of the bishops is to work out in practice’. Vischer noted that the document ‘affirms the doctrine of the Primate and the universal [^c28-88] jurisdiction of the Pope with a clearness which can hardly be surpassed’. He also does not spare his criticism against _Presbyterorum Ordinis_: ‘For what—theologically compelling—reason can the priest be [^c28-89] subordinated to the bishop?’

[^c28-86]: Lukas Vischer, ‘After the Fourth Session of the Second Vatican Council’, _Ecumenical Review_ 18 (1966): 150–89, at 154.

[^c28-87]: Nissiotis, ‘Report on the Second Vatican Council’, 196.

[^c28-88]: Vischer, ‘After the Fourth Session of the Second Vatican Council’, 158.

[^c28-89]: Ibid., 162.

During the last session there were a few dead moments when the final revision of the texts was being prepared in small commissions. The coordinating commission had programmed a discussion on a document on indulgences which had been prepared by the Apostolic Penitentiary. The Lutheran observer Warren A. Quanbeck paid quite a bit of attention to the discussion of this document in his report: ‘Some thought it nothing less than scandalous that such a document could be introduced, as it ignored completely the results of the Council’s work, and demonstrated once again how thoroughly curial officials could insulate [^c28-90] themselves not only from the world but from fairly spectacular happenings within the Church.’ The Lutheran observer Wolfgang Dietzfelbinger was shocked to see that the discussion which Luther initiated [^c28-91] 450 years ago ‘had until today not taken place in the Roman Church’. The observers also remained interested in the evolution of the planned motu proprio on mixed marriages. A representative group of observers had prepared a document on the basis of the _votum_ discussed _in aula_ during the previous session. It was their profound conviction that ‘the spirit of the Decree on Ecumenism and of the Declaration on Religious Liberty calls for freedom for responsibly Christian parents to decide as to the confession in which [^c28-92] their children are to be baptized and reared’. The issue was so important to them that they even **[p. 490]** exceptionally submitted a common petition to the pope on 1 October 1965 which was signed by twenty- [^c28-93] two observers.

[^c28-90]: Warren A. Quanbeck, ‘Report no. 6: The Discussion on Indulgences, November 10–11, 1965’, 2 (WCC Archives 4201.3.12).

[^c28-91]: Wolfgang Dietzfelbinger, ‘Chronicle of the Fourth Session of the Vatican Council’, in _Challenge … and Response: A_ _Protestant Perspective of the Vatican Council_, ed. Warren A. Quanbeck (Minneapolis: Augsburg, 1966), 3–21, at 15.

[^c28-92]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 614.

[^c28-93]: Vischer, ‘The Council as an Event in the Ecumenical Movement’, 488.

The pope’s proposal to organize the annual meeting with the observers in the form of an ecumenical prayer service at first met with hesitation on the part of the observers. Oscar Cullmann, however, faced the project with great enthusiasm as long as the pope would not preside at the service. The location of St Paul Outside the Walls was carefully chosen, since it was the church from which Pope John XXIII chose to announce the ecumenical council. The pope spoke highly of the very visible and important presence of the observers during the council: ‘Your departure leaves us in a solitude which we did not experience before the Council and which now saddens us; we would like to see you with us always!’[^c28-94]

[^c28-94]: Ibid., 486.

The joint declaration by Pope Paul VI and Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras, revoking the mutual excommunications of 1054, had a profound impact on the observers as well. Vischer, however, was also aware of the limitations of the event: ‘There was a widespread expectation that dialogue could begin [^c28-95] immediately and lead quickly to tangible results. The image was deceptive; the reality was more complex.’ Also, Nissiotis anticipated that it would take a lot of time to set up official Orthodox–Roman Catholic relations: ‘The Council gave me the impression that the discussion between Roman Catholics and Protestants is in many ways easier than between Roman Catholics and Orthodox, because both parties use [^c28-96] the same language when discussing the same problems.’ He welcomed ‘the act of revoking the anathema of 1054’ but knew that ‘the real motives [for the schism] still exist’ and could be found by Orthodox ‘in the [^c28-97] third chapter of _De Ecclesia_ and in the Decree on the Oriental Churches’. Still, he was aware that ‘all criticisms against certain positions must be accompanied by a sincere self-criticism of our own unilateral, [^c28-98] conservative or radical positions’.

[^c28-95]: Ibid., 527.

[^c28-96]: Nissiotis, ‘Report on the Second Vatican Council’, 202.

[^c28-97]: Ibid., 203.

[^c28-98]: Ibid., 206. The following article pays attention to the position of this interesting observer in a more extensive manner: De Mey, ‘Growth in Criticism? Comparing Orthodox Responses to Vatican II’, _The Ecumenical Review_ 73 (2021): 8–28.

### 7. Preparing Future Relations

The Secretariat for Christian Unity benefited greatly from the presence of the observers during the final session of the council to intensify structures of cooperation among the Christian churches. After the Joint Working Group was formally launched during a first meeting in Bossey in May 1965, a second meeting took place on 17–20 November in Rome in preparation for a first common statement in February 1966.[^c28-99]

[^c28-99]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 601–5.

**[p. 491]** That Catholics believed Anglicans could play a mediatory role in ecumenical relations with the churches of the Reformation appears from the special audience they received on 13 November, during the fourth session. Preparations were made for the creation of an Anglican Centre in Rome and for a visit of Archbishop Ramsey [^c28-100] in Rome. During this visit in March 1966, a more intensive dialogue between the two churches was announced. The group of Anglican observers also published a common volume with reactions on the most [^c28-101] important documents of the council. The mixed Lutheran–Catholic commission which gathered in April 1966 chose to work on the theme of the relationship of Gospel and Church. The two volumes edited by the [^c28-102] Lutheran observers can be considered a Lutheran commentary on the council. After the council, Hébert Roux took the initiative to publish a book in France gathering the reactions of many Protestants in his [^c28-103] country to the council. In Germany, Edmund Schlink introduced the results of the council at important meetings of the Evangelical Church in Germany (EKD), such as the _Kirchenkonferenz_ of 16 December 1965 and the synod of the Western part of the EKD, which met in West Berlin in March 1966. The synod showed itself ready to pursue the way of dialogue ‘with an open spirit’ but was aware that ‘fundamental differences in the understanding of the Gospel, which have led to the separation of our churches during the [^c28-104] Reformation, have not yet been overcome’. The Orthodox had only been fragmentarily present in Rome. [^c28-105] As a result, for a more thorough assessment of the council, one had to wait until the end of the decade.

[^c28-100]: Ibid., 606–8, 653–57.

[^c28-101]: Bernard Pawley, ed., _The Second Vatican Council: Studies by Eight Anglican Observers_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1967).

[^c28-102]: George A. Lindbeck, ed., _Dialogue on the Way: Protestants Report from Rome on the Vatican Council_ (Minneapolis: Augsburg, 1965); Quanbeck, _Challenge … and Responses._

[^c28-103]: Hébert Roux, ed., _Points de vue de théologiens protestants: Études sur les décrets du Concile Vatican II_ (Paris: Cerf, 1967).

[^c28-104]: Velati, _Separati ma fratelli_, 669.

[^c28-105]: Damaskinos Papandreou, ed., _Stimmen der Orthodoxie zu Grundfragen des II. Vatikanums_ (Freiburg: Herder, 1969).

### 8. Conclusion

This historical overview of the way the observers fully participated in the event of the council and reacted to (the evolution of) its documents shows that their presence was crucial. The documents of the council owe their final shape to the remarks that the observers formally and informally shared with the staff and members of the Secretariat for Christian Unity who were their primordial conversation partners and (often through them) with a far larger group of council fathers. The experiences of the first session, along with the many positive but also painful experiences that were to follow, changed the theological views of the **[p. 492]** observers and their communities and have had a positive impact on ecumenical relations up to the present day. For this reason, it will be useful to continue studying the reports and reflections of the observers to gain a better understanding of both the events and the documents of the Second Vatican Council.
