## 29. The Reception of Vatican II by the Orthodox Church

Radu Bordeianu

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 493]** [^c29-1] ‘The voices which the Council had uncovered give it dimensions that transcend the Catholic Church’, wrote Bishop Cassien (Bezobrazov), one of the Orthodox participants at the Second Vatican Council. His words still ring true today, given the main questions that Orthodox theology has addressed in the decades since the [^c29-2] council and how Vatican II has influenced the life of the Orthodox Church. Whether criticizing or applauding the council and its aftermath, Orthodoxy shaped its life and thought dialogically, taking into account the Catholic renewal set into motion at Vatican II.

[^c29-1]: Cited in Giuseppe Alberigo and Joseph A. Komonchak, eds., _History of Vatican II_, 5 vols. (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1995–2006), 2:522–23.

[^c29-2]: Throughout its documents, Vatican II used ‘Churches’ in reference to Orthodoxy, and not the singular. While appreciating the Council’s unambiguous recognition of the Orthodox as Churches, the Orthodox observers saw this use of the plural as a Catholic presupposition that a Church cannot have unity without the papacy. Unless I refer to the sum of autocephalous churches, I use the singular ‘Church’ in reference to the Orthodox world.

In order to assess the reception of Vatican II by the Orthodox Church, one cannot search for major official statements by either individual national Orthodox churches or by a body representing the entire Orthodoxy. This is not how Orthodoxy operates. On the one hand, national Orthodox churches use their autocephaly (the authority of self-governance) only in administrative matters, and not to issue statements with **[p. 494]** doctrinal importance, which would impact the rest of Orthodoxy. On the other hand, a pan-Orthodox assessment was simply impossible in the decades following the council, when Orthodoxy was separated by the Iron Curtain.

The process of reception of Vatican II involved primarily the reactions of individual Orthodox theologians, some of whom were present as observers or guests of the pontifical Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity (SPCU), and others who reacted after the council. The reception of Vatican II’s theology was a matter both of intellectual assessment and of theological influence. The first simply looks at the decisions of the council through an Orthodox lens; the second accepts the insights of the council into Orthodox theology and further develops them in a communion ecclesiology that emphasizes pneumatology, the local Church with all its ministries gathered in the Eucharist, synodality, and primacy. These reactions set the stage for several practical ways in which the Orthodox Church received Vatican II in its own life, including the lifting of the anathemas of 1054, the establishment of bilateral Orthodox–Catholic dialogues, liturgical reforms based on a common understanding of the communion between clergy and laity, and a renewed impetus for pan- Orthodox conciliarity.

### 2. Orthodox Theology

As Vatican II was unfolding, the first Orthodox theologians to react to it were the ecumenical observers and scholars who could not serve as official observers for reasons of an ecclesiastical nature but were invited as guests of the SPCU; the distinction between observers and guests was nominal. These delegates did not speak in plenaries, but they influenced the council informally, attended public sessions and general congregations, had access to draft documents, and were informed of the results of various commissions at weekly meetings organized by the SPCU. As a result of the fruitful interactions of Orthodox and Catholic theologians at the Dominican Ecumenical Centre Istina in Paris and the monastery of Chevetogne, the SPCU [^c29-3] was determined to bring Orthodox observers to the council. Constantinople was tasked to ask all Orthodox churches to send observers. The Ecumenical Patriarchate started out willing to do so and encouraged the other Orthodox churches to do the same. At Moscow’s insistence, the first Rhodes conference (1961) decided that all Orthodox should act in unison, but Moscow opposed sending observers, so it seemed that no Orthodox Church would do so. However, after dealing directly with the Vatican and going against its own insistence on a unifled Orthodox attitude, Moscow became the only Orthodox Church that sent observers to the first session. Its delegation consisted primarily of Vladimir Kotliarov and Vitaly Borovoi, whose reports **[p. 495]** were quite positive. Based on the positive experience of its observers at the first session, Moscow [^c29-4] encouraged the other Orthodox churches to send observers. But Constantinople, still feeling too hurt by the actions of Moscow and the Vatican before the first session, refused to send representatives. The attitude shifted again when the new Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras embraced each other during a common pilgrimage in Jerusalem in 1964; with this gesture, Rome recognized the pre-eminent place of Constantinople within the Orthodox world. This prompted the Ecumenical Patriarchate to send the following observers to the last two sessions: Panteleimon Rodopoulos, Ioannis Romanides, Maximos [^c29-5] Aghiorgoussis, and André Scrima. Among other theologians who later attended Vatican II as observers, the following stand out: Paul Evdokimov and Nicholas Afanasiev from St Serge in Paris, and Alexander Schmemann and Nicholas Arseniev from St Vladimir’s Seminary in Yonkers, New York. The most influential among them was Afanasiev.

[^c29-3]: Emmanuel Lanne, ‘La Perception en Occident de la participation du Patriarcat de Moscou à Vatican II’, in _Vatican II in_ _Moscow (1959–1965): Acts of the Colloquium on the History of Vatican II; Moscow, March 30–April 2, 1995_, edited by Alberto Melloni (Leuven: Library of the Faculty of Theology K. U. Leuven, 1997), 122–23.

[^c29-4]: Mauro Velati, _Separati ma fratelli: Gli osservatori non-cattolici al Vaticano II (1962–1965)_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2014), 234–35.

[^c29-5]: The Romanian monk André Scrima so impressed Cardinal Suenens with his view of the relationship between Scripture and the Liturgy that the cardinal suggested that the pope consult Scrima directly before concluding the discussions on _Dei_ _Verbum_. Moreover, Scrima’s essay on the role of role of Virgin Mary was widely circulated at the council and, when _Orientalium Ecclesiarum_ (_OE_) was ready to restore _communicatio in sacris_ with the East, Scrima asked Congar to convince the Pope to freeze the approval process, since the Orthodox do not allow it even in extremis. As a result, _OE_ 29 allows Eucharistic sharing with the East only after consultation with ‘the ordinaries of the separated churches’.

[^c29-6] Afanasiev’s essay on ‘The Church which Presides in Love’ was referenced in the preparatory drafts of _De Ecclesia_; its mention was removed from the final document only in an effort to limit all citations to biblical and patristic sources. His works influenced the discussions about the Church as communion, the contrast between universalist and eucharistic ecclesiologies, the role of the bishop in the Eucharistic assembly, and [^c29-7] the nature of the Eucharistic community. Moreover, he attended the fourth session as SPCU’s guest, and his work was recommended for further study to the participating bishops. Thus, it is not surprising that _Lumen Gentium_ (_LG_) bears a striking resemblance to his Eucharistic ecclesiology that affirmed the fullness of the local Church gathered around its bishop in the Eucharistic assembly, with all its ministries: ‘This Church of Christ is really present in all legitimately organized local groups of the faithful, which, insofar as they are united to their pastors, are also quite appropriately called Churches in the New Testament. For these are in [^c29-8] fact, in their own localities, the new people called by God, in the power of the Holy Spirit’ (_LG_ 26). Unfortunately, Afanasiev died less than a year after the close of the council, so his own reception of Vatican II remains incomplete.

[^c29-6]: In _The Primacy of Peter: Essays in Ecclesiology and the Early Church_, ed. John Meyendorff (Crestwood, NY: St Vladimir’s Seminary Press, 1992), 91–143; originally published as ‘L’Église qui préside dans l’amour’, in _La Primauté de Pierre dans_ _l’Eglise orthodoxe_, ed. N. Afanassieff et al. (Neuchâtel: Ed. Delchaux et Niestlé, 1960), 57–110.

[^c29-7]: _AS_ I/4, p. 87, n. 2; II/1, p. 252, n. 57; III/1, p. 254. See Anastacia Wooden, ‘The Limits of the Church: Ecclesiological Project of Nicolas Afanasiev’, PhD diss., Catholic University of America, 2019, 125–26.

[^c29-8]: While applauding such passages, John Meyendorff pointed out that others contradict this eucharistic ecclesiology, as for example when particular churches are characterized as ‘constituted after the model of the universal Church’ and ‘portions of the universal Church’ (_LG_ 23). Moreover, Meyendorff was critical of intercommunion as a consequence of Afanasiev’s Eucharistic ecclesiology, as well as of _Unitatis Redintegratio_’s third chapter, which allows for intercommunion, although for different reasons. John Meyendorff, ‘Vatican II: A Preliminary Reaction’, _St Vladimir’s Theological Quarterly_ 9, no. 1 (1965): 29–31.

**[p. 496]** Another observer—the lay theologian and World Council of Churches (WCC) delegate Nikos Nissiotis— wrote some of the most detailed analyses of the council. Early on, he was among the sceptics who wondered why a pope who could speak infallibly would convene a council. He also wished that the council had not been called ‘ecumenical’, since in the current divided context, no church can hold an ecumenical council by itself. Moreover, he considered that all churches should be represented by bishops with full voting rights at least when discussing ecumenism—an unrealistic desire, in retrospect. He regarded the work of the council with [^c29-9] great admiration, especially for the bishops who conveyed the comments of the observers to the plenaries.

[^c29-9]: Nissiotis considered that the Catholic bishops present went through ‘a veritable school of ecumenism’. Nikos Nissiotis, ‘Comité Central du Conseil œcuménique, Genève, 8–17 février 1966: Rapports sur le 2e Concile du Vatican’, _Istina_ 11, nos. 2–3 (1966): 255–56.

[^c29-10] However, he persistently criticized the conciliar documents for being weakly rooted in pneumatology. The conversation that Yves Congar had with him and Schmemann is by now well known. The two observers said: ‘If we were to prepare a treatise _De Ecclesia_, we would draft a chapter on the Holy Spirit, to which we would [^c29-11] add a second chapter on Christian anthropology, and that would be all.’ The pneumatological turn of the council, while insufficient by contemporary Catholic and Orthodox standards, was certainly momentous.

[^c29-10]: See e.g. Nikos Nissiotis, ‘The Main Ecclesiological Problem of the Second Vatican Council and the Position of the Non- Roman Churches Facing It’, _Journal of Ecumenical Studies_ 2, no. 1 (1965): 49–50.

[^c29-11]: Yves Congar, _I Believe in the Holy Spirit_, vol. 2, _He Is Lord and Giver of Life_, trans. David Smith (New York: Seabury, 1983), 66.

The positive experience of the observers began the process of a favourable reception of Vatican II in later Orthodox theology. Between 1964 and 1968, Dumitru Staniloae published ten articles that dealt directly with [^c29-12] Vatican II. Given his political isolation and five-year incarceration during communism, the level of his familiarity with conciliar debates is astounding. While he appreciated the affirmation that all bishops— including the pope—share in the same episcopal ordination, Staniloae considered that Vatican II strengthened papal infallibility and primacy compared to Vatican I; while Vatican I did not earnestly address the episcopal college, Vatican II explicitly subordinated the bishops to the pope on juridical grounds. While Staniloae appreciated _Lumen Gentium_’s stipulation that the bishops are not merely vicars of the pope, but exercise a power that is proper to them, he criticized the pope’s interventions over the episcopal majority, indicating that the bishops are conditioned by the pope, but not the other way around. The understanding **[p. 497]** that a bishop cannot exercise his ministry unless he is part of the College of Bishops is a positive step towards communion ecclesiology, as is the affirmation that the infallibility of the Church belongs to all the members—hierarchy and laity alike, the latter being endowed with a ‘supernatural appreciation of the [^c29-13] faith’ (_LG_ 12). When commenting on the fourth and fifth sessions, Staniloae appreciated the council’s openness to the world. And yet, he detected some competition between the conservative and progressive factions, reflected in the documents on religious liberty, freedom of conscience and its relationship to truth, and the dual purpose of marriage, namely procreation and conjugal love. He was particularly disturbed that Paul VI did not allow an earnest discussion of priestly celibacy. Nevertheless, Staniloae esteemed the departure from the two-source theory of Revelation (Scripture and Tradition) and the recognition of the ecclesial status of Protestants reflected in the expression ‘ecclesial communities’. Perhaps under pressure from communist censure, Staniloae highly praised the council’s promotion of peace and its refusal to [^c29-14] condemn communism.

[^c29-12]: The only article available in English appears in Dumitru Staniloae, _Theology and the Church_, trans. Robert Barringer (Crestwood, NY: St Vladimir’s Seminary Press, 1980), 45–72. This is a representative sample where the Orthodox author begins with observations concerning Vatican II and then creatively develops Orthodox theology in dialogue with the council.

[^c29-13]: Dumitru Staniloae, ‘Doctrina Catolica a infailibilitatii la I-iul si al II-lea Conciliu de la Vatican [The Catholic Doctrine of Infallibility at the First and Second Vatican Councils]’, _Ortodoxia_ 17, no. 4 (1965): 459–92.

[^c29-14]: Dumitru Staniloae, ‘Dezbaterile si hotaririle sesiunii a patra a Conciliului al II-lea de la Vatican [The Debates and Decisions of the Fourth Session of the Second Vatican Council]’, _Ortodoxia_ 18, no. 1 (1966): 8–34.

Already in the elements briefly sketched above, two important theological themes develop in Orthodox and Catholic theologies: _pneumatology_ and _communion ecclesiology_. Naturally, these topics did not first emerge at the council but were anchored in the rediscovery of the patristic and biblical roots of theology in _la nouvelle théologie_, the early pneumatological ecclesiology of Johann Adam Möhler, the theology of the Church as _sobornost_ of Alexei Khomiakov, and the ecumenical engagements of the Paris School involving Georges Florovsky and Vladimir Lossky, to give just a few examples. These authors and schools of thought represented the catalysts of significant theological development across denominational lines, coming into full prominence after the Second Vatican Council. Thus, the interchange between Orthodox and Catholic theologies continued, bringing the pneumatologies and ecclesiologies of the two churches closer together. For example, the parallels between the thought of Yves Congar and John Zizioulas are unmistakable. Their early ecclesiologies were markedly Christocentric, as were Vatican II’s early schemata. But later on, the two theologians and the council took a pneumatological turn. The council—as Zizioulas contended—could not completely abandon its Christological structure, but it was only able to add the references to the Holy Spirit more as an afterthought than a constitutive structure; a future Vatican III should make pneumatology constitutive of both Christology and ecclesiology, which in turn would make communion into the condition [^c29-15] of ecclesiological existence, of the very being of the Church. Zizioulas attempted—with varying degrees of **[p. 498]** success—to give an equally prominent role to the Son and the Spirit in the life of the Church, which [^c29-16] ‘breathes’ the Spirit continuously, calling upon the Spirit to descend upon it as in the _epiclesis_, in contrast with the view of the Church as the Christologically constituted perfect society. This Eucharistic approach to ecclesiology remains prominent in Zizioulas’s address to the 2005 International Synod of Bishops in Rome:

[^c29-15]: In this same context, Zizioulas writes a positive evaluation of Vatican II, which ‘has given hope and promise to many people that something can be done. … [T]he introduction of the notion of communion into ecclesiology … combined with the rediscovery of the importance of the _laos_ of God and the local Church, can help even the Orthodox themselves to be faithful to their identity.’ John D. Zizioulas, _Being as Communion: Studies in Personhood and the Church_, Contemporary Greek Theologians 4 (Crestwood, NY: St Vladimir’s Seminary Press, 1985), 123, 39–42.

[^c29-16]: Ibid., 185.

The ecclesiology of communion promoted by Vatican II and deepened further by eminent Roman Catholic theologians can make sense only if it derives from the Eucharistic life of the Church. The Eucharist belongs not simply to the _bene esse_ (well-being) but to the _esse_ (being) of the Church. The whole life, word and structure of the Church is Eucharistic in its very essence.[^c29-17]

[^c29-17]: ‘Synodus Episcoporum Bulletin: XI Ordinary General Assembly of the Synod of Bishops 2-23 October 2005’. This quote is a return to Zizioulas’s earlier contention that the Eucharist makes a Church—a statement originating with Henri de Lubac, and then Vatican II. See Paul McPartlan, _The Eucharist Makes the Church: Henri de Lubac and John Zizioulas in Dialogue_ (Edinburgh: T&T Clark, 1993).

These interchanges between Catholic and Orthodox theologies represent a solid foundation for addressing the most contested issue within communion ecclesiology, namely the reform of papal primacy, which [^c29-18] Nissiotis regarded as a practical impossibility during the council, but with hope for the future. As Peter De Mey shows, Vatican II’s treatment of the papacy elicited varied Orthodox responses. On the one hand, Nissiotis was surprised by how openly the bishops discussed collegiality and how they did not regard conciliarity as automatically counteracting papal primacy. Similarly, Zizioulas engages with Ioannis Karmiris’s recognition of a primacy of honour for the bishop of Rome; however, Zizioulas remarks, this kind of primacy of honour remains ambiguous and no longer exists in Orthodoxy (an allusion to Constantinople’s claim of a real primacy within Orthodoxy, not recognized by Moscow), and both conciliarity and primacy are of divine right. On the other hand, Schmemann regarded the ecclesiologies of Vatican II as presenting only one of the many historical ecclesiological models. Karmiris and Basil Krivocheine, while regarding Vatican II as a positive first step in regard to the relationship between the pope [^c29-19] and the College of Bishops, were unhappy that Vatican II did not depart enough from Vatican I. Despite these mixed reactions, Joseph Famerée shows that Orthodox and Catholics have progressed significantly since Vatican II: the two churches spoke in unison at Ravenna in 2007 on equality among the bishops and their intricate connection with the local Eucharistic assembly. According to Famerée, the statements of the **[p. 499]** Catholic bishops at Vatican II or of the Orthodox experts mentioned above are not as important as the Ravenna declaration that speaks with one voice, as part of the common reception made possible by the [^c29-20] openness that Vatican II initiated.

[^c29-18]: Nikos Nissiotis, ‘Mouvement œcuménique et Vatican II, un point de vue orthodoxe’, _Istina_ 11, nos. 2–3 (1965–66): 316–17.

[^c29-19]: Peter De Mey, ‘Conciliarité et autorité au niveau universel dans l’Église: de _Lumen Gentium_ au _Document de Ravenne_’, _Irénikon_ 83, no. 2 (2015): 202–6.

[^c29-20]: Joseph Famerée, ‘L’Église locale selon Lumen Gentium: Réactions orthodoxes à l’époque du concile’, _Irénikon_ 88, no. 2 (2015): 164–80.

Clearly, recent Orthodox ecclesiology has focused on Trinitarian, Eucharistic, and communion ecclesiologies as a result of the questions raised by theologians writing on Vatican II (Lossky, Florovsky, Staniloae, Zizioulas), or even present as observers (Afanasiev, Nissiotis, and Schmemann). The themes discussed at Vatican II became central for Orthodox theology, too. Having highlighted some of the Orthodox theological developments related to Vatican II, it is now important to turn to the influence that the council had upon the life of the Orthodox Church.

### 3. The Life of the Orthodox Church

As we saw above, the relationship between Rome and Constantinople varied greatly between 1961 and 1965, reaching unimaginable levels towards the end of the council. Although Athenagoras was unable to visit Vatican II as he intended, he initiated the lifting of the mutual excommunications of 1054. A moment of grace occurred at the concluding vigil of the council, on 7 December 1965. After the reading of the decision to ‘lift the sentences of excommunication, remove them from the midst of the Church, and consign them to [^c29-21] oblivion’, Pope Paul VI and Metropolitan Meliton of Heliopolis (representing Patriarch Athenagoras) embraced each other, to the enthusiastic applause of the assembly.

[^c29-21]: Alberigo and Komonchak, _History of Vatican II_, 5:472–78.

This dialogue of love set the tone for the Orthodox–Catholic theological dialogues to follow. Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew does not hesitate to affirm that, as a result of Vatican II, Catholic and Orthodox churches have experienced in common a significant spiritual renewal; a ‘return to the sources’ through the study of the Bible, the Fathers, and the Liturgy; the liberation from the rigid limits of scholasticism in favour of the openness of ecumenical encounters; the mutual annulment of the anathemas of 1054; the frequent exchange of annual visits and salutations; the return of relics, and the establishment of theological [^c29-22] dialogues. The oldest and most prolific among regional dialogues is the North American Orthodox– Catholic Theological Consultation, whose first meeting took place on 9 September 1965. Among the numerous documents that this consultation has produced, the statements on _Baptism and Sacramental Economy_ (1999) and _The Filioque: A Church Dividing Issue?_ (2003) are noteworthy. The former is the only **[p. 500]** official statement that affirms explicitly that Orthodox and Catholic churches recognize each other’s baptisms—a recognition that many take for granted, even though in ultra-Orthodox circles, rebaptisms still occur. The latter statement’s (mostly tacit) reception put to rest the thorny issue of the Filioque (i.e., the addition, in the usage of the Western Church, to the creed of Nicaea Constantinople of the phrase ‘the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father [and the Son]’), which is no longer the subject of ecumenical dialogues. Without an official recognition, it would be an exaggeration to state that this issue has been completely resolved, but the silence on this subject speaks loudly: the Filioque ‘need no longer divide us’.

[^c29-22]: Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew I, ‘Greeting by his All-Holiness Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew on the Occasion of the 50th anniversary of the Opening of the Second Vatican Council; Rome, St. Peter’s Square, October 22, 2012’, _Greek_ _Orthodox Theological Review_ 57, nos. 1–4 (2012): 380.

Other regional dialogues followed, culminating in the establishment of the Joint International Commission for Theological Dialogue between the Roman Catholic Church and the Orthodox Church in 1979. In its initial stage, the international dialogue focused on sacramental theology, especially the Eucharist and Holy Orders. In its second stage, it responded to the new context created after the fall of communism but entered a period of crisis in the late 1990s, when the Orthodox protested at the re-emergence of Byzantine Catholic churches in Eastern Europe. After a six-year hiatus, the international dialogue resumed in 2006, in this third stage focusing on issues of primacy and synodality.

Beyond the theological significance of these statements, one cannot underestimate the importance of pan- Orthodox participation in international dialogues. While the Orthodox churches that enjoyed political freedom had participated in the ecumenical movement since 1948 with the establishment of the WCC, the churches under communism were forbidden to enter into dialogue with the West. They opposed ecumenism until 1961, when the Vatican invited observers from all Orthodox churches. To offer a unifled response to this invitation, all autocephalous Orthodox churches participated in three Rhodes conferences of 1961, 1963, and 1964, which gradually opened up the possibility for the churches under oppressive communist regimes to be involved in ecumenism—most immediately in the dialogue with the Catholic Church, but also in ecumenism in general, through the WCC and bilateral dialogues. The importance of Vatican II for Orthodox ecumenism cannot be overstated: Orthodox churches from the Eastern Bloc owe their ecumenical participation to Rome’s invitation to send observers to Vatican II.

Besides official dialogues, Nicholas Denysenko documents ‘the cross-pollinating exchanges between the [^c29-23] Orthodox and Catholic Churches’. These were informal exchanges between Orthodox and Catholic theologians such as Afanasiev, Schmemann, and Congar, who influenced each other as they studied the liturgy together. Their agreement on the communitarian nature of lay and ordained priesthoods rooted in a common baptism is what gave rise to _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ (_SC_)’s affirmation that ‘all the faithful should be led to that full, conscious, and active participation in liturgical celebrations which is demanded by the **[p. 501]** very nature of the liturgy, and to which the Christian people, “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a redeemed people” (1 Pet 2:9, 4–5) have a right and obligation by reason of their baptism’ (_SC_ 14). Vatican II’s stature, in turn, influenced several liturgical reforms in the Orthodox Church. Thus, on the one hand, Orthodox theologians used the historical-critical methods of the West to study the liturgy and initiated profound liturgical reforms, even though they also cautioned against chaotic changes, as they perceived the reforms that _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ set in motion in Catholicism. It became common to change from liturgical prayers said silently to being read out loud; from laborious church architecture and Byzantine-style iconography to more simple, modern architecture and modest iconography; from prominent roles assigned to the priest and the cantor to active participation of all the faithful who often practise frequent communion. On the other hand, looking favourably to the role of the Spirit in the Orthodox liturgy, Catholicism revived the split _epiclesis_, added three new Eucharistic prayers, and emphasized the role of the Spirit in the sacrament of confirmation. Catholics experienced a renewed role of the laity in the liturgy, including assistance with the distribution of communion, frequent reception of communion, and prayer in vernacular languages.[^c29-24]

[^c29-23]: Nicholas E. Denysenko, _Liturgical Reform after Vatican II: The Impact on Eastern Orthodoxy_ (Minneapolis, MN: Fortress, 2015), 9.

[^c29-24]: Ibid., 357–65.

Unexpectedly, the Second Vatican Council also became a catalyst for pan-Orthodox synodality. For obvious political reasons, pan-Orthodox synodality was impossible for much of the second millennium. But the early twentieth century saw the first efforts to convene a pan-Orthodox council. Interrupted by two world wars and the emergence of militant atheist communist regimes, these efforts were reignited by the Vatican’s invitation to send ecumenical observers. As stated above, the 1961, 1963, and 1964 Rhodes conferences attempted to offer a common response to this invitation and to begin in earnest the preparations for a pan-Orthodox council. These latter efforts led to the Holy and Great Council of Crete (2016), which ended up being attended by only ten of the fourteen autocephalous churches. The Moscow Patriarchate and three other churches under its sphere of influence announced their withdrawal from Crete just days before its opening. Although not the pan-Orthodox council that was intended, Crete remains the most notable instance of Orthodox conciliarity in recent times.

Vatican II not only reignited pan-Orthodox synodality but was also the model for Crete regarding the invitation of ecumenical observers. The Vatican delegated Cardinal Kurt Koch and Bishop Brian Farrell, president and secretary respectively of the pontifical Council for Promoting Christian Unity. Their role, however, was limited to being passive spectators at the opening and closing sessions. While this invitation is an encouraging sign of ecumenical openness, Vatican II remains the standard for consultation with other churches and the prominent role of observers in the conciliar process.

Another practice that Vatican II consecrated in modern times—but is in fact the tradition of the ancient councils—was the involvement of _periti_ or theological experts, even though they did not have a vote. The influences of then-deacon Athanasius of Alexandria on the First Ecumenical Council, or of Congar and Karl **[p. 502]** Rahner on Vatican II, are amply documented. Orthodox theologians attempted to bring their contributions to Crete as well. For example, the Orthodox Theological Society in America produced a set of responses to the drafts of Crete, which were read by some participating bishops. Moreover, churches were encouraged to include theological experts in their delegations, as some did. Sadly, the four absent churches held Crete captive by not allowing it to deviate in a meaningful way from the previously agreed conciliar drafts, which had the overall approval of the missing churches. Even so, the absent churches have not recognized Crete. This was a lost opportunity for Orthodox theologians to influence a council as Catholic theologians influenced Vatican II—a model difficult to emulate.

Looking at the theologies of Crete and Vatican II, two elements stand out. When Vatican II was first announced as an ecumenical council, the Orthodox reaction was swift: in our divided context, none of our [^c29-25] churches can convene an ecumenical council, since we do not recognize each other fully as Church. Recent Catholic theology distinguishes between the seven ecumenical councils of the largely undivided Church and [^c29-26] the general councils that the Catholic Church held afterwards. Similarly, Crete did not regard itself as an ecumenical council. But a minority faction of participating bishops challenged the ecclesiological principle behind this affirmation; their understanding that Orthodoxy alone can be called ‘Church’ was based on a narrow understanding of the limits of the Church. Under their influence, Crete only timidly refers to non- [^c29-27] Orthodox as churches, and it makes the distinction between ‘churches’ and ‘confessions’. Up until Crete, Orthodoxy had never made this distinction, with one exception: in a pre-conciliar draft entitled ‘The Relationship of the Orthodox Church to Other Christian Churches and Communities’ (1976). Neither did Catholic theology do so before Vatican II, when it introduced the distinction between ‘churches’ and ‘ecclesial communities’ (_Unitatis Redintegratio_ 22); in the case of the latter, the emphasis fell on ‘ecclesial’— of the Church—as opposed to the negative connotation that this expression received subsequently, as a non-recognition of Protestants and Anglicans as Church. It is thus surprising that this distinction was introduced at Crete by the participants who oppose ecumenism; they were probably unaware that their distinction was an innovation from Vatican II and later misappropriated to diminish the ecclesial character of others. Ironically, they applied this term even to the Catholic Church. Vatican II remains a model of coexistence of competing factions and a standard of conciliar theological profundity.

[^c29-25]: Nikos Nissiotis, ‘Is the Vatican Council Really Ecumenical?’, _The Ecumenical Review_ 16, no. 4 (1964): 367.

[^c29-26]: Richard R. Gaillardetz, _Teaching with Authority: A Theology of the Magisterium in the Church_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 1997), 198–99.

[^c29-27]: Holy Great Council of Crete, ‘Relations of the Orthodox Church with the Rest of the Christian World’ (2016): no. 6, https://www.holycouncil.org/-/rest-of-christian-world.

Having begun with the words of one Orthodox participant at the Second Vatican Council, it is appropriate to conclude with the words of another observer. Nissiotis considered that Vatican II had an ecumenical **[p. 503]** character in the sense of challenging other churches to critical self-examination, renewal leading to a [^c29-28] new evangelism, and repentance for our lack of common action in the world. The reception of Vatican II by the Orthodox Church in its theology and life makes Nissiotis’s ecumenical task achievable. Catholic and Orthodox churches will hopefully continue to unite in a new evangelism and common action in the world.

[^c29-28]: Nissiotis, ‘The Main Ecclesiological Problem’, 62.

## 30. The Reception of Vatican II by Anglicans

Mark D. Chapman

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 504]** Anglicans have never found it easy to define the essence of Anglicanism. For much of its history, they have embraced a wide diversity of opinions and have often seen a virtue in comprehensiveness. From the beginnings of Anglicanism, it has always been weak on canon law and on clear definitions of doctrine: even during times of religious upheaval, the vast majority of the laity have never had to subscribe to confessions. This diversity has meant that Anglicans have often told different stories about their origins and have [^c30-1] elevated different periods of church history into their defining myths of origin. Some, particularly the High Church divines of the seventeenth century and the Anglo-Catholics from the nineteenth, have located their identity in the Early Church and stress the importance of continuity from the Church of the Fathers. Others, particularly those of a more Puritan or Evangelical persuasion, have emphasized the Protestant nature of the Church of England and its sister churches and have located the Church’s identity in the cardinal doctrines of the Reformation, such as _sola scriptura_ and _sola gratia_. Yet, partly because Anglicans never had a magisterial reformer of the stature of a Luther or a Zwingli or a Calvin, the Protestant identity of Anglicanism has always been contested: even when it was verging on adopting Calvinist confessions in the [^c30-2] 1590s, it avoided incorporating them into its official teachings. This situation has continued into the present: an outsider looking on might find very few similarities between two Anglican churches, one of **[p. 505]** which might look like a Pentecostal gathering and another like an unreformed Tridentine mass.

[^c30-1]: See Mark D. Chapman, _Anglican Theology_ (London: T&T Clark, 2012).

[^c30-2]: See ibid., 139. Alec Ryrie, ‘The Reformation in Anglicanism’, in _The Oxford Handbook of Anglican Studies_, ed. Mark D. Chapman, Sathianathan Clarke, and Martyn Percy (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2015), 34–45.

Even though there might seem to be little that unites Anglicans, for much of the history of Anglicanism after the separation from Rome in the 1530s there was one thing that provided a link across the breadth of the Anglican Church: shared opposition to the pope and the Roman Catholic Church. The very first English liturgical text, Cranmer’s Litany of 1544, implored deliverance from the ‘detestable enormities’ of the [^c30-3] bishop of Rome, and the most important apologist of the Elizabethan Settlement, Bishop John Jewel of Salisbury (1522–71), formulated his theology in opposition to the Church of Rome, which he felt had [^c30-4] ‘forsaken the fellowship of the Holy Fathers’. England (and, following the Act of Union of 1707, Britain) was a Protestant nation with a Protestant monarch. This situation was to last for a long time: the Act of Settlement of 1701 meant that the Supreme Governor would always be a Protestant—somewhat confusingly, for quite a period after the accession of the Hanoverians to the British throne in 1714, the monarch and Supreme Governor of the Church of England was a Lutheran.

[^c30-3]: Eric J. Hunt, ed., _Cranmer’s First Litany, 1544 and Merbeckes Book of Common Prayer Noted, 1550_ (London: SPCK, 1939).

[^c30-4]: John Jewel, _The Works of Bishop John_ Jewel, 4 vols (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press for the Parker Society, 1845– 50), 4:901.

Things changed only very gradually, and even then, there was little questioning of the Protestant identity of the Church of England. Thus, although there was a change in tone in relation to Roman Catholics— [^c30-5] especially during the Napoleonic Wars—which culminated in Catholic Emancipation in 1829, the Protestant nature of British society and the hegemony of the Church of England in the main power bases of [^c30-6] the Establishment, including the ancient universities, remained largely untouched. At the same time, some Anglicans, who formed the so-called Oxford Movement or ‘Tractarianism’ after the series of tracts they produced, moved towards an understanding of the Anglican Church that downplayed the role of Protestantism and the Reformation and emphasized the apostolic inheritance from the Church of the Fathers. Yet even they, for the most part, were hostile to Rome and especially towards what they saw as the system of papalism, which challenged the authority of the Early Church with the visible Church of the [^c30-7] present. Many key members of the bench of bishops were resolutely opposed to Rome. For instance, **[p. 506]** Christopher Wordsworth, bishop of Lincoln and author of the official Church of England response to the [^c30-8] First Vatican Council, maintained that the Roman Church was the Babylon of the Apocalypse; he campaigned against the establishment of a Roman Catholic hierarchy in England in 1850, which was often [^c30-9] referred to by its opponents as the ‘Papal aggression’.

[^c30-5]: See E. R. Norman, _The English Catholic Church in the Nineteenth Century_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1984); Sheridan Gilley, ‘The Roman Catholic Church in Britain’, in _A History of Religion in Britain: Practice and Belief from Pre-Roman Times_ _to the Present_, ed. Sheridan Gilley and W. J. Sheils (Oxford: Blackwell, 1994), 346–62; John Bossy, _The English Catholic_ _Community, 1570–1850_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1976).

[^c30-6]: Linda Colley, _Britons: Forging the Nation 1707–1983_, 2nd ed. (New Haven: Yale University Press, 2005), 321–63.

[^c30-7]: See Mark D. Chapman, _Fantasy of Reunion: Anglicans, Catholics, and Ecumenism, 1833–1880_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014), 27–67.

[^c30-8]: See Robert Fitzsimons, ‘The Church of England and the First Vatican Council’, _Journal of Religious History_ 27 (2003): 29–46.

[^c30-9]: Christopher Wordsworth, _Union with Rome: Is Not the Church of Rome the Babylon of the Book of Revelation?_ (London: Rivington, 1850). On British anti-Catholicism, see John Wolffe, _The Protestant Crusade in Great Britain 1829–1860_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1991) and Denis G. Paz, _Popular Anti-Catholicism in Mid-Victorian England_ (Stanford, CA: Stanford University Press, 1992).

From the other side there was an equal reluctance from most Roman Catholics to offer concessions to the Church of England, even if a few Romantic medieval enthusiasts made overtures to it, or at least to a few [^c30-10] equally enthusiastic Anglo-Catholics. There was sometimes particular vitriol from some of those who had been received into the Roman Catholic Church. For instance, Henry Edward Manning, who had converted from the Church of England in 1851, was vehement in his opposition to the Church of his baptism. Answering Edward Bouverie Pusey’s call for a united front against liberalism following the publication of [^c30-11] the controversial collection _Essays and Reviews_ in 1860, he wrote a strong defence of the uniqueness of the [^c30-12] Roman Catholic Church. In 1864, shortly before he became archbishop of Westminster, he published _The Workings of the Holy Spirit in the Church of England_, which took the form of a letter to Pusey. Although he was ready to admit the possibility of grace outside the Roman Catholic Church, he nevertheless felt that the Church of England was a teacher of nothing more than ‘fragmentary truths, shattered, disjointed from the [^c30-13] perfect unity of the Christian revelation’. He rejoiced to ‘watch with satisfaction every change, social and [^c30-14] political, which weakens [the] hold [of the Church of England] on the country’. That meant that for Manning, the Church of England was ‘not only no part of the Church, but no church of divine foundation. It is a human institution, sustained as it was founded by a human authority, without priesthood, without [^c30-15] sacraments, without absolution, without the real presence of Jesus upon its altars.’ The Roman Catholic approach to reunion was thus simply one of return.

[^c30-10]: Chapman, _Fantasy of Reunion_, 27–67.

[^c30-11]: See Mark D. Chapman, _Theology and Society in Three Cities_ (Cambridge: James Clarke, 2014), 65–77.

[^c30-12]: Chapman, _Fantasy of Reunion_, 74–76.

[^c30-13]: Henry Edward Manning, _The Workings of the Holy Spirit in the Church of England: A Letter to the Rev. E. B. Pusey, D.D._ (London: Longmans, 1864), 21. See also James Pereiro, _Cardinal Manning: An Intellectual Biography_ (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1998), 184–99.

[^c30-14]: Manning, _The Workings of the Holy Spirit_, 29.

[^c30-15]: Ibid., 42.

This understanding was replicated in the teachings emanating from the Vatican which focused on returning home to mother. In his Apostolic Letter _Praeclara Gratulationis Publicae_ of 20 June 1894, for instance, Pope Leo XIII issued an invitation to other Christians to return to ‘the Unity which has ever existed in the Catholic **[p. 507]** Church and can never fail … The Church, as the common mother of all, has long been calling you back to her.’ Two years later, the bull _Apostolicae Curae_ of 18 September 1896 (‘On the Nullity of Anglican Orders’) declared Anglican Orders ‘absolutely null and utterly void’, which made all Anglican clergy nothing more than laymen. From that point, even the most ardent of Anglican ecumenists held out little realistic hope for reunion with Roman Catholics.

Even though there were secret conversations from 1921 to 1927 between Anglicans—under the leadership of Lord Halifax, the most prominent lay Anglo-Catholic—and Roman Catholics—under Désiré Joseph Cardinal [^c30-16] Mercier, archbishop of Malines and Fernand Portal—these could never have resulted in anything concrete. The Roman position was once again asserted by Pius XI in the encyclical _Mortalium Animos_ (_MA_) of 6 January 1928, which outlawed any Roman Catholic participation in ecumenical assemblies (_MA_ 8) and affirmed unequivocally that in the ‘one Church of Christ no man can be or remain who does not accept, recognise and obey the authority and supremacy of Peter and his legitimate successors’ (_MA_ 11). All that was left to non- Catholics was thus ‘to draw nigh to the Apostolic See, set up in the City which Peter and Paul, the Princes of the Apostles, consecrated by their blood’ (_MA_ 12). Even though there were some studies of Anglicanism by Roman Catholics, including Yves Congar, who particularly admired its liturgy, the official position remained [^c30-17] immovable.

[^c30-16]: See Viscount Halifax, _Notes on the Conversations at Malines 1921–1925: Points of Agreement_ (London: Mowbray, 1928); R. J. Lahey, ‘The Origins and Approval of the Malines Conversations’, _Church History_ 43, no. 3 (1974): 366–84; Bernard Barlow, _‘A_ _Brother Knocking at the Door’: The Malines Conversations 1921–1925_ (Norwich: Canterbury, 1996). H. R. McAdoo, ‘Anglican/Roman Catholic Relations 1717–1980: A Detection of Themes’, in _Rome and the Anglicans: Historical and_ _Doctrinal Aspects of Anglican–Roman Catholic Relations_, ed. Wolfgang Haase (Berlin: Walter de Gruyter, 1982), 195–210.

[^c30-17]: See Yves Congar, _Divided Christendom: A Catholic Study of the Problem of Reunion_ (London: G. Bles, 1939), 181.

### 2. The Run-up to Vatican II

What is obvious is that, despite any talk of an ecumenical winter, relations between the Church of England, the wider Anglican Communion, and the Roman Catholic Church have changed completely from this approach. The election of Pope John XXIII in October 1958 marked the beginning of a sea change in relationships between the churches. This affected not just the Roman Catholic Church but also other denominations, especially the Anglican Communion, which was singled out from other Protestants in the ecumenical decree _Unitatis Redintegratio_ (_UR_) as a separate form of historic Christianity which held a ‘special [^c30-18] place’ (_UR_ 13). The ecumenical mood which had developed through the twentieth century, beginning with **[p. 508]** the Edinburgh World Missionary Conference in 1910, had affected the nature and practice of Anglicanism and had led several Anglican churches to unite with other Christians, most importantly on the Indian [^c30-19] subcontinent. The tone of the debate between Anglicans and Roman Catholics changed quickly. Within the Anglican churches (with rare exceptions), the polemics of the Reformation period began to disappear [^c30-20] through the century, even among the most Protestant-minded. Over the course of the Second Vatican Council, Roman Catholic rhetoric and practice was also completely transformed: where Roman Catholicism experienced a quick defrosting, other communions had long been experiencing a slow thaw through much of the twentieth century.

[^c30-18]: For the general history of recent Anglican–Roman Catholic relations, see Mary Reath, _Rome and Canterbury: The Elusive_ _Search for Unity_ (Lanham, MD: Rowman and Littlefield, 2007).

[^c30-19]: See Charlotte Methuen, ‘Ecumenism’, in Chapman, Clarke, and Percy, _The Oxford Handbook of Anglican Studies_, 464–78; and Sathianathan Clarke, ‘Ecumenism and Post-Anglicanism, Transnational Anglican Compactism and Cosmo- transAnglicanism’, ibid., 341–56.

[^c30-20]: Executive Committee of the Evangelical Fellowship, ‘Open Letter to the Anglican Communion’, in _Anglicans and Roman_ _Catholics: The Search for Unity_, ed. Christopher Hill and Edward Yarnold, SJ (London: SPCK/CTS, 1994), 283–97; Martin Davie, ‘Anglican Ecumenism: The Liberal Catholic Consensus and the Conservative Evangelical Challenge’, in _Paths to_ _Unity: Explorations in Ecumenical Method_, ed. Paul Avis (London: Church House, 2004), 29–51.

The first signs of a significant closer fellowship between Anglicans and Roman Catholics can be detected from the time of the visit of the archbishop of Canterbury, Geoffrey Fisher, to Pope John XXIII on 2 December 1960. This took place very soon after the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity (SPCU) was [^c30-21] established under Augustin Cardinal Bea as its first president. This was the first visit of an archbishop of Canterbury to a pope since the Reformation and, despite the many efforts to treat it simply as a courtesy [^c30-22] visit, it gained a deep symbolic meaning. According to Adrian Hastings, Fisher was ‘a firm Protestant, [^c30-23] almost intuitively suspicious of Rome’; few expected much to come out of the meeting. Fisher was, however, also a committed ecumenist, even if his energies were principally directed towards the World [^c30-24] Council of Churches (WCC) and the quest for full organic unity with Protestant denominations in Britain.

[^c30-21]: See William Purcell, _Fisher of Canterbury_ (London: Hodder & Stoughton, 1969); Edward Carpenter, _Archbishop Fisher: His_ _Life and Times_ (Norwich: Canterbury, 1991); David Hein, _Geoffrey Fisher: Archbishop of Canterbury_ (Cambridge: James Clarke, 2008); Andrew Chandler and David Hein, _Archbishop Fisher 1945–1961: Church, State and World_ (Farnham, NC: Ashgate, 2012).

[^c30-22]: Peter Staples, ‘Archbishop Geoffrey Francis Fisher: An Appraisal’, _Nederlands Theologisch Tijdschriff_, 28 (1974): 239–63; Andrew Chandler and Charlotte Hansen, _Observing Vatican II: The Confidential Reports of the Archbishop of Canterbury’s_ _Representative, 1961–1964_ (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press for the Royal Historical Society, 2011), 1–20.

[^c30-23]: Adrian Hastings, _A History of English Christianity, 1920–1985_ (London: Collins, 1986), 522.

[^c30-24]: See Carpenter, _Archbishop Fisher_, 309–70; Hein, _Geoffrey Fisher_, 74–77; Chandler and Hein, _Archbishop Fisher_, ch. 6.

Pope John had communicated his willingness to meet Fisher in Rome to Johannes (Jan) Willebrands, secretary of the new SPCU. Willebrands sent a formal letter on 27 October 1960 to John Satterthwaite (1925– 2014), general secretary of the Church of England’s Council for Foreign Relations from 1955 to 1970 when he became bishop of Fulham and Gibraltar, with formal responsibility for European chaplaincies of the Church [^c30-25] **[p. 509]** of England. Willebrands had earlier met Fisher at the WCC assembly in St Andrews, Scotland, in August 1959, although he denied planning the meeting on that occasion. The invitation provoked a modest amount [^c30-26] of opposition from some Protestant-minded Anglicans and free churchmen.

[^c30-25]: Carpenter, _Archbishop Fisher_, 707; Staples, ‘Archbishop Geoffrey Francis Fisher’, 260–61.

[^c30-26]: Owen Chadwick, ‘The Church of England and the Church of Rome, from the Beginning of the Nineteenth Century to the Present Day’, in _Anglican Initiatives in Church Unity_, ed. E. G. W. Bill (London: SPCK, 1967), 102.

At the same time, there was a sense of ignorance about the Church of England among many in Rome. To address this, the SPCU asked Bernard Leeming for a page about Fisher (whom he described as ‘not much of a theologian but I think a very sincere man, more led by feeling than cold reason’), a page about the history of [^c30-27] the Church of England, and a page about present-day Anglicanism. The Vatican Secretary of State, Domenico Cardinal Tardini, tried to introduce a press blackout and resisted a press release to ensure the visit was as low key (‘a courtesy visit’) as possible, and, lest there should be any misunderstanding about the nature of Anglican orders, the archbishop was simply to be called ‘Dr Fisher’. Similarly, there were to be no official photographs. However, it proved impossible to silence the press corps, who had realized the importance of the visit and who assembled at the airport in large numbers to greet Fisher’s arrival.

[^c30-27]: William Purdy, _The Search for Unity: History of Relations Between the Anglican and Roman Catholic Churches from the 1960s_ _to the First ARCIC_ (London: Chapman, 1996), 27.

At sixty-seven minutes, the visit was significantly longer than expected, and it was clear that Pope John and Fisher struck up an immediate rapport with one another: both were practical-minded churchmen and found [^c30-28] theologians a source of much frustration. In a conversation with Bernard Pawley, canon treasurer of Ely Cathedral, who was to become the first Anglican representative in Rome shortly after the meeting, Pope John remarked that theologians ‘have got us into this mess, and we have got to get ourselves out of it; it is [^c30-29] practical men like you and me who will deliver us from it’. Although there were no official records of the [^c30-30] visit, Fisher dictated an account to Satterthwaite very shortly afterwards. Discussing the forthcoming council, Fisher had commented to the pope that other churches were just as interested in what was happening in the Roman Catholic Church as the Catholic Church itself was. Fisher described the pope’s response: ‘in due course he expected that they would be able to take up matters concerning other Churches’, both Orthodox and Protestant. It was at this point that Fisher intervened to insert a special ‘plea for Anglicans too as falling in neither of these categories’. ‘The Pope’, Fisher observed, ‘readily accepted the distinction of Anglicans having a different position from Protestant bodies generally.’ The idea of Anglicanism being _sui generis_ and a communion that was not to be included under the Protestant umbrella was later to become enshrined in the council’s Decree on Ecumenism, _Unitatis Redintegratio_. Fisher also noted that he said to the pope that they were both ‘going forward together’ rather than returning to an **[p. 510]** [^c30-31] imagined past. That meant that ‘we will never remain quite the same as we were before’. Fisher then recalled that when John XXIII quoted from his own address about the importance of returning to ‘Mother Church’, he had immediately responded: ‘Your holiness, not _return_! None of us can go backwards, only forwards. Our two Churches are now running on parallel courses and we may look forward to their meeting one day.’ Pope John is reported to have replied: ‘You are quite right’, to which Fisher added, ‘I never heard [^c30-32] him speak again of “returning”.’

[^c30-28]: Staples, ‘Archbishop Geoffrey Francis Fisher’, 263; Purdy, _The Search for Unity_, 30–31.

[^c30-29]: Cited in Frederick Bliss, _Anglicans in Rome_ (Norwich: Canterbury Press, 2006), 44.

[^c30-30]: Carpenter, _Archbishop Fisher_, 734–36.

[^c30-31]: Ibid., 735.

[^c30-32]: Geoffrey Fisher, _Touching on Christian Truth: The Kingdom of God, the Christian Church and the World_ (London: Mowbray, 1971), 187–8; Carpenter, _Archbishop Fisher_, 737.

This visit was crucial in helping change the ecumenical tone, at least in the new SPCU, even before the council had begun. Consequently, despite the fact that the meeting was downplayed in Rome—_L’Osservatore_ [^c30-33] _Romano_ simply commented: ‘Dr. Geoffrey Francis Fisher had an audience with His Holiness’ —it was nevertheless to have major and lasting implications for relations between the churches. Two implacable foes had become conversation partners overnight: they were running on parallel courses. Fisher commented in the sermon he preached at the English church of All Saints in Rome during the visit: ‘The period of the [^c30-34] cold war between Churches is not altogether past. But it is passing.’ Looking back in retirement, he [^c30-35] observed that it was ‘the personality of Pope John’ that led to the change of attitude and allowed them to trust one another. The personal rapport became crucial for the future of ecumenism: ‘It is by such easy conversation between people who trust each other that fixed ideas from the past get unfrozen and [^c30-36] liquidated.’ In an article written shortly afterwards, Cardinal Bea also noted ‘the change of atmosphere’ brought about by the meeting before concluding: ‘We are sincerely convinced that his visit of last December [^c30-37] will bear fruit, though we have no wish to specify its nature.’

[^c30-33]: In Carpenter, _Archbishop Fisher_, 739.

[^c30-34]: Chadwick, ‘The Church of England and the Church of Rome’, 104.

[^c30-35]: William Purcell, _Fisher of Canterbury_ (London: Hodder & Stoughton, 1969), 273.

[^c30-36]: Fisher, _Touching on Christian Truth_, 188.

[^c30-37]: Augustin Bea, _The Unity of Christians_ (London: Chapman, 1963), 64–72, esp. 71.

### 3. The Second Vatican Council and Anglicanism

This change in mood between Anglicans and Roman Catholics is also clear from the course of the Second Vatican Council itself, especially the modifications that were made to the Decree on Ecumenism. The approach to ecumenism fundamentally changed during the council, as was observed at the time by a young Joseph Ratzinger: the word ‘ecumenical’, he felt, should mean that ‘one must cease to see non-Catholics **[p. 511]** merely as opponents against whom one must defend oneself; that one tries to recognise them as brothers, with whom one speaks and from whom one may also learn something’. The idea of walking together was embraced very early on. He continued: ‘ “Ecumenical” means taking everything into account, and not merely that one aspect which at the moment calls for condemnation or correction. It means setting forth the inner complex unity of the faith and in consequence making our separated brothers aware that [^c30-38] everything that is truly Christian is contained in Catholicism.’ As is well documented, the presence of the ecumenical observers ensured that this process was at the very heart of the conciliar method. The somewhat unexpected extent of the hospitality extended to them was obviously important in shaping the conciliar debates: even though they remained apart from the official process of deliberation, there was, nonetheless, as Cardinal Bea noted, a sense in which their very presence undoubtedly helped moderate the tone and mood [^c30-39] with which the council was conducted—other Christians are looking on.

[^c30-38]: Joseph Ratzinger, ‘The Second Vatican Council: The First Session’, _The Furrow_ 14, no. 5 (1963): 282.

[^c30-39]: Bea, _The Unity of Christians_, 9. On the theological role of the observers, see Christopher Thomas Washington, _The_ _Participation of Non-Catholic Observer Guests and Fraternal Delegates at the Second Vatican Council and the Synods of_ _Bishops: A Theological Analysis_ (Rome: Editrice Pontifica Università Gregoriana, 2015).

In the aftermath of the meeting between Pope John and Fisher, Canon Pawley became Anglican representative in Rome in 1961; he set about making friends in the Vatican and helping to dispel some of [^c30-40] their misunderstandings about the Anglican Communion. He noted that ‘the Pope’s lack of objective [^c30-41] information about the Church of England was immediately evident’ in his audiences. Soon afterwards, these friendships, especially with Cardinal Bea, were to prove crucial for all the observers at the council, not [^c30-42][^c30-43] just the Anglicans. The observers very quickly built up a close friendship with members of the SPCU. Before long, there was a strong group identity among all the observers who met regularly over coffee and [^c30-44] who were frequent guests of the SPCU. Several Roman Catholics, including Yves Congar and Georges H. [^c30-45] Tavard, began serious studies of Anglicanism during the council.

[^c30-40]: Chandler and Hansen, _Observing Vatican II_, 15–19.

[^c30-41]: Chandler and Hein, _Archbishop Fisher_, 108; Bernard Pawley and Margaret Pawley, _Rome and Canterbury through the_ _Centuries_ (London: Mowbray, 1974), 335–36.

[^c30-42]: Purdy, _The Search for Unity_, 37–38.

[^c30-43]: Bliss, _Anglicans in Rome_, 63–69; Purdy, _The Search for Unity_, 58–61; Chandler and Hansen, _Observing Vatican II_, 282.

[^c30-44]: John Moorman, _Vatican Observed: An Anglican View of Vatican II_ (London: Darton, Longman and Todd, 1967), 17–24.

[^c30-45]: Yves Congar, _Dialogue Between Christians: Catholic Contributions to Ecumenism_ (London: Geoffrey Chapman, 1964), 249– 84; George H. Tavard, _The Quest for Catholicity: A Study in Anglicanism_ (London: Catholic Book Club, 1963).

Following the invitations, Pawley’s presence and contacts in Rome meant that the Anglican observers were [^c30-46] the first to accept the offer. Three official Anglican observers were drawn from across the Communion: **[p. 512]** this was crucial in showing the global reach of Anglicanism. They were led by Bishop John Moorman of Ripon, a church historian and expert in Franciscan studies who had been raised in an Evangelical household; he was later to play a key role in the Anglican–Roman Catholic International Commission (ARCIC). Others who served for a period were Eugene Fairweather, professor of theology at Trinity College, Toronto; Ernest John from New Delhi; Clement Welsh of the College of Preachers in Washington, DC; Bishop Najib Atallah Cuba’in of Jordan, Lebanon, and Syria; Harold de Soysa, archdeacon of Colombo; and William J. Wolf, of the Episcopal Theological School at Cambridge, Massachusetts. Substitutes included Bishop Stanley W. Eley of Gibraltar; Bishop Alpheus Zulu, coadjutor bishop of St John’s, with his headquarters in Umtata, South Africa; Howard Root, dean of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and later professor of theology at the University of Southampton; Massey Hamilton Shepherd of the Church Divinity School of the Pacific in Berkeley, California; and Bernard Pawley himself. Pawley was succeeded by John Findlow, who followed him as representative in Rome and also as director of the new Anglican Centre. There were also Anglicans among the observers who were members of other delegations. Patrick Rodger, general secretary of Faith and Order [^c30-47] and later bishop of Oxford, represented the WCC.

[^c30-46]: David M. Paton and R. M. C. Jeffery, _Christian Unity and the Anglican Communion_, 2nd ed. (London: Church Information Office, 1966), 45.

[^c30-47]: See Bliss, _Anglicans in Rome_, 62–63; Bernard Leeming, SJ, _The Vatican Council and Christian Unity: A Commentary on the_ _Decree of Ecumenism of the Second Vatican Council, with a Translation of the Text_ (London: Darton, Longman and Todd, 1966), 312–17; Bernard Pawley, ed., _Second Vatican Council: Some Anglican Views_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1966); Peter Webster, _Archbishop Ramsey: The Shape of the Church_ (Farnham, NC: Ashgate, 2015), 31.

The Anglican observers were in general very favourable to the course of the council and especially to the frequent changes of direction from the conservative thrust of many of the original texts: Bishop Moorman [^c30-48] had observed that the urge to further reform appeared to be irresistible. Similarly, in his introduction to a volume produced by eight of the Anglican observers, Bernard Pawley noted that ‘the theologians therefore were sent back by the bishops to their text books and told to work out the implications of baptism for the [^c30-49] whole question of Christian membership’. On _Dei Verbum_, there was a general acceptance by the Anglican [^c30-50] observers of the new direction taken with the importance of Scripture and critical study. Similarly, both Moorman and Massey Shepherd felt that the liturgical changes were moving the Roman Catholic Church [^c30-51] into line with the vernacular traditions of Anglicanism. Shepherd even placed excerpts from the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy and the Preface to the 1549 Book of Common Prayer in parallel [^c30-52] columns.

[^c30-48]: Jan Grooataers, ‘Ebb and Flow Between Two Seasons’, in _History of Vatican II_, vol. 2, _Formation of the Council’s Identity:_ _First Period and Intersession_, ed. Giuseppe Alberigo and Joseph A. Komonchak (Leuven: Peeters, 1997), 523.

[^c30-49]: Pawley, _Second Vatican Council: Some Anglican Views_, 7.

[^c30-51]: Moorman, _Vatican Observed_, 46–48. Massey H. Shepherd, ‘The Liturgy’, in Pawley, _Second Vatican Council: Studies by Eight_ _Anglican Observers_, 149–74.

[^c30-52]: Shepherd, ‘The Liturgy’, 171–72.

**[p. 513]** The Decree on Ecumenism provoked a great deal of discussion from the Anglican observers. Although chapter 9 of the first schema on the Church had mentioned Protestant churches, Pope John had asked the [^c30-53] SPCU to prepare a text on ecumenism for discussion. The original preparatory document on ecumenism, ‘The Unity of the Church’, prepared by the Commission for the Oriental Churches, mentioned only the Eastern churches; it was scuppered after only three days of debate on 1 December 1962 on the grounds that it did not meet the ecumenical challenge presented by a significant number of Christians. This ecumenical discussion followed soon after the momentous debate on Revelation, which, according to Ratzinger, marked [^c30-54] the ‘turning point’ of the council. The assembled bishops showed a degree of trust in the SPCU, which went on to draft a new schema in collaboration with the Commission for the Oriental Churches.

[^c30-53]: George H. Tavard, _Vatican II and the Ecumenical Way_ (Milwaukee, WI: Marquette University Press, 2006), 31, 41–42.

[^c30-54]: Ratzinger, ‘The Second Vatican Council: The First Session’, 284.

The schema was eventually replaced with the draft of what became _Unitatis Redintegratio_, which showed far more openness towards other churches. Ratzinger felt that the greater openness to the other Christians marked the way forward into the future: ‘The Council, then, will be unable to bring about the union of Christendom; but it will make us aware in a new way of how much we have in common already and how widely we agree on fundamentals if only we bother to notice this and, instead of staring at the barriers that [^c30-55] divide us, observe the large amount that unites us.’ A draft was circulated in June 1963 which generally met with an enthusiastic response from the observers and the majority of the bishops. For Anglicans, however, there was a significant problem, which had earlier been highlighted by Fisher. While the draft spoke warmly and extensively of the Orthodox churches, all the other Christian communities ‘arising from the sixteenth century onwards’ were lumped together. This offended many Anglicans, for whom the idea of [^c30-56] continuity was central to their identity. Howard Root observed: ‘If this division was taken at face value the Anglican Communion, at least according to its own self-understanding, was not included in the schema at [^c30-57] all.’ While this observation might well have failed to satisfy more Protestant-minded Anglicans who would have been happy to have been included among the Protestants, it was clear that the Anglican observers saw themselves as something different.

[^c30-55]: Ibid., 287–88.

[^c30-56]: See Purdy, _The Search for Unity_, 71–72.

[^c30-57]: Howard E. Root, ‘Ecumenism in the Dogmatic Constitution on the Church and in the Decree on Ecumenism’, in Pawley, _Second Vatican Council: Studies by Eight Anglican Observers_, 121.

In the light of pleading from the Anglican observers, several bishops at the council sought to change the text, although it was the French and not the English bishops who championed the Anglican cause. Indeed, in the earlier debate, Cardinal William Godfrey of Westminster had counselled against any special acknowledgement of Anglicans, least of all Anglo-Catholics, on the grounds of laxity in doctrine and [^c30-58] **[p. 514]** morals. The only English bishops who spoke on the debate on ecumenism were George Dwyer of Leeds and John Heenan, archbishop of Liverpool. In his recollection of the council, Moorman noted that those bishops ‘who had taken the trouble to find out something about Anglicanism realised that, in spite of its curious habits, it was obviously something quite different from other Protestant communities, and that it [^c30-59] ought not, therefore, to be lumped together with them in the post-Reformation group’. During the debates on the decree in December 1963, Paul Gouyon, coadjutor of Rennes and titular archbishop of Pessinus, for instance, noted that ‘we look in vain’ in the schema for ‘any clear allusion to the great Anglican community, which in its origins is certainly quite distinct and different from the communities of the Reformation’. He continued: ‘It would satisfy me better if there were different and separate chapters for the Orthodox [^c30-60] Churches, for the Anglican Communion, and for the communions which grew out the Reformation.’ The branch theory of the Anglo-Catholics was quietly being accepted by at least one French Roman Catholic bishop; this may point back to the lasting influence of the Gallican tradition which had led to close relations [^c30-61] between the Church of England and French Catholics in the eighteenth century.

[^c30-58]: Chandler and Hansen, _Observing Vatican II_, 179.

[^c30-59]: Moorman, _Vatican Observed_, 98.

[^c30-60]: _AS_ II/6, 117; translated into English in Hans Küng, Yves Congar, and Daniel O’Hanlon, eds., _Council Speeches of Vatican II_ (Glen Rock, NJ: Paulist, 1964), 175–76.

[^c30-61]: See Paul Avis, _Anglicanism and the Christian Church_, 2nd ed. (London: T&T Clark, 2002), 121–29.

Similarly, Bishop Jean-Édouard-Lucien Rupp of Monaco went so far as to quote Newman’s opinion that ‘the fact that the Anglican Church had for three centuries produced so many holy people, and accomplished so much good, [meant] that it could be explained only by a special intervention of Divine Providence’. He also observed that ‘in the Anglican Church many beautiful and inspiring things were to [be] found on bishops [^c30-62] and their place in the church’. From a different background, Bishop Ernest Arthur Green of Port Elizabeth even suggested that it would be worthwhile to reopen the issue of Anglican orders since ‘local secretariats for Christian unity cannot be expected to solve a problem of this magnitude. It must be resolved on the [^c30-63] highest level between the supreme authorities of the Roman Catholic and the Anglican Churches.’ Similarly, Dom Christopher Butler of Downside, a former Anglican, who was the only voice from Britain to contribute to this part of the debate, felt it appropriate to single out the Anglican Church from the others since it was ‘so wide-spread, so devoted to patristic antiquity and which has deserved so well of the [^c30-64] ecumenical movement’.

[^c30-62]: Paraphrase in Chandler and Hansen, _Observing Vatican II_, 282.

[^c30-63]: Ibid., 285.

[^c30-64]: _AS_ II/6, 253. Howard E. Root, ‘Ecumenism in the Dogmatic Constitution on the Church and in the Decree on Ecumenism’, in Pawley, _Second Vatican Council: Studies by Eight Anglican Observers_, 121. See Christopher Butler, _A Time to Speak_ (London: McCrimmon, 1972), ch. 13.

Eventually the text noted that ‘among those in which the Catholic traditions and institutions in part survive, [^c30-65] the Anglican Communion occupies a special place’ (_UR_ 13). This insertion amounts to an explicit recognition of Anglicanism as something different from other Protestant churches. The model of **[p. 515]** Anglicanism which stressed continuity and which found its essence in the historic episcopate was that accepted by the Vatican Council, which had an important effect on Anglican self-definition, especially as it was to develop through the ecumenical process of ARCIC. _Unitatis Redintegratio_, which was promulgated by Pope Paul VI on 21 November 1964, became crucial in changing the mood in relations between the churches, as well as within the Roman Catholic Church itself. It became one of the most important achievements of Vatican II, marking a complete reversal—what it called a ‘change of heart’ (_UR_ 7)—of the polemical caricatures which had dominated earlier discussions between Roman Catholics and other Christians: while for Anglicans these had been shifting beforehand, the explicit recognition of the Anglican Communion as a distinct type of church cleared the decks for further discussions.

[^c30-65]: See Leeming, _The Vatican Council and Christian Unity_, 12.

In a new spirit of receptivity, openness, and even humility—a characteristic usually absent from the discipline of apologetics—‘all the Catholic faithful were to recognise the signs of the times and to participate skilfully in the work of ecumenism’ (_UR_ 4). This imperative required the Roman Catholic Church to begin discussions with what it called ‘our separated brethren’ (_UR_ 9), in the acknowledgement that, even though communion might be imperfect, members of other churches and ecclesial communities ‘are properly regarded as brothers in the Lord by the sons of the Catholic Church’ (_UR_ 3). ‘The Spirit’, it goes on, ‘has not refrained from using them as means of salvation which derive from the very fullness of grace and truth entrusted to the Catholic Church’ (_UR_ 3). Since non-Catholics could display ‘truly Christian endowments’, it was ‘right and salutary to recognise the riches of Christ and virtuous works in the lives of others bearing witness to Christ’ (_UR_ 4). What this reveals is that by the end of Vatican II there had been a complete about-face from the sort of polemics undertaken by Henry Manning in the 1860s: non-Catholics could undoubtedly display Christian endowments.

### 4. The Aftermath of the Council

Following the council there were rapid moves towards closer cooperation between Roman Catholics and their new ecumenical partners. With their special status as a church that was neither Protestant nor Orthodox, Anglicans were to feature prominently in early ecumenical discussions. This had become apparent in the year after the end of the council, when Geoffrey Fisher’s successor, Michael Ramsey, visited Pope Paul VI on 22–4 March 1966. Ramsey was a prominent theologian who held John XXIII in very high esteem and had even celebrated a Requiem Mass in John’s memory, which irritated a number of more [^c30-66] Protestant-minded Anglicans. Despite his Anglo-Catholic sympathies, however, Ramsey was initially [^c30-67] reluctant to visit Rome for fear of further upsetting the Protestant faction. There were also anxieties from **[p. 516]** English Roman Catholics who were busy pleading for the beatification of the forty martyrs of the Reformation, which they felt might be held up by talks between Ramsey and Pope Paul. Others, including John Heenan, who had become archbishop of Westminster in 1963, were anxious that a focus on Rome [^c30-68] might stall local discussions.

[^c30-66]: Webster, _Archbishop Ramsey_, 31.

[^c30-67]: Chadwick, ‘The Church of England and the Church of Rome’, 315.

[^c30-68]: Purdy, _The Search for Unity_, 92–93.

Ramsey was clear, however, that the global dimension of Anglicanism, which had become increasingly apparent at the council, be kept in view: he was adamant that dialogue should be international and [^c30-69] controlled by the SPCU rather than by the local Catholic bishops in England. He feared a return to the sort [^c30-70] of siege mentality that had frequently characterized the pre-conciliar period. His visit to Rome was [^c30-71] principally to emphasize the global dimension of his ministry; it was quite different from Fisher’s only six years beforehand and was marked by a great deal of publicity. The meeting, which was held on 23 March 1966 in the Sistine Chapel, took the form of a carefully prepared discussion during which the two men [^c30-72] quickly built up respect for one another. As they spoke about remaining differences on such matters as mixed marriages and orders, they proposed setting up a commission to address difficulties in doctrine and ecclesiology.

[^c30-69]: Letter of 26 January 1966 to Oliver Tomkins, in Webster, _Archbishop Ramsey_, 183.

[^c30-70]: Purdy, _The Search for Unity_, 40–41.

[^c30-71]: Webster, _Archbishop Ramsey_, 189–90; Chadwick, ‘The Church of England and the Church of Rome’, 315–17.

[^c30-72]: Purdy, _The Search for Unity_, 94–95; Chadwick, ‘The Church of England and the Church of Rome’, 321.

The day following the meeting, after the shared service of prayer in the basilica of St Paul’s Outside the Walls which had concluded with a joint blessing, Pope Paul gave Ramsey an episcopal ring. It felt to Ramsey as if the Pope was ‘giving me a piece of himself’. Asked by reporters whether this was a tacit recognition of the validity of his orders, Ramsey replied: ‘Not at all; but what it does betoken is the official recognition of the Church of England as an official Church with its rightful ministers. That from Rome means a great [^c30-73] deal.’ This memory stayed with Ramsey through the remainder of his life, and it is reported that he died [^c30-74] wearing the ring. Ramsey also opened the Anglican Centre in Rome in the Palazzo Doria Pamphilj. The address was given by Cardinal Willebrands, who felt that the meeting marked the beginning of ‘real dialogue’: the archbishop of Canterbury had led ‘the Anglican Communion into dialogue with Rome which [^c30-75] had opened its doors to him. He had brought the Anglican Communion into joint prayer with our church.’

[^c30-73]: Chadwick, ‘The Church of England and the Church of Rome’, 322.

[^c30-74]: Ibid., 322 Gordon Wakefield, ‘Michael Ramsey and Ecumenical Theology’, in _Michael Ramsey as Theologian_, ed. Robin Gill and Lorna Kendall (London: DLT, 1995), 63.

[^c30-75]: Jan Willebrands, ‘The Ecumenical Significance of the Visit of the Archbishop of Canterbury’, _Unitas_ 19 (1967): 14.

After their meeting, Pope Paul and Ramsey signed the _Common Declaration_. This established the Anglican– Roman Catholic International Commission, which was to address ‘not only theological matters such as [^c30-76] **[p. 517]** Scripture, Tradition and Liturgy, but also matters of practical difficulty felt on either side’. The _Common Declaration_ called somewhat ambitiously on both churches to promote the development of ‘respect, esteem and fraternal love’ in the hope of reaching ‘unity in truth’ and the ‘restoration of complete communion of [^c30-77] faith and sacramental life’. In the years that followed, ARCIC proved to hold perhaps the most fruitful ecumenical discussions emerging from the implementation of _Unitatis Redintegratio_. Eventually, the commission would produce a series of reports on Eucharist and ministry and two reports on authority which [^c30-78] were drawn together into the Final Report of 1982, revealing what was called a ‘substantial’ unity.

[^c30-76]: Paton and Jeffery, _Christian Unity and the Anglican Communion_, 47.

[^c30-77]: Paul VI and Michael Ramsey, ‘The Common Declaration [1966]’, in Hill and Yarnold, _Anglicans and Roman Catholics: The_ _Search for Unity_, 10–11.

[^c30-78]: Ibid., 13.

The tone of the Final Report retains the optimism of _Unitatis Redintegratio_ and reflects something of the mood in which the discussions were undertaken, which was one of openness, humility, and trust. In 1980, Pope John Paul II summarized the method as going ‘behind the habit and thought and expression born and nourished in enmity and controversy to scrutinise together the great common treasure, to clothe it in a language at once traditional and expressive of the insights of an age which no longer glorifles in strife but [^c30-79] seeks to come together in listening to the quiet voice of the Spirit’. There seemed a real desire to walk together as a ‘pilgrim church’ and to learn from one another: ‘contemporary discussions of conciliarity and [^c30-80] primacy in both communions indicate that we are not dealing with positions destined to remain static’.

[^c30-79]: Cited ibid., 96.

[^c30-80]: Anglican–Roman Catholic International Commission, ‘The Final Report [1992] 33’, ibid., 75.

However, this sort of optimism was soon challenged, not least by the Congregation for the Doctrine of the [^c30-81] Faith (CDF), under its prefect from 1981, Joseph Ratzinger. In many ways, this sought to slow the pace of ecumenical discussion.
