It was the pre-existing unity of the Catholic Church, and not a mutual exploration between partners walking together, that was to function as the criterion for identity. ‘Unity’, claimed Ratzinger, ‘is a fundamental, hermeneutic principle of all theology … a superficial unity which jumps the [^c30-82] gun without inward preparation through actual living could only prove harmful.’ It is possible to see Anglicanism and consequently the ARCIC process, with its stress on the collegial nature of authority, as a significant challenge to the unitive model being upheld by the CDF. Interestingly, the deepest criticism of [^c30-83] Ratzinger’s intervention came from some of the French bishops.

[^c30-81]: Ibid., 79–91.

[^c30-82]: Joseph Ratzinger, ‘Anglican–Catholic Dialogue: Its Problems and Hopes [1983]’, ibid., 261, 267.

[^c30-83]: Cited ibid., 171–84. See also the English and Welsh Bishops, ibid., 94–110.

In a postscript to the response to ARCIC, Ratzinger noted that the singularity of truth remained central to any conception of the Church which meant a return to the idea of reunion of the past: ‘Our quarrelling ancestors were in reality much closer to each other when in all their disputes they still knew that they could **[p. 518]** only be servants of one truth which must be acknowledged as being as great and as pure as it has been [^c30-84] intended for us by God.’ By the year 2000, _Dominus Iesus_ (_DI_) suggested that ‘the ecclesial communities which have not preserved the valid Episcopate and the genuine and integral substance of the Eucharistic mystery, are not Churches in the proper sense’ (_DI_ 17). This looked more like a return to something resembling Manning’s position in 1864 than a continuation of the idea of partnership pioneered at Vatican II.

[^c30-84]: Cited ibid., 281.

### 5. Conclusion

The relationships between Roman Catholics and Anglicans, which developed rapidly though the period of the council and up to the ARCIC Final Report, display something of the optimism of _Unitatis Redintegratio_. There was a fundamental change in relations between the two communions which was in part the result of Anglicanism’s special status in the decree. That meant, somewhat accidentally, that the council was to give a boost to those Anglicans who had tried to downplay the Reformation and disliked the idea of seeing Anglicanism as a form of Protestantism, a move which would have surprised many in earlier generations. On this post-Vatican II model, Anglicanism could easily be elevated into a kind of ecumenical ‘bridge [^c30-85] church’, standing between the Reformation and Roman Catholicism. The See of Canterbury now possesses an episcopal ring as proof of its special status: it was worn by Justin Welby on his first visit to Pope Francis [^c30-86] in June 2013. This ‘special relationship’ between Catholics and Anglicans proved immensely fruitful in the early ARCIC dialogues which stemmed from Vatican II. It undoubtedly has much to commend it, however much it might deviate from historic Protestant Anglican identity.

[^c30-85]: Aidan Nichols, _The Panther and the Hind: A Theological History of Anglicanism_ (Edinburgh: T&T Clark, 1993), ix, 179.

[^c30-86]: Anglican–Roman Catholic Dialogue, ‘Archbishop Justin meets Pope Francis in Rome [2013]’, https://iarccum.org/2013/archbishop-justin-meets-pope-francis-in-rome.

Things changed on both sides during the 1990s and the early part of the twenty-first century. On the one hand, some Anglicans, especially in parts of Africa, have sought to return to a more Protestant understanding of the Church to combat a perceived doctrinal and moral vacuum in the liberal churches of [^c30-87] the global North. On the other hand, many Roman Catholics have been looking to go back before the council and have sought what Pope Benedict XVI, in the 2005 ‘Address of His Holiness Benedict XVII to the Roman Curia Offering Them His Christmas Greetings’, called a ‘hermeneutic of continuity’, which challenges the major decisions of Vatican II. But with Pope Francis the situation has changed once again to the more positive mood struck by Vatican II. As John Paul II said in his address at the twenty-fifth anniversary of the SPCU on 28 June 1985: ‘_the Catholic Church is committed to the ecumenical movement with_ **[p. 519]** _an irrevocable decision_, and desires to contribute to it with all its possibilities’. This provided the basis for the encyclical _Ut Unum Sint_ of 1995. This might mean that the ecumenical achievement of Vatican II might [^c30-88] only really be in its infancy.

[^c30-87]: See Mark D. Chapman, _Anglican Theology_ (London: T&T Clark, 2012), 199–210.

[^c30-88]: See Gerard Mannion, ‘Pope Francis and Hope in the Ecumenical Future: A Papacy of Encounter’, in _The Hope of Things to_ _Come_, ed. Mark D. Chapman (New York: Palgrave Macmillan, 2017), 103–32.

### Suggested Reading

Bliss, Frederick. _Anglicans in Rome_. Norwich: Canterbury Press, 2006.

Chandler, Andrew, and Charlotte Hansen. _Observing Vatican II: The Confidential Reports of the Archbishop of Canterbury’s Representative, 1961–1964_. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press for the Royal Historical Society, 2011.

Hill, Christopher, and Edward Yarnold, SJ, eds. _Anglicans and Roman Catholics: The Search for Unity_. London: SPCK/CTS, 1994.

Pawley, Bernard, and Margaret Pawley. _Rome and Canterbury through the Centuries_. London: Mowbray, 1974.

Purdy, William. _The Search for Unity: History of Relations Between the Anglican and Roman Catholic Churches from the 1960s to the First ARCIC_. London: Chapman, 1996.

## 31. The Reception of Vatican II by Lutheran Churches

William G. Rusch

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 520]** In order to explore this theme adequately within the confines of the available space, some comments are necessary about the title of this chapter. First, there is the question of the definition of ‘reception’. In recent years, this word has gained considerable importance in ecumenical theology. There has also been extensive discussion about the exact definition of the word and concept. Although a number of suggested [^c31-1] interpretations of the word and concept have been offered, they share many common characteristics. In view of the present context, the definition proposed by Gilles Routhier seems to be the most appropriate: ‘Reception is a spiritual process by which the decisions proposed by a council are received and assimilated [^c31-2] into the life of a local church and become for that church a living expression of the apostolic faith.’ Second, there is the definition of ‘Vatican II’. Is the reference here all sixteen conciliar documents, the entire process of the council, or an event from 1962 to 1965 that could be described as ‘Vatican II’? Third, there is the issue of ‘Lutheran churches’. Globally, there are some hundreds of national or regional Lutheran churches so self-described. The variety among them in theology, in worship, in relation to the ecumenical movement and the contemporary cultural and social scene is enormous by any standard of discernment. Even the membership of the Lutheran World Federation, the global communion of Lutheran churches, numbers over 140 national and regional churches. These churches, in spite of their common confessional position, put forth in the constitution of the federation, exhibit no unifled stance on many issues.

[^c31-1]: William G. Rusch, _Ecumenical Reception: Its Challenge and Opportunity_ (Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 2007), 58–62.

[^c31-2]: Gilles Routhier, _La Réception d’un concile_ (Paris: Cerf, 1993), 69.

### 2. A ‘Reception’ of Vatican II by the Lutheran World Federation

**[p. 521]** Despite these factors, it is possible to address the topic of this chapter if a few cautions are kept in mind. No Lutheran church has officially or juridically ‘received’ the teachings or documents of the Second Vatican Council. That could hardly be expected. But Routhier’s definition does not call for this type of action. As will be seen, the Second Vatican Council has patently had a spiritual impact on a number of Lutheran churches, primarily those which are members of the Lutheran World Federation. This outcome has dramatically altered earlier perceptions of the Roman Catholic Church. In fairness, it must also be pointed out that for many other Lutheran churches, the council has had no positive or negative effect at all. For the present context, it will be appropriate to regard ‘the Second Vatican Council’ not as a meeting or a collection of documents, but rather as an event with its prehistory that included a number of meetings and finally a corpus of texts.

In regard to ‘Lutheran churches’, the primary focus will be on the membership of the Lutheran World Federation. How did these churches and the federation respond to this council of the Roman Catholic Church? In considering this question, it is critical to point out that in the early twenty-first century, both the federation and its member churches are not what they were in the 1960s, when the council was in session.

The Lutheran World Federation was established in 1947. At that time, its constitution declared that it was a free association of Lutheran churches. The intent of the language was to convey that the locus of authority and decision making resided in the member churches, not in the federation. In 1990, the constitution was amended to read that the federation was a communion of churches. Clearly, many factors went into this hotly debated change. These included an increasing sense of pulpit and altar fellowship among the member churches, statements about the nature of the federation from earlier assemblies, and actions of ecclesial discipline taken in 1984 regarding membership of certain churches in South Africa. An additional element was an increased awareness of the role the federation was playing in the ecumenical movement as, for example, in the selection of participants in international dialogues and ultimately in a decision-making role in the evaluation of this dialogue work. Here at least an indirect influence of the Second Vatican Council can be seen.

Changes in this period can also be seen in the churches themselves. Between the 1960s and the 2000s, many Lutheran churches in traditional Lutheran countries in North America and Europe witnessed a decline in membership and a diminishment of authority in their societies. Their characteristics of Lutheran identity were eroded under the pressures of secularism. With an increased generally positive value of pluralism, a unifled national Lutheran position proved impossible in many settings. Simultaneously, in Africa and Asia, Lutheran membership was increasing. Conciliar ecumenism, with its stress on social issues and cooperation between churches, was acknowledged in many of these churches, but it made little impact on their internal life or external relations.

**[p. 522]** At the same time, interestingly enough, the ecumenical movement, with its goal of the visible unity of Christ’s Church, was gaining prominence in many Lutheran churches. Two factors can be viewed as contributing to this situation: the entrance of the Roman Catholic Church after the Second Vatican Council into the one ecumenical movement, and the rise of bilateral dialogues with their recommendations for new relations between Lutheran churches and the Roman Catholic Church. Other Lutheran dialogues with non- Catholic churches also played their role in this regard. The result is that the commitment and openness to ecumenical advance, especially with the Roman Catholic Church, is greater at the present time than when the first session of the council opened. This situation must be regarded as part of the reception of the council within Lutheran churches.

### 3. Lutheran Observers at Vatican II

In addition, there is clear evidence of this non-technical reception of the council or openness to it by Lutherans even prior to the inauguration of the council. On 25 January 1959, Pope John XXIII revealed his intention to call a ‘general Council for the Universal Church’. By this terminology, the pope clearly meant a council for the Roman Catholic Church. He made this decision less than ninety days after his election to succeed Pius XII. On 11 October 1962, the Second Vatican Council formally began. The period between early 1959 and late 1962 was a time of intense preparation for the council event. Countless decisions were being made and pages of texts beyond number were being drafted. Correspondence to and from Rome flowed. Journeys by many individuals from and to Rome occurred. Most of that activity lies outside the scope of this chapter.

There is one exception to this description of the council as a Roman Catholic event: the thinking and activity to invite non-Catholics to the upcoming council. Clearly, this possibility arose slowly in the minds of those individuals preparing for the council, as did questions about the role and function of such non-Catholics. Of appropriate interest here is the question of inviting Lutherans to the council. A positive response to such an invitation would be evidence of at least some type of affirmative Lutheran reception of the council.

The question of non-Catholics at a Roman Catholic council was not a new issue in the twentieth century. It [^c31-3] had been raised earlier on several occasions, but the context now was quite different. Now in an upcoming **[p. 523]** council, whose purpose was announced to be pastoral as opposed to dogmatic, some members of the Roman Curia were actively seeking such participation.

[^c31-3]: See Christopher Thomas Washington, _The Participation of Non-Catholic Christian Observers, Guests, and Fraternal_ _Delegates at the Second Vatican Council and the Synod of Bishops: A Theological Analysis_, Testi Gregoriana, Serie Teologia 213 (Rome: Editrice Pontificia Università Gregoriana, 2015).

Kurt Schmidt-Clausen, the general secretary of the Lutheran World Federation, met with Monsignor Johannes Willebrands of the recently created Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity. This meeting occurred in late 1961 in Geneva. Willebrands encouraged Schmidt-Clausen to make a visit to Rome in the near future. This visit, which would not have been possible without the encouragement of the membership of the federation, took place in November of the same year. Schmidt-Clausen met with Cardinal Bea of the secretariat. This encounter was the first time that the idea of non-Catholic observers at the council was discussed. Bea proposed that an official invitation be extended to the groups of confessional churches. Both Schmidt-Clausen and Bea realized that there would be many problems to be resolved.

In addition to Schmidt-Clausen, there was another Lutheran presence in Rome prior to the official start of the council. Edmund Schlink, a Lutheran with long ecumenical experience and a professor of dogmatic and ecumenical theology at the University of Heidelberg, also met with Cardinal Bea in 1961. This meeting was at the cardinal’s invitation, and its purpose was to discuss the council. Schlink would be present at all four sessions of the council and would become a recognized leader of the group of observers. Although Schlink was appointed as an observer by the Evangelical Church in Germany, he clearly saw his role as that of a Lutheran. The Evangelical Church in Germany is a federation of twenty-seven autonomous Protestant territorial churches, not all of which are Lutheran. In 1961, prior to the opening of the council, Schlink published _Der kommende Christus und die kirchlichen Traditionen._[^c31-4]

[^c31-4]: See _Edmund Schlink Works_, vol. 1, _The Coming Christ and Church Traditions After the Council_, ed. Matthew L. Becker (Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 2017). Also valuable is Eugene M. Skibbe, _A Quiet Reformer: An Introduction to_ _Edmund Schlink’s Life and Ecumenical Theology_ (Minneapolis, MN: Kirk House, 1999).

In September 1962, Cardinal Bea of the Secretariat for Christian Unity released the list of observers who had been appointed by their church communities. The Lutherans selected by the Lutheran World Federation as observers were Dr Kristen E. Skydsgaard, professor of theology from Denmark, and Dr George A. Lindbeck, professor of theology from the United States; Dr Vilmos Vajta of the Office of Studies of the Lutheran World Federation and Dr Walter Leibrecht from the United States were designated as substitutes. As indicated above, Dr Schlink’s appointment as an observer was from the Evangelical Church of Germany. Skydsgaard, Lindbeck, and Schlink would be at almost all of the subsequent sessions of the council. They would play critical roles in the activities of the observers at the council. By publications and regular reports, they [^c31-5] provided an interpretation of the council to their home constituencies. These efforts are certainly signs of a Lutheran reception of the council as its work unfolded.

[^c31-5]: In addition to the regular reports to the Lutheran World Federation and the Evangelical Church in Germany, Skydsgaard edited in 1961 a collection of essays, published in English as _The Papal Council and the Gospel: Protestant Theologians_ _Evaluate the Coming Vatican Council_ (Minneapolis, MN: Augsburg, 1961). Before the conclusion of the council, Lindbeck edited a similar volume, _Dialogue on the Way: Protestants Report from Rome on the Vatican Council_ (Minneapolis, MN: Augsburg, 1965). Schlink published regular reports on the Council in _Ökumenische Rundshau_ and _Kerygma und Dogma._ See e.g. Edmund Schlink, ‘Zum Abschluss der 2. Sitzungsperiode des II Vatikanischen’, _Ökumenische Rundschau_ 13 (1964): 149–56, and ‘Das Ergebnis des konziliaren Ringens um den Ökumenismus der römischen katholischen Kirche’, _Kerygma_ _und Dogma_ 11 (1965): 177–93.

**[p. 524]** The Secretariat for Christian Unity directly appointed as a guest professor Oscar Cullmann, a French-born Lutheran who was a recognized scholar of the New Testament and the Early Church with ecumenical interests. Cullmann would be present at all four sessions and would play a significant role in the discussion [^c31-6] and determination of several council texts.

[^c31-6]: Cullmann also published during and after the Council. See e.g. Oscar Cullmann, ‘Die Reformbestrebungen des 2. Vatikanischen Konzils im Lichte der Geschichte der katholischen Kirche’, _Theologische Literaturzeitung_ 92, no. 1 (1967): 1– 22.

The first session of the council took place between October and December of 1962. It was a time for the council to organize itself and consider preliminary drafts of a number of documents and for the observers to discern their unparalleled role in this context. Between the conclusion of the first session and the opening of the second, significant work was done on revising the earlier texts and the preparation of material for the next session. Many observers continued to play an active role between the two sessions in commenting on texts and making critical suggestions. This interval was also the time of the death of Pope John XXIII and the election of Pope Paul VI.

The second session of the council began on 29 September 1963. New regulations were in place. Debate resumed about a document dealing with the Church and a first draft of a text on ecumenism that included relations with the Jewish community and the topic of religious liberty. Texts on the liturgy and mass communication were promulgated by Paul VI. The Lutheran World Federation again appointed Dr Skydsgaard and Dr Lindbeck as observers. Dr Vajta, who been a substitute at the first session, was also appointed as an observer. The substitutes were Bishop Sven Silen of Sweden and Dr Warren A. Quanbeck of the United States. Dr Schlink continued as an appointee of the Evangelical Church in Germany, and Dr Cullmann as a guest of the Secretariat for Christian Unity. The second session finished its work on 4 December 1963.

The third session of the council commenced on 14 September 1964. It was occupied with debate on several texts including on the Church, religious liberty, and divine revelation. At the conclusion of this session on 21 November 1964, Pope Paul VI promulgated texts on the Church and on ecumenism. The Lutheran World [^c31-7] Federation appointed Dr Skydsgaard, Dr Quanbeck, and Bishop Silen as observers. Dr Lindbeck and Dr Vajta were named substitutes. The World Council of Churches appointed an American Lutheran, Dr Jerald Brauer, **[p. 525]** as an observer. The Evangelical Church in Germany continued with Dr Schlink as an observer and named Dr Wolfgang Dietzfelbinger as a substitute. Dr Cullmann continued as a guest of the Secretariat for Christian Unity. For the first time, the Secretariat named as a guest a member of the Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod in the United States, Dr Oswald Hoffmann. The third session adjourned on 21 November 1964.

[^c31-7]: Like others already mentioned, Quanbeck took seriously the task of interpreting the council to a Lutheran audience. See Warren A. Quanbeck, ed., _Challenge … and Response: A Protestant Perspective of the Vatican Council_ (Minneapolis, MN: Augsburg, 1966). The volume includes essays by Skydsgaard, Vajta, Lindbeck, and Schlink.

The fourth and final session of the council assembled on 14 September 1965. This session saw approval of the texts on non-Christian religions, divine revelation, the ministry and life of priests, missionary activity, and the Church in the modern world. On 4 December, Paul VI led a service with the observers and guests at St Paul’s Outside the Walls. Four days later, on 8 December 1965, a solemn closing of the council took place in the piazza of St Peter’s. For this session, the Lutheran World Federation appointed as observers Skydsgaard, Quanbeck, Vajta, and Silen. Substitutes included Dr Seppo Antio Teinonen of Finland, Brauer of the United States, Dr Hagen A. K. Staack of the United States, and Dr Friedrich Kantzenbach of France. The Evangelical Church in Germany appointed Schlink as an observer and Dietzfelbinger as a substitute. Guests of the Secretariat for Christian Unity included Cullmann and three members of the Lutheran Church– Missouri Synod in the United States: Hoffmann, Dr Carl S. Meyer, and Dr Walter F. Wolbrecht.

The significance of these Lutheran observers at the council cannot be overestimated. They are a visible indication of a reception of the aims and purposes of the Second Vatican Council by a prominent part of global Lutheranism. They not only fulfilled their original purpose of informing and interpreting the council in Lutheran circles, but also in quiet, unofficial, and often unnoted ways they helped shape many conciliar texts and decisions. This is a story that cannot be told here.[^c31-8]

[^c31-8]: An unparalleled source for the history is Mauro Velati, _Separati ma fratelli: Gli osservatori non-cattolici al Vaticano II (1962–_ _1965)_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 2014).

### 4. Founding an Institute for Ecumenical Research

Another example within the context of the Lutheran World Federation where the influence of the council can be noted is in the establishment and work of the Institute for Ecumenical Research in Strasbourg, France. This institute is closely related to the Lutheran World Federation but independent from it.

In 1963, at the Helsinki Assembly of the Lutheran World Federation, action was taken to establish a Lutheran Foundation for Interconfessional Research. The purpose of such a foundation was envisioned to assist Lutheran churches to fulfil their ecumenical responsibility in the area of theology. This was to be accomplished by four activities: research in areas where churches were divided in doctrine and church order **[p. 526]** and where theological issues were causing controversy; sponsorship of scholarly conferences and seminars; contacts and communication with non-Lutheran theologians; and appropriate publication of research and conferences.

The foundation established the Institute for Ecumenical Research in Strasbourg to accomplish these purposes. This French city was selected because of several factors: the fact that it was a cultural and historical centre; its significant Catholic, Lutheran, and Reformed presence; and its historic role in the sixteenth century. The institute began its work on 1 February 1965. Over the years, it has had an international staff of two to six theologians. It has provided staff and expertise to several international dialogues. It was a resource for the development of the _Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification_ between Lutherans and Roman Catholics, approved by the Lutheran World Federation and the Roman Catholic Church in 1999. The staff of the institute played a critical role in the Lutheran–Mennonite Study Commission that resulted in the Lutheran World Federation in 2010 taking action to repent of the legacy of Lutheran persecution of Anabaptists.

The timing of the authorization and creation of the foundation and the institute should not be seen as coincidental. The fact that they occurred in the midst of the Second Vatican Council is a sign of the recognition and importance of this council for global Lutheranism.

### 5. The Establishment of Lutheran–Catholic Theological Dialogue

A final instance of a reception of the council by Lutheranism is the Lutheran–Roman Catholic dialogue, whose origins can be located within the council itself. Even prior to the conclusion of the council, a Lutheran observer had raised with the Secretariat for Christian Unity the possibility of a theological dialogue. This conversation ultimately led to the establishment of an international Lutheran–Roman Catholic dialogue and several national dialogues.

Already in 1965, a Joint Working Group between the federation and the Secretariat for Christian Unity proposed an international dialogue. This dialogue commenced its work in 1967 and in 1972 published the _Malta Report_ or _The Gospel and the Church._ This report was clear, broad, and bold in its work and conclusions. It set the tone for subsequent reports.

This initial report was followed over the years with a publication in 1978 entitled _The Eucharist_, which concluded that Lutherans and Catholics share a consensus on Eucharistic presence and sacrifice. The next report, in 1980, of a somewhat different mode offered a picture of the purpose of the dialogue: it had the title _Ways to Community._ That same year, the dialogue observed the 450th anniversary of the Augsburg Confession with the text _All Under One Christ._ A critical topic for all ecumenical endeavours, ministry, was the **[p. 527]** focus of the next report, _Ministry in the Church_ of 1981. Following on this report, the dialogue offered a process for the establishment of a joint Lutheran–Roman Catholic ministry in _Facing Unity_, released in 1984.

Ten years later, in 1994, the document _The Church and Justification_, examining the ecclesiological implications of the doctrine that became so significant at the time of the Reformation, was published. In 2006, the dialogue issued its first study document, _The Apostolicity of the Church_.[^c31-9]

[^c31-9]: The reports of the dialogue can be found in the series of volumes entitled _Growth in Agreement._ Harding Meyer and Lukas Vischer, eds., _Growth in Agreement: Reports and Agreed Statements of Ecumenical Conversations on a World Level_ (New York: Paulist Press; Geneva: World Council of Churches, 1985); Jeffrey Gros, FSC, Harding Meyer, and William G. Rusch, eds., _Growth in Agreement II: Reports and Agreed Statements of Ecumenical Conversations on a World Level, 1982–1998_ (Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans; Geneva: World Council of Churches, 2000); Jeffrey Gros, FSC, Thomas F. Best, and Lorelei F. Fuchs, SA, eds., _Growth in Agreement III: International Dialogue Texts and Agreed Statements, 1998–2005_ (Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans; Geneva: World Council of Churches, 2007); Thomas F. Best et al. eds., _Growth in Agreement IV, 1 and 2, 2005–_ _2013_ (Geneva: World Council of Churches, 2017). See also _Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification_ (Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 2000); _From Conflict to Communion: Lutheran–Catholic Common Commemoration of the Reformation in 2017_ (Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 2017).

Over the years of the dialogue, two texts were released either as part of the dialogue’s direct work or deeply influenced by it. They are the _Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification_ of 1999 and _From Conflict to Communion: Lutheran–Catholic Common Commemoration of the Reformation in 2017._

The signing of the _Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification_ on 31 October 1999 was a unique ecumenical event. Representatives of the Lutheran World Federation and the Vatican signed a text that expressed a common, although not total, understanding of this doctrine. As a result of this common understanding, the mutual condemnations of the sixteenth century between these Lutheran and Roman Catholic churches no longer apply to the churches in question.

To observe the upcoming 500th anniversary of the Reformation, the dialogue published a text in 2013 with the title _From Conflict to Communion._ This study document offered new perspectives on Luther and the Reformation and gave suggestions to Lutherans and Roman Catholics on how to observe in an ecumenical age an event that had divided the Western Church in the sixteenth century.

### 6. Conclusion

It is impossible even to conjecture about the above activities—Lutheran observers at the Second Vatican Council, the Institute for Ecumenical Research in Strasbourg, and an ongoing Lutheran–Roman Catholic dialogue on international and national levels running for decades—without attributing all of these developments to a reception in Lutheran churches of an event that can be portrayed as the Second Vatican Council.

**[p. 528]** Yet other aspects of this reception are more difficult to record. Still, they are no less real. They include the warm relations between Lutheran and Roman Catholic parishes, the cooperation in addressing social needs in the twenty-first century, and friendships on theological faculties and among church leaders of both traditions. There is no doubt that these less documented examples of this type of reception will continue to bear fruit as the century enfolds. The topic of this chapter is not static, but will continue. It offers the hope of greater Lutheran–Roman Catholic theological consensus in areas of continuing difference where the weight of these differences on visible unity requires further examination. It offers the expectation of fuller expressions of the unity that can be claimed by Lutherans and Roman Catholics. None of this is imaginable without the Second Vatican Council and a Lutheran openness to accept the genuine invitation to be there as _dilectissimi observatores_, an expression often heard in the _aula_ from the lips of the council fathers during their debates.

One way to measure the Lutheran reception of this council is to note a book published in 1959. In that year a young but already promising Lutheran professor, Jaroslav Pelikan, published _The Riddle of Roman Catholicism._ This award-winning book disclosed a learned Lutheran perception of the faith of the Roman Catholic Church in the mid-twentieth century. This volume is dated today because of both the Second Vatican Council and a Lutheran willingness to engage and receive that council.[^c31-10]

[^c31-10]: Jaroslav Pelikan, _The Riddle of Roman Catholicism: Its History, Its Beliefs, Its Future_ (New York: Abington, 1959).

### Suggested Reading

_Centre d’études œcuméniques: 1965–2015_. Strasbourg: Lutheran Foundation for Interconfessional Research, 2015.

Dietzfelbinger, Hermann. _Veränderung und Beständigkeit: Erinnerungen_, especially chap. 14, ‘Das Ökumenische Institut in Straßburg’, 240–49. Munich: Claudius, 1984.

Lindbeck, George A. _The Future of Roman Catholic Theology: Vatican II—Catalyst for Change_. Philadelphia: Fortress, 1970.

Rusch, William G. _Towards a Common Future: Ecumenical Reception and a New Consensus_. Eugene, OR: Cascade, 2019.

Schjørring, Jens Holger, Prasanna Kumari, and Norman A. Hjelm, eds. _From Federation to Communion: The History of the Lutheran World Federation_. Minneapolis, MN: Fortress, 1997.

## 32. Reformed Reception of Vatican II

Donald W. Norwood

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 529]** Before going into more detail, it is important to consider a few brief points concerning Reformed churches, the process of ecumenical reception, and why reception of a Roman Catholic council matters to non-Roman Catholics.

Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists, and Reformed Christians all constitute world communions of approximately equal size, each with 80-100 million members. Of the four, the Reformed churches are the least unifled and coordinated globally. Locally and in the World Council of Churches (WCC), especially in the decade of Vatican II, they have often been the ecumenical leaders. The first two general secretaries and an early director of Faith and Order were Reformed churchmen. But because of their global diversity, it is hard to generalize about Reformed reception. It is equally hard to define Reformed other than saying it is an ethos, a way of being church, which is more or less common to member churches of the World Communion of Reformed Churches. Our roots are in the European Reformation led by Calvin, Zwingli, Bucer, and company, yet in no case was any of these theologians a founding father to be compared with Martin Luther for the Lutherans or John and Charles Wesley for the Wesleyans and Methodists. And unlike Anglicans, we are not related to any particular place or nation. Mena Prestwich wrote of ‘International Calvinism 1541– 1715’_:_ ‘We are international. We can be found anywhere, but not everywhere. We like to think that our leading theologians belong to the whole Church.’ The Anglican historian Diarmaid MacCulloch described Calvin as ‘the Fifth Latin Doctor of the Church’, in the succession of Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory. Karl Barth, our best-known Reformed theologian of the twentieth century, preferred to be described as ‘catholic’ rather than ‘Protestant’. Calvin and Barth both wrote theology for the whole Church, **[p. 530]** not just for their particular part of it. All of which means that in theory, but not always in practice, the Reformed might be expected to be more ‘open’—a key concept in Barth—to receive what Rome or any other great Church tradition has to offer, provided what is offered is consistent with the mind of Christ and the Word of God, discerned in Scripture.

Like all other churches, we, the Reformed, received an invitation to share in the Vatican council. In our case this was addressed to the World Alliance of Reformed Churches and the International Congregational Council, two bodies that united in 1970 to form what later became the World Communion of Reformed Churches. We responded by sending some of our most ecumenically committed theologians: Robert McAfee Brown and Douglas Horton of the United States, Marc Boegner and Hébert Roux of France, Gerrit Berkouwer of the Netherlands, George Caird and William Shaw of Britain, and Lukas Vischer of Switzerland (also representing the WCC) to join the company of some 200 non–Roman Catholic observers. They were soon made to feel that they were not simply observers but active participants behind the scenes and a clearly visible presence that could not be ignored by the council fathers, the bishops, in their debates. Personal invitations were also extended to Oscar Cullmann, Karl Barth, and brothers Roger Schutz and Max Thurian of Taizé, all key thinkers in the Reformed tradition.

The observers’ views were sought and often heeded, especially on key issues like Scripture and Tradition, worship, Church unity, Christians and Jews, laypeople in the Church, and the Virgin Mary. Why? Because when Reformed theologian Willem Visser ’t Hooft, then the first general secretary of the WCC, attended one of the sessions, he immediately realized this and responded appropriately in Latin: ‘nostra res igitur’. Vatican business was ours also. But it is also the case ecumenically that the views of half the world’s Christians, represented by their bishops in an ecumenical council, ought to be taken seriously even if on some points we beg to differ. The observers and the Roman Catholic experts, _periti_ like Yves Congar, Hans Küng, Karl Rahner, and Joseph Ratzinger, helped make the whole experience of Vatican II an open university where all present had much to learn from each other, an exemplar of ‘Catholic learning and receptive ecumenism’.

### 2. A Set of Documents or an Experience of an Experience of an Ecumenical Council—or Both?

In the judgement of Reformed participants like Roux, McAfee Brown, Horton, and Vischer, the experience of Vatican II as an ecumenical event is as important as the documents. Simply being together in Rome was a life-changing experience which has continued to transform relationships with Roman Catholics almost **[p. 531]** everywhere. Vischer, in the final volume of Giuseppe Alberigo’s _History of Vatican II_, writes about ‘The [^c32-1] Council as an Event in the Ecumenical Movement’. This is also Alberigo’s line. The council is much more than the sum of its documents. Roux said, ‘It is impossible to give account of this lived experience. It was an event of which we were the witnesses.’ For Barth, the Church itself is a dynamic event, something that happens because God the Holy Spirit brings Christians together. Jürgen Moltmann became more ecumenically involved because of the council but rarely cites its documents. Gerrit Berkouwer valued the debates more highly than the council’s decisions.

[^c32-1]: Lukas Vischer, ‘The Council as an Event in the Ecumenical Movement’, in _History of Vatican II_, vol. 5, ed. Giuseppe Alberigo and Joseph A. Komonchak (Leuven: Peeters, 2006), 485–540.

Barth was to his dying day one of the council’s staunchest advocates; his comments are always perceptive. In the early stages, he advised his colleagues not to expect too much ecumenically. The council’s main purpose was its own internal renewal. If, in the process, Rome became more ecumenical, this was a bonus, not its main purpose. And he would know from Hans Küng’s _The Council and Reunion_ that Pope John’s original intention was to make the Roman Catholic Church more attractive so that other Christians would have less excuse to stay apart: ‘Look brothers, this is the Church of Christ. Come, here the way lies open for meeting and for homecoming; come, or take or resume that place which is yours.’ The same motive is evident in the first document approved by the Council (December 1963), _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ (_SC_):

The sacred Council has set out to impart an ever-increasing vigour to the Christian lives of the faithful; to adapt more closely to the needs of our age those institutions which are subject to change; to encourage whatever can promote the union of all who believe in Christ; to strengthen whatever serves to call all of humanity into the Church’s fold. … The liturgy daily builds up those who are in the Church … At the same time it marvelously enhances their power to preach Christ and thus show the Church to those who are outside as a sign lifted up among the nations, a sign under which the scattered children of God may be gathered together until there is one fold and one shepherd. (_SC_ 1–2)

The model here is still that of a call to return to Rome: Rome is home! As so often in council documents, it is not clear whether the ‘one shepherd’ here refers to the pope or to Christ, the Good Shepherd. Perhaps both. The council became more ecumenical as it evolved, thanks in part, I would argue, to the non-Roman Catholic observers. When England’s Roman Catholic archbishop spoke of ‘return’, one can almost hear Yves Congar in his _Journal_ shouting him down. His entry for 30 November 1962 reads: ‘Heenan, he spoke at [^c32-2] length to say little. HE SPOKE IN TERMS OF A RETURN.’ The US Presbyterian observer McAfee Brown made the same point. But despite the good intentions in the reforming of the liturgy and the fact that nothing is now said in the text of the Mass that conscientious Anglicans or Protestants need object to, it is sadly still **[p. 532]** the case that if we wish to receive communion in a Roman Catholic church, even if married to a Roman Catholic partner, we must first return to Rome. Or at least this remained the official view.

[^c32-2]: Yves Congar, _My Journal of the Council_, trans. M. J. Ronayne and M. C. Boulding, ed. Denis Minns (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2012), 221; emphasis in the original; originally published as _Mon journal du concîle_, 2 vols. (Paris: Cerf, 2002). For Heenan’s speech, see _AS_ I/3, 726–28.

Such rejection hurts more because now we are among friends. The importance of ecumenical friendship is not something noted in the documents. It could easily be undervalued as a non-theological factor. Douglas Horton noted this and had this to say in response to the welcome to the observers:

There are differences in theology and organisation that have developed between the Roman Catholic Church and us over the centuries, in which we have striven to remain apart. We should have to wait generations, if not centuries, in order to resolve them, but clearly the friendship that you have shown us has prepared the ground in which reconciliation can grow. As theologians, you may call friendship a non-theological factor, but theological or not, friendship must have a part to play in the future of the church.[^c32-3]

[^c32-3]: Citation of S. Schmidt by Julian Charley, ‘Friendship: The Forgotten Factor in Ecumenism’, in _Communion et réunion:_ _Mélanges Jean-Marie Roger Tillard_, ed. G. R. Evans and Michel Gourgues, OP (Leuven: Peeters, 1995), 113.

Congregationalist Horton is here quoted by Anglican Julian Charley. Charley writes about the importance of friendship in a festschrift for Jean-Marie Tillard, OP, who was also his close friend. Tillard, who was active in several key dialogues and in the WCC’s Faith and Order commission, had many other ecumenical friends. So did Gustave Weigel, SJ, in the US, among them Presbyterian Robert McAfee Brown. Visser ’t Hooft and Cardinal Willebrands found much in common because both came from the same province in Holland and were each ecumenically committed. Marc Boegner and Henri de Lubac had worked together in defence of Jews in Nazi-occupied France. Oscar Cullman loved Cardinal Bea because he was such a lovely man anchored in his love for Christ. In Britain, many of the ecumenical pioneers, like Presbyterian Lesslie Newbigin and Anglican Oliver Tomkins, became friends through the Student Christian Movement. Who dares to say now that friendship is a non-theological factor in Church unity! If one were only to read the council documents, neglecting its very human story, one might ignore that non-Roman Catholics were there or that over the course of its four sessions, lasting friendships were formed as people from very different traditions worked and worshipped together. Nor would one see the real significance of the council as a genuinely ecumenical event.

### 3. Conciliar Reception

One almost spontaneous effect of the calling of the Second Vatican Council was to revive and receive **[p. 533]** ecumenical interest in councils. This, too, was a ‘nostra res igitur’ matter for all churches, but especially for those that pride themselves on being conciliar, the Orthodox and Reformed in particular. John Calvin and Martin Luther once hoped that a free reforming council would resolve disputes at the Reformation and avoid divisions. All that happened was Trent, too little and too late. Calvin was scathing about the calibre of its bishops. He would be more complimentary about Vatican II. In some ways, his conciliar convictions may even have inspired it, or so Roman Catholic scholar Alexandre Ganoczy once suggested in _Calvin und_ [^c32-4] _Vaticanum II: Das Problem der Kollegialität_. In turn, Vatican II prompted the WCC to initiate studies of _Councils and the Ecumenical Movement_ (1968) and in its 1968 Uppsala assembly to propose that ‘The members of the World Council of Churches, committed to each other, should work for a time when a genuinely universal council may once more speak for all Christians, and lead the way into the future.’ It would be fair to claim that Reformed people like Lukas Vischer, director of Faith and Order, were among its leading advocates. They pursued the notion further in talk of ‘conciliar fellowship’. Lutheran general secretary Konrad Raiser, a close colleague of Vischer, made it part of the WCC’s Common Vision document in the 1990s and hoped it might even be a goal for the new millennium. Roman Catholics who contemplate a Vatican III realize it would have to be a very different council next time. The Reformed would insist that it include women and laypeople.

[^c32-4]: Alexandre Ganoczy, _Calvin und Vaticanum II: Das Problem der Kollegialität_ (Mainz: Institut für Europäische Geschichte, 1965).

### 4. Sharing the Experience of Vatican II

The observers not only participated in the formulations of the council’s sixteen documents but were also required by those who appointed them to report back. With one exception, our Reformed observers did so thoroughly and enthusiastically. I write as one who was inspired by what Professor Caird told us, his students in Oxford. He also published his findings as a Congregational Lecture, _Our Dialogue with Rome._ Karl Barth discovered in his final years, 1965–68, that what people most wanted to hear about was what he made of the council. An entire volume of his _Gesamptausgabe_ is taken up with his lectures and interviews. We also [^c32-5] have his appraisal of Vatican II, _Ad Limina Apostolorum_. Hébert Roux published reports to various French synods. Lukas Vischer kept the WCC fully informed. In the United States and beyond, Robert McAfee Brown and Douglas Horton offered their own detailed accounts. Horton kept a diary. Only the Waldensian professor Vittorio Subilia seems more sceptical. Congar comments in _My Journal of the Council_: ‘Subilia with whom the [^c32-6] World Alliance of Reformed Churches has replaced H Roux is VERY anti-Catholic.’ One might guess at **[p. 534]** this from the critical study Subilia made of Roman Catholicism even before the council, _The Problem of Catholicism_ (1962). He doubted if Rome was capable of reform.

[^c32-5]: Karl Barth, _Ad Limina Apostolorum: An Appraisal of Vatican II_, trans. Keith R. Crim (Eugene, OR: Wipf & Stock, 2016); originally published as _Ad Limina Apostolorum_ (Zurich: EVZ, 1967).

[^c32-6]: Congar, _My Journal of the Council_, 675.

This fact about Reformed reception is important to note. The Reformed, like other confessional groupings, embrace a wide spectrum of views. In Britain and Ireland, Revd Dr Ian Paisley, an Irish Presbyterian minister and MP, was for years notorious for his anti-Catholic and anti-ecumenical views. He mellowed dramatically and all Ireland benefited! Some Reformed congregations in Latin America are very anti- Catholic, which is not surprising if their Spanish and Portuguese ‘conquerors’ were very anti-Protestant. For such groups, the hard-fought struggle in the council for religious freedom after years of suppression was a matter of life and death. But Congar also noted that another Waldensian professor, Valdo Vinay, was [^c32-7] ‘less anti’. So was Paulo Ricca, who could rejoice in the fact that a tiny minority church like his could be taken so seriously in such a Roman Catholic country as Italy, not least in discussions about mixed marriages.

[^c32-7]: Ibid.

Rome’s commitment to the ecumenical movement opened up numerous possibilities of sharing something of the Vatican II experience. Two ways had been anticipated. One was the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, first inaugurated in 1909 and made more generous and open by the Roman Catholic Abbé Paul Couturier in 1937. The other is the Taizé Ecumenical Community, founded in war-torn France by four Reformed brothers, including Schutz and Thurian, who were guests at Vatican II. Taizé still gathers together thousands of young people for days of prayer and communal living across national and confessional frontiers. In one respect, it excels where Vatican II and Rome officially remain more cautious. Roman Catholics and Protestants can and do share communion together, though on one condition: the presiding priest is always Roman Catholic. This is short-circuit ecumenism that no serious dialogue would accept, except that it works and few seem to mind! And though there may never be another Vatican council, Roman Catholics are now active in many of the activities of the WCC and in most regional and national ecumenical councils. In the 1950s, we could not even pray together. Now we eat together, talk together, and wonder what still keeps us apart. After the good experience of Pope John, Reformed stalwarts like McAfee Brown could even contemplate _A Pope for All Christians_ (1976). Why not? Especially one like Francis!

### 5. Reformed Reception of Some Key Documents of Vatican II

Before reporting some Reformed responses to key documents, I have first tried to reread the texts and hear **[p. 535]** what each document has to say. This prompts three very different reactions. First, as a non-Roman Catholic reader, one becomes very conscious that a document was written by Roman Catholics for Roman Catholics. But second, most documents answer questions we non-Roman Catholics have been asking or should be asking. Third, Good Pope John and the council fathers invited us to the council and urged us to help them be the People of God that God wants us all to be. Years later, Pope John Paul II, in _Ut Unum Sint_ (_UUS_) (1995), asked Reformed Protestants and others to help him be a better pope. We all need each other’s help and are mutually accountable. We begin as the council did: with worship.

_Sacrosanctum Concilium_, the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy, was the first document considered and agreed by the council, on 4 December 1963. The council believed its most important act was to worship God. Each day began with a celebration of the Mass. Here observers observed but could not participate fully. What they could also observe was that worship was much more varied than they had assumed. Rome is truly the most international of all churches and is not monochrome. So in the two months leading up to this decision in December 1963, Horton experienced and appreciated six different rites, including Syrio-Antiochene, Mozambic, Coptic, and Malankara. This is worth knowing, because _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ is much more cautious about deviations from a norm. But he would also note that the council takes up many of the questions posed by the sixteenth-century Reformers.

Contrary to what is often assumed, John Calvin encouraged more frequent and active participation in the Eucharist than was customary in the medieval Catholic Church. He still fails to persuade most Reformed churches that the Eucharist should be celebrated each Sunday and that the full service is one of word and sacrament. _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ agrees with Calvin! So does St Giles’ Reformed Cathedral in Edinburgh.

The Reformers also pleaded for worship to be in the vernacular, the language of the people. This was strongly contested in the council debates. Hence what now seems an overcautious suggestion: ‘Since the use of the vernacular, whether in the Mass, the administration of the sacraments or in other parts of the liturgy, may frequently be of great advantage to the people, a wider use may be made of it’ (_SC_ 36.2). What is still being challenged by Roman Catholics themselves is the assumption that some remote higher authority knows best what the local vernacular is. This provoked John Wilkins’s angry protest about un-English English, _Lost in Translation_.[^c32-8]

[^c32-8]: John Wilkins, ‘Lost in Translation: The Bishops, the Vatican, and the English Liturgy’, _Commonweal_ 132, no. 21 (2 December 2005): 12 {.. See also Gerald O’Collins and John Wilkins, _Lost in Translation: The English Language and the_ _Catholic Mass_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2017).

A common Catholic criticism of Vatican documents is that they make no provision for implementing council [^c32-9] decisions. The point is made by the Dominican Hervé Legrand.  _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ is a welcome exception. It sets out forty-nine normative principles, among them the reform of the Mass: ‘It is the wish of **[p. 536]** the church to undertake a careful general reform of the liturgy in order that Christian people may be more certain to derive an abundance of graces from it’ (_SC_ 21). As a fruit of the wider ecumenical and liturgical movement which predates the council, there is now what Max Thurian of Taizé describes as _Ecumenical Convergence in Celebration_. Liturgies in different communities now have a marked similarity of structure. Reformed Christians would also welcome its more comprehensive understanding of Christ’s presence. Nothing is said about transubstantiation, even though ecumenically minded Reformed theologians like England’s Nathaniel Micklem could accept this scholastic attempt to expound a mystery. Christ, we are told, is also present in the word and in the hymns and prayers (_SC_ 7). Alleluia! The Reformation in Geneva and elsewhere was once marked by the abolition of the Mass. Professor Janos [^c32-10] Pasztor of the Hungarian Reformed Church reminds us that the classic Heidelberg Catechism stated: ‘The mass is fundamentally a complete denial of the once for all sacrifice and passion of Jesus Christ and as such an idolatry to be condemned.’ Reformed have no good reason to do so now, and this, as Pasztor notes, is all part of the positive response and reception of Vatican II. We may not talk about ‘the sacrifice of the Mass’ or ask the Blessed Virgin to pray for us, but we have listened to the explanations behind such convictions and can treat them with respect, if not total agreement.

[^c32-9]: Hervé Legrand, ‘Forty Years Later: What Has Become of the Ecclesiological Reforms Envisaged by Vatican II?’, in _Vatican II:_ _A Forgotten Future_, ed. Alberto Melloni and Christoph Theobald (London: SCM, 2005), 57–72.

[^c32-10]: Janos Pasztor, ‘Catholicity of Reformed Theology’, in _Toward the Future of Reformed Theology: Tasks, Topics, Traditions_, ed. David Willis and Michael Welker (Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 1999), 21–38.

In any case, for most Reformed congregations, total agreement with every word in a liturgical text is never expected. The Reformed tradition prefers ‘directories’ of public worship rather than authorized service books. Celebrants are free to write and revise prayers in different services, including the Eucharist, according to agreed principles about what should be said and done. So Max Thurian, as a Reformed theologian and liturgist, was free to write a liturgical text, the Lima Liturgy, which he hoped all traditions, including the Orthodox and Roman Catholics, could accept since it was based on agreements reached in responses to the WCC’s Faith and Order document _Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry_ (1982). Ironically, when, towards the end of his life, Thurian became a Roman Catholic, he was no longer free to be so bold.

_Sacrosanctum Concilium_ promises ‘to promote that warm and lively appreciation of sacred Scripture’ (_SC_ 24). Following the council, a three-year lectionary of readings for the Sunday Masses has been developed which is now widely followed in the Common Lectionary in many Reformed and other Protestant and Anglican [^c32-11] congregations. As such, it is for most worshippers the most obvious example of the reception of Vatican II. The point has been noted and welcomed by renowned Reformed liturgical scholars like Horace T. Allen Jr. of Boston and Yale. But in good Reformed fashion, the use of any lectionary is a matter for serious debate and discussion. Many congregations might welcome the fact that over the course of three years they may receive **[p. 537]** a much more comprehensive range of the ‘whole counsel of God’ in the witness of the Old and New Testaments than when subject to the arbitrary choice of texts by those who preside and preach. But questions arise. Who has authority to tell God’s people what parts of the Bible they can read? The magisterium? No way! Roman Catholics in Latin America wanted more attention given to the radical teachings of Old Testament prophets. In a review of American and Church of Scotland Reformed liturgies, John Goldingay notes that the choice of psalms is very selective. Half the Psalter consists of psalms of lamentation, but these are rarely included. On a more general note, Karl Barth rejoiced that whereas Roman Catholics were once warned not to read the Bible, now they are told they must do so. The Reformed would welcome more positive appreciation of hymns.

[^c32-11]: Consultation on Common Texts, _Revised Common Lectionary_, 20th Anniversary ed. (Minneapolis: Fortress, 2012).

### 6. The Decree on Ecumenism

If _Sacrosanctum Concilium_’s advocacy of a lectionary became the most obvious and common example of Reformed reception by local congregations, the Decree on Ecumenism (_Unitatis Redintegratio_ (_UR_)) changed every tradition’s prospects for better and closer relationships with Rome. When Roman Catholics had once been told not to read the Bible and, in _Mortalium Animos_ (1928), not to get too involved with other Christians, now they are urged to do both. The document begins: ‘The restoration of unity among all Christians is one of the principal concerns of the Second Vatican Council’ (_UR_ 1). The council believes, or certainly hopes, that ‘almost everyone, though in different ways, longs for the one visible Church of God, a Church truly universal and sent forth to the whole world that the world may be converted to the Gospel’ (_UR_ 1). Its call to unity is, in good Reformed fashion, biblically based: John 17 and Jesus’s prayer that all may be one, Ephesians 4 about the overcoming of divisions, and more general references to 1 Corinthians. Present generations are not to be blamed for divisions of the past ‘for which, often enough, people on both sides were to blame’ (_UR_ 3). Appeal is then made to ‘the signs of the times’, which include throughout the world many signs of movements to unity, and so ‘This sacred council, therefore, exhorts all the Catholic faithful to recognise the signs of the times and to take an active and intelligent part in the work of ecumenism’ (_UR_ 4). Praise the Lord, many priests and laity have done and are doing just that. So have some popes. But it should also be admitted, sixty years later, that Vatican documents are not timeless but reflect, as here, the optimism of the 1960s, when unity was much more fashionable.

Reformed theologians would hear their own distinctive convictions quoted when the council fathers, too, describe the Church as _semper reformanda_: ‘Christ summons the Church as she goes her pilgrim way to that continual reformation of which she always has need’ (_UR_ 6). Many of us have quoted this for years, unaware of its source. Appropriately, it was only in one of our oldest dialogues—that founded by Abbé Paul Couturier **[p. 538]** in 1937, the Groupe des Dombes, with French-speaking churches, Roman Catholic and Reformed—that we learned that the Pietist Jodocus von Lodenstein was probably the first to use the expression and did so in 1675.

The council here repeatedly (_UR_ 4, 9, 19) urges us all to dialogue. It met with an almost immediate positive response from Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists, and Reformed, all in the years 1965 to 1968 when two great ecumenical leaders, Cardinal Bea and Karl Barth, were still alive to add their comments. Barth had his own personal dialogues with Pope Paul VI, Yves Congar, Karl Rahner, Joseph Ratzinger, and others in Rome and gives us his report in _Ad Limina Apostolorum_ (1967). He also engaged in dialogue with his Swiss colleague in Basel, Hans Urs von Balthasar, in 1968. The _Growth in Agreement_ volumes prepared by the WCC currently list eighty major dialogues from 1972 to 2014, twenty of them involving Reformed churches. Those with Rome deal first with ‘The Presence of Christ in Church and World’ (1977) and ‘Toward a Common Understanding of the Church’ (1984–90). In addition, the Disciples of Christ entered into ‘Conversations with Rome’ in 1981 and on ‘The Church as Communion in Christ’ (1992). All dialogues—apart from the unofficial Malines Conversations, initiated by Cardinal Mercier in 1921, the Groupe des Dombes in 1937, and the Anglican–Old Catholic Bonn Agreement of 1931—post-date Vatican II and can be seen as a response to _Unitatis Redintegratio_’s appeal and the council’s lead.

The council also stimulated a wider discussion of the meaning of catholicity by admitting that ‘the divisions among Christians prevent the Church from realising the fullness of catholicity proper to her in those of her sons who, though joined to her by baptism, are yet separated from full communion with her’ (_UR_ 4). This is a big and bold confession. The Roman Catholic Church cannot be fully catholic without us! Barth and others had often claimed that it was because the Reformed had neglected that fuller catholicity confessed in the Creed of 381 that Rome usurped the title and called herself _the_ Catholic Church.

On two further points about this decree, it helps to know some background to the debates. Barth asked: ‘Why is the most grievous, the fundamental schism—the opposition of Church and Synagogue (Romans 9– 11; Ephesians 2)—not dealt with here?’ The answer is that the question of the Church’s relationship with the Jews was initially included as part of Bea’s commission, along with the discussion of religious freedom, but the council fathers found the addition of these two themes too much to handle in one document. Barth had earlier made the same point in a final volume of _Church Dogmatics_: ‘Even the modern ecumenical movement suffers more seriously from the absence of Israel than of Rome or Moscow.’ He said this in 1959, before the council and before the Russian Orthodox Church joined the WCC in 1961. These matters were ultimately treated in two additional documents: the Declaration on the Relation of the Church to Non-Christian Religions, _Nostra Aetate_, and the Declaration on Religious Freedom, _Dignitatis Humanae._

The second background note concerns what Stjepan, in his biography of Bea, _The Cardinal of Unity_, describes as a ‘bombshell’ and the _History of Vatican II_ describes as ‘The Black Week of Vatican II’. Someone in higher authority, presumably Pope Paul VI, insisted that some parts of the Decree on Ecumenism be altered even **[p. 539]** after the council fathers had debated and voted for them. The council fathers accepted that Protestants ‘find’ God in the Scriptures. How could they without the guidance of the magisterium! So, the text (_UR_ 21) was altered to say: ‘Invoking the Holy Spirit, they _seek_ in these very Scriptures God as he speaks to them in Christ.’ Roman Catholic commentators like Congar and Hebblethwaite make light of the changes. Reformed observers like Cullmann, Boegner, and Thurian were clearly upset but were comforted a little by the fact that Willebrands and Stransky were, too. Roux realized that the question of the pope’s authority in the Church remained an unresolved issue. It still is. Horton felt it was tragic that a lot of Protestants would now thank God they were not Roman Catholics. Visser ’t Hooft feared such actions might put an end to dialogue. Barth was unaware of the changes, as he had only the final text to go on. Matters were made worse when the pope unilaterally, without the agreement of the council, declared that Mary is ‘Mother of the Church’. Congar, in his posthumously published _Journal_ (22 November 1964), says he does not know what this means. With his customary emphasis, he writes, ‘THE SEPARATED BRETHREN HAVE GONE BACK TO HAVING DOUBTS [^c32-12] ABOUT US.’ Fortunately, most recovered, but the shock ought still to be recorded, as later popes were tempted to expound the council in their own words. It is also crucial in any serious dialogue that we allow the other partner to speak for herself. Reformed churches _are_ churches and in them _we do_ find God in Scripture and we do experience Christ’s presence in communion. Alleluia!

[^c32-12]: Congar, _My Journal of the Council_, 697; emphasis in original.

### 7. Significant Reformed Observations on Some Other Documents

Ideally, there ought not to be a separate document on Church unity, _Lumen Gentium_ (_LG_), since unity is of the very nature of the Church. Nor should there be another on the laity, _Apostolicam Actuositatem_, because in the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, _laos theou_ embraces all the People of God, not just the clergy. But the council fathers did agree that there should not be a separate document about Mary, for Mary belongs to the Church, even though Pope Paul and the council were not sure how.

Mary was not a contentious issue at the Reformation. She had become such by Vatican II. On what to say about Mary, the council was more divided than on any other issue. This is partly because in the 400 years since the Reformation, Roman Catholics, Protestants, Anglicans, and Orthodox had, with few exceptions, ceased to listen to and consult each other. The pope was infallible, and what he said about Mary must be taken as Gospel truth. Prior to another key document, _Dei Verbum_, Scripture and Tradition might have equal claims as Revealed Truth. The Reformers and the Reformed would not agree, but who cared what they **[p. 540]** thought? Their ministers were not ministers, their churches not churches, and their grasp of the faith deficient. It hurts to say all this, but such are the hurts this great council sought to heal, and praise the Lord, it partially succeeded.

The council fathers agreed that the Church is Christ with all the People of God, among whom a few are ordained as bishops, priests, and deacons (_LG_ 1–4, 9–17): ‘Hence the universal Church is seen to be a people made one by the unity of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit’ (_LG_ 4). Agreed! They wanted to say more about the collegiality and authority of the bishops (_LG_ 8, 18, 21–28) to offset the imbalance of Vatican I, when the council fathers had been prevented from fuller discussion of the papacy and the bishops by the outbreak of the Franco-Prussian War in 1870. Collegiality and the role of the Curia remain unfinished business or insoluble problems! They knew that any suggestion that the Blessed Virgin was Co-Redeemer, as many of them wished to state, was totally unacceptable to most other Christians and that even the Orthodox preferred respect and devotion for Mary to dogmatic assertions about the mysteries of our salvation. Barth, in his conversations with Pope Paul and some theologians, asked for reassurance: ‘Are the predicates of Mary—Advocate, _Auxiliatrix_, _Adjutrix_, and _Mediatrix_ (_LG_ 62)—to be understood only in the context of pious invocation? (Thus Ratzinger.) If so, is this interpretation to be extended to all Mariology?’

Because Vatican II was so sensitive to our Reformed reservations, it met with a much more sympathetic response. George Caird, for example, says, ‘We Protestants cannot be too grateful for the courage and generosity with which the Council Fathers have grasped this particular nettle. They have recognised what a serious obstacle their Mariology has been to Protestants, and they could hardly have done more to allay our [^c32-13] suspicions without seriously imperilling the simple faith of millions of loyal Catholics.’ Even before the council met, Max Thurian of Taizé had published a scholarly and very balanced account, _Mary, Mother of the Lord, Figure of the Church_. It is news to some of us, including me, that some of the Reformers had no difficulty in accepting Mary’s Immaculate Conception and Bodily Assumption even before these became official Roman Catholic dogma in 1870 and 1950 respectively.

[^c32-13]: George B. Caird, _Our Dialogue with Rome_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1967), 45–46.

On the laity, it is good to note that old Protestant slogans like ‘the priesthood of all believers’ were now being corrected and adopted in an ecumenical consensus on the common priesthood of all the baptized, and that for many of us, baptisms in different traditions are now recognized as something we have in common. Yves Congar’s groundbreaking study _Lay People in the Church_ (1956) is matched by _A Theology of the Laity_ (1957) by Hendrik Kraemer (the Reformed theologian and director of the WCC’s Ecumenical Institute at Bossey). But we would all have to agree with Roman Catholic theologian Paul Lakeland, whom I met at the First Receptive Ecumenism Conference in Durham, that the laity are still being forgotten and their convictions too often ignored.

In the 1960s, _Gaudium et Spes_ (_GS_) delighted many Roman Catholics and Protestants because of its bold **[p. 541]** attempt to read ‘the signs of the times’ and positively engage with the modern world. Forty years on, Lukas Vischer and many Roman Catholics would agree it is dated, time-bound to the ethos of Western liberalism and democracy. Even at the time, Barth wondered why it was so much more optimistic about human flourishing than St Paul. Read today, it says nothing about the current crisis of the environment or much about women.

### 8. Critical Reception: The Question of Woman

Cardinal Suenens observed that half the human race was female. Observer Douglas Horton wondered where they were. So, unlike the Reformed synods, he was more used to accepting that even there, men still dominated. In the final two sessions, a few carefully selected women were welcomed as ‘Guests in their own House’. Some took part in the commission in the Church in the Modern World, which is one reason why women get a brief but very non-committal reference in _Gaudium et Spes_: ‘At present women are involved in nearly all spheres of life; they ought to be permitted to play their part fully in ways suited to their nature’ (_GS_ 60; see also 29), which the celibate fathers of Vatican II, unlike us married men, presumed to understand!

There is nothing here for Reformed churches to receive: not even a challenge. Challenges would come later, when successive popes would tell us that the Church has no authority to ordain women. My own church had done so in 1917; Congregationalists in the US had done this even earlier, in 1853. Anglicans who were still dithering would later be told that ordaining women only made reunion more difficult. Maybe, but for the past century, their male priests had not been accepted either. But, as I have argued, the experience of the council is better than its documents. According to Roman Catholic author Mary Malone: ‘despite the bishops’ almost complete lack of concern for women, the Council had enormous consequences for them’, and not just Roman Catholic women. Once we accept that renowned feminist theologians like Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza and Rosemary Radford Ruether were stimulated by reports of the council and provoked by the documents, we can agree with Malone. Reformed feminist literature rarely mentions the documents, but no serious theologian can ignore these women or Mary Daly and many more. It is rather sad that few note the fact they are Roman Catholics who may look to women and men in other churches for support. Ecumenism is not about being non- denominational but about being able to say where we are coming from [^c32-14] and engage together in ‘receptive ecumenism and the call to catholic learning’. And to be fair, when the **[p. 542]** council fathers first met together in 1962, feminism, the environment, and ecofeminism were not live issues. Times have changed, but reception of what needs to be changed takes longer.

[^c32-14]: Paul Murray, ed., _Receptive Ecumenism and the Call to Catholic Learning_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2008).

### 9. Critical Reception: A Reformed Comment on Rwanda

Thirty years after the Council, fifty years after the Holocaust, Christians in Rwanda hacked to death their fellow Christians just because they belonged to a different tribe. The genocide in which nearly a million people were killed exposed the shameful weaknesses of the international community and of the churches. Some accounts ignore the churches’ role. Presbyterian scholar Tharcisse Gatwa does not. All the major churches—Roman Catholic, Anglican, and Reformed—were complicit in political policies which favoured the Hutus against the Tutsis and Twa people. The Reformed had poorly educated local leaders. Roman Catholic bishops were too often spokesmen for the government. But Vatican II did mean that in the slow and ongoing reconciliation process, Catholics and Protestants worked together as never before. Gatwa himself took a lead in this. But the same process exposed a failing that was clear even at Vatican II. Rome finds it impossible to admit that the Church, as distinct from some individual members, has sinned. Vatican II, as Barth noted, never confessed her anti-Semitism. The pope never asked forgiveness for the Rwanda genocide. Reconciliation requires repentance. Reformed theologians like Moltmann discovered after their Stuttgart Declaration of German guilt that confession can be liberating. All Catholics know this. Why not say so?

### 10. Concluding Summary

When the bishops representing the faithful voted almost unanimously for its sixteen documents, they transformed the face of the Roman Catholic Church and made her more attractive and comprehensible to that other half of the world’s Christians who are not Roman Catholics. We Reformed and other outsiders, once considered ‘heretics’, may now be thankful to be ‘in some, though imperfect communion with the Catholic Church’ (_UR_ 3). Pope John XXIII’s hope and prayer in the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity (1959) is now being answered and fulfilled. Alleluia! Little in the documents may change our faith, but most make it easier to engage in ongoing dialogue where we help each other and the whole Church to grow. We, the heirs of John Calvin and other Reformers, can agree with Pope John Paul II and the council that ‘Christ summons the Church, as she goes her pilgrim way, to that continual reformation of which she always has need’ (_UR_ 6; **[p. 543]** _UUS_ 16). Sunday by Sunday, many of us study the same Bible lessons and are helped by Catholic and Protestant commentators. Jürgen Moltmann and Hans Küng opened up discussions for us all in journals like _Concilium_ as others meet together in local ecumenical councils. We journey on, no longer as separated sisters and brothers but as ‘pilgrims together’. Another Alleluia even when the going is tough.

### Suggested Reading

Alberigo, Giuseppe, ed. _History of Vatican II_, English version edited by Joseph A. Komonchak. 5 vols. Maryknoll, NY: Orbis; Leuven: Peeters, 1995–2006.

Barth, Karl. _Ad Limina Apostolorum: An Appraisal of Vatican II_. Translated by Keith R. Crim. Eugene, OR: Wipf & Stock, 2016. Originally published in German as _Ad Limina Apostolorum_. Zurich: EVZ, 1967.

Caird, George B. _Our Dialogue with Rome_. London: Oxford University Press, 1967.

Norwood, Donald W. _Pilgrimage of Faith: Introducing the World Council of Churches_. Geneva: World Council of Churches, 2018.

Norwood, Donald W. _Reforming Rome: Karl Barth and Vatican II_. Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 2015.

## 33. The Methodist Reception of Vatican II

David Carter

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 544]** The Second Vatican Council marked a definitive turning point in the relationship between Methodists and Roman Catholics. Previously, almost all members of both communions had regarded the other with suspicion, often born of considerable mutual misunderstanding. In some countries, such as Britain, social relationships among Catholics and any Protestants were rare, and interchange on the sensitive subject of religion was usually avoided where contacts existed. Methodists regarded much Catholic faith and practice as unbiblical and even, in some cases, idolatrous; most Catholics thought of Methodism as just another heretical Protestant sect. The 1881 Oecumenical Methodist Conference, predecessor of today’s World Methodist Council, even defined popery, along with infidelity and intemperance, as one of the three great contemporary threats to evangelical religion.[^c33-1]

[^c33-1]: R. W. Perks et al., eds, _Proceedings of the Oecumenical Methodist Conference Held in City Road Chapel London, September_ _1881_ (Hamilton: S. G. Stone, 1882).

Very few indeed anticipated the changed relationships that were to come as a result of the council, especially in Britain and the US. Even Albert Outler, already an important voice in American Methodist theology, [^c33-2] doubted initially whether anything significant would come from the proposed council. However, well [^c33-3] beforehand, Maxim Piette, a French Catholic, had written appreciatively of the work of Wesley. On the eve of the council, but before it actually met and thus before there were any solid grounds for believing that key advances would be made, Rupert Davies, a leading British Methodist ecumenist, argued that the common **[p. 545]** concern of both communions for holiness gave grounds for hoping for closer rapprochement than hitherto. Davies’s was indeed a prophetic voice, his prophecy later receiving support from the emphasis placed on the universal call to holiness in _Lumen Gentium_. Both the atmosphere of the council and its call for dialogue stimulated Methodists to look for other similarities in emphasis between the two traditions.

[^c33-2]: Albert Outler, _A Methodist Observer at Vatican II_ (Westminster, MD: Newman Press, 1967).

[^c33-3]: Maxim Piette, _John Wesley in the Evolution of Protestantism_ (London: Sheed and Ward, 1937).

The World Methodist Council was invited to send observers to the council. These came mainly from the British and American conferences, but also included an Argentinian, José Miguel Bonino. It was their reports that would help change attitudes in both churches. From the Catholic side, the work of Outler, the American Methodist church historian, was particularly admired. In turn, several of the observers gave very positive reports to the subsequent meeting of the World Methodist Council in 1966, paving the way for its acceptance of the Catholic offer to initiate a formal international dialogue between the two communions.

It must be admitted that it is not always easy to determine which of the subsequent developments in Methodism, particularly in liturgy and in ecumenical practice, are primarily due to the influence of the council and which are due to more general ecumenical influences that were already operating, to varying extents, within Methodism as a result of the earlier Methodist entry into the ecumenical movement. Important elements in both churches were already influenced by the liturgical movement and by advances in modern biblical and historical research.
