Catholic liturgical changes resulting directly from Vatican II, such as the adoption of the Hippolytan Eucharistic prayer, were certainly to influence the revision of Eucharistic rites in both British and US Methodism, and Methodist liturgical scholars took a keen interest in the post-conciliar reforms.

The complexity of world Methodism must also be borne in mind when estimating the nature and extent of reception. In the 1960s, the British and American conferences both had the degree of self-confidence and the numbers of theologians to enter into constructive dialogue with Roman Catholics. Many other Methodist missions in Africa and Asia were receiving autonomous status from the American or British missions that had established them. In some countries, particularly in continental Europe, Methodist churches were small, often very pietistic, and critical of the established churches, Protestant as well as Catholic. In some places, their members had experienced discrimination, and relations with Roman Catholics remained extremely problematic despite the achievements of the council, a point observed in the tenth dialogue report of the international Methodist–Roman Catholic Commission in 2016; it contrasted the good relationships usually existing in Britain and the US between Catholics and Methodists with those in [^c33-4] some other countries, such as Brazil. It must be remembered that the World Methodist Council has no **[p. 546]** direct authority over the member churches, each of which is governed by its own conference. It was happy to commend the reports of the dialogues to the attention and study of the Methodist people, but evaluation at an official level was left to the conferences. In Britain, this did not occur until the 2006 report.

[^c33-4]: The World Methodist Council and the Roman Catholic Church, ‘The Call to Holiness: From Glory to Glory: Report of the Joint International Commission for Dialogue Between the World Methodist Council and the Roman Catholic Church’, Libreria Editrice Vaticana, 2016, http://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/pontifical_councils/chrstuni/meth-council- docs/rc_pc_chrstuni_doc_20171018_report-joint-commission_en.html.

### 2. The Observers: The Spirit of the Council

It was the spirit of the council as much as the debates and decrees that impressed the Methodist observers, including some who had not initially expected much. Albert Outler, a man of polymathic ability and the acknowledged doyen of the Methodist observers, initially expressed himself ill-suited to the task of being an observer, stating that his acquaintance with the contemporary Roman Catholic Church was ‘perfunctory and not very favourable’. He also admitted that he had shared many contemporary Protestant doubts as to Catholic understanding of the Gospel, the sovereignty of God, the vital role of faith, and the gratuitousness of grace.

Outler was soon to confess his mistake, arguing that he was ‘mightily impressed by the sights and sounds of two thousand bishops engaged in what seems an extraordinary exercise in re-education’. He became so impressed with the conciliar process that he ‘began to forget he was an outsider’ and began to think in terms of ‘we’ rather than ‘they’. He felt the challenge in daring ecumenical enterprise to the rest of Christendom, arguing that ‘the blunt truth is that Rome has leapfrogged over the rest of us on at least two fronts, church renewal and ecumenical action’.

Like many observers from other traditions, Outler was impressed with the warmth of the welcome given to all observers and the very real desire of so many of the council fathers and especially their accompanying _periti_ to learn from the observers’ reactions. In the attempts of both _periti_ and bishops to understand the Protestant mindset and possible reactions to conciliar proposals, Outler was frequently consulted. He also impressed the observers from other traditions.

The British Methodist minister in Rome at the time, Rex Kissack (not an official observer), felt challenged by the deep questioning of so much of their previous post-Tridentine tradition by the fathers. He recorded that he was led to question the state of public worship in Methodism and ask whether it faithfully ‘set forth the fullness of God or satisfled the deepest needs of the human soul’. There is no doubt that the spirit of openness to the wider world, not just the separated brethren and their churches, resonated with the Arminian Wesleyan spirit, with its stress on serving the present age and the duty of doing good to all people, but especially to them that are of the household of faith. Naturally, the acknowledgement of other Christians as separated brethren rather than, as traditionally, heretics and schismatics, was welcomed, as was the stress on being already united by the bonds of baptism, the Scriptures, and the basic credal **[p. 547]** confessions of the Primitive Church. Catholics were beginning to recover an emphasis on the doctrine of the royal priesthood of all the faithful, a doctrine precious to the reformers. The way was being opened up for collaboration in witness and service.

Kissack paid a particularly warm tribute to Cardinal Bea, ‘a personality with extraordinary powers of mind, heart and spirit, whose insight in detecting new tracks ahead and courage in thrusting into them, impressed [^c33-5] the observer as marks of authentic greatness’. Bishop Fred Corson, an American Methodist, developed a good personal relationship with Pope John, who, on one occasion, asked Corson how long he thought it would take to achieve unity. He hesitated as to how to respond only to hear, ‘Well, at any rate, between you and me, it’s done.’

[^c33-5]: Reginald Kissack, ‘Observing the Second Vatican Council’, _London Quarterly and Holborn Review_ 188 (1963): 204–9.

The council transformed Outler’s understanding of the Roman Catholic Church; as he later wrote, ‘the Council has proved that Rome is not a monolithic, conformist community’. He was, however, far too astute an observer of the scene to miss the acute tensions between the more conservative elements, particularly those who rather wished there had not been a council and those straining for reform. He knew that these acute tensions within the Catholic Church would not be easily resolved and that the progressives might not prevail, writing in 1964 that ‘If Bea and his cause predominate, the Ecumenical Movement will gain exciting new dimensions and momentum. If _semper eadem_ does, then there will be a regression into denominational ghettoes.’

Outler was particularly well qualifled to receive the council. Like so many of the council fathers and _periti_, he was a devotee of _ressourcement_, of reaching back into the common faith of the Great Tradition of the first millennium, a tradition that he sought to recover for a balanced renewal of his own Methodist tradition, in which there should be proper dialogue between Wesleyan perspectives and the earlier tradition that the Wesleys themselves had sought to perpetuate and renew in their own time. Outler was a scholar simultaneously at home with the fathers of the first few centuries and with the Wesleys, expanding the reception of both in American Methodism beyond previously narrower boundaries, seeking, in particular, to reinstate Wesley as a significant theologian rather than the cult hero he had become for Methodism everywhere. He thus had a natural affinity with what the fathers were trying to do and saw their successes as modelling an example of renewal for all the churches. He developed a vision of ‘a reformed Church of Rome forcing the wrangling fragments of non-Roman Catholic Christendom to face up to the scandal of divisions and risk a genuine _aggiornamento_ of their own’. What the Catholic Church was doing was paradigmatic for everyone else; it was, he repeatedly re-emphasized, not a change anyone had expected previously, but one which now represented a challenge to all.

Outler’s sophisticated understanding of the currents flowing within the council meant that he had no easy optimism about the task that would result from the council. He recognized that the potential of the council would have to be followed by thorough and systematic reception within the Roman Catholic Church at all **[p. 548]** levels. He had enough other ecumenical experience to realize that impetus can be lost; it is noteworthy that his eulogy of the Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, which he extolled as ‘the first full-orbed conciliar exposition of the doctrine of the Church in Christian history’, came with the warning that it should not suffer the fate of ‘being interred in the vast mausoleum of ecumenical literature’.

The council had a wide impact beyond the ranks of the immediate official observers. It was big news in the very secular English press. The author of this chapter was then an undergraduate. In his college, a group of enthusiastic Catholic students got a group of students together from other churches to discuss the events at the council, an event that transformed his earlier conception of the Catholic Church, based as it had been on reading a copy of the penny catechism which was in total contrast to the style of the conciliar documents. For a young Methodist, already interested in the earlier ecumenical movement, it marked the beginning of a lifelong creative dialogue with the Roman Catholic tradition. He remembers some older grass-roots Methodists being very intrigued by the news of the council and its implications for future and more positive relationships between the two communions.

In 1967, Cardinal Suenens visited Emory University in the United States and was told by Bishop Corson and (future) Bishop Cannon that the Methodist Church was closer to the Roman Catholic Church than any other [^c33-6] Protestant communion. Such was the change that had been wrought over the few years of the council. It owed much also to the developing awareness on both sides that Methodism and Roman Catholicism shared three key emphases: the universal vocation to holiness, the call to global mission, and the necessary interdependence and communion of all churches.

[^c33-6]: Joseph Suenens, _Memories and Hopes_ (Dublin: Veritas, 1991).

### 3. Reception of Particular Decrees

#### The Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, Lumen Gentium

Outler regarded the Dogmatic Constitution _Lumen Gentium_ as ‘the _fundamentum_’ of all the other fifteen documents of the council. ‘All of these rest back in the Constitution on the Church as the ground, and each of them, in one degree or another, provided signal development for one or other of its motifs.’[^c33-7]

[^c33-7]: Albert Outler, ‘A Response’, in _The Documents of Vatican II_, ed. Walter Abbott (London: Geoffrey Chapman, 1966), 102–6.

Outler saw _Lumen Gentium_ as ‘truly pastoral and ecumenical in spirit’, in contrast to the polemical spirit of the Vatican I decrees. It enlivened the prospect of dialogue both with the other churches and with the world. It breathed the spirit of those moderates like Contarini, who had been so marginalized by the sixteenth **[p. 549]** century’s aggressive reformers and papalists alike. The notion of the Church as mystery was fundamental. It lifted the discussion above the level of the instrumental. It established that ‘we belong to the Church, not the Church to us’. He welcomed the stress on collegiality, an understanding of leadership consonant upon the Wesleyan understanding of the corporate responsibility of the preachers ‘to watch over each other and the whole Connexion in faith and love’. The stress on the laity, the universal call to holiness, and the priesthood of all believers laid the ground for asserting their apostolate within the world.

Other points noted by Methodists at and after the council included the Trinitarian basis of its ecclesiology, the placing of emphasis upon the whole People of God before proceeding to the consideration of the role of the ordained ministry in the governance and leadership of the Church, and the stress upon the active and responsible role of the laity, which helped to dispel the widespread view of Methodists and many other Protestants that the laity had no capacity or role other than to ‘pay, pray, and obey’. The careful positioning of Mary within the communion of the Church was to bear fruit in the later pioneering dialogue between British Catholics and Methodists, _Mary, Mother of the Lord, Sign of Grace, Faith and Holiness_ (1995), aided by the participation of some Methodists in the Ecumenical Society of the Blessed Virgin Mary. The concept of the sacramental nature of the Church was also later to receive attention in the international dialogue. In the 1990s, Bishop Michael Evans, a member of both the Methodist–Roman Catholic International Commission (MRCIC) and the British dialogue, paid tribute to the draft British Methodist ecclesiological statement _Called to Love and Praise_ (officially approved by the conference in 1999) while noting that, from a Roman Catholic point of view, it needed more on ordained ministry; it did, however, indicate the British Methodist preparedness to make further progress on both episcopacy and the Petrine ministry.

#### The Decree on Ecumenism, Unitatis Redintegratio

Outler saw the Decree on Ecumenism as having fundamental importance for the whole ecumenical movement. He saw the statements in it on the Roman Catholic evaluation of the relative ecclesial status and the claims of the other churches as indicative of a clarifying approach which should be emulated by other churches in their relationships. Another Methodist observer, Claude Welch, noted a degree of convergence in the understanding of catholicity as a central concept. He argued that catholicity enabled both traditions to keep a firm grip on Church’s life as essentially participation in Christ and the Spirit, the term _katholikos_ pointing us to the fullness of God’s work in Christ and to the riches given by the Spirit. ‘The catholicity of the Church is the reflex of the catholicity of God’s grace in the creative and redemptive work of God. Catholicity allows us to be satisfled with nothing less than the most inclusive possible reception of the richness of Christ.’[^c33-8]

[^c33-8]: Claude Welch, ‘Catholicity’, _Ecumenical Review_ 16, no. 1 (1965): 33–42.

**[p. 550]** José Miguel Bonino identifled five points in the decree which Methodists could strongly affirm. They were the explicit affirmation of the ecumenical movement, the positive affirmation of the common baptism and devotion to Scripture, the guarded acceptance of some degree of communion _in sacris_, the recognition of a hierarchy of truths, and the distinction between essential doctrine and the mode of its expression. He felt, however, that there were remaining ambiguities in the document, including an ambiguity over whether it was a Christ-centred unity or a Rome-centred unity that was being sought. However, he also had the grace to accept that ‘if the primacy of the Bishop of Rome is not the right correlate for unity, where is it to be found?’[^c33-9]

[^c33-9]: José Bonino, ‘A Comment on the Decree on Ecumenism’, _Ecumenical Review_ 17, no. 2 (1965): 109–12.

#### The International Dialogue

One can argue that the Decree on Ecumenism is the decree that has been most faithfully and fully received by Methodism. The MRCIC began in 1967 and has continued through ten sessions, each covering a quinquennium. Both the rules and the spirit of dialogue as outlined in the decree have been honoured in practice. People appropriately qualifled both in their understanding of Methodism and in their appreciation of the Catholic tradition have been appointed to the international dialogue and to the four supporting national dialogues in Britain, the US, Australia, and New Zealand. In all cases, the spirit, on both sides, has been one of seeking to ‘understand the outlook of the separated brethren’ and of ‘treating each other on an equal footing’. It has been one of ‘searching together into the divine mysteries … with love for truth, charity and humility’. Dr Clare Watkins, a Catholic member of the tenth quinquennial dialogue, talked at an informal meeting of the relationship between the two teams as a genuinely _affiective_ one.

The real warmth and affection felt and expressed has not stopped the two teams from recording honestly remaining differences, such as that over the ordination of women, which thus far seem insoluble. It has thus fulfilled another requirement of the decree that both sides should clearly state their respective doctrinal positions and avoid ‘any false conciliatory approach’. At the same time, real advances in convergence have been made in ecclesiology and sacramental theology in accordance with the call of the council for dialogue on them. All this has been helped by Methodist reflection on connexionalism as a way of expressing practically the nature of the Church as _koinonia_, and a degree of re-reception of the Eucharistic theology of Charles Wesley’s hymns. It has also been helped by the Methodist tradition of a catholic reception of spiritual riches from other churches, dating back to Wesley’s time and his commendation of the spiritual classics of other traditions together with his emphasis on the catholic spirit, reasserted by the British Conference in 1820 with its call to ‘ever maintain the kind and catholic spirit of primitive Methodism towards all denominations of Christians, holding the Head’. Both churches can acknowledge that whatever **[p. 551]** they can accept as ‘being truly of the gospel in each other’, a mutual challenge in the report of the eighth dialogue (2006), belongs by that very fact to the catholic whole (Pontifical Council for Promoting Christian Unity, ‘The Grace Given You in Christ: Catholics and Methodists Reflect Further on the Church’). There is a clear consonance between the concepts of catholicity as held in both churches, despite continuing differences on some aspects of ministry. Both communions accept, as recorded in the 1986 report of the fourth international dialogue, that there is a case for a universal ministry of oversight, though, as yet, none as to the exact nature of its configuration and powers.

#### The National Dialogues

As mentioned above, there are four national dialogues—in Britain, in the US, in New Zealand, and in Australia—each with its own particular flavour relating to national relationships with other churches, not just to each other. Thus, the British dialogue has given particular attention to developments within the English local ecumenical partnerships, the famous _simultaneous Eucharists_ of Thamesdown being subject to particular practical and theological analysis in the early 1990s. The British dialogue has also given particular attention to the magisterial documents of both churches in Britain, such as _One Bread, One Body_ (Catholic bishops on the Eucharist, 1998) and _Called to Love and Praise_ (British Methodist statement on ecclesiology, 1999), as well as to papal ones such as _Ut Unum Sint_ (1995) and the reports of the international commission, which received attention from the dialogue well before it became standard for the British Methodist Faith and Order Committee to comment from. The British Committee has always included a representative of a mixed Catholic–Methodist marriage in both teams.

The American dialogue took particularly seriously the question of historically conditioned statements of both churches, such as the Twenty-Five Articles in Wesley’s revision of the Prayer Book for America and the question of their interpretation in modern times. Each of the first five rounds of the US dialogue produced major published reports, in contrast to the British dialogue, which produced short statements on authority (1978) and justification (1988) and only one significant consensus statement, in which it was a pioneer: _Mary_, _Mother of the Lord_, _Sign of Grace, Faith and Holiness_, in 1995. It preceded the later work of the Groupe des Dombes (_Mary in the Plan of God and the Communion of_ Saints, 1999) and the Anglican–Roman Catholic International Commission (_Mary: Grace and Hope in Christ_, 2004) and is a signal example of the call of _Unitatis Redintegratio_ to seek together with the separated brethren the divine mysteries.

In 2004, the American dialogue produced a report on the Eucharist, _Through Divine Love_, in which the major issue of remaining divergence related to the differing disciplines of admission to communion within the two communions. A later round of the dialogue was devoted to ‘the eucharist and the stewardship of God’s creation’, the latter indicating attention to a topic central for the pontificate of Francis.

**[p. 552]** The Australian dialogue tended to concentrate on pastoral issues, issuing an early report ‘Towards Agreement on Marriage’. It was continued after the formation of the Uniting Church in Australia in 1977, with the new church including both Congregationalists and some Presbyterians. The New Zealand dialogue was perhaps the feistiest in identifying points of ongoing disagreement, with both churches sensing a continuing weakness in the other: the Methodists thinking the Catholics too inflexible, and the Catholics feeling that Methodism gave way too easily to modern trends.

All the dialogues mentioned above illustrated to varying degrees the reception of the spirit and stipulations of Vatican II that the dialogue should be friendly and fraternal; that it should result in deeper appreciation of each other’s life, spirit, and teaching; and that it should seek the greatest possible convergence while remaining honest about continuing differences which seemed to offer no prospect of resolution within the foreseeable future. In all the dialogues, there has indeed been that ‘spirit of fraternal rivalry’ in ‘searching together into the divine mysteries’.

### 4. Reception of Other Decrees

Bishop Fred Corson welcomed the decree on bishops as ‘speaking to all bishops, Roman Catholic and non- Roman Catholic’, adding that ‘by New Testament standards it points out that charity, simplicity, holiness, [^c33-10] and humanity are the qualities of a true bishop of the Church’. He even suggested a meeting of bishops and chief pastors from all the churches. Certainly, the decree seems to have affected the understanding and practice of episcopacy in the present United Methodist Church, with a shift from the original stress on mission leadership and stationing of the preachers to one including teaching and transmission of the apostolic faith.

[^c33-10]: Fred Corson, ‘A Response to a Decree on the Bishops’ Pastoral Office in the Church (_Christus Dominus_)’, in Abbott, _The_ _Documents of Vatican II_, 430–34.

The Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation, _Dei Verbum_, was welcomed for its sturdy emphasis on the primacy of Scripture and the authority of tradition and magisterium as serving this rather than being either independent of it or above it. The beautiful meditation in chapter 8, which speaks of the Church constantly moving forward towards the fullness of divine truth until the words of God find their fulfilment in her, can be seen as on a convergent line with the American Methodist understanding of the Wesleyan Quadrilateral, with Scripture in prime place but with contributions to its understanding coming alike from Tradition, Reason, and Experience. It can also be seen as consonant with these lines from Charles Wesley: ‘words that endless bliss impart | kept in an obedient heart’.

_Gaudium et Spes_ was particularly welcomed for its engagement with the concerns and needs of the world. Its **[p. 553]** spirit of mission was seen as consonant with the Arminian Wesleyan approach. Much of its teaching, particularly on matters of social justice and access to adequate standards of living, can be paralleled from statements of the British Methodist Conference. It is widely recognized that Methodists and Catholics can cooperate freely and successfully on such matters relating to the common good.

### 5. The Consonance of Catholic and Wesleyan–Methodist Emphases and Insights

The post-conciliar relationship has enabled Methodists to recognize the consonance between similar, if differently expressed, emphases within their tradition and that of the Roman Catholic Church. The stress on the universal call to holiness in _Lumen Gentium_ and the link between holiness and unity inherent in the Decree on Ecumenism naturally resonate with the Methodist call to all the faithful to ‘press on to full salvation’ and the doctrine of Christian holiness. In the MRCIC dialogues, holiness was discussed in the third and tenth quinquennia. The essentially pastoral nature of ministry has been affirmed at several points in the international dialogue. The necessary interconnection and interdependence of all churches has been affirmed as at the root, alike in the Catholic understanding of Church as _koinonia_ and the Methodist practice of connexion; this was particularly addressed in the eighth dialogue report (2006). Differences continue as to the exact structures of ministry required for true connection/_koinonia_ across the _oikoumene_, though as early as the fourth dialogue report (1986) a vision was held out of a possible relationship in communion between the Catholic and Methodist episcopates, with a possible Methodist acceptance of a form on Petrine ministry. The ninth quinquennium of the international dialogue looked at the two major sacraments of baptism and Eucharist; both it and the American dialogue on the Eucharist referred to above showed considerable convergence on Eucharistic presence, sacrifice, and the eschatological aspect of the Eucharist (MRCIC, ‘Encountering Christ the Saviour: Church and Sacraments’, 2011). Most recently, in the teaching of Pope Francis in _Evangelii Gaudium_ and _Laudato Si’_, Methodists can see affirmation of Wesleyan principles and practice in the service of the poor and in the search for social justice. They see Francis carrying on from the conciliar teaching in _Gaudium et Spes_.

### 6. The Future and a Key Question

Francis’s pontificate gives solid ground of hope for further rapprochement between the two traditions. **[p. 554]** Francis is perhaps the easiest pope yet for Methodists to identify with, in gestures, practice, and teaching. They can see him as offering leadership on a global level on the key issues of the day for Christian witness and practice, delivering as, at more local levels, they expect their bishops (in US Methodism) and presidents of conference (in British and Irish Methodism) to do. Francis’s stress on collegiality and his practice, in encyclicals, in citing not just conciliar and previous papal teaching but also that of his brother bishops in their various conferences will appeal. His agreement to consider the possibility of ordaining women to the diaconate will be welcomed, though it will also be recognized that the persistent difference over the ordination of women as presbyters and bishops continues, with no sign of resolution on the horizon.

Reception remains a persistent problem, particularly at the grass-roots level. This has been slow and patchy, dependent particularly on the efforts of local leaders who are convinced ecumenists. Local church life in both communions, indeed in all, remains only too easily very parochial. Relatively few efforts have been made to promote reception at a popular level, though since the eighth report of the international commission more has been suggested in terms of appropriate material and questions for local study. As noted at the beginning, much still depends on the context of the particular Methodist churches and their particular ethos in each case. At the end of the council, the British Methodist minister Harold Roberts [^c33-11] asserted that it was important that dialogue should take place at every level. This has not happened widely in Britain or elsewhere. It remains a challenge for the various Methodist conferences to face: How do they keep ecumenical relationships and learning at the forefront of the agenda at all levels within their jurisdiction? If they cannot do so, then, sadly, the aim laid down from early on in the international dialogue of attaining full unity in faith, life, and mission indeed remains distant.

[^c33-11]: Harold Roberts, ‘Vatican II: Ecumenical Relations’, _London Quarterly and Holborn Review_ 192 (1967): 220–26.

Most recently, however, in October 2017 the pope received in audience a delegation of leaders from the World Methodist Council and the members of the Methodist Roman Catholic Commission to mark fifty [^c33-12] years of official dialogue. He affirmed the value of the work of John Wesley, the importance of the way in which ‘faith becomes tangible when it takes the concrete form of service to poor and marginalized people’, and the forthcoming quinquennium of the dialogue, which will be devoted to the theme of reconciliation. He expressed the hope that ‘your discussions about reconciliation may be a gift and not only for our communities but for the world’. With a pontiff perhaps closer in spirit to Methodism than any of his predecessors, hope remains despite the reservations expressed in the penultimate paragraph.

[^c33-12]: Hannah Brockhaus, ‘Pope to Methodists: Reconciliation Is More than Talk – It Needs Action’, _Catholic News Agency_, 19 October 2017, https://www.catholicnewsagency.com/news/pope-to-methodists-reconciliation-is-more-than-talk-it- needs-action-96674.

Gros, Jeffrey, William Rush, and Harding Myer, eds. _Growth in Agreement II: Reports and Statements of Ecumenical Conversations at World Level 1982–1998_. Geneva: WCC Publications, 2000.

## 34. Evangelicals and the Reception of the Second Vatican

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 556]** ‘What indeed has Wheaton to do with Rome? The Billy Graham Center with St Peter’s Basilica?’ Modelled after ‘What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem?’—the question posed rhetorically by Tertullian in the early third century—one might assume that the implied answer is the same as his: nothing at all. And for much of the last 250 years, that answer would have been true. Evangelicalism has been known for, among other things, its deep suspicion of all things Roman and its flerce commitment to the Protestant doctrinal definer: salvation is by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, to God alone be the glory. While evangelicals may quibble among themselves over the best way to unpack this sentence, they have been (with the rare exception) united that each ‘alone’ not only signals a break with Catholicism rightly understood, but also places Catholicism at odds with authentic Christianity. Evangelicals have traditionally regarded Catholics, in short, not so much in need of correction as of conversion.

That is, until the last fifty years. Since the 1960s, a slowly gaining thaw has taken place between (some) Catholics and (some) evangelicals, with conversations leading to friendships and to fraternal recognition. As Pope St John Paul II is once reported to have said to Billy Graham, ‘We are brothers!’ This chapter seeks to assess the role the Second Vatican Council played in this truly remarkable ecumenical turn of events. In the first section, I offer several examples of such interaction at academic, denominational, and para-church levels. The influence of the council in the Catholic turn towards evangelicals in each case is obvious. The council’s influence on the evangelical turn, however, is much more ambiguous. Accordingly, in the second section I evaluate academic and popular contemporaneous evangelical responses to the council, concluding **[p. 557]** that evangelicals as a whole simply were not aware of the momentous shift taking place. So, what then accounts for the evangelical turn of the last half-century? The final section offers an alternative explanation which, though more complex, is more compelling. This chapter will argue that, for evangelicals, the council’s role in the ecumenical improvement is at best minimal and indirect and that other, more personal factors are more important.

### 2. Cross-Confessional Cooperation

In the half-century since the council’s conclusion, evangelical/Catholic interaction has grown in several ways. It has grown in kind; it is not merely or exclusively an academic phenomenon. It has grown in warmth; as (some) evangelicals have interacted with (some) Catholics, they have come to find a surprising number of overlapping concerns in ecumenical, theological, social, and devotional areas that have led to conversation. And it has grown in frequency—and with that frequency, decreasing suspicion on both sides. Formal and informal interaction is taking place in the academy, in churches, and in para-church organizations.

In the academy, evangelical biblical scholars and theologians, whatever their disposition towards Catholicism, have come to take it for granted that interaction with Catholic scholarship (and, indeed, scholarship of all sorts) is simply part of their disciplinary tasks. Italian Reformed theologian Leonardo De Chirico, himself highly sceptical of such interaction, nevertheless documented just how mainstream it had [^c34-1] become by 2003. One can easily plot De Chirico’s evangelical spokesmen (they are all men) on a continuum, with Herbert Carson and Cornelius Van Til representing the traditional, anti-Catholic end of the spectrum, while John Stott and David Wells represent a more cautious middle, and Donald Bloesch and G. C. Berkouwer give voice to positive assessment. De Chirico’s point is not that such interaction is fawning, but that it is assumed to be an indispensable part of theological and biblical engagement across a theological spectrum.

[^c34-1]: Leonardo De Chirico, _Evangelical Theological Perspectcives on Post-Vatican II Roman Catholicism_ (Berne: Peter Lang, 2003). His scepticism is rooted in his argument that such interactions are too ad hoc and atomistic, and therefore fail to grapple with the (negative) factors Catholicism presents to (Reformed) evangelicalism as a system.

In the years following the publication of De Chirico’s study, academic engagement has continued, seeing evangelicals across denominational differences and theological disagreements engaging with the [^c34-2][^c34-3] encyclicals of John Paul II and the theology of Benedict XVI. Cross-confessional work on the Blessed Virgin **[p. 558]** Mary—a point of contention since the third generation of the Reformation—has pointed to long-overlooked and underappreciated areas of agreement without neglecting ongoing theological and [^c34-4] ecumenical challenges. The most daring proposal, however, comes from Presbyterian Peter J. Leithart, who has sharply criticized his fellow Protestants for allowing ‘not-Catholic’ to become their chief raison d’être. He bluntly avers that if this is all that constitutes Protestantism, then Protestantism has itself become antithetical to the Gospel and must die. In its place he proposes ‘Reformational Catholicism’, which begins from a position of fidelity to Reformation confession and concerns, and works towards the visible unity of [^c34-5] the Church.

[^c34-2]: Tim Perry, ed., _The Legacy of Pope John Paul II: An Evangelical Assessment_ (Downers Grove, IL: InterVarsity Press, 2007).

[^c34-3]: Tim Perry, ed., _The Theology of Benedict VXI: A Protestant Appreciation_ (Bellingham, WA: Lexham, 2019).

[^c34-4]: Tim Perry and Daniel Kendal, SJ, _The Blessed Virgin Mary_ (Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 2013); compare also Tim Perry, _Mary for Evangelicals_ (Downers Grove, IL: InterVarsity Press, 2006) with criticism found in Douglas J. Farrow, _Ascension_ _Theology_ (London: T&T Clark, 2011), 52–54.

[^c34-5]: Peter J. Leithart, _The End of Protestantism: Pursuing Unity in a Fragmented Church_ (Grand Rapids, MI: Brazos, 2016).

Formal conversations between Catholic bodies and evangelical para-church and Church organizations have also taken place. The following are especially noteworthy. A series of conversations between Catholics and evangelicals on mission and evangelization was held from 1977 to 1984; these in turn led to a formal [^c34-6] dialogue arranged under the World Evangelical Alliance (WEA) Theological Commission and the Pontifical [^c34-7] Council for Promoting Christian Unity (PCPCU). The fruit of the dialogue, released in 2005 as ‘Church, Evangelization, and the Bonds of Koinonia’, sought not only to clarify areas of agreement and disagreement, but also to overcome significant mutual misunderstanding, especially with regard to mission and evangelism. The document explicitly notes the influence of Vatican II on both the informal conversations and the dialogue itself, but stresses that such an influence extended only to the Catholic participants. The WEA also participated in a five-year trilateral conversation involving the World Council of Churches and the Pontifical Council for Interreligious Dialogue that resulted in the publication of a series of [^c34-8] practical guidelines on mission entitled ‘Christian Witness in a Multi-Religious World’ in 2011.

[^c34-6]: The WEA claims a global constituency ‘rooted in 129 national and seven regional alliances, 104 associate members, six affiliated specialised ministries and six commissions’. ‘World Evangelical Alliance History’, World Evangelical Alliance, worldea.org.

[^c34-7]: ‘Roman Catholic Dialogue with the World Evangelical Alliance’, christianunity.va.

[^c34-8]: ‘Christian Witness in a Multi-Religious World’, World Council of Churches, 18 June 2011, https://www.oikoumene.org/en/resources/documents/wcc-programmes/interreligious-dialogue-and- cooperation/christian-identity-in-pluralistic-societies/christian-witness-in-a-multi-religious-world.

Further, dialogue between the PCPCU and Pentecostals, ongoing since 1972, has passed through six phases [^c34-9] so far. Begun at the initiative of international Pentecostal leader David Du Plessis, a guest of the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity during the Second Vatican Council, the dialogues grew out of two factors: his **[p. 559]** experience of Vatican II as an observer and the charismatic renewal of the late 1960s, which gave Catholics, classical Pentecostals, and mainline Protestants a shared language of the Spirit. The first phase explored this shared language both experientially and theologically; the second sought to clarify divergences for the sake of greater mutual understanding. These then gave rise to the first sustained theological phase dealing with _koinonia_, or communion, as a means of understanding divergent ecclesiologies at work among the participants. The remaining three continued to build on this ecclesiological work, tackling, in turn, evangelism, conversion, and charisms (or spiritual gifts). The dialogue remains ongoing; given Pope Francis’s direct experience of and expressed appreciation for Pentecostalism in Argentina, it will no doubt continue for some time. Nevertheless, assessing the relative weight of these declarations is very difficult. They were, in their inception, driven by one man: David DuPlessis, who, in spite of his stature, simply did not and does not speak for all Pentecostals. The free-church ecclesiologies that define the various branches of Pentecostalism, further, mean that we simply [^c34-10] cannot gauge the scope or authority of these documents beyond the actual participants.

[^c34-9]: The resulting documents can all be found here: ‘Dialogue with Pentecostals, Pontifical Council for Promoting Christian Unity’, http://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/pontifical_councils/chrstuni/sub-index/index_pentecostals.htm.

[^c34-10]: As a result, the published reports very wisely include the adjective ‘some’, to avoid the accusation that the Pentecostal participants are speaking with movement-wide authority.

Finally, we consider Evangelicals and Catholics Together (ECT), the ongoing dialogue begun by evangelical Charles Colson and Catholic Fr. Richard John Neuhaus. ECT started as a conversation between its founders in [^c34-11] 1992 over mutually caused Catholic–evangelical antagonism in Latin America and culminated in 1994 [^c34-12] with the publication of ‘Evangelicals and Catholics Together: Christian Mission in the Third Millennium’. In subsequent declarations, ECT tackled both doctrinal and social matters, producing works on Scripture and Tradition, justification, the communion of saints, and Mary on the one hand, and holiness, the culture of life, religious freedom, and the nature of marriage on the other. While the socially oriented documents saw much greater areas of agreement than the doctrinal ones, all attempted to sketch out common areas and articulate areas of disagreement precisely and without rancour.

[^c34-11]: Mark A. Noll and Carolyn Nystrom, _Is the Reformation Over?: An Evangelical Assessment of Contemporary Roman_ _Catholicism_ (Grand Rapids, MI: Baker, 2005), 152.

[^c34-12]: The ECT declarations, along with helpful introductions from past participants, have been gathered together by Timothy George and Thomas G. Guarino, eds., _Evangelicals and Catholics Together at Twenty: Vital Statements on Contested Topics_ (Grand Rapids, MI: Brazos, 2015).

ECT’s influence persists beyond the deaths of its founders, as do its limitations. First, the documents carry little authority for either side; their influence extends only as far as the relative stature of the signatories within their communities permits. Second, while such conversations simply could not have taken place prior to the council, its influence extends only to the Catholic participants; there is no evidence that it was the council that moved evangelical participants to join in. Far more likely influences among evangelical signatories were the theme of co-belligerency in social concerns and the perceived need to move past simple repudiation, especially in regions where the communities were engaged alongside each other in **[p. 560]** mission and evangelism. Further, opposition to ECT among some evangelicals has been pronounced. ECT created a firestorm, which, while it did not split the evangelical movement, continued through the [^c34-13] publication of subsequent documents.

[^c34-13]: Noll and Nystrom, _Is the Reformation Over?_, 156–58.

From the academy and official and unofficial dialogues, we move to consider the changed dynamic at a more personal, popular level. The most-watched Canadian Christian television programme, _100 Huntley Street_, was founded by a Pentecostal minister, Revd David Mainse, and co-hosted for over a decade by a Jesuit priest, Fr Bob MacDougall. ‘Fr Bob’ in turn helped to launch the career of Baptist-raised, now Anglican, singer-songwriter Steve Bell. The annual ‘March for Jesus’, though not now nearly as popular as it was in the late 1990s, draws primarily from Catholic and evangelical churches. Since 1998, Trinity Western University, an interdenominational university with ties to the Evangelical Free Church, has worked cooperatively with the Catholic Redeemer Pacific College to offer Redeemer’s students degrees recognized [^c34-14] by Universities Canada. Today, Catholic dioceses and parishes across the country make wide use of the (evangelical Anglican) Alpha programme for evangelism and outreach as a complement to the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults. Billy Graham’s 1998 crusade in Ottawa was sponsored by the highest number [^c34-15] of Catholic parishes ever in the history of Graham’s global ministry. What is going on here? Noll and Nystrom point to the extraordinary findings of a 1996 Angus Reid poll that attempted to sketch evangelical identity:

[^c34-14]: Universities Canada (formerly the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada), although not an accrediting agency, does provide ‘quality assurance’ oversight to member institutions granting various degrees. See ‘Membership and Governance’, Universities Canada, https://www.univcan.ca/about-us/membership-and-governance.

[^c34-15]: Documented in Noll and Nystrom, _Is the Reformation Over?_, 10–12.

respondents were viewed as evangelical if, regarding the _Bible_, they agreed strongly that Scripture ‘is the inspired word of God’ or they agreed to any degree that ‘the Bible is God’s word and is to be taken literally, word for word’; if, regarding _conversion_, they strongly agreed that ‘I have committed my life to Christ and consider myself to be a converted Christian’; if, regarding _activism_, they agreed or agreed strongly that ‘it is important to encourage non-Christians to become Christians’; and if, regarding the centrality of the _cross of Christ_, they agreed strongly that ‘through the life, death and resurrection of Jesus, God provided a way for the forgiveness of my sins’. Of the Canadians who responded positively to all four of these evangelical markers, one-fourth were Roman Catholic. Of all Canadian Roman Catholics, 34 percent answered with the ‘evangelical’ response on at least three of the four questions. The same poll found that 11 percent of Canadian Catholics labelled themselves ‘evangelical’ or an equivalent term.[^c34-16]

[^c34-16]: Ibid., 12–13. Reid’s questions were based on David Bebbington’s _Evangelicalism in Modern Britain: A History from the_ _1730s to the 1980s_ (London: Routledge, 1988)and its description of the four marks of evangelical identity.

**[p. 561]** The anecdotal evidence stands alongside the academic and dialogical, whether formal or informal: there is no doubt that evangelical–Catholic relations have changed for the better since Vatican II.

This development is remarkable for two reasons. First, both evangelicalism and Catholicism were, until the mid-twentieth century, profoundly defensive, rendered that way by the damage done during the Reformation and, later, the perceived corrosions of modernity. Second, neither seems entirely comfortable with the modern ecumenical movement that is embodied, for example, in the World Council of Churches. In other words, their common encounters with modernity could have made both even more suspicious of each other. In many cases, it has not. The above account shows that the Second Vatican Council provided the foundation for the Catholic turn towards evangelicals at all levels. The question this chapter addresses, however, is different: To what degree did the reception of the Second Vatican Council by evangelicals contribute to this rapprochement?

### 3. Early Evangelical Responses to Vatican II

When we move to evangelical awareness of the council _at the time_, a straightforward answer to the question begins to emerge: the council simply was not received by evangelicals on any sort of large scale. Among evangelical academics, only two engaged with the council in full monographs, while in the popular evangelical press, it did not rate at all. Let us take the academy and the popular press in turn.

Of the two contemporaneous responses coming from the academy, the more accessible is David Wells’s _Revolution in Rome_. The title is not lightly chosen: ‘The Church That Never Changes’, Wells argues, had in fact changed in a profound way. Resisting any simplistic account, Wells notes that the council contained multiple voices—not simply conservatives (represented in particular by the Curia) ranged against progressives (found mainly among the younger theologians). Wells documented diversity among the progressives themselves: Küng and Schillebeekx, Daniélou and Congar, Bouyer and Rahner—no one can question their progressive credentials, but their contributions were hardly those of a _theologically or_ [^c34-17] _ideologically defined ‘party’._ It is therefore insufficient to say that the council moved the Catholic Church in a decidedly progressive direction, for at its end _which_ progressive direction would be embraced remained unclear. This remains Wells’s most trenchant observation.

[^c34-17]: David F. Wells, _Revolution in Rome_ (Downers Grove, IL: InterVarsity Press, 1972), 9.

Wells attributes the lack of clarity about future direction to the council’s documents themselves. When the various parties came into conflict—as often happened—one of three solutions was pursued. Occasionally, **[p. 562]** one side triumphed, and its ideas were adopted without modification. More likely and less satisfactorily, when neither side would back down, ‘the Council searched for a reconciling statement which would be [^c34-18] ambiguous enough to accommodate both schools of thought’. Finally, when neither victory nor ambiguity was possible, the council simply endorsed both sides, ‘as if their mutual incompatibility were no longer [^c34-19] glaringly obvious’. The bulk of Wells’s account traces this confusion through major conciliar debates. Is revelation found in the external sources of Holy Scripture and Tradition as interpreted by the magisterium, which are therefore to be regarded as authoritative? Or is it primarily located in a deep experience of the Spirit to which the above sources testify and according to which they can be corrected? Wells believes that [^c34-20] the council does not give a straightforward answer. Is God’s supernatural presence to be construed in primarily ‘heavenly’ terms—i.e., a turn away from the world and to the Church and her sacraments and finally in eternal life—or in primarily ‘earthly’ terms—i.e., working in the (secular) world for social [^c34-21] transformation with all people of goodwill? One may find both affirmed in conciliar documents. Does the [^c34-22] Church circumscribe ‘the limits within which God can be found’, or is she at the centre of a series of concentric circles, with Eastern churches, Protestant bodies, other religions, and even atheism circling in [^c34-23] orbit? Again, Wells charges the council with a lack of clarity. Finally, does teaching authority derive from the Holy Spirit and ascend through the people to the College of Bishops and from them to the pope, or does it descend from that same Spirit through the pope to the bishops, finally to be received by the faithful? On [^c34-24] Wells’s reading, _Lumen Gentium_ 3 gives the former answer, while the explanatory note gives the latter.

[^c34-18]: Ibid., 28.

[^c34-19]: Ibid., 31.

[^c34-20]: Ibid., 39–50.

[^c34-21]: Ibid., 51–77.

[^c34-22]: Ibid., 79.

[^c34-23]: Ibid., 79–87.

[^c34-24]: Ibid., 99–114.

Writing in 1972, Wells concluded that Protestants could only observe until the tensions were resolved. He [^c34-25] predicted a ‘Vatican III’, coming around 1980, that would realize one progressive vision. The third council, of course, has yet to materialize; nevertheless, Wells’s intuition that the post-conciliar years would be more about _which_ progressive perspective would definitively interpret and enact Vatican II’s documents has been vindicated.

[^c34-25]: Ibid., 35.

Unlike _Revolution in Rome_, G. C. Berkouwer’s _The Second Vatican Council and the New Catholicism_ was positively disposed towards those progressives who called for change based on biblical and patristic sources. Berkouwer had been engaging critically with contemporary Catholic thought for some time. _The Conflict with_ [^c34-26] **[p. 563]** _Rome_ is a thorough, if stale, recounting of the major Reformational divisions, while his _Recent_ [^c34-27] _Developments in Roman Catholic Thought_ is a thoughtful and surprisingly open engagement with _la nouvelle théologie_ of Jean Daniélou and others. In Berkouwer’s view, Vatican II represents official approval of the new theology’s biblical and patristic agenda. Traditional Protestants are presented neither with a capitulation to the Reformers nor with an embrace of liberal Protestantism, but with an opportunity to engage in an authentic and mutually transformative manner in the traditionally neuralgic points that separate the Roman Catholic Church from other ecclesial communities.[^c34-28]

[^c34-26]: G. C. Berkouwer, _The Conflict with Rome_ (Nutley, NJ: Presbyterian and Reformed, 1958).

[^c34-27]: G. C. Berkouwer, _Recent Developments in Roman Catholic Thought_ (Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 1958).

[^c34-28]: G. C. Berkouwer, _The Second Vatican Council and the New Catholicism_ (Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 1965), 32–33.

Berkouwer stressed the council’s focus on inner renewal: its call to turn outwards to the world undertaken for the sake of the ongoing vitality of Catholicism. It was a genuine, open-ended, and risk-laden invitation to dialogue that marked a ‘changed climate’. It is just this inward, penitential focus that poses the clear invitation and challenge to Protestantism, and especially those Protestants most tied to their Reformational confessions. If the Catholic Church is willing to take such a bold step _without ceasing to be what it has always claimed to be_, it is incumbent upon Protestants to respond in kind, lest the movement be exposed as merely a [^c34-29] determined and unthinking opposition to Rome in all things. His work sketches what is at stake in such a dialogue and what it might look like.

[^c34-29]: Ibid., 32–56.

Berkouwer arranges his early material in a familiar pattern of polarities—Scripture and Tradition, Exegesis [^c34-30] and Doctrinal Authority, the Pope and the Bishops —to accentuate how his ‘changed climate’ brings questions long thought settled back into play. If, as now seems obvious, Bible reading grows out of generations of reflection, then we can no longer tidily separate Scripture and Tradition into two separate spheres, whether we find in them two sources of revelation (as most Catholics understood Trent) or merely one (as most Protestants understood _Sola Scriptura_). If doctrinal authority is derived from sound scriptural exegesis, and such exegesis is always ongoing, in what ways might doctrines be said to be authoritative through time? If Catholics and Protestants now agree that there is no ‘contradiction between the free work of the Spirit and the established offices of the Church’, how can ‘the offices best serve the Church of Christ’? [^c34-31] The answers formerly accepted, whether by post-Tridentine Catholicism or Protestant scholasticism, are now seen to be insufficient to the challenges of the modern world. All sides have a stake in addressing them, from within their own churches and ecumenically in a careful way that neither surrenders to nor ignores the modern world.

[^c34-30]: Ibid., 89–111, 112–45, and 146–77 respectively.

[^c34-31]: Ibid., 177.

The ‘kernel of the problem’ that must be addressed in each of the preceding questions is historical [^c34-32] **[p. 564]** consciousness. While Truth may be eternal and unchanging, human perceptions thereof develop over time. For Catholicism’s ‘new theologians’, the solution is not in a special charism of infallibility that renders Church teaching immune to history or a straightforward embrace of historical relativism. Rather, the ‘association of the charism of infallibility with the complex evolution of dogma, with all its temporal aspects, can be understood only by way of an _a priori_ vision of the Church. The new theology is not preoccupied with a kind of changeability–unchangeability dialectic; it is concerned with the _a priori_ certain [^c34-33] unchangeability _within_ all the variations of history.’ Dogma therefore cannot be understood apart from its own historical context and must always be studied and restudied to discern the ‘essential intention’ of the Church that was clothed in ‘normally limited human speech’. While this commitment represents an authentic ecumenical opportunity, at the time of writing the outcome was by no means certain. The [^c34-34] traditionalist fear that ‘relativism will subtly become the master of dogma’, while perhaps unfair, was not without basis. The challenge for the Catholic Church in the modern world will be to articulate an understanding of the teaching office of the Church that can account for both infallibility and development of dogma through history. And this itself is _the_ most important ecumenical contribution of the council. ‘For the very problems that vexed this council are in large part problems that belong to all of us. And perhaps the relationship of divided Churches will be affected as they all recognize the depth and importance of the [^c34-35] problems they all share.’

[^c34-32]: Ibid., 57.

[^c34-33]: Ibid., 81.

[^c34-34]: Ibid., 82–86.

[^c34-35]: Ibid., 87–88.

Berkouwer attended Vatican II as an observer for the Dutch Gereformeerde Kerken, a small branch of the Reformed family. As the date of his publication shows, he published his account while the council was still in session—indeed, while some of the most important debates were taking place. At first blush, this may leave his final chapters on The Church and Mary looking anachronous in the light of _Lumen Gentium_ and _Gaudium et Spes_. In Berkouwer’s own reckoning, however, these are the most important chapters in the book and do retain their insightful character given the continued debates on the nature of the Church, including Mary’s place therein, among Roman Catholics following the council. He was grateful for the council’s willingness to raise questions that Protestants ought now to take up both on their own and in consultation with the Catholic Church. For him, the council represented no easy, common-denominator ecumenism, but one that was beginning to grasp just how serious the challenge of modernity was both for Catholicism and Christian faith as a whole. The only way forward is a common submission of these problems and all possible answers by all concerned to the Christ who will both protect and judge the churches in their reflective tasks. The Shepherd will give no rest to those bodies, and the Catholic Church is one, guilty of dispersing ‘His one flock and making a travesty of His one sheepfold’. Only insofar as we all stand under the cross can we hear, receive, and withstand the judgement of the Lord. Only under the cross is the assurance of Christ’s presence with the Church. Only under the Cross will the Church hear and be established by the Word of God.

**[p. 565]** If evangelical academic interaction with Vatican II was both insightful and rare, what of the popular movement as a whole? Mark Noll has documented a significant shift in evangelical perceptions of Catholicism through his survey of the contents of the movement’s flagship periodical, _Christianity Today_, from 1956 to 1968. Begun in 1956 by Billy Graham and Carl F. H. Henry, _Christianity Today_ was intended to be an evangelical counterweight to the liberal Protestant _Christian Century_. Its early issues stuck to careful reiterations of classical Protestant objections and expressed worry in political rather than theological terms. For example, while Pius XII was chastised over the dogmatic definition of Mary’s Assumption, far more ink was spilled over his rejection of the separation of Church and State and, later, the possibility that the United [^c34-36] States might elect its first Catholic president. And if the articles sought to be firm in their opposition, Noll observes that the letters were more strident and even extreme. Certainly, prior to 1960, the tenor of the evangelical popular press was anti-Catholic.

[^c34-36]: Mark A. Noll, ‘Evangelicals and John Paul II’, _The Legacy of John Paul II_ (Westmont, IL: InterVarsity Press, 2007), 25–26.

The shift, Noll argues, began around 1960 and the papacy of St John XXIII. His encyclical _Pacem in Terris_ was only gently chided for its optimism towards the United Nations. At his death, furthermore, the magazine both restated its commitment to classical Protestant principles and praised the late pope for his Christian devotion and charity. Here, Noll quotes an editorial at length: ‘In the final hours of his life, men marvelled at the strength of Pope John’s heart. Prior to that they had marvelled at its warmth … Perhaps history’s most universally beloved Pope, … John XXIII undoubtedly was largely responsible for a fresh spirit of charity [^c34-37] which created happier church relationship.’ The change in tone is, quite simply, remarkable; and it did not end with Pope John’s passing. While Pope Paul VI figured rarely in the pages of _Christianity Today_, whether he was praised or criticized, Noll detects a distinctly irenic approach not present prior to 1960.

[^c34-37]: Ibid., 27–28.

To point to the council as the pivot away from polemic and towards engagement, however, would be a mistake. Noll notes that _Christianity Today_ covered the council’s early phases only lightly and, for matters Catholic, was far more interested in the Kennedy presidency. A long silence in the popular press suggests that the council and its documents did not penetrate evangelical consciousness to any significant degree. Rather, Noll argues, the thaw is better attributed to two factors. First, the winsome personality and Christian devotion of John XXIII, when observed, was recognized by some as an expression of deep, authentic Christian commitment that required a reconsideration of traditional anti-papal epithets such as Antichrist. Second, there was a recognition—small in 1960, but growing steadily thereafter—of a common front with Catholics in what would come to be known as the culture wars.

To conclude this section, the following observations are in order. (1) The evangelical academy, insofar as it took notice of the council at all, did not receive it unanimously. Some, following Wells, were genuinely **[p. 566]** confused about its meaning, about its intent, and about the future. Others, with Berkouwer, were grateful for the unfiinching way the council faced the challenges of the modern world, providing thereby both an example of engagement to Protestant churches and an invitation to do so in conversation not simply with modernity, but with each other. Would the Catholic Church collapse into yet another variety of liberal Protestantism—albeit one with better vestments, art, and architecture? Or would it become more biblical, more faithful, and more recognizably Christian as it returned to the sources? (2) In the popular imagination, neither the council in particular, nor Catholicism in general, figured among the major concerns of most evangelicals. Beginning in 1960, both press coverage and popular responses began to warm, but there is simply no evidence that the council played a part in the change at the time.

### 4. A Concluding Alternative Account

So, if the council’s invitation was not taken up by evangelicals, what factors prompted the thaw? Mark Noll and Carolyn Nystrom posit four answers.

[^c34-38] The first is changes in World Christianity. Expansion of Christianity in the southern hemisphere, coupled with its decline in the northern one, has forced both Catholics and evangelicals away from settled certainties about each other and about the world. In Latin America and the Philippines, this has led to increased rivalry and sometimes hostility (where, this evangelical observes, Catholic teaching on mission both from the council and John Paul II needs still to be received by Catholics!). Elsewhere, especially in the northern hemisphere, it has led to greater cooperation ranging from begrudging to warm. Both communities have also been influenced by the global charismatic movement from years prior to the council. A new shared spirituality, worship, and music, all rooted in a common language and experience of the Holy Spirit, the experience of _glossolalia_ and ‘signs and wonders’, have blurred previously accepted theological [^c34-39] boundaries. The charming personality, warm piety, and obvious holiness of John Paul II—his papacy both a response to and an agent of global change—strengthened the ties so significantly as to be, now, rightly regarded as irreversible. Today, a Catholic apologist, Holly Ordway, teaches at a Houston Baptist [^c34-40] University; an evangelical publishing house—Baker Books—hosts the Catholic Commentary on Sacred Scripture, with its lead volume on the Book of Romans authored by an evangelical convert to Catholicism, [^c34-41] **[p. 567]** Scott Hahn. Examples could be multiplied, easily demonstrating that, at least in certain quarters, changes to global Christianity have produced a significant lessening of tensions.

[^c34-38]: Noll and Nystrom, _Is the Reformation Over?_, 63–67.

[^c34-39]: Ibid., 64–65.

[^c34-40]: See ‘Holly Ordway’, Houston Baptist University Contacts, https://www.hbu.edu/contact/holly-ordway.

[^c34-41]: Scott W. Hahn, _Romans_, ed. Peter Williamson and Mary Healy, Catholic Commentary on Sacred Scripture (Grand Rapids, MI: Baker Academic, 2017).

[^c34-42] Second, Noll and Nystrom point to changes in US politics and society. Catholics arrived en masse in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, generating xenophobia and open anti-Catholicism. The journey from there to the election of John F. Kennedy in 1960 was the journey of Catholic America into the mainstream of American social life. This marked the high point of the Catholic American experience. Since then, however, relations have improved because of the perception among certain Catholics, and widespread among evangelicals, that both communities are being pushed to the margins of the public square. Though its beginnings have been traced at least to 1960, certainly from 1973 on, evangelicals and Catholics have been thrown together on the same side of significant moral debates with a widely secularizing host culture [^c34-43] —what Baptist Timothy George has called an ‘ecumenism of the trenches’.

[^c34-42]: Noll and Nystrom, _Is the Reformation Over?_, 67–70.

[^c34-43]: See Timothy George, ‘Catholics and Evangelicals in the Trenches’, _Christianity Today_ (16 May 1994), 16.

[^c34-44] Third, the power of personal influence and cross-confessional friendships cannot be underestimated. David DuPlessis for Pentecostals, Billy Graham for Baptists, Roman Catholic Richard John Neuhaus, and evangelical Charles Colson—all these have provided a certain amount of personal vouchsafing for a community that places a great deal of trust, for good and for ill, in the word and example of its recognized leaders. The hiring of evangelical scholars by Catholic universities (Noll and Nystrom point to the broad visions of Fr Theodore Hesburgh and Fr Edward Malloy of Notre Dame) and, we might add, the appointment of Catholics in evangelical institutions (though less frequently and sometimes less happily) have led to [^c34-45] significant cross-pollination in various academic fields.

[^c34-44]: Noll and Nystrom, _Is the Reformation Over?_, 70–71.

[^c34-45]: e.g., the refusal of Wheaton College to renew Prof. Joshua Hochschild’s contract after his conversion to Catholicism in 2006. See Alan Jacobs, ‘To Be a Christian College’, _First Things_ (April 2006), https://www.firstthings.com/article/2006/04/to- be-a-christian-college.

[^c34-46] Last, Noll and Nystrom point to the healthy self-criticism within evangelicalism itself. Prompted by conversions of such evangelical scholars as Hahn, Peter Kreeft, and Thomas Howard, the last decade especially has seen a number of evangelicals willing to point out weaknesses in philosophy, aesthetics and literature, deep ecclesial life, and sacramental theology that need to be strengthened for the movement’s own sake. Some evangelicals have begun to interact with Catholic social teaching as a means to break segments of the movement away from the ‘cross and flag’ patriotism that sometimes verges on idolatry. Especially noteworthy here is the acceptance of the _Catechism of the Catholic Church_ among evangelicals as the source in which to discover what Catholics really believe and practise. Noll and Nystrom devote a chapter to the _Catechism_ as the accessible, authoritative means to correct misunderstanding and misinformation, to **[p. 568]** recover and celebrate areas of agreement, and to clarify and better comprehend those positions from [^c34-47] which evangelicals continue to dissent. It is an indispensable document, therefore, in the ongoing evangelical process of self-criticism and correction.

[^c34-46]: Noll and Nystrom, _Is the Reformation Over?_, 71–73.

[^c34-47]: Ibid., 116–50.

### 5. Conclusion

The image that Noll and Nystrom leave with their readers is of a web of relationships emerging in far more piecemeal, personal, and organic ways. Far more important to evangelicals than the council are convictions that they have Catholic allies in the struggles against militant secularism in the northern hemisphere and militant Islam in the South; that at least some Catholic leaders (notably John Paul II) share a recognizable, warm, and lively trust in the Lord Jesus; that ties of friendship built around Bible study and shared struggle can indeed be resilient and faith-strengthening. No thoughtful evangelical will move from these to the conclusion that the Reformation is over. Indeed, Noll and Nystrom answer their own question squarely in the negative. But it cannot be denied that the arena in which the doctrinal debates continue to take place is now different than it was in previous centuries, even in previous decades. Clearly, this web of relationships was and remains untidy, unsystematic, frustrating, and surprising. Indeed, because evangelicalism is a sometimes fractious, sometimes friendly grouping of family resemblances, its emergence and ongoing growth could have and continue to take place in no other way.

That the decades following the Second Vatican Council have seen a solid stream of two-way traffic between St Peter’s and Wheaton develop cannot be denied. For some on both sides, this is an achievement to be celebrated even as they acknowledge the need for more sustained and difficult conversations. For others, also on both sides, this is a tragic error or even a fiirtation with heresy. All, however, must acknowledge its reality. The evidence presented above clearly shows the significance of the council for those Catholics who have found in evangelical Protestants unlikely allies on several fronts; it also shows, however, its relative insignificance for evangelicals, who have entered into these conversations for their own, far more complex, reasons.
