## 35. Catholic–Jewish Relations in Light of Vatican II’s Nostra

### 1. The Origins of Nostra Aetate

**[p. 570]** After Pope John XXIII announced the convocation of an ecumenical council, Vatican officials began the work of preparing an agenda and preliminary texts. That original agenda contained nothing about interreligious relations, including the Church’s outlook on Judaism and the Jewish people. The eventual addition of the Church’s relationship with Judaism to the conciliar agenda resulted from a historic meeting between the French Jewish historian Jules Isaac, who lost most of his family in the Holocaust, and Pope John XXIII soon after the papal announcement of a forthcoming council. In the course of that meeting, Isaac made a strong plea to the pope to place the history of the troubled narrative of Catholic–Jewish relations on the list of [^c35-1] topics to be discussed at Vatican II. While the pope gave no firm assurance to Isaac during the meeting itself, shortly thereafter he ordered Cardinal Augustin Bea to begin work on the preparation of a statement on the Church and Judaism during the council.

[^c35-1]: Jules Isaac, _The Teaching of Contempt: Christian Roots of Anti-Semitism_ (New York: Holt, Rinehart and Winston, 1964). See also Norman C. Tobias, _Jewish Conscience of the Church: Jules Isaac and the Second Vatican Council_ (London: Palgrave Macmillan, 2017).

The initial draft of the proposed statement on the Church and the Jewish people did not come to the council **[p. 571]** for discussion until its second session. Its introduction sparked considerable debate on the floor of the council and beyond. Some bishops expressed strong opposition to what was seen as a major reformulation of the Church’s classical approach to Jews and Judaism. Others, especially bishops from Muslim-majority countries, felt that going home with a document that addressed only the Jewish question might have negative consequences for their small, often diminishing, Catholic communities. On a more positive note, some of these bishops had also come to appreciate religious insights in Islam and felt these values should be highlighted in the projected interreligious statement. So an ongoing debate ensued as to whether there should be some mention of the Jews in the anticipated theological document on the Church or whether the council should develop a separate declaration that would have a chapter on Catholic–Jewish relations and additional chapters on Islam, as well as a more general understanding of the value and principles of interreligious dialogue from a Catholic perspective. The latter eventually won the day; the document had four chapters, with the last chapter in the final version dealing with the Church and Judaism. Nonetheless, the idea of including something on the Jews in the theological statement on the Church which came to be known as the Constitution _Lumen Gentium_ was preserved. _Nostra Aetate_ in its present form eventually passed the council in its final session in October 1965 with an overwhelmingly positive vote.

Chapter 4 of _Nostra Aetate_ built its perspective relative to the Catholic–Jewish relationship on three central assertions using St Paul’s Letter to the Romans, chapters 9 to 11, as its foundation. The three core assertions can be summarized as follows: (1) Jews were not collectively responsible for the death of Jesus; (2) hence the covenant between God and Israel did not end with the Easter resurrection; and (3) in his preaching, Jesus drew significantly in a positive sense from important parts of the Jewish tradition current in his day. These three assertions turned the classical Christian perspective on Jews and Judaism upside down. From the time of the patristic writings, Jews had been seen as cast out of the covenantal relationship with God for their failure to acknowledge Jesus as the expected Messiah and had been replaced therein by the Church. It was St Augustine who crystallized this outlook on the Jews. He did not advocate their physical destruction. Rather, he advanced the notion that they were to be seen as ‘witness people’ who were to remain miserable and marginal in human society, never to have a homeland of their own. This perpetual Jewish condition was to serve as a reminder of what happens to a person who refuses to recognize Christ.

Overturning what has been known as the ‘deicide’ charge at Vatican II was key to the creation of a far more positive understanding of what John Paul II later termed the inherent bonding between Jews and Christians. The accusation of deicide against the Jews was ultimately the basis for the view that they had been expelled from the covenant. The Canadian theologian Gregory Baum, who was involved in the initial drafting of what became chapter 4 of _Nostra Aetate_, labelled this fundamental theological turnabout of Catholicism’s traditional outlook on Jews and Judaism the most dramatic change in the ordinary magisterium of the **[p. 572]** [^c35-2] Church to emerge from the council. While the term ‘deicide’ fell out of the final version of _Nostra Aetate_, repudiation of the term was clearly intended by the council.

[^c35-2]: Gregory Baum, _Amazing Church: A Catholic Theologian Remembers a Half-Century of Change_ (Toronto: Novalis, 2005).

With regard to the third central affirmation in _Nostra Aetate_—having to do with Jesus’s positive embrace of certain Jewish perspectives on theological issues, such as the understanding of God; key ethical issues; and an approach to worship—the document helped to generate widespread biblical research that has transformed our understanding of Jesus’s relationship with the Judaism of his day. The Church has moved away from a simplistic view that Jesus stood over against the Judaism of his time to a much more nuanced appreciation of a complex relationship, where it is now clear that he operated within the framework of what might be labelled the more ‘progressive’ forms of Jewish religious expression in the first century while proclaiming distinctive claims on some religious questions, such as the forgiveness of sins.

Nowhere is this fundamental change more evident than in the Church’s perspective on Jesus and the Pharisees. The classical view of the Pharisees as the arch-enemies of Jesus who were against the basic religious values Jesus made central in his preaching and public witness was officially replaced in Catholic teaching in the 1985 _Notes on the Correct Presentation of Judaism in Catholic Catechetics and Preaching_, issued for the twentieth anniversary of _Nostra Aetate._ In that document, Jesus is said to be closer to the Pharisees than to any other contemporary Jewish movement of his day. Unfortunately, there is widespread ignorance of this transformed view of Pharisaism and its basic teachings in the preaching in today’s Church. And Catholic theology has done little to incorporate this change into its statements on basic faith perspectives.

### 2. Official Catholic Statements in Light of Nostra Aetate

_Nostra Aetate_ has generated a number of official Catholic documents relevant to the discussion of Catholic– Jewish relations. In addition to the 1985 document mentioned above, there was a statement ten years earlier for the tenth anniversary of _Nostra Aetate_. That text stated a fundamental principle for all discussions between Catholic and Jews: Catholics must come to know Jews as they define themselves. Put another way, Catholics truly committed to dialogue with Jews to avoid creating ‘straw’ versions of what Jews believe, of building their understanding of Judaism on caricatures of Jewish belief and tradition. To go back to the previous issue of the portrayal of Pharisaism, here we find over the centuries one of the most evident examples of stereotyping that has undermined the Church’s outlook on Judaism in Jesus’s day, but even of contemporary Judaism, whose various movements are in one way or another all descendants of the Pharisaic tradition.

March 1998 saw the release of another important Vatican statement, titled _We Remember: A Reflection on the_ **[p. 573]** _Shoah_, published by the Pontifical Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews. It fulfilled a promise made to Jewish and Catholic leaders during John Paul II’s visit to Miami a decade later. There was some disappointment that _We Remember_ did not appear as a formal papal encyclical, something the pope seemed to indicate to the group assembled in Miami. The disappointment was somewhat softened by the inclusion of a strong statement from John Paul II in support of the document. Its greatest achievement was that it finally put the Shoah on the table as a central issue in Catholic–Jewish dialogue, something that both faith communities tended to avoid before the release of _We Remember_.

The document has had something of a chequered history. It ran into significant difficulties at several points during its ten-year incubation. Part of the initial difficulty had to do with the continued persistence within important sectors of Catholicism, particularly in Germany, of the notion that the Church was chiefly a victim of Nazism and that it was rather heroic in its opposition to National Socialism. So, to create a text which would move away from such a perspective to one in which critique of the Church, including the papacy, would play a central role faced formidable challenges. Cardinal Edward Idris Cassidy, who served as president of the Holy See’s Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews—created by Pope Paul VI to implement _Nostra Aetate_—finally took the lead in preparing a statement. As is the case with all such Vatican documents, the text needed approval from several major Vatican offices, in particular the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith. This congregation demanded certain major changes and additions to the text before it would approve _We Remember_’s release. Rather reluctantly, Cardinal Cassidy agreed to the requested changes, as it was made clear to him that the document would not see the light of day without them. Later, in a number of lectures on the document, Cardinal Cassidy tried to correct some of the statements with which he had serious concerns.

The principal changes in Cardinal Cassidy’s original draft included an inflation of the number of Jews saved by Catholics and a clear impression that only marginal Catholics were involved in collaborating with the Nazi programme of the incarceration and extermination of Jews. But this is definitely erroneous. As Cardinal Cassidy later insisted, Catholic leaders at various times clearly cooperated and stood by as the Nazis slaughtered the Jews of Europe, and the seeds of this actual or tacit cooperation were to be found in certain official Catholic teachings and representations of such teachings in art, such as the famous façade on the outer wall of the cathedral in Strasbourg, France.

The most important issue that _We Remember_ did not settle was the role of Pius XII during the Nazi era. This continues to be the case up to the present. Cardinal Cassidy had not included any reference to Pius XII in his draft version. But the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith insisted that it be made clear that what it termed ‘the Church as such’ could not be charged with collaboration and it was only ‘wayward’ preachers who led some Catholics astray.

Then, 2002 saw the release of a major document of some 200 pages on the depiction of Jews in the New Testament, _The Jewish People and Their Sacred Scriptures in the Christian Bible_. It was written by the Pontifical Biblical Commission, with an endorsement from Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, then president of the **[p. 574]** Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, who held ultimate jurisdiction over the text. Its public release was rather unusual. There was no formal announcement of the document; it merely began to appear in bookshops in Rome. The document offers a comprehensive analysis of how Jews and Judaism are presented in the various books that make up the Christian New Testament.

Two statements in particular are worth nothing. The first is the assertion that Jewish biblical interpretations are not in vain. While they may differ in some instances from Christian interpretations, they have a certain validity and need to be studied by Christians. This statement represents a genuine breakthrough from the traditional Christian perspective, which argued that texts in the Jewish Bible could be properly understood only in light of the New Testament. Jewish textual interpretation was considered incomplete in terms of the full revelatory meaning of what was traditionally understood in the Church as the ‘Old Testament’. Such an understanding is regrettably still present in the Easter Vigil, where the readings from the Hebrew Scriptures are presented while the church remains in darkness. It also can be seen in Monsignor John Oesterreicher’s annual volumes on Catholic–Jewish relations, which exclude any contributions by Jewish scholars on Old Testament texts prior to _Nostra Aetate_. Only in the final volume of the groundbreaking series published after Vatican II’s historic declaration were Jewish scholars invited to contribute interpretations of biblical texts.

The second key passage in this Pontifical Biblical Commission document states that when the Messiah finally appears, he will have the same traits which Christians have already seen in the person of Jesus Christ. Thus, the statement seems to maintain a certain ultimate coalescence between the Christian and Jewish Messianic visions. This assertion, which has significant theological meaning, needs further exploration in Christian theological circles, including the Vatican’s theological commission, since the Pontifical Biblical Commission does not engage in theological reflection as such.

For the fiftieth anniversary of _Nostra Aetate_, the Holy See’s Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews, now headed by Cardinal Kurt Koch, issued a statement entitled ‘The Gifts and the Calling of God are Irrevocable (Rom 11:29)’, that basically summarized a half-century of developments in Catholic–Jewish relations. The statement was released after some delay in early December 2015 with a note that it carried no magisterial authority, a rather unusual remark in a text from an official Vatican commission.

The 2015 document presented an overview of the major results from the personal dialogues and scholarly research generated by _Nostra Aetate_. It highlighted the continuing validity of the Jewish covenant after the Resurrection in the face of some challenges to such an understanding from scholars and church leaders such [^c35-3] as Cardinal Avery Dulles, SJ. However, the document sets the continuing reality of Jewish covenantal inclusion within a single covenantal framework embracing both Jews and Christians, without reflecting on **[p. 575]** how the two faith communities relate to each other within that single, shared covenant in the process of human redemption. The commission’s statement clearly maintains the universal significance of the Christ event in this regard. This question remains an ongoing challenge within the Christian–Jewish dialogue.

[^c35-3]: See e.g. Avery Dulles, ‘Who Can Be Saved?’, in _Church and Society. The McGinley Lectures, 1988–2007_ (New York: Fordham University Press, 2008), 522–34.

Other significant affirmations within the 2015 text include an understanding of two key passages in the Letter to the Hebrews which some have argued deny the continuing validity of the Jewish covenant. Referencing contemporary biblical scholarship, the document draws on the scholarly view that sees Hebrews as having a more limited, non-theological scope than Romans 9–11, which the authors of chapter 4 of _Nostra Aetate_ used as the theological foundation for their presentation of a far more positive picture of the Church’s relationship with Jews and Judaism than had been the case for centuries.

The fiftieth anniversary statement also addressed the issue of proselytizing of Jews, an issue that remains a raw nerve for many in the Jewish community. The statement clearly rejects any organized, deliberate efforts on the part of Catholics to convert Jews. This assertion received considerable attention in the Jewish media, which frequently misinterpreted it to mean that Catholicism has rejected Jewish conversion as such. While some individual Catholic theologians have called for such a formal repudiation, this statement rejects only organized, institutionally based efforts at conversion. It leaves open-ended the wider issue of whether Jews at some point must acknowledge the centrality of Christ in the salvific process. So, the discussion on this highly controversial topic will, and must, continue. It is far from fully resolved from the Catholic side, and Jewish participants in the conversation with Catholics must avoid giving the 2015 document a wider significance than it intends.

In addition to the above statements from Vatican offices, there is need to highlight the many statements by John Paul II. He spoke more often in a constructive way on the Christian–Jewish relationship than any previous pope. He called this relationship unique among the relationships the Church enjoys with non- Christian religious communities. He argued in a number of his speeches for an inherent bonding between Judaism and Christianity. And his papacy was the first to establish full diplomatic relations with the State of Israel. His visit to Israel in the year 2000, where he captured the attention and admiration of much of the population, proved an important source in the process of healing the historic Christian–Jewish rupture, as did his visit to the synagogue in Rome, breaking centuries of separation. While he did not follow through on the development of a comprehensive renewed theology of Jews and Judaism within the Catholic Church, he did create the atmosphere for individual theologians to pursue such a development. Cardinal Walter Kasper, whom John Paul II appointed as president of the Holy See’s Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews, took the lead in having theologians, including himself, focus on this effort. One result was the volume [^c35-4] **[p. 576]** _Christ Jesus and the Jewish People Today: New Explorations of Theological Relationships_, for which Cardinal Kasper wrote an important foreword. This volume attempted to address the major question ‘How can the Church integrate Covenantal continuity for Jews and yet maintain a universal significance for the Christ Event?’—a question that remains central to the ongoing theological challenge launched by the affirmation of ongoing covenantal inclusion for the Jewish people in _Nostra Aetate_. Finally, as previously indicated, the promised statement on the Shoah, _We Remember_, with John Paul II’s strong foreword, appeared during his papacy.

[^c35-4]: Philip A. Cunningham, et al., eds., _Christ Jesus and the Jewish People Today: New Explorations of Theological Relationships_ (Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 2011).

John Paul II’s two successors generally have reaffirmed his groundbreaking perspectives. Benedict XVI, in an address to Jewish leaders at the beginning of his papacy, committed himself to continued implementation of John Paul II’s vision. He himself seemed open to a new understanding of the reconciliation of Jews and Christians at the end of history. He also paid an important visit to the Rome synagogue where, in his address, he made positive reference to post-biblical Jewish texts, a way of affirming the continuing spiritual significance for Christians of post-biblical Jewish perspectives as well as continuing Jewish covenantal inclusion.

Pope Francis has tended in his papacy towards gestures more than texts. In this vein, there is a great significance in his long-standing relationship with his Argentinian rabbinic colleague Abraham Skorka, with whom he co-authored an important book on the Jewish–Catholic relationship while they worked [^c35-5] together in Buenos Aires. And in his initial papal encyclical, _Evangelii Gaudium_, Francis reaffirmed the post- _Nostra Aetate_ belief in the continuing validity of the Jewish covenant as well as the Jewish roots of Christianity. He insisted that Judaism cannot be regarded as ‘foreign’ to the Christian religion.

[^c35-5]: Jorge Mario Bergoglio and Abraham Skorka, _On Heaven and Earth_ (New York: Image, 2013).

### 3. Theological Developments in Light of Nostra Aetate

By affirming the continued validity of the Jewish covenant after the Christ event, Vatican II’s _Nostra Aetate_ posed a major challenge to classical Christian thought regarding Christology and ecclesiology. Central to this theological tradition in the Church was the belief that the Jewish failure to recognize Jesus as the authentic Messiah resulted in the loss of covenantal status for the Jewish people, leading them to be replaced by the Christian community. Whatever was good and true in Judaism was absorbed by the Church, leaving the Jewish religion an empty shell that was eventually to disappear from the earth. Images of the Jewish–Christian relationship such as the famous depiction on the façade of the cathedral in Strasbourg, France, graphically convey this traditional theological perspective. The Church is portrayed as a bright, beautiful young woman, while Judaism is depicted as a bent-over and blindfolded old woman. Clearly, such **[p. 577]** a theological understanding required a significant rethinking of the Christian perspective on its relationship with Judaism and the Jewish people in light of the affirmations found in _Nostra Aetate_.

The breakthrough in the Church’s understanding of Jews and Judaism began in the decades prior to Vatican II. This breakthrough was generated by several realities. First, modern biblical scholarship was beginning to look upon the relationship between the Old and New Testaments in a more positive light. Second, the experience of the Nazi attack on the Jewish population of Europe, and the realization by some Church leaders and scholars that the traditional negative views of Jews and Judaism in Christian theology contributed to the victimization of the Jews, particularly at grassroots level, enhanced this constructive turnabout in the Church’s outlook. Third, the pioneering work of several converted Jews (both Protestant and Catholic) such as John Oesterreicher aided this new development, which culminated in the overwhelming approval of chapter 4 of _Nostra Aetate_ by the council fathers. Finally, the enhanced collaboration of Jews and Christian in areas of social justice in the United States, while it did not directly involve discussions of the theological relationship between Jews and Christians, laid down fertile ground for the emergence of such a discussion by breaking down long-standing barriers between the Jewish and Christian communities on a personal level. Important names in the early theological effort included Charles Journet, Jean Daniélou, Karl Barth, Cardinal Augustin Bea, and Sister Rose Thering, OP, who produced a study of Catholic textbooks which revealed considerable distortions in the portrayal of Jews and Judaism. This study had an important influence on the American hierarchy at Vatican II, who played a central role in the eventual overwhelming approval of the document after several rocky years during the conciliar process.

Soon after the council, a number of Christian theologians in North America and Europe began to reflect on how the new understanding of Jewish covenantal continuity that emerged from the council might be integrated within a new Christological perspective in the Church. Initial contributors to this post-conciliar discussion included Gregory Baum, Rosemary Radford Ruether, Cardinal Carlo Martini, SJ, Monika Hellwig, A. Roy Eckardt, Paul van Buren (who produced a trilogy of volumes on the topic), and Clemens Thoma, SVD. With the exception of Ruether, all of these scholars held fast to a single covenantal link between Jews and Christians.

The initial attempts at theological reconstruction of the Christian–Jewish relationship began to chip away at two long and dominant trends in Christian thought. The first, which predominated in Catholicism (particularly in the liturgy), focused on the prophecy/fulfilment motif. Jesus fulfilled the Messianic prophecies found in the Jewish tradition and thus inaugurated the Messianic era for which Jews had hoped and prayed throughout the centuries. It was their own spiritual blindness that prevented most Jews from recognizing this fulfilment in the Christ event.

As a divine punishment for this boldness, Jews were displaced in the covenantal relationship by those baptized into the Church, the ‘new Israel’. As mentioned above, St Augustine saw the Jews as ‘witness **[p. 578]** people’ who needed to remain in a miserable and marginal state without ever again enjoying national sovereignty as a perpetual reminder to others of what happens to those who refuse to acknowledge Christ.

The second trend, strongly identifled with continental Protestant theology but with roots as well in Catholic thought, envisioned _freedom_ as the principal effect of the Christ event. Through his preaching and ministry, and in a very special way through his death and resurrection, Jesus paid a blood price to liberate humanity from the burden of Jewish law, which was spiritually inhibiting. As St Anselm and other Church Fathers put it, through the shedding of his blood on Calvary, Jesus washed humanity clean in a way that commitment to Torah on the part of the Jewish community could never accomplish. This interpretation of the ultimate meaning of the Christ event also tended to move the covenantal relationship with God away from a communal orientation towards a more individualistic, personal sense of human–divine bonding.

The initial efforts at rethinking the Christian–Jewish relationship theologically did not strongly challenge these more classical assertions about its nature except to say that the Jewish covenant had not been terminated. This certainly constituted a step forward, as it involved a clear rejection of total covenantal expulsion for Jews. How Christians could maintain more classical theological attitudes relative to the significance of the Christ event and now argue as well for continuing covenantal inclusion for Jews was generally relegated to the realm of the ‘mysterious’. God alone was privy to the process of reconciling these apparently contradictory claims, a process that would be realized only at the end of days. This, they felt, was the answer to the joint covenantal dilemma by St Paul in Romans 9–11, a central building block for _Nostra Aetate_.

The first group of Christian theologians to attempt a restatement of Christian theology endeavoured to put forth perspectives that tried to account directly for the validity for joint Christian–Jewish covenantal inclusivity. They felt that leaving it to ‘mystery’ remained too ambiguous. Their approaches vary, but all tend to see a constructive role for the Jewish tradition in the overall process of human salvation. And all are inclined to articulate a continuing positive role for the Jewish biblical tradition in the formulation of Christian self-identity rather than only a preparatory one rooted in an understanding that what Christians have traditionally termed ‘the Old Testament’ served in fact as ‘the Scriptures’ for Jesus in his preaching. Jesus himself knew of no ‘Old Testament’. His ministry was spiritually rooted in these biblical texts, particularly the prophetic literature such as Isaiah.

Various Christian theologians later began to explore the affirmations regarding Christian–Jewish relations in _Nostra Aetate_. One of the first was a leading post-Vatican II theologian, Monika Hellwig. Hellwig insisted that the covenant forged with Israel at Sinai was not obliterated with the coming of Christ. It in fact remains fully in force. This understanding forced Hellwig into a reconsideration of some claims embedded in classical Christology. She began to interpret the Christ event not primarily as the completion of the Messianic prophecies but as the now open possibility for Gentiles to enter the covenantal election first **[p. 579]** granted the Jewish people and to experience the intimacy with God that this election brought them. Hence, Christians must look to God’s continuing revelation in contemporary Jewish experience to grasp fully [^c35-6] God’s self-communication in our day.

[^c35-6]: See Monika Hellwig, ‘Christian Theology and the Covenant of Israel’, _Journal of Ecumenical Studies_ 7, no. 1 (1970): 37–51.

An interesting perspective on the Church’s theology of Judaism and the Jewish people appeared in the [^c35-7] writings of Cardinal Carlo Martini, SJ, a biblical scholar who served as archbishop of Milan (1980–2002). While his perspective was not as developed as those of other scholars in the dialogue with Judaism, Martini attempted to redefine the split between the Church and the Jewish people as the first major schism in Christianity. As with the other separations in Christian history, the break with Judaism deprived the Church of significant insights into the nature of human salvation. For Martini, Christianity cannot return to genuine wholeness without a reintegration with its Jewish foundation. The initial step in a post-_Nostra Aetate_ theology must be a recognition that the rupture that eventually came about in the Jewish–Christian relationship must be ended.

[^c35-7]: Carlo Maria Cardinal Martini, _The Catholic Church and the Jewish People: Recent Reflections from Rome_ (New York: Fordham University Press, 2007).

The Episcopalian scholar Paul van Buren, whose mentor was Karl Barth, contributed three volumes to the [^c35-8] ongoing theological discussion. For van Buren, ‘Israel’ consisted of two branches. Both are essential ingredients of any complete definition of the term, though each bears a distinctive character along with its inherent linkage. Christianity represents the community of Gentile believers drawn by the God of the Jewish people to worship him and to make known his love among the peoples of the world. For van Buren, it is not a question of the Church suddenly abandoning its historic proclamation of Jesus as the Christ and the Son of God. But Jesus was not the Christ in one crucial sense: he was not the long-awaited Jewish Messiah. And so, post-Easter Judaism remains a religion of legitimate Messianic hope rather than of spiritual blindness.

[^c35-8]: Paul van Buren, _Theology of the Jewish–Christian Reality_, 3 vols (London: Bloomsbury T&T Clark, 2000).

The shared Messianic vision of Judaism and Christianity led van Buren to advocate the notion of the ‘co-formation’ of the two faith communities. In saying this, he meant that both branches of ‘Israel’ must grow in tandem—alongside each other rather than in isolation. While each would retain a measure of distinctness, both would experience a growing mutuality characterized by understanding and love. This growing together in love would increase each partner’s freedom to be its distinctive self while maintaining an awareness of the necessity for mutual cooperation. Some in the Jewish community have been uncomfortable with the pronounced bondedness between Christianity and Judaism championed by van Buren; they prefer greater separation and distinctive integrity for the Jewish people in the renewed relationship. In several unpublished presentations shortly before his death, van Buren expressed the view that the ultimate meaning of Jesus’s ministry and death on Calvary was to make more _transparent_ the profound link between God and humanity.

**[p. 580]** The Swiss biblical theologian Clemens Thoma, SVD, added yet another perspective to the international [^c35-9] Catholic effort to rethink the Catholic–Jewish relationship theologically in light of _Nostra Aetate_. Thoma emphatically rejected any attempt to describe the basic theological tension between Judaism and Christianity as rooted in the acceptance/rejection of Jesus as Messiah. There existed no consistent, univocal notion of the Messiah in Jewish thought in Jesus’s time. Many diverse interpretations were floating about in a period which witnessed considerable creativity. Some Jews had even reached the conclusion that the notion of a personal Messiah should be discarded. Hence, there was no easy comparison to be made legitimately between Jewish Messianic expectations and the figure of Jesus, and therefore no grounds for alleging Jewish rejection of Jesus’s fulfilment of the purported Jewish Messianic vision.

[^c35-9]: Clemens Thoma, _A Christian Theology of Judaism_, trans. Helga Croner (New York: Paulist, 1980).

For Thoma, the uniqueness of Jesus was ultimately located in the unqualifled fashion in which he tied the kingdom of God to his own ministerial activities and his person. In so doing, he was following a trend present in apocalyptic interpretation of Judaism at the time. But his sense of intimacy with the Father went beyond what any sector of Judaism was prepared to acknowledge and endorse.

A central voice in the reconsideration on Christology, given his influential role in Catholic circles in [^c35-10] Germany, was that of Franz Mussner. His perspective bears many similarities to that of Clemens Thoma. The two shared a conviction about Jesus’s positive links to developing ideas within Judaism in the first century CE. Mussner joined Thoma in rejecting any interpretation of the Christ event over against Judaism based on a notion that Jesus fulfilled all the major Messianic prophecies. Mussner’s outlook does maintain a unique aspect in the revelation in and through Jesus as the Christ. But that uniqueness arises from the complete identity of Jesus’s work, as well as his words and actions, with the work of God. As a result of the revelatory vision accorded humanity through Christ, the New Testament is able to speak about God with an anthropomorphic boldness not found to the same degree in the Hebrew Scriptures.

[^c35-10]: Franz Mussner, _Tractate on the Jews: The Significance of Judaism for Christian Faith_ (Minneapolis: Fortress, 1984); originally published as _Traktat über die Juden_ (Kösel, 1979). See also _Dieses Geschlecht wird nicht vergehen: Judentum und_ _Kirche_ (Freiburg: Herder, 1991).

Mussner distinguished between the older ‘prophet Christology’ and the somewhat later development of what he terms ‘Son Christology’. Both have some roots in Judaism. His preference is definitely for the ‘Son Christology’ model. This model opts for a profound convergence between Jesus and God. For him, the uniqueness of Jesus is to be found in the depth of his imitation of God. And so, for Mussner the most distinctive feature of Christian thought relative to Jesus lies in the notion of the Incarnation rather than in any claim of total Messianic fulfilment.

A Catholic theologian whose work has had important impact in terms of a Christian theology of the Jewish [^c35-11] **[p. 581]** people is Johann Baptist Metz. A student of Karl Rahner, Metz is one of the few Catholic theologians who has attempted reconstruction of the Church’s theological approach to Jews and Judaism through the experience of the Holocaust. After the Shoah, Metz is convinced that Christian theology must be guided by the insight that Christians can form and understand their identity only in the face of the Jews. Jewish history and Jewish beliefs need to be reintegrated into Christian theological statements and consciousness. Jewish history is a continuing part of ecclesial history, not merely pre-Christian history.

[^c35-11]: See e.g. Johann Baptist Metz, ‘On the Way to a Christology after Auschwitz’, trans. Matthew Ashley, in _the End of Time? The_ _Provocation of Talking About God_, ed. Tiemo Peters and Claus Urban (New York: Paulist, 2004), 26–46; originally published as ‘Unterwegs zu einer Christologie nach Auschwitz’, _Stimmen der Zeit_ 218, no. 11 (2000): 755–60.

For Metz, the critical theological question in light of the Holocaust is the presence/absence of God. How we resolve the issue of divine existence in light of the Shoah will have a significant impact on how Christians express their belief in Jesus as the Christ. And in terms of Christological statement, Metz strongly feels that the Church needs to return to a more Hebraic form of Christological expression rooted in the Synoptic rather than in the Pauline biblical literature. This modal reorientation to a Hebraic consciousness will move Christology away from what Metz names ‘the victorious form of Christology’ that had all the answers and no longer needed the Jewish vision of religious reality. Such change will generate a future-oriented, open-ended approach to Christology in which the central theme will be discipleship. It will also be a Christology that provides an essential eschatological role for the Jewish people.

In recent years, the pace of theological developments relative to the Church’s understanding of Judaism and the Jewish people has slowed in comparison with the first several decades following Vatican II, and the orientation has somewhat changed. John Pawlikowski, Philip Cunningham, and Didier Pollefeyt are three scholars who have added their voices to the reformulation of Catholicism’s approach to Judaism, especially in the area of Christology.

Pawlikowski has argued for an incarnationally based Christology (rather than a prophetic/Messianic or blood Christology) as offering the best possibility for the creation of meaningful theological space for Judaism after the Christ event. In his view, the Christ event made more transparent the link between humanity and the Godhead. But, drawing upon some recent scholarship on ‘incarnationalism’ in first-century CE Judaism, he would maintain that this ‘new revelation’ built upon a developing trend in sectors of Judaism contemporaneous with Jesus rather than constituting a total replacement for Judaism.[^c35-12]

[^c35-12]: John Pawlikowski, ‘Christology, Anti-Semitism, and Christian–Jewish Bonding’, in _Restructuring Christian Theology_ (Minneapolis: Fortress, 1994), 245–68; ‘Christology after the Holocaust’, _Encounter_ 59, no. 3 (1998): 345–68; ‘Christology and the Jewish People’, _Sobornost_ 26, no. 1 (2004): 61–79; ‘Christology and the Jewish–Christian Dialogue: A Personal Theological Journey’, _Irish Theological Quarterly_ 72, no. 2 (2007): 147–67.

Cunningham and Pollefeyt, working as a team, also root their perspective in a notion of incarnationalism as [^c35-13] **[p. 582]** interpreted within Judaism by Michael Wyschograd. Christian belief in the Incarnation intensifled this existing Jewish view by relating it directly to a single person in Jesus. They describe their approach as a Logos-based Christology which, while emphasizing the special presence of the Logos in Jesus Christ, also acknowledges the continuing presence of the Logos in Judaism, albeit in a different way. Both Judaism and Christianity remain central to the eschatologically oriented process of human salvation.

[^c35-13]: Philip A. Cunningham and Didier Pollefeyt, ‘The Triune One, the Incarnate Logos, and Israel’s Covenantal Life’, in _Christ_ _Jesus and the Jewish People Today: New Explorations of Theological Interrelationships_, ed. Philip A. Cunningham, et al. (Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 2011), 183–201.

### 4. Unmet Challenges in Christian–Jewish Relations

Several major challenges await further reflection in the Christian–Jewish dialogue generated by _Nostra Aetate_. A major theological challenge results from the recent scholarship on the first several centuries of Christianity, which has clearly shown continuing links between the two faith communities well after Calvary. Biblical scholarship as well as Early Church historiography have clearly demonstrated that the separation of Judaism and Christianity was a lengthy process over several centuries. In that sense it is erroneous to argue, as the Church has often done, that Jesus ‘founded’ a new, totally separate religious institution in his own lifetime. Systematic theology has yet to catch up with this widespread new perspective among biblical scholars as it reflects on Christology and ecclesiology and their continuing links with Judaism.

As the Catholic Church becomes ever more global—with growth largely in Africa and Asia, where few Jewish communities exist—it will be necessary to demonstrate that chapter 4 of _Nostra Aetate_ has relevance everywhere and not merely in the North Atlantic area, as some have claimed. Part of the challenge here lies in the greater integration of Christian–Jewish discussions into the wider arena of interreligious dialogue. Unfortunately, too often in scholarly and Vatican circles, there has existed too much separation between the two sectors. The Christian–Jewish encounter, because it touches upon fundamental themes of self-identity, impacts Christian self-understanding in any and all interreligious dialogues.

The issue of evangelization also remains inadequately addressed. Individual Catholic leaders such as Cardinal Walter Kasper and Catholic documents such as the December 2015 Statement from the Holy See’s Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews have rejected any form of organized proselytizing of the Jewish people. But the more fundamental theological issues have hardly been discussed. It is one of the most challenging of the remaining issues and is not capable of easy resolution.

Finally, a new focus is necessary on the implementation of _Nostra Aetate_ in the liturgy, with regard to both Eucharistic celebration and the recitation of the hours. With the exception of a few liturgical scholars, such as Liam Tracey, OSM and Richard McCarron, almost nothing has been done to foster implementation of Vatican II’s new vision of the Catholic–Jewish relationship.
