## 36. Nostra Aetate: Ongoing Interreligious Dialogue Especially

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 584]** The purpose of this chapter is to present the measures taken in the Catholic Church to encourage the reception and implementation of _Nostra Aetate_ (_NA_). Special attention will be given to the work of the office set up to promote the new vision embodied in this declaration and to the documents it has produced.

### 2. A Dicastery for Dialogue

Even before the final vote had been taken on _Nostra Aetate_, Pope Paul VI decided to set up within the Vatican [^c36-1] an office for interreligious dialogue. He announced this publicly on Pentecost Sunday, 1964. Shortly afterwards, on 19 May 1964, there came into being what was first named the Secretariat for Non-Christians [^c36-2] **[p. 585]** (SNC), later to become the Pontifical Council for Interreligious Dialogue (PCID). As announced by Paul VI, Cardinal Paolo Marella, former diplomatic representative of the Holy See in Japan, was made the first president of this office. He called to work with him as secretary Fr Pierre Humbertclaude, a Marianist, who had been a missionary, also in Japan. One of the first persons to join the staff was Fr Joseph Cuoq, Missionary of Africa, who for two years had been in charge of a desk for Christian–Muslim relations within the Congregation for the Oriental Churches. Once the SNC was set up, Cuoq was immediately transferred there.

[^c36-1]: For this announcement, see Francesco Gioia, ed., _Interreligious Dialogue: The Official Teaching of the Catholic Church from_ _the Second Vatican Council to John Paul II (1963–2005)_ (Boston: Pauline Books & Media, 2006), n. 194. On the first years of this office, see Michael L. Fitzgerald, ‘The Secretariat for Non-Christians is Ten Years Old’, _Islamochristiana_ 1 (1975): 87–94; Michael L Fitzgerald, ‘Twenty-five Years of Dialogue: The Pontifical Council for Interreligious Dialogue’, _Islamochristiana_ 15 (1989): 109–20. For a brief account of the succeeding years, see Miguel Angel Ayuso Guixot, ‘50 Years in the Service of Interreligious Dialogue’, _Pro Dialogo_ 145, no. 1 (2014): 23–32. For a more complete history, see Maurice Borrmans, ‘Une brève histoire du Conseil pontifical pour le dialogue interreligieux’, in _Dialoguer avec les Musulmans: Une cause perdue ou_ _une cause à gagner?_ (Paris: Pierre Téqui, 2011), 157–82.

[^c36-2]: The change of title came with the Apostolic Constitution of John Paul II _Pastor Bonus_, promulgated on 28 June 1988. The change from secretariat to pontifical council indicated a more permanent place of this office within the structure of the Roman Curia. The choice of ‘Interreligious Dialogue’ to replace ‘Non-Christians’ can be seen as the avoidance of a negative term, thus showing greater respect for the followers of other religions. In the latest reform of the Roman Curia, by Pope Francis in _Praedicate Evangelium_ (19 March 2022) this body has been retained as an independent office and is now known as the Dicastery for Interreligious Dialogue.

Under Cardinal Marella (1964–73), the secretariat got slowly under way. It took up first the task of spreading the vision of Vatican II, showing Catholics that in relating respectfully to followers of other religions, they were not being untrue to their Christian faith. For this purpose, a modest journal was created, at first simply called _Bulletin_, but later renamed _Pro Dialogo._ In one of the first issues, Msgr Piero Rossano, who would later become the secretary of the office, published an article in Latin about the teaching of [^c36-3] Vatican II on relations with people of other religions. Another initiative was the production of small booklets providing guidelines for dialogue with Buddhists, Hindus, and Muslims. _Guidelines for Dialogue between Christians and Muslims_, first published in 1970, was republished in 1981 in a revised and augmented [^c36-4] edition. There was also a booklet entitled _Meeting the African Religions._ This aroused criticism on the part of some missionaries, who said: ‘We have been doing all we can to stamp out these religions, and here comes the Vatican saying that we have to promote them’. Of course, there is an exaggeration in this objection: showing respect and upholding values is not the same as promoting a religion. In any case, undaunted by this opposition, the secretariat established two new desks: one for Asian Religions and the other for Traditional Religions, particularly in Africa. The work of promoting dialogue continued in collaboration with the local hierarchies throughout the world.

[^c36-3]: Piero Rossano, ‘Quid de non Christianis Oecumenicum Concilium docuerit’, _Bulletin Secretariatus pro Non Christianis_ 1 (1964): 15–22.

[^c36-4]: Maurice Borrmans, O_rientations pour un dialogue entre chrétiens et musulmans_ (Paris: Cerf, 1981); translated by R. Marston Speight as _Guidelines for Dialogue between Christians and Muslims_ (Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 1990).

The 1970s were years of striking initiatives in dialogue, particularly between Christians and Muslims. The World Council of Churches (WCC) organized an international meeting in Broumana, Lebanon, in 1972, which I had the privilege of attending on behalf of the SNC. This was followed by regional meetings in Africa and Asia. In the years following, there were congresses in Cordoba, Tunis, and Tripoli, Libya. The SNC, now **[p. 586]** under the leadership of Cardinal Sergio Pignedoli (1973–80), took an active part in these meetings and also established relations with Al-Azhar in Egypt. Delegations of Muslims from Indonesia and Iran came to the Holy See, as also a delegation from Saudi Arabia, led by the minister of Justice, which was received in audience by Pope Paul VI.

In October 1974, Pope Paul VI established within the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity the Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews and, in a parallel way, the Commission for Religious Relations with Muslims. Since relations with the Jews was a special task, different from ecumenical [^c36-5] relations, it made sense to entrust this work to a semi-independent commission. Within the SNC, the situation was different. Christian–Muslim relations formed a large part of its ordinary concerns, so the existence of a distinct commission seemed less appropriate. Eventually, the commission was transformed into a think-tank on Christian–Muslim relations. It has produced some useful reflections, such as _Religious Liberty: A Theme for Christian–Muslim Dialogue_ (2006).

[^c36-5]: Note should be taken of the documents produced by this Commission: _Guidelines and Suggestions for Implementing the_ _Conciliar Declaration Nostra Aetate No. 4_ (1974); _Notes on the Correct Way to Present Jews and Judaism in Preaching and_ _Catechesis in the Roman Catholic Church_ (1985); and _We Remember: A Reflection on the Shoah_ (1998). On these documents and on Catholic–Jewish relations in general, see Edward Idris Cardinal Cassidy, _Ecumenism and Interreligious Dialogue_ (Mahwah, NJ: Paulist, 2005).

The short presidency of Archbishop Jean Jadot (1980–84), who had served as apostolic nuncio in Bangkok and subsequently in the United States, and the much longer presidency of Cardinal Francis Arinze (1984– 2002), offered a time for theological reflection on the foundations and practice of dialogue. It also brought in a new concern: the impact of new religious movements. An inter-dicasterial committee produced a [^c36-6] provisional report on this question in 1986. This led to the appointment within the PCID of a desk officer for new religious movements.

[^c36-6]: Extracts from this report, ‘The Phenomenon of Sects or New Religious Movements’, can be found in Gioia, _Interreligious_ _Dialogue_, nos. 852–53.

### 3. Dialogue and Mission

It is now time to present some of the documents published during this period. Twenty years after it had been set up, the Secretariat for Non-Christians produced its first official document: _The Attitude of the Church_ [^c36-7] _toward the Followers of Other Religions: Reflections and Orientations on Dialogue and Mission_ (1984).  _Dialogue and Mission_ (_DM_), to give it its short title, is a truly inspirational document which deserves revisiting.

[^c36-7]: For the full text, see Gioia, _Interreligious Dialogue_, nos. 808–51.

One of the most important statements in this short document is that mission is ‘a single but complex and articulated reality’ (_DM_ 13). Interreligious dialogue is then mentioned as one of the elements of this mission, which are given in this order: the simple presence and witness of the Christian life; the service of mankind **[p. 587]** and all forms of activity for social development; liturgical life and prayer and contemplation; dialogue in which Christians meet the followers of other religious traditions; and announcement and catechesis in which the good news of the Gospel is proclaimed. It could be observed that the element of prayer and liturgical life should come before that of service and that dialogue should be understood to cover ecumenical relations and relations with non-believers. These, however, are quibbles.

The inclusion of dialogue within this list is significant, since it means that interreligious dialogue, as well as other forms of dialogue, cannot be treated as a luxury, an optional extra, the concern of a few people with strange ideas. As Pope Paul VI had emphasized in _Ecclesiam Suam_, the Church cannot but be in relation with all people, with those who believe in Jesus Christ as well as those who do not. It cannot say that the latter are none of its concern, nor can its only mode of relation be to try to bring them into the Catholic faith. It must strive to meet the followers of other religious traditions ‘in order to walk together towards truth and to work together in projects of common concern’ (_DM_ 13).

One implication of this statement is that interreligious dialogue has its own validity and does not need to be justifled by reference to another element in the Church’s mission. To express this more clearly, such dialogue is not a form of pre-evangelization, a mere preparation for the proclamation of the Gospel; it is part of the evangelizing mission of the Church. This will become apparent if we compare dialogue with another element of the Church’s mission: service or _diakonia_. This _diakonia_, however much it may meet with suspicion on the part of the followers of other religious traditions, is an essential part of the Church’s activity and cannot be renounced. Yet, the hungry are not fed and the sick tended in order that they may become Christians; such care is simply an expression of love and compassion, especially for those who are suffering and in need. Similarly, dialogue, though it, too, may meet with suspicion, does not have any hidden motivation but is an expression of respect for the right to religious liberty, which is one of the most fundamental rights of the human person.

A further consequence of this teaching is that there can be vocations within the Church for the ministry of interreligious dialogue. Just as all the faithful have the duty to pray but some are called in a special way to a life of prayer and contemplation, and just as all Christians must show charity but some are called to dedicate their whole lives to particular works of mercy, so also all members of the Church should have an attitude of dialogue towards other believers, but some may be called to make this dialogue the central part of their activity. What is important is to see the whole as well as the parts, to preserve unity in the bonds of the Spirit, as St Paul says (see Eph. 4:3), so that all these various activities, including dialogue, are seen as an expression of the vitality of the Body of Christ.

In a very interesting passage, _Dialogue and Mission_ offers the Trinity as a model for dialogue: ‘In the mystery of the Trinity revelation helps us to perceive a life of communion and exchange’ (_DM_ 22). In the Father we contemplate a love which precedes everything, and which is not limited by space or time. In other words, the gifts of God are to be discovered in all peoples at all periods of history. The Ignatian principle of ‘Finding **[p. 588]** God in all things’ could be recalled here. It is the duty of the Church to discover, to bring to light, and to help to mature the riches that God has hidden in creation and in history. There is an ‘exchange of gifts’ to be pursued in interreligious dialogue just as in ecumenism.

God the Son, the Word made flesh, is the one who enlightens every human being. He is the Redeemer who is present with his grace in every human encounter, to free us from egoism and to help us to love one another as he has loved us. As John Paul II has written, echoing the teaching of Vatican II, Christ is in some way united with every single person (_Redemptor Hominis_ 14). This means that every person, whatever their religion, is to be treated with respect.

Finally, the Spirit is that force of life, development, and continuous renewal which is at work in the depths of individual consciences, accompanying them in the progress towards the Truth. As John Paul II was to point out later, the Spirit is active within the history of peoples, in cultures and religions (see _Redemptoris Missio_ 29). This Spirit works outside the visible boundaries of the Mystical Body of Christ. The Spirit anticipates and accompanies the Church as it goes on its way. So, the Church is impelled to discern the signs of the Spirit’s presence, to follow wherever the Spirit leads, and to serve the Spirit as a humble collaborator (_DM_ 24).

One of the merits of _Dialogue and Mission_ is that it broadens the concept of dialogue. When dialogue is mentioned, many people think immediately of theological discussions. They are often wary because they realize that in the past, such discussions have often turned to polemics. _Dialogue and Mission_, taking a lead from the bishops of Asia, distinguishes four different forms of dialogue: dialogue of life, dialogue of deeds, dialogue of discourse, and dialogue of religious experience (_DM_ 28–35). It might have been better to speak of ‘relations’ with other believers and to have kept the term ‘dialogue’ for formal exchanges, yet the line taken by this document can certainly be justifled. ‘Dialogue of life’ does not mean simply living side by side but indicates a readiness to enter into friendly conversation with one’s neighbours in order to live in harmony and peace. ‘Dialogue of deeds’, described as ‘collaboration with others for goals of a humanitarian, social, economic, or political nature which are directed toward the liberation and advancement of mankind’ (_DM_ 31), cannot come about without exchange on goals and means; we could say that there can be no cooperation without consultation. The ‘dialogue of discourse’, exchanges at the level of experts on matters concerning religion or on problems faced by humanity, can help to prepare the way for cooperation. The ‘dialogue of religious experience’ is a sharing at a deeper level on what is most precious to each religion. In this regard it may be remembered that words are not the only means of communication. Silence can also create communion, particularly that silence which allows the action of the Holy Spirit to be perceived. For the Spirit, as has been said, ‘acts in the depth of people’s consciences and accompanies them on the secret path of hearts towards the truth (cf. _Gaudium et Spes_ 22)’ (_DM_ 24).

This last form of dialogue has been given considerable encouragement by the Day of Prayer for Peace, celebrated in Assisi in October 1986 on the initiative of Pope John Paul II. It has also been taken up by religious of the monastic tradition, particularly of the Benedictine family, who have developed the [^c36-8] **[p. 589]** association Dialogue interreligieux monastique/Monastic Interreligious Dialogue (DIMMID). While prudence is required, so that the twin dangers of syncretism and indifferentism may be avoided, courage is also needed. Sharing the riches of religious traditions allows differences to be seen in a new light. In such a climate these differences, often fundamental, need not prevent dialogue. They can be ‘referred back in humility and confidence to God who “is greater than our heart” (1 John 3:20)’ (_DM_ 35).

[^c36-8]: For more information on DIMMID, see the online bulletin that it publishes, _Dilatato Corde._

### 4. The Contribution of Religious Men and Women

It may be useful to highlight one final passage from this document, where it speaks about ‘the many examples that could be drawn from the history of Christian mission’ (_DM_ 17). Reference is made to St Francis of Assisi and his _regola non bollata_, in which he encouraged his followers to go ‘among Muslims’ in a peaceful way. There is also mention of Charles de Foucauld, ‘who carried out mission in a humble and silent attitude of union with God, in communion with the poor, and in universal brotherhood’ (_DM_ 17).

It would have been possible to expand this paragraph by referring to other religious who have contributed to [^c36-9] interreligious dialogue. The example springs to mind of some pioneers in the task of establishing positive and constructive relations with people of other religions, such as the two Jesuits Matteo Ricci (1552–1610) and Roberto de Nobili (1577–1656), in China and India respectively. Their missionary methods had perhaps more to do with inculturation than with dialogue, yet in their adaptation to the milieu in which they operated, whether of mandarins or of Brahmins, they showed great respect for the religious sensitivities of the people to whom they were relating. We could also remember the Jesuits who, during the same period, engaged in dialogue with Muslim scholars at the court of the Mughal emperor Akbar (1556–1605).

[^c36-9]: For a fuller development of this point, see Michael L. Fitzgerald, ‘Religious Congregations and Their Contribution to Interreligious Dialogue’, _Centro Pro Unione Semi-annual Bulletin_ 77 (2010), 3–8.

In a later century, Charles Lavigerie (1825–92), founder of the missionary society to which I belong, the Missionaries of Africa (White Fathers), proposed a patient and painstaking approach to the Muslim milieu, with which he was familiar as archbishop of Algiers. He emphasized the need to influence society as a whole, overcoming hostility through attention to culture and through a witness of disinterested love and service. He encouraged dialogue on themes common to Christians and Muslims: the greatness of God, the relationship of creature to Creator, and the need for human beings to repent and receive forgiveness. In his writings he took up the ideas of Pope Gregory VII in his letter to the Muslim ruler al-Nasir, to which _Nostra Aetate_ refers (cf. NA 3, note 1). Lavigerie was in no hurry to have Muslims baptized but ‘wanted every **[p. 590]** conversion to be tested through one or two years of “spiritual” formation (the “Postulate”) to make sure [^c36-10] that the prospective convert was really under the influence of the Spirit and determined to go ahead’.

[^c36-10]: Cf. Jean-Marie Gaudeul, _Encounters and Clashes: Islam and Christianity in History_, vol. 1, _A Survey_ (Rome: Pontificio Istituto di Studi Arabi e d’Islamistica, 2000), 315.

In the dialogue with Hindus we should remember Henri Le Saux (1910–73), a Benedictine monk of the Abbey of Kergonan, in Brittany. Together with Jules Monchanin (1895–1957), not a religious but a priest of the diocese of Lyons, Le Saux founded the ashram Shantivanam, engaging in a profound dialogue with Hindu spirituality. Their work was continued by another Benedictine, Bede Griffiths (1906–93). Another monk who was influential in encouraging dialogue, in his case with Buddhists, was the prolific writer Thomas Merton (1915–68).[^c36-11]

[^c36-11]: For brief notes on Monchanin and Merton, see Michael L. Fitzgerald and John Borelli, _Interfaith Dialogue: A Catholic View_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2006), 232–37.

If we think of institutions rather than of individuals, mention could be made of the Institut des belles lettres arabes (IBLA), founded by the Missionaries of Africa in Tunis in 1926 to facilitate a continuous cultural dialogue. A similar institute was created in Cairo by the Dominicans. Originally planned as an extension of the École biblique in Jerusalem, but with a vocation to pay special attention to Islamic culture, the Institut dominicain d’études orientales (IDEO) was established as a separate entity in March 1953. The first director was Fr Georges Chehata Anawati, OP (1905–94), who deserves the title ‘pioneer’ in his own right but also for his collaboration with another scholar of Islam, Louis Gardet (Frère André of the Petits Frères de Jésus) (1904–86).[^c36-12]

[^c36-12]: Cf. Jean-Jacques Perennes, _Georges Anawati (1905–1994): Un chrétien égyptien devant le mystère de l’Islam_ (Paris: Cerf, 2008); Maurice Borrmans, _Louis Gardet (1904–1986): Philosophe chrétien des cultures et témoin du dialogue islamo-chrétien_ (Paris: Cerf, 2010).

These pioneers and these institutions prepared the way for _Nostra Aetate_, but there were also many religious engaged in the drafting of the conciliar declaration. Cardinal Augustine Bea, head of the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity, who had the duty of piloting the document through the Vatican Council, was a Jesuit. One of his first permanent collaborators, who was given the Jewish portfolio, was Thomas Stransky, an American Paulist priest. He was assisted by other religious: Gregory Baum, OSA; Georges Tavard, AA; and Leo Rudloff, OSB. As the document expanded to include relations with religions other than Judaism, other religious were called on to provide their expertise. For the paragraph on Islam we find George Anawati, OP; Robert Caspar, M.Afr.; Joseph Cuoq, M.Afr.; and Jean Corbon (a priest of the Greek Catholic Church in Lebanon, a former M.Afr.), with John Long, SJ, as the coordinator. With regard to Traditional Religions, Buddhism, and Hinduism, the team that was brought together included two Jesuits, Josef Neuner and Josef Pfister; a Dominican, Yves Congar; Thomas Stransky, the Paulist; and Msgr Charles Moeller, a diocesan **[p. 591]** priest working in the Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity. Without a doubt, the contribution of [^c36-13] religious to the composition of _Nostra Aetate_ was enormous.

[^c36-13]: I am grateful to Dr John Borelli, special assistant for interreligious dialogue to the President of the University of Georgetown, for supplying the details in this paragraph.

To complete this religious roll-call, I would like to recall the names of the religious who have worked or are working in the SNC/PCID. There was Pierre Humbertclaude, Marianist, as the first secretary, to be followed later by Marcello Zago, OMI, my own self from the Missionaries of Africa, and Miguel Angel Ayuso Guixot of the Comboni Missionaries, currently Cardinal President of the dicastery. A Japanese Salesian, John Bosco Masayuki Shirieda, served for many years as under-secretary. On the Islam desk there has been a Syrian Salvatorian, François Abou Mokh; a Brother of the Christian Schools from Egypt, Edouard Martin Sabanegh; and Thomas Michel, SJ, who served first on the Asian desk. At the Asian desk presently is Markus Solo, SVD. The Africa desk was for a time run by Giuseppe Butturini of the Comboni Missionaries. Religious women have been few, in fact only two: Sr Teresa Seouw, Canossian, and Sr Judith Zoebelein, Franciscan Sister of the Eucharist.

### 5. Dialogue and Proclamation

Perhaps it was thought that _Dialogue and Mission_ had said everything that needed to be said about the importance of dialogue, but almost immediately questions arose: What is the exact relationship between interreligious dialogue and the preaching of the Gospel? Is dialogue the new form of mission, rendering the proclamation of the Gospel message superfluous? These questions, which arose perhaps on account of some exaggerations on the part of those who were engaging enthusiastically in interreligious dialogue, but which also betrayed growing fears of relativism, could not be ignored. Consequently, a further document was produced by the PCID, in conjunction with the Congregation for the Evangelization of Peoples. The joint [^c36-14] authorship is significant, since it gives the document extra weight. _Dialogue and Proclamation_ (_DP_) was published in 1991, soon after _Redemptoris Missio_, the missionary encyclical of John Paul II.

[^c36-14]: For the text, see Gioia, _Interreligious Dialogue_, nos. 925–1013. For a commentary on _DP_ in relation to _Redemptoris Missio_, see Jacques Dupuis, ‘A Theological Commentary: Dialogue and Proclamation’, in _Redemption and Dialogue_, ed. William R. Burrows (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1993), 119–58. For commentaries on both _DM_ and _DP_, as well as on Vatican documents and other relevant material, see Denis C. Isizoh, ed., _Milestones in Interreligious Dialogue_ (Rome: Ceedee, 2002).

_Dialogue and Proclamation_ is a more ponderous document than _Dialogue and Mission_. It carefully defines the terms it is going to use: ‘evangelization’, ‘dialogue’, ‘proclamation’, ‘conversion’, ‘religious traditions’ (_DP_ 8–12). It states clearly that it is not covering relations with Jews, which deserve special treatment, nor does **[p. 592]** it take into account dialogue with the followers of ‘new religious movements’, which requires special discernment. Treating first of interreligious dialogue, it spells out the teaching of Vatican II and of the magisterium in the years since the council. It points to the positive values of other religious traditions, but it also remarks prudently: ‘To say that other religious traditions include elements of grace does not imply that everything in them is the result of grace. For sin has been at work in the world, and so religious traditions, notwithstanding their positive values, reflect the limitations of the human spirit, sometimes inclined to choose evil’ (_DP_ 31). Turning to proclamation, it insists on its urgency, yet it calls attention to the manner in which proclamation is to be carried out. It concludes that ‘the Church’s proclamation must be both progressive and patient, keeping pace with those who hear the message, respecting their freedom and even their “slowness to believe” (_Evangelii Nuntiandi_ 79)’ (_DP_ 69). The final section offers a reflection on both these elements of the Church’s evangelizing mission taken together. I wish to quote in full the first paragraph of this last section:

Interreligious dialogue and proclamation, though not on the same level, are both authentic elements of the Church’s evangelizing mission. Both are legitimate and necessary. They are intimately related, but not interchangeable: true interreligious dialogue on the part of the Christian supposes the desire to make Jesus Christ better known, recognized and loved; proclaiming Jesus Christ is to be carried out in the Gospel spirit of dialogue. The two activities remain distinct but, as experience shows, one and the same local Church, one and the same person, can be diversely engaged in both. (_DP_ 77)

Although expressed in what might be termed ‘Chalcedonian’ language, this reflection is useful insofar as it repeats the recognition of interreligious dialogue as a legitimate part of the Church’s evangelizing mission.

A feature of this document is its realism. It recognizes the difficulties facing both the proclamation of the Gospel message and interreligious dialogue. For instance, there is mention of socio-political factors. These could include majority–minority relations. It is difficult to engage in dialogue if being in a minority situation leads to the adoption of a defensive attitude. Such a difficulty can be overcome only by ensuring freedom and respect for each person’s rights. There is also mention of the burdens of the past. For relations with Muslims, these would include the Crusades and colonialism, which still have the capacity for rankling Muslims, but also the practice of slavery, which has aroused negative feelings towards Islam, especially among many peoples of Africa. Another obstacle mentioned is suspicion about the other’s motives in dialogue. Lack of reciprocity can also inhibit dialogue. Nevertheless, _Dialogue and Proclamation_ states: ‘despite the difficulties, the Church’s commitment to dialogue remains firm and irreversible’ (_DP_ 54) and that ‘to proclaim the name of Jesus and to invite people to become his disciples in the Church is a sacred and major duty which the Church cannot neglect’ (_DP_ 76).

In its conclusion, _Dialogue and Proclamation_ restates the aim of the document, which is ‘to provide some **[p. 593]** basic clarifications’. Recognizing that it remains at a general level, it calls for special attention to be [^c36-15] given to relations with the followers of each religion.

[^c36-15]: I have attempted to apply the teaching of _DP_ to Christian–Muslim relations; cf. ‘ “Dialogue and Proclamation”: A Reading in the Perspective of Christian-Muslim Relations’, in _In Many and Diverse Ways: In Honor of Jacques Dupuis_, ed. Daniel Kendal and Gerald O’Collins (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2003), 181–93.

### 6. A Document Never Published

The PCID intended to produce another document, this time on ‘the spirituality of dialogue’. Its aim was to encourage the practice of dialogue by clarifying the motivations for developing relations with people of other religions. This document never saw the light of day, yet a fair amount of work had been done in preparation for its publication. First, in November 1995, the PCID held a plenary assembly on the theme ‘The Dialogue of Spirituality and the Spirituality of Dialogue’. Ample time was given for a presentation of the idea of holiness in different religions: Hinduism, Buddhism, Islam, Traditional Religions of Africa, and Christianity. Then came a reflection on the dialogue of religious experience. Finally, Jean Vanier was invited [^c36-16] to share some thoughts on elements for a Christian spirituality of interreligious dialogue. Subsequently, in October 1998, in preparation for the Great Jubilee of the Year 2000, the PCID held another plenary assembly discussing the topic ‘Called to the Conversion of the Heart (_metanoia_)—Towards the Year 2000’. Previous to [^c36-17] this, some studies had been published on conversion/purification as seen in different religions. These were complemented by two talks: one on the call to a conversion of the heart and one on the spirituality of dialogue. This plenary resulted in a decision to prepare a document on the spirituality of dialogue; Cardinal Arinze, president of the PCID, was asked to write to the episcopal conferences of the world announcing this intention. In this letter, he suggested the following points to be developed in the future document: God is both love and communion; God communicates with human beings; we are called to convert to God; Christian identity; proclamation and dialogue; the need to understand other believers; prominent elements of Christian practice: faith, hope, and charity, prayer and sacrifice. He then asked for comments and [^c36-18] suggestions. On this basis, a draft document was prepared; it was also sent to the episcopal conferences for comment. A further draft, taking into account the comments and suggestions received, was then discussed in detail during another plenary assembly, held in November 2001.

[^c36-16]: All these presentations are found in _Pro Dialogo_ 92, no. 2 (1996).

[^c36-17]: See _Pro Dialogo_ 97, no. 1 (1998).

[^c36-18]: Cardinal Arinze’s letter, together with the text of the two talks mentioned, can be found in _Pro Dialogo_ 101, no. 2 (1999).

**[p. 594]** According to the regulations of the Roman Curia, laid down in the Constitution _Pastor Bonus_, any document of the Holy See which touched on doctrine had to receive the approval of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith. The proposed document on the spirituality of dialogue was thus submitted and examined, but never received the necessary approval. The reasons for this refusal are not clear, but the following can be suggested. The drafters of the document had opted to take _Dialogue and Mission_ and _Dialogue and Proclamation_ as read, and thus did not wish to summarize their teaching. It may therefore have been felt that the proposed document could prove misleading for those who came to it without a sufficient background knowledge. Although this document on the spirituality of dialogue was never published, all the elements of such a spirituality can be found in the preparatory papers that have been referred to here.

### 7. Dialogue in Truth and Charity

The PCID did produce a third official document in 2014, on the occasion of the fiftieth anniversary of its institution by Pope Paul VI. _Dialogue in Truth and Charity. Pastoral Orientations for Interreligious Dialogue_ is the result of the tenth plenary assembly of the PCID, held in June 2008. The first chapter on ‘The Church and Inter-religious Dialogue’ provides a summary of the official teaching of the Church on this subject. Chapter 2 treats of the ‘Dynamics of Inter-religious Dialogue’. It discusses the vocation to promote dialogue, formation in dialogue, and aspects and praxes [_sic_] of dialogue. Similar to chapter 1, this chapter is made up of a catena of quotations from church documents. Chapter 3 looks at ‘Specific Fields of Inter-religious Relations’. Here are to be found short reflections on defending human dignity and promoting the exercise of human rights, establishing bonds of trust and friendship among religious leaders, educating the youth for interreligious cooperation, interreligious cooperation in health-care services, concern for persons in interreligious marriages, prayer and symbolic gestures.

The reflections in this chapter are to some extent new, though it may be felt that they do not go far enough. As in the first two chapters, the references given are to magisterial documents only. For instance, with regard to interreligious marriages, reference is made to the Code of Canon Law and to the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches. On prayer, the reference is to the _Catechism of the Catholic Church._ Yet these two topics formed the subject of joint studies undertaken by the PCID and the corresponding office of the WCC. No reference is made to these studies, presumably because the ensuing joint publications are not considered to be the official teaching of the Catholic Church. This brings us to the final section of this chapter, precisely on collaboration with the WCC.

### 8. The Ecumenical Dimension of Interreligious Dialogue

**[p. 595]** The relationship between ecumenism and interreligious dialogue is fairly evident. On the one hand, the scandal of the divisions among Christians is an obstacle to the witness of Christians in a multi-religious world; conversely, as the Pontifical Council for Promoting Christian Unity’s _Directory for the Application of the Principles and Norms of Ecumenism_ notes, ‘interreligious relations are to be considered an important part of ecumenical cooperation’ (210). Very early on in its existence, the SNC entered into contact with the corresponding body of the WCC. Sharing concerns, through attendance at each office’s reflection meetings, led eventually to an annual joint meeting of the staff of the two bodies, the PCID and the Office on Interreligious Relations. This in turn led to common projects, some of which can be mentioned here.

A desire to contribute towards peace in the Middle East led to a collaborative effort of the PCID and the Holy See’s Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews together with the Office on Interreligious Relations of the WCC and the General Secretariat of the Lutheran World Federation. This took the form of two meetings of Jews, Christians, and Muslims, the first held in Glion, Switzerland, in May 1993, and the second in Thessaloniki, Greece, in 1996. Although these meetings were held in Europe, most of the participants came from Israel and Palestine.[^c36-19]

[^c36-19]: Hans Ucko, ed., _The Spiritual Significance of Jerusalem for Jews, Christians, and Muslims_ (Geneva: World Council of Churches, 1994), 81.

The increase in the number of marriages between Christians and people belonging to other religions led to a [^c36-20] common document of the PCID and the Office on Interreligious Relations. Another topic which held the attention of both offices was that of interreligious prayer. The project was carried out in three stages. First, a survey was conducted within local churches and different traditions on the practice of interreligious prayer. This was followed by a consultation bringing together some people experienced in this fleld who produced a common statement. Finally, a small group of theologians representing different churches and coming from different parts of the world met to examine the theological foundations for interreligious prayer; they also produced a concluding statement. A selection of papers and both of the above-mentioned statements are [^c36-21] included in a joint publication of _Pro Dialogo_ and the WCC’s _Current Dialogue._

[^c36-20]: ‘Reflections on Interreligious Marriage: A Joint Study Document’, _Pro Dialogo_ 96, no. 3 (1997): 324–39.

[^c36-21]: _Pro Dialogo_ 98 (1998).

How to give Christian witness in a multi-religious world also retained the attention of the PCID and the Office on Interreligious Relations and led them to reach out to the World Evangelical Alliance. Together **[p. 596]** these bodies were able to produce a formal agreement in 2011 on the essence of Christian mission: _Christian Witness in a Multi-Religious World: Recommendations for Conduct_. It is worth quoting the preamble to the document:

Mission belongs to the very being of the church. Proclaiming the word of God and witnessing to the world is essential for every Christian. At the same time, it is necessary to do so according to gospel principles, with full respect and love for all human beings. Aware of the tensions between people and communities of different religious convictions and the varied interpretations of Christian witness, the Pontifical Council for Interreligious Dialogue (PCID), the World Council of Churches (WCC) and, at the invitation of the WCC, the World Evangelical Alliance (WEA), met during a period of 5 years to reflect and produce this document to serve as a set of recommendations for conduct on Christian witness around the world. The document does not intend to be a theological statement on mission but to address practical issues associated with Christian witness in a multireligious world.

Since these three bodies—the Roman Catholic Church (through the PCID), the WCC, and the World Evangelical Alliance—have a combined membership of around 2 billion and represent nearly 90 per cent of the world’s Christians, this document can truly be seen as a major achievement. It deserves to be better known and especially to be put into practice.

### 9. Conclusion

What conclusion can be drawn from all that has gone before? First it can be asserted that _Nostra Aetate_ has been a blessing and that it has had a definite impact on the life of the Church, enabling it to fulfil its mission as described in _Lumen Gentium_: ‘The Church, in Christ, is in the nature of sacrament—a sign and instrument, that is, of communion with God and of unity among all human beings’ (_LG_ 1). Second, it is only right to recognize that the PCID has provided good guidance for relations with people of other religions. Its official documents are not many (this in itself is perhaps a good thing), but its other publications, including the journal _Pro Dialogo_, provide a wealth of material that can stimulate reflection and orientate action.

It is nevertheless necessary to add a further observation. Interreligious dialogue is not the monopoly of the Holy See. The real dialogue between Christians and people of other religions is carried out at local level. The task of the Dicastery for Interreigious Dialogue is to assist and support these local efforts. So to trace the growth of interreligious dialogue since the promulgation of _Nostra Aetate_, one would have to look at the role of national and regional commissions, the activities of different associations, and, of course, the role of religious congregations and institutes of consecrated life, which was beyond the scope of the present chapter.

### Suggested Reading

Chia, Edmund Kee-Fook, _World Christianity_ encounters _World Religions_. A Summa of Interfaith Dialogue, Collegeville, Minnesota, Liturgical Press Academic 2018.

## 37. Vatican II and Interreligious Dialogue: The Catholic

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 598]** By design, this chapter excludes from consideration Judaism and Islam in its study of the teaching of the Second Vatican Council on other religions, since they are treated in other chapters. I begin with a brief exposition of the pre-Vatican II teaching of the Catholic Church on religions other than Judaism and Islam to provide the context for understanding how Vatican II’s teaching on the relation of the Church to other religions represents a radical break from the Catholic Church’s previous theological tradition. The second section will examine in detail the council’s teaching on the Church’s relation to other religions other than Judaism and Islam. The chapter concludes with a brief consideration of issues that remain _quaestiones disputatae_ in the theology of religion and are especially relevant for Christian dialogue with Asian religions.

### 2. ‘From Confrontation to Dialogue’: Before Vatican II

The heading of this section is borrowed from Jacques Dupuis’s masterful overview of the developments in [^c37-1] **[p. 599]** the Catholic Church’s attitude towards other religions. ‘Confrontation’ is a helpful shorthand description of the overall theological posture of the Catholic Church, especially its papal and episcopal magisterium, towards religions other than itself from the beginnings of Christianity to the late 1960s. As these developments are examined in detail, however, ‘confrontation’ may arguably be too weak a descriptive term if it is taken to mean simply ‘a hostile or argumentative meeting or situation between [^c37-2] opposing parties’. Indeed, not rarely has confrontation led to wholesale condemnations, bloody persecutions, and protracted wars against believers of other religions, especially Jews and Muslims.

[^c37-1]: See Jacques Dupuis, _Christianity and the Religions: From Confrontation to Dialogue_, trans. Phillip Berryman (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2002). It is interesting that Dupuis does not use the common expression ‘Non-Christian Religions’ but simply ‘the Religions’ (original Italian: _le religioni_). As will be argued, this is not an innocent semantic variation but entails a significant shift in the theology of religions. On this, see n. 4 below.

[^c37-2]: _New Oxford American Dictionary_, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2005), 358.

#### Four Theological Principles

Armed confiicts and wars in the name of religion aside, pre-Vatican II Catholic theology of religions was by [^c37-3] and large negative. To appreciate its nuances, it is necessary to distinguish between two related but distinct issues. The first is the salvation of non-Christian individuals; the second, the salvific power of non- [^c37-4] Christian religions. Regarding the salvation of non-Christian individuals, the Catholic Church’s position is governed by four principles. The first is theological: God wants all to be saved. The second is Christological: salvation is achieved only through Jesus Christ. The third is ecclesial: the Church is the necessary means of salvation. The fourth is sacramental: baptism with water is the act by which a person enters the Church, [^c37-5] becomes its member, and has access to all the means of salvation.

[^c37-3]: For an overview, see Karl J. Becker and Ilaria Morali, eds., _Catholic Engagement with World Religions: A Comprehensive_ _Study_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2010), 21–125.

[^c37-4]: The use of ‘non’ as a prefix to refer to others different from oneself is perhaps an unavoidable anthropological and sociological shorthand to distinguish ‘us’ from ‘them’. But the negative naming of the other loses its innocence as an identity marker when it is used by a group that has consistently claimed to be superior to all others in all aspects of life. The ‘non’, then, when applied to others, implies the absence, or at best imperfect presence, of all the things that make this group the norm and standard of perfection for all others. Thus, during the height of empire and colonialism, sobriquets such as ‘non-Greek’, ‘non-Roman’, ‘non-Persian’, ‘non-Turkish’, ‘non-British’, ‘non-Russian’, ‘non-Han’ (Chinese), to cite a few, were powerful weapons in the imperial and colonialist arsenals to categorize other peoples as uncivilized and barbarian who therefore needed to be brought into the fold by means of the _mission civilisatrice_ (civilizing mission), often by conquest and subjugation. Such negative designation is by no means a neutral nomenclature but is part and parcel of the imperial politics of difference and power. Analogously, when ‘non-Christian’ is used to designate religions and believers other than Christianity and Christians, the pejorative connotation is also present, given the claim that Christianity is the only true religion. For convenience’s sake, I will occasionally use ‘non-Christian’ but with full awareness of its theological inappropriateness.

[^c37-5]: These four principles are purported to be based on key Scriptural texts, such as for the first: 1 Tim 2:4; for the second: John 14:6; Acts 4:12; for the third: Matt 16:18; 28:16–21; and for the fourth: Mark 16:15–16. Of course, a host of other biblical texts have been adduced to support these four principles. For helpful overviews of this theme, see Francis A. Sullivan, _Salvation Outside the Church? Tracing the History of the Catholic Response_ (New York: Paulist, 1992); Gerald O’Collins, _Salvation for All: God’s Other Peoples_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2008); and Ralph Martin, _Will Many Be Saved? What_ _Vatican II Actually Teaches and Its Implications for the New Evangelization_ (Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 2012).

**[p. 600]** Of these four principles, the second and third, which are inextricably intertwined, have remained constant. Not only is Christ always confessed to be the unique and universal saviour, but also the necessity of the Church for salvation is said to be not merely ‘of precept’—that is, only by a positive will of God who could in principle have decided otherwise—but also ‘of means’—that is, absolutely required for achieving the intended effect, without possibility of dispensation and exception. A terse Latin formula expresses this kind [^c37-6] of necessity: _extra ecclesiam nulla salus_ (outside the Church there is no salvation). Notably, this formula on the necessity of the Church for salvation first appeared in Origen and was forcefully enunciated by Cyprian, both writing from North Africa in the third century. It served to warn Christian heretics and schismatics who were encouraged to return to the ark of salvation—that is, the Church—if they wanted to be saved. In later centuries it was extended to Jews, Muslims, and the followers of all religions other than Christianity.

[^c37-6]: For the history of this maxim, see Sullivan, _Salvation Outside the Church?_, 3–11; Molly T. Marshall, _No Salvation Outside the_ _Church: A Critical Inquiry_ (Lewiston, NY: Edwin Mellen, 1993); and Bernard Sesboüė, _Hors de l’Église, pas de salut: Histoire_ _d’une formule et problèmes d’interprétation_ (Paris: Desclée de Brouwer, 2004).

Salvation of Non-Christian Individuals

By contrast, the first principle, God’s universal salvific will, and the fourth, the necessity of baptism, have been subjected to various reversals. God’s universal salvific will is denied by the so-called doctrine of double predestination, according to which God predestines, by an eternal and inviolable decree of God’s infallible [^c37-7] foreknowledge and sovereign will, some to salvation (the elect) and others to damnation (the reprobate). Needless to say, non-Christians by definition belong to the latter group. The Catholic Church’s episcopal magisterium, however, does not espouse double predestination. On the one hand, it affirms that God wills all humans to be saved, and in this sense God ‘predestines’ all to salvation. On the other hand, it admits the possibility of a person freely refusing God’s offer of salvation and thus incurring damnation. In this context, an important distinction is drawn between ‘causation’ and ‘permission’: God ‘permits’ but does not ‘cause’ a person’s will to refuse God’s offer of saving grace. In this way, the episcopal magisterium leaves open the [^c37-8] possibility of salvation for all, including non-Christians.

[^c37-7]: This teaching is generally associated with Calvin, but its roots are already found in Augustine, who nevertheless affirms human freedom. On the other hand, it was condemned by the Second Council of Orange (529); later, in 1653, Jansenism, which holds that Christ did not die for all, was condemned by Pope Innocent X.

[^c37-8]: _Catechism of the Catholic Church_ states concisely: ‘To God, all moments of time are present in their immediacy. When therefore he establishes his eternal plan of “predestination”, he includes in it each person’s free response to his grace. … For the sake of accomplishing his plan of salvation, God permits the acts that flowed from their [the damned’s] blindness’ (no. 600).

**[p. 601]** However, if non-Christians can be saved without baptism, does the fourth principle still hold? This principle, the absolute necessity of baptism for salvation, is predicated on the doctrine of original sin, according to which all humans, except Mary the Mother of God, are born in the state of enmity against God and without sanctifying grace; they therefore cannot be saved unless they are cleansed of this original sin and restored to friendship with God by the sacrament of baptism. In general, before the discovery of the ‘New World’ in the late fifteenth century, the Catholic Church’s episcopal magisterium and theologians rejected the possibility of salvation for non-Christians, even though they did not follow Augustine’s [^c37-9] teaching on double predestination and the fate of infants who die unbaptized.

[^c37-9]: Unlike Augustine, who thought that infants who die unbaptized suffer eternal punishments of hell, medieval theologians such as Peter Abelard, Peter Lombard, and Pope Innocent III made a distinction between lack of beatific vision and punishment of hell. Infants who die unbaptized suffer only the lack of beatific vision and not the eternal torments of hell, which are the punishment for actual personal sins. This fate of unbaptized babies gave rise to the doctrine of ‘limbo’.

Thomas Aquinas admits that in some cases, such as the Gentiles who lived _before_ the coming of Christ, an implicit faith in Christ, and thus baptism of implicit desire, would be sufficient for salvation. However, Thomas maintains that _after_ the coming of Jesus, explicit faith in Jesus is necessary for salvation, and that God would give grace necessary for salvation to those who do what they can, according to the theological principle that _facienti quod in se est, Deus non denegat gratiam_ (To one who does what lies in his power, God [^c37-10] does not deny grace). Indeed, Thomas suggests that God would send that person a preacher of the faith or give an interior revelation to help that person to make a decision about whether to explicitly believe in [^c37-11] God.

[^c37-10]: Another principle in support of the possibility of salvation without ritual baptism is: ‘God has not bound his power to the sacraments [_Deus suam potestatem sacramentis non alligavit_].’

[^c37-11]: For a detailed exposition of St Thomas’s view on this theme, see Sullivan, _Salvation Outside the Church?_, 47–62.

The problem of the salvation of non-Christians became an urgent issue after the ‘discovery’ of the New World towards the end of the fifteenth century: the Church became aware of the existence of huge populations outside Europe who had not heard the Gospel preached to them, or had heard the Gospel preached badly, or were offended by the scandalous behaviours of Christians, and for whom the possibility of eternal salvation required explanation. Notable Dominican and Jesuit theologians such as Francisco de Vitoria, Domingo Soto, Albert Pigge, Robert Bellarmine, Francisco Suarez, Juan de Lugo, and Juan Martínez de Ripalda attempted various explanations for the possibility of salvation of non-Christians.[^c37-12]

[^c37-12]: For an exposition of the views of these theologians, see ibid., 69–102; and Becker and Morali, _Catholic Engagement with_ _World Religions_, 6–90.

These theologians, while maintaining the necessity of baptism, attempted various explanations for the possibility of salvation of non-Christians without baptism by water, and hence without actual membership in the Church. First, it is argued that besides baptism by water, there is baptism by blood—that is, **[p. 602]** martyrdom—by which a person is saved if she or he, though not yet ritually baptized, dies in witness to the faith. Second, salvation is also possible by the baptism of _explicit_ desire when a person, such as a catechumen, has agreed to be baptized but dies before being able to do so. Third, salvation is also possible through baptism by _implicit_, even unconscious, desire (_votum_) when a person believes that God exists and rewards those who seek God (Heb. 11:5) and, not without divine grace, lives a morally good life but, without any fault on his or her part, does not know that baptism is necessary (‘invincible ignorance’). This baptism by implicit and unconscious desire was available to those who lived a good life before Christ: for instance, the patriarchs of Israel and the ‘holy pagans’ such as Melchizedek. It is of course also available to those who live after Christ who, through no fault of theirs, do not know Christ and the Church but with God’s grace live a good life. This possibility of salvation by the baptism of desire is taught by the Council of Trent (1545–63), which affirms the necessity of faith and ‘the bath of rebirth’, that is, baptism for justification, but also adds ‘or the desire for it’ (_aut eius voto_).[^c37-13]

[^c37-13]: Gerald O’Collins insightfully points out that beside this text on justification by means of baptism, either actual or by desire, the Council of Trent in its decree on the sacrificial nature of the Mass also has a positive appreciation of the Jewish sacrifices (‘under the regime of the Law’) and the sacrifices of other religions (‘under the regime of nature’). See Gerald O’Collins, _The Second Vatican Council on Other Religions_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2013), 38–39.

The most explicit formulation of the sufficiency of baptism by implicit, even unconscious, desire for salvation occurred in the controversy involving the Jesuit priest Leonard Feeney. Interpreting the axiom _extra ecclesiam nulla salus_ in the strictest sense possible, Feeney asserts that no one is saved who does not live and die as a Roman Catholic, thus excluding not only non-Christians but also non-Catholic Christians. In 1949, the Holy Office sent a letter to Richard Cushing, then archbishop of Boston, in which it states:

To gain salvation it is not always required that a person be incorporated in reality [_reapse_] as a member of the Church, but it is required that one belong to it at least in desire and longing [_voto et desiderio_]. It is not always necessary that this desire be explicit, as it is with catechumens. When one is invincibly ignorant, God also accepts an implicit desire, so called because it is contained in the good disposition of soul by which a person wants his or her will to be conformed to God’s will.[^c37-14]

[^c37-14]: Jacques Dupuis, ed., _The Christian Faith in the Doctrinal Documents of the Catholic Church_ (Boston: St Pauls, 2001), 329. The Letter invokes the teaching of Pope Pius XII in his encyclical _Mystici Corporis_ (1943), in which the Pope mentions those, though not actual members of the Body of Christ, who are ‘ordained [_ordinantur_] to the mystical Body of the Redeemer by some kind of unconscious desire or longing’. See ibid., 330. Before Pius XII, Pius IX had affirmed the possibility of salvation for non-Christians who, through no fault on their part, do not know Christ and his church (‘invincible ignorance’). Thus, the axiom ‘outside the church there is no salvation’ is now reformulated as ‘There is no salvation for those who _culpably_ remain outside the church’. For the texts of Pius IX’s two documents in which he states this teaching, namely _Singulari_ _quadam_ (1854) and _Quanto conficiamur moerore_ (1864), see Dupuis, _The Christian Faith_, 423–25.

**[p. 603]** Non-Christian Religions vs. Christianity

So far, we have followed the twists and turns in the Catholic Church’s teaching on the possibility of salvation for non-Christian _individual_s up to Vatican II. While holding fast to the four theological principles mentioned above, this teaching ends in a positive affirmation of this possibility in virtue of the non- Christian’s implicit ‘desire’ (_votum_) and ‘longing’ (_desiderium_) for Jesus, the Church, and baptism. By contrast, there has been no favourable appreciation of the non-Christian _religions_ in themselves, since the salvation of non-Christians is affected by their ‘relatedness’ to Christ and the Church and is not attributed to anything belonging to the non-Christian religions themselves. Indeed, prior to Vatican II, the attitude of the Catholic Church towards religions other than itself—except Judaism, with which it acknowledges to possess intrinsic ties but which it claims to have superseded—is uniformly negative and even condemnatory.

In the patristic era, with the rare appreciation for Greek philosophy in Justin, Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius of Caesarea, and Augustine, Roman religions were severely condemned for their alleged atheism, [^c37-15] polytheism, myths, rituals, superstitions, and immorality. Christianity is proclaimed to be the only true religion (_vera religio_); if there is anything good in the Roman religions, it is deemed to be purloined from the Bible and is seen as stepping stones towards Christianity (_praeparatio evangelica_). Consequently, the goal of Christian missions is to destroy the errors and evil of other religions and to convert ‘pagans’ or ‘heathens’ to the Church.

[^c37-15]: For a survey of the Early Church’s attitude to pagan religions, see Joseph Carola, ‘Non-Christians in Patristic Theology’, in Becker and Morali, _Catholic Engagement with World Religions_, 21–48.

There are, of course, exceptions to this general condemnation of non-Christian religions, such as Pope Gregory VII’s letter to Anzir, the Muslim king of Mauritania (1076). In this letter the pope, after thanking Anzir for his gifts, states that Christians and Muslims ‘believe and confess one God, although in different ways, and praise and worship him daily as the creator of all ages and the ruler of this world’ and assures the king that he and others ‘greatly admire and praise’ the king’s ‘goodness and virtues’. Gregory ends his letter with the prayer that God may lead Anzir to ‘the abode of happiness, to the bosom of the holy patriarch [^c37-16] Abraham, after long years of life here on earth’. Another important text is the statement by the First Plenary Council of India, which met in Bangalore in 1950. The statement, after rejecting indifferentism and syncretism, acknowledges that ‘there is truth and goodness outside the Christian religion, for God has not left the nations without a witness to himself, and the human soul is naturally drawn towards the one true [^c37-17] God’. This text from the plenary council’s documents, approved by Pope Pius XII in 1951, is particularly **[p. 604]** significant, as it is the first magisterial statement that clearly and explicitly acknowledges the truths and spiritual values of non-Christian religions as such, and not merely of non-Christian individuals.

[^c37-16]: Dupuis, _The Christian Faith_, 419. Interestingly, the letter is referred to in Vatican II’s _Nostra Aetate_ 3.

[^c37-17]: Dupuis, _The Christian Faith_, 428. It must be pointed out, however, that the First Plenary Council of India also says that these non-Christian religions have also been infected with ‘serious errors’ and that now ‘Christ being constituted the one Mediator between God and human beings, there is no salvation by any other name’ (ibid., 423).

Admittedly, these respectful statements about the existence of ‘truth and goodness’ in non-Christian religions are extremely rare before Vatican II. Most assessments of religions other than Christianity, including Judaism and Islam, are profoundly negative. Perhaps the most trenchant expression of the Catholic Church’s negative attitude towards non-Christian religions in general is found in the Decree for the Copts at the General Council of Florence (1442):

[The Holy Roman Church] firmly believes, professes and preaches that ‘no one remaining outside the Catholic Church, not only pagans’, but also Jews, heretics or schismatics, can become partakers of eternal life; but they will go to the ‘eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels’ (Mt 25:41), unless before the end of their life they are joined [_aggregati_] to it. … No one can be saved, no matter how much alms one has given, even if shedding one’s blood for the name of Christ, unless one remains in the bosom and unity of the Catholic Church.[^c37-18]

[^c37-18]: Ibid., 321.

It is against the background of this solemn magisterial teaching, which is the first to extend the axiom _extra ecclesiam nulla salus_ beyond heretics and schismatics to ‘pagans’ and Jews, that the novelty of the teaching of Vatican II on non-Christian religions can be fully appreciated.[^c37-19]

[^c37-19]: This text is composed of quotations from the book of Fulgentius of Ruspe (467–533), _De fide liber ad Petrum_, 38, 79, 80. ‘Pagans’ refers not to Jews but to the followers of antique religions. It cannot refer to Muslims, since Fulgentius lived before the rise of Islam in the seventh century. The Council of Florence (1442) might have Muslims in mind though it is highly unlikely since Muslims were referred to as Mohammedans, nor can it refer to the followers of religions of the New World since the Council of Florence took place before 1492. Today, ‘pagans’ may be broadly understood to comprise the believers of religions other than Judaism and Islam.

### 3. Vatican II on Asian Religions

As mentioned above, we leave out of consideration Vatican II’s teaching on the relation of the Church with Judaism and Islam and concentrate on what the council says about the relation of the Church to other Asian religions. Of Vatican II’s sixteen documents, three will be closely examined: the Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, _Lumen Gentium_ (_LG_), the Declaration on the Relation of the Church to Non-Christian Religions, _Nostra Aetate_ (_NA_), and the Decree on the Mission Activity of the Church, _Ad Gentes_ (_AG_), in the chronological order of their promulgation. Other documents of Vatican II that touch on, albeit tangentially, this theme include the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy (_Sacrosanctum Concilium_ (_SC_)) and the Pastoral Constitution **[p. 605]** on the Church in the Modern World (_Gaudium et Spes_ (_GS_)). Only passing references will be made to them. Again, for clarity’s sake, we will treat two issues separately; namely, the salvation of non-Christian [^c37-20] individuals and the validity of non-Christian religions.

[^c37-20]: Studies on Vatican II’s teaching on non-Christian religions are legion. Most of them deal with Judaism and Islam; a lot fewer treat the so-called Asian religions. Among helpful English studies, we note O’Collins, _The Second Vatican Council on_ _Other Religions_; Martin, _Will Many Be Saved?_; and Gavin D’Costa, ed., _The Catholic Church and the World Religions: A_ _Theological and Phenomenological Account_ (London: T&T Clark, 2011).

#### Salvation of Non-Christian Asian Individuals

The first conciliar document to be promulgated is the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy, _Sacrosanctum Concilium_, on 4 December 1963. The document does not speak of non-Christians and non-Christian religions explicitly. However, it does have non-Christians in mind in three places. The first is its opening statement, which says that one of the purposes of the council is ‘to strengthen whatever can help to call the whole of humankind into the household of the church’, thus including non-Christians (_SC_ 1). The second is its restoration of the ‘Prayer of the Faithful’ to the Mass, in which intercession is made for the Church, civil authorities, the needy, the whole humanity, and ‘for the salvation of the entire world’, thus for non- Christians as well (_SC_ 53). The third is where it highlights the role of Christ as the High Priest who as the incarnate ‘choirmaster’ sings on earth the eternal song he sings in ‘the halls of heaven’ and associates ‘the entire community of humankind to himself’, including therefore non-Christians (_SC_ 83).[^c37-21]

[^c37-21]: On this point, see O’Collins, _The Second Vatican Council on Other Religions_, 61–68.

While _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ refers to non-Christians only implicitly, _Lumen Gentium_, promulgated on 21 November 1964, is the first magisterial document that speaks explicitly about the salvation of non- Christians. The first ever comprehensive treatise on the Church by an ecumenical council, _Lumen Gentium_ presents the Church as a mystery acting in history as a sacrament—that is, a sign and an instrument—of the Mystery of the Triune God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (_LG_ 1–4). Accordingly, the council describes the Church by means of three major biblical images, corresponding to the three divine Persons: ‘People of God’, ‘Body of Christ’, and ‘Temple of the Holy Spirit’ (_LG_ 6–7). It also makes a very important distinction (not separation) between the kingdom/reign of God and the Church: the Church is not identical to the kingdom of God but is its seed, sign, and instrument. As to where the one Church of Christ is to be found, Vatican II does not, as Pope Pius XII did in his encyclical _Mystici Corporis_, equate the Church of Christ with the Roman Catholic Church. Instead, it intentionally affirms that the one Church of Christ, ‘constituted and organized as a society in the present world, subsists in the Catholic Church’ (_LG_ 8). The term ‘subsists’ is intentionally used instead of ‘is’ to leave room for the possibility that elements of ‘truth and grace’ may be found outside **[p. 606]** the visible boundaries of the Catholic Church in non-Catholic Christian churches and ecclesial communities and, as we will see below, outside Christianity itself in other religions.

After these clarifications on the nature of the Church as sacrament of the Trinity in history and as the People of God on the march towards the kingdom of God, _Lumen Gentium_ explains how different groups of people relate to the Catholic Church in several consecutive paragraphs (_LG_ 13–17), which must be read as a whole. Paragraph 13 speaks of the catholicity (with lower-case c), or universality, of Christianity, to which all people are called to belong in various ways.

Paragraph 14 speaks of Catholics as being ‘fully incorporated’ (_plene incorporantur_) into the Church and gives a list of the essential elements that constitute a Catholic. It adds that catechumens, who have the explicit intention to be incorporated into the Church by baptism, are ‘joined’ (_coniunguntur_) with it. Paragraph 15 speaks of non-Catholic Christians and affirms that the Catholic Church is ‘joined’ (_coniuntam_) to them, and that, depending on the essential elements constitutive of Christianity they possess, they may be said to be ‘church’ or ‘ecclesial community’. This paragraph on non-Catholic Christians being joined with the Catholic Church foreshadows the council’s later Decree on Ecumenism, _Unitatis Redintegratio_.

Of central concern to our theme is paragraph 16, which speaks of people ‘who have not yet accepted the Gospels’—that is, non-Christians—as ‘related’ or ‘ordered’ (_ordinantur_) in various ways to the People of God. _Lumen Gentium_ classifles them in four groups: (1) Jews; (2) Muslims; (3) ‘those who in shadows and images seek the unknown God’—that is, believers in God or theists—those people who ‘do not know the Gospel of Christ or his Church, but who nevertheless seek God with a sincere heart and, moved by grace, try in their actions to do his will as they know it through the dictates of their conscience’; and (4) ‘those who, without any fault of theirs, have not yet arrived at an explicit knowledge of God and who, not without grace, strive to live a good life’—that is, unbelievers and even atheists. These four groups of people are said to be ‘ordered’ or ‘related’ to the Church, with descending degrees of relatedness to it. The Catholic Church categorically affirms, for the first time in a solemn pronouncement, that they may achieve salvation. Though _Lumen Gentium_ does not state so explicitly, clearly the likelihood of this possibility corresponds with the degree of each group’s relatedness to the Church.

It is to be noted that here _Lumen Gentium_ does not address the issue of the salvific significance of non- Christian religions as such; hence, it is not proposing a theology of religions, but only speaks of the possibility of salvation of non-Christian individuals. Leaving aside Jews and Muslims, who together with Christians form the three so-called Abrahamic religions, into which of the third and fourth categories do individual Asian non-Christians fall? _Lumen Gentium_ does not spell this out, but it may be helpful to do so with some examples. It is not clear whether _Lumen Gentium_ includes in the third category God-seekers or theists, both monotheists and polytheists. Both can be said ‘to seek the unknown God in shadows and images’. Among Asians, the Sikhs are strict monotheists, whereas Hindus have been classifled as monotheists, polytheists, henotheists, or pantheists, depending on which traditions of Hinduism they **[p. 607]** adhere to. Obviously, monotheists stand closer to Christians, but henotheists, polytheists, and pantheists do not seem to be excluded from salvation since they, too, ‘in shadows and images seek the unknown God’.

Buddhists and Jains fall into the fourth category, though somewhat loosely since they do not deny God as such but only consider the metaphysical discourse on God a distraction from the essential task of alleviating suffering (_dukkha_). Both Confucianists and Daoists also belong to this fourth category, again somewhat uneasily, because they do not explicitly deny God as such. Rather, for the former, God is not one of the five [^c37-22] relations essential for full human flourishing, and for the latter, God is not distinct from cosmic harmony. Practitioners of Shinto, literally the Way of the Gods, may also be placed in this fourth category, as they believe that _kami_ (in the plural, designating spirits or gods) are present in both animate and inanimate objects. However, the Japanese word _kami_ can also be understood in the singular and refers to the singular Deity manifesting itself in a variety of objects, both spiritual and material. Next, the followers of the so-called primal or indigenous religions may also be grouped in this fourth category, since they ‘have not yet arrived at an explicit acknowledgement [_expressam agnitionem_] of God’ but believe in ‘spirits’, both benevolent and malevolent, who control their lives. Lastly, even atheists may be included in this fourth category. Admittedly, atheists, especially those who mount arguments against the existence of God, have gone a step further by explicitly denying God’s existence; still, in a sense, they can be counted among ‘those [^c37-23] who have not yet arrived at an explicit acknowledgement of God’.

[^c37-22]: Confucius does speak occasionally of ‘Heaven’ and the ‘Mandate of Heaven’, which can be interpreted in the theistic sense, but he does not make human relationship to Heaven a part of human flourishing. Dao or the Cosmic Dao is a creative source constantly generating ‘the ten thousand things’—that is, the world—but it is not a transcendent supreme creator God, whether personal or impersonal, creating things out of nothing.

[^c37-23]: To support its teaching on the possibility of salvation for the third group, _Lumen Gentium_ invokes 1 Tim 2:4, Acts 17:25–28, and the Letter of the Holy Office to the archbishop of Boston mentioned above. On Vatican II’s treatment of atheism, its various causes and kinds, and the Church’s attitude towards it, see also _GS_ 19–21.

Of all the people included in the fourth group, Vatican II explicitly affirms that they may be saved. _Lumen Gentium_ does not make use of the traditional concept of the baptism of implicit desire to explain the possibility of salvation for non-Christian believers and non-believers. Rather, it affirms the possibility of their salvation based on three different levels of ‘belonging’ to the Church: (1) ‘being fully incorporated’ for Catholics, (2) ‘being joined’ for non-Catholic Christians, and (3) ‘being related’ for non-Christians, both believers and non-believers. Thus, it is in virtue of their ‘relatedness’ (_ordinatio_) to the Church, and through it to Christ, that non-Christian believers and non-believers can be saved.

The council, however, makes several important qualifications. First, non-Christian believers and non-believers must do everything in their power to come to the knowledge of God, and therefore their ignorance must be inculpable. Second, they must strive to lead a morally good life according to the dictates of their **[p. 608]** conscience. Third, in all cases, the grace of God is necessary for them to be able to lead an upright life. Fourth, whatever goodness and truth is found in them is considered by the Church as ‘a preparation for the gospel’, a phrase taken from the title of Eusebius of Caesarea’s work _Praeparatio Evangelica_.

The council hastens to point out that the fact that non-Christian believers and non-believers may be saved does not invalidate the Church’s mission to preach the Gospel. Paragraph 17 invokes Matthew 28:19-20 to affirm that ‘the church has received from the apostles Christ’s solemn command to proclaim the truth which saves, and it must carry it to the very ends of the earth’ (_LG_ 17). Through this mission, ‘whatever good is found sown in people’s hearts and minds, or in the rites and customs of peoples, is not only saved from destruction, but is purifled, raised up, and perfected for the glory of God, the confusion of the devil, and the happiness of humanity’ (_LG_ 17). This concept of mission will be elaborated in the Decree on the Mission Activity of the Church (_Ad Gentes_), which will be examined below.

Christianity and Asian Non-Christian Religions: _Nostra Aetate_

So far, Vatican II has dealt only with the issue of the salvation of non-Christian believers and non-believers as individuals, and not with Asian religions as such. The place where _Lumen Gentium_ comes closest to broaching this theme is when it refers to the ‘rites and customs of peoples’ (_ritibus et culturis populorum_) that will be ‘purifled, raised up, and perfected’ through evangelization (_LG_ 17), though these rites are not explicitly designated as religious. The first conciliar document that deals explicitly with non-Christian religions as such is _Nostra Aetate_, which was promulgated on 28 October 1965. The shortest of the sixteen conciliar documents, with only 1,141 words in forty-one sentences and five paragraphs in the original Latin, it has a complex history of composition, starting as a draft document on the Jews (_De Iudaeis_) and ending with a declaration on the relation of the Church to all religions; in the aftermath of the council, it has had an [^c37-24] impact on interreligious dialogue beyond all expectations. Obviously, this document is of central importance for our study.

[^c37-24]: Among innumerable commentaries and critical evaluations of _Nostra Aetate_, two English-language works deserve notice: Charles L. Cohen, Paul F. Knitter, and Ulrich Rosenhagen, eds., _The Future of Interreligious Dialogue: A Multireligious_ _Conversation on Nostra Aetate_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2017); and Pim Valkenberg and Anthony Cirelli, eds., _Nostra Aetate_: _Celebrating 50 Years of the Catholic Church’s Dialogue with Jews and Muslims_ (Washington, DC: The Catholic University of America Press, 2016). Despite its subtitle, the latter book has a rich section on Asian religions (41–89). On the history of the composition of _Nostra Aetate_, see John Borelli, ‘_Nostra Aetate_: Origin, History, and Vatican II Context’, in Cohen, Knitter, and Rosenhagen, _The Future of Interreligious Dialogue_, 23–43.

Again, leaving Judaism and Islam aside, only one paragraph, no. 2, of _Nostra Aetate_ deals with specifically Asian religions. The first paragraph mentions two reasons why in our time the Catholic Church devotes special attention to its relations to other religions: first, the strengthening of the bonds of friendship among different peoples, and second, the mission of the Church to foster love and unity among individuals and nations. The council intends to do so by reflecting on ‘what people have in common and what tends to bring **[p. 609]** them together’ (_NA_ 1). What humans have in common, according to the council, are three: first, one and the same origin, namely God, the creator of the one stock from which all humans originate; second, God’s providence, evident goodness, and saving designs which are extended to all; and third, one and the same destiny, namely God, the fulfilment of all. _Nostra Aetate_ cites Acts 17:26 for the first commonality; Wisdom 8:1, Acts 14:17, Romans 2:6–7, and 1 Timothy 2:4 for the second; and Revelation 21:23–24 for the third.

In addition to these three commonalities, _Nostra Aetate_ notes that people commonly look to their own religions for answers to ‘the unsolved riddles [_reconditis aenigmatibus_] of human existence’ (_NA_ 2). The council lists seven existential ‘riddles’ or enigmas: (1) What is the nature of the human being? (2) What is the meaning and purpose of human life? (3) Which behaviour is good and which is evil? (4) What is the origin and purpose of suffering? (5) How can genuine happiness be attained? (6) What happens at death and after death, such as reward and punishment? and (7) What is the ‘ultimate mystery [_ineffiabile mysterium_], beyond human explanation, from which we take our origin and towards which we tend’? (_NA_ 2). By the ultimate/ineffable mystery, _Nostra Aetate_ refers to God, who is incomprehensible and inexpressible, and is our Alpha and Omega, our Beginning and End.
