**[p. 638]** Considering the vastness of the Asian continent, the uneven distribution of the Catholic presence, the plurality of cultures and religions, and differences in economic, political, and social conditions, it is not an easy task to present a comprehensive view of the reception of Vatican II in Asia.

Asia is the birthplace of the world’s major religions. Considering the intra-ecclesial reality as well, Asia is marked by plurality and diversity. Although Christianity was born in Asia and spread to many Asian countries in the first centuries, Christianity did not arrive in some countries until the colonial period. Only in a few Asian countries are Christians the majority; in others, they are an insignificant minority. And while in most countries the Latin Church is predominant, in some countries there is a strong presence of the Eastern churches. From a historical point of view, colonial rule by various European countries has had a profound impact on Asia. Many Asian countries are theocratic, having some other religion as the official religion; others are communist regimes, where the freedom of the Church is limited. In some parts of Asia, Christians are persecuted. And yet, in spite of being a minority, the Church is very active and alive in many countries.

### 2. The Reception of Vatican II in Asia

In this chapter, we shall highlight the reception of documents which have been particularly relevant for Asia, though we may refer to the reception of other documents as well. Moreover, the reception of different **[p. 639]** documents or teachings in different countries shall be mentioned according to their relevance, instead of separately discussing the reception of Vatican II in each country. Before getting into the details, let us examine some of the events and facts which facilitated the reception of the council in Asia.

Immediately after Vatican II, most Asian countries undertook a serious process of reflecting on the teaching [^c39-1] of the council. The All India seminar on ‘Church in India Today’, organized by the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of India (CBCI) in 1969 in Bangalore, was the culmination of a long process of study of the council documents. Similarly, the Plenary Councils of the Philippines (PCP), especially the Second Plenary [^c39-2] Council of 1991 (PCP-II), played a significant role in the reception of the council. In the decades following the council, many countries have undergone such processes of study and implementation of its teachings. Also, conferences and seminars were conducted on important anniversaries of the council, and the papers were subsequently published.

[^c39-1]: CBCI, _All India Seminar on Church in India Today_ (New Delhi: CBCI Centre, 1969).

[^c39-2]: PCP-II, _Acts and Decrees of the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines (20 January–17 February 1991)_ (Pasay City: Paulines, 1992).

Theological, liturgical, and catechetical centres were established in many countries to study the council’s teachings and to implement them. From the 1970s, catechetical texts in many countries were prepared in light of Vatican II. There were attempts to take the message of the council to the people, for example, in the training programmes for catechists and in competitions (essay contests, cultural programmes, etc.) organized for students.

Since English is the second language in some Asian countries (e.g., the Philippines, India), the English translations of Vatican II documents were immediately accessible to many Asians. In addition, translations of the council documents into the vernacular were made available in the years following it, making the teachings of the council readily available even to those who did not have a solid grasp of English. Some of the translations into Asian languages include Malayalam—the language of Kerala, India—(translation in 1967 by Dharmaram College, Bangalore; published by Dharmaram Publications; 10th revised edition in 2012) and Korean (the first (1969), second (2002), and third (2007) versions published by the Catholic Conference of Korea). A Vietnamese translation was published in 1972. The first translation into Chinese was published in Hong Kong in 1975. A translation into Chinese published in Taiwan was introduced to the mainland Church in 1987. The Church in mainland China independently published the translations in 2001. The most recent Chinese translation was published in 2012; the Japanese translation was done by Nanzan University in 1986, and a revised edition was published by the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Japan in 2013. Besides helping people to access the teaching of the council more easily, translation of the documents into the vernacular helped in developing theological terms and concepts in those languages.

Vatican II was the first ecumenical council in modern times in which Asian bishops participated, though not all of them were Asian-born. This helped the immediate reception of the council when they returned to their dioceses in Asia after the council. As Archbishop Leonardo Legaspi of Caceres in the Philippines said, ‘It can **[p. 640]** then, be said that the first converts of the Council are its members themselves … In this way did Christ [^c39-3] prepare and shape us to become the first evangelizers of the message of the Council to our people.’

[^c39-3]: Ibid., lxxxiii.

In the 1960s, many Asians were undergoing higher studies in the pontifical faculties in Rome which offered them direct experience of the council. Those who studied in Rome and in Europe immediately after the council also could imbibe the spirit of the council in a special way. When they returned to their homelands to teach in the faculties and major seminaries, they became spokespersons of the council. In many countries, as early as the 1970s, ecclesiastical education was structured in light of Vatican II.

The Federation of Asian Bishops’ Conferences (FABC), established in 1972, can be said to be the child of Vatican II. It was Vatican II that brought the Asian bishops together, and their interactions during the council led them to form an identity as bishops of the Asian Church. The FABC became the most effective instrument of the reception of Vatican II in Asia. It was during Pope Paul VI’s visit to Manila in November 1970, where 180 Asian bishops had gathered for ‘the Asian Bishops’ Meeting’, that the idea of FABC was [^c39-4] proposed; on 16 November 1972, the structures and statutes of the FABC were approved. ‘Its purpose is to [^c39-5] foster among its members solidarity and co responsibility for the welfare of Church and society in Asia.’ According to its statutes, one of the purposes of the FABC is ‘to study ways and means of promoting the apostolate, especially in light of Vatican II and post-conciliar official documents, and according to the needs of Asia’.

[^c39-4]: Peter C. Phan, ‘ “Reception” or “Subversion” of Vatican II by the Asian Churches? A New Way of Being Church in Asia’, _Australian eJournal of Theology_ 6 (2006): 8–10.

[^c39-5]: FABC, ‘Theses on the Local Church: A Theological Reflection in the Asian Context’, _FABC Papers_ 60 (1991), http://www.fabc.org/fabc%20papers/fabc_paper_60.pdf.

### 3. Theology of the Local Church

One of the main features of Vatican II ecclesiology is its theology of the local Church. This is closely related to the communion ecclesiology of the council. In the words of the Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, _Lumen Gentium_ (_LG_), the Church is a sacrament, a sign and instrument of ‘communion with God and of unity among all men’ (_LG_ 1). The 1985 Synod of Bishops, held on the twentieth anniversary of the closing of Vatican II, stated that ‘the ecclesiology of communion is the central and fundamental idea of the Council’s documents’.

The universal Church is a communion of local churches. In Vatican II, there is a shift of emphasis to the local churches with their diversity and legitimate autonomy. The local Church is the concrete manifestation of the universal Church. It is fully the Church, not just an administrative unit of the universal Church. Vatican **[p. 641]** II documents did not give a precise definition of the local Church. The term can refer to a basic Christian community, a Eucharistic assembly, a parish, a diocese, an individual _sui iuris_ Church, a regional Church, a national Church, etc. ‘Particular Church’ is used twenty-four times in the documents—twelve times to refer to the diocese and other times to refer to organic groupings of churches (e.g., _Unitatis Redintegratio_ (_UR_) 14; _Orientalium Ecclesiarium_ (_OE_) 2–4, 10, 16, 17, 19). ‘Local Church’ is used eight times to refer to the diocese, groupings of churches, and the parish. Sometimes ‘particular’ and ‘local’ are used as synonyms (e.g., _UR_ 14). [^c39-6] By its communion with other local churches, a local Church becomes Catholic and universal. The theology of the local Church continues to be the subject of attention in the post-conciliar documents. For example, Paul VI, in _Evangelii Nuntiandi_ (_EN_, 1975) says: ‘Nevertheless this universal Church is in practice incarnate in the individual Churches’ (_EN_ 62). It is interesting to note how this theology is reaffirmed by Pope Francis in his Apostolic Exhortation _Amoris Laetitia_ (_AL_), which underscores that though unity of teaching and practice is necessary, it does not exclude a variety of interpretations: ‘Each country or region, moreover, can seek solutions better suited to its culture and sensitive to its traditions and local needs’ (_AL_ 3). In fact, the Pope is referring here to the teaching of _Gaudium et Spes_ (44), and various other post-Conciliar documents.

[^c39-6]: Kuncheria Pathil, ‘Theology of the Local Church’, _Jeevadhara_ 28, no. 166 (1998): 257–78.

The theology of local churches had a particular significance for Asia, since in the post-colonial period Asian countries were rediscovering and reasserting their cultural, religious, political, and social heritage and identity. In the wake of coming-to-be ‘new nations’ with ‘Third World consciousness’, the ‘new world of Asia’ found great inspiration in the theology of the local churches. This theology was further developed by the FABC. FABC Paper 60 is an excellent example of this: ‘A local Church emerges from the encounter between a people and the Gospel’; it is the ‘historical actualization of the mystery of God in Christ.’[^c39-7]

[^c39-7]: FABC, ‘Theses on the Local Church’, 5, 12.

National bishops’ conferences in Asian countries have been instrumental in strengthening the consciousness of local churches. These conferences, which meet regularly, have various commissions working on different areas of ecclesial life. There are other initiatives as well to strengthen local identities. The National Incentive Convention for Evangelization (NICE) of the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Japan is [^c39-8] one such initiative. Greater emphasis on inculturation, dialogue, contextual theologies, more autonomy for Eastern Oriental churches, new centres of ecclesiastical education and publications, development in missions, and other areas are signs of a developing theology of local churches. In countries like the Philippines, the theology of the local Church has led to initiatives like the emergence of basic ecclesial [^c39-9] communities (BECs).

[^c39-8]: Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Japan, ‘The Catholic Church in Japan Today’, https://www.cbcj.catholic.jp/english/japan/history/1994-2016.

[^c39-9]: Ferdinand Dagmang, ‘From Vatican II to PCP II to BEC Too: Progressive Localization of a New State of Mind to a New State of Affairs’, in _Revisiting Vatican II: 50 Years of Renewal_, ed. Shaji George Kochuthara, 3 vols. (Bangalore: Dharmaram, 2015), 2:317–26.

### 4. Dialogue: Key to the Reception of Vatican II

**[p. 642]** The key to understanding the reception of Vatican II in Asia is ‘dialogue’. FABC has called for triple dialogue, considering the three main Asian realities of life: dialogue with the vibrant religious traditions, ancient [^c39-10] cultures, and teeming millions of Asian poor. In the post-colonial Asian Church, there is a conviction that its existence will be meaningful only through dialogue.

[^c39-10]: Franz-Josef Eilers, ed., _For All the Peoples of Asia_, vol. 1, _Federation of Asian Bishops’ Conferences Documents from 1970 to_ _1991_ (Quezon City: Claretian, 1992), 14–15; vol. 2, _Federation of Asian Bishops’ Conferences Documents from 1992 to 1996_ (Quezon City: Claretian,1997), 2.

#### Dialogue with Religions

In the post-colonial period, there is a deeper conviction that the Spirit of God is at work in other religions as well. In the words of the Declaration on the Relation of the Church to Non-Christian Religions, _Nostra Aetate_ (_NA_), ‘The Catholic Church rejects nothing of what is true and holy in these religions … The Church, therefore, urges her sons and daughters to enter with prudence and charity into discussion and collaboration with members of other religions’ (_NA_ 2). Subsequent Vatican documents continue this spirit of dialogue. In _Fides et Ratio_ (_FR_), John Paul II says, ‘In India, particularly, it is the duty of Christians now to draw from this rich heritage the elements compatible with their faith, in order to enrich Christian thought’ (_FR_ 72). This work of discernment finds its inspiration in _Nostra Aetate_. Similarly, the post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation _Ecclesia in Asia_ (_EA_, 1999) acknowledges that the most striking feature of Asia is the plurality of cultures and religions and reaffirms the Church’s respect for them (_EA_ 6). It also invites theologians to strengthen existing means of dialogue (_EA_ 21, 24, 31).

Asian churches have vigorously taken up this theology of religions and dialogue with other religions. FABC’s contribution in this regard is noteworthy. Summarizing the FABC theology of religions, Michael Amaladoss says: ‘All religions can facilitate salvific divine–human encounter, so that people belonging to other [^c39-11] religions are saved, not merely in spite of, but because of practicing those religions.’ ‘Therefore, the only practical option before us is a third alternative: dialogue, positive relationship, collaboration and common [^c39-12] pilgrimage and search for truth in view of the welfare, salvation and unity of the whole humanity.’

[^c39-11]: Michael Amaladoss, ‘The FABC Theology of Religions’, in _Harvesting from the Asian Soil: Towards an Asian Theology_, ed. Vimal Tirimanna (Bangalore: Asian Trading Corporation, 2011), 53.

[^c39-12]: Kuncheria Pathil, CMI, ‘Pluralism, Dialogue and Communion’, in Kochuthara, _Revisiting Vatican II: 50 Years of Renewal_, 1:329.

**[p. 643]** In post-colonial Asia, especially following the Second Vatican Council, a number of initiatives were undertaken to promote interreligious dialogue. Many theologians tried to develop a theology of religions and dialogue. Study of the scriptures, philosophy, and theology of other religions became part of the curriculum in theological faculties. Many centres for interreligious dialogue were established. Christian Ashrams were founded in India, integrating the spirituality of other religions with that of Christianity. In many South East Asian countries, dialogue with indigenous religious traditions like Shamanism was undertaken. In Japan, Thailand, and many other countries, dialogue with Buddhism became an integral part of theology and church life. Catholics became interested in Zen Buddhism; many began to use methods of [^c39-13] Zen meditation in their own prayer life. Indigenous forms of music, dance, art, architecture, and so on were used to make the Christian message more intelligible and meaningful to the context. There were also attempts to form basic human communities where people could come together and collaborate irrespective of religious affiliations.

[^c39-13]: Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Japan, ‘The Catholic Church in Japan Today’.

One of the recent questions in interreligious theology is that of multi-religious belonging. Many Asian theologians challenge the exclusivist or pluralist models of dialogue, which ‘assume a Christian starting point and a certain degree of Christian uniqueness and incompatibility with other faiths’. Instead, they propose dual or plural belonging. For example, can one be Christian and Buddhist at the same time? ‘The [^c39-14] starting point is accepting a “real” experience of and relationship with both Buddha and Christ.’ Many Christians in China continue with ancestor worship. Christians who continue their Shamanistic tradition are another example. Though it needs further exploration, this points to a new direction in which interreligious theology in Asia is developing.

[^c39-14]: Edmund Tang, ‘Identity and Marginality: Christianity in East Asia’, in _The Oxford Handbook of Christianity in Asia_, ed. Felix Wilfred (New York: Oxford University Press, 2014), 95–96; Albertus Bagus Laksana, ‘Multiple Religious Belonging or Complex Identity? An Asian Way of Being Religious’, ibid., 493–509.

#### Dialogue with Cultures

During the colonial period, Christianity was often introduced in Western cultural garb; attempts to replace indigenous cultures were not rare. This is one of the major reasons behind the continuing perception that Christianity is a foreign/Western religion. This does not mean that the Church in Asia from the beginning did not try for indigenisation and inculturation. For example, according to Podipara, the Syro-Malabar [^c39-15] Church was ‘Hindu in culture, Christian in Religion, Oriental in Worship’. Chinese Christians tried to **[p. 644]** integrate the Christian faith into their culture. The Rite controversy in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries—that is, efforts to integrate traditional ancestor worship into the Christian faith—was such an attempt. Throughout the history of Christianity in Japan, a number of attempts were made to use Buddhist [^c39-16] concepts and terms to communicate the Christian faith to the people.

[^c39-15]: Placid Podipara, ‘Hindu in Culture, Christian in Religion, Oriental in Worship’, _Ostkirchliche Studien_ 8 (1959): 89–104.

[^c39-16]: Nozomu Miyahira, ‘Christian Theology under Feudalism, Nationalism and Democracy in Japan’, in _Christian Theology in_ _Asia_, ed. C. H. Sebastian Kim (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2008), 109–27; Osamu Takeuchi, ‘The Heart of _Wa_ and Christian Ethics’, _Asian Horizons_ 4, no. 1 (2010): 114–27.

In the post-colonial period, there has been an emphasis on the need for inculturation and indigenization. The teachings of the Second Vatican Council, especially the teaching on culture in _Gaudium et Spes_ (_GS_ 53– 62), gave momentum to this. _Gaudium et Spes_ clearly says that the Church ‘is not tied exclusively and indissolubly to any race or nation, to any one particular way of life’ and hence ‘enter[s] into communion with different forms of culture, thereby enriching both itself and the cultures themselves’ (_GS_ 58). Taking their cue from such a positive view of culture and inculturation, Asian churches have contributed greatly to the dialogue with Asian cultures. _Ecclesia in Asia_ underscores how inculturation and evangelization are interrelated (_EA_ 21).

FABC, from its inception, has given prime importance to dialogue with Asian cultures. This can be seen in many of its documents. These attempts have taken place especially in the areas of liturgy, theology, and spirituality. Translation of liturgical texts into the vernacular helped lead to more lively participation of the faithful in the liturgy and facilitated inculturation in liturgy.

Inculturation also means ‘redeeming’ the vernacular. ‘Vernacular interpretation makes use of the reader’s cultural resources and social experiences to understand the biblical narratives and the broader Christian [^c39-17] tradition’. In many countries, there have been attempts to develop theology using the vernacular and ‘to [^c39-18] re-articulate the faith’.

[^c39-17]: Agnes M. Brazal, ‘Redeeming the Vernacular: Doing Post-Colonial-Intercultural Theological Ethics’, _Asian Horizons_ 4, no. 1 (2010): 50.

[^c39-18]: Rebecca Cacho, ‘Faith as Dialectical Interplay of Affection and Cognition in Newman and “_Pandama_” (Integrative Sensing) of Filipino Christians’, _Asian Horizons_ 7, no. 3 (2013): 595–621, at 596.

#### Dialogue with the Poor

In many of the council documents, the Church’s concern for the poor is visible. For example, _Lumen Gentium_ says: ‘Just as Christ carried out the work of redemption in poverty and oppression, so the Church is called to follow the same path if it is to communicate the fruits of salvation to humanity’ (_LG_ 8). _Gravissimum Educationis_ (9), _Apostolicam Actuositatem_ (8), and others underscore the Church’s commitment to the poor. The opening statement of _Gaudium et Spes_ shows the Church’s preferential option for the poor: ‘The joys and hopes, the grief and anguish of the people of our time, especially of those who are poor or affiicted, are the joys and hopes, the grief and anguish of the followers of Christ as well’ (_GS_ 1). The council’s emphasis on justice and equity and its stance against excessive inequality (_GS_ 63–72) inspired Asian churches in their **[p. 645]** preferential option for the poor of Asia. Moreover, the Declaration of Religious Freedom, _Dignitatis Humanae_, was instrumental in the Church’s commitment to religious liberty and human rights. Clearly, subsequent documents in Catholic social teaching have immensely strengthened the Church’s commitment for the poor.

In the post-conciliar period, we find a growing conviction that there cannot be a relevant theology for Asia that overlooks the poor. FABC’s Fifth Plenary Assembly states: ‘Our challenge is to proclaim the Good News of the Kingdom of God: to promote justice, peace, love, compassion, equality and brotherhood in these [^c39-19] Asian realities.’ Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle (formerly archbishop of Manila, the Philippines; since 2019 prefect of the Congregation for the Evangelization of Peoples) affirms that ‘the very identity and credibility or “authority” of the Church in Asia rests heavily on how it dialogues with the poor in the spirit of [^c39-20] kenosis’. In the decades following the council, Asian churches undertook many initiatives to dialogue with the poor. Besides the invitation given by Vatican II, the influence of liberation theology can also be seen here. In India, various branches of theology, such as Dalit theology, subaltern theology, and tribal theology, have developed from the conviction that Christian commitment requires a determined commitment to the poor. Theologians also address the issue of the caste system in India and other inhuman social structures. [^c39-21] Minjung theology of Korea is another example of the liberationist perspective in the post-colonial period. In 1975, the Japanese Bishops’ Conference set up the Japan Catholic Council for Justice and Peace, which was actively involved in helping war refugees (from Vietnam) and migrant workers. By the 1980s, the Japanese Church had become more involved in human rights issues, such as against the discrimination suffered by [^c39-22] Buraku minorities and by Korean residents in Japan. In the Philippines, during the reign of Marcos, a theology of struggle developed, and finally even the hierarchy took a stance against Marcos. The Plenary Council of the Philippines-II placed great emphasis on the commitment to the poor: ‘As we approach the [^c39-23] year 2000, Christ bids this community … to be a Church of the Poor.’

[^c39-19]: Eilers, _For All the Peoples of Asia_, 1:275.

[^c39-20]: Luis Antonio Tagle, ‘The Mission of the Church in Asia: Living the Incarnation in Poverty and Plurality’, in _Harvesting from_ _the Asian Soil: Towards an Asian Theology_, ed. Vimal Tirimanna (Bangalore: Asian Trading Corporation, 2011), 130.

[^c39-21]: Michael Amaladoss, ‘Asian Theological Trends’, in Wilfred, _The Oxford Handbook of Christianity in Asia_, 113.

[^c39-22]: Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Japan, ‘The Catholic Church in Japan Today’.

[^c39-23]: PCP-II, _Acts and Decrees of the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines_, no. 96.

The Church’s educational and social apostolate have taken a liberation perspective, especially in the postcolonial period. In the social apostolate, besides financial assistance, empowering the people has become a major focus. Many Catholic educational institutions reserve a percentage of places for students belonging to marginalized groups.

**[p. 646]** Gender justice and the empowerment of women are treated as integral dimensions of liberation. Perhaps Asia, in general, has been slower to respond to the council’s call to ensure the just participation of women in society (_GS_ 29, 60). Although the struggle for gender equality is a worldwide phenomenon, in Asia this assumes a vital importance, as most Asian societies are deeply rooted in the patriarchal system.

Globalization has resulted in new faces in the struggle for justice and the preferential option for the poor. Though globalization is welcomed as international collaboration and cooperation, it becomes another tool for the market-driven economy to exploit the poor and weaker sections of the society. Asian theologians call for globalization with solidarity.[^c39-24] However, this process of triple dialogue has not been always a pleasant task. Many such attempts have been met by scepticism and resistance on the part of the hierarchical Church. Many theologians have faced discouraging and painful experiences; some were censored, especially in the 1980s—sometimes officially, sometimes unofficially. Attempts to develop the ‘Indian Liturgy/Mass’ were suppressed. Doubt has been cast upon efforts to integrate indigenous religious practices. Such attitudes and actions on the part of the authorities have hindered the process of dialogue promoted by Vatican II. Nonetheless, in recent years, enthusiasm for dialogue has been rediscovered.

[^c39-24]: Shaji George Kochuthara, ‘Globalization in Solidarity: Reflections on Globalization from India’, _Political Theology_ 15, no. 1 (2014): 53–73.

### 5. Orientalium Ecclesiarum

In its Decree on the Catholic Churches of the Eastern Rite, _Orientalium Ecclesiarum_, the council declared that it ‘values highly the institutions of the Eastern Churches, their liturgical rites, ecclesiastical traditions and their ordering of Christian life’ (_OE_ 1). This affirmation of their uniqueness and dignity has been received with enthusiasm by the Eastern churches as well as by the Latin Church, though sometimes with tensions and confiicts. Bishop Basil Losten, the Greek Catholic bishop of New York and New England, rightly observes, ‘One of our most important ecclesiological gains in the twentieth century among Catholics is the [^c39-25] recovery of the “_equalis dignitas_” of the autonomous Churches in the Catholic communion.’ Although this recognition predates the council, it was Vatican II that solemnly proclaimed it. The communion ecclesiology of the council can be said to be the result of the interaction between the Eastern and Western Church council fathers. The pluralistic ecclesiology, spirituality, and diversity of traditions were duly recognized by the [^c39-26] council.

[^c39-25]: Bishop Basil, ‘Preface’, in _The Vatican and the Eastern Christian Churches: Papal Encyclicals and Documents Concerning the_ _Eastern Churches_ (Fairfax, VA: Eastern Christian Publications, 1996), 1:2.

[^c39-26]: Francis Thonippara, ‘_Orientalium Ecclesiarum_: Second Vatican Council Decree on the Eastern Catholic Churches—A Historical Survey’, _Asian Horizons_ 8, no. 1 (2014): 15.

**[p. 647]** The reception of the council has been visible in the restoration and reform of liturgies and in the relationship with the Latin Rite, especially in terms of jurisdiction and its extension outside the proper territories of the Eastern churches. _Orientalium Ecclesiarum_ has been of particular importance for Asia, since most of the Eastern Oriental Catholic churches are found there. This is especially visible in India, though not much is widely known outside India concerning its reception in that country.

Before Vatican II, the term ‘churches’ in the plural was not in common usage. For example, Pope Benedict XV, on 1 May 1917, founded a special Congregation for the Oriental Church, separating it from the Congregation of the _Propaganda Fide_. In 1967, after the Second Vatican Council, it was renamed the Congregation for the Oriental Churches. This change from singular to plural itself is due to the new theological vision initiated by the council.[^c39-27]

[^c39-27]: Ibid., 9.

_Orientalium Ecclesiarum_ invited the Eastern churches to ‘preserve their own lawful liturgical rites and way of life’ (_OE_ 6). In some churches, this led to conflict. One such conflict within the Syro-Malabar Church—one of the two Oriental churches present in India—has been over the restoration of the liturgy. Following a series of attempts, the restored rite of the Eucharistic liturgy was finally introduced in February 1986. One positive effect of this process was that it led to greater interest in the study of tradition and of the Vatican II documents, since that was the immediate context and inspiration for this renewal. In the Syro-Malankara Church, such confiicts did not happen, since it had not been Latinized to the same extent as the Syro- Malabar Church.

_Orientalium Ecclesiarum_ directs that ‘Provision must be made therefore everywhere in the world to protect and advance all these individual churches. For this purpose, each should organize its own parishes and hierarchy, where the spiritual good of the faithful requires it’ (_OE_ 4). This implied that in many places, multiple jurisdictions would have to be permitted. Here, _Orientalium Ecclesiarum_ has been of particular importance to the Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara churches in India. Many of the statements and instructions in _Orientalium Ecclesiarum_ are intended to correct the injustice and Latinization that these [^c39-28] churches had undergone during the colonial period and afterwards. For example, Johannes M. Hoeck, commenting on the decree, observes: ‘The real reason as to why the right to preach the gospel … is specially mentioned among the rights and obligations of all the Individual Churches is to be traced to the situation in India, where the Malabar Church, which has a large surplus of priests, was until recently only permitted to [^c39-29] convert people to the Latin rite.’ Pospishil expresses the same opinion: ‘the situation is different for the flourishing Catholics of the two Syrian rites in South India … [who] were not permitted to extend their **[p. 648]** missionary activity … because the territory had been assigned to Latin rite missions, which rite after all [^c39-30] reached that part of the globe hardly a few hundred years back.’ Similarly, Walter Abbott, in his translation of the decree notes: ‘In the past, the apostolate in the missions has been conducted exclusively in the Latin rite. This practice has been resented by some easterners, mostly in India where the priests of the ancient [^c39-31] Malabar rite were always obliged to adopt the Roman rite to undertake missionary apostolate.’

[^c39-28]: Thomas Anchukandam, SDB, ‘_Orientalium Ecclesiarum_: Decree on the Catholic Eastern Churches’, in _Towards a Deeper_ _Understanding of Vatican II and the Post-Conciliar Documents_, ed. Thomas Anchukandam, Dominic Veliath, and Jose Kuttianimattathil (Bangalore: Kristu Jyothi, 2001), 123.

[^c39-29]: Johannes M. Hoeck, ‘Decree on Eastern Catholic Churches’, in _Commentary on the Documents of Vatican II_, vol. 1, ed. Herbert Vorgrimler (London: Burns & Oates, 1967), 307–31, at 315.

[^c39-30]: Victor J. Pospishil, _Orientalium Ecclesiarum: Decree on the Eastern Catholic Churches of the II Council of Vatican_ (New York: Fordham University, 1965), 13–14.

[^c39-31]: Walter M. Abbott, ed., _The Documents of Vatican II_ (London: Geoffrey Chapman, 1966), 375 n. 7.

The promulgation of the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches on 18 October 1990 was another landmark. The Code was a definite sign of the recognition of the identity, uniqueness, and legitimate autonomy of the Eastern churches.

The reception of _Orientalium Ecclesiarum_, especially with regard to the equal right of the individual churches, has been rather slow. However, we must acknowledge that in spite of resistance, the vision of _Orientalium Ecclesiarum_ has been consistent and steady.

On 8 September 1978, Pope John Paul I appointed Archbishop Mar Antony Padiyara as Apostolic Visitor to examine the conditions of the Syro-Malabar Christians living in the Latin dioceses of India outside Kerala; his report was submitted in 1980. In 1987, John Paul II wrote to the members of the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of India, saying that the Church in India consisted of three individual churches and that there should be catechesis in each Church concerning the other churches. He also pointed out that these three churches should have their own conferences or synods, but the CBCI should remain the national conference for all. Moreover, he said that it is necessary to provide pastoral care according to the rite to which each person belongs, and therefore he intended to establish the Syro-Malabar diocese of Kalyan for the Bombay- [^c39-32] Pune region. ‘This was indeed a real follow up action of the Council.’ The eparchy of Kalyan was erected on 30 April 1988.

[^c39-32]: Archbishop Joseph Powathil, ‘_Orientalium Ecclesiarum_: A Breakthrough in History’, in Kochuthara, _Revisiting Vatican II: 50_ _Years of Renewal_, 1:346.

In 1992, the Syro-Malabar Church was raised to the status of a major archiepiscopal Church, followed by the Syro-Malankara Church in 2005. On 26 May 2012, the diocese of Faridabad was erected for the Syro- Malabar Catholics living in six states of the surrounding territory. On 10 October 2017, Pope Francis erected two new eparchies for the Syro-Malabar Church (Shamsabad and Hosur) and extended the territories of two existing dioceses. This initiative was accompanied by a letter from the pope addressed to the bishops of [^c39-33] India, which is significant when we reflect on the reception of _Orientalium Ecclesiarum_. By this letter, the [^c39-34] pope established the jurisdiction of the Syro-Malabar Church in all of India, one of their repeated demands in the process of the reception of _Orientalium Ecclesiarum_. Although the letter is rather brief, Pope Francis **[p. 649]** quotes extensively from _Lumen Gentium_ and _Orientalium Ecclesiarum_, underscores the equal dignity of all the individual churches (para. 4; cf. _OE_ 1, 3), and affirms that ‘differences do not diminish unity’ (_LG_ 13). Francis also points out that this measure is to be understood as the completion of a process initiated especially with _Orientalium Ecclesiarum_ and followed by successive popes since Vatican II (para. 7). It is also worth recalling that a number of dioceses of Eastern Catholic churches have been established in Europe, North America, and Australia in the decades following Vatican II in order to provide adequate pastoral care for their members. The latest addition may be the eparchy of Mississauga in Canada (22 December 2018).

[^c39-33]: Pope Francis, ‘Letter of the Holy Father Francis to the Bishops of India’, _Bollettino, Sala Stampa della Santa Sede_ 0687 (10 October 2017): 1–9, http://press.vatican.va/content/salastampa/it/bollettino/pubblico/2017/10/10/0687.pdf.

[^c39-34]: Ibid.

### 6. Theology of Mission

The reception of the Decree on the Mission Activity of the Church, _Ad Gentes_ (_AG_), in Asia has been complex for various reasons. Many Christians themselves rejected the colonial model of mission. In most Asian countries, Christianity remains a minority religion. Moreover, traditional religions and cultures of Asia were opposed to the colonial model of mission. In the post-colonial period, the rediscovery and reassertion of indigenous traditions resulted in resistance to Christian mission aimed at conversion. Adding to this, the rise of fundamentalist ideas in the majority religions in some Asian countries has made conversion difficult or even impossible. Along with these issues, debate on the theology of mission has created confusion among Christian missionaries. Engaging in dialogue with other religions and cultures was considered urgent.

_Ad Gentes_ itself presents divergent views of mission. It must be remembered that one-third of the council’s participants came from the ‘mission’ world. They were aware that the situation in the former colonies had changed. But there was also a concern that the positive view of other religions expressed in documents like _Lumen Gentium_, _Nostra Aetate_, and _Dignitatis Humanae_ would diminish missionary zeal. ‘The resultant decree … introduced a clear rupture with much of the Western mission theology and practice of colonial times. … Nonetheless, tension between “direct proclamation of the Good News” and “inter-faith dialogue” [^c39-35] was not resolved on the council floor nor in the decree _AG._’  _Ad Gentes_ makes it clear that the Church is by ‘its very nature missionary’ (_AG_ 2). Mission is the work of God, who wishes to unite the whole of humanity (_AG_ 9). This mission is to transform the world through forming a new humanity characterized by love and fellowship, justice and peace, freedom and wholeness, solidarity and sharing, together with all people of [^c39-36] good will. The second chapter of _Ad Gentes_ presents the incarnational principle of mission: ‘Christ, by his incarnation, committed himself to the particular social and cultural circumstances of the women and men **[p. 650]** among whom He lived’ (_AG_ 10). Thus, the mission is oriented towards establishing Christian communities (_AG_ 15) and developing indigenous theologies (_AG_ 22). However, the three last chapters of _Ad Gentes_ ‘largely leave the cosmic vision, incarnational principle and centrality of the local church’ and ‘work [^c39-37] on practicalities’. This difference in theology and approach is reflected in the post-conciliar period as well.

[^c39-35]: John Mansford Prior, SVD, ‘New Daybreak in Mission: From _Ad Gentes_ to _Inter Gentes_’, in Kochuthara, _Revisiting Vatican II_, 1:396.

[^c39-36]: Ibid., 398.

[^c39-37]: Ibid., 400.

Paul VI’s 1975 Apostolic Exhortation _Evangelii Nuntiandi_ carried forward the incarnational principle of mission: ‘Evangelization loses much of its force and effectiveness if it does not take into consideration the actual people to whom it is addressed, if it does not use their language, their signs and symbols, if it does not answer the questions they ask, and if it does not have an impact on their concrete life’ (_EN_ 63). John Paul II’s 1990 encyclical _Redemptoris Missio_ (_RM_) reaffirms the centrality of Jesus Christ (_RM_ 4–11) and rejects attempts to consider parallel ways of salvation other than that which is offered in Jesus Christ (_RM_ 29). However, _Redemptoris Missio_ also notes that responding to the new social realities is an integral dimension of the mission (e.g., _RM_ 37b). John Paul II’s post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation _Ecclesia in Asia_ (1999) reaffirms that ‘evangelization and inculturation are naturally and intimately related to each other’ (_EA_ 21).

The challenge has been, thus, to develop a new theology of mission, rooted in dialogue and inculturation respecting the manifold religious and cultural traditions of Asia and proclaiming the good news. The FABC took up this challenge. The report of the 1974 meeting of the FABC says: ‘In Asia especially this [^c39-38] [evangelization] involves a dialogue with the great religious traditions of our peoples.’ It also underscores: ‘The primary focus of our task of evangelization, then, at this time in our history, is the building up of a [^c39-39] truly local Church.’ To carry out this mission, the Asian churches should be authentic subjects, active agents of evangelization—no longer ‘mere recipients’ of a Western Christendom, no longer mere clones of [^c39-40] the Church in Europe with its historically conditioned forms and theologies. So, the primary task of mission is not the salvation of souls or the planting of the Church but, without neglecting these, it is first of all to engage in dialogue and to form the local churches through the incarnational principle. As Karotemprel points out, the ecclesiology of Vatican II presented in _Lumen Gentium_, _Ad Gentes_, and _Nostra Aetate_ is gradually developing into a mission theology in Asia while helping to conceive new methods of missionary activity. In the context of poverty and a plurality of faiths and cultures, the Church in Asia is called to a triple [^c39-41] dialogue and solidarity. Asian theologians have resisted efforts to make dialogue a _means_ of mission, as [^c39-42] they believe that dialogue is itself evangelization.

[^c39-38]: Franz-Josef Eilers, ed., _For All the Peoples of Asia_, 1:14.

[^c39-39]: FABC, _Evangelization in Modern Day Asia: The First Plenary Assembly of the Federation of Asian Bishops’ Conferences (FABC)_: Statement and Recommendations of the Assembly: Taipei, Taiwan, 22–27 April 1974 (Hong Kong: Office of the Secretary- General, FABC, 1974).

[^c39-40]: FABC, ‘Theses on the Local Church’, 3.

[^c39-41]: Sebastian Karotemprel, ‘Chiesa e missione oggi’, in _Il Concilio Vaticano II: Recezione e attualita’ alla luce del Giubileo_, ed. Rino Fisichella (Milan: San Paolo, 2000), 301.

[^c39-42]: Felix Wilfred, ‘The Reception of Vatican II in a Multireligious Continent’, _Concilium_ 3 (2012): 119.

**[p. 651]** In the last few decades, a number of institutes were established in Asia, especially in Sri Lanka, the Philippines, India, Indonesia, and Korea, which offer specializations in missiology. The courses offered address not only mission in one’s own country, but also global mission. Asia, although it continues to be a mission continent, is sending missionaries worldwide. Many theological journals in missiology are published from Asia: for example, _East Asian Pastoral Review_ (Manila), _Japan Missionary Bulletin_ (Tokyo), _Third Millennium_ (Rajkot, India), _South Asian Journal of Missiological Research—Jnanadeepika_ (Pune), _Ishvani Mission Digest_ (Pune), and _Mission Today: A Journal of Missiological and Ecumenical Research_ (Shillong, India). New organizations and networks were established to pray for the missions, to help missionaries, and to collaborate in missionary work. A number of ‘mission’ dioceses were established in various countries in Asia; that is, for ‘direct’ evangelization. Vatican II’s positive outlook on inculturation has prompted different mission initiatives, such as initiatives to learn from the spirituality of yoga and Zen, as well as the [^c39-43] establishment of Christian ashrams. Many missionary congregations have been founded in the post-conciliar period, including the Mission Society of the Philippines, the Missionary Society of St Thomas the Apostle, the Missionary Society of Heralds of Good News, the Missionaries of Mary Immaculate (India), the Catholic Foreign Mission Society of Korea, and the Missionary Society of Thailand. Many of the existing congregations have placed a particular focus on mission.

[^c39-43]: Karotemprel, ‘Chiesa e missione oggi’, 299–300.

One development in the theology of mission in Asia is the shift from _missio ad gentes_ (mission to the nations) to _missio inter gentes_ (mission among the nations). ‘The focus of the Asian local church’s _missio_ [^c39-44] _inter gentes_ is identifled with Jesus’ own mission of bringing about the Reign of God _among_ his people.’ The principal means of this mission is the triple dialogue. It is a process of ‘mutual conversion’, of learning from the other and communicating with the other’s own faith experience through listening, reflection, contemplation, and action. Divergent approaches of mission in _Ad Gentes_ and subsequent documents and FABC teachings need not be seen as confusions, but as part of the process of developing a new theology of mission initiated by Vatican II.

[^c39-44]: Jonathan Yun-Ka Tan, ‘_Missio Inter Gentes_: Towards a new Paradigm in the Mission Theology of the Federation of Asian Bishops’ Conferences’, _FABC Papers_ 109 (2004): 36. Prior, ‘New Daybreak in Mission’, 403–4.

### 7. The Role of the Laity

A major contribution of Vatican II is its recognition of the role of the laity in the Church and their equal dignity. Both the laity and the clergy share in the one priesthood of Christ (_LG_ 10, 31). All the faithful ‘from the bishops down to the last of the lay faithful’ share the prophetic office of the People of God so that it **[p. 652]** ‘cannot err in matters of belief’ (_LG_ 12). The council’s new approach to the laity is based on its communion theology, envisioning the Church as a mystery, as People of God (_LG_ ch. 2). The Decree on the Apostolate of the Laity, _Apostolicam Actuositatem_ (_AA_), develops further the theology of the laity and says that they have to act like leaven in the world (_AA_ 2); they must actively engage in the social, economic, political, and cultural areas of life and infuse them with Gospel values (_AA_ 7). The Synod of Bishops of 1987 on the ‘Vocation and Mission of Laity in the Church and World, Twenty Years after Vatican II Council’, and the subsequent Apostolic Exhortation _Christifideles Laici_ (_CL_), continues the Vatican II theology of the laity. It acknowledges that ‘In giving a response to the question “Who are the lay faithful”, the Council went beyond previous interpretations which were predominantly negative’ (_CL_ 9).

In post-conciliar Asia, greater participation of the laity in various fields is visible. New ecclesial movements like the Community of Sant’Egidio, Focolare, Couples for Christ, Worldwide Marriage Encounter, and others in which laypeople have leadership roles are active in Asian countries. Many laypeople exercise preaching and healing ministries in the charismatic movement. They also engage in charity work, individually and collectively. In parishes and at the diocesan level, many organizations for laity have been formed, and many lay faithful actively participate in them. Bishops’ conferences have offices of the laity. In countries like the [^c39-45] Philippines, laypeople take on leadership roles in basic ecclesial communities. They study theology and teach in schools or theological faculties, though their numbers are still very low. The Catholic Bishops’ Conference of the Philippines declared 2014 the Year of the Laity.

[^c39-45]: Dagmang, ‘From Vatican II to PCP II to BEC Too’, 317–18.

In spite of all these initiatives, the extent to which the equality of all the faithful and their equal responsibility are actualized needs to be evaluated. It seems that even now, clericalism and the hierarchical model of the Church exert considerable influence. In many countries, in practical terms, the laity are considered only a substitute to the clergy. When it comes to the administration of the Church, often the role of the laity is only to serve and obey the hierarchy.

### 8. Ecumenism

The council’s teaching on ecumenism is found primarily in the Decree on Ecumenism, _Unitatis Redintegratio_. However, it must be understood in light of _Lumen Gentium_. _Orientalium Ecclesiarum_ also discusses relationships with the separated Eastern churches (Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches). _Lumen Gentium_’s renewed vision of the Church as mystery, as communion, and as People of God, as well as the lesser emphasis on the hierarchy and papal primacy and greater emphasis on collegiality, have prepared **[p. 653]** the ground for new possibilities in ecumenical relations. _Unitatis Redintegratio_ highlights the plurality of the churches and underscores that the ‘Church of Christ’ is one, but exists in the many churches (_UR_ 1, 3). The Church of Christ can exist outside the boundaries of the Roman Catholic Church. Different churches have ‘different ways’, ‘different methods and approaches’, and ‘different theological expressions’, which are ‘complementary and not conflicting’ (_UR_ 14, 16, 17). It also acknowledges that ‘Far from being an obstacle to the Church’s unity, such diversity of customs and observances only adds to the beauty of the church’ (_UR_ 16). Dialogue among the churches is the means of strengthening and maintaining communion among them.

The plurality of churches is also an Asian reality. In some Asian countries, the number of Catholics is lower than that of other Christians. China is said to have 12 to 15 million Catholics and around 50 million other Christians. According to the 2005 census in South Korea, 29.2 per cent of the population are Christians: 18.3 per cent are Protestants and 10.9 per cent are Catholics. India has more than 10 million Christians belonging to other churches. There is a profound conviction that the disunity of Christians is a scandal and an anomaly. Various initiatives have been undertaken for dialogue and cooperation among the churches. Bishops’ conferences have commissions or offices for church unity which organize regular meetings and programmes. Steps taken by the Asia Ecumenical Committee between the FABC and the Christian Conference of Asia are significant. The Week of Prayer for Christian Unity is celebrated solemnly in many dioceses and parishes in collaboration with various churches. Courses on ecumenism are included in the curriculum at theological faculties, and many faculties recognize courses offered by the faculties of other churches.

The relationship among the churches has improved considerably. However, in spite of the council’s sincere call for dialogue and communion, no substantial change has occurred in the ecumenical scenario even fifty [^c39-46] years after. One of the main reasons for this is the continuing Catholic attitude that while the Roman Catholic Church possesses the fullness of ecclesial reality, other communities have only some ‘ecclesial elements’. Another important development in recent decades is the growth of Pentecostal churches. Ecumenical dialogue is still mostly limited to the more traditional churches.

[^c39-46]: Kuncheria Pathil, ‘Ecumenism beyond _Unitatis Redintegratio_’, _Asian Horizons_ 8, no. 3 (2014): 413–36.

### 9. Asia’s Growing Significance in the Universal Church

In the decades following the council, Asia witnessed a boom of vocations to priestly and religious life. Of the priests and religious in Asia, very few are non-Asians. Moreover, as mentioned above, Asia now sends missionaries to other continents. Some major religious congregations, such as the Society of Jesus, have **[p. 654]** their largest number of members in Asia. Many Indigenous religious congregations were founded in the post-conciliar period, and the existing congregations have grown considerably. Although theological and religious formation still has many Western elements, there has been a growing awareness of their identity as Asians—to be ministers of Christ in Asia, as Asians for an Asian Church. Moreover, their formation programmes, both religious and theological, were developed in light of Vatican II teachings and subsequent documents, emphasizing dialogue with cultures, religions, and the poor, and promoting greater involvement in the socio-cultural life in their particular contexts.

Many ecclesiastical faculties were established in Asia after the council, for example, by the Congregation for Catholic Education: India (11), Philippines (3), Japan (2), Israel (1), Taiwan (1). Many more institutions are affiliated with faculties in Europe or in their own country. In some countries, theology faculties or departments or chairs are part of the State universities. In some Asian countries, most of the students are seminarians, priests, and religious, but in others a good number are laypeople. Evidently, the curriculum in these faculties was developed in light of the directions given by Vatican II in the Decree on the Training of Priests, _Optatam Totius_ (especially 13–22) and the Declaration on Christian Education, _Gravissimum Educationis_, and the subsequent Apostolic Constitution of John Paul II, _Sapientia Christiana_ (1979). Some faculties and theological institutions were founded with a specific focus on Vatican II theology. For example, in 1966, the East Asian Pastoral Institute was founded at Ateneo de Manila University to educate clergy and [^c39-47] laity on the new direction in which Catholic theology was moving. Some faculties in India have a special emphasis on inculturation, dialogue with religions, and contextual theological education. Many faculties and theological institutions also asked thousands of Asians to specialize in ecclesiastical studies, so they could teach in those institutions. This means that in each Asian country there are many theologians who have been trained in the spirit of Vatican II and are training students accordingly. Thus, these institutions became heralds of the reception of the council in Asia. In addition to the various institutions, the role of individual theologians, theological organizations, and theological journals are to be particularly acknowledged.

[^c39-47]: Terence J. Fay, SJ, ‘Decolonization of the Filipino Church after Vatican II’, _History Research_ 5, no. 1 (2015): 29.

### 10. The Reception of Vatican II in Some Other Areas of Ecclesial Life

The Decree on the Mass Media _Inter Mirifica_ (_IM_) has a special relevance due to the technological developments in the last half-century. Evidently, the situation today is very different from the time when the document was written. The Asian churches make a ‘concerted effort to ensure that the means of **[p. 655]** communication are utilized in the many works of the apostolate’ (_IM_ 13). Besides making use of the Internet and social media, Asian churches have established media centres and institutes of training in media.

Vatican II’s call for active involvement in public and political life (_GS_ 73–76) has been received positively. However, for Christians in most Asian countries, being a minority, and with the interplay of religion and politics, involvement in politics is a difficult task. In countries where Christians are the majority, there have been confiicts between church authority and the laity over the stances taken on issues, though it is recognized that the ‘political community and the Church are autonomous and independent of each other in [^c39-48] their own fields’ (_GS_ 76). The Reproductive Health Bill in the Philippines (2012) is a recent example. Concrete ways of critical engagement in politics are yet to be developed.

[^c39-48]: Eric Marcelo O. Genilo, ‘Epilogue: The Church of PCP II after the RH Bill Debate’, in _The Second Plenary Council of the_ _Philippines: Quo Vadis_, ed. Eric Marcelo O. Genilo, Agnes M. Brazal, and Daniel Franklin Pilario (Quezon City: Ateneo de Manila University Press, 2015), 169–89.

_Lumen Gentium_ chapter 6, the vocation of religious, and the Decree on Renewal of Religious Life, _Perfectae Caritatis_, as well as subsequent documents such as the post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation _Vita Consecrata_ (1996) and _Starting Afresh from Christ_ (2002), have had a great impact on the Asian churches, especially as Asia has been experiencing a boom in religious vocations in the past half-century. Responding to the call of the council to return to the sources as well as to adapt ‘to the changed conditions of our time’ (_PC_ 2), religious have been particularly involved in the ‘triple dialogue’, working for integral human development.

### 11. Concluding Remarks

We may rightly say that an ecumenical council has three phases: preparation, the actual event, and reception. Of these, obviously, the longest phase is that of reception. Although Vatican II was concluded in 1965, considering the time usually taken for the reception of a council, fifty years is not a long period. Moreover, we must consider that Vatican II did not try to define any doctrine which needed immediate reception, but rather was trying to give new directions to the Church, which would need a long time for gradual assimilation. That is to say, the reception of the council is ongoing.

On the whole, we could say that as a single document, _Gaudium et Spes_ had the greatest impact on Asia, both on account of what it taught and on account of its spirit of ‘reading the signs of the times’. For the Oriental churches in Asia, _Orientalium Ecclesiarum_ had a special significance. We cannot, however, argue that the reception of the council in Asia has been merely linear. Opposition, resistance, and interventions on the part of authorities, misunderstandings, doubts, and so on have been part of the process. On the one hand, these have slowed down reception. On the other hand, they have been helpful at least to a certain extent in **[p. 656]** promoting the dialogue further and moving forward in the spirit of communion, studying more profoundly the council’s teachings and new ways of implementing them.

The reception of the council in Asia goes far beyond simply implementing the council’s teachings. Asia has imbibed the spirit of the council—the spirit of communion and theology of the local churches; the spirit of dialogue; the spirit of evangelization; and, above all, the spirit of ‘reading the signs of the times’ and responding to them in the Asian context. This spirit has helped the Asian churches to respond to situations and contexts that the council did not fully envisage more than fifty years ago. This spirit is one of the most important contributions of the council to Asian churches and of Asian churches to the universal Church and to humanity.

Eilers, Franz-Josef, ed. _For All the Peoples of Asia_. Volume 1, _Federation of Asian Bishops’ Conferences Documents from 1970 to 1991_. Quezon City: Claretian, 1992.

Eilers, Franz-Josef, ed. _For All the Peoples of Asia._ Volume 2, _Federation of Asian Bishops’ Conferences Documents from 1992 to 1996_. Quezon City: Claretian, 1997.

Kochuthara, Shaji George, ed. _Revisiting Vatican II: 50 Years of Renewal_, 3 vols. Bangalore: Dharmaram, 2014–15.

Pathil, Kuncheria. ‘Theology of the Local Church’. _Jeevadhara_ 28, no. 166 (1998): 257–78.

## 40. The Impact, Reception, and Implementation of Vatican II

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 657]** The renowned Catholic theologian and bishop of Lilongwe, Malawi, Patrick Kalilombe (1933–2012), wrote of Africa’s role in the Second Vatican Council:

The presence of Africa at Vatican II was marginal and by proxy … Although technically and juridically the Church was no longer ‘missionary’, it is hardly possible to imagine that the African Church counted very much as an influence on the Council. Apart from regular interventions from the principal spokesman, Cardinal L. Rugambwa, only sporadic voices were heard from Africa.

It is obvious from an examination of the sixteen documents that the council was largely a forum for the concerns of the churches of Europe and America in the 1960s. Africa’s problems and preoccupations, therefore, came only indirectly: they did not determine the central perspective from which the council’s deliberations were moving. Moreover, real acquaintance with the documents must not be exaggerated, even though efforts were made to publish them and diffuse their message widely in the African continent. After all, Africa was at the time of the council largely a non-literate continent.[^c40-1]

[^c40-1]: Patrick A. Kalilombe, ‘The Effect of the Council on World Catholicism: Africa’, in _Modern Catholicism: Vatican II and After_, ed. Adrian Hastings (London: SPCK, 1991), 310–11. Much of what follows is a revised version of an article that first appeared as ‘ “After All, Africa is a Non-Literate Continent”: The Reception of Vatican II in Africa’, _Theological Studies_ 74, no. 1 (2013): 284–301.

**[p. 658]** Kalilombe’s assessment remains largely incontestable, considered in its historical context. Yet, with the benefit of hindsight, a more positive valuation of Vatican II, its reception, impact, and significance for the Church in Africa is possible, as I attempt to demonstrate in this chapter.

### 2. The Context

To describe and assess the reception, impact, and implementation of the Second Vatican Council in Africa requires an understanding of the social and political context of the continent during the period of the announcement, convocation, deliberation, and conclusion of the council (1959–65). Viewed from the perspective of contemporary events in Africa, the council did not happen in a vacuum. ‘For the Catholic Church in Africa the vast internal revolution set in motion by Pope John more or less coincided with the [^c40-2] political and cultural revolution of Independence.’ Vatican II occurred at a momentous time in the history of Africa, as nationalist tumult and agitation slowly and intensely rose to a combustible crescendo. During the conciliar years, that movement would culminate in the precipitated transfer of political power from bewildered and beleaguered colonialists to exuberant and inexperienced African leaders.

[^c40-2]: Adrian Hastings, _A History of African Christianity, 1950–1975_ (New York: Cambridge University Press, 1979), 167–68.

Thus, the religious excitement occasioned by the sudden announcement and convocation of the council coincided with the secular excitement over Africa’s political emancipation. Symbolically, Pope John XXIII’s radical objective of _aggiornamento_ bore a notable resemblance to aspirations for political independence in several African countries in the 1960s. In the Church as in secular society, the promise of change and a future of hope struck a deep and optimistic resonance in the hearts and minds of Africans. This parallel movement offers a first clue to the impact of Vatican II in Africa:

Probably in no other continent did the Vatican Council coincide quite so neatly and sympathetically with a major process of secular change as in Africa. … The conciliar themes of localization and pluralism, of the recognition of the positive values of different cultures and even other religious traditions, the new use of the vernacular in the liturgy, the ecumenical rapprochement, all this conformed with the general early 1960s stress on African political and cultural values, on decolonization, on the social necessity of cooperation and unity across the division of tribe, race and religion.[^c40-3]

[^c40-3]: Adrian Hastings, ‘The Council Came to Africa’, in _Vatican II: By Those Who Were There_, ed. Alberic Stacpoole (London: Geoffrey Chapman, 1986), 315–16.

**[p. 659]** Yet, this correlation of the promise and hope of Vatican II for the Church and the wave of socio-political change in Africa needs to be critically examined before being adopted as the basis for analysing and assessing Africa’s reception of the council.

For setting this positive evaluation in context, two points are noteworthy. First, we may not overlook the fact that nationalism/independence and the conciliar event represented distinct interests and divergent preoccupations in Africa. Whereas the former interest was orchestrated by mission-bred and mission-educated Africans who hardly distinguished colonial adventure from missionary agenda, the latter interest was led by missionary ecclesiastics and clergy suspicious of the pulsating waves of political emancipation and self-determination. In the aftermath of independence, tension surfaced promptly between the missionary Church and nascent political regimes around issues of schools, the political system of one-party [^c40-4] rule, and an elitist cast of ideologues eager to appropriate the spoils of independence. Second, Adrian Hastings, to whom is credited these positive impressions of Vatican II in relation to Africa, wrote at a time much closer to the council and, as I will point out in this chapter, from the perspective of arguably the most vigorous promoter and advocate of the directives of Vatican II. Much has transpired on the continent since then. Looking back sixty years, the temptation is strong to conclude that just as the promise and hope of political independence failed to deliver progress and development, so too did the _aggiornamento_ of Vatican II become tepid in Africa.

[^c40-4]: Hastings, _History of African Christianity_, 151–52.

This chapter examines some of the factors that have conditioned and shaped Africa’s reception of Vatican II. It premises this exploration on the thesis that, due to a complex interplay of personalities, attitudes, events, and contexts, what was heralded as a radical renewal and change in direction, or an _aggiornamento_, for the Church has progressed along a chequered path on the African continent.

I begin by analysing three primary factors that were determinant of Africa’s role during the sessions of Vatican II. These factors fall under the broad categories of demography, ecclesiology, and theology. Following this analysis, I will give a concise account of the reception and principal achievement of Vatican II for the Church in Africa—using appropriate examples—and indicate paths to the future inspired by the spirit of the council.

It is important to concede the spatial limitation of this analysis, focusing as it does primarily on Eastern Africa—an option influenced largely by the relative scarcity of materials covering the entire continent of [^c40-5] **[p. 660]** Africa. Besides, considering the characteristic diversity of the continent, any account of Vatican II’s reception, impact, and implementation would be of necessity partial and offer only a basic overview.

[^c40-5]: The following are useful sources: Alfred Guy Bwidi Kitambala, _Les Évêques d’Afrique et le Concile Vatican II: Participation,_ _contribution et application jusqu’à l’Assemblée spéciale du synode des évêques de 1994_ (Paris: L’Harmattan, 2010); Jean- Paul Messina, ‘L’Église d’Afrique au concile Vatican II: Origines de l’Assemblée spéciale du synode des évêques pour l’Afrique’, _Mélanges de sciences religieuses_ 51, no. 3 (1994): 279–95; Tharcisse Tshibangu, _Le Concile Vatican II et l’Église_ _africaine (1960–2010): Mise en œuvre du Concile dans l’Église d’Afrique_ (Kinshasa: L’Épiphanie; Paris: Karthala, 2012).

### 3. Factors Influencing Africa’s Participation at Vatican II

#### Counting Bodies and Weighing Voices

If we proceed from the assumption of the adage that _synodus episcoporum est_ (‘the synod/council is of the bishops’), we could perhaps form a preliminary impression of Vatican II and its impact on _ecclesia in Africa._ In the first place, African bishops constituted a small percentage of the overall composition of the council. The presence of Africa in terms of representation by so-called native bishops and ecclesial leaders was numerically insignificant. Besides the question of meagre representation, an additional focal point of analysis is the influence that this minority had on the proceedings and outcomes of the council. It would not be an exaggeration to contend that none of the African bishops present at Vatican II had a major voice or played a decisive role, a factor routinely attributed to their unpreparedness in regard to the complex themes, [^c40-6] documents, and conciliar process. Those who had a major voice as council fathers or as _periti_ were [^c40-7] primarily expatriates.

[^c40-6]: Albert de Jong, _The Challenge of Vatican II in East Africa: The Contribution of Dutch Missionaries to the Implementation of_ _Vatican II in Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, and Malawi, 1965–1975_ (Nairobi: Paulines, 2004), 28; Hastings, _History of African_ _Christianity_, 168.

[^c40-7]: African voices at the council raised issues of pertinence to the continent that unfortunately were not reflected adequately in the final documents. An example of this was the matter of tribalism and ‘the feminist cause’ reputedly championed at the council by Archbishop Malula of Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo (formerly Leopoldville, Zaire). See Denis Hurley, _Vatican II: Keeping the Dream Alive_ (Pietermaritzburg: Cluster, 2005), 105–6. Overall, however, the intervention of African bishops was limited to pithy comments and reactions to particular issues. See e.g. ibid., 108, 109, 129, 138. By far the most active in terms of number of oral interventions and written submissions at the council were Archbishop Denis Hurley (Durban, South Africa) and the first African cardinal, Laurean Rugambwa (Bukoba, Tanzania). See Philippe Denis, ‘The Historical Significance of Hurley’s Contribution to Vatican II’, in _Vatican II: Keeping the Dream Alive_, ed. Denis Hurley (Pietermaritzburg: Cluster, 2005), 207–8. That the voices of African bishops at Vatican II had limited impact or influence is further confirmed by the fact that no African bishop appears in John W. O’Malley’s list of ‘Council Participants Frequently Mentioned’, in _What Happened at Vatican II_ (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2008), 321–28.

Historical accounts of Africa’s presence and participation at Vatican II identify some of the leading figures who flew the banner of the continent. Expectedly, almost all of them were expatriates. One of the leading bishops at Vatican II from Africa was the charismatic and energetic Bishop Joseph Blomjous of Mwanza, Tanzania. Alongside him was Bishop Vincent McCauley of Fort Portal, Uganda, variously characterized by [^c40-8] **[p. 661]** Richard Gribble as a ‘driving force’, ‘catalyst’, and ‘spokesman’ of the bishops from East Africa. The insignificant participation of African-born bishops at the council would appear to be confirmed by Dutch church historian Albert de Jong’s claim that Dutch bishops ghost-wrote the interventions of African [^c40-9] bishops. This claim, however, should not be generalized. Archbishop Denis Hurley’s account of events at the council proffers some qualification of de Jong’s assertion. While Hurley—himself a leading figure from Africa at the council—received help from some prominent European _periti_, his interventions reflected his own authorship and his untiring appeal for a council that is pastoral in its approach to the issues of the [^c40-10] day. Yet, contrary to Hastings’s contention that the participation and contribution of Africa was ‘not [^c40-11] insignificant’, the view held by Philippe Denis—and shared by Patrick Kalilombe, noted above—is representative of the consensus among scholars regarding the influence of African bishops at Vatican II:

[^c40-8]: Richard Gribble, _The Implementation of Vatican II in Eastern Africa: The Contribution of Bishop Vincent McCauley, CSC_ (Lewiston, NY: Edwin Mellon, 2009), 70, 74.

[^c40-9]: de Jong, _The Challenge of Vatican II in East Africa_, 30.

[^c40-10]: Hurley, _Vatican II_, 30, 162–78.

[^c40-11]: Hastings, _History of African Christianity_, 173.

Most observers agree, however, that the African bishops failed significantly to influence the work of the Council itself. The African representation—260 of a total 2,358 at the first session in 1962— had relatively little weight in the final outcome of the Council. The themes discussed were perceived as ‘too European’ not only by the 61 African-born bishops present at the opening of the Council, but also by the missionary bishops.[^c40-12]

[^c40-12]: Denis, ‘Historical Significance of Hurley’s Contribution’, 197–98.

Notwithstanding the numerical insignificance and theological unpreparedness of African council fathers, the accounts also concur in stressing that the modus operandi of African bishops during the conciliar [^c40-13] sessions was well organized and highly efficient. A minor but highly symbolic fact was the presence of a lay auditor from Togo, Eusebe Adjakpley.

[^c40-13]: A first-hand account by Hurley corroborates the claim of organizational superiority of African bishops at the council: ‘The African Bishops had not wasted any time in getting themselves organised. South Africa had taken the lead in regard to the English-speaking African bishops and secured the use of a very convenient hall in a street oft the Via della Conciliazione … The African bishops got together in two groups, the Anglophone (i.e. English-speaking) and the Francophone (the French- speaking).’ Hurley, _Vatican II_, 23–24. See also O’Malley, _What Happened at Vatican II_, 122.

As mentioned in the Introduction, it is possible, with the benefit of hindsight, to read the event, outcomes, and impact of Vatican II in regard to the Church in Africa in a more positive light. It is interesting, for example, to note the divergent views of Matthew Hassan Kukah, Bishop of Sokoto (Nigeria), who argues that Vatican II was a ‘catalyst’ for the growth of the Church in Africa. For Kukah, although

10% of the 2000 Council Fathers came from Africa … some of the fruits of the Council … were, in **[p. 662]** turn, positive developments for the Church in Africa. These include the emergence of the local clergy; the translation of the Bible into local languages; ecumenical and interreligious dialogue; [^c40-14] the involvement of the lay faithful in the Church and society.

[^c40-14]: Cited in Catholic Information Service for Africa (CISA).

Kukah’s appraisal contrasts remarkably with that of another eminent African theologian, Laurenti Magesa. When Magesa asks, ‘was the African theological and pastoral view present at the Council?’ his response is unequivocal: ‘quite frankly, not really!’[^c40-15]

[^c40-15]: Laurenti Magesa, _The Post-Conciliar Church in Africa: No Turning Back the Clock_ (Nairobi: CUEA, 2016), 1.

#### A Church in the Making

The second factor is ecclesiological. In the early 1960s, the Church in Africa could hardly be qualifled as ‘African’. As the preceding point demonstrates, in terms of leadership and direction, the Church in Africa prior to and during Vatican II represented a native outpost of a Eurocentric ecclesial organization. Understandably, therefore, the concerns of the universal Church as outlined and debated at the council barely intersected with the pressing issues that the ‘young’ churches in places like Africa had to contend with. Thus, as the conciliar drama unfolded in the _aula_, and European and North American ecclesiastical grandees fought running battles across doctrinal and ideological lines, African bishops watched with bemusement and fascination variously as spectators, cheerleaders, and a voting bloc.[^c40-16]

[^c40-16]: O’Malley, _What Happened at Vatican II_, 291–95.

#### African Theology en route

The third and final point concerns the status of theology in Africa as local production. In the 1960s, African theology was still in its formative years. This perception of provisionality remains an important criterion for [^c40-17] assessing the history and development of theological scholarship in Africa. At the time of Vatican II, the popular debate centred on the desirability, feasibility, and possibility of African theology as a viable discipline. Consequently, at this watershed event, Africa lacked the theological expertise and institutional capacity to engage the pertinent issues on Vatican II’s agenda. A telling illustration of this lacuna appears in the composition of the African delegation. Alongside the majority of expatriate bishops, the corps of _periti_ [^c40-18] was exclusively European and North American. Unlike ‘the bishops of the Western European bloc’, the **[p. 663]** council’s African contingent did not have ‘the advantage of this magnificent pool of theologians and also of Scripture scholars, historians, liturgical experts and prominent promoters of lay apostolates, social [^c40-19] concern and catechetics’. Regrettable as this observation might seem at first glance, upon closer examination it contains a positive element in regard to the topic under consideration. It can be argued that to a large extent, the impetus to develop an African theology came from the council: ‘Vatican II brought to Africa a theology and a catechesis whose central themes showed how the power of Jesus Christ supplanted the power of local gods. This theology became concrete in the church’s sacramental system where signs and [^c40-20] words expressed initiation, maturity, healing, forgiving, and nourishment.’

[^c40-17]: Agbonkhianmeghe E. Orobator, ‘The Sky Is Wide Enough: A Historico-Critical Appraisal of Theological Activity and Method in Africa’, _Hekima Review_ 40 (2009): 34–44.

[^c40-18]: Hastings, ‘The Council Came to Africa’, 316.

[^c40-19]: Hurley, _Vatican II_, 71–72.

[^c40-20]: Bede Jagoe, ‘Vatican II Comes to Africa’, _Worship_ 79 (2005): 548.

The factors outlined above provide some evidence of the unpreparedness of the Church in Africa for Vatican II. The cadre of ecclesial leadership and, even less, the body of the Church in Africa was not prepared for the council.

### 4. Reception and Implementation

Richard McBrien defines reception as the ‘process by which the body of the faithful, or a significant portion [^c40-21] thereof, accepts and abides by an official teaching or disciplinary decree of the hierarchical Church’. Reception, however, is not a straightforward process; in Church history, councils have encountered objections, resistance, and rejection. Norman Tanner, a historian of church councils, notes that ‘other major councils, such as Nicaea I or Chalcedon, had laboured receptions precisely because of the importance [^c40-22] and challenging nature of their teaching. So too with Vatican II.’

[^c40-21]: Richard P. McBrien, _The Church: The Evolution of Catholicism_ (New York: HarperOne, 2008), 322.

[^c40-22]: Norman Tanner, ‘How Novel Was Vatican II?’ _Asian Horizons_ 6 (2012): 408.

As mentioned above, the event of Vatican II paralleled significant historic political events in Africa in the 1960s. The intersection of events held out fresh promise for Church and society in Africa. ‘The fresh new breeze of _aggiornamento_ and the new energy of the political and cultural revolutions in Eastern Africa made [^c40-23] Vatican II quite acceptable to the African Church.’ This assertion calls for a twofold qualification. First, it presupposes a homogeneous and established reality called the ‘_African_ Church’. At the time of the council, such a reality did not exist; like African theology, at best, it was still in the making. Second, acceptability would have been limited to the hierarchy, largely comprised of expatriate missionary bishops and clergy, and not to any recognizable, informed, and active community of African Christians. The general assessment is that in ‘the rather untheological world of the Catholic Church in Africa’, Vatican II had very little impact [^c40-24] **[p. 664]** on the ground, beyond academic circles and hierarchical concerns. Yet de Jong’s contention that Vatican II ‘formed the starting point for the self-reliance, the inculturation and the renewal of the African [^c40-25] Church’ is largely correct, if interpreted in a strict sense, that is, as a task that was yet to be fully accomplished rather than as a finished product.

[^c40-23]: Gribble, _Implementation of Vatican II in Eastern Africa_, 77.

[^c40-24]: Hastings, ‘Council Came to Africa’, 317.

[^c40-25]: de Jong, _The Challenge of Vatican II in East Africa_, 30.
