The reception and implementation of Vatican II in Africa can be assessed in the context of a broad set of factors that either facilitated or impeded this process. These factors are not exhaustive. The following represents and illustrates some of the most important considerations.

#### The Challenge of Literacy

Vatican II produced a corpus of constitutions, decrees, and declarations of varying themes, degrees of authority, lengths, and styles for dissemination, study, and implementation in the Church. ‘Indeed the texts [^c40-26] of Vatican II, in words, amount to twice that of all the first seven councils taken together.’ For a continent steeped in orality and unremarkable for its literacy levels, this factor constituted a formidable challenge. The texts of Vatican II, delivered in high ecclesiastical Latin, would have been incomprehensible to the vast majority of African Christians and clergy in the post-conciliar years. ‘The average lay person with no understanding of English had no possibility whatever of reading and studying the Vatican II documents [in [^c40-27] Latin].’

[^c40-26]: Tanner, ‘How Novel Was Vatican II?’, 404.

[^c40-27]: de Jong, _The Challenge of Vatican II in East Africa_, 34.

The linguistic challenge was equally true for bishops and priests, as Hastings points out: ‘The bishops returned to their dioceses with a heap of Latin documents to redirect a clergy far less informed about what had been going on than their counterparts in Europe but also, for the most part, far more willing to be [^c40-28] redirected. The laity, of course, were still more uninformed.’ The clergy (and laity) were as unprepared for the implementation of Vatican II as the latter’s documents were inaccessible and incomprehensible. This [^c40-29] situation, however, was mitigated by approximations of translation in English and Swahili.

[^c40-28]: Hastings, ‘Council Came to Africa’, 316.

[^c40-29]: Bishop Vincent McCauley of Fort Portal, Uganda, for example, published and distributed English texts of the documents of Vatican II. Yet, when it came to accessibility and familiarisation with the documents of Vatican II, De Jong suggests they were ‘probably the least read and studied books in the presbyteries’. See de Jong, _The Challenge of Vatican II in East Africa_, 33.

To extend this argument on literacy, from a historical perspective, the reception of Vatican II and the realization (or lack thereof) of its promise in Africa were the result of an absence of a sustained initiative to [^c40-30] inform the people of God ‘on the mind of the Church, as expressed in Vatican II’. There is, however, evidence that some bishops created platforms in their dioceses to speak informally about their experiences [^c40-31] **[p. 665]** at Vatican II to a mixed audience of clergy, religious, and laypeople. While this practice would have been common in the post-conciliar years, it gradually declined as the excitement of renewal and reform ebbed, and interest in the study of Vatican II’s documents receded to the exclusive domain of seminary formation.

[^c40-30]: Alex B. Chima, ‘Africanising the Liturgy: Where Are We Twenty Years after Vatican II?’, _African Ecclesial Review_ 25 (1983): 291.

[^c40-31]: Hurley, _Vatican II_, 32.

#### Semper Idem: Resistance of Bishops and Priests

A recurring theme in the assessment of the reception and implementation of Vatican II in Africa concerns the attitude of bishops and priests. De Jong lambastes African bishops and clergy for deliberately mounting resistance against orientation sessions and the implementation of Vatican II. The reasons he adduces for their formidable resistance stem from various factors. Steeped as they were in a legalistic, clericalist, and Ultramontane theological upbringing, they showed little sympathy for indigenous religion and culture as useful sources of the inculturation of liturgy and catechetical reform. Nor were they enamoured of the prospect of the diminishment of clerical authority, social status, and living standard that a post-conciliar ecclesiology seemed to indicate with the recognition of the important roles of the laity in the Church. The reactions of African bishops and clergy to Vatican II seemed an exercise in surreptitious self-preservation [^c40-32] and safeguarding of ecclesiastical and clerical privileges. This is de Jong’s account; while it is too biased to form the basis of a general statement on the attitude and positions of African ecclesiastics and clergy vis-à-vis Vatican II, it merits further critical consideration, as will become clear further on.

[^c40-32]: de Jong, _The Challenge of Vatican II in East Africa_, 83–89.

Notwithstanding the challenges posed by the illiteracy of ill-informed laity and the opposition of conservative and ill-prepared bishops and priests, evidence exists of credible attempts at propagating and implementing the directives and orientations of Vatican II in Africa. By way of illustration, three such attempts are noteworthy: the writings of Adrian Hastings, the publications of the _African Ecclesial Review_, and the work of the Pastoral Institute of the Association of Member Episcopal Conferences of East Africa (AMECEA) in Gaba, Uganda.

#### Adrian Hastings

Available resources on the reception and implementation of Vatican II in Africa, particularly in East Africa, give considerable credit to the initiative, effort, and ingenuity of British Roman Catholic priest, theologian, and historian Adrian Hastings. ‘Hastings personally stoked the fires of Vatican II enthusiasm through his [^c40-33] publication of a fortnightly bulletin.’ In response to the initiative of the AMECEA bishops to launch a **[p. 666]** programme of post-conciliar re-education and reorientation for Kenya, Malawi, Tanzania, Uganda, and Zambia, Hastings produced critically acclaimed study guides and commentaries on the documents of the council pared down to the level of comprehension of missionary priests and religious, Indigenous clergy, and laypeople. Over a period of two years, this fortnightly bulletin, ‘Post Vatican II: A Guide to the Documents of the Second Vatican Council’, became the staple of conferences, seminars, workshops, meetings, and discussion groups on Vatican II of priests and religious, and, in some cases, of catechists and laypeople in several parts of Africa and beyond. One beneficiary of Hastings’s publication attests to its [^c40-34] significant impact: ‘If there has been one factor that made Vatican II known, then that is it!’ Regrettably, Hastings’s initiative was short-lived.

[^c40-33]: Gribble, _Implementation of Vatican II in Eastern Africa_, 77; see also 155.

[^c40-34]: Cited in de Jong, _The Challenge of Vatican II in East Africa_, 35.

#### African Ecclesial Review

Hastings himself noted two other major factors that created ‘a real wave of pastoral renewal’ in Africa following the conclusion of Vatican II; namely, the founding of the _African Ecclesial Review_ (_AFER_) and the [^c40-35] Pastoral Institute at Gaba. Regarding the former, ‘in addition to the Council documents and the authorized commentary by Hastings, the pastoral theological periodical, _African Ecclesial Review_ … was an important [^c40-36] factor in the process of assimilating Vatican II’. In the wake of Vatican II, _AFER_ gained prominence as the leading journal of theology in English-speaking Africa.

[^c40-35]: Hastings, ‘Council Came to Africa’, 319.

[^c40-36]: de Jong, _The Challenge of Vatican II in East Africa_, 35.

Prior to and during the council, _AFER_ published columns on happenings at Vatican II. In the first two decades following the council, some of the most critical and incisive analyses of conciliar documents, themes, and innovations appeared in _AFER_. It would later include full texts of the conciliar documents and critical commentaries. Articles in _AFER_ treated topics as varied as catechetics, sacraments, liturgy, interreligious dialogue, inculturation, ecumenism, and seminary formation in the context of the Church in Africa.

Regrettably, the publications would fizzle out as the years went by, giving credence to Hastings’s poignant observation about the fleeting lifespan of Vatican II’s reception and implementation in Africa: ‘By the late 1970s the period of post-conciliar innovation was well-nigh over … Clericalism at the top but congregationalism at the bottom proved the _de facto_ compromise of the post-conciliar African Church.’[^c40-37]

[^c40-37]: Hastings, ‘Council Came to Africa’, 322.

#### AMECEA Pastoral Institute

One institution that bears lasting testimony to the legacy of Vatican II for Africa is the AMECEA Pastoral **[p. 667]** Institute. The launch of this initiative responded to the need to communicate the vision, promote the teaching, and implement the guidelines of Vatican II in all parts of the nascent African Church. In the words of one eyewitness:

The decision of the AMECEA Bishops to launch a pastoral and catechetical institute was a deliberate attempt to meet the needs made more urgent by the context described above: the need to bring to grass-root level the doctrinal and pastoral renewal of Vatican II; the need to help pastoral workers to update themselves in the fleld of catechetical and pastoral work; the need for personal renewal.[^c40-38] He continues: ‘The academic input (of Gaba) would be geared towards updating and deepening the existing wealth of knowledge, in the light of the teaching of Vatican II.’[^c40-39]

[^c40-38]: Jean-Claude Lemay, ‘Gaba: A Story of Renewal’, _African Ecclesial Review_ 26 (1984): 23.

[^c40-39]: Ibid., 24.

Concretely, this programme included ‘a two-week period set aside for the study of the Vatican II documents’. With time, it expanded into a three-week course on the documents of Vatican II. The profile of the initial participants in this programme reflected ‘the mixity [_sic_] of the local church … priest, religious, [^c40-40] women and men, and laity, African and non-African’. In addition to pastoral and catechetical training, for a few short years, the Pastoral Institute conducted experimentation in appropriately adapted and creative African liturgies in response to the inspiration and directives of _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ (_SC_), the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy.

[^c40-40]: Ibid.

As with the previous efforts considered in this chapter, with the passing of the years, the impact of this institute as a prime facilitator and effective vehicle for the implementation of the directives and teaching of Vatican II would gradually diminish. Interestingly, this decline is attributable to the manifest conservatism within the Church in Africa that resisted the orientation of Vatican II. Considering its status as a tool for implementing Vatican II, the Pastoral Institute owed its establishment and existence to the bishops of AMECEA. Curiously, however, the latter took exception to the ‘liberal’ and ‘progressive’ direction of the Institute and adopted measures that not only curtailed the effectiveness of its programmes, but would also essentially engineer its gradual and eventual demise.[^c40-41]

[^c40-41]: de Jong, _The Challenge of Vatican II in East Africa_, 189; Gribble, _The Implementation of Vatican II in Eastern Africa_, 159.

### 5. Sixty Years On: The Council’s African Legacy

The legacy of Vatican II is a matter of contention and debate among theologians in the world Church. The **[p. 668]** same situation holds in Africa. Quite clearly, as is evident in the foregoing, the perspectives of historians on Vatican II and Africa differ. These perspectives are not straightforwardly descriptive, but thematic and fragmentary, and they contain multiple points of convergence and divergence. One major factor of interpretation lies in the fact that, so far, most of the accounts and interpretations are written by expatriates, reflecting interests, adopting methodology, and applying criteria that, far from being false, are [^c40-42] radically partial. Unsurprisingly, favourable and flattering portrayals of the contributions of expatriate [^c40-43] bishops and clergy dominate existing historical accounts. A comprehensive, critical, and scholarly account of Vatican II and Africa awaits realization; such an undertaking would avoid the pitfall of simply narrating Africa’s presence and encounter with Vatican II in broad strokes. Conflicting perspectives aside, the positive impulses released by Vatican II for the Church in Africa are beyond dispute:

[^c40-42]: An important exception is Magesa’s _The Post-Conciliar Church in Africa._

[^c40-43]: Notably, de Jong, _The Challenge of Vatican II in East Africa_; Gribble, _Implementation of Vatican II in Eastern Africa._ De Jong’s bias is unmistakable in his claim that ‘Dutch missionaries and their colleagues from other countries were the reformers and renewers of the Church, while the African clergy in general remained dismissive of the renewals because of their clinging to conservative ecclesiological positions’ (187).

For Bishops of the Catholic Church in East Africa, as for Bishops everywhere, the Council was not only an impressive assembly of the Universal Apostolic College; it was also a deep experience of learning, at times challenging and even disturbing, but also liberating and rewarding … For the leaders of the Church in East Africa, the sharing of the Council’s experience became a priority. How could such renewal as they lived at Vatican II be brought to their people and in particular to their close collaborators in the ministry?[^c40-44]

[^c40-44]: Lemay, ‘Gaba: A Story of Renewal’, 23.

Still, there are those, like Vincent Donovan, who contended that Vatican II’s programme for ‘young churches’ produced a carbon copy of Eurocentric ecclesiology laden with all the trappings and flaws of the [^c40-45] Western Church. Donovan’s unflattering characterization should not surprise us. As mentioned above, an ‘African’ Church could hardly be said to exist at the time of Vatican II.

[^c40-45]: Vincent J. Donovan, _Christianity Rediscovered: 25th Anniversary Edition_, 2nd ed. (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2003), 97, 131.

Nevertheless, there are several useful areas for positively assessing the impact of Vatican II on the Church in Africa in the past, at present, and for the future. Three such areas may be found distributed in the analyses of African theologians since Vatican II.

#### Dining with the Devil

In the missionary Church, a key challenge of Christianity is how to fashion a constructive relationship with **[p. 669]** indigenous African religion. Despite the deliberate attempts of Eurocentric missionaries and evangelists, Christianity could neither circumvent nor suppress the claims of indigenous religion in Africa. In general, ‘the encounter between Christianity and indigenous beliefs, rituals, and customs involved a massive and [^c40-46] continuous process of interpretation and reassessment’. In many instances, ignorance and antagonism dominated the relationship and skewed the process, judging by the approach of missionaries’ obstinate commitment to their avowed mission to demonize, oppose, and eliminate all manifestations of indigenous religion and worship. Vatican II inaugurated a new approach that acknowledged the claims of ‘other religions’ and attempted fresh interpretation and reassessment of interreligious encounter, while simultaneously tenaciously asserting the superiority of Christianity and the pre-eminence of the Roman Catholic Church as the sacrament of salvation.

[^c40-46]: Richard Gray, _Christianity, the Papacy, and Mission in Africa_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2012), 155.

_Nostra Aetate_ (_NA_), the Declaration on the Relation of the Church to Non-Christian Religions, and _Ad Gentes_ (_AG_), the Decree on the Mission Activity of the Church, provided the basis for adopting a fresh approach to non-Christian religions in the missionary context of Africa. In particular, _Nostra Aetate_, as Emmanuel Ifesieh has noted, ‘is in some ways one of the Council’s most radical and far-reaching products, and it has many implications for the Church in Africa’.[^c40-47]

[^c40-47]: Emmanuel I. Ifesieh, ‘Vatican II and Traditional Religion’, _African Ecclesial Review_ 25 (1983): 230.

Although African religion—perhaps glibly subsumed under the category of people who seek God ‘in shadows and images’ (_Lumen Gentium_ 16)—did not get a mention in these seminal documents, it is reasonable to argue that if one reads between the lines, Vatican II led to a shift in attitude vis-à-vis indigenous religion in Africa. The fundamental attitude of considering the latter solely and merely as _preparatio evangelii_ remained dominant, but Vatican II opened the way for the emergence of a marginally more sensitive approach that acknowledges goodness, truth, and holiness in other religions (_AG_ 3, 9, 11, 22; [^c40-48] _NA_ 2; _SC_ 37–40). Furthermore, the openness towards dialogue with and respect for indigenous African religion as contained in the analysis that exists in the corpus of African theology owes its origins to Vatican [^c40-49] II.

[^c40-48]: Eugene Hillman, _Toward an African Christianity: Inculturation Applied_ (New York: Paulist, 1993), 38–40.

[^c40-49]: Laurenti Magesa, ‘On Speaking Terms: African Religion and Christianity in Dialogue’, in _Reconciliation, Justice, and Peace:_ _The Second African Synod_, ed. Agbonkhianmeghe E. Orobator (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2011), 26.

#### Inculturation—To Drum or Not to Drum

In light of the preceding point, within the wider fleld of theological scholarship, a central topic that claims the attention of the post-conciliar generation of African theologians concerns defining the meaning, delineating the scope, and regulating the application of the principle of inculturation. The primary aim of **[p. 670]** this process, as Eugene Hillman put it, is to determine ‘whether and to what extent Christian faith is [^c40-50] supposed to bypass, negate or affirm the claims any culture has on the loyalty of its people’. Viewing it as a theological initiative or project, we can rightly trace the origins of inculturation of the Church to the teaching, guidelines, and direction of Vatican II. De Jong emphatically argues that ‘the foremost driving force for inculturation of the Church in this region [East Africa] consists in the new theological perceptions [^c40-51] of Vatican II’. The scope is continental. Yet, ironically, the direction of this project, at least in the initial phase of the implementation of the council, was not only attenuated but also strongly contested by a constellation of local factors and personalities.

[^c40-50]: Hillman, _Toward an African Christianity_, 29.

[^c40-51]: de Jong, _The Challenge of Vatican II in East Africa_, 187. See Gribble, _Implementation of Vatican II in Eastern Africa_, 78–82.

De Jong also argues that the inculturation issuing from Vatican II was superficial. Not only does he regret this superficiality, but also, as already mentioned, he lays the blame squarely at the feet of a conservative African episcopate and clergy. Credit for whatever simulacrum of post-conciliar adaptation, Africanization, or inculturation that existed belonged to European bishops and clergy, not to—if I might paraphrase—their [^c40-52] inferior, illiterate, and retrograde African counterparts bereft of theological imagination. This statement oversimplifles attitudes, facts, and processes in the Church in Africa vis-à-vis Vatican II. It is largely biased, even though it identifles some exceptional cases of outright resistance. It is possible and necessary to perceive things in a different optic.

[^c40-52]: de Jong, _The Challenge of Vatican II in East Africa_, 186–90; Gribble, _Implementation of Vatican II in Eastern Africa_, 80–81.

Hastings, who wields incontestable authority on this matter, contradicts de Jong’s claims and provides a list of outstanding African ecclesial leaders, pioneers, and reformers inspired by the spirit of Vatican II, which de Jong’s partial and biased account does not consider. The post-conciliar movement of inculturation, reform, and renewal benefited immensely from the activities of African ecclesial leaders who ‘were men of [^c40-53] imaginative commitment, exuberance and charism’. The cast of post-conciliar reformers included Bishops Joseph Malula (Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo), Christopher Mwoleka (Rulenge, Tanzania), Peter Sarpong (Kumasi, Ghana), Denis Hurley (Durban, South Africa), Patrick Kalilombe (Lilongwe, Malawi), Peter Dery (Wa, Ghana), and Emmanuel Milingo (Lusaka, Zambia). These ecclesial leaders understood post-conciliar liturgical, sacramental, and theological inculturation as constitutive of the mission of the Church in Africa.

[^c40-53]: Hastings, ‘Council Came to Africa’, 321.

Naturally, inculturation has created a rich terrain for evaluating the depth and extent of renewal generated by Vatican II in Africa. A much-debated and celebrated quintessence of this renewal was the introduction of African music and instrumentation into Catholic liturgy, the focal point of which was the African drum. [^c40-54] While some would dismiss this as superficiality, others would perceive it as an initiative of immense **[p. 671]** symbolic value for the identity of the African Church. ‘The drum was the great symbol of post-Vatican II liturgy—a symbol at once of cultural pluralism and popular participation, the arrival of an active laity, but still more the arrival of Africa in all its vibrant, populist, rhythmic vitality as a major reality within [^c40-55] Catholicism.’

[^c40-54]: de Jong, _The Challenge of Vatican II in East Africa_, 181–85, 189.

[^c40-55]: Hastings, ‘Council Came to Africa’, 320.

Taking account of the liturgical innovation inspired by Vatican II, especially via _Sacrosanctum Concilium,_ opinion on the progress in liturgical adaptation and inculturation in Africa has been consistently divided. Twenty years after Vatican II, Alex Chima made the following assessment: ‘Our liturgy is still far from having African “flesh and blood”, as Vatican II, indirectly, says it should.’ He concluded: ‘It seems we have [^c40-56] not gone much further than the stage of relatively insignificant adaptations.’ To recall de Jong’s position, if Chima’s analysis is correct, African bishops and priests are to blame for resisting post-conciliar liturgical adaptation, whereas Dutch missionaries led the process of creative liturgical adaptation. Through de Jong’s lens, one sees that it was only European ecclesiastics who presided over the presence of Africa at Vatican II and controlled the implementation of the teaching and directives of the council in some parts of Africa.

[^c40-56]: Chima, ‘Africanising the Liturgy’, 283, 290.

As shown above, however, it may be questioned whether de Jong’s perspective does justice to the wider continental context. The situation in West and Central Africa could hardly be described as superficial, uninspiring, and lacking creativity or imagination. In these regions, it can be argued that Vatican II created a [^c40-57] liturgical revolution in Africa of immense practical and pastoral significance. In Central Africa, for example, in the aftermath of Vatican II, the legendary African ecclesiastic Cardinal Malula of Kinshasa initiated and led liturgical reforms that have lasted well into the twenty-first century, particularly in the _Missel romain pour les diocèses du Zaïre_. Undoubtedly, the impetus for this reform emanated from the inculturation movement triggered by Vatican II. A first-hand account from Nigeria in West Africa corroborates this claim: ‘Led by the themes of Vatican II, sensitivity to popular religion and culture and a commitment to inculturation made it possible to refashion liturgy, celebrating rites to be relevant and familiar, intelligible, and also emotionally stimulating … Now there was permission for Africans to be [^c40-58] Africans.’

[^c40-57]: Hastings, ‘Council Came to Africa’, 320. For examples from West, Central, and East Africa, see Elochukwu E. Uzukwu, _Worship as Body Language: Introduction to Christian Worship: An Orientation_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 1997), 270– 317.

[^c40-58]: Jagoe, ‘Vatican II Comes to Africa’, 550. See also Brian Hearne, ‘Conciliar Fellowship and the Local Church: A Catholic View from Africa’, _Ecumenical Review_ 29 (1977): 129.

In contemporary African theology and ecclesiology, inculturation represents an effective methodology of reflection, analysis, and praxis.[^c40-59]

[^c40-59]: See Laurenti Magesa, _Anatomy of Inculturation: Transforming the Church in Africa_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2004).

#### Ecclesial Pan-Africanism and Results-Oriented Particular Churches

**[p. 672]** Another significant development that owes its origins to Vatican II is the awareness of African ecclesial [^c40-60] leaders ‘that they belonged together and should work in collaboration’. The immediate outcome of this realization was the creation of continental and regional forums. ‘The collegiality experienced by the African bishops at Vatican II generated action for some form of permanent episcopal association, linking all African [^c40-61] countries’. One example of this episcopal association is the Symposium of Episcopal Conferences of Africa and Madagascar (SECAM), founded in 1969. For several decades, SECAM has served as the umbrella body for episcopal conferences on the continent in to coordinate activities in the areas of evangelization, theological formation, social action, leadership development, and pastoral initiative.

[^c40-60]: Kalilombe, ‘Effect of the Council on World Catholicism: Africa’, 311.

[^c40-61]: Gribble, _Implementation of Vatican II in Eastern Africa_, 164.

The momentum for creating and sustaining pan-African movements inspired the establishment and development of fledgling regional and national bodies. An example of a highly effective regional body is AMECEA. This association of bishops’ conferences in East Africa has developed an admirable profile in the African Church in the area of regional ecclesiastical collaboration. Arguably, the most concrete and best achievement of AMECEA is its pioneering role in developing small Christian communities as a new way of [^c40-62] being Church and establishing a flagship higher education institution, the Catholic University of Eastern Africa in Nairobi, Kenya.

[^c40-62]: See Joseph G. Healey and Jeanne Hinton, eds., _Small Christian Communities Today: Capturing the New Moment_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2005). Joseph Healey, ‘1961–2015 Timeline in the History and Development of Small Christian Communities (SCCs) in Africa Especially Eastern Africa’, _Small Christian Communities Global Collaborative Website_, accessed 6 May 2019, http://smallchristiancommunities.org/1961-2015-timeline-in-the-history-and-development-of-small-christian- communities-sccs-in-africa-especially-eastern-africa/.

Taken as a whole, these organs, forums, or platforms of ecclesiastical collaboration stand as structural, [^c40-63] contextual, and appropriate expressions of the conciliar idea of ‘particular churches’ (_AG_ 22). Yet, reflecting on the six decades of ecclesial growth and development in Africa since Vatican II, such optimistic characterization would seem contradicted by the intense centralization and concentration of the understanding of Church in hierarchical structures of governance and control. At least in Africa, the promise or optimism of national and regional ecclesial structures as credible and vibrant loci of the Church and embodiment of catholicity has been fulfilled only partially. This, however, is in contrast to the growing prominence of national episcopal conferences in dealing with domestic socio-economic and political issues since the 1980s. National conferences continue to be active in the public sphere. Examples of their zones of **[p. 673]** influence include facilitating political transitions, resolving social conflict, and negotiating peace and reconciliation in situations of armed violence. Such focus ad extra remains imbalanced in the absence of a commensurate focus ad intra on organizational and ecclesial matters affecting the Roman Catholic Church.

[^c40-63]: Hearne, ‘Conciliar Fellowship and the Local Church’, 133.

### 6. Conclusion

‘The Church in Africa is greatly indebted to Pope John XXIII and to the Council that he convoked: the Second Vatican Council.’ Thus began Ifesieh’s assessment of two decades of receiving Vatican II and its impact on traditional religion in Africa. His conclusion pays glowing tribute to the legacy of Vatican II for Christianity and the Church in Africa: ‘Vatican II, by its openness to the God-given values in African traditional religion and culture, has initiated a new era for the Church in Africa, when Christianity will no longer appear as a [^c40-64] foreign religion but as one that brings to fulfilment the deepest longings of African religiosity.’ Sixty years after the council, this positive and optimistic assessment bears the endorsement of several theologians and historians in Africa. Although numerically and theologically insignificant, Africa’s dignifled presence and participation at the council contributed to what historian of Vatican II Alberto Melloni designates as ‘multi- [^c40-65] coloured universality’ of the Church.

[^c40-64]: Ifesieh, ‘Vatican II and Traditional Religion’, 230, 236.

[^c40-65]: Alberto Melloni, ‘The Second Vatican Council’, _Asian Horizons_ 6, no. 3 (2012), 431.

The currents of renewal and reform unleashed by the central affirmations of Vatican II continue to wax and [^c40-66] wane against the retaining wall of legalism, clericalism, and conservatism. It goes without saying that all the accounts of the experience and reception of Vatican II in Africa focus on bishops as key players, primary implementers, authoritative interpreters, and incontestable guardians of the legacy of the council. There is nothing surprising about this approach in a Church that continues to labour under clericalist and hierarchical tutelage and where the vast majority of the people of God minister, serve, and worship at the behest of the clergy. Clearly, certain features of the Church in Africa continue to resist and hold out against the renewal and reforms inaugurated by Vatican II. Forms of this resurgent clericalism and conservatism exist in matters of sexual morality, control of liturgical development, gender discrimination, and the exercise of ecclesial authority. This trend directly impacts two aspects of the life of the Church in Africa and beyond. The first concerns the role of the laity, which continues to be subservient to clericalist domination. The second relates to the role of women, which is affirmed with a rhetorical flourish that barely conforms to **[p. 674]** lived reality. Perhaps not unsurprisingly, Bishop Kukah, as many an African bishop would contend, holds a more positive view of the legacy of Vatican II in relation to laity and women:

[^c40-66]: See Adrian Hastings, ‘Opting for Vatican II Plus’, _Journal of Theology for Southern Africa_ 41 (1982): 26.

[Vatican II’s] opening up to the laity has enabled them to bring their academic and professional gifts to the Church, enriching the Church in every aspect and enabling many lay faithful to make major contributions in almost every area of the Catholic Church’s life … More astonishing for the Church has been the vitality of women groups. In most parts of Africa, women remain the most [^c40-67] powerful and most forceful expression of the life and energy that holds the Church.

[^c40-67]: Cited in Catholic Information Service for Africa (CISA).

On both counts, the bishop’s statement represents a piece of historical fiction, not a fact of history.

As I see it, ‘in theory, Vatican II empowered the people of God. However, such empowerment founders at the bridgeheads of clericalism, androcentric opposition to women’s role and contribution in the church, and a fluid definition of the theological self-understanding of the church’.[^c40-68]

[^c40-68]: Agbonkhianmeghe E. Orobator, ‘Did the Council Really Empower the People of God? The Wall of Separation between _Apostolicam Actuositatem_ and _Presbyterorum Ordinis_’, in _The Letter and the Spirit: On the Forgotten Documents of Vatican II_, ed. Annemarie C. Meyer (Leuven, Peeters: 2018), 194. See also Agbonkhianmeghe E. Orobator, _Religion and Faith in Africa:_ _Confessions of an Animist_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2018), 127–51.

As should be clear to a keen observer of the history of Christianity in Africa, notwithstanding the multiple negative factors that have conditioned the reception and limited the implementation of Vatican in the African Church, the impact of this ecclesial watershed limns more than just a trajectory of decline. Since Vatican II, studies in African Christianity provide incontrovertible evidence of demographic progress, [^c40-69] theological creativity, and religious effervescence. In this sense, the Second Vatican Council is best understood within the currents of change and growth in African Christianity. While the council cannot be facilely credited for this growth, nevertheless it laid the foundation for the emergence and existence of a truly local African Church and continues to inspire contextualized theological production.

[^c40-69]: See Philip Jenkins, _The Next Christendom: The Coming of Global Christianity_ (New York: Oxford University Press, 2002); John L. Allen, _The Future Church: How Ten Trends are Revolutionizing the Catholic Church_ (New York: Doubleday, 2009); Kwame Bediako, _Christianity in Africa: The Renewal of a Non-Western Religion_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1995).

Although the ‘letter’ of the Second Vatican Council proved somewhat esoteric, indecipherable, and incomprehensible to the majority of Catholics on a largely non-literate continent, the ‘spirit’ of the council continues to animate, motivate, and support the demographic and theological flourishing of the African Church. Adopting Adrian Hastings’s words, we can sum up the theological and ecclesiological achievement of Vatican II in Africa as follows: ‘The Catholic Church of Africa of the 1980s is unthinkable without Vatican [^c40-70] II and the many great endeavours which followed close upon it.’ Hastings’s claim holds true not only for the 1980s but also for present times.

[^c40-70]: Hastings, ‘Council Came to Africa’, 322.

### Suggested Reading

**[p. 675]** Lowery, Stephanie A. _Identity and Ecclesiology: Their Relationship among Select African Theologians_. Eugene, OR: Pickwick, 2017.

Magesa, Laurenti. _The Post-Conciliar Church in Africa: No Turning Back the Clock_. Nairobi: CUEA Press, 2016.

O’Malley, John W. _What Happened at Vatican II_. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2008.

Orobator, Agbonkhianmeghe E., ed. _The Church We Want: African Catholics Look to Vatican III_. Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2016.

Orobator, Agbonkhianmeghe E. _Religion and Faith in Africa: Confessions of an Animist_. Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2018.

Schultenover, David, ed. _50 Years On: Probing the Riches of Vatican II_. Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2015.

## 41. Reception of Vatican II in Latin America and the

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 676]** To write about the council’s reception in the churches of a continent is a task that calls for a sharp awareness of its limitations. On the one hand, the work of Vatican II encompasses a vast range of topics regarding the life of the Church and its regional theologies. On the other, an enhanced awareness concerning the complexities and diversity of socio-cultural realities including not only national differences, but also the variegated subcultures of each country, has been on the rise, especially in Latin America and the Caribbean. Notwithstanding the multifarious and complex character of these situations, common features of Church life are recognizable enough to allow one to speak of a Latin American and Caribbean reality.

Reflecting upon the council’s continental reception, one immediately notices the growing awareness of being a regional Church with its own singular features, differentiated from the reality of other continents, especially Europe; this awareness finds its starting point in the conciliar event and its immediate reception during the Second General Conference of the Latin American Episcopate, celebrated in Medellín, Colombia, in 1968, an event that various authors describe as the official birth of the Latin American and Caribbean Church.

An almost unanimous consensus prevails as to the decisive and positive value of the council for the life of the Church. This can be verifled in the widest array of texts, such as episcopal documents—both individual and collegial—and the countless pastoral and theological contributions of a number of collectives, especially groups of priests belonging to different countries, religious congregations, and so on. As a whole, **[p. 677]** Vatican II soon became a symbol of renewal. The significance of this event was highlighted by several studies that compared it to a new Pentecost. The most typical expressions of post-conciliar Latin American Catholicism—such as the ecclesial base communities (EBCs/CEBs), popular reading of the Bible, the positive assessment of popular religiosity, and liberation theology itself—are acknowledged as theological-pastoral realities derived from the conciliar event. Such realities allow one to assert the selective, creative, and faithful reception in the region.

Another general aspect typifying the nature of this reception is that the Vatican II documents have not been directly examined to the same degree as they have been in other languages and regions. Yet the study of the council’s reception must be undertaken even in those areas where its links to Vatican II are not fully evident. We may thus speak of a mediated connection that should not be dismissed as superficial. Unlike research undertaken in other latitudes, two facts are attested in a significant portion of our continent’s theological bibliography. Vatican II is generally understood in relation to the Medellín conference as a unique major event of celebration and reception. Perhaps the council’s European rootedness, as evinced by its priorities and neglected topics, has fuelled this dynamism. Hence, after its fiftieth jubilee, we continue to hear about a ‘twofold memory’: the council and Medellín. On the other hand, the reception of the council’s legacy is largely linked to several important magisterial texts published afterwards. A case in point is Paul VI’s Apostolic Exhortation on the proclamation of the Gospel, _Evangelii Nuntiandi_ (1975), which proved essential to the outlook of the Third General Conference of Latin American and Caribbean Bishops, held in Puebla, México (1978). Treating matters scarcely discussed by Vatican II, the encyclical On the Development of Peoples, _Populorum Progressio_ (1967) had a considerable impact on the Medellín conference.

### 2. Signs of the Times: The ‘See, Judge, Act’ Method

The methodological approach espoused by the magisterial discourse, in the scheduling of the Church’s pastoral activities, and in the theological elaboration of these decades, reveals one of the chief guidelines in the council’s continental reception. Victor Codina rightly considers the Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World, _Gaudium et Spes_, as ‘the text that has had a stronger impact over Latin America [^c41-1] because of its call to scrutinise and discern the signs of the times’. Vatican II was only a first step in this direction which, as is known, was highly debated during the preparation of the Pastoral Constitution. **[p. 678]** Among the novelties introduced in the final version of the so-called Schema XIII during the council’s fourth session was the document’s hermeneutical structure, which, according to Christoph Theobald, ‘was grounded on the inductive “See, Judge, Act” method belonging to the Catholic Action movement and [^c41-2] introduced as structuring scheme on the spring of 1965’. From that moment onwards, the interpretation of the ‘signs of the times’, a biblical and pastoral expression that symbolizes such a method, became a theological criterion to organize the constitution as a whole. This inductive method, joined with a trilogy dialectically forged by Joseph Cardijn, founder of the Young Christian Workers (or Juventud Obrera Cristiana, JOC), had been frequently employed by churches in Latin America and the Caribbean prior to the [^c41-3] council.

[^c41-1]: Víctor Codina, ‘Las iglesias del continente 50 años después del Vaticano II: cuestiones pendientes’, in _50 años del Vaticano_ _II: Análisis y perspectivas_, ed. Congreso Continental de Teología (Bogotá: Paulinas, 2013), 84.

[^c41-2]: Christoph Theobald, _Le Concile Vatican II: Quel avenir?_ (Paris: Cerf, 2015), 228.

[^c41-3]: Agenor Brighenti, ‘Método ver-julgar-agir’, in _Dicionário do Concílio Vaticano II_, ed. Joāo Decio Passos and Wagner Lopes Sanchez (São Paulo: Paulinas, 2015), 608–15.

The Medellín conference creatively adopted the theological method of the Pastoral Constitution _Gaudium et Spes_. A major feature distinguishing it from the council resides in the fact that this method permeated not only a single document, but also the ‘working mechanism’, as it was called, of the entire conference, and is reflected in the final documents. In the years that followed Medellín, one can observe the impact of this method in the construction of recognizable a Latin American ecclesial identity. According to Agenor Brighenti, this method lies at the root of the popular ecclesial activities that led to the adoption of the preferential option for the poor and vulnerable, the creation of ecclesial base communities, the practice of the popular reading of the Bible, and the development of a pastoral life that integrates concern for social justice, civil militancy, and liberation theology itself. Alongside its richness and limitations, all these ecclesial expressions epitomize a qualitative theological and pastoral novelty in the history of the Church and point to the originality of the Latin American style and identity.

### 3. God’s Irruption in the Irruption of the Poor

Because of its richness and complexity, it is difficult to summarize the core of the ecclesial process and the theological originality of these decades generated in the continent since Medellín. Several authors suggest that the novelty lies in the irruption of the poor and in the irruption of God among them. Fifty years later, what in the 1960s was a budding certainty has come to inspire the self-understanding of the Latin American and Caribbean Church, sparking the first contextual non-European theology: liberation theology. From that point on, the poor become a matter of crucial concern for the continent, a _locus theologicus_ from which to **[p. 679]** understand the Gospel. The expression ‘close to the poor, close to God’ sums up a key and decisive [^c41-4] criterion for evangelical discernment.

[^c41-4]: Gustavo Gutiérrez, ‘Cerca del pobre, cerca de Dios’, _Páginas_ 220 (2010): 6–15.

Narrowly interconnected from the start, liberation theology and the post-conciliar Latin American episcopal magisterium developed an original reflection on these topics. Especially at Medellín (1968), the theological foundation of what the Puebla conference (1979) would later call the ‘preferential option for the [^c41-5] poor’ (_Documento de Puebla_ (_DdeP_) 1134–65) is emphatically proclaimed, even if in a somewhat rudimentary manner.

[^c41-5]: ‘Documento de Puebla’ or ‘Conferencia general del episcopado latinoamericano: Puebla de los Ángeles, México, Enero– Febrero 1979’, in CELAM, _Río de Janeiro, Medellín, Puebla, Santo Domingo: Documentos pastorales; Introducción, textos,_ _índice temático_ (Bogotá: Kimpres, 1994), 241–565.

The poverty alluded to by the Latin American Church of the 1960s and 1970s was chiefly that of rural peasants, those immigrating into the great cities, and industrial labourers. In any case, it was ascribed to people who were poor from a socio-economic viewpoint; namely, Latin Americans lacking food, healthcare, housing, and education: the unemployed and the exploited masses. As many countries lost their democracies and endured military dictatorships, the victims of human rights violations (the persecuted, the tortured, and those gone missing) and their relatives clamouring for justice came to be regarded as a new category of poor by the Latin American Church. Insecurity, lack of freedom, humiliation, and abandonment added to the aforementioned miseries (_DdeP_ 49, 314, 347).

Throughout those years, Latin America was also the scene of a Cold War battle between the great powers of the United States and the Soviet Union. Latin American countries, belonging to the so-called Third World, were aligned—some willingly, others by coercion—with either capitalism or Marxism. The Cuban revolution (1959) was a milestone that determined the 1960s until the democratic ascent to power of Salvador Allende in Chile (1970) offered a new paradigm for viable socialism. The military coup that overthrew Allende added this country to the long list of Latin American nations that in those years were led by military dictatorships (Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay). In Chile, Pinochet’s dictatorship (1973–90) pioneered in testing out the sort of neoliberalism that quickly prevailed over the rest of the continent. The fall of the Berlin Wall (1989)—a sort of triumph of Western capitalist society—impacted social and political movements of the Latin American Left, as well as liberation theology.

Struggling to understand poverty and its causes, liberation theologians in the 1960s adopted the shift that had taken place in the social sciences, abandoning the prevailing ‘development policy’—which assumed that underdeveloped countries would naturally follow the course of developed ones—to embrace the ‘dependency theory’. That theory presupposed the need to ‘liberate’ poor countries from rich ones, given that their very bond was what generated the riches of one and the poverty of the other.

**[p. 680]** The concept of poverty gained thicker theological density after Medellín and Puebla; liberation theology distinguished, following the Scriptures, between ‘material’ (socio-economic) poverty and ‘spiritual’ poverty (the solidary commitment for the poor). Gustavo Gutiérrez coined the expression ‘with the poor against poverty’. In this manner, the poor became a theological subject, given their epistemological advantage for understanding the Gospel and the value ascribed to the wisdom of their theological reflection. Magisterial and theological reflections value the agonizing struggle of the poor to simply survive as well as their capacity to testify and evangelize, revealing God as the God of the poor.

In the following decades, the quest to understand and explain the persistence of poverty together with its growing complexities has motivated a number of conceptualizations and terminologies in an attempt to reach for strategies and tentative solutions to its structural problems. Poverty is spoken of in increasingly diverse ways. Particularly important has been the enhanced awareness of the racial problem alongside the ‘public appearance’ of Indigenous cultures and the ‘emergence’ of women-specific gender issues. On the other hand, a new vision of ecology from the perspective of the poor has emerged.

### 4. A Regional Church and an Ecclesiology in Quest for Renewal

[^c41-6] Victor Codina rightly warns against Romantic idealizations of the Latin American Church. Newcomers to the continent often expect to find ecclesial base communities at work in every parish, bishops like Oscar Romero in each diocese, exemplary laymen and laywomen preaching the word to the point of martyrdom in each church, or genuinely prophetic people among the poor in every religious community. The facts are quite different and at times even disappointing. On the contrary, a great Christian majority continues to live under traditionalist, even pre-conciliar ecclesial structures. Machismo in general, and clericalism in particular, deeply pervade the mentalities and practices of countless bishops, priests, and pastoral workers. Stagnating parish structures are no exception. Diocesan networks such as presbyteral or pastoral councils possess a rather nominal than operative existence. A paucity of synodal processes at all levels is a well-established and widespread reality. They all represent personal life forms and institutional practices that appear to resist transformation. To be sure, gender inequalities, so evident in ecclesial structures, find a strong ally in the notably patriarchal cultural mores of our countries that are invariably present in all social classes and in the most varied contexts: familial, political, corporate, labour unions, universities, etc.

[^c41-6]: Víctor Codina, _Para comprender la eclesiología desde América Latina_ (Estella: Verbo Divino, 1990), 107.

#### Continental Episcopal Collegiality: CELAM

**[p. 681]** The first general conference of the Latin American episcopate, held in Rio de Janeiro (1955), went down in history for one of its resolutions: the creation of the Latin American Episcopal Council (CELAM). In its last chapter, the final document states: ‘It is by unanimity that the General Conference of the Latin American Episcopate agrees to bid, attentively requesting the Holy Apostolic See, for the creation of a Latin American Episcopal Council … to be composed of the Representatives of the National Episcopal Conferences.’ A few weeks later, on 24 September, the Holy See informed the pontifical representatives in Latin America that Pius XII had saluted the initiative. The institution of a Latin American Episcopal Council was approved on 2 November of the same year. CELAM constituted a totally new kind of institution. Though it is true that some conferences, limited to regional or provincial representation, existed in a few European countries such as Spain and Italy, their institutional task was not, unlike CELAM’s, to promote and synchronize the activities of national episcopal conferences. ‘Completely new is the recognition of the need to insert the national organizations of the episcopate in the broader context of collaboration at continental and intercontinental [^c41-7] levels, which finds an institutional expression for the first time in the history of the _conventus episcoporum._’ It should be noted, however, that CELAM is not a continental conference. It is rather a point of contact and a means of collaboration for the episcopal conferences; in itself, it lacks any legal authority.

[^c41-7]: Giorgio Feliciani, _Le conferenze episcopali_ (Bologna: Il Mulino, 1974), 291.

If CELAM was created in the years immediately preceding the council, its organization was solidifled during the years of Vatican II through the bishops’ lived experience of episcopal collegiality. Its subsequent positive impact on the churches of the continent cannot be underestimated. Its major achievements—the general conferences from Medellín (1968) to Aparecida (2007)—are pivotal outcomes that have defined the lives of the churches. A general positive consensus prevails regarding the importance of these events for the construction of a Church with a shared language and orientation in the continent.

The celebration of the First Ecclesial Assembly of Latin America and the Caribbean (2021), with not only episcopal participation as in previous conferences, but with the representation of all the people of God, and the creation of a new regional institution, the Ecclesial Conference of the Amazon Region, because of the Synod of 2019, constitute new events of ecclesiological relevance in the region.

#### Ecclesial Base Communities

The rise of ecclesial base communities (EBCs) is regarded as a typical phenomenon of the Latin American **[p. 682]** church in the post-conciliar period. Their birthplace, however, can be located in Brazil in the 1950s. Despite their common ground, their historic diversity makes it difficult to speak of EBCs in univocal terms. As Codina has observed, their history differs in each of their respective countries. The EBCs of Brazil, Mexico, or Chile, with a long-established tradition, are not easily comparable to those of relatively recent origin in the British and French Caribbean, nor are their communal practices the same in Brazil and Peru. The EBCs of Central American countries that have undergone war situations, such as El Salvador, Nicaragua, and Guatemala, are deeply marked by cases of martyrdom. Moreover, great differences prevail within a single country between the rural EBCs and those in the slums of great cities, or between modern EBCs and [^c41-8] those of Indigenous or African American culture.

[^c41-8]: Víctor Codina, ‘La sabiduría de las comunidades de base de América Latina’, _Concilium_ 254 (1994): 688.

Despite all the differences, it is possible to recognize a common imaginary that has characterized this ecclesiological reality. Awareness of the novelty and relevance of this form is a crucial factor. If liberation theology has understood itself from its inception as ‘a new way of doing theology’, EBCs have conceived of themselves as ‘a new way of being Church’. There is an awareness of a paradigmatic change of model. Medellín described EBCs as a ‘focus of evangelisation and starting cell for ecclesial structuration, presently [^c41-9] an essential factor for humanitarian promotion and development’. As a predominantly lay community understanding themselves as a ‘base’ in ecclesial terms, in relation to the Church’s hierarchical structure, a critical aspect is that they are also ‘base’ from a sociological perspective, since their membership is composed mainly of poor people. EBCs have flourished especially in such socio-economic environments.

[^c41-9]: ‘Documento de Medellín’, 15, 10, https://www.celam.org/documentos/Documento_Conclusivo_Medellin.pdf

A representative sample is Leonardo Boff’s book _Ecclesiogenesis: The Base Communities Reinvent the Church_. According to Boff, EBCs do not present themselves as an ‘alternative to the Church institution’ but rather constitute a ‘permanent source of renewal’, being ‘beyond doubt one of the greatest driving forces for the [^c41-10] renewal of the Church in the entire world’. In the words of Brazilian priest Jose Marins, perhaps the most important author to promote this ecclesial form, they represent the ‘initiation of a new historical project of [^c41-11] Church’.

[^c41-10]: Leonardo Boff, _The Base Communities Reinvent the Church_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1986), 14; originally published as _Eclesiogénesis: Las comunidades de base reinventan la iglesia_ (Santander: Sal Terrae, 1980).

[^c41-11]: José Marins, ‘Comunidades eclesiales de base en América latina’, _Concilium_ 104 (1975): 29.

EBCs understand themselves as heirs to the twentieth-century renewal movements, initially sharing Vatican II’s ecclesiology of communion. To this, a number of factors must be added: the biblical movement acclaimed in _Dei Verbum_; the pastoral experiences of Catholic Action; the use of the ‘See, Judge, Act’ method; the promotion of the laity and the willingness to create new ministries; the ecumenical spirit and **[p. 683]** interreligious dialogue fostered by the council; the Christian involvement in politics encouraged by _Gaudium et Spes_; and the reformulation of Christology emphasizing the historic proximity of Jesus of Nazareth to the needs of the poor and marginalized that calls for a committed and testimonial following. The scarce number of priests and religious vocations is a pastoral problem endemic to the continent with an impact on the genesis of the EBCs.

The EBCs’ breeding grounds have been diverse, such as forms of parish renewal, the establishment of Bible study groups, and goal-specific groups with a keen social and political awareness for the betterment of everyday life, particularly that of the poor. Whatever the originating drive may have been, the creation of EBCs has always presupposed ‘a coordination of the _religious_ with the _social_ sphere. One of the two may have had precedence over the other or have been dominant at first, but a real ecclesial base community only [^c41-12] emerges after both aspects are integrated.’ The orientation towards praxis and social change constitutes a key aspect.

[^c41-12]: Marcelo Azevedo, ‘Comunidades eclesiales de base’, in _Mysterium liberationis: Conceptos fundamentales de la teología de_ _la liberación_, 2 vols., ed. Ignacio Ellacuría and Jon Sobrino (Madrid: Trotta, 1990), 2:251.

Throughout these decades, EBCs have naturally experienced the impact of the different cultural situations of their countries together with those changes taking place within the ecclesial context. Changes in the traditional features of EBCs are attested throughout the 1970s and 1980s, and a crisis regarding their quality and demographic increase is attested in the 1990s. The cultural turn of the1990s, which to some extent affected all forms of ecclesial socialization correcting the one-sidedness of previous decades, cannot be deplored as a negative development. One observes a transition from sheer social analysis towards the inclusion of cultural mediations, from a patriarchal Church towards a familiar community with an increasingly feminine face, from an ecclesial elitist complex towards a greater appraisal of popular religiosity, and so on. A major trend, ratifled in the following years, was already discernible then: the Latin American poor no longer belong to EBCs but many have moved to the Pentecostal churches.

Under the pontificates of John Paul II and Benedict XVI, the Catholic Church seems to have promoted a ‘new springtime’ favouring international ecclesial movements over EBCs. Consequently, two opposite ecclesiological projects coexisted in Latin America throughout these decades. The cultural climate of the new millennium and Francis’s pontificate have diminished the prominence of these movements.

On the other hand, parochial structures do not seem to have renewed under the ecclesiological vision of Vatican II. Like Medellín had done forty years earlier, the Documento de Aparecida (_DA_) speaks of a ‘pastoral [^c41-13] ministry of mere conservation’ (_DA_ 370): in other words, pastoral structures still focused on sacramental and administrative affairs.

[^c41-13]: The ‘Documento de Aparecida’ is found in CELAM, _Documento conclusivo de Aparecida_ (Bogotá: Centro de publicaciones del CELAM, 2007).

#### The Theological Concept of People of God

**[p. 684]** The council’s theological concept of the people of God, developed especially in chapter 2 of the Dogmatic Constitution _Lumen Gentium_, was immediately greeted with an overwhelming acceptance in the ecclesial, magisterial, theological, and pastoral discourses of the continent. A case in point is the Medellín document, where the category is featured some thirty times. But Medellín addresses the issue in somewhat different terms than Vatican II, not by arguing for it from its Trinitarian roots, as _Lumen Gentium_ had done, but by taking into account the perspective of _Gaudium et Spes_, which characterizes the whole ecclesiological approach. A key point differentiating Medellín from the teaching of the council is _Lumen Gentium_’s omission of the foundational and liberating experience of the Exodus, advocated by Medellín and subsequently adhered to as a central and determining idea in the ecclesiological reflections of later decades. The positive consensus with regard to the category of the People of God, easily verifled in the different schools of thought across the continent, was accompanied by the critical assessment of its neglect in subsequent Roman documents.

The relevance of the concept of the People of God was downplayed in the Final Report of the extraordinary Synod of Bishops meeting in 1985, to mark the twentieth anniversary of Vatican II. The final document refers only once to the Church as People of God, listing it as one among several other concepts. The eclipse of this concept is also confirmed by several later magisterial documents. Recently, the Argentinian theologian Carlos Maria Galli has thoroughly demonstrated the relevance of this absence. Identifying the only reference to this category in the _Relatio Finalis_ (1985) ‘as just another expression of the mystery’, he observes that ‘if the diagnosis focused upon the concept’s crisis, a reasonable remedy would be to reaffirm its genuine meaning. According to this text, one would never guess that this category had formed an architectural column of _Lumen Gentium_ or was the title for one of its chapters.’[^c41-14]

[^c41-14]: Carlos María Galli, ‘El retorno del pueblo de dios misionero: Un concepto-símbolo de la eclesiología del concilio a Francisco’, in _La Eclesiología del Concilio Vaticano II_, ed. Virginia Azcuy, José Carlos Caamaño, and Carlos María Galli (Buenos Aires: Agape, 2015), 413.

On the contrary, some authors point to the ‘return’ of the category of the People of God as confirmed by Francis and _Evangelii Gaudium_ (_EG_) (2013). The pope himself states that he ‘would like to dwell briefly on this way of understanding the Church’ (_EG_ 111), mentioning the category twenty-one times in the document —more times than any other concept to describe the Church. He thereby underscores the ‘historic character’ of the Church’s ‘mystery’ together with the inclusion of all the baptized with a variety of faces and large cultural differences. In line with the Latin American reception of the council, we may therefore say that _Evangelii Gaudium_ distances itself from the ecclesiology of 1985 Synod, which, in reinterpreting the council, had highlighted the concept of _communio_ while eclipsing that of the People of God.

### 5. The Popular Reading of the Bible and the Biblical Animation of the

### Whole Pastoral Ministry

**[p. 685]** Different endeavours focused on God’s word developed in Latin America and the Caribbean over these decades, openly seeing themselves as heirs to the renewal ushered in by the twentieth-century biblical movement, especially by the Dogmatic Constitution _Dei Verbum_. The 1993 document _The Biblical Interpretation of the Church_, issued by the Pontifical Biblical Commission, also had important effects. If the biblical movement in the continent had been unleashed by the conciliar constitution, this text confirmed many insights of the Latin American biblical journey, such as the interdisciplinary scope of biblical interpretation, the importance of the reader’s context, liberationist and feminist readings, the critique of [^c41-15] fundamentalism, the praiseworthiness of _lectio divina_, and so on. Of course, the use of the vernacular in liturgical celebrations also favoured the appropriation of the Bible by the People of God.

[^c41-15]: Gabriel Naranjo Salazar, ‘El camino de la pastoral bíblica antes y después del concilio en América Latina’, _Medellín_ 137 (2009): 23.

Among all the achievements of these decades, one must be particularly highlighted. ‘The Council’s legacy finds its most creative and meaningful expression in the Popular Reading of the Bible, a wide communal appropriation of God’s Word that has nurtured the path of ecclesial base communities and social pastorals [^c41-16] throughout these years with great input from the laity, especially from women.’ Many authors would agree with this statement by José Oscar Beozzo. In the words of Pablo Richard, one of its chief advocates: ‘The aim of the Latin American Biblical movement is precisely to return the Bible to the people of God, to lay it on their own hands, hearts and minds. As the Bible’s genuine “owner” and personal interpreter, the [^c41-17] people of God retrieve their divine right to read and interpret the Holy Scriptures.’ Biblical sciences and the Church’s magisterium are at its service. Carlos Mesters, the main exponent of this endeavour, thinks that beyond the regional and national differences that restrict its realization, the novelty of this experience resides in its aims, social location, and human subjects of interpretation. The goal is not to compile information about the past but to illumine the present with the light of God’s presence among us and interpret our lives with the help of the Bible. The human subject is not the specialist, since scriptural interpretation is a communitarian activity where all participate, including the exegete who fulfils that **[p. 686]** special role within the community. If the role of the poor is primordial, the contribution of Indigenous people and women is also increasingly noteworthy. The poor and marginalized constitute the social locus of interpretation. It is the critical social awareness that modifles the outlook. It consists of an ecumenical interpretation not because of its theoretical debates, but due to the quest for liberation and the universal commitment of the faithful to defend all life under threat. The ‘See, Judge, Act’ method, in particular, [^c41-18] fostered what its authors have called a ‘new vision on the revelation: God speaks in the present day’. Its pastoral reading distinguishes between the Book of Life and the Book of the Bible, granting priority to the Book of Life as the first Book of God. Evidently, the so-called popular reading of the Bible is narrowly connected to other post-conciliar experiences typical of Latin America; namely, the option for the poor, base communities, and the inductive methodology inherited from the specialized Catholic Action.

[^c41-16]: José Oscar Beozzo, ‘Vaticano II: 50 años después en América Latina y el Caribe’, _Concilium_ 346 (2012): 442.

[^c41-17]: Pablo Richard, ‘Interpretación latinoamericana de la biblia: Realidad, método, prospectiva’, in _Comentario bíblico_ _latinoamericano: Nuevo testamento_, ed. Armando Levoratti (Estella: Verbo Divino, 2007), 11.

[^c41-18]: Carlos Mesters and Francisco Orofino, ‘Leitura popular da Bíblia’, in _Dicionário do Concílio Vaticano II_, ed. Joāo Decio Passos and Wagner Lopes Sanchez (São Paulo: Paulinas, 2015), 534.

Another relevant aspect related to God’s word in the life of the Church is the paradigm shift effected by the biblical pastoral, moving from a specialized pastoral (educational pastoral, health care pastoral, etc.) towards a biblical animation of pastoral life as a whole. The meaningful expression ‘a biblical impetus to pastoral ministry’ was received by the Latin American magisterium (_DA_ 248) and, at a later stage, by the post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation of Benedict XVI, _Verbum Domini_ (2010).

Summing up, the assessment of Chilean biblical scholar Pablo Uribe appears to be justifled. The general reception of the biblical movement and of the teaching of the conciliar constitution _Dei Verbum_ is more apparent in practical pastoral experiences than in theoretical works. ‘The reception does not divert from the orthodox formulation of the _sensus fidei_, but its adherence to it is realized within _praxis_, generating a theoretical reflection that works out certain levels of appropriation of the teachings present in the Constitution.’[^c41-19]

[^c41-19]: Pablo Uribe Ulloa, ‘Recepción bíblica de la Constitución _Dei Verbum_ en América Latina’, _Medellín_ 162 (2015): 298.

### 6. Trends in Latin American and Caribbean Theology

#### Liberation Theology

It was in the 1960s that the inductive ‘See, Judge, Act’ method developed and acquired prominence. The interpretative key for base communities, priestly movements, and religious congregations was the Latin American reality read in a critical, liberationist perspective. In this methodology, the second step was a **[p. 687]** reflection grounded in faith and serving as a prophetic denunciation. The third step was to orient pastoral endeavours towards the transformation of ecclesial and socio-political realities. This inductive methodological quest, undertaken by multiple ecclesial groups, merged with the work of a number of theologians and pastoralists, giving birth, in the early 1970s, to liberation theology. According to its advocates, this was not just another theological school among others but a new way of doing theology. Its method distinguished it from other theologies. Gustavo Gutiérrez defines it as ‘a critical reflection on [^c41-20] historical _praxis_ in the light of the Word’. Its theology was understood as a ‘second act’ within the believer’s experience, integral to a praxis of liberation, the ‘first act’. Praxis constituted not only a verifying criterion but also a moment internal to theological knowledge. Socio-analytical mediation—that is, the integration of the social sciences within theological reflection—became prominent in order to aid in understanding the sources of oppression. The perspective of the poor proved essential to the new methodology, where the poor were no longer spoken about as objects or recipients but became the subjects and even the socio-theological locus par excellence. According to Jon Sobrino, poverty gives rise to thought. Poverty shapes thought, teaches people to think in a different manner, and becomes the generating and organizing principle of the theological task. Jorge Costadoat’s remarks on this matter are meaningful; above all, the great novelty contributed by this theological school is ‘to have accorded the poor an unprecedented [^c41-21] epistemological relevance in the history of theology’.

[^c41-20]: Gustavo Gutiérrez, _Teología de la liberación: Perspectivas_ (Salamanca: Sígueme, 1972), 38; translated as _A Theology of_ _Liberation: History, Politics, and Salvation_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1973).

[^c41-21]: Jorge Costadoat, ‘Identidad de la teología latinoamericana y la teología de la liberación’, _Perspectiva Teológica_ 50 (2018): 37.

The leitmotif of this new way of doing theology was liberation, conceived as the correlate of the socio-analytical concept of dependency (where underdevelopment does not represent a backward stage of capitalist development but its direct aftermath), surpassing the idea of development that prevailed in the 1970s. The accent shifted from development to liberation. Although the incorporation of dependency theory and Marxist analysis testifled to the seriousness of its historic commitment, it is worth noting that both represented a limited approach to the reality under analysis. Gutiérrez himself recognized in a 1988 reissue of his famous book, _A Theology of Liberation_, that the historic interpretation of those early years of liberation theology reinforced a structural socio-economic perspective strongly influenced by dependency theory. Without disregarding the socio-economic factor, Gutiérrez’s renewed interpretation underscores the cultural and historic mediations that, in his opinion, enhance our understanding of a complex and global reality.

Liberation theology found itself in a very challenging situation from the 1990s on. Liberation theologians were confronted with the question ‘Is liberation theology dead?’ There were several causes for this doubt: the enthusiasm that had characterized the immediate post-conciliar period had vanished; the socialist **[p. 688]** experience in Eastern European countries had failed; the politics of episcopal nominations was marked by a distinctively conservative bias; theological and ecclesial attention had been deflected towards other areas, such as the theology of religions; there was an absence of Latin American issues in international agendas related to politics and the economy; and more. In response, theologians such as Gutiérrez, Sobrino, and Trigo maintained that so long as poverty continued to cry for justice, a theology steeped in the _principium liberationis_ would not become outmoded.

Two important aspects must not be overlooked. Liberation theology has shown a strong connection to spirituality even within its own methodology, as confirmed by such influential works as Gutiérrez’s _Beber en su propio pozo_ (_We Drink from Our Own Wells_, 1984) and Segundo Galilea’s _El futuro de nuestro pasado_ (1985). This theological school is also inextricably linked with many experiences of martyrdom on the continent. These are decisive aspects of the movement of liberation theology.

#### Latin American Feminist Theologies

Liberation theology is often charged with failing to realize, especially in its beginnings, the importance of gender issues and of the continent’s cultural convolutions related to Indigenous and African American peoples. To be sure, the analytical apparatus it employed emphasized the socio-economic factor to the detriment of other marginalized and emerging human groups. Alongside the theoretical evolution of liberation theologies, the development of global feminism and the growing number of women theologians within the liberationist school triggered, in the late 1970s, the rise of a Latin American feminist theology.

We note the continental development of theological feminism through the organization of congresses in different locations of Latin America and the Caribbean. The starting point for this movement is usually ascribed to the Mexico event of 1979. Even though any survey is bound to remain inadequate and therefore partial, we nonetheless recognize the contributions of the following authors: Maria Pilar Aquino (San Diego, California), Elsa Tamez (Costa Rica), Ivone Gebara (Brazil), Maria Clara Luccetti Bingemer (Brazil), Olga Consuelo Vélez Caro (Colombia), and Virginia Azcuy (Argentina), to name but a few.

The vast majority of these writers express their dissatisfaction, if not their disappointment, with the results achieved thus far regarding the recognition of women’s place in the life of Latin American churches. As for theologies developed by women, it is noteworthy that female theologians have gradually diversifled their approaches—not only with respect to their theological, epistemological, and methodological choices, but also in accordance with the personal experiences undergone by women. An awareness concerning the vital context and the specific character of women’s experiences in relation to their geographic, historic, political, and cultural reality has been greatly enhanced. Many formulations characteristic of these movements have shaped theologies elaborated by women, theologies from women’s perspectives, feminist theologies, **[p. 689]** womanist theology (following the model of Black theology), and _mujerista_ theology (grounded in the experiences of Latin female immigrants in the United States). Regardless of their different perspectives, they all critique forms of theology that claim to be neutral while concealing androcentric and patriarchal biases. They thus aim to make a constructive contribution to a new rationality of a different order, complementing and enriching the theology elaborated in male circles.

Notwithstanding the progress that has been achieved, great challenges remain in store for society, for the churches, and even for Latin American feminist movements. A conspicuous sign of the times appears on this fleld as we acknowledge that the pastors and theologians of the churches of Latin America and the Caribbean were not leading supporters of the process for feminine liberation, which have caught fire and developed more consistently in other geographical regions of the world. In Latin America and the Caribbean, theological feminism emerged much later than social feminism.

#### Indigenous and African American Theologies

One of the most outstanding events of recent decades is the rise of Indigenous peoples as specific subjects with long-standing demands for recognition. In this respect, the ‘theological emergence’ of Indigenous peoples recognizes itself as indebted to Vatican II ‘for at least two reasons: the dialogue with the modern world emphasising the evangelical commitment for justice and the poor, and the theological openness to acknowledge religious and socio-cultural differences and diversities, as epitomised by the indigenous [^c41-22] peoples themselves’. Occurring before the Medellín conference thanks to the initiatives promoted by CELAM’s Missionary Department, which was created in 1966, the first ecclesial encounters played a major role through the promotion of Indigenous pastoral meetings. Despite the antiquity of its religious wisdom, a Latin American current of theology coordinating the reflection of contemporary natives and the so-called Indigenous or Amerindian theology is a rather recent phenomenon. Meeting in Mexico (1990), the first workshop on Indigenous theology drew attention to its emergence. Various encounters, many of which were convened by CELAM itself, have followed since 2002. The reticence shown in earlier years by the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, which discouraged attempts to speak of an Indigenous theology, was perceived by its proponents as a persistent token of a colonial mentality in the Church opposed to the transformations fostered by Vatican II.

[^c41-22]: Roberto Tomichá, ‘Teologías de la liberación indígenas: Balances-y tareas pendientes’, _Horizonte_ 32 (2013): 1779.

Grounded in the historic memory that expresses the cultural roots of the people, and aimed at retrieving the mythic-symbolic and bodily languages narrowly linked to the daily struggle for life, Indigenous theology **[p. 690]** conceives itself as a collective task aimed at a radical questioning of existing theologies, social lifestyles, and the Church in general.

African American theologies denote two theological expressions born out of the African experience in the American continent. Black theology was developed by Black theologians in the United States beginning in the 1970s. African American theology, on the other hand, encompasses the ‘African’ theology that has taken root in Latin America as well as in the Caribbean, a vast geographical region full of religious and cultural peculiarities. Its genesis is related to the effervescence of popular movements, the emergence of a Black awareness within the continent, and the result of an intense pastoral base activity. It has developed over more than thirty years, with its main theological centres in Quito and São Paulo. This current is a tributary of the same liberation theologies that it criticizes for having neglected ethnic, gender, and cultural issues. It differentiates itself from other liberationist strands by prioritizing the social reality of racism above all other concerns, considering skin colour as the root cause for a person’s social location among the poorest. Grounded in specific communal experiences that diverge from those of whites or mestizos, this theological reflection underscores the need to realize and create an identity that rises above racial differences. The congruence between these theologies with Vatican II is stated explicitly.

#### People’s Theology

Considered by some as a specific current among the liberation theologies which emerged at the same time as that initiated by Gutiérrez, the so-called theology of the people has gained notoriety following the election of Cardinal Jorge Bergoglio as bishop of Rome. Among the factors that were instrumental in generating and developing this theological and pastoral trend, three may be mentioned. First, as V.
