Azcuy reminds us, ‘the Argentinian historic experience together with its popular movements are foremost among the great strands of reflection that have roused an interest for the people, their culture and religion’. Second, according to the biography of its chief exponent, Lucio Gera, another ‘strand of reflection derives from the socio-cultural strata of those who joined this collective theological quest’ in Argentina; namely, immigrants, whose experience sparked the question of identity, giving rise to the specific grounding of this theology in the popular world. The third factor is the pastoral character of Vatican II itself, which aroused [^c41-23] great interest in Argentina. Works by Juan Carlos Scannone, Carlos María Galli, and Victor Manuel Fernández feature among the most important representatives of this school, which bears conspicuous fruit in Pope Francis’s 2013 Apostolic Exhortation _Evangelii Gaudium_.

[^c41-23]: Virginia Azcuy, ‘Introducción’, in _La teología argentina del pueblo_, ed. Lucio Gera (Santiago: Universidad Alberto Hurtado, 2015), 13–14.

### 7. The Liturgical Reform and Popular Religiosity

**[p. 691]** The council’s liturgical reform was probably the most tangible radical change in the concrete lives of countless ecclesial communities throughout the continent. The use of vernacular languages made Vatican’s II pastoral intention and its process of _aggiornamento_ particularly manifest. In this respect, the active participation of the faithful, a pivotal aspect to the liturgical reform, gathered significant momentum. Despite isolated cases of abuse, including the defective observance of liturgical norms or stubborn resistance towards renewal, historically speaking these do not seem to epitomize the continent’s reception of the council’s liturgical reform.

Serious weaknesses in the council’s reception can be seen in the only recently initiated process of inculturation. They are also apparent in the liturgical reform’s distant and timid relationship to popular religiosity, the keystone of religious experience for millions of believers in the continent, but which received little attention in _Sacrosanctum Concilium_. The authoritative opinion of the Uruguayan liturgical scholar Roberto Russo is clear with respect to the issue of inculturation: the initial conviction that fostered dialogue between the Roman liturgy and the diverse cultures appears to have been curtailed. ‘The language barrier has been sorted with substantial success. Pending, however, is the idiomatic issue, which remains even more complex and must be expressed in the texts as well as in symbols and in music.’[^c41-24]

[^c41-24]: Roberto Russo, ‘_Sacrosanctum concilium_ e reforma litúrgica in América Latina’, in _Il Concilio vaticano II y la liturgia:_ _Memoria y futuro_, ed. Pierangelo Chiaramello (Rome: Liturgiche CLV, 2013), 245.

From Medellín in 1968 to Aparecida in 2007, popular piety has been a recurrent theme in all conferences organized by the continent’s episcopates. At Aparecida, it certainly attained a prominent place, with two novel expressions that speak of a genuine ‘people’s mysticism’ or ‘popular spirituality’ (_DA_ 62, 263), stressing the importance of pilgrimages, festivals, chants, costumes, dances, and so on. Given the aforementioned shortcomings in the inculturation of the Roman rite, a narrower bond between liturgy and popular piety seems a desideratum. This need becomes all the more critical when one considers the particular significance of Marian devotion reflected in important sanctuaries across the continent (Guadalupe, Aparecida, Luján, etc.) which attract millions of believers annually.

To sum up, although the liturgical reform is seen as a positive and very significant impetus for renewal, the relevance of Roberto Russo’s severe assessment becomes apparent when the limitations of the churches’ practices are acknowledged. He rightly observes: ‘the great guidelines that break through the sheer reformation of the rites and the texts solicited by _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ have not been fully assimilated nor **[p. 692]** [^c41-25] developed in the Latin American continent’. The inspiring principles of the liturgical reform have not developed to their full potential.

[^c41-25]: Russo, ‘_Sacrosanctum concilium_ e reforma litúrgica in América Latina’, 245.

### 8. The Ecumenical Dialogue and Religious Pluralism

Given the continent’s religious landscape, the ecumenical reception of the council followed a singular path largely diverging from other regions of the Catholic Church. Ecumenical endeavours have been characterized by a resistance to the various political dictatorships of the continent, serving those movements that promote social change. These unofficial ecumenical groups remained somewhat detached from official ecclesial institutions. Since the collapse of Latin American dictatorships, their endeavours have been gradually redefined. Organizations such as the Latin American Council of Churches (CLAI) or the Conselho Nacional de Igrejas Cristas do Brasil (CONIC) have acquired increasing relevance in the new scenario. As a result, ecumenism has historically been associated with the struggles for political liberation and with revolutionary social movements typical of the 1970s and 1980s.

A positive outcome of the ecumenical work over these years is rooted in its links to the biblical movement, the encouragement of common scriptural readings, and the joint preparation of translations on a continental level. This is seen most clearly in CELAM’s activities and in joint endeavours such as those shared with the United Bible Societies.

The itinerary of these decades also reveals a growing awareness of the loss of Catholicism’s factual or alleged hegemony and its power to homogenize the religious culture, due largely to the momentous demographic growth of Latin American Pentecostalism. The growth of traditional “mainline” Protestant churches, too, has stagnated, leading to a slow but persistent demographic decline.

Notwithstanding all the progress achieved in these decades, a cautious assessment of the path trodden must also highlight the many tasks pending in the continent.

Mutual ignorance, conceptual confusion, and a stagnating conformity to Catholic hegemony in cultural and religious matters have hindered bishops, priests, religious and the Christian folk in general from embracing ecumenism as a constitutive dimension of evangelisation. This has generally discouraged the attendance and continuity of the ecumenical endeavours fostered by CELAM, which has led to an impression of disinterest and even dismay.[^c41-26]

[^c41-26]: Patricio Merino Beas, ‘El diálogo ecuménico animado desde el Celam’, _Theologica Xaveriana_ 184 (2017): 405.

### 9. Closing Remarks

**[p. 693]** An assessment of the council’s reception in Latin America and the Caribbean must include several other relevant aspects. The fleld of catechesis, for instance, represents a dynamic and creative area for pastoral activity guided by a conciliar spirit with great reach and impact over Christian communities. Largely absent from the consideration of the council, this theme, decisive since Medellín, is strongly developed by the post-conciliar dynamic in Latin America and beyond. The educational fleld, on the other hand, has also progressed independently, distinguishing itself at an early stage from the general proposal expressed by the Vatican II declaration on Christian Education, _Gravissimum Educationis_. Medellín’s liberating concept of education evinces a different understanding of the educational issue.

A good synthesis of the processes undergone in these decades is aptly expressed by Víctor Codina. In the case of Latin America and the Caribbean, the reception of the council has not been merely a spirited assimilation, much less a simple application of Vatican II to Latin America:

Rather, it has constituted an original recreation, a creative loyalty, a rereading of the council by a continent at once Christian and infested with poverty and injustices. This reception has contributed to the progress of the conciliar doctrine eliciting its latent intuitions and offering a very concrete historic and geographic translation of the Council’s _aggiornamento_. For all these reasons and in spite of being wrought in full communion with the universal Church, this reception has been troublesome for certain segments of the civil society and the Church incapable of appreciating the novelty and dynamism of the Spirit. It has been a martyrial reception in the strong sense of the word, faithfully received by witnesses of the Gospel who in many cases have lived out their loyalty to the Lord to the extent of shedding their own blood. For these reasons, the Latin American reception of Vatican II deserves respect: we must remove our shoes, for we are walking on holy ground.[^c41-27]

[^c41-27]: Codina, ‘Las iglesias del continente 50 años después del Vaticano II’, 82.

Codina rightly observes that no one could have foreseen the living forces that have been unleashed. ‘It has been a time of grace, a _kairos_, an authentic Pentecost as was Vatican II itself.’[^c41-28]

[^c41-28]: Ibid.

## 42. Reception of Vatican II in North America

Brian P. Flanagan

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 695]** Attempting to write a history of the reception of the Second Vatican Council in North America is a daunting task. Within the United States and Canada, the very particular experiences of different communities— particularly in distinct linguistic communities in Canada, and in different racial, linguistic, regional, and socio-economic communities in both countries—make it difficult to tell a single unifled story without blurring the distinctive histories of conciliar reception in North America or reinforcing overly simplistic narratives of ‘liberals’ vs. ‘conservatives’ or ‘progressives’ vs. ‘traditionalists’ that obscure as much as they explain. And we are only at the beginning of a period where the necessary granular research on what occurred even in the earliest periods of the reception of the council has been carried out; to attempt a comprehensive synthesis seems mistaken at best and useless at worst.[^c42-1]

[^c42-1]: Gilles Routhier, ‘Pour un programme de recherche sur la réception de Vatican II’, in _Réceptions de Vatican II: Le Concile au_ _risque de l’histoire et des espaces humains_, ed. Gilles Routhier (Leuven: Peeters, 2004), 5–17.

And yet, even if we must be aware of the limitations of the current state of research, we can still begin to survey some of the major moments and characteristics of conciliar reception in North America while creating space for the stories of conciliar receptions, in the plural, that are the real story of this period. Overall, this chapter argues that one can identify at least two distinct phases of early conciliar reception in North America that recur across regional, national, and ethnic differences. The first phase, rooted in the pre-conciliar life of Catholics in North America and other major socio-political factors of the early 1960s, was a period of enthusiastic optimism, broadly open to the way in which the Church seemed to be **[p. 696]** modernizing in ways that fit the experience and optimism of many North American Catholics. In a second phase, corresponding in many places to the upheavals of the late 1960s and lay Catholics’ disappointment with _Humanae Vitae_ in 1968, one finds a period of increasing disagreement over the pace and priorities of conciliar reception, between and among clergy and laity across North America. In this period of contested reception, energies and anxieties unleashed by the initial phase of conciliar reception found expression both in continued enthusiastic reception and in differences of opinion over the nature of that reception. In this period the categories of ‘progressives’ vs. ‘traditionalists’ make sense in some contexts, as clergy, religious, and lay Catholics, newly aware of the possibility of ecclesial change, disagreed, sometimes publicly and sometimes bitterly, over the possibilities and limits of such change.

The chapter therefore proceeds as follows. First, it reviews the ecclesial and socio-political context of Catholicism in North America in the pre-conciliar period. Since that which is to be received is received according to the capabilities of the receiver, the experience of Catholics in the United States and in anglophone and francophone Canada in the period leading up to the council was a constituent element of conciliar reception. Second, it outlines the initial phase of conciliar reception, which through media coverage and other forms of communication began even as the work of the council continued. Third, it looks at the contested reception of the council that begins in the late 1960s; while the sheer fact of conciliar reception was never in question in North America, more lasting confiicts over _how_ to receive the council came to new prominence in this period.

Within this broad framework, however, there will be some examples of ‘micro-receptions’, bringing to the forefront moments, communities, and stories that complicate or sit uneasily with any dominant narrative. Precisely through such interruptions, the reader will get a sense of the incompleteness of the current state of research into reception of the council in North America, the provisionality of most conclusions regarding that reception, and the difficulty of generalizing across the diverse constitutive communities that make up the Catholic Church in Canada and the United States.

### 2. Pre-conciliar Catholicism in the United States and Canada

Unlike at other times in history when general councils of the Church were called to respond to a particular crisis, at the time of the Second Vatican Council Roman Catholicism was, by many different metrics, apparently thriving, both internally and in its relations with the wider culture. After the Second World War, seminaries and houses of formation for religious life were full and growing; Mass attendance, and reception of the sacraments at those Masses, was high. In the United States, many newly affiuent and educated Euro- American Catholics joined their Protestant neighbours in the move to the suburbs, and, while substantive **[p. 697]** anti-Catholic attitudes and discrimination continued in many ways and places, the election of John F. Kennedy to the presidency in 1960 seemed to many white US Catholics to symbolize their acceptance as fully American. Even without specific Hispanic ministries, long-standing Mexican American communities in the US Southwest and newer immigrants from Mexico, Puerto Rico, Cuba, and other predominantly Spanish-speaking countries were present in this largely white-dominated US Catholic Church, even as most white Catholic institutions in the US actively or passively participated in the structures of institutional racism that marginalized African American Catholics. While Catholics in the two solitudes of anglophone and francophone Canada pursued distinct paths in this period, they also experienced the fruits of a similar postwar economic boom and increasing integration as Catholics in Canadian public life. This was true even if, under the Duplessis government, Catholics in Quebec and francophone Catholics outside Quebec maintained more institutional distance from their anglophone co-religionists, and while First Nations Catholics, Ukrainian and other Eastern Catholics, and more recently arrived Canadians found themselves at the margins of Catholic life in Canada.

One false narrative that must be countered, however, is that the institutional strengths, such as they were, of pre-conciliar Catholicism in North America were rooted primarily in stability and immovability in the face of modernity. Pre-conciliar Catholic life in North America was not dormant or stagnant but was in fact in the midst of a period of rapid development and even experimentation, particularly in the areas of liturgy, theology, and ecumenical and interreligious dialogue. Pre-conciliar Catholicism was never as backward-looking or frozen in time as some might suggest, either in praise or critique of that period. Rather, we can find numerous developments in ecclesial practice and in Catholics’ relations to their wider social, political, and cultural contexts. Rather than frozen ground needing to be tediously broken up and melted, preconciliar Catholicism in North America was often fertile soil made ready to receive the council in the decades that preceded it.[^c42-2]

[^c42-2]: Claude Ryan, ‘L’Église du Québec à la veille de Vatican II et de la Révolution tranquille’, in _Vatican II au Canada:_ _Enracinement et réception_, ed. Gilles Routhier (Montreal: Fides, 2001), 163–75; Kathleen Cummings, Timothy Matovina, and Robert Orsi, ‘Preface’, in _Catholics in the Vatican II Era: Local Histories of a Global Event_, ed. Kathleen Sprows Cummings, Timothy Matovina and Robert Orsi (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2018), ix–xxiii.

One major place of pre-conciliar energy inside the Church was in the area of prayer and spirituality more broadly. The European liturgical movement had a major effect in institutions like St John’s Abbey in Collegeville, Minnesota, which had connections with European monasteries and theologians and had a growing effect upon Catholics in the United States and Canada through its publications and seminars. Growing use of ‘dialogue Masses’ and other forms of lay participation in the liturgy, encouragement of frequent communion, the printing and dissemination of missals in various forms, and increasing Bible reading and attention to Scripture all characterize pre-conciliar liturgical practices that prepared the [^c42-3] **[p. 698]** ground for reception of the council’s teaching on the liturgy. Rather than an imposition upon an unwilling and unprepared populace, most evidence suggests that Catholics in the United States and Canada were well prepared to receive the post-conciliar liturgical reforms; in Quebec, for example, according to Gilles Routhier, the idea that the faithful were unprepared or resistant arose only in the second half of the 1970s; in the immediate post-conciliar period, rather than calls to slow down liturgical renewal, one finds [^c42-4] more often expressions of impatience with the slow pace of implementation.

[^c42-3]: Joseph Chinnici. ‘The Catholic Community at Prayer, 1926–1976’, in _Habits of Devotion, Catholic Religious Practice in_ _Twentieth-Century America_, ed. James O’Toole (Ithaca, NY: Cornell University Press, 2004), 9–87; Christine Laflèche and Gilles Routhier, ‘Le Mouvement liturgique au Québec: Attentes et espérances de l’aggiornamento conciliaire’, in Routhier, _Vatican II au Canada_, 129–61.

[^c42-4]: Gilles Routhier, ‘La Réception de Vatican II au Canada’, in _Vatican II: Herméneutique et réception_, ed. Gilles Routhier (Quebec: Fides, 2006), 269–318.

Connected with these liturgical and spiritual practices were new institutions and forms of religious activity that greatly expanded lay Catholic participation in ecclesial life in the first half of the twentieth century and that peaked in the immediate post-war era. In Quebec, the various branches of Catholic Action provided institutions in which Catholics engaged with Catholic social teaching and developed some of the leadership skills they would use during and after the Quiet Revolution—the intense process of secularization that characterized the 1960s. In the United States and Canada, in addition to other forms of Catholic Action, the Christian Family Movement, various sodalities, and the catechetical movement all became locations in which lay Catholics, together with clergy and religious, solidifled their Catholic identity while looking to new forms of spiritual and social activity in addition to the parish. This ‘pedagogy of participation’, as Joseph Chinnici names it, prepared the way for the later reception of the council’s expansive vision of the Church as the People of God and of a ‘universal call to holiness’ lived out not only within rectories and cloisters, but also in families, workplaces, schools, and public life.[^c42-5]

[^c42-5]: Chinnici, ‘The Catholic Community at Prayer, 1926–1976’, 39–51.

In addition to these internal factors, wider social and political trends also shaped the ground into which the council would be received. One major factor looming over the council and its reception was the fact of the Cold War; indeed, it is nearly impossible to underestimate the influence upon Catholics in both the US and Canada of the possibility of mutually assured nuclear annihilation, a nightmare that, in the Cuban Missile Crisis, veered dangerously close to becoming reality during the first session of the council in October 1962. But beyond this, the constituent Catholic communities in the United States and Canada differed from each other in their social, political, and cultural situations in the pre-conciliar period in ways that resist broad generalization.

For many white US Catholics, the post-war period was a time of upward economic mobility and, often, physical mobility out of urban enclaves into more prosperous, and more religiously and ethnically mixed, suburbs. In ways not true for their African American and Latino counterparts, white Catholics benefited **[p. 699]** from this trend and, in the process, were increasingly influenced by the dominant patterns of post-war US culture. Especially among upwardly mobile working-class, middle-class, and newly upper-class white US Catholics, the mid-twentieth century before the Second Vatican Council was already a time of growing [^c42-6] assimilation to the norms, values, and patterns of behaviour of US culture outside the Church. For these communities descended from the European migrations of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the election of John F. Kennedy, the first Catholic to hold the office of the US presidency, in 1960 marked the culmination of a process of growing acceptance of Catholics as ‘real Americans’, and, simultaneously, a growing acceptance of the US suburban way of life. And, with that process of assimilation, white Catholics increasingly counted Jews and Protestants of various churches as their neighbours, friends, and relations in a way that would not have been possible in the earlier, more homogenous Catholic enclaves.

[^c42-6]: Scott Appleby, ‘Decline or Relocation: The Catholic Presence in Church and Society, 1950–2000’, in _The Church Confronts_ _Modernity_, ed. Leslie Woodcock Tenter (Washington: The Catholic University of America Press, 2007), 209–10.

In addition, long-standing Mexican Catholic communities in the south-western border states as well as newer post-war Mexican migrants formed the backbone of a vibrant and diverse Hispanic Catholic community that, in the early 1960s, was beginning to claim its voice and its rights. In the same year that the council opened, 1962, César Chávez and Dolores Huerta founded the union that would eventually become the United Farm Workers. At the same time, migrants from Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic were changing the culture and demographics of the Catholic Church, especially in cities like New York and Chicago, which were dominated by Euro-American Catholic institutions and leaders. The 1959 revolution in Cuba led to the migration of thousands of Cubans, including many of the most active members and leaders [^c42-7] of Cuban Catholic institutions. In addition to these large pre-conciliar migrations of Spanish-speaking Catholics, the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 dramatically changed the magnitude and countries of origin of new immigrants to the US. New migrations to the United States from elsewhere in Latin America, from Asia, and from Africa ensured that the Church in which Vatican II was received would include Catholics from throughout the global South rather than only from the European countries privileged under the previous immigration quota systems. These developments meant that the post–Vatican II Church in the United States was an immigrant Church again, at the same time that the descendants of older Euro- American communities were consolidating their economic, political, and ecclesial power as ‘fully American’.

[^c42-7]: Timothy Matovina, _Latino Catholicism: Transformation in America’s Largest Church_ (Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press, 2011), 6–41.

Numerous other events and factors could be listed here: the movement for civil rights for African Americans in the United States; the assassinations of John F. Kennedy, Robert Kennedy, and Martin Luther King, Jr; the initial steps of US military involvement in Vietnam; and the demographic changes that resulted from the **[p. 700]** post-war baby boom. Routhier rightly warns that not every post-conciliar event ought to be identifled as a direct result of the council; not everything that happened _post concilium_ ought to be identifled as _propter_ [^c42-8] _concilium_, and it seems clear that while the council may have contributed to the overall sense of the cultural, economic, and political flux that marked the second half the 1960s, the council should not be viewed in isolation from the rapid changes in North American society throughout the 1960s and 1970s and [^c42-9] their wider context.

[^c42-8]: Routhier, ‘Pour un programme de recherche sur la réception de Vatican II’, 9.

[^c42-9]: Thomas Sugrue, ‘The Catholic Encounter with the 1960s’, in _Catholics in the American Century: Recasting Narratives of U.S._ _History_, ed. R. Scott Appleby and Kathleen Sprows Cummings (Ithaca, NY: Cornell University Press, 2012), 61–79.

Canadian Catholics as well shared some of the same sense of accelerating socio-cultural change, but three factors distinguished the Canadian context into which the council was received. The first was the Quiet Revolution, the series of major social and political transitions that occurred in the province of Quebec in the early 1960s. The election of Jean Lesage of the Liberal Party as premier of Quebec in 1960 led to the provincial government taking responsibility for numerous institutions that had been run by the Catholic Church in Quebec—especially education, health care, and social services. This rapid process of secularization, unlike some comparable processes in Europe, was not marked by animus towards the Catholic Church or demonstrative anticlericalism. In the nearly homogenous Catholic society of francophone Quebec, this secularization was carried out by committed lay Catholics, many of whom gained their leadership abilities in the various organizations of Catholic Action, and with the cooperation, or at least without the active opposition, of clergy and bishops. As one historian describes this secularization, ‘it was not at the hands of modern doubters and scoffers at religion that the core of Québec society was evacuated of the Catholic Church’s once-dominant presence, but rather through the faith-filled intentions of religious motivated and socially committed Catholic laypersons and of onetime professional operatives of [^c42-10] the Church itself’. Nevertheless, Québécois society changed rapidly in the early 1960s, becoming more urban, more self-consciously nationalist, and more secular. In this context, the coming changes of the Second Vatican Council would often be embraced in continuity with the movements for ‘modernisation’ or [^c42-11] ‘adaptation’ already occurring on the ground in Quebec.

[^c42-10]: Kevin J. Christiano, ‘The Trajectory of Catholicism in Twentieth-Century Québec’, in _The Church Confronts Modernity_, ed. Leslie Woodcock Tenter (Washington: The Catholic University of America Press, 2007), 45.

[^c42-11]: Terence J. Fay, _A History of Canadian Catholics_ (Montreal: McGill-Queen’s University Press, 2002), 278–302.

A second factor in the Canadian context that distinguishes its reception of the council was wide-scale postwar immigration to Canada, especially from Eastern Europe, that made it an increasingly multicultural society. For the Catholic Church in particular, reception of the council could not but be affected by the presence of a large Ukrainian Catholic population, both in the long-standing agricultural communities of **[p. 701]** western Canada and in the newer communities in the urban centres of eastern Canada. By comparison to the United States, Eastern Catholics comprised a larger percentage of the Catholic population, and their experiences and voices, particularly in relation to ecumenism and to their distinctive liturgical, theological, [^c42-12] and cultural identity, need to be taken into account as part of the story of conciliar reception. And, as in the United States, changes in post-war immigration patterns, particularly the rising numbers of new Canadians from Asia and Africa by comparison to the mostly white European migrants of the pre-war period, made the Catholic Church in Canada a more self-consciously multicultural Church.

[^c42-12]: Myroslaw Tataryn, ‘Canada’s Ukrainian Catholics and Vatican II: A Guide for the Future or Struggling with the Past?’, in _Vatican II: Expériences canadiennes/Canadian Experiences_, ed. Michael Attridge, Catherine Clifford, and Gilles Routhier (Ottawa: University of Ottawa Press, 2011), 239–52.

A third factor, present in a far more limited way among Native Americans in the US, was the culmination of decades of organization and activism by Indigenous Canadians. The late 1960s and 1970s were marked by increasing governmental re-evaluation of policies affecting Indigenous communities as well as growing recognition of Aboriginal treaty rights. Within the Catholic context, the participation of the Catholic Church in sometimes coercive missionary activities and in the residential school system meant that the Church was beginning to experience some of the critique that would grow in the following decades as the mistakes made in Canadian treatment of Indigenous Canadians were brought to public consciousness. In the immediate period of conciliar reception, these forms of pan-Canadian Indigenous rights activism were at their beginning, but the fact of a large yet largely misunderstood and undervalued Indigenous Catholic community would form part of the context in which the council, especially in regard to inculturation, would be received in Canada.

In summary, therefore, pre-conciliar Catholicism in both the United States and Canada was marked by deep vibrancy and institutional strength. At the same time, pre-conciliar Catholics were members of a rapidly changing society and of particular communities whose social and political locations were increasingly mutable, and recognized as such. Rather than stagnation or nostalgia taking hold, however, Catholics were already responding creatively to these changes and adapting their Catholicism before the council, often in and through the institutions of their local Catholic communities. These activities inside the Church largely prepared Catholics well for the _aggiornamento_ initiated by John XXIII. Many, if not most, Catholics in North America, if they were aware of the coming council, looked towards it in hope that changes within the Church might help their communities better adapt to their newer social and cultural locations. Finally, the accelerating pace of societal transformations throughout the 1960s and early 1970s contributed to a sometimes welcomed, sometimes worrying sense of change, which would lead first to a broad welcome of the conciliar renewal as a necessary response to changing times, but also, in some cases, to a reactionary pushback against change within and without the Church.

### 3. Initial Reception: Enthusiasm and Implementation

**[p. 702]** On 29 November 1964, the First Sunday of Advent, English-speaking Catholics in many parts of the United States encountered extensive use of the vernacular in the Mass for the first time; English- and French-speaking Catholics in Canada began experiencing widespread use of the vernacular in the following year. There are dangers of assigning the ‘reception’ of the council, or even of its liturgical adaptations, to a particular date, since the liturgical renewal should be seen as the intensification of a process that was set in motion earlier, and since the liturgical changes occurred piecemeal over a longer period of time. Nevertheless, the liturgical changes that began on that date provide a helpful symbol for the overall sense of change that marked reception of the council in North American Catholicism, since these changes were often the most obvious initial indicator of the impact of the council at the local level.

As noted earlier, these changes were in most cases neither unexpected nor unwanted. Not unexpected, in that forms of greater lay participation in the liturgy had been growing throughout the first half of the twentieth century in forms of missal usage, vernacular preaching, dialogue Masses, and other aspects of the liturgical movement. As the first and in many ways best-prepared document of the council, _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ built upon both scholarship and new forms of popular piety in its call for ‘full, conscious, and active participation’ in the liturgy. Nor, in most cases, were the changes unwanted. While some individuals and communities raised questions about the speed or the scope of the changes, the overall response to liturgical renewal was one of welcome, and even of impatience at delays and limitations in the [^c42-13] implementation processes. With some significant individual exceptions, the process of liturgical revision that began in 1964 was broadly welcomed by Catholics in the fast-changing societies of the US and Canada, particularly by communities like upwardly mobile Euro-American Catholics who wanted to fit in with their neighbours and in francophone communities of Canada for whom French-language usage was increasingly being reclaimed as a mark of socio-cultural and political identity.

[^c42-13]: Chinnici, ‘The Catholic Community at Prayer, 1926–1976’, 82–87; Routhier, ‘La Réception de Vatican II au Canada’, 285–86.

The broadly enthusiastic welcome given to these liturgical reforms, therefore, provides a helpful symbol for the reception of the council as a whole in the US and Canada. While such a top-down implementation was primed to succeed in a community deeply formed to ‘pay, pray, and obey’, that reception was aided not only by habits of obedience but also by experiences and expectations formed before and during the meeting of the council. As the most reported-upon council in Church history, the role of secular and Catholic **[p. 703]** journalists in the reception of the council cannot be overestimated. In the words of Routhier, ‘the bishop and his official intermediaries were no longer the only ones to convey information to the faithful. Thanks to the media, the faithful had gradually built up a new idea of the Church, of its activity, of its work, of its [^c42-14] reform, and of its future.’ The liturgical reforms were not simply something that ‘happened’ to many North American Catholics; rather, they were something that many Catholics had been waiting for, and in some cases allowed them to assimilate more easily into the structures of a secularizing society in which they [^c42-15] found themselves. At the same time, Catholics made active choices regarding their practices; as many Catholics embraced the new Eucharistic liturgy, one can point to the ‘collapse of confession’ in the post- [^c42-16] conciliar period as a response both to past practice and to a new-found sense of individual agency.

[^c42-14]: Routhier, ‘La Réception de Vatican II au Canada’, 291.

[^c42-15]: Appleby, ‘Decline or Relocation’, 208–35; James Davidson, ‘The Catholic Church in the United States: 1950 to the Present’, in _The Church Confronts Modernity_, ed. Leslie Woodcock Tentler (Washington: The Catholic University of America Press, 2007), 177–207.

[^c42-16]: James O’Toole, ‘In the Court of Conscience’, in _Habits of Devotion, Catholic Religious Practice in Twentieth-Century_ _America_, ed. James O’Toole (Ithaca, NY: Cornell University Press, 2004), 168–85.

The same is true for many other aspects of conciliar reception that were less immediately obvious then and now. Three seem most broadly universal in the North American experience, each of which can be understood through both the shared experiences and some of the ‘micro-receptions’ of distinct communities of North American Catholics. The first and most powerful was the change in the understanding of the nature of the Church and of the relation of the baptized faithful to the clergy. In its teachings in _Lumen Gentium_ on the universal call to holiness, on the Church as the pilgrim people of God, and on the relations between ordained and lay Catholics as a shared if differentiated call to mission, the council opened up pathways to intensifled lay involvement and co-responsibility in the Church. The change in style of the council had much to do with this opening; as John O’Malley notes, the language of the conciliar documents moved ‘from commands to invitations, from laws to ideals, from threats to persuasion, from coercion to conscience, from monologue to conversation, from ruling to serving, from withdrawn to [^c42-17] integrated, from vertical and top-down to horizontal’. But this movement was one prepared for, and even eagerly anticipated, by Catholics involved in the various organizations of Catholic Action, in the Christian Family Movement, and in the catechetical movement. This ‘pedagogy of participation’ prepared lay Catholics for greater involvement in their Church, and the language of the time often used the metaphors of [^c42-18] maturity, of ‘growing up’, of ‘becoming adults’ to describe this change in perspective.

[^c42-17]: John O’Malley, ‘Vatican II: Did Anything Happen?’, in _Vatican II: Did Anything Happen?_, ed. David G. Schultenover (New York: Continuum, 2007), 81.

[^c42-18]: Chinnici, ‘The Catholic Community at Prayer, 1926–1976’, 39–51.

One community of reception in which this is particularly clear is the experience of Catholics in Quebec. The council’s call for co-responsibility in the Church mirrored the experience of the Quiet Revolution’s claiming of co-responsibility for all sorts of social services previously administered by the institutional Church. **[p. 704]** Without the angry anticlericalism or the reactionary ecclesial resistance found in some European contexts, this process of secularization in Quebec was perceived and experienced as fitting harmoniously with the conciliar call for lay Catholics’ active leadership in secular matters. In Quebec, the assumption of the responsibility for health care, education, and many social services by lay Catholics through the mechanisms of the state was seen not as anti-Church or anti-Catholic but as a proper division of labour [^c42-19] through which Catholic teaching combined with lay expertise would reach its fullest extent.

[^c42-19]: Gilles Routhier, ‘La Réception de Vatican II au Canada’, 269–318.

Another distinct place of reception of conciliar teaching on lay co-responsibility for the Church can be seen in the history of ministry to and with Hispanic Catholics in the US. Central to this story is the history of the Encuentros, beginning with Primer Encuentro Hispano de Pastoral in 1972. These wide-scale gatherings were inspired in part by forms of the new theologies of liberation being developed in Latin America, but in the US context they brought together clergy, religious, and laypeople to claim a collective voice for Latinos within the US Catholic Church and for the future of pastoral ministry to and with Latinos throughout the United States. The Encuentros have been marked by intentionally participatory processes which were themselves anticipated by the See–Judge–Act method of the Young Christian Workers movement. In these meetings over the following decades, US Latinos co-created a new form of grassroots synodality; that is, a new form of collective ecclesial decision-making that was enabled by the conciliar call for lay co-responsibility in the Church.[^c42-20]

[^c42-20]: Matovina, _Latino Catholicism_, 74–97; Mario J. Paredes, _The History of the National Encuentros_ (New York: Paulist, 2014).

A second, nearly universally received theme of the council was the new perspective on the relations of Catholics to other Christians, to members of other religious traditions, and to the non-Catholic world most broadly. In contexts marked by assimilation to mainstream culture, like that of Euro-American Catholics in the United States, the new opening to non-Catholics was enthusiastically welcomed. In a culture in which so-called mixed marriages were stigmatized and Catholics had been officially forbidden from participating in the ecumenical activities pioneered by their Protestant and Orthodox neighbours, forms of ecumenical engagement were enthusiastically welcomed. While, as elsewhere, much unofficial encounter and groundwork had been done in the pre-conciliar period, after the council parishes and dioceses entered into official relations with local councils of churches and other ecumenical organizations. But the reception also occurred at grass-roots level: one programme begun in 1965 was the ‘living room dialogues’ which brought together Catholic, Protestant, and Orthodox neighbours for conversation and faith sharing; within two years, 5,000 of these groups had met throughout the US and Canada. In terms of interreligious dialogue, the shared immigrant and Americanization trajectory of Euro-American Catholics and Jews led to increased communication, dialogue, and cooperation, particularly in interreligious charity efforts and local interfaith religious services. Furthermore, the declaration on religious liberty, _Dignitatis Humanae_, rooted in the **[p. 705]** thought of American Jesuit John Courtney Murray and championed at Vatican II by the US bishops, was for many US Catholics an endorsement of their way of negotiating religious identity in a pluralist democracy and a bookend to the election of John F. Kennedy: now, just as the United States had accepted them as [^c42-21] participants in US culture, their Church had ratifled the way in which they had done so.

[^c42-21]: Joseph Chinnici, ‘Ecumenism, Civil Rights, and the Second Vatican Council: The American Experience’, _U.S. Catholic_ _Historian_ 30 (2012): 21–49.

Another important micro-reception of the council was the Catholic Charismatic Renewal. Related to the modern Pentecostal movement and churches that are conventionally dated to the Azusa Street Revival in the first decade of the twentieth century, Pentecostalism began as a renewal movement within the Protestant churches; by the mid-century, it had a major and growing community throughout the US and Canada. In mostly lay-led prayer groups in the immediate post-conciliar period, Catholics began to experience baptism in the Spirit and forms of charismatic gifts in ways similar to classical Pentecostalism and started organizing para-liturgical prayer services and organizations. By drawing upon the language of a universal call to holiness and Pope John XXIII’s own call for ‘a new Pentecost’, the Catholic Charismatic Renewal was cautiously welcomed by church authorities as an unexpected fruit both of ecumenical dialogue and of the openness to new forms of spirituality and mission that the council promoted. The Charismatic Renewal became a major voice not only in the Euro-American communities of the Midwest, where it began in the late 1960s, but also among Latino and African American Catholics. It stands as a further indicator that conciliar reception of the value of dialogue in North America involved much creative reappropriation of conciliar teaching by individuals and communities rather than a simplistic adaptation or fully controlled implementation by ecclesial leaders.[^c42-22]

[^c42-22]: Fay, _A History of Canadian Catholics_, 297–301; Susan A. Maurer, _The Spirit of Enthusiasm: A History of the Catholic_ _Charismatic Renewal, 1967–2000_ (Lanham, MD: University Press of America, 2010).

A third broadly shared aspect of North American reception of the council was the renewal of Catholic social teaching in relation to the political and economic issues of the day. Rooted in _Gaudium et Spes_ as well as recent papal teaching, including John XXIII’s encyclical _Pacem in Terris_, North American attention to the socio-political implications of the Gospel became a defining feature of post-conciliar Catholicism. As elsewhere, re-reception of Catholic social teaching was prepared by much pre-conciliar work, including the organizations of Catholic Action and small, yet vocal, communities like Dorothy Day’s Catholic Worker Movement. But the implementation of a Catholic vision of shared social life, and a confidence in the mechanisms of government as an instrument of that implementation, characterized post-conciliar Catholicism, especially among lay Catholics looking to exercise their vocation within the worlds of politics, business, and education. Quebec provides the clearest example, in which the secular government took on many of the social initiatives previously administered by the Church, but throughout North America Catholics increasingly saw their social and political activities as duties of both their citizenship and their **[p. 706]** baptism. This was not without disagreement, however, and intra-Catholic conflict over the Vietnam War in the United States, ranging from the pro-military work of Cardinal Francis Spellman to the radical pacifism and protest of the Berrigan brothers, indicated the intensity with which Catholics disagreed about [^c42-23] how Catholic social teaching should be interpreted.

[^c42-23]: Mark S. Massa, _The American Catholic Revolution_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2010), 103–28.

A leading place for the reception of the council’s social teaching, as well as its return to the Church’s sources of spiritual and theological renewal, was the reception of the council by communities of religious life in North America, especially by women religious. Perhaps more than any other document, the conciliar decree _Perfectae Caritatis_ (_PC_) most clearly advocated for a grass-roots appropriation of conciliar _ressourcement_ and _aggiornamento_ at the level of local communities. This can be seen in its very title, ‘Decree on the Adaptation and Renewal of Religious Life’, in addition to its explicit instruction that religious communities’ ‘manner of life, prayer, and work should be suitable to the physical and psychological conditions of today’s religious; it should also, in so far as this is permitted by an institute’s character, be in harmony with the demands of the apostolate, with the requirements of culture and with the social and economic climate’ (_PC_ 3). This call, along with _Perfectae Caritatis_’ instruction that religious communities return to the sources of their own distinctive charisms and to the spirit and aims of their founders, led many religious communities to re-evaluate their life and practice in the immediate post-conciliar period in the light of their histories and of the ‘signs of the times’ in their local communities.

In North America, this call was widely and, in most cases, positively received, especially by communities of women religious who had been quietly yet consistently re-evaluating their communities’ priorities, experimenting with innovative leadership styles and decision-making processes, and educating their members in a variety of fields and competencies, including theology. Not without controversy, including within their own communities, women religious revised their constitutions, began working in ministries beyond the traditional fields of education and health care to engage more directly in social services and justice-related organization, and moved away from some of the structures, regulations, and forms of organization that they judged more rooted in medieval and early modern societal norms than in the genuine charisms of their founders. In Quebec, the secularization of many of the services previously rendered by religious communities, especially education and health care, further intensifled this rethinking of charisms and even crises of identity, in some cases. The modifications or even abandonment of traditional habits that were the most visible indication for many Catholics that something about religious life was changing symbolized a wider paradigm in religious women’s sense of identity with and within the wider Church.

Those changes were not without conflict, however, and this final example of micro-reception provides a helpful anticipation of the next section’s analysis of how conciliar reception became increasingly confiictual in the decades following the council. Two kinds of conflict predominated. First, as Mark Massa’s case study **[p. 707]** of the Sisters of the Immaculate Heart of Mary in Los Angeles demonstrates, the rethinking by women religious of their ministries and priorities was not always welcomed by bishops and other ecclesial [^c42-24] authorities who had long counted on women religious to staff ‘their’ schools and hospitals. Further, the pace and scope of changes led to confiicts within communities, often along generational lines, between women whose security of identity and practice over the course of their lifetimes was being critiqued and [^c42-25] even overturned in the service of ‘renewal’.

[^c42-24]: Ibid., 75–102.

[^c42-25]: Margaret M. McGuinness, _Called to Serve: A History of Nuns in America_ (New York: New York University Press, 2013), 154–79.

This crisis in identity coincided with a dramatic drop in the numbers of women entering religious life, particularly in contrast to the seemingly anomalous spike in vocations to the priesthood and religious life in the post-war period. Between 1958 and 1962, approximately 23,302 women entered religious orders; at the [^c42-26] end of the following decade, between 1976 and 1980, only 2,767 women made the same choice. At the same time, thousands of members of religious orders, male and female, as well as seminarians and clergy, also left active ministry, contributing to the impression of a collapse not only of religious communities, but also of some of the structures of Catholic institutional identity thought previously to be unshakeable. It is to the consequences of the further confiicts over conciliar reception that began in the late 1960s that this chapter now turns, but the experiences of communities of women religious, which functioned as early laboratories of conciliar renewal, already indicate that conflict over the content, scope, and pace of ecclesial change would mark a distinct second phase of conciliar reception in North America.

[^c42-26]: Chester Gillis, _Roman Catholicism in America_ (New York: Columbia University Press, 1999), 97.

### 4. Continuing Reception of the Council: Conflict over Change

The year 1968 often serves as a symbolic date for the upheavals of cultural, political, and religious life that occurred throughout the late 1960s and early 1970s in many societies, including the United States and Canada. The symbolism can be overdrawn in a way that inflates the importance of that year in relation to what occurred before and after. But 1968 was a year marked by the Tet Offensive in Vietnam, the assassinations of Robert Kennedy and Martin Luther King, Jr in the United States, the founding of the Parti Québécois in Canada, and protests, sometimes violently suppressed, in Prague, Paris, Mexico City, and college campuses throughout the United States. In the Roman Catholic world, 1968 is best known as the year of the release of Pope Paul VI’s final encyclical, _Humanae Vitae_ (On the Regulation of Birth). While it should **[p. 708]** similarly not be isolated from its pre- and post-history, the reception, and non-reception, of _Humanae Vitae_ in the North American Catholic context marks a turning point in the reception of the council. _Humanae Vitae_, as much as any of the other crucial theological and cultural factors, signifled a transition to a more contentious phase in the reception of the council, where different understandings and expectations of ecclesial renewal came into focus, and in which the longer-term awareness of change as a possibility in Roman Catholic life began to have institutional consequences. At the same time, as Routhier suggests, Catholics in North America faced the challenge that the more gradual conciliar _aggiornamento_ was quickly [^c42-27] overtaken by the cultural revolutions occurring at the same time.

[^c42-27]: Routhier, ‘La Réception de Vatican II au Canada’, 300.

The complicated history of _Humanae Vitae_ begins during the Second Vatican Council, when, rather than having the issue of birth control raised in the conciliar discussions, John XXIII established a commission to study the issues; it was later renewed and enlarged by Paul VI. In addition to curial officials, bishops, and theologians, the commission eventually included the voices of lay Catholics, most notably Patty and Pat Crowley of Chicago, leaders in the Christian Family Movement who were able to survey their membership and bring the experiences of married committed Catholics to the awareness of the commission. The commission submitted its report in 1966, with a majority of the members recommending changes to the full condemnation of birth control, while a minority report signed by four of the sixty-nine commission members advised against any revision of the teaching. Both reports were leaked to the media in 1967, leading to heightened expectations among many North American Catholics that the use of contraception for some regulation of births would no longer be considered sinful. _Humanae Vitae_, released in July 1968, disappointed many lay Catholics, theologians, and clergy in North America, leading to statements by theologians like moral theologian Fr Charles Curran and by some priests of the Archdiocese of Washington, DC, against the directives of their bishop, and the remarkable Winnipeg Statement of the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, which attempted to maintain space for contraception-using Catholics within the life of the Church. In Catholic media as well as in the wider secular press, deeply divided Catholics debated both the pastoral and theological sense of the document, as well as the ecclesiological questions regarding conscience, magisterial teaching authority, and development of doctrine that it raised.[^c42-28]

[^c42-28]: Massa, _The American Catholic Revolution_, 29–48; Robert McClory, _Turning Point: The Inside Story of the Papal Birth Control_ _Commission and How Humanae Vitae Changed the Life of Patty Crowley and the Future of the Church_ (New York: Crossroad, 1995); Leslie Woodcock Tentler, _Catholics and Contraception: An American History_ (Ithaca, NY: Cornell University Press, 2004).

In many ways, the preparation for _Humanae Vitae_ and its reception structurally paralleled the preparation and reception of the Second Vatican Council. Much of the theological and pastoral reflection on the issues had been done in the decades preceding the encyclical both in theological scholarship and in careful **[p. 709]** reflection by married Catholic laypeople. And as with liturgical reform, ecumenical and interreligious dialogue, and religious liberty, many North American Catholics had high expectations for what they thought was a long-overdue _aggiornamento_ of Catholic teaching to the realities of modern married living. Unlike the conciliar reforms, however, _Humanae Vitae_ marks a point at which the expectations of many North American Catholics for continuing reform and renewal were met instead with an authoritative rejection of those hopes. This contrast experience—between a conciliar experience which met and in some cases exceeded expectations for adaptation of the Church to North American cultures and mores and a post-conciliar experience which established a firm line beyond which adaptation would go no further—explains as much about the swiftness and intensity of the reaction as the particular content of _Humanae Vitae_.

_Humanae Vitae_ intersects with the reception of the council in North America in at least two substantial ways. First, practically, reception or non-reception of _Humanae Vitae_ concretized and solidifled divisions between Catholics over how to interpret and receive the council. Most North American Catholics, clergy and lay, were broadly supportive of, or at least went along with, the implementation of conciliar teaching, and outside some very small traditionalist communities, few Catholics would be found outright rejecting the council or its teachings. But just as religious communities like the Sisters of the Immaculate Heart of Mary and others experienced tensions regarding the pace and scope of the changes that accompanied that implementation, North American Catholics as a whole now found an issue that became an effective sign of the divisions between more ‘progressive’ Catholics expecting a continuing trajectory of reform and change and more ‘conservative’ Catholics who thought that the pace and scope of reform needed to be slowed and curtailed. A strict binary is overly simplistic—as in the initial reception, many Catholics in many different communities were facing different challenges and having different arguments than an argument over the legitimacy of contraception. But in Catholic media in this period, in the relations between lay Catholics and clergy, between priests and their bishops, and between the churches in North America and Rome, the divisions that _Humanae Vitae_ made evident played a major role in further reception of the council. Conflict over liturgical renewal and divisions over whether such changes had ‘gone too far’ first arise in the post-1968 Church; arguments about identity, clerical formation, and the place of religious life, and discussion of the continuing place of conscience and religious liberty, would all mark the following decades.

In the extreme, some Catholics from then on viewed the conciliar reception either as a lost opportunity for further reform or as a Pandora’s box of reforms that got out of hand; while most Catholics’ views were more moderate, _Humanae Vitae_ sowed the seeds of further polarization within the Catholic Church in North America, especially within the United States. As Stephen Schloesser has noted, the council did an excellent job of responding to modernity and meeting the expectations of many Catholics to the questions they had been raising and practices they had been experimenting with in the pre-conciliar period; however, _Humanae Vitae_ marks what he names the collision of conciliar teaching with ‘biopolitics’, with the issues regarding **[p. 710]** sexuality and gender about which the council was broadly uninterested and unprepared to address— [^c42-29] issues that would dominate intra-ecclesial debates and divisions in the decades to come.

[^c42-29]: Stephen Schloesser, ‘ “Dancing on the Edge of the Volcano”: Biopolitics and What Happened after Vatican II’, in _From_ _Vatican II to Pope Francis: Charting a Catholic Future_, ed. Paul J. Crowley (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2014), 3–26.

A second way in which the debates over the reception or non-reception of _Humanae Vitae_ affected reception of the council is in relation to the historical consciousness, and particularly the consciousness of change, that the Second Vatican Council fostered, intentionally or not, among North American Catholics. As Mark Massa has written, Vatican II changed not just Catholic teaching and practice but also the broader horizon within which Catholics thought about the historicity of their community’s teachings and practices. Quoting Garry Wills, he restates that the council ‘let out the dirty little secret, in the most startling way, the fact that [^c42-30] the _church changes_’. Massa continues in his own words, identifying the debates over the reception of the council as intensifled by growing Catholic recognition of the fact of ecclesial change. He writes, ‘If the debates within the American Catholic community set oft by the decrees of Vatican II were actually based on the unintended consequence of allowing, or even encouraging, Catholic believers to face the long-delayed implications of historical development and contingency, then the battles suddenly become more important [^c42-31] and the stakes become higher.’

[^c42-30]: Massa, _The American Catholic Revolution_, 7.

[^c42-31]: Ibid., 9.

From that perspective, therefore, the conflict over the proper reception of the council that reached a turning point in the reception and non-reception of _Humanae Vitae_ was connected with a variegated reception of the conciliar reality of ecclesial change. The debates over _Humanae Vitae_ brought into the open differences between Catholics who had embraced change and expected that historical consciousness and the possibility of further renewal would be a continuing component of Catholic life from then onwards, and those Catholics who were concerned by the pace or scope of ecclesial change and were expecting magisterial action to clarify the limits of reform and renewal. After _Humanae Vitae_, Catholics of the former perspective who had expected a more dramatic change in Catholic teaching on birth control were deeply disappointed and, in some cases, disillusioned in their expectation of continued Catholic adaptation to the norms of their North American cultures. At the same time, Catholics of the latter perspective found their footing on a bedrock of immutable Catholic teaching from which they began to critique other forms of unlimited or overly rapid change in their understanding of how to be Catholic.

In the decades of reception of the council after 1968, then, while continuing to differ significantly from place to place and from community to community, one finds some common forms of reception across Catholics in North America that develop and, in some ways, solidify these differing views on the overall reception of the council. First, generally across geographical, linguistic, and ethnic lines, the adaptation of **[p. 711]** structures, institutions, liturgy, and ways of being Catholic continued at a steady pace. In addition to some of the developments already mentioned, there were further translations and adaptations of liturgical forms, continued renewal of religious communities, the establishment of new diocesan and parochial pastoral structures, and increased lay involvement in ministries, new religious communities, the Catholic charismatic renewal, and theological education. All of these developments, in which Catholics received and claimed the initiatives of the council in often surprisingly creative and diverse ways in their local contexts, made the council a ‘done deal’, an irrevocable aspect of Catholic life in North America. Direct opposition to the council was small, isolated, and largely irrelevant to wider Catholic life in North America, even if forms of mass and social media would later allow them to speak with an outsized voice in the early decades of the twenty-first century.

The fault line between ‘progressive’ and ‘conservative’ Catholics that debates over _Humanae Vitae_ brought to the forefront and symbolized, however, hardened into lines of continued conflict over conciliar reception, adaptation, and renewal, particularly at the institutional levels of theological faculties, Catholic media, and leadership in dioceses and religious communities. Under the later years of the papacy of Paul VI, and particularly under the long papacy of John Paul II, the conflict was never over _whether_ to receive Vatican II but over _how_ to receive Vatican II. Among those labelled ‘conservative’, the consensus was that the period of adaptation and experimentation after the council had got out of hand and needed to be reined in; in North America, in the face of the Roe v. Wade, the women’s liberation movement, rapidly changing norms of sexual behaviour, and the increasing irrelevance of religious voices in a secularizing public sphere, many Catholics concluded that earlier attempts at conciliar reception that had adapted Catholic teaching and [^c42-32] practice to the outside culture needed to be slowed, stopped, or even reversed. At the same time, many more ‘progressive’ Catholics expected ecclesial change to be the continuing narrative of Catholic life and were frustrated by the slowing down or reversal of continuing adaptation, not only in the area of birth control, but also regarding expectations of greater lay involvement in ecclesial life and decision-making, increased and more prominent roles for women at all levels of Catholic life, and more robust Catholic participation in movements for civil rights and greater equality for African Americans, Latinos, and others. These tensions were more polarized in the United States, but still present in various ways in Canada.

[^c42-32]: Appleby, ‘Decline or Relocation’.

Finally, this post-1968 period of ecclesial reception was marked by the rhetoric of ecclesial ‘crisis’. One area of crisis involved the demographics of clerical and religious life, as numbers of new seminarians and vocations to religious life dropped precipitously by comparison to the pre-conciliar period and as numerous women and men left communities or priestly ministry. Arguably, some of this, especially with regard to religious women, resulted from the renewed valuation of lay ministry and, ironically, of women’s liberation, as ministries and jobs once requiring ordination or consecration to religious life could now be **[p. 712]** pursued by laypeople, and as additional professional opportunities became possible for women outside the convent. Similarly, contemporaries identifled a ‘crisis’ regarding Mass attendance and religious practice. While outside Quebec, Mass attendance remained high compared to many other countries, it and other forms of participation decreased compared to pre-conciliar levels. Whether or not these post-conciliar ‘crises’ were in fact caused by the conciliar reforms, they further exacerbated continuing polarization regarding conciliar reception, shaping competing, often adversarial patterns of thought and institutional structures, especially in the United States, for decades to come.

## 43. Reception of Vatican II in Europe

Mathijs Lamberigts

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 713]** In 1963, during the period of the Second Vatican Council, Anglican bishop John A. T. Robinson published his book entitled _Honest to God_. The book became a bestseller and was quickly translated into seventeen languages, selling over a million copies. It was an accessible book that was read by clergy, theologians, and laypeople. And though initially it provoked consternation, it was soon used as a standard text in theological [^c43-1] colleges and universities. Writing at a time when regular attendance in the Anglican Church was in rapid decline, Robinson was struggling with traditional expressions of Christianity and searching for a new kind of language to communicate the Christian faith. Harvey Cox’s _The Secular City_ (1965) claimed that through [^c43-2] the process of secularization—a concept that has itself been problematized since the 1980s, with valuable [^c43-3] statistics that still remain valid —the faithful were increasingly unconvinced by previous religious certitudes. Two years later, Peter Berger argued in _The Sacred Canopy_ (1967) that all religious ideas, despite their presentation as both objective and absolute, were nothing more than the constructs of human beings longing for meaning in their lives. Like Robinson’s book, Cox’s and Berger’s became bestsellers. All three authors were convinced that the ‘good old days of traditional doctrine’ were over. The advent and proliferation of these and other similar works, written by Anglican and Protestant authors yet appearing **[p. 714]** [^c43-4] even in Catholic circles, announced the end of conventional Christianity.

[^c43-1]: C. Slee, ed., _Honest to God: 40 Years On_ (Canterbury: SCM, 2004).

[^c43-2]: C. G. Brown, ‘The Secularisation Decade: What the 1960s Have Done to the Study of Religious History’, in _The Decline of_ _Christendom in Western Europe, 1750–2000_, ed. H. McLeod and W. Ustorf (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2003), 29–46.

[^c43-3]: Y. Lambert, ‘New Christianity, Indifference and Diffused Spirituality’, in H. McLeod and W. Ustorf, _The Decline of_ _Christendom in Western Europe, 1750–2000_ (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2003), 63–78.

[^c43-4]: W. H. Van de Pol, _Het einde van het conventionele christendom_ (Roermond: J.J. Romen & Zonen, 1966).

[^c43-5] During the 1960s, Christian religiosity of most denominations underwent a simultaneous change in most if [^c43-6] not all countries in Western Europe —a change that remains visible up to the present day. Secularization found its way, and neither the organization of a synod on evangelization in 1974 nor the publication of the Apostolic Exhortation _Evangelii Nuntiandi_ in 1975 had a great impact on Catholic life in Europe. The same should be said for John Paul II’s project against the culture of death and Benedict XVI’s second evangelization of especially Europe. Christianity gradually lost its monopoly; Roman Catholicism became, like other Christian denominations, an important minority religion in a pluralizing world. Pluralism was always present within Christianity and Roman Catholicism, but the pluralism of the mid-1960s was often characterized by an a- or anti-Christian/Catholic attitude. In Western Europe, the position of the Roman Catholic Church was gradually weakened in countries such as Spain, the Netherlands, and Germany and regions such as Flanders. In Ireland, complaints could be heard about growing absenteeism and [^c43-7] materialism. France and French-speaking Belgium were already mission lands long before Vatican II. Even in Italy, the approval of the law on divorce in 1970 made clear that Catholics were no longer obedient to the papal authority. In 1974, the attempt to abrogate the law ended in a massive defeat: 68 per cent of the [^c43-8] inhabitants of Rome were opposed to it. Being Roman Catholic thus became an individual choice: the Church no longer decided for her members how they were to vote, whom they were to marry, or how they were to behave. The faithful often became clients, with the freedom to choose and to ‘construct’ their own religion and religious practices. In this way, Vatican II happened at a time when the Roman Catholic Church in Europe was still a _Grosskirche_, but its implementation would take place at a time when she was confronted with internal crises and secularization, two key factors that would have an immense impact on the reception of the council. Nevertheless, Catholics remain an important demographic: in 2010, 50 per cent of all European Christians were (Roman) Catholic according to the European Values Surveys.

[^c43-5]: H. McLeod, _The Religious Crisis of the 1960s_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2007).

[^c43-6]: Brown, ‘The Secularisation Decade’, 29–30.

[^c43-7]: V. A. McClelland, ‘Great Britain and Ireland’, in _Modern Catholicism: Vatican II and After_, ed. A. Hastings (London: SPCK, 1991), 365–76, 370.

[^c43-8]: P. Chenaux, _Paul VI: Le Souverain éclairé_ (Paris: Cerf, 2015), 248–249.

These changes along with cultural changes came about during a period when leaders of the Roman Catholic Church were attempting to concretize the _aggiornamento_ or updating that, according to John XXIII, was needed in the Church and its relationship to the world. Yet they were either unforeseen or underestimated [^c43-9] **[p. 715]** by the council fathers, with the result that the conciliar documents were sometimes responding to the challenges of the 1950s and not dealing directly with problems that were under way in 1965.

[^c43-9]: J. Kerkhofs, ‘Western Europe’, in Hastings, _Modern Catholicism: Vatican II and After_, 357–76.

Furthermore, half of Europe had been under the influence of communism since 1945, a primary objective of [^c43-10] which was the complete eradication of religion. Strategies to attain this objective might differ, with the Soviet Communist Party being sensitive to local traditions and historical differences, for example. Regions such as Eastern Germany and the Czech Republic gradually became areligious. In other countries, such as Poland, the Catholic Church protected her identity by acting against the communist regime. On the other hand, in countries like Bulgaria, Estonia, and Romania, Roman Catholics suffered under communist constraints, as they formed but a small minority. This was also the case for important parts of Yugoslavia, Macedonia, the USSR, Belarus, Moldavia, and Ukraine. At the same time, regions such as Croatia, Slovenia (in Yugoslavia), and Slovakia (in Czechoslovakia) remained predominantly Roman Catholic. On the whole, bishops from communist countries were a small group at the council: only two bishops from Hungary, four from Czechoslovakia (several were still imprisoned when the council began in 1962), twenty-four from Yugoslavia, and twenty-six from Poland participated, just over 2 per cent of all bishop participants. Needless to say, the council would be perceived and implemented differently in those parts of Europe, where Roman Catholics had to struggle for survival. Thanks to the Vatican’s Ostpolitik, successfully developed by the Secretary of State, Cardinal Agostino Casaroli, agreements were reached with communist Hungary [^c43-11] (1964) and communist Yugoslavia (1966). These agreements resulted, in Yugoslavia, in a free exercise of religious rites, the safeguarding of freedom of conscience and freedom of religion, and competency of the [^c43-12] Holy See with regard to ecclesiastical matters. There was a revival of religious life in which _Glas Koncila_, a bulletin that published news about the council, played an important role. In 1970, the bulletin had about [^c43-13] 180,000 subscriptions, making it the most widely read weekly in Yugoslavia. In Croatia, the creation of a Centre for Conciliar Research, Documentation, and Information, the ability to build new churches, and mass gatherings such as the Thirteenth Marian Congress in Marija Bistrica (1971) with more than 100,000 participants, all had an impact during the first period after Vatican II. However, Tito’s coup against reform-minded Croatian leaders at the end of 1971 would result in a long period of ‘Croat silence’, when the Catholic [^c43-14] Church was accused of helping the ‘nationalists’.

[^c43-10]: G. Sikorska, ‘Eastern Europe’, in Hastings, _Modern Catholicism: Vatican II and After_, 345–56, 345.

[^c43-11]: P. H. Kosicki, ‘Introduction’, in _Vatican II Behind the Iron Curtain_, ed. P. H. Kosicki (Washington, DC: The Catholic University of America Press, 2016), 1–26, 22.

[^c43-12]: I. Banac, ‘Vatican II and Yugoslavia’, in Kosicki, _Vatican II Behind the Iron Curtain_, 75–98, 87-88.

[^c43-13]: Sikorska, ‘Eastern Europe’, 348.

[^c43-14]: Banac, ‘Vatican II and Yugoslavia’, 94–97.

The political climate had an impact on Catholic Church life. Because Cardinal Josef Beran’s critique of the Czech regime—Beran was allowed to participate in the final session of the council, but not to return to **[p. 716]** Prague—Czechoslovakian efforts to implement the conciliar decisions were blocked by the regime, at least until 1967. During the Prague Spring in 1968, several initiatives were undertaken to implement the council. Because the Prague Spring was short-lived, the Church, its press, and its associations were soon brought again under strict State control. From the early 1970s, the Church in the Czech Republic had to fight [^c43-15] to survive. Readers had to wait until the early 1980s to see Czech translations of the Vatican II documents. It was only in 1988 that Cardinal František Tomášek received permission to import Bibles and breviaries in [^c43-16] Czech. A Slovak edition had been published in 1968-70, thanks to the help of the Academia Christiana in Rome, the same institution that would help with the printing of the Czech edition. Similar restrictions existed in Romania and Bulgaria. Even in Poland, where people were well informed about conciliar activities and bishops like Karol Wojtyła regularly published about the council and its meaning, a bilingual Polish– Latin edition of the documents in 1968 was prevented from reaching a wide audience through the intervention of the secret police. Thus, average Polish readers had to wait until 1986 to see the documents of [^c43-17] Vatican II in their own language. In Hungary, the agreement between the State and the Vatican did not end the persecution of the Church. Only in 1975 were the council documents translated into Hungarian, thanks [^c43-18] to the abbey of Pannonhalma. In Lithuania, Latvia, and Belarus, the conciliar documents were not available before the fall of the Iron Curtain. In countries under the communist regime, religious education and thus adequate instruction about Vatican II remained a problem, as education was highly controlled by the communist parties.

[^c43-15]: J. R. Felak, ‘Vatican II and Czechoslovakia’, in Kosicki, _Vatican II Behind the Iron Curtain_, 99–126, 120.

[^c43-16]: Sikorska, ‘Eastern Europe’, 349.

[^c43-17]: P. H. Kosicki, ‘Vatican II and Poland’, in Kosicki, _Vatican II Behind the Iron Curtain_, 127–98.

[^c43-18]: Á. Von Klimó, ‘Vatican II and Hungary’, in Kosicki, _Vatican II Behind the Iron Curtain_, 50–74, 70.

In sum, the post-Vatican II attempts to implement conciliar ideas were confronted with a growing crisis and constant decline of religious life in Western Europe and firm opposition in Central and Eastern Europe, an opposition that also resulted in the decline of religious life.

### 2. Liturgical Renewal

The implementation of the Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy, _Sacrosanctum Concilium_, began during the council itself. From the beginning, there existed a tension between the activities of the Council for the Implementation of the Constitution on Sacred Liturgy (_Consilium ad exsequendam Constitutionem de sacra liturgia_) and the Sacred Congregation of Rites, due primarily to the fact that the respective competencies of [^c43-19] the two were not clearly defined. The publication of the motu proprio, initially prepared by the **[p. 717]** secretariat of the council and the Congregation of Rites, immediately caused unrest, critique, and disappointment in several European countries, including Germany, Austria, and France, for local European episcopal conferences had hoped for a liturgical renewal under the responsibility of local episcopal conferences. According to bishops and experts, the approach of the Congregation for Rites did not respect the council’s spirit.

[^c43-19]: P. Marini, _Challenging Reform: Realizing the Vision of the Liturgical Renewal_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2007).

Thanks to the efforts of Cardinal Giacomo Lercaro and Annibale Bugnini, supported by Paul VI’s instruction _Inter Oecumenici_ (26 September 1964), the Consilium was prepared to initiate the implementation of the constitution independently of the congregation. The instruction made possible a broad interpretation of the norms for the use of the vernacular and a more decentralized approach to the reform.
