Bishops’ conferences received more autonomy, sharing responsibility with the Holy See. Soon, the use of the vernacular was accepted everywhere. The fact that bishops’ conferences were granted greater autonomy was just one side of the coin. Indeed, local communities dared to act autonomously, as well, at times resulting in conflict. The _Paroisse et liturgie_ incident (the editor-in-chief was convoked by Cardinal Leo Jozef Suenens because he had suggested that _Sacrosanctum Concilium_ was only the beginning of a process, a position that upset many, including Paul VI) made clear that European bishops claimed autonomy when speaking with Rome, but sometimes acted like ‘Romans’ at home. The expectations of the local faithful often went beyond the intentions of the approved constitution, and thus bishops were urged to intervene. However, the use of the vernacular, deeply related to the concept of active participation, became more and more extensive, with the result that the conciliar restrictions soon disappeared.[^c43-20]

[^c43-20]: M. Lamberigts, ‘Entwicklungen nach dem II. Vatikanum in den Niederlanden: Die liturgische Entwicklung als Fallstudie’, in _Das Zweite Vatikanische Konzil und die Zeichen der Zeit heute_, ed. P. Hünermann (Freiburg: Herder, 2006), 283–312.

Resistance to the liturgical renewal became visible when Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre, former superior general of the Spiritans, established, with the permission of the bishop of Fribourg-Lausanne (Switzerland), the International Seminary of St Pius X in Écône, Switzerland. Lefebvre wanted to return to the Tridentine Mass. His action, initially tolerated if not accepted, would ultimately result in a schism under Pope John Paul II, albeit for reasons other than liturgical ones. However, Lefebvre’s liturgical concerns were taken seriously by Paul VI’s successors. The so-called Tridentine rite was accepted as an alternative to the Revised Roman Missal and functioned as a way to help bring traditionalists back to the Roman Catholic Church. At times, resistance to the use of the vernacular was the result of specific contextual and cultural factors. For example, mixed Catholic communities in the Soviet Union, consisting of various nationalities, considered the use of the vernacular as a contribution to a further Russification among national minorities, and thus continued to celebrate Mass in Latin.

Yet, all in all, the liturgical renewal was well received, not only in Western but also in Eastern Europe, where it had an important impact on the life of the Church. The use of the vernacular and the renewed Liturgy of **[p. 718]** the Word provided greater opportunities for the preaching of the faith and the preparation for the sacraments. In Czechoslovakia, a country with a long tradition of liturgy in the vernacular (such as the Slavonic liturgy and the Hussite movement), this process began in early 1965: folk singing at Mass, liturgical training of the laity, the introduction of the vernacular, the adaptation of liturgical space, and the [^c43-21] simplification of rites were all promoted. In 1965, provisional translations were in use. In 1969, the final texts of the parts of the revised Mass were published, but, because of the communist regime, people had to [^c43-22] wait until 1985 for a complete missal in Czech. It was printed in Rome. In Yugoslavia, the Croatian and Slovenian vernaculars were soon introduced, with both Croatia and Slovenia being dominantly Roman [^c43-23] Catholic. In Hungary, liturgical participation was promoted through the introduction of reformed rites. Liturgical changes gradually and without controversy found their way into common practice. Mass was celebrated in the vernacular as early as 1966. Bulgarian authorities refused the necessary permission to publish the new liturgical books, which thus circulated in the form of loose-leaf copies. Catholics had to wait until 1988 before the liturgical books in Bulgarian would find their way into circulation. In Romania, the State authorities used liturgical reform to undermine the unity in the Catholic Church by arbitrarily favouring sometimes the Romanians, sometimes the Hungarians, sometimes the Germans. In Poland, things were more complicated: Cardinal Wyszyński was opposed to the use of Polish in missals, Mass, and breviary, and the request that priests face the congregation during Mass was rejected, even as late as 1967. Reforms took effect beginning only in 1968, and the first post–Vatican II missal was still bilingual. In fact, it took until 1986 before the first full Polish-language missal was made available to the faithful. Needless to say, communist resistance—which refused to make paper available for printing liturgical books—was also [^c43-24] not helpful in the implementation process.

[^c43-21]: Felak, ‘Vatican II and Czechoslovakia’, 116–117.

[^c43-22]: Sikorska, ‘Eastern Europe’, 350.

[^c43-23]: Von Klimó, ‘Vatican II and Hungary’, 70.

[^c43-24]: Sikorska, ‘Eastern Europe’, 350.

In Western Europe, things went well. In Ireland, the vernacular was introduced in 1965, on the first Sunday of Lent. In 1968, full use was made of the vernacular in the Roman canon and the new Eucharistic Prayers. [^c43-25] The Irish and English versions were approved by Rome in 1969. In Scotland, also, most people appreciated the liturgical renewal. According to a poll of 1980, only 15 per cent were still in favour of the high Tridentine Latin Mass. More complicated was the situation in England and Wales, where the Catholic Church was confronted with the phenomenon of older Catholic families, who had once converted from Anglicanism, and for whom the use of Latin was part of their identity. In 1965, the Latin Mass Society was founded, not only as an organization in favour of Latin but also in opposition to any form of change. The reaction of the English and Welsh bishops was respectful, and Cardinal John Heenan succeeded in obtaining permission to celebrate the Tridentine Mass in circumstances where converted faithful were asking for this ministry, even though **[p. 719]** many Catholics in Wales were happy with the new rite. Thanks to this decision to make the Tridentine Mass possible, England would not be confronted with Lefebvre and the Pius X movement. In fact, it seems that twenty years after the council, people did not make much use of this opportunity, thus giving the impression that the initial opposition had gradually disappeared.

[^c43-25]: McClelland, ‘Great Britain and Ireland’, 366.

On the Continent, the liturgical renewal also found its way. Surely, confiicts between experimental and traditional liturgists, as in the Netherlands (with an intervention from Bugnini) or debates about the ‘correct’ language between Dutch- and Flemish-speaking people caused tensions at times, but all in all one could accurately say that the liturgical implementations became one of the most visible results of Vatican II.[^c43-26]

[^c43-26]: Lamberigts, ‘Entwicklungen nach dem II. Vatikanum’, passim.

### 3. Synods and Pastoral Councils

#### The Internationalization of the Curia: From Italianization to Europeanization

During the preparations for the council, a good number of bishops had asked for a reform of the Roman Curia. This request was repeated several times during the council. However, changes did not come as quickly [^c43-27] as some hoped, partly because members of the Curia were not in favour of reform. The first post-conciliar initiatives could be read as an expression of anxiety and suspicion, as became clear in the attempts of Spanish Cardinal Arcadio Larraona to centralize the needed reform of the Curia and to limit international [^c43-28] representation in the Curia to 30–35 per cent of non-Italians and Cardinal Ottaviani’s questionnaire on [^c43-29][^c43-30] doctrinal confusion after the council in 1966. Paul VI shared Ottaviani’s concerns. Although the replies of the French bishops, for example, to the questionnaire were prudent, it became clear that Vatican II’s reception had become polarized among the French clergy. Jacques Maritain’s _Le Paysan de la Garonne_ (1966) did not help to calm the rising emotions, for it considered the post-Vatican II period as worse than the time of high modernism. The change of the name of the Congregation of the Holy Office to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (1965) and the abolition of the _Index librorum prohibitorum_ (Index of Forbidden **[p. 720]** Books, 1966) did not have an immediate impact on the mindset of members of the Curia. Initiatives of Paul VI (_Regimini Ecclesiae Universae_, 1967) and John Paul II (_Pastor Bonus_, 1988) aimed to internationalize the [^c43-31] Curia, but whether they contributed to the _aggiornamento_ process remains a point of debate.

[^c43-27]: G. Alberigo, ‘Transition to a New Age’, in _History of Vatican II_, vol. 5, _The Council and the Transition—The Fourth Period and_ _the End of the Council September 1965–December 1965_, ed. G. Alberigo and J. A. Komonchak (Leuven: Peeters, 2006), 573– 644.

[^c43-28]: Philippe Chenaux, ‘La Réception du Concile Vatican II dans la Curie romaine’, in _The Transformation of the Christian_ _Churches in Western Europe 1945–2000_ / _La Transformation des églises chrétiennes en Europe occidentale_, ed. L. Kenis and P. Pasture, KADOC Studies on Religion, Culture and Society 6 (Leuven: Leuven University Press, 2010), 255–66, 260–261.

[^c43-29]: C. Sorrel, _Renouveau conciliaire et crise doctrinale: Rome et les Églises nationales (1966–1968); Actes du colloque_ _international de Lyon (12–13 mai 2016)_, Chrétiens et sociétés: Documents et mémoires 32 (Lyons: Laboratoire de la recherche historique Rhône-Alpes, 2017).

[^c43-30]: Chenaux, _Paul VI_, 223.

[^c43-31]: Chenaux, ‘La Réception du Concile Vatican II dans la Curie romaine’, 265–266.

In the first decade following the close of the council, the appointments of new prefects to important Roman congregations remained quite European in character. The French Cardinal Gabriel-Marie Garrone succeeded Cardinal Giuseppe Pizzardo in 1968 as head of the Congregation for Seminaries and Universities. The Yugoslavian Franjo Seper replaced Cardinal Ottaviani in 1968 as prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith; Jean-Marie Villot of France was appointed as prefect of the Congregation for the Council in 1967 and two years later became Secretary of State; and in 1968 the Belgian Maximilien de Furstenberg succeeded Cardinal Gustavo Testa as prefect of the Congregation for the Oriental Churches. In this context, the appointment of the American Cardinal John Joseph Wright of Pittsburgh as prefect of the Congregation for the Clergy in 1969 was one of the few exceptions.

Paul VI’s desire to promote dialogue with others became clear in the creation of the Secretariat for Non- Christians (1964) and for Non-believers (1965), and later the Pontifical Council for the Laity and the Pontifical Commission for Justice and Peace (1967). For two decades, more or less, the two secretariats, like the Secretariat for the Promotion of Christian Unity, would be led by Europeans. The same was true of the International Theological Commission, which was founded in 1969, where eighteen out of thirty members were Europeans; in the period 1974-1979, it was twenty-two out of thirty. Suenens had suggested the need for greater cultural diversity among the members of the Roman Curia during the synod of 1967, a measure which the Curia feared. The idea was supported by Paul VI in the aftermath of the crisis caused by the publication of _Humanae Vitae_. The one exception was the Pontifical Council Cor Unum (founded in 1971). Europeans would head the International Theological Commission from its creation (1969) up to the beginning of the third millennium, thus making clear that Europe was still considered an important player when it came to reform and renewal, setting the tone for the others. Vatican II is often described as a European council. Its implementation remained—in the period immediately following the council— predominantly in the hands of European church leaders, at least at central level.

#### Synods and Collegiality

The autonomy of local bishops and episcopal collegiality were, at least by the conciliar majority, considered **[p. 721]** an important aspect of Vatican II’s teaching, when they were rediscovered after having fallen into oblivion after Trent. However, the post-Vatican II synods, announced in the motu proprio _Apostolica Sollicitudo_ of September 1965, had only a consultative function: in vain the bishops would ask during the [^c43-32] extraordinary synods of 1969 and 1985 for a more deliberative competency. The first synod, held in Rome in 1967, discussed the crisis of faith. The result—a ‘profession of faith’, read by Paul VI on 30 June 1968— was, in essence, written by Jacques Maritain, who was consulted in this matter by Charles Journet. Needless [^c43-33] to say, some commentators considered this profession a kind of new syllabus. The first synods could not be qualifled as great successes. Both the extraordinary synod of 1969 and the second synod of 1971 were [^c43-34] strongly marked by an atmosphere of crisis. The synod of 1969 made clear that the struggle for correct [^c43-35] interpretation had begun in Europe. Its focus was collegiality including the relations between bishops’ conferences and the pope on the one hand, and relations between local bishops and their own conference on the other. During the preparation process, the Swiss theologian Hans Küng explicitly questioned the existing centralization and made a plea for greater respect of local churches. In the run-up to the 1969 synod, Cardinal Suenens, in a well-prepared interview in _Documentation catholique_, strongly criticized the absence of collegiality in the Church. Suenens, mindful of the devastating impact the publication of _Humanae Vitae_ had on the local faithful, was of the opinion that the pope was failing to govern collegially. In the end, the synod concluded that a more profound theological study of collegiality was needed. The synod of 1971 focused on the priesthood in a period when thousands were leaving the priesthood or the religious [^c43-36] life in Europe. To the great disappointment of European bishops, the Tridentine model was reaffirmed. Today it is commonly accepted that because of this decision, the Church lost a generation of intellectual priests across Western and Central Europe. Although the synods were intended to increase the reciprocity between centre and periphery, one gets the impression that they gradually became a means for communication from the centre to the periphery. While the extraordinary synod of 1985 was intended as an evaluation of the reception of Vatican II twenty years after it closed, Cardinal Ratzinger, in an interview with the journalist Messori on the eve of the synod (translated and published simultaneously in many languages; in English, ‘The Ratzinger Report’), criticized both collegiality and episcopacy. Although the initiative met with critique, centralization would in the end be more pronounced in the synod’s final report than participants wished. The final report, emphasizing communion and neglecting the conciliar idea of the Church as the People of God (see _Lumen Gentium_), did not do justice to the synodal discussions. People **[p. 722]** complained time and again about the procedures that were followed, and the role played by the secretaries general (from the establishment of the synod, they all were Europeans). Synods seldom became icebreakers, as they were rigorously and logistically prepared and controlled. It became clear that episcopal conferences [^c43-37] were considered as being at the service of the college together with the pope and of the individual bishops. The implementation of collegiality can thus be considered the Achilles heel of the council. The organization of the synods made clear that of the three principles of ecclesial life (community, collegiality, presidency), the presidency regime remained dominant: the way from the centre to the periphery was dominating the [^c43-38] way from the periphery to the centre. In this regard, it is interesting to mention that the first special synod in the aftermath of Vatican II dealt with the Church in the Netherlands, a polarized Church and a polarized [^c43-39] episcopacy, in a Church in crisis. This synod, dealing with local problems, was held in Rome.

[^c43-32]: J. Grootaers, ‘Collégialité et primauté dans l’application de Vatican II’, in Kenis, Billiet, and Pasture, _The Transformation of_ _the Christian Churches in Western Europe 1945–2000_, 267–80.

[^c43-33]: For the details, see Chenaux, _Paul VI_, 222–229.

[^c43-34]: Jan Grootaers, _Heurs et malheurs de la collégialité: Pontificats et synodes face à la réception de Vatican II_, Annua Nuntia Lovaniensia 69 (Louvain: Peeters, 2012).

[^c43-35]: Joseph Famerée, ‘La Collégialité au synode extraordinaire de 1969: Un premier conflit d’interprétation de Vatican II’, in _L’Autorité et les autorités: L’Herméneutique théologique de Vatican II_, ed. G. Routhier and G. Jobin, Unam Sanctam 3 (Paris: Cerf, 2010), 95–123.

[^c43-36]: Chenaux, _Paul VI_, 239–244.

[^c43-37]: Grootaers, ‘Collégialité et primauté dans l’application de Vatican II’, 277–280.

[^c43-38]: Bernard Sesboüé, _Le magistère à l’épreuve_: _autorité, vérité et liberté dans l’Église_ (Paris: Desclée de Brouwer, 200), 237– 242.

[^c43-39]: Kerkhofs, ‘Western Europe’, 358.

#### Local Pastoral Synods and Councils

The Pastoral Council of the Dutch Church Province

The organization of the Pastoraal Concilie van de Nederlandse Kerkprovincie (the Pastoral Council of the Dutch Church Province) made the Netherlands an interesting test case for the implementation of Vatican II. The pastoral council was an initiative of the Dutch bishops, who wanted priests and laity to be actively involved and engaged in the Church’s life, thus creating a kind of local collegiality. In 1970, the council approved a resolution that distinguished priesthood and celibacy. The resolution was supported by the [^c43-40] Dutch bishops but met with criticism in Rome. Through the nomination of conservative bishops such as Simonis (1970) and Gijsen (1972)—the latter being ordained by the pope himself in Rome—Paul VI made clear what he thought about the situation in the Netherlands. By his episcopal appointments, he actively contributed to the growing polarization in the Dutch Catholic Church. Meanwhile, the Vatican rejected the creation of a permanent National Pastoral Council (1972) and the National Pastoral Consultation, replacing [^c43-41] it quickly so that it no longer met yearly.

[^c43-40]: Chenaux, _Paul VI_, 242.

[^c43-41]: Kerkhofs, ‘Western Europe’, 358.

At the time of this pastoral council, the publication of the _Nieuwe Katechismus_ (_New Catechism_), drawn up on behalf of the Dutch Episcopal Conference and meant for adults, caused problems. This catechism was very much influenced by the conciliar event and was seen as a concrete implementation of Vatican II, a council that had invited local communities to invest in the training and formation of laity. It was a huge success. **[p. 723]** More than 400,000 copies were sold in the Netherlands. The catechism was translated into several international languages and was well received by many priests and laypeople. However, right-wing Dutch Catholics complained about the catechism’s treatment of topics such as Mary’s virginity, original sin, Christ’s presence in the Eucharist, and the existence of angels. The attempt to translate Catholic doctrine into contemporary language was thus confronted with disapproval, revealing growing polarization in the Dutch Church. The matter caused concern in Rome. With regard to Christ’s presence in the Eucharist, Paul VI published the encyclical _Mysterium Fidei_ (3 September 1965), in the midst of a Dutch debate on that matter, thus presenting himself as the true defender of the faith. After years of discussion which involved [^c43-42] not only Piet Schoonenberg, Edward Schillebeeckx, and W. Bless, but also a commission of cardinals who, during the council, had opted for _aggiornamento_ and collegiality (cardinals Frings, Lefèbvre, and Jäger), the Dutch Episcopal Conference refused to change the catechism but approved the publication of a supplement, [^c43-43] explaining the points under discussion. In passing, both Cardinal Charles Journet and Joseph Ratzinger [^c43-44] played a significant role in the attempts to revise the catechism. The authoritarian way in which the central office intervened, however, resulted not only in further polarization but also in disapproval of Rome’s interventions in the (then flourishing) Church life in the Netherlands.

[^c43-42]: W. Bless, ed., _Witboek over de Nieuwe Katechismus_ (Utrecht: Ambo, 1969).

[^c43-43]: A. Chiaruttini, ed., _Il dossier del Catechismo olandese_ (Milan: Mondadori, 1968); Bless, _Witboek over de Nieuwe_ _Katechismus_; E. Dhanis, _Aanvulling bij de Nieuwe Katechismus_ (Bussum: Brand, 1969).

[^c43-44]: Chenaux, _Paul VI_, 226.

The Synods in Germany

In the Federal Republic of Germany, a national synod would also be prepared: the most important national synod in Europe of its time. Inspired by the Dutch Pastoral Council and the diocesan Synod of Hildesheim (1968), the bishops’ conference decided to reflect on how to apply Vatican II in Germany. After a careful period of preparation, the national synod took place in the cathedral of Würzburg, where clergy (164 participants) and laity (153 participants), met during eight sessions between 1971 and 1975 to discuss documents on liturgy, marriage and the family, pastoral structures, co-responsibility, education, and ecumenism. With regard to progress in ecumenical issues, optimism was high, but participants were disappointed at the refusal of the bishops to discuss the ordination of married men to the Catholic priesthood. In regard to _Humanae Vitae_ and the problem of remarried divorced Catholics, participants had expected more progress, but saw none.[^c43-45] Other Synods[^c43-46]

[^c43-45]: Kerkhofs, ‘Western Europe’, 359.

[^c43-46]: Kerkhofs, ‘Western Europe’, 359–362.

In 1969, a diocesan synod was also held in Denmark, consisting of only one diocese, as Catholics were a **[p. 724]** minority in the country. For this occasion, the laity were also in the minority. Given the situation of Catholics in Denmark, the synod focused on ecumenism and issues related to it, such as mixed marriages. The synod also stressed the importance of co-responsibility and asked for a more open approach to issues like optional celibacy, sacraments for remarried divorced Catholics, and family planning (it was the year after _Humanae Vitae_). At the beginning of the 1970s, synods were held in Austria (where the bishops refused to approve anything they considered as not being in line with tradition) and in Switzerland. The Swiss had prepared their local pastoral synod well. The final session of November 1975 was celebrated in the cathedrals of the seven dioceses. The points of debate were the same as in the Netherlands and in Germany. While the bishops intended to create a permanent Inter-diocesan Pastoral Forum, this was disapproved by Rome, thus discouraging post-conciliar enthusiasm. In Luxembourg, a diocesan synod in 1971 resulted in the creation of a permanent Diocesan Pastoral Council. With the foundation of a permanent Inter-diocesan Pastoral Consultation, in which people from all relevant backgrounds had a seat, the Flemish Church founded a consultancy board of 125 members that met on a regular basis, but whether it had a real impact on the life of the Church in Flanders remains to be seen.

In England, pastoral consultations were held, resulting in a national pastoral meeting in 1980. This meeting was preceded by the widest consultation ever held in the Catholic Church of England and Wales: 100,000 people submitted their replies on the preparatory documents. In Liverpool, more than 2,000 delegates participated in the National Pastoral Congress, which concentrated on the Church as People of God and co-responsibility. Attention was paid to liturgical renewal, ecumenism, and in-service training of priests. The delegates also opted for a more positive teaching on sexuality, suggesting a re-examination of official Church teaching on contraception and the remarriage of divorced people. As elsewhere, people in England requested the ordination of married men and that women be ordained as permanent deaconesses. In their message _The Easter People_, the bishops approved most proposals, but the practical implementation of the last series of desired actions did not really succeed.[^c43-47]

[^c43-47]: Kerkhofs, ‘Western Europe’, 360.

Regional and local synods were organized in Italy, Spain, and France (especially as of 1985), but at that moment the French Church was already suffering from polarization. Two major events were organized by the Church in Italy on the themes of Evangelisation and Human Promotion (1976) and Christian Reconciliation and the Human Community (Loreto, 1985). At both meetings, it became clear that the Italian Church was also suffering from polarization in regard to Christian involvement in political life. The older Catholic Action movement opted for dialogue in a pluralizing world, while the new movements promoted a Church-centred approach.

### 4. Crises with Regard to Marriage and Celibacy

#### Humanae Vitae

**[p. 725]** The year 1968 was one of resistance against institutions and authorities in both Western and Eastern Europe. The student revolts in France and Germany often favoured communist regimes, unaware of or neglecting their at-times horrifying impact on the life of the faithful in Eastern Europe. Even before Vatican II, intellectuals in Western Europe considered communism, certainly in its mitigated form as present in Italy, as a possible foundation for new political reflections. Among Christians, sympathy for communist ideas was growing. The movement Christians for Socialism had, at least in the 1970s and 1980s, some success in Western Europe. Philosophical atheism found its way throughout Western Europe. After the second half of the 1960s, the dialogue with culture, an important issue in _Gaudium et Spes_, became a challenging task. The violent intervention by members of the Warsaw Pact at the time of the Prague Spring (1968) was not treated as a major issue of concern in Western Europe, not even when Jan Palach protested against this oppressive communist aggression in 1969 by self-immolation.

During this period of protests, _Humanae Vitae_ was published. Paul VI had withdrawn the birth control issue from the conciliar agenda. During the debate on _Gaudium et Spes_ it was announced that the pope would make a statement on this question after the council. Paul VI did not follow the advice of the majority of members of the commission he himself had established to study the issue. The publication of this encyclical in the midst of turmoil was experienced as a kind of contempt for the growing maturity of the faithful in general and women in particular: the farewell to Roman Catholic pontifical sexual guidelines was impressive. One of the most faithful adherents of Paul VI, Msgr Gérard Philips, prepared the Belgian reaction to the encyclical, appealing to the conscience of the faithful and thus referring back to the spirit of Vatican II. Several [^c43-48] European episcopal conferences would be inspired by this Belgian reaction. Cardinals Alfrink, Döpfner, Heenan, König, and Suenens disapproved of the encyclical, which was far from the intentions of Vatican II, [^c43-49] where the pope and bishops, the magisterium and theologians worked together. In England, people emphasized the primacy of conscience and suggested that the encyclical lacked an understanding of the modern world. The duty of obedience to the magisterium was questioned; among other reactions, fifty-five people signed a letter of protest, published in _The Times_ in August 1968. Although disappointed, Cardinal Heenan, together with his colleagues in the Church of England and Wales, felt compelled to save the [^c43-50] **[p. 726]** obedience to the magisterium. Guidelines were drawn up and priestly opposition was broken. Peace was restored, but at the expense of great disappointment and disillusionment. Vatican II’s momentum seemed to be over.

[^c43-48]: L. Declerck, ‘La Réaction du cardinal Suenens et de l’épiscopat belge à l’encyclique _Humanae Vitae_’, _Ephemerides_ _Theologicae Lovanienses_ 84 (2008): 1–68.

[^c43-49]: Chenaux, _Paul VI_, 232–234.

[^c43-50]: McClelland, ‘Great Britain and Ireland’, 373.

The division among theologians was enormous. Hans Küng, supported by Edward Schillebeeckx, Yves Congar, and Karl Rahner, disagreeing with the encyclical, made a plea for academic freedom, an initiative that would be supported by thirty-eight theologians of the group around the journal _Concilium_. Jean Daniélou and Henri de Lubac defended the encyclical. The first became cardinal in April 1969, the second refused such nomination, at least that year.

#### The Crisis of Priestly and Religious Life

With Vatican II, the priest was expected to become someone who was close to the parish community. That most priests and religious gave up the soutane or religious habit helped to overcome the former distance. Furthermore, some priests were of the opinion that they ought to take care of their own income and be [^c43-51] engaged among the workers, eventually taking on political responsibilities, a clear change in the priestly profile of that time.

[^c43-51]: É. Fouilloux, ‘Essai sur le devenir du catholicisme en France et en Europe occidentale de Pie XII à Benoît XVI’, _Revue_ _théologique de Louvain_ 42 (2011): 526–57.

In Western Europe, the fact that the debate on mandatory celibacy was removed from the conciliar agenda but reaffirmed in the encyclical _Sacerdotalis Caelibatus_ (24 June 1967) had an enormous impact. Many young priests left the priesthood, for they had hoped that soon celibacy and priesthood would be separated based on local sensitivities and developments. People all over Western Europe protested against the reaffirmation of the Tridentine model of priesthood. The Dutch bishops engaged in defending the possibility of married priests at Rome. In the Netherlands, France, and Germany, a position in favour of optional celibacy was not experienced as revolutionary, for many Catholics lived in a context where the Protestant minister went to a liturgical celebration with his wife and children. Old Catholics did the same. Serious research had shown that ordained ministry and marriage went hand in hand in the early Church, and that this practice was common at all levels of the hierarchy. The positive attitude towards marriage and sexuality promoted in _Gaudium et Spes_ challenged the idea that a life of celibacy was to be considered as better than marriage.

[^c43-52] The decline of vocations and ordinations was dramatic; France and the Netherlands were good examples. But even in countries where the number of vocations to the secular clergy remained stable, such as in Ireland (where, like elsewhere, the decline in vocations to religious life was considerable), people were [^c43-53] concerned about the intellectual qualities of candidates following the close of the council.

[^c43-52]: Chenaux, _Paul VI_, 240–243.

[^c43-53]: McClelland, ‘Great Britain and Ireland’, 370.

**[p. 727]** The council’s Decree on Renewal of Religious Life, _Perfectae Caritatis,_ was the result of a flerce debate between those fathers who considered religious as part of the _ecclesia militans_ (renewal should be supervised and directed by Rome) and those who were more focused on the mission of religious communities for Church and world (often referring to the life of the Early Church). The decree was written without the [^c43-54] substantial involvement of women, while among women religious and lay brothers the decrease in [^c43-55] vocations was already highly visible before the opening of the council. For that reason, Pius XII and bishops like Suenens (1963) had already asked for a rethinking of religious life, especially in the case of the active apostolate. When the council opened, 30 per cent of the nuns in the diocese of Tournai who were involved in this work were older than 65, and only 10 per cent were younger than 30. Similar data could be found for French and other Belgian dioceses.

[^c43-54]: J. Schmiedl, ‘Reception and Implementation of the Second Vatican Council: Religious Institutes’, in Kenis, Billiet, and Pasture, _The Transformation of the Christian Churches in Western Europe 1945–2000_, 296–311.

[^c43-55]: D. Claes, ‘Aan de vooravond van het concilie: De “Vota Antepraeparatoria” van de Belgische, Luxemburgse en Nederlandse bisschoppen voor het Tweede Vaticaans Concilie’, licentieverhandeling Katholieke Universiteit Leuven, Louvain, 1992; (this study was realized in the Flemish part of the country, not in Louvain-la-Neuve); J. Schmiedl, _Das Konzil und die Orden:_ _Krise und Erneuerung des gottgeweihten Lebens_ (Vallendar Schöntstatt: Patris, 1999).

Soon after the council, Paul VI, in his Apostolic Letter _Ecclesiae Sanctae_ (1966), asked all congregations and religious orders to organize a special general chapter that would draw up legislation and provide spiritual [^c43-56] and apostolic revitalization of their specific charisms, undoubtedly a challenging task. These general chapters were organized between 1967 and 1971., The publication of _Renovationis Causam_ by the Congregation for Institutes of Consecrated Life was influential in this reflection, for it invited institutions to rethink their processes of education and formation. Countless documents were prepared to rediscover the identity and self-identity of congregations and orders. However, many orders and congregations no longer had qualifled personnel to offer such training. In Germany, the number of religious formation colleges decreased from thirty to six (five still had a full faculty of theology). By 1968, the Flemish congregations and orders had already concentrated theological formation in one place (Louvain).

[^c43-56]: Janica Prunty, ‘Reception of the Call of Vatican II for Renewal of Religious Life: Case Study of the Irish Federation of the Sisters of Our Lady of Charity’, in Dermot A. Lane (ed.), _Vatican II in Ireland. Fifty Years On. Essays in Honour of Pádraic_ _Conway_. Studies in Theology, Society and Culture, 12 (Oxford-Bern-Berlin-Brussels: Peter Lang, 2015) 121–149.

These reflections on formation and education had an impact on the form of the rule or constitutions and on concrete ways of living. The most visible result of this reform was the simplification of the religious habit. The invitation to adapt the way of living to the new needs of the apostolate at a time when the Church was invited to dialogue with the world was a great challenge, especially in those orders and congregations that combined spiritual life and concrete apostolates. In this period, characterized by dialogue with the world **[p. 728]** and with the members of the orders and congregations, a new type of governance was needed. Community building and sharing of each other’s lives resulted in concepts of co-responsibility, respect, and sometimes chaos. Leadership was rethought: authoritarian governance no longer worked as the children of 1968 entered the cloisters. Subsidiarity, a respectable concept, could also result in claims for autonomy and freedom. They reflected what was happening in the post-1968 era. The reappreciation of sexuality, secularization, and mass media thus found their way into the cloisters.

[^c43-57] In the midst of this renewal process and its implementation, many members left their communities, sometimes while continuing their public activities; this was the case with the Jesuit Oosterhuis of the Ecclesia of Amsterdam, the Benedictine abbot of Siegburg, Alkuin Heising, the Dominican Otto Hermann Pesch, and others. Orders and congregations were separated from their intellectual members, who were often their ‘possible’ (intended?) future leaders. The decrease in numbers had an enormous impact on the visibility of orders and congregations: many Catholic schools had to be handed over to the laity; orders and congregations had often dominated the theological landscape in the 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s, but religious theologians of the calibre of Schillebeeckx, Rahner, Congar, and Chenu were absent from the 1990s onwards. Once-flourishing houses such as that of the Jesuits in Fourvière near Lyons or the Dominicans of Le Saulchoir near Paris closed. Over the years, the number of religious and religious houses constantly decreased; diocesan commissions for religious reflected on closing houses, merging diocesan religious congregations, and what to do with the material and spiritual legacy of all these congregations and orders.

[^c43-57]: H. Punsmann, ‘Zur Komplexität religiöser Orden heute’, _Wissenschaff und Weisheit_ 61 (1998): 137–69.

At the time of the council and during its aftermath, attempts were made to develop new forms of religious life. Secular institutes were created. New movements started, such as the Neocatechumenate in Spain; Communione e Liberazione, the Community of Sant’Egidio, and the Community of Bose in Italy; or the [^c43-58] communities of Emmanuel and Chemin neuf in France. These movements were distinct in their origins and ambitions, and some have proven to be successful. Often, they supported Roman politics and received Rome’s support, the Legionaries of Christ being a good example. Against all odds, John Paul II supported and even officially recognized them shortly before his death. It remains one of the black marks on his career, however, especially because the founder was already suspected of paedophilia and the abuse of power. Some of the new movements caused unrest in local communities and were distrusted by local bishops and clergy because they contributed to a growing polarization in the Church. They were considered (and considered themselves) an antidote to what John Paul II described as a Western European culture of death. A good number of new episcopal appointments had a background in these new movements.

[^c43-58]: O. Landron, _Les Communautés nouvelles: Nouveaux visages du catholicisme français_ (Paris: Cerf, 2004).

### 5. The Return of the Inquisition?

**[p. 729]** Vatican II is often described as a council of (European) theologians. But these theologians soon began to disagree on both the spirit and the legacy of Vatican II. This dispute did not have a great impact on the life of the Roman Catholic Church in Central and Eastern Europe, where local churches were confronted, if not struggling, with communist regimes.

In 1965, the international journal _Concilium_ was founded by a group of theologians, many of whom had been present at the council as official (or unofficial) _periti_. They wanted to create a forum that would continue the theological process started at the council. Members of the executive editorial committee included the likes of Edward Schillebeeckx, Karl Rahner, Yves Congar, and Henri de Lubac. Joseph Ratzinger was one of the members of the editorial board for the dogmatic theology section, Hans Küng was editor-in-chief for the ecumenism section, and Hans Urs von Balthasar, a former Jesuit but not a _peritus_, was on the editorial board for the spirituality section. Soon, some, like von Balthasar and Ratzinger, began to consider developments in the journal too radical and not sufficiently in line with tradition. In 1972, von Balthasar and Ratzinger, with the support of de Lubac—all three of them were members of the International Theological Commission —founded the journal _Communio_. Even during the council, de Lubac and Ratzinger had shared concerns [^c43-59] about the overly optimistic views of the council fathers with regard to dialogue with the world. Now they made it clear that they did not consider the post-conciliar developments as correct implementations of the council they had experienced. This split in the ranks of conciliar theologians would mark the beginning of a long-term debate over the correct interpretation of Vatican II.

[^c43-59]: L. Figoureux, _Henri de Lubac et le concile Vatican II (1960–1965)_, Bibliothèque de la Revue d’histoire ecclésiastique 102 (Turnhout: Brepols, 2017).

Meanwhile, theologians such as Schillebeeckx and Küng were investigated by the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (CDF). While in 1968 the CDF agreed that Karl Rahner would come to Rome to defend Schillebeeckx’s orthodoxy, in 1979 Schillebeeckx had to travel in person to Rome to defend himself. This was the year Bernhard Häring was asked to stop publishing critiques of _Humanae Vitae_, Küng lost his _nihil obstat_ as professor at the Catholic Faculty of Theology in Tübingen, and Jacques Pohier was condemned for his book _Quand je dis Dieu_, a book published in 1977. It will come as no surprise that people spoke of a new [^c43-60] inquisition. Schillebeeckx was not condemned, which is not the same as receiving approval. His colleague Piet Schoonenberg was publicly attacked by Jean Galot, examiner of Schillebeeckx’s positions, for his [^c43-61] **[p. 730]** Christology. No wonder that both within and outside theological milieus, people wondered openly [^c43-62] whether the CDF wanted to put an end to the academic freedom of thought and speech.

[^c43-60]: P. Hebblethwaite, _The New Inquisition? Schillebeeckx and Küng_ (London: Collins, 1980).

[^c43-61]: P. Schoonenberg, ‘Antwoord aan p. Jean Galot’, _Tijdschriff voor Theologie_ 20, no. 1 (1980): 86–92.

[^c43-62]: ‘De zaak Schillebeeckx: Reflecties en reacties’, _Tijdschriff voor Theologie_ 20, no. 4 (1980): 340–426.

In 1981, Joseph Ratzinger, archbishop and cardinal of Munich, was appointed prefect of the CDF, a position he would hold until 2005, when he was elected pope. In this position, he was official controller of the orthodoxy of candidates for the office of bishops, and head of the congregation that sought to protect and defend official Roman Catholic doctrine. The number of European ‘heretics’ that the CDF confronted was [^c43-63] impressive; Schillebeeckx received a notification in 1984 for his book on ministry.

[^c43-63]: Rubén Aguilar Valenzuela, ‘Los teólogos herejes de Roma’, _Nexos_ 35 (2013): 24f.

It goes without saying that the initial enthusiasm was far away in the 1980s, with an ageing clergy on the one hand and secularization on the other. Attempts to develop new forms of lay and ordained ministry did not prove to be successful.

### 6. Ecumenism and Religious Liberty

#### Ecumenism

The promulgation of _Unitatis Redintegratio_ in 1964 was the beginning of active and attentive dialogue with other Christian denominations in Europe. Even though the Roman Catholic Church did not become a formal member of the World Council of Churches (WCC), it became a full member of the WCC’s Faith and Order Commission. Especially with the Anglican Church, the contacts improved greatly, following the visit of the archbishop of Canterbury, Michael Ramsey, to the pope in 1966. The results achieved by the Anglican– Roman Catholic International Commission (ARCIC), created in 1969, were encouraging, although its activities were sometimes considered to be the work of ‘the elite discussing the exotic’.[^c43-64]

[^c43-64]: McClelland, ‘Great Britain and Ireland’, 374.

Especially in the first period (up to 1981), Catholic and Anglican bishops discussed issues such as authority, the Eucharist, intercommunion, and priestly ministry, resulting in mutual recognition of baptism, and agreement on the doctrines of Eucharist and ministry. Anglicans experienced _Humanae Vitae_ as a hindrance to dialogue, and English Catholics were concerned about Anglican positions on the ordination of women, remarriage in church of divorcees, the rights of homosexual priests, and the like. However, the positive role of Cardinal Hume and Archbishop Worlock cannot be underestimated. The National Pastoral Congress in Liverpool (1980), the ecumenical visit of John Paul II to England in 1982 (where he signed a common declaration with Robert Runcie, archbishop of Canterbury), and the firm will to collaborate with the British **[p. 731]** Council of Churches, resulting in the Swanwick Declaration of 1987, created an atmosphere of mutual trust and respect. Hume clearly considered the declaration to be the fruit of Vatican II’s Decree on [^c43-65] Ecumenism.

[^c43-65]: McClelland, ‘Great Britain and Ireland’, 375–376.

Elsewhere in Western Europe, local episcopal conferences created councils that were expected to engage actively in dialogue with other Christian denominations. After the council, local ecumenical councils were established everywhere. Common liturgical celebrations became a custom during the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity. The dialogue with the Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches received great encouragement when Paul VI spoke of ‘sister churches’ in his letter to Patriarch Athenagoras of Constantinople, _Anno Ineunte_ (1967). Immigrants from Eastern Europe were welcomed in the West, making the presence of Orthodox faithful more visible. Coal miners from Ukraine found a safe home and employment in the West.

Eastern Europe has a long history of denominational divisions, and communist regimes typically set denominations against one another. However, this strategy was sometimes counterproductive. In Lithuania, Hungary, and the German Democratic Republic (GDR), people from different denominations helped each other in the struggle against the communists. In the GDR, Catholics, living in isolation, [^c43-66] sometimes benefited from the pastoral care offered by local Protestant pastors. In the Czech context (Catholics, Hussites, Protestants), the Decree on Ecumenism, _Unitatis Redintegratio_, was well received; between 1967 and 1969, ecumenical seminars were organized in which the ideas of people like Congar, [^c43-67] Küng, and Rahner were discussed. However, the end of the Prague Spring also meant the end of this experiment.

[^c43-66]: Sikorska, ‘Eastern Europe’, 351.

[^c43-67]: Felak, ‘Vatican II and Czechoslovakia’, 118–119.

Ecumenism can be very concrete, as is the case with mixed marriages: in England and Wales, the number of mixed marriages increased from 30 per cent in the 1950s to 67 per cent in the 1970s. In 1985, in the Federal Republic of Germany, more than 30 per cent of marriages were mixed; in the German Democratic Republic, the number was more than 50 per cent. The situation seems to be similar in Switzerland and in the Netherlands. Ecumenism could also be very challenging, if not daring, as could be observed in Northern Ireland, where the violent conflict between citizens was also a conflict between Catholics and Protestants.[^c43-68]

[^c43-68]: McClelland, ‘Great Britain and Ireland’, 371.

#### Religious Liberty

Religious liberty was an important issue for council participants from Central and Eastern Europe, yet Catholics from most countries in the region would not see a visible change in their reality until the fall of the Iron Curtain. Vatican II meant more to Central and Eastern Europe than just the election of the Polish Pope **[p. 732]** John Paul II, although Catholic Poles considered his election God’s reward for Polish faithfulness to Christ and his Church. Ten months after the first visit of John Paul II to Poland, the Solidarność (Solidarity) movement was born, based largely on Christian values. The communist regime proved ineffective in resisting this Christian movement and would collapse at the end of the 1980s. A Catholic, Tadeusz Mazowiecki, would become the first non-communist prime minister of Poland since the end of World War II. Similar things happened in Russia during glasnost and in Czechoslovakia. During the council, the Czech cardinal Beran pleaded for a halt to the suppression of religious freedom, but in reaction to the boldness of [^c43-69] his speech, the regime refused to talk with the Holy See. During the Prague Spring (1968), the Catholic journal _Via_ became a platform for theological debate. Representatives from all over Czechoslovakia, including fourteen bishops, wrote a charter for religious freedom. The Association for Conciliar Renewal promoted the spiritual renewal of the Church and service to society. The August 1968 invasion by Soviet [^c43-70] troops put an end to these and other initiatives. Later, laypeople and priests involved in the Charter 77 human rights movement, found inspiration in the conciliar documents. Cardinal Tomášek of Prague, who was initially opposed, would change his mind in the 1980s regarding the movement in favour of religious freedom and human rights in Czechoslovakia. In 1988, he endorsed a petition that was drawn up by Catholic laypeople and signed by 600,000 people. This action, which was in line with Vatican II, would contribute to [^c43-71] the fall of the regime. The pro-communist priests’ movement Pacem in Terris was dissolved at the end of 1989, but it evidently caused problems in Spain, where the Church found it hard to come to terms with parliamentary democracy and pluralism. The Spanish Church had benefited greatly from the Franco regime and after his death, it underwent a transformation.

[^c43-69]: Felak, ‘Vatican II and Czechoslovakia’, 106.

[^c43-70]: Sikorska, ‘Eastern Europe’, 346.

[^c43-71]: Felak, ‘Vatican II and Czechoslovakia’, 110–113; 125.

In Western Europe, the Declaration on Religious Freedom, _Dignitatis Humanae_, had an impact in Spain and Italy where, in 1976 and 1984 respectively, the relationship of Church and State continued to evolve, moving away, in different ways, from the framework of Catholicism as official religion of the State. At the time of the Franco regime, Paul VI had developed a rather critical attitude, asking Franco to stop intervening in episcopal appointments. In Italy, where he was on positive terms with people inside the Democrazia Cristiana (Christian Democratic Party), Paul deplored but had to accept the political party’s move to the Left. In any case, the final traces of a form of civil anti-reformation politics had disappeared in the West.

### 7. The Laity

With the Decree on the Apostolate of the Laity, _Apostolicam Actuositatem_, Vatican II offered a new insight on **[p. 733]** the role and involvement of the laity in the life of the Church and in the world. However, even at the time of the council, Catholic Action, an instrument for the laity’s engagement in the world, was in crisis. The Italian branch decreased from 3 million members in 1962 to 700,000 in 1969. In France, the movement would opt for socialism, if not Marxism—a choice that alienated the movement from the French hierarchy.

The laity was willing to take up responsibility, as was made clear in the Dutch Pastoral Council of Noordwijkerhout. That council discussed at length and in depth issues such as liturgy, ministry, laity, and celibacy, and as a result more of the lay faithful than ever before were active in the Church after 1965. The faithful were involved in catechesis, liturgy, parish councils, pastoral teams, prayer and Bible study groups, justice and peace groups, and so on, giving Vatican II a visible public face. Given the fact that many parishes no longer had a parish priest, parochial life could only continue thanks to their commitment. Because of a shortage of priests and religious, the laity gradually also took over the lead in schools and hospitals. At theological faculties, the number of lay students (men and women) soon outnumbered priests and seminarians, first in their capacity as students, then as teaching staff.

Laypeople critically followed the investigation of theologians such as Schillebeeckx, and a good number were convinced that investing time and energy in the Church had become a waste. Still, often inspired by Vatican II, critical movements continued to plead for a Church ‘de base’, a Church in the hands of the faithful: the lay movement Wir sind Kirche (We are the Church) was, in many senses, the echo of Vatican II’s appeal to the laity.

The laity was highly active in Central and Eastern Europe, where the many restrictions on entering seminaries or functioning as a priest and the dissolution of monastic orders resulted in a greater engagement and commitment of the laity. _Apostolicam Actuositatem_ indirectly helped Catholics. In Hungary, a programme was developed for laypeople to perform pastoral services; the programme was supported by [^c43-72] the hierarchy, but it never succeeded due to the opposition of the older clergy. In Croatia, in the Zagreb [^c43-73] Catholic Theological Faculty, an Institute for the Theological Culture of the Laity, was founded in 1968. The institute, like church choirs, religious instruction groups, and student movements, played an important role in the democratization of Croatian society during the period 1967 to 1971. In Czechoslovakia, laypeople got the opportunity to study theology at Olomouc, at least during the first two years of its reopening (in 1968). During protests against the regime in the 1980s, organizers called for independent lay associations [^c43-74] and parish councils. In the Soviet Union, priests were reduced to the status of parish employees. Parish councils were often infiltrated by local communists. It was not easy for Catholic laypeople to bear witness to their faith, as promotion of the faith confiicted with communist anti-religious legislation. But Catholicism survived thanks to the firm commitment of the laity. In Poland, young people especially joined the Light- **[p. 734]** Life Movement, received Christian instruction, and witnessed disappointment with State ideology. Informal discussion groups, Weeks of Christian Culture, and academic courses came into existence. In Lithuania, where the repression was more severe, laypeople took on responsibility, publishing in a clandestine way (samizdat). The same happened, even more substantially, in Czechoslovakia—a trend that has continued since the mid-1970s. Religious samizdat was larger than all the secular samizdat put together. In Eastern Germany, married men were allowed to hold services in isolated places. The initiative received support from the authorities and the Vatican. Lay ministry sprang up, and laypeople assumed responsibility for the pastoral care of elders and the sick. In addition, programmes of Christian education [^c43-75] were developed. The Pax Christi movement became the most influential peace movement in Europe and was, for many years, one of the key bridges, if not the only one, between Roman Catholicism and the [^c43-76] Russian Orthodox churches.

[^c43-72]: Sikorska, ‘Eastern Europe’, 351.

[^c43-73]: Banac, ‘Vatican II and Croatia’, 92.

[^c43-74]: Felak, ‘Vatican II and Czechoslovakia’, 125.

[^c43-75]: Sikorska, ‘Eastern Europe’, 351–353.

[^c43-76]: Kerkhofs, ‘Western Europe’, 363–364.

In most countries of Western and Central Europe, churches continued to make great efforts to reach the youth, however in vain. The fact that in the Czech Republic only 1 per cent of youth belongs to Christian denominations today is due in part to the influence of the communist regime, while the fact that the average [^c43-77] age of persons who go to church in France is over 50 is probably not. Some of the faithful—a minority— who are not happy with post-conciliar developments long for a return to the ‘good old days’, when truth was guaranteed, doctrine was immutable, and priests wore ‘uniforms’. Needless to say, the tensions between them and the more open-minded faithful remain a challenge and cause difficulties for those priests who aspire to be shepherds for all the faithful.

[^c43-77]: Fouilloux, ‘Essai sur le devenir du catholicisme en France et en Europe occidentale de Pie XII à Benoît XVI’, 527.

### Suggested Reading

Chenaux, Philippe. _Paul VI_: _Le Souverain éclairé_. Paris: Cerf, 2015.

Hastings, Adrian. _Modern Catholicism: Vatican II and After_. London: SPCK; New York: Oxford University Press, 1991.

Kenis, Leo, Jaak Billiet, and Patrick Pasture, eds. _The Transformation of the Christian Churches in Western Europe 1945–2000 / La transformation des églises chrétiennes en Europe occidentale_. KADOC Studies on Religion, Culture and Society, 6. Leuven: Leuven University Press, 2010.

Kosicki, Potr H. ed. _Vatican II Behind the Iron Curtain_. Washington, DC: The Catholic University of America Press, 2016.

Lamberigts, Mathijs. ‘The Dechristianisation of Europe: A Challenge for the Church’. In _La Chiesa, mistero e missione: A cinquant’anni dalla Lumen Gentium (1964–2014)_, edited by G. Tangorra, 221–49. Centro studi sul Concilio Vaticano II 6. Vatican City: Lateran University Press, 2016.

Schmiedl, Joachim. _Das Konzil und die Orden: Krise und Erneuerung des gottgeweihten Lebens_. Vallendar Schönstatt: Patris, 1999.

## 44. Receiving the Vision of Vatican II in Oceania

Ormond Rush

### 1. Introduction

**[p. 735]** The area called ‘Oceania’ constitutes one-fifth of the surface of the globe. It includes the earth’s largest ocean, the Pacific, and a continent, Australia. This chapter will explore reception of the vision of Vatican II in this widely diverse geographical, cultural, and ecclesiastical region that includes Australasia (Australia and Aotearoa New Zealand), Papua New Guinea, and the Pacific islands (grouped as Melanesia, Micronesia, and Polynesia). Over the four sessions of Vatican II, the official number of bishops coming from the six subregions within the ecclesiastical region of Oceania totalled seventy-four: thirty-eight from Australia, six from Melanesia, three from Micronesia, thirteen from New Guinea, six from New Zealand, and eight from Polynesia.[^c44-1]

[^c44-1]: See Segreteria Generale del Concilio, _I padri presenti al concilio ecumenico Vaticano II_ (Rome: Segreteria Generale del Concilio, 1966), 167–71.

Today, politically, the area includes nineteen nations, ranging in population from 25 million (Australia) to countries as small as 11,000 inhabitants (Tuvalu), with a total population of around 40 million. There are eighty-one Catholic dioceses in the region, including Eastern Catholic eparchies, ordinariates, apostolic prefectures, and missions _sui iuris_. In terms of subregional ecclesiastical structures, there are four episcopal conferences: the Episcopal Conference of the Pacific (Conferentia Episcopalis Pacifici—CEPAC); the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands; the New Zealand Catholic Bishops Conference; and the Australian Catholic Bishops Conference (ACBC). In 1990, for the sake of greater regional collaboration and coordination, these four conferences formed the Federation of Catholic Bishops’ **[p. 736]** Conferences of Oceania (FCBCO). In 1998, a Special Assembly of the Synod of Bishops for Oceania met in Rome. The preparation for this synod, its deliberations, and the resulting Apostolic Exhortation _Ecclesia in Oceania_ proved to be an important litmus test for assessing the reception of Vatican II across Oceania.

### 2. A Structuring Framework and Overview

The seventy-four bishops of Oceania who participated in the debating and drafting processes throughout Vatican II each made their own considered decisions regarding the various elements of the final vision of the [^c44-2] council, as delineated throughout the laborious drafting and voting on the sixteen final documents. We have no way of reconstructing exactly how each of these Oceanic bishops voted throughout the council. However, that the majority of the Oceania bishops, like the vast majority of the world’s bishops, were in favour of the final vision is generally true. When the council closed on 8 December 1965, the ecclesial responsibility of each of those bishops was to bring the conciliar vision home and implement it, albeit within widely diverse contexts. The history of the reception of Vatican II in Oceania, therefore, begins with, but goes well beyond, the immediate implementation by these Oceanic bishops in their own dioceses upon their return from the council. As Gilles Routhier insists, this official dimension of reception is still ‘just a [^c44-3] little part of the story’.

[^c44-2]: Jeffrey J. Murphy, ed., _Australian Bishops at Vatican II: Their Written and Spoken Interventions; From the Acta Synodalia,_ _Series I–IV (October 1962 to December 1965) Vatican Polyglot Press, 1970–1983_, trans. Bronwen Niel and Russell Davies (Brisbane: unpublished, 2000); Jeffrey J. Murphy, ‘The Australian Hierarchy and Vatican II: 1959–1965’, (PhD diss., Griffith University, 2001); Mikaele Pāunga, _The Oceania Bishops: Remote Preparation and Contribution to the Second Vatican_ _Council 1959–1965_ (Suva, Fiji Islands: The Bluebird Printery, 2006); Ormond Rush, ‘The Australian Bishops of Vatican II: Participation and Reception’, in _Vatican II: The Reception and Implementation in the Australian Church_, ed. Neil Ormerod et al. (Melbourne: John Garrett, 2012), 4–19.

[^c44-3]: Gilles Routhier, ‘Reception of Vatican II and Elements for Further Studies’, in _The Living Legacy of Vatican II: Studies from_ _an Indian Perspective_, ed. Paul Pulikkan (Bengaluru, India: ATC, 2017), 95.

A broader understanding of the reception of Vatican II throughout the local churches of Oceania can be conceived as taking place at three levels, beyond just the perspectives and plans of diocesan bishops. Alois Grillmeier’s framework of conciliar reception in the Early Church can be used to structure the analysis here of renewal and reform in the wake of Vatican II: _official reception_ (by local bishops and national/regional episcopal conferences); _theological reception_ (by theologians); and _spiritual reception_ (by the baptized [^c44-4] **[p. 737]** faithful). These three levels necessarily overlap (since the hierarchy and theologians are to be included in ‘the faithful’), but the distinction is important, since the hierarchy and theologians among the faithful, and the others among the faithful, have distinct but complementary roles in the Church.

[^c44-4]: Alois Grillmeier, ‘The Reception of Chalcedon in the Roman Catholic Church’, _Ecumenical Review_ 22 (1970): 383–411; Alois Grillmeier, _Christ in Christian Tradition,_ vol. 2, _From the Council of Chalcedon (451) to Gregory the Great (590–604); Part One,_ _Reception and Contradiction: The Development of the Discussion about Chalcedon from 451 to the Beginning of the Reign of_ _Justinian_ (Atlanta, GA: John Knox Press, 1987), 7–10.

In assessing how deeply the conciliar vision has been received at these three levels, the council’s _communio_ ecclesiology will be another useful criterion for evaluation. The council spoke of three dimensions of ecclesial communion brought about by the Holy Spirit: _communio fidelium_, the bond uniting all the faithful; _communio ecclesiarum_, the bond uniting all dioceses, at a national, regional, and universal level; and _communio hierarchica_, the bond uniting dioceses of the world Church through the communion among their [^c44-5] bishops, with and under the bishop of Rome. The sense of the Church as a communion of local churches (_communio ecclesiarum_) has very much taken root in Oceania, where there is a strong sense of local Church and of communion between the eighty-one dioceses in the Oceania region, as well as with the worldwide communion of churches. Moreover, when all the principles that make up the vision of Vatican II are taken [^c44-6] into account, three motifs resonating across many of those principles come to the fore as particularly pertinent when examining the reception of the conciliar vision throughout Oceania: the motifs of ‘participation’, ‘dialogue’, and ‘adaptation’.

[^c44-5]: Ormond Rush, ‘Inverting the Pyramid: The _Sensus Fidelium_ in a Synodal Church’, _Theological Studies_ 78, no. 2 (2017): 312– 20.

[^c44-6]: Ormond Rush, _The Vision of Vatican II: Its Fundamental Principles_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2019).

The time frame of reception since the close of the council can arguably be divided into three periods. In the 1980s, Walter Kasper, following Hermann Pottmeyer, proposed a three-phase analysis of the reception of [^c44-7] Vatican II worldwide. This is still generally appropriate for describing the time frame of reception in Oceania up to the present moment. There was an initial phase of ‘exuberance’: ‘The Vatican II years were a springtime in Catholicism. To many it seemed that the Church was at last shaking oft outmoded accretions from the past, and that it was becoming more relevant to contemporary men and women, and hence more [^c44-8] Christian’. The description by New Zealand theologian Neil Darragh of the situation in his country was certainly true elsewhere, at least in Australia:

[^c44-7]: Hermann J. Pottmeyer, ‘A New Phase in the Reception of Vatican II: Twenty Years of Interpretation of the Council’, in _The_ _Reception of Vatican II_, ed. Giuseppe Alberigo, Jean Pierre Jossua, and Joseph A. Komonchak (Washington, DC: The Catholic University of America Press, 1987), 27–43; Walter Kasper, ‘The Continuing Challenge of the Second Vatican Council: The Hermeneutics of the Conciliar Statements’, in _Theology and Church_ (New York: Crossroad, 1989), 166–76.

[^c44-8]: Edmund Campion, _Rockchoppers: Growing up Catholic in Australia_ (Ringwood, Australia: Penguin, 1982), 172.

The reception of Vatican II was very positive in New Zealand through the 1970s and 1980s. There was a lot of discussion, meetings, and changes in parishes. Maori theology began to emerge, and the Pasifika migrations to New Zealand continued this positive interpretation of Vatican II with a **[p. 738]** good deal of inculturation that was very lively, especially in liturgy and in community [^c44-9] participation. There was some resistance to the council, but this was strong only in small pockets.

[^c44-9]: Neil Darragh, correspondence with the author.

Then there was a second phase of ‘disappointment’: ‘People were alienated to both the left and the right in the years that followed. Some radicals left the Church—or retreated into apathy—because the Church did not change fast enough. Others were perplexed and alienated by the speed of change, especially in the [^c44-10] liturgy.’ This alienation characterized the so-called ‘culture wars’ during the pontificates of John Paul II [^c44-11] and Benedict XVI. For Australia, the divide between ‘conservative’ and ‘progressive’ views has been [^c44-12] documented in the research of Janet Curtis. Once again, Darragh’s description of the New Zealand experience captures _in nuce_ what was true in other areas:

[^c44-10]: Elizabeth Isichei, ‘Australia and New Zealand’, in _Modern Catholicism: Vatican II and After_, ed. Adrian Hastings (London: SPCK, 1991), 335.

[^c44-11]: For two contrasting examples, see Paul Collins, _Mixed Blessings: John Paul II and the Church of the Eighties_ (Ringwood, Australia: Penguin, 1986), and Michael Gilchrist, _Lost! Australia’s Catholics Today_ (Melbourne: Freedom, 2006).

[^c44-12]: Janet Crosby Curtis, ‘ “Across the Gulf”: A Historical and Psychological Study of Differences of Opinion in the Reception of the Second Vatican Council (1962–1965) in Australia’ (PhD diss., Monash University, 2015).

[The situation] all changed through the 1990s with the big influx of Catholic migrants from the Philippines, India, and to a lesser extent China, Vietnam, and Korea. These migrations brought an already established ‘reception’ in their own countries which they brought to New Zealand, presumably coloured too by migrant conservatism. A migration of priests from these countries followed them. At about the same time, New Zealand-born Catholics became enthusiastic about Catholic schools but began to disappear from Sunday Eucharist. This brought a more universalized Catholicism that fitted with the centralization under John Paul II and very nearly eliminated the first few decades of contextualization in New Zealand.[^c44-13]

[^c44-13]: Neil Darragh, correspondence with the author.

The present phase of Vatican II’s reception in Oceania is strongly marked by Pope Francis’s movement away from a revisionism that downplays the _novum_ that the council ardently desired, towards a more comprehensive implementation of the council’s radical vision of renewal for the Church ad intra and ad extra. In particular, the conciliar elements of _participation_, _dialogue_, and _adaptation_ that have seen particular appropriation in Oceania now find support in Pope Francis’s notion of a synodal and missionary-oriented Church that is creatively responsive to the signs of the times, such as climate change and the negative effects of globalization on the underprivileged.

Following this general overview, specific examples will now be selected, using the three levels of official, theological, and spiritual reception to structure the discussion.

### 3. Official-Institutional Reception

**[p. 739]** Grillmeier’s first level of reception (what he calls ‘kerygmatic reception’) is that by the hierarchy (the pope and the Roman Curia, and local bishops and priests), especially through their promotion (or otherwise) of all principles of the council’s vision. Gilles Routhier defines ‘kerygmatic reception’ as ‘the totality of the efforts of the pastors in view of proclaiming, promoting and putting in practice the teaching of the [^c44-14] Council’. While it is ultimately at the level of ‘spiritual reception’ that the ‘success’ of Vatican II is to be assessed, it is necessary to start with its official reception and implementation because, since the council itself was an official ecclesial event—the most authoritative in the previous 150 years—initially, the official implementation of its vision, perhaps necessarily, was basically a ‘top-down’ affair. But it is mostly a positive story to be told.

[^c44-14]: Routhier, ‘Reception of Vatican II and Elements for Further Studies’, 94.

One aspect of official reception relates to the responsibility of the local bishop and the bishops as a nation or region to implement the conciliar vision, including setting up the structures envisaged by the council for enabling participation and dialogue among all the faithful and their more open engagement with the world. How each of the local bishops in each of the eighty-one dioceses of Oceania have enthusiastically (or otherwise) personally embraced the principles of Vatican II’s vision and sought to inculcate those principles in the hearts and minds of the faithful is still an area requiring future research. But, from the current evidence, the vast majority of bishops over the last half-century have seen Vatican II in a positive light, even though there is also evidence that such endorsement has been muted, and even refused, in places.

Immediately after the council, those bishops who were enthusiastic participants at the council were generally enthusiastic in bringing the vision home. In New Zealand, for example, the bishop of Auckland, Reginald Delargey, can be highlighted for both his engagement during the council and its implementation [^c44-15] upon his return. Likewise, Guilford Young, archbishop of Hobart, Australia, was not only a founding member during the council of the International Commission for English in the Liturgy but also an early promoter of the liturgical reforms and the participation of laity and dialogic structures such as parish and [^c44-16] pastoral councils. In Adelaide, Matthew Beovich inculcated a tradition of participation and dialogue that [^c44-17] continued in the leadership style of the archbishops who followed him.

[^c44-15]: Nicholas Reid, _The Life and Work of Reginald John Delargey_ (Auckland, New Zealand: Catholic Diocese of Auckland, 2008).

[^c44-16]: W. T. Southerwood, _The Wisdom of Guilford Young_ (George Town, Tasmania: Stella Maris, 1989).

[^c44-17]: Josephine Laffin, ‘The Archbishop of Adelaide at Vatican II’, _Australasian Catholic Record_ 80, no. 3 (2003): 319–33. Josephine Laffin, _Matthew Beovich: A Biography_ (Kent Town, Australia: Wakefield, 2008); Josephine Laffin, ‘ “Sailing in Stormy Waters”: Archbishop Matthew Beovich and the Catholic Archdiocese of Adelaide in the 1960s’, _Journal of Religious_ _History_ 34 (2010): 289–311.

**[p. 740]** Throughout Oceania, the liturgical renewal was introduced quickly by the decrees of the episcopal conferences and then implemented by individual bishops. In Australia, this began in 1964, while the council [^c44-18] was still in session. In New Zealand, there was a similar early introduction of the liturgical reforms, with [^c44-19] both an English and a Maori translation of the texts. Generally, there was little education and preparation of the parishioners beforehand. Nevertheless, local liturgical commissions were soon set up to deepen people’s knowledge of the principles behind ‘the changes’.

[^c44-18]: Clare Johnson, ‘A Deep and Vast Renewal of the Church’s Inmost Life’, in Ormerod et al., _Vatican II: The Reception and_ _Implementation in the Australian Church_, 35–43.

[^c44-19]: See the timeline in Joseph Grayland, _It Changed Overnight! Celebrating New Zealand’s Liturgical Renewal, 1963 to 1970_ (Auckland: Te Hepara Pai, 2003), x–xiii.

A striking initiative was taken in New Guinea within six years of the council’s close, a year before national independence was achieved. The bishops initiated a nationwide renewal in 1971 in a deliberate attempt to inculcate the spirit of Vatican II and to formulate a common pastoral strategy. Between 1972 and 1975, this ecclesial review, called a ‘Self-Study’ of the church in New Guinea, involved workshops and meetings ‘in the villages, hamlets, towns, schools and special organizations like teachers’ colleges, university, police and army … It is estimated that a third of all Catholic faithful in PNG (at least 250,000 people) participated in [^c44-20] some way.’ In particular, several aspects of the conciliar vision came to the fore. The dominant image that emerged was ‘We are the Church’ (_Yumi yet i Sios_), along with a strong sense of local Church, indigenization, and inculturation, themes which redefined the self-identity not only of the local peoples, but also of the foreign ‘missionary’ priests and religious. Important for this developing sense of local Church and indigenization had been the establishment in 1963 of Holy Spirit Regional Seminary; now the participation of Indigenous laity was foregrounded, with the local catechist emerging as the backbone of ecclesial life in rural areas. Philip Gibbs, however, notes the tensions that arose from these initiatives in later decades: ‘Bishops attempt to consult with the laity, but then find it difficult to deal with the laity’s response.’ He points to ‘an ongoing tension between different models of Church: a hierarchical/sacramental model versus a people of God/_communio_ model’.[^c44-21]

[^c44-20]: Philip Gibbs, ‘Global Influences in the Growth of the Catholic Church in the Pacific Region’, in _The Catholic Church in Asia-_ _Pacific and Globalisation_, ed. Jose Casanova and Peter Phan (Oxford: Oxford University Press, forthcoming).

[^c44-21]: Philip Gibbs, ‘The Catholic Church in Papua New Guinea after World War II’, in _Alive in Christ: The Synod for Oceania and the_ _Catholic Church in Papua New Guinea 1998–2005_, ed. Philip Gibbs (Goroka, Papua New Guinea: Melanesian Institute, 2006), 26.

In Australia, in the initial phase of reception, participatory and dialogic bodies such as diocesan pastoral councils and parish councils were very much promoted—something that in recent decades has significantly diminished. Another aspect of the conciliar vision that the bishops were initially quick to implement was [^c44-22] **[p. 741]** creating structures to promote and support the social justice mission of the Church, each year publishing [^c44-23] a ‘Social Justice Sunday Statement’ and initiating a series of major listening and consultation projects on the distribution of wealth, the role of youth, and the participation of women. However, as with other conciliar challenges, ‘the call of the Second Vatican Council for greater engagement by Catholics with the [^c44-24] great social issues of the day met with mixed responses in Australia’.

[^c44-22]: Michael Costigan, _Social Justice and the Australian Catholic Bishops_ (Mulgrave, Australia: John Garratt, 2009).

[^c44-23]: Australian Catholic Bishops Conference, _Building Bridges: Social Justice Statements from Australia’s Catholic Bishops, 1988_ _to 2013_ (Alexandria, Australia: Australian Catholic Bishops Conference, 2014).

[^c44-24]: Bruce Duncan and Sandie Cornish, ‘The Council’s Call to Renewed Social Engagement’, in Ormerod et al., _Vatican II: The_ _Reception and Implementation in the Australian Church_, 114.

A further aspect of ‘official reception’ relates to implementation of the council’s vision of collegiality among bishops of a nation or region, as well as the collegial relationship of local bishops with the bishop of Rome, as mediated by the Roman Curia. Throughout Oceania, the bishops have embraced the ‘collegial spirit’ encouraged by the council regarding communion between dioceses within a region (_LG_ 23). When Pope Paul VI visited Australia in 1970, all the bishops of Oceania met with him, coming together for the first time since the council. This informal meeting highlighted the value of such interaction as a concretization of the council’s _communio_ ecclesiology, even at regional level. Accordingly, in 1990, the bishops created the Federation of Catholic Bishops’ Conferences of Oceania. This group has continued to meet every four years in a plenary assembly in various locations throughout the region.

Vatican II’s teaching on episcopal collegiality was among the council’s great achievements. Complementing the vision of Vatican I regarding the pope’s ‘primacy’ over the bishops, Vatican II saw the world’s bishops as a ‘college’, like the apostles, ‘with Peter and under Peter’ (_AG_ 38). Accordingly, it called for a reform of the Roman Curia (_CD_ 9–10), something which Pope Paul VI nevertheless undertook as his papal prerogative. Since the council, the collegial relationship between individual bishops of Oceania and Rome (de facto, the Roman Curia) has been tense on occasion. Bishops have spoken at times of a patronizing and domineering [^c44-25] attitude on the part of curial officials in regular communications and during the _ad limina_ visits to Rome. An articulation of this tension came during the 1985 Synod of Bishops, called by Pope John Paul II to evaluate the twenty years of reception of Vatican II. The president of the Australian Catholic Bishops’ Conference, Archbishop Francis Rush, reported on the perspective from Australia:

[^c44-25]: For the perspective of a New Zealand bishop, see Peter J. Cullinane, _Openings to Renewal: Letters to the Church_ (Hindmarsh, Australia: ATF, 2011).
