The question of collegiality and the relationship of the local church to the universal church are major internal questions, which are causing sufficient anxiety and wasting enough energy to distract the church from what should be its major concerns. … Diversity among the local churches and the principle of subsidiarity argue that local solutions should be found for local problems, as long as these solutions do not jeopardise the unity of the local churches with and under the Holy Father. Bishops and theologians sometimes get the impression that their orthodoxy is questioned **[p. 742]** lightly and that their difficulties and industry are not appreciated. This leads to a loss of trust, which only damages the church … We see the need for an even more refined theology, and more [^c44-26] effective use, of episcopal conferences.

[^c44-26]: Francis Rush, ‘Speech at the 1985 Extraordinary Synod of Bishops, Rome, 27 November 1985’, in _Life to Me Is Christ:_ _Selected Talks and Homilies of Archbishop Francis Rush_, ed. Ormond Rush and Mary Coman (Strathfield, Australia: St Pauls, 2010), 92–93.

Something of this tension was evident during the 1998 _ad limina_ visit to Rome of the Australian bishops. Part of that visit was a meeting of the heads of the six major curial dicasteries with the bishops chairing the six major committees of the Australian Catholic Bishops Conference. The result of the meeting was a [^c44-27] document commonly referred to as the Statement of Conclusions. As Richard Lennan remarks:

[^c44-27]: Dicasteries of the Roman Curia, ‘The Situation of the Church in Australia’, _Origins_ 28 (1999): 507–16.

The _Statement of Conclusions_ identifles both positive and negative aspects of the Catholic Church in Australia. The positives, especially as they relate to a concern for social justice, tolerance, and the search for authenticity provide grounds for thanksgiving. The relationship between the positive and the negatives, however, is not articulated. A more comprehensive review of the Australian church would need to grapple with the dynamics of this relationship.[^c44-28]

[^c44-28]: Richard Lennan, ‘Perceptions, Realities, and Possibilities’, _Compass_ 33 (1999): 27.

It was the negative view of liturgical, ministerial, and spiritual life in Australia that disappointed many. The Curia’s negativity was seemingly influenced by communication from conservative voices in Australia, ‘the unrepresentative minority who had been bombarding Rome with letters of complaint—in one period of time [^c44-29] more complaint mail was arriving from Australia than from the United States’. The unfavourable assessment of the apostolic nuncio played a role, too. The concluding paragraph of the Statement of Conclusions is telling; it describes the meeting between the representatives of the Australian bishops and the heads of the Curia’s dicasteries as ‘the meeting … between the Church in Australia and _the primary collaborators of the Roman Pontiffi_’. In one sentence, the council’s doctrine of collegiality, regarding the world’s bishops as the primary collaborators with the bishop of Rome, had been negated.

[^c44-29]: Barry Brundell, ‘By What Authority?’, _Compass_ 33 (1999): 34.

Immediately after the _ad limina_ visit, however, a much more positive experience of collegiality and of the Church as a _communio ecclesiarum_ occurred in Rome: the Special Assembly of the Synod of Bishops for Oceania took place from 22 November to 12 December 1998. Its origins lay in Pope John Paul II’s call to start the new millennium with a Jubilee Year in 2000. ‘The best preparation’, he said in _Tertio Millennio Adveniente_ (_TMA_), ‘can only be expressed in a renewed commitment to apply, as faithfully as possible, the teachings of Vatican II to the life of every individual and of the whole Church … [Accordingly] an **[p. 743]** examination of conscience must consider the reception given to the Council, this great gift of the Spirit at the end of the second millennium’ (_TMA_ 20, 36). To that effect, he called for a series of ‘continental synods’, naming in particular one for Oceania (_TMA_ 38). In preparation, a series of questions were sent out to the bishops of the region in 1997, and the following year the results of that survey were collated, becoming the [^c44-30] _instrumentum laboris_ or working document to start oft the synod’s discussion. It constitutes a snapshot of the Church in Oceania at the turn of the millennium. When the synod finally gathered, every bishop from Oceania was present. Discussion throughout the synod remained focused on local concrete challenges and local practical solutions.

[^c44-30]: General Secretariat of the Synod of Bishops, ‘_Instrumentum Laboris_: Synod of Bishops Special Assembly for Oceania. Jesus Christ and the Peoples of Oceania: Walking His Way, Telling His Truth, and Living His Life [1998]’, Libreria Editrice Vaticana, http://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/synod/documents/rc_synod_doc_24081998_oceania-instrlabor_en.html.

Pope John Paul II’s post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation _Ecclesia in Oceania_ (_EO_) uses as its structuring principle the conciliar motif of the three offices of Christ as prophet, priest, and king (shepherd). The council’s _communio_ ecclesiology likewise echoes throughout; the word _communio_ (either in Latin or English) appears fifty-nine times in the relatively short document. Among the multiple challenges it lists are threats to the health of the Pacific Ocean and

the harmful policies of some industrialized nations and increasingly powerful transnational corporations which can lead to deforestation, despoliation of the land, pollution of rivers by mining, over-fishing of profitable species, or fouling the fishing-grounds with industrial and nuclear waste. The dumping of nuclear waste in the area constitutes an added danger to the health of the indigenous population. (_EO_ 31)

Throughout the region, the document was positively received.[^c44-31]

[^c44-31]: For Australia, see Terence Kennedy, ‘The Synod for Oceania’, _Compass: A Review of Topical Theology_ 36, no. 2 (2002): 1–4. For Papua New Guinea, see Philip Gibbs, ‘Reception of _Ecclesia in Oceania_’, in Gibbs, _Alive in Christ_, 160–81.

Thirty years after the council, the Australian bishops embraced in a concrete way two key planks of the council’s vision, _participation_ and _dialogue_, with regard to a topic that the council had rarely addressed explicitly: the participation of women in the Church. The few key conciliar texts are _Gaudium et Spes_ (_GS_) 29, 52, and 60, and _Apostolicam Actuositatem_ 9. However, in the reception of the council, these meagre conciliar acknowledgements have taken on major significance in the reception of the council’s comprehensive vision throughout Oceania. In that more comprehensive interpretation, other conciliar emphases allow interpreters to expand on those minor acknowledgements, especially in the light of Vatican II’s emphasis on the equal dignity of all human beings and the rightful participation of all the baptized, regardless of any distinction, in the inner and outer life of the Church. And so, recognition of the equal dignity of women and **[p. 744]** men, and their equal ecclesial role in transforming the spiritual, familial, social, economic, cultural, and political life of human communities, has been a slowly received element of the conciliar vision in Oceania. Feminist theologians in Australia have played an important role in challenging perceptions and demanding [^c44-32] greater participation. In 1996, the Australian bishops commissioned an enquiry into the participation of women in the Church of Australia. It was intended to be a listening exercise in accord with the council’s call for dialogue within the Church (_GS_ 92). As well as inviting written submissions, the process involved listening sessions throughout the major cities and towns of Australia. According to one of the women on the Research Management Group: ‘In every way and at every stage, the process was one of purposeful and [^c44-33] effective collaboration.’

[^c44-32]: Maryanne Confoy, Dorothy Lee, and Joan Nowotny, eds., _Freedom and Entrapment: Women Thinking Theology_ (North Blackburn, Australia: Dove, 1995).

[^c44-33]: Sonia Wagner, ‘_Woman and Man: One in Christ Jesus_: A Retrospective’, in _Women in the Catholic Church in Australia:_ _Reflections on ‘Woman and Man’ Ten Years On_, ed. David Brennan (Alexandria, Australia: Australian Catholic Social Justice Council, 2010), 7.

The results were published as _Woman and Man: One in Christ Jesus_. It starkly stated:

The dominant issue arising from the research was gender equality, recognising the equal dignity of women and men created in the image and likeness of God … The very limited participation of women in decision-making at present and the need to increase women’s involvement in decision-making at all levels were constant and major themes. Involvement in decision-making was often linked with a call to promote opportunities for women to participate in leadership in the church.[^c44-34]

[^c44-34]: Marie Macdonald and Research Management Group, _Woman and Man: One in Christ Jesus; Report on the Participation of_ _Women in the Catholic Church in Australia_ (Sydney: HarperCollins Religious, 1999), viii.

The following year, the bishops’ annual Social Justice Sunday Statement for 2000 celebrated the study and made known the bishops’ decisions in the light of the document’s recommendations. They called for ‘a better balance’ of men and women on existing oversight bodies as well as in ecclesial leadership positions [^c44-35] and professional roles. The statement announced that the bishops would set up a Commission for Australian Catholic Women within the ACBC to advise the bishops on ministry and pastoral life matters (in 2006, it was renamed the Council for Australian Catholic Women). On the tenth anniversary of _Woman and_ [^c44-36] _Man_, there were calls for the further realization of what the document intended.

[^c44-35]: Australian Catholic Bishops’ Conference, ‘Woman and Man: The Bishops Respond. Social Justice Sunday Statement 2000’, in _Building Bridges: Social Justice Statements from Australia’s Catholic Bishops, 1988 to 2013_ (Alexandria, Australia: Australian Catholic Bishops Conference, 2014), 172.

[^c44-36]: Kimberly Davis and Brian Lucas, ‘The Australian Catholic Bishops Conference and the Participation of Women in the Catholic Church: Ten Years On’, _Australasian Catholic Record_ 86, no. 2 (2009): 145–60; Brennan, _Women in the Catholic_ _Church in Australia_.

If the Church was slow to facilitate greater female participation, there was soon to come a crisis which **[p. 745]** highlighted the dire consequences of the Church’s refusal to address the issue—the twin scandal of [^c44-37] clergy child abuse and episcopal responses to their crimes. The Australian government in 2012 called for a Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse. It turned out to be one of the most devastating challenges to the credibility of the Catholic Church in Australia; even the onslaught of secularism seemed to pale in significance. Many causes of the twin problem were highlighted throughout the proceedings. But two were among the more significant: clericalism and the absence of women in the governance of the Catholic Church. Fifty years after Vatican II, the clericalism decried by the council had still, obviously, remained embedded in Australian Church life, despite its cultural egalitarianism; similarly, the full participation of women in the three offices of Christ (teaching, worship, and governance) had not been realized. This external challenge from a secular authority may very well be, in the history of the Church in Australia, one of the most effective stimuli to the Catholic Church to reform itself. In its final recommendations, the Report of the Royal Commission spoke of the importance of women in church leadership positions:

[^c44-37]: Neil Ormerod, ‘Clergy Sexual Abuse: What Difference Did Vatican II Make?’ in Ormerod et al., _Vatican II: The Reception and_ _Implementation in the Australian Church_, 213–25.

The exclusion of lay people and women from leadership positions in the Catholic Church may have contributed to inadequate responses to child sexual abuse. In accordance with contemporary standards of good governance, we encourage the Catholic Church in Australia to explore and develop ways in which its structures and practices of governance may be made more accountable, more transparent, more meaningfully consultative and more participatory, including at the diocesan and parish level.[^c44-38] While the Royal Commission was still in session, in 2017 the Australian bishops called for a plenary council [^c44-39] to be held in Australia. It was seen as an opportunity for purification, renewal, and reform in the wake of the scandals revealed throughout the Royal Commission. But the pastoral initiative was also a direct response to the renewed emphasis on Vatican II’s fundamental principles by Pope Francis, in particular the council’s participatory and dialogic notion of the Church, as captured in his ‘Address at the Ceremony Commemorating the 50th Anniversary of the Institution of the Synod of Bishops’ (2015): ‘A synodal Church is a Church which listens’. The bishops envisaged three phases for the plenary council: preparation, celebration, and implementation. Of particular importance was the preparation phase of ‘open listening and dialogue sessions’ throughout Australia, when every Catholic was invited to respond freely to the question ‘What do you think God is asking of us in Australia at this time?’

[^c44-38]: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, ‘Final Report. Volume 16: Religious Institutions, Book 2 [2017]’, 680, https://www.childabuseroyalcommission.gov.au/sites/default/files/final_report_- _volume_16_religious_institutions_book_2.pdf.

[^c44-39]: This was initially scheduled to take place over two assemblies, in 2020 and 2021. However, because of the COVID pandemic, this was eventually changed to two assemblies in 2021 and 2022.

**[p. 746]** All these official-institutional aspects of reception have been highly significant. But assessing reception by an exclusive focus on the initiatives of official and institutional reception is limited. Lennan notes this with regard to the 1998 Statement of Conclusions from the Roman Curia: ‘The document tends towards an exclusive emphasis on the bishops’ responsibility for the faith and a corresponding lack of emphasis on the church’s—understood as the whole People of God—responsibility. This issue crystallises a weakness of the [^c44-40] entire document: its concentration on ordained leadership and action.’

[^c44-40]: Richard Lennan, ‘Perceptions, Realities, and Possibilities’, _Compass_ 33 (1999): 27.

A fuller assessment of Vatican II’s reception in Oceania requires attention to other levels of ecclesial life.

### 4. Theological Reception

A vibrant story can be told about the _theological_ reception of Vatican II’s vision across Oceania. This level involves the research and writings of scholars in all the related disciplines of ‘theology’, their meeting annually to share research, and the dissemination of their work through publication nationally and internationally.

Perhaps inspired by the positive relationship the Australian bishops saw modelled at Vatican II between the [^c44-41] bishops and the _periti_ of the council, in the post-conciliar years the bishops have generally supported theological scholars and their work. In Australia, biblical scholars formed a national association as early as 1963, later known as the Australian Catholic Biblical Association. At the explicit request of the episcopal conference, the Australian Catholic Theological Association was established in 1975. In 2003, the region-wide Association of Practical Theology in Oceania was formed, with the deliberate aim of theologizing in the spirit of the Decree on the Mission Activity of the Church, _Ad Gentes_, and the Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World, _Gaudium et Spes_—by engaging with the concrete issues facing the diverse [^c44-42] areas of Oceania. The establishment of the ecumenical Melanesian and South Pacific Associations of Theological Schools also provided opportunities for sharing theological engagement with culture and context.

[^c44-41]: Francis Rush, ‘Australian Catholic Theological Association Mass, Banyo Seminary, 6 July 1989’, in Rush and Coman, _Life to_ _Me Is Christ_, 141–43.

[^c44-42]: Gerard Hall, ‘Australia and Oceania’, in _The Wiley Blackwell Companion to Practical Theology_, ed. Bonnie J. Miller- McLemore (Chichester, UK: Wiley Blackwell, 2014), 549–50.

Several journals became vehicles for disseminating this post-conciliar theological scholarship. In the Pacific, the above associations established the _Melanesian Journal of Theology_ and the _Pacific Journal of Theology_. In Papua New Guinea, the journal _Point_ has played a significant role. In New Zealand, theologians tended to publish in overseas, particularly Australian, journals, but in 1997 the monthly magazine _Tui Motu_ **[p. 747]** _—InterIslands_ was set up to publish theological reflection for a theologically aware but not necessarily academic New Zealand readership. With a similar intent, in 2002 the Catholic Institute of Theology in Auckland instigated a series of monographs of theological reflection by New Zealanders for a distinctly New Zealander readership. In Australia, some journals were formed to be more scholarly in focus, and others more popular in style, but no less influential in educating clergy and laity in the theological foundations and reception of the council’s vision. Here are some examples: in biblical studies, the _Australian Biblical Review_; in theology generally, _Compass Theology Review_, _Catholic Theological Review_, _Faith and Culture_, _Pacifica_, and the _Australian eJournal of Theology_; in liturgy, _The Summit_, _Liturgy News_, and the _Australian Journal of Liturgy_; as well as _Bioethics Outlook_ and the long-established _Australasian Catholic Record._ The journal _Eureka Street_ has been particularly important in addressing current social issues through the lens of Catholic social teaching.

Highly effective in promoting knowledge and reception of the council were the programmes of education provided either informally in parishes or formally through institutes of higher education. Here, Vatican II’s vision for theological education being made available to the laity as well as seminarians quickly became a reality. In Papua New Guinea, the ecumenical Melanesian Institute and the Catholic Church’s Liturgical Catechetical Institute, both in Goroka, became models for an inculturated and contextually based theological education. The curriculum of the Pacific Regional Seminary in Suva, Fiji, aims to prepare students for the priesthood in engaging with contemporary cultural, social, political, and economic issues. In Australia, church-sponsored theological colleges led the way for decades after the council in providing theological education for laypeople and not just seminarians. However, in recent years, publicly funded universities such as Australian Catholic University have become more prominent.[^c44-43]

[^c44-43]: Anthony Kelly, ‘Theology and Theological Education in Australia in the Wake of Vatican II’, in Ormerod et al., _Vatican II: The_ _Reception and Implementation in the Australian Church_, 271–73.

To be included within the theological reception of Vatican II is the role played by formal ecumenical [^c44-44] dialogues that have taken place in direct response to Vatican II’s ecumenical vision. Since these dialogues have involved scholars from both partners in the bilateral dialogues, the resulting statements can be counted among the best theological work from Oceania over the last half-century. Generally, the Catholic dialogue partners refer primarily to the documents of Vatican II as the benchmark for Catholic teaching on [^c44-45] any particular topic.

[^c44-44]: Raymond K. Williamson, ed., _Stages on the Way: Documents from the Bilateral Conversations between Churches in Australia_ (Melbourne: Joint Board of Christian Education, 1994); Williamson, ed., _Stages on the Way,_ vol. 2, _Documents from the_ _Bilateral Conversations between Churches in Australia 1994–2007_ (Strathfield, Australia: St Pauls, 2007).

[^c44-45]: Gerard Kelly, ‘The Reception of Vatican II’s Decree on Ecumenism’, in Ormerod et al., _Vatican II: The Reception and_ _Implementation in the Australian Church_, 226–39.

It is a truism to state that the theologies emerging in Oceania since Vatican II have been a direct result of conciliar principles, especially those related to revelation, faith and culture, ecumenism, dialogue, and a more dynamic understanding of ‘adaptation’. The council spoke of the Trinitarian God’s revelatory **[p. 748]** presence in the ever-shifting contexts of history and culture and of the Church’s consequent need to discern that presence—and to ‘adapt’ the Church’s response to the realities of the present in the light of the Gospel. Theology now was to be no longer merely about interpreting past doctrines for the present, but also about discerning God’s revealing and saving plan within the shifting conditions of society, culture, and political-economic circumstance. Throughout Oceania, the council’s challenge has been creatively [^c44-46] embraced in diverse ways by ‘contextual theologies’ that are ecumenically sensitive. As Gerard Hall notes: ‘in dealing with such a diversity of local cultures and situations, it is not possible to speak of _an_ Oceanic theology’. He goes on to remark:

[^c44-46]: See the extensive surveys in Neil Darragh, ‘Contextual Theology in Aotearoa New Zealand’, in _Asian Christian Theologies: A_ _Research Guide to Authors, Movements, Sources,_ vol. 1, ed. John C. England et al. (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2002), 541–98; Clive Pearson, ‘Australian Contextual Theologies’, in England et al., _Asian Christian Theologies_, 1:599–657.

Nonetheless, by the beginning of the third millennium, a new energy for grounding theology in the practical, political, and cultural realities of people’s lives was emerging. Not theology, but theologies. Not simply ‘adapting’ the gospel to cultures, but bringing gospel and cultures into mutual critical engagement. In particular, postcolonial contextual theologies critique the once assumed identification of gospel with European cultural forms. The now emerging practical theologies of Oceania apply a more radical gospel culture dialectic to all cultures while engaging with local and global challenges.[^c44-47]

[^c44-47]: Gerard Hall, ‘Australia and Oceania’, in _The Wiley Blackwell Companion to Practical Theology_, ed. Bonnie J. Miller- McLemore (Chichester, UK: Wiley Blackwell, 2014), 548.

The challenges of post-colonialism have brought forth creative responses throughout the Pacific.[^c44-48]

[^c44-48]: Upolu Lumā Vaai and Unaisi Nababo-Baba, eds., _The Relational Self: Decolonising Personhood in the Pacific_ (Suva, Fiji: University of the South Pacific Press and Pacific Theological College, 2017); Upolu Lumā Vaai and Aisake Casimira, eds., _Relational Hermeneutics: Decolonising the Mindset and the Pacific Itulagi_ (Suva, Fiji: University of the South Pacific Press and Pacific Theological College, 2017).

Much of this finds its inspiration in Vatican II. As noted, one example of the theological reception of particular conciliar themes is the appropriation in Papua New Guinea of the ecclesiological notion of the People of God, of the integrity of the local Church, of the necessity of inculturation, and of a heightened sense of the apostolate of the laity in the mission of the Church. The importance of inculturation and the value of Indigenous peoples was brought to the fore during the visit of Pope John Paul II to Oceania in 1986. In an address that echoed themes from _Ad Gentes_, the pope spoke to Aborigines and Torres Strait islanders at Alice Springs, Australia. In referring to Aboriginal Dreamtime legends, he said: ‘It is wonderful to see how people, as they accept the Gospel of Jesus, find points of agreement between their own traditions and those of Jesus and his people.’[^c44-49]

[^c44-49]: Pope John Paul II, ‘Address to Aborigines and Torres Strait Islanders’, in _The Pope in Australia: Collected Homilies and Talks_ (Homebush, Australia: St Pauls Publications, 1986), 168.

**[p. 749]** Particular themes and sensibilities from the conciliar vision have been developed by systematic theologians. [^c44-50] The council’s Trinitarian emphasis (_LG_ 2–4) has seen particular treatment. Paralleling a focus in Oceanic theological writings, a striking feature of the Apostolic Exhortation _Ecclesia in Oceania_ was its _communio_ ecclesiology, which had come to the fore at the 1998 Synod for Oceania. Feminist theologians have brought to clearer expression conciliar principles such as human dignity, equality, justice, and the necessary [^c44-51] participation of all in the inner and outer life of the Church. Other theologians have developed particular [^c44-52][^c44-53][^c44-54][^c44-55] conciliar themes such as revelation and tradition, eschatology, ecclesiology, ecumenism, [^c44-56][^c44-57][^c44-58] interreligious dialogue, dialogue with the world, the _sensus fidelium_, as well as themes not directly addressed by the council but emerging since the council, such as the ecological crisis, music as theology, [^c44-59] and others.

[^c44-50]: Anthony Kelly, _The Trinity of Love: A Theology of the Christian God_ (Wilmington, DE: Michael Glazier, 1989); David Coffey, _Deus Trinitas: The Doctrine of the Triune God_ (New York: Oxford University Press, 1999); Patricia A. Fox, _God as Communion:_ _John Zizioulas, Elizabeth Johnson, and the Retrieval of the Symbol of the Triune God_ (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2001); Anne Hunt, _Trinity: Nexus of the Mysteries of Christian Faith,_ Theology in Global Perspective Series (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2005); Neil Ormerod, _The Trinity: Retrieving the Western Tradition_, Marquette Studies in Theology 48 (Milwaukee, WI: Marquette University Press, 2005).

[^c44-51]: Confoy, Lee, and Nowotny, _Freedom and Entrapment_; Gideon Goosen, _Australian Theologies: Themes and Methodologies_ _into the Third Millennium_ (Strathfield, Australia: St. Pauls, 2000), 227–53.

[^c44-53]: Anthony Kelly, _Eschatology and Hope_ (Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 2006).

[^c44-55]: Michael Putney, _My Ecumenical Journey_, ed. Elizabeth Delaney, Gerard Kelly, and Ormond Rush (Adelaide, Australia: ATF Theology, 2014); Antonia Pizzey, _Receptive Ecumenism and the Renewal of the Ecumenical Movement: The Path of Ecclesial_ _Conversion_ (Boston: Brill, 2019).

[^c44-56]: Gerald O’Collins, _The Second Vatican Council on Other Religions_ (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2013); Edmund Kee-Fook Chia, ed., _Interfaith Dialogue: Global Perspectives_ (New York: Palgrave Macmillan, 2016).

[^c44-57]: James Gerard McEvoy, _Leaving Christendom for Good: Church-World Dialogue in a Secular Age_ (Lanham, MD: Lexington, 2014).

[^c44-58]: Ormond Rush, _The Eyes of Faith: The Sense of the Faithful and the Church’s Reception of Revelation_ (Washington, DC: The Catholic University of America Press, 2009).

Peter Malone Homebush, 89–102 (Strathfield, Australia: St Pauls, 1988); Maeve Louise Heaney, _Suspended God: Music and a_ _Theology of Doubt_ (New York: T&T Clark, 2022); Danielle Lynch, _God in Sound and Silence: Music as Theology_ (Eugene, Oregon: Pickwick Publications, 2018).

The related conciliar themes of faith-history, gospel-culture, and dialogue-‘adaptation’ have stimulated [^c44-60] theologizing out of one’s local context and created an ‘Australian theology’. Particularly inspired by Pope John Paul II’s 1986 address to Australia’s Indigenous peoples, Indigenous theologies have emerged, such as [^c44-61] **[p. 750]** Rainbow Spirit theology. A similar focus on reception from a particular context has given rise in [^c44-62] Aotearoa New Zealand to a rich Maori inculturation within the Church. The tragic history of violence against Australian Aborigines since the arrival of English settlers in 1788, as well as the forced relocation of children from their homes (‘the stolen generations’), have challenged Australian Catholic theologians to [^c44-63] promote a genuine reconciliation with the Indigenous peoples of the land, which remains unfinished business.

### 5. Spiritual Reception

One of theology’s tasks is to bring to expression the lived faith of local communities. We now turn to the ‘_spiritual_ reception’ of Vatican II and the role the various perspectives of Indigenous, feminist, lay, and other ‘spiritualities’ have played in realizing the council’s pastoral vision.

Only a small minority of the faithful in Oceania have viewed Vatican II negatively and resisted its vision. The vast majority have perceived the event and its vision in a positive way, even despite the fact that for many of the younger generations today, the council is a faraway historical event. But how profoundly have ‘the faithful’ (understood by the council as all baptized Catholics, including those ordained) appropriated in their minds and hearts the major principles of the council’s vision and allowed those principles to shape their inner Catholic imagination and direct their daily Christian life and practice? Although the council envisaged reform on the level of institutional structures and programmes, such change must go hand in hand with personal conversion and conviction by each individual Catholic, ordained or lay. The council fathers knew this, hence their concern that the council be ‘pastoral’; personal conversion and ecclesial [^c44-64] conversion must go together. They spoke of ‘the universal call to holiness’ (_LG_, chapter 5). The term ‘spiritual reception’ describes this broad level of individual and communal engagement with God and with the mission of the Church in one’s local context.

[^c44-64]: Ormond Rush, ‘Ecclesial Conversion after Vatican II: Renewing the Face of the Church to Reflect the Genuine Face of God’, in _50 Years On: Probing the Riches of Vatican II_, ed. David G. Schultenover (Collegeville, MN: Liturgical Press, 2015), 155–74.

One case in particular highlights the power of reception at local level. The 1968 encyclical _Humanae Vitae,_ on the transmission of human life, received diverse reactions in Oceania. The council had spoken of the **[p. 751]** inviolability of conscience and of the dignity of a person’s sense of faith (_sensus fidei_). According to a New Zealand historian, ‘_Humanae Vitae_ impinged more profoundly on the life of the average lay person than all [^c44-65] the deliberations of Vatican II.’ According to sociological research, ‘the trigger that led Catholics’

[^c44-65]: Elizabeth Isichei, ‘Australia and New Zealand’, in Hastings, _Modern Catholicism: Vatican II and After_, 339.

independent thinking about these [moral] issues was the publication of _Humanae Vitae_ in the new climate produced by Vatican II’.[^c44-66]

[^c44-66]: Robert Dixon et al., _Research Project on Catholics Who Have Stopped Attending Mass: Final Report February 2007_ (Fitzroy, Australia: Australian Catholic Bishops Conference, 2007), 320.

Ironically, paralleling negative features of the post-conciliar years, such as the downturn in Mass attendance and a suspicion of the institutional Church, interest in ‘spirituality’ has increased. Moreover, there has been an embrace of the council’s teaching that faith’s response to revelation (God’s self-disclosure) is always embedded in particular historical, cultural, relational, and societal contexts (_Ad Gentes_ and _Gaudium et Spes_). This is evident in the flowering of contextual ‘spiritualities’ throughout Oceania.

Indigenous Oceanic peoples have embraced this incarnational Christian vision. Emboldened by the council’s vision, as concretized in Pope John Paul II’s address at Alice Springs, Aboriginal Australian Catholics have [^c44-67] more confidently expressed their Christian faith from the horizon of their distinctive culture. This has often been coupled with a prophetic spirituality in resistance to their people’s experience of violence and [^c44-68][^c44-69] racism. Similarly, in Aotearoa New Zealand, there has emerged a consciously Catholic Maori spirituality. In Papua New Guinea and elsewhere, in an example of fusion of local and imported spiritualities, the charismatic movement was particularly vibrant and influential in the 1980s. In recent decades, interest in [^c44-70] ‘Australian spirituality’ has emerged, often with explicit reference to Indigenous spiritualities.

[^c44-67]: Joan Hendriks and Gerry Hefferan, eds., _A Spirituality of Catholic Aborigines and the Struggle for Justice_ (Brisbane: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Apostolate, 1993); Joan Hendriks and Gerard Hall, ‘The Natural Mysticism of Indigenous Australian Traditions’, in _Fullness of Life_, ed. K. Acharya et al. (New Delhi: Somaiya, 2008), 491–518.

[^c44-68]: Vicki Clark and Matthew Digges, ‘Joyfully Giving and Receiving: Aboriginal People and the Church in Australia since Vatican II’, in Ormerod et al., _Vatican II: The Reception and Implementation in the Australian Church_, 117–36.

[^c44-69]: Henare Tate, ‘Stepping into Maori Spirituality’, in _Spirituality in Aotearoa New Zealand: Catholic Voices_, ed. Helen Bergin and Susan Smith (Auckland, New Zealand: Accent, 2002), 37–53.

[^c44-70]: Anthony Kelly, _A New Imagining: Towards an Australian Spirituality_ (Melbourne: Collins Dove, 1990) and Veronica Brady, _Caught in the Draught_ (Sydney: Angus & Robertson, 1994).

For many Catholic women, despite the council’s muted attention to women in the Church, feminist spiritualities have led them either to leave altogether or to give prophetic resistance to clericalism and [^c44-71] sexism in the Church. And, ‘on the whole, the response by religious women in Australia to the documents [^c44-72] and directives of Vatican II has been overwhelmingly positive’. Among the laity in general, there has been **[p. 752]** a greater consciousness of their right to participate in the inner and outer life of the Church, although [^c44-73] clericalism persists.

[^c44-71]: Confoy, Lee, and Nowotny, _Freedom and Entrapment_.

[^c44-72]: Margaret Beirne, ‘ “Old Habits Die Hard”: The Experience of Australian Religious Women in the Wake of Vatican II’, in Ormerod et al., _Vatican II: The Reception and Implementation in the Australian Church_, 154–75.

[^c44-73]: Michael Pender, ‘A Lay Perspective on Catholic Spirituality’, in _Spirituality in Aotearoa New Zealand: Catholic Voices_, ed. Helen Bergin and Susan Smith (Auckland, New Zealand: Accent, 2002), 71–85; Neil Ormerod, ‘The Laity in the Australian Church’, in Ormerod et al., _Vatican II: The Reception and Implementation in the Australian Church_, 62–75.

Perhaps one of the most striking features of the spiritual reception of Vatican II throughout Oceania is the self-awareness among the majority of laypeople of being the major protagonists in the inner and outer life of the Church. Without in any way diminishing the service role of the hierarchy, this was central to the council’s vision. It has been overwhelmingly embraced by ordained and laity, despite the enduring clericalism among some. In a scan of parish life since the council, we find deeply faith-filled laypeople involved in various ‘ministries’: liturgy, sacramental programmes, the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults, governance (pastoral and financial councils), spiritual direction, adult education, chaplaincy in hospitals and prisons, social justice advocacy. Although before Vatican II the ‘apostolate of the laity’ had certainly been an emerging vision, none of this ‘participation’ was possible without the radical reimagining of Vatican II. And Oceania has embraced the new imagining.

### 6. Conclusion

Our investigation of the three levels of reception has examined the reception of Vatican II by the pilgrim People of God in Oceania. There have been highlights and many signs of deep appropriation, but also many signs of a continuing need for purification, renewal, and reform. The election of Pope Francis in March 2013 has been seen, by both critics and supporters, as a circuit-breaker in the reception of Vatican II in Oceania— a new phase has begun. Symbolic of the pope’s vision of a world Church renewed according to Vatican II is the fact that Tonga, Papua New Guinea, and New Zealand each have a cardinal overseeing a major diocese, and Australia does not. The pope frequently states that the council remains the compass for the world Church and that there is need for an even greater commitment to its prophetic vision. Noting the need for a pastoral and missionary conversion of the Church in his exhortation _Evangelii Gaudium_, Francis emphasizes the missionary nature of the Church. He has issued impassioned pleas to care for the poor and for the planet. He contends that if creative solutions to such issues are to be found, the Church needs to be more synodal [^c44-74] and become ‘a church that listens’ to the _sensus fidelium_ in order to listen to the Spirit. The Australian bishops’ grounding the 2021–22 plenary council precisely on such a vision gives cause for hope.

[^c44-74]: Pope Francis, ‘Address at Ceremony Commemorating the 50th Anniversary of the Institution of the Synod of Bishops [2015].’
